edibleParts.text: Young stems, while they are still tender and no thicker than about 1.5 cm — the fibrous outer skin peels off with a potato peeler. Also the leafy side stalks, young leaves, the flowering heads, and the black seeds. Once the plant has flowered the stems go woody and are not worth the trouble.

identification.text:
Smyrnium olusatrum is a stout, glabrous (hairless) biennial growing to 150 cm tall (exceptionally 180 cm), with a solid stem up to 22 mm in diameter, which becomes hollow and grooved with age. It has a tuberous taproot which can be 60 cm long, as well as fibrous lateral roots.

The stem leaves are arranged in a spiral (although the upper cauline ones are often opposite and sometimes in whorls of 3), with an inflated, purple-striped, fleshy petiole that has papery margins towards the base. The compound leaves are broadly diamond-shaped, 2- or 3-times ternately (sometimes pinnately) divided. Sometimes they are slightly hairy towards the base. The individual leaflets are dark green above, pale green below, flat, lobed and serrated with obtuse teeth that have a tiny white hydathode at the tip.

Inflorescences are terminal or in the leaf axils and consist of a compound umbel of individual umbels, the former 6–7 cm in diameter, with 5–25 peduncle rays which are glabrous, ridged and 2–4 cm long. There are 3–4 bracts, which are small, pale and inconspicuous (or absent), and the peduncle is usually longer than its rays. The individual umbels are 1–2 cm across with 10–20 flowers and 1–5 tiny bracteoles. The actinomorphic flowers are small, with 5 yellowish petals and 5 tiny, green sepals, 5 stamens and (if present) 2 styles.
Sometimes there are 4 or 5 peduncles branching from the top of the stem, giving the impression of an umbel of umbels of umbels. Generally, it is only the terminal umbel that has 100% bisexual flowers; the lateral ones have both bisexual and male-only flowers (typically with the male umbellules in the centre), and the tertiary umbels often have only male flowers. This is best seen at maturity, when the male-only flowers wither without producing fruit.

The mature fruit is a black schizocarp 6.5–8 mm long, which splits into two single-seeded mericarps, revealing a stalk (the carpophore) that runs between them. Each mericarp has 3 ridges and numerous vittae (oil tubes), which exude a pungent oil which smells of capsicum or diesel. A single plant may produce between 3,000 and 9,000 seeds in a single year.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock's flowers are white; alexanders' are yellowish. Hemlock's leaves are divided two to four times, finely cut and lacy; alexanders' are divided in threes (sometimes pinnately) into flat, lobed and toothed leaflets. Hemlock's stem is hollow between the joints and usually spotted or blotched purple, most of all towards the base — but not every plant is marked, so a stem without blotches does not rule hemlock out. Alexanders' stem starts solid but becomes hollow and grooved with age, so a hollow stem does not rule alexanders out. Purple on the leaf stalks does not separate them: alexanders' stalks are purple-striped and hemlock's are purple-blotched when mature. Crushed hemlock gives off a foul, mousy smell. Ripe hemlock fruits are dark brown and 2.5–3 mm long; alexanders' are black and 6.5–8 mm. Both are largely hairless and both can reach about 1.5 m, so neither hairiness nor height helps. If the flowers are white or the leaves finely divided, do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild celery's flowers are greenish white and about 1 mm across; alexanders' are yellowish. Wild celery's umbels are 2–5 cm across, almost stalkless and set opposite a leaf, with no bracts; alexanders' are 6–7 cm across, on rays 2–4 cm long. Wild celery's lower leaves are once or twice pinnate, but its stem leaves can be in threes, so leaves divided in threes do not rule it out. All parts of wild celery smell strongly of celery. Wild celery's fruits are dark brown and 1.5–2 mm long; alexanders' are black and 6.5–8 mm. Both grow in waste places. Wild celery is eaten too (see its page).

Monica Wilde, 'Alexanders Soup'
preparation.text: Sits between celery, lovage and angelica in flavour — sweet, with a tang that carries. Peel the stems and cook them like celery; the leafy side stalks steam in a few minutes. Leaves are strong enough to treat as a herb rather than a salad green, and the black seeds grind to a peppery, myrrh-scented spice that is best set against citrus or chocolate.

recipes.method: Serves 6. 4 large heads of alexanders, stems peeled; 1 large parsnip; 1 bunch of wild garlic or wild leeks; 6 strands of dulse; 2 onions; 1 tbsp coconut oil; 2 litres good stock; 1 tbsp birch bolete or porcini powder; salt and pepper. Lightly scrape the alexanders stems and the parsnip with a potato peeler to take off the outer fibres, and trim any roots off the wild garlic. Chop the onions and fry them gently in the coconut oil until translucent. Add the chopped parsnip and fry 3 minutes, then add the stock and the rest of the ingredients. Bring to the boil and simmer 10 minutes. Take off the heat, let it cool a little and blend. Season with salt, pepper and the bolete powder, and reheat to serve, garnished with a sprig of alexanders leaf.
recipes.title: Alexanders soup

recipes.method: The side stalks, the smaller branching stalks and the leaves; butter; salt and pepper. Peel the side stalks and cut off the smaller branching stalks, and steam them with the leaves for 7 minutes. Then add butter, salt and pepper.
recipes.title: Steamed alexanders stalks

recipes.method: 200 g alexanders stems, 5 mm–1.5 cm thick, 100 g golden or brown granulated sugar. Wash, dry and finely chop the stems. Cook in a heavy-based pan over medium-high heat for about 8 minutes, until the liquid they give off has gone. Stir in the sugar and cook a further 10 minutes, until it crystallises around the pieces. Cool in the pan, then store in a dry jar — they keep about 6 months. Makes roughly 120 g.
recipes.title: Candied alexanders stems

recipes.method: 1 heaped tbsp alexander seeds, 500 g white or wholemeal flour (or half of each), a pinch of sea salt, 1 tsp quick yeast, 1 tsp sugar or honey, 400 ml warm water, 15 ml olive oil (optional). Grind or chop the seeds roughly — you want texture, not powder; dry-roasting them at 140 °C for 10–20 minutes first makes them easier to grind, so long as they do not burn. Mix them through the flour and salt. Dissolve the yeast and honey in the warm water, stir into the dry mix and combine well. Knead about 10 minutes, until the dough springs back when pressed. Leave covered somewhere warm until doubled, knock it back, drop it into an oiled tin and prove again until doubled. Bake at 200 °C for 40–45 minutes, until the loaf sounds hollow tapped underneath. Rest 10 minutes in the tin, then cool on a rack before slicing.
recipes.title: Alexander seeded bread

recipes.method: Makes about 25. 100 g salted butter, 40 g demerara sugar, a heaped tsp of orange zest, 1 tsp roughly ground alexander seeds, 125 g plain flour, 1/4 tsp baking powder. Heat the oven to 180 °C (160 °C fan) and grease a large tray. Cream the butter and sugar, then beat in the zest and seeds. Mix the flour and baking powder separately and work them in, stopping as soon as it comes together — overworking makes the shortbread tough. Flatten the dough to roughly 20 x 15 cm and cut about 25 rectangles. Lift them onto the tray with a palette knife, at least 1 cm apart, and prick each with a fork. Bake 8–10 minutes, until light brown. Cool 5 minutes before moving them to a rack. They keep a week in an airtight tin.
recipes.title: Alexander and orange shortbread

recipes.method: Built from leftover alexander seed cake. 150 g of the cake (undrizzled), 125 g mascarpone or another soft cream cheese, 120 g dark cooking chocolate, and 1/2–1 tsp roughly ground alexander seeds if you want more of them. Crumble the cake into small pieces rather than crumbs and work in the cheese and seeds. Roll into balls about 2.5 cm across on greaseproof paper and chill for an hour. Melt the chocolate in a bowl set over a little simmering water, taking it off the heat when about half has melted and letting the rest come on its own. Dip each ball with a teaspoon until fully coated, return it to the paper, and leave to set hard. They keep several days.
recipes.title: Alexander seed and chocolate truffles

summary.text:
Smyrnium olusatrum, common name alexanders (or alisander), is an edible flowering plant of the family Apiaceae (Umbelliferae) which grows on waste ground and in hedges around the Mediterranean and Atlantic coastal regions of Europe. In north Africa it is restricted to the Mediterranean and Atlantic regions, including the Canary Islands.

It is recorded as an introduction in New Zealand, Australia and Bermuda.

The conservation status of alexanders in Britain and France is Least Concern, and it is not considered to be threatened in any region, although it is rare in some countries, such as Belgium.
In Ireland it is common around the south and east coasts, but rare inland and to the west. More generally in Europe, it occurs throughout the Mediterranean, where it is recorded in all coastal areas, including the islands, and it extends as far as Crimea and the Black Sea. It is also found along the Atlantic coast of the continent from the Iberian Peninsula northwards through France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and (recently) into Norway; and westwards to the Azores.
Alexanders is widespread in Britain, where it is frequent in coastal areas in the south, becoming progressively rarer towards the north of Scotland, and absent from Orkney and Shetland. Inland, it is often found close to the sites of medieval monastery gardens and other historical places such as castles.
It is a strictly lowland plant in northern Europe. In Britain, it is recorded no higher than 290 m, at Davidstow Airfield in Cornwall.
In New Zealand, iNaturalist holds 22 wild records (19 research grade, 28/10/2026), most of them on the Wellington south coast around Houghton Bay, with a few from Auckland, Lincoln, Upper Moutere and Dunedin.

warnings: Hemlock, one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand, belongs to the same family and also grows in waste places. Check every plant against Lookalikes before you pick it.

edibleParts.text:
Leaves and flower heads, raw or cooked: boiled, or after soaking for several hours in salty water. The petals, pulled apart, are sprinkled into salads or onto biscuits, cakes and desserts as a garnish. The dried flower heads and seeds can be ground into flour.
The fresh flowers are eaten as a snack, sucked for their nectar.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, 'Trifolium hybridum' factsheet (Webb et al. 1988; Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY 3.0 NZ, https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Trifolium-hybridum.html, retrieved 09/11/2026) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Perennial; stems glabrous, erect or ascending, not rooting at nodes. Leaves glabrous; petioles about 10–100 mm long; leaflets elliptic to obovate, usually obtuse, cuneate at base, finely serrate, about 10–35 mm long; lateral veins thin and straight to leaflet margin; petiolules up to about 1 mm long, more or less equal; stipules ovate, acuminate. Inflorescences axillary, racemose, globose, pedunculate, longer than leaves; flowers numerous; pedicel up to 6 mm long; bracts subtending flowers free. Calyx glabrous or sparsely hairy, 10-veined but 5 veins often indistinct, not inflated at fruiting; throat open, glabrous or sparsely hairy; calyx teeth somewhat unequal (2 upper slightly longer), shorter than corolla, narrowly triangular, usually much longer than tube, sometimes only slightly longer, erect at fruiting; sinuses obtuse. Corolla usually pink, persistent, 5–10 mm long. Pod glabrous, straight, more or less equal to calyx, 3–4 mm long, 1–4-seeded; seeds about 1–1.5 mm diameter.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover's flower head is usually stalkless, sitting directly on the leaves beneath it, whose stipules partly wrap the young head; alsike's heads rise from the leaf axils on stalks, above the leaves. Red clover's stems are sparsely hairy low down and moderately to densely hairy higher up, and its leaf stalks are usually moderately hairy; alsike's stems and leaves are hairless, though its upper stem can be hairy. Red clover's leaflets usually carry a crescent-shaped spot towards the base; alsike's are described as unmarked. Red clover's corolla is 10–16 mm long, alsike's 5–10 mm. Colour is not a safe test: red clover is pink to purple-pink and rarely cream, alsike usually pink. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are hairless or nearly so on stem and leaf, and both hold round heads on stalks that rise above the leaves, so the head settles little: white clover is usually white but occasionally pink to reddish, and alsike is usually pink, so colour overlaps. Follow the stem: white clover creeps and roots at the nodes, while alsike's stems are erect or ascending and do not root at the nodes. White clover's leaflets often carry light or dark markings; alsike's are described as unmarked. With a hand lens, alsike's calyx teeth are usually much longer than the calyx tube, where white clover's are shorter than the tube. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats; alsike clover's hairless stems stand erect or rise from the base and do not root at the nodes. Least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long, alsike clover's 10–35 mm long. Out of flower, leaflet size is a guide, as the published ranges do not meet. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Least yellow sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Creeping wood sorrel's stems lie along the ground or rise a little and often root at the nodes; alsike clover's hairless stems stand erect or rise from the base and do not root at the nodes. Creeping wood sorrel's leaflets are 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm), alsike clover's 10–35 mm long. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: both have three leaflets, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Its stems are erect or ascending and do not root at the nodes, and its leaflets are c. 10–35 mm long. Leaflet size overlaps between 10 and 16 mm, so it does not separate them. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pale-pink wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long. Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Alsike clover's stems are hairless, erect or ascending; suckling clover's are sparsely to densely hairy and lie along the ground or rise a little. Neither roots at the nodes. Alsike clover's three leaflet stalks are more or less equal; on most suckling clover leaves the middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the side ones (under 1 mm). Leaflet size overlaps between 10 and 12 mm (alsike clover about 10–35 mm long, suckling clover about 3–12 mm), so it does not separate them. Suckling clover has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Suckling clover

NOTE 15/10/2026 (owner asked whether red clover and alsike clover recipes are interchangeable): searched and read Practical Plants, PFAF, Useful Temperate Plants, Edible Wild Food, Nature's Restaurant Online (Southwestern Ontario), Creative Canning, Cosmopolitan Cornbread, Practical Self Reliance, Homestead Heroine and Flatcap Forager. NO source found says red-clover (or white-clover) recipes can be used with alsike, and no recipe written for alsike was found. Clover-jelly and clover-flour pages name only red, white and crimson clover. What sources do say for alsike: leaves and flower heads raw or cooked, a tea of the dried heads, and flour of the dried heads and seeds (Practical Plants/PFAF, after Facciola 1990; Edible Wild Food). Nature's Restaurant Online: 'The dried flower heads of the Alsike and White clover can ground into flour… I've done it, but found the effort wasn't worth the result'; of all four Ontario clovers, 'All are edible, but don't eat much of any of them raw', and leaves other than white clover's need 10–15 minutes' simmering — a forager's site, not used for the page. A reader comment on Homestead Heroine ('Red clover and Aslike clover are toxic') is unsourced and contradicts the botanical sources; not used. So no recipes were copied to this entry.

summary.text:
Alsike clover (Trifolium hybridum) is a perennial clover of the pea family (Fabaceae), native from southern Europe to the Caucasus and naturalised in New Zealand.
In New Zealand: North Island: Northland, Waikato, southern Hawke's Bay, Wellington Province; South Island: scattered throughout but most common in eastern coastal areas; Chatham Islands. Naturalised from southern Europe to Caucasia, first recorded in 1883. Alsike clover is cultivated in pasture and in general appearance resembles white clover, from which it is easily distinguished by the more erect habit and obtuse sinuses of the calyx teeth.

warnings: The plant can irritate skin if handled.

There is limited evidence of T. hybridum having toxic effects on horses including photosensitisation and Alsike clover poisoning. A diet in horses of at least 20% T. hybridum over the course of four weeks could lead to poisoning which includes deleterious neurological effects and liver failure.

identification.text:
Stoloniferous herb, sometimes forming mats. Stems densely hairy on the angles, purplish. Petioles to about 8 cm long, slender, hairy. Lamina 3–8 × 2.5–6 cm, sometimes smaller near base of shoots, ovate, or broad-ovate, often rhombic-ovate on flowering stems, with hairs scattered above, more densely hairy below, coarsely crenate or crenate-serrate, with large pale silvery greyish areas on either side of midrib above; base truncate or subcordate; apex more or less obtuse. Calyx 8–10 mm long, hairy. Corolla 2–2.5 cm long from base to apex of upper lip, yellow, hairy outside; upper lip 1.2–1.4 cm long, elliptic; lower lip with middle lobe about 7 mm long, narrow-triangular, streaked brown, acute; lateral lobes rounded. Filaments puberulent, the longer pair longer than style. Nutlets not seen.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Galeobdolon luteum Huds.]
A mat-forming ground cover under 50 cm tall, spreading by runners. The leaves are mint-like and aromatic, with silvery-grey patches on top; the yellow, hairy, tubular flowers are in dense whorls in the leaf joints from December to May. The upper lip of each flower is hood-shaped and fringed with eyelash-like hairs; the lower lip has three lobes and reddish-brown markings. It has sometimes been misnamed spotted deadnettle (Lamium maculatum), whose flowers are purple.

summary.text:
Lamium galeobdolon, the yellow archangel or golden dead-nettle, is the only deadnettle with yellow flowers. In New Zealand it is called the aluminium plant or artillery plant. Its variegated subspecies (subsp. argentatum) is invasive in several European countries outside its native range and in New Zealand, Canada and the United States.
It is native to Europe and western Asia, and was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1988. It was planted as a ground cover for shady places and has escaped from gardens; the wild plants here are the variegated garden form, which seldom reverts to green leaves, and it is likely to spread further. No seed is known from New Zealand plants: it spreads by runners and by fragments moved in soil. In 1988 it was known wild from Little Barrier Island, Levin, Hanmer, Christchurch and Hokitika. It is on the National Pest Plant Accord and on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds, under sustained control in Auckland and an organism of interest in Southland.

warnings: It is a pest plant controlled with herbicide sprays such as metsulfuron-methyl. Pick only where you know it has not been sprayed.

It must not be bred, sold, distributed or released anywhere in New Zealand (National Pest Plant Accord). It spreads from runners and fragments in moved soil and dumped garden waste, so carry no living pieces elsewhere: put trimmings in a weed bag, green waste or landfill.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Sandy and stony beaches near high water mark, mostly eastern coasts.

On northern Chatham Island an annual growth builds up each summer on the beach edge of the dune (DOC, restated).

Well drained, sandy soil is preferred. It is likely to be found in areas midway up beaches, out of the range of waves and tides, which can destroy individuals, especially through storm events. (Wikipedia)

It often grows in patches well out on sandy beaches, usually the plant closest to the high tide line (New Brunswick, Canada; 1left, restated).

identification.text:
Stems 30–60 cm tall, much-branched from base, stout, glabrous, sprawling to suberect, forking; main stem often flexuous. Rosette leaves fleshy, obovate to oblanceolate, shallowly pinnatifid, petiolate, 4–6 × 1.5–3 cm; margins serrate; stem leaves narrower and shorter, oblanceolate, obtuse, bluntly serrate. Inflorescence axis flexuous, thickening and elongating at fruiting. Pedicels suberect to spreading, 1–3 mm long. Flowers 6–8 mm in diameter, clustered. Petals 4–6 × 1–1.5 mm. Silique erect, (12)–15–22 × 4–7 mm; upper segment ovate, acuminate, tapering to a narrow winged beak, emarginate, 4-angled or 8-ribbed, somewhat flattened, frequently persistent if lower segment seedless, 8–13 mm long; lower segment terete, barrel-shaped, often obconic, (4)–6–9 mm long, without lateral horns.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Check the ripening fruit. In American sea rocket the lower fruit segment has no horns and the upper segment is ovate, acuminate, notched at the tip, 4-angled or 8-ribbed, somewhat flattened, with a narrow winged beak; in sea rocket the lower segment has 2 spreading to deflexed horns at its tip and the upper segment is mitre-shaped, acute and 4-angled. The flowering stem is flexuous in American sea rocket, whose main stem is also often flexuous, and straight in sea rocket. Petals are 4–6 mm long in American sea rocket against 7–9 mm, flowers 6–8 mm across against c. 1 cm, and rosette leaf margins are serrate against entire, rarely crenate or sinuate. American sea rocket stems are 30–60 cm tall, sea rocket's 10–30 cm. Fruit length and leaf lobing do not separate them: the fruit lengths overlap, and sea rocket plants can have entire or pinnatifid leaves. Sea rocket's leaves, stems, flower buds and immature pods are eaten, but it is very bitter.

preparation.text: Use the younger leaves and shoots in salads; mix older leaves with milder greens and cook them as a potherb. Stems, leaves and pods can go into salads, or be boiled for 5 to 10 minutes for a milder taste. The leaves are best cooked and eaten only in small quantities. For the root flour, dry and grind the root and mix it with cereal flour. Dice the fleshy leaves small: they taste like a milder, saltier horseradish. The leaves between the seedling stage and the old plant are the nicest; seedlings and old leaves are less pleasant, and the flavour may get stronger later in the season. Use the leaves raw as a peppery garnish, chopped over seafood, in sandwiches and salads, or in a stir-fry; the flowers make a spicy garnish. Pick leaves and stem tips with fingers or scissors, from well above the high-tide mark and away from boat ramps and heavily walked areas, and wash them well.

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1 large handful young sea rocket leaves and tender pods; 1 handful other coastal greens, such as sea celery leaves or New Zealand spinach (warrigal greens); 40 ml olive oil; 20 ml lemon juice; 5 ml agave or maple syrup; salt and pepper; 40 ml toasted sunflower seeds. Rinse the sea rocket well in cold water and dry it. If using New Zealand spinach, blanch it in boiling water for 1 minute, cool it in cold water and squeeze it dry. Toss the greens together in a bowl. Whisk the oil, lemon juice, syrup, salt and pepper into a dressing, toss the salad gently in it, and scatter the sunflower seeds over to serve.
recipes.title: Sea rocket salad with coastal greens

recipes.method: Ingredients: about 250 ml young sea rocket leaves; a splash of white vinegar; salt and pepper. Rinse the leaves and blend them with the vinegar and a little salt and pepper to a paste, tasting as you go. Serve it as you would mustard or wasabi.

summary.text:
Cakile edentula, the American searocket, is a species of the flowering Cakile plant. This plant is native to North America. It is also a non-native, invasive species in other parts of the world, especially Japan and Australia, and on the west coast of North America. Cakile edentula has the life cycle of an annual plant in Northern latitudes. In warmer climates, it survives as a biennial if possible. Cakile edentula grows roots more aggressively and intensively if a nearby competitor is sensed. The plant does not react this way if the nearby competitor is kin. (Wikipedia)

In New Zealand it is naturalised from the east coast of North America, first recorded as naturalised in 1935, and New Zealand plants belong to var. edentula; the Flora records it from the North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands (Flora of New Zealand, restated). From its first New Zealand record in 1921 it spread over 30 to 40 years along the eastern coasts of the North and South Islands; where European sea rocket has since arrived, American sea rocket is now rarely found, which the authors read as one species displacing a close relative (Cousens & Cousens 2011, restated). On northern Chatham Island it was a major weed at the front of a dune being restored for Chatham Island oystercatcher nesting; it spreads along the coast by wave action and also sets copious seed that germinates locally, and hand pulling alone did not clear it (DOC, restated).

Its original name is Bunias edentula Bigelow (1814) (Flora of New Zealand Online). Cakile is an old Arabic name for the plant, and edentula is Latin for 'without teeth' (Eat The Weeds; GardenWorld). The fruit splits in two: the lower segment stays on the parent plant, is buried by shifting sand over winter and sprouts in place, often in crowded clumps, while the rocket-shaped upper segment breaks off and can be carried by the sea to distant shores (New Brunswick, Canada; 1left, restated).

Museum specimens include one from the foreshore at the base of Farewell Spit, collected 23/05/1977 (Auckland Museum AK143045), and one from Owhiro Bay, Wellington, collected 13/11/1994 by Phil Garnock-Jones and Sabrina Malcolm (Te Papa SP092663).

warnings: Eat the leaves only in small quantities.

It is controlled as a weed in New Zealand dune restoration: on northern Chatham Island, live and pulled plants were sprayed with Roundup Extra herbicide, so plants on dunes under restoration may have been sprayed.

edibleParts.text:
This edible plant is widely valued for its culinary versatility. Its leaves can be consumed raw in fresh salads, offering a crisp and refreshing texture, or used as an ingredient in a variety of dishes, such as pizzas, sandwiches, and soups.
D. muralis exhibits a spicy and pungent flavour profile, characteristic of the edible plants of this genus, which are frequently used in cooking.

identification.text: It is an annual, but sometimes grows as a perennial, with ascending to erect, branching stems (10–)30–40(–60) cm tall. It has lobed leaves, which form a rosette at the base of the plant. The lower leaves are obovate with wavy margins to pinnatifid, (3–)5–15 cm long and 1–4 cm wide. The flowers are yellow, with oblong sepals and longer, obovate petals. Later, it produces a fruit capsule, long cylindrical with a short beak. It contains 2 rows of yellow brown seeds, which are ovoid or ellipsoid shaped.

lookalikes.howToTell: Perennial wall-rocket's pod sits on a short stalk (gynophore) (0.5–)1–2 mm long between the sepal scars and the pod; annual wall-rocket's pod has none. Perennial wall-rocket's petals are 7–12 mm long against 3–7 mm, so flowers with petals about 7 mm long are not separated by size. Perennial wall-rocket is not foetid and its leaves are mostly on the stem; annual wall-rocket is foetid and its leaves are mostly basal, forming a rosette. Leaf division does not reliably separate them in New Zealand: perennial wall-rocket's leaves run from toothed to deeply pinnatifid, and annual wall-rocket's from sinuate-margined to pinnatifid. Height (perennial 30–100 cm, annual (10–)30–40(–60) cm) and pedicel length (perennial 1.5–4 cm, annual 0.5–2 cm) overlap. Both have yellow petals, a seedless beak and seeds in two rows in each half of the pod. Perennial wall-rocket's leaves are eaten raw in salads or lightly cooked; it is the rocket grown commercially and sold as wild rocket.

preparation.text:
The flavour profile of D. muralis leaves evolves significantly with their stage of development. Younger leaves are tender and have a mild, slightly peppery taste, making them ideal for raw preparations like salads or as delicate garnishes. In contrast, mature leaves present a more intense, spicy, and pungent flavour, which enhances their appeal in robust dishes like soups, sauces, or as a garnish for hot meals.
They can also be processed, such as dried or frozen, to extend their shelf life and broaden their applications in different culinary contexts.

The scope of the warning, so it is not read as more than it says. The quoted sentences are about Brassicaceae as a family, not about this species in particular, and the paper makes no claim about roadside plants: its own D. muralis was grown in soil and irrigation water analysed before planting, and those leaves came in below the EU maximum levels for lead, cadmium and mercury (Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915). The warning is on this page because the habitat field above it records the plant growing on waste ground, beside railways and roads and on tips; the inference from one to the other is the reader's to draw and a person's to write, so it is not written here.

months comes from the iNaturalist month-of-year histogram for Diplotaxis muralis in New Zealand (place_id 6803, verifiable records, n=110), read 08/10/2026, taking every month at or above a quarter of the peak month (April, 20 records; threshold 5). That admits ten months and excludes March (4 records) and July (3). Recorded because those two gaps are an artefact of a thin per-month sample rather than a seasonal break — a single observation either way moves them — and because the 34 flowering-annotated records are too few to set a season from. Read it as recorded essentially year round.

summary.text:
Diplotaxis muralis, the annual wall-rocket, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.
It is native to temperate regions of North Africa, Europe and parts of western Asia.
It is found in North Africa, within Algeria, Libya, Morocco and Tunisia, in addition to Ethiopia in East Africa. Within Asia it is found in the Caucasus, Georgia and Turkey. In middle Europe, it is in Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands, Poland, Slovakia and Switzerland. In southeastern Europe, within Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Italy, Malta, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia and Ukraine. Also in southwestern Europe, it is found in France, Portugal and Spain.
It has naturalised in the UK since 1778, when it was found in a field of oats raised from imported seeds from a ship wrecked on the Kent coast.
In New Zealand it was first recorded naturalised in 1899 and is found throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands (Flora of New Zealand, restated).

warnings: Brassicaceae plants are known for their tendency to accumulate heavy metals, a trait that makes them valuable for the phytoremediation of contaminated soils. However, this same ability necessitates careful monitoring, as the accumulation of heavy metals can also pose potential health risks.

The leaves of this plant can be used to make apple mint jelly, as well as a flavouring in dishes such as apple mint couscous.
Leaves, raw or cooked as a potherb, and as a flavouring in salads or cooked foods; a herb tea is made from the leaves.
In New Zealand apple mint is often used as a substitute for, or even in preference to, spearmint, for its sweeter flavour.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous, densely hairy perennial with erect, branched stems to about 70 cm tall. Leaves sessile or nearly so, smaller below inflorescence, 1.5–4.5 × 0.8–3 cm, broad, usually elliptic, sometimes ovate or oblong-ovate, rugose, crenulate or crenulate-serrate, often grey-tomentose at least below, with oil globules below; base cordate or subcordate and often more or less amplexicaul. Inflorescence of several narrow elongated terminal spikes, densely hairy, freely branching at base; central spike to about 8 cm long, the others shorter; flowers pedicellate. Calyx 1.5–2.5 mm long, broad-campanulate, more or less green, glandular, hairy; teeth equal, acuminate, equal to tube at anthesis. Corolla 3–3.5 mm long, pale pink or whitish; lobes more or less hairy; tube exserted. Stamens exserted or included. Nutlets about 0.8 mm long, ovoid, bluntly angled, reticulate. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: No single character separates every plant, so use several together. Apple mint's leaves are broad, usually elliptic and wrinkled, 1.5–4.5 × 0.8–3 cm; spearmint's are lanceolate to ovate, 2.5–9 × 0.7–2 cm, so leaf sizes overlap. Apple mint is densely hairy and often grey-woolly beneath; spearmint ranges from nearly hairless to densely hairy and grey-woolly beneath, so hairiness alone does not decide it. Both have stalkless or nearly stalkless leaves; apple mint's leaf base is heart-shaped or nearly so and often clasps the stem, spearmint's ranges from tapered to heart-shaped. Apple mint's calyx is more or less green and its corolla pale pink or whitish; spearmint's calyx is more or less purple, its corolla mauve or pinkish, and its stems are often tinged red. Apple mint has a fruity, minty flavour, and spearmint a minty, green, cooling, spicy smell, but smell is a clue, not a test. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Wild spearmint

lookalikes.howToTell: Smell does not separate them: crushed pennyroyal leaves have a very strong fragrance like spearmint, and infants have been made ill by tea made from pennyroyal thought to be mint. Apple mint is often spearmint-scented too. Look at where the flowers are: apple mint's are in several narrow, densely hairy spikes at the stem tips, the central spike to about 8 cm long; pennyroyal's are densely packed in spaced rings in the leaf joints along the stem, with a cluster of leaves at the shoot tip. Apple mint's stems are erect, to about 70 cm tall; pennyroyal's creep along the ground and ascend, to about 30 cm long. Apple mint's leaves are stalkless or nearly so, broad, wrinkled, 1.5–4.5 × 0.8–3 cm, often grey-woolly beneath, with a heart-shaped or nearly heart-shaped base that often clasps the stem; pennyroyal's are stalked, sometimes shortly, not wrinkled, usually 0.6–2 × 0.4–1 cm, so the smallest apple mint leaves overlap pennyroyal's in size. Apple mint's calyx is more or less green and its corolla pale pink or whitish, 3–3.5 mm long; pennyroyal's calyx is purple and its corolla mauve, 4–6 mm long. Both grow in pasture. Pennyroyal is poisonous to the liver; do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Pennyroyal

lookalikes.howToTell: No single character separates every plant, so use several together. Apple mint's calyx is more or less green and 1.5–2.5 mm long, and its corolla pale pink or whitish, 3–3.5 mm long; peppermint's calyx is purple and 3–4 mm long, and its corolla mauve or lilac, 5–6 mm long. Apple mint is densely hairy, its leaves often grey-woolly at least beneath; peppermint's stems are hairless or sparsely hairy and its leaves hairy or hairless. Apple mint's leaves are stalkless or nearly so, with a heart-shaped or nearly heart-shaped base that often clasps the stem; peppermint's usually have a distinct stalk (nearly stalkless on some shoots in water) and a tapered to rounded base. Crush a leaf: apple mint has a fruity, minty flavour and is not peppermint- or lemon-scented; peppermint smells of peppermint, or of lemon in the bergamot-mint form. Their leaf sizes overlap (apple mint 1.5–4.5 × 0.8–3 cm, peppermint 1–6 × 1–3.5 cm), so size does not separate them. Both are edible.

preparation.text: It is also often used to make a mint tea, as a garnish, or in salads.

recipes.method: A kilo of green cooking apples; a small bunch of apple mint; 250 ml cider vinegar; 500 g sugar for every 500 ml of juice; 60 ml finely chopped apple mint leaves. Simmer a kilo of green cooking apples, quartered but not peeled or cored, with a small bunch of apple mint under water until tender, about 40 minutes. Strain overnight through a jelly bag, stir the 250 ml cider vinegar into the juice and measure it, then add 500 g sugar for every 500 ml. Dissolve the sugar gently, boil hard to setting point, about 10 minutes, and stir the 60 ml finely chopped leaves through off the heat before potting into warm sterilised jars.
recipes.title: Apple mint jelly

recipes.method: Five apple mint leaves; a tablespoon of muscovado sugar; two shots of rum; 100 ml soda water; a lime; ice. Squeeze two lime wedges over the sugar in the glass, add the leaves and muddle them into it, pour the rum over, fill with ice, top with soda and stir.

summary.text:
Mentha suaveolens, the apple mint, pineapple mint, woolly mint or round-leafed mint (synonyms M. rotundifolia, Mentha macrostachya, Mentha insularis), is a member of the mint family Lamiaceae.

Apple mint is native to southern and western Europe and is naturalised in central and northern parts of Europe.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North, South and Stewart Islands: scattered throughout. Native to southern and western Europe; first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1935. Throughout New Zealand plants of apple mint are fairly uniform; they form nutlets but these are generally, or possibly always, inviable. This plant is treated as M. rotundifolia (L.) Hudson in many Floras but true M. rotundifolia is now considered to be a hybrid between M. longifolia (L.) Hudson and M. suaveolens.

warnings: Large quantities of mint essential oil can cause abortion; this caution is given for mints in general, not recorded for this species.
Apple mint hybridises freely with other mints, so wild plants may not match the description exactly.
Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed. Pick from ground you know.

habitat.text:
By far the commonest and most widespread wild bamboo in New Zealand: the Volcanic Plateau and most lowland country southwards, thinning out only in the south of the South Island, which roughly tracks where it was planted. Look on roadsides and riverbanks, in and around plantations, in scrub and along forest margins, and especially where a garden boundary meets rough ground — on abandoned sections and in waste places. Spread here is by rhizome and not by seed, so a stand is one clone creeping outwards from something somebody planted.
In Marlborough and Canterbury it grows mostly near the coast.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Medium-sized and forming dense thickets; rhizomes running extensively from periphery. Culm 3–5 m, dark green; banded white just below nodes. Culm-sheath green or greenish purple, eventually very pale, internodes almost all hidden in lower and middle parts of culm; ligule 2–3 mm, broad and prominent, truncate. Branches 1 per node, sometimes 2–3 at upper nodes. Leaf-sheath glabrous, often purplish above. Ligule minutely puberulent. Leaf-blade (1)–3–5–(7) on each branch, to 25–(30) × 3.5–(4) cm, broadly linear or linear-oblong, abaxially upper ⅓ green and lower ⅔ glaucescent, adaxially shining dark green, acuminate. Inflorescence more or less purple, at least on exposed side. Spikelets 4–9 cm, flattened; florets to about 12, distichous. Glumes 2. Lemma 10–13 mm, including short awn, ciliate, obscurely tessellate. Fig. 1.
[From: Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the lower part of several canes in the stand. On some of fishpole bamboo's canes the lower nodes are crowded together and sometimes zigzag, with swollen, often lopsided internodes; not every cane shows it, so check more than one. Fishpole's canes are green in their first year and yellow afterwards; arrow bamboo's are dark green. Arrow bamboo's cane is round, not notched, with the internodes in its lower and middle parts mostly hidden by sheaths; fishpole bamboo's internodes are flattened or grooved on alternate sides above each node, though usually round below the lowest branches. Arrow bamboo has one branch per node, sometimes two or three at the upper nodes; fishpole usually has two markedly unequal branches with a small or missing third. Arrow bamboo's leaf blades reach 25–30 cm long and 3.5–4 cm wide and are glossy dark green above; fishpole's are usually 5–13 cm long and under 3 cm wide. Height does not separate them (fishpole usually 3–6 m, arrow bamboo 3–5 m), and both have a white band just below the nodes (on fishpole, on young canes). Both have edible young shoots, cooked.
lookalikes.name: Fishpole bamboo

lookalikes.howToTell: Black bamboo's canes are 4–7 m. In var. nigra they turn black or heavily black-blotched in their second year, but the green-caned var. henonis is naturalised here too, so a green stand does not rule it out. Arrow bamboo's canes are 3–5 m and dark green. Both have a white band or waxy ring just below the nodes (on black bamboo, on young canes), so that does not separate them. Black bamboo's internodes are flattened or grooved on alternate sides above each node, though usually round below the lowest branches; arrow bamboo's are round, not notched. Black bamboo usually has 3 branches per node with the middle one small or missing; arrow bamboo has 1 per node, sometimes 2–3 at upper nodes. Black bamboo's leaf-blades are usually 5–9 cm long (up to 13 cm); arrow bamboo's reach 25 cm (up to 30 cm). Black bamboo's cane sheaths are purple or purple-flushed and fall away; arrow bamboo's are green or greenish purple, fade very pale, and stay on, hiding most of the lower and middle internodes. Raw bamboo shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides, which must be destroyed by thorough cooking.
lookalikes.name: Black bamboo

preparation.text: The toxins must be destroyed by thorough cooking, and for this reason, fresh bamboo shoots are boiled before being used in other ways. The shoots of some species contain cyanide that must be leached or boiled out before they can be eaten safely. Slicing the bamboo shoots thinly assists in this leaching.

recipes.method: Cut the shoots when they stand about 8–10 cm above the ground, taking them 5 cm or more below the soil. Handle the husk with care: it is many overlapping brown layers covered in fine, sharp hairs. Run a knife up the side of the shoot to slit it, then unwrap and throw away the layers until you reach the pale core; cut off the pointed tip and the fibrous base. They have a rather bitter flavour: cover the core with water and boil for 20 minutes, change the water and simmer until tender, then boil again in fresh water for 5 minutes, repeating until the flavour is milder.
recipes.title: Preparing fresh shoots

That entry also carries 'Do not use during pregnancy', cited to the same reference as the species' medicinal leaf use, and it is left off this page because it is unclear whether it attaches to the shoots or to the medicine. Habitat: Weedbusters. 'Arrow bamboo' weed information sheet. © Weedbusters, all rights reserved. Retrieved 02/10/2026. https://www.weedbusters.org.nz/what-are-weeds/weed-list/arrow-bamboo/ — paraphrased, not quoted. Source of the habitats-invaded list and of the vegetative-spread note.

Months: Auckland Council, 'Bamboo species' pest page, https://www.tiakitamakimakaurau.nz/protect-and-restore-our-environment/pests-in-auckland/pest-search/phyaur/ — © Auckland Council, all rights reserved, retrieved 08/10/2026. Fact restated, not quoted. The page covers six bamboos and names this one, Arrow Bamboo, among them, and its control advice is to remove young shoots in spring while they are soft because running types only shoot in spring. Spring in New Zealand is September to November, which is the whole of this field. This is a weed-control page, so what it dates is when the shoots are soft enough to pull, which is the same moment they are worth eating, but the page has no interest in eating them.

Months, two routes that were NOT used, recorded so they are not retried. Ken Fern's entry (above) has the shoots cut in late spring, but that is the northern hemisphere, and converting it would land on November here by arithmetic rather than by observation. Forest Floor, 'Bamboo for cane production', http://forestfloor.co.nz/ff/bambooshoot.htm, no licence stated, so all rights reserved, retrieved 08/10/2026, has running bamboos in New Zealand shooting spring to early summer, but that page is about growing bamboo for cane and names Phyllostachys aurea and P. nigra, two of this page's lookalikes, not this species. The usual method does not work here either: an iNaturalist NZ month histogram dates the records, and the records are of canes and leaves, which stand all year, so they cannot date the shoots.

NOT YET ON THE PAGE, and it is the owner's to write: the same Auckland Council page states that these six bamboos, this one included, may not be bred, distributed, released, sold or planted in Auckland, with an exception for relocating an existing plant within the same property, and lists the species as Sustained Control across the whole region under the Regional Pest Management Plan. That bears on a forager — taking shoots is fine and is arguably control, but carrying live rhizome home is not — and it is not yet written anywhere on this entry. The council page is all rights reserved, so it cannot be quoted, and a restatement of a legal rule is safety text. Check it against the Regional Pest Management Plan itself rather than the council's summary of it.

summary.text: Pseudosasa japonica, the arrow bamboo (Japanese: metake), is a species of bamboo in the grass family Poaceae native to Japan and Korea, but planted worldwide as a horticultural plant. The common name "arrow bamboo" results from the Japanese samurai using its hard and stiff canes for their arrows. Introduced to New Zealand as an ornamental and naturalised since 1968, it is the most widespread wild bamboo in the country and is named on DOC's list of environmental weeds.

warnings: Raw bamboo shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides, natural toxins also contained in cassava. The toxins must be destroyed by thorough cooking, and for this reason, fresh bamboo shoots are boiled before being used in other ways.

identification.text:
Perennial herb; taproot cylindric, to about 2 cm diameter, often divided; caulorrhiza short and stout, bearing a number of flowering stems. Hairs variable, the longer ones mostly curved or bent near base. Petiole of basal leaves to about 30 cm long; hairs denser distally and mostly appressed to ascending. Lamina to about 9 cm diameter, reniform to orbicular, lobed to 3/4-⅞ way to midrib; lobes usually 5–7, obovate, sparsely hairy on both sides, obtuse, mucronate, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; median and longer lateral teeth oblong-obovate. Cauline leaves similar to basal but smaller, with few lobes. Flowering stem glabrescent; hairs mostly appressed to ascending; bracteoles more or less linear; flowers in pairs. Outer sepals 3–3.5 × about 2.5 mm, ovate-elliptic; inner sepals narrower, with hyaline margins; hairs short and appressed. Petals about 4.5 × 3 mm, obovate, pale pink. Mericarps hairy; beak to 12 mm long. Seed about 2 × 1.2 mm, oblong, reddish brown; dorsal alveolae mostly rectangular, rather shallow.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped, cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Australasian cranesbill differs from Solander's geranium on three characters: the middle teeth of its leaf lobes are about as long as broad (mostly longer than broad in Solander's geranium); the pale, see-through border of its inner sepals is mostly more than 0.3 mm wide near the tip (mostly less than 0.3 mm); and its seeds are red-brown with rather shallow rectangular pits (red-brown to dark brown, with rather deep rectangular to polygonal pits). Its sepals are mostly elliptic to obovate, against ovate. The lobing does not separate them (both are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way), and both have paired flowers. Solander's geranium's root is recorded as food.
lookalikes.name: Solander's geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Australasian cranesbill differs from turnip-rooted geranium on three characters: the middle teeth of its leaf lobes are about as long as broad (mostly longer than broad in turnip-rooted geranium); the pale, see-through border of its inner sepals is mostly more than 0.3 mm wide near the tip (mostly less than 0.3 mm); and its seeds are red-brown with rather shallow rectangular pits (red-brown to dark brown, with rather deep rectangular to polygonal pits). Its sepals are mostly elliptic to obovate, against ovate. The lobing does not separate them (both are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way), and both have paired flowers. No source read records turnip-rooted geranium as food, and it is nationally Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable (2023 assessment).

lookalikes.howToTell: Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Cinquefoil geranium is separated from Australasian cranesbill on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in Australasian cranesbill, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in Australasian cranesbill. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of Australasian cranesbill overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Cinquefoil geranium's root is recorded as food.
lookalikes.name: Cinquefoil geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Cut-leaved cranesbill is an annual, usually with a thin fibrous taproot and glandular hairs prominent in the flower clusters, while Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a rather stout to tuberous rootstock and no, very few, or short and inconspicuous glandular hairs on the flower clusters. Cut-leaved cranesbill's leaves are cut almost to the leaf stalk into linear segments; Australasian cranesbill's are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into broader lobes. Both have pink petals. Older floras placed Australasian cranesbill under Geranium dissectum (Allan's 1961 Flora of New Zealand treated it as Geranium australe and Geranium dissectum var. glabratum Hook.f.), so older records may use that name. Cut-leaved cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food.

summary.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island; South Island: rare south of Nelson and Marlborough. Also indigenous to Australia.
It is mainly found in modified habitats, and so may have greatly increased in frequency during the last 2 centuries. G. homeanum was treated by Allan (1961) as G. australe.

identification.text:
An annual, much-branched, grey-green, glaucous to red-green saltbush up to 1 m tall and 2 m across, with male and female flowers on the same plant. Main stems four-angled, widely spreading to nearly erect, woody at the base and otherwise firmly fleshy to succulent, deeply ribbed and stout, up to 15 mm thick, grey-green to glaucous at first and turning purple-red to maroon with age; upper stems much branched, ribbed and more or less slender. Leaf stalks stout and fleshy, up to 20 mm long. Leaves 20–100 mm long and 30–60 mm wide, very fleshy to almost succulent, broadly lance-shaped, broadly triangular or broadly arrow-shaped, with a broadly wedge-shaped base and a blunt to pointed tip. On young plants the leaves are more or less entire, usually with one or two deep, forward-pointing lobes near the base, often on one side only; mature leaves are entire or deeply but irregularly lobed to almost coarsely toothed, the lobes broadly triangular, blunt and pointing forward. Flowers in long, branched spikes that arch and hang in fruit, in dense clusters that at first touch and later become separated. Female flowers are enclosed by bracteoles 1.5–2 mm long at flowering. Fruiting bracteoles 3–4 mm long and 2–5 mm wide, triangular, joined near the base, entire or with one or two teeth, smooth or warty, very fleshy, grey-green to glaucous and turning black and much thickened with age. Fruits mostly 2.5–4 mm across, round and flattened; seed coat glossy black and smooth. Flowers November to April; fruits December to May.
Told from common orache by its much wider, often deeply toothed or lobed leaves, its more robust build and its much fleshier, more glaucous foliage; young plants often have entire leaves or leaves lobed once or twice near the base.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at mature plants and the fruit. Australian orache is robust, up to 1 m tall and 2 m across, with stout main stems up to 15 mm thick and woody at the base; its leaves are very fleshy to almost succulent, 20–100 mm long and 30–60 mm wide, broadly lance-shaped to broadly triangular or arrow-shaped with a broadly wedge-shaped base, and on mature plants often deeply but irregularly lobed or coarsely toothed, the lobes blunt and pointing forward. Common orache has ribbed, more or less slender stems and leaves 20–70 mm long and 3–40 mm wide, mostly narrowly lance-shaped to elliptic with a narrowly wedge-shaped to wedge-shaped base, and nearly always entire. In fruit, Australian orache's bracteoles are 3–4 mm long and very fleshy, turning black and much thickened with age; common orache's are thin, green or grey-mealy, and usually 2.5–8.5 mm long. Young Australian orache often has entire leaves or leaves lobed once or twice near the base, like common orache, so go by mature plants and the fruit. Many botanists treat the two as one species. Common orache is eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Common orache

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaf bases, the stems and the fruit. Spear-leaved orache's lower leaves are mostly triangular-arrow-shaped and toothed above the basal lobes, with a base usually squared off (sometimes broadly wedge-shaped or arrow-shaped), on slender stalks 1–2.5 cm long; Australian orache's leaves have a broadly wedge-shaped base and blunt, forward-pointing lobes, on stout, fleshy stalks up to 20 mm long. Australian orache has stout main stems up to 15 mm thick and woody at the base; spear-leaved orache's stems are more or less slender. In fruit, Australian orache's bracteoles are 3–4 mm long, entire or with one or two teeth, very fleshy, turning black and much thickened with age; spear-leaved orache's reach 9 mm, are usually toothed and generally have small outgrowths. Spear-leaved orache's bracteoles are extremely variable in New Zealand, so check more than one character. Spear-leaved orache also grows around the Chatham Islands lagoon. Spear-leaved orache is eaten (see its page).

Name: 'Australian orache' is the vernacular in Flora of New Zealand Online (https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Atriplex-australasica.html, retrieved 09/11/2026) and iNaturalist's preferred common name; NZPCN gives only the generic 'orache, saltbush', and NZTCS gives 'spreading orach', which Wikipedia uses for A. patula, so neither was taken. No Māori name in NZPCN, NZTCS, Flora of New Zealand Online or Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga, so none given.

Agrees with NZPCN ('Indigenous', 'Endemic taxon No'; '2023 | At Risk – Relict | Qualifiers: RR, SO') and Flora of New Zealand Online ('Indigenous (Non-endemic)'). No food use is recorded, so the 'There is no reason to pick this plant' sentence is used, not the At Risk one, following the Kermadec pōhutukawa and Chatham Island ice plant entries (owner's harvest-ethics rule). No recipes (none sourced; At Risk entries carry none).

Summary, habitat and identification: NZPCN 'Atriplex australasica' (de Lange; all rights reserved), retrieved 09/11/2026 — detailed description, similar taxa, distribution ('South Island (known from a 1770 collection from the Marlborough Sounds, possibly from two 1860 collections made from south Canterbury by Haast and Kirk), Chatham Islands (abundant). Also Australia (southern coast) and Tasmania'), habitat, threats ('Only recently rediscovered on the Chatham Islands where it is very common'), flowering November–April, fruiting December–May, dispersal (Thorsen et al. 2009) and etymology, all restated. There is no Flora of New Zealand description of this species: Flora vol. IV (1988) sank the name into A. patula ('A. patula has been known as A. angustifolia, A. australasica and A. erecta in N.Z.', https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/b95f3b1c-398d-4f55-8548-8252f2bb9dfc), and Biota of New Zealand keeps 'Atriplex australasica sensu early New Zealand Botanists' as a synonym of A. patula alongside the accepted A. australasica Moq. Not used: Plants of South Eastern New South Wales' description (Australian; its bracteoles 'free from each other from midway or to the base' differ from NZPCN's 'fused near base').

Common orache (both ways): NZPCN's named confusion above and its test ('differs consistently by its much wider, often deeply toothed or lobed leaves … more robust stature and much more fleshy-glaucous foliage'), with the NZPCN description of this species and Flora of New Zealand vol. IV's A. patula description (lamina 2–7 × 0.3–4 cm, nearly always entire, base narrow-cuneate to cuneate; stems ribbed, ± slender; fruiting bracteoles (1.5)–2.5–8.5–(11) mm, thin, green or grey-farinose; 'Ch.' in its distribution). summary.text:
Atriplex australasica, Australian orache, is an annual saltbush in the amaranth family (Amaranthaceae), native to New Zealand and to the southern coast of Australia and Tasmania.
In New Zealand it is abundant on the Chatham Islands, where it was only recently rediscovered. On the South Island it is known from a 1770 collection from the Marlborough Sounds, and possibly from two 1860 collections from south Canterbury. In the 2023 national assessment it is At Risk – Relict, with a restricted range, and secure overseas.
It has been confused with common orache, Atriplex patula, in New Zealand writing, and many botanists regard the two as one species, in which case the name A. patula has priority. Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (1988) noted that common orache had been known in New Zealand as A. australasica.
Its seeds are spongy nutlets, spread by water and possibly also by wind and seed-eating animals. Australasica means 'of or from Australasia'.

warnings: No record of Australian orache as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

On the Chatham Islands it grows near spear-leaved orache, and common orache has been recorded there too. Australian orache has been confused with common orache in New Zealand writing, and spear-leaved orache is easily confused with both. Check the leaves and fruit before picking any orache there (see the lookalikes).

NatureSpot, 'Autumn Hawkbit' (all rights reserved — restated)
identification.text:
Perennial with stout rootstock. Stems erect, branching, 20–75 cm tall, glabrous or with sparse simple hairs. Leaves all basal, linear to ovate, pinnatifid with narrow-triangular or linear, patent or recurved lobes, rarely simple, toothed, (3)–5–15–(40) × (0.3)–1.5–5–(8) cm; hairs simple, sparse or 0. Stem bracts numerous, especially above, narrow-triangular to linear. Capitula turbinate, erect in bud. Involucral bracts linear-lanceolate, acute, with fine pale hairs and usually longer dark hairs also; outer bracts about ½ length of inner bracts; inner bracts 8–12 mm long. Florets yellow, 1½–2× length of involucre. Stigmas greyish green. Achenes reddish brown, all similar, wrinkled, not beaked, fusiform to cylindric, 4–5 mm long. Pappus in 1 row; hairs plumose, widened at base.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4. as Leontodon autumnalis L.]
In the field (NatureSpot, restated): the stem swells just below the head, so the bracts narrow into the stalk rather than forming a bell; the outer florets are striped red underneath; leaf hairs, if any, are simple, never forked; there are no scales among the florets. A photo taken from the side, showing head and stem, is what confirms it — one looking down on the flower is not enough.

lookalikes.howToTell: A dandelion's flower stem is unbranched, hollow and leafless, with a single head; autumn hawkbit's stems branch, carry many small narrow bracts, especially near the top, and bear several heads, and they are not hollow. A dandelion's leaf stalk and the base of its midrib are hollow too. Leaves alone do not separate them: both form a rosette of lobed leaves that are hairless or sparsely hairy. In seed, a dandelion's achenes carry a slender beak 7–10 mm long under a parachute of fine white hairs; autumn hawkbit's have no beak and a feathery parachute. Both have yellow heads and milky sap. The dandelion's leaves, flowers and roots are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Dandelion

lookalikes.howToTell: Autumn hawkbit's stems branch, carry many small narrow bracts and hold their buds erect; hawkbit's stem is unbranched, with a single head, none to a few small scale-like bracts, and nodding buds. Under a hand lens, hawkbit's leaf hairs fork into two or three at the tip; autumn hawkbit's are simple, sparse or absent. Autumn hawkbit's stigmas are greyish green, hawkbit's yellow. Turned over, autumn hawkbit's outer florets are striped red underneath, hawkbit's usually greyish violet. In seed, autumn hawkbit's achenes are all alike, unbeaked, with a single row of feathery hairs; hawkbit's outer achenes have only a ring of tiny scales. Both have yellow heads, basal rosettes of lobed leaves and milky sap. Hawkbit's leaves are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Hawkbit

lookalikes.howToTell: Pull a head apart: catsear has thin, tapering, nearly transparent scales with yellow tips among its florets, easy to miss; autumn hawkbit has none. This is the best feature for telling them apart. Catsear's leaves have moderately dense, stiff, pale hairs; autumn hawkbit's are hairless or sparsely hairy. Autumn hawkbit's stems carry many small narrow bracts, especially above, where catsear's have only a few minute ones. Leaf shape does not help: autumn hawkbit's is remarkably variable. Both usually have branched stems with several yellow heads, a rosette of leaves and milky sap. Catsear's young leaves and roots are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Catsear

lookalikes.howToTell: Mouse-ear hawkweed has one head on a stem with no more than one scale-like leaf, (2)–5–10–(15) cm tall at flowering and lengthening up to about five times as the seed ripens; autumn hawkbit's stems are 20–75 cm, branched, with numerous small bracts and several heads. Mouse-ear hawkweed's leaves are untoothed or very obscurely toothed with a very dense coat of star-shaped hairs that makes the underside white, and it spreads by creeping runners; autumn hawkbit's are usually cut into narrow lobes, with sparse simple hairs or none. Mouse-ear hawkweed's achenes are about 2 mm with simple bristles; autumn hawkbit's are 4–5 mm with feathery pappus hairs. Both have yellow heads and milky sap. No food use of mouse-ear hawkweed is recorded; its traditional uses are medicinal (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mouse-ear hawkweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Autumn hawkbit's stems branch, carry many small narrow bracts and hold their buds erect; microseris's flower stems are leafless and unbranched, with a single head, and its buds nod. Autumn hawkbit's outer involucral bracts are about half as long as the inner ones and its florets a darker yellow; microseris has a single row of involucral bracts with a few small bracteoles at the base. In seed, autumn hawkbit's achenes carry a single row of feathery hairs; microseris's pappus hairs are stiff, brownish and minutely barbed. Leaf hairs do not separate them: both have leaves that are hairless or nearly so. Both have yellow heads, basal rosettes of often lobed leaves and milky sap. Microseris is a native plant whose roots are edible, though eating them rests on two tastings and no Māori food use is recorded; murnong, the Australian 'yam daisy' eaten for its tuber, is a different species (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Microseris

preparation.text: No source gives a method written for this species. Its leaves go to the same uses as dandelion's: raw in salad or cooked as a green. Dandelion greens are bitter; if you dislike bitterness, cook them rather than eating them raw, and season them with salt, lemon or chilli. The recipes below are written for dandelion or for wild greens in general.

recipes.method: Written for any wild greens, dandelion among them. Serves 2–4. About 225 g cooked wild greens; a medium clove of garlic (about 5 g); 2 tbsp olive oil, plus more to serve; a pinch of chilli flakes; salt, or a finely chopped anchovy fillet or a dash of fish sauce; lemon wedges. Blanch the greens in boiling salted water until they taste good to you — for wild greens this can take 10–15 minutes — and chop long ones coarsely; you want about 225 g cooked. Slice a medium clove of garlic (about 5 g) as thinly as you can and cook it in 2 tbsp olive oil in a 20 cm pan over medium-low heat for 4–5 minutes, until lightly browned and fragrant but not burnt. Add a pinch of chilli flakes, then the greens; season, stir to coat and heat through; with bitter greens, a finely chopped anchovy fillet or a dash of fish sauce can stand in for the salt. Serve with lemon wedges and more olive oil.
recipes.title: Wild greens with garlic and chilli

recipes.method: Written for dandelion greens. Garlic; 2 tbsp olive oil; 4 tbsp pine nuts; about 1.25 litres (loosely packed) greens; 1 tbsp balsamic vinegar; about 45 g grated Parmesan; salt and pepper. Gently cook garlic in 2 tbsp olive oil over medium-low heat for 3–4 minutes without letting it burn, then lift it out onto a paper towel. Toast 4 tbsp pine nuts in the same oil over low heat for 3–4 minutes until browned and lift them out too. Add about 1.25 litres (loosely packed) of greens cut into 5 cm pieces and cook on low for 2–3 minutes until wilted. Stir in 1 tbsp balsamic vinegar, the pine nuts and garlic, then about 45 g grated Parmesan; season with salt and pepper.
recipes.title: Sautéed greens with pine nuts

recipes.method: Written for dandelion leaves. For the salad: 1.75 kg butternut pumpkin; olive oil; salt and pepper; about 60 ml pumpkin seeds; garlic salt; 200 g washed leaves. For the dressing: 60 ml honey; 2 tbsp balsamic vinegar; 1 tbsp olive oil. Heat the oven to 250 °C. Cut 1.75 kg butternut pumpkin into 2 cm-thick pieces, toss with olive oil, salt and pepper, and roast in one layer on two lined trays for about 20 minutes, turning once, until golden and tender; let it cool. Toast about 60 ml pumpkin seeds, tossed in olive oil and garlic salt, in a moderate oven for about 5 minutes. Tear 200 g washed leaves into bite-sized pieces and sauté in a hot oiled pan until cooked. Shake 60 ml honey, 2 tbsp balsamic vinegar and 1 tbsp olive oil in a jar (warm the honey first if it is stiff). Combine the greens and pumpkin, scatter with the seeds, dress, and season.
recipes.title: Roast pumpkin and sautéed greens salad

summary.text:
Scorzoneroides autumnalis, commonly called autumn hawkbit, is a perennial plant species, widespread in its native range in Eurasia (from Europe east to western Siberia), and introduced in North America.
The plant is sometimes called fall dandelion, because it is very similar to the common dandelion (one of the main differences being a branched stem with several capitula), but "yellow fields", covered by this plant appear much later than dandelions, towards the autumn in Eastern Europe.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Wairarapa (one early collection); South Island: Canterbury, Otago, Southland. Naturalised from Europe, Asia and North Africa, first recorded in 1867.
New Zealand specimens belong to subsp. autumnalis. Leontodon autumnalis may sometimes resemble forms of the native Microseris scapigera, but is distinguished by the branching stems bearing stem bracts, the outer involucral bracts about ½ the length of inner bracts, the darker yellow florets and plumose pappus hairs.
