identification.text:
Passiflora tarminiana is a high climbing vine with hairy stems and petioles. Where the petioles join the stem it has stipules which are 4–7 by 2–3 mm and are soon deciduous. The leaves are three-lobed and hairy below but usually hairless above. The flowers are solitary and hang downwards. The base of the flower has pale green bracts enclosing a swollen nectary chamber. The floral tube (hypanthium) is 6–8 × 0.7–1 cm and pale green, while the sepals and petals are 3–6 cm long, pink and perpendicular to the floral tube, or reflexed. Fruits taper at both ends, are 10–14 cm long by 3.5–4.5 cm wide and ripen to yellow or light orange. The fruit contain many seeds which are embedded in an edible, orange aril.
Passiflora tarminiana is distinguished from P. tripartita var. mollissima by a number of features. P. tarminiana has small deciduous stipules while P. tripartita var. mollissima has larger, persistent stipules. The sepals and petals in P. tarminiana are perpendicular to the floral tube or are reflexed, whereas they are never so open in P. tripartita var. mollissima. They are also both much shorter in relation to the length of the floral tube in P. tripartita var. mollissima than in P. tarminiana.

lookalikes.howToTell: The flowers separate them: black passionfruit's petals are white and its corona threads white with a purple base, and it has no conspicuous floral tube; banana passionfruit's flowers are pink, hang down, and sit on a pale green floral tube whose reported length varies by source (up to 6 cm, 6-8 cm, or 6-9.5 cm). Black passionfruit's fruit is dull purple, broadly ellipsoid to nearly round, 5-6.25 cm long and 4.75-5.75 cm across, with black seeds; banana passionfruit's is slender and tapers at both ends, ripening yellow to light orange, with dark red seeds, and reported lengths run from up to 9 cm to 14 cm depending on the source. Black passionfruit has narrow stipules 10-15 mm long; banana passionfruit's are small and soon fall, so mature stems lack them. Both fruits are edible.
lookalikes.name: Black passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are vigorous climbing vines with three-lobed leaves and pink flowers, and both have sweet, edible orange pulp, so leaf outline and flower colour do not separate them. Go to the stipules where the leaf stalk meets the stem: pink-flowered passionfruit's are pinnate — a very narrow central strip fringed almost to its base with dark thread-like segments. Banana passionfruit's are small, about 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and fall early, so a mature stem usually has none. The ripe fruit also helps: pink-flowered passionfruit's is round or slightly flattened, 4–7 cm across, yellow and finely downy; banana passionfruit's is slender and tapers at both ends. Floral-tube length is not a safe test: pink-flowered passionfruit's is about 4–5 cm, and banana passionfruit's is given as anything from up to 6 cm to 9.5 cm depending on the source. Pink-flowered passionfruit's corona threads are violet-blue, but the sources checked do not describe banana passionfruit's corona, so do not use colour there as a comparison. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Pink-flowered passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube about 6–8 cm long (published figures run from up to 6 cm to 8 cm), with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and published lengths run from up to 9 cm to 14 cm. Banana passionfruit (P. tarminiana) has small stipules that soon fall, while P. tripartita's are larger and stay on. In flower, P. tarminiana's sepals and petals spread flat or bend back, while P. tripartita's never open that far and are much shorter compared with the floral tube, and P. tripartita's tube is the longer one, about 8–10 cm against 6–7 cm, though P. tarminiana's is also given as up to 8 cm, so a tube near 8 cm does not decide it. P. tripartita var. mollissima's leaves are moderately to densely hairy on the upper surface, where P. tarminiana's are usually hairless above. P. tarminiana hybridises with other members of its subgenus, Tacsonia, and the hybrid P. tarminiana × tripartita has been recorded wild in New Zealand, so an in-between plant may be neither. P. tripartita's other New Zealand variety, var. azuayensis, has leaves hairless or nearly so above, so upper-leaf hairs alone do not separate it from P. tarminiana. Both have 3-lobed leaves, pink hanging flowers and edible yellow-orange fruit, so leaf outline, flower colour and fruit colour do not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube about 6–8 cm long (published figures run from up to 6 cm to 8 cm), with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and published lengths run from up to 9 cm to 14 cm. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia's leaves are undivided and leathery and its flowers under 2 cm across, while banana passionfruit (P. tarminiana)'s leaves are 3-lobed. Kōhia is dioecious: only female plants bear fruit, and only after pollen reaches them from a male plant, so a vine without fruit can still be kōhia; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Kōhia

recipes.method: 20–30 banana passionfruit; around 1–1.5 litres water; the juice of 2 lemons (6–8 tbsp); up to 1.1 kg sugar. Halve the fruit and scrape the pulp and seeds into a pot, then drop the empty skins in with them — in the hope they release pectin into the juice. The author notes you might not want to add the skins if the fruit is not organic. Add just enough water to cover, around 1–1.5 litres, bring to the boil and simmer 30–45 minutes, stirring now and then. Strain, pressing the pulp to get all the juice out, and throw away the skins and spent seeds. Return the juice to the pot with the lemon juice and sugar, and boil until it reaches setting point — allow another half hour, longer if it started watery. Pour into clean jars and water-bath 15 minutes to seal. Makes about six 250 ml jars. The author says the sugar can come down from 1.1 kg if that is too sweet, but some is needed for the pectin to set.
recipes.title: Banana passionfruit jelly

recipes.method: 12 ripe fruit, 240 ml water, about 300 g sugar, 2 litres milk, 60 ml cream, ice. Halve the fruit and scoop the pulp into a blender with the water, and blend to a cream. Add the milk, the sugar and a little crushed ice and blend at medium speed, then add the cream and blend one minute more. Strain out the seeds if you like, and serve cold.
recipes.title: Curuba milk drink (jugo de curuba en leche)

recipes.method: 8 fruit; 240 ml water; 4 tablespoons sugar; 480 ml milk; a 200 g pot of cream; a little ice, if you like; a bar of chocolate. Blend the pulp with 240 ml water and strain out the seeds. Blend the juice again with the sugar, the milk and 6 tablespoons of the cream, with a little ice if you like. Melt the chocolate, coat the inside of each glass and chill to set it. Whip the rest of the cream until firm, pour the sorbete into the glasses and top with the cream.
recipes.title: Curuba sorbete with chocolate

recipes.method: 10 fruit, 600 ml water, about 400 g sugar, 2 cloves, the juice of 1 lemon. Scoop out the pulp, blend it for only about 3 seconds with 120 ml of the water, and strain to keep the liquid. In a large pot put the remaining 480 ml water, the sugar, the cloves and the lemon juice, add the strained liquid and cook over medium-low heat for about 40 minutes, until it thickens. Take out the cloves before it comes off the heat, and let it cool. Good on bread.

Lookalike cards among the five Passiflora entries (written by the assistant on the owner's instruction (owner, 22/10/2026: /goal "find all you can about Passiflora and fill in following the rules")): each card restates the two species' descriptions and Flora of New Zealand's Passiflora key — Webb, C.J. et al. 1988, Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Flora of New Zealand Series, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/0e0cc34b-28b7-4b4a-8a94-9b059b1af976 — couplet 1 'Hypanthium cylindric and strongly elongated' against 'Hypanthium 0 or saucer-shaped and inconspicuous'; couplet 2 'Stipules pinnate with filiform segments; fr. ± globose' (pinnatistipula) against 'Stipules simple, ovate and toothed or subulate and entire; fr. ellipsoid'; couplet 3 '× rosea' 'Stipules with lanceolate rachis; stamens abnormal and ± petaloid'; couplet 6 'Lvs entire, coriaceous; perianth < 2 cm diam. when fresh' (tetrandra) against 'Lvs lobed, membranous or submembranous; perianth > 4 cm diam. when fresh'. Descriptions: Webb 1988 for P. edulis, P. pinnatistipula, P. tetrandra and P. mollissima (= P. tripartita var. mollissima; Flora of New Zealand Online files Webb's P. mollissima description under that name); for P. tarminiana, which Webb did not separate, Wikipedia 'Passiflora tarminiana' (revision 1352787405, CC BY-SA 4.0), NZPCN's P. tarminiana page (all rights reserved; facts restated) and Flora of New Zealand Online's weed profiles (CC BY 3.0 NZ: tube '6-7 cm' for P. tarminiana, '8-10 cm' and leaves 'moderately to densely hairy on the upper surface' for P. tripartita var. mollissima). The tarminiana–tripartita test follows Wikipedia's 'distinguished from P. tripartita var. mollissima' paragraph and NZPCN ('Can be distinguished from P. tarminiana by the large persistent stipules, and the long hypanthium'); var. azuayensis 'leaves glabrous to glabrate on upper surface' is NZPCN after Heenan & Sykes 2003; the hybrid is iNaturalist taxon 1645626, Passiflora tarminiana × tripartita (43 wild New Zealand records on 22/10/2026). Blue passionflower: NZPCN 'Most similar to P. caerulea in flower'; Webb 1988 'Lvs 5-lobed almost to base', 'pulp scanty and inedible'. × rosea: Webb's key and NZPCN's P. pinnatistipula page. Kōhia's fruit only on female plants: Wikipedia 'Passiflora tetrandra' (revision 1324332696). Risk `edible` every way, because every page carries a food record. Not carded: black passionfruit ↔ pink-flowered passionfruit — Webb gives black passionfruit 'N.: N. Auckland … Great Barrier Id; K.' and pink-flowered 'S.: Banks Peninsula (widespread), Otago (Palmerston)', so their wild ranges do not meet in the Flora. Recipes 'Curuba milk drink', 'Curuba sorbete with chocolate' and 'Tumbo jam' (written by the assistant on the owner's instruction, owner, 22/10/2026: /goal "find some recipies for passionara"; restated in English, metric, no text reproduced; Spanish-language sources are used for facts only, as for the mallows): (1) 'Jugo de Curuba o Sorbete de Curuba', El Rincón Colombiano (filed under Gastronomía de Cundinamarca), © all rights reserved, retrieved 22/10/2026, https://elrinconcolombiano.com/jugo-de-curuba/ — its '1½ taza de azúcar' is given here as about 300 g and '1 taza' as 240 ml; (2) and (3) '+10 recetas con tumbo o curuba', Comida Peruana Web, © all rights reserved, retrieved 22/10/2026, https://comidaperuanaweb.org/gastronomia/recetas-con-tumbo/ — the sorbete is its 'Sorbete de curuba', and the jam its 'Mermelada de tumbo'. The jam's ingredient list omits the sugar its method adds ('2 tazas de azúcar', given here as about 400 g) and lists '1/2 cucharadita de canela en polvo' that its method never uses, so the cinnamon is left out. The page's '1 taza de agua (240 ml)' sets the cup used. summary.text:
Passiflora tarminiana is native to the uplands of tropical South America but the exact native range is uncertain as it has been widely cultivated in this region. It is found in the Colombian highlands and the Venezuelan, Peruvian and southern Ecuadorean Andes where it is cultivated from around 2000 – 3000 metres.
It has naturalised in Australia, Guam, Hawaii, New Zealand and Zimbabwe. In both Hawaii and New Zealand it is regarded as an invasive species. It is widely cultivated throughout the world, including California, Réunion, Mexico, Panama and Papua New Guinea.
Passiflora tripartita var. mollissima and P. tarminiana were until recently considered to be one species, P. mollissima.

warnings: An unwanted organism under the National Pest Plant Accord. It cannot be sold, propagated, distributed or released, and regional rules require control in places — sustained control across the Bay of Plenty, site-led management on Otago Peninsula and around Dunedin's West Harbour.

edibleParts.text:
The pulp surrounding the seeds is eaten. The fruit is yellow-orange when ripe and contains a sweet edible orange-colored pulp with black seeds.
The fruits of this species are a pale yellow colour, the pulp is more aromatic and tart and has a somewhat superior flavour to the flesh of the deep yellow to orange fruits of Passiflora tarminiana.

identification.text:
Vigorous vine; shoots densely hairy, weakly angular when young. Leaves 3-lobed; petioles 1.5–5 cm long, densely hairy, with (4)–6–12 stalked or subsessile glands; stipules 5–10 mm wide (excluding subulate apex when present), subreniform, with glandular teeth; lamina lobes usually 5–14 cm long, extending 1/2-⅔ of the distance in from the margin, usually more or less tomentose below, hairy or glabrate above, elliptic or elliptic-ovate, narrow-lanceolate on juvenile shoots, serrate or serrulate, acute; middle lobe largest, 4–9 × 2–5 cm. Flowers bisexual, solitary. Pedicels longer than petioles, densely hairy. Bracts 1.5–3.75 cm long, ovate or broad-ovate, more or less tomentose outside, entire or slightly toothed, united for lower 1/4–1/2 until anthesis. Hypanthium 8–9.5 cm long, glabrous outside. Sepals 2–3.8 cm long, elliptic, green on reverse, pink or rose inside, rounded and with short horn near apex; petals similar but pink on both sides; corona a ring of purple, white-tipped scales 1–2 mm long. Filaments 1.5–2 cm long, pale, often scarcely longer than anthers; anthers (7)–10–12 mm long. Ovary white-villous. Fruit (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow, puberulent; pulp sweet and orange, edible. Seed 4.5–5.5 mm long, broad-obovoid, dark red to black, alveolate.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Passiflora mollissima (Kunth) L.H.Bailey.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube given in different descriptions as up to 6 cm, 6–7 cm or 6–8 cm, with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and is given as up to 9 cm long or as 10–14 cm. Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Banana passionfruit (P. tarminiana) has small stipules that soon fall, while P. tripartita's are larger and stay on. In flower, P. tarminiana's sepals and petals spread flat or bend back, while P. tripartita's never open that far and are much shorter compared with the floral tube, and P. tripartita's tube is the longer one: 8–10 cm against 6–7 cm, though one description gives P. tarminiana 6–8 cm, which reaches the bottom of that range, so a tube near 8 cm does not decide it. P. tripartita var. mollissima's leaves are moderately to densely hairy on the upper surface, where P. tarminiana's are usually hairless above. P. tarminiana hybridises with other members of its subgenus, and wild hybrids of the two have been recorded in New Zealand, so an in-between plant may be neither. P. tripartita's other New Zealand variety, var. azuayensis, has leaves hairless or nearly so above, so upper-leaf hairs alone do not separate it from P. tarminiana. Both have 3-lobed leaves, pink hanging flowers and edible yellow-orange fruit, so leaf outline, flower colour and fruit colour do not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Pink-flowered passionfruit has downy young shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, grey- or white-felted underneath and dark shining green above; its stipules are pinnate, with dark thread-like segments almost to the base of a very narrow central strip; its flowers have a floral tube (4)–4.5–5 cm long, pink petals and violet-blue corona threads; its fruit is 4–7 cm across, round or slightly flattened, yellow and finely downy. Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Pink-flowered passionfruit's stipules are pinnate, with thread-like segments, and its fruit is more or less round; a banana passionfruit's stipules are simple — either ovate and toothed or awl-shaped and untoothed — and its fruit is ellipsoid. Both have pink flowers and edible orange pulp, so flower colour does not separate them. A hybrid, Passiflora × rosea, which has no entry here, looks very like pink-flowered passionfruit, but the central strip of its stipules is lanceolate and its stamens are usually abnormal. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Pink-flowered passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. The fruit separates them too: black passionfruit's is dull purple and nearly round; the fruit of banana passionfruit (P. tripartita) is yellow or orange when ripe and elongated. Blue passionflower, which has no entry here, has a flower much like black passionfruit's, but its leaves are 5-lobed and its pulp is scanty and inedible. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Black passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia has undivided, leathery leaves and flowers under 2 cm across, against lobed leaves and flowers over 4 cm across in the passionfruits it keys out beside, and banana passionfruit (P. tripartita)'s leaves are 3-lobed. Only female kōhia plants bear fruit (the plant is dioecious), so a fruitless kōhia is common; use the leaves. Both are edible.

preparation.text: Fruit - eaten raw or used in ice creams, fruit salads, pies, jellies, to make drinks etc.

recipes.method: 20–30 banana passionfruit; around 1–1.5 litres water; the juice of 2 lemons (6–8 tbsp); up to 1.1 kg sugar. Halve the fruit and scrape the pulp and seeds into a pot, then drop the empty skins in with them — in the hope they release pectin into the juice. The author notes you might not want to add the skins if the fruit is not organic. Add just enough water to cover, around 1–1.5 litres, bring to the boil and simmer 30–45 minutes, stirring now and then. Strain, pressing the pulp to get all the juice out, and throw away the skins and spent seeds. Return the juice to the pot with the lemon juice and sugar, and boil until it reaches setting point — allow another half hour, longer if it started watery. Pour into clean jars and water-bath 15 minutes to seal. Makes about six 250 ml jars. The author says the sugar can come down from 1.1 kg if that is too sweet, but some is needed for the pectin to set.
recipes.title: Banana passionfruit jelly

recipes.method: 12 ripe fruit, 240 ml water, about 300 g sugar, 2 litres milk, 60 ml cream, ice. Halve the fruit and scoop the pulp into a blender with the water, and blend to a cream. Add the milk, the sugar and a little crushed ice and blend at medium speed, then add the cream and blend one minute more. Strain out the seeds if you like, and serve cold.
recipes.title: Curuba milk drink (jugo de curuba en leche)

recipes.method: 8 fruit; 240 ml water; 4 tablespoons sugar; 480 ml milk; a 200 g pot of cream; a little ice, if you like; a bar of chocolate. Blend the pulp with 240 ml water and strain out the seeds. Blend the juice again with the sugar, the milk and 6 tablespoons of the cream, with a little ice if you like. Melt the chocolate, coat the inside of each glass and chill to set it. Whip the rest of the cream until firm, pour the sorbete into the glasses and top with the cream.
recipes.title: Curuba sorbete with chocolate

recipes.method: 10 fruit, 600 ml water, about 400 g sugar, 2 cloves, the juice of 1 lemon. Scoop out the pulp, blend it for only about 3 seconds with 120 ml of the water, and strain to keep the liquid. In a large pot put the remaining 480 ml water, the sugar, the cloves and the lemon juice, add the strained liquid and cook over medium-low heat for about 40 minutes, until it thickens. Take out the cloves before it comes off the heat, and let it cool. Good on bread.
recipes.title: Tumbo jam (mermelada de tumbo)

Checked 22/10/2026: Weedbusters and Bay of Plenty Regional Council both give flowers from January to December, followed by fruit; NZPCN and Webb give flowering in every month; iNaturalist New Zealand wild records annotated 'fruiting' (n = 89) reach at least a quarter of the peak month in all twelve months; and ripe yellow fruit shows in research-grade photos from July (obs 89283504) and August (obs 30666880).

Lookalike cards among the five Passiflora entries (written by the assistant on the owner's instruction (owner, 22/10/2026: /goal "find all you can about Passiflora and fill in following the rules")): each card restates the two species' descriptions and Flora of New Zealand's Passiflora key — Webb, C.J. et al. 1988, Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Flora of New Zealand Series, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/0e0cc34b-28b7-4b4a-8a94-9b059b1af976 — couplet 1 'Hypanthium cylindric and strongly elongated' against 'Hypanthium 0 or saucer-shaped and inconspicuous'; couplet 2 'Stipules pinnate with filiform segments; fr. ± globose' (pinnatistipula) against 'Stipules simple, ovate and toothed or subulate and entire; fr. ellipsoid'; couplet 3 '× rosea' 'Stipules with lanceolate rachis; stamens abnormal and ± petaloid'; couplet 6 'Lvs entire, coriaceous; perianth < 2 cm diam. when fresh' (tetrandra) against 'Lvs lobed, membranous or submembranous; perianth > 4 cm diam. when fresh'. Descriptions: Webb 1988 for P. edulis, P. pinnatistipula, P. tetrandra and P. mollissima (= P. tripartita var. mollissima; Flora of New Zealand Online files Webb's P. mollissima description under that name); for P. tarminiana, which Webb did not separate, Wikipedia 'Passiflora tarminiana' (revision 1352787405, CC BY-SA 4.0), NZPCN's P. tarminiana page (all rights reserved; facts restated) and Flora of New Zealand Online's weed profiles (CC BY 3.0 NZ: tube '6-7 cm' for P. tarminiana, '8-10 cm' and leaves 'moderately to densely hairy on the upper surface' for P. tripartita var. mollissima). The tarminiana–tripartita test follows Wikipedia's 'distinguished from P. tripartita var. mollissima' paragraph and NZPCN ('Can be distinguished from P. tarminiana by the large persistent stipules, and the long hypanthium'); var. azuayensis 'leaves glabrous to glabrate on upper surface' is NZPCN after Heenan & Sykes 2003; the hybrid is iNaturalist taxon 1645626, Passiflora tarminiana × tripartita (43 wild New Zealand records on 22/10/2026). Blue passionflower: NZPCN 'Most similar to P. caerulea in flower'; Webb 1988 'Lvs 5-lobed almost to base', 'pulp scanty and inedible'. × rosea: Webb's key and NZPCN's P. pinnatistipula page. Kōhia's fruit only on female plants: Wikipedia 'Passiflora tetrandra' (revision 1324332696). Risk `edible` every way, because every page carries a food record. Not carded: black passionfruit ↔ pink-flowered passionfruit — Webb gives black passionfruit 'N.: N. Auckland … Great Barrier Id; K.' and pink-flowered 'S.: Banks Peninsula (widespread), Otago (Palmerston)', so their wild ranges do not meet in the Flora. Blue passionflower, P. × rosea, P. mixta and P. antioquiensis have no entries (owner, 22/10/2026: blue passionflower 'Skip it').

Photos (the owner's curation in the editor, seen 22/10/2026; this line replaces the assistant's earlier description of a set the owner has since changed): -8 hanging flowers (obs 45728051, John Barkla, Port Chalmers, CC BY — var. azuayensis), -9 ripe fruit (obs 30666880, Amy Balkin, Careys Bay, CC BY-NC), -1 flower (obs 96184531, Alice Shanks, Redcliffs, CC BY), -2 leaf (obs 105382150, Mark, Ruby Bay, CC BY). Every observation re-checked by the iNaturalist API 22/10/2026 (taxon, research grade, wild, photo licence) and every frame checked by eye against its caption.

Self-audit of the Passiflora cards, 22/10/2026 (assistant): every number in each card was checked mechanically against the source text it restates; two hedges were then added — the tarminiana–tripartita tube test now says Wikipedia's 6–8 cm for P. tarminiana reaches the bottom of P. tripartita's 8–10 cm, and the kōhia–black passionfruit cards say a young black passionfruit's leaves are undivided ('Lvs deeply 3-lobed, but entire on young plants', Webb 1988) so texture decides ('coriaceous' against 'submembranous').

Recipes 'Curuba milk drink', 'Curuba sorbete with chocolate' and 'Tumbo jam' (written by the assistant on the owner's instruction, owner, 22/10/2026: /goal "find some recipies for passionara"; restated in English, metric, no text reproduced; Spanish-language sources are used for facts only, as for the mallows): (1) 'Jugo de Curuba o Sorbete de Curuba', El Rincón Colombiano (filed under Gastronomía de Cundinamarca), © all rights reserved, retrieved 22/10/2026, https://elrinconcolombiano.com/jugo-de-curuba/ — its '1½ taza de azúcar' is given here as about 300 g and '1 taza' as 240 ml; (2) and (3) '+10 recetas con tumbo o curuba', Comida Peruana Web, © all rights reserved, retrieved 22/10/2026, https://comidaperuanaweb.org/gastronomia/recetas-con-tumbo/ — the sorbete is its 'Sorbete de curuba', and the jam its 'Mermelada de tumbo'. The jam's ingredient list omits the sugar its method adds ('2 tazas de azúcar', given here as about 400 g) and lists '1/2 cucharadita de canela en polvo' that its method never uses, so the cinnamon is left out. The page's '1 taza de agua (240 ml)' sets the cup used. Not used: its 'esponjado de curuba', whose ingredient list gives no amount of fruit; its cocktail (alcohol); and the health claims on both pages. WHICH SPECIES: 'curuba' and 'tumbo' are names Wikipedia gives to both P. tripartita ('also called curuba, tumbo, curuba de Castilla, tumbo serrano and poro poro') and P. tarminiana ('curuba, curuba de Castilla, or curuba sabanera blanca (Colombia)'; 'tumbo or curuba (Bolivia)'; 'tacso, tumbo, tumbo del norte' (Peru)), and neither recipe names a species, so the same three recipes are on both banana passionfruit entries.

summary.text:
Passiflora tripartita, also called curuba, tumbo, curuba de Castilla, tumbo serrano and poro poro, is a species of Passiflora from Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, and Brazil in areas at elevations of 2000 – 3200 meters. P. tripartita var. mollissima and P. tarminiana were until recently considered to be one species, P. mollissima.
Banana passionfruit is the commonest naturalised species of the genus in New Zealand. North and South Islands: Auckland to Otago Harbour, particularly just N. of Wellington, coastal Marlborough, including the Sounds, and coastal parts of Nelson.
Two varieties grow wild in New Zealand, var. mollissima and var. azuayensis; var. azuayensis has leaves hairless or nearly so on the upper surface.

identification.text:
Glabrous, evergreen or semi-deciduous shrub to about 7 m high. Shoots terete, grey or yellowish grey; reproductive shoots often pendent. Spines to 2.3 cm long, sometimes single, sometimes 3-partite. Leaves with short petiole to 5 mm long. Lamina mostly 2.5–7.5 × 1–2.5 cm, oblanceolate, elliptic to obovate and often very variable on one plant, entire or spiny serrate (often remotely so), more or less shining above and often turning reddish in autumn, reticulate, subcoriaceous, sometimes almost membranous in shadier and moister habitats; base attenuate; apex spiny. Flowers foetid, arranged in simple or compound racemes to 6 cm long; bracts 2–3 mm long, lanceolate-acuminate; bracteoles sometimes about 1/2 way along pedicel, otherwise near base, shorter than bracts. Pedicels 0.6–1.5 mm long. Perianth segments yellow, sometimes the outer red-tinged, 4–7 mm long; outer sepals shorter; inner sepals broadly obovate and petals slightly emarginate, with 2 prominent basal oblong nectaries. Stamens 3–4 mm long. Ovules 4. Berry 7–12 mm long, broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, reddish black, strongly whitish pruinose; juice dark red; fruiting style about 1 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Barberry's leaves are mostly 2.5–7.5 cm long, entire or spiny-toothed (often only sparsely), and very variable on one plant; Darwin's barberry's are small, 1–3 (rarely 3.5) cm long, obovate with two spiny lobes at the tip (shoots that are not flowering sometimes carry extra teeth below). Barberry's flowers are yellow (the outer parts sometimes red-tinged) and smell unpleasant; Darwin's barberry's are orange-yellow. Barberry is hairless, with single or three-parted spines up to 2.3 cm long; Darwin's barberry's shoots are densely brown-hairy and its spines split into five. Barberry's berries are 7–12 mm long and broadly ellipsoid to nearly round, with a style about 1 mm long; Darwin's barberry's are 5–7 mm across and round, with a conspicuous style 1.5–3 mm long. An evergreen spiny shrub with dark, white-bloomed berries does not separate them. The garden hybrid B. × stenophylla (Darwin's barberry × B. empetrifolia) has three-parted spines and narrow linear-lanceolate leaves but fruit like Darwin's barberry's, so the spine and leaf tests do not settle it.
lookalikes.name: Darwin's barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Barberry's berries are reddish black under a heavy whitish bloom, with dark red juice; European barberry's are scarlet to crimson-scarlet, shining and without bloom, oblong, 9–11 mm long. Barberry is evergreen or partly deciduous, its leaves shining above, somewhat leathery (almost thin in shady, moist places) and often turning reddish in autumn; European barberry is plainly deciduous, its leaves thin, dull green above and usually finely toothed. Barberry grows to about 7 m with spines up to 2.3 cm long; European barberry to about 2 m, its spines under 1.5 cm. Leaf size (2.5–7.5 against 2–8 cm long, both 1–2.5 cm wide), yellow flowers in clusters up to about 6 cm, and a place around old homesteads and plantations do not separate them. In New Zealand barberry has usually been called B. vulgaris, even in Allan's 1940 flora, so a name in print is no guide.
lookalikes.name: European barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Barberry's leaves are unlobed, 2.5–7.5 cm long, smooth-edged or spiny-toothed, and very variable on one plant; hawthorn's are deeply cut into 3–7 lobes. Barberry is evergreen or partly so; hawthorn loses its leaves in winter. Barberry's flowers are yellow and smell unpleasant; hawthorn's are white, rarely pink. Barberry's berries are reddish black under a heavy whitish bloom, with dark red juice; hawthorn's haws are dark red and shining, 7–11 mm across, crowned by the bent-back sepals and holding usually one stone, which must not be crushed. Barberry's spines are single or three-parted, up to 2.3 cm; hawthorn's are single, up to 12–(20) mm. A thorny hedge shrub with berries in autumn does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Hawthorn

preparation.text: Eat the berries raw, soak any that have shrivelled before using them, or scatter them over a cooked vegetable stir-fry at the table.

recipes.method: Written for barberry (Berberis glaucocarpa) by the New Zealand forager who picked it. ½ cup (125 ml) barberries; ¾ cup (185 ml) dates; ¾ cup (185 ml) almonds; ¼ cup (60 ml) sunflower seeds; ¼ cup (60 ml) dried peaches; a pinch of salt; a pinch of cinnamon; 1 tablespoon carob powder; ¼ cup (60 ml) desiccated coconut, plus more to coat. Soak ½ cup (125 ml) barberries if they have shrivelled, and soak ¾ cup (185 ml) dates. In a food processor, grind ¾ cup (185 ml) almonds and ¼ cup (60 ml) sunflower seeds to crumbs. Add the barberries, dates, ¼ cup (60 ml) dried peaches, a pinch of salt, a pinch of cinnamon, 1 tablespoon carob powder and ¼ cup (60 ml) desiccated coconut, and process until the mixture holds together. Roll into balls and coat them in more coconut. The source leaves out the unit for the almonds, barberries and coconut; cups are assumed here, matching its other lines. Millilitres use the 250 ml metric cup.
recipes.title: Barberry and peach bliss balls

summary.text:
Berberis glaucocarpa, sometimes called common barberry or simply barberry, is a species of flowering plant, a barberry, native to the western Himalaya in central Asia, to west central Nepal. It is considered invasive in New Zealand, where it is found in the North and South Island. It has also been introduced to Great Britain. The species is listed as banned in South Africa.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: throughout in modified lowland areas; S.: as far S. as Canterbury and Westland.
Barberry is very commonly cultivated as a hedge in the lowland parts of N.Z. except for colder parts of the South Island. The plants fruit abundantly and the large branches of glaucous-white frs are a characteristic sight on many farms in autumn. In N.Z. barberry or Himalayan barberry has usually been called B. vulgaris although this name should be applied to a very different sp. in another section of the genus. Thus, the short description and diagram in Allan (1940) really refer to B. glaucocarpa. B. glaucocarpa has also occasionally been called B. aristata in N.Z.; this is a related Himalayan sp.
The fruits are spread by birds and mammals, including brush-tailed possums and rodents. The birds which most often spread this plant in New Zealand are themselves exotic frugivores, namely Silvereyes (which self-introduced from Australia), Song Thrush, Common Blackbird, and Common Starling. New Zealand Bellbirds ignore barberry fruits.

identification.text:
Large shrub or small tree to about 7 m with many smooth trunks; vegetative parts glabrous or nearly so. Leaves aromatic; petioles 5–13 mm long, often purplish. Lamina 4–13 × 1.5–4.5 cm, narrow-elliptic or elliptic, shining above; base cuneate; apex acute, cuspidate or acuminate. Umbels in upper leaf axils; peduncles about 5 mm long, glabrous or puberulent. Involucral bracts about 5 mm long, strongly imbricate, glabrous or puberulent. Pedicels more or less puberulent. Perianth 3–4 mm long, cream or whitish. Male flowers with 8–12 stamens. Berry 1.3–1.5 × 0.6–1.3 cm, narrow- to broad-ellipsoid, glossy black.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaf edge: bay's leaves are untoothed, on some leaves wavy; cherry laurel's have a few distant, short, sharp teeth toward the tip and are more or less smooth toward the base. Bay's flowers are cream or whitish, 3–4 mm long, in small umbels in the upper leaf joints; cherry laurel's are greenish white to cream, 20–35 on an erect, dense spike 80–120 mm long, and its fruits hang in grape-like clusters along the spike. Bay's leaves are aromatic; cherry laurel's can smell of almonds when crushed. Both are evergreen with shining leaves of overlapping length (bay 4–13 cm, cherry laurel 7.5–18 cm), and both have dark fruit, bay's glossy black and 1.3–1.5 cm long, cherry laurel's dark purple and about 10 mm long, so leaf size, shine and fruit colour do not tell them apart. Cherry laurel's leaves and seeds release cyanide: do not eat any part of it.
lookalikes.name: Cherry laurel

preparation.text: The leaves are most often used whole (sometimes in a bouquet garni) and removed before serving (they can be abrasive in the digestive tract). Bay leaves can also be crushed or ground before cooking. Crushed bay leaves impart more fragrance than whole leaves, but are more difficult to remove and thus they are often used in a muslin bag or tea infuser. Ground bay laurel may be substituted for whole leaves and does not need to be removed, but it is much stronger.

recipes.method: For the shortbread: 3 small dried bay leaves; 200 g sugar; 454 g soft butter; 1 tsp lemon zest; ⅛ tsp salt; 480 g flour. For the icing: 5 small bay leaves; 67 g sugar; 120 g icing sugar; 1 tbsp meringue powder; 3 tbsp lemon juice. Grind 3 small dried bay leaves with 1–2 tbsp of 200 g sugar to a powder, sifting out any stubborn bits. Beat with 454 g soft butter, the rest of the sugar, 1 tsp lemon zest and ⅛ tsp salt, then work in 480 g flour a little at a time to a soft dough. Shape 25 g rounds and bake at 175 °C for 18–20 minutes, until lightly browned at the edges. For the icing, grind 5 small bay leaves with 67 g sugar, then beat with 120 g icing sugar, 1 tbsp meringue powder and 3 tbsp lemon juice at medium speed for 4–5 minutes, until thick but still pourable. Dip the cooled biscuits and leave on racks 12–24 hours to set.
recipes.title: Bay leaf and lemon shortbread

summary.text:
Laurus nobilis is an aromatic evergreen tree or large shrub with green, glabrous (smooth) leaves.
Laurus nobilis is a widespread relict of the laurel forests that originally covered much of the Mediterranean Basin when the climate of the region was more humid. With the drying of the Mediterranean during the Pliocene era, the laurel forests gradually retreated, and were replaced by the more drought-tolerant sclerophyll plant communities familiar today. Most of the last remaining laurel forests around the Mediterranean are believed to have disappeared approximately ten thousand years ago, although some remnants still persist in the mountains of southern Turkey, northern Syria, southern Spain, north-central Portugal, northern Morocco, the Canary Islands and in Madeira.
In New Zealand it is an exotic, naturalised since 1983 and named on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.

warnings: Some members of the laurel family, as well as the unrelated but visually similar mountain laurel and cherry laurel, have leaves that are poisonous to humans and livestock.

While some visually similar plants have poisonous leaves, bay leaves are not toxic. However, they remain stiff even after cooking and may pose a choking hazard or cause harm to the digestive tract if swallowed whole or in large pieces.

habitat.text: Coastal to montane. Mostly coastal: on cobble and sand beaches, in coastal forest and shrubland, and in wind-shorn vegetation on cliffs and rock stacks. Now and then it grows well inland, sometimes in barberry hedges on farmland or on limestone and calcareous sandstone outcrops in otherwise dense forest. It climbs where it has support.

identification.text: Trailing or lianoid herb or subshrub with terete branching softly woody stems up to about 3 m long. Leaves on flattened petioles up to 1 cm long; lamina fleshy, papillose, (1)–2–3–(5) × 1–3 cm, obtuse, deltoid to broad-ovate to ovate-rhomboid, rather abruptly narrowed to petiole. Flowers on slender peduncles about 5 mm long, solitary or occasionally paired, occasionally unisexual; perianth yellow. Calyx tube subglobose; stamens 10–20; ovary 2–(3)-celled; styles 2–(3). Fruit 5–7 mm diameter, subglobose, succulent, bright to dark red, not horned; seeds 1–3.

lookalikes.howToTell: Check the fruit first. Beach spinach's fruit is a round, succulent berry 5–8 mm long, pink to dark red, without horns, holding 1–3 seeds. New Zealand spinach's fruit is typically top-shaped and angled, 8–10(–15) mm long, with 2–4 hardened horns and 4–10 seeds. Without fruit, look at the flowers: beach spinach's sit on slender stalks, 5–30 mm long, while New Zealand spinach's are stalkless or nearly so. Thick, fleshy leaves covered in tiny bumps (papillae), diamond to triangular leaf shapes and yellow flowers are common to both, so none of those separates them.

summary.text: Tetragonia trigyna, kōkihi or native spinach, is a trailing, scrambling subshrub of the ice-plant family, Aizoaceae. It is native to New Zealand (Kermadec Islands, Three Kings, North, South and Chatham Islands) and to Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands, and is widespread and common around most of the New Zealand coast. Its 2023 national assessment is Not Threatened.

warnings: Its oxalate content has not been measured; its close relative New Zealand spinach is high in oxalates. Blanch the leaves in boiling water and discard the water before eating them in quantity.

identification.text:
Annual or biennial. Stems erect or ascending, branching, ribbed to grooved, 15–75–(100) cm tall; hairs both white, slender, crinkly, subappressed, and red-based, stout, straight, spreading. Rosette and lower stem leaves thick, petiolate, oblong to oblanceolate, usually deeply runcinately 1–2-pinnatifid, rarely simple and shallowly pinnatifid or toothed, (7)–10–20–(35) × (2)–4–8–(12) cm; hairs pale, 0.2–0.5 mm long, on both surfaces and margins; lobes slightly recurved, toothed or divided. Stem leaves similar, deeply pinnatisect to not lobed, toothed, sessile, subauriculate or lobed at base. Capitula campanulate; buds erect. Involucral bracts with pale subappressed cobwebby hairs and often dark, spreading glandular hairs on outer surface, and fine appressed straight hairs on inner surface; outer bracts 6–12, lanceolate to ovate-lanceolate, ?-1/2 length of inner bracts; inner bracts lanceolate, not keeled, (6)–9–12 mm long, with pale to scarious glabrous margins. Receptacle areoles with raised ciliate margins. Corolla yellow, sometimes with red stripe on outer face of ligule. Achenes brown, 10-ribbed, fusiform, scabrid, all long-beaked, 6–9 mm long. Pappus bristles in 1–(2) rows, fine, white. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: A dandelion's leaves are all in the basal rosette, and its flower stems are hollow and leafless, each carrying a single flower head. Beaked hawksbeard sends up an erect or ascending, ribbed stem, 15–75 cm and sometimes to 100 cm tall, that branches and carries leaves of its own. Before the stems appear, the leaves are similar: both usually have leaves cut into lobes that point back towards the centre, beaked hawksbeard's usually deeply. Beaked hawksbeard's leaves carry short pale hairs on both surfaces and the margins, where a dandelion's are hairless or have only sparse short hairs, mostly on the midrib above — a clue, not a test. Milky sap does not separate them: both belong to the dandelion tribe, the Cichorieae, all of which have milky latex. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Dandelion

lookalikes.howToTell: Leaf shape does not separate them: catsear's leaves are usually shallowly to deeply lobed, rarely simple and toothed, and beaked hawksbeard's are usually deeply lobed with lobes pointing back, rarely simple and shallowly lobed or toothed. Look at the flowering stem. Catsear's leaves are all in the basal rosette, its stems carry only a few tiny bracts, and they are hairless or have a few sparse hairs low down; beaked hawksbeard's stems carry leaves and are hairy, with fine crinkly white hairs and stout, spreading, red-based ones. Under the flower head, catsear's bracts are hairless except for a row of stiff hairs along the midrib; beaked hawksbeard's have pale cobwebby hairs and often dark glandular hairs. Catsear's seed parachute has an inner row of feathery hairs; beaked hawksbeard's is of fine white bristles. Hairy leaves, branched stems and height (catsear 4–60 cm, sometimes to 150 cm; beaked hawksbeard 15–75 cm, sometimes to 100 cm) do not separate them. Catsear has milky sap; sap is not a test.
lookalikes.name: Catsear

lookalikes.howToTell: Smooth hawksbeard's leaves are thin and often hairless, or hairy only along the middle beneath; beaked hawksbeard's are thick, with short pale hairs on both surfaces and the margins. The seed is the firmest test: smooth hawksbeard's achenes are not beaked and are 2–2.5 mm long, and its parachute does not stand above the bracts in fruit; beaked hawksbeard's are long-beaked and 6–9 mm long — though beaked hawksbeard sometimes has outer achenes without a beak, so check the inner ones. Smooth hawksbeard's bracts are hairless on the inner surface and the pits of its flower base have flat, hairless rims; beaked hawksbeard's bracts have fine flattened hairs inside and the pits of its flower base have raised, fringed rims. Smooth hawksbeard's inner bracts are 5–8 mm long, beaked hawksbeard's (6)–9–12 mm, so they overlap. Both have branching, ribbed stems, erect buds and yellow heads that may be striped red or pink beneath. Smooth hawksbeard's leaves are eaten in salads and soups in Tuscany (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Smooth hawksbeard

preparation.text: Leaves raw in salads, or cooked: boiled, in soups, stews, omelettes and potajes, or pan-fried. In Crete the leaves are usually eaten boiled, in salads.

recipes.method: For 4: about 450 g freshly picked young greens; 3 tbsp kosher salt, for the cooking water; olive oil; lemon wedges; about ½ tsp finishing salt. Soak about 450 g of freshly picked young greens in cold water for 10 minutes. Bring about 3.8 L of water and 3 tbsp kosher salt to the boil in a large lidded pot, add the greens, cover and bring back to the boil. Uncover and cook for 60 seconds, stirring until all are wilted, then taste one — some greens take longer — and drain in a colander once tender. Let them drain for a minute, turning them over, then tip into a warmed serving bowl, drizzle with olive oil and serve with lemon wedges and about ½ tsp finishing salt to taste.

summary.text:
Crepis vesicaria is a European species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae with the common name beaked hawk's-beard.

Crepis vesicaria subsp. taraxacifolia, the beaked hawksbeard, is a subspecies of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It is native to Europe and northwest Africa. It has become naturalized in scattered locations in the United Kingdom, North America, and Oceania.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Northland, Manawatu, Hawke's Bay, Wairarapa, Wellington; S.: Nelson, Canterbury, Otago. Naturalised from western Europe and North Africa, first recorded in 1870. New Zealand plants are referable to subsp. taraxacifolia.

identification.text:
Perennial herb, apparently acaulous but with underground stolons bearing numerous bulbils near the apex; contractile roots thick, fleshy, glassy white; bulb to about 3 cm long, ovoid; tunic pale brown, 5–7-nerved. Leaves 3-foliolate, radical. Petiole 6–22 cm long, more or less hairy; stipules membranous, glabrous or nearly so. Lamina sessile (that of terminal leaflet somewhat larger than laterals), 10–32 × 12–35 mm, shallowly to deeply 2-lobed to about 1/2 way, glabrous above, more or less sericeous and finely reticulate below; base narrow-cuneate; lobes oblong to almost obovate; apex rounded. Flowers (1)–3–18, in pseudoumbels, pendent; peduncles (7)–15–45 cm long, glabrous to sparsely hairy; pedicels to 2 cm long, densely clothed in glandular hairs. Bracts at base of pedicels, about 2.5 mm long, lanceolate, hairy, with apical calli. Sepals 5–6.5 mm long, lanceolate or oblong-lanceolate, with glandular hairs mainly towards base, or nearly glabrous; calli 2, apical, usually orange, sometimes yellow. Petals (1.5)–2–2.8 cm long, obovate with narrow claw, golden, sometimes red-margined, with appressed hairs outside or almost glabrous. Stamens at 2 levels, glabrous; filaments appendaged below, about 7 mm long in the 2 common stylar morphs, 5 mm long in the rare long-style morph. Styles either shorter than or nearly equal to lower stamen whorl (short-styled clone), longer than lower stamen whorl (mid-style clone), or equal to or longer than upper stamen whorl (long-style clone), hairy. Capsule not seen. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

It is a tall robust species (15-30 cm.) that develops numerous bulbils and has bright yellow flowers in an umbel. The leaves are trifoliate, often with purple edges or dots.

lookalikes.howToTell: In flower: white clover packs numerous flowers, each with a corolla 8–12 mm long, usually white and occasionally pink to reddish, into a globe-shaped head. Bermuda buttercup has separate golden flowers with petals (1.5)–2–2.8 cm long, usually 3–18 of them (occasionally 1) hanging from the top of a stalk (7)–15–45 cm long. Out of flower it can be mistaken for clover, and the leaves do not settle it: white clover's leaflets are obovate to elliptic or nearly round with a blunt to notched tip, so they can look notched like Bermuda buttercup's two-lobed leaflets, and the sizes overlap (white clover c. 5–25 mm long, Bermuda buttercup 10–32 mm). Both often carry leaf markings — light or dark on white clover, purple or purplish-brown flecks, dots or edges on Bermuda buttercup. Look instead at how the plant grows: white clover's stems creep along the ground and root at the nodes, while Bermuda buttercup grows upright, its leaves rising from a short vertical stem at the soil surface (or above it in shade or dense growth) over an underground bulb, and its runners, which carry the bulbils, are underground. Season is no help: in New Zealand white clover flowers July to March and Bermuda buttercup is recorded flowering in every month.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have yellow flowers and three heart-shaped leaflets, and both can have purple in the leaf, so none of those separates them; leaflet sizes overlap too (creeping wood sorrel (2.5)–5–18 mm long, Bermuda buttercup 10–32 mm). Look at how the plant grows: creeping wood sorrel has slender, branched stems up to c. 40 cm long that lie along the ground or rise a little, carry the leaves, and often root at the nodes; Bermuda buttercup is an upright plant from an underground bulb, apparently stemless, its leaves all rising from the base on stalks 6–22 cm long. Then the flowers: creeping wood sorrel carries 1–5 on a stalk 1–4 cm long (to 9.5 cm in fruit), with petals 4.5–10–(13) mm long; Bermuda buttercup usually carries 3–18 (occasionally 1), hanging, on a stalk (7)–15–45 cm long, with golden petals (1.5)–2–2.8 cm long. The petal lengths do not overlap; flower number does. Creeping wood sorrel sets cylindrical capsules, usually hairy, (6)–10–18–(20) mm long; no capsule has been seen on Bermuda buttercup in New Zealand.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have yellow flowers and three notched leaflets, and both can have purple in the leaf, so none of those separates them. Least yellow sorrel creeps: its stems are more or less thread-like, prostrate or nearly so, root at the nodes and often form mats. Bermuda buttercup appears stemless, with its leaves all rising from the base on stalks 6–22 cm long, and grows from a bulb with underground runners that bear many small bulbils. Size helps, but the ranges meet: least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long and 1.5–12 mm wide, Bermuda buttercup's 10–32 mm long and 12–35 mm wide; least yellow sorrel's petals are 4.5–9 mm long (up to 13 mm), Bermuda buttercup's golden petals 2–2.8 cm (from 1.5 cm). Least yellow sorrel's flowers are solitary, rarely paired; Bermuda buttercup usually carries 3–18 (occasionally 1), hanging, on a stalk 15–45 cm long (from 7 cm). Least yellow sorrel sets a capsule 7–10 mm long (3–13 mm at the extremes); no capsule has been seen on Bermuda buttercup in New Zealand.

preparation.text: The leaves have a pleasant acid flavour and make a pleasant addition to salads. Use the leaves in moderation. In South Africa it is a traditional ingredient in dishes such as waterblommetjiebredie ('water flower stew').

recipes.method: For the filling: about 680 g leafy greens (spinach, Swiss chard leaves, nettles, lamb's quarters, amaranth or quickweed); 3 egg yolks; 1 egg; 250 ml (1 cup) crème fraîche or sour cream; 125 ml (½ cup) whipping cream; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt, plus more if needed; plenty of black pepper; 45 ml (3 tbsp) chopped Bermuda buttercup stems. For the pastry: 560 ml (2¼ cups) plain flour; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt; 125 ml (½ cup) extra virgin olive oil; 125 ml (½ cup) tepid water. Make the filling first; the pastry needs no resting. Bring 2.5 cm of water to the boil in a large pot, pack in about 680 g of leafy greens (spinach, Swiss chard leaves, nettles, lamb's quarters, amaranth or quickweed), cover and cook on high for 2 minutes, stir, then cook 2 minutes more until just tender but still bright green. If you use nettles, cover them in boiling water instead and cook about 5 minutes. Drain, refresh in cold water, squeeze as dry as you can, roll in a clean tea towel to press out the rest, and chop roughly. Beat 3 egg yolks and 1 egg with 250 ml (1 cup) crème fraîche or sour cream, 125 ml (½ cup) whipping cream, 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt and plenty of black pepper, then stir in the greens and 45 ml (3 tbsp) chopped Bermuda buttercup stems, adding more salt if needed. For the pastry, stir 560 ml (2¼ cups) plain flour, 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt, 125 ml (½ cup) extra virgin olive oil and 125 ml (½ cup) tepid water together and form a ball. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Roll the pastry into a disc about 30 cm across on an oiled or lined baking tray, turn up and crimp the edge into a lip, spread in the filling and bake 40–45 minutes, until the pastry is crisp and the centre is set.
recipes.title: Leafy green tart with Bermuda buttercup

recipes.method: Pasta of your choice; olive oil or butter; shredded parmesan (or any cheese); a couple of handfuls of Bermuda buttercup leaves; salt and pepper. Cook pasta of your choice as the packet directs, drain and return it to the pot. Stir in olive oil or butter until melted, then add shredded parmesan (or any cheese), a couple of handfuls of Bermuda buttercup leaves, and salt and pepper to taste. Toss and serve.

summary.text:
Oxalis pes-caprae is a species of tristylous yellow-flowering plant in the wood sorrel family Oxalidaceae. Some of the most common names for the plant reference its sour taste owing to oxalic acid present in its tissues. Indigenous to South Africa, the plant has become a pest plant in different parts of the world that is difficult to eradicate because of how it propagates through underground bulbs. In the non-native range the plants largely reproduce vegetatively and many populations have only one style length and the plants never produce seed.
In New Zealand: North Island: a common to abundant weed in lowland areas; South Island: Marlborough, Nelson, less common in coastal Canterbury. Naturalised from South Africa, first recorded in 1883.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

All parts contain oxalate, and eaten in quantity the plant poisons livestock: sheep grazing it have died of oxalate poisoning in Australia and Italy, and miniature horses with access to it have been poisoned. It has not been reported poisoning livestock in New Zealand. It is mildly toxic to people, especially eaten in large quantities.

habitat.text:
Leccinum scabrum is a European species that has been introduced to various areas of the world, mostly appearing in urban areas. In New Zealand, it associates solely with Betula pendula.
It grows in association with birch. It has been found in association with ornamental birch trees planted outside of its native range, such as in California.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Leccinum scabrum' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The cap is 4–10 cm wide and convex before flattening. The skin of the cap is tan or brownish, usually with a lighter edge; it is smooth, bald, and dry to viscid.
The pores are whitish at a young age, later gray. In older specimens, the pores on the pileus can bulge out, while around the stipe they dent in strongly. The pore covering is easy to remove from the skin of the pileus. The spore print is brown. The spores measure 13–16 by 4–4.5 μm and are elliptical.
The stipe is 5–15 cm long and 1–3.5 cm wide and slim, with white and dark to black flakes; it tapers upward. The basic mycelium is white.
The flesh is whitish, sometimes darkening following exposure. In young specimens, the meat is relatively firm, but it very soon becomes spongy and holds water, especially in rainy weather. When cooked, the meat turns black.


Similar species
Several different species of Leccinum mushrooms are found in mycorrhiza with birches, and can be confused by amateurs and mycologists alike. L. holopus is paler and whitish in all parts. L. alaskanum, common with birch in Alaska, has a dark and light, streaked or mottled cap. L. variicolor has a bluish stipe. L. oxydabile has firmer, pinkish flesh and a different pileus skin structure.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): A very common weed of open, disturbed sites, in arable land, waste ground, roadsides, dry riverbeds, and pastures. Recorded elevations range from 0 to 1525 m.
Veronica persica is a common ruderal and arable weed associated with disturbed habitats such as cultivated fields, gardens, lawns and roadsides. The plant prefers moist conditions and grows well in loamy, nutrient-rich soil.
In New Zealand it is a common weed of crops, gardens and pasture, quick to colonise bare soil (Massey, Yates). In lawns, mowing tends to keep it down (Yates).

identification.text:
Annual herb to 0.1 m tall. Stems prostrate to decumbent and rooting at nodes, eglandular-pubescent; hairs uniform. Leaf bud indistinct; leaves separating while very small, opposite-decussate, erecto-patent to spreading; lamina thin, ovate to broad ovate, sometimes deltoid, 6–35 mm long, 5–30 mm wide, dull green above, paler beneath, midrib and palmate secondary veins evident; surfaces eglandular-hairy; margin pubescent, serrate; teeth in 3–8 pairs; apex rounded to sub-acute; base truncate; petiole 0.5–7.0 mm long. Inflorescence a terminal raceme, 200–500 mm long; flowers distant, 12–50, all bisexual; bracts alternate, leaf-like; pedicels spreading, 5–15 mm long, up to 40 mm long and incurved at fruiting, with short, antrorse, eglandular hairs and scattered longer eglandular or occasionally glandular hairs. Calyx lobes 4, tapered to narrow obtuse apex, sub-equal, 5–7 mm long, with short, antrorse hairs on margins and a few longer ones on calyx tube. Corolla 8–12 mm diameter; tube white and yellow, about 1 mm long, much shorter than calyx, eglandular-hairy inside; lobes 4, usually sky-blue, rarely white, erecto-patent to spreading, unequal, orbicular to broadly elliptical, 5–8 mm long, rounded; nectar guides dark blue or purple, rarely absent. Stamen filaments white or pale blue, 2–3 mm long; anthers dark blue. Style glabrous, 1.5–3.0 mm long. Capsules angustiseptate, didymous with prominent veins, diverging obtuse lobes and broad sinus between, eglandular- and glandular-hairy in distal half, 3.5–4.0 mm long, 6–7 mm at widest point. Seeds ellipsoid, smooth and concave on funicle side, wrinkled and convex on back, straw-yellow to brown, 1.5–1.8 mm long.
Veronica persica is distinctive among the common weedy speedwells in New Zealand. Plants can be identified by their coarsely toothed leaves, lax terminal inflorescences of alternate leaf-like bracts and pedicellate blue flowers, and distinctive capsules, which are broader than long, with widely spreading lobes, shallow sinus, and ciliate margins. The anterior corolla lobe is usually, but not always, paler than the other three lobes, and the short stamens are curved and more or less erect alongside the style.
The stems are round, and the whole plant is quite hairy, on stems and leaves (Massey). The flowers fall off very easily once the plant is picked (Massey).
Other speedwells grow in the same places. Field speedwell (Veronica arvensis), the commonest speedwell in lawns, is very similar but a bit smaller, with tiny pale blue flowers that are not on stalks (Massey, Yates). Creeping speedwell (Veronica filiformis) is a perennial with runners and small, oval, hairy leaves; turf speedwell (Veronica serpyllifolia) is a perennial with runners, smooth thyme-like leaves and small white flowers (Massey, Yates).

lookalikes.howToTell: Ground-ivy's leaves are round to kidney-shaped, 1–3.5 cm long, with a heart-shaped base and scalloped edges, and its flowers are tubular and two-lipped, 1–1.5 cm long, blue or blue-violet with purple spots on the lower lip. Bird's-eye speedwell's leaves are ovate, 6–35 mm long, with 3–8 pairs of coarse teeth and a squared-off base; its flowers are flat, 8–12 mm across, with four sky-blue lobes striped dark, each alone on a long, slender stalk, and its seed capsules are two-lobed and broader than long. Both creep and root at the joints and both have blue flowers, so neither tells them apart. Ground-ivy grows mostly in shade below trees and around buildings, speedwell in open, disturbed ground. Ground-ivy's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked; they are bitter.
lookalikes.name: Ground-ivy

lookalikes.howToTell: Field woundwort's flowers are two-lipped, 6–7 mm long, pink or lilac, and grow in clusters around the stem up a leafy spike; bird's-eye speedwell's are flat, 8–12 mm across, with four sky-blue lobes (rarely white) striped dark, each alone on a long, slender stalk. Field woundwort's stem is square; speedwell's is round. Both are hairy, sprawl across the ground, have paired, toothed leaves of much the same size, flower all year, and grow in gardens, fields, waste places, roadsides and river beds, so none of these tells them apart. Field woundwort poisons livestock (staggers); no record of it being eaten by people has been found, so do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Field woundwort

lookalikes.howToTell: Field speedwell's flowers are tiny, 2–3 mm across, and sit almost stalkless (stalks 0–2 mm) among small bracts at the stem tips; bird's-eye speedwell's are 8–12 mm across, each alone on a long, slender stalk (5–15 mm, longer in fruit). Field speedwell's leaves are 5–20 mm long with 3–6 pairs of teeth; bird's-eye speedwell's are 6–35 mm with 3–8 pairs. Out of flower they look much the same: both are hairy, with paired, toothed leaves of similar shape, and both grow in gardens, crops, lawns and waste ground. Size alone does not separate them, as field speedwell can grow large in gardens. No record of field speedwell being eaten has been found.
lookalikes.name: Field speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Turf speedwell's flowers are pale blue fading to whitish, 3–5 mm across, on short stalks (1–3 mm) up a spike at the stem tips; bird's-eye speedwell's are sky-blue, 8–12 mm across, each alone on a long, slender stalk. Turf speedwell's leaves are almost hairless, 5–17 mm long, with shallow, rounded teeth; bird's-eye speedwell's are hairy, 6–35 mm long and coarsely toothed. Turf speedwell is a perennial that stays below the mower in lawns and damp pasture; bird's-eye speedwell is seldom in mown turf and is commoner in gardens and crops. Both creep and can root at the joints, and both have paired leaves and dark-striped flowers, so neither tells them apart. Turf speedwell's record as food is thin, so it is not given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Turf speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the petals: scarlet pimpernel's flowers have five lobes, (2–)6–15 mm across, orange or orange-red; bird's-eye speedwell's have four, 8–12 mm across, usually sky-blue (rarely white) with dark stripes. Scarlet pimpernel's leaves have no stalk, smooth edges and often faint black dots underneath; bird's-eye speedwell's have a short stalk and 3–8 pairs of coarse teeth. Scarlet pimpernel's stem is square and hairless; speedwell's is round and hairy. Both sprawl across the ground, carry their flowers singly on long, slender stalks, have leaves of overlapping size, flower all year and grow in gardens and crops, so none of these tells them apart. Blue-flowered plants are blue pimpernel (see that card). Scarlet pimpernel is poisonous: eating it can cause nausea, headache and bodily pain.
lookalikes.name: Scarlet pimpernel

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the petals: blue pimpernel's flowers have five lobes, 6–15 mm across, blue, with finely scalloped edges; bird's-eye speedwell's have four, 8–12 mm across, usually sky-blue (rarely white) with dark stripes. Blue pimpernel's leaves have no stalk, smooth edges and often faint black dots underneath; speedwell's have a short stalk and 3–8 pairs of coarse teeth. Blue pimpernel's stem is square and hairless; speedwell's is round and hairy. Both sprawl, carry blue flowers singly on long, slender stalks, have leaves of overlapping size and grow in cultivated land and waste places, so none of these tells them apart. Do not eat blue pimpernel: it was long treated as a blue form of scarlet pimpernel, which is poisonous.
lookalikes.name: Blue pimpernel

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping speedwell's leaves are round to kidney-shaped, 3–8 mm long and 5–12 mm wide, with rounded teeth and a squared-off to slightly heart-shaped base; bird's-eye speedwell's are generally slightly narrower than long, ovate, 6–35 mm long, coarsely toothed, with a squared-off base. Leaf size overlaps at 6–8 mm long, so look at the shape. Both have flat, four-lobed blue flowers of much the same size (8–10 mm across in creeping speedwell, 8–12 mm in bird's-eye speedwell), each alone on a slender stalk, so the flower alone does not separate them. Creeping speedwell's flower stalks are thread-like, 15–40 mm long; bird's-eye speedwell's are stouter and shorter (5–15 mm in flower, up to 40 mm in fruit), and its front lobe is usually distinctly paler than the other three. Creeping speedwell sets no fruit in New Zealand; bird's-eye speedwell sets two-lobed seed capsules, broader than long. Creeping speedwell is a perennial that forms dense mats in lawns; bird's-eye speedwell is an annual seldom found in mown turf. Both creep and root at the joints. No food use of creeping speedwell has been confirmed; see its page.

preparation.text: Add the young leafy stems to salads, pesto or smoothies, or cook them in soups and casseroles. In Udhampur district, India, the young leaves and shoots are made into a vegetable dish with yogurt. For tea, bring a handful to the boil and let it steep. The flowers make a pretty decoration, if you have the patience to pick them. They fall off very easily once the plant is picked.

Wild Botanica, 'Speedwell ~ Veronica persica' (New Zealand, published 24/08/2024), https://www.wildbotanica.co.nz/blogs/articles/speedwell-veronica-persica, read via r.jina.ai (Shopify blocks curl), retrieved 30/10/2026 — leaves, stalks and flowers edible, slightly bitter, pick young; salads, pestos, smoothies, juices, teas, cooked; flowers as decoration. Eat The Weeds, Veronica persica tag page (ground ivy article), https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/veronica-persica/, read via r.jina.ai (mod_security blocks curl), retrieved 30/10/2026 — 'Of these four all but the Persian Speedwell are edible.' No reason given; the same sentence says none of the four has creeping stems that root at the nodes, which NZFO contradicts for V. persica ('Stems prostrate to decumbent and rooting at nodes'). Recorded in the thin-evidence warning as a conflicting statement; not used otherwise.

Useful Temperate Plants (Ken Fern): no record for Veronica persica (retrieved 30/10/2026). Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga: no results for 'Veronica persica'. NZPCN 'Veronica persica': exotic, naturalised 1867, origin C. and S. Europe, W. Asia — agrees. edibleplantdb.org (aggregator citing Bhatia 2018) blocked by a captcha; the primary paper was read instead.

Months [9, 10, 11] → [4–12], 30/10/2026: no NZ source dates the leaves; NZFO says it flowers and fruits all year, so 'before flowering' is no calendar limit here. iNaturalist API, NZ (place 6803) research-grade wild, taxon 55666, month-of-year histogram (January–December): 71, 50, 69, 237, 98, 85, 194, 309, 351, 237, 117, 105. Months at or above a quarter of the September peak (351): April–May and July–December; June (85) falls just short and is filled in between May and July. April's 237 is inflated by the City Nature Challenge. January–March are low (50–71): an annual mostly dying back in late summer. Langlands' [9, 10, 11] sits inside this window. Julia Sich (Bay of Plenty, 04/11/2014): 'Speedwell is plentiful now in spring'.

Ground-ivy card (both directions): characters from NZFO (V. persica, Garnock-Jones 2023) and Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988, CC BY-NC-SA, restated) 'Glechoma hederacea L.': 'Lamina 1-3.5 × 1-4.5 cm, suborbicular to reniform … shallowly to deeply crenate; base cordate', 'Corolla 1-1.5 cm long, blue or blue-violet, hairy outside; lower lip with purple spots', 'Usually in shady places below trees and around buildings', 'local in many southern North Id and South Id localities'. Confusion named by Eat The Weeds (Persian speedwell 'somewhat similar in appearance to Ground Ivy').

Lead review (30/10/2026): Eat The Weeds' 'not edible' for Persian speedwell not repeated in the warnings (no reason given, and the same sentence wrongly says it does not root at the nodes); 'no record of toxicity was found' not used (absence of a record is not evidence of safety). Months [9–11] (Langlands) widened to [4–12]: the young leaves and shoots are the harvest, not the flowers (owner, 28/10/2026), dated by the iNat histogram in the line above.

Photos (30/10/2026, the owner's set): iNaturalist research-grade, wild, New Zealand observations, each checked against the iNaturalist API (taxon Veronica persica, not captive) and by eye — birds-eye-speedwell-5.heic = https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/16353042 (no rights reserved; Dunedin); birds-eye-speedwell-2.heic = https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/298355184 ((c) Saryu Mae 前 朝琉, CC BY; Waiuku); birds-eye-speedwell-3.heic = https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/249087494 ((c) Sandra Keller, CC BY; Ngatea); birds-eye-speedwell-4.heic = https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/257430364 ((c) Jonas Sielenkämper, CC BY; Tasman). Captions written from the images. Not shown: the seed capsule (two-lobed, broader than long).

Bird's-eye speedwell card (both directions, 30/10/2026): the confusion is named by Massey University's New Zealand weeds database, 'Scrambling speedwell' (https://www.massey.ac.nz/about/colleges-schools-and-institutes/college-of-sciences/our-research/themes-and-research-strengths/plant-science-research/new-zealand-weeds-database/scrambling-speedwell/, retrieved 30/10/2026, restated: staggerweed 'can be confused with it, but it has a square stem, compared with the round stem of scrambling speedwell'). Field woundwort characters from Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988, CC BY-NC-SA) 'Stachys arvensis': 'Corolla 6-7 mm long, pink', 'upper lip small, not hooded, < lower lip', 'Lamina of basal and upper lvs 1-4 × 0.7-2.5 cm … evenly crenate; base truncate to cordate', 'A weed of gardens, fields, waste places, roadsides, and river beds', 'FL Jan-Dec'; lilac in New Zealand, square stem and scrambling habit from Massey 'Staggerweed'; flowers in false whorls up a terminal spike with leaf-like bracts from the field-woundwort identification (Wikipedia, 'Stachys arvensis'). Speedwell characters from Flora of New Zealand Online (Garnock-Jones 2023): leaves 6–35 mm long, 5–30 mm wide, serrate, base truncate; corolla 8–12 mm diameter, lobes 4, usually sky-blue, rarely white; pedicels 5–15 mm; stems prostrate to decumbent; round stem from Massey; habitat includes dry riverbeds; flowers all year. Leaf sizes overlap (woundwort 10–40 mm), so size is named as not separating.

Owner's links (30/10/2026), retrieved 30/10/2026: NZ Flora Online factsheet https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/taxon/Veronica-persica.html, Wild Botanica https://www.wildbotanica.co.nz/blogs/articles/speedwell-veronica-persica and Eat The Weeds https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/veronica-persica/ re-read — already used above, nothing new.

NZPCN, 'Veronica persica' https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/veronica-persica/ retrieved 30/10/2026 — common names scrambling speedwell, Persian speedwell; Exotic; naturalised 1867; origin C. and S. Europe, W. Asia (summary line). Its St Veronica etymology not used.

Its 'Similar species' list also links chickweed, scarlet pimpernel and scrambling fumitory, without saying how they are confused — no cards made from the list alone.

Not used: 'thrives in moist, shady areas' (said of speedwells as a group; Massey and the Flora put this one in open ground); control advice.

New Zealand Lawn Addicts, 'Speedwell in Lawns' https://www.newzealandlawnaddicts.com/weed-guides/speedwell/ retrieved 30/10/2026 — herbicide resistance agrees with Massey. Not used: 'don't root along the nodes' (contradicts the Flora: 'rooting at nodes'), turf speedwell as 'Veronica sublata' (it is V. serpyllifolia), control advice.

Biota of NZ, 'Veronica persica Poir.' https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/d9f48b7f-acf3-4e77-862e-8ef538425a61 retrieved 30/10/2026 — biostatus Exotic, Wild, New Zealand (agrees). Its vernacular 'creeping speedwell' not used: in New Zealand that name belongs to Veronica filiformis (Massey, Yates).

Persian speedwell; habitat in Texas lawns); the rest is behind a subscriber wall and was not read.

Ashley Adamant, Practical Self Reliance, 'Identifying Speedwell (& Ways to Use It)' (03/06/2023) https://practicalselfreliance.com/speedwell-veronica-sp/ retrieved 30/10/2026 — names ground-ivy as a lookalike of the creeping speedwells (ground-ivy card) and notes the roadside pollution risk (spray warning).
