Field speedwell card (both directions with bird's-eye speedwell, 30/10/2026): confusion named by Massey University's weeds database, 'Field speedwell' (https://www.massey.ac.nz/about/colleges-schools-and-institutes/college-of-sciences/our-research/themes-and-research-strengths/plant-science-research/new-zealand-weeds-database/field-speedwell/, retrieved 30/10/2026, restated: 'looks very similar to scrambling speedwell', 'much the same … when vegetative, only smaller', 'Size is not a good characteristic', flowers and fruits 'simply grow at the base of leaves') and Yates NZ 'Speedwell'. Characters from Flora of New Zealand Online (Garnock-Jones 2023): V. arvensis corolla 2–3 mm diameter, pedicels 0–2 mm, leaves 5–20 mm, teeth 3–6 pairs, habitats incl. lawns, arable land, waste places; V. persica corolla 8–12 mm, pedicels 5–15 mm (to 40 mm in fruit), leaves 6–35 mm, teeth 3–8 pairs.

Turf speedwell card (both directions with bird's-eye speedwell, 30/10/2026): the two compared as lawn speedwells by Massey 'Turf speedwell' (https://www.massey.ac.nz/about/colleges-schools-and-institutes/college-of-sciences/our-research/themes-and-research-strengths/plant-science-research/new-zealand-weeds-database/turf-speedwell/, retrieved 30/10/2026) and 'Scrambling speedwell' ('Turf speedwell has different shaped leaves and small whitish flowers') and by Yates NZ 'Speedwell'. Characters from Flora of New Zealand Online (Garnock-Jones 2023): V. serpyllifolia corolla 3–5 mm, pale blue fading to whitish, pedicels 1–3 mm, raceme terminal, leaves 5–17 mm, almost glabrous, shallowly crenate, stems rooting at nodes below; V. persica as above, 'Stems … rooting at nodes', 'coarsely toothed leaves'. 'Seldom found in turf … too large to escape the mower blades' (Massey).

Scarlet pimpernel ↔ bird's-eye speedwell card (30/10/2026): Massey 'Scarlet pimpernel' (https://www.massey.ac.nz/about/colleges-schools-and-institutes/college-of-sciences/our-research/themes-and-research-strengths/plant-science-research/new-zealand-weeds-database/scarlet-pimpernel/, retrieved 30/10/2026) calls it 'similar in size and growth habit to weeds such as scrambling speedwell', notes 'a variant of the species which has blue flowers', 'a square, hairless stem', leaves with 'no stalks' and black gland dots, 'commonly found in flower gardens and crops'; Massey 'Scrambling speedwell' and 'Field speedwell' list it under similar species. Pimpernel characters from Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988) 'Anagallis' (genus: 'glabrous except for corolla and stamens', leaves 'entire', 'Corolla deeply 5-lobed') and 'Anagallis arvensis' ('Lvs sessile, (2)-5-25 × …mm', 'often indistinctly dotted with sessile black glands beneath', 'pedicels (0.5)-1-2 cm long', 'Corolla (2)-6-15 mm diam., orange, orange-red or deep blue', 'FL Jan-Dec', 'Poisonous (Connor 1977)'); nausea and diarrhoea from the scarlet-pimpernel entry's warning. Speedwell characters from Flora of New Zealand Online (Garnock-Jones 2023; petiole 0.5–7 mm, serrate, teeth 3–8 pairs, corolla lobes 4, 8–12 mm, pedicels 5–15 mm, flowers all year) and Massey (round, hairy stem). Leaf sizes overlap (5–25 vs 6–35 mm), as do flower stalks. Note: Flora of New Zealand Online now treats blue-flowered plants as a separate species, Lysimachia loeflingii (Flora IV's var. coerulea).

Blue pimpernel cards (30/10/2026): bird's-eye speedwell — Massey 'Scarlet pimpernel' (https://www.massey.ac.nz/about/colleges-schools-and-institutes/college-of-sciences/our-research/themes-and-research-strengths/plant-science-research/new-zealand-weeds-database/scarlet-pimpernel/, retrieved 30/10/2026) calls the species 'similar in size and growth habit to … scrambling speedwell' and notes 'a variant of the species which has blue flowers'; chickweed — the same page names chickweed as similar ('white flowers, round stems and a single line of hairs'). Pimpernel characters: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988) 'Anagallis' (glabrous, leaves entire, corolla deeply 5-lobed), 'Anagallis arvensis' (leaves sessile, (2)–5–25 mm, black glands beneath, pedicels (0.5)–1–2 cm, corolla (2)–6–15 mm diameter) and 'var. coerulea' ('Corolla blue; margin distinctly crenulate', grows with var. arvensis in the same habitats — 'cultivated land, waste places and most other open disturbed sites'); square hairless stem — Massey. Speedwell characters as on the scarlet pimpernel card (Flora of New Zealand Online, Garnock-Jones 2023; Massey). Chickweed characters as on the chickweed ↔ scarlet pimpernel card (Flora of New Zealand Online 'Stellaria media'); chickweed edible parts from its own entry.

Creeping speedwell card (04/11/2026, new draft entry; owner, 04/11/2026: 'sure if they both actually exist in nz in the wild' — 35 wild New Zealand iNaturalist records, naturalised per Flora of New Zealand): Confusion named by Flora of New Zealand Online, 'Veronica filiformis' (https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Veronica-filiformis.html), Recognition ('Plants of V. persica have a spreading growth form, blue flowers, and leaf-like bracts, but…'); Massey University, New Zealand weeds database, 'Creeping speedwell' (https://www.massey.ac.nz/about/colleges-schools-and-institutes/college-of-sciences/our-research/themes-and-research-strengths/plant-science-research/new-zealand-weeds-database/creeping-speedwell/, read via r.jina.ai, retrieved 04/11/2026: 'The flowers of creeping speedwell look very similar to scrambling speedwell, but this annual weed has larger leaves and it is seldom found in turf') and 'Scrambling speedwell' (https://www.massey.ac.nz/about/colleges-schools-and-institutes/college-of-sciences/our-research/themes-and-research-strengths/plant-science-research/new-zealand-weeds-database/scrambling-speedwell/: 'only likely to be confused with other speedwell species, such as the stoloniferous perennial species creeping speedwell'); NZPCN, 'Veronica filiformis' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/veronica-filiformis/: 'Flower similar to V. persica but plant creeping with reniform (not pointed) leaves. V. persica has abundant fruit with divergent capsule lobes'). Characters: V. filiformis from Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (Garnock-Jones 2023, Flora of New Zealand – Seed Plants Fascicle 9; CC BY 3.0 NZ), 'Veronica filiformis' (https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Veronica-filiformis.html), retrieved 04/11/2026: perennial herb to 0.05 m tall; stems creeping and prostrate, sometimes ascending at tips, rooting at nodes; lamina broadly ovate to orbicular or reniform, 3–8 mm long, 5–12 mm wide, surfaces and margins hairy, crenate or crenate-serrate, base truncate to sub-cordate; pedicels filiform, 15–40 mm; corolla 8–10 mm diameter, lobes 4, blue; capsules not seen in New Zealand ('sterile in New Zealand'); lawns, golf courses. Dense mats — Massey 'Creeping speedwell'. V. persica from Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (Garnock-Jones 2023, Flora of New Zealand – Seed Plants Fascicle 9; CC BY 3.0 NZ), 'Veronica persica' (https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Veronica-persica.html): annual; stems prostrate to decumbent and rooting at nodes; lamina ovate to broad ovate, 6–35 mm long, serrate, base truncate; pedicels 5–15 mm, up to 40 mm at fruiting; corolla 8–12 mm diameter, usually sky-blue; capsules didymous, 3.5–4.0 mm long, 6–7 mm wide. 'Seldom found in turf' — Massey 'Turf speedwell' and 'Creeping speedwell'. The leaf-shape, pedicel, paler anterior lobe and fruit tests are the V. filiformis Recognition paragraph's own comparison with V. persica. Risk unknown: creeping speedwell has no confirmed food record (no Plants For A Future record; see its entry).

summary.text:
Veronica persica is a flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae.
Veronica persica is native to the Caucasus and northern Iran, but it has become widely naturalised elsewhere. It now has a near cosmopolitan distribution, having been introduced to Europe, North Africa, the Americas, East Asia, Australia and New Zealand.
The species was first recorded in Britain in 1825. It rapidly extended its range during the 1800s and was ubiquitous throughout lowland Britain and Ireland by 1960.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: widespread in all districts. South Island: widespread but not yet recorded in Western Nelson and Fiordland. Kermadec Islands, Chatham Islands, Stewart Island, Campbell Island, local.
Other names in New Zealand (NZPCN, Massey): scrambling speedwell, Persian speedwell. In New Zealand 'field speedwell' is Veronica arvensis, although some overseas pages use that name for this species. Naturalised in New Zealand by 1867 (NZPCN).

warnings: Its record as food is thin: young leaves and shoots cooked with yogurt in one district of northern India, and a handful of foraging pages, two of them from New Zealand.
Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed. It survives many common lawn weedkillers (MCPA, 2,4-D, clopyralid), so a healthy-looking patch may still have been sprayed. Pick from ground you know.

identification.text:
Open thicket-forming with rhizomes running extensively. Culm 4–7 m (often much taller in cultivation), green, remaining so or becoming black or heavily blotched black in 2nd year, erect, with white waxy ring beneath nodes when young; nodes all more or less evenly spaced. Culm-sheaths uniformly purple or purple-flushed, sometimes dark blotched above; auricles on main shoots prominent, dark; oral bristles long, caducous; sheath-blade linear, undulate. Branches green or black, spreading widely (giving an open network). Leaf-sheath with very short auricles. Oral bristles present. Leaf-blade usually 5–9–(13)× 0.5–2–(3) cm, lanceolate, abaxially glaucescent, adaxially moderately shining, acuminate.
[From: Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Arrow bamboo's canes are 3–5 m and dark green, with a white band just below each node; black bamboo has a white waxy ring there on young canes too, so the band does not separate them. Arrow bamboo's internodes are round, not notched; black bamboo's are flattened or grooved on alternate sides above each node, though usually round below the lowest branches. Arrow bamboo has 1 branch per node, sometimes 2–3 at upper nodes; black bamboo usually has 3, with the middle one small or missing. Arrow bamboo's leaf-blades reach 25 cm (up to 30 cm) and are shining dark green above; black bamboo's are usually 5–9 cm (up to 13 cm). Arrow bamboo's cane sheaths stay on and hide most of the lower and middle internodes; black bamboo's fall away. Arrow bamboo forms dense thickets, black bamboo open ones. Arrow bamboo's young shoots, cooked, have a rather bitter flavour.
lookalikes.name: Arrow bamboo

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the lower part of several canes. On some of fishpole bamboo's canes the lower nodes are crowded together and sometimes zigzag, with swollen, often lopsided internodes; black bamboo's nodes are all more or less evenly spaced. Not every fishpole cane shows the crowding, so check more than one. Fishpole's canes are green in their first year and yellow afterwards; black bamboo's are green and either stay green or turn black or heavily black-blotched in their second year. The cane sheaths differ: fishpole's are light mauve-brown or pinkish brown mottled dark purple, with no auricles or bristles; black bamboo's are uniformly purple or purple-flushed, with prominent dark auricles on the main shoots. Height does not separate them (fishpole usually 3–6 m, black bamboo 4–7 m), and both have a white waxy ring below the nodes on young canes. Both have edible young shoots, cooked.

preparation.text: Somewhat acrid when raw, they are prepared for eating by boiling in one change of water, the water being changed after 8 - 10 minutes. The toxins must be destroyed by thorough cooking, and for this reason, fresh bamboo shoots are boiled before being used in other ways. The shoots of some species contain cyanide that must be leached or boiled out before they can be eaten safely. Slicing the bamboo shoots thinly assists in this leaching.

recipes.method: Cut the shoots at about 8 cm above the ground, 5 cm below the soil. Handle the husk with care: it is many overlapping brown layers covered in fine, sharp hairs. Run a knife up the side of the shoot to slit it, then unwrap and throw away the layers until you reach the pale core; cut off the pointed tip and the fibrous base. The shoots are wide — about 5 cm across — so slice them before boiling if you want the leaching to reach the middle. They are somewhat acrid raw: cover with water, boil, and change the water once after 8–10 minutes, then simmer until tender. They keep a distinct taste and smell of their own.
recipes.title: Preparing fresh shoots

recipes.method: For two: 200 g of shoots already boiled, 1 chicken thigh (about 200 g), 3 snow peas and 15 ml oil; for the seasoning, 15 ml sake, 30 ml mirin, 5 ml sugar, 22.5 ml soy sauce, 2.5 ml granulated dashi and 200 ml water. Cut the tips into 4–5 cm lengths and halve them lengthways; slice the rest 7 mm thick. Cut the chicken into bite-sized pieces and fry it in the oil over a medium heat until it changes colour. Add the seasoning and the shoots, bring to the boil, cover and simmer on a low heat for 10–15 minutes. Top with the snow peas, blanched. Written for hachiku, the green-caned var. henonis, which is naturalised here.
recipes.title: Hachiku simmered with chicken

summary.text: Phyllostachys nigra, commonly known as black bamboo or purple bamboo (Chinese: 紫竹), is a species of bamboo, native to Hunan Province of China, and is widely cultivated elsewhere. Two forms have naturalised in New Zealand: var. nigra since 1991 and the green-caned var. henonis since 1993.

warnings: Raw bamboo shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides, natural toxins also contained in cassava. The toxins must be destroyed by thorough cooking, and for this reason, fresh bamboo shoots are boiled before being used in other ways.

habitat.text:
Prunus serotina is a pioneer species. In the Midwest, it is seen growing mostly in old fields with other sunlight-loving species, such as black walnut, black locust, and hackberry. Gleason and Cronquist (1991) describe P. serotina as "[f]ormerly a forest tree, now abundant as a weed-tree of roadsides, waste land, and forest-margins". The tree is hardy and can tolerate poor soils and oceanic salt sprays.
In New Zealand: forest, plantations, shrubland, grassland, riparian areas and roadsides (Auckland Council, restated).

identification.text:
a medium-sized tree, up to 15 m high, deciduous, with a tall trunk and erect or spreading branches. its leaves are alternate, thin, green, about 10 cm long, and have toothed margins. its white flowers (about 1 cm across) are spreading and borne in dense terminal racemes.. its fleshy black-purple fruit (up to 1.5 cm long) have a stony centre and resemble a cherry.

The leaves are 5–13 centimetres long, ovate-lanceolate in shape, with finely toothed margins. The fall leaf color is yellow to red. The flowers are small, white and 5-petalled, in racemes 10–15 cm long which contain several dozen flowers. For about its first decade the bark of a black cherry tree is thin, smooth, and banded, resembling a birch. A mature tree has very broken, dark gray to black bark. An almond-like odour is released when a young twig is scratched and held close to the nose, revealing minute amounts of cyanide compounds produced and stored by the plant as a defense mechanism against herbivores.

preparation.text: It must be fully ripe or else it will have a bitter flavour. The fruit can taste sweet or bitter. The better fruits have a thin skin and a juicy flesh with a pleasant vinous flavour. The fruit can also be used as a flavouring in liquors.

recipes.method: 5 cups fully ripe cherries; 15 cups cold water; 5 cups raw cane sugar; 2 tsp citric acid (or 8 tbsp lemon juice). Use fully ripe cherries, so dark purple they look black; red ones are under-ripe. If they need cleaning, float 5 cups of cherries in a large pot of cold water, pour off whatever rises, and drain. In a large glass jar (about 7.5 L) crush the raw cherries by hand to break every skin — hands are gentler on the stones than a masher. Add 15 cups cold water, 5 cups raw cane sugar and 2 tsp citric acid (or 8 tbsp lemon juice) and stir until the sugar dissolves; any left will dissolve over the next day. Cover with cheesecloth or a linen towel tied on with string, so it can breathe but fruit flies cannot get in, and keep it in a cool spot out of direct sun, such as a kitchen counter. Stir vigorously with a clean spoon about once every 12 hours (at least once a day) and taste a teaspoon after each stir. After 2–3 days it should be bubbly; fewer days give a sweeter, less fizzy drink, more days a drier, fizzier one — the recipe's authors bottle theirs after 5–7 days. Strain out the stones, skins and pulp, finishing through a fine-mesh strainer, pour into swing-top bottles or jars (not plastic or metal) and refrigerate at once. Never store the bottles at room temperature: the fermentation keeps building pressure and they can burst. It keeps in the fridge for months, and is lightly alcoholic, probably about 1–2.5%.

summary.text: Prunus serotina, commonly called black cherry, wild black cherry, rum cherry, or mountain black cherry, is a New World deciduous tree or shrub in the rose family, Rosaceae. Despite its common names, it is not very closely related to commonly cultivated cherries. The species is widespread and common in North America and Central America. Prunus serotina was widely introduced into Western and Central Europe as an ornamental tree in the mid-20th century, where it has become locally naturalized. It has acted as an invasive species there, negatively affecting forest community biodiversity and regeneration.

warnings: Like apricots and apples, the seeds of black cherries contain cyanogenic glycosides (compounds that can be converted into cyanide), such as amygdalin. These compounds release hydrogen cyanide when the seed is ground or minced, which releases enzymes that break down the compounds.
The foliage, particularly when wilted, also contains cyanogenic glycosides, which convert to hydrogen cyanide if eaten by animals.

The plant (especially the seed and young shoots) contains cyanogenic glycosides, especially amygdalin and prunasin. When ingested, these compounds break down in the digestive tract to release cyanide.

identification.text:
Deciduous tree, to 25 m high; twigs puberulent when young, angled, usually with stout scattered stipular spines up to about 1 cm long. Leaves glabrous to puberulent particularly below, petiolate; leaflets ovate to elliptic, acute or obtuse, sometimes shortly mucronate, in 4–10 more or less opposite pairs, (10)–20–40–(50) mm long, stipellate; petiolules 2–5 mm long. Raceme with numerous flowers; pedicels 5–10 mm long. Calyx puberulent; calyx teeth unequal, broadly triangular. Corolla white with the base of standard greenish or yellowish, 15–23 mm long. Pod glabrous, irregularly oblong, 2–8-seeded, 35–80 mm long; seeds smooth, brown- spotted, oblong. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers, the pods and the leaves. Black locust's flowers are white, 15–23 mm long, many to a cluster; honey locust's are small, greenish or creamy-yellow, with petals 4–6 mm long, in golden-hairy spikes 5–10 cm long. Black locust's pods are 35–80 mm long with 2–8 seeds; honey locust's are 15–40 cm long and 3–4 cm wide, dark brown when ripe, with 15–25 seeds set in pulp. Black locust's leaves are once divided, with 4–10 pairs of leaflets; honey locust's are more often twice divided, though some are once divided with 5–15 pairs. Black locust's spines are up to about 1 cm long, scattered on the twigs; honey locust's are 2–10 cm long or more, often branched, on the trunk and branches. Both are planted in forms without spines and in golden-leaved forms, so missing spines or leaf colour do not tell them apart. Honey locust's pod pulp is eaten (see its page).

preparation.text: Pick the flower clusters when the flowers have just opened. The flowers are dipped in batter and fried as fritters, made into jam, cakes or pancakes, or made into a drink. They have also been eaten raw, mostly by children for the nectar.

recipes.method: Makes about 20–25 fritters. 250 g plain flour, 2 eggs, 200 ml milk, 150 ml beer, 50 g granulated sugar, 1 tsp vanilla extract, 1 tbsp rum (optional), ½ tsp fine salt, 625 ml vegetable oil for frying, icing sugar to dust, and black locust flower clusters picked when just open. If you rinse the flowers, dry them well before frying. Mix everything except the flowers into a smooth batter, cover and rest for 30 minutes to an hour. Heat oil 2.5–4 cm deep in a saucepan; it is ready when a few drops of batter sizzle and turn golden within seconds. Dip the flowers in the batter, drain slightly and fry about 3 at a time for 2–3 minutes a side, until golden brown. Drain on paper towel and dust lightly with icing sugar.
recipes.title: Black locust flower fritters

recipes.method: Makes about 30. 350 g plain flour, 250 ml (1 cup) milk, 2 eggs, 80 g sugar, 1 sachet baking powder, 2 tbsp sunflower oil, more sunflower oil for frying, icing sugar to dust, and 2 cups (500 ml) black locust flowers. Clean the flowers and strip them from the central stalk. Mix the flour with the sifted baking powder, the sugar, eggs, milk and the 2 tbsp oil into a batter, stir in the flowers and let it rest while the frying oil heats. Fry until well browned, drain on paper towel and dust with icing sugar. Best freshly made, but also good cold. For a vegan batter use sparkling water instead of the milk and aquafaba instead of the eggs; for a savoury one leave out the sugar, add 1 tsp salt and salt the fritters when they come out.
recipes.title: Black locust flower fritters, Italian style

recipes.method: Makes 10–12 fritters, for 2. 60 g (½ cup) plain flour, ½ tsp baking powder (optional; more makes the fritters bitter), 120 ml (½ cup) light-coloured or non-alcoholic beer, 10–12 freshly picked black locust flower clusters, 1 tbsp brown sugar, ½ lemon, and vegetable oil for frying. Shake and look over the flowers to remove dirt and insects. Whisk the flour, the baking powder if using, and the beer into a smooth batter, slightly thick but still runny. Holding each cluster by its stalk, dip it in the batter and let the excess run off. Heat enough oil to cover the base of a large frying pan; it is ready when a drip of batter fizzes and starts to brown. Fry over medium-high heat until golden underneath, turn and brown the other side, adding oil between batches. Eat soon after cooking, sprinkled with the brown sugar and a squeeze of lemon. Pull the stalks out as you eat; they are not eaten.
recipes.title: Beer-batter black locust fritters (vegan)

summary.text: Black locust or false acacia, a deciduous tree of the pea family (Fabaceae) from central and eastern North America, naturalised in New Zealand by 1870. In the North Island it is locally common throughout; in the South Island it is occasional in Nelson, Marlborough, Westland, Canterbury and Otago. False acacia is used in soil conservation, and grown as an ornamental tree. The species suckers freely and forms small thickets from plantings; it has become a problem in some reserves and parks in the North Island. Cultivars include forms with golden or gold-green leaves, and forms without spines, but almost all naturalised material is green-leaved and spiny. New Zealand nurseries sell the golden-leaved cultivar 'Frisia' as a street tree, tolerant of heat, drought and pollution. It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds in New Zealand.

warnings: The bark, leaves and seeds are poisonous. They contain toxalbumins (robin and phasin) and can cause nausea, weakness, flushing, lethargy and vomiting; larger amounts or more chewing can bring a weak or irregular pulse, fever, seizures, and in bigger doses paralysis and coma, with possible gut bleeding and liver and kidney damage.
Children have been poisoned after chewing the bark or eating the seeds.
Only the flowers are eaten. Every other part of the tree, especially the bark, should be treated as toxic.
Twigs usually carry stout spines up to about 1 cm long. Punctures from them can cause pain, swelling and rash, and a few reports describe worse outcomes.

habitat.text:
Gardens, cultivated ground, compost heaps, disturbed soil.
Generally abundant, especially in open places such as arable land, waste places, dry riverbeds and roadsides, particularly much-disturbed areas.

identification.text: An annual or short-lived perennial herb to about 75 cm tall, usually hairy, sometimes nearly glabrous, with oval, slightly wavy leaves. Small white five-pointed star flowers with a yellow centre, in small, usually few-flowered clusters, then berries in clusters, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow.

lookalikes.howToTell: Poroporo is a hairless, soft-wooded shrub to about 3 m; black nightshade is a herb to about 75 cm, usually hairy. Poroporo's flowers are usually 4–5 cm across and violet, though white ones are recorded; black nightshade's are 10–13 mm across, usually white, sometimes pale mauve. The other native poroporo, Solanum aviculare, has flowers 10–40 mm across in white, lavender or dark blue, so flower size and colour alone do not settle it. Poroporo's berries are 23–30 mm long, egg-shaped to ellipsoid and hanging, usually yellow or pale orange; black nightshade's are 7–10 mm across and round, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow. Poroporo is poisonous too: its green and yellow berries and its leaves are poisonous, and ripe orange berries lose much of their toxicity; the fruit can be eaten when ripe, orange and with its skin bursting.
lookalikes.name: Poroporo

lookalikes.howToTell: Before flowers or fruit appear, the only character here is the coating: fat hen's leaves may be green or grey-mealy, the meal denser underneath when present, and very rarely a plant is bright green, while no mealy coating is recorded on black nightshade, whose leaves usually carry scattered short hairs. Leaf shape and toothing overlap and do not separate them. In flower they differ: black nightshade has flowers 10–13 mm across, often star-shaped, usually white (sometimes pale mauve) around a yellow cone of anthers, in small, usually few-flowered clusters, then round berries 7–10 mm across, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow. Fat hen's flowers are tiny and green with no petals, usually packed in dense spikes and panicles, and it forms no berry: its fruit stays wrapped in the flower parts around a glossy black seed (1.0–)1.1–1.4(–1.6) mm across.
lookalikes.name: Fat hen

lookalikes.howToTell: Field mustard's flowers are bright yellow with four petals 6–10 mm long, and its fruit are long, thin pods, not berries; black nightshade's flowers are usually white with yellow anthers, followed by clusters of round berries. Field mustard's lower leaves have a large end lobe and 1–3 pairs of side lobes and are bristly; black nightshade's are oval to lance-oval, entire to coarsely toothed, only sometimes slightly lobed. Field mustard starts as a rosette at ground level; black nightshade is a tall, upright, usually much-branched plant.
lookalikes.name: Field mustard

lookalikes.howToTell: Both can have white flowers. Wild radish's have four petals 13–20 mm long, usually veined with mauve, and its fruit are pods pinched between the seeds, not berries; black nightshade's flowers are 10–13 mm across with yellow anthers in the centre, followed by round berries 7–10 mm across. Wild radish's rosette and lower leaves are divided into an end leaflet and 1–8 pairs of side leaflets, and are bristly; black nightshade's are oval to lance-oval, entire to coarsely toothed, only sometimes slightly lobed.
lookalikes.name: Wild radish

Wikipedia contributors. 'Solanum nigrum', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solanum_nigrum Corroborates the solanine and adds the delay. Symptoms may follow eating raw immature green fruit or mature leaves, with 'typically a delay of 6 to 12 hours after ingestion for symptoms to occur', beginning with fever, sweating, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, confusion and drowsiness; death from large amounts comes through cardiac arrhythmia and respiratory failure, though the plant 'is rarely fatal'. Most suspected poisonings involve leaves or unripe fruit. Solanine is practically insoluble in water and can be destroyed by boiling but not by baking, though 'S. nigrum's leaves may be different from this perspective'; there are ethnobotanical accounts of the young leaves and shoots being boiled as a vegetable with the water discarded and replaced several times. Livestock have also been poisoned by nitrate from grazing the mature leaves and green berries.

The confusion this page does not currently card, and the test for it. Solanum nigrum is sometimes mistaken for the far more toxic deadly nightshade, Atropa belladonna, which is a different genus. Two differences: black nightshade berries grow in bunches while deadly nightshade's grow individually, and black nightshade's flowers have white petals. Wikipedia contributors. summary.text:
A common garden weed with white star flowers and black berries. Its green parts are poisonous, and it is too easily confused with poroporo and fat hen to treat as food.
Native to Eurasia, it was first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1853 and now grows throughout the North and South Islands and on the Kermadec, Chatham and Campbell Islands.

warnings: Leaves and green berries contain solanine: vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness, and in children worse. Fully ripe berries are eaten in some cuisines, but telling ripe from nearly ripe in the field is not a bet this guide makes.
Keep children away from the black berries — they look like tiny blackcurrants.

identification.text:
Vigorous vine, glabrous except for pistil and stamens. Shoots slightly angular. Leaves deeply 3-lobed, but entire on young plants; petiole 1–3 cm long, with 2 sessile glands near apex; stipules 10–15 mm long, linear-subulate, entire; lamina lobes more or less elliptic, submembranous, deep shining green above, rounded at base; middle lobe largest, 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm, serrate or serrulate, obtuse to acute. Flowers ☿, solitary. Pedicels 4–6 cm long at flowering. Bracts 1.5–2 cm long, ovate, free, coarsely serrate. Hypanthium inconspicuous. Sepals 2.5–3 cm long, oblong, green on reverse, white inside; petals white, similar to sepals; corona threads 2–2.5 cm long, white with purple base. Filaments puckered, purple towards base, otherwise white; anthers 8–10 mm long, longer than filaments. Ovary puberulent. Fruit 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broad-ellipsoid or subglobose, dull purple; pulp orange, sweet. Seed about 5 mm long, ovate, black, pitted. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. The fruit separates them too: black passionfruit's is dull purple and nearly round; the fruit of banana passionfruit (P. tripartita) is yellow or orange when ripe and elongated. Blue passionflower, which has no entry here, has a flower much like black passionfruit's, but its leaves are 5-lobed almost to the base and its pulp is scanty and inedible. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia's leaves are undivided and leathery and its flowers under 2 cm across, while black passionfruit's leaves are 3-lobed. A young black passionfruit's leaves are undivided too, so on a young plant go by texture: kōhia's are leathery, black passionfruit's thin. Kōhia is dioecious: only female plants bear fruit, and only after pollen reaches them from a male plant, so a vine without fruit can still be kōhia; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Kōhia

The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. The fruit separates them too: black passionfruit's is dull purple and nearly round; the fruit of banana passionfruit (P. tarminiana) is yellow or orange when ripe and elongated. preparation.text:
The ripe aromatic fruit is allowed to wrinkle and develop its sweetness, it is then eaten raw, juiced, made into a syrup or used in sauces, cakes, ice creams, sherbets etc.
In Australia and New Zealand, it is available commercially both fresh and tinned. It is added to fruit salads, and fresh fruit pulp or passion fruit sauce is commonly used in desserts, including as a topping for pavlova (a regional meringue cake) and ice cream, a flavouring for cheesecake, and in the icing of vanilla slices.

recipes.method: The pulp of about 12 passionfruit (250 ml), 125 g unsalted butter, 165 g caster sugar, 5 eggs and 2 extra yolks. Whisk the pulp to loosen it and push it through a sieve, then stir half the seeds back into the juice. Put the juice, butter and sugar in a heatproof bowl over a pan of simmering water, keeping the bowl clear of the water, and stir until the butter melts. Beat the eggs and yolks lightly, whisk them in gently, and keep stirring for 20–25 minutes until it thickens: it is ready when a finger drawn across the curd on the back of a spoon leaves a line that holds. Pour into warm sterilised jars, seal, cool, and keep in the fridge for up to 8 weeks.
recipes.title: Passionfruit curd

recipes.method: 880 g caster sugar, 500 ml water, 250 ml passionfruit pulp, 1 teaspoon citric acid. Put everything in a saucepan over medium heat and stir until the sugar dissolves, bring to the boil, take off the heat and let it cool. Keep it in the fridge for up to 4 weeks. Serve over crushed ice, topped up with water or soda water. Makes about 1.25 litres.

summary.text:
Passiflora edulis, commonly known as passion fruit, is a vine species of passion flower native to southern Brazil, through Paraguay, and northern Argentina.
This sp. is the black passionfruit of commerce and is widely cultivated in warmer parts of the country. All wild and virtually all cultivated plants in N.Z. belong to f. edulis, and not the less hardy, yellow-fruited f. flavicarpa Degener which is the usual form grown in tropical Polynesia.
N.: N. Auckland (plantations at Waitangi and Silverdale), near Auckland (Waitakere Range), Great Barrier Id; K.: well-established on Raoul Id where it grows so abundantly on and near the forest margin in some places that attempts have been made to eliminate it.

habitat.text: Sphaeropteris medullaris is common in lowland forest throughout the North Island of New Zealand. It is fairly common in wetter coastal areas, but rare in the drier eastern parts and absent in Canterbury and Otago.

identification.text: Rhizomes erect, forming a woody trunk up to about 20 m tall, 150–300 mm in diameter, covered in black, hexagonal stipe scars; bearing scales near the apex. Rhizome scales conform, acicular, bearing dark-coloured setae on margins, blackish-brown, shining. Fronds 3000–5000 mm long, arching upwards from the crown; dead fronds usually falling, but up to 5 occasionally persistent. Stipes 160–1650 mm long, 40–95 mm wide and 40–60 mm deep at the base, black, sometimes becoming dark brown distally, weakly tuberculate and slightly rough; blackish-brown or dark brown scales with dark-coloured setae on margins densely covering base of stipe, up to 50 mm long and 2 mm wide, becoming pale brown, smaller and more scattered distally. Laminae deeply 2-pinnate-pinnatifid to 3-pinnate-pinnatifid, elliptic or obovate, 3000–4000 mm long, 600–2000 mm wide, dark green on adaxial surface, pale green on abaxial surface, coriaceous; adaxial surfaces of rachis and primary pinna midribs abundantly covered in fine, acicular, colourless or pale brown hairs up to 1 mm long, more scattered on secondary pinna midribs and tertiary pinnae; abaxial surfaces bearing ovate scales with attenuate apices and dark red marginal and apical setae, up to 2 mm long and 1 mm wide on the pinna midribs, and acicular scales up to 5 mm long and 0.5 mm wide on the rachis; rachis blackish-brown on abaxial surface, becoming yellow-brown or pale brown distally, often yellow-brown or yellow-green or green on adaxial surface especially when young, tuberculate. Primary pinnae in 20–25 pairs, ovate, narrowly ovate or narrowly triangular; the longest at or above the middle, 350–950 mm long, 125–300 mm wide, short to long-stalked, abaxial surfaces of costae tuberculate. Secondary pinnae narrowly ovate or narrowly triangular, the longest 65–185 mm long, 12–37 mm wide, short-stalked or sessile. Longest tertiary pinnae 7–20 mm long, 2–4 mm wide, adnate to decurrent; apices acute; margins serrate or divided up to half way to costa. Sori 0.7–1.1 mm in diameter; paraphyses as long as sporangia; indusia completely covering sori before maturity, splitting irregularly at maturity.

summary.text:
Sphaeropteris medullaris,  synonym Cyathea medullaris, commonly known as mamaku or black tree fern, is a large tree fern up to 20 m tall with a trunk up to 20 cm diameter at breast height.
The species is found across many southwestern Pacific Ocean islands, including New Zealand, Fiji, the Marquesas Islands, Tahiti, the Austral Islands, and Pitcairn Island. It is not present in the Kermadec Islands. In the South Island, its distribution is more localised. In New Zealand it also occurs on the Three Kings Islands in the far north, on Stewart Island / Rakiura in the far south and in the Chatham Islands.

habitat.text:
Roadsides, riverbanks, gullies, forest margins, abandoned farmland. Forms impenetrable thickets.
Coast and lowlands, especially in high-rainfall country: pasture that is only lightly grazed, orchards and forestry blocks, hedgerows, roadsides and waste ground, scrub, forest edges and clearings, riverbeds, stream banks, swamps, sand dunes and gardens (NZPCN, restated).

harvestEthics.text: A declared pest plant in most regions. There is no such thing as taking too much.

Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988), 'Rubus fruticosus', via NZ Flora Online (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — leaflets '(3)–5–(7)', fruit 'black, usually shiny or rarely pruinose drupelets'
identification.text: Arching thorny canes, compound leaves of usually five (three to seven) toothed leaflets with a pale underside, white or pink five-petalled flowers, and clustered berries ripening green to red to black, usually shiny.

lookalikes.howToTell: Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Raspberry's leaves are pinnate, with side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk, where blackberry's are palmate, all leaflets spreading from one point; raspberry's are densely white-felted underneath. A ripe raspberry comes away from its core when picked and is hollow; a blackberry keeps its core.
lookalikes.name: Red raspberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. The flowers separate them: blackberry's are 15–60 mm across and have stamens and carpels together, while bush lawyer's are 8–15 mm across, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Ripe blackberry is black and bush lawyer's yellow to orange or red, but blackberry is red before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit. The native lawyers lack the long, glandular, bristly hairs some introduced brambles carry on their young stems; not every blackberry has them, so their absence does not rule blackberry out.
lookalikes.name: Bush lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. The flowers separate them: blackberry's are 15–60 mm across and have stamens and carpels together, while white-leaved lawyer's are 8–15 mm across, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Ripe blackberry is black and white-leaved lawyer's yellow to orange or red, but blackberry is red before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit. The native lawyers lack the long, glandular, bristly hairs some introduced brambles carry on their young stems; not every blackberry has them, so their absence does not rule blackberry out.
lookalikes.name: White-leaved lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet, where blackberry's have (3–)5(–7); creeping lawyer creeps along the ground, blackberry arches and scrambles. Ripe creeping lawyer fruit is red, but blackberry is red too before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit.
lookalikes.name: Creeping lawyer

preparation.text: Raw, or into jam, crumble, cordial and vinegar. Fully black and pulling away from the plant with no effort means ripe.

recipes.method: Written for blackberries; the page names no species. Makes about 8 jars. 1.8 kg blackberries, 1.5 kg jam sugar (sugar with added pectin), the juice and pips of 1 lemon, and a fingertip-sized knob of butter (optional). The night before, layer the berries and sugar in a very large bowl, cover and leave at room temperature so the sugar starts to dissolve; stir once in the morning. Put a small saucer in the freezer. Tip everything into a preserving pan or a large, wide pan and stir in the lemon juice; tie the lemon pips in muslin or a tea strainer and add them, because they give up pectin and help the set. Warm gently until all the sugar has dissolved, then bring to the boil and simmer for 5 minutes. Take off the heat and put a little on the cold saucer: once it is cool, push it with a finger, and if it wrinkles it has set. If not, boil 2–3 minutes more and test again, until it wrinkles. Skim, stir in the butter if using, and leave 15 minutes so the fruit settles before ladling into sterilised jars (wash them in hot soapy water and dry them in an oven at 170 °C, 150 °C fan, for at least 10 minutes). Keeps at least 6 months somewhere cool and dark; refrigerate once open.
recipes.title: Blackberry jam

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries. Makes about 200 ml. 350 g blackberries, 115 g caster sugar, 3 strips of pared lemon rind, 2 slices of ginger each about 0.5 cm thick, and 125 ml water. Wash and drain the berries and put them in a non-reactive pan with the sugar, lemon rind and ginger, then pour over the water. Bring gently to the boil and simmer for 15–20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the fruit is completely soft and the juice is starting to thicken. Take out the rind and ginger and press the pulp through a sieve with a wooden spoon (or use a mouli) to remove the seeds. Pour into a small sterilised bottle or jar, close it and leave to cool. Keeps up to a month in the fridge. Use it as a cordial with sparkling water, over ice cream, or folded into yoghurt or whipped cream.
recipes.title: Blackberry syrup

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the author notes many roadside patches are sprayed, so pick only where you know they aren't, or use frozen. Serves 10. Dough: 200 g softened butter, 200 g caster sugar, 4 eggs, ½ teaspoon vanilla essence, 400 g plain flour and ¼ teaspoon baking powder. Filling: 4 medium cooking apples (Granny Smith will do), peeled and cored, 200 g blackberries, 80 g caster sugar, the zest of a lemon, 50 g butter, plus caster sugar for sprinkling. Butter a pie dish about 24 cm across and 4 cm deep and swirl caster sugar round to coat it. Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla; sift in the flour and baking powder and stir until just combined. Cover and chill for at least an hour. Heat the oven to 190 °C (170 °C fan). Roll two-thirds of the dough between sheets of baking paper and line the base and sides of the dish; roll the rest for the lid and keep it chilled. Cut the apples into thick slices, toss with the 80 g sugar, the blackberries and the lemon zest, and fill the case. Dot with the butter, lay on the lid, press the edges to seal, cut a slit in the top and dust with caster sugar. Bake in the middle of the oven for 40–50 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean. Cool before serving with whipped cream or vanilla ice cream.
recipes.title: Apple and blackberry shortcake

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. 500 g blackberries, 250 g plain or wholemeal flour (or 200 g flour and 50 g rolled oats), 150 g soft brown sugar and 180 g cold unsalted butter, cubed. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan). Put the berries in a lightly buttered ovenproof dish, with a sprinkle of sugar if they are sharp. Rub the flour and butter together with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs, then stir in the sugar (and the oats). Spread the topping evenly over the fruit and bake on the middle shelf for about 30 minutes, until golden. Serve with cream or custard.
recipes.title: Blackberry crumble

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. Makes 12. 150 g blackberries, 2 eating apples, 50 g caster sugar plus extra for sprinkling, 2 tablespoons water, 1 beaten egg and 500 g shortcrust pastry. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan) and line a baking tray with baking paper. Peel and chop the apples small and cook them with the sugar and water over medium heat for 5 minutes; add the blackberries and cook 5 minutes more on low, then tip into a bowl to cool. Roll the pastry 5 mm thick on a floured surface and cut 12 equal rectangles. Lay 6 on the tray, brush the edges with egg, spoon the fruit into the middle, cover with the other 6 and press the edges firmly with a fork. Cut a few slits in each, brush with egg, sprinkle with sugar and bake for 20 minutes, until golden and bubbling.
recipes.title: Blackberry and apple hand pies

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. Makes 12. 100 g blackberries, 250 g jumbo rolled oats, 125 g unsalted butter, 125 g light brown sugar and 2 tablespoons golden syrup. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan) and line a 20 × 20 cm tin with baking paper. Melt the butter, sugar and syrup in a pan over low heat, stir in the oats until coated, and press the mixture into the tin. Scatter the blackberries on top and press down firmly so it is level. Bake for 20–25 minutes, until golden, then cool before cutting into 12.
recipes.title: Blackberry flapjacks

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. Blackberries alone or mixed with other summer fruit (raspberries, blackcurrants, redcurrants; frozen is fine) — enough to fill your pudding basin one and a half times — plus about 3 tablespoons caster sugar, sliced day-old white bread and a little butter. Butter the basin. Cut the crusts off the bread and line the basin with it, pressed firmly with no gaps, keeping a couple of slices for the lid. Heat the fruit and sugar gently in a pan until it simmers and runs with syrupy juice; taste carefully (it is very hot) and add sugar if it is sharp. Fill the basin with the fruit, keeping back some syrup and fruit. Put on the bread lid, press a plate on top and weigh it down with a can. Once cool, refrigerate overnight so the juice soaks into the bread. Turn out onto a plate, pour over the rest of the syrup and decorate with the leftover fruit.
recipes.title: Summer pudding

recipes.method: Written for wild brambles in Essex, England; the page names no species. Serves 1. A handful of young blackberry leaves; freshly boiled water; honey, to taste. Wash the leaves well, watching for insects. Chop them roughly, or scrunch them in your hands to bruise them. Put about 2 tablespoons (30 ml) of the chopped leaves in a tea infuser, pour over freshly boiled water and cover the cup. Steep for 5 minutes, taste, and give it another 5 minutes if you want it stronger. Stir in a teaspoon of honey if you like. To keep leaves for later, remove any stems, lay the leaves flat on a baking sheet and dry them in the oven at its lowest setting until brittle, then store them in a clean jar in a dark cupboard. Use 1 teaspoon of dried leaf per cup and taste after 2–3 minutes, because dried leaf infuses faster than fresh. The author finds the fresh tea grassy and slightly citrusy, like a green tea, and more tannic the longer it brews.
recipes.title: Blackberry leaf tea

sources: Langlands, Peter. Foraging New Zealand (Penguin Random House NZ, 2024), 'Blackberry' entry.

Its actual legal status, which 'declared pest' summarises. Blackberry is a Sustained Control pest in regional pest management plans rather than an eradication target, because it is too widespread to contain — Hawke's Bay, Bay of Plenty, Auckland and Tasman–Nelson all list it that way, with the occupier responsible for control and rules commonly requiring destruction within 10 m of a boundary where the neighbour is also controlling it. Breeding, distributing, releasing or selling it is an offence under the Biosecurity Act 1993. It is **not** a National Pest Plant Accord species. Hawke's Bay Regional Council, pest hub: 'Blackberry'. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.hbrc.govt.nz/environment/pest-control/pest-hub/pests/pest/21

What it is sprayed with and when, which is what the spray warning is really about. Hawke's Bay Regional Council's guidance for large patches is to spray in summer to autumn, before the leaves go brittle, with metsulfuron-methyl, Tordon Brushkiller or triclopyr 600 EC. Small patches are dug out year-round. Goats control it effectively where they are confined with it. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.hbrc.govt.nz/environment/pest-control/pest-hub/pests/pest/21

Why the scientific name carries 'agg.' — Rubus fruticosus L. is an ambiguous name that has been applied in several ways, which is why the European blackberries are treated as an aggregate rather than a species. Wikipedia contributors. 'Rubus fruticosus', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubus_fruticosus

IV (Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) — species pages australis https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/39c4783c-2d71-492a-ac53-7b451f760db3, parvus https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/dcac1cba-8672-42b4-a1bc-7fe526408c24, schmidelioides https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/7d1a26e8-60eb-4d9c-a61c-34f2da095dce, idaeus https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/143de0f8-b564-439e-a48e-2fad7375e125, fruticosus https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/10a24c18-75dd-4a10-b29b-757623bde62e; the pair tests restate its Rubus key (https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/ec381da4-4d7f-42c3-a4fb-e53e5d76b192: flowers 15–60 mm and ⚥ with fruit finally black for blackberry, against 8–15 mm and unisexual with yellow to red fruit for the native lianes; pinnate against palmate leaves; '< 10 teeth on each side' for R. australis; juvenile and inflorescence leaves sometimes reduced to one leaflet) and its notes on R. parvus ('relatively large ⚥ fls whereas the other indigenous spp. have small fls and are dioecious') and R. schmidelioides (juvenile leaflets 'much narrower and usually glabrous'). The hollow-raspberry test is Wikipedia, 'Rubus idaeus' (CC BY-SA 4.0, revision 1365353396): 'the drupelets separate from the core when picked, leaving a hollow fruit, whereas in blackberries and most other species of Rubus, the drupelets stay attached to the core' — used only on the raspberry–blackberry pair, because 'most other species' does not cover the native lawyers by name. The glandular hairs sentence restates NZPCN's similar-taxa notes for R. australis and R. schmidelioides (ARR); Webb's blackberry key confirms some blackberries lack long-stalked glands. 'Red before it turns black' rests on this catalogue's blackberry identification text ('ripening green to red to matte black', Langlands). No card joins red raspberry and creeping lawyer: Flora of New Zealand puts creeping lawyer only west of the Main Divide from Nelson to South Westland, and lists no raspberry station there. Every number was checked against the saved Flora text. The commonest native lawyers, R. cissoides (bush lawyer, 3,367 wild NZ iNaturalist records on 21/10/2026) and R. squarrosus (leafless lawyer, 541), have no entries, so no card can open them.

identification.text:
Ribes nigrum is a medium-sized shrub, growing to 1.5 by 1.5 metres. The leaves are alternate, simple, 3 to 5 centimetres broad and long with five palmate lobes and a serrated margin. All parts of the plant are strongly aromatic. The flowers are produced in racemes known as "strigs" up to 8 cm long containing 10–20 flowers, each about 8 millimetres in diameter. Each flower has a hairy calyx with yellow glands, the five lobes of which are longer than the inconspicuous petals. There are five stamens surrounding the stigma and style and two fused carpels. The flowers open in succession from the base of the string and are mostly insect pollinated, but some pollen is distributed by the wind. They are somewhat self-pollinating, but produce more fruit when pollinated by another plant of a different variety. A pollen grain landing on a stigma will germinate and send a slender pollen tube down the style to the ovule. In warm weather, this takes about 48 hours, but in cold weather, it may take a week, and by that time, the ovule may have passed the stage where it is receptive. If fewer than about 35 ovules are fertilised, the fruit may not be able to develop and will fall prematurely. Frost can damage both unopened and open flowers when the temperature falls below −1.9 °C. The flowers at the base of the strig are more protected by the foliage and are less likely to be damaged.
In midsummer the strigs of green fruit ripen to edible berries, very dark purple in colour, almost black, with glossy skins and calyxes at the apex (the calyxes being persistent), each containing many seeds. An established bush can produce about 4.5 kilograms of fruit each year.
Plants from Northern Asia are sometimes distinguished as a separate variety, Ribes nigrum var. sibiricum, of which R. cyathiforme is considered a synonym.


Phytochemicals
Polyphenol phytochemicals present in the fruit, seeds, and leaves are being investigated for their potential biological activities. Major anthocyanins in blackcurrant pomace – delphinidin-3-O-glucoside, delphinidin-3-O-rutinoside, cyanidin-3-O-glucoside, and cyanidin-3-O-rutinoside, which are retained in the juice concentrate – are among other polyphenols.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree; twigs ribbed, glabrous to densely hairy. Leaves reduced to phyllodes, alternate; phyllodes glabrous, narrowly obovate, elliptic and symmetric or falcate, usually obtuse, sometimes shortly mucronate, entire, (40)–60–100 × 8–20 mm, with 3–4 prominent veins; stipules triangular, 1–2 mm long, conspicuous in young plants only. Inflorescence of few to numerous, many-flowered, pale creamy yellow, globose heads; heads solitary or in axillary racemes usually longer than the leaves. Flowers 5-merous, sessile. Pod glabrous, twisted or spiralled, 8–10 cm long (up to 4 cm diameter), 5–8 mm wide; aril pink to crimson or red, encircling seed. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Racosperma melanoxylon (R.Br.) Mart.]
Flowers August–November. Young plants may have feathery, twice-divided (bipinnate) leaves, and some leaves are intermediate, with bipinnate leaflets on a well-developed phyllode.
It is easily told from the other naturalised wattles with large phyllodes by its 5-parted flowers in round heads and the large aril enfolding the seed. Told from Sydney golden wattle (Acacia longifolia) by its flowers in round heads (Sydney golden wattle's are in cylindrical spikes) and, at fruiting, by the large red aril enfolding the seed (Sydney golden wattle's aril is slightly folded and cup-shaped).

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers: blackwood's are pale creamy yellow, in round heads; Sydney golden wattle's are pale to golden yellow, in cylindrical spikes. At fruiting, look at the seed: blackwood's has a large pink to crimson or red aril encircling and enfolding it; Sydney golden wattle's aril is not much folded, thickened and cup-shaped below the seed. Blackwood's pods are twisted or spiralled; Sydney golden wattle's are straight or slightly curved, but its coastal subspecies sophorae has extremely contorted pods, so pod shape does not always separate them. The leaves do not separate them: both have narrow, flat phyllodes with several prominent veins, blackwood's (40)–60–100 × 8–20 mm with 3–4 veins, Sydney golden wattle's (60)–80–130 × 6–22 mm with 2–4. Both grow in waste places, often near the coast. Sydney golden wattle's seeds are eaten (see its page).

summary.text:
Blackwood (Acacia melanoxylon), also called Tasmanian blackwood, is a shrub or tree, growing up to 30 m tall, of the pea family (Fabaceae), native to eastern Australia and Tasmania and naturalised in New Zealand.
In New Zealand: North Island: Northland, established in the vicinity of Auckland City, Hauraki Plains, the vicinity of Whakarewarewa and Rotorua, at Halcombe (Manawatū) and near Palmerston North; South Island: Christchurch and coastal North Canterbury, Otago Peninsula, also collected once from Te Waewae Bay, Southland. Naturalised from eastern Australia and Tasmania, first recorded in 1918.
It is used in forestry and for soil conservation, so it can be expected to spread further. Its hard, dark timber is used for furniture, boats and musical instruments, and it is increasingly planted in New Zealand for it.
It is on the Department of Conservation's list of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024, but is not in any regional pest management plan. The common names wattle and acacia are used for many species of its genus, 13 of which are naturalised in New Zealand.

warnings: Many wattles are considered poisonous, and 13 wattle species are naturalised in New Zealand. Be sure of the species before eating any wattle seed or flower: Sydney golden wattle (Acacia longifolia) has similar leaves (see the lookalikes).
Eat only the seeds and flowers. The bark and twigs were used to stupefy fish.
The wood can cause hand dermatitis, and its sawdust is a problem particularly for furniture makers; occupational asthma from blackwood has been reported.

habitat.text:
Subtidal, anchored on rocky bottoms in water about 3–20 m deep, on open coasts sheltered from direct wave action and in calm bays, harbours and sheltered offshore waters, where it forms beds with floating canopies. It tolerates strong tidal currents. Smaller plants grow in shallow pools and channels.
In New Zealand it forms large forests in the deep sheltered waters of the south.

harvestEthics.text:
This species is at risk. If you harvest it, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.
Removing a plant's floating surface canopy sharply cuts the number of reproductive blades it makes and can leave it sterile for weeks.
Attached bladder kelp may not be taken from the East Otago taiāpure; kelp that is unattached and cast ashore is exempt. In the Kaikōura Marine Area (Te Whata Kai o Rakihouia i Te Tai o Marokura) it may be gathered by hand only, within a daily limit. Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.

identification.text: Huge: up to 45 m long in New Zealand. Long cylindrical stipes carry the blades up towards the surface, where the fronds form a floating canopy. Blades are long and leaf-like, wrinkled, with small teeth along the edges and a single oval gas bladder where each blade joins the stipe. New blades split off one after another from a growing point near the top of each frond. The holdfast is a massive dome of intertwined cylindrical haptera. Golden brown. Reproductive blades are smooth, have no bladders and sit in a cluster just above the holdfast, with darker patches where spores form. Blades from wave-exposed sites are thicker, narrower and corrugated; those from sheltered sites are smooth.

preparation.text: Chop fresh blades into roasted vegetables, marinate them for salads, or dry them and sprinkle them into soups and stews. Dried blades can be oven-baked and eaten like crisps, or ground into a seasoning. Cooked blades turn bright green and can be used to wrap seafood. Small slices soaked in light vegetable stock for a few hours can be blended into a purée for soups and stews. Dried and ground, it is made into kelp powder and kelp salt.

summary.text:
Bladder kelp, known as giant kelp elsewhere, is New Zealand's largest kelp — a native brown seaweed whose gas-filled floats hold its blades up to form floating canopies.
In New Zealand it grows around the southern North Island, the South Island, and Stewart, Chatham, Bounty, Antipodes, Auckland and Campbell Islands. Its current northern limit appears to be D'Urville Island in the western Marlborough Sounds, near Mana Island on the North Island's west coast and Palliser Bay on its east coast; it does not persist where the sea stays above 18–19 °C for several days. It is also widespread in cool southern hemisphere waters and in the Americas from Alaska to Mexico and from Peru to Argentina and Uruguay.
It is assessed as At Risk – Declining, with low confidence because the data are poor. Range retraction and declines are linked to warmer seas, reduced light and sediment from land runoff, and, in parts of its range, invasion by wakame (Undaria pinnatifida). Its beds along the Canterbury coast shrank after the 2017–18 marine heatwave and recovered quickly once the sea cooled. It has retreated in the Marlborough Sounds to cool-water refuges in Queen Charlotte Sound, and a forest that once stretched 20 km between Brighton and Taieri Mouth, south of Dunedin, has gone.
Attached bladder kelp has been in the Quota Management System since 01/10/2010 in the South East, where commercial cutting is limited to the top 1.2 m of water. In New Zealand it has been harvested to make kelp powder and kelp salt. It is hand-gathered commercially in Akaroa Harbour, then dried and milled for food products, supplements and gin distilling.

warnings: Bladder kelp is a brown seaweed, and brown seaweed can contain very high levels of iodine. High levels of iodine can cause thyroid problems, so eating it more than every once in a while may be unsafe, especially when pregnant or breastfeeding.
A single gram of dried bladder kelp can hold about 2.7 mg of iodine — about 18 times an adult's daily need of 0.15 mg, and more than twice the adult upper limit of 1.1 mg a day.
Harvest only from clean water — never near stormwater drains, in harbours, or where there is heavy boat traffic.
Seaweed absorbs pollutants as well as minerals and nutrients.
Cut blades with scissors — never pull seaweed up by its base; leave the holdfast in the water.

identification.text:
Annual; stems trailing or prostrate, (2)–5–40 cm long, sometimes mat-forming. Leaves sessile, (2)–5–25 × (1.5)–3–18 mm, ovate, elliptic, or elliptic-ovate, sometimes very broad-ovate, often indistinctly dotted with sessile black glands beneath; base rounded or subcordate; apex more or less obtuse. Flowers solitary; pedicels (0.5)–1–2 cm long. Calyx (3)–3.5–4.5 mm long; lobes lanceolate, acuminate; margins scarious. Corolla (2)–6–15 mm diameter, conspicuous; lobes about 3–7 mm long, elliptic or obovate, with numerous minute red to black-tipped glandular hairs on margin. Stamens about (1)–2 mm long; filaments much longer than anthers, more or less purple except for white-hairy dilated base. Capsule (2.5)–3–5 mm diameter, more or less equal to calyx; style persistent. Seed 0.7–about 1.4 mm long, reticulate, flattened on 1 side, convex and keeled on the other.
Blue pimpernel (Flora of New Zealand): Corolla blue; margin distinctly crenulate.
It has a square, hairless stem, and its stalkless leaves grow in opposite pairs, often with small black dots underneath (Massey). Apart from the flower colour it is the same plant as scarlet pimpernel, whose flowers are orange or orange-red.

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the petals: bird's-eye speedwell's flowers have four lobes, 8–12 mm across, usually sky-blue (rarely white) with dark stripes; blue pimpernel's have five, 6–15 mm across, blue, with finely scalloped edges. Speedwell's leaves have a short stalk and 3–8 pairs of coarse teeth; blue pimpernel's have no stalk, smooth edges and often faint black dots underneath. Speedwell's stem is round and hairy; blue pimpernel's is square and hairless. Both sprawl, carry blue flowers singly on long, slender stalks, have leaves of overlapping size and grow in cultivated land and waste places, so none of these tells them apart. Bird's-eye speedwell's young leaves and shoots are eaten, but its record as food is thin.
lookalikes.name: Bird's-eye speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Chickweed's stems are round with a single line of hairs; blue pimpernel's are four-angled (square in section) and hairless. Chickweed's petals are white and divided almost to the base (rarely absent), in usually loose clusters at the stem tips; blue pimpernel's flowers are blue, with five lobes, borne singly in the leaf axils on stalks (0.5)–1–2 cm long. Chickweed's lower leaves have a stalk about as long as the blade; blue pimpernel's leaves are stalkless and often indistinctly dotted with black glands underneath. Leaf size and the sprawling habit overlap and do not separate them. Chickweed's leaves, stems and flowers are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Chickweed

summary.text:
Blue pimpernel was long treated as a blue-flowered variety of scarlet pimpernel (Anagallis arvensis var. coerulea); Flora of New Zealand Online now treats it as a separate species, Lysimachia loeflingii, described in 2022.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands, in coastal and lowland areas, at least as far south as Canterbury, but rare south of Nelson. Naturalised from Europe and Asia Minor, first recorded in 1904.

warnings: Do not eat it. It was long treated as a blue form of scarlet pimpernel, which is poisonous: its saponins cause nausea and diarrhoea, and handling can irritate skin. No separate study of the blue plant was found.
It grows through chickweed and speedwell mats and has blue flowers like speedwell's — check every stem before picking (see the lookalikes).

edibleParts.text: Technically edible, but unpalatable.

habitat.text:
Xerocomellus cisalpinus was reported to grow mainly under broad-leaved trees (Quercus, Fagus, Populus, Betula) as well as under conifers (Pinus, Abies, Cedrus, Picea).
Though Xerocomellus cisalpinus is mainly associated with broad-leaved trees such as Quercus, Fagus, Betula, Populus especially of Quercus spp. Association with some coniferous trees such as Pinus and Juniperus were also presented.
In New Zealand it grows on the ground, mostly under introduced trees — most often oak, and also cedar, lime, silver birch, European beech and pine.

sources: Karaduman, Uzun, Yeşilyurt & Kaya (2024), 'First record of Xerocomellus cisalpinus for Turkish Mycobiota', Biological Diversity and Conservation 17(2) (CC BY 4.0)
identification.text:
Pileus 30-50 mm in diameter, at first hemispherical, then convex to almost plane, surface dry, velvety, somewhat areolate in age, blackish to dark brown when young, pale brown to ochraceous at maturity with a reddish tint at marginal zone. Flesh whitish to creamy, soft, slightly blueing when injured. Tubes creamy yellow to pale yellow, slightly blueing when bruised. Pores almost concolorous with the tubes to olivaceous yellow, slightly blueing when injured. Taste and smell not distinctive. Stem 3−6.6(−7) × 5−9 mm, cylindrical without a ring, some slightly tapering towards the base, some slightly curved at the base or bulbose, yellow to olivaceous yellow in the upper half, gradually becoming dull red to ocher brown downwards, white fuzzy at the base, Context fibrillose and brittle, blueing when cut or bruised especially towards the base.
Basidia 32–43 × 10–11.5 µm, clavate, 2-4 spored (mainly 4). Basidiospores (10.1−)10.4−12.5(−14.3) × (3.8−)3.9−4.8(−5) µm, subfusiform, thick walled, 1-3 guttulate.
This species may have similar morphological appearance with X. chrysenteron, but the smooth spore surface of X. chrysenteron differs it from this species. Xerocomellus pruinatus also have similar spore ornamentation with X. cisalpinus. But it lacks the ability of blueing.

lookalikes.howToTell: These two are hard to tell apart in the field: macroscopic characters such as colour and cap cracking tend to intergrade between species in this group, both caps often crack, both stain blue, and both have been collected in New Zealand under silver birch. Riverine bolete's cap is described as bright red, carmine, dark red or reddish brown, often fading with age to apricot or ochre with a reddish tint; bluefoot's is usually ochre to brown, grey-brown or blackish brown, but can have a reddish tint or be entirely red. Habitat may help: riverine bolete grows in wet woodland, and its New Zealand collections are under poplar, goat willow and silver birch; about half of bluefoot's New Zealand collections are under oak, and others under cedar, lime, beech, pine and silver birch.

identification: boletales.com, 'Xerocomus cisalpinus' — cap to 7 cm, dry and velvety but soon cracking to reveal pinkish flesh; tubes and pores lemon yellow blueing when bruised; stipe bright yellow above grading to bright red below and blueing; flesh blueing on exposure, most notably in the stipe; spores 10.5–16 × 4–5.5 µm and striate. Separated from X. chrysenteron by its more gracile form and striate spores, and from X. pruinatus by more frequent cap cracking and smaller spores. 'Copyright © 2026 boletales.com - All Rights Reserved', so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://boletales.com/genera/xerocomus/x-cisalpinus/

The Foraging Course Company, 'Foraging guide: blue foot bolete' — cap 5–10 cm cracking to show yellow flesh flushed red; pores lemon yellow ageing green-yellow and slowly bruising blue; stem 4–8 cm, yellow above and red at the base; flesh bruising blue-green slowly, particularly in the stem base. Names X. chrysenteron as the lookalike, separated by blueing less intensely in the stem base, and says both are edible. '© 2026 The Foraging Course Company Ltd', so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.foragingcoursecompany.co.uk/post/foraging-guide-blue-foot-bolete

lookalikes: the lookalike the overseas sources name, Xerocomellus chrysenteron, is all but absent from New Zealand — 2 iNaturalist NZ records, below the bar this catalogue sets for an entry, so there is no page to card. X. pruinatus has 0. The congener that is actually here is Xerocomellus ripariellus, 47 records, which the catalogue holds as a draft. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/438013

identification: Kibby, G. (2023). 'Fungal Portrait 96: Xerocomellus cisalpinus and some lookalikes'. Field Mycology 24(4): 111–112, British Mycological Society. In copyright — facts restated, no text reproduced. Field characters when fresh and young: the two-toned yellow and red stem, the cap often cracking with reddish tones in the cracks, and in particular an intense blue stain in the stem when scratched. Spores 11.5–15.0 × 4.5–5.7 µm with very faint longitudinal lines. Described in 2003 as a Xerocomus; the epithet means 'on this side of the Alps', after the Italian holotype, and the author calls it a misnomer because the species is common through much of Europe. Usually with Quercus, also other deciduous hosts.

identification: Kibby, G. (2023). 'Fungal Portrait 96: Xerocomellus cisalpinus and some lookalikes'. Field Mycology 24(4): 111–112, British Mycological Society. In copyright — facts restated, no text reproduced. Warns that old, faded Xerocomellus should rarely be identified at all, because all the species look very similar with age.

summary: Kibby, G. (2023). 'Fungal Portrait 96: Xerocomellus cisalpinus and some lookalikes'. Field Mycology 24(4): 111–112, British Mycological Society. In copyright — facts restated, no text reproduced. X. cisalpinus, X. ripariellus, X. chrysenteron and X. pruinatus have all been much confused and together formed the composite 'red-cracked bolete' of the older field guides — the same conflation this catalogue's deleted 'Red-pored boletes' entry made.

A description under an open licence does exist, but not in English: French Wikipedia, 'Xerocomellus cisalpinus', carries description, habitat, comestibilité and confusions sections under Creative Commons attribution, partage dans les mêmes conditions (CC BY-SA). It is not quoted here because a translation is not a verbatim copy, and the catalogue has no precedent for translated description text. Checked 07/10/2026. https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xerocomellus_cisalpinus

edibleParts: French Wikipedia (CC BY-SA) is a fourth voice and agrees it is edible, adding a preparation detail none of the others give — cooked, preferably with the stipe removed, choosing young firm specimens whose tubes are not well developed. Facts noted; the sentence is not translated into the page. Checked 07/10/2026. https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xerocomellus_cisalpinus

lookalikes: Kibby, G. (2023). 'Fungal Portrait 96: Xerocomellus cisalpinus and some lookalikes'. Field Mycology 24(4): 111–112, British Mycological Society. In copyright — facts restated, no text reproduced. Separations from the three congeners. X. ripariellus also stains strongly and has striated spores, but has a bright blood-red cracked cap and prefers wetter woodland — pond edges and boggy ground — especially with Salix and Alnus. X. chrysenteron has a more uniformly red stem, flesh that rarely bruises intense blue and is more often dull red in the stem, and spores that are not striated and are broader, 11.8–16.5 × 4.8–6.8 µm. X. pruinatus often does not crack, has a dark plum-red to blackish brown cap with a distinct thin red marginal zone, flesh flushing only slowly pale blue, and prefers Fagus.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Lowland to montane wet places, especially tarns, streams, bogs, lagoons.
It is an adaptable plant which grows in many types of damp, wet, and aquatic habitat.
In Britain (Useful Temperate Plants): Moist places, especially where water stands only in the winter.
NZPCN rates it an obligate wetland plant: almost always found growing in water or wet ground, rarely on dry land.
In the USA (MSU Extension) it is also a weed of plant nurseries.
