harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In the Wellington region (Regionally Vulnerable), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it. In Northland (Regionally Naturally Uncommon), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text:
Perennial, rarely annual, taprooted herb. Stems erect, rarely decumbent, glabrous or hairy, (3)–20–40–(100) cm tall. Leaves glabrous or hairy; margins toothed. Rosette leaves petiolate, auriculate at base, deeply pinnatifid to pinnate, (2)–4–7–(10) × 1–3 cm. Stem leaves similar to rosette leaves, auriculate at base, becoming smaller with narrower lobes above, the uppermost sometimes simple. Pedicels glabrous or sparsely hispid, erecto-patent at flowering, spreading at fruiting, (2)–4–7 mm long. Sepals 1.5–2–(2.5) mm long. Petals yellow, equal to sepals. Silicle glabrous, oblong to elliptic, curved, (2)–4–7 × 2–3 mm; valves not veined; style 0.5–1 mm long. Seeds pale brown, about 0.8 mm long, finely colliculate, in 2 rows per locule. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In plain terms (MSU Extension): small, light yellow four-petalled flowers in clusters at the stem tips, followed by small pods shaped like a globe or a short cylinder, curving slightly upward.

lookalikes.howToTell: Watercress has white petals, about twice as long as the sepals, and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes; its leaflets are rounded, with smooth or wavy edges. Bog yellow cress has yellow petals only about as long as the sepals (1.5–2.5 mm), usually stands upright from a taproot, and its leaves are deeply lobed with toothed edges. Its pods are short and plump, 2–7 mm long; watercress's are narrow, 8–18 mm. Both grow at the edges of streams and other wet places, and both have small lobes at the base of the leaf stalk, so place and leaf base do not separate them. Watercress is edible; cook it if it comes from water below grazing land.
lookalikes.name: Watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Narrow-fruited watercress has white petals, about twice as long as the sepals, and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes; its leaflets are rounded, with smooth or wavy edges. Bog yellow cress has yellow petals only about as long as the sepals (1.5–2.5 mm), usually stands upright from a taproot, and its leaves are deeply lobed with toothed edges. Its pods are short and plump, 2–7 mm long; narrow-fruited watercress's are slender, 10–30 mm. Both grow in streams, ditches and other wet places, so place does not separate them. Narrow-fruited watercress is edible; cook it if it comes from water below grazing land.
lookalikes.name: Narrow-fruited watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have small yellow flowers and deeply lobed, toothed leaves with small lobes at the base, and both grow in damp ground, so colour, leaves and place do not separate them. The flowers do: creeping yellowcress's petals are 3–5 mm long, about twice the length of the sepals; bog yellow cress's are only about as long as the sepals (1.5–2.5 mm). Creeping yellowcress spreads into patches by creeping underground parts; bog yellow cress grows from a taproot. Creeping yellowcress's pods, when they form, are slender, 10–15 mm long; bog yellow cress's are short and plump, 2–7 mm. Creeping yellowcress often sets no pods at all, because a patch is often a single plant that cannot fertilise itself. Creeping yellowcress has no reliable food record.
lookalikes.name: Creeping yellowcress

lookalikes.howToTell: Land cress has much larger flowers: its yellow petals are 6–8 mm long, while bog yellow cress's are only about as long as the sepals (1.5–2.5 mm). Land cress's pods are long and narrow, 30–70 mm, with the seeds in one row; bog yellow cress's are short and plump, 2–7 mm, with the seeds in two rows. Both have yellow flowers and deeply lobed leaves, and both can grow by rivers and streams, so colour, leaves and place do not separate them. Land cress's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Land cress

preparation.text: Young leaves, stems and seedlings go raw into salads or are cooked, and the plant can stand in for watercress. The taste is like peppery lettuce or radish. Māori boiled the leaves and ate them like cabbage. The plant can be dried for storage. Raw only from clean water with no sheep or cattle grazing nearby; otherwise cook it.

summary.text:
Rorippa palustris, marsh yellow-cress, bog yellow-cress or common yellow-cress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.
Rorippa palustris is native to, or naturalized across much of the globe.

Native range
AFRICA: in Egypt and Ethiopia.
ASIA and EURASIA: in Afghanistan; Bhutan; the Caucasus (in Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Russia) and Ciscaucasia (in Dagestan); much of China and Taiwan; India (in the states of Assam, Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, and West Bengal); Indonesia (in Papua province, Java, the Lesser Sunda, and Maluku Islands); Japan (in the prefectures of Hokkaido, Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, and the Ryukyu Islands); Kazakhstan; the Korean Peninsula; Kyrgyzstan; Mongolia; Pakistan; Papua New Guinea; eastern and western Siberia; Tajikistan; northeastern Turkey; Turkmenistan; Uzbekistan; and Yemen.
EUROPE: grows natively in most regions.
NORTH AMERICA: in every province and territory (excluding Nunavut) of Canada; Puerto Rico; the District of Columbia and every state (excluding Hawaii) in the United States; Mexico
The CARIBBEAN: in Cuba and Haiti.
AUSTRALASIA: New Zealand

Naturalized range
AUSTRALASIA: Australia and New Zealand
MEZO- and SOUTH AMERICA: in Argentina; Brazil; Chile; Ecuador; Panama; Peru; and Suriname.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) it grows throughout the North and South Islands, and NZPCN also records it on the Chatham Islands. It has probably also been introduced, but it is almost certainly a native plant as well. Allan's 1961 Flora treated it as Rorippa islandica. It is assessed Not Threatened (2023). Regionally it is rarer: Regionally Naturally Uncommon in Northland (2026) and Regionally Vulnerable in the Wellington region (2025); Data Deficient in Auckland and Not Threatened in Otago (2025) (NZPCN).
Māori names recorded for it include hānea, kōwhitiwhiti and poniu (Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga).
In New Zealand it flowers mainly in December and January (from October to February), and fruits mainly in January and February (from October to May) (Flora of New Zealand Online).
The name palustris is from the Latin palus, 'swamp'; Rorippa is a Latinised form of Rorippen, a Saxon name used by the 16th-century botanist Euricius Cordus (NZPCN). Achille Richard named New Zealand plants Nasturtium sylvestre in his 1832 Essai d'une flore de la Nouvelle-Zélande, and Kirk's 1899 Students' Flora used Nasturtium palustre (Flora of New Zealand Online).
Auckland Museum holds a specimen from T. F. Cheeseman's herbarium collected at Lake Ketenikau, Whangārei, in March 1878 (AK4404); Te Papa holds 37 collection objects, and Manaaki Whenua's herbarium about 110 databased New Zealand records, most from Canterbury (22) and Wellington (17) (Biota of NZ). It is a recorded New Zealand host of white rust (Albugo candida) (Biota of NZ).

warnings: Never eat plants from sites with polluted water.

Liver fluke risk: Rorippa species, the genus of bog yellow cress, are among the wild freshwater plants recorded as sources of human liver fluke (Fasciola) infection when eaten raw, mostly where infected cattle or sheep graze. Heat kills the cysts; cook plants from such ground.

identification.text:
Densely branched evergreen shrub, 1–6 m high. Shoots and young leaves with minute glandular scales. Leaves subsessile or shortly petiolate, alternate on young shoots but on mature stems mostly in fascicles on short spurs along the rigid branch spines. Lamina 5–43 × 3–12 mm, oblong, linear-oblong or spathulate; base attenuate; apex rounded-truncate. Flowers 1–2–(3) together, on short spurs. Pedicels slender, about 5 mm long at flowering, to 2 cm long at fruiting. Calyx 4–8 mm long, tubular-campanulate; teeth triangular, obtuse to acute. Corolla 10–13 mm long; tube broad-cylindric; lobes 4–5 mm long, obovate, pale mauve or cream; apex rounded. Filaments hairy at base. Fruit 5–12–(14) mm diameter, globular or somewhat obovoid, scarlet. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Boxthorn's leaves are small, 5–43 mm long, unlobed and oblong to spoon-shaped, mostly in clusters on short spurs along the rigid branch spines; hawthorn's are 25–70 mm and deeply cut into 3–7 lobes. Boxthorn is evergreen; hawthorn loses its leaves in winter. Boxthorn's flowers are tubular, pale mauve or cream, 10–13 mm long, one to three together; hawthorn's are white, rarely pink, open and five-petalled, many together in flat clusters. Boxthorn's berries are scarlet, round or slightly egg-shaped, on stalks up to 2 cm long; hawthorn's haws are dark red and crowned by the bent-back sepals, holding usually one stone. A thorny hedge shrub with red berries does not separate them.

summary.text:
Lycium ferocissimum, the African boxthorn or boxthorn, is a shrub in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) indigenous to South Africa.
It has also been recorded in the Free State, but these may represent introductions. It has been widely introduced in South Africa and elsewhere in Africa, as far north as Morocco. It has been recorded in Sardinia, Italy. This shrub is found in other Mediterranean countries such as Tunisia and Spain. There is one record in France from 2020.
It has become naturalised in Australia and New Zealand. It is listed in Australia's Weed of National Significance list and is a declared noxious weed in the United States.

warnings: The orange-red berries are probably poisonous.
The green spines are easy to miss until you brush against the bush.

habitat.text:
Open scrub, hillsides, forest margins, regenerating farmland — mostly in the open, but also under podocarp, broadleaved and beech forest, under mānuka and kānuka, in coastal and other scrub, and under pine plantations.
It is found in rough and reverting pasture, on road cuttings and banks, in ditches, on lake and forest margins, in peat bogs, on old sand dunes, on cliff faces, in forest clearings and disturbed ground, along river beds and terraces, in tussock land, and on heated ground.

identification.text: A tall coarse fern to 2 m with fronds divided three times into stiff, leathery, triangular blades on a strong dark stalk, forming dense stands rather than single plants. New shoots emerge singly from the ground as tightly coiled brown-hairy fists, unlike pikopiko's clusters of soft green koru on an existing plant.

lookalikes.howToTell: Pikopiko (hen and chicken fern) grows from a short, stout, upright rhizome; bracken has long-creeping underground rhizomes and forms extensive stands. Pikopiko's stalks and fronds carry scales, and its fronds lack hairs; bracken's fronds carry hairs and lack scales, and its stalks become woody and chestnut brown at the base. Pikopiko's fronds usually bear small bulbils (plantlets) on the upper surface, which usually make it readily recognised; bracken's description has none. Habitat helps but is not a test: pikopiko grows in wetter, shaded places on the forest floor, in gullies and on streamsides; bracken grows mostly in the open but also under forest, scrub and pine plantations. The young, unopened fronds of pikopiko are a traditional Māori food.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pteridium_esculentum On the toxin: it contains ptaquiloside, concentrations in New Zealand 'vary greatly, and in a high proportion of stands ptaquiloside is not found', with the higher and very high concentrations in the areas where bovine enzootic haematuria or acute haemorrhagic syndrome was known to occur, and traditional Māori cooking techniques 'may have lessened the content'. It also carries silica structures that ground down teeth — visible in many Māori archaeological sites — and is known to cause constipation.

Aruhe, and why 'were once eaten' undersells it. The rhizome was a staple Māori food, especially for groups away from permanent settlements, and alongside kūmara was often the primary carbohydrate — particularly in the south, where tropical Pacific crops would not grow. Much of the plant's present distribution in New Zealand follows prehistoric deforestation and the deliberate tending of aruhe stands on the richest soils. It was associated with Haumia-tiketike, atua of uncultivated foods, and carried by warriors. The forms are named separately: aruhe the rhizome, roi its roasted product, rauaruhe the fronds, mōkehu the new shoots, and rārahu, rarauhe or rahurahu the whole plant. Wikipedia contributors. summary.text: The common coarse fern of open country. Its rhizome, aruhe, was a staple Māori food, often the main carbohydrate alongside kūmara, and its young shoots look like pikopiko, but the plant contains a carcinogen and is now left alone.

warnings: Contains ptaquiloside, which caused tumours in rats; bracken fern is possibly carcinogenic to humans, with sufficient evidence of cancer in animals. Ptaquiloside levels in New Zealand bracken vary greatly and many stands carry none, but nothing in the field shows which. Cooking does not make it safe: processed bracken, and boiling-water extracts of it, still caused tumours in rats.

Do not gather any fern shoot from open, dry, sunny ground — that is bracken country. Bracken also grows under forest, in scrub and under pine plantations, so a fern shoot in shade can still be bracken.

identification.text:
This siphonous green alga is of two subspecies in Ireland and Great Britain. They are similar, both are dark green in color. It forms long erect finger-like fronds. These grow to 40 cm or more long branching dichotomously. The cortex of the branches is formed by closely packed utricles, these are small cylindrical club-shaped structures formed from a single cell up to 1200 μm (micrometres) long. The rounded tips of these closely packed utricles give the frond a velvety texture. The fronds hang down from rocks during low tide, hence the nickname "dead man's fingers". The "fingers" are branches up to a centimeter wide and sometimes over 30 centimeters long.
Codium fragile occurs in the low intertidal zone, and subtidal on high-energy beaches.
It has no gametophyte stage, and male and female gametes are both produced on separate plants.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Usually near habitations, also common to abundant elsewhere in pastures, river banks and open moist places, and a major weed of gardens and arable land.
Plants grow very large around stockyards, cowsheds and other places with very high nitrogen levels.
It is abundant throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands, and grows on the Kermadec, Chatham and Campbell Islands.
It copes with poorly drained soil better than many plants, so it is often thickest in low-lying parts of paddocks.

identification.text:
Stout, tap-rooted bisexual or monoecious perennial; stems usually 30–100 cm tall, erect. Petiole of lower leaves usually much shorter than lamina and with long, white, membranous ochreae. Lamina of lower leaves to 35–(50) × 15–(20) cm, more or less oblong or oblong-ovate, more or less membranous, often puberulent below, especially on veins; margins more or less undulate; base cordate to rounded; apex obtuse or subacute. Cauline leaves becoming progressively smaller, narrower, and more tapered at base and apex. Inflorescence usually with several spreading branches; Whorls 10-many-flowered, usually contiguous, sometimes some rather remote; pedicels more or less recurved, slender, glabrous, the lower subtended by a small leaf; flowers dense, strongly protandrous. Perianth 1.5–3 mm long, generally green at first, often becoming red where exposed to strong light; segments with hyaline margins; outer segments more or less oblong or elliptic-oblong, not reflexed at fruiting; inner segments erect, greatly enlarged at fruiting. Fruiting valves 3.5–5 mm long, more or less triangular with truncate base; margins with some teeth 1–1.7 mm long, but usually several shorter; apex rounded to obtuse; tubercle prominent, rosy, more or less oblong, 2–2.5 mm long. Nut about 2.5 mm long, glossy brown, sharply angled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In spring it starts as a low rosette of large, broad, oval leaves, heart-shaped where they meet the stalk and often red-veined; some lower leaves have red stalks. The upper surface is hairless. Each leaf stalk is wrapped at its base by a thin, papery sheath (ochrea), a mark of the dock family. Seedlings have oval leaves on red stalks, with new leaves unrolling from the centre. Young leaves are slippery with mucilage when picked, and bruised leaves can turn red. In mown lawns it can hang on as a small rosette of flat-lying leaves. Its seed leaves are round-tipped and taper to a stalkless base.
Each spring an upright flowering stem grows from the crown. The fruits start green, turn red and dry dark brown, so by late summer the whole seed head is rust-red to chocolate brown. Usually only one of the three fruit valves carries a large tubercle; the other two have smaller ones or none. The taproot is thick, tough and yellowish-brown, and can go more than a metre deep.

lookalikes.howToTell: Foxglove is deadly. Its leaves are matt and hairy, grey-felted beneath (sometimes almost hairless above), with scalloped edges and a base that narrows into a long winged stalk; broad-leaved dock's are glossy, hairless above, with smooth, slightly wavy edges and a heart-shaped to rounded base. Foxglove's side veins curve forward to run almost parallel with the midrib; dock's run out to the edge. Every dock leaf stalk is wrapped at its base by a papery sheath (ochrea). If a leaf is felted or hairy underneath, leave it.
lookalikes.name: Foxglove

lookalikes.howToTell: Curled dock's lower leaves are narrow — 6–30 × 1.5–6.5 cm — with strongly wavy, curled edges, and taper into the stalk; broad-leaved dock's are much broader, up to 35 × 15 cm (rarely 50 × 20), with a heart-shaped to rounded base, a blunt tip and only slightly wavy edges. In fruit, broad-leaved dock's valves have a few teeth 1–1.7 mm long on their edges; curled dock's are entire or finely scalloped. Young curled dock has rounder, less curly leaves, so check several. The two hybridise, and the hybrids look halfway between, so a plant that fits neither description well may be a cross. Both are eaten the same way.
lookalikes.name: Curled dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Broad-leaved dock's basal leaves are widest near the base and narrow towards the tip; clustered dock's stay much the same width end to end. Judge by the basal leaves — those on the flower stems are often not the typical shape. Clustered dock's lower leaves are only 1–3.5 cm wide; broad-leaved dock's reach 15 cm (rarely 20). Clustered dock's flower whorls are all spaced apart, on branches that twist as they fruit, and its fruit valves (2–3.2 mm) are entire, each with a large tubercle; broad-leaved dock's whorls are usually packed together, and its valves have teeth 1–1.7 mm long on their edges and usually one large rosy tubercle, the other two smaller or absent.
lookalikes.name: Clustered dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Fiddle dock's lower leaves are pinched in the lower half above two large rounded lobes, like a fiddle (occasionally plain and oblong), and are 1–8 cm wide; broad-leaved dock's are broad ovals up to 15 cm wide (rarely 20), not pinched. Fiddle dock's fruiting branches spread wide and tangle into a mass, with distant whorls and tiny narrow leaves under 1 cm long right to the tips; broad-leaved dock's branches don't twist and its whorls are usually packed together. Both have toothed fruit valves: fiddle dock's spines reach 2 mm, broad-leaved dock's teeth 1–1.7 mm. Fiddle dock's flowering branches also stand out more nearly at right angles to the stem. Judge by the basal leaves; those on the flower stems are often not the typical shape.
lookalikes.name: Fiddle dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Lesser burdock's basal leaves are broadly triangular, 25–40 cm long (up to 55), sparsely hairy above and whitish and densely felted beneath, with scalloped to bluntly toothed edges and hollow stalks; broad-leaved dock's are oblong ovals, hairless above and at most finely downy on the veins beneath, with smooth, slightly wavy edges and a papery sheath (ochrea) round the base of each stalk. Burdock leaves are matt; dock's are glossy.
lookalikes.name: Lesser burdock

lookalikes.howToTell: New Zealand dock's leaves are narrow, 3–15 × 0.4–2.5 cm, usually brown, rarely green, on low sideways-spreading zig-zag branches with small flower whorls spaced well apart; broad-leaved dock's are big ovals up to 35 × 15 cm with a heart-shaped to rounded base, on erect stems 30–100 cm tall. Both have toothed fruit valves, but New Zealand dock's usually have no swelling (tubercle); broad-leaved dock's have one prominent rosy tubercle 2–2.5 mm long. New Zealand dock is native, uncommon in the north and now gone from Auckland, and is often pulled out as a weed by mistake, so leave plants that fit its description.
lookalikes.name: New Zealand dock

preparation.text: Pick the two to six youngest leaves from the centre of each plant, before the flower stalk grows, when they are still slippery with mucilage at the base. The new leaves of early spring are the mildest, and plants put out a second flush of young leaves in autumn. Very young leaves can go raw into salads and sandwiches; take off the slimy stalks first. Cook older leaves like spinach, in at least one change of water to draw out the bitterness, and cut out tough midribs; they shrink to about a quarter of their volume and turn dull green. Large leaves, blanched for 30 seconds, wrap fillings like vine leaves. The leaves can be dried, or blanched and frozen. Chopped young stems can be simmered with honey like rhubarb. The seeds can be boiled into a porridge or toasted and ground into flour; the papery husk is high in fibre and hard on the gut in quantity, so mix dock flour with other flour.

recipes.method: Written for dock generally — the page does not say which; the same author names curled and broad-leaved dock as New Zealand's commonest docks. The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard. 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: Written for dock generally — the page does not say which; the same author names curled and broad-leaved dock as New Zealand's commonest docks. The author's greens were dock, onion weed, nasturtium, plantain, baby wild mustard, dandelion, sow thistle and a violet leaf. 2 crushed garlic cloves; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 500 ml (2 cups) firmly packed wild greens, sliced very thinly; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper; 125 ml (½ cup) roughly chopped pistachios, walnuts, almonds or brazil nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp hearts, pumpkin or sunflower seeds; and 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, hemp seed oil or a mix. Makes about 750 ml (3 cups). To slice the greens, sort them into similar shapes, bunch and twist a few leaves together and slice as thinly as you can — this suits the tougher, stringier ones such as plantain, mustard and dock. Toss everything together. Good as a side or salad, in a wrap or sandwich, or with pasta, risotto, eggs, or sausages and mash. It keeps at least 4 days in a sealed jar in the fridge.
recipes.title: Weedolata (wild-greens gremolata)

recipes.method: Written for docks generally (the author names curly and broad-leaved dock). 12 large dock leaves; ½ diced onion; 2–3 diced garlic cloves; 2–3 tbsp olive oil, plus more if needed and to drizzle; 500 ml (2 cups) cooked rice; the juice of 1 large lemon (about 60 ml); a large handful of chopped mint and parsley; any chopped dried fruit, nuts or leftover meat; seasoning; coarse sea salt. Blanch 12 large dock leaves in boiling water, one or two at a time, for 30 seconds, and drain them on paper towels. Sweat ½ diced onion and 2–3 diced garlic cloves in 2–3 tbsp olive oil over a medium heat. Stir in 500 ml (2 cups) cooked rice, lower the heat, and add the juice of 1 large lemon (about 60 ml), a large handful of chopped mint and parsley, and any chopped dried fruit, nuts or leftover meat; season, add more oil if needed, and take it off the heat. Put two spoonfuls of the rice on each leaf, fold in the sides and roll up like a burrito. Drizzle with olive oil and sprinkle with coarse sea salt.
recipes.title: Dock dolmas

recipes.method: Written for curled and broad-leaved dock. Dock leaves; oil; salt or other seasonings. Wash the leaves and dry them very well, toss them in oil and lay them in a single layer on a baking tray. Season with salt or other seasonings and bake at 150 °C for 10–15 minutes, until crisp. Don't let them brown, which makes them more bitter; if they don't crisp, they were not dry enough.
recipes.title: Dock chips

recipes.method: Written for curled and broad-leaved dock (from Edible Garden Weeds of Canada, 1978). 2 tbsp butter; 1 chopped onion; 750 ml (3 cups) washed, shredded dock leaves; 750 ml (3 cups) milk; 750 ml (3 cups) fresh clams or oysters (or cod); 2 large potatoes, cooked and cubed but still slightly firm; salt and pepper. Melt 2 tbsp butter and cook 1 chopped onion until lightly browned. Add 750 ml (3 cups) washed, shredded dock leaves and cook 1–2 minutes until wilted. Add 750 ml (3 cups) milk, 750 ml (3 cups) fresh clams or oysters (or cod), and 2 large potatoes, cooked and cubed but still slightly firm. Cover and simmer over a low heat for 10–15 minutes, until the seafood is cooked. Season with salt and pepper.
recipes.title: Dock chowder

recipes.method: Written for curled and broad-leaved dock (from Edible Garden Weeds of Canada, 1978). 500 ml (2 cups) washed dock leaves; 60 ml (¼ cup) butter; 2 tbsp grated onion; 2 pressed garlic cloves, if you like; 2 tbsp flour; 250 ml (1 cup) milk; seasoning; 3 sliced hard-boiled eggs; 125 ml (½ cup) panko; 125 ml (½ cup) grated aged cheddar. Bring 60 ml (¼ cup) water to the boil, add 500 ml (2 cups) washed dock leaves and simmer 3–4 minutes, then drain. Melt 60 ml (¼ cup) butter, cook 2 tbsp grated onion (and 2 pressed garlic cloves, if you like) for 1 minute, stir in 2 tbsp flour, then slowly stir in 250 ml (1 cup) milk; season and cook until thick. In a greased small casserole dish, layer the dock with 3 sliced hard-boiled eggs, pour the sauce over, and top with 125 ml (½ cup) panko and 125 ml (½ cup) grated aged cheddar. Bake at 180 °C for 20–25 minutes.
recipes.title: Dock casserole

recipes.method: Written for the seeds of broad-leaved and curled dock. Makes about 30. 250 ml (1 cup) dock flour (from about 625 ml, 2½ cups, of dried seed); 250 ml (1 cup) oat flour; ½ tsp salt; 1 tsp onion powder; 1 tbsp yeast flakes; up to 125 ml (½ cup) water. Spread the gathered seeds on a baking tray and dry them in a low oven until slightly toasted, without burning them (about 625 ml, 2½ cups, of dried seed makes 250 ml, 1 cup, of flour); soaking them overnight first takes out some bitterness. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Grind the seeds in a coffee grinder or food processor, and mix 250 ml (1 cup) of the dock flour with 250 ml (1 cup) oat flour, ½ tsp salt, 1 tsp onion powder and 1 tbsp yeast flakes. Add up to 125 ml (½ cup) water a little at a time until it holds together without sticking, knead, cover and rest 10 minutes. Roll half the dough out about 2 mm thick on a greased, floured tray, cut into crackers or leave whole, and bake for 15 minutes; repeat with the rest. Cool completely. They keep a week in an airtight container.
recipes.title: Dock seed crackers

recipes.method: Written for broad-leaved dock, with dandelion; the author says any dock picked in spring, before flowering, will do, and so will other strong-tasting spring greens such as nettle, plantain or watercress. Makes about 35 small puddings or one large one. For the puddings: 400 g pearl barley; 4 eggs; 2 large leeks; a little oil; about half a supermarket bag of washed dock and dandelion leaves; 3 raw eggs, plus 1–2 more if needed; seasoning. For the coating: flour; 1 beaten egg; 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs; 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle, if you like; garlic mayonnaise, to serve. Boil 400 g pearl barley until tender, drain and cool. Hard-boil 4 eggs and chop finely. Finely chop 2 large leeks and soften them in a little oil. Blanch about half a supermarket bag of washed dock and dandelion leaves in boiling water for 20 seconds, then plunge into iced water (skip this and the puddings are more bitter and less green); squeeze out every drop of water and chop finely. Mix the chopped eggs, leeks, barley and greens with 3 raw eggs, and season very well. Wrap the mixture tightly in a tray covered with cling film, set in a larger tray of hot water, or seal it in a pudding bowl with baking paper, foil and string and stand it in a pan of water reaching at least halfway up. Steam for 45–60 minutes, in a 160 °C oven or on the hob, until it holds together; if it won't roll into balls, mix in 1–2 more raw eggs and steam longer. Turn out and serve as one pudding, or roll into small balls while warm and chill them (they freeze individually at this stage). Roll the chilled balls in flour, then in 1 beaten egg, then in 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs (mixed, if you like, with 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle), and deep-fry for 1–2 minutes until browned; or simply flour and fry them. Serve warm, with garlic mayonnaise.
recipes.title: Dock, dandelion and nettle puddings

recipes.method: Written for dock generally — the author thinks his leaves were most likely curled dock, not broad-leaved; the New Zealand version below names broad-leaved and curled dock; use young leaves. Serves 4. You need 170 g young dock leaves, washed; salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to finish; 50 g (¼ cup) basmati or other long-grain rice; 1 small onion, chopped; 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped garlic; 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped fresh oregano; a pinch of ground cumin; 1 litre chicken or vegetable stock; 1 large egg, beaten; black pepper; and plenty of fresh lemon juice. Drop the dock leaves into boiling salted water for a few seconds until just wilted, cool them in cold water and squeeze them dry (about 180 ml). Toast the rice on a tray in a 175 °C oven until just golden, then simmer it, covered, with a pinch of salt and 125 ml water until tender. Chop the dock both ways so no long strands are left. In a 3-litre pot, soften the onion and garlic in the oil over medium heat for about 10 minutes, until just browning at the edges. Add the stock, dock, oregano and cumin, bring to a simmer and season, then add the rice and simmer gently for about 10 minutes. Pour the beaten egg in a spiral over the surface without stirring and let it heat through. Serve with a drizzle of olive oil, black pepper and enough lemon juice that the soup tastes lemony. For a simpler version without egg (Wild Botanica, New Zealand): soften the onion and garlic, wilt the chopped leaves (central veins removed) in the pot, add the stock, cumin, oregano and salt, simmer for 10 minutes, then stir through about 50 g cooked rice and finish with lemon juice.

summary.text:
Broad-leaved dock, also called bitter dock or butter dock, is often simply called dock, and in heavily modified places it is the commonest of the genus. It is native to Europe and was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1864. Its Māori names include paewhenua, paenehua and rungarunga. 'Butter dock' comes from the old use of its leaves to wrap butter for market.
One plant can shed tens of thousands of long-lived seeds — about 60,000 by an Australian estimate — so large seed banks build up in the soil, and taproots left after digging or cultivation regrow. Tannins make the leaves unpalatable to cattle and horses, though sheep eat them, so it is a particular weed of dairy farms. It hybridises with curled dock, giving plants that look halfway between the two.

warnings: It contains oxalic acid, which gives the leaves their sharp taste. A little is fine, but large amounts can lock up calcium and other minerals in food; cooking lowers the oxalic acid. Take particular care, or leave it alone, if you are prone to rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.
Large amounts of dock leaves that are not properly cooked can cause nausea, stomach cramps, vomiting and headache.
Docks are routinely sprayed in New Zealand pastures, orchards, lawns and gardens, so pick them only where you know no herbicide or pesticide has been used.

Young foxglove rosettes, which are deadly, can look like dock leaves. Foxglove leaves are matt and hairy, grey-felted beneath, with scalloped edges; dock leaves are smooth and glossy. Check every leaf you pick.
Handling the leaves can cause mild dermatitis in some people, and the plant can set off hay fever or asthma in some people.

identification.text:
Scrambling perennial; stems glabrous, somewhat angled, broadly winged. Leaves glabrous; tendril branched in upper leaves, sometimes reduced and simple in lower leaves; leaflets in 1 pair, narrowly to broadly elliptic, acute to acuminate, 30–100–(120) mm long; veins parallel; stipules ovate-lanceolate with 1–(2) basal lobes, usually about as wide as or wider than stem, but at least 1/2 as wide ((3)–5–15 mm wide), 15–35 mm long. Inflorescence longer than leaves, (4)–8–14-flowered; pedicels 5–12 mm long. Calyx glabrous, slightly or not gibbous at base; calyx teeth somewhat unequal, triangular; lower teeth equal to or longer than tube; upper teeth shorter. Corolla usually magenta or purple-pink, rarely white, (15)–20–30 mm long. Pod glabrous, light brown, 10–15-seeded, 60–110 mm long; seeds reddish brown, reticulate-rugose; hilum ⅕-⅓ of circumference.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Narrow-leaved everlasting pea (Lathyrus sylvestris), established only locally in South Canterbury and North and Central Otago, is very similar; it has smaller flowers, 13–17 mm long, usually lanceolate to linear leaflets, and narrow stipules about 1–3 mm wide, less than half as wide as the stem. Tangier pea (Lathyrus tingitanus) may grow with it: Tangier pea has 1–3 flowers to a stalk and smooth seeds with a short hilum (⅙–⅕ of the circumference).

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stipules, the leafy flaps where each leaf joins the stem: broad-leaved sweet pea's are broad, (3)–5–15 mm wide, usually about as wide as the stem or wider and at least half as wide; narrow-leaved everlasting pea's are lance-shaped to linear, about 1–3 mm wide and less than half as wide as the stem. Broad-leaved sweet pea's flowers are larger, (15)–20–30 mm long, (4)–8–14 to a stalk; narrow-leaved everlasting pea's are 13–17 mm long, (2)–5–8 to a stalk. Broad-leaved sweet pea's leaflets are narrowly to broadly elliptic, 30–100 mm long (to 120 mm); narrow-leaved everlasting pea's are usually lance-shaped to linear, rarely narrowly elliptic, 50–130 mm long. Broad-leaved sweet pea's shoots late in the flowering season may have narrow, almost linear leaves and as few as 2 flowers, so go by the stipules. Broad-leaved sweet pea's lower calyx teeth are as long as the calyx tube or longer; narrow-leaved everlasting pea's are all shorter than the tube. Broad-leaved sweet pea's pods are 60–110 mm long, narrow-leaved everlasting pea's 40–70 mm. Both are scrambling perennials with broadly winged stems, one pair of leaflets and branched tendrils. Narrow-leaved everlasting pea is established only locally, in South Canterbury and North and Central Otago. Neither is eaten.

summary.text: Broad-leaved sweet pea, also called everlasting pea or perennial pea (Lathyrus latifolius), is a scrambling perennial of the pea family, Fabaceae, introduced to New Zealand from central and southern Europe and first recorded here in 1872. It is locally common to abundant throughout the North Island and in the South Island, though not recorded from central and south Westland or Fiordland, and is recorded at Halfmoon Bay on Stewart Island. It is a persistent perennial with thick fleshy roots that forms extensive patches, and patches in flower are a conspicuous part of the roadside weed flora in many areas. The flowers are typically deep pink, but white- and light-pink-flowered plants are common in many populations. Though often called sweet pea, it is not the annual garden sweet pea (Lathyrus odoratus). It is sold in New Zealand nurseries as a perennial climber for fences, trellises and arches, including the cultivars 'Red Pearl' and 'Pink Pearl'. It is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds in New Zealand.

warnings: Broad-leaved sweet pea is not given here as food. Its pods and seeds are recorded as toxic, and the parts recorded as food contain toxic amino acids that cooking does not completely remove.
A nerve-active amino acid, diaminobutyric acid, has been isolated from this plant and measured in its seeds.
Like all members of the genus Lathyrus, it contains toxic amino acids (lathyrogens). Eating them often or in quantity can cause serious nerve or skeletal disorders, neurolathyrism and osteolathyrism.

It is poisonous to animals. Its seeds contain an amino acid that the body converts to a toxin causing paralysis of the legs or skeletal and blood-vessel damage. Horses are particularly sensitive; cattle, sheep and dogs are also affected, and death is possible in severe cases.
It is a pest plant in New Zealand: it is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (NZPCN): on rock and in rock pools on the lower shore, and in the shallow subtidal zone.
In New Zealand (Waikato Regional Council): along the coast, in estuaries and even brackish water, but not in very deep water, as it needs sunlight. It grows attached to rocks, shells and other seaweeds, and can also break free and live as a floating mass that piles up on beaches and in sheltered bays.

harvestEthics.text:
Pick at low tide. Cut the fronds with a knife or scissors, taking the upper two-thirds and leaving the holdfast and lower third on the rock so it regrows, and take a little from each place rather than a lot from one.
New Zealand's rules come first. Nothing may be taken from a marine reserve, and some areas are closed to seaweed gathering, such as the Oaro-Haumuri Taiāpure near Kaikōura. In the Kaikōura Marine Area the fishing rules count sea lettuce as karengo: gather it by hand only, and within the daily karengo limit, which MPI's 2024 notice set at 5 litres of wet volume (what fits in a 5-litre bucket). Check MPI's fishing rules for the area before you pick.

identification.text:
Ulva lactuca is a thin flat green alga growing from a discoid holdfast. The margin is somewhat ruffled and often torn. It may reach 18 centimetres or more in length, though generally much less, and up to 30 cm across. The membrane is two cells thick, soft and translucent, and grows attached, without a stipe, to rocks or other algae by a small disc-shaped holdfast.
Green to dark green in colour, this species in the Chlorophyta is formed of two layers of cells irregularly arranged, as seen in cross-section. The chloroplast is cup-shaped in some references but as a parietal plate in others with one to three pyrenoids. There are other species of Ulva which are similar and not always easy to differentiate.
In New Zealand, sea lettuce forms thin, bright green sheets up to 30 cm across with wavy, ruffled edges; the sheets are tough and translucent and can look like wilted lettuce. Other Ulva species here look very similar, and a genetic survey of New Zealand Ulva found several species that cannot be told apart by their form alone.

preparation.text: Wash the fronds in several changes of fresh water, until the water runs clear, to get rid of sand and the small amphipods that hide in them, and pick out anything that is not clean, living frond. The taste is very mild, slightly bitter and clean; the darker the green, the more bitter it is. Eat it raw, add it to soups at the end of cooking, or blanch it: 10–30 seconds in boiling water, then into iced water, keeps the colour bright, and 1–2 minutes makes it more tender for a salad. Dried in a dehydrator, in a low oven or in the sun, which takes a few hours, it turns crisp and flaky and only a little salty, for crumbling over food as a seasoning or adding in strips to miso soup. Fresh fronds keep about 3 days in the fridge. Washed and patted dry, they freeze for up to 6 months; thaw them in hot water, drain and use them straight away.

recipes.method: The author gives no amounts. Fresh sea lettuce; sesame seeds; good salt. Wash the sea lettuce in two changes of fresh water and pat it dry. Spread it on a tray and dry it slowly in a very low oven, the bottom of a wood stove or a sunny spot; it takes a few hours. Blend the dry sea lettuce with the sesame seeds and salt, or pound them in a mortar and pestle, and keep it in a jar to sprinkle over anything, from noodles to beans.
recipes.title: Sea lettuce sesame salt

recipes.method: The author gives no amounts. Washed sea lettuce; sesame seeds; tamari, if you like. Spread the sea lettuce out on a dehydrator tray, sprinkle it with sesame seeds, and dry it in the sun for a day or two. It comes out sweet and nutty. A sprinkle of tamari before drying would make it better. It takes a lot of sea lettuce to make one sheet, so these are a snack rather than a nori substitute for sushi.
recipes.title: Sea lettuce sheets with sesame

recipes.method: 55 g (2 oz) fresh sea lettuce; 80 ml (⅓ cup) coconut aminos; 7.5 ml (½ tbsp) garlic powder; 7.5 ml (½ tbsp) ground ginger; the juice of 1 lime; 5 ml (1 tsp) chilli garlic sauce. Heat the oven or an air fryer to 165 °C. Wash the sea lettuce well in fresh water, squeeze out as much water as you can, and air-dry or spin it until fluffy. Mix the other ingredients into a sauce, toss the sea lettuce in it and leave it for up to 15 minutes. Lay it as flat as you can on a baking tray and bake for 15 minutes, turning it halfway; in an air fryer, 10 minutes, fluffing and turning it halfway. Leave it to cool and crisp in the air, then serve.
recipes.title: Sea lettuce zesty bliss chips

recipes.method: For the salad: 20 g fresh sea lettuce; 1 head of cos lettuce; 1 avocado; 1 carrot, cut in matchsticks; 60 ml (¼ cup) spring onions; 1 apple, thinly sliced; 115 g (4 oz) goat cheese; 30 ml (2 tbsp) sunflower seeds. For the dressing: 60 ml (¼ cup) tahini; 60 ml (¼ cup) pistachio oil; 30 ml (2 tbsp) water; 15 ml (1 tbsp) soy sauce; 15 ml (1 tbsp) rice vinegar; 15 ml (1 tbsp) maple syrup; 30 ml (2 tbsp) lemon juice; 15 ml (1 tbsp) lemon zest; 1 garlic clove, minced; salt to taste. Blanch the sea lettuce in boiling water for 10–15 seconds, then straight into iced water; drain it and squeeze out the water. Stir the dressing together, adjusting it to taste. Toss the sea lettuce, cos, carrot and spring onions with the dressing (the method also tosses in rocket, which the list leaves out), and top with the avocado, apple, goat cheese and sunflower seeds.
recipes.title: Sea lettuce green salad with tahini dressing

recipes.method: Written for sea lettuce and gutweed together; the author gives no amounts, and any tender seaweed will do. Sea lettuce and gutweed; reduced-salt soy sauce; rice vinegar; the juice of half a small lime; sugar; finely grated fresh ginger; garlic; toasted sesame oil; chilli flakes; toasted white and black sesame seeds. Wash the seaweed well, cover it with boiling water and blanch it for 1–2 minutes. Meanwhile whisk the soy sauce, vinegar, lime juice, sugar, ginger, garlic, sesame oil and chilli flakes together in a bowl. Drain the seaweed, rinse it under cold water and squeeze out as much water as you can. Toss it with the dressing and serve straight away, or chill it for 30 minutes first; the longer it sits, the more tender it gets. Scatter the sesame seeds over to serve. Leftovers keep 3 days in the fridge.
recipes.title: Sea lettuce and gutweed salad

Edibility, preparation, harvest and recipes, all restated: Milkwood (https://www.milkwood.net/2016/08/08/seaside-sandwich-foraging-eating-sea-lettuce/) — intertidal rocks, low tide, knife, spare the holdfast, a little from each place, nutrient-loaded water near outfalls and river mouths, wash in a couple of rounds of fresh water, eat fresh, blanched in salads, in soups at the end, dried as a sprinkle; sesame salt and the sesame 'faux nori' sheets (no amounts given); bait for blackfish (luderick) in NSW, where it is the one seaweed that may be picked live — NSW rules, not New Zealand's. National Seaweed Hub, University of Connecticut (https://seaweedhub.extension.uconn.edu/ocean-farm-to-table/sea-lettuce-profile-recipes/; profile written for 'Ulva spp.') — tide pools, pilings, docks, driftwood; 'Very mild, slight bitterness'; darker is more bitter; crisp when dried; blanch 10–30 seconds then ice bath; fridge 3 days; freeze or dehydrate; two recipes by Jules Marsh (Kelpful), US measures converted (oz to g, cups by volume, 325 °F to 165 °C; scallions written as spring onions, romaine as cos; the salad's method adds arugula its list omits, said so in the recipe). 'Harvest Season: Year round' is for tank-farmed sea lettuce in the US, so not used for months. Sibel's Recipe (https://www.sibelsrecipe.com/post/seaweed-salad) — sea lettuce as U. lactuca or U. rigida, gutweed as U. intestinalis or U. linza; wash until the water runs clear; avoid stagnant water, unrefreshed rock pools and busy harbours; cut the upper two-thirds; blanch 1–2 minutes; freeze up to 6 months; the salad (its 'Printable Recipe' box is empty live and in the Wayback copy of 03/10/2022, so no amounts). The Forager's Year (https://foragersyear.wordpress.com/2012/07/24/sea-lettuce-ulva-lactuca-the-miraculous-multipurpose-sea-herb/) — amphipods in the fronds, dried 'only a tiny bit salty', strips in miso soup, dehydrator better than oven; it rinses only in seawater, while Milkwood and Sibel wash in fresh water — the preparation follows the two that wash. Also blackfish bait.

Not used from the links: Sibel's 'early spring - late summer' season (a UK forager's general seaweed advice, and the Waikato factsheet says growth stalls above 20 °C in summer, so it is no safe guide to a New Zealand window; months are left as they were); Sibel's iodine and thyroid caution (written for seaweed in general; nothing in these sources gives sea lettuce's iodine content); Sibel's 'no toxic seaweeds that can be picked on foot in UK waters' (UK only); UConn's nutrition and 'antioxidant and antiviral' ulvan claims, and The Forager's Year's digestibility remark (health claims, out of scope); Milkwood's gutweed note (gutweed has no entry here). summary.text:
Ulva lactuca, also known by the common name sea lettuce or broadleaf sea lettuce, is an edible green alga in the family Ulvaceae.
The distribution is worldwide: Europe, North America (west and east coasts), Central America, Caribbean Islands, South America, Africa, Indian Ocean Islands, South-west Asia, China, Pacific Islands, Australia and New Zealand.
In New Zealand it is counted as introduced. A 2009 genetic survey of 581 New Zealand Ulva samples found 24 distinct taxa and concluded that at least five had been introduced, U. lactuca among them, judging partly by how often they turned up in highly modified places and areas with frequent vessel traffic. NZPCN and Biota of NZ list it as Exotic (Biota's earlier status was indigenous); Biota's databased collections are from the Canterbury and Wellington land districts.
Sea lettuce shelters small marine animals and is food for them and for some birds. It needs cool water and nutrients: above about 20 °C in summer its growth slows or stops, and added nitrogen and phosphorus drive blooms that can smother seagrass and shellfish.
In 2021 Ulva was not cultivated in New Zealand; a study isolated 24 Ulva cultivars from wild Bay of Plenty populations as a first step towards land-based farming.
Life cycle
The sporangial and gametangial thalli are morphologically alike. The diploid adult plant produces zoospores by meiosis – making them haploid. These settle and grow to form haploid male and female plants similar to the diploid plants. When these haploid plants release gametes they unite to produce the zygote which germinates, and grows to produce the diploid plant.

warnings: Sea lettuce grows especially well in nutrient-rich water, near ocean outfalls and at river mouths below cities or farmland, and at some sites it is contaminated with toxic heavy metals. Prolific growth often indicates sewage pollution. Pick it only from clean, open water: never near an outfall or river mouth, in a busy harbour, or from stagnant pools that the tide does not refresh.
Never collect rotting sea lettuce from piles on the shore. Bacteria rotting it can give off hydrogen sulphide, a poisonous gas; keep away from large rotting piles.

habitat.text: Dead wood in native forest and scrub, most often mānuka, kānuka and gorse. It also grows on karaka, kōwhai, pōhutukawa, cabbage trees and pine, and has been seen on tōtara, which few mushrooms can decay. Sometimes it fruits from living trees, or from the ground off buried roots. It copes with surprisingly dry conditions and is often found in the drier parts of a forest, where few other mushrooms grow.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

identification.text:
A fleshy, shell- to fan-shaped mushroom growing from wood, with a short, stubby stem off to one side; the stem can be almost central, or missing so the cap joins the wood directly. The cap is 2.5–15 cm across, occasionally to 18 cm, smooth with a silky sheen when dry, and brown with olive, yellow or reddish tints — can be purplish, especially when young. The margin is strongly rolled under, especially in young caps, and can be wavy.
The gills are white to cream or pale creamy yellow, broad, and run down the stem, where their ends form a network of criss-crossed ridges. The stem is cream to white and woolly towards the base, and the base is often darker. The flesh is white, thin at the edge and firm where the cap joins the stem. The spore print is white, drying pale buff to tan. The smell is often nothing, or sweetish, or faintly of grass.
Unlike many oyster mushrooms it often grows singly or in twos and threes rather than in big clusters. The other New Zealand oyster mushrooms (velvet oyster, Pleurotus parsonsiae, and phoenix oyster, P. pulmonarius) have caps from cream to brown, and can only be told apart reliably under a microscope.

lookalikes.howToTell: Olive oyster is rubbery, with a dark brown to purplish-brown polished cap and pale grey gills. Brown oyster is not rubbery, and its gills are cream to yellow; darker brown oyster caps can become dark brown and shiny, so check the texture and the gill colour, not the cap. Olive oyster mostly grows on dead southern beech and is commoner in the South Island; brown oyster is commonest in the upper North Island, mostly on mānuka, kānuka and gorse.

preparation.text: A medium to large, meaty mushroom with plenty of flavour, earthy with a nutty note. Use it in any dish that calls for wild mushrooms; the larger caps suit mushroom steaks or schnitzel. Slice it and fry in a little oil until it starts to brown, or lay pieces in a hot pan in one layer and leave them unturned until one side is golden and crisp, then season. Trim off the hard base of the stem. Check the gills and flesh for fly larvae: in Australia wild ones are often riddled with them, and they go fly-blown quickly.

recipes.method: Written for oyster mushrooms generally: the author's were pink oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus djamor) from a grow bag, and the author says wild-foraged oysters would be even better. 1 large cluster of oyster mushrooms; 80 ml (⅓ cup) extra-virgin olive or refined coconut oil; 50 g butter, dairy or plant-based; 5–10 ml (1–2 tsp) wild salt or smoky chipotle seasoning; 10 ml (2 tsp) smoked paprika; 5 ml (1 tsp) cracked black pepper; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt (less if your seasoning is salty); the leaves of a small stick of rosemary, chopped. Sauce: 500 ml vegetable stock, 150 ml smoky barbecue sauce, 15 ml (1 tbsp) liquid smoke and 4 finely chopped garlic cloves. Makes 2 steaks. Simmer the stock for 10 minutes, add the barbecue sauce, liquid smoke and garlic and simmer 15 minutes more, until it thickens. Keep the cluster's stems together and tear it into two or three hand-sized pieces. On high heat, melt 60 ml (¼ cup) of the oil with 30 ml (2 tbsp) of the butter in a cast-iron pan, press each piece in and weigh it down with another cast-iron pan or a heavy pot; cook about 8 minutes, until golden. Flip, press again and cook until golden, then flip, season the top generously, add the rest of the oil and butter, and cook pressed for 5 minutes a side. Leave the pieces in the sauce for 5 minutes. Heat the oven to 180 °C, put the steaks on a lined tray, baste with half the remaining sauce and bake 15 minutes; flip, baste with the rest and bake 15 minutes more. Serve with mashed potato or kūmara and greens or a salad.
recipes.title: BBQ oyster mushroom steaks

recipes.method: Written for oyster mushrooms generally; the author grows and sells oyster mushrooms in New Zealand. Serves 2. 200 g fresh oyster mushrooms; 30 g butter; 2 garlic cloves, thinly sliced; black pepper and salt; 50 ml cream (optional); a handful of parsley, spinach or spring onion, roughly chopped; a squeeze of lemon juice (optional); ricotta (optional); sliced good bread. Melt the butter in a heavy frying pan and cook the garlic until soft. Tear the mushrooms into strips (the stems can be discarded or chopped small and used), add them and cook until soft. Add the cream if using and turn the heat down. Stir in the greens and the lemon. Spread toast or fresh bread with butter or ricotta, pile the mushrooms on top and season with pepper and salt. For a variation, use a dash of tamari and sesame oil in place of the cream and lemon.
recipes.title: Sautéed oyster mushrooms on toast

recipes.method: Written for mixed mushrooms: oyster mushrooms are one of three in the mix, with flat and Swiss brown mushrooms. Serves 4. 375 g shortcrust pastry; 2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil; 500 g mixed mushrooms, including oyster mushrooms; 2 garlic cloves, finely grated; ½ bunch of parsley; 100 g gruyère; 4 eggs; 200 ml cream; salt and pepper. Heat the oven to 170 °C. Roll the pastry into a tart tin, weigh it down with baking weights or rice and blind-bake for 5–10 minutes, then remove the weights and bake until just golden; leave to cool. Heat the oil in a frying pan over high heat and sauté the mushrooms until golden and cooked down. Toss in the parsley and garlic and take off the heat. Whisk the eggs with a pinch of salt and some pepper, then whisk in the cream until just combined. Spread the gruyère over the base of the tart, put the mushrooms on top and carefully pour the custard over. Bake for 30–40 minutes.
recipes.title: Mushroom tart

recipes.method: Written for blue oyster mushrooms grown from a kit; the recipe is by Zach Papaleoni of Spore to Fork. Makes 6–8 sandwiches. Slaw: 50 g (¼ cup) sugar; 60 ml (¼ cup) red wine vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 250 ml (1 cup) water; 125 ml (½ cup) each of cucumber matchsticks, shredded cabbage and carrot matchsticks; 60 ml (¼ cup) thinly sliced sweet onion; salt and pepper. Mushrooms: about 900 g oyster mushrooms, pulled into shreds; 60 ml (¼ cup) olive oil; 1 tbsp smoked paprika; 1 tbsp onion powder; 1 tsp cumin; 1 tsp dried oregano; 1 tsp mustard powder; ½ tsp cayenne; 1 tbsp salt; 1 tsp ground black pepper; 1 tsp liquid smoke; 250 ml (1 cup) barbecue sauce; fresh buns. Whisk the sugar, vinegar, oil and water in a large bowl, add the vegetables, season and leave to marinate. Heat the oven to 220 °C. Toss the mushrooms with the oil, spices, salt, pepper and liquid smoke, spread them on a tray and roast for 20 minutes; toss, then roast 10 minutes more, until they begin to crisp. Drizzle the barbecue sauce over, toss with tongs and roast 5 minutes more. Pile the mushrooms into the buns and top with the slaw and more barbecue sauce.
recipes.title: Pulled oyster mushroom sandwiches with fresh slaw

recipes.method: Written for blue oyster mushrooms grown from a kit; the recipe is by Zach Papaleoni of Spore to Fork. Makes 8 small (15 cm) tortillas. Marinade: a packed 80 ml (⅓ cup) fresh coriander; the juice of 1 orange; the juice of ½ lemon; the juice of 1 lime; 1 tbsp minced canned chipotle pepper; 1 tbsp fresh oregano, minced (or ½ tsp dried); 3 tbsp soy sauce; 1 tbsp minced garlic; 60 ml (¼ cup) minced white onion; 1 tsp cumin; 1 tsp chilli powder; 1 tsp ground black pepper. Also: about 450 g oyster mushroom clusters; cooking spray; salt; tortillas; toppings such as chopped lettuce or watercress, sliced red onion, diced tomato, avocado, cheese, sour cream, pico de gallo, citrus and coriander. Whisk the marinade ingredients together in a large bowl, add the mushroom clusters, toss gently to coat, cover and refrigerate for 1 hour. Lay heavy-duty foil over the grill bars, heat the grill on high and spray the foil. Lift the clusters onto the foil with tongs, salt both sides and sear until golden brown. Turn the heat down to low–medium and cook with the lid down until most of the liquid has come out and evaporated. Take the mushrooms off, remove the foil and quickly grill the tortillas. Slice the mushrooms if you like and assemble the tacos.
recipes.title: Oyster mushroom asada tacos

recipes.method: Written for blue oyster mushrooms grown from a kit; the recipe is by Zach Papaleoni of Spore to Fork. Serves 6. 4 tbsp unsalted butter; about 450 g oyster mushrooms, torn or cut into bite-sized pieces; 1 head of garlic, minced; fresh herbs, minced (the authors prefer sage); salt and cracked black pepper; 60 ml (¼ cup) dry white wine; about 475 ml cream; about 450 g wide egg noodles, cooked. Heat the butter in a large non-stick pan over medium heat; once it stops bubbling, add the mushrooms and toss to coat. After a few minutes their liquid will come out and evaporate; then add the garlic, herbs, salt and pepper, and cook, stirring now and then, until golden brown. Add the wine and stir to deglaze the pan, reduce it a little, then slowly stir in the cream. Simmer to the consistency you want, taste and re-season. Toss in the noodles and garnish with more herbs and black pepper.
recipes.title: Oyster mushroom cream sauce with noodles

recipes.method: Written for blue oyster mushrooms grown from a kit; the recipe is by Zach Papaleoni of Spore to Fork. Makes 4 burgers. About 450 g oyster mushrooms, finely diced; 2 tbsp olive oil; ½ tsp salt; ¼ tsp ground black pepper; about 450 g beef mince; about 7 g dried morels, crushed and finely minced (optional); seasoned salt and cracked black pepper. Heat the oven to 220 °C. Toss the mushrooms with the oil, salt and pepper, spread them on a tray and roast for 20 minutes; toss, then roast 10 minutes more, and set aside. Mix the roasted mushrooms thoroughly with the beef and the morels, shape into 4 patties and season with seasoned salt and pepper. Grill on high heat until done to your liking.
recipes.title: Half beef, half oyster mushroom burgers

summary.text:
Pleurotus australis, the brown oyster mushroom, is a gilled fungus native to Australia and New Zealand.
It is one of four Pleurotus species indigenous to New Zealand, and is most abundant in the upper half of the North Island. DNA from New Zealand and Australian collections is intermixed, so they are the same species. Like a few other oyster mushrooms it has an asexual stage: growing caps can carry coremia, a black, slimy smear of asexual spores. It can be grown at home on kānuka or gorse logs, and is sold in New Zealand as a grow kit.

warnings: In Australia it grows in the same places as the poisonous ghost fungus (Omphalotus nidiformis), and the two look very similar there; eating ghost fungus causes hours of vomiting. Ghost fungus has no iNaturalist record in New Zealand, but anywhere it might occur, rule it out: ghost fungus glows faintly in the dark, and brown oyster's gills form a network of ridges right down the stem to the wood.

harvestEthics.text:
Not a legally declared pest, but on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds: birds spread its seed, and it may outcompete and displace native plants. Harvest as much as you like, and do not spread the seed: put it in green waste or landfill.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text:
Large shrub or small tree to c. 10 m high; bark smooth, light grey; pneumatophores absent. Branchlets ± pendent, angular. Leaves aromatic when crushed; petiole < 10 mm long. Lamina mostly 4–10–(13) × 1–3.5–(4) cm, sometimes smaller near base of branchlets and below inflorescence, often narrowly elliptic, sometimes elliptic or obovate, glossy, slightly undulate; veins numerous, conspicuous and parallel; base attenuate or narrowly cuneate; apex mostly cuspidate to acuminate, but sharply acute in obovate leaves. Cymes with 3–25 flowers, terminal or in the upper axils of short leafy branchlets, to c. 15 cm diameter; peduncles to c. 4 cm long; pedicels shorter, slender, angular. Hypanthium 4–6 mm long at anthesis, obconic, generally dark red at least on exposed side; pseudopedicel hardly evident; calyx lobes 2–4 mm long, broadly triangular-ovate, sometimes dark red, persistent on fruit. Petals c. 4 mm diameter, free, suborbicular, white, caducous. Stamens to c. 13 mm long, white. Style ± = longest stamens. Fruit 1–2–(2.5) × 0.7–1.5–(2) cm, oblong to obovoid, crimson to crimson-purple, ± glossy. Seed 1 or few, large; cotyledons green.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In S. australe the strong young shoots are ± 4-winged with the wings joining just above the node to form a pocket or protuberance and the seeds contain a single embryo. [From the notes in Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Lilly pilly's fruit is pinkish mauve or white, nearly round to broadly oblong or obovoid and often slightly flattened, with a hollow at the tip, and its calyx lobes fall off; brush cherry's fruit is crimson to crimson-purple, oblong to obovoid and glossy, with its calyx lobes (2–4 mm long) still on the tip. Lilly pilly's flowers are smaller, with petals about 2 mm long and stamens to about 3 mm; brush cherry's petals are about 4 mm across and its stamens to about 13 mm long. Lilly pilly's leaves are broader for their length (ovate or elliptic-ovate, usually 2–5 cm wide); brush cherry's are often narrowly elliptic, mostly 1–3.5 cm wide, on branchlets that more or less hang down. In New Zealand lilly pilly flowers from October to January, brush cherry from January to July. Look at the young branchlets: only brush cherry has a small pocket just above where each pair of leaves joins the stem; lilly pilly has none. Angles alone do not separate them, as both can be four-angled or shortly four-winged. Otherwise the two are very similar, with glossy, aromatic leaves, parallel veins and reddish new leaves. Lilly pilly's fruit is eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Lilly pilly

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the strong young shoots: brush cherry's are more or less four-winged, the wings running down from each leaf stalk and joining just above the next pair of leaves in a small pocket or hump; magenta lilly pilly's shoots are at most angled, with smooth internodes and no pocket. This works even on young plants. Cut a fruit open: brush cherry's seed has a single embryo, while magenta lilly pilly's usually shows lines of division marking its several embryos. Brush cherry's fruit is oblong to obovoid and crimson to crimson-purple; magenta lilly pilly's is round to egg-shaped and usually magenta, but can be white, pink or purple, so colour alone is not reliable. Leaf size and the white flowers overlap. Magenta lilly pilly is sometimes sold in New Zealand under brush cherry's scientific name, so a garden label does not settle it. Brush cherry is much less often planted than magenta lilly pilly, and its wild seedlings are uncommon. Magenta lilly pilly's fruit is eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Magenta lilly pilly

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: tree privet's berries are bluish or purplish black with a powdery bloom, no more than 6 mm long, each with a ribbed seed about 5 mm long; brush cherry's fruit is crimson to crimson-purple and glossy, oblong to obovoid, usually 1–2 cm long (up to 2.5 cm), with its calyx lobes still on the tip. Brush cherry's new leaves are reddish, unlike tree privet's. Tree privet's flowers are small and tubular, with four reflexed white lobes 2–2.5 mm long and only two stamens, in dense clusters up to 25 × 20 cm; brush cherry's have free, round white petals about 4 mm across and numerous white stamens up to about 13 mm long, in clusters of 3–25. Tree privet's leaves are not described as aromatic, are 3–6 cm wide and sit on stalks mostly 1–2 cm long; brush cherry's are aromatic when crushed, mostly 1–3.5 cm wide (up to 4 cm), so the widths overlap a little, on stalks under 10 mm. Tree privet's shoots are more or less round, with prominent lumpy warts; brush cherry's strong young shoots are more or less four-winged. Both are evergreen trees with glossy, opposite leaves of overlapping length (brush cherry mostly 4–10 cm, up to 13 cm; tree privet 5–13 cm), and both grow on roadsides, in scrub and at forest margins. Tree privet's berries are poisonous.

preparation.text: Eaten fresh, or made into jam, jelly or cordial. Each fruit holds one or a few large seeds.

recipes.method: 2 kg brush cherry fruit; 1 litre (4 cups) water; 1 kg sugar. Pick off any stalks, wash the fruit and drain it in a colander. Put it in a saucepan with the water, bring to the boil over a moderate heat, then cover and simmer for 20 minutes until soft. Let cool. When it is cool enough to handle, strain it through a jelly bag, or a sieve lined with two layers of flannelette, squeezing out as much juice as you can. Bring the juice to the boil over a high heat in a preserving pan or large, wide saucepan, stir in the sugar and bring back to a rapid boil, stirring and skimming off any scum. Boil until it sets, about 20–30 minutes. To test, put a teaspoonful on a saucer chilled in the freezer and let it cool for a couple of minutes: if the surface wrinkles clearly when pushed, it is ready. Pour into hot, sterilised jars and seal. Makes about five 250 g jars.
recipes.title: Brush cherry jelly

recipes.method: 1 kg brush cherry fruit; 750 ml (3 cups) water; juice of 2 lemons; 750 ml (3 cups) sugar; 3 teaspoons citric acid. Pick off any stalks and wash the fruit. Put it in a large saucepan with the water and bring to the boil, then cover and simmer for 20 minutes until cooked. Let cool. Line a sieve with a jelly bag or flannelette and set it over a large clean saucepan; tip in the cooked fruit and its juice and pour in the lemon juice. Gather the bag around the fruit and squeeze and twist it until all the juice is forced out, then discard the remains. Bring the liquid to a rapid boil, stir in the sugar and citric acid, and when they have completely dissolved, pour through a funnel into hot, clean bottles and seal. To drink, put 1–2 tablespoons in a glass and dilute with tap or soda water. Refrigerate after opening. Makes about two 750 ml bottles.

summary.text:
A large shrub or small tree of the myrtle family from Queensland and New South Wales. In New Zealand it has been recorded wild in eastern Northland from Mangonui to near Whangārei, in Auckland, and in the Marlborough Sounds at Canoe Bay and Deep Bay, where seedlings were found invading shady bush margins; wild plants usually come up near where it is grown, from seed spread by birds. Wild New Zealand plants were once recorded as S. paniculatum (magenta lilly pilly), and magenta lilly pilly is sometimes sold here under brush cherry's scientific name.
It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds, but is not a legally declared pest plant.

warnings: Tree privet, a weed tree with poisonous purple-black berries, can look similar. Brush cherry's berries are reddish-pink to crimson and its new leaves are reddish; tree privet's new leaves lack that red colour.

habitat.text:
Coastal ground, where it is widely naturalised, and inland around lowland lakes, in waste places and other modified ground. Overseas it grows on sandy or gravelly ground and in cracks in rock, in sunny, dry places, usually near the sea.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Abundant on sand and mud flats in and around estuaries and lagoons, common around lowland lakes inland, and in waste places in and around the main cities, also along railway tracks, roadsides and in many other open modified habitats, as far inland as Central Otago.

identification.text:
Hairy annual or perennial with persistent taproot. Leaves all radical, rosulate; petiole ill-defined, with silky tuft of hairs at base. Lamina (10)–30–120–(200) × 1–5–(10) mm, linear, 1–(2)-pinnatisect, rarely entire, with 1–4 pairs of linear, acute to subulate lobes or teeth, hairy, particularly on the margins, sometimes only sparsely ciliate; main vein usually 1. Scapes 3–45 cm long, not ribbed, usually densely clothed in antrorse hairs. Spikes 0.5- about 8 cm long, usually cylindric, shortly oblong in very small plants. Bracts almost equal to calyx, ovate-acuminate; keels prominent, hairy, herbaceous; margins hyaline in lower part. Sepals unequal, about 2 mm long, broad-ovate, with green, herbaceous, hairy or glabrous keel and exposed margins ciliate, remainder of sepal hyaline. Corolla tube equal to or longer than sepals, hairy in lower 1/2; lobes 1–1.2 mm long, ovate, spreading. Stamens glabrous, exserted. Style hairy, long, longer than corolla. Capsule mostly 1.5–2 mm long, broad-ellipsoid or subglobose, usually 4-seeded. Seeds 0.8–1 mm long, ovoid-ellipsoid, pinkish brown, convex on both sides; margin hyaline. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
A flat, star-shaped rosette of narrow leaves, often with one to four pairs of narrow side lobes or teeth, like antlers. The leaves are hairy, especially along the edges, and usually have a single main vein. The tiny flowers are packed into a cylindrical spike on a hairy, unribbed stalk 3–45 cm long, with the stamens sticking out. It flowers from July to April. Plants vary a great deal in leaf shape, size, hairiness and colour, some with red tints; what marks it out from the other plantains here is the combination of lobed or toothed leaves, all from the base, and a spike of many flowers.

lookalikes.howToTell: Narrow-leaved plantain's leaves are entire or only slightly toothed, 5–48 mm wide, with 3–7 veins running their length; buck's-horn plantain's usually have one to four pairs of narrow lobes or teeth and a single main vein, and are 1–5 mm wide (up to 10). Narrow-leaved plantain's flower stalk is strongly ribbed and 12–70 cm long; buck's-horn's is not ribbed and is 3–45 cm long. Buck's-horn leaves are rarely without lobes, so on a plant with plain leaves count the veins and feel the stalk. Both are hairy rosettes that flower from July to April, so neither tells them apart.
lookalikes.name: Narrow-leaved plantain

lookalikes.howToTell: Both form flat rosettes of narrow, deeply cut leaves on open ground, including near the sea, and twin cress can be mistaken for buck's-horn plantain. Twin cress is hairless or nearly so, smells foetid when crushed, sends out leafy stems along the ground, and bears tiny white (or petal-less) flowers in short clusters followed by paired pods about 1.5 mm long. Buck's-horn plantain leaves all grow from the base, are hairy at least on the margins with a silky tuft of hairs at the base, and its flowers are in dense cylindrical spikes on leafless stalks with protruding stamens. Twin cress leaves are eaten raw or cooked for their hot, cress-like taste; see its own entry.

preparation.text: The leaves are fairly tender, with a mild, sweetish, nutty taste and a slight bitterness. Trim off the lower ends, which can be stringy. Use them raw in salads, or blanch them in boiling water for a few seconds first to make them more tender, or cook them.

recipes.method: Written for buck's-horn plantain. Buck's-horn plantain leaves; wild rocket; sliced mushrooms; walnuts; olive oil; vinegar. Trim the stringy lower ends off the leaves and toss them with wild rocket, sliced mushrooms and walnuts; the mild leaves balance the spicy rocket. Dress with olive oil and vinegar.

summary.text:
Plantago coronopus, the buck's-horn plantain, is a herbaceous annual to perennial flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae.
In New Zealand it is also called Capuchin's beard, crowfoot plantain and cut-leaved plantain. It is native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia, from the Azores and Canary Islands east to Afghanistan and Pakistan. It arrived here by accident and was first recorded growing wild in 1873. It is highly salt tolerant, grows from seed, and is spread in moved soil and by people. In Britain it has been spreading inland along main roads, where it tolerates winter salting.
It is grown as a salad leaf, sold in Italy as minutina, erba stella or barba dei frati, and is one of the leaves in misticanze, a salad of wild and cultivated leaves from the Marche region of Italy. Growers value it as a frost-hardy winter crop.

harvestEthics.text:
This species is at risk. If you harvest it, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.
Rimurapa is culturally significant, particularly for pōhā tītī in the south. Some beds are subject to customary management or rāhui. Ask locally before harvesting.
It may not be taken from the East Otago taiāpure unless it is unattached and cast ashore, and bull kelp may not be taken between Marfells Beach and the Conway River, out to 4 nautical miles from shore. The Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998 protects bull kelp from commercial harvesting within Ngāi Tahu's traditional seaweed-gathering grounds.
Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.
