identification.text:
Massive, flattened blades, thick and rubbery, growing to 5 m long or sometimes up to 10 m, often divided into strap-like portions. Inside, the blade has a honeycomb of air-filled tissue that keeps it buoyant. On more exposed sites the blades become narrower and more whip-like, but they always stay rounded or oval in cross-section; the more exposed the site, the more divided the fronds. A short, cylindrical, unbranched stipe grows from a large, dome-shaped holdfast. Golden to dark brown to olive green.
Told from Durvillaea poha, which also has a honeycomb, by blades that stay rounded or oval in cross-section and a cylindrical stipe: D. poha's blades stay broad and flattened in cross-section and its orange-yellow stipe becomes flattened towards the tip. Told from Durvillaea willana by the honeycomb and the unbranched stipe: D. willana has no honeycomb, does not float, and its stipe produces side branches.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have thick, leathery blades with an internal honeycomb, so the honeycomb does not separate them. Look at a blade in cross-section: Durvillaea poha's blades are broad and flattened, and stay flattened even where the tips become whip-like; bull kelp's always remain rounded or oval in cross-section, even where they become narrower and whip-like on more exposed sites. Durvillaea poha's short stipe is orange-yellow and becomes flattened towards the tip; bull kelp's is cylindrical. Colour helps only a little: Durvillaea poha's blades are orange-brown to golden and can look more orange, bull kelp's are golden to dark brown to olive green. Size does not separate them: Durvillaea poha is usually 5–10 m long, bull kelp grows to 5 m and sometimes up to 10 m. Durvillaea poha often grows in a band above bull kelp, or further back on rock platforms and in more sheltered bays, but in southern New Zealand the two frequently grow next to one another. Durvillaea poha is found mainly on the southern South Island, Stewart Island and the Snares and Auckland Islands, and at low frequencies along the Wellington coastline; it was not found on the northern South Island north of the Kaikōura Peninsula. No record of Durvillaea poha as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Durvillaea poha

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or tear a blade: bull kelp's has an internal honeycomb, full of air, that keeps it buoyant; Durvillaea willana's has no honeycomb, and it does not float. Look at the holdfast: bull kelp's is extensively burrowed and hollowed out; Durvillaea willana's is solid, woody and not burrowed, and grips the rock so firmly that storms usually snap its stipe instead, so fewer than a third of cast-up Durvillaea willana plants still have a holdfast, against more than three-quarters of cast-up bull kelp. Durvillaea willana is also stiffer and more upright than bull kelp. Bull kelp's short stipe is cylindrical and unbranched; Durvillaea willana's is thick and cylindrical and produces side branches. Colour overlaps: Durvillaea willana is dark brown, darker than all other bull kelps, while bull kelp ranges from golden to dark brown to olive green. Durvillaea willana usually grows lower on the shore, from the low intertidal to the upper subtidal; bull kelp grows in the low intertidal, so the two can meet there. Durvillaea willana grows 5–6 m long and has smaller blades than bull kelp, which grows to 5 m and sometimes up to 10 m, so size alone does not separate them. In the North Island Durvillaea willana is found only near Castle Point on the northern Wairarapa coast, not in Cook Strait; bull kelp grows from the Three Kings Islands to Stewart Island. No record of Durvillaea willana as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Durvillaea willana

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or tear a blade: bull kelp's has an internal honeycomb, full of air, that keeps it buoyant; Durvillaea chathamensis's blades are solid, with no honeycomb, and do not float. Very small plants are difficult to identify, so check a full-grown blade. Bull kelp's blades are often divided into strap-like portions; Durvillaea chathamensis's are flattened, with parallel sides, wavy edges and very noticeable pale margins, and are usually not divided. Division alone does not separate them, because on exposed coasts Durvillaea chathamensis's blades can also split into many narrow straps: there, bull kelp's strands are inflated and whip-like, rounded or oval in cross-section, while Durvillaea chathamensis's are solid straps. Shallow, crater-like dents up to 25 mm across are common on Durvillaea chathamensis's blades, especially near the margins; the study that described it never saw them on bull kelp. Both have an unbranched stipe growing from a large, dome-shaped holdfast, so the stipe does not separate them. Colour overlaps: bull kelp is golden to dark brown to olive green, Durvillaea chathamensis dark brown. Size does not separate them: bull kelp grows to 5 m and sometimes up to 10 m, Durvillaea chathamensis up to about 3.5 m, so a plant shorter than 3.5 m can be either. Bull kelp grows in the low intertidal; Durvillaea chathamensis grows from the low intertidal to about 2 m deep, often in a band just below bull kelp, so the two meet there. Durvillaea chathamensis is found only in the Chatham Islands; bull kelp grows there and from the Three Kings Islands to Stewart Island. No record of Durvillaea chathamensis as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Durvillaea chathamensis

preparation.text: Roast the blade. Dried blade is soaked in plenty of cold water for at least 2 hours, ideally about 12 hours, rinsed, then simmered from cold for 20–30 minutes, or 40 minutes to 1 hour for thick pieces, until tender. Hot soaking water does not speed it up.

Which species you are actually cutting, because there are two. A 2012 revision split Durvillaea poha out of D. antarctica on genetic, morphological and ecological evidence, and it is the only other species in the genus with the same honeycombed buoyant structure. D. poha occurs only in southern New Zealand and the subantarctic islands, grows higher up or further back on the rock platforms and in more sheltered bays where wave force is weaker, has generally wider and more orange-looking fronds, and — this is the point for this entry — **pōhā are made from both**. In southern New Zealand the two grow together, so a southern blade is as likely to be D. poha. Wikipedia contributors. 'Durvillaea antarctica', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. summary.text:
The massive leathery kelp of the southern coast — traditionally made into pōhā, the bags that preserved tītī.
In New Zealand it grows on exposed coasts from the Three Kings Islands to Stewart Island, and on the Chatham, Bounty, Snares, Antipodes, Auckland and Campbell Islands. In northern New Zealand it grows only on very exposed headlands; it becomes more common in the cooler waters south of Cook Strait. It also grows in the Southern Ocean, South America and southern Atlantic islands. It is At Risk – Declining.
Bull kelps are fucoids, not true kelps. Four species of bull kelp grow around New Zealand; Durvillaea poha and Durvillaea willana share its coasts.
Ngāi Tahu split open and inflated the blades to make pōhā, which were filled with tītī (muttonbird) chicks and sealed with hot fat; birds kept this way for up to six years. The narrow stalk between holdfast and blade was made into a flute.

warnings: Bull kelp grows in the low intertidal of exposed, wave-battered coasts. Watch the sea for at least ten minutes before going onto the rocks, never turn your back on it, never go alone, and keep off wet rocks that waves and spray are sweeping over.

Take only drift, or cut from the blade tip, well away from the holdfast. Never cut through the stipe or remove the holdfast: fronds cannot regrow from a holdfast left behind, and fronds cut close to the holdfast may not regrow.

Bull kelp is a brown seaweed, and brown seaweed can contain very high levels of iodine. High levels of iodine can cause thyroid problems, so eating it more than every once in a while may be unsafe, especially when pregnant or breastfeeding.
Collect only from clean coast, away from wastewater outfalls, sewage discharges and farm run-off. Seaweed from water contaminated with human sewage can carry norovirus.

identification.text:
Scrambling liane; stems stout, terete, finely tomentose when young, sometimes becoming glabrous, often only sparsely hairy in juveniles; armature of numerous, small, slender, wide-based, reddish prickles. Leaves palmate; leaflets 3–5, mostly glabrous but often with weak hairs on major veins on both surfaces and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly serrate, thin and submembranous and with veins darkened and conspicuous in juveniles; terminal leaflet lamina elliptic to ovate or suborbicular, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, with petiolule usually about equal to or longer than lamina, rarely shorter. Inflorescence a many-flowered panicle up to 20 cm long. Petals white to cream, occasionally pinkish. Drupelets pale yellow to orange-red. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
This sp. is easily distinguished by the rounded, almost glabrous, coarsely toothed, relatively small, long-petiolulate terminal leaflets.

lookalikes.howToTell: Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. The flowers separate them: blackberry's are 15–60 mm across and have stamens and carpels together, while bush lawyer's are 8–15 mm across, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Ripe blackberry is black and bush lawyer's yellow to orange or red, but blackberry is red before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit. The native lawyers lack the long, glandular, bristly hairs some introduced brambles carry on their young stems; not every blackberry has them, so their absence does not rule blackberry out.
lookalikes.name: Blackberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Raspberry's leaves are pinnate, with side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk; bush lawyer's are palmate, all leaflets spreading from one point. Raspberry is an erect shrub with flowers 20–25 mm across; bush lawyer is a climbing liane with flowers 8–15 mm across, male and female on separate plants.
lookalikes.name: Red raspberry

lookalikes.howToTell: White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Leaves: bush lawyer's end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, hairless except often on the veins and margins, with fewer than 10 coarse or irregular teeth on each side; white-leaved lawyer's is felted underneath or, if hairless (mostly in the lowland eastern South Island), narrow-lanceolate or linear and coarsely toothed. Juvenile white-leaved lawyer leaflets are much narrower and usually hairless. Their fruit colours overlap, so fruit does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: White-leaved lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet; bush lawyer's have three or more. Young plants and flowering shoots of other brambles sometimes have single-leaflet leaves too, so judge by the leaves on mature stems.
lookalikes.name: Creeping lawyer

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. Makes 6 jars of 250 ml. The recipe is somewhere between a jam and a jelly: the juice is pressed rather than dripped through a bag, so it sets cloudy. 1 litre berry juice (fresh or thawed frozen berries put through a cold-press juicer), 300 ml cold-pressed apple juice, the juice of 3 lemons, 1.3 kg white sugar, 10 whole cloves and the zest of an orange. Wash the jars and dry them, open end up, in a 120 °C oven for about 15 minutes, leaving them in the warm oven until needed; boil the lids for 5 minutes and let them air-dry. Put the berry, apple and lemon juices and the sugar in a jam pan, dissolve the sugar over low heat, then bring to the boil. Add the cloves and orange zest, skim off foam as it rises, and boil to setting point — about 30 minutes for the author, giving a soft set. Ladle the hot jelly into the hot jars and seal.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry jelly

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. 400 g berries, 500 ml white wine vinegar and 100 g white sugar. Warm the vinegar with the sugar until it has dissolved. Put the berries in a large clean jar or a non-reactive bowl, pour the warm vinegar over them and leave overnight. Strain gently through a fine sieve or muslin and pour into a sterilised bottle or jar. The author uses it to quick-pickle wafer-thin slices of raw beetroot (3 tablespoons of vinegar and ¼ teaspoon of sea salt for 2 small beetroot, soaked at least 15 minutes) served with goat's cheese.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry vinegar

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. Muddle a big handful of berries (fresh or frozen) in a cocktail shaker, add 60 ml tequila blanco, 30 ml Cointreau, 60 ml fresh lime juice and 60 ml sugar syrup, shake hard over ice and pour. Strain it if you don't want the seeds.

summary.text: Rubus australis, commonly called swamp lawyer, is a climbing plant species found in New Zealand. It is endemic, and grows throughout the North and South Islands (rarely in the drier east) and on Stewart Island.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In the Auckland region (Regionally Endangered), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it. In Northland (Regionally Naturally Uncommon), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text: An erect native nettle 15–60 cm tall that spreads by rhizomes. Leaves are light green, triangular to triangular-ovate, 2–6 cm long (up to 12 cm in the Flora of New Zealand), with a squared-off to slightly heart-shaped base and 9–10 (sometimes 12) regular teeth on each side, on stalks 3–7 cm long. The stinging hairs are most numerous on the leaf stalks, fewer on the leaf blades and stem. Male and female flowers grow on the same plant: the lowest flower clusters are all male, the upper ones all female. Its sting is generally less painful than other native nettles', though it varies from plant to plant and from person to person.

lookalikes.howToTell: Ongaonga is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m, with numerous long-stalked white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long, pale green triangular to ovate-triangular leaves usually 7–12 cm long (4–18 cm), and 2 stipules at each node. Bush nettle is a soft herb 15–60 cm tall, with leaves 2–6 cm long (sometimes up to 12 cm, overlapping ongaonga's) and 4 stipules at each node. Both grow at forest margins. Young ongaonga can be confused with the other native nettles, so size is not reliable on a young plant. Its sting has killed: in 1961 a young man died of paralysis and breathing problems several hours after walking through tree nettles. If it is woody, walk away.
lookalikes.name: Ongaonga

lookalikes.howToTell: Stinging nettle grows to 1.5 m with leaves 5–25 cm long, and its male and female flowers are usually on separate plants; bush nettle is 15–60 cm with light green, triangular leaves 2–6 cm long (sometimes up to 12 cm), and carries both sexes on one plant, male clusters below female. Stinging nettle grows in waste places, cultivated land and grassland; bush nettle in forest, forest margins and shaded places.
lookalikes.name: Stinging nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf nettle is an annual with a short taproot and ovate to elliptic leaves 2–8 cm long, and its flower clusters usually carry male and female flowers together; bush nettle is a perennial that spreads by rhizomes, with triangular leaves, the lowest flower clusters all male and the upper ones all female. Dwarf nettle grows in gardens, farms and waste ground; bush nettle in forest, forest margins and shaded places.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf stinging nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Southern nettle is a stout, bushy native up to about 1 m whose branches lie down and root before turning upright, with broadly ovate, dark green leaves 10–20 cm long, the leaf stalk often carrying a pair of small leaflets near its base; its stinging hairs are mainly on the leaf edges and the veins underneath, and are often few or none. Bush nettle is a soft herb 15–60 cm tall that spreads by rhizomes, with light green, triangular leaves 2–6 cm long (sometimes up to 12 cm). Both grow on Stewart Island. No record of southern nettle being eaten has been found, and it is At Risk – Declining.
lookalikes.name: Southern nettle

recipes.method: Written for common stinging nettle (Urtica dioica and similar nettles) in North America, not for this species. Serves 6. About 225 g nettles; 1 cup diced celery; 2 cups diced leeks; 2 diced shallots; 1 small diced onion; 3 tbsp butter; about 1 litre chicken stock; 2 cups diced potato; 120 ml cream; salt and white pepper; crème fraîche; chopped dill or mint. Blanch about 225 g nettles in salted boiling water until just wilted, about 30 seconds, cool them in cold water, squeeze dry and finely chop a handful to finish the soup. Sweat 1 cup diced celery, 2 cups diced leeks, 2 diced shallots and 1 small diced onion in 3 tbsp butter over medium heat for 5 minutes. Add about 1 litre chicken stock and 2 cups diced potato and simmer until tender, about 15 minutes. Add the blanched nettles and blend, then stir in the chopped nettles and 120 ml cream and season with salt and white pepper. Serve with crème fraîche and chopped dill or mint.
recipes.title: Classic stinging nettle soup

recipes.method: Written for common stinging nettle (Urtica dioica and similar nettles) in North America, not for this species. Serves 2. About 225 g young nettle tops; 3 large crushed garlic cloves; 3 tbsp olive oil, plus more to serve; salt and pepper; a pinch of chilli flakes; ½ cup ricotta; lemon wedges. Wash about 225 g young nettle tops and steam them, covered, over boiling water for 2–3 minutes until tender. Meanwhile warm 3 large crushed garlic cloves in 3 tbsp olive oil over medium heat for at least 10 minutes until browned, then discard the garlic. Add the steamed nettles to the oil, season with salt, pepper and a pinch of chilli flakes, gently fold in ½ cup ricotta and warm through. Serve warm or at room temperature with olive oil and lemon wedges.
recipes.title: Steamed nettles with ricotta

recipes.method: Written for stinging nettle in Britain; the recipe does not name the species. Serves 6. 25 g butter; 150 g nettle leaves, washed; 200 g feta, crumbled; 50 g parmesan, grated; the zest and juice of a lemon; 1 egg, beaten; grated nutmeg; seasoning; 7 filo sheets; 75 g melted butter; 1 tbsp sesame seeds. Brown 25 g butter in a large frying pan, add 150 g washed, still-damp nettle leaves and cook for about 6 minutes until wilted; cool, squeeze out the liquid and chop roughly. Mix with 200 g crumbled feta, 50 g grated parmesan, the zest and juice of a lemon, two-thirds of a beaten egg, grated nutmeg and seasoning. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan). Lay 3 filo sheets end to end, overlapping by about 5 cm, brush with some of 75 g melted butter, add 3 more sheets and more butter, then a seventh sheet in the middle. Spoon the filling in a line about 2 cm wide along one long edge, tuck in the ends, roll into a long sausage and coil it into a spiral about 20 cm across in a shallow round pan or on a buttered baking tray. Brush with the rest of the egg, scatter with 1 tbsp sesame seeds and bake for 40–45 minutes until golden.
recipes.title: Nettle spanakopita

recipes.method: Written for stinging nettle in Britain; the recipe does not name the species. Serves 4. 200 g nettle leaves; 1 tbsp olive oil; a 200 ml tub of crème fraîche; 1 tsp wholegrain mustard; 140 g blue cheese, crumbled; seasoning; 4 slices of sourdough. Wilt 200 g nettle leaves in 1 tbsp hot olive oil for 1 minute, cool briefly and chop roughly. Mix with a 200 ml tub of crème fraîche, 1 tsp wholegrain mustard, half of 140 g crumbled blue cheese, and seasoning. Toast 4 slices of sourdough on both sides under the grill, spread with the nettle mix, top with the rest of the cheese and grill until golden and bubbling.
recipes.title: Nettle and blue cheese rarebit

Name: 'native nettle, bush nettle' from NZPCN 'Urtica sykesii' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/urtica-sykesii/, P.J. de Lange 2016, retrieved 24/10/2026) and Wikipedia. Origin 'native': NZPCN Biostatus 'Native', 'Indigenous. Australia and New Zealand'. Status: NZTCS 2023 'Not Threatened', qualifier SO (de Lange et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0, via NZPCN); regionally, Northland 2026 'Regionally At Risk – Regionally Naturally Uncommon' (NZPCN, seen 24/10/2026), Auckland 2025 'Regionally Threatened – Regionally Endangered', Otago and Wellington 2025 'Regionally Not Threatened'. harvestEthics is the standard Not Threatened sentence.

Name history, which the edibility rests on: NZPCN 'Taxonomic notes' — 'Urtica sykesii is the species previously treated (incorrectly it transpires see Grosse-Veldmann et al. 2016) by New Zealand botanists as Urtica incisa Poir., an Australian species that is sparingly naturalised in New Zealand'; Grosse-Veldmann, Conn & Weigend 2016, Phytotaxa 245(4): 251–261 (not read). So older New Zealand records of 'Urtica incisa' — Flora of New Zealand vols I and IV, Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga, Crowe 1990 — are of this plant.

'Wear gloves' and 'cooking destroys the sting' are UTP's general nettle lines on the same page.
maoriName left empty on purpose: Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga gives 'ongaonga' for 'Urtica incisa', but on this app ongaonga names the tree nettle, which can kill.

Identification: NZPCN 'Urtica sykesii' description and 'Similar taxa' (description based on Grosse-Veldmann et al. 2016; all rights reserved, restated): 'Erect, perennial, rhizomatous herb 0.15–0.60 m with elongating rhizomes, aerial stems usually unbranched', 'Leaf lamina 20–60 × 20–50 mm triangular to triangular-ovate', 'leaf base truncate to subcordate; margins regularly dentate with 9–10(–12) teeth on each side', 'lamina light greenish', 'petioles 30–70 mm long', 'Plants monoecious; lowest inflorescences pure male, upper ones pure female', 'The impact of the stinging hairs seems to vary from plant to plant and in the way people react to them. Generally this species has a less painful sting than our other indigenous Urtica'. Wikipedia's 'stinging hairs … 0.2–0.3 mm long' is not used: NZPCN gives that length for the simple hairs, and stinging hairs with setae 1.3–2.2 mm.

summary.text:
Urtica sykesii, commonly known as native nettle and bush nettle, is a species of nettle native to Australia and New Zealand. In Australia, the species is restricted to Victoria. In New Zealand, it is found in the North and South Islands.
Until 2016 New Zealand botanists called it Urtica incisa, an Australian nettle now known to be only sparingly naturalised here. It is widespread, though scarce north of Auckland.

warnings: Young ongaonga can be confused with the herbaceous native nettles. Never pick from a plant with a woody stem.
Use only young leaves. Older leaves develop gritty crystals (cystoliths) that are widely held to irritate the kidneys.

edibleParts.text:
The stems and fleshy rhizomes of C. australis are high in natural sugars and were steam-cooked in earth ovens (umu tī, a large type of hāngī) to produce kāuru, a carbohydrate-rich food used to sweeten other foods. The growing tips or leaf hearts were stripped of leaves and eaten raw or cooked as a vegetable, when they were called kōuka—the origin of the Māori name of the tree.
Edible shoots - a cabbage substitute. The leaves are very fibrous even when young.

habitat.text:
Forest margins, open places, abundant near swamps.
Generally a lowland species, it grows from sea level to about 1,000 metres, reaching its upper limits on the volcanoes of the central North Island, where eruptions have created open spaces for it to exploit, and in the foothills of the Southern Alps in the South Island, where deforestation may have played a part in giving it room to grow.
Cordyline australis is a light-demanding pioneer species, and seedlings die when overtopped by other trees. To grow well, young plants require open space so they are not shaded out by other vegetation. Another requirement is water during the seedling stage. Although adult trees can store water and are drought resistant, seedlings need a good supply of water to survive. This stops the species from growing in sand dunes unless there are wet depressions present, and from hillsides unless there is a seepage area. The fertility of the soil is another factor—settlers in Canterbury used the presence of the species to situate their homesteads and gardens. Another factor is temperature, especially the degree of frost. Young trees are killed by frost, and even old trees can be cut back. This is why C. australis is absent from upland areas and from very frosty inland areas.
Today it is common across farmland, open places, wetlands and scrub in both main islands, but rare on Stewart Island; it likes full sun, so it is scarce inside unbroken forest though common on its edges (DOC, restated). It grows from the coast to montane forest, most of all on alluvial river terraces, and seedlings often come up unbidden in gardens from bird-dropped seed (NZPCN, restated).

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Cabbage trees should not be cut for exploitation.

identification.text:
Plant to 12–(20) m high; young unbranched stems 5–10 cm diameter; older trees with massive trunk to 1.5m diameter, much-branched above. Leaves 30–100 × 3–6 cm, only slightly narrowed above base; midrib indistinct, nerves fine. Panicle lax, 60–150 cm long. Flowers fragrant, white; segments 5–6 mm long. Berry whitish.
[From: Healy and Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Forest cabbage tree grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Cabbage tree (Cordyline australis) grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Cabbage tree grows to the size of a small tree with a thick trunk and many branches, and its leaf stalk is flat and ill-defined, at least three-quarters as wide as the widest part of the blade; forest cabbage tree rarely approaches tree form and, if tall, usually has several more or less equal main stems, and its leaf stalk is narrow, long (up to a quarter of the blade's length) and deeply channelled, widening rather abruptly into a much wider blade that droops at the tip, with a prominent midrib and several stronger side nerves. Both have white, scented flowers, so flower colour does not separate them. Where the two overlap at about 300–1,000 ft (90–300 m) on the northern tip of the Tararua Range, about half the plants cannot be put strictly in either species.
lookalikes.name: Forest cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf cabbage tree is rarely more than 2 m tall and often flowers while its short stem is still leafy to the ground; its leaves are 30–60–(100) × 1–2 cm, more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base; its panicle is very open, up to about 60 cm long, with slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers that are whitish or pink outside, and its berries are bluish or flecked with blue, 4–5 mm across. Cabbage tree (Cordyline australis) grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Dwarf cabbage tree is usually no more than 1–(2) m tall with a main stem 1–2 cm across and leaves rarely over 2 cm wide, its flower cluster large for the plant but with very slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers; cabbage tree's main stem soon exceeds 2 cm across even on a young plant, and its leaves are mostly over 2 cm wide. Hybrids between the two have been described from the far north (C. × matthewsii, Carse 1926), some almost enlarged copies of dwarf cabbage tree, so an in-between plant there may be neither.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain cabbage tree grows to about 8 m with massive, rather sparingly branched stems; its leaves are up to 1–2 m × 10–15 cm, broadly sword-shaped, drooping only with age, glaucous underneath, narrowed above the base to a short stalk, with a broad, conspicuous midrib that is often reddish, the stronger nerves often reddish too; its panicle is tightly compact, 60–160 cm long, its crowded, rather fleshy flowers on longer stalks than in the other species, and its berries are bluish, about 6 mm across. Cabbage tree (Cordyline australis) grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Mountain cabbage tree stands apart from all the others on its leaves: up to 10–15 cm wide, glaucous underneath, with a strong, often reddish midrib and main nerves, and a tightly compact flower cluster. The other species' leaves are rarely over 10 cm wide, often much less, not or scarcely glaucous underneath, and their flower clusters are lax and open. Garden plants sold as 'Cordyline indivisa' or 'Dracaena indivisa' are often young cabbage trees, so a nursery label does not settle it.

preparation.text:
If the spike of unopened leaves and a few outer leaves is gripped firmly at the base and bent, it will snap off. The leaves can be removed, and what remains is like a small artichoke heart that can be steamed, roasted or boiled to make kōuka, a bitter vegetable available at any time of the year. Kōuka is delicious as a relish with fatty foods like eel, muttonbirds, or pigeons, or in modern times, pork, mutton and beef. Different trees were selected for their degree of bitterness, which should be strong for medicinal use, but less so when used as a vegetable.
Peel back the tough outer leaves of a leaf head until the paler shoot and heart show, stripping too few rather than too many at first. Boil or bake the heart for 6 minutes or less, depending on its size, and then treat it like an artichoke heart, for example adding it to a tray of baked vegetables for about the last 10 minutes.
After drying, the harvested stems or rhizomes were steamed for 24 hours or more in the umu tī pit. Steaming converted the carbohydrate fructan in the stems to very sweet fructose. Kāuru could also be dipped in water and chewed and was said to smell and taste like molasses.
Proper kāuru was the side-shoot; "when it was taken the tree did not die, as it did if its root (more-tī) was taken."

summary.text:
Cordyline australis, commonly known as the cabbage tree, or by its Māori name of tī or tī kōuka, is a widely branched monocot tree endemic to New Zealand.
Cordyline australis occurs from North Cape to the very south of the South Island, where it becomes less and less common, until it reaches its southernmost natural limits at Sandy Point (46° 30' S), west of Invercargill near Oreti Beach. It is absent from much of Fiordland, probably because there is no suitable habitat, and is unknown on the subantarctic islands to the south of New Zealand, probably because it is too cold. It occurs on some offshore islands—Poor Knights, Stewart and the Chathams—but was probably introduced by Māori. In the Stewart Island region, it is rare, growing only on certain islands, headlands and former settlement sites where it may have been introduced by muttonbird collectors, while on the Chatham Islands it is also largely "a notable absentee".
Early European explorers of New Zealand described "jungles of cabbage trees" along the banks of streams and rivers, in huge swamps and lowland valleys. Few examples of this former abundance survive today—such areas were the first to be cleared by farmers looking for flat land and fertile soil. In modern New Zealand, cabbage trees usually grow as isolated individuals rather than as parts of a healthy ecosystem.
The cabbage tree's year begins in autumn among the tight spike of unopened leaves projecting from the centre of each tuft of leaves. Some of the growing tips have changed from making leaves to producing inflorescences for the coming spring, and around these, two or three buds begin to produce leaves. The inflorescence and the leaf buds pass the winter protected by the enveloping spike of unopened leaves. Months later in spring or early summer, it bears its flowers on the outside of the tree, exposed to insects and birds.
Flowering takes place over a period of four to six weeks, giving maximum exposure to pollinating insects. The flowers produce a sweet perfume which attracts large numbers of insects. The nectar produced by the flowers contains aromatic compounds, mainly esters and terpenes, which are particularly attractive to moths. Bees use the nectar to produce a light honey to feed their young and increase the size of the hive in the early summer. It takes about two months for the fruit to ripen, and by the end of summer a cabbage tree can have thousands of small fruits available for birds to eat and disperse. The strong framework of the inflorescence can easily bear the weight of heavy birds like the New Zealand pigeon, which was formerly the major disperser of the seeds.
The berries of C. australis are enjoyed by bellbirds, tūī, and kererū. Māori sometimes planted groves of cabbage trees (pā tī) to attract kererū which could be snared when they came to eat the berries. Reminiscing in 1903 about life in New Zealand sixty or more years earlier, George Clarke describes how such a tapu grove of cabbage trees would attract huge numbers of pigeons: "About four miles from our house, there was a great preserve of wood pigeons, that was made as tapu as the native chiefs could devise. At a certain season, the pigeons came in vast flocks to feed on the white berries of the Ti tree (bracœna) [sic] and got so heavy with fat that they could hardly fly from one tree to another. No gun was allowed in the place. The Māoris, with a long slender rod and a slip noose at the end, squatted under the leaves and noiselessly slipped the noose over the necks of the stupid pigeons as they were feeding." As the native birds have vanished from much of New Zealand with the clearing of forests, it is now flocks of starlings which descend upon the fruit.
In the central North Island, it has evolved a much sturdier form (with the Māori name tī manu, meaning "with branches bearing broad, straight upright leaves"). This form resembles that found in the far south of the South Island, suggesting that they are both adapted to cold conditions. The fallen leaves of the tree also help to raise the fertility of the soil when they break down.
A quote from Philip Simpson sums up the wide range of habitats the cabbage tree occupied in early New Zealand, and how much its abundance and distinctive form shaped the impression travellers received of the country:
"In primeval New Zealand cabbage trees occupied a range of habitats, anywhere open, moist, fertile and warm enough for them to establish and mature: with forest; around the rocky coast; in lowland swamps, around the lakes and along the lower rivers; and perched on isolated rocks. Approaching the land from the sea would have reminded a Polynesian traveller of home, and for a European traveller, conjured up images of the tropical Pacific".

edibleParts.text: Flowers — mainly the petals (ray florets) — and the young leaves. Fresh petals are chopped into salads or used as a garnish. Dried petals have a more concentrated flavour and season soups, stews and cakes, and they colour rice and soups in place of saffron; in Mallorca the dried petals are used for their colour, not their flavour. A tea is made from the petals and flowers; tea made from the petals alone is less bitter. The tender leaves are eaten raw in salads: they taste first sticky-sweet, then strongly salty and penetrating, and they are generally not considered palatable. There is no record of the seed being eaten.

identification.text:
Erect or ascending, annual or short-lived perennial herb, sometimes somewhat woody toward base, (10)–15–50 cm tall. Stems densely clothed in short, erect, glandular hairs, usually becoming glabrous below, much-branched. Basal and lower cauline leaves sparsely to moderately clothed in simple and glandular hairs, ciliate, usually narrow-obovate, sometimes elliptic or more or less orbicular, entire, with few minute scattered marginal teeth, or rarely remotely dentate, obtuse to acute and mucronate, apetiolate and long-cuneate, 6–20 × 1.5–5 cm; upper cauline leaves similar to lower but becoming smaller, oblong to lanceolate, broad-based and often more or less amplexicaul. Capitula solitary, 35–85 mm diameter. Involucral bracts in 2 rows, glandular and ciliate, lanceolate, acuminate, 10–15 mm long, the inner with more conspicuous membranous margins. Ray florets (20)–40–60, in 1-several rows; ligules usually orange, sometimes pale orange or yellow, clearly exceeding bracts, (8)–12–30 mm long; disc florets numerous, usually orange, sometimes pale orange or yellow, rarely brownish black. Achenes glabrous or sparsely hairy, usually of 3 types; outermost achenes strongly incurved, long-beaked, 12–18 mm diameter, with small stout spines on back, usually alternating with shorter, short-beaked, broadly 3-winged, tuberculate or smooth-backed achenes; inner achenes enclosed by outer, tuberculate on back, 4–7 mm diameter 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The striking heteromorphic achenes distinguish Calendula species from all other Asteraceae in New Zealand.
Field marigold (Calendula arvensis), known in New Zealand only from around Napier, is generally smaller in all its parts: heads 10–15 mm across, with about 11–22 ligules about equal to or not much longer than the bracts; involucral bracts 6–9 mm long; outer wingless achenes short-beaked, 7–10 mm long (Flora of New Zealand, restated).

preparation.text: Pick flowers after the dew has dried, and only from plants that have not been sprayed with pesticides or other chemicals. Pull the petals from the heads, rinse and dry them. Use fresh petals raw in salads, egg salad and spring rolls or as a garnish, or toss them through rice when it has finished cooking and let them steam for a few minutes. To dry petals for seasoning and tea, pick fully open flowers and dry them quickly in the shade; store dried petals in a glass jar. Young leaves: raw in salads.

recipes.method: 3 tablespoons olive oil; 2½ cups (about 625 ml) hot chicken stock; 1 small onion, minced; salt to taste; ½ cup (125 ml) white rice; ½ cup (125 ml) calendula petals; ½ cup (125 ml) orzo. Heat the oil in a heavy saucepan and stir in the onion, rice and orzo, stirring constantly so the rice and orzo toast and the onion cooks lightly. When the rice turns opaque, add the stock and salt and stir well. Cover and turn the heat to low. After 15 minutes check whether the rice is tender but not mushy; if not, cook 5 minutes more and check again. When it is tender, add the calendula petals and toss gently, then cover and leave off the heat for about 5 minutes to steam before serving.
recipes.title: Calendula pilaf

recipes.method: By Susan Belsinger, from The Herb Society of America's calendula guide. Serves 6. 12 hard-boiled eggs; ½ cup (125 ml) mayonnaise; 2 teaspoons Dijon-style mustard; 2 tablespoons each chopped sweet pickles and pickle juice; ¼ cup (about 60 ml) thinly sliced spring onions or minced onion; ⅓ cup (about 80 ml) finely diced celery; 2 tablespoons snipped chives; 2 tablespoons snipped dill; ½ teaspoon Hungarian paprika; salt and freshly ground pepper; a handful of fresh calendula petals, coarsely chopped, plus more petals to garnish. Dice the eggs into a bowl. Add the mayonnaise, mustard, pickle juice, onions, celery, 1 tablespoon of the chives, the paprika, and salt and pepper, and toss well. Stir in the chopped calendula petals. Refrigerate for half an hour, then let it stand at room temperature for 5–10 minutes. Garnish with calendula petals and the remaining chives and dill and serve at once. The method mentions only the pickle juice, not the chopped pickles.
recipes.title: Egg salad with calendula and chives

recipes.method: Written for purslane, with chickweed, parsley and calendula petals; the author gives no amounts. Tear leafy salad greens — lettuce, mizuna, rocket, chickweed, parsley — into a bowl and add chopped purslane, cherry tomatoes and alfalfa sprouts. Decorate it with heartsease pansy flowers and calendula petals, and dress it with lemon juice, olive oil and salt.
recipes.title: Purslane salad

summary.text:
Calendula officinalis, Mary's gold, common marigold, the pot marigold, Scotch marigold, or ruddles, is a flowering plant in the daisy family, Asteraceae.
It is probably native to southern Europe, though its long history of cultivation makes its precise origin unknown. It is also widely naturalised further north in Europe (as far north as southern England) and elsewhere in warm temperate regions of the world.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Auckland City, vicinity of Hamilton, Hawke's Bay, Wellington Province; South Island: Nelson City, Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago, Southland, near settlements. Origin unknown; naturalised in New Zealand by 1883.
Marigold, or pot marigold as it is also called, is widely cultivated; ligules of cultivars vary from pale yellow to deep orange with the disc wholly or partly coloured yellow, orange, brownish black or green. Wild plants occur as casuals or are locally well-established, and include a range of disc and ray colours although most have wholly orange or yellow capitula.

warnings: Avoid calendula if you are allergic to plants of the daisy family (Asteraceae), including ragweed: allergic reactions and skin sensitisation are reported.
Avoid calendula when pregnant or breastfeeding: its safety in pregnancy and lactation has not been established.

identification.text:
Annual or perennial herb. Habit various, from a tufted rosette to an erect many-stemmed herb with the rosette stage almost completely suppressed. Stems ribbed, erect, glabrous, 10–30–(40) cm tall. Leaves much dissected; petiole longer than lamina; lamina to 10 × 10 cm in rosette leaves, usually much smaller in stem leaves. Pedicels ribbed, 5–10 cm long. Calyx hood apiculate. Petals obovate, yellow to orange, or yellow with orange base, rarely white, cream or red, (1)–2–3.5 cm long. Anthers longer than filaments. Capsule ribbed, straight or slightly curved, 25–90 × 3–4 mm. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

preparation.text: Pick young leaves before they become tough or too bitter, from clean, unsprayed plants. Boil them as greens, discarding the cooking water, or roast them, then lay them in water before eating. The leaves are bitter, with a latex-like flavour that can persist after boiling. Use the petals raw as a garnish, a few at a time. Eat it as an occasional small green, never as a meal-sized portion or a staple.

summary.text:
California poppy (Eschscholzia californica) is an annual or perennial herb of the poppy family (Papaveraceae), native to the western United States and naturalised in New Zealand since 1878.
It grows throughout the North and South Islands and is commonest in Hawke's Bay, Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury and Otago; in the eastern South Island it covers large areas of some riverbeds and shingly hillsides, making brilliant displays when it flowers. It is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds in New Zealand, though no regional pest management plan lists it. It contains several alkaloids and is used as a calming, sleep-aiding herbal medicine.

warnings: California poppy contains several alkaloids, prominent in the leaves, and is a calming, sedative herbal medicine: eat only small amounts, and not regularly.
Do not eat it if you are pregnant or breastfeeding: its safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established.
Do not give it to children, and avoid it if you take sedatives or other medicines that act on the nervous system.
As a herbal medicine it may impair your ability to drive or use machines.

habitat.text: It grows in forests, forest edges, and riparian areas. It grows at high elevations of 500–3,000 m in its native region, but may also be found at sea level in Oceania and Pacific islands where it occurs widely in subtropical and warm, temperate conditions. Its latitude range is about 45°S to 60°N, and its altitude range is generally from sea level to 3,000 m.

identification.text:
Annual or short-lived, sprawling or spreading perennial, (15)–20–150–(200) cm tall, densely hairy. Leaves petiolate. Lamina 5–16–(20) × 3–10–(17) cm, usually broadly ovate, entire or slightly sinuate-dentate; base subcordate or cordate; apex acuminate. Flowers solitary. Calyx densely hairy outside; teeth 3–5 mm long, narrow-triangular, acuminate. Corolla 15–22 mm diameter, pale yellow with purplish patch towards base; teeth very shallow, more or less acute. Anthers 3–3.5 mm long, violet. Fruiting calyx 3–5 cm long, 10-ribbed, hairy. Berry 10–20 mm diameter, orange; flesh sweet. Seed 1.5–2 mm diameter, broadly oblong-ellipsoid. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Physalis peruviana is a South American species of plant in the nightshade family (Solanaceae).
The species is reportedly native to Chile and Peru. Its center of genetic diversity is in the Andes Mountains of Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, and Peru.
The plant has become invasive in some natural habitats, forming thickets, particularly in Hawaii and on other Pacific islands.
There are believed to be dozens of ecotypes worldwide that differentiated by plant size, calyx shape, and the size, color, and flavor of the fruit. Wild forms are thought to be diploid with 2n = 24 chromosomes, while cultivated forms include varieties with increased ploidy and 32 or 48 chromosomes.

identification.text:
A flat rosette like dandelion, but the leaves are rough with stiff hairs, where dandelion's are hairless and jaggedly toothed. Flower stalks are solid, wiry and branch into several yellow flowers; dandelion's are hollow, unbranched and carry one flower each.
Perennial. Stems ascending to erect, usually branched, glabrous or with a few sparse hairs below, 4–60–(150) cm tall. Leaves all basal, oblanceolate to linear-oblanceolate, usually shallowly to deeply pinnatifid, rarely simple and toothed, (2)–4–20–(40) × (0.5)–0.8–4–(9) cm, with moderately dense pale strigose hairs. Stem bracts few, minute. Capitula turbinate to campanulate. Involucral bracts linear-lanceolate with narrowly acute apex, 6–15 mm long at flowering, up to 20 mm long at fruiting, glabrous except for a row of strigose hairs on midrib (the distal hairs dark), herbaceous or with narrow scarious border. Florets yellow, about 1½× length of involucre. Achenes dark brown, scabrid, fusiform, beaked, 8–16 mm long, sometimes the outer achenes not or shortly beaked and then shorter. Pappus in 2 rows, the outer hairs short, slender, scabrid to plumose, the inner up to 12 mm long, plumose.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Beaked hawksbeard's flowering stems are ribbed to grooved and carry leaves of their own; catsear's leaves are all in the basal rosette and its stems carry only a few tiny bracts. Beaked hawksbeard's stems are hairy, with fine crinkly white hairs and stout, spreading, red-based ones; catsear's are hairless or have a few sparse hairs low down. Under the flower head, beaked hawksbeard's bracts have pale cobwebby hairs and often dark glandular hairs; catsear's are hairless except for a row of stiff hairs along the midrib. Beaked hawksbeard's seed parachute is of fine white bristles; catsear's is feathery. Leaf shape does not separate them: beaked hawksbeard's leaves are usually deeply lobed with lobes pointing back, and catsear's are usually shallowly to deeply lobed. Hairy leaves, branched stems and height do not separate them either.
lookalikes.name: Beaked hawksbeard

lookalikes.howToTell: A dandelion's flower stem is hollow, leafless and unbranched, with a single head; catsear's stems are usually branched, solid, carry a few tiny bracts and can carry several heads. A dandelion's leaves are hairless or carry sparse short hairs, mostly on the midrib above; catsear's have moderately dense, stiff, pale hairs. Both have a rosette of lobed leaves, yellow heads and milky sap, so none of those separates them. The dandelion's leaves, flowers and roots are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Dandelion

lookalikes.howToTell: Out of flower the two are strikingly similar. Use a hand lens on the leaf hairs: hawkbit's fork into two, sometimes three, at the tip; catsear's are simple. In flower, hawkbit's stem is unbranched, with a single head and at most a few tiny bracts; catsear's stems are usually branched and can carry several heads, so an unbranched stem alone does not settle it. Pulling a head apart also works: catsear has thin scales among the florets on the flower base, hawkbit has none. Both have hairy rosette leaves that are often lobed, yellow heads and milky sap. Hawkbit's leaves are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Hawkbit

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the bracts under the flower head. Catsear's carry a row of stiff hairs along the midrib — dark near the tip, usually pale near the base — like a miniature cock's comb; smooth cat's ear's are always hairless, the inner ones with broad papery margins. Catsear's florets stand about one and a half times as long as the bracts, smooth cat's ear's about as long, and smooth cat's ear's heads are narrowly cylindrical where catsear's are top-shaped to bell-shaped. Catsear's leaves have moderately dense stiff pale hairs; smooth cat's ear's are hairless or sometimes sparsely hairy, so leaf hair is a clue, not a test. Catsear is a perennial; smooth cat's ear is an annual, rarely perennial. Stems do not separate them: catsear's are usually branched, smooth cat's ear's sparingly branched or not. Catsear's heads are larger, 2–4 cm across against 0.5–1.5 cm (measured on British plants). The seeds differ: catsear's are beaked and 8–16 mm long, though the outer ones are sometimes short- or unbeaked; smooth cat's ear's outer seeds are never beaked and 4–5 mm long, and only the inner ones carry a beak, up to 8 mm long. The two hybridise, so a plant with mixed features may be neither. Both have yellow heads and milky sap. Smooth cat's ear's young leaves are eaten, though somewhat bitter (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Smooth cat's ear

lookalikes.howToTell: The surest test is inside the head: catsear has thin, tapering scales among the florets on the flower base, nearly transparent apart from their yellow tips and easily missed; autumn hawkbit has none. Autumn hawkbit's leaves are hairless or have sparse simple hairs, nowhere near as many or as stiff as catsear's. Its branched stems carry many small narrow bracts, especially near the top, where catsear's carry only a few minute ones, and its head tapers gradually into the stem, where catsear's narrows more abruptly. Both usually have branched stems with several yellow heads, rosettes of lobed leaves, and milky sap. Autumn hawkbit's leaves are used like dandelion and catsear leaves (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Autumn hawkbit

lookalikes.howToTell: Mouse-ear hawkweed's leaves are untoothed or very obscurely toothed, with a very dense coat of star-shaped hairs that makes the underside white, and the plant spreads by creeping runners; catsear's leaves are usually lobed, rarely just toothed, with moderately dense pale bristly hairs. Mouse-ear hawkweed has a single head on each stem; catsear's stems are usually branched. Catsear has thin scales among the florets on the flower base, mouse-ear hawkweed none. Catsear's achenes are 8–16 mm and mostly beaked with feathery inner pappus hairs; mouse-ear hawkweed's are about 2 mm, unbeaked, with simple bristles. Both form hairy rosettes with yellow heads and milky sap, and stem heights and leaf lengths overlap. No food use of mouse-ear hawkweed is recorded; its traditional uses are medicinal (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mouse-ear hawkweed

preparation.text:
Leaves are bitter and hairy raw — better wilted or in soup. Buds can be pickled. Treat it as a coarser dandelion.
In Spain the rosette leaves were eaten cooked: at El Atazar and Cervera (Madrid) they were stripped down to the midrib, which was boiled, then fried and eaten in scrambled eggs or stews. In the Serranía de Cuenca the plant was eaten in salads, and at Reinosa (Cantabria) the young leaves were eaten during the war.
Young leaves are slightly bitter to bland; older ones are stringy. Eat them raw in salads, steamed, or tossed in a pan with oil and garlic and finished with lemon and salt. Some Greek households use it as the green in hortopita. The flowers can be infused in honey or coated in flour for fritters, and the petals make a garnish.
Cooking reduces the bitterness but never removes it.

recipes.method: Dig up the roots, scrub them, roast them lightly in the oven, then grind them and brew to taste. No temperature, time or quantity is given; the dandelion root coffee on the dandelion page has them, for dandelion root.
recipes.title: Catsear root coffee

recipes.method: Flowering catsear stems with their buds and flowers; extra virgin olive oil; garlic salt, or whatever seasoning you like; petals from a fresh flower. Pick flowering stems with their buds and flowers; a good patch gives enough for dinner in a couple of minutes. Wash them and put them in a pot with a shallow layer of water, cover, and steam over medium heat until soft. Then fry them in extra virgin olive oil with garlic salt, or whatever seasoning you like, over medium-high heat until lightly golden. Scatter with petals from a fresh flower to serve.
recipes.title: Steamed and fried catsear buds

summary.text:
Flatweed. The dandelion lookalike with hairy leaves and branched, wiry flower stalks. It is edible too.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): throughout the North and South Islands; Stewart Island; Kermadec, Chatham and Campbell Islands. Naturalised from Europe and North Africa, first recorded in 1867.
Often more common than dandelion.

warnings: Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed. Pick from ground you know.

edibleParts.text: The leaf stalks, raw or cooked. The leaves, raw in salads or as a garnish, or as a flavouring in soups and stews, fresh or dried; they have a mild, peppery taste. The seeds (strictly tiny fruits), whole or ground, as a spice. Wild celery is more bitter than the garden vegetable, whose sap was bred over centuries to be less bitter and sweeter.

identification.text:
Erect terrestrial biennial, not rooting at nodes. Stems hollow, grooved, striate, up to 80–(100) cm high. Basal leaves 1–2-pinnate, with a leaf stalk; ultimate segments deltate or rhombic, lobed and crenate or dentate near apex, 2–4 cm long, more or less without a stalk; stem leaves similar to basal but often without a leaf stalk and becoming 1-pinnate or 3-foliolate with elliptic-obovate, entire or lobed segments. Umbels 2–5 cm in diameter, compound, more or less without a stalk and leaf-opposed, and so appearing bracteate; rays 4–15; bracts and bracteoles 0. Flowers numerous, greenish white, about 1 mm in diameter. Fruit broadly ovoid, dark brown, 1.5–2 mm long; ribs light brown, thread-thin.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
All parts of the plant smell strongly of celery. Descriptions differ on the stems: Flora of New Zealand gives them as hollow, British floras as solid, so do not lean on that.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand; all parts are poisonous if eaten. Look under the umbels: hemlock has about 4–8 narrow, pointed, down-turned bracts beneath each umbel and 3–6 bracteoles on the outer side of each small umbel; celery has none, though its umbels sit almost without a stalk opposite a leaf and so can look as if they had a bract. Hemlock grows up to 2–(3) m, its hollow stems usually purple spotted or blotched; celery reaches 80–(100) cm. Hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided into segments 5–40 mm long, celery's 1–2 times divided into lobed segments 2–4 cm long. Hemlock's flowers are white, about 2 mm across, and its fruit 2.5–3 mm long; celery's flowers are greenish white, about 1 mm across, and its fruit 1.5–2 mm long. Hemlock smells foetid when crushed and celery smells strongly of celery, but no source here treats smell as a reliable test on its own. Both grow in damp waste places, so place does not rule hemlock out.
lookalikes.name: Hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: Look under the small umbels: water celery always has 4–8 small bracteoles there, and celery has none. Water celery lies along the ground or rises from it and roots at its lower nodes; celery stands erect and does not root at the nodes. Water celery's leaves are once-pinnate, with 2–8 pairs of toothed leaflets 1–8 cm long (up to 12); celery's are 1–2-pinnate, with lobed segments 2–4 cm long. Both grow in wet ground, so place does not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Water celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Garden celery found wild can look very similar to sea celery, including on the Chatham Islands. Celery is an erect biennial up to 80–(100) cm tall; sea celery lies along the ground or rises from it. Celery has no bracts or bracteoles under its umbels, and sea celery usually has none (at most a single bract that soon falls), so that check does not separate them. The surest difference is the ripe fruit: celery's are dark brown with thread-thin ribs, sea celery's have broad, spongy ribs. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Sea celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Alexanders' flowers are yellowish; wild celery's are greenish white and about 1 mm across. Alexanders' umbels are 6–7 cm across, on rays 2–4 cm long; wild celery's are 2–5 cm across, almost stalkless and set opposite a leaf, with no bracts. Alexanders' leaves are divided in threes into flat, lobed, toothed leaflets, but wild celery's stem leaves can be in threes too, so leaf shape alone does not separate them. Alexanders' fruits are black and 6.5–8 mm long; wild celery's are dark brown and 1.5–2 mm. Both grow in waste places. Alexanders is eaten too (see its page).

preparation.text: Pull the tough strings off the stalks before cooking; a stalk separates readily into them. Chopped with onion and carrot, celery is the base of many soups and sauces. The stalks can be pickled: take off the leaves, boil the stalks in water, then add vinegar, salt and oil. Dry the leaves in a single layer in the oven at 180 °C for 5–7 minutes, or in a pan over medium-low heat, until crisp but not browned. Ground seeds mixed with salt, or crumbled dried leaves mixed with salt, make celery salt. It flowers from November to March, and the seeds follow the flowers.

recipes.method: Written for shop-bought celery. Makes about 240 ml, depending on the leaves. 1 bunch of celery, for its leaves; an equal volume of flaky sea salt. Pick the leaves off the stalks, outer and inner, leaving the stems behind. Rinse them in a sieve under cold water, shake off as much water as you can and pat them dry in a clean tea towel, so they toast rather than steam. Spread them in a single layer on a baking tray and bake at 180 °C for 5–7 minutes, or toast them in a large frying pan over medium-low heat, until dry and crisp but not browned. Let them cool completely, crumble them with your fingers, discarding any that aren't crisp, and mix with an equal amount of salt in a jar. The author prefers flaky salt, whose flakes match the crumbled leaves in size.
recipes.title: Homemade celery salt

recipes.method: Written for shop-bought celery. Serves 3–4. 30 ml (2 Tbsp) olive oil; 300 g celery, sliced, tough strings removed; 1 garlic clove, peeled; 200 g potatoes, peeled and cut into chunks; 500 ml vegetable stock; 100 ml milk; crusty bread, to serve. Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat, add the celery, garlic and potatoes and stir to coat. Add a splash of water and a big pinch of salt and cook for 15 minutes, stirring often and adding a little more water if the vegetables start to stick. Pour in the stock, bring to the boil, then simmer for 20 minutes until the potatoes fall apart and the celery is soft. Blend smooth with a stick blender, add the milk and blend again. Season and serve with crusty bread.
recipes.title: Celery soup

recipes.method: Written for shop-bought celery. Serves 6. 200 g bulgur wheat; 1 bunch celery, with its leaves; 1 apple; juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (4 Tbsp) olive oil; a handful of toasted hazelnuts, roughly chopped; 1 red chilli, deseeded and chopped; a large handful of pomegranate seeds; a small bunch each of parsley, mint and tarragon, chopped. Put the bulgur in a large bowl, just cover it with boiling water, cover the bowl and leave for 30 minutes to absorb the water. Meanwhile separate the celery stalks, set the leaves aside, slice the stalks very finely and roughly chop the leaves. Cut the apple into fine matchsticks and toss them in a little of the lemon juice. Whisk the rest of the lemon juice with the oil and some seasoning. Fluff the bulgur with a fork, then mix in the sliced celery and apple, then the nuts, chilli, pomegranate seeds and herbs. Pour over the dressing, toss gently and scatter with the celery leaves. It keeps in the fridge for a few days.
recipes.title: Celery and bulgur salad

recipes.method: Written for shop-bought celery; the recipe is by Ignacio Mattos. Serves 8 with grilled fish. 360 ml (1½ US cups) finely chopped parsley; 120 ml (½ US cup) finely chopped celery leaves; 1 garlic clove, finely grated; ½ lemon; ½ tsp mild red pepper flakes, such as Aleppo; 180 ml (¾ US cup) extra-virgin olive oil; salt and black pepper. Mix the parsley, celery leaves and garlic in a bowl. Finely zest the lemon into the bowl and squeeze in its juice. Add the pepper flakes, stir in the oil and season with salt and pepper. Leave for 10 minutes for the flavours to come together. The author serves it with whole turbot grilled in foil, and aioli.
recipes.title: Celery leaf salsa verde

recipes.method: Written for shop-bought celery; the recipe is by Najmieh Batmanglij, a vegetarian version of a stew traditionally made with lamb. Serves 6. 120 ml olive oil; 675 g cremini mushrooms, cleaned and thickly sliced; 8 celery stalks, washed and cut into sticks about 6 mm by 5 cm; 1 medium onion, thinly sliced; 2 garlic cloves, thinly sliced; 1 jalapeño, finely chopped, or ½ tsp red pepper flakes; 2 tsp sea salt; ½ tsp ground black pepper; 710 ml water; ½ tsp ground saffron dissolved in 30 ml water (optional); 45 ml (3 Tbsp) lime juice; 80 g chopped parsley; 40 g chopped mint, or 15 ml (1 Tbsp) dried mint; 45 ml (3 Tbsp) dried fenugreek leaves; Persian rice, to serve (optional). Heat the oil in a heavy pot over high heat and sauté the mushrooms for 5 minutes. Add the celery, onion, garlic and jalapeño and sauté 10 minutes more, then stir in the salt and pepper. Add the water, bring to the boil, then cover and simmer over medium heat for 40 minutes. Stir in the saffron, lime juice, parsley, mint and fenugreek, cover and simmer over medium-low heat for another 5 minutes, or until the celery is tender. Adjust the seasoning and keep warm until you serve it.
recipes.title: Persian celery stew with mushrooms (khoresh-e karafs)

recipes.method: Written for plantain and dandelion, with celery leaves and parsley (the page does not say which plantain). A small handful of celery leaves; 4 branches of parsley (go easy: it can take over); 4 leaves each of plantain, dandelion and kale. Blend the greens in 750 ml–1 litre (3–4 cups) water, then add 1 banana, 250 ml (1 cup) frozen blueberries, 1 kiwifruit and ½ avocado and blend again.

summary.text:
Apium graveolens, commonly known as celery, is an Old World species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae.
Wild celery is native to much of Eurasia, ranging from Ireland in the west, through Europe north to Scotland, Denmark and Poland, and east to the Caucasus and Central Asia, and as far as the western Himalayas, and also through Macaronesia and North Africa to West Asia and the Arabian Peninsula. It is widely naturalised outside this range, including in Scandinavia, North and South America, Africa, India, central, eastern and southern Asia, and New Zealand. The cultivar groups may also be naturalised.
In New Zealand it is an exotic from Eurasia, called wild celery, and not common. Flora of New Zealand (1988) records it in the North Island from the Three Kings Islands, Kaitaia and Kaitara in Northland, Rangitoto Island, Coromandel and the west coast of Wellington Province; in the South Island from the Marlborough Sounds and Christchurch; and on the Chatham Islands and Campbell Island. Its first New Zealand record, from 1832, was most probably native sea celery misidentified. The garden vegetable, grown for its leaf stalks, is a form of this species, and garden celery is reported growing wild.

warnings: Hemlock, one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand, also has white flowers in compound umbels and grows in the same damp waste places. Before you pick, check under the umbels and along the stems as described in Lookalikes.
Celery is a food allergen: in people allergic to it, it can cause a potentially fatal anaphylactic reaction, and it has caused skin rashes and cross-reactions with carrot and ragweed.

Celery sap on the skin followed by sunlight can cause phytophotodermatitis: 24–48 hours later the skin turns red and inflamed and often blisters, and dark marks can stay for several years. Vegetable pickers get it on their hands and fingers; gloves prevent it. Eating plants rich in the same chemicals can make the skin more sensitive to sunlight generally, and celery seeds have caused it.

habitat.text: It is found growing by Nothofagaceae (beech).

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to harvest this mushroom, you can look at it and photograph it without disturbing.

identification.text: Cap is 3–5.5 cm in diameter. Golden yellow, apricot or occasionally reddish orange, dry and finely felted. Stalk is 2–3.5 cm long and 5–8 mm in diameter. It has no gills, the under part has dull red pores and looks spongy.

lookalikes.howToTell: Do not decide on the tree. This endemic grows under native beech, but the introduced peppery bolete, usually found with fly agaric under pines and introduced broadleaved trees, also turns up in beech forest where fly agaric has become naturalised. Cap colour helps but the ranges meet at orange. This one's cap is golden yellow, apricot or occasionally reddish orange, dry and finely felted. The peppery bolete's is fawn to light brown, brownish orange or cinnamon brown, and slightly slimy when wet. Look at the stem. The peppery bolete's stem is golden yellow at the base, with yellow flesh. This one's stem matches the cap or is reddish, pale yellow at the very top, with pale reddish-brown flesh. A crumb of the peppery bolete, chewed and spat out, is acrid and peppery; this one's taste is not distinctive.
lookalikes.name: Peppery bolete

New Zealand Plant Conservation Network, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus' — biostatus native; recorded from Nelson and Southland; gregarious or caespitose under Nothofagus; fruiting March and May. No common name is given. All rights reserved, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/chalciporus-aurantiacus/

Virtual Mycota, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus' — the McNabb description, in copyright, so the prose cannot be rendered and only its data is taken here. Cap 3–5.5 cm; tubes to 3 mm; pores 0.5–1 mm; stipe 2–3.5 cm long by 5–8 mm; spores 7.2–9 × 4.2–5.2 µm per McNabb and 7–9 × 4.2–6 µm per Pegler & Young; basidia 32–45 × 8–10 µm; cystidia 42–60 × 5.5–10 µm. Cap golden yellow, apricot or reddish orange; hymenophore dull red; stipe concolorous with the cap or reddish, pallid yellow at the apex; context sordid pallid fawn to yellowish fawn. Gregarious or caespitose under Nothofagus. The accounts are McNabb 1968, New Zealand Journal of Botany 6(2): 137–176, and Pegler & Young 1981, Transactions of the British Mycological Society 76(1): 103–146. The page's E. Horak photograph is Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial 3.0 New Zealand — a licence this project accepts — so it is the first real candidate for the photo this entry is blocked on. Checked 07/10/2026. https://virtualmycota.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/vM_Species_Details.aspx?pk=27591

New Zealand Organisms Register, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus (McNabb) Pegler & T.W.K. Young' — endemic; basionym Xerocomus aurantiacus McNabb. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.nzor.org.nz/names/169c81df-1fb4-4b19-9e3e-35ac5693f7c6

Conservation, global. IUCN/Global Fungal Red List assessment by J.A. Cooper, 26/07/2019 — Data Deficient, because the population size is uncertain and a decline is possible. Known from 23 records at 13 localities, with only 5 confirmed sightings since 2013 against 52 for the invasive C. piperatus in the same period; an estimate of up to 15,000 mature individuals across roughly 1,000 unrecorded sites. Recorded from both the North and South Islands, in beech forest. Ecology: likely a parasite on indigenous ectomycorrhizal fungi rather than mycorrhizal with the beech itself, host unknown, which may be what restricts it — so habitat prose should not say it partners with Nothofagus, only that it grows under it. Threat: displacement by the introduced C. piperatus and its host Amanita muscaria, which now occupy all but one recorded location of this species. No open licence on the page, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://redlist.info/iucn/species_view/112183/

Biota of New Zealand, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus (McNabb) Pegler & T.W.K. Young 1981' — endemic and present. A third synonym beyond the basionym: Boletus aurantiacus (McNabb) G. Stev. 1982. Hosts given as Nothofagus menziesii and N. truncata. Recorded from Buller, Fiordland, Marlborough Sounds, Nelson, Taupo, Wairarapa and Wellington, with historical records from Southland — a much wider range than the Nelson and Southland the NZPCN page gives, so the habitat text should not be written to the narrower claim. Images are under varying copyright and no blanket licence is stated, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/1cb1d0b5-36b9-11d5-9548-00d0592d548c

Landcare Research Fungal Guide, genus Chalciporus — the genus is characterised by reddish pores and bright yellow mycelium at the stipe base, with a viscid cap and a cinnamon to flesh-brown spore print. Two species here: C. aurantiacus, endemic, under native Nothofagus, with a golden yellow, apricot or reddish brown cap and a dull red pore surface; and C. piperatus, exotic, under pines and introduced broadleaves, usually close to Amanita muscaria. That contrast — native beech versus pine, and cap and pore colour — is the axis a person can write the lookalike guidance on. No licence statement, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://fungalguide.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/FG_Genus.aspx?Group=Chalciporus&pk=24737

Queensland Mycological Society, 'Queensland Fungal Record: Chalciporus aff. aurantiacus', P. Leonard, last updated 09/10/2017 — NOT this species. It is an Australian collection growing with Eucalyptus, and the record's own notes say the Queensland material is distinct from the New Zealand fungus: smaller, with pinkish red pores and narrower spores. Its measurements must not be used to describe the endemic. Recorded here only so the next person knows the near-relative exists and why it was set aside. © Queensland Mycological Society. Checked 07/10/2026. https://qldfungi.org.au/wp-content/uploads/FoQs/C-Misc/Chalciporus-aff-aurantiacus.pdf

Wikipedia contributors, 'Chalciporus' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — genus of Boletaceae, suborder Boletineae, about 25 species, erected by Frédéric Bataille in 1908. Boletoid fruit bodies with pores in shades of red to pink, stipes lacking reticulation, yellow mycelium and smooth oval spores. C. aurantiacus appears in the species list but the article carries no description of it and does not mention New Zealand at all. The genus prose is openly licensed and could be quoted verbatim as genus context if that is wanted, but there is no species prose here to render. Retrieved 07/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalciporus
