Two of its claims are wrong or stale and are recorded here so they are not picked up again. It gives the basionym as Xerocomelus aurantiacus; Index Fungorum and NZOR both give Xerocomus aurantiacus McNabb, which is the one to use, with Boletus aurantiacus (McNabb) G. Stev. an illegitimate later name. And it reports an NZTCS status of Nationally Critical, which is the superseded Hitchmough 2002 listing — see the NZTCS 38 entry below. The four language Wikipedias linked (Cebuano, Swedish, Silesian, Waray-Waray) are bot-generated stubs; there is no English article for the species. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q10448162

Kaimai Bush, 'Chalciporus' — a small bolete, 30–60 mm across, dry, cap yellowish to apricot, pores dull red, yellow mycelium at the stipe base, under native beech. Gives the former name as Xerocomelus aurantiacus, agreeing with Wikidata against NZOR. Sets C. piperatus beside it as the introduced one under Pinus radiata, fawn to light brown, 40–70 mm, dull brown-red pores. No licence statement, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.kaimaibush.co.nz/Fungi/C/chalciporus.html

New Zealand Plant Conservation Network, factsheet PDF generated 05/06/2026 — the print version of the species page already cited above, with no facts beyond it. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/site/assets/files/0/20/990/chalciporus-aurantiacus.pdf

Conservation, national — THIS SETTLES IT. Cooper, Buchanan, Leonard, Allison-Cooper, Johnston, Padamsee, McKenzie & Michel, 'Conservation status of selected species of non-lichenised agarics, boletes and russuloid fungi in Aotearoa New Zealand, 2021', New Zealand Threat Classification Series 38, Department of Conservation, October 2022. ISSN 2324-1713, ISBN 978-1-99-116195-6. Licensed CC BY 4.0 — the only openly licensed source on this entry, so its text may be quoted verbatim with credit. Chalciporus aurantiacus is NOT THREATENED, listed with a status change of 'Better': it is one of nine taxa previously assessed as Threatened – Nationally Critical under Hitchmough 2002 whose status improved 'because of a better understanding of their potential distributions'. The Nationally Critical figure that Wikidata still carries is the 2002 listing and is twenty years out of date. Note the national and global assessments disagree in tone and that is not an error: Not Threatened here, Data Deficient globally in 2019. Retrieved 07/10/2026. https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/nztcs38entire.pdf

MOSTLY RESOLVED, and the resolution favours Cooper: whether this species has yellow mycelium at the stipe base. Cooper's IUCN assessment says C. aurantiacus 'has more persistent orange/red colours and lacks the yellow mycelium at the stipe base', making its absence the separator from C. piperatus. The Landcare Fungal Guide genus page says the genus is characterised by 'the base of the stipe with bright yellow mycelium', and Kaimai Bush gives this species yellow basal mycelium outright. The MycoKeys revision of the subfamily settles the genus-level half of it: across the Chalciporoideae species it describes, basal mycelium is white in five and yellowish in one, so yellow basal mycelium is NOT a genus character and the Fungal Guide's claim is a generalisation from New Zealand's two species. That leaves the specialist who assessed this species against an amateur site repeating a genus page. McNabb's description does not mention basal mycelium at all, so it cannot arbitrate. Cooper is the better authority, but the character has not been checked on a specimen, so the lookalike guidance is safer on cap colour and host tree — which every source agrees on. Checked 07/10/2026.

REJECTED, recorded so it is not used: The Hidden Forest, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus'. It calls the species 'Exotic (Introduced)' and 'Australasian' where NZOR, Biota NZ, the Fungal Guide and the IUCN assessment all have it endemic to New Zealand; gives a season of spring to summer against iNaturalist's January–May records; and gives a cap of 20–60 mm and a stipe of 30–70 mm against McNabb's 3–5.5 cm cap and 2–3.5 cm stipe. Its figures appear to describe something else. Nothing from it is used. It also repeats the yellow-basal-mycelium claim as a key Chalciporus trait, which the MycoKeys revision contradicts. No licence statement either. Checked 07/10/2026. http://hiddenforest.co.nz/fungi/family/boletaceae/bolet03.htm

Zhang, Li, Liang, Mu, Yu, Wu, Chen, Pu & Zeng (2025), 'The subfamily Chalciporoideae (Boletaceae, Boletales) in China', MycoKeys 124: 123–157, DOI 10.3897/mycokeys.124.165901, CC BY 4.0 — openly licensed and quotable, but it does not mention C. aurantiacus anywhere, so there is no description here to use. Two things it does give. Basal mycelium is white in five of the species it describes and yellowish in one, which is the evidence that yellow basal mycelium is not a genus character — see the mycelium note above. And on trophic mode: unlike most Boletaceae, Chalciporoideae species 'may adopt various nutritional strategies, including ectomycorrhizal, saprotrophic, or mycoparasitic modes', with C. piperatus now thought 'more likely a mycoparasitic or saprotrophic fungus' on isotopic and synthesis evidence. That independently supports Cooper's reading of this species as a parasite on other fungi rather than a beech partner. Retrieved 07/10/2026. https://mycokeys.pensoft.net/article/165901/

SEARCH EXHAUSTED for an openly licensed description, 07/10/2026 — recorded so it is not re-searched blind. Checked and came up empty: English Wikipedia (no species article; the CC BY-SA genus article carries no species text and never mentions New Zealand); the new-record-paper route that filled bluefoot-bolete (inapplicable — the species is endemic, so there is no 'first record for X' literature); the CC BY MycoKeys revision of the subfamily (does not include it); GBIF (no description attached to the species in any of its eight checklist datasets); Zenodo and the Biodiversity Literature Repository (no treatments); NZTCS 38 (CC BY 4.0 but a status assessment, no description). Everything descriptive that exists is all rights reserved — McNabb via the Virtual Mycota, NZPCN, Kaimai Bush — or wrong, as with The Hidden Forest. CONCLUSION: there is no openly licensed description of this species to copy. The summary, habitat and identification have to be written for this guide from the facts above, which README:267 permits with an empty sources array. The protologue itself is McNabb 1968, New Zealand Journal of Botany 6(2): 137–176, DOI 10.1080/0028825X.1968.10429056 — paywalled at Taylor & Francis, and the thing to read if the basal mycelium question is ever worth settling properly.

sourcingNote: An endemic species with no openly licensed description. The Virtual Mycota carries McNabb's account and it is in copyright; there is no English Wikipedia article, only a CC BY-SA genus article that never mentions the species or New Zealand; and the one openly licensed source here, NZTCS 38 (CC BY 4.0), is a status assessment with no description in it. So the summary, habitat and identification have to be written, from the facts gathered in the sources above. The conservation question is now settled and it went the permissive way: NZTCS 38 lists this species as Not Threatened, upgraded from the Nationally Critical of 2002 that Wikidata still shows, so harvesting guidance is not ruled out on status grounds. It still has to reckon with the IUCN picture behind that status — 5 confirmed sightings since 2013 against 52 for the introduced bolete that is displacing it, and now present at all but one of this species' recorded sites. The lookalike card to peppery-bolete has the material it needs in cap colour and host tree: apricot to reddish orange under native beech, against fawn under pine. It must NOT be written on yellow basal mycelium, which three sources contradict each other on — see the unresolved note in the sources. Photos are attached, so the only remaining blockers are prose: summary, habitat, identification, a warning or the lookalike card, and the harvesting and tikanga guidance. The lookalike card to the other Chalciporus is the assistant's restatement of the Fungal Guide and Kaimai Bush on the owner's instruction, not the owner's words.

identification.text:
Trailing herb. Stem flattened, 2-angled, glabrous. Leaves 3-angled, acute, tapering to connate base, (4)–10–15–(30) × 5–6 mm; margins papillate. Flowers 2–4 cm diameter. Petals uniformly white to purple, in 3–5 rows, 1–3 cm long. Stamens 5–6 mm long; inner filaments hairy at base. Stigmas 5–(6). Capsule valves with widely divergent expanding keels; placental tubercle present, 2-lobed or reduced to a ridge. Seeds yellowish brown to brown, obovoid, distinctly papillate, about 1 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Flowering: November–January; fruiting: December–April.
Told from the other New Zealand ice plants by its stems, which are papillate and 2-angled rather than smooth and terete, and by its distinctly papillate rather than wrinkled or smooth seeds.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stem: Chatham Island ice plant's is flattened, 2-angled and rough with tiny pimples (papillae); native ice plant's is round and smooth. Chatham Island ice plant's leaf edges are pimply too, where native ice plant's are usually smooth but rarely pimply, so go by the stem. Its leaves are mostly shorter, 10–15 mm long (4–30 mm) against mostly 20–30 mm (6–40 mm) on native ice plant, but the ranges overlap. Its seeds are yellowish brown to brown and distinctly pimply; native ice plant's are brown and wrinkled; both are about 1 mm long. Both are trailing succulents with 3-angled, pointed leaves and flowers 2–4 cm across with 3–5 rows of petals, white to purple here and white to deep pink on native ice plant, so flower colour does not separate them. Both grow on the coasts of the Chatham Islands, and Chatham Island ice plant grows nowhere else. On the Kermadec Islands native ice plant (subspecies stricticaule) also has pimply leaf edges, but its stem is round and smooth. Chatham Island ice plant was once counted as part of native ice plant. Native ice plant's leaves and fruit are eaten (see its page).

summary.text:
Disphyma papillatum, the Chatham Island ice plant, is a trailing succulent herb in the ice plant family Aizoaceae, endemic to the Chatham Islands.
It grows on Chatham, Pitt, South East, Mangere, Little Mangere, Rabbit and Castle Islands, the Forty Fours, the Star Keys, the Sisters and Western Reef. In the 2023 national assessment it is At Risk – Naturally Uncommon, as an island endemic with a restricted range.
Chinnock described it in 1971; before that it was counted as part of the normal variation of native ice plant, Disphyma australe, which also grows on the Chatham Islands.
Its fleshy capsules are spread by animals that eat them, and possibly by wind and water. It is grown as a groundcover in exposed coastal gardens, as it tolerates wind and salt spray. It is easily raised from rooted pieces and fresh seed.

warnings: No record of Chatham Island ice plant as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
It grows with native ice plant on the Chatham Islands and was once counted as part of that species, so any ice plant there may be either. Check the stem before picking (see the lookalikes).

edibleParts.text: Leaves - raw or cooked as a potherb. A mild pleasant flavour, they make a very acceptable alternative to lettuce in salads. Immature seeds - raw or cooked. They are used to make a creamed vegetable soup that resembles pea soup. A few leaves are also added for colouring. The seeds have a pleasant nutty flavour, though they are too small for most people to want to collect in quantity.

identification.text:
M. parviflora has a decumbent or erect habit, growing up to 50–80 cm in height. The broad leaves have 5–7 shallow lobes. The lobe edges are round-toothed, with varying hairiness. It has small white or pink flowers at the base of leaf stalks. The 2 mm seeds are reddish-brown and kidney-shaped.
Newly sprouted plants have hairless, heart-shaped cotyledons with long stalks. These cotyledons are 3–12 mm long and 3–8 mm wide. Stalks usually do have hairs. The first leaf is rounder and larger than the others. True leaves are round and weakly lobed with wavy, shallow-toothed edges and a red spot at the leaf base. The plant rapidly grows a deep taproot.
M. parviflora has a diploid chromosome count of 42.
M. parviflora is distinguished from M. neglecta by shorter petals, enlarged fruiting calyx, and reticulately veined mericarps with winged edges.

Annual, procumbent to erect herb. Stems sparsely to moderately hairy with mostly stellate hairs. Leaves sparsely to densely clothed in mostly stellate hairs above, moderately clothed in mostly stellate hairs below, reniform to orbicular, cordate, shallowly or moderately 5–7-palmately lobed and crenate, 1–8 cm diameter; petioles 1.5–10 cm long; stipules ovate-triangular, 2–6 mm long. Flowers in axillary clusters of (1)–2–5; fruiting pedicels 2–10–(20) mm long; epicalyx segments linear, somewhat shorter than calyx; calyx teeth more or less orbicular with acute apex, glabrous or sparsely clothed in stellate hairs and ciliate, greatly enlarged and spreading at fruiting; petals white, pale mauve or pink towards tips, more or less equal to or only slightly longer than calyx, 3–5 mm long. Mericarps (9)–10–(11) per fruit, glabrous or hairy, strongly reticulately veined on back; edges slightly winged and sometimes toothed.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Both have strongly net-veined fruit segments, so the veining does not separate them; use the petal length, the calyx in fruit and the edges of the fruit segments. Leaf shape and size overlap (cheeseweed mallow 1–8 cm across, common mallow 1–15(–20) cm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. The two are separated by cheeseweed mallow's shorter petals, enlarged fruiting calyx and net-veined fruit segments with winged edges. Both are low herbs with round to kidney-shaped, lobed leaves of overlapping size (1–8 cm and 1–7(–8) cm across) and flowers in clusters in the leaf joints, so the leaves do not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. They are separated by the edges of the fruit segments (squared in French mallow, slightly winged in cheeseweed mallow) and French mallow's longer petals. Both have strongly net-veined fruit, so the veining does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and are unchanged in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Both have palmately lobed, toothed leaves whose sizes overlap (island mallow 2–15(–20) cm across, cheeseweed mallow 1–8 cm), so use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Both have round, palmately 5–7-lobed, round-toothed leaves, so the leaves do not separate them; use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Tree mallow

preparation.text: Leaves raw in salads or cooked as a potherb; immature seeds raw or cooked, or in a creamed soup. In Jaén, Spain, the little fruits, shaped like bread rolls, have been eaten as a snack (Andújar, Quesada).

recipes.method: Written for mallow in general; the author says little mallow is the kind most eaten in Morocco. Serves 4. About 225 g mallow leaves and stems (about 2 litres, packed), 120 ml olive oil, about 120 ml chopped parsley and/or coriander leaves, 4 cloves garlic, pressed or finely chopped, 1½ tsp paprika, 1½ tsp ground cumin, ¼ tsp salt, ¼ tsp cayenne pepper (optional), 2 tbsp lemon juice, the chopped pulp of 1 preserved lemon, and preserved lemon rind and a handful of red olives to garnish. Wash the mallow thoroughly, drain, chop the leaves and stems and steam over simmering water for 15–20 minutes, until tender; it shrinks a lot and darkens. Press out the extra water against the side of the steamer basket. Meanwhile, fry the oil, garlic, herbs and spices over medium or medium-low heat for several minutes, until the herbs wilt and the garlic smells fragrant, without burning the garlic, then take off the heat. Add the mallow, preserved lemon pulp and lemon juice and cook over medium heat for 5–10 minutes. Taste and adjust the seasoning, and serve warm or at room temperature with the olives and preserved lemon rind, usually as a dip with bread. Without preserved lemon, use a little more lemon juice; the same method works with spinach, kale or purslane, with the steaming time adjusted.
recipes.title: Moroccan mallow salad (khoubiza or bakkoula)

recipes.method: Written for cheeseweed, which the author names as Malva parviflora, in the US Southwest. Several handfuls of cheeseweed leaves (about 1 litre once chopped), 1 large onion, diced, cooking oil (the author suggests bacon fat or butter), and salt and pepper, or lemon or vinegar. Strip the leaves from the main stem and wash them; the leaf stalks can stay but chop them small, as they can be tough (chopped stems add a celery-like crunch). Chop the leaves coarsely. Brown the onion in a large frying pan or wok as much as you like (spring onions or garlic chives also work), add the greens and cover with a lid so their own moisture steams them as they shrink. Season and serve as a side dish or on pasta.
recipes.title: Sautéed cheeseweed

summary.text:
Malva parviflora is an annual or perennial herb that is native to Northern Africa, Southern Europe, and Western and Central Asia and is widely naturalized elsewhere. Common names include cheeseweed, cheeseweed mallow, Egyptian mallow, least mallow, little mallow, mallow, marshmallow, small-flowered mallow, small-flowered marshmallow, and smallflower mallow.
Its native range extends from the Mediterranean, through West Asia, and to Central Asia and can be found in Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, Tunisia, Kuwait, Afghanistan, Cyprus, Iran, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Greece, Croatia, Italy, Malta, Spain, France, and Portugal. The species is widely naturalized elsewhere, including in North America since the 19th century. It is a naturalized weed in Australia.
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North Island, throughout the South Island except Westland and Fiordland, and on the Kermadec Islands. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1883.

warnings: M. parviflora accumulates pollutants such as cadmium and chromium. In nitrogen-rich soils, the plant's leaves and seeds can be toxic to cattle and poultry due to an accumulation of nitrates. If consumed in large amounts, the plant can damage energy homeostasis in horses, possibly due to its cyclopropene fatty acids.
It has often caused staggers in sheep, and less often in cattle and horses, in Australia and to a lesser extent South Africa; no cases have been confirmed in New Zealand.

harvestEthics.text:
An environmental weed that can invade intact native forest and reduces native recruitment. Harvest as much as you like, and do not spread the seed.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text:
Large shrub or small tree to 6 m high. Trunk smooth, pale brown. Shoots terete or subterete, puberulent when young. Petioles 7–10 mm long, puberulent. Lamina 4–8 × 2.5–4.5 cm, obovate, ciliolate toward base of margins and midrib, at least when young, otherwise glabrous, dotted with glands beneath, glossy and dark green above; lateral veins fairly conspicuous in dried material but not impressed or markedly raised; base cuneate, often narrowly so; apex usually obtuse, sometimes rounded. Flowers solitary, often produced in nearly all axils of upper leaves; pedicels 7–10 mm long, puberulent, jointed near apex with very small, caducous, ovate bracteoles. Hypanthium and calyx limb glandular-punctate; lobes usually 5, 3–4 mm long. Petals c. 5 mm long, elliptic, white, more or less glandular-punctate. Stamens longer than petals. Style c. 4 mm long, stout. Fruit more or less globose, c. 2 cm diameter, becoming dark purple, occasionally yellow; flesh usually purple, occasionally whitish, sweet. Seeds numerous.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Psidium cattleianum Sabine.]

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psidium_cattleyanum A small, highly branched tree usually 2–4 m and at most 13 m. Both the thin skin and the juicy interior are soft and edible, though the skin is often removed for a sweeter flavour; it also makes jam and juices, and the leaves can be brewed for tea. On how aggressive it is, which is this entry's framing: it is considered the most invasive plant in Hawaii, and is among the worst on Réunion and Madagascar, where it threatens endemic forest — and it was introduced to most of the places it now invades precisely because people wanted the fruit.

On how fast the fruit goes over. Commercial products are not made from it partly for want of a market but also because of the heavy presence of fruit flies, which renders the fruit inedible soon after picking. summary.text:
Psidium cattleyanum, commonly known as Cattley guava, strawberry guava or cherry guava, is a small tree (2–6 m tall) in the Myrtaceae (myrtle) family. It is an invasive plant in many areas and is considered the most invasive species in Hawaii, although it has some economic uses, including its edible fruit.
In New Zealand it was first recorded naturalised in 1977, as an escape from cultivation; by 1988 it was known wild near Whangārei, in Auckland and on Raoul Island. Auckland Council's regional pest plan lists it for sustained control across the whole region.

identification.text:
Evergreen, wide spreading shrub or tree, up to about 10 m high when mature, not armed, glabrous or almost so; trunks often several, usually short, often forming large thickets. Leaf petiole 5–10–(12) mm long; blade coriaceous, oblanceolate to narrow-elliptic or narrow-oblong, (75)–90–150–(180) × (23)–30–50–(55) mm, acute to very short-acuminate but often splitting at tip and appearing emarginate, especially when dried, cuneate to rounded at base, shining above with prominent paler veins, less shining below; margin somewhat recurved, more or less entire toward base, with distant, short, acute teeth toward apex; stipules long-triangular, deciduous. Inflorescence an axillary or terminal, erect, dense raceme (80)–100–(120) mm long, with 20–30–(35) fragrant flowers; pedicels 2–2.5–(5) mm long, elongating slightly after anthesis. Hypanthium broad; sepals broadly triangular, about 1 mm long, acute, green, more or less erect. Petals 5, spreading, orbicular, 2.5–5 × 2–4 mm, rounded, greenish white to cream. Stamens longer than petals; filaments pale. Fruit about 10 mm long, ovoid, glabrous, dark purple, very bitter; stone smooth.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is told from other cherries and from Portugal laurel by being evergreen, by its flowers on long spikes rather than in small clusters, and by its leaves having only a few short, distantly spaced teeth, toward the tip. The fruits hang in grape-like clusters and look like dark purple to black cherries. The leaves can have the scent of almonds when crushed.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaf edge: cherry laurel's leaves have a few distant, short, sharp teeth toward the tip and are more or less smooth toward the base; bay's leaves are untoothed, on some leaves wavy. Cherry laurel's flowers are greenish white to cream, 20–35 on an erect, dense spike 80–120 mm long, and its fruits hang in grape-like clusters along the spike; bay's flowers are cream or whitish, 3–4 mm long, in small umbels in the upper leaf joints. Bay's leaves are aromatic; cherry laurel's can smell of almonds when crushed. Both are evergreen with shining leaves of overlapping length (bay 4–13 cm, cherry laurel 7.5–18 cm), and both have dark fruit, cherry laurel's dark purple and about 10 mm long, bay's glossy black and 1.3–1.5 cm long, so leaf size, shine and fruit colour do not tell them apart. Bay's leaves are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Bay tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Taiwan cherry is deciduous, with thin leaves finely and sharply toothed along the edge; cherry laurel is evergreen, with leathery leaves shining above and only a few distant, short teeth toward the tip. Taiwan cherry's flowers are bell-shaped, deep pink to rose-magenta, and hang in clusters of 1–5 (July–September); cherry laurel's are greenish white to cream, 20–35 on an erect spike 80–120 mm long (August–September). Taiwan cherry's fruit is glossy scarlet, up to 12 × 10 mm; cherry laurel's is dark purple, about 10 mm long, very bitter, and hangs in grape-like clusters along the spike. The fruits are of similar size, and cherry laurel fruits from November to January, when Taiwan cherry is also in fruit, so check the leaves and how the fruit is borne, not size. Taiwan cherry's fruit is eaten.
lookalikes.name: Taiwan cherry

Wikipedia, 'Bay leaf' (same day): cherry laurel 'certainly does contain dangerous concentrations of cyanogenic glycosides together with the enzymes to generate the hydrogen cyanide from the glycosides if the leaf is physically damaged'.

Plants For A Future, 'Prunus laurocerasus' (all rights reserved), https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Prunus+laurocerasus, retrieved 04/11/2026 — Known Hazards: hydrogen cyanide 'found mainly in the leaves and seed', 'any very bitter seed or fruit should not be eaten', 'In excess, however, it can cause respiratory failure and even death' (genus-level cyanide text, used for the death clause in warnings). Edible Uses: 'Fruit - raw or cooked. Sweet and reasonably pleasant when fully ripe' (refs 65, 74 and the author's own eating), 'Some sources suggest the fruit is poisonous, this probably refers to the unripe fruit', seed 'raw or cooked', leaf water as an almond flavouring 'poisonous in large amounts'. Not given as food here (see the open question). NOT used: medicinal uses. Other uses seen (for the useful-plants candidates table): green dye from the leaves, dark grey to green dye from the fruit, hedging, wood for turnery.

OPEN QUESTION (owner, 04/11/2026): the ripe fruit flesh is eaten in some sources. Plants For A Future eats it (see above); Wikipedia says 'The fruits are astringent but edible' (citing Fruitipedia, a dead link, and PFAF, so not independent); Kolayli et al. (2003), 'Chemical and antioxidant properties of Laurocerasus officinalis Roem. (cherry laurel) fruit grown in the Black Sea region', J Agric Food Chem 51(25):7489–94, PMID 14640604 (abstract via PubMed E-utilities, retrieved 04/11/2026): 'a summer fruit highly characteristic of the Black Sea region. The edible parts of the fruit were tested'. Against: Flora of New Zealand describes New Zealand fruit as 'very bitter', and PFAF and Wikipedia both say bitter fruit should not be eaten; the stone is poisonous; NZPCN and Flora of New Zealand flag the species as poisonous. Bay tree: Flora of New Zealand Online 'Laurus nobilis' (CC BY 3.0 NZ, https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Laurus-nobilis.html): 'Lvs aromatic', 'Lamina 4–13 × 1.5–4.5 cm', 'Umbels in upper lf axils', 'Perianth 3–4 mm long, cream or whitish', 'Berry 1.3–1.5 × 0.6–1.3 cm … glossy black'; Wikipedia 'Laurus nobilis' (CC BY-SA 4.0): leaves 'with an entire (untoothed) margin. On some leaves the margin undulates.' Cherry laurel: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV / NZFO as above (teeth toward apex, raceme (80)–100–(120) mm with 20–30–(35) flowers, petals greenish white to cream, fruit c. 10 mm, dark purple, very bitter), NZFO weed profile (leaves 7.5–18 cm), Weedbusters (grape-like clusters), Wikipedia (almond scent). No card to the other Prunus entries (black cherry, Japanese cherry, cherry-plum, European plum): no trusted source read names a confusion with cherry laurel specifically. Weedbusters' cherry laurel page says it is told 'from other cherries' — generic, not a named pair — so it was not used for a card.

Not given: Portugal laurel (Prunus lusitanica), the closest lookalike in New Zealand (Weedbusters; Wikipedia: 'distinguished by its sharply toothed leaves and red petioles'), has no entry in this guide; it is not eaten either.

summary.text:
Prunus laurocerasus, also known as cherry laurel, common laurel and sometimes English laurel in North America, is an evergreen species of cherry (Prunus), native to regions bordering the Black Sea in southwestern Asia and southeastern Europe, from Albania and Bulgaria east through Turkey to the Caucasus Mountains and northern Iran.
The common names of P. laurocerasus refer to the similarity of foliage and appearance to bay laurel (Laurus nobilis, the true laurel, in the family Lauraceae), and like the bay laurel, Prunus laurocerasus was used for making laurel wreaths, but the two plants are not closely related.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands. Naturalised from south-east Europe, first recorded in 1958. Flowering August to September, fruiting November to January. P. laurocerasus is frequently grown as a hedge plant for its dense, evergreen habit and relics of cultivation are very common in settled areas, especially around old homesteads, domains and parks.
Its seed is spread by birds, and it also spreads by suckers from the roots. It is named on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds and is an Organism of Interest in the Tasman-Nelson regional pest management plan.

warnings: Do not eat any part of cherry laurel. Its leaves and seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides, including amygdalin, which release hydrogen cyanide when the leaf is damaged. The leaves are poisonous to people and livestock; eating the leaves or seeds may cause severe discomfort, and in excess cyanide can cause breathing failure and death.
The fruit of New Zealand plants is very bitter, and in this plant bitterness indicates larger amounts of hydrogen cyanide. The stone inside the fruit is poisonous like the leaves.
Its leaves look like bay leaves and its fruit like cherries. Check any 'bay tree' or wild cherry before picking (see the lookalikes).

identification.text: Wild types are large shrubs or small trees reaching 8–12 metres tall, sometimes spiny, with glabrous, ovate deciduous leaves 3–7 cm long. It is one of the first European trees to flower, often before the leaves have opened. The flowers are white or pale pink and about 2 cm across, with five petals and many stamens. The fruit is an edible drupe, 2–3 cm in diameter, ripening to yellow or red.

lookalikes.howToTell: No single test settles it; most of these ranges overlap. Young shoots: cherry plum's are hairless and shining; the plum's are usually hairy and dull, though sometimes hairless, so a hairy shoot points to the plum. Size: a plum is 25–45 mm long, sometimes only 20 mm, and a cherry plum 15–30 mm, sometimes only 10 mm, so a fruit over 30 mm points to the plum, and anything smaller is not settled by size (the plum can be as small as 15 mm). Colour overlaps: plums are green, yellow, red or blackish purple, usually bloomed; cherry plums yellow to orange-red or scarlet, sometimes dark crimson, slightly bloomed. Do not use the midrib — cherry plum's can be densely hairy on its lower third underneath. Cherry plum fruits from November to January and the plum from January to February. Both flower in August and September, and their petals and flower stalks overlap in size.

preparation.text:
The fruits are edible. Some varieties have sweet fruits that can be eaten fresh, while others are sour and better for making jam. Cherry plums are a key ingredient in Georgian cuisine where they are used to produce tkemali sauce, as well as a number of popular dishes, such as kharcho soup and chakapuli stew.
In Middle Asia and Caucasus considerable quantities are processed to preserves, jam, pie and 'lavas' (fruit-flesh dried in thin layers).

recipes.method: 1.8 kg cherry plums, 1.8 kg brown cane sugar and about 285 ml water. Put everything in a large, flat-bottomed pan, stir, and bring to the boil. Boil until the skins start to come off and the fruit comes away from the stones. Pour the mixture into a large piece of muslin and squeeze the pulp through it back into the pan. Keep boiling until it reaches setting point, which can take as long as 30 minutes. To test, chill a couple of saucers in the fridge before you start; drip a little jam onto one, let it cool for a moment, then push it sideways with a finger — it is ready when it wrinkles and feels tacky. Pour into sterilised jars and screw on the lids. Makes about 7 jars.
recipes.title: Cherry plum jam

recipes.method: 2.8 kg cherry plums, 1.4 kg sugar, about 4 litres water, 1 sachet wine yeast (any red wine yeast will do), 1 tsp yeast nutrient and 1 tsp pectolase. Boil 1 litre of the water, pour it over the fruit and crush the fruit with the end of a rolling pin until no lumps are left. Leave it a few hours, then add the rest of the water and the pectolase — plums are rich in the pectin that sets jam and also clouds wine. Leave a couple of days, then strain through a fine sieve. Bring the juice quickly to the boil in a saucepan and turn off the heat straight away; the author once skipped this and lost the whole batch to acetobacter. Pour the hot juice over the sugar and stir until it dissolves, cool to room temperature, then add the yeast and yeast nutrient. Top up to 4.5 litres if necessary, funnel into a demijohn and fit an airlock. Rack into a clean demijohn after four to six weeks, and again a few weeks later if you want. Bottle when clear — or, if it will not clear completely, bottle it anyway.
recipes.title: Cherry plum wine

recipes.method: Written for plums in general rather than cherry plums. Makes a 1-litre jar. 250 g granulated sugar, 420 ml apple cider vinegar, ½ tsp crushed coriander, 1 tsp ground cardamom, 750 g plums, stoned and halved, 1 small cinnamon stick, 1 red chilli cut into quarters and 1 star anise. In a large saucepan, bring the sugar, vinegar, coriander and cardamom to a gentle simmer and cook for 5 minutes to infuse. Add the plums and cook for about 2 minutes, until just softened but still holding their shape. Put the cinnamon, chilli and star anise in a sterilised 1-litre jar (or two or three smaller ones), scoop in the plums and pack them tightly, leaving about 1.25 cm at the top, then pour the vinegar over until they are completely covered. Seal while still warm, leave to cool at room temperature, then refrigerate for 2 weeks before serving. They keep about a couple of weeks in the fridge; for longer storage they can be processed in a water bath. Good on toast with farmhouse cheese, on savoury porridge, in salads, or with pork chops, chicken or turkey.

summary.text:
Prunus cerasifera is a species of plum known by the common names cherry plum and myrobalan plum.
It is native to Southeast Europe and Western Asia, and is naturalised in the British Isles and scattered locations in North America. It is also naturalized in parts of Southeast Australia where it is considered to be a mildly invasive weed of bushland near urban centers.
They are self-fertile but can also be pollinated by other Prunus varieties such as the Victoria plum. The plant propagates by seed or by suckering, and is often used as the rootstock for other Prunus species and cultivars.

warnings: The plant (especially the seed and young shoots) contains cyanogenic glycosides, especially amygdalin and prunasin. When ingested, these compounds break down in the digestive tract to release cyanide.

edibleParts.text: Whole aerial plant — leaves, stems, flowers.

sources: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA)
habitat.text:
Damp shaded garden beds, under hedges, cultivated soil. Grows in dense low mats.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Grassland, waste land, roadsides, coastal sandy sites, damp sites, cultivated land, disturbed stony sites, riverbeds.

identification.text: Small oval opposite leaves on a weak sprawling stem. The giveaway: a single line of fine hairs running along one side of the stem, switching sides at each node. Tiny white flowers with five deeply split petals that look like ten.

lookalikes.howToTell: Snap a stem: petty spurge bleeds white milky sap, and no milky sap is recorded for chickweed. Spurge sap irritates skin and has caused serious eye inflammation, so keep it away from your face. Petty spurge's stems are hairless, where chickweed's carry a line of hairs down one side; its leaves are alternate, where chickweed's are in opposite pairs; and its small green flower heads have no petals, where chickweed has white petals split almost to the base (rarely none). Both are weeds of gardens and cultivated ground.
lookalikes.name: Petty spurge

lookalikes.howToTell: Scarlet pimpernel's stems are four-angled (square in section) and hairless; chickweed's are round with a single line of hairs. Pimpernel's flowers are orange or orange-red, borne singly in the leaf axils on stalks (0.5)–1–2 cm long; chickweed's petals are white and divided almost to the base (rarely absent), in usually loose clusters at the stem tips. Pimpernel's leaves are stalkless and often indistinctly dotted with black glands underneath; chickweed's lower leaves have a stalk about as long as the blade. Leaf size and the sprawling habit overlap and do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Scarlet pimpernel

lookalikes.howToTell: Blue pimpernel's stems are four-angled (square in section) and hairless; chickweed's are round with a single line of hairs. Blue pimpernel's flowers are blue, with five lobes, borne singly in the leaf axils on stalks (0.5)–1–2 cm long; chickweed's petals are white and divided almost to the base (rarely absent), in usually loose clusters at the stem tips. Blue pimpernel's leaves are stalkless and often indistinctly dotted with black glands underneath; chickweed's lower leaves have a stalk about as long as the blade. Leaf size and the sprawling habit overlap and do not separate them. Do not eat blue pimpernel.
lookalikes.name: Blue pimpernel

preparation.text: Raw in salads, blitzed into a pesto, or wilted briefly.

recipes.method: Chickweed and Italian parsley, roughly half and half, long stems removed; 1 small garlic clove, crushed with salt; freshly shelled walnuts (or other nuts); extra virgin olive oil; a little grated parmesan (optional); lemon juice. Fill a food processor with the chickweed and parsley leaves and chop them; they reduce down a lot. Add the garlic, then the walnuts, and pour in olive oil until it becomes a purée. Mix in a little parmesan if you want it creamier, then add lemon juice a squeeze at a time, tasting as you go; it keeps the pesto bright green and balances it. Finish with a drizzle of oil for gloss. The author keeps it for at least a week in the fridge and uses it in sandwiches, on pizza, through pasta or to lift other dishes. She notes that picked chickweed itself does not keep in the fridge, so make the pesto the day you pick it.
recipes.title: Chickweed pesto

recipes.method: Chickweed, as large and lush as you can find; freshly shelled walnuts; a few olives; halloumi; a squirt of lemon juice; a splash of avocado oil. Fry the halloumi. Add the walnuts, olives and fried halloumi to the chickweed. Dress it simply with the lemon juice and avocado oil. Eat it the day you pick the chickweed; the author finds it does not keep in the fridge. She makes the chickweed the star of the bowl rather than an extra.
recipes.title: Chickweed salad

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard. 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: Written for the author's mixed wild leaves. Of his lists, this catalogue covers dandelion and hairy bittercress (pungent), chickweed and hawthorn leaves (mild), and gorse flowers and flowering currant blossom (extras). He warns to be extra careful identifying leaves before the plants flower. Pungent leaves; mild leaves; a few extras; walnut oil; elderberry vinegar; salt and pepper; a little mustard; fermented greens; pickled buds. Mix pungent and mild leaves about 1 to 3, then scatter a few extras over the top. Dress simply with walnut oil, elderberry vinegar, salt, pepper and a little mustard; he finishes it with fermented greens and pickled buds.
recipes.title: Wild summer salad

recipes.method: Written for chickweed, with sweet chestnuts. Makes 2. Boil chestnuts in water for 10 minutes, drain them and let them cool a little, then halve them and scoop out the flesh; process it to a fine flour. Mash a heaped 125 ml (½ cup) of this chestnut flour with ½ avocado and a little salt. Spread it on 2 nori sheets, add fenugreek sprouts and a bunch of chickweed, and roll them up.
recipes.title: Chickweed and chestnut nori wraps

recipes.method: Written for chickweed, nasturtium and onion weed. Soak 500 ml (2 cups) chickpeas overnight, drain and rinse them well, and sprout them for 48 hours, rinsing twice a day, until the tails are as long as the peas; or cook them, as the author also allows. 500 ml (2 cups) sprouted chickpeas; 185 ml (¾ cup) tahini (the author grinds whole sesame seeds instead); 2–4 garlic cloves, minced; the juice of 2 large lemons and 1 orange; 125 ml (½ cup) olive oil; 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt; 5 ml (1 tsp) cumin; a big handful of chickweed, some nasturtium leaves, a small bunch of onion weed leaves and a sprig of parsley or another herb. Process the chickpeas with the citrus juice until still slightly chunky, then add everything else and process to the consistency you want.
recipes.title: Raw chickpea hummus with wild greens

recipes.method: Written for cleavers, violet leaves, chickweed, red deadnettle and bittercress. A small handful of cleavers; 4 violet leaves; a handful of chickweed; 3 or 4 stems of red deadnettle; a small handful of bittercress; a big handful of bok choy, kale or silverbeet; 1 banana, peeled; 1 apple (whole without the stalk if organic, otherwise peeled); 1 mandarin (with its peel if organic, otherwise peeled); 1 or 2 kiwifruit, peeled; 1 small or ½ large avocado; 500 ml (2 cups) water, more if the blender struggles. Wash the weeds and greens, put them in the blender, snip them up a bit with scissors and add the water. Blend on low until the greens break down, then on high until smooth. Add the fruit and avocado and blend again, low and then high, until creamy.
recipes.title: Winter health boosting smoothie

sources: Langlands, Peter. Foraging New Zealand (Penguin Random House NZ, 2024), 'Chickweed' entry.
Knox, Johanna. A Forager's Treasury: A New Zealand guide to finding and using wild plants (Allen & Unwin, 2013).

summary.text:
Mild, sweet and abundant in every neglected garden bed in the country.
Stellaria media, chickweed, is an annual flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae. It is native to Eurasia and naturalised throughout the world, where it is a weed of waste ground, farmland and gardens.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands and on the Kermadec, Chatham, Antipodes, Auckland and Campbell Islands; naturalised from Europe, first recorded wild in 1832.

warnings: Always break a stem and check for milky sap before picking a mat — petty spurge is almost everywhere in New Zealand gardens, where chickweed grows too.
The leaves contain saponins, so do not eat large quantities: paralysis has been reported from eating too much.

edibleParts.text: The fruit and the leaves. The fruit is eaten raw; it is a juicy, berry-like fruit 17–20 mm long, green to yellowish, that stays closed when ripe and is full of tiny seeds in a dark, sweet, thick jelly. The leaves are eaten baked or pickled; raw, they are harshly tannic and barely edible.

harvestEthics.text: Not a legally declared pest, but on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and it hybridises with the native ice plant. Harvest as much as you like, but do not damage the dunes while gathering, and spread no stem fragments or garden waste: even small pieces can grow into new plants.

identification.text:
Mat-forming trailing perennial herb. Stems to 6 m long, glabrous, 2-angled, subwoody at base. Leaves smooth, sharply 3-angled, linear, acute, scarcely tapered to connate base, 35–90 × 5–12 mm, 5–12× as long as wide; keel denticulate near apex. Flowers 6.5–8 cm diameter. Calyx glabrous; longest sepals 25–45 mm long. Petals spreading, purple, paler near base, 10–35 mm long. Stamens 4–10 mm long; filaments yellow or pinkish, hairy at base; anthers pale yellow. Stigmas 8–11. Seeds brown, often asymmetrically obovoid, 1–1.3 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Carpobrotus aequilaterus sensu (Haw.) N.E.Br.]
Stems occasionally root where they touch the ground.
Leaves bitter-tasting. Fruit indehiscent, fleshy, mucilaginous; locules as many as stigmas. [Genus description, from: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Very similar to South African ice plant, but easily told apart when flowering: this plant has smaller, purple flowers.
Hybrids with the native ice plant have flowers 4–5.2 cm across, with purplish petals that later turn purplish pink.

lookalikes.howToTell: Best told apart in flower. South African ice plant has pale yellow petals that turn pinkish orange or dull pink with age, on flowers 8–10 cm across; this plant's petals are purple, paler near the base, on flowers 6.5–8 cm across. South African ice plant's leaves are 70–120 × 12–17 mm, against 35–90 × 5–12 mm here, but the ranges overlap, so do not rely on leaves out of flower.
lookalikes.name: South African ice plant

lookalikes.howToTell: Native ice plant is smaller in every part. Its flowers are 2–4 cm across, with petals uniformly white to deep pink, against 6.5–8 cm and purple here. Its leaves are mostly 20–30 mm long (6–40 mm) and 4–6 mm wide (up to 9 mm), against 35–90 × 5–12 mm here. Its stems are round in section, not 2-angled, and its fruit is a capsule whose cells have lids, where this plant's fruit stays closed. Plants with purplish flowers 4–5.2 cm across may be hybrids between the two.
lookalikes.name: Native ice plant

summary.text:
Carpobrotus chilensis, the Chilean sea fig, also called purple-flowered ice plant or angled pigface, is a mat-forming succulent in the ice plant family Aizoaceae, naturalised in New Zealand since 1969.
New Zealand sources give its origin as California and Chile, or South America, and it was brought in as a garden ornamental. In New Zealand it was long called Carpobrotus aequilaterus, the name of a very different-looking Western Australian endemic.
The Flora of New Zealand (1988) recorded it at Patea in Taranaki and Pukerua Bay near Wellington, and in Canterbury and Otago. Herbarium specimens have since recorded it wild on beaches in Golden Bay. It is not a legally declared pest, but it is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. It forms natural hybrids with the native ice plant, Disphyma australe.
Animals eat the fruit and spread the seed. Its stems root where they touch the ground, and stem pieces moved in soil or dumped with garden waste grow into new plants.

identification.text:
Large, suckering, spiny shrub up to 3–(4) m high when mature and several m diameter; stems brownish olive, smooth, shining and glabrous when young, often forming dense thickets. Leaves distributed along length of first-year, non-flowering stems, and in fascicles on short shoots on older flowering stems; petiole 6–12 mm long, green or red-tinged, glabrous; blade obovate to elliptic, finely serrate to crenate, (30)–50–80–(100) × 20–50 mm, acute and often curled at tip, attenuate to petiole at base, glabrous, more or less shining and deep green on upper surface, paler below; leaves of short shoots on flowering stems similar but smaller; stipules prominent, reniform, up to 12 × 20 mm, crenate. Flowers in fascicles of (3)–4–5, 25–35 mm diameter, more or less sessile. Sepals fused at base; lobes broadly ovate to oblong, 3–5 mm long, green, glabrous, with hyaline ciliate margins. Petals 5, more or less overlapping, suberect or spreading, broad-ovate to orbicular, 12–20 mm diameter, shortly clawed; limb white to bright pink to scarlet. Stamens shorter than petals; filaments coloured as in petals. Fruit up to 60 mm diameter, more or less broadly ovoid to subglobose but often misshapen, yellowish and often brown-speckled, indented at base and apex. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Genus Chaenomeles (Flora of New Zealand): Flowers solitary or fascicled, distributed along stems, those on older wood appearing before leaves and those on younger wood usually appearing with or after leaves. Stamens 40–60. Chaenomeles species have more or less spiny branches, usually glabrous leaves, sometimes hairy on midrib beneath, the flowers few in fascicles, mainly produced before the leaves but with scattered flowers later, erect sepals, and the fruit less than 70 mm long.
The flowers mostly open on bare branches, before the glossy leaves; garden cultivars run from white and green-tinged white through pink and coral to vermilion and scarlet. The fruit is green to yellow, about the size of a small lemon, and stays rock hard even when ripe.

lookalikes.howToTell: Quince is unarmed, or only rarely slightly spiny; flowering quince is a spiny shrub. Flowering quince leaves are finely toothed, hairless, and more or less shining deep green above; quince leaves have entire margins and are white- to grey-woolly beneath. Flowering quince flowers come in clusters of (3)–4–5, 25–35 mm across, mostly before the leaves, with erect sepals; quince flowers sit singly at the ends of short leafy shoots, 30–50 mm across, with sharply bent-back, densely woolly sepals that stay on the fruit. Flowering quince fruit is up to 60 mm across, often misshapen and brown-speckled; quince fruit is usually 80–150 mm long and more or less finely downy. Flower colour helps only at the red end: flowering quince can be white, pink or scarlet, quince white to pink. Height does not separate them (both are suckering shrubs that can form thickets, flowering quince up to 3–(4) m and quince up to 5–(8) m), and both fruits are yellowish and fragrant. Quince fruit is eaten cooked.

preparation.text: Leave the fruit on the shrub until it begins to fall, until the skin turns yellow, or until after a frost. Raw, the fruit is rock hard and sour; cooking softens it and brings out its fragrance. For jelly, quarter the fruit, just cover it with water, boil until soft and mushy, strain off the juice and boil it with sugar to setting point. Ripe fruit is tart and needs more sugar than apple. Freezing the fruit first softens it for cutting. Cut fruit browns, so drop the pieces into water with lemon juice as you chop. The fruit is high in pectin, so jams and jellies set without added pectin. Sources differ on texture: chopped small it can soften in 5–10 minutes, or keep some crunch even after long stewing. For a clear jelly, let the juice drip through cloth overnight without squeezing; a longer boil with sugar alone turns the jelly reddish. Quince recipes can be used, but the fruit is much smaller than ordinary quince, so go by weight or volume rather than by number of fruit.

recipes.method: Written for japonica (Chaenomeles, the red-flowered shrub with yellow-green apple-like fruit). Ingredients: japonica fruit (the author gathered about a kilo of windfalls), water, and sugar — jam (setting) sugar or ordinary sugar — at a kilo for every litre of juice. Keep the fruit for a few days in a bowl in a warm room. Quarter it, put it in a large pot, just cover with water and boil until soft and mushy. Strain the juice off the pulp; the author skips the jelly bag and accepts a cloudy jelly. Measure the juice and boil it with the sugar: with jam sugar, boil vigorously for one minute; with ordinary sugar, keep boiling until a teaspoonful on a cold saucer wrinkles into a set after a few seconds. The source gives no jarring instructions.
recipes.title: Japonica jelly

recipes.method: Written for Japanese quince (Chaenomeles japonica). Ingredients: 750 g Japanese quince, water to cover, 3 large stalks of tarragon plus 3 more sprigs for chopping, and caster sugar at 400 g for every 600 ml of juice; 3 jam jars and wax discs. Sterilise the jars and lids. Quarter the fruit and take out the seeds; wrap about half the seeds in muslin (for pectin) and put the bag in a pan with the fruit. Cover with water, bring to the boil and simmer until tender, 40 minutes to an hour and a half depending on how bletted the fruit was. Strain through muslin, keeping the liquid (the pulp can go into jam). Measure the liquid and weigh out the sugar. Heat the liquid, sugar, tarragon stalks and the seed bag gently, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then bring to a rolling boil without stirring until it reaches 104.5 °C, or passes the fridge test. Take off the heat, lift out the seed bag and tarragon stalks, stir in the finely chopped tarragon and leave to cool for 10–15 minutes so the herb spreads evenly. Pour into the sterilised jars to within a couple of mm of the top, lay the wax discs on wax side down and screw the lids on tightly while hot.
recipes.title: Japonica and tarragon jelly

recipes.method: Written for flowering quince (Chaenomeles speciosa), fruit about the size of a small lemon; adapted by the author from a Simply Recipes quince jam. Ingredients: 10–12 flowering quinces (about 950 ml, 4 packed cups, once minced), 830 ml (3½ cups) water, 30 ml (2 tablespoons) lemon juice, the zest of one lemon and 700 g (3½ cups) sugar. Makes about three 250 ml jars. Wash the fruit and cut it in half; remove the core, seeds and any blemished bits, rinse, and do not peel. Mince the fruit finely with a large knife or a food processor. Put two small plates in the freezer for testing the set. Bring the water to the boil in a large heavy pan, add the minced fruit, lemon juice and zest, lower the heat and simmer until the fruit is soft, about 10 minutes. Add the sugar, bring back to the boil and stir until it has all dissolved. Lower the heat to medium-high and cook uncovered, stirring now and then, until the jam turns pink and thickens, about 30–50 minutes. To test, dab a little hot jam on a cold plate, wait a few seconds and run a finger through it: if the streak stays, it is ready; if not, cook a few minutes more and test again. Mash with a potato masher for a less chunky jam. Ladle into sterilised jars, wipe the rims clean, and screw on lids sterilised in boiling water. Turn the jars upside down under a tea towel; when cool, turn them upright and press the lids. A lid that springs back has not sealed: keep that jar in the fridge.
recipes.title: Flowering quince jam

recipes.method: Written for Japanese flowering quince (Chaenomeles japonica); the author's own recipe, loosely based on a Greek quince jam. Makes 1 litre. Ingredients: 800 g whole fruit (about 600 g once cored and chopped), 400 g sugar, 1 lemon (zest and juice), 4–6 whole cloves and 1 tablespoon rosewater (optional). Put the jars in an oven at 75 °C until needed. Put half the lemon juice in a large bowl and half-fill it with cold water. Wash, quarter, core and slice the fruit thinly, dropping each handful into the lemon water as you go so it does not brown. Drain and weigh the fruit; if it is not 600 g, use sugar at 2 parts to 3 parts fruit. Put the fruit in a stainless steel pan with just enough water to nearly cover it and bring to the boil; cook 5–10 minutes until soft. Add the sugar, cloves, zest and half the remaining lemon juice, lower to medium heat and cook, stirring now and then with a wooden spoon, until the fruit breaks down and the liquid reduces to the thickness you want. Add the last of the lemon juice and the rosewater and boil 15 minutes more. Take off the heat and leave to stand 15–30 minutes, then ladle into the hot jars and seal. Lower the sealed jars into a tall pot of hot (not yet boiling) water, bring to the boil and process for 5–10 minutes, then cool on a wooden board. After 12–24 hours, check the seals: any jar that has not sealed goes in the fridge and is eaten within a week. This makes a soft jam; for a firmer set, use less water at the start or cook the fruit until about half the water has evaporated before adding the sugar.
recipes.title: Flowering quince jam with cloves and rosewater

summary.text:
Chaenomeles speciosa, the flowering quince, Chinese quince or Japanese quince, is a thorny deciduous or semi-evergreen shrub native to eastern Asia.
The fruit is a fragrant, hard pome that resembles a quince.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Japonica or Japanese quince is one of our commonest cultivated shrubs, but is not common as a fully naturalised plant. However, it is frequently a long-persistent, suckering relic in abandoned gardens. A number of cultivars, mainly distinguished by flower colour, are grown and wild plants can be expected to reflect this range of colour. Naturalised in North Auckland (Mangamuka Hill), Nelson (Little Wanganui) and Christchurch; native to China, first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1988.
In New Zealand it is also called japonica, a name also used for the related Japanese quince (Chaenomeles japonica), which is grown here but not naturalised. 'Chinese quince' is also the name of a different tree, Pseudocydonia sinensis. Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and wild, with herbarium records from North Auckland, Taranaki, Wellington, Nelson, Westland and Canterbury. The name speciosa means handsome. It is sold in New Zealand garden centres as a flowering shrub and hedge plant.

warnings: The raw fruit is very harsh, sour and acid and is not eaten raw; cook it.

No seed analysis for this species was found. The seed is likely to contain cyanogenic glycosides, which release cyanide when digested: the seeds of the related Japanese quince (Chaenomeles japonica) contain them, and eating Chaenomeles seeds without pretreatment may be hazardous. Remove the seeds, or strain them out with the pulp.

identification.text:
In the most common variety, the fruit is roughly pear-shaped, somewhat flattened and with coarse wrinkles, ranging from 10–25 cm long, with thin green skin fused with green to white flesh, and a single, large, flattened stone. This seed or stone can be up to 10 cm long by 7 cm wide. Some varieties have spiny fruits. Depending on the variety, a single fruit can weigh up to 1.2 kg. Most New Zealand chokos are green, and smooth or covered in small spines. It flowers as the days shorten, so in New Zealand flowers may not appear until late summer or early autumn.
The chayote vine can be grown on the ground, but as a climbing plant, it will grow onto anything, and can easily rise as high as 12 m when support is provided. It has heart-shaped leaves, 10–25 cm wide and tendrils on the stem. The plant bears male flowers in clusters and solitary female flowers.
Told from moth plant (Araujia sericifera), whose pods look like choko fruit, by its more grape-like leaves and its tendrils: moth plant climbs by twining, its leaves are opposite and greyish-downy underneath, and its leathery pods hold kapok-like pulp and many seeds with silky tufts, not one large stone.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at how it climbs: choko holds on with tendrils on the stem; moth plant's stems twine. Look at the leaves: choko's are heart-shaped, 10–25 cm wide and more grape-like; moth plant's are 1.5–6 cm wide, ovate-oblong or oblong, in opposite pairs, dark green above and glaucous-white and downy underneath. Cut the fruit open: choko's holds a single large, flattened stone in firm green to white flesh; moth plant's thick, leathery pod holds kapok-like pulp and many dark brown seeds, 7–8 mm long, each with a silky tuft 3–5 cm long. In flower, moth plant's are white, deeply bell-shaped, about 2–2.5 cm long, sometimes streaked pinkish mauve inside, usually 2–4 together; choko's are small, white or greenish, the male ones in clusters and the female ones single. The fruits are of much the same pear shape and size (choko's 10–25 cm long, moth plant's pods up to 10, sometimes 12, cm long), and both grow around gardens and over hedges in the Auckland area and the Bay of Plenty. Moth plant is poisonous: its milky sap is poisonous in every part.
lookalikes.name: Moth plant

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: māwhai's are only about 6–10 mm long, egg-shaped, and densely covered in spines 1.6–3.6 mm long with backward-pointing barbs; choko's is a pear-shaped, pale green fruit 10–25 cm long holding a single large, flattened stone, and even the spiny kinds grown in New Zealand carry only small spines. The two have been confused when not in fruit: choko's leaves are larger and darker green, heart-shaped and 10–25 cm wide; māwhai's are grey-green, 3.5–19.5 × 4.5–20 cm, sharply 5- or 7-lobed with toothed edges and rough to the touch, and its stems carry harsh hairs. Māwhai's white male flowers, 4.5–7.8 mm across, come 8–19 along a long stalk, and its female flowers 8–11 together in a head; choko's male flowers are in clusters and its female flowers single. Both grow in the northern North Island: māwhai in coastal and lowland forest, scrub and bracken, and spreading into farmland and urban wasteland; choko near gardens and over hedges and fences. No record of māwhai as food was found, and it is At Risk – Naturally Uncommon.

preparation.text: Pick the fruit from about 5–7 cm long, before the seed has enlarged, when it is most tender, up to about 10–20 cm; smaller fruit are less sweet and suit savoury dishes, and larger, sweeter fruit can go into jams and preserves. Eat young fruit raw like cucumber. Steam, boil, bake, fry, mash or stir-fry older fruit, peeled and cut up with the central seed removed; it need not be peeled to be cooked or fried in slices. The seed is nutty when cooked and can be deep-fried. Pick the shoots down to the second leaf from the growing tip and cook them, with the young leaves, as a green vegetable, like asparagus: steam them or add them to stir-fries. Boil, bake, roast or fry the tuberous root like a potato, or candy it in syrup.

recipes.method: 1 choko, peeled with the seed removed; 1 scrubbed yacon; a quarter of a red cabbage; the juice of 1 lime; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) coconut sugar; 60 ml (¼ cup) coconut thread; 60 ml (¼ cup) raisins; 60 ml (¼ cup) mung bean sprouts; 4 sprigs of mint; 45 ml (3 tbsp) aioli (egg, aquafaba or tofu based); black pepper. Grate into a large bowl 1 choko, peeled with the seed removed (peel it whether you eat it raw or cooked; it is firm), and 1 scrubbed yacon. Add a quarter of a red cabbage, sliced as finely as you can, the juice of 1 lime, 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and 2.5 ml (½ tsp) coconut sugar, and toss; adding the lime and salt straight away takes away the choko's slightly astringent feel. Then add 60 ml (¼ cup) coconut thread, 60 ml (¼ cup) raisins, 60 ml (¼ cup) mung bean sprouts, 4 sprigs of mint, 45 ml (3 tbsp) aioli (egg, aquafaba or tofu based) and some black pepper, and toss well. Serves 4. It keeps well in the fridge.
recipes.title: Choko and yacon slaw

recipes.method: 1 kg choko (4–6 fruit); 30 ml (2 tbsp) plain salt; 750 ml (3 cups) cider vinegar; 125 ml (½ cup) raw sugar; 5 ml (1 tsp) pickling spice, or 5 ml (1 tsp) yellow mustard seed and a sprig of dill per jar, or a bay leaf and a few whole peppercorns per jar. Peel the chokos, take out the seed, cut them into quarters and then into spears about as thick as your thumb. Put them in a glass, plastic or stainless steel bowl, mix in the salt, cover and leave for an hour to dry-brine. Meanwhile heat six clean glass jars of about 400 ml in the oven at 125 °C for 30 minutes, and boil their lids in a pan of water for 10 minutes. Bring the vinegar, sugar and spices to the boil and simmer for 5–10 minutes. Drain the liquid off the chokos without rinsing them. Take the jars out with tongs and stand them on a wooden board or tea towel; put any dill or bay leaves straight into the jars. Pack the spears evenly into the jars, ladle the hot vinegar over them, and screw the boiled lids on tightly. Store in a cool, dark place and wait at least three weeks before eating. They keep for about two years.
recipes.title: Choko pickle

recipes.method: 12–18 g (2–3 tbsp) dried shrimp; 600 g choko; 22 ml (1½ tbsp) canola, vegetable or almond oil; 35 g shallots or onion, sliced; 2 cloves garlic, smashed; a few slices of ginger; 300 ml water or broth; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) sea salt (1.25 ml, ¼ tsp, if using broth); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) chicken bouillon powder (optional); sliced spring onions and toasted sesame seeds to serve. Rinse the dried shrimp and soak them in cold water for 30 minutes (or hot water for 15–20 minutes), then drain. Peel the chokos, cutting the skin off any deep ridges with a paring knife. Slice off the top, stand each one cut side down and halve it, trim any skin left on the bottom ridges, and dig out the seed. Cut each half lengthwise into two, slice 6–12 mm thick, and rinse and drain the slices. Heat the oil in a wok over medium-high heat and cook the shallots, garlic, ginger and shrimp for 1–2 minutes. Add the choko, water or broth, salt and bouillon powder and stir. Cover and cook for 7–8 minutes, until the choko is fork-tender but still a little firm. Taste the broth and add salt if needed. Serve topped with spring onions and sesame seeds. Serves 2. For a vegan version, cook a few diced shiitake mushrooms with the choko and use vegetable broth.
recipes.title: Chinese stir-fried choko

recipes.method: 500 g choko (2 medium); 22 ml (1½ tbsp) oil; 1 cm ginger, sliced; 2–3 large cloves garlic, sliced; 1 green or red chilli, chopped (optional); 2.5 ml (½ tsp) chilli powder or flakes; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) sea salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground cumin; a pinch (⅛ tsp) of turmeric (optional); 1 small tomato, deseeded and chopped (about 80 ml, ⅓ cup); 30 ml (2 tbsp) unsweetened desiccated coconut; 15 ml (1 tbsp) toasted sesame seeds or 30 ml (2 tbsp) roasted, skinned peanuts; 30 ml (2 tbsp) chopped coriander leaves. Peel the chokos over a bowl of water, rinsing them often to wash off the slippery sap, then trim both ends, halve them lengthwise, take out the seed and pith, and cut into pieces about 2 cm across. Heat the oil in a pan and fry the ginger, garlic and chilli for a minute. Add the choko and salt and stir-fry over medium-high heat for 4 minutes. Stir in the chilli powder, cumin and turmeric, add the tomato and stir-fry for another 4–5 minutes. Add about 80 ml (⅓ cup) water (very young chokos may not need it), cover and cook for about 10 minutes, adding a splash more water if the pan dries out, until tender but still a little crunchy. Taste for salt. Lightly crush the sesame seeds or peanuts in a mortar, then stir them in with the coconut and coriander. Serves 4, with rice, dal or flatbreads.
recipes.title: Spiced choko

recipes.method: 3 chokos (about 225 g each); 45 ml (3 tbsp) vegetable oil; 3 cloves garlic, finely chopped; 1 medium brown onion, finely diced (about 250 ml, 1 cup); 25 ml (1 tbsp plus 2 tsp) fish sauce; freshly ground black pepper. Peel the chokos and halve them lengthwise. With the tip of a knife or a spoon, take out the seed and the white part around it. Lay each half cut side down, cut it in half lengthwise, then slice it thinly across. Heat the oil in a 30 cm non-stick or cast-iron frying pan over medium heat until it shimmers. Cook the garlic, stirring now and then, for about 2 minutes, until it just starts to brown. Add the onion and cook for about 3 minutes, until it begins to soften. Add the choko and cook, stirring often, for about 10 minutes, until tender and cooked through. Stir in the fish sauce and season with pepper. Serves 6.
recipes.title: Sautéed choko

summary.text:
Choko (Sicyos edulis, long known as Sechium edule), also called chayote, is a climbing vine of the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae) from Central America, introduced to New Zealand.
It is grown in gardens, where it was once a common cover for backyard sheds and bare fences, and was recorded as naturalised in 1989. It is a perennial: frost kills the leaves back in late autumn and winter, but it resprouts from the crown in spring, and in the lower South Island it usually needs cover to ripen fruit. Herbarium specimens from the North Auckland, South Auckland and Nelson land districts and the Bay of Plenty include plants growing wild near gardens, some described as apparently naturalised, and it is not uncommon around Tauranga. It is not on the Department of Conservation's list of environmental weeds or in any regional pest management plan.

warnings: The sap that oozes from the fruit when it is peeled can irritate the skin: wear gloves when peeling and handling it.
Choko is a strong diuretic: eating it in large amounts has caused severe low blood potassium in a pregnant woman, which returned to normal once she stopped. Eat it in moderation.
