identification.text:
Perennial herb, with slender or sometimes fairly stout caulorrhiza. Hairs soft, retrorse or antrorse, generally appressed and often short, sometimes spreading. Stems slender, prostrate or spreading, with more or less retrorse hairs; branches usually many. Basal leaves rarely persistent through growing season; petioles to 12–(19) cm long; hairs retrorse and dense. Lamina usually to 3–(4) cm diameter, reniform to orbicular or broadly ovate, lobed 3/4-⅞ way to midrib; lobes (3)–5, narrowly to broadly obovate-cuneate, obovate-elliptic, obovate-oblong, or oblong, with appressed hairs on both sides or glabrous above, rounded to acute or mucronate at apex; larger lobes usually with 2 more or less oblong or elliptic secondary lobes. Cauline leaves smaller, with fewer lobes. Peduncles (with pedicels) usually 1–3–(4) cm long, filiform, with dense, retrorse hairs; bracteoles subulate or linear-subulate; flowers 1–(2). Sepals 3–5–(6) × 1–2.5 mm, lanceolate to elliptic, broadly elliptic or more or less ovate, usually with green margin, sometimes completely purple; hairs more or less spreading, often very short and antrorse towards apex, sometimes few. Petals 4–5 × 2–2.5 mm, broadly obovate, pink. Mericarps 2–3 mm long, with more or less dense hairs; beak (6)–7–10 mm long. Seed 1.5–1.9 mm long, oblong, distinctly alveolate.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped or cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Cinquefoil geranium and Solander's geranium are separated on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in Solander's geranium, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in Solander's geranium. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of Solander's geranium overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Solander's geranium's root is recorded as food.
lookalikes.name: Solander's geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Cinquefoil geranium and turnip-rooted geranium are separated on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in turnip-rooted geranium, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in turnip-rooted geranium. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of turnip-rooted geranium overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. No source read records turnip-rooted geranium as food, and it is Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable.
lookalikes.name: Turnip-rooted geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Cinquefoil geranium and Australasian cranesbill are separated on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in Australasian cranesbill, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in Australasian cranesbill. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of Australasian cranesbill overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Australasian cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food.

summary.text:
Geranium potentilloides, belongs to the family Geraniaceae, and is a small prostrate perennial herb that can grow up to 60cm high. The species is commonly referred to as Soft Cranesbill or Cinquefoil geranium.
Geranium potentilloides is native to the south-east of Australia, New Zealand and Indonesia.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Auckland southwards, widespread and common; South Island: Nelson, Marlborough, and collected once between Akatore and Glenledi (South Otago).

habitat.text:
Hedges, garden edges, fence lines, damp waste ground; scrambles over anything nearby.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): commonest among shrubs and tall herbs around cultivated areas, in waste places, forest margins, clearings and scrub, sometimes on newly exposed surfaces, rough pastures and cliff faces.

preparation.text: Cook — the hooks make it unpleasant raw. Wilt like spinach, blend into soup, or steep the fresh plant as a tea.

recipes.method: Fresh cleavers stems and leaves, enough to loosely fill a 1-quart (about 950 ml) jar; boiling water; ice and a sprig of mint, to serve. Loosely fill the jar with the cleavers and pour boiling water over them. Put the lid on and leave to steep for 4–6 hours. Strain, keep it in the fridge, and drink it over ice with a sprig of mint.
recipes.title: Cleavers tea

recipes.method: Written for Galium aparine in the UK. Serves 6. 100 g bunch of cleavers tops; 2 tablespoons olive oil; 2 garlic cloves, finely chopped; 2 medium onions, finely chopped; 2 red capsicums, roughly chopped; 1 red chilli, finely chopped; 400 g can of plum tomatoes; 50 ml elderberry pontack or Worcestershire sauce; ½ teaspoon hot pepper sauce; 1 tablespoon toasted seaweed such as nori or dulse; 1.5 litres hot water; salt and black pepper. Rinse the cleavers and snip off the roots with scissors. Warm a little of the oil in a saucepan and sweat the garlic and onions for 5 minutes, until they start to soften. Stir in the capsicums, then hold the bunch of cleavers over the pan and snip it in with scissors in 1–2 cm lengths, so the stems can't wind round the blender later. Cook for 5 minutes more. Pour in the hot water and add all the seasonings, then simmer for 15 minutes, until the capsicums are tender. Take the pan off the heat, let it cool and adjust the seasoning. Blend the cooled soup until completely smooth, with a stick blender or in a jug blender. Reheat and serve with finely chopped chives or wild garlic on top. The author sometimes adds a little crème fraîche or crumbled feta.
recipes.title: Cleavers and red pepper soup

recipes.method: The author's greens, picked from roadsides around Whangaroa Harbour, were nasturtium, kawakawa, fennel, samphire, fat hen, wild mustard, cleavers and clover. The author warns that New Zealand roadsides are still sprayed with glyphosate, so pick with care. 1 garlic clove (or 4 peeled onion weed bulbs); 60 ml (¼ cup) macadamia nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) grated parmesan, dairy or plant-based (or 125 ml, ½ cup, macadamias and no parmesan); 750 ml (3 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml extra-virgin olive oil; salt and pepper. Makes about 350 g. Blend in a food processor to the texture you like. Good on crackers or toast, as a side, or stirred through soup, pasta or rice.
recipes.title: Wild Whangaroa pesto

recipes.method: Written for cleavers, violet leaves, chickweed, red deadnettle and bittercress. A small handful of cleavers; 4 violet leaves; a handful of chickweed; 3 or 4 stems of red deadnettle; a small handful of bittercress; a big handful of bok choy, kale or silverbeet; 1 banana, peeled; 1 apple (whole without the stalk if organic, otherwise peeled); 1 mandarin (with its peel if organic, otherwise peeled); 1 or 2 kiwifruit, peeled; 1 small or ½ large avocado; 500 ml (2 cups) water, more if the blender struggles. Wash the weeds and greens, put them in the blender, snip them up a bit with scissors and add the water. Blend on low until the greens break down, then on high until smooth. Add the fruit and avocado and blend again, low and then high, until creamy.
recipes.title: Winter health boosting smoothie

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Often on or near hedges in settled areas, spreading to waste sites, roadsides, and footpaths, also gardens.
It also grows on bush and shrubland margins, along streams and on the coast, and invades tussockland, fernland, bare ground and dunes. It grows most strongly in open, sunny places.
Look for it near the coast, especially from Northland to the Bay of Plenty and south to Wellington, and around Tasman Bay (Nelson), with occasional plants near Blenheim and Picton.

identification.text:
Climbing or scrambling, dioecious or monoecious perennial with tuberous woody rootstock; stems to about 3 m long, glabrous, flexuous. Leaves all similar. Petioles slender, equal to or often longer than lamina. Lamina 3–8 × 2–6 cm, more or less triangular or hastate with 2 long basal lobes at 45° to petiole, otherwise entire, slightly puberulent on main veins below when young; sinus broad and rounded; apex acuminate to cuspidate. Panicle pyramidal, with small leaves in the lower axils only. Pedicels filiform, long, glabrous. Perianth 1.5–2 mm long, green; outer segments more or less ovate-oblong, becoming strongly reflexed in female flowers. Fruit valves (4)–6–9–(9.5) mm diameter, orbicular, entire, prominently reticulate, cordate, yellow, pink to crimson; tubercles 0. Nuts about 3 mm long, glossy light brown; keels almost winged. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It scrambles over hedges, shrubs and fences on stems up to about 3 m long, from brown, woody, beet-like tubers that in old plants can be more than 10 cm across. The arrowhead-shaped leaves have pointed basal lobes; the ribbed stems start green and turn red with age. Small green to pink flowers in clusters at the top of the plant become papery, three-winged, heart-shaped fruit, yellow, pink or crimson.
In New Zealand the tubers are kūmara- or beetroot-like, 5–20 cm long with yellow flesh, with long weak rhizomes running from them. The stems are short-lived, growing each year from the tubers, and zigzag as they climb; they redden with age, drought or cold. The light green, soft, slightly fleshy leaves have basal lobes pointing downwards. Flowers come at the top of the plant from November to March. The fruit is green at first, then pink to crimson, and ends straw-coloured to pale brown in large cascading clusters. No other climber here has both tubers and showy pink seed capsules.

lookalikes.howToTell: Climbing dock's stems are ribbed and it scrambles over its support rather than twining round it. Its flowers are tiny (1.5–2 mm), green to pink, in large branched clusters at the top of the plant, followed by masses of papery, heart-shaped, three-winged fruit, yellow, pink or crimson. Its leaves are 3–8 cm long with pointed basal lobes and a broad, rounded notch, and it grows from brown tubers with yellow flesh. Pink bindweed's stems are smooth and twine round other plants; its flowers are single pink trumpets, usually 5–6 cm long (3–7 cm), each with two large bracts hiding its base; its leaves are 3–14 cm long (rarely 17), the basal lobes usually rounded and the notch deep; its roots are white. Both have arrowhead-shaped leaves and both smother hedges and scrub on coastal, lowland and town land, so leaf shape alone does not separate them.

preparation.text: Strip the leaves off the stems, which can be woody. Use them raw in salads and green sauces or as a sharp garnish. Cooked, they lose some sharpness and colour and become silky and sweet-sour; in Indonesia they are baked with fish in place of tamarind.

recipes.method: Written for climbing (rambling) dock in Australia, with farmer's friend and dandelion leaves. Makes about 8 servings. 500 ml (2 cups) climbing dock leaves; 125 ml (½ cup) farmer's friend leaves; 125 ml (½ cup) dandelion leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) parsley leaves; 2 crushed garlic cloves; 2 tbsp drained capers; 125 ml (½ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; a dash of red wine vinegar; 1 tsp Dijon mustard; the juice of 1 lemon; sea salt and pepper. Put 500 ml (2 cups) climbing dock leaves, 125 ml (½ cup) farmer's friend leaves, 125 ml (½ cup) dandelion leaves, 250 ml (1 cup) parsley leaves, 2 crushed garlic cloves and 2 tbsp drained capers in a food processor and chop finely. With the motor running, add 125 ml (½ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, a dash of red wine vinegar, 1 tsp Dijon mustard and the juice of 1 lemon, and process until combined. Season with sea salt and pepper and leave it to stand for 10 minutes. Serve as a dipping sauce, condiment or marinade.

summary.text:
Rumex sagittatus, synonym Acetosa sagittata, commonly known as turkey rhubarb or rambling dock or potato vine, is a herbaceous perennial plant native to southern Africa, which has become a weed in Australia and New Zealand.
The plant is native to southern Africa, where it occurs from Malawi and Zambia south to South Africa. It has become naturalised in many parts of Australia near urban areas, from Queensland to eastern Tasmania, and warmer locales in New Zealand.
It spreads by seed or by resprouting from the tuber. The seeds float on water and hence may be conveyed far from the parent plant. Tubers may be broken up by tractors or road graders and each fragment may be able to regrow; they can also be difficult to find with removal of plants by hand. Rumex sagittatus may grow and smother other plants it covers.
It was brought to New Zealand as an ornamental and recorded wild by 1935. It is sometimes grown for its colourful fruit, and has been used to dye wool. It is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds and under sustained control across the Auckland region, where it smothers native plants and stops seedlings establishing.
A young plant can fruit within its first year and set thousands of seeds, which can lie dormant in the soil for at least two years. Seeds and tubers travel on the wind, in fresh and salt water, in moved soil and in dumped garden waste. It copes with wet and drought, dying back to its tubers in drought and, in cooler places, over winter, then regrowing in spring; after fire it resprouts from the tubers. Other names include arrow dock and arrowhead vine.

warnings: It contains oxalic acid, which gives the leaves their sharp taste. Do not eat it in large amounts, and leave it alone if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.
It is a pest plant controlled with herbicide sprays such as metsulfuron-methyl or glyphosate. Pick only where you know it has not been sprayed.

In the Auckland region it must not be bred, sold, distributed, released or planted. It regrows from its tubers and rhizomes and spreads by seed, so carry no living pieces elsewhere: rot them in a covered barrel of water, burn them, or send them to green waste, a refuse transfer station or landfill.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Usually damp places such as river banks and beds, ditches, drains and swampy places, also pastures and waste places in high rainfall areas, sometimes just above high tide level on beaches.
It grows throughout the North and South Islands.
New Zealand's national wetland plant list rates it FAC (facultative): it is common both in wetlands and on dry land.

identification.text:
Glabrous, short-lived, tap-rooted perennial; stems rather thin, wiry, flexuous, spreading, green to dark red, to about 1 m tall. Petioles of basal leaves often very long, particularly in subaquatic plants. Lamina of lower leaves (3)–7–20–(23) × (1)–1.5–3.5 cm, oblong or ovate-oblong, more or less membranous; margin often undulate and crisped; base broad-cuneate, rounded or cordate; apex acute or subacute. Stem leaves progressively smaller and extending about ⅔ along inflorescence branches. Inflorescence many-branched, spreading and flexuous, becoming twisted. Whorls all distant; flowers probably protandrous, bisexual, small, dense. Pedicels slender, reddish. Perianth (0.7)–1–5 mm long; outer segments ovate, obtuse, not reflexing at fruiting; inner segments greatly enlarging at fruiting. Fruiting valves 2–2.8–(3.2) mm long, ovate, reticulate, entire, rounded at apex, generally becoming dark red, each with a large tubercle occupying ?-3/4 valve width. Nut 1.5–2 mm long, dark glossy brown or reddish brown, acutely angled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Its flower whorls are all spaced well apart along spreading branches that twist as the fruit ripens, and small leaves run about two-thirds of the way up the branches. Each of the three fruit valves carries a large, smooth, oblong swelling (tubercle), all three well developed. Plants can be very reddish, especially in fruit.
It usually branches from below the middle of the stem, and its stiff branches spread wide rather than standing upright; the stems zig-zag. The stalks of the basal leaves are usually about as long as the blade. The fruiting heads turn rusty brown and stand out, and the ripe fruits snap off their slender jointed stalks when brushed.

lookalikes.howToTell: Curled dock's flower whorls are mostly packed together on erect branches, with few or no leaves among them; clustered dock's are all spaced apart along spreading branches that twist as they fruit, with small leaves about two-thirds of the way up. Curled dock's fruit valves are larger (3–4.5 mm), often with only one much larger tubercle; each of clustered dock's (2–3.2 mm) has a large tubercle. Curled dock's leaf base tapers into the stalk; clustered dock's is broadly wedge-shaped, rounded or heart-shaped. Both can have wavy, curled leaf edges.
lookalikes.name: Curled dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Broad-leaved dock's lower leaves reach 15 cm wide (rarely 20); clustered dock's are only 1–3.5 cm wide. Broad-leaved dock's flower whorls are usually packed together and its fruit valves have teeth 1–1.7 mm long on their edges and a prominent rosy tubercle; clustered dock's whorls are all spaced apart, on branches that twist as they fruit, and its valves (2–3.2 mm) are entire, each with a large tubercle.
lookalikes.name: Broad-leaved dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Fiddle dock's lower leaves are flat and pinched in the lower half above two large rounded lobes (occasionally plain and oblong); clustered dock's are oblong, often wavy and curled, and sometimes slightly pinched part way down, but usually not as sharply. Both have spaced whorls on branches that twist as they fruit, but fiddle dock's fruit valves have spines up to 2 mm long on their edges, while clustered dock's are entire.

preparation.text: Pick the leaves young, before the flower stalk rises, when they become more bitter and astringent. Take out the central vein, boil the leaves and throw the water away: this softens the bitterness and lowers the oxalic acid. Use them as cooked greens. Grind the seeds into a powder and add it to flour for bread or biscuits.

recipes.method: Written for dock generally — the author thinks his leaves were most likely curled dock but is not certain; the New Zealand version below names broad-leaved and curled dock; clustered dock is very bitter, more so as it ages, so use only young leaves. Serves 4. You need 170 g young dock leaves, washed; salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to finish; 50 g (¼ cup) basmati or other long-grain rice; 1 small onion, chopped; 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped garlic; 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped fresh oregano; a pinch of ground cumin; 1 litre chicken or vegetable stock; 1 large egg, beaten; black pepper; and plenty of fresh lemon juice. Drop the dock leaves into boiling salted water for a few seconds until just wilted, cool them in cold water and squeeze them dry (about 180 ml). Toast the rice on a tray in a 175 °C oven until just golden, then simmer it, covered, with a pinch of salt and 125 ml water until tender. Chop the dock both ways so no long strands are left. In a 3-litre pot, soften the onion and garlic in the oil over medium heat for about 10 minutes, until just browning at the edges. Add the stock, dock, oregano and cumin, bring to a simmer and season, then add the rice and simmer gently for about 10 minutes. Pour the beaten egg in a spiral over the surface without stirring and let it heat through. Serve with a drizzle of olive oil, black pepper and enough lemon juice that the soup tastes lemony. For a simpler version without egg (Wild Botanica, New Zealand): soften the onion and garlic, wilt the chopped leaves (central veins removed) in the pot, add the stock, cumin, oregano and salt, simmer for 10 minutes, then stir through 60 ml (¼ cup) cooked rice and finish with lemon juice.
recipes.title: Dock soup with rice, egg and lemon

summary.text:
Rumex conglomeratus, known as clustered dock and sharp dock, is a plant of the family Polygonaceae; an older name for it is Rumex acutus. It is native to Europe, North Africa and Asia Minor and was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1867. Kew's Plants of the World Online gives a wider native range, east to Central Asia and the western Himalaya and also South Africa, and lists it as introduced in the Americas, Japan, Korea, Tasmania and Norfolk Island as well as both main islands of New Zealand.
It is a weed of pasture and cultivated ground, though in Australia it is less aggressive than curled dock. It spreads by seed: ripe fruits break off when people, animals or machinery brush the dry branches, and travel on the wind (the valves act as sails), in mud, and on water (the tubercles act as floats). Pieces of the crown and upper taproot cut up by cultivation can regrow. Red-veined dock (Rumex sanguineus) has been reported from New Zealand, but the Flora of New Zealand (1988) found no specimens and suggests plants so named may have been clustered dock, which can also be very reddish.

warnings: It contains oxalic acid, which gives the leaves their sharp taste. A little is fine, but large amounts can lock up calcium and other minerals in food; cooking lowers the oxalic acid. Take particular care, or leave it alone, if you are prone to rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.
Large amounts of dock leaves that are not properly cooked can cause nausea, stomach cramps, vomiting and headache.

habitat.text:
Lactarius glyciosmus is a common mushroom and is found under broad-leaved trees, particularly birch—often inside of sphagnum moss. It grows in soil individually or in scattered groups.
In New Zealand it is one of several introduced species associated with birch (Betula spp.).

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to pick this mushroom. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.

identification.text:
Lactarius glyciosmus is a small to medium-sized agaric, which typically has a convex cap measuring between 2 and 6 centimetres, with a small central depression developing with age. Sometimes there is a central pimple, and the cap is typically coloured a greyish lilac, sometimes varying to a pale buff. It is thin fleshed, with an incurved margin in younger specimens. The stem measures between 25 and 65 millimetres in height, with a width between 4 and 12 mm. The cylindrical stem is typically widest at the bottom becoming narrower towards the top, or sometimes club shaped. The stem is concolorous with the cap, but sometimes is a little paler or with a yellowish hue. The stem is particularly soft and easily broken, and can become hollow. The flesh is buff. The gills are decurrent and crowded, and vary in colour from a pale yellowish to a pale flesh, turning to a greyish lilac with age. The milk is white with an initially mild, later hot and acrid taste. The mushroom has a strong smell of coconuts.
The spore print is a creamy white colour, and the spores themselves are broadly elliptic in shape, and covered with small warts. The warts are connected by thin ridges in an incomplete network. The spores measure between 8 and 9 by between 5 and 6 micrometres.


Similar species
It is similar to L. vietus, the grey milk cap, but is differentiated by the fact L. vietus milk dries grey, while L. glyciosmus milk dries white. It can also be confused with L. cocosiolens, which also smells of coconuts, but L. cocosiolens has a slimy brown or orange cap and is not found among birch.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. Coconut milk cap's milk is white, rather watery and unchanging, its cap is greyish lilac, pale greyish brown or brownish grey with leaden tints rather than orange, and it smells of coconut - faintly, in the New Zealand description. It grows under silver birch; saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine.

edibleParts.text: Young leaves, flower buds, petals and flower stalks; the roots are also listed among the parts used for food. The young leaves are eaten raw in salads or cooked as a potherb, and become increasingly astringent with age; their flavour is variously described as somewhat acrid, pleasantly sour, mild and agreeable, lettuce-like, or bitter with a medicinal aftertaste. Flower buds and petals are eaten raw in sandwiches, soups and salads, and the buds are pickled in vinegar as a substitute for capers. The flowers are also used for tea, on their own or with the leaves.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Mostly in lawns and pastures especially in wetter areas, also waste places, forest margins and clearings, stream banks, seepages, cultivated land, dunes and tussock grassland.
In New Zealand it does best in moist soil and copes well with shade, and it is best suited to sheep-grazed pasture and closely mown lawns, where its small size keeps it below the height of grazing or mowing (Massey University, restated).
It prefers field-like habitats.

identification.text:
Stoloniferous rosette perennial. Basal leaves cuneately narrowed to a petiole more or less equal to lamina, mostly spathulate, obovate or elliptic-oblong, crenate-serrate with 2–6 pairs of teeth or remote denticles, almost glabrous to moderately hairy on both surfaces, often more hairy on lower, with 1 main vein, (10)–20–60–(80) × (4)–8–20–(25) mm. Peduncle moderately to densely hairy, leafless, 3–15–(25) cm long. Capitula 15–25 mm diameter at anthesis; receptacle conic. Involucral bracts ovate- to elliptic-oblong, usually obtuse, rarely subacute, sparsely to moderately hairy. Ray florets in 1–(5) rows; ligules linear, white, often tinged pink to reddish purple on lower surface or at apex, rarely wholly pink to reddish purple, 5–8–(11) mm long. Disc florets yellow. Achenes hairy, brown with pale ribs, 1–1.3–(1.6) mm long; pappus 0. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The rosettes stay small and flat and often grow in patches joined by short, stout rhizomes; each leaf is spoon-shaped, and the head, about 2 cm across, sits alone on an unbranched, leafless stalk (Massey University, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Lawn daisy's flower stalk is leafless, 3–15 cm long (up to 25 cm), and rises from a flat rosette with a single head 15–25 mm across. Ox-eye daisy's flowering stems are leafy and erect, up to about 1 m tall, with one or a few heads usually 30–60 mm across (25–65 mm at the extremes), so the two meet only at about 25 mm. Ox-eye's upper stem leaves are stalkless, narrow and clasp the stem, often with ear-like lobes at the base; its basal leaves are long-stalked, coarsely toothed, scalloped or shallowly lobed, and up to 12 cm long (rarely 18 cm). Lawn daisy's leaves are spoon-shaped to oblong, usually 20–60 mm long (10–80 mm at the extremes), with 2–6 pairs of shallow teeth and one main vein. Lawn daisy's rays are often tinged pink to reddish purple underneath or at the tip; ox-eye's are white. What does not separate them: white rays around a yellow disc, and young rosettes — both have spoon-shaped, scalloped basal leaves, though ox-eye's rosettes grow into taller clumps while lawn daisy's stay small and flat. Ox-eye daisy is eaten too — its young leaves, shoots and flower buds (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Ox-eye daisy

lookalikes.howToTell: Roman chamomile's leaves are cut three times into narrow, thread-like segments that point in different directions, giving a feathery look, and its hairy, leafy stems creep or rise to about 20 cm, branching from the base. Lawn daisy's leaves are undivided, spoon-shaped to oblong, with 2–6 pairs of shallow teeth, all in a basal rosette, and its flower stalk is leafless. Roman chamomile is sweetly aromatic. Inside the head, Roman chamomile's receptacle carries small, blunt scales among the florets; lawn daisy's has none. What does not separate them: head size (Roman chamomile about 8–20 mm across, up to 30 mm; lawn daisy 15–25 mm), white rays around a yellow disc, and place — both grow in lawns, and Roman chamomile is planted as a lawn. Roman chamomile's fresh or dried flowers are used for herb tea and its young sprigs as a seasoning (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Roman chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: Stinking mayweed is an annual with leafy stems, usually much-branched from the base, standing or rising usually 30–40 cm tall (5–60 cm at the extremes), and its leaves are cut three times into narrow segments with a somewhat feathery look. Lawn daisy has undivided, spoon-shaped, toothed leaves in a basal rosette and a leafless flower stalk. Stinking mayweed is strongly foetid. Its receptacle carries narrow, pointed scales, usually only in the inner two-thirds; lawn daisy's has none. Its white rays bend back as the head ages. What does not separate them: head size (stinking mayweed about 15–30 mm across, up to 35 mm; lawn daisy 15–25 mm), white rays around a yellow disc, and place — both grow in lawns and pasture. Stinking mayweed is not a food plant: its juice is acrid, touching or eating it can cause allergies in some people, the foliage may irritate skin, and there are reports of toxicity.

preparation.text: Leaves: pick young ones, as older leaves are more astringent — they are most tender in spring, though regularly mown lawns put up fresh, tender growth at any time of year; eat them mixed with other salad leaves to soften the bitter aftertaste, or cook them — wilted in butter with a splash of stock, or as a potherb. Buds: pack unopened buds into a jar, cover them with hot salted vinegar (spices optional) and leave them four to six weeks to mature. Flowers and petals: raw over salads and sandwiches, as a garnish, or steeped in boiled water for tea — pour boiling water over the flowers and leaves and leave them about 10 minutes. Whole daisy chains can be laid over fish, dressings, salads or cooked greens as an edible decoration. The whole plant, roots included, can be chopped, sautéed and simmered in a soup.

recipes.method: Written for the lawn daisy, Bellis perennis. 1 cup (250 ml) unopened daisy flower buds; ½ teaspoon black peppercorns; 4 allspice berries; a few sprigs of rosemary or lavender, or another herb you like; 1 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste; ½ teaspoon mustard seeds; 1 garlic clove, finely sliced; ½ tablespoon honey; 1 cup (250 ml) white wine vinegar. Wash the buds, trim the stems and let them dry well, so no water dilutes the vinegar. Put the peppercorns, allspice, salt, mustard seeds and garlic in the bottom of a 500 ml jar (or two 250 ml jars) and pack the buds in on top. Heat the vinegar until it is almost boiling, take it off the heat and pour it over the buds to fill the jar to the rim. Seal with vinegar-proof lids, label, and keep in a cool, dark cupboard for four to six weeks to mature. The page lists the honey and herb sprigs among the ingredients but its steps do not say when to add them. Use them in pasta, chicken piccata, egg sandwiches or potato salad.
recipes.title: Daisy flower capers

recipes.method: Serves 2 as a starter or side. 12 medium-sized daisy leaf rosettes; 8 baby beetroots; 4 large garlic cloves, peeled and left whole; a small handful each of fresh thyme and sage, chopped; light olive oil; rosehip syrup or balsamic vinegar; chicken stock; butter; pepper. The page gives no amounts for the oil, syrup, stock, butter or pepper. Wash the daisy greens and spin or pat them dry. Scrub the beetroots, top and tail them but keep them whole. Lightly crush the garlic with the back of a knife. Lay the beetroots in a row on a large sheet of thick foil with a garlic clove between each, drizzle with enough oil to glaze them, then with syrup or vinegar as you would dress a salad, and sprinkle over the herbs. Fold the foil to seal and bake at 200 °C (gas 6) for an hour, or until the beetroots are tender. Unwrap, keeping the juices; pour the juices into a saucepan with a good knob of butter, melt it, add the whole daisy greens and keep stirring, then add a splash of stock and reduce quickly. Serve with the beetroots.
recipes.title: Sautéed daisy greens with roasted baby beetroots

recipes.method: Written for Bellis perennis. About 6–8 oz (about 170–225 g) of whole daisy plants — roots, leaves and flower heads — (use the roots only where daisies are plentiful); a few drops of olive oil; half a cup (125 ml) of white wine or apple cider; 1 litre of vegetable broth; salt and pepper; a dash of cream; croutons to serve. Clean the plants well (soil clings to the roots on heavy clay) and chop them, not too small. Sauté them quickly in a heavy pan with the oil, add the wine or cider and let the alcohol cook off, then stir in the broth. Season to taste, finish with a dash of cream and serve with croutons. The page gives no simmering time.
recipes.title: Daisy soup

summary.text:
Bellis perennis ( BEL-iss pə-REN-iss), the daisy, is a European species of the family Asteraceae, often considered the archetypal species of the name daisy.
Bellis perennis is native to western, central and northern Europe, including remote islands such as the Faroe Islands, but has become widely naturalised in most temperate regions, including the Americas and Australasia.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island, South Island, Stewart Island; Chatham, Auckland and Campbell Islands: locally abundant throughout. Native range Europe to western Asia; naturalised in New Zealand by 1867.
B. perennis is an extremely common lawn weed and its stoloniferous habit allows it to form dense patches. The species is also cultivated and selected forms with coloured ligules and semi-double heads are occasionally found wild.
In New Zealand pastures it seldom causes problems, though in Southland and Otago it can become aggressive and dominate pasture; livestock generally avoid eating it, and it is often one of the few plants left in pasture badly damaged by porina caterpillars (Massey University, restated).
In New Zealand it is also called English daisy (NZPCN) and daisy or double daisy (Biota of NZ), and it is sold as a garden bedding plant with double or single heads in pink, rose and white (Yates, restated).
The Department of Conservation lists it among New Zealand's environmental weeds (2024), as a fully naturalised plant with more than minor impacts in natural ecosystems (restated).

warnings: People allergic to plants of the daisy family (Asteraceae) can react to it. Few side effects are recorded from eating it, but eat it in moderation.
In herbal medicine the plant is classed as laxative and purgative.
Daisies in lawns and turf can be controlled with herbicides — clopyralid, triclopyr/picloram and 2,4-D/dicamba mixes — so plants picked from a lawn may have been sprayed.

identification.text:
Common mallow is a herbaceous perennial with an erect or decumbent branched stem up to 1.5 metres tall. The minutely ridged stems are covered with fine soft hairs, sometimes with a slightly bulbous base. The leaves are alternate, with a petiole up to 20 centimetres long, simple but palmate, with stellate hairs (i.e. several strands radiating from a common center) and prominent veins on the underside. 

The flowers are reddish-purple with dark stripes and occur in axillary clusters along the main stem with the flowers at the base opening first. There are 5 petals, and 5 sepals, 3–6 mm long, which are fused in the lower half, and have broadly triangular lobes. There is also an epicalyx (or false calyx) with oblong segments, two-thirds as long as calyx lobes (2–3 mm long x 1.5 mm wide).


Fruits
Nutlets strongly reticulate (usually without hair, with sharp angle between dorsal and lateral surfaces, 5–6 mm in diameter.


Seeds
Also called 'cheeses', the seeds are brown to brownish green when ripe, about 2.5 mm long and wide.


Chemistry
M. sylvestris contains malvin and malonylmalvin. It also contains the naphthoquinone malvone A, which is also a phytoalexin.

The large-flowered mallow is very variable in size, particularly of the flowers, and petals may vary in colour from pale pink through to a deep bluish purple. Small-flowered plants appear similar to M. nicaeensis but are distinguished by the slightly longer petals, longer fruiting pedicels, and the presence of hairs at the base of the calyx tube.

Perennial, ascending to erect herb. Stems glabrous to densely hairy with simple and stellate hairs. Leaves more or less glabrous to densely hairy, reniform to suborbicular, obtuse to cordate at base, shallowly or moderately 3–5–(7)-palmately lobed and crenate, 1–15–(20) cm diameter; petioles 1–15–(30) cm long; stipules narrowly to broadly ovate with acute apex, 3–10 mm long. Flowers 2–10 in axillary clusters or irregular racemes; fruiting pedicels 10–45 mm long; epicalyx segments narrow-oblong to elliptic-ovate, somewhat shorter than calyx; calyx teeth broadly ovate with acute apex, sparsely to densely hairy with stellate or simple hairs and ciliate, not enlarged at fruiting; petals from deep pink to reddish or bluish purple with darker markings, 2–5× as long as calyx, 12–30 mm long. Mericarps 8–12–(15) per fruit, usually glabrous, strongly reticulately veined on back; edges sharply angled but not winged.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Both have strongly net-veined fruit segments, so the veining does not separate them; use the petal length, the calyx in fruit and the edges of the fruit segments. Leaf shape and size overlap (cheeseweed mallow 1–8 cm across, common mallow 1–15(–20) cm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cretan mallow is often confused with forms of common mallow whose epicalyx segments are slightly joined at the base; it is separated by its round-edged, more or less smooth-backed fruit segments (net-veined and sharply angled in common mallow), its long-pointed calyx teeth (acute in common mallow) and its generally broader epicalyx segments. Petal colour and length overlap. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Petal lengths overlap between 12 and 15 mm, and common mallow can have pale pink flowers, so on a pale, mid-sized flower use the fruit: hairy and smooth-backed in dwarf mallow, usually hairless and strongly net-veined in common mallow. Dwarf mallow lies flat or ascends and common mallow ascends or stands upright, so an ascending plant fits both. Leaf shape and size overlap. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. French mallow is separated from small forms of common mallow by the hairless base of the calyx tube (hairy in common mallow); common mallow also has slightly longer petals and longer fruiting stalks. Both have strongly net-veined fruit segments, so the veining does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and are unchanged in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Island mallow's petals (30–40 mm) and common mallow's (12–30 mm) only meet at 30 mm, and both are pink to purple with darker veins or markings, so the flower colour does not separate them; check the calyx, long and tube-shaped in island mallow, and the fruit, smooth with one low rib against strongly net-veined. Leaf size overlaps. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. They are separated by the upper stem leaves (cut almost to the base in musk mallow, shallowly lobed in common mallow) and the fruit (densely hairy and smooth-backed against usually hairless and net-veined). Petal lengths overlap ((15–)20–30 mm against 12–30 mm), so the flower does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. The flowers overlap: both are pink to purple with darker veins or markings, and tree mallow's 15–20 mm petals sit inside common mallow's 12–30 mm range. Use the epicalyx, which is longer than the calyx and enlarged in fruit in tree mallow but shorter than the calyx in common mallow (whose epicalyx segments may be somewhat joined at the base, so joining alone is not a test), and the fruit, ribbed crosswise against net-veined. Both have lobed leaves that can reach 20 cm across. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.

preparation.text: In Morocco, Tunisia and Palestine, Malva leaves are steamed with garlic and tomatoes, and eaten as an appetizer or salad. In Egypt, the leaves are made into a stew-like vegetable dish, known as khobeiza, which is similar to Molokheia. In Spain the tender leaves are eaten fresh in salads, alone or with other plants (Alt Empordà, Córdoba), or blanched (Alt Empordà, central Valencia, Mallorca); they have also been eaten fried, and in Cabo de Gata stewed alone or with other greens. In Albanchez de Mágina (Jaén) they are boiled and then sautéed. More rarely the petals are eaten raw in salads. The flowers are infused as a cooling drink (La Garrotxa), and flowers and fruits go into homemade ratafia liqueurs in Catalonia. The commonest use is the fruits, eaten on the spot as a snack, slightly unripe or ripe, even as they start to dry on the plant; their shape gives them names such as panecillos (little bread rolls) and quesitos (little cheeses). The fruits can be very constipating.

recipes.method: Written for mallow in general; the page names no species. Serves 2. 450 g mallow leaves, 2 tbsp (30 ml) olive oil, 1 medium onion, diced, and 1 medium lemon. Pull the leaves off the stems and soak them in water with a small pinch of salt, then rinse well under running water to remove any dirt or grit and drain completely. Fry the onion in the oil until soft and translucent, then lift it out. In the same pan, cook the leaves with a splash of water over medium heat, stirring now and then, until they wilt and shrink. Once they are tender, stir the onion back in, tip onto a plate and finish with lemon juice, to taste, and a drizzle of olive oil. The source notes that young leaves are best; older ones are tougher and have less flavour. Good with vermicelli rice or fresh pita bread.
recipes.title: Sautéed mallow with onions (khobeizeh)

recipes.method: Written for Malva sylvestris. 6 large eggs (or more, to fill the tray); 3 tbsp milk; grated Parmigiano Reggiano; salt and freshly ground nutmeg to taste; and freshly picked mallow leaves (the page gives no amount). Heat the oven to 180 °C. Cook the leaves in boiling water for a few minutes, rinse, and blend to a purée. Whisk the eggs, milk, cheese, salt and nutmeg in a small bowl, stir in the mallow purée, and pour into a prepared muffin tray. Bake until cooked through and golden, 30–35 minutes. Leave to cool, then keep in a container in the fridge until eaten.
recipes.title: Egg muffins with mallow

recipes.method: Written for common mallow (Malva sylvestris) picked in Andalusia, as a mallow version of the Granada tapa of spinach with chickpeas. A bag of mallow leaves; a large jar of chickpeas (drained); 4 tsp (20 ml) cumin seeds; half a bulb of garlic (crushed); the juice of 1 lemon; olive oil; and salt. Rinse the leaves, roll them into a tight bunch and slice roughly at about 1 cm. Steam them gently, covered, over low heat with a small cup of water until wilted, then set aside; mallow goes dry if only fried, so steam it first. Dry-toast the cumin seeds in a large frying pan until lightly browned and grind them. Fry the cumin in olive oil over medium heat for a minute, add the garlic and stir for about two minutes, then stir in the chickpeas to coat them, and then the mallow. Cover and simmer gently for 10–15 minutes, adding a little water if it dries out. Season with salt and lemon juice. Serve on its own or with bread.
recipes.title: Mallow with chickpeas (espinacas con garbanzos style)

recipes.method: Written for common mallow, used in place of jute mallow in an adaptation of the Egyptian green soup molokhia. Serves 4. 200 g mallow leaves (plus a few flowers to decorate), 2 tbsp (30 ml) olive oil, 1 small onion, finely chopped, salt, 4 garlic cloves, chopped, 2 tsp (10 ml) ground coriander, 500 ml well-flavoured stock and 4 tbsp (60 ml) natural yoghurt. For the dukkah: 2 tbsp (30 ml) hazelnuts; 1 tbsp (15 ml) sunflower seeds; 2 tsp (10 ml) sesame seeds; 1 tsp (5 ml) each of cumin, fennel, nigella and coriander seeds; and ½ tsp (2.5 ml) sweet paprika. Strip and rinse the leaves and chop roughly. Soften the onion with a pinch of salt in the oil over low heat for 5 minutes, add the garlic until lightly golden, then the coriander until fragrant, then the stock, and bring to the boil. For the dukkah, roast the hazelnuts at 160 °C for 10 minutes, rub off their skins in a tea towel, toast the seeds for 5–10 minutes until lightly browned, then crush everything roughly in a mortar and mix in the paprika. Add the leaves to the boiling stock and cook about 5 minutes, until tender but still bright green, then purée and season. Serve with a spoonful of yoghurt, the dukkah and the flowers, with rice or flatbread.
recipes.title: Mallow soup with hazelnut dukkah

recipes.method: Written for common mallow (Malva sylvestris), cooked to a molokhia recipe. 800 g common mallow leaves, 6–8 garlic cloves, crushed, about 1 litre of chicken broth, 1 tbsp (15 ml) vegetable or olive oil, ½ tsp (2.5 ml) salt and a pinch of black pepper. Bring the broth to the boil, add the washed leaves, return to a mild boil, then simmer gently without boiling, stirring now and then, until the leaves have melted (15–20 minutes); simmer about 5 minutes more and take off the heat. Fry the garlic in the oil over medium heat until golden, without burning it, add the pepper, then ladle soup into the pan a little at a time — it should sizzle — until it is all mixed in. Salt to taste and eat as it is, or poured over rice and toasted pita.
recipes.title: Garlic mallow soup (molokhia style)

summary.text:
Malva sylvestris is a species of the mallow genus Malva, of which it is the type species. Known as common mallow to English-speaking Europeans, it acquired the common names of cheeses, high mallow and tall mallow (mauve des bois by the French) as it migrated from its native home in Western Europe, North Africa and Asia through the English-speaking world.
One of the major areas that it grows in is northeast and central Iran. It is also found in North Africa and grows as a biennial in the Mediterranean; it grows as a perennial elsewhere. It has been introduced to and has become naturalised in eastern Australia, in the United States, Canada, and Mexico as an invasive species.
Palearctic:
Macaronesia: Azores, Madeira Islands
Northern Africa: Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco
Arabian Peninsula: Saudi Arabia
Western Asia: Afghanistan, Sinai, Iran, Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey
Caucasus: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Ciscaucasia, Dagestan, Georgia
Soviet Middle Asia: Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan
Mongolia: Mongolia
China: Xinjiang
Indian Subcontinent: Bhutan, India, Pakistan
Northern Europe: Denmark, Finland, Ireland, Norway, Sweden, United Kingdom
Middle Europe: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Netherlands, Poland, Slovakia, Switzerland
East Europe: Belarus, Central Russia, Central Black Earth, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova, Northern Russia, North Caucasus, Northwestern Russia, Volga, Urals, Volga-Vyatka, Ukraine
Southeastern Europe: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Italy, Macedonia, Montenegro, Sardinia, Serbia, Sicily, Slovenia, Romania, Cyprus
Southwestern Europe: Balearic Islands, Corsica, France, Portugal, Spain
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North Island except Taranaki, in Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury and Otago, and on the Chatham Islands. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1870.

warnings: When grown on nitrogen rich soils (and particularly when these are cultivated inorganically), the plant tends to concentrate high levels of nitrates in its leaves.

identification.text: Cerastium fontanum is a low growing plant covered with small hairs which are not sticky, that is, without glandular tips. The erect flowering stems up to 45 cm long and leaves, opposite, up to 20 mm long without stalks. It has prostrate branches which do not bear flowers. The 5 petals are shorter than the sepals or a little longer and are deeply divided. The flowers have 10 stamens with 5 separate styles.

sources: Knox, Johanna. A Forager's Treasury: A New Zealand guide to finding and using wild plants (Allen & Unwin, 2013).

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Poor stony or gravelly pastures, screes, stony river beds, roadsides and railways, shingle river banks and beds, dry waste places, sea level to about 1000 m.
Great mullein most frequently grows as a colonist of bare and disturbed soil, usually on sandy or chalky ones. It grows best in dry, sandy, or gravelly soils, although it can grow in a variety of habitats, including banksides, meadows, roadsides, forest clearings, and pastures.

identification.text:
Annual or biennial, with greyish or white tomentum of stellate hairs; stems to about 1 m tall, usually simple, sometimes with a few branches from near base. Rosette leaves shortly petiolate, 7–20 × 3.5–10 cm, elliptic-ovate to elliptic-obovate, crenulate; base attenuate; apex obtuse to acute. Cauline leaves sessile, often more elongated, oblong, to about 30 cm long; base decurrent. Inflorescence dense, woolly, to about 80 cm high, simple or sometimes with 1–2 branches. Bracts lanceolate, acuminate. Flowers subsessile or very shortly pedicellate, 1-several in each axil. Calyx 8–12 mm long, deeply lobed; lobes triangular-acuminate. Corolla 1.5–2.5–(3) cm diameter, yellow, hairy; lobes rounded. Stamens 5; upper 3 stamens with white-villous filaments; lower 2 stamens glabrous or nearly so, and with anthers decurrent. Capsule 8–10 mm long, broad-ovoid, exserted from calyx. Seeds cylindric-oblong, rugose; apex truncate. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
V. thapsus is a dicotyledonous plant that produces a rosette of leaves in its first year of growth. All parts of the plants are covered with star-shaped trichomes. This cover is particularly thick on the leaves, giving them a silvery appearance.
Each flower is open for a single day, opening before dawn and closing in the afternoon.
Of the five mulleins naturalised in New Zealand, only this one keeps its stems and leaves woolly. The others have stems and leaves that are not woolly and stamens with purple hairs, except Verbascum pulverulentum, whose wool thins with age and whose flower spike has many slender branches.

lookalikes.howToTell: Foxglove is deadly. Its rosette leaves are hairy to almost hairless on top and grey-felted only underneath, and narrow into a long, winged stalk; common mullein's are covered all over in greyish or white star-shaped hairs that stay woolly, and are only shortly stalked. Both have finely scalloped edges, their leaf sizes overlap (foxglove 10–25 cm long, mullein rosette leaves 7–20 cm), and both grow on poor pastures, stony river beds and roadsides, so none of those tells them apart. In flower there is no confusion: mullein carries a dense, woolly spike of flat, yellow, five-lobed flowers 1.5–2.5 cm across (to 3 cm); foxglove a spike of nodding bells mostly 3.5–5 cm long, usually pinkish purple with dark spots, sometimes white. A foxglove with greenish-yellow flowers (Digitalis lutea) is grown in gardens; it had not been reported growing wild by 1988, and its plants are hairless or nearly so. If a rosette leaf is not woolly on top as well as underneath, or narrows into a long, winged stalk, leave it.

preparation.text: For leaf tea, infuse dried leaves in boiling water for 5–10 minutes; the tea is aromatic and slightly bitter. The leaves are taken from first-year rosettes. Pick young, tender leaves, and pass over any that are brown or spoiling. Fresh leaves give a lighter, greener tea; dried leaves are mellower and strain clearer. Fresh or dried flowers make a sweeter tea. The flowers are thin and bruise easily, and go mouldy readily while drying; a cup is 1.5–2 g of dried flowers in 150 ml of boiling water. For root tea, clean, peel and dice the root first. Strain every drink through a fine cloth: the tiny hairs on the leaves and on the stamens irritate the throat and can set off a cough. The leaves also go into shrubs, syrups and fizzy fermented sodas (see the recipes). The raw flowers can be scattered over salads, and in Catalonia they were nibbled as a treat. In New Zealand it flowers from July to April, mostly December to April; the rosette leaves are there all year.

recipes.method: Written for dried mullein leaves. Hot: 1 tbsp dried mullein leaves per 200 ml cup; boiling water. Cold: 1–2 tsp dried leaves per cup, or 4–8 tsp for 1 litre; cold filtered water. Optional: a teaspoon of honey; a squeeze of lemon or lime; a few dried peppermint or lemon balm leaves, or a slice of fresh ginger. For hot tea, put the leaves in the cup, pour boiling water over them and steep for 10–15 minutes, then strain. For cold tea, cover the leaves with cold water in a jar, stir so they are all under, cover and steep in the fridge for 8–12 hours or overnight, then strain and serve over ice; it is smoother and less bitter. The page strains through a fine mesh or sieve, or cheesecloth for the cold tea; strain through a fine cloth, which catches the leaf hairs (see the warnings).
recipes.title: Mullein leaf tea, hot or cold-brewed

recipes.method: 250 ml loosely packed fresh mullein leaves (or 125 ml dried); 250 ml apple cider vinegar; 250 ml sugar or honey; optional: 125 ml thinly sliced lemon, orange or lime, or sliced ginger. Rinse the leaves gently, pat them dry and, if fresh, chop roughly. In a clean glass jar, muddle the leaves, citrus or ginger (if using) and sugar, then pour the vinegar over. Stir to dissolve the sugar and close the jar tightly. Keep in a cool, dark place for 3–5 days, shaking daily. Strain through a fine cloth, pressing the solids gently, and bottle. Keep in the fridge for up to 6 months. Use it in drinks and mocktails.
recipes.title: Mullein leaf shrub

recipes.method: 60 ml loosely packed fresh or dried mullein leaves; 1–2 tbsp chopped ginger or citrus zest; 250 ml sugar; juice of ½ lemon; 1 litre filtered water; optional: a grape or a few raisins, to start the wild yeast. Combine everything in a clean 2-litre glass jar and stir to dissolve the sugar. Cover with a thin cloth or coffee filter held on with a rubber band. Leave at room temperature, out of direct sun, for 2–4 days, stirring once a day, until it bubbles and is lightly fizzy. Strain out the solids through a fine cloth and pour into swing-top bottles, leaving 2.5 cm of air at the top. Keep in the fridge, release the pressure every few days, and drink within 2 weeks.
recipes.title: Mullein and ginger soda

recipes.method: 250 ml water; 250 ml sugar or honey; 125 ml fresh mullein leaves (or 60 ml dried); optional: 4–5 slices fresh ginger, lemon peel or a handful of fresh mint. Bring the water to the boil and take it off the heat. Add the leaves and any flavourings, cover and steep for 15–20 minutes. Strain through a fine cloth, then stir in the sugar until it dissolves. Bottle, cool, then refrigerate; use within 1 month. Drizzle over baked goods, pancakes or fruit, or stir into lemonade and mocktails.

The tests come from Flora of New Zealand vol. IV for both species: mullein 'Rosette lvs shortly petiolate, 7-20 × 3.5-10 cm … crenulate', 'Stem and lvs persistently woolly', 'Corolla 1.5-2.5-(3) cm diam., yellow'; foxglove 'Petiole long and winged', 'Lamina 10-25 × 3.5-12 cm … hairy to glabrate above, ± grey-tomentulose with crisped hairs beneath, crenate or crenulate', 'Corolla mostly 3.5-5 cm long … usually pinkish purple with dark purple white-ringed spots … sometimes pure white', habitat 'poor pastures … stony river beds, roadsides'. Ruled out as tests: leaf edges (both scalloped), leaf size (overlap), habitat, flowering season (Jul–Apr and Oct–Jan overlap). Ranges overlap: both widespread on the North and South Islands.

summary.text:
Verbascum thapsus, the great mullein, greater mullein or common mullein, is a species of mullein native to Europe, northern Africa, and Asia, and introduced in the Americas, Australia and New Zealand.
V. thapsus has a wide native range including Europe, northern Africa, and Asia, from the Azores and Canary Islands east to western China, north to the British Isles, Scandinavia, and Siberia, Kashmir and south to the Himalayas.
It has been introduced throughout the temperate world, and is established as a weed in Australia, New Zealand, tropical Asia, La Réunion, North America, Hawaii, Chile, Hispaniola, and Argentina. It has also been reported in Japan.
In the United States, it was imported very early in the 18th century and cultivated for its medicinal and piscicide properties. By 1818, it had begun spreading so much that Amos Eaton thought it was a native plant. In 1839, it was already reported in Michigan and in 1876, in California. It is now found commonly in all the states. In Canada, it is most common in the Maritime Provinces and southern Quebec, Ontario, and British Columbia, with scattered populations in between.
In northern Europe, it grows from sea level up to 1,850 m altitude, while in China it grows at 1,400–3,200 m altitude.
This ability to grow in a wide range of habitats has been linked to strong phenotype variation rather than adaptation capacities.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands: abundant and often conspicuous in open drier parts throughout, much less common in wetter parts; Kermadec Islands: Raoul Island, but not persisting.
It is named on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds in New Zealand.
Other names in New Zealand: woolly mullein (NZ Plant Conservation Network; the Department of Conservation weed list), mullein, Aaron's rod, great mullein and flannel mullein (Herb Federation of New Zealand). The name mullein comes from the Latin mollis, soft, for the flannel-like leaves.
It was naturalised in New Zealand by 1867 (NZ Plant Conservation Network), and is especially plentiful in paddocks right through Hawke's Bay and in the South Island (Herb Federation of New Zealand).
One plant can set 100,000 to 240,000 seeds, which may stay alive in the soil for up to 100 years. It is poisonous to stock, but they seldom eat it because the dense hairs irritate their skin and mouths, so it can take over a large share of a pasture (Weeds Australia).

warnings: Strain every drink made from it through a fine cloth. The fine hairs on the leaves and flowers irritate the mouth and throat, and they can lodge in the skin. Some people wear a dust mask and gloves when handling a lot of leaves.
Do not eat the seeds. They are slightly narcotic, and they contain saponins, coumarin and rotenone, which are toxic to fish; crushed seed heads have been widely used to poison fish.
The leaves have also been reported to contain rotenone, an insecticide, and coumarin; the amounts are not known.
Mullein flower tea, as a medicine, is not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding, because its safety has not been established, or for children under 12.
Foxglove, which is poisonous, is the most important lookalike: before either flowers, a foxglove rosette can be taken for a mullein rosette. See the lookalike card.

identification.text:
Much-branched, prostrate or widespreading to suberect, farinose, monoecious annual, often with erect main stem and stiff horizontal branches, sometimes mat-forming. Stems ribbed, more or less slender. Petiole to 1.5 cm long; lamina 2–7 × 0.3–4 cm, mostly linear-lanceolate, lanceolate or elliptic, sometimes ovate and then often hastate, rarely lobed on 1 side only, otherwise lamina nearly always entire, green or grey-green; base narrow-cuneate to cuneate; apex acute to obtuse. Inflorescence leaves (even down to base of branches) smaller, narrower, with shorter petioles. Inflorescence long, spicate; flowers in glomerules; upper glomerules sometimes subtended by small bract-like leaves. male flowers: perianth about 0.5 mm long; segments green with hyaline margin. female flowers: bracteoles 1–1.5 mm long at anthesis, sessile, triangular or rhombic-triangular, often triangular-hastate, otherwise entire or with a few marginal or sometimes central dorsal teeth, sometimes with appendages. Fruiting bracteoles (1.5)–2.5–8.5–(11) × 1–5–(6) mm, sometimes unequal, thin, green or grey-farinose, the lower part united; apex acute or acuminate. Fruit enclosed or apex exserted from bracteoles, 1.4–2.2–(3.2) mm diameter, circular, laterally flattened; pericarp easily removed. Testa shining black, almost smooth.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Some plants have all their leaves more or less linear.
Stems 0.3–1.2 m long. The lower leaves are mostly in opposite pairs, especially on young shoots; leaves higher up can be alternate.

lookalikes.howToTell: Compare the leaves below the main flower spikes, at flowering. Common orache's middle and lower leaves are mostly narrowly lance-shaped to lance-shaped with a wedge-shaped base, sometimes ovate and then often arrow-shaped; spear-leaved orache's are mostly triangular to arrow-shaped with a squared-off base, though the base varies from broadly wedge-shaped to arrow-shaped. In fruit, common orache's two bracteoles are joined in their lower part; spear-leaved orache's are almost free or joined only at the base. Where common orache's leaves have basal lobes, these often point forward. The bracteoles of both are extremely variable in New Zealand, so check more than one character.
lookalikes.name: Spear-leaved orache

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers and fruit. Common orache's female flowers usually have no sepals or petals: each fruit is held between two bracteoles that grow with it, up to about 8.5 mm long (rarely 11 mm), entire or with a few teeth. Fat hen's flowers are mostly bisexual and its fruit is wrapped in small sepals, 0.5–3 mm long, with no bracteoles. The leaves do not separate them reliably: both plants are mealy and variable, and fat hen's leaves can be lance-shaped with a wedge-shaped base too.
lookalikes.name: Fat hen

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the habit and the fruit. Garden orache is erect, usually over 75 cm tall, with a stout, rigid, angled main stem; its lower leaves are 5–30 cm long on stalks up to 5 cm, triangular-arrow-shaped or ovate, with a heart-shaped to squared-off base. Common orache is prostrate or spreading, sometimes with an erect main stem but otherwise lax, with ribbed, more or less slender stems and leaves 2–7 cm long, mostly narrowly lance-shaped to elliptic with a wedge-shaped base. In fruit, most of garden orache's female flowers sit between two free, round, untoothed bracteoles with no bumps or appendages, 6–15 mm across; common orache's bracteoles are triangular, joined in their lower part and usually 2.5–8.5 mm long.
lookalikes.name: Garden orache

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at mature plants and the fruit. Common orache has ribbed, more or less slender stems and leaves 20–70 mm long and 3–40 mm wide, mostly narrowly lance-shaped to elliptic with a narrowly wedge-shaped to wedge-shaped base, and nearly always entire. Australian orache is robust, up to 1 m tall and 2 m across, with stout main stems up to 15 mm thick and woody at the base; its leaves are very fleshy to almost succulent, 20–100 mm long and 30–60 mm wide, broadly lance-shaped to broadly triangular or arrow-shaped with a broadly wedge-shaped base, and on mature plants often deeply but irregularly lobed or coarsely toothed, the lobes blunt and pointing forward. In fruit, common orache's bracteoles are thin, green or grey-mealy, and usually 2.5–8.5 mm long; Australian orache's are 3–4 mm long and very fleshy, turning black and much thickened with age. Young Australian orache often has entire leaves or leaves lobed once or twice near the base, like common orache, so go by mature plants and the fruit. Australian orache is strictly coastal and in New Zealand is abundant only on the Chatham Islands, where common orache has also been recorded. Many botanists treat the two as one species. No record of Australian orache as food was found (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Australian orache

summary.text:
Atriplex patula (spear saltbush; common orache; spear orach; spreading orach) is a ruderal, circumboreal species of annual herbaceous plant in the genus Atriplex naturalized in many temperate regions.
The species accumulates salt from the environment in its tissues. Unlike other Atriplex species, it lacks notable salt bladders to excrete salt onto the leaves.
In New Zealand it has been recorded wild since 1853: in the North Island from Auckland City and Opotiki, and in the South Island in eastern areas from Marlborough to Southland and in Central Otago, as well as on Stewart Island and the Chatham Islands. Most early New Zealand records of it probably refer to forms of spear-leaved orache, and it has also been known here as A. angustifolia, A. australasica and A. erecta.
The native Atriplex australasica (At Risk – Relict), strictly coastal and abundant on the Chatham Islands, has been confused with common orache in New Zealand writing, and many botanists treat the two as one species. It has much wider, often deeply toothed or lobed leaves, though young plants often have entire leaves or leaves lobed once or twice near the base.
Its name comes from an ancient Latin plant name of uncertain origin, possibly from the Greek a- 'without' and traphein 'nourishment', because many saltbushes grow in arid desert soils; patula means spreading. Herbarium specimens determined as common orache come from the North Auckland, Hawke's Bay, Wellington, Canterbury and Otago land districts, most of them from Canterbury.

warnings: Plants grown on fertilised ground can concentrate harmful amounts of nitrate in their leaves.
Eating very large quantities has been linked to photosensitivity, in a single report.
The just-ripe seeds have a reputation as a strong laxative.

Native saltbushes grow on the same coasts and saline ground, and all of them are Threatened or At Risk: do not pick them. Atriplex buchananii (Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable) and grey saltbush, A. cinerea (Threatened – Nationally Critical, one natural population left), are perennials with small, entire, silvery-grey or whitish leaves, round to broadly oval in A. buchananii and narrow in grey saltbush. On the Chatham Islands, A. billardierei (Threatened – Nationally Endangered) grows on sandy beaches; its fleshy leaves are densely covered in small bladder-like swellings. Holloway's crystalwort, A. hollowayi (Threatened – Nationally Critical), survives naturally only on two beaches at Te Paki in Northland. On the Chatham Islands, Atriplex australasica (At Risk – Relict), strictly coastal, grows on beaches, clay banks and cliff faces; its leaves are much wider than common orache's and often deeply toothed or lobed, though young plants often have entire leaves.

identification.text:
Medium-sized to tall tree with rough shallowly fissured, dark grey bark, about 6–12 m high (to about 15 m in cultivation); branches erect when young but later spreading. Young shoots shining brown or reddish brown, becoming glabrous, sometimes with branch spines on older shoots. Leaves very variable and mostly crowded on short shoots; petiole 15–65–(80) mm long; glabrate to pilose; blade broadly ovate, elliptic, broad-elliptic, or suborbicular, (25)–35–80–(100) × (20)–30–60–(80) mm, apiculate to acuminate, rounded at base, bright green, glossy and glabrous above when mature, paler below and sometimes pilose when young, crenulate-serrate; stipules attenuate. Inflorescence of usually 5–10 flowers; pedicels 18–30 mm long, glabrate or softly pilose. Sepals triangular, brown- or grey-tomentose, recurved. Petals broadly obovate or obovate-oblong, 14–22 × 10–18 mm, concave, white; apex rounded. Anthers more or less purple. Fruit usually pyriform or broadly obovoid, less commonly subglobose or globose, usually 40–80 mm long (longer in some cultivated plants), sweet, with a gritty texture when ripe; skin green to yellow, sometimes brown. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Flowers in early spring, after plums and peaches but before apples. Ripe fruit is soft and sweet; nashi (Asian pear) fruit is round and crisp like an apple.

lookalikes.howToTell: Quince leaves have entire margins and are white- to grey-woolly beneath; pear leaves are finely round-toothed, bright green, glossy and hairless above when mature, and only sometimes hairy beneath when young. Quince flowers sit singly on short leafy shoots, 30–50 mm across, white to pink; pear flowers come in clusters of usually 5–10, white, with more or less purple anthers. Quince fruit is usually 80–150 mm long, yellow, more or less finely downy and fragrant, and stays hard when ripe; pear fruit is usually 40–80 mm long (longer in some cultivated plants), with green to yellow, sometimes brown skin, and is sweet when ripe. Shape does not separate them: both fruits can be pear-shaped or nearly round, both have gritty flesh, and size overlaps in cultivated pears. Quince fruit is eaten cooked.
