preparation.text: Pick when the fruit is full size but before it softens, and ripen it off the tree; fruit left to ripen on the tree often drops and bruises. Hard wild-type fruit sweetens in storage, and late (May) pears keep well for winter eating. A ripe pear gives a little when pressed gently near the stem; for poaching, underripe pears never soften properly or take up the flavour, and overripe ones go mushy. Fruit with sawdust-like frass and mushy trails has been bored by codling moth larvae. Discard the core and pips.

recipes.method: Ingredients: 8 ripe pears, cored and finely diced; 250 ml tamarind sauce (the method calls it tamarind purée); 250 ml soft brown sugar; 2 tbsp finely grated fresh ginger; 4 tsp mustard seeds; 1/2 tsp salt. Put everything in a pot and simmer gently, stirring often so it doesn't stick, until the sauce is thick and the pears are tender, about 30 minutes. Bottle while hot into sterilised jars and seal with screw-top lids. Makes 2 jars. Suggested use: on crostini with creamy blue cheese and a slice of pear.
recipes.title: Pear & Tamarind Chutney

recipes.method: Ingredients: 3 brown pears, quartered, cored and thinly sliced lengthways; 2 tbsp rice vinegar or lemon juice; 1 1/4 cups (about 310 ml) plain flour; 1/2 cup (125 ml) walnut flour; 2 tsp baking powder; 1 packed cup (250 ml) soft brown sugar; 150 g butter, melted, plus extra to grease; 1 cup (250 ml) milk; 1 tsp baking soda; 1 egg; 1 1/2 tsp freshly grated nutmeg; 1 1/2 tsp ground ginger; 3/4 cup walnut pieces; 1 tbsp raw sugar. Heat the oven to 170°C fanbake; line the base of a 22 cm springform tin and grease the sides. Keep the pear slices in cold water with the vinegar or lemon juice so they don't brown. Mix the flour, walnut flour, baking powder and sugar, then mix in the butter. Press 1 rounded cup of this into the tin as a base. Warm the milk and whisk in the baking soda; add it to the rest of the flour mixture with the egg, nutmeg and ginger, mix until smooth and fold in the walnuts. Pour half the batter over the base, lay half the drained, patted-dry pears on top in one layer, add the rest of the batter and fan the remaining pears over the top without pressing them in. Sprinkle with raw sugar and bake 40–45 minutes, until risen, golden and a skewer comes out clean. Cool in the tin. Walnut flour can be made by blitzing walnut pieces. Keeps 2–3 days in a sealed container, or up to a week in the fridge.
recipes.title: Pear, Nutmeg & Walnut Cake

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1 sheet frozen puff pastry, thawed just before use; 2 ripe pears, unpeeled, cored and finely diced; 115 g (4 oz) crumbled Gorgonzola; 3/4 cup (180 ml) walnut halves, chopped; 1/2 tsp kosher salt; 1/4 tsp freshly ground black pepper; 1 tsp minced fresh thyme. Heat the oven to 190°C (375°F) with a rack in the upper third. Roll the pastry out slightly on a lightly floured board until smooth, cut into 16 squares and halve each diagonally into 32 triangles; space them about 1 cm apart on a baking sheet. Put a little pear in the centre of each, top with Gorgonzola and walnuts, and season with salt and pepper. Bake until puffed and golden, 15–20 minutes. Sprinkle with thyme and serve warm. Makes 32.
recipes.title: Pear, walnut and Gorgonzola puffs

recipes.method: Ingredients: 4 bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs; 1 1/2 tsp fennel seeds, crushed (optional); 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided (1 tsp + 1/2 tsp); 3/4 tsp freshly ground black pepper, divided (1/2 tsp + 1/4 tsp); 3 large pears, unpeeled, cored and cut into 1 cm (1/2 inch) slices; 1 medium red onion, cut into 1 cm wedges; 1 tbsp olive oil; 1/2 cup (125 ml) walnut halves; 8 cups (about 2 litres) rocket or baby spinach; juice of 1/2 lemon; 55 g (2 oz) crumbled Gorgonzola or other blue cheese. Heat the oven to 230°C (450°F) with a rack in the middle. Toss the chicken in a bowl with the fennel seeds, 1 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp pepper and lay it on a large rimmed baking sheet. Toss the pear, onion, oil and remaining salt and pepper in the same bowl and arrange around the chicken. Bake 25 minutes, scatter the walnuts over and bake 5 minutes more, until the chicken is browned and crisp (a few minutes longer if not). Spread the greens on a platter, top with the pears, onion and walnuts, squeeze over the lemon, then add the chicken and the blue cheese. Serves 4.
recipes.title: Sheet-pan chicken with pears, onion, walnuts and blue cheese

recipes.method: Filling: 1.1 kg (2 1/2 lb, about 5 large) firm, tart apples; 680 g (1 1/2 lb, about 3 large) ripe pears; 1/4 cup (60 ml) sugar; 3 tbsp lemon juice; 2 tbsp plain flour; 1 1/2 tbsp chilled salted butter, in 1 cm cubes. Topping: 1 cup (250 ml) plain flour; 1 cup (250 ml) fine cornmeal (not stone-ground); 3 tbsp plus 2 tsp sugar; 2 1/2 tsp baking powder; 1 tsp kosher salt; 1 tsp finely grated lemon zest; 1 1/2 tbsp chilled salted butter, in small pieces; 1 cup plus 2 tbsp chilled cream. Use a deep ovenproof dish with sides at least 9 cm high (or ramekins). Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Peel and core the fruit; slice the apples 6 mm thick and the pears 1 cm thick. Toss in the dish with the sugar, lemon juice, flour and butter and bake uncovered for 20 minutes. Meanwhile whisk the flour, cornmeal, 3 tbsp sugar, baking powder, salt and zest; rub in the butter into thin flakes, stir in 1 cup cream with a fork until the dough just comes together, pat out 2 cm thick on a well-floured surface and cut 5–7.5 cm biscuits, re-rolling scraps. Chill them while the fruit cooks. Stir the fruit (it should look softer and glossy), overlap the biscuits on top in circles, brush with the remaining 2 tbsp cream and sprinkle with the 2 tsp sugar. Bake uncovered about 35 minutes, until golden and bubbling. Cool at least 20 minutes and serve warm. The fruit can be done up to a day ahead (drain off excess juice); make the biscuits just before baking. Serves 8.
recipes.title: Apple-pear cobbler with lemon-cornmeal biscuits

recipes.method: Ingredients: 2 cups (500 ml) red wine; 1/2 cup (125 ml) sugar; 1 vanilla bean, split lengthwise; 1 cinnamon stick; zest and juice of 1 orange; zest of 1 lemon; 1 bay leaf; 6 ripe pears, stems on; raspberries to garnish (optional). Use pears that are heavy for their size and give a little near the stem. In a medium saucepan over medium heat, stir the wine, sugar, vanilla, cinnamon, orange zest and juice, lemon zest and bay leaf until the sugar dissolves. Peel the pears carefully, leaving the stems on, and cut 6 mm off the bottoms so they stand upright. Add them to the pan, bring to the boil, then simmer, turning gently, until a paring knife slides in easily, about 15 minutes. Cool the pears in the liquid, then lift them out and chill, covered, about 2 hours. Strain the liquid into a clean pan and boil until reduced to a thick syrup, about 20 minutes; cool to room temperature. Serve the pears drizzled with the syrup. Serves 6.
recipes.title: Red wine poached pears

recipes.method: Ingredients: 3 ripe pears (about 570 g / 1 1/4 lb; about 2 1/4 cups chopped); 1 1/2 cups (375 ml) Riesling; 3 tbsp chopped fresh ginger; 1 cup (250 ml) sugar; 1–2 tsp lemon juice, to taste; 1/2 tsp kosher salt. Put the pears, wine and ginger in a medium saucepan, cover and bring to the boil over high heat, then cook covered on very low heat for 20 minutes. Transfer to a blender with the sugar, cover very tightly and purée until smooth, about 30 seconds. Strain into an airtight container, stir in lemon juice and salt to taste, and refrigerate until very cold, about 4 hours. Churn in an ice-cream maker, then freeze in an airtight container at least 4–5 hours before serving. Makes about 1 litre (1 quart).
recipes.title: Pear, Riesling and ginger sorbet

recipes.method: Ingredients: 2 ripe pears, divided; 1 vanilla bean; 1 cup (250 ml) brandy; 1 cup (250 ml) sugar; 1 cup (250 ml) water. Wash and chop one pear, leaving the skin on and discarding the core and pips. Split and scrape the vanilla bean. Put the pear and vanilla in a sealable glass jar with room for another cup of liquid, cover with the brandy, seal, shake and leave 2 days. Remove the vanilla and leave 3 more days. Chop the second pear (core and pips discarded) and bring it to the boil with the sugar and water over medium heat, about 5–7 minutes; simmer 5 minutes more and cool. Add the syrup and fruit to the jar, shake and leave 2 days. Taste, and when the flavour is right strain through a fine sieve and then a coffee filter into a bottle. Makes about 2 1/4 cups (560 ml).
recipes.title: Pear liqueur

recipes.method: Ingredients: 4 tbsp unsalted butter, divided, plus more to serve; 2 semi-firm pears, grated (about 1 cup / 250 ml); 2 tbsp sugar; 1/4 cup (60 ml) rum; 1 cup (140 g / 5 oz) plain flour; 2 tsp baking powder; pinch of salt; 1 cup (250 ml) milk; 2 eggs, beaten; 1 tsp vanilla extract; maple syrup. Melt 2 tbsp butter in a medium frying pan over medium-high heat, add the grated pear and cook, stirring often, until it starts to soften, about 4 minutes. Add the sugar and rum and cook until the liquid has evaporated and the pear is soft, about 6 minutes; cool. Mix the flour, baking powder and salt; whisk the milk, eggs and vanilla, add to the dry ingredients and whisk smooth, then whisk in the pear. Melt 1 tbsp butter in a large frying pan over medium-high heat and ladle in 1/4-cup (60 ml) portions. Cook until bubbles appear, about 3 minutes, flip and cook until browned and cooked through, about 3 minutes more. Repeat with the remaining butter and batter. Serve hot with butter and syrup. Serves 4.
recipes.title: Rum and pear pancakes

summary.text:
Pyrus communis, the common pear, is a species of pear native to central and eastern Europe, and western Asia.
It is one of the most important fruits of temperate regions, being the species from which most orchard pear cultivars grown in Europe, North America, and Australia have been developed.
European pears arrived in Northland with the missionaries in the early 1800s; one of the original trees is now over 200 years old, and the Samuel Marsden Pear Tree in Kerikeri is the oldest surviving exotic fruit tree in New Zealand. Nashi, or Asian pear (Pyrus pyrifolia), grown in New Zealand since 1982, is a separate species.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island; South Island: local but probably scattered throughout; generally very infrequent in any one locality. P. communis is widespread in cultivation and long persists as a relic of cultivation. Many cultivars are grown in New Zealand. Healy, A. J., Trans. Roy. Soc. N.Z. 85: 545 (1958), commented that its wild distribution in New Zealand is similar to that of Malus domestica, the apple, but it is much less common and usually occurs as single trees. As with apples, pears are often spread by people throwing away cores containing seeds, particularly from moving vehicles.
A very large, old wild-type pear in Canterbury, with small, bright yellow, very tannic fruit that keeps its star-shaped flower remains, was identified in 2025, from its fruit and leaves in the field, as most likely the European wild pear, Pyrus pyraster (also treated as P. communis subsp. pyraster). Perry pears, usually hybrids of the two, are very rare in New Zealand.

warnings: Pear pips contain amygdalin, which the body breaks down into cyanide. Swallowing the pips from one core whole is unlikely to cause harm; chewing or crushing pips, or swallowing several at once, raises the risk of cyanide poisoning, and symptoms can be delayed. Discard the core, and keep pips away from children and pets.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Usually amongst grass on moist roadsides, very local.
It is known wild from the Maungatungaroa Stream (Manawatū), Christchurch, Dunedin, the Pourakino Valley (Southland) and Halfmoon Bay (Stewart Island).
On New Zealand's national wetland plant list it is rated facultative: it grows as readily in wetlands as on dry ground.

identification.text:
Slightly puberulent, dioecious perennial; rootstock more or less woody; stems to about 1 m tall, reddish towards base. Lower leaves with long slender petioles several times longer than lamina; uppermost leaves shortly petiolate or subsessile, somewhat amplexicaul. Lamina 3.5–12 × 1–3 cm, narrowly oblong to more or less lanceolate, pleasantly sour to taste, entire except for 2, more or less downwards-directed, basal lobes to about 1.3 cm long; apex obtuse. Inflorescence to about 30 cm long, reddish, with several simple branches, leafless. Flowers in fascicles; pedicels slender. Perianth of male flowers 1.5–2 mm long. Outer perianth of female flowers about 0.5 mm long, soon strongly reflexed; valves orbicular-cordate, winged, entire and lacking tubercles, enlarging to 2.8–3.5–(4) mm at fruiting, more or less rose-red. Nut about 2–(2.3) mm long, dark shining brown, acutely angled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The leaves taste pleasantly sour, but so do sheep's sorrel and fiddle dock, and curled dock a little, so taste alone does not identify it. Cultivated French sorrel (Rumex scutatus) has wider, shield-shaped basal leaves nearly as broad as long, and its upper leaves are clearly stalked rather than clasping the stem.
The leaves start as a low basal rosette, each on its own long stalk; in early summer a tall, sparsely leaved flowering stem rises, often marked with red, with small maroon to crimson flowers. Only female plants set fruit, which is tinged red and three-winged and carried off by the wind. Field bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis), also wild in New Zealand, has similar arrow-shaped leaves and grows in the same places, but it trails and scrambles, with many leaves spaced along each stem instead of single long-stalked leaves from a rosette.

lookalikes.howToTell: Sheep sorrel is much smaller: leaf blades 1.5–5 cm long, with the two basal lobes standing out at about right angles, on flowering stems 3–30 cm tall, and it often spreads by slender yellow underground stems. Common sorrel's blades are 3.5–12 cm, its basal lobes point downwards, its upper leaves partly clasp the stem, and its stems reach about 1 m. On female plants, common sorrel's fruit is wrapped in round, winged, rose-red valves 2.8–4 mm across; sheep sorrel's valves are 1.2–1.5 mm and wingless. Both are sour and eaten the same way.

preparation.text:
Eat the leaves on their own as a thirst-quenching snack, or use them in salads, as a potherb, or puréed in soups. They can be overpowering in quantity, so use them as a flavouring in mixed salads, and sparingly. The leaves can be dried, though they lose much of their flavour; they freeze better. The root is dried, ground and made into noodles; the seed can be ground and mixed with other flour for bread.
Young leaves suit salads, sandwiches, egg dishes (omelettes, scrambled eggs, quiche) and herb butters; cook older leaves like spinach, or in soups, stews and sauces. Cooked, the leaves quickly lose their bright green and turn dark olive or brown, which doesn't affect the flavour. The acid reacts with cast iron and blackens the leaves, so cut them with a stainless-steel knife, shred them just before use, and avoid cast-iron pans. The leaves wilt soon after picking, so pick them as you need them; in a bag in the fridge they keep for a couple of days at most. Large, coarse leaves can be wrapped around meat or fish while it cooks.

recipes.method: Written for common sorrel (Rumex acetosa). 2 large handfuls of sorrel leaves; 1 onion; 1 potato; 500 ml homemade stock. Rinse 2 large handfuls of sorrel leaves and dry them in a salad spinner. Coarsely chop 1 onion and dice 1 potato, and fry them gently in a pressure cooker for about 3 minutes. Add 500 ml homemade stock and the sorrel, bring up to pressure and cook for 3 minutes. When it has cooled enough to open, blend with a hand blender. Serve with bread.
recipes.title: Sorrel soup

recipes.method: Written for sorrel bought at a market; the author doesn't name the species. 225 g soft unsalted butter, in thin slices; 1½ cups (about 375 ml) finely chopped sorrel leaves; 1 teaspoon fine salt; 1 teaspoon ground black pepper; the finely grated zest of 1 lemon. Put half of 225 g soft unsalted butter, in thin slices, in a food processor, add 1½ cups (about 375 ml) finely chopped sorrel leaves, 1 teaspoon fine salt, 1 teaspoon ground black pepper and the finely grated zest of 1 lemon, then the rest of the butter. Process until evenly mixed, scraping down once or twice. Roll into a log about 4 cm across in baking paper or plastic wrap, twist the ends and chill. It keeps 5 days in the fridge or 3 months frozen. Set a slice on each salmon fillet before it cooks, or use it on chicken and steamed vegetables.
recipes.title: Sorrel butter

recipes.method: Written for sorrel bought at a market; the author doesn't name the species. For the pastry: 1¼ cups (about 160 g) plain flour; ¼ teaspoon salt; 115 g cold cubed butter; 1 tablespoon cider vinegar; 3–5 tablespoons iced water; 1 egg white. For the filling: 1 large leek, sliced (white and pale green parts); 2 tablespoons olive oil; 3 eggs; ¼ cup grated parmesan; ½ cup milk; ½ cup half-and-half (or equal parts milk and cream); ¼ cup ricotta; 1 teaspoon salt; ½ teaspoon pepper; 2 tablespoons chopped dill; 1 tablespoon chopped rosemary; 2 cups washed, dried raw sorrel leaves. Pastry: pulse 1¼ cups (about 160 g) plain flour with ¼ teaspoon salt, add 115 g cold cubed butter and pulse to fine crumbs, then with the motor running add 1 tablespoon cider vinegar and 3–5 tablespoons iced water until it just comes together. Flatten, wrap and chill 1 hour. Roll out to line a 23 cm tart or pie tin, line with foil and baking beans and bake 20 minutes at 190 °C; remove the beans, brush with 1 egg white, prick the base and bake 5 minutes more. Filling: cook 1 large sliced leek (white and pale green parts) in 2 tablespoons olive oil, covered, over medium-low heat until golden and caramelised, 20–25 minutes. Whisk 3 eggs with ¼ cup grated parmesan, ½ cup milk, ½ cup half-and-half (or equal parts milk and cream), ¼ cup ricotta, 1 teaspoon salt, ½ teaspoon pepper, 2 tablespoons chopped dill and 1 tablespoon chopped rosemary. Spread the leeks in the case, pour the egg mixture over and bake about 30 minutes, until puffed and just set. Cool about 12 minutes, then scatter 2 cups of washed, dried raw sorrel leaves over the top just before slicing (on a hot quiche they brown). The recipe is at its best the same day.

summary.text:
Common sorrel, also called garden sorrel or sour dock, is native to temperate Eurasia and was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1855. It was probably brought in deliberately, being grown for its sour leaves, but it has stayed surprisingly uncommon in the wild. The name acetosa comes from the Latin for sour.
Its native range runs across Europe and temperate Asia as far as Japan and Taiwan, and into Morocco. People have gathered it for thousands of years: its seeds and charred remains turn up at Mesolithic and Neolithic settlement sites across Europe. French gardeners began improving it in the late 1600s, giving the large-leaved cultivar 'Belleville'; 'Profusion', from 1993, never flowers or sets seed. Garden forms are sold under names such as French sorrel, which is also the name of a different species, Rumex scutatus, and much of the garden sorrel in cultivation is a form some botanists treat as a species of its own, Rumex rugosus.
Plants are either male or female, and wild stands usually hold more females than males.

warnings: It contains oxalic acid, which gives the leaves their sharp taste. A little is fine, but large amounts can lock up calcium, iron and other minerals in food and add to the risk of kidney stones. Larger, older leaves and the stems hold the most. Eat raw leaves only occasionally or in small amounts; cooking lowers the oxalic acid a great deal. Take particular care, or leave it alone, if you are prone to rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney or bladder stones, or hyperacidity.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): coastal and lowland. Roadsides, waste places, building sites, railways, riverbeds, cultivated ground, lawns, poor and dry pastures to over 1000 m.

identification.text:
Annual, at first stemless, later usually with 1 or more hairy stems; plant extremely variable in size, from prostrate to about 50 cm high and about 75 cm wide, not musk-scented. Leaves to about 15 cm long, pinnate, hairy, sometimes densely so, sometimes glandular; petiole longer in rosette and lower cauline leaves. Leaflets sessile, ovate, deeply and finely pinnately dissected with linear to lanceolate lobes, often densely covered in white hairs. Stipules triangular, often broad, membranous, ciliate, silvery; midrib green, forming an acute or mucronate apex. Umbels (2)–5–12-flowered; bracts broad-ovate, membranous, with green keeled midrib forming an acute to short-acuminate apex. Peduncles densely covered in glandular hairs, often longer than upper cauline leaves; pedicels more or less equal to calyx at anthesis. Sepals (2.5)–3–5 mm long at anthesis, lanceolate, hirsute or glandular, mucronate. Petals 4–6 mm long, elliptic or oblong-elliptic, usually pink or mauve-pink, rarely white; claw short, hairy. Stamens about 3 mm long; filaments widened at base, without lateral teeth, usually pinkish; anthers dark purple. Staminodes narrow-lanceolate. Fruit beak 3–3.5 cm long, with appressed hairs. Mericarps densely hirsute with hairs of differing lengths; apical pits eglandular, with a prominent shallow glabrous furrow beneath.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In open, exposed habitats, especially on poor or stony soils, the plants are usually more or less red, as well as being very small and depauperate.
Common stork's-bill is a herb that typically grows in rosettes pressed flat to the ground, with a deep tap root that allows it to survive through the summer on dry soils. It can develop stems up to 60 cm long that are sometimes red and sometimes green, and may be erect or prostrate, and have simple or glandular hairs which become more abundant towards the top. Plants with glandular hairs are sticky, but those with simple hairs are much less so. It has no scent. The stems bear bright pink flowers which often have dark spots on the bases. The long seed-pod, shaped like the bill of a stork, bursts open in a spiral when ripe, sending the seeds (which have long tails called awns) into the air.
Musky storksbill (Erodium moschatum) looks very similar. It smells of musk when bruised, is clammy with dense glandular hairs, and its leaflets are lobed into more or less ovate, toothed lobes rather than finely cut; its stipules and bracts are blunt to rounded, not acute to short-pointed. In flower, musky storksbill's fertile stamens usually have a small tooth on one or both sides of the widened base (rarely none); common storksbill's have none. Common storksbill's seed segments have glandless pits at the top; musky storksbill's pits are glandular.

lookalikes.howToTell: Young plants of both are rosettes of finely divided, fern-like leaves, and both grow in waste places and riverbeds. Common storksbill's leaves and stems are hairy, sometimes densely so; hemlock is hairless throughout, and its leaf stalks have no hairs. Crush a leaf: hemlock smells foetid; common storksbill has no scent. Hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided, with segments 5–40 mm long; common storksbill's are once divided into stalkless leaflets that are themselves deeply and finely cut, up to about 15 cm long in all. Stem colour is not a safe test: common storksbill's stems can be red, and hemlock's are usually spotted or blotched purple. Grown on, hemlock stands erect, up to 2–(3) m, with hollow stems and many white flowers about 2 mm across; common storksbill lies along the ground or rises to about 50 cm, with clusters of (2–)5–12 flowers, petals 4–6 mm long, usually pink or mauve-pink but rarely white, followed by fruits with a beak 3–3.5 cm long. Mistakes are likeliest with very young plants; if a rosette is hairless or smells foul, do not eat it. Hemlock is deadly poisonous; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: Musky storksbill looks very similar and grows in the same places, though common storksbill tends to grow on drier, less fertile sites. Crush a leaf: musky storksbill usually smells of musk, though not always strongly; common storksbill has no musky smell. Musky storksbill is densely glandular and clammy; common storksbill is usually much less clammy. Common storksbill's leaflets are deeply and finely cut into narrow, linear to lanceolate lobes, giving fern-like foliage; musky storksbill's are lobed into more or less ovate, toothed lobes. Common storksbill's stipules and bracts end in an acute to short-pointed tip; musky storksbill's are blunt to rounded. In flower, look at the fertile stamens: musky storksbill's filaments usually have a small tooth on one or both sides of the widened base (rarely none); common storksbill's have none. Petal colour and the 3–3.5 cm fruit beak do not separate them. Musky storksbill's leaves are eaten too; see its own entry.

summary.text:
Erodium cicutarium, also known as common stork's-bill, redstem filaree, redstem stork's bill or pinweed, is a herbaceous annual – or in warm climates, biennial – member of the family Geraniaceae of flowering plants. It is native to Macaronesia, temperate Eurasia and north and northeast Africa, and was introduced to North America in the eighteenth century, where it has since become naturalized, particularly in the deserts and arid grasslands of the southwestern United States. It is also naturalized elsewhere, including South America and southern Africa.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands and the Chatham Islands, very common throughout. Naturalised from Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia, first recorded in 1855. It flowers from September to May. New Zealand plants are subspecies cicutarium. It is also called storksbill, alfilaria, common crowfoot, pin clover and pin grass.
It is a weed of turf and pasture. Its sharply pointed fruits can pierce the skin of sheep and work into the flesh, more often than those of musky storksbill. The long awn of each fruit winds and unwinds with the humidity, burying the seed in the soil.
Sheep and lambs that eat a lot of storksbill can become sensitive to sunlight (photosensitisation): it has been seen in lambs grazing herbage that was mainly storksbill in Australia and New Zealand (North Canterbury and Hawke's Bay). The agent responsible has not been identified.

warnings: Young plants are rosettes of finely divided, fern-like leaves, like those of hemlock, which is deadly. Common storksbill's leaves and stems are hairy; hemlock is hairless throughout and smells foetid when crushed. Do not pick very young plants you are unsure of; flowering and fruiting plants are much easier to name (see the lookalikes).

Sheep and lambs that graze mostly storksbill can become sensitive to sunlight (photosensitisation). The substance responsible has not been identified, and whether it affects people is not known. No source gives a safe quantity for people.

In lawns and pastures it is controlled with herbicides such as MCPA, 2,4-D, dicamba, picloram with triclopyr, and bentazone. Avoid plants on roadsides, heavily grazed ground or sprayed areas, and pick it only where you know none has been used.

identification.text:
Slender to stout scrambling or tufted annual; stem sparsely hairy. Leaves sparsely to densely hairy; tendrils branched; leaflets in (3)–4–8 pairs, often alternate, linear to elliptic to obovate, (5)–10–30–(40) mm long; stipules simple or with 1, adaxial, basal lobe, or dentate, usually with a dark spot. Inflorescence much shorter than leaves, 1–2–(4)-flowered. Peduncle much shorter than flowers, rarely more or less equal to flowers. Pedicel 1–5 mm long. Calyx somewhat gibbous at base; calyx teeth more or less equal, shorter than, equal to, or longer than the tube. Corolla usually purple, reddish purple or rose, sometimes white or pink, (8)–12–28 mm long; limb of standard longer than claw. Pod more or less glabrous or puberulent, blackish or brownish black, constricted or not between seeds, 5–12-seeded, (20)–30–60 mm long; seeds light or dark brown with dark spots; hilum ⅙-⅕ of circumference.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Flowers or seeds are needed to identify vetches. Common vetch is told from other vetches by its leaves with 4–8 pairs of leaflets, its large flowers in short clusters, and its more or less equal calyx teeth. Yellow vetch (Vicia lutea), established only on Banks Peninsula, is very similar but has a pale yellow corolla, sometimes tinged purple, and unequal calyx teeth.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers and pods. Yellow vetch's corolla is pale yellow, sometimes tinged purple, and its calyx teeth are unequal: the lower teeth about as long as the calyx tube, the upper ones much shorter. Common vetch's corolla is usually purple, reddish purple or rose, sometimes white or pink, and its calyx teeth are more or less equal. Yellow vetch's pods are moderately hairy and hold 3–6 seeds; common vetch's are more or less hairless or finely downy and hold 5–12. The leaves do not separate them: both have tendrils and several pairs of leaflets, and leaflet sizes overlap, so flowers or seeds are needed. Both grow on Banks Peninsula, the only place yellow vetch is established. Yellow vetch's only food records are for its seeds, which are not given as food here (see its page).

preparation.text: Pick only young, tender shoots and leaves, taking a little from many plants rather than stripping one, and leave plants that are dusty or growing in contaminated places. Young shoots can be eaten raw, as in pesto or salad, but only a small helping at a time; cooking them as a green vegetable is the more cautious way to try them. Cook young pods before eating them. Do not eat the seeds (see warnings).

recipes.method: 2 packed cups (500 ml) young common vetch shoots and leaves, 1 tbsp olive oil, 1 small garlic clove, finely chopped, 1 tsp lemon juice, salt and black pepper; toasted sesame seeds or grated parmesan are optional. Wash the vetch well under running water and remove tough stems. Blanch the greens in a saucepan of boiling water for 2–3 minutes and drain well. Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat, cook the garlic briefly, then add the greens and sauté for another 2–3 minutes until tender. Season with a little salt and pepper and finish with the lemon juice. Serve as a small side dish.
recipes.title: Lemon-garlic vetch greens

recipes.method: 100 g pine nuts, 2 garlic cloves, 2–3 good handfuls of very young, tender common vetch shoots, a generous splash of olive oil and 50 g grated parmesan. Pound the pine nuts, garlic, vetch shoots and oil together in a large mortar and pestle, or blend them in a food processor, and work in the parmesan. Serve on pasta, stir through risotto, spread on bruschetta or serve alongside meat.

summary.text: Common vetch, also called vetch or tare (Vicia sativa), is a scrambling or tufted annual of the pea family, Fabaceae, introduced to New Zealand from western and southern Europe to western Asia and North Africa and first recorded here in 1867. It is a very common weed throughout New Zealand: common to abundant throughout the North and South Islands, in lowland disturbed areas on Stewart Island and Codfish Island, and on the Kermadec and Chatham Islands. It varies greatly in leaf form, in the number of flowers in a cluster, and in flower and pod size; reduced, narrow-leaved plants grow in dry stony sites and more robust, broader-leaved plants in wet places, and one plant can bear several leaf forms as it develops. Some New Zealand plants fit var. sativa, a stout plant with broad leaflets and a corolla over 18 mm long, or the narrow-leaved vetch, var. angustifolia (also treated as subsp. nigra), a slender plant with narrow leaflets and a corolla under 18 mm long, but many plants are intermediate. Its seed is long-lived in the soil and is scattered when the pods burst open. It is not a listed pest plant.

warnings: The seeds contain the nerve toxins γ-glutamyl-β-cyanoalanine and β-cyanoalanine, and cyanogenic glycosides. They are toxic to animals with a simple stomach, people included, and damage the nervous system, with signs such as convulsions and leg paralysis.

Soaking does not lower the main seed toxin enough and boiling only reduces it; in the vetch varieties tested it remains too high for animals with a simple stomach. The seeds are not given here as food.
The seeds also contain vicine and convicine, the compounds that cause favism from broad beans: in people with G6PD deficiency they break down red blood cells, and favism can be fatal.

habitat.text: Cow parsley grows in sunny to semi-shaded locations in meadows and at the edges of hedgerows and woodland. It is a particularly common sight by the roadside and with its frothy early-flowering white blooms is regarded as the most important springtime landscape wildflower in Britain.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Anthriscus sylvestris' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Cow parsley is an upright herbaceous (non-woody) perennial, growing to 60–170 centimetres tall. The stems are hollow, striate (striped with parallel, longitudinal lines), furrowed, and green in colour with flushes of purple, with a diameter up to 1.5 cm. It has tiny hairs on the stem, rachis, and leaf stalks which are difficult to see but can easily be detected by touch. The petioles clasp the stem around the base and are broad and flattened with a downy margin. The rachis has a deeply grooved channel.
The leaves are triangular, 2–3 pinnate, roughly 30 cm wide and 45 cm long, green, and fern-like or feathery in appearance with hair on the underside. The lowest primary division is much smaller than the rest of the leaf.
The flowers are arranged in compound umbels on short pedicels (<1 cm) with a ring of short, stout hairs at the apex. There are downy oval bractioles with red pointy tips on the umblets, arranged on 4–10 rays 1.5–3 cm long. The rays are glabrous (smooth and hairless), with no bract present. Peduncles are similar in length to rays, more or less glabrous and furrowed. Each flower has 5 white petals, 2 stamens and 2 styles with an enlarged base forming a swelling at the apex of the ovary (stylopodium).
The main stem meets the roots in a single primary taproot which can branch further below the surface. From the roots lateral rhizomes can form.  Flowering time in the UK is April to early June.

summary.text:
Anthriscus sylvestris, known as cow parsley, wild chervil, Queen Anne's lace or keck, is a herbaceous biennial or short-lived perennial plant in the family Apiaceae (Umbelliferae).
However, the plant is also sufficiently common and fast-growing to be considered a nuisance weed in gardens.  Cow parsley's ability to spread rapidly by means of rhizomes and to produce large quantities of seeds in a single growing season has made it an invasive species in many areas of the United States. Vermont has listed cow parsley on its "Watch List" of invasive species, while Massachusetts has banned the sale of the plant. It is classed as a Class B Noxious Weed in the State of Washington since 1989, where its sale is also banned. In Iceland, where cow parsley is now commonly seen overgrowing lupine fields, it has been classified as an alien invasive species.

identification.text:
Low-growing shrub; creeping stems up to 1 m long, rooting at nodes, terete, glabrous; armature of small prickles restricted to young stems. Leaves reduced to a single leaflet; leaflet lamina coriaceous, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20)–25–90 × 5–22 mm, sometimes with a pair of obscure lobes near base, glabrous on both surfaces or with sparse scattered hairs on midrib, veins and margins, bronze-green on upper surface, paler on lower, sharply serrate-dentate. Inflorescence a few-flowered panicle or flowers solitary. Petals white. Drupelets red. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
R. parvus has relatively large bisexual flowers whereas the other indigenous spp. have small flowers and are dioecious.
NZPCN's newer description gives separate male and female flowers instead, and calls them smaller and usually solitary (NZPCN, restated).
The sterile hybrid R. ×barkeri is often sold as this species; it has three-leaflet leaves and does not flower (NZPCN).

lookalikes.howToTell: Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet, where blackberry's have (3–)5(–7); creeping lawyer creeps along the ground, blackberry arches and scrambles. Ripe creeping lawyer fruit is red, but blackberry is red too before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit.
lookalikes.name: Blackberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet; bush lawyer's have three or more. Young plants and flowering shoots of other brambles sometimes have single-leaflet leaves too, so judge by the leaves on mature stems.
lookalikes.name: Bush lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet; white-leaved lawyer's have three or more. Young plants and flowering shoots of other brambles sometimes have single-leaflet leaves too, so judge by the leaves on mature stems.
lookalikes.name: White-leaved lawyer

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. Makes 6 jars of 250 ml. The recipe is somewhere between a jam and a jelly: the juice is pressed rather than dripped through a bag, so it sets cloudy. 1 litre berry juice (fresh or thawed frozen berries put through a cold-press juicer), 300 ml cold-pressed apple juice, the juice of 3 lemons, 1.3 kg white sugar, 10 whole cloves and the zest of an orange. Wash the jars and dry them, open end up, in a 120 °C oven for about 15 minutes, leaving them in the warm oven until needed; boil the lids for 5 minutes and let them air-dry. Put the berry, apple and lemon juices and the sugar in a jam pan, dissolve the sugar over low heat, then bring to the boil. Add the cloves and orange zest, skim off foam as it rises, and boil to setting point — about 30 minutes for the author, giving a soft set. Ladle the hot jelly into the hot jars and seal.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry jelly

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. 400 g berries, 500 ml white wine vinegar and 100 g white sugar. Warm the vinegar with the sugar until it has dissolved. Put the berries in a large clean jar or a non-reactive bowl, pour the warm vinegar over them and leave overnight. Strain gently through a fine sieve or muslin and pour into a sterilised bottle or jar. The author uses it to quick-pickle wafer-thin slices of raw beetroot (3 tablespoons of vinegar and ¼ teaspoon of sea salt for 2 small beetroot, soaked at least 15 minutes) served with goat's cheese.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry vinegar

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. Muddle a big handful of berries (fresh or frozen) in a cocktail shaker, add 60 ml tequila blanco, 30 ml Cointreau, 60 ml fresh lime juice and 60 ml sugar syrup, shake hard over ice and pour. Strain it if you don't want the seeds.

identification.text:
Much-branched, prostrate, spreading to suberect, more or less farinose annual monoecious herb. Stems more or less slender; ribs and nodes often purplish or dark red. Petiole of lower leaves usually 1–2.5 cm long, slender; lamina of lower leaves 1–9 × 0.75–8 cm, mostly narrowly to broadly triangular-hastate, sometimes more or less ovate or rhombic-ovate, green, glaucous or sometimes reddish, sparsely to prominently and deeply dentate above basal lobes; base usually truncate, sometimes broad- cuneate or sagittate; apex acute or subacute. Inflorescence leaves smaller and more often ovate to lanceolate. Inflorescence of long reddish or brownish spikes; flowers in glomerules. male flowers: perianth 0.5–0.8 mm long with margins hyaline. female flowers: bracteoles 1–2 mm long at anthesis, sessile, triangular-hastate, broad-ovate or rhombic-ovate, usually dentate, less commonly entire, generally with appendages. Fruiting bracteoles to 9 × 6.5 mm, sometimes unequal, almost free or shortly united. Fruit enclosed by bracteoles, 1–2.5 mm long, more or less circular, laterally flattened; pericarp easily removed; larger-fruited plants with bracteoles often larger and lacking appendages. Testa shining black or deep brown, smooth. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is very variable in habit, colour, leaf shape and bracteoles. Plants exposed to sun, salt-laden wind and drought are often quite prostrate and somewhat succulent; in waste places, on roadsides and in similar modified places near the coast, plants are generally larger and green rather than glaucous. The lowermost leaves are opposite; the upper ones are alternate.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers and fruit. Spear-leaved orache's female flowers usually have no sepals or petals: each fruit is held between two bracteoles that grow with it, reaching up to 9 × 6.5 mm, usually toothed and generally with small outgrowths. Fat hen's flowers are mostly bisexual and its fruit is wrapped in small sepals, 0.5–3 mm long, with no bracteoles. The leaves do not separate them: both plants are mealy and very variable, and fat hen's leaves, usually wedge-based, can also be triangular with a squared-off base.
lookalikes.name: Fat hen

lookalikes.howToTell: Compare the leaves below the main flower spikes, at flowering. Spear-leaved orache's middle and lower leaves are mostly triangular to arrow-shaped with a squared-off base, though the base varies from broadly wedge-shaped to arrow-shaped; common orache's are mostly narrowly lance-shaped to lance-shaped with a wedge-shaped base, sometimes ovate and then often arrow-shaped. In fruit, spear-leaved orache's two bracteoles are almost free or joined only at the base; common orache's are joined in their lower part. Where common orache's leaves have basal lobes, these often point forward. The bracteoles of both are extremely variable in New Zealand, so check more than one character.
lookalikes.name: Common orache

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the habit and the fruit. Garden orache is erect, usually over 75 cm tall, with a stout, rigid, angled main stem; its lower leaves are 5–30 cm long on stalks up to 5 cm. Spear-leaved orache is prostrate or spreading to nearly erect, with more or less slender stems; its lower leaves are 1–9 cm long on slender stalks 1–2.5 cm long, mostly triangular-arrow-shaped and toothed above the basal lobes. In fruit, most of garden orache's female flowers sit between two free, round, untoothed bracteoles with no bumps or appendages, 6–15 mm across; spear-leaved orache's are triangular-arrow-shaped to ovate, usually toothed and generally with appendages, up to 9 mm long. Large-fruited spear-leaved orache can have bigger bracteoles without appendages, so check the habit and leaves too.
lookalikes.name: Garden orache

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaf bases, the stems and the fruit. Spear-leaved orache's lower leaves are mostly triangular-arrow-shaped and toothed above the basal lobes, with a base usually squared off (sometimes broadly wedge-shaped or arrow-shaped), on slender stalks 1–2.5 cm long; Australian orache's leaves have a broadly wedge-shaped base and blunt, forward-pointing lobes, on stout, fleshy stalks up to 20 mm long. Spear-leaved orache's stems are more or less slender; Australian orache has stout main stems up to 15 mm thick and woody at the base. In fruit, spear-leaved orache's bracteoles reach 9 mm, are usually toothed and generally have small outgrowths; Australian orache's are 3–4 mm long, entire or with one or two teeth, very fleshy, turning black and much thickened with age. Spear-leaved orache's bracteoles are extremely variable in New Zealand, so check more than one character. Both grow around the Chatham Islands lagoon, and in New Zealand Australian orache is abundant only on the Chatham Islands. No record of Australian orache as food was found (see its page).

preparation.text: Add young leaves to salads and cook older ones like spinach; mature leaves are good wilted with butter. Strip the leaves from the tougher stems. Mix them with stronger-tasting leaves if they seem bland, and go easy on the salt, as they are salty already. Grind the seed into a powder to thicken soups, or add it to wheat flour for bread or muffins; it is small and very fiddly to collect. Young, soft seeds can be sprinkled over food; take only a few so the plant can regenerate.

recipes.method: Written for spear-leaved orache, this plant. Serves 4. 2 kg mussels, cleaned and de-bearded (foraged ones need thorough cleaning and checking); a basket of very dry pine needles; malted barley, enough to cover the tray; a splash of whisky (the source uses Bowmore 12 Years Old); 1 garlic clove; 2 handfuls of orache leaves; a knob of butter; 15 ml (1 tbsp) olive oil; salt and pepper. Outside, scatter a layer of malted barley over a large metal tray, about 40–50 cm across. Lay the mussels hinge side up, side by side, in a big circle, and pile pine needles about 20 cm high over them. Light the needles in several places, upwind of the tray, and blow on them to get them going; the fire is dramatic, so choose the spot with care. When the needles have burnt down, after 5–10 minutes, pick the mussels out of their shells, carefully, as the shells can be hot. Heat the butter, olive oil and garlic in a pan over a medium heat for 1 minute, add the orache, cover and cook for 2–3 minutes. Add the mussels, season with salt and pepper and heat through. Mussels must be properly cooked: if in any doubt, bring them to a simmer and cook for 2 minutes. Serve in clean oyster shells. The source lists the whisky but its method never says where it goes, and it uses the malted barley without listing it.

summary.text:
Atriplex prostrata, called the spear-leaved orache, hastate orache, thin-leaf orache, triangle orache, and fat hen, is a widespread species of flowering plant in the saltbush genus Atriplex, native to Europe, Macaronesia, northern Africa, Ethiopia, the Middle East, western Siberia, and Central Asia, and introduced to temperate North America, South America, Australia, New Zealand, Korea, Japan, and Primorsky Krai in far eastern Russia.
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North and South Islands and on Stewart Island. It was first recorded wild here in 1878, and it was plentiful in places by the late nineteenth century. New Zealand plants were once named as a native species, Atriplex novae-zelandiae, but no character separates them from A. prostrata elsewhere, and the species is probably introduced, since early botanists apparently did not collect it. It has also been known in New Zealand as A. hastata and A. triangularis. It is a facultative halophyte: it can grow on salty ground but does not need it.
In Australia, where creeping saltbush is one of its common names (one it shares there with the native berry saltbush, A. semibaccata), it is an environmental weed of wet, somewhat saline ground such as creek margins, estuaries and the edges of inland salt lakes.
Its name comes from an ancient Latin plant name of uncertain origin, possibly from the Greek a- 'without' and traphein 'nourishment', because many saltbushes grow in arid desert soils; prostrata means prostrate.

warnings: Plants grown on fertilised ground can concentrate harmful amounts of nitrate in their leaves.
The seeds have emetic and purgative properties.

Native saltbushes grow on the same coasts and saline ground, and all of them are Threatened or At Risk: do not pick them. Atriplex buchananii (Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable) and grey saltbush, A. cinerea (Threatened – Nationally Critical, one natural population left), are perennials with small, entire, silvery-grey or whitish leaves, round to broadly oval in A. buchananii and narrow in grey saltbush. On the Chatham Islands, A. billardierei (Threatened – Nationally Endangered) grows on sandy beaches; its fleshy leaves are densely covered in small bladder-like swellings. Holloway's crystalwort, A. hollowayi (Threatened – Nationally Critical), survives naturally only on two beaches at Te Paki in Northland. On the Chatham Islands, Atriplex australasica (At Risk – Relict), strictly coastal, grows on beaches, clay banks and cliff faces; it has wide, often deeply toothed or lobed leaves, though young plants often have entire leaves.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Lawns, golf courses. Recorded elevations range from 30 to 120 m.

identification.text:
Perennial herb to 0.05 m tall. Stems creeping and prostrate, sometimes ascending at tips, rooting at nodes; hairs eglandular, somewhat retrorse, uniform, also a few longer glandular hairs sometimes present. Leaf bud indistinct; leaves diverging while still small, opposite-decussate but sub-distichous on prostrate stems, spreading; lamina thin, broadly ovate to orbicular or reniform, 3–8 mm long, 5–12 mm wide, dull green above, pale green beneath; midrib and lateral veins visible; surfaces and margins with mixed long eglandular and glandular hairs; margin crenate or crenate-serrate; teeth in 2–5 pairs; apex obtuse to rounded; base truncate to sub-cordate; petiole 1–3 mm long. Inflorescence a terminal raceme, 50–300 mm long, sometimes resuming vegetative growth with opposite leaves after flowering; flowers distant, 5–20, all bisexual; minute, undeveloped flowers sometimes present in axils of lower bracts; bracts alternate, leaf-like; pedicels filiform, erect, often deflexed at fruiting, 15–40 mm long, with mixed short eglandular and longer glandular hairs all around. Calyx lobes 4, obtuse, 2.5–3.5 mm long, sub-equal, mixed glandular- and eglandular-hairy on outer surface and margins, glabrous within. Corolla 8–10 mm diameter; tube white and yellow, 0.5 mm long, shorter than calyx, eglandular-hairy inside; lobes 4, blue, spreading, sub-equal, elliptic to orbicular, 3.0–4.5 mm long, rounded; nectar guides dark blue. Stamen filaments white, 2.5–3.0 mm long; anthers blue. Style glabrous, 2–4 mm long. Capsules and seeds not seen in New Zealand material.
The creeping growth form and solitary flowers on long filiform pedicels are distinctive. Veronica lilliputiana plants are similar in being prostrate and creeping and having blue flowers, but their leaves are very much smaller, greyish-green, and entire, and flowers are carried on very short stalks, each with a pair of bracts. Veronica jovellanoides plants are also prostrate and have similar leaves, but their flowers are in short racemes and the corolla is white. Plants of Veronica persica have a spreading growth form, blue flowers, and leaf-like bracts, but their leaves are generally slightly narrower than long, ovate, truncate, and toothed (rather than circular, sub-cordate, and crenate), their pedicels are stouter and shorter, and the anterior corolla lobe is usually distinctly paler than the other 3 lobes. In addition they set fruit, whereas Veronica filiformis plants are sterile in New Zealand. Plants of Veronica hederifolia have a similar growth form although not so strictly prostrate, and they differ in leaf shape and size, pedicel hairs in 1 row, distinctive cordate triangular fringed calyx lobes, smaller and paler corolla, and by producing capsules, which contain large, cup-shaped seeds.
When not in flower, Veronica filiformis might be confused with unrelated small creeping plants, especially Glechoma hederacea (Lamiaceae), which is locally naturalised throughout New Zealand. Glechoma stems are 4-angled and have longer hairs than Veronica filiformis stems. Glechoma hederacea leaves are usually larger, more deeply cordate, and have deeper and rounder crenations. Glechoma flowers are sub-sessile in axillary clusters, and the corolla is long-tubed and 2-lipped.
Its small, kidney-shaped leaves are quite hairy, and in flower it carries fairly large bluish flowers on long stalks. Turf speedwell also creeps on rooting stems, but its leaves are a different shape and tend not to be hairy, and its flowers are whitish; creeping speedwell forms much denser mats. Its flowers look very like bird's-eye speedwell's, but that annual has larger leaves and is seldom found in turf. Field speedwell has no creeping stems (Massey).

lookalikes.howToTell: Bird's-eye speedwell's leaves are generally slightly narrower than long, ovate, 6–35 mm long, coarsely toothed, with a squared-off base; creeping speedwell's are round to kidney-shaped, 3–8 mm long and 5–12 mm wide, with rounded teeth and a squared-off to slightly heart-shaped base. Leaf size overlaps at 6–8 mm long, so look at the shape. Both have flat, four-lobed blue flowers of much the same size (8–12 mm across in bird's-eye speedwell, 8–10 mm in creeping speedwell), each alone on a slender stalk, so the flower alone does not separate them. Bird's-eye speedwell's flower stalks are stouter and shorter (5–15 mm in flower, up to 40 mm in fruit), and its front lobe is usually distinctly paler than the other three; creeping speedwell's stalks are thread-like, 15–40 mm long. Bird's-eye speedwell sets two-lobed seed capsules, broader than long; creeping speedwell sets no fruit in New Zealand. Bird's-eye speedwell is an annual seldom found in mown turf; creeping speedwell is a perennial that forms dense mats in lawns. Both creep and root at the joints. Bird's-eye speedwell's young leaves and shoots are eaten, but its record as food is thin.
lookalikes.name: Bird's-eye speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Turf speedwell's leaves are almost hairless; creeping speedwell's are hairy on both faces and edges. Turf speedwell's flowers are pale blue fading to whitish, 3–5 mm across, on short stalks (1–3 mm) up a spike at the stem tips; creeping speedwell's are blue, 8–10 mm across, each alone on a thread-like stalk 15–40 mm long. Turf speedwell's stems creep and root only at the base, then rise to flower; creeping speedwell's lie flat, sometimes rising at the tips. Turf speedwell sets small notched capsules; creeping speedwell sets no fruit in New Zealand. Both are perennials that creep, root at the joints and form mats in lawns, and their leaves overlap in size (turf speedwell 5–17 mm long, creeping speedwell 3–8 mm), so habit and leaf size do not separate them. Turf speedwell's record as food is thin, so it is not given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Turf speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Field speedwell's flowers are tiny, 2–3 mm across, and sit almost stalkless (stalks 0–2 mm) among small bracts at the stem tips; creeping speedwell's are 8–10 mm across, each alone on a thread-like stalk 15–40 mm long. Field speedwell is an annual with no creeping stems; creeping speedwell is a perennial whose stems creep flat and root at the joints, forming dense mats. Field speedwell sets small heart-shaped capsules; creeping speedwell sets no fruit in New Zealand. Both are hairy, both have small, toothed leaves of overlapping size (field speedwell 5–20 mm long, creeping speedwell 3–8 mm) and both grow low in lawns, so hairiness, leaf size and habitat do not separate them. No record of field speedwell being eaten has been found.
lookalikes.name: Field speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Out of flower the two are easily confused: both creep and root at the joints, have round to kidney-shaped, scalloped, hairy leaves and grow in lawns. Ground-ivy's stems are four-angled and carry longer hairs than creeping speedwell's. Ground-ivy's leaves are usually larger, 1–3.5 cm long and 1–4.5 cm wide, with a deeper heart-shaped base and deeper, rounder scallops; creeping speedwell's are 3–8 mm long and 5–12 mm wide, with a squared-off to slightly heart-shaped base. Ground-ivy's flowers are tubular and two-lipped, 1–1.5 cm long, blue or blue-violet with purple spots on the lower lip, almost stalkless in clusters in the leaf joints; creeping speedwell's are flat, with four blue lobes, 8–10 mm across, each alone on a thread-like stalk 15–40 mm long. Ground-ivy's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked; they are bitter.
lookalikes.name: Ground-ivy

Dense mats — Massey 'Creeping speedwell'. Field speedwell card (both directions, 04/11/2026): Contrasted by Massey University, New Zealand weeds database, 'Field speedwell' (https://www.massey.ac.nz/about/colleges-schools-and-institutes/college-of-sciences/our-research/themes-and-research-strengths/plant-science-research/new-zealand-weeds-database/field-speedwell/, read via r.jina.ai, retrieved 04/11/2026: 'Creeping speedwell has different shaped leaves, roots along its stems and long stalks under each flower in spring', and it lists creeping speedwell under similar species); Yates NZ, 'Speedwell' (https://www.yates.co.nz/problem-solver/weeds/speedwell/, retrieved 04/11/2026) names the four as New Zealand's common lawn speedwells, which 'all share a similar growth habit'. Dense mats — Massey 'Creeping speedwell'. No creeping stems — Massey 'Field speedwell' ('it doesn't produce creeping stems like the closely related turf speedwell or creeping speedwell').

Characters: V. filiformis from Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (Garnock-Jones 2023, Flora of New Zealand – Seed Plants Fascicle 9; CC BY 3.0 NZ), 'Veronica filiformis' (https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Veronica-filiformis.html), retrieved 04/11/2026: perennial herb to 0.05 m tall; stems creeping and prostrate, sometimes ascending at tips, rooting at nodes; lamina broadly ovate to orbicular or reniform, 3–8 mm long, 5–12 mm wide, surfaces and margins hairy, crenate or crenate-serrate, base truncate to sub-cordate; pedicels filiform, 15–40 mm; corolla 8–10 mm diameter, lobes 4, blue; capsules not seen in New Zealand ('sterile in New Zealand'); lawns, golf courses. Glechoma hederacea from Flora of New Zealand Online, 'Glechoma hederacea' (Webb et al. 1988; CC BY 3.0 NZ; https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Glechoma-hederacea.html): non-flowering stems hairy, creeping and rooting at nodes; lamina 1–3.5 × 1–4.5 cm, suborbicular to reniform, sparsely to densely hairy, crenate, base cordate; corolla 1–1.5 cm long, blue or blue-violet, lower lip with purple spots. Four-angled, longer-haired stems, usually larger and more deeply cordate leaves with deeper, rounder crenations, sub-sessile axillary flowers and a long-tubed two-lipped corolla: the V. filiformis Recognition paragraph. Ground-ivy in lawns: the ground-ivy entry's habitat (Wikipedia, 'Glechoma hederacea'); range overlap: the V. filiformis Recognition paragraph calls Glechoma 'locally naturalised throughout New Zealand', and Flora of New Zealand vol. IV gives it 'local in many southern North Id and South Id localities', which includes the Palmerston North area where creeping speedwell grows.

summary.text:
Veronica filiformis is a species of flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae. It is known by many common names, including slender speedwell, creeping speedwell, threadstalk speedwell and Whetzel weed.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Auckland (in and near Auckland City, Hamilton), Southern North Island (Palmerston North). Exotic; indigenous to Caucasus, Crimea, and SW Asia. First recorded by Sykes in 1981, from a specimen collected by A.E. Esler at Mt Eden. Flowers August–November; fruits not seen in New Zealand.
Veronica filiformis has spread around the temperate world as a cultivated plant and has escaped and become a troublesome weed in many places. The plants are self-incompatible and spread vegetatively, probably establishing freely from small fragments when lawns are mowed. It is possible a single clone was introduced in New Zealand; in any case, self-incompatibility is the reason fruits are not produced in places where Veronica filiformis is naturalised.
It is very local in New Zealand, establishing only from pieces of the plant, and was naturalised by 1981, perhaps as an ornamental but probably by accident in soil with other plants (NZPCN).
It is a major problem in turf, found mainly around Palmerston North and Auckland but slowly spreading through the country. It is thought to set no seed here, and is probably carried about in clods of soil on footwear and equipment. It tolerates most turf herbicides (Massey).

warnings: No food use for creeping speedwell has been confirmed. Plant databases list none, and the only claims found are informal web pages that give no part or preparation, so it is not given as food here.
It grows in lawns and golf courses, which are often sprayed, and it survives most turf weedkillers, so a healthy-looking patch may still have been sprayed.

Its creeping, rooting stems and small round leaves look like turf speedwell's and ground-ivy's, its flowers like bird's-eye speedwell's, and it grows in lawns with field and turf speedwell. Check the flowers and leaves before picking any of them (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
A perennial with a slender main root and no bulbs. Its slender, weak, branched stems, up to about 40 cm long, lie along the ground or rise a little, are covered in spreading hairs and often root at the nodes. Each leaf has three equal, broadly heart-shaped leaflets, (2.5–)5–18 mm long, notched up to halfway down, on a hairy stalk (0.5–)1–7 cm long. The leaves are green or purple.

The flowers are yellow, with petals 4.5–10(–13) mm long, in clusters of 1 to 5 on a stalk 1–4 cm long (up to 9.5 cm in fruit). The fruit is an upright, cylindrical capsule (6–)10–18(–20) mm long, usually densely hairy, which bursts to throw out its seeds.

In New Zealand two forms are told apart: the typical form, with green leaves and stems, and var. atropurpurea, with purple-green leaves and stems, purple flower stalks and sepals, and a thicker taproot.

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping wood sorrel spreads on slender, branched stems up to c. 40 cm long that lie along the ground or rise a little, carry the leaves, and often root at the nodes. Bermuda buttercup is an upright plant from an underground bulb and apparently stemless; its leaves all rise from the base on stalks 6–22 cm long. Its flower stalks are (7)–15–45 cm long, against creeping wood sorrel's 1–4 cm in flower (to 9.5 cm in fruit), and usually carry 3–18 hanging flowers (occasionally 1) with golden petals (1.5)–2–2.8 cm long; creeping wood sorrel carries 1–5 flowers with petals 4.5–10–(13) mm long, so petal length separates them where flower number does not. Creeping wood sorrel sets cylindrical capsules, usually hairy, (6)–10–18–(20) mm long; no capsule has been seen on Bermuda buttercup in New Zealand. Yellow flowers, heart-shaped leaflets, leaflet size and purple in the leaf do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Bermuda buttercup

lookalikes.howToTell: Least yellow sorrel looks like a smaller creeping wood sorrel, with much the same leaves, creeping stems and yellow flowers, so size and flower count are the tests, and size changes with growing conditions. Least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long and its leaves typically under 10 mm across; creeping wood sorrel's leaflets are 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm) and its leaves normally about 20 mm across. Count the flowers on a stalk: least yellow sorrel's are solitary, rarely paired; creeping wood sorrel carries 1 to 5, usually at least two. Least yellow sorrel's capsule is mostly 7–10 mm long, creeping wood sorrel's mostly 10–18 mm, though the ranges meet. Least yellow sorrel is more often in lawns, creeping wood sorrel in garden beds and nurseries. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Least yellow sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. White clover's leaflets are 5–25 mm long, creeping wood sorrel's 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm). Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves or stems: both creep and root at the nodes, both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually stalkless on the leaves beneath it, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Red clover's hairy stems stand erect or lie along the ground at the base and do not root at the nodes; creeping wood sorrel's stems lie along the ground or rise a little and often root at the nodes. Red clover's leaflets are 15–40 mm long, creeping wood sorrel's 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm). Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Alsike clover's hairless stems stand erect or rise from the base and do not root at the nodes; creeping wood sorrel's stems lie along the ground or rise a little and often root at the nodes. Alsike clover's leaflets are 10–35 mm long, creeping wood sorrel's 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm). Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: both have three leaflets, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have yellow flowers and three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and both grow in lawns and gardens. Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long, its florets staying on the head around tiny pods 2–3 mm long. Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets, and sets cylindrical capsules (6)–10–18–(20) mm long. On most suckling clover leaves the middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the side ones (under 1 mm); creeping wood sorrel's three leaflets are equal, on very short stalks. Suckling clover's stems do not root at the nodes; creeping wood sorrel's often do. Leaflet size overlaps (suckling clover about 3–12 mm long, creeping wood sorrel (2.5)–5–18 mm), and both have hairy stems that lie along the ground or rise a little. Suckling clover has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Suckling clover

preparation.text: Add the leaves to salads, cook them as a pot herb with milder greens, or use them to give a sour taste to other food. For a drink, steep the leaves in hot water for about 10 minutes, sweeten and chill. The leaves are very small and fiddly to pick.

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) lemon juice and 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) maple syrup or honey. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the sorrel and stir for 1–2 minutes, until it wilts. Put it in a blender or food processor with the lemon juice and the syrup or honey and blend until well combined. Serve it straight away, or refrigerate it and warm it before use; the author finds it even better the next day. The author serves it on fish, or as a dipping sauce for grilled prawns.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel sauce

recipes.method: About 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, stems or flowers, or a mix, about 250 ml (1 cup) water, and maple syrup or another sweetener to taste. The amounts are rough: use as much sorrel as you like and enough water to cover it. Blend the sorrel and water until well combined, strain through a fine sieve and sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel 'lemonade'

recipes.method: Equal parts wood sorrel, sugar, and water; the author usually uses 250 ml (1 cup) of each. Put everything in a saucepan and bring it to a simmer, stirring. Simmer for 15–30 minutes, strain through muslin (cheesecloth) and pour into sterilised bottles. The author uses it in tea, topped up with soda water, over ice cream or fresh strawberries, or in vinaigrettes and marinades.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel syrup

recipes.method: The recipe uses one part leaves to three parts water. Fresh wood sorrel leaves; boiling water; sweetener to taste (optional). Put the leaves in a container, pour the boiling water over them and leave to steep for 5–15 minutes. Strain out the leaves and sweeten to taste if you like. Drink it hot, or pour it over ice for an iced tea.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel tea

recipes.method: 2 cloves garlic, minced; olive oil for cooking; 2 spring onions, chopped; 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock; 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish; 3 medium mint leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk; salt and pepper. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks. Heat a little olive oil in a small saucepan and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the spring onions. Cover with the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, then add the sorrel for about 30 seconds. Take it off the heat, add the mint and blend smooth with a stick blender (or an ordinary blender). Stir in the coconut milk and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until well chilled, a couple of hours, and serve garnished with the sorrel flowers.
recipes.title: Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

recipes.method: About 450 g (1 lb) Italian or breakfast sausage; 1 medium spaghetti squash; several cups of wood sorrel, washed and drained, stems removed (the recipe gives no closer amount); olive oil; 1 red onion, halved and sliced; 1 egg; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk or any milk; 1 garlic clove, minced; 15 ml (1 tbsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) tarragon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) black pepper; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground sage. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Halve the squash, spoon out the seeds and stringy threads, set the halves cut side up on a baking tray, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and bake for 20–25 minutes, until the flesh gives a little when pressed. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts. Take the squash out of the oven and scrape out the flesh with a fork (careful, it will be hot). Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.
recipes.title: Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel

recipes.method: Two handfuls of wood sorrel, chopped; potato and kūmara, boiled first and sliced; cream. Layer the sorrel with the sliced potato and kūmara in a baking dish, pour cream over the top and bake at 180 °C until it starts to brown.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel, kūmara and potato gratin

recipes.method: Chop a big handful of wood sorrel leaves, stalks and flowers and mix them through a potato salad dressed with a cream dressing.
recipes.title: Potato salad with wood sorrel

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: The author's greens were puha, sow thistle, nasturtium, onion weed, wild fennel, oxalis, wild mustard and wild celery; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 1 diced onion; 1 potato, scrubbed and diced; 2 sliced garlic cloves; 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 1.3 litres water; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked pepper; extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil, to serve; edible weed flowers. Serves 4. Cut the vegetables and greens to similar sizes. Fry the onion in the oil for a minute, then add the potato and garlic (the method also adds fennel bulb and celery stalks, which the ingredient list leaves out) and fry for another minute. Add the water, cover, bring to the boil and simmer until the potato is soft. Add the greens with the salt and yeast and cook for 3 minutes, until just tender — added at the end, they keep their colour. Blend until smooth (push it through a sieve if your blender isn't powerful), season with the pepper and more salt if needed, and serve drizzled with extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil and scattered with edible weed flowers.
recipes.title: Wild greens soup

The card follows Flora of New Zealand. Risk edible because the Bermuda buttercup page says the plant is palatable and eaten, with an oxalate warning.

Sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, 'Oxalis pes caprae' (Webb et al. 1988 / Edgar & Connor 2000 / Allan 1961 text; CC BY 3.0 NZ), https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Oxalis-pes-caprae.html | Flora of New Zealand Online, 'Oxalis corniculata' (Webb et al. 1988 / Edgar & Connor 2000 / Allan 1961 text; CC BY 3.0 NZ), https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Oxalis-corniculata.html | Weeds Australia, 'Soursob (Oxalis pes-caprae)', https://weeds.org.au/profiles/soursob/ — 'small, upright, perennial herb ... with an underground bulb'; leaves 'often with purplish brown flecks, speckles or markings on the upper surface'; 'Aerial growth commences as a rosette of leaves' (saved pages/b5-weedsaus-Oxalis-pes-caprae.txt) | Wikipedia 'Oxalis pes-caprae' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — 'in modest quantities is reasonably harmless'; runners eaten raw or boiled (supports edible risk, with oxalate caution) UNRESOLVED: Bermuda buttercup 'edible' rests on Wikipedia ('in modest quantities is reasonably harmless'); oxalate caution applies. proposed_risk was null; final_risk is the current catalogue risk (edible), checked.

Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (cups at 250 ml, 1 tbsp = 15 ml, 1 tsp = 5 ml; every page all rights reserved; retrieved 15/10/2026; supplied by the owner). None is written for this species: each is written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally. The sauce, 'lemonade' and syrup from Kate MacQuarrie, 'Wood Sorrel Recipes', PEI Untamed, 09/07/2023 (https://www.pei-untamed.com/post/wood-sorrel-recipes) — written for 'the Wood Sorrels' of Prince Edward Island, no species named; 'grilled shrimp' given as prawns; the lemonade's 'leaves, stems, and/or flowers' and its note that the author does not measure are kept. 'Wood sorrel cooler' is Sunny Savage's 'Oxalis Cooler' as given in Green Deane, 'Oxalis: How To Drown Your Sorrels', Eat The Weeds (dated 16/01/2018 on the page, with reader comments from 2012; https://www.eattheweeds.com/oxalis-how-to-drown-your-sorrels/; the owner's second link, https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/oxalis-deppei/, is a tag page showing the same article) — written for Oxalis generally, the article naming the Florida species including O. corniculata; 1 US quart is about 946 ml; the recipe does not strain the drink and neither does this. 'Wood sorrel tea' from Jesse, 'Wood Sorrel: Identification, Uses, and Precautions', Feral Foraging, 11/07/2024 (https://feralforaging.com/wood-sorrel/) — written mainly for O. stricta and O. violacea; the page gives the ratio only as '1:3' after 'Gather wood sorrel leaves' and 'Pour over boiling water', without saying by volume or by weight, so 'one part leaves to three parts water' is this guide's reading.
