summary.text:
Oxalis corniculata, the creeping woodsorrel, procumbent yellow sorrel or sleeping beauty, is a somewhat delicate-appearing, low-growing herbaceous plant in the family Oxalidaceae.
This species probably comes from southeastern Asia. It was first described by Linnaeus in 1753 using specimens from Italy, and it seems to have been introduced to Italy from the east before 1500. It is now cosmopolitan in its distribution and is often regarded as a weed in gardens, agricultural fields, and lawns.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Gardens, market gardens, cultivated and swampy land, riverbeds and damp pasture.
It grows at the edges of water bodies and as a weed of cultivated ground and wet pasture. It forms dense stands on low-lying pasture and other ground beside rivers, where its rhizomes can smother the pasture, and is particularly common in the Waikato.
On the national wetland plant list it is rated facultative: it grows in wetlands and on dry ground alike.

identification.text:
Glabrous perennial rhizomatous herb. Stems erect, often flexuous, 30–70 cm tall. Leaves variable in shape; margins toothed. Rosette leaves petiolate, auriculate at base, deeply pinnatifid, 4–10–(25) × 2–4 cm. Middle and upper leaves smaller, 1–2-pinnatifid, linear to ovate; lobes narrow-lanceolate to linear, entire or toothed; basal auricles present. Pedicels erecto-patent at flowering, spreading at fruiting, 5–15 mm long. Sepals 2–2.5 mm long. Petals yellow, (3)–4–5 mm long. Silique glabrous, linear, curved, 10–15 × 1–1.5 mm, but often not or poorly developed; valves with median vein weak or 0; style about 0.5 mm long. Seeds brown, about 0.6 mm long, finely colliculate, in 2 rows per locule.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Its rhizomes creep underground and put down roots at the nodes, so it grows in dense patches. The flowers are about 4–6 mm across, with four separate petals, and sit at the tops of thin upright stems. The lower, rosette leaves are cut deeply into as many as ten lobes (2 to 5 pairs); the leaves up the flowering stems are smaller, with fewer and narrower lobes.
Marsh yellow cress (Rorippa amphibia, also called tall yellow cress) is similar: it also spreads by rhizomes and often sets no seed. In New Zealand it grows only in Northland, Auckland, Waikato and the Bay of Plenty, and its pods, when they form, are short and oval, 1.5–3 mm long (sometimes up to 4 mm), not slender and 10–15 mm long.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have small yellow flowers and deeply lobed, toothed leaves with small lobes at the base, and both grow in damp ground, so colour, leaves and place do not separate them. The flowers do: bog yellow cress's petals are only about as long as the sepals (1.5–2.5 mm); creeping yellowcress's are 3–5 mm long, about twice the length of the sepals. Bog yellow cress grows from a taproot; creeping yellowcress spreads into patches by creeping underground parts. Bog yellow cress's pods are short and plump, 2–7 mm long; creeping yellowcress's, when they form, are slender, 10–15 mm, but it often sets none. Bog yellow cress's young leaves and stems are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Bog yellow cress

lookalikes.howToTell: Watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes; its leaflets are rounded, with smooth or wavy edges. Creeping yellowcress has yellow flowers on upright stems and spreads by creeping underground parts; its upper leaves are cut into narrow, toothed or untoothed lobes. Both grow in wet ground and both have petals about twice as long as the sepals, so place and petal length do not separate them. Watercress is edible; cook it if it comes from water below grazing land.
lookalikes.name: Watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Land cress has larger flowers, with yellow petals 6–8 mm long against 3–5 mm in creeping yellowcress. Land cress's pods are 30–70 mm long with the seeds in one row; creeping yellowcress's, when they form, are 10–15 mm with the seeds in two rows, and it often sets none. Land cress grows from a stout taproot; creeping yellowcress spreads into patches by creeping underground parts. Both have yellow flowers and deeply lobed leaves and grow on riverbeds and cultivated or waste ground, so colour, leaves and place do not separate them. Land cress's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Land cress

Creeping yellowcress has yellow flowers on upright stems and spreads by creeping underground parts; its upper leaves are cut into narrow, toothed or untoothed lobes. Both grow in wet ground and both have petals about twice as long as the sepals, so place and petal length do not separate them. Narrow-fruited watercress is edible; cook it if it comes from water below grazing land.

summary.text:
Rorippa sylvestris (the creeping yellowcress, keek, or yellow fieldcress; syn. Radicula sylvestris (L.) Druce ) is an invasive species of plant in the United States, likely entering from Europe before 1818 from ballast water and spreading throughout North America through contaminated nursery seed stock.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) it is locally common throughout the North and South Islands, naturalised by 1952 from temperate Eurasia.
R. sylvestris, like R. amphibia, is self-incompatible and colonies of only one genotype are often established. In such cases the plants do not set seed.
It probably arrived as a seed or soil contaminant. Its seed and pieces of rhizome are carried by water and on contaminated machinery. Rorippa is a Latinised form of Rorippen, a Saxon vernacular name used by Euricius Cordus.
Most of Landcare Research's databased herbarium specimens come from Canterbury (18) and Wellington (13), then Nelson 3, Hawke's Bay 2, Marlborough 2, North Auckland 1 and South Auckland 1; 21 more are not placed in a land district.

warnings: Liver fluke risk: Rorippa sylvestris is one of the plants called wild watercress, which has been reported as the main source of human liver fluke (Fasciola) infection where the disease is common in farm animals. Infection comes from eating such plants raw; heat kills the cysts.

edibleParts.text: Eaten in Spain and Morocco. In Spain the small fruits have been eaten as a snack, especially by children, who call them panecillos ("little bread rolls"), the same way as common mallow's, and in Petra, Mallorca, the round leaves are eaten steamed. In the countryside around El Jadida, Morocco, it is the wild food plant people name most often.

identification.text:
Stout annual to biennial up to 2 m high but frequently smaller, often branched from base.  Stems densely clothed in stellate hairs when young, becoming more or less glabrous and often woody at base when older.  Leaves densely clothed in stellate hairs when young, becoming sparsely so when older, suborbicular, cordate to obtuse at base, shallowly 3–5-palmately lobed and crenate or serrate, 1–15 cm diameter;  petioles 1–15 cm long;  stipules ovate-triangular, 3–6 mm long.  Flowers in axillary clusters of (1)–2–6–(8);  fruiting pedicels 5–25 mm long;  epicalyx segments ovate to broadly ovate, united for lower 1/4, about ⅔-4/5 length of calyx, unchanged at fruiting;  calyx shallowly campanulate;  calyx teeth more or less equal to tube, ovate, acuminate, densely clothed in stellate hairs, usually more or less connivent at fruiting;  petals lilac or pink with darker veins, (8)–10–18 mm long.  Mericarps 8–10 per fruit, glabrous, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on back and with a single low longitudinal rib;  edges usually rounded, rarely more or less sharply angled.
[From:  Webb et al.  (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Lavatera cretica L.]
L. cretica is often confused with the forms of Malva sylvestris in which the bases of the epicalyx segments are slightly fused. L. cretica can be distinguished by the round-edged, more or less smooth-backed mericarps, the acuminate calyx teeth, and generally broader epicalyx segments.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Cretan mallow is often confused with forms of common mallow whose epicalyx segments are slightly joined at the base; it is separated by its round-edged, more or less smooth-backed fruit segments (net-veined and sharply angled in common mallow), its long-pointed calyx teeth (acute in common mallow) and its generally broader epicalyx segments. Petal colour and length overlap. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and are unchanged in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. summary.text:
Malva multiflora (previously known as Lavatera cretica) is a species of flowering plant in the mallow family known by the common names Cornish mallow and Cretan hollyhock. It is native to western Europe, North Africa, and the Mediterranean Basin, and it is naturalized in areas with a Mediterranean climate, such as parts of Australia, South Africa, and California.
In New Zealand it grows in Auckland City, Waikato, Coromandel, Napier and from Palmerston North to Wellington, and in Nelson, lowland Canterbury and North Otago. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1940.

edibleParts.text: Young leaves, raw or cooked; the stems, raw or cooked, peeled for the inner part; and the seeds, raw or cooked. Young leaves are milder than broad-leaved dock's, sour and lemony, and grow tough and bitter once the plant flowers. The roasted seed has been used as a coffee substitute.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Mostly damp places such as lakesides, river beds, ditches, swamps, moist dune slacks near the coast, and wet pastures, sometimes drier ground in waste places, pastures and other modified habitats.
It is a widespread and often abundant weed in all but the mountains, on the North, South and Stewart Islands and the Chatham, Campbell and Macquarie Islands.
New Zealand's national wetland plant list rates it facultative: it grows as readily on dry ground as in wetlands.

identification.text:
Perennial herb with stout taproot; stems to about 1 m tall, more or less erect, often somewhat flexuous. Petiole much shorter than lamina, the anterior side flattened with raised margins so as to appear concave, sometimes ciliolate. Lamina of lower leaves 6–30 × 1.5–6.5 cm, narrow-lanceolate, oblong or lingulate, more or less membranous, strongly undulate with more or less crisped margins, minutely puberulent on midrib towards base below; base attenuate; apex acute. Upper leaves similar but much smaller. Inflorescence branches many, more or less erect, often simple; whorls mostly contiguous, the lower sometimes with a small subtending leaf, rarely leaves present towards apex. Flowers bisexual or unisexual, strongly protandrous, dense. Pedicels slender, minutely puberulent. Perianth 1–2.5 mm long; segments of outer whorl more or less elliptic, obtuse, not reflexing at fruiting; segments of inner whorl much longer, greatly enlarging at fruiting. Fruiting valves 3–4.5 × 3–5 mm, broad-ovate to orbicular, sometimes wider than long, strongly reticulate with raised veins, entire, sinuate or crenulate; tubercles 1–3, generally broad-ovoid, more or less deep red and often 1 much larger and occupying up to 1/2 length of valve. Nuts 2–2.5 mm long, dark brown, sharply angled.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The leaves are long and narrow — often no more than about 8 cm wide — with strongly wavy, curled edges, and taper into the stalk. Young plants have less curly, slightly rounder and broader leaves, so look at several. Each leaf stalk is wrapped at its base by a thin, papery sheath (ochrea), and young leaves are slippery with mucilage when picked. The root is a large, yellow, forking taproot. Older leaves often turn yellow or red. In fruit the whole head turns a conspicuous rusty brown, and the stiff dead stems can stay standing into winter.

lookalikes.howToTell: Foxglove is deadly. Its leaves are matt and hairy, grey-felted beneath, with scalloped edges; curled dock's are smooth (finely downy only on the midrib near the base beneath), with strongly wavy, curled edges. Both leaves narrow into the stalk, so the base does not separate them. Foxglove's side veins curve forward to run almost parallel with the midrib; dock's run out to the edge. Every dock leaf stalk is wrapped at its base by a papery sheath (ochrea). If a leaf is felted or hairy underneath, leave it.
lookalikes.name: Foxglove

lookalikes.howToTell: Broad-leaved dock's lower leaves are much broader — up to 35 × 15 cm (rarely 50 × 20) — with a heart-shaped to rounded base, a blunt tip and only slightly wavy edges; curled dock's are narrow, 6–30 × 1.5–6.5 cm, strongly wavy and curled, and taper into the stalk. In fruit, broad-leaved dock's valves have a few teeth 1–1.7 mm long on their edges; curled dock's are entire or finely scalloped. Young curled dock has rounder, less curly leaves, so check several. Both are eaten the same way.
lookalikes.name: Broad-leaved dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Clustered dock's flower whorls are all spaced apart along spreading branches that twist as they fruit, with small leaves about two-thirds of the way up; curled dock's whorls are mostly packed together on erect branches, with few or no leaves among them. Each of clustered dock's fruit valves (2–3.2 mm) has a large tubercle; curled dock's valves are larger (3–4.5 mm) and often only one has a much larger tubercle. Clustered dock's leaf base is broadly wedge-shaped, rounded or heart-shaped; curled dock's tapers into the stalk. Both can have wavy, curled leaf edges.
lookalikes.name: Clustered dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Fiddle dock's lower leaves are flat and pinched in the lower half above two large rounded lobes (occasionally plain and oblong); curled dock's are narrow, strongly wavy and curled, and taper into the stalk. Fiddle dock's fruit valves have spines up to 2 mm long on their edges; curled dock's are entire or finely scalloped.
lookalikes.name: Fiddle dock

lookalikes.howToTell: New Zealand dock is low and spreads sideways on slender zig-zag branches together about 50 cm long, with many small flower whorls spaced well apart; curled dock stands upright to about 1 m, its whorls mostly packed together. New Zealand dock's leaves are smaller, 3–15 × 0.4–2.5 cm, usually brown, rarely green; curled dock's are 6–30 × 1.5–6.5 cm. Both have wavy, curled leaf edges. In fruit, New Zealand dock's valves have 1–4 straight teeth on each edge and usually no swelling (tubercle); curled dock's have smooth or finely scalloped edges and 1–3 deep red tubercles. New Zealand dock is native, uncommon in the north and now gone from Auckland, and is often pulled out as a weed by mistake, so leave plants that fit its description.
lookalikes.name: New Zealand dock

preparation.text: Use only the youngest leaves, ideally before the flower stalk grows; even these can be bitter, and those picked in spring and autumn are the most pleasant. Add them raw to salads in moderation, or cook them as a potherb or in soups — older, tougher leaves are better wilted or sautéed than raw; boiling in more than one change of water takes out more of the sour oxalic acid and bitterness. The stalks of the young central leaves, still slimy with mucilage, are juicy and tart; the flower stalk, picked before it flowers, can be peeled and eaten raw or cooked and tastes of green beans. The seeds can be ground into flour for pancakes and the like, or toasted first to make the husk easier to rub off; the husk is high in fibre and hard on the gut in quantity. To gather seed, run your fingers down the stems to strip it off. To toast it, spread it no more than about 6 mm deep in a dry cast-iron pan over a medium-high heat and stir often until it browns and smells nutty, about 10 minutes. Toasted seed tastes tart and nutty, rather like rye, and can be eaten as a snack or used in granola and crackers. For seed flour, strip the seed heads into a paper bag once the seeds have turned dark brown, pick out any leaves and stems, and dry the seeds until cracker-dry (6–8 hours in a dehydrator at about 63 °C, or briefly in a low oven at about 95 °C). Grind seed and husk together, as finely as you can, in a spice grinder or high-speed blender — there is no need to winnow, and most of the flour is husk. It tastes a little like buckwheat and has no gluten, so use it for about a quarter of the flour in baking. For doughs, soak it first: pour 60 ml (¼ cup) boiling water over 125 ml (½ cup) dock flour, cover and leave to cool, which stops the dough cracking or tearing. A handful of green seeds can be cooked with rice for a mild tartness. Dried, powdered leaves season fish.

recipes.method: Written for dock generally — the page does not say which; the same author names curled and broad-leaved dock as New Zealand's commonest docks. The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard. 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: Written for dock generally — the page does not say which; the same author names curled and broad-leaved dock as New Zealand's commonest docks. The author's greens were dock, onion weed, nasturtium, plantain, baby wild mustard, dandelion, sow thistle and a violet leaf. 2 crushed garlic cloves; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 500 ml (2 cups) firmly packed wild greens, sliced very thinly; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper; 125 ml (½ cup) roughly chopped pistachios, walnuts, almonds or brazil nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp hearts, pumpkin or sunflower seeds; and 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, hemp seed oil or a mix. Makes about 750 ml (3 cups). To slice the greens, sort them into similar shapes, bunch and twist a few leaves together and slice as thinly as you can — this suits the tougher, stringier ones such as plantain, mustard and dock. Toss everything together. Good as a side or salad, in a wrap or sandwich, or with pasta, risotto, eggs, or sausages and mash. It keeps at least 4 days in a sealed jar in the fridge.
recipes.title: Weedolata (wild-greens gremolata)

recipes.method: Written for docks generally (the author names curly and broad-leaved dock). 12 large dock leaves; ½ diced onion; 2–3 diced garlic cloves; 2–3 tbsp olive oil, plus more if needed and to drizzle; 500 ml (2 cups) cooked rice; the juice of 1 large lemon (about 60 ml); a large handful of chopped mint and parsley; any chopped dried fruit, nuts or leftover meat; seasoning; coarse sea salt. Blanch 12 large dock leaves in boiling water, one or two at a time, for 30 seconds, and drain them on paper towels. Sweat ½ diced onion and 2–3 diced garlic cloves in 2–3 tbsp olive oil over a medium heat. Stir in 500 ml (2 cups) cooked rice, lower the heat, and add the juice of 1 large lemon (about 60 ml), a large handful of chopped mint and parsley, and any chopped dried fruit, nuts or leftover meat; season, add more oil if needed, and take it off the heat. Put two spoonfuls of the rice on each leaf, fold in the sides and roll up like a burrito. Drizzle with olive oil and sprinkle with coarse sea salt.
recipes.title: Dock dolmas

recipes.method: Written for curled and broad-leaved dock. Dock leaves; oil; salt or other seasonings. Wash the leaves and dry them very well, toss them in oil and lay them in a single layer on a baking tray. Season with salt or other seasonings and bake at 150 °C for 10–15 minutes, until crisp. Don't let them brown, which makes them more bitter; if they don't crisp, they were not dry enough.
recipes.title: Dock chips

recipes.method: Written for curled and broad-leaved dock (from Edible Garden Weeds of Canada, 1978). 2 tbsp butter; 1 chopped onion; 750 ml (3 cups) washed, shredded dock leaves; 750 ml (3 cups) milk; 750 ml (3 cups) fresh clams or oysters (or cod); 2 large potatoes, cooked and cubed but still slightly firm; salt and pepper. Melt 2 tbsp butter and cook 1 chopped onion until lightly browned. Add 750 ml (3 cups) washed, shredded dock leaves and cook 1–2 minutes until wilted. Add 750 ml (3 cups) milk, 750 ml (3 cups) fresh clams or oysters (or cod), and 2 large potatoes, cooked and cubed but still slightly firm. Cover and simmer over a low heat for 10–15 minutes, until the seafood is cooked. Season with salt and pepper.
recipes.title: Dock chowder

recipes.method: Written for curled and broad-leaved dock (from Edible Garden Weeds of Canada, 1978). 500 ml (2 cups) washed dock leaves; 60 ml (¼ cup) butter; 2 tbsp grated onion; 2 pressed garlic cloves, if you like; 2 tbsp flour; 250 ml (1 cup) milk; seasoning; 3 sliced hard-boiled eggs; 125 ml (½ cup) panko; 125 ml (½ cup) grated aged cheddar. Bring 60 ml (¼ cup) water to the boil, add 500 ml (2 cups) washed dock leaves and simmer 3–4 minutes, then drain. Melt 60 ml (¼ cup) butter, cook 2 tbsp grated onion (and 2 pressed garlic cloves, if you like) for 1 minute, stir in 2 tbsp flour, then slowly stir in 250 ml (1 cup) milk; season and cook until thick. In a greased small casserole dish, layer the dock with 3 sliced hard-boiled eggs, pour the sauce over, and top with 125 ml (½ cup) panko and 125 ml (½ cup) grated aged cheddar. Bake at 180 °C for 20–25 minutes.
recipes.title: Dock casserole

recipes.method: Written for the seeds of broad-leaved and curled dock. Makes about 30. 250 ml (1 cup) dock flour (from about 625 ml, 2½ cups, of dried seed); 250 ml (1 cup) oat flour; ½ tsp salt; 1 tsp onion powder; 1 tbsp yeast flakes; up to 125 ml (½ cup) water. Spread the gathered seeds on a baking tray and dry them in a low oven until slightly toasted, without burning them (about 625 ml, 2½ cups, of dried seed makes 250 ml, 1 cup, of flour); soaking them overnight first takes out some bitterness. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Grind the seeds in a coffee grinder or food processor, and mix 250 ml (1 cup) of the dock flour with 250 ml (1 cup) oat flour, ½ tsp salt, 1 tsp onion powder and 1 tbsp yeast flakes. Add up to 125 ml (½ cup) water a little at a time until it holds together without sticking, knead, cover and rest 10 minutes. Roll half the dough out about 2 mm thick on a greased, floured tray, cut into crackers or leave whole, and bake for 15 minutes; repeat with the rest. Cool completely. They keep a week in an airtight container.
recipes.title: Dock seed crackers

recipes.method: Written for curly (curled) dock — the author does not vouch for broad-leaved dock seed. 125 ml (½ cup) dock seed flour; 60 ml (¼ cup) boiling water; 500 ml (2 cups) flour; 5 eggs; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 125 ml (½ cup) water. Soak 125 ml (½ cup) dock seed flour in 60 ml (¼ cup) boiling water, covered, until cool (see Preparation). Combine it with 500 ml (2 cups) flour, 5 eggs, 5 ml (1 tsp) salt and 125 ml (½ cup) water into a dough, and make pasta from it as usual; unsoaked dock flour can make the pasta brittle or tear. The author served it with brown butter, morels and wild greens. The recipe's proportions also work for a dock seed porridge or polenta.
recipes.title: Dock seed pasta

recipes.method: Written for curly (curled) dock; dandelion or other greens work too. Serves 4. For the gnocchi: 900 g golden potatoes, halved; 60 ml (¼ cup) lightly beaten egg; 185 ml (¾ cup) plain flour, plus up to 60 ml (¼ cup) more. For the sauce: 375 ml (1½ cups) low-salt chicken stock; 20 g rinsed dried porcini; 1 tbsp olive oil, plus another 1 tbsp; 1 minced small shallot; 1 sliced garlic clove; 80 ml (⅓ cup) dry white wine; 2 tbsp chopped parsley. To serve: a few handfuls of washed, trimmed dock leaves; olive oil; salt and pepper; parmesan shavings. Gnocchi: boil 900 g golden potatoes, halved, in salted water until tender, 25–30 minutes, and keep the water. Lift them out one at a time, peel while hot and fluff with a fork without overmashing. Cool 5 minutes, then drizzle over 60 ml (¼ cup) lightly beaten egg, scatter over 185 ml (¾ cup) plain flour and fold together; knead very gently, adding up to 60 ml (¼ cup) more flour if it is gummy. Cut into 8, roll each into a thumb-thick log and cut every 2 cm; press each piece lightly with a fork and dust with flour. Sauce: heat 375 ml (1½ cups) low-salt chicken stock with 20 g rinsed dried porcini to a simmer, cover off the heat for 5 minutes, then lift out and dice the mushrooms, keeping the liquid. Fry them in 1 tbsp olive oil over a medium heat with 1 minced small shallot and 1 sliced garlic clove until lightly browned, 2–4 minutes. Add the liquid, 80 ml (⅓ cup) dry white wine and another 1 tbsp olive oil, scraping up the browned bits, and boil hard, whisking now and then, about 5 minutes. Stir in 2 tbsp chopped parsley, season and keep warm. To serve: bring the potato water back to the boil and cook the gnocchi in small batches, lifting them out about 10 seconds after they rise. Lay them straight onto a platter of a few handfuls of washed, trimmed dock leaves, which wilt in the heat. Top with the sauce, a drizzle of olive oil, salt, pepper and parmesan shavings.
recipes.title: Potato gnocchi with porcini sauce and wilted dock

recipes.method: Written for broad-leaved dock; the author says any dock picked in spring, before flowering, will do, and so will other strong-tasting spring greens such as nettle, plantain or watercress. Makes about 35 small puddings or one large one. 400 g pearl barley; 4 eggs, hard-boiled; 2 large leeks; a little oil; about half a supermarket bag of washed dock and dandelion leaves; 3 raw eggs, plus 1–2 more if needed. To finish: flour; 1 beaten egg; 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs; 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle (optional); garlic mayonnaise. Boil 400 g pearl barley until tender, drain and cool. Hard-boil 4 eggs and chop finely. Finely chop 2 large leeks and soften them in a little oil. Blanch about half a supermarket bag of washed dock and dandelion leaves in boiling water for 20 seconds, then plunge into iced water (skip this and the puddings are more bitter and less green); squeeze out every drop of water and chop finely. Mix the chopped eggs, leeks, barley and greens with 3 raw eggs, and season very well. Wrap the mixture tightly in a tray covered with cling film, set in a larger tray of hot water, or seal it in a pudding bowl with baking paper, foil and string and stand it in a pan of water reaching at least halfway up. Steam for 45–60 minutes, in a 160 °C oven or on the hob, until it holds together; if it won't roll into balls, mix in 1–2 more raw eggs and steam longer. Turn out and serve as one pudding, or roll into small balls while warm and chill them (they freeze individually at this stage). Roll the chilled balls in flour, then in 1 beaten egg, then in 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs (mixed, if you like, with 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle), and deep-fry for 1–2 minutes until browned; or simply flour and fry them. Serve warm, with garlic mayonnaise.
recipes.title: Dock, dandelion and nettle puddings

recipes.method: Written for dock generally — the author thinks his leaves were most likely curled dock but is not certain; the New Zealand version below names curled and broad-leaved dock; use young leaves. Serves 4. You need 170 g young dock leaves, washed; salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to finish; 50 g (¼ cup) basmati or other long-grain rice; 1 small onion, chopped; 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped garlic; 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped fresh oregano; a pinch of ground cumin; 1 litre chicken or vegetable stock; 1 large egg, beaten; black pepper; and plenty of fresh lemon juice. Drop the dock leaves into boiling salted water for a few seconds until just wilted, cool them in cold water and squeeze them dry (about 180 ml). Toast the rice on a tray in a 175 °C oven until just golden, then simmer it, covered, with a pinch of salt and 125 ml water until tender. Chop the dock both ways so no long strands are left. In a 3-litre pot, soften the onion and garlic in the oil over medium heat for about 10 minutes, until just browning at the edges. Add the stock, dock, oregano and cumin, bring to a simmer and season, then add the rice and simmer gently for about 10 minutes. Pour the beaten egg in a spiral over the surface without stirring and let it heat through. Serve with a drizzle of olive oil, black pepper and enough lemon juice that the soup tastes lemony. For a simpler version without egg (Wild Botanica, New Zealand): soften the onion and garlic, wilt the chopped leaves (central veins removed) in the pot, add the stock, cumin, oregano and salt, simmer for 10 minutes, then stir through about 50 g cooked rice and finish with lemon juice.
recipes.title: Dock soup with rice, egg and lemon

sources: Filled 25/10/2026 under the owner's goal 'do websearches and fill anything about Rumexes that you can find. remember to stick to our rules'. New entry: curled dock, 338 research-grade wild NZ observations (iNaturalist, 25/10/2026); with broad-leaved dock 'the most common here in New Zealand' (The Veggie Tree). Name: Flora of New Zealand Online 'Curled dock; Yellow dock'; NZPCN 'curled dock, yellow dock'.

Flora of New Zealand Online 'Rumex crispus' (https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Rumex-crispus.html, retrieved 25/10/2026) — description. Flora vol. IV (https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/e6e913f8-cfee-4a29-b00d-0fbf74b785e3): habitat verbatim; 'N.; S.; St.; Ch., C., M.: widespread and often abundant weed in all but montane regions'; 'Europe, N. Africa, W. Asia 1832'. RHS 'Docks' (https://www.rhs.org.uk/weeds/docks): 'often no more than 8cm (3in) wide'. Backyard Forager (above, on broad-leaved dock): young leaves less curly, rounder; mucilage; ocrea; 'The root of curly dock is yellow and intensely bitter'. Wikipedia 'Rumex crispus' (CC BY-SA 4.0, retrieved 25/10/2026): 'a large, yellow, forking taproot'; 'hybridizes readily with other Rumex species including Rumex obtusifolius'; Armenian aveluk ('During drying fermentation takes place to make it less bitter'); leaves boiled 'in several changes of water'; 'Both the leaves and root may be laxative in some individuals, though not in all, and generally it is mild' (warning 5).

summary.text:
Curled dock, also called curly dock or yellow dock, is native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia and was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1832. It hybridises readily with other docks, including broad-leaved dock.
One plant can shed tens of thousands of seeds — about 60,000 by an Australian estimate. The ripe fruits snap off easily when brushed and travel on clothing, animals, machinery and mud, and on wind and water: the papery valves act as sails and the tubercles as floats. Pieces of crown and taproot broken up by cultivation regrow, and in Australia the root has been recorded 3 m deep. Seedlings overwinter as rosettes. In Armenia the young plants are dried in braids, fermenting as they dry, to make aveluk, which is boiled back to life for soups and salads.

warnings: It contains oxalic acid, which gives the leaves their sharp taste. A little is fine, but large amounts can lock up calcium and other minerals in food; cooking lowers the oxalic acid. Take particular care, or leave it alone, if you are prone to rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity. Large amounts can kill: in a published case, a 53-year-old man died three days after eating curled dock, with severely low blood calcium and liver failure.
Large amounts of dock leaves that are not properly cooked can cause nausea, stomach cramps, vomiting and headache.
Pick docks only where you know no herbicide or pesticide has been used.

Young foxglove rosettes, which are deadly, can look like dock leaves. Foxglove leaves are matt and hairy, grey-felted beneath, with scalloped edges; dock leaves are smooth and glossy. Check every leaf you pick.
The leaves and the root can be mildly laxative in some people.
Avoid it when pregnant or breast-feeding.

identification.text:
Hairy, annual, taprooted herb, with large basal leaf rosette and more or less ascending branches to about 50 cm long. Stems more or less densely hairy with the hairs more or less retrorse. Petioles to about 20 cm long, longest in rosette leaves, with hairs as on stems. Lamina 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, orbicular or suborbicular, with appressed hairs, especially on veins below; lobes 5–7, extending almost to the petiole, again pinnately lobed or 3-lobed, especially in rosette leaves; ultimate segments linear or narrow-oblong, acute. Flowers usually in pairs; peduncles usually longer than pedicels, both densely hairy with eglandular and often pink-tipped glandular hairs. Sepals 5–8 mm long (excluding awn), ovate, densely clothed in long, white, eglandular and short glandular hairs, aristate with awn (1)–2–3 mm long. Petals 3.5–5 mm long, obovate, pink or rose, emarginate; claw short. Filaments whitish; anthers blue. Mericarps 2.5–3 mm long, with white, patent hairs. Seeds prominently isobilaterally alveolate.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Dove's-foot cranesbill is an annual densely covered in short or long hairs; its leaves are 1.5–5 × 1.5–6 cm, kidney-shaped to round, cut about 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes, usually with 3 rounded secondary lobes towards the tip; its sepals are 2–3.5 mm long and end in a short point; its petals are rosy pink or pink, (3)–4–6 mm long and deeply notched, its anthers mauve, and its fruit segments (mericarps) about 1.5 mm long, hairless, with prominent pale cross-ridges. Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. The fruit separates them: dove's-foot cranesbill's fruit segments (mericarps) are hairless on the outer face and ridged, cut-leaved cranesbill's hairy and smooth. Without fruit, use the leaves: cut-leaved cranesbill's are divided nearly to the base into linear segments, dove's-foot cranesbill's to about 3/4 of the way into broader lobes. The anthers differ too (blue against mauve). Both are hairy annuals with a basal rosette and small, notched pink petals, and both have glandular hairs in the flower clusters, so none of those separates them. Dove's-foot cranesbill's fruits are recorded as eaten by young people in Spain as a nibble.
lookalikes.name: Dove's-foot cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped, cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Cut-leaved cranesbill is an annual, usually with a thin fibrous taproot and glandular hairs prominent in the flower clusters, while Solander's geranium is a perennial with a rather stout to tuberous rootstock and no, very few, or short and inconspicuous glandular hairs on the flower clusters. Cut-leaved cranesbill's leaves are cut almost to the leaf stalk into linear segments; Solander's geranium's are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into broader lobes. Both have pink petals. Older floras placed Solander's geranium under Geranium dissectum (its synonyms include Geranium dissectum var. pilosum Hook.f. and var. australe Benth.), so older records may use that name. Solander's geranium's root is recorded as food.
lookalikes.name: Solander's geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Cut-leaved cranesbill is an annual, usually with a thin fibrous taproot and glandular hairs prominent in the flower clusters, while Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a rather stout to tuberous rootstock and no, very few, or short and inconspicuous glandular hairs on the flower clusters. Cut-leaved cranesbill's leaves are cut almost to the leaf stalk into linear segments; Australasian cranesbill's are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into broader lobes. Both have pink petals. Older floras placed Australasian cranesbill under Geranium dissectum (Allan's 1961 Flora of New Zealand treated it as Geranium australe and Geranium dissectum var. glabratum Hook.f.), so older records may use that name. Australasian cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food.
lookalikes.name: Australasian cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Small-flowered cranesbill is a taprooted annual densely clothed in short hairs; its leaves are 1–3.5 × 1.5–4.5 cm, kidney-shaped to almost round, cut 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes that are themselves 2–3-lobed; its sepals are 2–3 mm long (to about 4 mm in fruit) and end in a short point; its petals are pale mauve, 2.5–3.5 mm long and notched; only 5–6 of its 10 stamens carry anthers (mauvish brown); and its fruit segments (mericarps) are 1.5–2 mm long, densely clothed in hairs pressed flat on the outer face. Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. They are separated on the leaves and stamens: cut-leaved cranesbill's lower leaves are divided nearly to the base into linear segments, its sepals end in an awn and all 10 stamens are fertile; small-flowered cranesbill's are divided to about 3/4 of the way into oblong to ovate segments, its sepals end in a point under 0.5 mm, and 4–5 of its 10 stamens lack anthers. Both have hairy fruit segments (mericarps), so the fruit alone does not separate them, though cut-leaved cranesbill's hairs spread and small-flowered cranesbill's are pressed flat. Its petals are pink or rose and 3.5–5 mm long against small-flowered cranesbill's pale mauve 2.5–3.5 mm, and its anthers blue against mauvish brown. No source read records small-flowered cranesbill as food.

summary.text:
Geranium dissectum or cut-leaved crane's-bill is a plant species of the genus Geranium. It is native to Europe.
It can be found on other continents as well, in some instances as an introduced species.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: commonest from Taranaki northwards; South Island: Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury (at least south to Ashburton); Kermadec Islands (Raoul, but not collected recently), Chatham Islands. G. dissectum has recently become a prominent weed of arable land in northern and eastern South Island.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Waste places, river beds, gardens.
It is found growing in open areas, gardens, fields and meadows, and widely in uncultivated areas in urban habitats.
In northern Europe it is mainly a weed of ploughed vegetable fields and cultivated land, gardens, soil heaps, rubbish dumps, roadsides and waste ground, and is rarely seen away from them.

identification.text:
Annual herb with slightly hairy, ascending stems. Petioles slender, to at least 4 cm long. Lamina 1.5–4 × 2–5 cm (inflorescence leaves often smaller), broad-ovate or almost reniform, irregularly and deeply dentate or crenate, hairy; base cordate or subcordate. Bracts similar to leaves but petiole short and lamina to 3.5 × 5 cm. Calyx 8–10 mm long, hairy; teeth equal to tube, subulate, prominently ciliate. Corolla 11–15 mm long, purplish; tube with at most an inconspicuous basal ring of hairs inside; upper lip 3–4 mm long, tomentose outside; lower lip about 2 mm long, deeply emarginate. Nutlets about 2.5 mm long, patterned white, sharply angled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The base of the corolla is nearly hairless, unlike L. purpureum where it is obviously ringed with hairs.
Its leaves are usually a little narrower than red deadnettle's and more deeply toothed, irregularly so: neighbouring teeth are often of different sizes, where red deadnettle's are even and shallow. The upper leaves have short, winged stalks. The plant is a little less downy than red deadnettle and has an unpleasant smell.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut-leaved deadnettle's leaves are irregularly and deeply toothed, and its flower tube has at most a faint ring of hairs inside near the base; red deadnettle's leaves have even, rounded teeth, and its flower tube has a conspicuous ring of hairs inside. Neighbouring teeth on a cut-leaved deadnettle leaf are often of different sizes. They look alike and often grow together, and cut-leaved deadnettle is probably often overlooked because it is so like red deadnettle.
lookalikes.name: Red deadnettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Henbit's bracts — the leaves under the upper flower clusters — are stalkless, broadly ovate and clasp the stem; cut-leaved deadnettle's bracts are like its deeply toothed leaves, with short stalks. Henbit's flower is about 15 mm with a long, narrow tube; cut-leaved deadnettle's is 11–15 mm. Both grow on waste ground and in gardens.
lookalikes.name: Henbit deadnettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Field woundwort's flowers are small — 6–7 mm long, with a small upper lip that is not hooded and is shorter than the lower lip, the tube no longer than the calyx; cut-leaved deadnettle's are 11–15 mm long with a hooded upper lip. Field woundwort's stem is much hairier, and its bracts are stalkless. Both are weeds of gardens, crops, waste places and river beds, and young plants are easily confused. Field woundwort poisons livestock (staggers); no record of it being eaten by people has been found, so do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Field woundwort

Useful Temperate Plants has no entry for it; a seed seller's 'some people eat the young leaves' (True Harvest Seeds) was not used. No recipes: no source writes one for it, and its edibility rests on one source.

summary.text:
Lamium hybridum, the cut-leaved dead-nettle, is a species of Lamium native to western and northern Europe and northwestern Africa.
Villars reduced it to a variety of the similar red dead-nettle Lamium purpureum, but recently, genetic evidence has shown it is genetically distinct from L. purpureum and should stand as a distinct species.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1957. The Flora of New Zealand (1988) knew it only from the South Island, commonest in Nelson and also found in South Canterbury and Otago, and called it apparently uncommon but probably often overlooked because it looks so like red deadnettle. It now grows in both islands: it has been found from Northland to Wellington, mostly since 2022, and most records come from Canterbury, especially Christchurch, and from Nelson and Tasman.
It mainly pollinates itself.

warnings: Field woundwort (staggerweed), which poisons livestock, grows in the same places and looks alike when young. Check for the larger flowers with a hooded upper lip.

identification.text:
Flat rosette of jagged backward-pointing lobed leaves. A single flower per hollow, leafless stem. Every part bleeds white milky sap. An unbranched, leafless stem with one head rules out catsear and the hawksbeards, but not hawkbit, the native dandelion or mouse-ear hawkweed, which have one too (see the lookalike cards).
Perennial rosette herb. Leaves all basal, linear-oblanceolate to obovate, runcinate-pinnatifid to not lobed, toothed, glabrous or with sparse short multicellular hairs especially on midrib above, 5–30–(60) × 1–10–(12) cm; terminal lobe triangular to deltoid, acute or obtuse, truncate or hastate at base; lateral lobes narrowly to broadly triangular, usually recurved, often toothed, especially on distal margin; petiole and proximal part of midrib hollow. Scape stout, hollow, glabrous or cobwebby, 3–35–(60) cm tall. Capitula 3–5 cm diameter. Involucral bracts glabrous; outer bracts narrowly obovate, attenuate, dull green or reddish, strongly reflexed to recurved at flowering and fruiting, with margins not scarious; inner bracts narrowly triangular to linear, acute, green, erect, with scarious margins at least at base. Florets golden yellow. Achene body cream to greenish brown, ribbed, clavate, 2.5–3.5 mm long; ribs each with 3–(5) teeth on distal ⅓, the distal teeth longest; cone tapering, 0.5–1 mm long, concolorous with body; beak usually white to cream, rarely dark, slender, 7–10 mm long. Pappus white, 5–7 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Catsear's leaves carry moderately dense, stiff pale hairs; a dandelion's are hairless or only sparsely hairy. Catsear's flower stems are usually branched, solid and almost leafless, with only a few tiny bracts, and can carry several flower heads; a dandelion's are hollow, unbranched and leafless, with one flower head each. Both have a rosette of leaves, yellow flower heads and milky sap, so none of those separates them. Catsear is edible: its young leaves are bland and can be eaten raw or cooked, though older leaves can be tough.
lookalikes.name: Catsear

lookalikes.howToTell: Beaked hawksbeard's stem branches and carries leaves, and stands 15–75 cm tall, sometimes to 100 cm; a dandelion's flower stem is hollow, leafless and unbranched, with a single flower head — the same check as for catsear. The rosettes alone do not separate them: both usually have leaves with backward-pointing lobes, and both have milky sap.
lookalikes.name: Beaked hawksbeard

lookalikes.howToTell: Look under the flower head. A dandelion's outer bracts are strongly bent back at flowering and fruiting and have no papery margins; the native dandelion's stand erect at flowering, spread a little in fruit, and usually have pale papery (scarious) margins. The seed separates them too: each rib of a dandelion's achene has 3–(5) teeth on its top third, the native dandelion's (3)–5–7 teeth on its top third to two-thirds. Leaf shape does not settle it: the native dandelion's leaves are usually toothed and sometimes cut into back-pointing lobes, and in lowland South Canterbury and the Chatham Islands they are deeply lobed. Both have a hollow, leafless flower stem with one head, a hollow leaf stalk, and leaves that are hairless or sparsely hairy. The native dandelion is usually the smaller, with heads 1.5–3 cm across and sometimes 4 cm, against 3–5 cm, so head size alone does not settle it either. It grows mostly in montane to alpine grassland and herbfield, but also in lowland grassland, forest margins and dunes. Its leaves were eaten by Māori; it is At Risk – Declining (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Native dandelion

lookalikes.howToTell: Hawkbit's flower stem is also unbranched and leafless, with a single head, so that test does not separate them. Look at the leaf hairs with a hand lens: hawkbit's leaves carry sparse to dense hairs that fork into two, sometimes three, at the tip — the feature that tells hawkbit from the similar plants of the dandelion tribe here — while a dandelion's leaves are hairless or have sparse short hairs, mostly on the midrib above. A dandelion's flower stem is stout, fleshy and hollow; hawkbit's is thinner and more wiry, and solid or not as hollow. In seed, hawkbit's outer seeds carry only a ring of tiny scales and its inner seeds a feathery parachute on a short beak; a dandelion's seeds carry a parachute of fine white hairs on a slender beak 7–10 mm long. Both have yellow heads, rosettes of lobed leaves whose lobes can point back, and milky sap. Hawkbit's leaves are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Hawkbit

lookalikes.howToTell: Autumn hawkbit's flower stems branch, carry many small narrow bracts — most of them near the top — and bear several heads; a dandelion's are unbranched, leafless and hollow, with one head. Autumn hawkbit's stems are not hollow. The leaves do not settle it: both have a basal rosette of lobed leaves whose lobes can point back, and autumn hawkbit's are hairless or have sparse simple hairs, much like a dandelion's. In seed, autumn hawkbit's achenes have no beak and carry a feathery parachute; a dandelion's carry a parachute of fine white hairs on a slender beak 7–10 mm long. Both have yellow heads and milky sap. In New Zealand autumn hawkbit is known mainly from Canterbury, Otago and Southland. Its leaves are used like dandelion leaves (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Autumn hawkbit

lookalikes.howToTell: Smooth hawksbeard's flowering stem branches, carries leaves of its own — the upper ones narrow, stalkless and usually toothed at the base — and bears several heads; a dandelion's is hollow, leafless and unbranched, with one head. Hawksbeards also have a solid leaf stalk and midrib, where a dandelion's leaf stalk and the base of its midrib are hollow. Smooth hawksbeard's seed has no beak and is only 2–2.5 mm long; a dandelion's carries a slender beak 7–10 mm long. The two are often confused; smooth hawksbeard's multiple, branched flower stems are the difference. Before the stems rise the rosettes are alike: both can have back-pointing lobes, and smooth hawksbeard's leaves are often hairless. Both have yellow heads and milky sap. Smooth hawksbeard's leaves are eaten in salads and soups in Tuscany (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Smooth hawksbeard

lookalikes.howToTell: Turn a leaf over: mouse-ear hawkweed's leaves are white beneath with a very dense coat of star-shaped hairs, carry long bristly hairs above, and are untoothed or only very obscurely toothed; a dandelion's are toothed, usually cut into back-pointing lobes, hairless or with sparse short hairs, with a hollow leaf stalk and midrib base. Mouse-ear hawkweed spreads by slender creeping runners (stolons), as several other hawkweeds in New Zealand do. A dandelion's achene carries a slender beak 7–10 mm long; mouse-ear hawkweed's are about 2 mm and not beaked. Both make rosettes with one yellow head on a leafless stem, leaf lengths overlap at 5–7 cm, and stem heights overlap. No food use of mouse-ear hawkweed is recorded; its traditional uses are medicinal (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mouse-ear hawkweed

preparation.text:
Young leaves raw; older leaves boiled to cut bitterness. Flowers battered or made into syrup. Roots roasted as a coffee substitute.
Each part is at its best at a different time in New Zealand: leaves in spring before the plant flowers, while they are tender and less bitter; flowers when fully open, in late spring and early summer; roots in autumn and early winter.

recipes.method: Makes about 500 ml. About 475 ml small, tight, unopened dandelion buds; 300 ml vinegar (5% acidity); 60 ml water; 1 tsp canning or fine salt. Pick the smallest, tightest unopened buds — under the first bud of a plant there are often several pea-sized younger ones deeper in the rosette. Bring 300 ml vinegar, 60 ml water and 1 tsp salt to the boil, stirring until the salt dissolves. Pack about 475 ml of buds into a jar and pour the hot brine over them. Cap and keep in the fridge, or process in a water-bath canner for 10 minutes with about 1 cm headspace.
recipes.title: Pickled dandelion buds

recipes.method: Wash the roots, trim off any blemished parts and thin strands, and chop into small pieces of even size. Roast at 200 °C for 30–45 minutes on a tray lined with baking paper (or in an air fryer lined with foil), checking and shaking every 5–8 minutes and taking out any pieces that are done early. Cool completely and store airtight in a cool, dry place. Steep the pieces like tea, or grind them and use them like ground coffee in a plunger, with about the same number of scoops. Or bring 2 tsp of roasted root to the boil in about 475 ml water, simmer for 15 minutes and strain, as LifeSource Natural Foods brews it. From LifeSource Natural Foods: ten or more roots per cup.
recipes.title: Dandelion root coffee

recipes.method: For 6: about 900 g dandelion leaves; 4–6 tbsp olive oil; 60 ml chopped or sliced garlic; a pinch of chilli flakes (optional); salt and pepper; lemon juice (optional). Cut the tough base off about 900 g of dandelion leaves, cut them into bite-sized pieces and swish them in a bowl of cold water, rinsing until no grit is left. To take out some of the bitterness, blanch the leaves first in salted boiling water — even a minute helps — then plunge them into iced water and squeeze out as much water as you can before sautéing. Warm 4–6 tbsp olive oil with 60 ml chopped or sliced garlic and a pinch of chilli flakes if you like in a large pan over medium heat, until the garlic softens, colours lightly and smells fragrant. Add the leaves, in batches if needed, and cook for a few minutes, stirring now and then, until as tender as you like and the liquid has cooked off; add a splash of water or cover the pan to steam if it gets dry. Season with salt and pepper and serve hot or at room temperature, with lemon juice if you like.
recipes.title: Sautéed dandelion greens

recipes.method: Written for cleavers and dandelion together. A handful of cleavers; a few dandelion flowers; 1 lemon (the author uses an organic one), sliced with its skin; filtered water. Put them in a jug, top it up with filtered water and leave it overnight to steep before drinking.
recipes.title: Cleavers and dandelion cold infusion

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard. 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: The author's greens were dock, onion weed, nasturtium, plantain, baby wild mustard, dandelion, sow thistle and a violet leaf. 2 crushed garlic cloves; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 500 ml (2 cups) firmly packed wild greens, sliced very thinly; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper; 125 ml (½ cup) roughly chopped pistachios, walnuts, almonds or brazil nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp hearts, pumpkin or sunflower seeds; and 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, hemp seed oil or a mix. Makes about 750 ml (3 cups). To slice the greens, sort them into similar shapes, bunch and twist a few leaves together and slice as thinly as you can — this suits the tougher, stringier ones such as plantain, mustard and dock. Toss everything together. Good as a side or salad, in a wrap or sandwich, or with pasta, risotto, eggs, or sausages and mash. It keeps at least 4 days in a sealed jar in the fridge.
recipes.title: Weedolata (wild-greens gremolata)

recipes.method: Written for climbing (rambling) dock in Australia, with farmer's friend and dandelion leaves; the dandelion is a quarter of the leaves. Makes about 8 servings. 500 ml (2 cups) climbing dock leaves; 125 ml (½ cup) farmer's friend leaves; 125 ml (½ cup) dandelion leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) parsley leaves; 2 crushed garlic cloves; 2 tbsp drained capers; 125 ml (½ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; a dash of red wine vinegar; 1 tsp Dijon mustard; the juice of 1 lemon; sea salt and pepper. Put 500 ml (2 cups) climbing dock leaves, 125 ml (½ cup) farmer's friend leaves, 125 ml (½ cup) dandelion leaves, 250 ml (1 cup) parsley leaves, 2 crushed garlic cloves and 2 tbsp drained capers in a food processor and chop finely. With the motor running, add 125 ml (½ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, a dash of red wine vinegar, 1 tsp Dijon mustard and the juice of 1 lemon, and process until combined. Season with sea salt and pepper and leave it to stand for 10 minutes. Serve as a dipping sauce, condiment or marinade.
recipes.title: Climbing dock salsa verde

recipes.method: Written for dandelion and broad-leaved dock together; the author says other strong-tasting spring greens such as nettle, plantain or watercress can replace them. Makes about 35 small puddings or one large one. 400 g pearl barley; 4 eggs, hard-boiled; 2 large leeks; a little oil; about half a supermarket bag of washed dock and dandelion leaves; 3 raw eggs, plus 1–2 more if needed. To finish: flour; 1 beaten egg; 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs; 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle (optional); garlic mayonnaise. Boil 400 g pearl barley until tender, drain and cool. Hard-boil 4 eggs and chop finely. Finely chop 2 large leeks and soften them in a little oil. Blanch about half a supermarket bag of washed dock and dandelion leaves in boiling water for 20 seconds, then plunge into iced water (skip this and the puddings are more bitter and less green); squeeze out every drop of water and chop finely. Mix the chopped eggs, leeks, barley and greens with 3 raw eggs, and season very well. Wrap the mixture tightly in a tray covered with cling film, set in a larger tray of hot water, or seal it in a pudding bowl with baking paper, foil and string and stand it in a pan of water reaching at least halfway up. Steam for 45–60 minutes, in a 160 °C oven or on the hob, until it holds together; if it won't roll into balls, mix in 1–2 more raw eggs and steam longer. Turn out and serve as one pudding, or roll into small balls while warm and chill them (they freeze individually at this stage). Roll the chilled balls in flour, then in 1 beaten egg, then in 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs (mixed, if you like, with 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle), and deep-fry for 1–2 minutes until browned; or simply flour and fry them. Serve warm, with garlic mayonnaise.
recipes.title: Dock, dandelion and nettle puddings

recipes.method: Written for the author's mixed wild leaves. Of his lists, this catalogue covers dandelion and hairy bittercress (pungent), chickweed and hawthorn leaves (mild), and gorse flowers and flowering currant blossom (extras). He warns to be extra careful identifying leaves before the plants flower. Pungent leaves; mild leaves; a few extras; walnut oil; elderberry vinegar; salt and pepper; a little mustard; fermented greens; pickled buds. Mix pungent and mild leaves about 1 to 3, then scatter a few extras over the top. Dress simply with walnut oil, elderberry vinegar, salt, pepper and a little mustard; he finishes it with fermented greens and pickled buds.
recipes.title: Wild summer salad

recipes.method: Written for dandelion, with clover leaves (the page does not say which clover) and violet leaves. 250–500 ml (1–2 cups) watermelon; 2 peaches; 1 banana; 12 dandelion leaves; a handful of clover leaves; a handful of violet leaves; 2 kale leaves; 500 ml (2 cups) water; 15 ml (1 tbsp) chia seeds; 15 ml (1 tbsp) pumpkin seeds; 2 cardamom pods. Grind the chia, pumpkin seeds and cardamom. Blend the greens with the water, then add the fruit and the ground seeds and blend again until smooth.
recipes.title: Peach, melon and dandelion smoothie

recipes.method: Written for dandelion, chickweed and parsley leaves; the author gives no amount for the leaves. Dandelion, chickweed and parsley leaves; 2 garlic cloves; salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) oil; 125 ml (½ cup) macadamia nuts or pine nuts. Process the garlic with the salt, add the nuts and process again, then add the leaves and oil and process to the consistency you like, adding more oil if needed. Decorate it with dandelion flowers.
recipes.title: Dandelion pesto

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taraxacum_officinale Corroborates all three edible parts and refines how to use them: the young leaves and unopened buds are usually eaten raw in salads while older leaves are cooked, raw leaves being slightly bitter and closest in character to mustard greens. The leaves are high in vitamins A and C, iron, phosphorus and potassium. Native to Eurasia, introduced to New Zealand, and growing in lawns, roadsides, disturbed banks and waterway shores — which is this entry's habitat, independently.

summary.text:
Entirely edible, and growing in every lawn in the country.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North, South and Stewart Islands; Kermadec, Chatham and Campbell Islands. Naturalised from Europe, first recorded in 1852. T. officinale is a common weed of lawns and cultivated land. Plants can sprout from dislodged pieces of root.
Flora of New Zealand treats it broadly, to include probably several microspecies that are hard to tell apart because they vary so much with season and place (restated).

warnings: Lawn and verge plants are the most likely of any wild food to have been sprayed. Ask before harvesting from anywhere council-maintained.
There are reports that some people have suffered dermatitis as a result of touching the plant, this is probably caused by the latex in the leaves and stems.
There is conflicting evidence about whether dandelion causes an allergic reaction in people who are sensitive to related plants like ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds, and daisies.

sources: Useful Temperate Plants (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0)
edibleParts.text: Fruit - raw or cooked and used in preserves. An acid but very pleasant flavour, children seem particularly fond of the fruit. When fully ripe, the fruit loses most of its acidity and makes very pleasant eating. Unfortunately there is a lot of seed compared to the amount of flesh and this does detract somewhat from the pleasure of eating it.

identification.text:
Evergreen shrub to about 4 m high. Shoots densely clothed in brown hairs, terete or nearly so. Spines palmately 5-partite, hairy. Leaves subsessile or nearly so. Lamina 1–3–(3.5) × 0.5–1.5–(2) cm, obovate with 2 spiny apical lobes (leaves of vegetative shoots sometimes with additional spiny teeth below), glabrous, glossy dark green above; base cuneate. Inflorescence usually a simple pendulous raceme to about 7 cm long, occasionally slightly paniculate. Bracts lanceolate, reddish, much shorter than pedicels. Pedicels 5–15 mm long at anthesis, reddish. Perianth segments 5–8.5 mm long except in the much shorter outermost whorl, orange-yellow except for reddish flush on outermost segments, usually oblong or oblong-obovate; innermost whorl (petals) slightly emarginate. Nectaries inconspicuous. Stamens slightly shorter than petals. Ovules up to 8. Style equal to or longer than ovary at anthesis. Berry 5–7 mm diameter, subglobose or globose, black or nearly so, more or less pruinose; fruiting style conspicuous, 1.5–3 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Darwin's barberry's leaves are small, 1–3 (rarely 3.5) cm long, obovate with two spiny lobes at the tip (shoots that are not flowering sometimes carry extra teeth below); barberry's are mostly 2.5–7.5 cm long, entire or spiny-toothed (often only sparsely), and very variable on one plant. Darwin's barberry's flowers are orange-yellow, barberry's yellow. Darwin's barberry's shoots are densely clothed in brown hairs and its spines split into five like a hand; barberry is hairless, its spines single or three-parted and up to 2.3 cm long. Its berries are 5–7 mm across and round, with a conspicuous style 1.5–3 mm long left at the tip; barberry's are 7–12 mm long, broadly ellipsoid to nearly round, with a style about 1 mm long. Dark berries with a whitish bloom, an evergreen habit and a tall spiny shrub do not separate them. The garden hybrid B. × stenophylla (Darwin's barberry × B. empetrifolia) has three-parted spines and narrow linear-lanceolate leaves but fruit like Darwin's barberry's, so the spine and leaf tests do not settle it.
lookalikes.name: Barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Darwin's barberry is evergreen and its berries are black or nearly so, with a whitish bloom, 5–7 mm across and round; European barberry is deciduous and its berries are scarlet to crimson-scarlet, shining, without bloom, oblong and 9–11 mm long. Darwin's barberry's leaves are glossy dark green above, with spiny lobes, up to about 3.5 cm long; European barberry's are thin, dull green, usually finely toothed and 2–8 cm long. Darwin's barberry's spines split into five; European barberry's are mostly three-parted and under 1.5 cm long. Spiny stems and yellowish flowers in clusters do not separate them. Red berries alone do not mark European barberry: the deciduous B. wilsonae (red, round berries without bloom; adult leaves entire) grows wild at three New Zealand sites, and garden B. thunbergii also has scarlet berries.
lookalikes.name: European barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Darwin's barberry has simple leaves, 1–3 (rarely 3.5) cm long, in clusters on stems armed with five-parted spines; Oregon grape's leaves are compound, up to about 25 cm long, of 3–7 pairs of holly-like leaflets 5–9.5 cm long plus one at the tip, and its stems carry no spines (in Mahonia the leaves are never modified to form spines). Darwin's barberry's berries are 5–7 mm across with a conspicuous style 1.5–3 mm long left at the tip; Oregon grape's are about 10 mm across. Glossy, spiny-edged, holly-like foliage, dark berries with a bloom and yellow to orange flowers do not separate them.

preparation.text:
The fruit goes very well raw in a muesli or cooked in a porridge.
Berberis microphylla and B. darwinii (both known as calafate and michay) are two species found in Patagonia in Argentina and Chile. Their edible purple fruit are used for jams and infusions.

recipes.method: Written for Darwin's barberry (Berberis darwinii) by the horticulturist who grew it. 900 g ripe berries; 2 litres of water; the juice of one lemon; about 400 g (2 cups) sugar. Simmer 900 g ripe berries in 2 litres of water until soft. Push the fruit and liquid through a sieve to hold back the skins and most of the seeds, then squeeze the pulp through muslin to get as much juice as you can. Heat the juice with the juice of one lemon, stirring in about 400 g (2 cups) sugar a cupful at a time as it warms. Boil hard for about 25 minutes, until it starts to set, then spoon into sterilised jars and cover. The author got two good-sized jars. The source calls its strained liquid both '3 cups' and '1.5 L', which do not agree, so measure your own. Metric sugar is converted from the source's cups.

summary.text:
Berberis darwinii, Darwin's barberry, is a species of flowering plant in the family Berberidaceae. It is native to southern Chile and Argentina and naturalized elsewhere. Regional vernacular names include michay, calafate, and quelung. Growing to 3–4 m tall, it is an evergreen thorny shrub.
Berberis darwinii was first described in 1835 by Charles Darwin during the voyage of the Beagle. It was one of many named in honour of Darwin. The berries of this species are known to have been consumed by prehistoric native peoples in the Patagonian region over millennia.
Berberis darwinii is regarded as an invasive plant pest in New Zealand that escaped from gardens into indigenous plant communities via its bird-dispersed seeds. It is considered a serious threat to indigenous ecosystems throughout New Zealand and is listed on the National Pest Plant Accord.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: locally common in Wellington and the Wairarapa; S.: extensively naturalised from C. Canterbury to Foveaux Strait; St.: Halfmoon Bay, very common.
B. darwinii is a variable sp. with several described vars; N.Z. material can be referred to the type var. One New Zealand collection represents the commonly cultivated hybrid B. × stenophylla Lindley (B. darwinii × B. empetrifolia Lam.). This has long arching branches, 3-parted spines and linear-lanceolate leaves. It has frs similar to B. darwinii and sets viable seed.
Brought to New Zealand as an ornamental, it was naturalised in 1946 (NZPCN) and is now common from the central North Island to Stewart Island (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research). Birds and possums eat the berries and spread the seed; soil and water movement occasionally carry it too (NZPCN, Weedbusters). Two weevils were approved in 2012 for its biological control: one destroys the flower buds, the other damages the fruit and seeds. The fruit-and-seed weevil was first released in 2015 and is established at a number of sites in Southland and Wellington (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research).
A rust fungus, Puccinia berberidis-darwinii, was approved for release against it in 2025, with its first release planned for Canterbury in spring 2026 (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research).

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.

identification.text:
Plants grow up to 20 cm high, usually shorter: a swollen, blunt-tipped main stem with side branches of the same shape, each narrowed where it joins and rounded at the tip. The branches are filled with clear, jelly-like slime, which oozes out in quantity when the plant is touched. Older branches can look leathery rather than swollen. It is attached by a small disc, from which several stems may arise. Golden to mid-brown; younger plants can be greenish brown and pale yellow at the tips, older plants dark brown. The reproductive structures show as small holes in the surface of the branches.
Touch tells it apart: its tubular fronds are full of sticky gum, so once touched it cannot be mistaken for another seaweed.
