summary.text:
Deadman's fingers or gummy weed (Splachnidium rugosum) is a small native brown seaweed whose swollen, finger-like branches are filled with clear slime.
It grows on intertidal rocks all around the coast of the North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands, and is also known from Australia, South Africa and the Juan Fernández Islands. It is the only species in its genus.
It is assessed as Not Threatened in New Zealand, and secure overseas.
The name dead man's fingers is also used for Codium fragile, a green seaweed (branching velvetweed in this catalogue).

warnings: No record of deadman's fingers (Splachnidium rugosum) as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
The name dead man's fingers is also used for Codium fragile, a green seaweed (see branching velvetweed), so food advice found under that name may be for Codium, not this seaweed.

edibleParts.text: None.

habitat.text: On the ground under introduced trees, as a root partner: above all oaks, including English oak and holm oak, and also sweet chestnut and European beech, especially in older plantings of oak. In New Zealand it turns up in parks, botanic gardens and arboreta, often beside paths and tracks under the trees, and in suburban gardens, in beds and on lawns. There is, however, evidence of it associating with mānuka (Leptospermum) and kānuka (Kunzea) in New Zealand, so a mushroom under native trees is not ruled out.

harvestEthics.text: Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.

identification.text: Smooth greenish, yellowish or bronze cap, often with a faint radial sheen; young caps can be almost white, and an all-white form occurs. Gills white and free of the stem, turning cream with age, sometimes with a slight pinkish or greenish tint. White stem with a skirt-like ring, and — the critical feature — a membranous cup (volva) around the swollen base, frequently hidden below the leaf litter. Spore print white.

lookalikes.howToTell: Field mushroom's gills are deep pink at first and turn chocolate brown to almost black; it has no volva, and its thin ring often disappears. Death cap's gills are white, turning cream, sometimes with a faint pink or green tint, as it ages, but not the deep pink then chocolate-brown of a field mushroom. Its stem has a skirt-like ring, and the swollen base sits in a white, sack-like volva that is sometimes underground. Cap colour does not separate them. Death caps are usually yellow-green, olive or bronze, but young caps can be almost white and an all-white form occurs. In a closed button a white veil hides a field mushroom's gills, so never judge a button. Dig up the whole base of every mushroom and check the gills of every one, every time. A spore print confirms it: field mushroom deep chocolate brown, death cap white.
lookalikes.name: Field mushroom

lookalikes.howToTell: Horse mushroom's gills stay pale for a long time — whitish, pale grey or pale pink — before turning chocolate brown, so a young one can look white-gilled. It has no volva; under its thick double ring is a circle of cogwheel-like patches; and it smells strongly of aniseed or almond, where young death caps have almost no smell. Death cap's gills stay white to cream, its base sits in a sack-like volva that may be buried, and its spore print is white, against horse mushroom's dark chocolate brown. Both can be white with a ring, and horse mushroom has been collected under oak and pine in New Zealand. Dig up the whole base and check every one.
lookalikes.name: Horse mushroom

lookalikes.howToTell: Shaggy parasol also has free white gills, a ring, a swollen stem base and a white spore print. Its cap breaks into coarse, shaggy brown scales on a white background with a smooth brown centre, its buttons are round with a smooth brown skin, and its base is a bulb with no sac (sometimes abruptly swollen with a rim on top). Its flesh turns orange to red within moments when cut. Death cap's cap is smooth, its buttons are white eggs inside a veil, and its base sits in a ragged, white, sac-like volva that may be hidden in leaf litter. Dig up the whole base of every mushroom and check it.
lookalikes.name: Shaggy parasol

lookalikes.howToTell: A young death cap is a white egg inside a veil and has been mistaken for a puffball. A giant puffball has no stem, cap or gills: cut in half from top to bottom it is solid, even, pure white flesh all the way through, while a death cap egg shows the outline of a cap, gills and stem inside. Giant puffballs grow mostly in pasture and lawns; death caps with trees, especially oak.
lookalikes.name: Giant puffball

summary.text: Listed so you can recognise it. Established in New Zealand, and responsible for most fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide. It was apparently introduced to New Zealand with exotic trees such as oak or spruce. Most New Zealand records are from the North Island — Auckland, the Waikato (above all Hamilton), the Bay of Plenty, Gisborne and Whanganui — and there are research-grade records from Motueka and Upper Moutere in Tasman.

warnings: In New Zealand most serious death-cap poisonings are people from Asia who picked it believing it was the paddy straw mushroom (Volvariella volvacea): as it starts to open, a death cap looks like the Asian straw mushroom and other Asian edible mushrooms. Straw mushrooms are almost never found wild in New Zealand, so treat any 'straw mushroom' you find here as a death cap, and buy them instead.

Symptoms usually begin 6 to 12 hours after eating it, sooner in serious cases and as late as 2–3 days in milder ones. The first stomach symptoms often fade for several hours or a day or two, a deceptive period of apparent recovery, before liver and kidney damage shows. By the time you feel ill, damage is underway.
If ingestion is even suspected, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766 immediately. Do not wait for symptoms.
Keep children and dogs away from mushrooms under oak trees from summer to late autumn.

identification.text:
Clump-forming, fountain-like; rhizomes not running. Culms initially erect and wand-like, later arching over, 2–2.5 m, glaucous-white when young, becoming medium to deep green. Culm-sheath uniformly green or purplish green; ligule 1–5 mm, puberulent; auricles and bristles 0; sheath-blades linear-subulate. Branches many at each node, small, densely tufted. Leaf-sheath green or purplish, glabrous excepting margins sometimes ciliate. Ligule prominent, oblong, minutely puberulent. Leaf-blade usually 4–12–(15) × 0.4–0.8–(1.3) cm, narrow lanceolate or linear-lanceolate, long acuminate. Panicles large and diffuse. Spikelets 8–12 mm, often purple or strongly flushed purple. Glumes shorter than florets, unequal, minutely puberulent; lower ¾ - ⅚ length of upper. Lodicules about 2 × 2 mm, ciliate. Caryopsis 6–7 mm, blackish.
[From: Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

edibleParts.text: Young shoot tips in spring, raw, as a tea or as a flavouring. Older needles all year, as a tea or flavouring; they are tougher, more tannic and less aromatic. Young or older needles can also be infused in oil or vinegar.

habitat.text: Naturalised abundantly, sometimes forming an understorey in areas adjacent to plantations, and often regenerating on banks and paths around and downwind of cultivation sites. Lowland, montane and subalpine, on sites of low to moderate fertility, in scrub, forest margins, shrubland, tussockland and light wells in forest. Seedlings establish most readily on well-lit, sheltered sites without competing plants; it seldom spreads where the vegetation cover is dense. It is more shade-tolerant than other conifers but does not tolerate drought. Planted, it grows best in cool, higher-rainfall sites at 350–950 m on moist, free-draining soils.

identification.text:
Large or very large tree; branches more or less horizontal; branchlets tending to droop. Bark thick, reddish brown beneath. Shoots light to dark brown, with short hairs, ridged. Winter resting buds to 1 cm long, shining purplish brown, long, narrow and sharply acute. Leaves 1.5–3.8 cm × 1–2 mm, often revolute, glaucous-banded below, orange-scented when crushed, 2-ranked on juvenile and other vegetative shoots in deep shade; apex obtuse. Male cones 1.2–2 cm long. Mature female cones (4)–5–10 cm long, cylindric-ovoid. Bract scale with exserted part pointed towards cone apex; central lobe longer, 5–15 mm long, subacute; ovuliferous scales much wider than long, entire. Seed mottled brown beneath.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Young spontaneous saplings of Douglas fir usually have smaller, pectinate leaves in 2 ranks and thus resembling saplings of Abies and Picea species, but the scent of oranges when crushed and the Fagus-like buds readily distinguish this species from all other conifers in New Zealand. Also, unlike the commoner Abies and Picea species, cones are often produced on young plants as small as 1–2 m high.
Branches grow in irregular whorls, and the bark becomes rough and furrowed with age. The male cones are catkin-like; the female cones are papery and hang downwards. Douglas fir lacks the persistent leaf bases of the hemlocks (Tsuga). Bigcone Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga macrocarpa), also cultivated in New Zealand, has longer cones, 10–18 cm.

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a few needles: Douglas fir's smell of oranges; yew's have no real scent. Turn a shoot over: Douglas fir's needles have two whitish, silvery bands beneath; yew's have two broad pale green bands, never silver. Douglas fir's shoots are light to dark brown with short hairs and end in long, narrow, sharply pointed, shining purplish-brown buds up to 1 cm long; yew's shoots are green and ribbed. Douglas fir carries woody cones 4–10 cm long that hang down, with three-pointed bracts sticking out between the scales; female yews carry soft crimson berry-like arils 10–15 mm long around a single seed, and yew has no woody cones. Most yews are male or female trees, so a tree without red arils can still be yew. Needle size and arrangement do not separate them: Douglas fir's are 1.5–3.8 cm long and yew's 1.2–2.5 cm, and both can lie in two flat rows, especially on shaded or young shoots.

preparation.text: Pick the tips once their papery brown bud scales have fallen off, when they are about 1–4 cm long. Take them from side branches rather than the leading shoot, and not too many from one part of the tree. Steep tips or needles in hot water for tea, or in cool water for several hours to overnight. Use the needles as you would rosemary, in bread, marinades and roasts. Use them on the day you pick them, as their aroma fades quickly. Finely chopped young tips can go into salads, pesto and cures for meat or fish, and needles blended with caster sugar flavour shortbread. When using older needles, strip them off the brownish-orange stems, which are bitter and taste of resin. A cut Christmas tree kept a month in a warm room has lost most of its flavour.

recipes.method: Written for Douglas fir. 500 ml (2 cups) water; 750 ml (3 cups) white sugar; 500 ml (2 cups) Douglas fir tips. Heat the water in a saucepan over medium heat. Slowly add the sugar and bring it to the boil, then take it off the heat and add the tips. Leave the syrup to cool before straining it. Keep it in a glass jar in the fridge for up to 2 months; adding 30 ml (2 tablespoons) of vodka or brandy makes it keep for up to a year.
recipes.title: Douglas fir syrup

recipes.method: Written for Douglas fir. Cut a handful of young tips where they join the stem, or pluck older needles off the stems so no stem goes in. Chop the needles finely with a rocking motion and put them in a mug or tea infuser. Bring water to the boil, take it off the heat until it stops boiling, then pour it over the needles. Steep 5 minutes, or 10 minutes if you will not sweeten it. Add a little honey if you like, and steep another 5 minutes.
recipes.title: Douglas fir needle tea

recipes.method: Written for Douglas fir. 250 ml (1 cup) young Douglas fir tips; 250 ml (1 cup) water; 250 ml (1 cup) sugar, or to taste; 5–10 ml (1–2 teaspoons) fresh lemon juice. Rinse the tips in cold water and throw out any that are dry, tough or browned. Stir the water and sugar in a small pot until the sugar dissolves, add the tips and bring to a very gentle simmer; do not boil. Keep it on low heat for 15–20 minutes, then take it off the heat and leave 10–15 minutes more for a stronger flavour. Strain through a fine sieve or cheesecloth and stir in the lemon juice. Cool, pour into a sterilised jar or bottle and keep in the fridge for 3–4 weeks. Use it in sparkling water or cocktails, over waffles or yoghurt, or in a glaze for roast carrots or salmon.
recipes.title: Douglas fir tip syrup with lemon

recipes.method: Written for Douglas fir. 1 kg apples; 100 ml water; 40 g Douglas fir needles; caster sugar (the same weight as the cooked apple); juice of 2 lemons. Peel and core the apples and simmer them in the water until soft, about 30 minutes. Blitz the needles in a food processor, or strip them from the stalks and chop them. Mash the apples, weigh them, add the same weight of sugar and heat until it dissolves. Add the lemon juice and needles and simmer about 30 minutes. Press the paste through a sieve to remove the needles, return it to the pan and cook about 30 minutes more, until it is thick, red and a wooden spoon leaves a trail. Pour it into a 15 cm dish lined with baking paper, wrap tightly in a tea towel and leave somewhere cool and dark for 14 days to set. Wrapped, it keeps a few months. Serve with cheese and crackers.

summary.text:
Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), also called Oregon pine, is a very large, resinous, evergreen conifer in the pine family (Pinaceae), native to western North America and brought to New Zealand for forestry.
Pseudotsuga menziesii var. menziesii, the coast Douglas-fir, grows in the coastal regions from west-central British Columbia southward to Central California. In Oregon and Washington, its range is continuous from the eastern edge of the Cascades west to the Pacific Coast Ranges and Pacific Ocean. In California, it is found in the Klamath and California Coast Ranges as far south as the Santa Lucia Range, with a small stand as far south as the Purisima Hills in Santa Barbara County. One of the last remaining old growth stands of conifers is in the Mattole Watershed, and is under threat of logging. In the Sierra Nevada, it ranges as far south as the Yosemite region.
Another variety exists further inland, Pseudotsuga menziesii var. glauca, the Rocky Mountain Douglas-fir or interior Douglas-fir. Interior Douglas-fir intergrades with coast Douglas-fir in the Cascades of northern Washington and southern British Columbia, and from there ranges northward to central British Columbia and southeastward to the Mexican border, becoming increasingly disjunct as latitude decreases and altitude increases. Mexican Douglas-fir (P. lindleyana), which ranges as far south as Oaxaca, is often considered a variety of P. menziesii.
Fossils (wood, pollen) of Pseudotsuga are recorded from the Miocene and Pliocene of Europe (Siebengebirge, Gleiwitz, Austria).
It is also naturalised throughout Europe, Argentina and Chile (called Pino Oregón). In New Zealand it spreads as a wilding conifer: its seed is easily blown by the wind and carried a long way, and it is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds. A mature tree can shed about 20,000 seeds a year, in autumn and winter.
The oldest planting in New Zealand, at Peel Forest Estate near Geraldine, was raised from seedlings brought out in a Wardian case and planted about 1859. Its tallest tree measured 69.6 m in 2013, the tallest cultivated Douglas fir known in the world.
In New Zealand it is naturalised in the North Island on the Volcanic Plateau, particularly the Rotorua area, and in the South Island in Canterbury (inland areas to about 800 m) and Central Otago (mainly Queenstown Hill and Naseby); it was first recorded wild in 1925.
Herbarium specimens also record it growing wild in the Nelson, Marlborough, Wellington and Hawke's Bay land districts, for example self-sown under plantations north of Hope Saddle and in Lismore Forest near Whanganui, and abundantly naturalised on the Kaweka Range.
Douglas fir is one of the commonest cultivated conifers in New Zealand south of the Volcanic Plateau, and is grown in forests, plantations, parks, domains and gardens throughout settled areas and sometimes beyond to about 1000 m. It is one the most important timber species after Pinus radiata. In New Zealand it is rather variable, mainly in cone size and foliage colour. Some planted trees look like the Rocky Mountain variety (var. glauca), a smaller tree with completely blue-grey foliage and smaller cones, but that variety has not been seen wild here.

warnings: Yew, a deadly poisonous conifer, has flat needles like Douglas fir's. Check every tree before you pick (see the lookalikes).
Take extra care in pregnancy: many sources recommend against eating or drinking any conifer, including conifer-needle teas, while pregnant.
Try only a little the first time: allergic reactions to conifers are not common, but are more likely than with most foods.
Do not pick from trees that may have been sprayed. Wilding conifers are controlled with herbicide, and urban trees may have been sprayed with pesticides or exposed to other pollutants.

identification.text:
Taprooted, annual herb, with basal rosette of leaves, densely covered in short or long hairs. Stems decumbent or more or less ascending, pinkish, to about 50 cm long. Petiole of rosette and lower cauline leaves to 14 cm long, densely covered in patent white hairs. Lamina palmately lobed, 1.5–5 × 1.5–6 cm, reniform to orbicular, densely covered in long white hairs; lobes 5–9, extending to about 3/4 way to petiole, usually with 3 oblong to obovate, obtuse to rounded, secondary lobes towards apex. Upper leaves smaller and simpler with shorter petioles. Flowers numerous, usually paired; peduncles with dense, long, white, eglandular and short glandular hairs; pedicels similar but often shorter than peduncles and curving upwards after flowering. Sepals 2–3.5 mm long, ovate, with hairs as on pedicels, mucronate. Petals (3)–4–6 mm long, obovate, rosy pink or pink, deeply emarginate; claw very short. Filaments whitish; anthers mauve. Mericarps about 1.5 mm long, broad, glabrous, with prominent pale transverse ridges. Seeds smooth. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Dove's-foot cranesbill is an annual densely covered in short or long hairs; its leaves are 1.5–5 × 1.5–6 cm, kidney-shaped to round, cut about 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes, usually with 3 rounded secondary lobes towards the tip; its sepals are 2–3.5 mm long and end in a short point; its petals are rosy pink or pink, (3)–4–6 mm long and deeply notched, its anthers mauve, and its fruit segments (mericarps) about 1.5 mm long, hairless, with prominent pale cross-ridges. The fruit separates them: dove's-foot cranesbill's fruit segments (mericarps) are hairless on the outer face and ridged, cut-leaved cranesbill's hairy and smooth. Without fruit, use the leaves: cut-leaved cranesbill's are divided nearly to the base into linear segments, dove's-foot cranesbill's to about 3/4 of the way into broader lobes. The anthers differ too (blue against mauve). Both are hairy annuals with a basal rosette and small, notched pink petals, and both have glandular hairs in the flower clusters, so none of those separates them. Cut-leaved cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food.
lookalikes.name: Cut-leaved cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Small-flowered cranesbill is a taprooted annual densely clothed in short hairs; its leaves are 1–3.5 × 1.5–4.5 cm, kidney-shaped to almost round, cut 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes that are themselves 2–3-lobed; its sepals are 2–3 mm long (to about 4 mm in fruit) and end in a short point; its petals are pale mauve, 2.5–3.5 mm long and notched; only 5–6 of its 10 stamens carry anthers (mauvish brown); and its fruit segments (mericarps) are 1.5–2 mm long, densely clothed in hairs pressed flat on the outer face. Dove's-foot cranesbill is an annual densely covered in short or long hairs; its leaves are 1.5–5 × 1.5–6 cm, kidney-shaped to round, cut about 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes, usually with 3 rounded secondary lobes towards the tip; its sepals are 2–3.5 mm long and end in a short point; its petals are rosy pink or pink, (3)–4–6 mm long and deeply notched, its anthers mauve, and its fruit segments (mericarps) about 1.5 mm long, hairless, with prominent pale cross-ridges. The two are similar in habit but can always be told apart by the fruit: small-flowered cranesbill's fruit segments (mericarps) are hairy but otherwise smooth, dove's-foot cranesbill's hairless with cross-ridges. Small-flowered cranesbill also has only 5–6 fertile anthers where dove's-foot cranesbill's 10 stamens all carry one, is usually less hairy, and generally has smaller petals (2.5–3.5 mm against (3)–4–6 mm). Both are hairy annuals with round leaves cut about 3/4 of the way into 5–9 lobes, so the leaves do not separate them. No source read records small-flowered cranesbill as food.

summary.text:
Geranium molle, the dove's-foot crane's-bill or dovesfoot geranium, is an annual herbaceous plant of the family Geraniaceae.
It is native to the Mediterranean and sub-Mediterranean areas, but has naturalized in other parts of Europe, in southwestern and central Asia and in North Africa, though it may have already been in those parts and areas, just not properly identified. It is considered an introduced species in North America, where it is known as Dovefoot Geranium or Awnless Geranium. Although non-native in parts of its range, this species poses little threat to native ecosystems.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island; South Island; Stewart Island; Kermadec Islands, Chatham Islands, Campbell Island: a common weed throughout, but not collected recently from the Kermadec Islands and Campbell Island.
In New Zealand it has been recorded as naturalised since 1852; it is exotic and grows wild, and 53 databased New Zealand collections are held, 30 of them from Canterbury. It now spreads mostly as a contaminant of clover seed, and has travelled from Western Europe, the Mediterranean and the Near East to most of Europe, the Americas, Australia, New Zealand and the Far East.

identification.text:
The cap is 2.5–10 cm wide, obtuse to convex, becoming broadly convex with a depressed centre. The margin (cap edge) is rolled inward and bearded with coarse white hairs when young. The cap surface is dry and fibrillose except for the center, which is sticky and smooth when fresh, azonate, white to cream, becoming reddish-orange to vinaceous (red wine-coloured) on the disc with age. The gills are attached to slightly decurrent, crowded, seldom forked, whitish to pale yellow with pinkish tinges, slowly staining brownish ochraceous when bruised.
The stem is 2–6.5 cm long, 6–13 mm thick, nearly equal or tapered downward, silky, becoming hollow with age, whitish when young, becoming ochraceous from the base up when older, apex usually tinged pinkish, often with a white basal mycelium. The flesh is firm and whitish; the odour is faintly like geraniums or sometimes pungent, and taste is acrid. The latex is white upon exposure, unchanging, not staining tissues, taste acrid. The spore print is cream with a pinkish tint. The edibility of Lactarius pubescens has been described as unknown, poisonous, and even edible.
The spores are 6–8.5 by 5–6.5 μm, elliptic, ornamented with warts and ridges that sometimes form a partial reticulum, prominences up to 1.5 μm high, hyaline (translucent), and amyloid. The cap cuticle is a layer of thin-walled hyphae.


Varieties
Lactarius pubescens var. betulae (A.H. Sm.) Hesler & A.H. Sm. 1979
Lactarius pubescens var. betularum (Bon) Bon 1985
Lactarius pubescens var. scoticus (Berk. & Broome) Krieglst. 1991


Ectomycorrhizae
The ectomycorrhizae that L. pubescens forms in association with Betula pendula and Populus tremuloides has been grown in pure culture and described scientifically.


Similar species
Lactarius scoticus Berk. & Broome is a small morphological mimic of L. pubescens, growing in arctic-alpine birch. L. pubescens is often mistaken for L. torminosus which has larger spores (7–10 by 6–8 μm). Certain identification may require microscopic or genetic analysis.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Downy milk cap's milk is white and does not change colour or stain the flesh. Downy milk cap's cap margin is rolled in and bearded with coarse white hairs when young, and the cap is white to cream, reddening at the centre with age; saffron milk cap's cap is orange to salmon. The trees differ too: in New Zealand and Australia downy milk cap grows with birch, saffron milk cap only with pine.

Lactarius pubescens, commonly known as the downy milk cap, is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

The fungus is common all over temperate Europe and has been reported from eastern North America, the Pacific Northwest, Arizona, California, Colorado, Idaho, and western Canada; its frequency of appearance is occasional. It is also found in Greenland, and was reported for the first time in Rome, Italy, in 1997.

identification.text:
Plants to 4–5 m high, often with thick cylindric trunk. Stem segments to about 30 cm long, often much less, more or less ovate to oblong or obovate, flattened; base narrowed. Areoles villous and with brownish glochids; spines 1–2 per areole, 1–4 cm long. Flowers on margins of stem segments, 5–9 cm diameter. Sepals and petals 3–4 cm long, yellow, with red tinge or median red stripe on outside of outer petals, ovate. Filaments white or greenish. Stigmas about 5 mm long. Fruit 5–7.5 × 3–4.5 cm, obovoid, reddish purple, fleshy, spineless; apex with large round depression. Pulp pale green or greenish white.
Larger plants have a drooping habit.
Told from prickly pear (O. ficus-indica) by its green stems, never more than two spines per cluster and red-tinged flowers: prickly pear has blue-green stems, up to six spines in each cluster and completely yellow flowers.

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the spines in each cluster on the pads: prickly pear has one to six, drooping prickly pear never more than two, so clusters of three or more point to prickly pear, while ones and twos do not separate them. Prickly pear's stems are blue-green and its flowers completely yellow; drooping prickly pear's stems are green and its yellow flowers have a red tinge or a red stripe on the outside of the outer petals. The fruit does not reliably separate them: prickly pear's can be yellow, orange or red, drooping prickly pear's is reddish purple. Both are large cacti of beaches and coastal places, up to about 5 m tall, with flat egg-shaped pads up to about 30 cm long and a drooping habit when large. Prickly pear's ripe fruit and young pads are eaten.

preparation.text: No preparation written for this species was found. For prickly pears (Opuntia) in general: pick the fruit with long-handled tongs, wearing gloves, eye protection, long sleeves and sturdy footwear, and choose firm, fully coloured fruit that comes away from the pad easily. Shaking the fruit in a half-full paper bag knocks many of the spines off. The glochids can be burnt off over a gas flame or with a kitchen torch, which takes about a minute; the thick skin protects the fruit underneath. Scrub off the singed skin under running water, then peel the fruit or cook it for juice. Fruit can be washed, dried and frozen for up to 12 months, but frozen fruit still carries its spines, so handle it with tongs.

recipes.method: Written for prickly pears (Opuntia) in general; the guide names no species. Handle the fruit with tongs throughout. Singe the spines off the whole fresh fruit over the high flame of a gas stove or grill, turning it so the flame reaches as much of the skin as possible, then scrub the fruit with a vegetable brush under running water to remove the singed skin. Halve the fruit, put it in a large pan with enough water to cover and boil for about 20 minutes, until tender. Line a colander with two layers of closely woven muslin, cheesecloth or coffee filters, set it over a bowl, and crush the fruit in it with a potato masher or large spoon to collect the juice. Juice from unripe fruit holds more pectin, so collect it separately. The juice keeps 3 days in the fridge or up to 12 months frozen in a labelled, sealed container.
recipes.title: Prickly pear juice

recipes.method: Written for prickly pears (Opuntia) in general; the guide names no species. Makes about 1.25 litres. 625 ml water; about 650 g (3¼ cups) sugar; 625 ml prickly pear juice; 1 teaspoon lemon juice. Heat the water and sugar in a 2-litre pot over a medium heat and bring to the boil. Add the prickly pear juice and lemon juice, stir for one minute, then take it off the heat. Use straight away, or keep it in a sealed container up to 5 days in the fridge or 12 months in the freezer. It is a heavy syrup for drinks or canning: for a pink lemonade (two large glasses), boil 125 ml water with 100 g sugar, cool it, and stir it in a jug with 250 ml fresh lemon juice (about 6 lemons), 30 ml of the prickly pear syrup and 250 ml cold water; serve over ice with lemon slices and mint if you like.
recipes.title: Prickly pear syrup

recipes.method: Written for prickly pears (Opuntia) in general; the guide names no species. Makes about five 250 ml jars. 1 litre prickly pear juice (fresh or frozen); 1 packet (3 tablespoons) low-sugar powdered pectin; 2 tablespoons bottled lemon juice; about 600 g (3 cups) sugar. Read and follow the pectin instructions. Put the juice and pectin in a 5-litre pot and bring to a rolling boil, stirring all the time. Add the lemon juice and sugar, bring back to a hard boil and boil 3–4 minutes. Test for a set: the most dependable test is to cook it to 4.5 °C above the temperature at which water boils where you are; or let it run off the side of a metal spoon, where at setting point the drops join into a sheet that breaks cleanly from the edge; or chill a little on a cold plate in the freezer for a few minutes to see whether it gels. Take it off the heat, let it stand about a minute, and skim off the foam. Ladle into hot, clean jars one at a time, leaving 6 mm headspace, and put on the lids and bands. Process 10 minutes in a boiling-water bath (the guide's time for 300–1,800 m above sea level; 15 minutes from 1,800 to 3,000 m). Lift the jars out onto a clean, dry cloth and leave them to cool overnight (12–15 hours), then take off the bands, dry the lids and put on clean, dry bands. Store in a cool, dry place for up to 12 months.
recipes.title: Prickly pear jelly (low sugar)

recipes.method: Written for prickly pears (Opuntia) in general; the guide names no species. Makes 1–1.25 litres; it gives pickles a pink colour and a flavour the guide likens to watermelon and kiwifruit. 1 litre prickly pear juice (fresh or frozen); 1 litre white vinegar (5% acidity); about 1.2 kg (6 cups) sugar; 4 teaspoons pickling salt. Stir the juice, vinegar, sugar and salt together in a 5-litre pot and bring to the boil. Pour into clean jars and put on the lids; it keeps up to 2 weeks in the fridge. Or pour it hot over prepared fruit or vegetables in place of the brine in another pickle recipe, and process as that recipe says. For refrigerated jicama pickles (about eight 250 ml jars), peel 1.8 kg jicama and cut it into strips about 6 mm wide and 8–10 cm long, pack them tightly into clean jars, pour about 1.25 litres of the boiling brine over, put on the lids and leave to cool before refrigerating; they keep up to 2 weeks in the fridge.

summary.text:
Drooping prickly pear (Opuntia monacantha) is a large cactus of the cactus family, Cactaceae, native to southern Brazil and Argentina and naturalised in New Zealand.
It was brought here as an ornamental and was first recorded as naturalised in 1855. The Flora of New Zealand (1988) treats it as Opuntia vulgaris and records it from the south side of Hokianga Harbour, near Mangonui, Napier and Nelson, and once at Lowburn in Central Otago; it noted then that the plant had not spread significantly, thriving where established in warmer areas. Herbarium specimens collected wild since then add Auckland, North Canterbury (Waipara, Conway Flat), Banks Peninsula (Birdlings Flat, Summit Road near Evans Pass), Whanganui, Koitiata Beach and Alexandra in Central Otago; several had grown from dumped garden waste or spread from nearby plantings. It reproduces by stem pieces and by seed, which people, birds and soil movement disperse. It is the prickly pear most often recorded wild in New Zealand, with 102 research-grade iNaturalist records against 22 for prickly pear (O. ficus-indica). It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. Auckland's Regional Pest Management Plan lists it for sustained control across the whole region and as a Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area Notice pest: in the Auckland region it must not be bred, distributed, released, sold or planted. Bay of Plenty Regional Council lists prickly pear cacti, naming this species, as advisory pest plants.

warnings: The stems carry spines and tufts of tiny barbed bristles (glochids) that irritate the skin on contact. In prickly pears generally, the glochids are almost invisible, and once they pierce the skin the barb breaks off and stays embedded.

Prickly pear juice tastes tart but is a low-acid food (pH 5 to 7). To can the juice or fruit, it must be acidified and processed in a boiling-water bath, or pressure processed. Written of prickly pears in general.

identification.text:
Plants grow up to about 3.5 m long, with massive blades that are flattened, with parallel sides and wavy edges, and usually not divided. The blades are solid inside, with no honeycomb of air-filled tissue, and do not float. Their pale margins are very noticeable, and shallow, crater-like dents up to 25 mm across are common on the blade surface, especially near the margins. On exposed coasts the blades can split into many narrow straps; with increasing shelter they become less divided, and in very sheltered places may be undivided. A short, solid, unbranched stipe, usually cylindrical and flattening towards the blade, grows from a large, dome-shaped holdfast; holdfasts are commonly fused together. Dark brown. Very small plants are difficult to identify.
Told from bull kelp by its solid, non-buoyant blades: bull kelp's blades have an internal honeycomb that keeps them buoyant.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or tear a blade: bull kelp's has an internal honeycomb, full of air, that keeps it buoyant; Durvillaea chathamensis's blades are solid, with no honeycomb, and do not float. Very small plants are difficult to identify, so check a full-grown blade. Durvillaea chathamensis's blades are flattened, with parallel sides, wavy edges and very noticeable pale margins, and are usually not divided; bull kelp's are often divided into strap-like portions. Division alone does not separate them, because on exposed coasts Durvillaea chathamensis's blades can also split into many narrow straps: there, bull kelp's strands are inflated and whip-like, rounded or oval in cross-section, while Durvillaea chathamensis's are solid straps. Shallow, crater-like dents up to 25 mm across are common on Durvillaea chathamensis's blades, especially near the margins; the study that described it never saw them on bull kelp. Both have an unbranched stipe growing from a large, dome-shaped holdfast, so the stipe does not separate them. Colour overlaps: Durvillaea chathamensis is dark brown, bull kelp golden to dark brown to olive green. Size does not separate them: Durvillaea chathamensis grows up to about 3.5 m long and bull kelp to 5 m, sometimes up to 10 m, so a plant shorter than 3.5 m can be either. Durvillaea chathamensis grows from the low intertidal to about 2 m deep, often in a band just below bull kelp, which grows in the low intertidal, so the two meet there. Durvillaea chathamensis is found only in the Chatham Islands, where bull kelp also grows. Bull kelp's blades are eaten.

summary.text:
Durvillaea chathamensis — a large bull kelp endemic to the Chatham Islands, with solid blades that lack bull kelp's air-filled honeycomb and do not float.
It was named as a species in 1979. It grows alongside bull kelp (Durvillaea antarctica) on Chatham Island, and the two are so similar genetically that its status was questioned, but a 2016 genome-wide study found it is a reproductively isolated species that differs from bull kelp ecologically as well as in form.
It is At Risk – Naturally Uncommon, as an island endemic.

warnings: No record of Durvillaea chathamensis as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
In the Chatham Islands it grows with bull kelp, often in a band just below it, so check every plant before cutting (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text:
Found in the intertidal in exposed areas, often in a band above D. antarctica, around southern South Island, Stewart, Snares and Auckland Islands.
It grows alongside bull kelp over much of its range, but of the two it is the bull kelp of less exposed sites; bull kelp takes the most wave-beaten rock.

harvestEthics.text:
This species is at risk. If you harvest it, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.
Bull kelp (Durvillaea species) may not be taken between Marfells Beach and the Conway River, out to 4 nautical miles from shore. The Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998 protects bull kelp (Durvillaea species) from commercial harvesting within Ngāi Tahu's traditional seaweed-gathering grounds.

identification.text:
Plants usually 5–10 m long, and are made up of massive blades, broad and flattened, with an internal honeycomb structure. Blades can become whip-like at the tips, but always remain broad and flattened in cross-section. Short stipe is orange-yellow and becomes flattened towards the tip. Holdfasts may join together with several stipes growing out of a clump. Blades orange-brown to golden. Fertile structures are scattered over the blades but are not easily visible.
[From: Neill & Nelson (2016) Beautiful browns, NIWA.]
The stipes are unbranched.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or tear a blade: Durvillaea poha's has an internal honeycomb; Durvillaea willana's has none, and it does not float. Look at the holdfast: Durvillaea poha's is extensively burrowed and hollowed out; Durvillaea willana's is solid, woody and not burrowed, and grips the rock firmly. Durvillaea poha's short stipe is orange-yellow, unbranched and flattened towards the tip; Durvillaea willana's is thick and cylindrical and produces side branches. Durvillaea poha's blades are orange-brown to golden; Durvillaea willana is dark brown, darker than all other bull kelps. Durvillaea poha grows in the intertidal, often in a band above bull kelp; Durvillaea willana grows lower, from the low intertidal to the upper subtidal. Durvillaea willana grows 5–6 m long and Durvillaea poha is usually 5–10 m long, so size does not separate them. Both grow on exposed coasts of the South Island and Stewart Island. No record of Durvillaea willana as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Durvillaea willana

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have thick, leathery blades with an internal honeycomb, so the honeycomb does not separate them. Look at a blade in cross-section: Durvillaea poha's blades are broad and flattened, and stay flattened even where the tips become whip-like; bull kelp's always remain rounded or oval in cross-section, even where they become narrower and whip-like on more exposed sites. Durvillaea poha's short stipe is orange-yellow and becomes flattened towards the tip; bull kelp's is cylindrical. Colour helps only a little: Durvillaea poha's blades are orange-brown to golden and can look more orange, bull kelp's are golden to dark brown to olive green. Size does not separate them: Durvillaea poha is usually 5–10 m long, bull kelp grows to 5 m and sometimes up to 10 m. Durvillaea poha often grows in a band above bull kelp, or further back on rock platforms and in more sheltered bays, but in southern New Zealand the two frequently grow next to one another. Durvillaea poha is found mainly on the southern South Island, Stewart Island and the Snares and Auckland Islands, and at low frequencies along the Wellington coastline; it was not found on the northern South Island north of the Kaikōura Peninsula. Bull kelp's blades are eaten.

summary.text:
Durvillaea poha — a large, buoyant bull kelp endemic to New Zealand, with broader, flatter blades than bull kelp (Durvillaea antarctica).
It was long recognised as genetically, morphologically and ecologically distinct, as the shorter and broader 'cape' form of D. antarctica, and was named as a species in 2012. No hybrids with D. antarctica have been seen where the two grow together.
It grows around the southern South Island, Stewart Island and the Snares and Auckland Islands. Genetic sampling in 2021 found it at four North Island sites, about 150 km north-east of the nearest South Island population, but not on the northern South Island north of the Kaikōura Peninsula. It is At Risk – Declining.
Bull kelps (Durvillaea species) are threatened by events such as the 2016 Kaikōura earthquake, whose uplift killed intertidal bull kelp along about 120 km of coast from Oaro to Cape Campbell, and the 2017/18 Tasman Sea marine heatwave, after which bull kelp stands near Christchurch had died.
Bull kelp (rimurapa, Durvillaea species) blades are made into pōhā, the bags Ngāi Tahu used to preserve tītī.

warnings: No record of Durvillaea poha as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
In southern New Zealand it frequently grows next to bull kelp, and both have honeycombed blades, so check every plant before cutting (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text:
Found in the low intertidal to upper subtidal on exposed coasts of the southeastern corner of the North Island (but not Cook Strait), South Island and Stewart Island.
It grows mostly on wave-exposed rocky shores, from between neap and spring low water down into the shallow subtidal: usually 0.5–1.5 m below low water where the sea is murky, sometimes to about 4 m where it is clear. On cliff coasts it favours ledges, small shelves and gutters; elsewhere it forms a conspicuous band on shallow offshore reefs, stable boulder shores and broad wave-cut platforms, staying half-submerged in the surge. It goes only a short way into harbours and bays, tolerates some scouring by sand and gravel, and grows in dense beds near the mouths of large rivers. Wherever it has been recorded it grows close to bull kelp, Durvillaea poha or both.

This species is at risk. If you harvest it, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.
It may not be taken from the East Otago taiāpure unless it is unattached and cast ashore. Bull kelp (Durvillaea species) may not be taken between Marfells Beach and the Conway River, out to 4 nautical miles from shore. The Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998 protects bull kelp (Durvillaea species) from commercial harvesting within Ngāi Tahu's traditional seaweed-gathering grounds.

identification.text:
Plants grow up to 5 m high and consist of massive blades, tough and leathery, sometimes divided into straps, with no internal honeycomb structure. Stipe is thick, cylindrical, and produces side branches. Holdfast a dome-shaped disc. Dark brown. Fertile structures are scattered over the blades but are not easily visible.
[From: Neill & Nelson (2016) Beautiful browns, NIWA.]
It is 5–6 m long and can weigh over 40 kg. Its blades are solid and leathery and sink, unlike the honeycombed, buoyant blades of bull kelp and Durvillaea poha. The stiff, upright stipe is 1–2 m long and bears side branches; it rises from a solid, woody, dome-shaped to pyramidal holdfast up to 0.5 m wide, and neighbouring holdfasts often merge to carry several plants. The holdfast is not burrowed and grips the rock firmly, so storms usually snap the stipe at the holdfast rather than tear the holdfast free: fewer than a third of cast-up plants still have one. Plants at the top of the kelp band are often battered down to a stump with side branches. It is stiffer and more upright than bull kelp.
This species is chocolate brown in colour and is darker than all other bull kelp species.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or tear a blade: Durvillaea poha's has an internal honeycomb; Durvillaea willana's has none, and it does not float. Look at the holdfast: Durvillaea poha's is extensively burrowed and hollowed out; Durvillaea willana's is solid, woody and not burrowed, and grips the rock firmly. Durvillaea poha's short stipe is orange-yellow, unbranched and flattened towards the tip; Durvillaea willana's is thick and cylindrical and produces side branches. Durvillaea poha's blades are orange-brown to golden; Durvillaea willana is dark brown, darker than all other bull kelps. Durvillaea poha grows in the intertidal, often in a band above bull kelp; Durvillaea willana grows lower, from the low intertidal to the upper subtidal. Durvillaea willana grows 5–6 m long and Durvillaea poha is usually 5–10 m long, so size does not separate them. Both grow on exposed coasts of the South Island and Stewart Island. No record of Durvillaea poha as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Durvillaea poha

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or tear a blade: bull kelp's has an internal honeycomb, full of air, that keeps it buoyant; Durvillaea willana's has no honeycomb, and it does not float. Look at the holdfast: bull kelp's is extensively burrowed and hollowed out; Durvillaea willana's is solid, woody and not burrowed, and grips the rock so firmly that storms usually snap its stipe instead, so fewer than a third of cast-up Durvillaea willana plants still have a holdfast, against more than three-quarters of cast-up bull kelp. Durvillaea willana is also stiffer and more upright than bull kelp. Bull kelp's short stipe is cylindrical and unbranched; Durvillaea willana's is thick and cylindrical and produces side branches. Colour overlaps: Durvillaea willana is dark brown, darker than all other bull kelps, while bull kelp ranges from golden to dark brown to olive green. Durvillaea willana usually grows lower on the shore, from the low intertidal to the upper subtidal; bull kelp grows in the low intertidal, so the two can meet there. Durvillaea willana grows 5–6 m long and has smaller blades than bull kelp, which grows to 5 m and sometimes up to 10 m, so size alone does not separate them. In the North Island Durvillaea willana is found only near Castle Point on the northern Wairarapa coast, not in Cook Strait; bull kelp grows from the Three Kings Islands to Stewart Island. Bull kelp's blades are eaten.

summary.text:
Durvillaea willana is a bull kelp endemic to New Zealand, and the largest seaweed of its order (Fucales) here. The specific epithet willana honours Eileen Alice Willa who collected many algal species for Lindauer.
It grows on the South Island and Stewart Island/Rakiura, with a small North Island population near Castle Point on the northern Wairarapa coast. It reaches north to Cape Farewell in the west; warm summer seas keep it out of western Cook Strait, the Marlborough Sounds and Nelson, and it is not found on the Snares, Auckland or Campbell Islands. Within that range it is conspicuously absent from three long stretches of rocky shore: Wellington's south coast, the southern and central Wairarapa coast, and South Westland. It does not float and disperses poorly. Plants are male or female, take at least two years to become fertile and can live 8–10 years. Dense beds shelter many smaller seaweeds and animals and soften the waves, protecting more fragile species inshore and reducing coastal erosion. The 2016 Kaikōura earthquake did it less harm than the intertidal bull kelps, but where the shore rose 2–3 m every plant lifted into the new intertidal zone died. It is At Risk – Naturally Uncommon.

warnings: No record of Durvillaea willana as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
Wherever it has been recorded it grows close to bull kelp, Durvillaea poha or both, and it looks superficially like bull kelp, so check every plant before cutting (see the lookalikes).

identification.text: Cordyline pumilio is a plant rarely exceeding 2 metres tall. It is a very narrow-leaved species, and does not develop into the large tree-like form of C. australis. It often flowers while its short stem is leafy to the ground. In older plants the bare part of stem is up to 1 metre long and 1.5 cm wide, and not usually very erect. The leaves are 30 cm to 1 metre long and 1 to 2 cm wide, and may narrow above the base into a channelled petiole. The midrib is prominent abaxially, or at least proximally and the leaf margins are slightly recurved. The flower spike or panicle appears in November or December and is up to 60 by 30 cm, very open with slender axes, branched to the second order, with small white or bluish-white flowers irregularly scattered along the branches. The bracts are often small and inconspicuous. The tepals are narrow, recurved and have three nerves. The stigma is short and trifid.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cabbage tree grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Dwarf cabbage tree (Cordyline pumilio) is rarely more than 2 m tall and often flowers while its short stem is still leafy to the ground; its leaves are 30–60–(100) × 1–2 cm, more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base; its panicle is very open, up to about 60 cm long, with slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers that are whitish or pink outside, and its berries are bluish or flecked with blue, 4–5 mm across. In short: dwarf cabbage tree is usually no more than 1–(2) m tall with a main stem 1–2 cm across and leaves rarely over 2 cm wide, its flower cluster large for the plant but with very slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers; cabbage tree's main stem soon exceeds 2 cm across even on a young plant, and its leaves are mostly over 2 cm wide. Hybrids between the two have been described from the far north (C. × matthewsii, Carse 1926), some almost enlarged copies of dwarf cabbage tree, so an in-between plant there may be neither.
lookalikes.name: Cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Forest cabbage tree grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Dwarf cabbage tree (Cordyline pumilio) is rarely more than 2 m tall and often flowers while its short stem is still leafy to the ground; its leaves are 30–60–(100) × 1–2 cm, more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base; its panicle is very open, up to about 60 cm long, with slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers that are whitish or pink outside, and its berries are bluish or flecked with blue, 4–5 mm across. In short: dwarf cabbage tree is usually no more than 1–(2) m tall with a main stem 1–2 cm across and leaves rarely over 2 cm wide, its flower cluster large for the plant but with very slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers; forest cabbage tree's main stem soon exceeds 2 cm across even on a young plant, and its leaves are mostly over 2 cm wide. A hybrid between the two has been described (C. × gibbingsae, Carse 1929) that looks like a small, stemless forest cabbage tree, so an in-between plant may be neither.

preparation.text:
Young seedlings were carefully selected and planted out, and after perhaps three years the roots were dug up, stacked in small piles, and dried in the sun. As they dried, the fibrous roots were burned off, and then the roots were scraped and baked slowly in an umu or hāngī, requiring twelve to eighteen hours to cook. The cooked roots were chewed, or pounded and washed and squeezed to extract the sugar, which was eaten with fern root as a relish.
Roots tied separately for baking in bundles of hangehange, Geniostoma rupestre.
Roots dug up and dried, sometimes eaten raw.

summary.text:
Cordyline pumilio, commonly known as the dwarf cabbage tree, pygmy cabbage tree or by its Māori names tī koraha or tī rauriki, is a narrow-leaved monocot shrub endemic to the North Island of New Zealand.
It has long leaves and can easily be mistaken for a grass or a sedge. C. pumilio grows in the north of the North Island from North Cape at 34°S to Kawhia and Ōpōtiki at about 38°S, generally under light forest and scrub.

edibleParts.text: This plant is often consumed as a food, with its leaves, stalks and seed all being considered edible. Leaves and young shoots - raw or cooked. They can be added in quantity to salads, and make an excellent lettuce substitute, they can also be cooked as greens. The leaves are mucilaginous. Some people find this mucilaginous texture unpleasant, especially if the leaves are cooked. Immature seeds - raw or cooked. The seeds can be eaten raw or cooked and have a nutty flavor. Mature seeds can be cooked like rice or grains.

identification.text:
Dwarf mallow is a prostrate, downy, herbaceous plant, growing to approximately 60 cm.
The leaves are alternate with long, strongly channeled petioles and narrowly triangular stipules.
It is a broadleaf winter annual that also persists through a biennial or perennial life cycle if environmental conditions are favorable.
Each leaf is reniform or with 5–7 shallow lobes, the basal leaves are 3–7 cm.
It grows a tough taproot.
The flowers are single-stalked and occur in clusters of 2–5 in the leaf axils.
The flower stalks are shorter than the leaf stalks, with the leaves partially obscuring the flowers.
The fruits are schizocarps, which split into mericarps (nutlets) and are smooth and hairy.
In addition to daily phototropic movements, leaves show epinasty, geotropism and sleeping behaviors. Leaves joined to the stem on the east side of the plant bend abaxially and leaves on the west side of the plant bend adaxially, while leaves on the north and south sides turn sideways. Overnight, leaves were observed returning to their morning position.

The smooth-backed mericarps clothed in short hairs distinguish this species. It has often been recorded in New Zealand as M. rotundifolia.

Annual or short-lived perennial, procumbent to ascending herb. Stems sparsely to densely clothed in stellate hairs. Leaves sparsely to moderately clothed in mostly stellate hairs above, densely hairy below, reniform to orbicular, cordate, shallowly 5–7-palmately lobed and crenate, 1–7–(8) cm diameter; petioles (2)–4–20 cm long; stipules triangular, 3–6 mm long. Flowers in axillary clusters of 2–5; fruiting pedicels 1–8 cm long; epicalyx segments linear to narrowly ovate-oblong, shorter than calyx; calyx teeth ovate-triangular, acuminate, with stellate hairs and ciliate, not enlarged at fruiting; petals white to lilac, often with lilac to pink veins, usually at least twice as long as calyx, (7)–8–15 mm long. Mericarps 12–15 per fruit, hairy, rarely sparsely so, smooth or faintly reticulate on back; edges sharply angled but not winged.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. The two are separated by cheeseweed mallow's shorter petals, enlarged fruiting calyx and net-veined fruit segments with winged edges. Both are low herbs with round to kidney-shaped, lobed leaves of overlapping size (1–8 cm and 1–7(–8) cm across) and flowers in clusters in the leaf joints, so the leaves do not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Petal lengths overlap between 12 and 15 mm, and common mallow can have pale pink flowers, so on a pale, mid-sized flower use the fruit: hairy and smooth-backed in dwarf mallow, usually hairless and strongly net-veined in common mallow. Dwarf mallow lies flat or ascends and common mallow ascends or stands upright, so an ascending plant fits both. Leaf shape and size overlap. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. The fruit separates them: strongly net-veined on the back in French mallow, smooth or faintly veined (and hairy) in dwarf mallow. Petal lengths overlap (6–10 mm against (7–)8–15 mm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and are unchanged in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Both have palmately lobed, toothed leaves whose sizes overlap (island mallow 2–15(–20) cm across, dwarf mallow 1–7(–8) cm), so use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Both have round, palmately 5–7-lobed, round-toothed leaves, so the leaves do not separate them; use the petal length, the epicalyx and the fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.

preparation.text: In culinary applications, it is cooked similar to spinach, or used for thickening soups, as the leaves release a thickening agent similar to okra which is also in the mallow family. In Morocco leaves are known as Bakola or Khobiza, braised as a side dish (called salad, but cooked) or used as a sauce over couscous. The root can be ground and used as a meringue substitute by boiling in water, simmering until thickened, and then whisked like egg whites. In Spain the unripe fruits are eaten raw as a treat (Arraia-Maeztu, Álava), and in Cazorla and Santiago-Pontones (Jaén) people eat the little fruits, called panecillos.

recipes.method: Written for mallow in general; the author gives khobiza as Malva neglecta or Malva parviflora. Serves 2. ½ tbsp olive oil, 1 small onion, thinly sliced, about 500 ml roughly chopped mallow leaves, a pinch of salt and black pepper, and a squeeze of lemon. Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat and fry the onion for 2–3 minutes. Add the mallow, toss, and season with salt and pepper. Add the lemon and serve straight away. Keep leftovers in the fridge for a couple of days only.
recipes.title: Palestinian sautéed mallow (khobiza)

recipes.method: Written for mallow (Malva neglecta and other species) by herbalist Erin Smith. 2–3 large handfuls of mallow leaves, 2 tbsp (30 g) butter, 1 large or 2 small onions, finely sliced, 1 large carrot, chopped, 2 celery sticks, chopped, 1 large garlic clove, crushed, about 1 litre of good chicken or vegetable stock, 1 medium potato, 2 tbsp (30 ml) yoghurt or crème fraîche (optional), a pinch of grated nutmeg, salt and black pepper, and chopped herbs (chives, parsley, rosemary or thyme). Soften the onion, carrot, celery and garlic in the butter without browning. Add the stock (and the potato, chopped — the page lists it but does not say when it goes in), bring to the boil and simmer until the potato and carrot mash with a fork. Add the mallow leaves and simmer 5–10 minutes. Season with salt, pepper and nutmeg, purée with a hand blender, return to the pan, stir in the cream and warm through. Serve with a little yoghurt or cream and chopped herbs (chives, parsley, rosemary or thyme).
recipes.title: Blended mallow soup

recipes.method: Written for mallow generally; the post shows dwarf mallow. 250 ml (1 cup) sunflower seeds, soaked and dried; 250 ml (1 cup) pumpkin seeds or cashews, soaked; 250 ml (1 cup) chopped mallow greens; 250 ml (1 cup) mallow water; the juice of 1 lemon; 1 small garlic clove; 10 ml (2 tsp) salt. For the mallow water, steep chopped mallow leaves and stems in cold water for several hours or overnight, until the water is as thick as egg white. Process everything in a food processor or blender until smooth. Serve it with carrot or celery sticks or on crackers, and keep it in an airtight container in the fridge.
recipes.title: Mallow spread

summary.text:
Malva neglecta is a species of plant of the family Malvaceae, native to most of the Old World except sub-Saharan Africa. It is known as common mallow in the United States and also as buttonweed, cheeseplant, cheeseweed, dwarf mallow, and roundleaf mallow.
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North Island, in eastern areas of the South Island from the Marlborough Sounds to Southland, where it is common, and on the Chatham Islands. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1867.

warnings: When grown on nitrogen rich soils (and particularly when these are inorganic), the plant tends to concentrate high levels of nitrates in its leaves.
It has a high nitrate content, similar to that of arugula.

identification.text:
Shallowly taprooted, erect monoecious annual, moderately clothed in short-stalked stinging hairs, otherwise sparsely to densely hairy. Stem with lateral branches usually present, up to 60 cm high. Leaves ovate or elliptic, acute, obtuse to truncate at base, coarsely serrate, (1)–2–8–(10) cm long. Petiole about ⅔ as long as lamina. Stipules 4 per node, entire, 1–3 mm long. Racemes with numerous male and female flowers, up to 1.5–(3) cm long. Perianth segments of female flowers extremely unequal, glabrous to hairy; margins ciliate. Achene ovoid, light brown, 1.5–2 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Ongaonga (tree nettle) is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m tall; dwarf nettle is a soft, branched annual herb up to 60 cm. Ongaonga's leaves are pale green and triangular to ovate-triangular, with white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long on the leaf teeth, young stalks and leaf veins; ongaonga's stinging hairs are long-stalked and dwarf nettle's short-stalked. Ongaonga has 2 stipules at each node, dwarf nettle 4. Its sting has killed: in 1961 a young man died of paralysis and breathing problems several hours after walking through tree nettles. Young ongaonga can be confused with other native nettles, so do not touch a stinging plant unless you are sure it is not woody.
lookalikes.name: Ongaonga

lookalikes.howToTell: Stinging nettle is a perennial up to 1.5 m that spreads by rhizomes into patches and seldom branches; dwarf nettle is a branched annual up to 60 cm with a short taproot. Stinging nettle's leaves are 5–25 cm, the end tooth longer than the teeth beside it; dwarf nettle's are 2–8 cm and rounder, the end tooth about as long as its neighbours. Stinging nettle's flower clusters, up to 9 cm, are one sex, usually on separate plants; dwarf nettle's clusters, up to 3 cm, usually carry male and female flowers together. Both sting, and both are eaten young and cooked.
lookalikes.name: Stinging nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush nettle is a native perennial that spreads by rhizomes, with light green, triangular leaves 2–6 cm long (sometimes up to 12 cm), a squared-off to slightly heart-shaped base and 9–10 (sometimes 12) teeth on each side; its lowest flower clusters are all male and the upper ones all female. Dwarf nettle is an annual with a short taproot and ovate to elliptic leaves 2–8 cm long, and its flower clusters usually carry male and female flowers together. Bush nettle grows in forest, forest margins and shaded places; dwarf nettle in gardens, farms and waste ground.
lookalikes.name: Bush nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Southern nettle is a stout, bushy native up to about 1 m whose branches lie down and root before turning upright, with broadly ovate, dark green leaves 10–20 cm long, the leaf stalk often carrying a pair of small leaflets near its base; its stinging hairs are mainly on the leaf edges and the veins underneath, and are often few or none. Dwarf nettle is an annual up to 60 cm with a short taproot and leaves 2–8 cm long. Both grow on the Chatham Islands; dwarf nettle is absent from Fiordland. No record of southern nettle being eaten has been found, and it is At Risk – Declining.
lookalikes.name: Southern nettle

preparation.text: Wear stout gloves to pick, and use only the young leaves. Cooking or thoroughly drying the leaves destroys the stinging hairs; pouring boiling water over them stops the sting. Blanching in salted water for 30–60 seconds, or steaming, removes the sting; leaves to be dried need no blanching first. Tops that have started to set seed are tougher. To freeze, blanch, drain, squeeze out the water and bag.

recipes.method: Written for common stinging nettles in North America (Urtica dioica 'and similar'); Forager Chef's nettle guide counts Urtica urens among the common nettles it covers. Serves 6. About 225 g nettles; 1 cup diced celery; 2 cups diced leeks; 2 diced shallots; 1 small diced onion; 3 tbsp butter; about 1 litre chicken stock; 2 cups diced potato; 120 ml cream; salt and white pepper; crème fraîche and chopped dill or mint, to serve. Blanch about 225 g nettles in salted boiling water until just wilted, about 30 seconds, cool them in cold water, squeeze dry and finely chop a handful to finish the soup. Sweat 1 cup diced celery, 2 cups diced leeks, 2 diced shallots and 1 small diced onion in 3 tbsp butter over medium heat for 5 minutes. Add about 1 litre chicken stock and 2 cups diced potato and simmer until tender, about 15 minutes. Add the blanched nettles and blend, then stir in the chopped nettles and 120 ml cream and season with salt and white pepper. Serve with crème fraîche and chopped dill or mint.
recipes.title: Classic stinging nettle soup

recipes.method: Written for common stinging nettles in North America (Urtica dioica 'and similar'); Forager Chef's nettle guide counts Urtica urens among the common nettles it covers. Serves 2. About 225 g young nettle tops; 3 large crushed garlic cloves; 3 tbsp olive oil, plus more to serve; salt and pepper; a pinch of chilli flakes; ½ cup ricotta; lemon wedges. Wash about 225 g young nettle tops and steam them, covered, over boiling water for 2–3 minutes until tender. Meanwhile warm 3 large crushed garlic cloves in 3 tbsp olive oil over medium heat for at least 10 minutes until browned, then discard the garlic. Add the steamed nettles to the oil, season with salt, pepper and a pinch of chilli flakes, gently fold in ½ cup ricotta and warm through. Serve warm or at room temperature with olive oil and lemon wedges.
recipes.title: Steamed nettles with ricotta

recipes.method: Written for stinging nettle in Britain; the recipe does not name the species. Serves 6. 25 g butter; 150 g nettle leaves, washed; 200 g feta, crumbled; 50 g parmesan, grated; the zest and juice of a lemon; 1 egg, beaten; grated nutmeg; seasoning; 7 filo sheets; 75 g melted butter; 1 tbsp sesame seeds. Brown 25 g butter in a large frying pan, add 150 g washed, still-damp nettle leaves and cook for about 6 minutes until wilted; cool, squeeze out the liquid and chop roughly. Mix with 200 g crumbled feta, 50 g grated parmesan, the zest and juice of a lemon, two-thirds of a beaten egg, grated nutmeg and seasoning. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan). Lay 3 filo sheets end to end, overlapping by about 5 cm, brush with some of 75 g melted butter, add 3 more sheets and more butter, then a seventh sheet in the middle. Spoon the filling in a line about 2 cm wide along one long edge, tuck in the ends, roll into a long sausage and coil it into a spiral about 20 cm across in a shallow round pan or on a buttered baking tray. Brush with the rest of the egg, scatter with 1 tbsp sesame seeds and bake for 40–45 minutes until golden.
recipes.title: Nettle spanakopita

recipes.method: Written for stinging nettle in Britain; the recipe does not name the species. Serves 4. 200 g nettle leaves; 1 tbsp olive oil; a 200 ml tub of crème fraîche; 1 tsp wholegrain mustard; 140 g blue cheese, crumbled; seasoning; 4 slices of sourdough. Wilt 200 g nettle leaves in 1 tbsp hot olive oil for 1 minute, cool briefly and chop roughly. Mix with a 200 ml tub of crème fraîche, 1 tsp wholegrain mustard, half of 140 g crumbled blue cheese, and seasoning. Toast 4 slices of sourdough on both sides under the grill, spread with the nettle mix, top with the rest of the cheese and grill until golden and bubbling.
recipes.title: Nettle and blue cheese rarebit

recipes.method: Written for stinging nettles; the recipe says Urtica dioica or U. urens will do. About 450 g nettle leaves, stripped from their stems; 4 tbsp ghee, olive oil or coconut oil; 4 finely chopped garlic cloves (or 1 tsp asafoetida); a 2.5 cm piece of fresh ginger, finely chopped; 1 small jalapeño or serrano chilli, finely chopped (optional); 1 tbsp turmeric powder; 1 tsp ground coriander; 1 tsp whole cumin seed; about 450 g coarsely chopped spinach or chard; salt; 120 ml cream (or crème fraîche or coconut cream). Bring about 4 litres of water to the boil, add about 450 g nettle leaves stripped from their stems and boil for 5 minutes, then drain in a colander. In a frying pan, heat 4 tbsp ghee, olive oil or coconut oil and fry 4 finely chopped garlic cloves (or 1 tsp asafoetida), a 2.5 cm piece of finely chopped fresh ginger, 1 small finely chopped jalapeño or serrano chilli if you like, 1 tbsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp ground coriander and 1 tsp whole cumin seed. Add about 450 g coarsely chopped spinach or chard and stir to coat in the spices, then add the nettles and a few pinches of salt. Cover and cook, stirring every few minutes and adding a little water if it sticks, until the greens are soft but not mushy. Take off the heat, stir in 120 ml cream (or crème fraîche or coconut cream), adjust the salt and serve warm with dal and rice or chapati.
recipes.title: Nettle saag

recipes.method: Written for nettles: the author eats both perennial and annual (dwarf) nettle, and gives this soup from Richard Mabey's Food for Free (1972). 4 large handfuls of nettle tops, picked with gloves; 1 large onion; 50 g butter or coconut oil; 2 potatoes; 1 litre vegetable stock; 15 ml (1 tbsp) crème fraîche or yoghurt; salt, pepper and grated nutmeg. Strip the nettles from the thicker stalks and wash them. Melt the butter and cook the chopped onion gently until translucent. Add the nettles and the chopped potatoes and cook 2–3 minutes, then add the stock and simmer 20 minutes, crushing the potatoes now and then with a wooden spoon. Season, with a little grated nutmeg, and finish with a swirl of crème fraîche or yoghurt; blend it first if you want a smoother soup.
recipes.title: Nettle and potato soup

recipes.method: Written for nettles: the author eats both perennial and annual (dwarf) nettle. Put 30 g dried nettle leaves, or two handfuls of cut-up fresh leaves, in a 1-litre preserving jar, fill it with boiling water, put the lid on and leave it to steep overnight at room temperature. The author drinks 1 or 2 cups a day. For an ordinary cup of tea, steep about a teaspoon of leaves in a teapot for 5 minutes.
recipes.title: Overnight nettle infusion

summary.text:
Urtica urens, commonly known as annual nettle, dwarf nettle, small nettle, dog nettle, burning nettle, or bush nettle is a herbaceous annual flowering plant species in the nettle family Urticaceae.
The native distribution of Urtica urens includes most of Europe except the British Isles, northern Asia, north and northwest Africa.
In the British Isles, Urtica urens is an archaeophyte, an ancient introduction. It has been introduced to all other continents of the world except Antarctica.
It is reputed to sting more strongly than Urtica dioica (common nettle).
In New Zealand it is the commonest nettle, usually just called stinging nettle. First recorded wild here in 1846, it is locally common throughout both main islands — except Northland and Taranaki, Westland and Fiordland — and on the Chatham Islands.
The genus name Urtica comes from the Latin verb urere, 'to burn'. The name bush nettle is also used for this species overseas; in this guide, Bush nettle is the native Urtica sykesii, a different plant.
In New Zealand its leaves feed the caterpillars of the red admiral and yellow admiral butterflies.

warnings: Use only young leaves. Older leaves develop gritty crystals (cystoliths) that are widely held to irritate the kidneys.
Nettles in paddocks, along fence lines and under trees may be sprayed with MCPA, 2,4-D or glufosinate. Pick from ground you know.
