identification.text:
Annual herb. Stems erect, softly hairy, to 1 m tall. Leaves sparsely to densely hairy. Rosette and lower stem leaves lyrate-pinnatifid or pinnatifid to almost lyrate-pinnate, 5–10–(30) × (1)–2–8–(15) cm; terminal lobe ovate to triangular to hastate; lateral lobes in 1–5 pairs, narrow-lanceolate or triangular, entire, sinuate or coarsely toothed. Upper stem leaves usually smaller with narrower, but not linear-filiform lobes, or hastate, or ovate and not lobed. Racemes often flexuous, ebracteate, glabrous or sparsely hairy, 20–40–(60) cm long. Pedicels 3–5 mm long, elongating to about 10 mm long at fruiting, sparsely hairy. Sepals usually hairy, 3–5 mm long, not horned. Petals yellow, 6–10 mm long. Anthers 1–1.5 mm long; filaments longer than sepals. Silique glabrous or hairy, spreading, linear-cylindric, (40)–60–100 × 1–1.5 mm; style 0.5–2 mm long. Seeds oblong, brown, about 1 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The stems are wiry and branch at about 45 degrees. The very long, slender pods stick out from the stem at 45–90 degrees, on short stalks almost as thick as the pod. As a seedling it is almost identical to hedge mustard; in the rosette its end lobe is longer and more pointed.

lookalikes.howToTell: As seedlings the two are almost identical. In the rosette, hedge mustard's end lobe is short and rounded; eastern rocket's is longer and more pointed. In flower, hedge mustard's petals are 3–4 mm long, against eastern rocket's 6–10 mm, and its sepals about 2 mm, against 3–5 mm. Hedge mustard's pods are short, 10–15–(20) mm, and pressed flat against the stem; eastern rocket's are (40)–60–100 × 1–1.5 mm and spread away from it.
lookalikes.name: Hedge mustard

lookalikes.howToTell: Flowers do not separate them: both have yellow petals 6–10 mm long. Field mustard's stems are hairless and its upper leaves are smooth, bluish-green, not lobed and clasp the stem; eastern rocket's stems are softly hairy and its leaves sparsely to densely hairy. Field mustard's pods are (30)–40–60 × 2–5 mm and end in a seedless beak 6–10 mm long; eastern rocket's are longer and thinner, (40)–60–100 × 1–1.5 mm, with no beak or a very short one.
lookalikes.name: Field mustard

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild radish's flowers are larger: its petals are 13–20 mm long, usually pale yellow or white and usually veined with mauve, against eastern rocket's yellow 6–10 mm. Wild radish's pods are (2)–3–8–(9) mm wide, pinched between the seeds, on stout stalks 1–2 cm long; eastern rocket's are slender, 1–1.5 mm wide and (40)–60–100 mm long, on stalks 3–5 mm long that lengthen to about 10 mm.
lookalikes.name: Wild radish

summary.text:
Sisymbrium orientale is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae known by the common names Indian hedgemustard and eastern rocket. It is native to Europe, Asia, and North Africa, and it can be found throughout much of the temperate world as an introduced species and in some areas a common roadside weed.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) it grows throughout the North and South Islands and on the Kermadecs, naturalised by 1932 from southern Europe, Asia Minor and North Africa. It is also called Indian hedge mustard and oriental mustard.
In Britain it arrived mainly as a contaminant of grain, was found growing wild by 1858, and has since become more frequent in some areas.
New Zealand fungus collections record it as a host of Albugo candida, Leptosphaeria maculans, Mycosphaerella brassicicola and Pleospora herbarum.

warnings: Do not gather it from heavily fertilised ground or places that catch run-off: the leaves may be full of nitrates, which are toxic in high doses.

Brassicaceae plants are known for their tendency to accumulate heavy metals, a trait that makes them valuable for the phytoremediation of contaminated soils. However, this same ability necessitates careful monitoring, as the accumulation of heavy metals can also pose potential health risks.

identification.text: Small tree with opposite compound leaves of five to seven toothed leaflets, corky warty bark, and large flat-topped sprays of tiny cream flowers, followed by drooping clusters of small purple-black berries.

lookalikes.howToTell: Tutu is highly poisonous, and eating its fruit has been linked with many deaths of children in New Zealand. Both have opposite leaves (tutu occasionally in whorls of three), so leaf arrangement does not separate them. Tutu's leaves are simple, (30)–50–80–(100) mm long, dark shining green above, with flat or slightly wavy margins; elder's are compound, of (3)–5–7 leaflets toothed except towards the base. Tutu's flowers hang in slender drooping strings (10)–15–20–(30) cm long, followed by fruit of succulent dark purple petals about 4 mm long around the seeds; elder's tiny white flowers are in large flat-topped clusters mostly 10–20 cm across, followed by round berries 4–8.5 mm across, usually shining black. Season does not separate them: tutu flowers October to March and fruits November to April. If you are unsure which you are looking at, harvest neither.

preparation.text: Flowers into cordial, fritters or a sparkling wine. Berries MUST be cooked and strained — cooked into syrup, jelly or wine. Never eat raw berries.

recipes.method: Makes just over 1 litre. 20 elderflower heads (more if they are small or you want a stronger taste); 1 litre boiling water; 75 g citric acid; 1 kg sugar; 4 lemons. Pick heads whose flowers are white, not yellow or brown, and fully open, ideally mid-morning on a sunny day, and use them as soon as you can; left too long they start to smell sour. Pick out insects, large leaves and brown bits, but don't rinse the flowers, or the cordial loses flavour. Put the flowers in a large pot and pour the boiling water over them. Add the citric acid and sugar and stir until they dissolve. Grate in the lemon zest, cut the lemons into quarters, add them and stir. Cover the pot and leave to infuse for at least 24 hours. Strain through muslin or a fine strainer into another pot, squeezing the pulp hard to get all the flavour out. Sanitise bottles or jars by washing them in soapy water, rinsing, then filling them with boiling water for 5 minutes and emptying them. Funnel in the cordial, filling to overflowing so little air is left, and keep it in a cool, dark place; refrigerate once opened. It is strong: dilute it with still or sparkling water, or mix it into drinks or cakes.
recipes.title: Elderflower cordial

recipes.method: Written for elderflowers in Britain; the page names no species. Serves 4. 12 freshly picked large elderflower heads, each cut with a length of stalk; sunflower oil, for deep-frying; icing sugar, to dust; 1 lemon, quartered, to serve. For the batter: 80 g plain flour; 20 g cornflour; 1 tablespoon caster sugar; 225 ml chilled sparkling water; 1 egg white. Put the flour, cornflour and sugar in a large bowl, add the sparkling water and mix very briefly and lightly, just until combined. Leave it to stand for an hour. Meanwhile, shake any insects out of the flower heads without washing them, and trim each stalk to about 5 cm below the head to use as a handle. When you are ready to fry, whisk the egg white to soft peaks and fold it gently into the batter with a metal spoon. Heat the oil to 190 °C in a deep-fryer; or use a wide, deep pan no more than a third full, over high heat, until a drop of batter rises at once in a ring of bubbles. Hold a flower head upside down by its stalk, dip it into the batter and let the excess drip off. Lower it gently into the oil, where it will spread and float, and use the stalk to push it under a little so all the batter cooks. Fry one at a time until light golden and crisp, then lift out by the stalk and rest on kitchen paper for a moment. Dust with icing sugar and serve with lemon wedges to squeeze over. Eat the flowers off the stalk, not the stalk itself (see Warnings).
recipes.title: Elderflower fritters

recipes.method: Written for elderberries in England; the page names no species. 900 g Bramley (cooking) apples, washed but not peeled or cored, quartered, bruises cut out; 450 g elderberries, washed and stripped from the stalks; 900 ml water; 1 cinnamon stick and 5 cloves, tied in muslin; granulated cane sugar (450 g for every 600 ml of juice). Snip each berry cluster off the tree with scissors. At home, hold a cluster by its stalk and push the berries off with the prongs of a dinner fork. Put the fruit, the bag of spices and the water in a preserving pan, bring to the boil, then lower the heat and cook gently until the fruit is soft. Crush the fruit with the back of a wooden spoon to release the juice and keep cooking until it is a soft pulp, then take out the spices. Tip the pulp into a jelly bag or muslin tied with string and hang it over a large bowl somewhere cool overnight. Don't squeeze the bag, or the jelly will be cloudy. Next day, measure the juice and allow 450 g sugar for every 600 ml. Put the juice and sugar in a clean preserving pan over low heat and stir until the sugar dissolves, then raise the heat and boil until setting point: 105 °C on a sugar thermometer, or a teaspoon dropped on a chilled saucer wrinkles when pushed once it has cooled. Skim if needed, pour into sterilised jars and seal. To sterilise the jars, run them through the hottest dishwasher cycle, or wash them by hand and dry them in the oven at 120 °C for 20 minutes. The author serves it with autumn game.
recipes.title: Elderberry jelly

recipes.method: Written for elderberries in the UK; the page names no species. Makes about 250 ml. 250 g ripe elderberries; 250 ml apple cider vinegar; ½ star anise; 3 cloves; 2 black peppercorns; a small shaving of mace; 1 cm fresh ginger, bruised; ½ small shallot, thinly sliced; 20 g soft brown sugar, or to taste. Strip every berry off its stalks with a fork and rinse them well. Put the berries in a casserole dish with the vinegar, cover, and bake in a slow oven at 100 °C until the berries are soft. Strain the liquid into a jug, then push the rest of the juice through the sieve with a potato masher. Put the juice in a pan with the spices and shallot, cover, and simmer on a very low heat for 25 minutes. Strain again and return the liquid to the pan. Add the sugar and warm it until it dissolves, then boil hard for 2–3 minutes until it turns syrupy. Cool, bottle and store in a dark place. The author leaves it to mature for years before use.
recipes.title: Pontack (elderberry ketchup)

recipes.method: 10–16 large elderflower heads (or 1 tablespoon dried elderflowers for each fresh head); 650 g sugar; 4.5 litres of cold water; 1 lemon; 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar. Pick 10–16 large elderflower heads in full bloom, on a sunny morning if you can. Shake out the insects but don't wash them. To be careful, snip the flowers off the thick stalks. Dissolve 650 g sugar in 4.5 litres of cold water — warm a little of the water to dissolve the sugar, cool it, then mix it into the rest. In a large bucket or bowl, combine the sweetened water with the flowers, the juice and quartered skin of 1 lemon, and 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar. Cover and leave for 4 days, somewhere cool; if mould forms, scrape off the mat of flowers on top and carry on. Fine-strain into clean screw-top plastic fizzy-drink bottles, leaving a few centimetres of air at the top. Never use corked bottles, and avoid glass flip-tops: you can't feel the pressure through them, and they are far more dangerous if they burst. Leave at room temperature for 6–14 days. From day 6, squeeze the bottles every day, and as soon as the bases start to round out, ease the caps to let off some (not all) of the pressure; a forgotten bottle can explode. Once it tastes right, move it to the fridge to slow the fermentation, and keep checking the pressure. The author uses whole heads, green stalks and all, as is traditional. The source says one tablespoon of dried elderflowers replaces one good-sized fresh head. The author drinks it between 2 and 4 weeks; it is lightly alcoholic after a week and starts turning vinegary at 5–6 weeks. The source notes that the yeast comes from the flowers, so in a cool room it can take a while to get going. The author sometimes uses an infused vinegar, such as pineapple weed vinegar, for a twist.
recipes.title: Elderflower champagne

recipes.method: If a batch of elderflower champagne goes flat and vinegary, mix it with some live vinegar (with its mother). Leave it in an open container covered with cheesecloth, somewhere dark, for 2–3 months, until it reaches about 3–4% acidity. Use it for pickling.
recipes.title: Elderflower champagne vinegar

recipes.method: Ripe elderberries; apple cider vinegar (or white wine vinegar), 500 ml for every 350 g of berries; sugar, 350 g for every 260 ml of liquid. Strip the ripe berries off every stalk — freezing the heads first makes this easier — and weigh them. For every 350 g of berries add 500 ml apple cider vinegar (or white wine vinegar) in a jar or tub. Cover and leave for 5 days, stirring now and then. Strain, pressing the berries, and throw them away. Add 350 g sugar for every 260 ml of liquid, simmer for 10 minutes, and bottle. The recipe's final simmer is essential: raw elderberries are not safe to eat. The recipe works with less sugar too, if you want it less sweet.

summary.text:
Two harvests from one tree — cordial in early summer, syrup in autumn. The berries must be cooked.
Native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa, elder was first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1867. It grows wild from Auckland to Wellington, though uncommon north of the Volcanic Plateau, is very common in many parts of Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago and Southland, and reaches Stewart Island. It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.

warnings: Raw berries, leaves, bark and stems contain cyanogenic glycosides and can cause vomiting. Cooking destroys them in the fruit.
Strip the berries fully off the green stalks before cooking — the stalks are the toxic part most often left in.
Shake flower heads to evict insects; do not wash them or you rinse away the aromatic pollen.

sources: Langlands, Peter. Foraging New Zealand (Penguin Random House NZ, 2024), 'Oak' entry.

SPLIT 28/10/2026 (owner, 28/10/2026: "ahh yes split them", after being told a genus entry cannot carry one true bio status): this entry was the genus entry 'oak' (Quercus spp.), from Langlands' 'Oak' entry, which names no single species. Basis for the species kept: Flora of New Zealand Online factsheet 'Quercus robur' (description from Webb et al. 1988, Flora of New Zealand vol. IV, which treats naturalised plants) and 'Quercus ilex'; iNaturalist NZ research-grade, not-captive records (API species_counts, place 6803, retrieved 28/10/2026): Q. robur 563, Q. ilex 98, Q. palustris 71, Q. cerris 18, Q. rubra 11, Q. coccinea 8. Fruit - raw or cooked. Rich in vitamin C, the fruit has a very acid flavour and is mainly used in preserves, though children and some adults seem to like it raw when it is fully ripe.
Young leaves - used as a flavouring or as an acid nibble. They can be used in much the same way as sorrel (Rumex acetosa).

identification.text:
Glabrous, deciduous shrub to about 2 m high. Shoots angled. Spines generally 3-partite, shorter than 1.5 cm long on adult shoots. Petiole to 1 cm long; lamina 2–8 × 1–2.5 cm (often some very small leaves on flowering spurs), elliptic to obovate, membranous, dull green above, usually serrulate, sometimes entire; base attenuate; apex obtuse. Flowers in racemes to about 6 cm long at anthesis. Bracts 1–2 mm long, ovate or lanceolate-ovate. Pedicels 5–10 mm long. Perianth segments medium yellow, those of outermost whorl smaller, ovate; innermost sepals about 5 mm long, obovate; petals about 5 mm long, obovate, more or less rounded at apex. Nectaries about 1 mm long, prominent, orange. Stamens 2–3 mm long. Ovules 2. Stigma sessile. Berry 9–11 mm long, oblong, scarlet or crimson-scarlet, shining.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: European barberry is deciduous and its berries are scarlet to crimson-scarlet, shining, without bloom, oblong and 9–11 mm long; Darwin's barberry is evergreen and its berries are black or nearly so, with a whitish bloom, round and 5–7 mm across. European barberry's leaves are thin, dull green, usually finely toothed and 2–8 cm long; Darwin's barberry's are glossy dark green above, with spiny lobes, up to about 3.5 cm. European barberry's spines are mostly three-parted and under 1.5 cm long; Darwin's barberry's split into five. Spiny stems and yellowish flowers in clusters do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Darwin's barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: European barberry's berries are scarlet to crimson-scarlet, shining and without bloom, oblong, 9–11 mm long; barberry's are reddish black under a heavy whitish bloom, with dark red juice. European barberry is plainly deciduous, its leaves thin, dull green above and usually finely toothed; barberry is evergreen or partly deciduous, its leaves shining above, somewhat leathery (almost thin in shady, moist places) and often turning reddish in autumn. European barberry grows to about 2 m with spines under 1.5 cm; barberry to about 7 m with spines up to 2.3 cm. Leaf size, yellow flowers in clusters up to about 6 cm, and old homestead and plantation sites do not separate them. In New Zealand barberry has usually been called B. vulgaris, even in Allan's 1940 flora, so a name in print is no guide.

preparation.text:
The dried fruit is still often used as a condiment, it is very popular in Uzbekistan, for example, where it is used to make the national dish known as 'Plov'.
A refreshing lemon-like drink can be made from the fruit.
The dried young leaves and shoot tips make a refreshing tea.
In Europe, the berries have been traditionally used as an ingredient in making jam. The berries are high in pectin which makes the jam congeal as it cools after having been boiled. In southwestern Asia, especially Iran, the berries are used for cooking, as well as for jam-making. In Iran, barberries are commonly used as a currant in rice pilaf.
Eaten raw, European barberries are usually flavoured with something, because they can be very sour; cooking or drying mellows the sourness.
Wear gloves to pick them, as the shrubs are very thorny, and strip the berries from their stalks indoors. The seeds are large for the size of the berry: for jam, cook the berries until soft and press them through a fine sieve to hold back the seeds, stalk bits and the small black flower remains at the tip of each berry.

recipes.method: From a German herbal page about the common barberry (Berberis vulgaris). 1 kg washed berries; 500 ml water; 500 g jam-setting sugar of the 2:1 kind. Bring 1 kg washed berries to the boil with 500 ml water and simmer for about 20 minutes. Pour through a sieve and catch the juice. Mix the juice with 500 g jam-setting sugar of the 2:1 kind (Gelierzucker 2:1, sugar with added pectin for twice its weight of fruit), bring back to the boil, boil hard for about 4 minutes and pour into sterilised jars.
recipes.title: Barberry jelly

recipes.method: Written for European barberry (Berberis vulgaris) by a forager who picks it wild from hedgerows in Vermont. 450 g stemmed barberries (about 3 cups); 250 ml water; sugar, the same volume as the pulp (about 375 ml). Put 450 g stemmed barberries (about 3 cups) in a saucepan with 250 ml water and simmer gently for about 5 minutes, mashing, until the berries fall apart and release their juice. Press through a fine sieve to remove the seeds, stalk bits and black flower remains; sieve again through a finer sieve or muslin for a smoother jam; expect about 375 ml of pulp. Return it to a clean pan with the same volume of sugar (about 375 ml for 375 ml of pulp), bring to a rolling boil over high heat and boil, stirring all the time, for 2 to 3 minutes, until it starts to gel; test on a plate chilled in the freezer; it sets soft and spoonable. Ladle into two hot, sterilised 250 ml jars, leaving 6 mm headspace. Keep in the fridge or freezer, or process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes (15 minutes above about 1,800 m) and leave undisturbed for 12 to 24 hours before checking the seals. Keeps 12 to 18 months in sealed jars; once opened, refrigerate and use within 2 to 3 weeks.

summary.text:
Berberis vulgaris, also known as common barberry, European barberry or simply barberry, is a shrub in the genus Berberis native to the Old World. It produces edible but sharply acidic berries, which people in many countries eat as a tart and refreshing fruit.
The shrub is native to central and southern Europe, southern England, northwest Africa and western Asia; it is also naturalised in northern Europe and North America. In the United States and Canada, it has become established in the wild over an area from Nova Scotia to Nebraska, with additional populations in Colorado, Idaho, Washington state, Montana, and British Columbia. It is also cultivated in many countries.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): South Island: Canterbury, Otago, especially inland.
European barberry was introduced to New Zealand in the early period of European settlement, and seems to have been mainly planted in the South Island.
B. vulgaris is the alternate host species of the wheat stem rust fungus (Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici), a grass-infecting rust fungus that is a serious fungal disease of wheat and related grains.
In New Zealand, where it has been naturalised since 1875, it spreads both by seed and by suckering; it sets a great deal of seed, which birds and people carry (NZPCN).

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.

identification.text:
Deciduous, generally small tree up to about 6–(9) m high when mature, sometimes forming thickets, not or sparsely armed; trunk short to fairly tall; secondary branches erect to spreading. Lf petiole (10)–15–30 mm long, pilose at least when young; blade moderately thin, obovate to broadly elliptic or suborbicular, 30–70–(120) × 15–45–(60) mm, acute or short-apiculate at apex, cuneate at base, glabrous and more or less slightly shining above, duller below, hairy at first and usually with at least some hairs remaining on major veins and lower part of margins, otherwise glabrous, serrulate, almost 2-serrate or crenate, sometimes with teeth glandular; stipules short, oblong-triangular, deciduous. Flowers 1–2–(4), in fascicles on short shoots, not fragrant; pedicels (5)–10–25–(30) mm long, pendent or spreading, glabrous or hairy, greenish. Hypanthium broad; sepals oblong-lanceolate, about 3 mm long, obtuse, glabrous or glabrate except on inner face, mostly green, often becoming reflexed, with or without marginal, stalked glands. Petals 5, spreading, more or less orbicular or elliptic-obovate, (8)–10–15 mm long, rounded, more or less undulate, white or greenish white. Stamens shorter than petals; filaments whitish. Fruit (20)–25–45 mm long (to about 60 mm in cultivation), globose, subglobose, broadly ellipsoid or broadly ovoid-oblong, sulcate, glabrous, green, yellow, red or blackish purple in flesh and skin, usually pruinose, somewhat sweet to dry or slightly bitter; stone smooth. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The subspecies that grows wild here, subsp. insititia (damsons and greengages), is sometimes spiny, with hairy young twigs and flower stalks, and roundish fruit that is green, yellow, red or blackish purple, the flesh usually clinging to the stone. Subsp. domestica (true plums) is spineless, with fruit longer than wide, reddish or purple, the flesh usually free or partly free from the stone, and rarely grows wild (Flora of New Zealand, restated). Plums from seed vary widely in their fruit.

lookalikes.howToTell: No single test settles it; most of these ranges overlap. Young shoots: the plum's are usually hairy and dull, though sometimes hairless; cherry plum's are hairless and shining, so a hairy shoot points to the plum. Size: a cherry plum is 15–30 mm long, sometimes only 10 mm, and a plum 25–45 mm, sometimes only 20 mm, so a fruit over 30 mm points to the plum, and anything smaller is not settled by size (the plum can be as small as 15 mm). Colour overlaps: cherry plums are yellow to orange-red or scarlet, sometimes dark crimson, and only slightly bloomed; plums green, yellow, red or blackish purple, usually bloomed. The midrib does not help, because cherry plum's can be densely hairy on its lower third underneath. Cherry plum fruits from November to January and the plum from January to February. Both flower in August and September.

preparation.text: Halve and remove the stones. For jam, soften the fruit before adding the sugar, or the skins toughen. Strong spices such as star anise, cloves, vanilla, cinnamon and black pepper suit poached plums.

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1 kg plums, halved and stoned; juice of 1 large lemon or 1 orange; 700 g granulated sugar. Simmer the plums gently with the juice and 150 ml water for about 5 minutes, until they begin to soften; softening them before the sugar goes in keeps the skins from toughening. Add the sugar a third at a time, stirring until it dissolves, then take the pan off the heat, cover and leave for a couple of hours or overnight while the plums sink into the syrup. Bring back to the boil, stirring off any sugar stuck to the base, and boil rapidly for about 10 minutes to setting point: the pale froth has almost gone, the surface is glossy, the boil slows, and a drop on a cold plate sets to a light gel. Rest 5 minutes so the fruit settles, then fill four sterilised 300 ml jars to the brim and seal at once. Store cool and dark; best eaten within a year. Variations: 2–3 star anise or a couple of cinnamon sticks in the poaching fruit (remove at the end), 1–2 tsp brandy in each jar, or 75–100 g walnut pieces towards the end of the boil.
recipes.title: Plum Jam

recipes.method: Ingredients (serves 4): filling: 30 g butter; 1 vanilla pod, split; 1 star anise; 1 small cinnamon stick; 1 Bramley apple, peeled, cored and roughly chopped; 50 g light brown sugar; 6 plums, stoned and quartered; 250 g blackberries. Crumble: 50 g blanched hazelnuts, blitzed; 60 g plain flour; 40 g polenta; 50 g caster sugar; 75 g unsalted butter. Custard: 200 g toasted hazelnuts, roughly crushed; 250 ml evaporated milk; 400 ml whole milk; 8 egg yolks; 3 tbsp cornflour; 150 g light brown sugar. Heat the butter with the vanilla, star anise and cinnamon for 2 minutes, add the apple and sugar and cook 5 minutes, then add the plums and blackberries and simmer gently for 15 minutes, until soft but holding their texture; keep warm. Heat the oven to 200°C (180°C fan). Mix the hazelnuts, flour, polenta and sugar, rub in the butter, scatter on a baking tray and chill at least 30 minutes, then bake 25 minutes until coloured; cool and break up. For the custard, simmer the crushed hazelnuts in both milks, then cook gently for 30 minutes; strain out the nuts and return the milk to the pan. Mix the yolks with the cornflour and sugar, pour into the hot milk and stir over a medium heat until thick, 5–8 minutes; let it boil a few minutes to lose the floury taste, then strain and keep warm. Put the filling in a dish, scatter over the crumble, warm through in the oven and serve with the custard.
recipes.title: Blackberry, Plum & Apple Crumble with Toasted Hazelnut Custard

recipes.method: Ingredients (about 4): 170–200 g plums or damsons (or prunes); a cinnamon stick (or ground cinnamon); 250 ml (1 cup) red wine; 2–4 tbsp sugar; about 2 tbsp chopped fresh ginger (less if ground). To serve: a slice of white bread toasted or fried in olive oil, or a shortcrust pie case. Cook the washed, stoned plums in the red wine (with a little extra water if using prunes) until soft. Strain through a colander, or blend for a smoother texture, and add very fine sugar, cinnamon and ginger to taste. Serve hot or cold as a fruit mousse, spooned on the toast (a 'sop', after Bartolomeo Scappi, 1570), or in a blind-baked shortcrust case. A modern reading of a sixteenth-century recipe: 'Put your prunes into a pot and put red wine or claret wine, and a little fair water … Strain them with sugar, cinnamon and ginger.'
recipes.title: Tudor Plum Tart

recipes.method: Ingredients (serves 8): pavlova: 5 egg whites; 1 tsp ground cinnamon; 250 g caster sugar; 1 tsp white wine vinegar. Cherries: 100 g dried cherries; 100 ml kirsch. Spiced plums: 200 ml red wine; juice of 1 orange; 75 g light brown sugar; 1 cinnamon stick; a few cardamom pods and allspice berries, lightly crushed; 1 piece pared orange zest; 8 ripe plums, stoned and quartered. To assemble: 300 ml double or whipping cream, whipped; 1 tbsp icing sugar; 1/2 tsp cinnamon (optional). Heat the oven to 150°C (130°C fan) and line a tray with baking paper marked with a 23 cm circle. Whisk the egg whites to soft peaks, then beat in the cinnamon-sugar a spoonful at a time until stiff and glossy; fold in the vinegar. Pile into the circle with a slight hollow in the middle and peaks round the side, bake 1 1/4–1 1/2 hours until crisp at the sides with some give in the middle, then turn the oven off and leave to cool completely. Simmer the cherries in the kirsch until plump and most of it is absorbed. Warm the wine, orange juice, sugar, spices and zest, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then simmer a few minutes until syrupy; poach the plums a few minutes, until soft but holding their shape. Lift them out, slipping off the skins, and strain the liquid. Stir the icing sugar and cinnamon into the cream, and a couple of tablespoons of the plum liquid into the cherries. Spread the cream over the meringue, top with the plums and cherries and drizzle with the remaining liquid.
recipes.title: Spiced Pavlova with Plums

recipes.method: Ingredients (serves 4): 1 tbsp olive oil; 2 onions, thinly sliced; 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped; 10 plums, quartered and stoned; 4 cm fresh ginger, peeled and finely chopped; 8 boneless, skinless chicken thighs; 2 tbsp soy sauce (tamari for gluten-free); a large pinch of caster sugar; 150 g long-grain white rice; 1 large head broccoli, in florets; a handful of coriander, chopped. Heat the oven to 200°C (180°C fan). Soften the onions and garlic in the oil in a casserole over a medium heat. Stir in the plums, ginger, chicken, soy sauce, sugar and 100 ml water, cover and bring to the boil, then bake 30–40 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through and the plums have collapsed into a sauce; season with more soy if needed. Meanwhile cook the rice and steam the broccoli until just tender. Serve the chicken over the rice with the broccoli, scattered with coriander.
recipes.title: Chinese Plum Chicken

recipes.method: Dried plums: use freestone plums. Halve them, pop out the stones, turn the halves inside out with your thumbs, and dip in citrus juice if you want to keep the colour. Dehydrate for about 16 hours at a medium setting (55°C). Make sure they are completely dry before storing, or they go mouldy. Fruit leather: blend stewed plums (thawed from the freezer is fine) half-and-half with soft, overripe bananas and a splash of citrus juice or syrup left over from bottled or canned fruit. Spread on oiled, solid dehydrator trays and dry for about 10 hours at 55°C.
recipes.title: Dried Plums & Plum Fruit Leather

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prunus_domestica The pulp is edible and usually sweet, though some varieties are sour enough to need cooking with sugar. On the hybrid sign in the scientific name: the parentage was long held to be Prunus spinosa with P. cerasifera, but recent cytogenetic evidence seems to implicate P. cerasifera as the sole wild stock from which the cultivated plant could have evolved. Greengages and damsons are subspecies of the same plant, and Wikipedia says (without citation) that the subspecies cross easily.

The kernels, and the chemistry behind the warning. Plum kernels contain amygdalin, a cyanogenic glycoside that releases hydrogen cyanide when broken down in the small intestine — the same compound as in apple seeds and peach kernels. 'Amygdalin: Toxicity, Anticancer Activity and Analytical Procedures for Its Determination in Plant Seeds', PMC8069783. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8069783/

summary.text:
Prunus domestica is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. A deciduous tree, it includes many varieties of the fruit trees known as plums in English, though not all plums belong to this species. The greengages and damsons also belong to subspecies of P. domestica.
In New Zealand the plum is an exotic, a cultivated hybrid introduced for agriculture and naturalised by 1922; it is named on DOC's 2024 list of 386 environmental weeds. It can sucker into small thickets but spreads mainly by seed, each plum holding viable seed, carried by people and birds. Of the two subspecies here, subsp. insititia (damsons and bullaces) grows wild and subsp. domestica is only casual. Two native mistletoes, Ileostylus micranthus and Peraxilla tetrapetala, are recorded growing on it.
The most common commercial plum varieties in New Zealand are Japanese plums (Prunus salicina) and their hybrids, such as Black Doris, which are not this species; European plums come second (Tree Crops, restated).

warnings: Never eat the stones or kernels — they contain cyanogenic compounds.

habitat.text: Short grass in open, sunny places: lawns, parks, roadside verges, sports fields, pasture, meadows and grassy coastal dunes, and occasionally woodland edges. It grows from the ground, never from wood, and copes with lawns that are walked on often. In New Zealand it forms conspicuous rings in pasture and also grows on lawns and in other urban grassland.

identification.text:
A small, plain, tan mushroom of short grass, usually in troops, arcs or rings.
The cap is 1–5 cm across, bell-shaped with a slightly inrolled edge at first, then flattening out but keeping a broad central bump (umbo); very young caps may lack the bump. It is smooth and dry, pale orange-tan, buff or reddish tan, often a little darker at the centre, and fades to cream or almost white as it dries. The edge is sometimes faintly lined and often frays with age.
The gills are white to cream, fairly thick and widely spaced, and free of the stem or only just attached. Short gills that stop well short of the stem are mixed in with long ones, and some fork.
The stem is 2–8 cm long and only 2–6 mm thick, off-white to buff, sometimes darker and downy at the base, with no ring. It is tough and pliant: you can bend and twist it without it snapping. This is one of the best tests, as most similar lawn mushrooms have brittle stems that snap.
The flesh is thin and white and does not change colour when cut. The smell is mild and mushroomy; the gills have also been described as smelling of bitter almonds. The spore print is white.
The spring fieldcap (Agrocybe praecox), common in New Zealand lawns, can look similar while young, but it has no central bump, and its gills darken to brown and give a brown spore print.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both come up in lawns and other short grass. Make a spore print: a fairy ring champignon's is white, a mower's mushroom's deep brown, sometimes purplish. A fairy ring champignon's gills are white to cream and widely spaced; a mower's mushroom's are brown with paler edges and go mottled as the spores ripen. A fairy ring champignon's stem is tough and pliant and bends without snapping; a mower's mushroom's is fragile and hollow.
lookalikes.name: Mower's mushroom

preparation.text:
Cut the stems off with a sharp knife or scissors, in the field or at home; the stems are tough and the caps tear easily, so pulling hard rips the cap. Brush the caps clean, or rinse off any grass in cold water and dry them between towels in the fridge. Picking enough is slow work, but they often come up in large numbers.
They are firm and slightly chewy, with a rich, nutty, slightly sweet flavour. A simple first way to try them: fry them in butter for about 5 minutes, add a good squeeze of lemon juice and simmer for another 10 minutes. They suit soups, stews, pasta sauces, risotto and omelettes, and their sweetness suits baking: dried and powdered, they go into biscuits and cakes.
They are among the easiest mushrooms to dry. Leave the caps whole on paper for a few days, thread them on a string to hang, or use a dehydrator. Soaked, they come back with the texture and flavour of fresh ones, and the soaking water can go into the dish.
Late in the season they are often full of maggots.

recipes.method: Written for fairy ring champignons. Serves 4. 400 g fairy ring champignons; a pinch of coriander seeds; 50 g butter; salt; black pepper; hot buttered toast. Brush the mushrooms clean, paying attention to the gills, and trim off the stems. Crush the coriander seeds. Melt the butter in a large, wide frying pan over medium heat, add the coriander and then the mushrooms, and stir to coat them. Cook over medium heat for 5–7 minutes, until cooked through but still holding their shape; any hotter and the coriander burns. Season and serve on hot toast with the buttery juices spooned over.
recipes.title: Coriander-fried fairy rings on toast

recipes.method: Written for fairy ring champignons. Makes 1 omelette. 2 large eggs; salt; black pepper; a pinch of cayenne pepper; 2–3 wild garlic leaves; 4–5 common sorrel leaves; about 60 g fairy ring champignons; 15 g (1 tbsp) butter; a few drops of lemon juice; a wild garlic flower to garnish (optional). Beat the eggs with a little seasoning and the cayenne. Trim the stalks off the wild garlic and sorrel, shred the leaves finely and stir them into the egg; leave to infuse. Clean the mushrooms and trim the stems to a couple of millimetres below the cap. Melt half the butter in a small frying pan over medium heat; when it foams add the mushrooms, turn up the heat and toss them for a couple of minutes until soft. Turn the heat down to keep them warm and season with salt, pepper and a little lemon juice. Heat the rest of the butter in an 18 cm frying pan over low heat. When it foams, pour in the eggs, swirl for a few seconds, then leave to cook over the lowest heat until just set on top. Tip the mushrooms onto one half, fold the other half over and slide onto a warm plate. Scatter with wild garlic flowers, if using.
recipes.title: Herb omelette with fairy ring champignons

recipes.method: Written for dried fairy ring mushrooms, or the same amount fresh. Serves 4 as a starter or 2 as a main. The author's method does not say when the hot sauce, salt and pepper go in. 250 ml (1 cup) dried fairy ring caps; 375 ml (1½ cups) peeled, diced tomatoes (a tin unless you have vine-ripened ones); 2.5 ml (½ tsp) herbes de Provence; 60 ml (¼ cup) chopped flat-leaf parsley; 15 ml (1 tbsp) extra virgin olive oil; 15 g (1 tbsp) butter; about 1 ml (¼ tsp) hot sauce, to taste; salt; pepper; 225 g pasta such as farfalle, fusilli or penne. Soak the dried mushrooms in hot water until soft, then drain, keeping the liquid. Heat the butter and oil in a frying pan, add the mushrooms and herbes de Provence and cook slowly for 15 minutes. Add the soaking liquid and boil hard until about three-quarters of it has gone. Add the tomatoes and parsley and cook 3–4 minutes. Cook the pasta in boiling salted water until al dente and serve the sauce over it.
recipes.title: Fairy ring mushroom pasta sauce

recipes.method: Written for dried fairy ring mushrooms, or the same amount fresh. Serves 4–6 as a side or 2–3 as a main. 250 ml (1 cup) dried fairy ring caps; 375 ml (1½ cups) Arborio rice; 1.25 litres (5 cups) chicken or vegetable stock, or a mix, including the mushroom soaking liquid; 30 ml (2 tbsp) chopped shallot; 45 g (3 tbsp) butter; 45 ml (3 tbsp) extra virgin olive oil; 160 ml (⅔ cup) grated Parmesan; 60 ml (¼ cup) balsamic vinegar. Soak the mushrooms in hot water until soft, drain them and use the liquid as part of the stock. Fry the mushrooms slowly in half the butter and oil for 10 minutes and set aside. Meanwhile bring the stock to a simmer. In a heavy pan, soften the shallot in the rest of the butter and oil until lightly coloured. Add the rice and stir for about a minute until coated. Add 125 ml (½ cup) of simmering stock and stir over medium heat until the rice has taken it up; keep adding stock this way, stirring, until the rice is creamy but still al dente, about 30 minutes. If the stock runs out, use hot water. About 10 minutes before the end, add the mushrooms; about 5 minutes before the end, stir in the Parmesan and balsamic vinegar. Serve straight away.
recipes.title: Fairy ring mushroom risotto

recipes.method: Written for fairy ring mushrooms. 100 g fairy ring mushrooms; 2 spring onions; soy sauce; sesame oil; fresh ginger; oyster sauce or mirin; vegetable stock; olive oil; udon noodles. Wipe the mushrooms clean with kitchen paper and remove the stems. Slice the spring onions thinly, keeping the white and green apart. Put the udon into boiling water; it takes about 10 minutes. Meanwhile fry the caps in olive oil for a few minutes, add the white of the spring onion and fry a minute more. Turn the heat down and add some grated ginger, soy sauce and sesame oil, and about a teaspoon of oyster sauce or mirin to bring out the mushrooms' sweetness; taste and add more if needed, without drowning their flavour. Lift the udon straight from the pan into the mushrooms, toss and leave a minute or two, adding a little stock so the noodles are glossy and well coated. Finish with more grated ginger, a dash of sesame oil and the green of the spring onion.
recipes.title: Fairy ring mushrooms with udon

recipes.method: Written for Scotch bonnets (fairy ring champignons). Serves 6. 30 ml (2 tbsp) sunflower or olive oil; 1 onion; 2 garlic cloves; 200 g fairy ring caps, stems removed; 2 carrots; a handful (about 1 cup) of frozen peas; 5 ml (1 tsp) paprika; salt; pepper; 1 dried bay leaf; 45 ml (3 tbsp) sour cream, or more; 15 ml (1 tbsp) plain flour; a handful of small soup pasta; fresh parsley; a little lemon juice or vinegar; 1.5 litres water or stock. Snap the caps off the tough stems, rinse them in a big bowl of cold water, lift them out and repeat if needed. Slice the carrots into thin discs and finely chop the onion and garlic. Soften the onion and garlic in the oil over low heat until translucent. Take the pan off the heat, stir in the paprika, then pour in half the water and add the carrots, bay leaf, salt and pepper. Cook a couple of minutes, until the carrots are half done. Add the mushrooms and peas and cook over medium heat for about 10 minutes, adding the pasta halfway so that it is cooked by the end. Mix the sour cream and flour until smooth, stir in a ladle of the hot soup, then pour it all into the boiling soup and stir until it thickens. Serve with chopped parsley and a splash of lemon juice or vinegar.
recipes.title: Hungarian Scotch bonnet mushroom soup

Daniel Winkler, 'New Zealand Fungi', MushRoaming (24/05/2017, edited 13/06/2021; photographed in the South Island, April 2017): apparently introduced, also known in NZ as Scotch bonnet; excellent edible, tedious to pick, rich nutty taste, dries and reconstitutes easily. Sage Journal, 'Forager's favourites | 6 interesting edible fungi to find in Aotearoa' (25/03/2025, updated 04/09/2026), words extracted from Ruben Mita, A Naturalist's Guide to the Fungi of Aotearoa New Zealand (John Beaufoy): cap 1–5 cm, height 2–6 cm; umbo, frayed and striate margin, pale orangeish-tan fading to cream; gills cream, adnexed to free; spore print white; fields and urban grassy areas, often in rings, summer to autumn; 'dangerously nondescript in appearance, although still identifiable' (warning 1). Jenny, 'Fairy Ring Mushroom: Identification, Foraging, and Edibility', Mushroom Appreciation (30/05/2023, modified 25/07/2024): many mushrooms form rings; species can be intermixed in a ring; ground only, never wood; untreated lawns only; long and short gills; bitter-almond gill odour; pliant stem; white unchanging flesh; lookalikes fool's funnel (no umbo, closely spaced gills), Inocybe (brittle stems, distinctive odour, brown spore print), spring fieldcap (gills turn brown, no umbo); sweet, firm, chewy, nutty; dried and powdered for baking; cut stems with a knife; rinse and dry between towels in the fridge; soups, stews, pasta sauces, omelettes; linked recipes (Wild Food UK coriander-fried, Cook and Drink udon, Hungarian Tidbits soup used). Wild Food UK, 'Fairy Ring Champignons': gills not crowded, free of the stem; stem thin, fibrous, tough, no skirt; short grass on lawns, verges, parks and pasture; Clitocybe rivulosa/dealbata in the same habitats and rings towards the middle and end of the season, decurrent gills, in-turned cap edge, lighter to white; maggots late in the season; dries whole on paper and rehydrates to fresh; its linked recipes are recipes 1 and 2. Totally Wild UK, 'Fairy Ring Mushrooms (Marasmius Oreades)' (25/11/2021): meadows, lawns, occasionally sand dunes and woodland edges; cap fades almost white when old or dry; gills widely spaced, thick, free; lookalikes in the same rings; caps traditionally threaded on string and dried. Pat O'Reilly, First Nature 'Marasmius oreades': trehalose and revival after drying, producing new spores; Marasmius from marasmos 'drying out', oreades from the Oreads; never identify by the ring, a specimen failing any characteristic is something else; cap 2–5 cm, stem 4–8 cm × 2–6 mm, tough and pliant, darker downy base; odour mushroomy but not distinctive, taste mild, slightly nutty; thrives in public lawns and parks; spring fieldcap buff gills darken, brown spores; extra care from midsummer as Clitocybe rivulosa and dealbata appear, not umbonate, stiffer stems; soups, stews, pasta sauces, omelettes; dries and reconstitutes well. Michael Wood, 'Fairy Ring Mushroom Recipes', MykoWeb (1998): butter, 5 minutes, lemon juice, 10 more minutes (preparation); cut stems with scissors; dried and reconstituted keep the texture and flavour of fresh; pasta sauce and risotto are recipes 3 and 4. Alan Bergo, 'Fairy Ring Mushrooms / Mousserons (Marasmius oreades)', Forager Chef (13/07/2015, modified 02/11/2023; 403 to curl, read via the Internet Archive copy of 15/05/2026): sunny, open grassy places, not deep woods; tough, pliable stem the easiest test, most lookalikes brittle; widely spaced, forked gills, some not reaching the stem; the cap tears if the stem is pulled too hard; rinse in cold water and dry between towels in the fridge; dries on the counter or in a dehydrator.

Also used (29/10/2026): Wikipedia 'Clitocybe rivulosa' revision 1364581221 (CC BY-SA 4.0) — renamed Collybia rivulosa (He et al. 2023); funnel-shaped whitish cap, decurrent crowded white gills, white spore print; grassy habitats, often in fairy rings, where children may find them; muscarine, symptoms within 15–30 minutes, larger doses abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhoea, blurred vision, laboured breathing, death rare (warning 2). Wikipedia 'Inocybe' revision 1313826113 (CC BY-SA 4.0) — many species contain large doses of muscarine; small conical caps with a pronounced umbo; musty or spermatic odour; gills become grey-brown or ochre-brown; brown spores (warning 3). iNaturalist API, retrieved 29/10/2026: Marasmius oreades (taxon 118240) has 322 research-grade wild NZ observations, 141 in Canterbury (79 in Christchurch) and 93 in Otago; of the 83 with notes, the commonest habitat words are grass (28), ring (12), pasture (7), lawn (6), dune (3) and field (3) (summary, habitat). Collybia rivulosa (taxon 1525557) has 3 NZ research-grade records (Wellington, Auckland, Gisborne), Inocybe (taxon 58679) 181 and Agrocybe praecox (taxon 118391) 408; Collybia dealbata and Marasmius nigrodiscus have none, so the ivory funnel is not named in the warning and Wikipedia's M. nigrodiscus is not used.

Not used, with reasons: northern-hemisphere seasons (Wikipedia May–November in the UK, Mushroom Appreciation June–November, Wild Food UK April–November, First Nature June–November, Forager Chef mid-June in Minnesota, Cook and Drink 'early spring until late autumn') — months come from New Zealand sources; Mushroom Appreciation's cap up to 5 inches, rings over 100 or 700 years old and folklore; Wikipedia's Collybia, Marasmiellus, Micromphale and Strobilurus lookalikes (no species named); Stevenson's 'appears to be parasitic on grass roots' kept only as weakened grass inside the ring; the readers' comments on Wild Food UK and Forager Chef (raw eating, cyanide production after picking, sprays, bacon-like flavour); Forager Chef's own recipe 'Capellini With Fairy Ring Mushroom Sauce' — its ingredient list has a diced shallot the method never uses and its method finishes with garlic chives the list omits, so it could not be restated without guessing; the Reddit fairy ring cookies and the YouTube fried Scotch bonnets linked from Mushroom Appreciation (not recipe pages); First Nature's 'Fairy Ring Champignons that appear early in the year are pretty safe'. summary.text:
Marasmius oreades, also known as the fairy ring mushroom, fairy ring champignon or Scotch bonnet, is a mushroom native to North America and Europe.
It is introduced in New Zealand, probably brought in with seed or straw, and has been recorded here since at least 1937. Material collected in rough grass at Karori in 1948 was first described as a new species, Collybia subclusilis, before it was recognised as this one. Most of its 322 research-grade New Zealand iNaturalist records are from Canterbury and Otago.
Many other mushrooms also grow in fairy rings, so the common name causes confusion. In a ring, the living mycelium at the edge makes the grass grow taller and greener, while the grass inside is weakened or dies back to brown.
The genus name comes from the Greek marasmos, 'drying out': it can dry out completely in the sun and revive when rain soaks it, even going on to make new spores. A sugar, trehalose, protects its cells while dry and probably gives it its sweet taste. The species name refers to the Oreads, the mountain nymphs of Greek myth.

warnings: Never identify a mushroom by its ring: many mushrooms grow in fairy rings, poisonous ones among them, and poisonous species can come up in the same ring mixed in with fairy ring champignons. This is a plain little brown mushroom, so check every one you pick against the whole description; if it fails on any point, it is something else.

The fool's funnel (Clitocybe rivulosa, now also called Collybia rivulosa), recorded in New Zealand, grows in grass, often in rings, and contains muscarine. Within 15–30 minutes it causes heavy salivation, sweating and watering eyes, and in larger amounts stomach pain, severe nausea, diarrhoea, blurred vision and difficult breathing; deaths are rare. It is whitish to greyish, with no central bump, an edge that stays rolled under, crowded gills that run down the stem a little or are only just attached, and a stiff stem. A fairy ring champignon is tan, keeps a central bump, and has widely spaced gills that are free of the stem or only just attached, and a pliant stem.

Fibrecaps (Inocybe), many of which contain muscarine, include little brown mushrooms with a pointed central bump like a fairy ring champignon's. They have brittle stems, often a musty or unpleasant smell, gills that turn grey-brown or brown, and a brown spore print. Make a spore print: a fairy ring champignon's is white.
Pick only from lawns, parks and verges you know have not been sprayed with weedkiller or other chemicals.

identification.text:
Plant without onion smell. Bulb subglobose, 1–3 cm diameter, with numerous sessile offset bulbs; tunic smooth, white. Leaves 20–40 cm × 5–15 mm, dull, light green, flat. Scapes 20–60 cm high, terete, hollow; spathe-valves 2, connate below, red-tinged. Flowers 8–20, umbellate, 1–1.5 cm long, about 1.5 cm diameter, campanulate, fragrant, dull white; segments with greenish base and reddish midvein; pedicels erect or spreading, longer than flowers. Capsule 5–8 mm long, 3-lobed. Seeds about 2 mm long, many, sharply angled, minutely wrinkled.
[From: Healy & Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]
In general aspect N. inodorum resembles an Allium but lacks the characteristic onion smell.
Some descriptions give the leaves a faint onion-like smell, so a weak smell does not rule it out. A mature plant has a large main bulb with many small bulblets clustered around it.

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: onion weed smells strongly of garlic or onion; false garlic has no onion smell, or only a faint one. Onion weed's flower stalk is sharply three-angled; false garlic's is round in section and hollow. Onion weed's leaves are strongly channelled; false garlic's are flat, dull and light green. Onion weed's white bells have a green stripe down the centre of each segment, 3–15 to a head on drooping stalks; false garlic's are dull white, each segment with a greenish base and a reddish midvein, 8–20 to a head on erect or spreading stalks. Flower size (10–15 mm long, up to 20, against 1–1.5 cm), a 20–60 cm flower stalk, offset bulbs, garden ground and flowering at the same time (onion weed October–November, false garlic October–December) do not separate them. Onion weed's leaves and bulbs are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Onion weed

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: Naples garlic smells of garlic; false garlic has no onion smell, or only a faint one. Naples garlic's flower stalk has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one; false garlic's is round in section and hollow. Naples garlic carries a many-flowered, roughly flat-topped umbel 5–8 cm across of pure white flowers 8–10 mm long on stiff stalks, with a single bract below it that stays on; false garlic carries 8–20 dull white flowers 1–1.5 cm long, each segment with a greenish base and a reddish midvein, above two bracts joined at the base and tinged red. Flat leaves of overlapping width (1–2 cm against 5–15 mm), a 20–60 cm flower stalk, offset bulbs and white bells do not separate them. Naples garlic's leaves and bulbs are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Naples garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: rosy garlic smells of garlic; false garlic has no onion smell, or only a faint one. Rosy garlic's flowers are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves; false garlic's are dull white, each segment with a greenish base and a reddish midvein. Rosy garlic often carries bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among its flowers, though plants without bulbils also occur. Rosy garlic has a single bract below the umbel that stays on; false garlic has two, joined at the base and tinged red. Dig one up: rosy garlic's offset bulbs sit on short stalks and the outer bulb skin has prominent round pits; false garlic's offset bulbs are stalkless and its bulb skin is smooth and white. A round flower stalk, flat leaves and spring flowering do not separate them. Rosy garlic's leaves and bulbs are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Rosy garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: wild garlic smells of garlic; false garlic has no onion smell, or only a faint one. Wild garlic's leaves are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical; false garlic's are flat. Wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils, its few flowers about 5 mm long, green to white and often purplish; false garlic carries 8–20 dull white flowers 1–1.5 cm long. Dig one up: wild garlic's offset bulbs sit on short stalks; false garlic's are stalkless. Spring flowering (wild garlic October–November, false garlic October–December) does not separate them. Wild garlic's leaves and bulbs are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Wild garlic

summary.text:
Nothoscordum gracile, also known as slender false garlic, or fragrant onion, is a bulbous plant belonging to the Amaryllidaceae family. Native from southern Mexico to western South America, the species is used as an ornamental plant due to its showy inflorescences and the fragrance of its flowers.
Flora of New Zealand (1980) described it as Nothoscordum inodorum, and it was earlier known in New Zealand as N. fragrans; Flora of New Zealand Online now names it Nothoscordum gracile and includes N. borbonicum in it. The name N. inodorum belongs to Naples garlic.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island, from Waipu to Wellington, and South Island, at Nelson, Christchurch and Timaru. Probably native to South America. An 1899 record may have been onion weed; the first sure record is from 1940. It was almost certainly introduced as an ornamental, is occasionally still seen in cultivation and can be troublesome in older gardens in scattered localities. N. inodorum reproduces both by offset bulbs and by seeds and in some overseas countries is a serious weed in gardens and cultivated land.

warnings: False garlic is not given here as food. It is not known to be poisonous, but its record as food is thin: a 1919 note that it was used as garlic in Jamaica to season smoked sausage, and plant-database lines compiled from older books that list the bulb as a garlic substitute.

The smell check that confirms onion weed and the other wild garlics is the way to tell them from false garlic, which has no onion smell or only a faint one and grows in the same gardens. A plant that looks like a wild garlic but does not smell strongly of garlic or onion when crushed may be false garlic, or snowflake, which is poisonous — leave it (see the lookalikes).

identification.text: Upright or spreading, 5–200 cm tall, with a stem sometimes streaked red or purple. Leaves are extremely variable: lance-shaped to ovate, diamond-shaped or triangular, and untoothed to coarsely toothed, and the young leaves and growing tips are coated in a white, mealy bloom that rubs off. Flowers are tiny, green and clustered, without petals.

lookalikes.howToTell: Before flowers or fruit appear, no reliable field test is recorded. Fat hen is green or grey-mealy, the mealy coating, when present, denser underneath, and very rarely the leaf is bright green; black nightshade's leaves have no white mealy coating and usually carry scattered short hairs. Leaf shape and toothing overlap and do not separate them. In flower and fruit: black nightshade has flowers 10–13 mm across, often star-shaped, usually white (sometimes pale mauve) around a yellow cone of anthers, in small few-flowered clusters, then round berries 7–10 mm across, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow. Fat hen's flowers are tiny and green with no petals, packed in dense spikes and panicles, and it forms no berry: its fruit stays wrapped in the flower parts around a glossy black seed 1.1–1.4 mm across.
lookalikes.name: Black nightshade seedlings

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers and fruit. Fat hen's flowers are mostly bisexual and its fruit is wrapped in small sepals, 0.5–3 mm long, with no bracteoles. Spear-leaved orache's female flowers usually have no sepals or petals: each fruit is held between two bracteoles that grow with it, reaching up to 9 × 6.5 mm, usually toothed and generally with small outgrowths. The leaves do not separate them: both plants are mealy and very variable, and fat hen's leaves, usually wedge-based, can also be triangular with a squared-off base, like spear-leaved orache's.
lookalikes.name: Spear-leaved orache

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers and fruit. Fat hen's flowers are mostly bisexual and its fruit is wrapped in small sepals, 0.5–3 mm long, with no bracteoles. Common orache's female flowers usually have no sepals or petals: each fruit is held between two bracteoles that grow with it, up to about 8.5 mm long (rarely 11 mm), entire or with a few teeth. The leaves do not separate them reliably: both plants are mealy and variable, and fat hen's leaves can be lance-shaped with a wedge-shaped base, like common orache's.

preparation.text:
Boil, and tip the cooking water away; boiling leaches out much of the soluble oxalate. Do not eat raw in quantity.
Soak the seed in water overnight and rinse it thoroughly before use, to remove its saponins.

recipes.method: Written for bathua, the north Indian name for fat hen; the author names it Chenopodium album. 250 g fat hen leaves; 1 green chilli (more if you want it hotter); 3 cups (about 720 ml) plain yoghurt; ¼ teaspoon salt, plus more to taste; ¼ teaspoon kala namak (black salt), or to taste; ½ teaspoon roasted ground cumin; 1 cup (about 240 ml) water, for boiling. Pick off and discard the tough stems, wash the leaves well and chop them roughly. Bring the water to the boil with ¼ teaspoon of the salt, add the leaves and boil them on low heat for 7–8 minutes. Let them cool to room temperature and drain off the excess water. Grind the boiled leaves with the chilli to a paste. Whisk the yoghurt until smooth, then mix in the paste, cumin, kala namak and salt; go easy on the salt, because the leaves were salted while boiling. Leave it to stand for an hour before serving, refrigerate it if serving later, and serve it cool. The author says the plant does not work raw and is tamed by boiling.
recipes.title: Fat hen raita

recipes.method: Written for fat hen in England; the page gives the common name only. Serves 4 as a side dish. 150 g quinoa; ½ teaspoon ground turmeric; 400 ml water; 100 g fat hen leaves, well washed; vinaigrette dressing; 1 red capsicum; a bunch of spring onions; ¼ cucumber; 2 sprigs of mint; a small handful of flat-leaf parsley. Bring the water to the boil with the turmeric, add the quinoa and simmer for 15 minutes, until the water is absorbed and the grains are soft. Tip it into a bowl, fork some dressing through and leave to cool. Steam the fat hen leaves over boiling water for 2–3 minutes, until they collapse like spinach, then chop them roughly. Halve the cucumber lengthways, scoop out the seeds with a teaspoon and dice it, and dice the capsicum the same size. Trim the roots off the spring onions and slice them, with some of the green. Chop the herbs fairly finely. Toss everything gently through the quinoa, adding more dressing if it seems dry, and serve.
recipes.title: Fat hen tabbouleh

recipes.method: The author's greens, picked from roadsides around Whangaroa Harbour, were nasturtium, kawakawa, fennel, samphire, fat hen, wild mustard, cleavers and clover. The author warns that New Zealand roadsides are still sprayed with glyphosate, so pick with care. The recipe uses fat hen raw; in a Lincoln University test of a raw fat hen pesto (22% leaves, with parmesan), the pesto held 58.5 mg of soluble oxalate per 100 g, 28.8% of its total oxalate, because the leaves are diluted and the calcium in the parmesan binds much of the rest (Savage & Vanhanen 2018). 1 garlic clove (or 4 peeled onion weed bulbs), 60 ml (¼ cup) macadamia nuts, 60 ml (¼ cup) grated parmesan (dairy or plant-based, or 125 ml (½ cup) macadamias and no parmesan), 750 ml (3 cups) roughly chopped wild greens, the zest and juice of 1 lemon, 125 ml extra-virgin olive oil, and salt and pepper. Makes about 350 g. Blend in a food processor to the texture you like. Serve on crackers or toast, as a side, or stirred through soup, pasta or rice.
recipes.title: Wild Whangaroa pesto

sources: Knox, Johanna. A Forager's Treasury: A New Zealand guide to finding and using wild plants (Allen & Unwin, 2013).

Savage, G.P. & Vanhanen, L. 2018, 'Oxalate Contents of Raw, Boiled, Wok-Fried and Pesto and Juice Made from Fat Hen (Chenopodium album) Leaves', Foods 8(1): 2 (Lincoln University, New Zealand). https://doi.org/10.3390/foods8010002 — measures what cooking actually does to the oxalate, and it is the reason this entry's preparation note now says to boil and tip the water away. Raw leaves held 1112.4 mg total oxalate per 100 g dry matter; boiling dropped that to 682.8 and wok-frying to 883.6. The soluble fraction is the one that matters for kidney stones, and it stayed at about three-quarters of the total in both raw and boiled leaves while falling to 53.4% in wok-fried ones. Making the cooked leaves into pesto, or juicing them, significantly reduced both total and soluble oxalate. Checked 06/10/2026.

Wikipedia contributors. 'Chenopodium album', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chenopodium_album On eating it: young shoots may be eaten raw or cooked, leaves are preferably cooked, and the flower buds and flowers can also be eaten cooked. A 100 g serving of cooked leaves is high in vitamin C (96% of the daily value), vitamin A (73%), riboflavin (37%), manganese (37%), calcium (31%) and vitamin B6 (21%). It is a close relative of quinoa, which is grown for the same kind of seed.

Nitrate accumulation, which is the entry's second warning. Fat hen is a known nitrate accumulator; drought, fertilisation and nutrient deficiency all drive nitrate up in the tissues, concentrations are generally highest in the stems, and animal metabolism converts nitrate to nitrite, which is the toxic form. Nitrate poisoning of cattle fed Chenopodium album hay is on record. Oxalate is highest in the fastest-growing plants and much higher in the leaves than the seeds or stems, and older foliage also carries saponins. Oregon State University Extension, 'Nitrate and Oxalate Poisoning'. Checked 06/10/2026. https://extension.oregonstate.edu/sites/extd8/files/documents/1/ppnitrateoxalatepoisoning0.pdf

summary.text:
A spinach relative and one of the most common garden weeds, recognised by the mealy white dust on its young leaves.
In New Zealand it is common throughout the North and South Islands and is also recorded from the Kermadec and Chatham Islands and Campbell Island. It is native to temperate Eurasia and North Africa and has been recorded wild here since 1867. It is poisonous to stock but eaten as a potherb by people.

warnings: Contains oxalates like spinach — eat cooked and in moderation, and not at all if you have kidney stones.
Accumulates nitrates from heavily fertilised or manured ground; avoid plants growing on muck heaps or freshly fertilised paddocks.

harvestEthics.text:
Overhanging fruit over a public footpath is legally the tree owner's. Knock on the door — most people are relieved.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

preparation.text: The fruit falls to the ground when ripe and at its fullest flavour, but it may be picked from the tree prior to falling to prevent bruising. Although the skin is edible, the fruit usually is eaten by cutting it in half, then scooping out the pulp with a spoon.

recipes.method: Ripe feijoas; acidulated water (water with lemon juice); coconut or a neutral oil such as rice bran, for the trays. Cut ripe feijoas in half across their width and scoop each half out whole. Dip them in acidulated water (water with lemon juice) before drying. Lightly oil perforated trays (pizza trays with holes work) with coconut or a neutral oil such as rice bran so they don't stick, and arrange the halves cut side down with space between them, one kind of fruit to a tray. Dry in a 60 °C oven for about 12 hours, or in a dehydrator, then store in sterilised glass jars.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Pastures, waste places, roadsides, railway yards and other habitats near settlements.
It favours dry, sunny places on sandy soils, and copes with drier ground than the other weedy docks.
It grows on the North and South Islands, and is usually the main dock in mown lawns and turf, because it stays smaller than the other docks and survives regular mowing.

identification.text:
Perennial herb; taproot thick; stems many, spreading, to about 60 cm tall. Petiole of lower leaves long and often longer than lamina, often puberulent. Lamina of lower leaves 3–20 × 1–8 cm, with basal 1/4 of lamina forming 2 large rounded cordate lobes with a rounded sinus at the junction with remainder of lamina and thus leaf constricted in basal 1/2, flat, occasionally simple, oblong, puberulent towards base beneath; apex obtuse to rounded. Upper cauline leaves much smaller, simple, oblong, entire, with cuneate base. Inflorescence branches spreading at a wide angle at flowering, later becoming twisted and forming a tangled mass. Whorls of flowers distant; subtending leaves present to the branch apex, reduced, narrow-linear, shorter than 1 cm long; pedicels slender, ciliolate. Flowers bisexual, strongly protandrous. Perianth 1–2 mm long, often reddish; segments of outer whorl more or less ovate-oblong, not reflexed at fruiting; segments of inner whorl becoming much elongated. Fruit valves 4.5–5.5 mm long, triangular, often narrowly so, with thick, raised reticulations; apex obtuse; marginal spines to 2 mm long, thick; tubercles unequal but prominent on each valve, oblong. Nut 1.8–3 mm long, deep shining brown, acutely angled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The lower leaves are pinched in the middle above two large rounded lobes, roughly the shape of a fiddle, which tells it from the other large weedy docks.
It grows as a rosette of leaves spreading from a crown at ground level. In mown lawns it lies very flat with smaller leaves than in rough ground, and seldom sets seed because the mower takes the heads. The flowering branches stand out nearly at right angles to the stem, more so than broad-leaved dock's. The flowering heads start green and turn reddish brown to rusty brown as they ripen; ripe fruits snap off the dry branches easily.

lookalikes.howToTell: Broad-leaved dock's lower leaves are broad ovals up to 15 cm wide (rarely 20), not pinched; fiddle dock's are pinched in the lower half above two large rounded lobes, like a fiddle (occasionally plain and oblong), and 1–8 cm wide. Broad-leaved dock's fruiting branches don't twist and its whorls are usually packed together; fiddle dock's spread wide and tangle into a mass, with distant whorls and tiny narrow leaves right to the tips. Both have toothed fruit valves: broad-leaved dock's teeth are 1–1.7 mm, fiddle dock's spines up to 2 mm. Fiddle dock's flowering branches also stand out more nearly at right angles to the stem.
lookalikes.name: Broad-leaved dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Curled dock's leaves are narrow, strongly wavy and curled, and taper into the stalk; fiddle dock's are flat and pinched in the lower half above two large rounded lobes (occasionally plain and oblong). Curled dock's fruit valves are entire or finely scalloped; fiddle dock's have spines up to 2 mm long.
lookalikes.name: Curled dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Clustered dock's leaves are oblong, often wavy and curled, and sometimes slightly pinched part way down, but usually not as sharply as fiddle dock's flat, fiddle-shaped leaves (fiddle dock's are occasionally plain and oblong too). Both have spaced whorls on branches that twist as they fruit, but clustered dock's fruit valves are entire, each with a large tubercle, while fiddle dock's have spines up to 2 mm long on their edges.
lookalikes.name: Clustered dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Sheep sorrel's leaves are small and narrow, blades 1.5–5 cm long and up to 2 cm wide, with a pair of narrow lobes at the base sticking out sideways like a spearhead; fiddle dock's are 3–20 cm long and 1–8 cm wide, with two large rounded lobes at the base and pinched in above them. Sheep sorrel is a low plant, flowering stems 3–30 cm, spreading by slender yellow underground stems, with nearly leafless flower spikes; fiddle dock has a thick taproot, stems to about 60 cm, and small leaves right to the branch tips. In fruit, sheep sorrel's valves are 1.2–1.5 mm, smooth-edged and without lumps; fiddle dock's are 4.5–5.5 mm with spines on the edges and a lump on each. Don't use taste: both are sour.

summary.text:
Fiddle dock, also called red dock or fiddleleaf dock, is named for its fiddle-shaped leaves. Flora of New Zealand gives its origin as southern and western Europe; its native range runs from the Atlantic islands and Britain through the Mediterranean and North Africa to Iran and Turkmenistan, and it is also native to South Africa's Cape. It was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1878. Massey University calls it a common dock found throughout New Zealand, though probably less common in pastures than broad-leaved dock; Flora of New Zealand (1988) put it behind the other large weedy docks.
It varies a good deal, and some authorities split it into several subspecies that are hard to tell apart; Flora of New Zealand does not. The ripe fruits break off when brushed, and their toothed valves carry them on wind, water, animals and people. The crown and the top of the taproot regrow from pieces dragged about by cultivation.

warnings: It contains oxalic acid, which gives the leaves their sharp taste. A little is fine, but large amounts can lock up calcium and other minerals in food; cooking lowers the oxalic acid. Take particular care, or leave it alone, if you are prone to rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.
Large amounts of dock leaves that are not properly cooked can cause nausea, stomach cramps, vomiting and headache.
Docks are routinely sprayed in New Zealand lawns, pastures and orchards, so pick them only where you know no herbicide has been used.

edibleParts.text: Cap and stem.

habitat.text: Fields and other grassy places, above all open grazed pasture and paddocks, and often lawns in suburban areas, in small groups, in fairy rings or singly. Rarely in woodland.

harvestEthics.text: Pasture is almost always private land, and often recently sprayed or fertilised. Ask the farmer.

identification.text: White cap, sometimes with fine scales. Gills start pink and mature to chocolate brown — never white at maturity. Stem is short with a thin ring and NO sac or bulb at the base. Flesh may bruise faintly pinkish, never bright yellow. Pleasant mushroom smell.

lookalikes.howToTell: Death cap's gills are white, turning cream, sometimes with a faint pink or green tint, as it ages, but not the deep pink then chocolate-brown of a field mushroom. Its stem base sits in a white, sack-like volva that is sometimes underground, so you must dig up the whole base to see it. It has a skirt-like ring that usually stays; a field mushroom's thin ring often disappears. Cap colour does not separate them. Death caps are usually yellow-green, olive or bronze, but young caps can be almost white and an all-white form occurs. In a closed button a white veil hides a field mushroom's gills, so never judge a button. Death cap grows with trees, especially oak (in New Zealand it is thought to have arrived with introduced trees such as oak or spruce), and field mushrooms are often found in fields bordered by trees that death cap can be associated with, so open grass is no guarantee. Half a mature cap is reportedly a lethal dose for an adult. Always dig up the whole mushroom and always check gill colour. A spore print confirms it: field mushroom deep chocolate brown, death cap white.
lookalikes.name: Death cap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut through the base of the stem, or scratch the cap edge. Yellow stainer turns bright chrome yellow almost at once, most strongly at the stem base (the change is most marked in young, fresh mushrooms), and smells of ink, phenol or iodine, especially at the cut base. Field mushroom does not turn yellow: its flesh reddens when cut and it smells pleasant. Field mushroom's stem narrows towards the base; yellow stainer's base is bulbous. White caps and pink-then-brown gills are shared, both can grow on lawns, and a spore print will not help - both drop dark brown. Check every stem base.
lookalikes.name: Yellow stainer

lookalikes.howToTell: Horse mushroom is bigger and stouter, with a thick double ring that has cogwheel-like patches underneath; it yellows slowly where bruised and smells of aniseed or almond. Field mushroom is smaller, its gills are pink when young, its ring is thin and simple and often disappears, its cut flesh blushes reddish, and it smells pleasant but not of aniseed. Both are edible, but horse mushroom's yellowing makes the yellow-stainer checks matter more: cut the stem base and smell every one.
lookalikes.name: Horse mushroom

lookalikes.howToTell: Wine cap can resemble Agaricus mushrooms such as the field mushroom: both have a ring and a dark spore print, so the print does not separate them. The gills do. The field mushroom's are free of the stem and start pink, then turn chocolate brown. Wine cap's are attached to the stem and go from whitish or pale grey to purplish grey and purple-black, never pink. Wine cap has a wine-red to tan cap, a thick, grooved, cogwheel-like ring and grows on wood chip and mulch; the field mushroom has a white cap and a thin ring, in open pasture.
lookalikes.name: Wine-cap stropharia
