preparation.text: Cook. Excellent fried.

recipes.method: Written for field mushrooms in the UK; the recipe links to the site's Agaricus campestris guide. Makes six 10 cm tartlets or one 25 cm tart. For the pastry: 175 g plain flour; 85 g fridge-cold unsalted butter, plus extra for the tins; a pinch of salt; 1 egg yolk; 1 tablespoon iced water. For the filling: 250 g field mushrooms; 1 tablespoon olive oil; salt and black pepper; 250 ml double cream; 1 egg; 3 egg yolks; 1½ tablespoons freshly grated parmesan; 1 tablespoon finely chopped chives. Rub or pulse the flour, butter and salt to fine crumbs, add the egg yolk and half the water and mix to a soft dough, adding more iced water if needed. Flatten the dough into a ball (for tartlets, cut it into 6 wedges, roll each into a ball and flatten it slightly), bag it and chill for at least 30 minutes. Brush the mushrooms clean and slice them thickly. Heat enough oil to cover the base of a large frying pan over a medium heat, add a single layer of mushrooms and let them fry undisturbed for about 2 minutes, until lightly browned, then turn and cook the other side. Drain them on kitchen paper, season, and fry the rest the same way. Heat the oven to 200 °C and butter the tins. Roll the pastry about 3 mm thick, line the tins, trim and prick the bases, and bake on a baking sheet for 15 minutes, until lightly golden. Turn the oven down to 180 °C. Beat the cream with the whole egg, the yolks, plenty of seasoning and 1 tablespoon of the parmesan, then stir in the chives. Share the mushrooms between the cases, pour the cream mixture over without overfilling them and scatter over the rest of the parmesan. Bake for 10–15 minutes, longer for one large tart, until risen, golden and set. Serve warm or cold.
recipes.title: Field mushroom tartlets

recipes.method: The author made it with foraged field mushrooms (Agaricus campestris) and says any mushrooms will do. 1 sliced onion; 500 ml (2 cups, 200 g) roughly chopped mushrooms; 2 sliced garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 15 ml (1 tbsp) balsamic reduction or brandy; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) walnuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) sunflower seeds; 15 ml (1 tbsp) tahini; 5 ml (1 tsp) smoked paprika; 5 ml (1 tsp) miso paste; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper; nasturtium leaves, flowers or herbs, to line the ramekin. Makes about 350 g. Fry the onion in the oil over medium heat for about 10 minutes, until it starts to caramelise. Add the mushrooms and garlic and cook 5 minutes more, then the balsamic or brandy and the lemon, and cook a couple of minutes until no liquid is left. Let it cool. Pulse the walnuts and sunflower seeds in a food processor, add the mushroom mixture and the rest, and pulse to the texture you like. Line a ramekin with a beeswax wrap or cling film, edges overhanging, then with nasturtium leaves, flowers or herbs; pack in the pâté, fold the edges over and chill for 2 hours before turning it out. Or keep it in a jar in the fridge for up to a week.
recipes.title: Field mushroom pâté

summary.text: Agaricus campestris is a widely eaten gilled mushroom closely related to the cultivated A. bisporus (button mushroom). A. campestris is commonly known as the field mushroom or, in North America, meadow mushroom. In New Zealand: Biota of New Zealand records Agaricus campestris here as recorded in error, because 'New Zealand records refer to several undescribed similar species' — the paddock mushrooms picked here as field mushrooms belong to species not yet formally described.

warnings: Dig up the entire base of every single mushroom. A buried volva is the difference between dinner and a liver transplant.
Never harvest a white-gilled mushroom. If the gills are white, put it down.
Amanita phalloides is established in New Zealand and is associated with oak and other introduced trees, such as sweet chestnut and European beech.

The mock meadow mushroom (Agaricus californicus), recorded in New Zealand mostly around Christchurch, is mildly poisonous and causes stomach upsets in many people. It resembles the field mushroom, with a white cap and a ring, and its yellowing where damaged is not always readily apparent, so a stem base that does not turn yellow does not rule it out.
Never eat a wild mushroom you have not confirmed with an experienced identifier. Photos are not identification.

edibleParts.text: The leaves, especially the younger, less bitter ones; the flower buds and flowers; young roots; and the seeds. The leaves are hot, but lose much of their taste and heat in cooking. The flowers are sweet with a slight mustardy bite. The root is smaller than a cultivated turnip, with a similar but stronger flavour. The root and seeds can also be eaten raw.

identification.text:
Annual with lax rosette. Stems erect or ascending, glabrous, to 1.5 m tall, sometimes becoming subwoody below. Lower leaves petiolate, lyrate-pinnatifid with large terminal and 1–3 pairs of lateral lobes, bright green, bristly, 15–25–(30) × 5–10 cm; margins sinuate, toothed. Upper leaves becoming amplexicaul, glaucous, not lobed, sessile, glabrous, narrowly triangular, entire, 2–10 × 1–2 cm. Racemes to 40 cm long; open flowers overtopping buds. Sepals narrow-oblong, (4)–5–7 × 1–1.5 mm. Petals bright yellow, 6–10 × 3–4 mm. Lateral stamens spreading. Silique terete, glabrous, linear-lanceolate, slightly constricted between seeds, (30)–40–60 × 2–5 mm; gynophore 0; valves with prominent median and weaker lateral veins; beak tapering, seedless, 6–10 mm long. Seeds reddish brown, 1–1.5 mm diameter 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The rosette leaves are covered in bristly hairs; the leaves near the top of the flowering stem are smooth. The open flowers sit above the unopened buds. Rape (Brassica napus) is similar, but its open flowers sit level with or below the buds, its leaves are all bluish-grey and its petals are 10–12 mm long. The root swells with age into a small turnip, much smaller than a cultivated one.

lookalikes.howToTell: Field mustard's upper leaves are smooth (hairless), bluish-green, not lobed and clasp the stem; wild radish's flowering stems and leaves stay bristly-hairy all the way up. Both have bristly rosette leaves, so a rosette alone does not separate them. Field mustard's petals are bright yellow and 6–10 mm long; wild radish's are 13–20 mm long, usually pale yellow or white (also pink, mauve or brownish) and usually veined with mauve.
lookalikes.name: Wild radish

lookalikes.howToTell: The rosettes are easily confused; tell them apart once they flower. Hedge mustard's flowers are smaller: its petals are yellow and 3–4 mm long, against field mustard's bright yellow 6–10 mm. Hedge mustard's pods are 10–15–(20) × 1–2 mm and pressed flat against the stem, so they are easy to miss; field mustard's are (30)–40–60 × 2–5 mm, with a seedless beak 6–10 mm long, and stand out from the stem. Hedge mustard's stem is hairy and its upper stem leaves are still deeply lobed, only the uppermost becoming simple; field mustard's stem is hairless and its upper leaves are smooth, bluish-green, not lobed and clasp the stem.
lookalikes.name: Hedge mustard

lookalikes.howToTell: Flowers do not separate them: both have yellow petals 6–10 mm long. Eastern rocket's stems are softly hairy and its leaves sparsely to densely hairy; field mustard's stems are hairless and its upper leaves are smooth, bluish-green and clasp the stem. Eastern rocket's pods are very long and thin, (40)–60–100 × 1–1.5 mm, with no beak or a very short one; field mustard's are (30)–40–60 × 2–5 mm and end in a seedless beak 6–10 mm long.
lookalikes.name: Eastern rocket

lookalikes.howToTell: Black nightshade's flowers are usually white, sometimes pale mauve, 10–13 mm across, with yellow anthers in the centre, and it bears round berries 7–10 mm across, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow; the unripe green berries are the most toxic. Field mustard's flowers are bright yellow with four petals, and its fruit are long, thin pods. Black nightshade's leaves are oval to lance-oval, entire to coarsely toothed, only sometimes slightly lobed, on stalks up to 7 cm; field mustard's lower leaves have a large end lobe and 1–3 pairs of side lobes and are bristly. Field mustard starts as a rosette at ground level; black nightshade is a tall, upright, usually much-branched plant, its stems and leaves sometimes tinged purple.
lookalikes.name: Black nightshade

preparation.text: Eat very young leaves raw in salads; older leaves soon turn fibrous and hairy and are better cooked or fermented. Use them like bok choy: they shrink fast as they cook, so fry or steam them for only a few seconds. Cook the flower buds like broccoli, again only briefly, and add the flowers to salads or use them as a garnish. Dig roots from first-year plants, before they send up a flowering stem; young, small ones may be tender enough to cook, and larger ones are fibrous but good in stock. For seed, spread the pods on a plate to dry in the sun until they split, and use the seeds like mustard seed; to make mustard, pound them with a little liquid, vinegar if you want the paste to keep.

recipes.method: Written for broccoli rabe (rapini), a cultivated form of the same species: use the young flowering shoots of field mustard. Serves 4. 1 bunch of young field mustard shoots; 15 ml (1 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for drizzling; 2 garlic cloves, sliced; ¼ teaspoon chilli flakes; sea salt and black pepper; a lemon wedge. Trim about 1 cm off the ends of the stems. Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil and have a large bowl of iced water ready. Blanch the shoots for 2 minutes, cool them in the iced water for about 15 seconds, drain and pat dry on paper towels. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat, add the garlic for 30 seconds, then the chilli flakes. Add the shoots and toss them for 3–5 minutes until tender, stems included. Lift them out, leaving any liquid behind, season with salt and pepper, squeeze over the lemon and serve as a side dish.
recipes.title: Sautéed field mustard shoots with garlic and chilli

summary.text:
Brassica rapa is an annual to biennial plant species native to Eurasia that is from the Brassicaceae family.
Brassica rapa is an early-season nectar and pollen source for a wide range of insects. Numerous pollinators are attracted to its bright yellow flowers, including bees, flies, and butterflies. A common visitor, the small white butterfly (Pieris rapae) uses the plant both as a nectar source and as a host for larval feeding. Conversely, insect pollination is also very important to the plant; insect pollination of B. rapa leads to 30% more yield when compared to self-fertilizing controls. Furthermore, B. rapa can undergo rapid genomic adaptations when selected on by bumblebees.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) it grows throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands, naturalised by 1864 from Europe. Wild plants here belong to subsp. sylvestris, which has also been called B. campestris and B. rapa var. campestris; the cultivated turnip is subsp. rapa. In New Zealand it is also called wild turnip.
Māori names include pōhata, pōwhata and paea. Its large white root and its leaves were eaten, and Shortland (1851) records that his party ate eel, fernroot and turnip tops (kōrau) at a Māori village on the Taieri Plain.
Unlike many crop weeds it can germinate at any time of year, mostly in autumn or spring, and it goes to seed very quickly.
It is native across Europe, Russia and Asia. It is found in most parts of the world, and has returned to the wild many times as a feral plant or weed. Other English names include turnip mustard, wild mustard, wild kale and bird rape. It can behave as a summer annual, winter annual, or biennial depending on the climate and management. The cultivated turnip (var. rapa) is itself recorded in New Zealand as a casual escape, with herbarium records from Canterbury and Wellington. The genus name Brassica is the Latin name Pliny the Elder used, from the Celtic bresic, cabbage.

warnings: Field mustard is classed as poisonous in New Zealand; the record gives no part or amount.
The seeds contain an oil that can cause irritation for some people.
Do not gather it from heavily fertilised ground or places that catch run-off: the plant takes up and holds nitrates, which are toxic in high doses.
It is a common weed of crops and is controlled with herbicides. Pick it only where you know none has been used.

Brassicaceae plants are known for their tendency to accumulate heavy metals, a trait that makes them valuable for the phytoremediation of contaminated soils. However, this same ability necessitates careful monitoring, as the accumulation of heavy metals can also pose potential health risks.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Open, modified and disturbed habitats, waste places, roadsides, arable land, short, poor, and depleted pasture, lawns, stream beds, and cliffs. Recorded elevations range from 0 to 1360 m.
In New Zealand it grows in gardens and arable crops, and it does better in lawns than bird's-eye speedwell, growing below the mower blades (Massey).
It is also found on open rocky ground and along rail corridors (NZPCN).

identification.text:
Annual herb to 0.45 m tall. Stems decumbent to erect; hairs of two types: dense, bifarious, antrorse, short, eglandular; and sparse, long, uniform, eglandular or sometimes glandular. Leaf bud indistinct; leaves separating while very small, opposite-decussate, erecto-patent to spreading; lamina thin, elliptic to ovate or sub-orbicular, becoming deltoid above, 5–20 mm long, 3–12 mm wide, dull green above, pale green to pinkish beneath; midrib and secondary veins distinct; surfaces eglandular-pubescent above and beneath, at least on veins; margin pubescent, serrate-crenate to serrate-dentate; teeth in 3–6 pairs; apex obtuse to sub-acute; base truncate to sub-cordate; petiole 0–4 mm rarely to 10 mm long. Inflorescence a terminal spike or raceme, 5–40 mm long; flowers crowded, distant at fruiting, 5–60, all bisexual; bracts alternate, lowest leaf-like, becoming lanceolate-elliptic, longer than pedicels; pedicels erecto-patent, 0–2 mm long, eglandular-pubescent all around. Calyx lobes 4, sub-acute to acute, unequal (the posterior ½–¾ the anterior), 1.5–3.0 mm long, elongating to 5–6 mm at fruiting, glandular- and eglandular-hairy. Corolla 2–3 mm diameter; tube white and yellow, 1 mm long, shorter than calyx, glabrous; lobes 4, blue, rarely white or pinkish, erecto-patent, unequal, elliptic to orbicular, 1.0–1.5 mm long, rounded; nectar guides dark blue. Stamen filaments white, 0.5–1.0 mm long; anthers blue. Style glabrous, about 0.5 mm long. Capsules angustiseptate, obcordate, glandular- or eglandular-ciliate on edges, 2.5–3.0 mm long, 3–4 mm at widest point. Seeds ellipsoid, flattened, smooth, pale brown, 1–1.2 mm long.
Veronica arvensis plants can be recognised by a combination of characters: short, bifarious, mixed with long, uniform stem hairs, leaves toothed but not deeply lobed, tiny bright blue (very rarely white) sessile flowers in a terminal inflorescence, small, obcordate ciliate capsules, and flattened seeds.
Veronica verna plants have a similar growth form, with sessile, small blue flowers and flattened seeds, but can be distinguished by having only short stem hairs (glandular above), upper leaves and lower bracts lobed to at least halfway, and pubescent faces on the capsules (glandular on capsule margins).Veronica triphyllos plants have rather larger blue flowers, digitately lobed leaves, densely glandular inflorescence and calyx, much longer pedicels at fruiting, larger capsules, and cup-shaped seeds.
Veronica arvensis plants have been misidentified as Veronica polita. Veronica polita plants have rather larger flowers with longer pedicels, and even their uppermost bracts are leaf-like. Their capsule lobes are rounded, only weakly flattened, and hairy all over. Their seeds are wrinkled and cup-shaped.
Out of flower it looks much the same as bird's-eye speedwell, only smaller, with similar leaves and hairs; size is not reliable, as it can grow quite large in flower gardens. In flower, its small blue flowers and heart-shaped fruits sit at the bases of the leaves without stalks. Unlike turf speedwell, it has no creeping stems (Massey).
Its lower bracts are leaf-like, so each flower looks as if it sits alone in a leaf base (NZPCN). Turf speedwell has hairless leaves and mainly white flowers (Massey).

lookalikes.howToTell: Bird's-eye speedwell's flowers are 8–12 mm across, each alone on a long, slender stalk (5–15 mm, longer in fruit); field speedwell's are tiny, 2–3 mm across, and sit almost stalkless (stalks 0–2 mm) among small bracts at the stem tips. Bird's-eye speedwell's leaves are 6–35 mm long with 3–8 pairs of teeth; field speedwell's are 5–20 mm with 3–6 pairs. Out of flower they look much the same: both are hairy, with paired, toothed leaves of similar shape, and both grow in gardens, crops, lawns and waste ground. Size alone does not separate them, as field speedwell can grow large in gardens. Bird's-eye speedwell's young leaves and shoots are eaten, but its record as food is thin.
lookalikes.name: Bird's-eye speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Turf speedwell's leaves are almost hairless; field speedwell's are hairy on both faces, at least on the veins, and its stems carry two kinds of hairs. Turf speedwell is a perennial whose lower stems creep and root at the joints; field speedwell is an annual with no creeping stems. Turf speedwell's flowers are pale blue fading to whitish, 3–5 mm across, on stalks 1–3 mm long; field speedwell's are bright blue, 2–3 mm across, almost stalkless. Both grow low in lawns throughout New Zealand, with small paired, toothed leaves and four-lobed flowers in a spike at the stem tips, so habitat and leaf shape do not separate them. Turf speedwell's record as food is thin, so it is not given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Turf speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping speedwell's flowers are 8–10 mm across, each alone on a thread-like stalk 15–40 mm long; field speedwell's are tiny, 2–3 mm across, and sit almost stalkless (stalks 0–2 mm) among small bracts at the stem tips. Creeping speedwell is a perennial whose stems creep flat and root at the joints, forming dense mats; field speedwell is an annual with no creeping stems. Creeping speedwell sets no fruit in New Zealand; field speedwell sets small heart-shaped capsules. Both are hairy, both have small, toothed leaves of overlapping size (creeping speedwell 3–8 mm long, field speedwell 5–20 mm) and both grow low in lawns, so hairiness, leaf size and habitat do not separate them. No food use of creeping speedwell has been confirmed; see its page.

summary.text:
Veronica arvensis, common names: wall speedwell, corn speedwell, common speedwell, rock speedwell, field speedwell, is an annual flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae. The species is native to Europe and a common weed in gardens, pastures, waste places, and cultivated land.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: throughout. South Island: throughout. Kermadec Islands, Chatham Islands, Stewart Island, Campbell Island/Motu Ihupuku. First recorded by Kirk in 1864.
In New Zealand it normally grows as a winter annual, germinating in autumn, flowering in spring and dying off in spring (Massey).
It is native to temperate Eurasia and North Africa, and was naturalised in New Zealand by 1864 (NZPCN). Colenso described a New Zealand plant as Veronica hirsuta in 1892; that name is now treated as the same species (Biota of New Zealand).

identification.text:
Field woundwort is an annual herb with branched, square stems up to 45 cm long, growing with a sprawling or erect habit. The stems are pale green and covered with patent, sparsely glandular hairs up to 2 mm long. Plants are easily uprooted to reveal a mass of short, white, fibrous roots at the base of the plant and sometimes along any horizontal stems close to the base. The leaves are arranged in opposite, decussate pairs, with no stipules, and petioles of up to 4 cm long; the blade is simple and oval, up to 4 cm long, with a truncate base and between 7 and 12 rounded teeth per side. They are dull, medium green on the upper surface and paler beneath, hairy on both sides.
The inflorescence consists of a terminal spike with up to 8 false whorls (actually two opposite clusters that look like a whorl) of 4 to 7 flowers, each with a short pedicel of up to 1.5 mm. The whorls are subtended by a pair of leaf-like bracts which are stalked at the base of the inflorescence, becoming sessile towards the top of the plant. There is also one tiny bracteole at the base of each cluster of flowers. The lower whorls are widely spaced, but the upper ones are more crowded towards the tip of the plant. The flowers are zygomorphic with a 5 lobed calyx tube 5 to 7 mm long, and two lipped corolla 6 to 8 mm. The upper lip is entire and the lower lip is three lobed, with the central lobe much larger. It can be white, pink or purple.
In New Zealand it tends to scramble across the ground rather than stand upright, and its flowers are lilac (Massey). In very dry, stony places such as river beds, plants are often only a few centimetres tall (Flora of New Zealand). Seedlings have stalked leaves (University of Queensland key).

lookalikes.howToTell: Field woundwort's flowers are small — 6–7 mm long, with a small upper lip that is not hooded and is shorter than the lower lip, the tube no longer than the calyx; red deadnettle's are 10–14 mm long with a hooded upper lip. Field woundwort's stem is much hairier, and its bracts are stalkless. Both are weeds of gardens, crops, waste places and river beds, and young plants are easily confused. Field woundwort poisons livestock (staggers); no record of it being eaten by people has been found.
lookalikes.name: Red deadnettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Field woundwort's flowers are small — 6–7 mm long, with a small upper lip that is not hooded and is shorter than the lower lip, the tube no longer than the calyx; henbit's are about 15 mm long with a hooded upper lip, on a long, narrow tube. Field woundwort's stem is much hairier. Henbit's leaves among the flowers are stalkless, broad and kidney-shaped, clasp the stem and look unlike its other leaves; field woundwort's are stalkless too, but oblong, oval or nearly round, like its upper leaves — so stalkless leaves alone do not separate them. Both are weeds of gardens, crops and waste places, and young plants are easily confused. Field woundwort poisons livestock (staggers); no record of it being eaten by people has been found.

Field woundwort's stem is much hairier, and its bracts are stalkless. Both are weeds of gardens, crops, waste places and river beds, and young plants are easily confused. Speedwell's stem is round; field woundwort's is square. Both are hairy, sprawl across the ground, have paired, toothed leaves of much the same size, flower all year, and grow in gardens, fields, waste places, roadsides and river beds, so none of these tells them apart. summary.text:
Stachys arvensis is a species of flowering plant in the mint family known by the common names field woundwort and staggerweed. It is native to Europe, Western Asia, and North Africa. It is known on other continents as an introduced species and widespread weed.
In New Zealand it is common to abundant throughout the North and South Islands, including offshore islands, and on Raoul Island in the Kermadecs (Flora of New Zealand); it was naturalised by 1867 (NZPCN). It can germinate at any time of year, mostly in spring and autumn, and many of the selective herbicides used in cereal crops do not kill it (Massey).

warnings: It poisons livestock: animals that eat too much of it develop staggers, and sheep have drowned after staggering into a creek. No record of it being eaten by people has been found.
Red deadnettle and henbit, which are eaten, grow in the same places and look alike when young.

identification.text:
The common forms of P. aurea are easily identified by their characteristic compressed internodes in the lower part of the canes which have a tortoise shell-like appearance.
Fairly dense thicket-forming with rhizomes running extensively. Culm usually 3–6 m (often taller in cultivation), glaucous when young, green during the first year, yellow afterwards, erect, with white waxy ring beneath nodes when young; nodes on some shoots congested and sometimes zigzag towards base; internodes swollen and often asymmetric. Culm-sheath light mauve-brown or pinkish brown, mottled dark purplish, especially towards apex; auricles and oral bristles 0; sheath-blade narrow linear, flat, often with greenish pink marginal band. Branches spreading widely to give an open network. Leaf-sheath with long oral bristles. Auricles 0. Ligule minutely puberulent. Leaf-blade usually 5–13–(15) × 0.7–2–(2.7) cm, lanceolate, abaxially glaucescent, acuminate.
[From: Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Check the leaves: arrow bamboo's blades reach 25–30 cm long and 3.5–4 cm wide, glossy dark green above, against fishpole's usually 5–13 cm and under 3 cm wide. Arrow bamboo has one branch per node, sometimes two or three at the upper nodes, where fishpole usually has three, the middle one small or missing and the other two markedly unequal. Its canes are round, not notched, and dark green; fishpole's internodes are flattened or grooved on alternate sides above each node (usually round below the lowest branches), and its canes turn yellow after the first year, with crowded nodes and swollen, often lopsided internodes near the base of some canes. Height does not separate them (arrow bamboo 3–5 m, fishpole usually 3–6 m), and both have a white band below the nodes (on fishpole, on young canes). Arrow bamboo's young shoots are edible cooked, with a rather bitter flavour.
lookalikes.name: Arrow bamboo

lookalikes.howToTell: Black bamboo's canes are green at first and either stay green or turn black or heavily black-blotched in their second year; fishpole's turn yellow after their first. Because some naturalised black bamboo stays green, a green stand does not rule it out — look at the nodes and sheaths instead. Black bamboo's nodes are all more or less evenly spaced; some of fishpole's canes have crowded, sometimes zigzag nodes and swollen, often lopsided internodes near the base. Black bamboo's cane sheaths are uniformly purple or purple-flushed, with prominent dark auricles on the main shoots; fishpole's are light mauve-brown or pinkish brown mottled dark purple, with no auricles. Both have a white waxy ring below the nodes on young canes, and their heights overlap (black bamboo 4–7 m, fishpole usually 3–6 m), so neither helps. Both have edible young shoots, cooked.
lookalikes.name: Black bamboo

preparation.text: The toxins must be destroyed by thorough cooking, and for this reason, fresh bamboo shoots are boiled before being used in other ways. The shoots of some species contain cyanide that must be leached or boiled out before they can be eaten safely. Slicing the bamboo shoots thinly assists in this leaching.

recipes.method: Cut the shoots at about 8 cm above the ground, 5 cm below the soil; the canes are slender, about 15 mm, thicker in their native China. Handle the husk with care: it is many overlapping brown layers covered in fine, sharp hairs. Run a knife up the side of the shoot to slit it, then unwrap and throw away the layers until you reach the pale core; cut off the pointed tip and the fibrous base. They are said to be the sweetest of the genus, with very little bitterness, but cook them: cover with water and boil for 20 minutes, change the water and simmer until tender. If they are still bitter, boil again in fresh water for 5 minutes, and repeat until the flavour is milder.

summary.text: Phyllostachys aurea is a species of bamboo, and is of the 'running bamboo' type, belonging to the diverse Bambuseae tribe. Brought here from south-eastern China as an ornamental and naturalised since 1977, it is named on DOC's list of environmental weeds.

warnings: Raw bamboo shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides, natural toxins also contained in cassava. The toxins must be destroyed by thorough cooking, and for this reason, fresh bamboo shoots are boiled before being used in other ways.

identification.text:
Perennial acaulous herb with thick, fleshy, glassy white, contractile root below the main bulb which is surrounded by numerous small bulbils; tunic brown; scales 3–7-nerved. Leaves 3-foliolate. Petiole (5)–10–50 cm long, glabrous or sparsely hairy; stipular wing broad, membranous, long-ciliate. Lamina of leaflets equal or nearly so, sessile, 12–50 × 18–80 mm, broadly fishtail-shaped, shallowly and broadly 2-lobed, glabrous except for more or less hairy base, finely reticulate beneath, not punctate; calli 0 or inconspicuous. Inflorescence about 10–50 cm tall, pseudoumbellate, about 5–15–(20)-flowered, glabrous or nearly so; pedicels very variable in length, more or less deflexed at first, usually glabrous. Bracts at pedicel base, about 3 mm long, lacking calli. Sepals 3–5.5 mm long, lanceolate-elliptic to elliptic, glabrous; calli 2, orange, prominent, apical. Petals about 1.2–1.5 cm long, oblong-obovate, pink, glabrous. Stamens at 2 levels; filaments of longer set about 4–5 mm long, hirsute above, glabrous and dilated below, shorter set sparingly hairy. Styles shorter than stamens, glabrous or hairy. Capsule not seen.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

Pale form: some plants have broadly heart-shaped (not fishtail-shaped) leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm, with a rather shallow notch, hairless above and hairy or hairless below, with no orange dots; flower clusters 7–26 cm long with 8–15 flowers, hairless or hairy; and petals 9–15 mm long, whitish or very pale mauve-pink. Flora of New Zealand vol. IV describes these as Oxalis vallicola and notes they are often confused with fishtail oxalis and pink shamrock; NZ Flora Online now includes them in this species.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, 'Oxalis vallicola'.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are pink-flowered sorrels with no leafy stem, their leaves all rising from the base, and several flowers in a cluster at the top of a tall stalk. Look at the base of the plant: fishtail oxalis grows from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, with a thick, fleshy, glassy white root below it; shamrock wood sorrel grows from a short, thick, fleshy rhizome, rough with old leaf-base scars, and has no true bulbils. Look at the leaflets: fishtail oxalis's are broadly fishtail-shaped, shallowly and broadly two-lobed, 12–50 mm long and 18–80 mm wide, hairless except near the base, with no orange dots or only faint ones; shamrock wood sorrel's are broadly heart-shaped with a narrow notch up to a third of their length, with flattened hairs on both faces, a tuft of hairs at the base and a band of orange dots along the edge. Fishtail oxalis's petals are about 1.2–1.5 cm long, pink and hairless; shamrock wood sorrel's are 9–16 mm long, usually rose with darker veins, with a band of flattened hairs on the outside, so length overlaps. Flower number overlaps too: fishtail oxalis about 5–15 (up to 20), shamrock wood sorrel (4)–7–35. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. The tests above that do not rest on leaflet shape or petal colour still hold for it. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Shamrock wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are pink-flowered sorrels with no leafy stem, growing from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, with a thick, fleshy, glassy white root below it, and both are weeds of cultivated and waste ground. They are alike in size and flower colour; the orange dots under the leaflets settle it. Pink shamrock's leaflets are broadly heart-shaped and rounded, 10–35 mm long and 12–48 mm wide, with a rather narrow notch, hairy beneath and finely dotted underneath with raised orange spots, especially round the edge; fishtail oxalis's are broadly fishtail-shaped, shallowly and broadly two-lobed, 12–50 mm long and 18–80 mm wide, hairless except near the base, with no orange dots or only faint ones. Pink shamrock's flower clusters carry long curly hairs; fishtail oxalis's are usually hairless or nearly so. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. Its leaflet shape and flower-cluster hairs then match pink shamrock's, but it still has no orange dots under the leaflets. Petals do not separate them safely: pink shamrock's are 1.5–2 cm long, pink to rose; fishtail oxalis's about 1.2–1.5 cm, pink. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pink shamrock

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel has leafy stems, spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and each flower stalk carries a single flower. Fishtail oxalis has no leafy stem: its leaves all rise from the base, from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, and it carries about 5–15 (up to 20) flowers in a cluster on a stalk about 10–50 cm tall. Pale-pink wood sorrel's petals are 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white; fishtail oxalis's are about 1.2–1.5 cm long, pink. Pale-pink wood sorrel's petals can be as short as 1 cm, so petal size alone does not separate them. Pale-pink wood sorrel's leaflets carry an irregular row of orange dots just inside the edge; fishtail oxalis's have none or only faint ones and are broadly fishtail-shaped. Leaflet size overlaps: pale-pink wood sorrel's are 4–16 mm long, fishtail oxalis's 12–50 mm. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. The tests above that do not rest on leaflet shape or petal colour still hold for it. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pale-pink wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Purple wood sorrel carries a single flower on each stalk, 1–11 cm long, forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base. Its leaflets are broadly obovate with a rounded tip, sometimes slightly notched, with long hairs fringing the edges, and its sepals carry a dense fringe of long white hairs and have no orange dots. Fishtail oxalis carries about 5–15 (up to 20) flowers in an umbel-like cluster on a stalk about 10–50 cm tall, its petals about 1.2–1.5 cm long, pink. Its leaflets are broadly fishtail-shaped, shallowly and broadly two-lobed, 12–50 mm long and 18–80 mm wide, and its sepals are hairless, with two prominent orange dots at the tip. What does not separate them: both have no leafy stem, with all the leaves rising from the base; both grow from bulbs that make bulbils, though purple wood sorrel's outer bulb scales are dark brown or blackish, shining and sticky and fishtail oxalis's are brown or pale fawn-brown; and fishtail oxalis's leaflets have no orange dots or only faint ones, so leaflet dots do not help. Purple wood sorrel's petals can be as short as 10 mm, so petal length points to purple wood sorrel only when the petals are longer than 16 mm. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. The tests above that do not rest on leaflet shape or petal colour still hold for it. Do not eat purple wood sorrel; see its own entry.

preparation.text: Eat the leaves and stems raw in salads, or cook them, with the bulbs, with other greens or potatoes as a leafy vegetable. The leaves are also made into chutney, soup, a cool drink or tea, and are pickled. Use it in moderation.

summary.text:
Oxalis latifolia is a species of flowering plant in the woodsorrel family known by the common names garden pink-sorrel and broadleaf woodsorrel. It is native to Mexico and parts of Central and South America. However, it has propagated to other parts of the world.
It is known on most other continents as an introduced species and a noxious weed and invasive species, as it infests many types of agricultural crops.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: widespread and often abundant; South Island: northern half; Kermadec Islands: Raoul Island. Naturalised from tropical South America, first recorded in 1958. O. latifolia is somewhat less widespread than the related O. debilis, but where it occurs is generally common and often abundant. If not checked it can cover recently cultivated soil with a dense mass of foliage which arises from the numerous small bulbils scattered during cultivation. O. intermedia A. Rich. is sometimes considered to be the correct name of this species.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

It spreads by the many small bulbils around its bulb, which are scattered when the soil is dug or moved; left unchecked it can cover freshly cultivated soil with a dense mass of leaves, and the bulbils can stay alive in the soil for several years. Dig it only where you mean to clear it, and do not move soil it grows in.
It grows with pink shamrock and shamrock wood sorrel, pink-flowered sorrels that look very like it (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
It is a deciduous shrub growing to 3 metres tall and broad. It is naturally multi-stemmed with an upright-arching to rounded habit, although it can be grown in tree form. The bark is dark brownish-grey with prominent paler brown lenticels.
The leaves are alternately arranged, simple, 2–7 centimetres long and broad, palmately lobed with five lobes. When young in spring, they have a strong resinous scent.
The flowers are produced in early spring at the same time as the leaves emerge, on dangling racemes 3–7 cm long of 5–30 flowers; each flower is 5–10 millimetres in diameter, with five red, pink, or white petals.
The fruit is a dark purple oval berry about 1 cm long; it has an insipid taste.

recipes.method: Flowering currant flowers and young leaves; equal parts sugar and water; lemon juice, citric acid or flowering currant vinegar, for a cordial. Use the flowers and young leaves; with flowers alone the results turn pink. For a syrup, infuse them into a syrup of equal parts sugar and water by heating gently, without boiling. Cool, and keep in sterilised jars in the fridge for a couple of weeks. Pour it over puddings or add it to gin. For a cordial, sharpen the syrup to taste with lemon juice, citric acid or the flowering currant vinegar below; this also helps it keep. Dilute to drink.
recipes.title: Flowering currant syrup and cordial

recipes.method: Flowering currant flowers and young leaves; cold white wine or apple cider vinegar; flowering currant syrup or cordial, or honey, for a shrub or oxymel. Use the flowers and young leaves; with flowers alone the results turn pink. Infuse them straight into cold white wine or apple cider vinegar for a week, then strain. Use it in salad dressings or as a pickling liquor — the author pickles magnolia petals and Japanese knotweed in it. Mix the vinegar with flowering currant syrup or cordial for a shrub, or with honey for an oxymel, to add fruity sourness to gin drinks.
recipes.title: Flowering currant vinegar and shrub

recipes.method: Flowering currant flowers and young leaves; vodka; flowering currant cordial, syrup or shrub, to sweeten. Use the flowers and young leaves; with flowers alone the results turn pink. Infuse them in vodka for no more than a week, strain, and sweeten to taste with flowering currant cordial, syrup or shrub.
recipes.title: Flowering currant liqueur

recipes.method: The author's elderflower champagne with flowering currant flowers in place of the elderflowers. He gives no amount; for a subtler flower he says to use more plant material than the 10–16 elderflower heads. Flowering currant flowers and young leaves; 650 g sugar; 4.5 litres of cold water; 1 lemon; 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar. Dissolve 650 g sugar in 4.5 litres of cold water — warm a little of the water to dissolve the sugar, cool it, then mix it into the rest. In a large bucket or bowl, combine the sweetened water with the flowers or leaves, the juice and quartered skin of 1 lemon, and 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar. Cover and leave for 4 days, somewhere cool; if mould forms, scrape off the mat of flowers on top and carry on. Fine-strain into clean screw-top plastic fizzy-drink bottles, leaving a few centimetres of air at the top. Never use corked bottles, and avoid glass flip-tops: you can't feel the pressure through them, and they are far more dangerous if they burst. Leave at room temperature for 6–14 days. From day 6, squeeze the bottles every day, and as soon as the bases start to round out, ease the caps to let off some (not all) of the pressure; a forgotten bottle can explode. Once it tastes right, move it to the fridge to slow the fermentation, and keep checking the pressure. The author drinks it between 2 and 4 weeks; it is lightly alcoholic after a week and starts turning vinegary at 5–6 weeks. The source notes that the yeast comes from the flowers, so in a cool room it can take a while to get going.
recipes.title: Flowering currant champagne

recipes.method: Written for the author's mixed wild leaves. Of his lists, this catalogue covers dandelion and hairy bittercress (pungent), chickweed and young hawthorn leaves (mild), and gorse flowers and flowering currant blossom (extras). He warns to be extra careful identifying leaves before the plants flower. Pungent leaves; mild leaves; a few extras; walnut oil; elderberry vinegar; salt and pepper; a little mustard; fermented greens; pickled buds. Mix pungent and mild leaves about 1 to 3, then scatter a few extras over the top. Dress simply with walnut oil, elderberry vinegar, salt, pepper and a little mustard; he finishes it with fermented greens and pickled buds.

summary.text:
Ribes sanguineum, the flowering currant, redflower currant, red-flowering currant, or red currant is a North American species of flowering plant in the family Grossulariaceae.
It is native to the western United States, Canada and Mexico. In western British Columbia, Washington, and Oregon, it is distributed widely in the moist regions west of the Cascades. In California it is restricted to areas near the coast, and can be found as far south as Santa Barbara County. In Mexico, it is only found on the Pacific island of Guadalupe, where it may be extirpated. Although its conservation status is secure across the rest of its range, in Idaho it is critically imperiled and is found only rarely in Bonner, Kootenai, Benewah, and Adams counties.
It is widely cultivated and naturalized throughout temperate Europe and Australasia.

habitat.text:
Forest margins.
Cordyline banksii tolerates a wide variety of habitats. It is common in coastal, lowland, and lower montane forests in the North Island, widespread in the northern half of the South Island and Westland as far south as Haast. It also occasionally occurs in subalpine regions in the South Island. In shrublands it occurs with Cordyline pumilio and may form hybrids with it.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Cabbage trees should not be cut for exploitation.

identification.text: Tī ngahere is a sparingly-branched cabbage tree up to 4 metres tall. The leaves are lanceolate (somewhat paddle-shaped), up to 2 metres long and from 40–80 millimetres wide. The leaves are broad in the mid portion and droop from there. A prominent flat midrib runs the whole length of the leaf. The fruiting panicle is up to 2 metres in length. The flowers are white and pleasantly perfumed. The globe-shaped fruit are up to 5 millimetres in diameter, and are white, bluish-white, or blue.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cabbage tree grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Forest cabbage tree (Cordyline banksii) grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Cabbage tree grows to the size of a small tree with a thick trunk and many branches, and its leaf stalk is flat and ill-defined, at least three-quarters as wide as the widest part of the blade; forest cabbage tree rarely approaches tree form and, if tall, usually has several more or less equal main stems, and its leaf stalk is narrow, long (up to a quarter of the blade's length) and deeply channelled, widening rather abruptly into a much wider blade that droops at the tip, with a prominent midrib and several stronger side nerves. Both have white, scented flowers, so flower colour does not separate them. Where the two overlap at about 300–1,000 ft (90–300 m) on the northern tip of the Tararua Range, about half the plants cannot be put strictly in either species.
lookalikes.name: Cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf cabbage tree is rarely more than 2 m tall and often flowers while its short stem is still leafy to the ground; its leaves are 30–60–(100) × 1–2 cm, more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base; its panicle is very open, up to about 60 cm long, with slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers that are whitish or pink outside, and its berries are bluish or flecked with blue, 4–5 mm across. Forest cabbage tree (Cordyline banksii) grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Dwarf cabbage tree is usually no more than 1–(2) m tall with a main stem 1–2 cm across and leaves rarely over 2 cm wide, its flower cluster large for the plant but with very slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers; forest cabbage tree's main stem soon exceeds 2 cm across even on a young plant, and its leaves are mostly over 2 cm wide. A hybrid between the two has been described (C. × gibbingsae, Carse 1929) that looks like a small, stemless forest cabbage tree, so an in-between plant may be neither.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain cabbage tree grows to about 8 m with massive, rather sparingly branched stems; its leaves are up to 1–2 m × 10–15 cm, broadly sword-shaped, drooping only with age, glaucous underneath, narrowed above the base to a short stalk, with a broad, conspicuous midrib that is often reddish, the stronger nerves often reddish too; its panicle is tightly compact, 60–160 cm long, its crowded, rather fleshy flowers on longer stalks than in the other species, and its berries are bluish, about 6 mm across. Forest cabbage tree (Cordyline banksii) grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Mountain cabbage tree stands apart from all the others on its leaves: up to 10–15 cm wide, glaucous underneath, with a strong, often reddish midrib and main nerves, and a tightly compact flower cluster. The other species' leaves are rarely over 10 cm wide, often much less, not or scarcely glaucous underneath, and their flower clusters are lax and open. Forms intermediate between these two have been recorded.

Cabbage trees in general give a leaf heart: peel back the tough outer leaves of a leaf head until the paler shoot and heart show, stripping too few rather than too many at first; boil or bake it for 6 minutes or less, depending on its size, and treat it like an artichoke heart.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Mostly open disturbed areas, especially poor pastures, scrub and forest margins, stony river beds, roadsides, tracksides.
It is very widespread on the North, South and Stewart Islands, but often absent from drier areas; it is abundant on the West Coast of the South Island, up to about 1000 m.
On the national wetland plant list it is an obligate upland plant: almost always on dry ground, rarely in wetlands.

identification.text:
Biennial or short-lived perennial. Basal rosette giving rise to densely hairy simple stems to about 2.5 m high. Petiole long and winged; upper stem leaves with much shorter petioles. Lamina 10–25 × 3.5–12 cm, lanceolate to elliptic or ovate, hairy to glabrate above, more or less grey-tomentulose with crisped hairs beneath, crenate or crenulate; base cuneate to attenuate. Racemes to about 60 cm long, with many nodding flowers. Bracts lanceolate, shortly glandular-hairy, decreasing in size upwards, longer than pedicels; pedicels tomentulose, 5–15 mm long. Calyx 8–17 mm long, shortly glandular-hairy, deeply lobed; lobes imbricate, ovate, obtuse or acute. Corolla mostly 3.5–5 cm long; tube campanulate and inflated above constricted base, usually pinkish purple with dark purple white-ringed spots in lower part, sometimes pure white, glabrous; lobes short and rounded. Stamens included. Capsule 10–15 mm long, ovoid. Seeds oblong, alveolate, truncate. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Before it flowers it is a rosette of matt, hairy leaves (grey-felted beneath) with scalloped edges, the base narrowing into a winged stalk. The side veins curve forward to run almost parallel with the midrib. White-flowered plants are often found among the purple ones. It flowers from October to January. In its first year it grows only the rosette, which stays green through winter; the flower spike rises from it the next spring. On wild plants the flowers hang along one side of the spike; garden strains may carry them all round it, and are also sold in white and apricot.

lookalikes.howToTell: Broad-leaved dock's leaves are glossy, hairless above, with smooth, slightly wavy edges and a heart-shaped to rounded base, and each leaf stalk is wrapped at its base by a papery sheath (ochrea); foxglove's are matt and hairy (sometimes almost hairless above), grey-felted beneath, with scalloped edges and a base that narrows into a winged stalk, and their side veins curve forward to run almost parallel with the midrib.
lookalikes.name: Broad-leaved dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Curled dock's leaves are smooth, with strongly wavy, curled edges, and each leaf stalk is wrapped at its base by a papery sheath (ochrea); foxglove's are matt and hairy (sometimes almost hairless above), grey-felted beneath, with scalloped edges, and their side veins curve forward to run almost parallel with the midrib. Both narrow into the stalk.
lookalikes.name: Curled dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Lesser burdock's basal leaves are broadly triangular, 25–40 cm long (15–55) and 13–30 cm wide, with a heart-shaped base and a hollow stalk; foxglove's are lance-shaped to oval, 10–25 cm long and 3.5–12 cm wide, narrowing gradually into a long, winged stalk, with side veins that curve forward to run almost parallel with the midrib. Both are felted beneath and have scalloped edges, so those don't separate them. Foxglove flowers from October to January in a tall spike of hanging bells; burdock flowers from January to April in thistle-like heads that become burs.
lookalikes.name: Lesser burdock

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mullein's rosette leaves are covered all over in greyish or white star-shaped hairs that stay woolly, on top as well as underneath, and are only shortly stalked; foxglove's are hairy to almost hairless on top, grey-felted underneath, and narrow into a long, winged stalk. Both have finely scalloped edges, their leaf sizes overlap, and both grow on poor pastures, stony river beds and roadsides, so none of those tells them apart. Mullein flowers in a dense, woolly spike of flat yellow flowers 1.5–2.5 cm (rarely 3 cm) across; foxglove in a spike of nodding pinkish-purple or white bells. Mullein's leaves and flowers are made into tea, strained of their irritating hairs; its seeds are not eaten.
lookalikes.name: Common mullein

summary.text: Foxglove is native to western Europe and Morocco and was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1867. It is a serious weed and one of the commonest naturalised plants in the wetter parts of the country, and it is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds. It was once grown in New Zealand as a source of the drug digitalin; its leaves are the source of digitoxin, still used for heart failure. It is still sold here by seed companies and nurseries as a garden flower, and it self-seeds freely. The genus name comes from the Latin digitus, finger, for the shape of the flowers, and purpurea means purple. It is now placed in the plantain family (Plantaginaceae); older New Zealand books put it in the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae).

warnings: Every part is poisonous, to people and to some animals. The leaves, flowers and seeds contain cardiac glycosides (digitoxin and digoxin) that cause a slow pulse, nausea, vomiting and an irregular heartbeat, and can stop the heart.
Its leaves have been eaten by mistake for edible greens: in Italy a woman needed cardiac intensive care after eating a homemade pie made with five foxglove leaves sold to her as borage.
Before the flower spike appears, the rosettes can look like dock and burdock.

identification.text:
Much-branched, usually evergreen shrub up to 2.5 m high; twigs villous, particularly when young, round and ribbed. Leaves usually sparsely to densely clothed in appressed hairs on both surfaces, sometimes subglabrous above, petiolate, 3-foliolate; leaflets shortly petiolulate, obovate, acute to obtuse and shortly mucronate, 7–20–(30) × (3)–4–10–(12) mm; terminal leaflet larger than lateral leaflets; stipules triangular to lanceolate, up to 2.5 mm long. Inflorescence a cluster, with axis shorter than 10 mm long, of 4–7 flowers, terminating short lateral branches; pedicels about 3 mm long. Calyx densely hairy, bilabiate; upper lip deeply 2-fid; lower lip shortly 3-lobed. Corolla yellow to golden yellow, 9–13 mm long; standard glabrous. Pod densely villous, oblong, 3–6-seeded, about 18–20 mm long; seeds green to black, ellipsoid or orbicular, flattened, about 2.5 mm diameter.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Teline monspessulana (L.) K.Koch]
Reduced forms of Montpellier broom with smaller leaves and fewer and smaller flowers sometimes occur in very dry situations.
It flowers from May to November. Older stems are ridged, woody and grey-brown. Ripe pods turn dark brown to black, and once they have burst open they twist into a coil.

lookalikes.howToTell: Sweet broom's flowers are in elongated racemes at the ends of the shoots, 10–30 or more on a stalk 10–130 mm long, and are 13–18 mm long; Montpellier broom's are in clusters of 4–7 at the ends of short side branches, on a stalk under 10 mm long, and are 9–13 mm long. Sweet broom can grow into a small tree up to 6 m high; Montpellier broom is a shrub up to 2.5 m. Both have leaves of three leaflets, and their hairiness overlaps, so leaves do not separate them. Plants with shorter, fewer-flowered racemes (stalk about 10–30 mm) are naturalised here; they may be the garden hybrid Cytisus × spachianus or hybrids between the two, and in hybrids the cluster stalk can reach about 4 cm, so a plant in between cannot be named from its flowers. Neither is eaten.
lookalikes.name: Sweet broom

lookalikes.howToTell: Gorse is sharply spiny: on a grown plant the leaves are reduced to spines, the main ones rigid, furrowed and 15–30 mm long. Montpellier broom has no spines, and its leaves have three leaflets all its life. Gorse's flowers are single, 13–20 mm long; Montpellier broom's are 9–13 mm long, in clusters of 4–7 at the ends of short side branches. Gorse seedlings have leaves of three hairy leaflets, so a seedling's leaves do not separate it from broom. Both grow in scrub, waste places and coastal places.
lookalikes.name: Gorse

lookalikes.howToTell: Scotch broom's twigs are green and more or less five-angled, it loses its leaves, and its flowers are single or paired in the leaf angles, 16–25 mm long, with a hairless calyx; its pods are black, 15–60 mm long, hairy only along the edges. Montpellier broom's twigs are round and ribbed, it is usually evergreen, and its flowers are 9–13 mm long in clusters of 4–7 at the ends of short side branches, with a densely hairy calyx; its pods are densely hairy all over, about 18–20 mm long. Both have leaves of three leaflets and yellow pea flowers, and grow in waste places and scrub.

summary.text:
Genista monspessulana, commonly known as French broom, Montpellier broom, or Cape broom (Australia), is a woody leguminous perennial shrub. It is native to the Mediterranean, Asia Minor and the Azores. While it may still be commonly sold in some garden stores, it is considered an invasive plant in most places where it has been introduced.
G. monspessulana and related plants are common in European shrublands.
In New Zealand: locally common throughout the North Island, and throughout the South Island except Westland; naturalised by 1872. The species has been previously known in New Zealand as Cytisus monspessulanus or C. candicans; early records of C. capensis are also referable to T. monspessulana.
Its pods burst open explosively on warm days, throwing the seed.
The plant begins seed production once it reaches a height of approximately 40 cm, and each plant can live for 10–20 years. One mature plant can produce 10,000 seeds per season. The generous seed production and the plant's ability to re-sprout after cutting or burning help it to invade new habitat vigorously when introduced.
It was brought to New Zealand as an ornamental. Other English names for it are Canary broom and soft broom.
It first flowers when about two years old. The bursting pods throw seed 1–5 m from the plant, and the seed is carried further by machinery, moving soil and water, and by ants and birds. The seeds are hard-coated and can stay alive in the soil for more than 20 years; fire and soil disturbance set off mass germination of this seed bank.
As a legume it fixes nitrogen. On gumland and other poor soils the extra nitrogen can let forest plants or further weeds crowd out the specialised orchids, ferns and herbs that grow there.
In South Africa, where it is not yet a major invader, soil under established stands held 909 to 22,727 seeds per square metre (median 1,970), and 60% of plants resprouted after being cut and their stumps treated with herbicide.
It is considered toxic to stock that graze it heavily, but no cases of poisoning have been reported in Australia.

warnings: French broom flowers, and perhaps all parts, are toxic.
French broom foliage and seeds contain a variety of quinolizidine alkaloids, especially in young leaves.
The leaves and seeds contain alkaloids which are poisonous to many large domestic animals.

It is a pest plant in New Zealand: it is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and the regional pest management plans of Auckland, Gisborne, Manawatū-Whanganui, Canterbury, Otago and the Chatham Islands name it.

edibleParts.text: The aerial parts and leaves, as a flavouring and in drinks. In Morocco the aerial parts are drunk; in Algeria they are boiled beneath couscous as it steams, to scent it; in Spain the aerial part is used to make a liqueur, and the leaves to season olives. Each use is recorded from a single area, by few people, and the main databases of useful plants list no edible use for this species.

identification.text:
Bushy shrub to about 1 m high, often grey and with stellate tomentum, strongly aromatic. Leaves sessile, linear to narrow-oblong, sometimes revolute, mostly 2–3 cm long, pinnate with obtuse leaflets to pinnatifid or crenulate, with scattered simple hairs in the stellate tomentum. Peduncle to 30 cm long, much longer than spike; spike 3–4.5 cm long, broad-cylindric, dense. Fertile bracts 7–11 mm long, broad-ovate, apiculate, purplish; sterile apical bracts 7–10 mm long, ovate, ovate-lanceolate, to nearly elliptic, mauve-blue. Calyx 5–7 mm long, tubular, more or less tomentose outside; dorsal appendage broadly reniform to suborbicular, more or less mucronate. Corolla 8–10 mm long; tube longer than calyx by about 2 mm; limb mauve, somewhat irregular; lobes 1.5–2.5 mm long. Nutlets about 1.5 mm long, oblong, not mucilaginous when wet.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is distinguished from all other species in section Stoechas by its pinnate or toothed leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: French lavender's leaves are toothed or cut along the edges (pinnate-dentate), much less commonly only scalloped; topped lavender's leaves are entire. French lavender's flowers are mauve; topped lavender's are dark purple. French lavender's flower stalk, up to 30 cm, is much longer than its spike; topped lavender's is about as long as its spike. The sterile bracts crowning the spike are 7–10 mm long in French lavender, 1–2 cm in topped lavender. Wetted, topped lavender's nutlets turn mucilaginous; French lavender's do not. Leaves that are often grey with star-shaped hairs, a strong aromatic smell and a crown of sterile bracts on the spike do not separate them: both belong to the same section of the genus.

summary.text:
Lavandula dentata, the fringed lavender or French lavender, is a species of flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae, native to the Mediterranean basin, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Yemen, and the Arabian Peninsula.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: naturalised around old house sites in 2 former settlements on Rangitoto Island. Toothed lavender is a very common cultigen in lowland areas of the North Island and northern parts of the South Island. The common name French lavender is sometimes wrongly applied to this species; it should be reserved for L. stoechas.
Other names: toothed lavender (Flora of New Zealand Online, NZPCN); fringed lavender (Wikipedia).

warnings: No toxicity study of this plant in people or other mammals was found. Its essential oil contains camphor, at 15.62% to 49.75% in Moroccan samples, and in some plants is mostly 1,8-cineole; its make-up varies widely between plants.

edibleParts.text: The leaves and stems are edible, and are widely collected for food. Leaves - raw or cooked. A very mild flavour with a mucilaginous texture, they make a very acceptable part of a mixed salad, or a good filling for a salad sandwich, though they are somewhat boring on their own. The cooked leaf has a rather slimy texture. Seed - raw. Best used before it is fully mature, the seed has a pleasant nutty taste but it is rather small and fiddly to harvest.

identification.text:
Annual or short-lived perennial, procumbent, ascending or erect herb. Stems sparsely to moderately hairy with usually simple hairs. Leaves glabrous to sparsely hairy with usually simple hairs and rarely stellate hairs above, sparsely to moderately hairy below, reniform to orbicular, obtuse to cordate at base, shallowly or moderately 5–7-palmately lobed and crenate, 1–10–(15) cm diameter; petioles 1–20–(30) cm long; stipules broadly ovate with acute apex, 2–8 mm long. Flowers in axillary clusters of (1)–2–6; fruiting pedicels 2–10–(15) mm long; epicalyx segments narrowly ovate-oblong to broadly ovate, more or less equal to calyx at flowering; calyx teeth broadly ovate-triangular, sparsely hairy with simple or stellate hairs and ciliate on teeth but lower tube more or less glabrous, slightly enlarged at fruiting; petals pale lilac or pink with darker veins and tips, about 2× length of calyx, 6–10 mm long. Mericarps 8–9–(10) per fruit, often hairy when immature but usually becoming glabrous, strongly reticulately veined on back; edges sharply angled but not winged.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
New Zealand material has petals shorter than the 10–12 mm given in European Floras, possibly indicating that plants have come from the eastern part of the species' range. M. nicaeensis is distinguished from small forms of M. sylvestris by the glabrous base of the calyx tube, from M. neglecta by the strongly reticulately veined mericarps, and from M. parviflora by the squared edges of the mericarps and longer petals.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. They are separated by the edges of the fruit segments (squared in French mallow, slightly winged in cheeseweed mallow) and French mallow's longer petals. Both have strongly net-veined fruit, so the veining does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. French mallow is separated from small forms of common mallow by the hairless base of the calyx tube (hairy in common mallow); common mallow also has slightly longer petals and longer fruiting stalks. Both have strongly net-veined fruit segments, so the veining does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. The fruit separates them: strongly net-veined on the back in French mallow, smooth or faintly veined (and hairy) in dwarf mallow. Petal lengths overlap (6–10 mm against (7–)8–15 mm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and are unchanged in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.

preparation.text: They make an excellent garnish when chopped and fried in olive-oil with onions and spices. A particularly famous preparation are the Khubeza patties. In Villarino de los Aires (Salamanca, Spain) the green, unripe fruits are eaten raw.

recipes.method: Written for mallow in general; the page names no species. The author was told by Turkish cooks that large mallow leaves are used as wrappers for dolma, and went looking for the biggest-leaved mallows they could find. Serves 8. Large mallow leaves, about 240 ml short- or medium-grain rice (not long-grain, which sets hard when cold), about 240 ml water, ½ onion, finely chopped, about 225 g fresh mushrooms, finely chopped, about 80 ml pesto, 3 tbsp (45 ml) olive oil, and salt. Prepare the leaves as you would grape leaves: boil them in salted water for a minute or two, cool them in iced water, and let them drip dry. Heat a large frying pan over high heat, add the mushrooms and shake the pan often until they give up their water. When most of it has gone, add the onion, oil and a little salt and fry until the onion starts to colour. Add the rice, toast it for a minute, then add about 240 ml water and a little salt, turn the heat to medium and cook until the water is absorbed. Take off the heat, let the rice cool, and stir in the pesto (with a little more oil if the pesto is dry). Lay a leaf smooth side down, base towards you, and put about a tablespoon of filling in a short log across the bottom, leaving at least 1 cm clear at each side. Fold the bottom up once, fold in the sides and roll up; leaves vary in size, so adjust the filling to suit. Pack the rolls seam side down and snug together in a steamer insert or on the bottom of a large pot, up to three layers deep; mallow rolls do not need weighing down. Add water to just below the rolls, cover, bring to the boil and steam gently for 40 minutes to an hour, until the rice is no longer crunchy. Serve warm or at room temperature; they keep a week in the fridge.

summary.text:
Malva nicaeensis is a species of flowering plant in the mallow family known by the common names bull mallow and French mallow. It grows in the Middle East, where it has variously served as food.
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North Island and in Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury and North Otago. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1957, though Flora of New Zealand says it was present much longer and had been confused with other mallows.

habitat.text: Monstera deliciosa is native to humid tropical forests, in lowlands and on lower mountains, in the south of Mexico and also in Costa Rica, Guatemala and Panama. The seeds fall to the ground, then the seedlings crawl (negative phototropism) until they meet a tree on which to attach. The many adjacent roots thus allow the plant to anchor against its new support and reach the canopy light (although it rarely grows in full sun and prefers a light dimmed by the foliage).

identification.text:
This member of the arum family (Araceae) is a hemiepiphyte with aerial roots. It is able to grow up to 20 m high in the wild, with large, leathery, glossy, pinnate, heart-shaped leaves 25–90 cm long by 25–75 cm broad. The leaves on young plants are smaller and entire with no lobes or holes, but soon produce lobed and fenestrate leaves as they grow. Although it can grow very tall in nature, it only measures between 2 and 3 m when grown indoors. The older the plant, the more the leaves are covered with its familiar large perforations. The exact purpose of the fenestrations remains unclear, but three main theories have been brought forth: increasing water absorption, limiting the damage done by the wind and reducing the impact of herbivores. 
Wild seedlings grow towards the darkest area they can grow until they find a tree trunk, then start to grow up towards the light, creeping up the tree.
The inflorescence is adorned with a cream-white spathe of uniform, velvety appearance, covering, like a hood, a yellowish white spadix 10 to 15 cm high and about 3 cm in diameter. Flowers are bisexual, containing both androecium and gynoecium, though protogynous development reduces self-pollination; in the wild they are pollinated mainly by nitidulid beetles.


Fruit

The fruit of Monstera deliciosa is up to 25 cm long and 3–5 cm diameter, and it looks like a green ear of maize covered with hexagonal scales. As the fruit ripens, these scales or platelets fall off the fruit, releasing a strong and sweet scent. The smell has been compared to a combination of pineapples and bananas. The fruit is edible and safe for humans.
Fruits of plants of the Araceae (Arum family) often contain raphides and trichosclereids – needle-like structures of calcium oxalate. In M. deliciosa, unripe fruit containing these needle-like crystalline structures can cause irritation of the mouth.
It takes longer than a year for fruits to reach maturity. The fruit first shows signs of ripening by the yellowing of its lowest scales. As it ripens, the starch that was stored in the green fruit is converted to sugar, giving it its sweet flavor. This mechanism is comparable to how banana fruits ripen. The strong odor the fruit produces becomes noticeable when it is half-ripe. As time passes and the fruit continues to ripen, the odor becomes stronger. After it becomes fully ripe, however, the scent deteriorates quickly.
