identification.text:
Gynodioecious, deciduous shrub or small tree, more or less erect and bushy or lianoid; trunk to about 20 cm thick when of tree form; bark more or less peeling. Branchlets hairy when young. Petioles slender, often filiform, 0.5–5.5 cm long, more or less hairy, particularly on upper side. Lamina (2)–3–8–(10) × (1)–2–4 cm, usually ovate to broad-ovate or ovate-oblong, less commonly suborbicular, elliptic or lanceolate-ovate, green above, glaucous or silvery beneath, often suffused with red or purple; midrib and sometimes main lateral veins hairy beneath; base usually broad-cuneate, truncate or rounded, occasionally subcordate; apex rounded to obtuse and mucronate, or acute to acuminate. Flowers solitary or few in clusters, on young shoots or more or less cauliflorous, usually pendulous; pedicels 7–15 mm long, filiform. Floral tube 8–20 mm long, more or less purple. Sepals 6–14 mm long, narrow-triangular, green or purplish, eventually more or less reflexed. Petals 1–5 mm long, dark purple, elliptic. Stamens of ☿ flowers well-exserted; filaments 6–10 mm long, more or less purple. Style 1.7–3.5 cm long, much longer than stamens; stigma capitate. Berry about 10 mm long, ellipsoid-oblong, dark purple or almost black.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
A shrub, much-branched from the base; branchlets slender, sometimes scandent; leaves ovate to orbicular, usually less than 5 cm long. Plants are intermediate in size and habit between tree fuchsia and scrambling fuchsia.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the trunk and branching: tree fuchsia is a tree with a distinct trunk, to about 12 m high with a trunk to 60 cm thick, and keeps its trunked form even when it is much reduced in exposed places; Fuchsia ×colensoi is a shrub much-branched from the base, with slender branchlets that sometimes climb, or a small tree with a trunk to about 20 cm thick. Look at the leaves: tree fuchsia's are usually lance-shaped to narrowly egg-shaped or oblong, usually more than 5 cm long, with a pointed to drawn-out tip; Fuchsia ×colensoi's are usually egg-shaped to broadly egg-shaped or oblong-egg-shaped, less often almost round, usually less than 5 cm long, with a rounded to blunt tip ending in a short point, or a pointed to drawn-out one. Leaf size and shape overlap (tree fuchsia 2–14 cm long, sometimes 1.5 cm; Fuchsia ×colensoi 3–8 cm, sometimes 2 cm or 10 cm, and both can have oblong-egg-shaped leaves), and tree fuchsia has smaller leaves in exposed places, so leaves alone do not separate them. Flowers and berries do not separate them: the floral tube (tree fuchsia 7–20 mm, Fuchsia ×colensoi 8–20 mm), the sepals (5–16 mm against 6–14 mm) and the berries (both about 10 mm long, ellipsoid-oblong, dark purple to almost black) overlap. Fuchsia ×colensoi is intermediate in size and habit between tree fuchsia and scrambling fuchsia, probably their hybrid though this is not confirmed, and in many areas grows with both. Tree fuchsia's ripe berries are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Tree fuchsia

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the main stems: scrambling fuchsia is a liane whose stout main stems, to about 5 m long and 5 cm thick, sprawl when they lack support; Fuchsia ×colensoi is usually a shrub or small tree whose branches may be slender and scrambling but not its main stems, though some plants are lianoid. Without support, both can form a somewhat similar ball-like shrub of interlacing branchlets. Look at the leaves: scrambling fuchsia's are broadly egg-shaped to almost round, usually 25–30 mm long, with a slightly heart-shaped to squared-off base; Fuchsia ×colensoi's are usually egg-shaped to broadly egg-shaped or oblong-egg-shaped, less often almost round, usually 3–8 cm long, with the base usually broadly wedge-shaped, squared-off or rounded, occasionally slightly heart-shaped. Leaf size overlaps (scrambling fuchsia 25–30 mm, sometimes 10 mm; Fuchsia ×colensoi 3–8 cm, sometimes 2 cm or 10 cm), so a plant with small, round leaves may be either. Flowers and berries do not separate them: the floral tube (scrambling fuchsia 7–15 mm, Fuchsia ×colensoi 8–20 mm), the sepals (6–10 mm against 6–14 mm) and the dark purple berries (5–10 mm against about 10 mm) overlap. Fuchsia ×colensoi is intermediate in size and habit between scrambling fuchsia and tree fuchsia, probably their hybrid though this is not confirmed, and in many areas grows with both. No food record written for scrambling fuchsia was found (see its page).

summary.text:
Fuchsia ×colensoi is an endemic New Zealand fuchsia, probably the hybrid of tree fuchsia (Fuchsia excorticata) and scrambling fuchsia (Fuchsia perscandens).
The hybrid nature of F. × colensoi has not been confirmed, but plants are intermediate in size and habit between the putative parents, F. excorticata and F. perscandens. In many areas it occurs with both putative parents, but is also sometimes found where one or both are absent. It is often commoner than F. perscandens but seldom commoner than F. excorticata.
Field evidence makes it almost certain that a number of forms attributed to F. colensoi are the progeny of the cross F. excorticata × perscandens.
It grows on the North Island, locally from the Waikato southwards, throughout much of the South Island, where it is common in many areas, and on Stewart Island. It has also been collected wild in Northland, in a small streamside swamp at Pipiwai.

warnings: Its food record is thin: a plant database and an overseas nursery record the berries as eaten, and no New Zealand record written for this fuchsia was found. That they are harmless also rests on a general record for all New Zealand's native fuchsias.
It often grows with tree fuchsia and scrambling fuchsia and is intermediate between them, so check the trunk, stems and leaves (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
Erect, monoecious annual, sparingly branched, farinose at least when young, sometimes brownish purple or reddish purple. Stems to 2.5 m high, much less in impoverished soil, stout, angular. Leaves below inflorescence (excluding those at base of plant) with petioles to 5 cm long; lamina 5–30 × 3–20 cm, triangular-hastate, ovate, or sagittate-ovate, narrower in inflorescence, irregularly dentate, sinuate, to almost entire; base deeply or shallowly cordate to truncate; apex rounded to acute. Inflorescence terminal, narrow-paniculate, to 40 cm long; branches slender. male flowers: perianth about 0.5 mm long, green with hyaline margin. female flowers: dimorphic, most with 2 bracteoles and perianth 0, otherwise with 5-lobed perianth and bracteoles 0. Bracteoles free, orbicular or suborbicular, very shortly stalked, entire, without appendages or tubercles, strongly accrescent, 6–12–(15) mm diameter at fruiting. Fruit circular to broad-elliptic, flattened, dimorphic: in perianth flowers 1.5–2.5 mm diameter and horizontal, in bracteolate flowers 2.5–4.3 mm diameter and vertical; pericarp removed fairly easily. Testa shining black, almost smooth.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The reddish purple form grows wild alongside the commoner green one, especially in Central Otago.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the habit and the fruit. Garden orache is erect, usually over 75 cm tall, with a stout, rigid, angled main stem; its lower leaves are 5–30 cm long on stalks up to 5 cm, triangular-arrow-shaped or ovate, with a heart-shaped to squared-off base. Common orache is prostrate or spreading, sometimes with an erect main stem but otherwise lax, with ribbed, more or less slender stems and leaves 2–7 cm long, mostly narrowly lance-shaped to elliptic with a wedge-shaped base. In fruit, most of garden orache's female flowers sit between two free, round, untoothed bracteoles with no bumps or appendages, 6–15 mm across; common orache's bracteoles are triangular, joined in their lower part and usually 2.5–8.5 mm long.
lookalikes.name: Common orache

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the habit and the fruit. Garden orache is erect, usually over 75 cm tall, with a stout, rigid, angled main stem; its lower leaves are 5–30 cm long on stalks up to 5 cm. Spear-leaved orache is prostrate or spreading to nearly erect, with more or less slender stems; its lower leaves are 1–9 cm long on slender stalks 1–2.5 cm long, mostly triangular-arrow-shaped and toothed above the basal lobes. In fruit, most of garden orache's female flowers sit between two free, round, untoothed bracteoles with no bumps or appendages, 6–15 mm across; spear-leaved orache's are triangular-arrow-shaped to ovate, usually toothed and generally with appendages, up to 9 mm long. Large-fruited spear-leaved orache can have bigger bracteoles without appendages, so check the habit and leaves too.
lookalikes.name: Spear-leaved orache

preparation.text: Leaves picked before the plant is about 15 cm tall make a mild, tender salad leaf; older leaves are better steamed, stir-fried, added to soups or cooked like spinach, and large ones can be wrapped around a filling. Pinch out the growing tips again and again and eat them as spinach. The taste is salty and spinach-like, and the red forms taste the same as the green but turn a dish pink. Cook it with sorrel to soften sorrel's sourness. Keep the leaves in a bag in the fridge and use them within a few days. Grind the seed into a meal for soups, or mix it with flour for bread; it is small and fiddly to harvest.

recipes.method: Written for red garden orache. Serves 4. 3 bunches of garden orache, red or green; 1 carrot; 1 onion; 100 g rice; 10 black peppercorns; 1–2 eggs; 250–500 ml (1–2 cups) borș (the Romanian fermented wheat-bran liquid), or lemon juice, vinegar or sauerkraut juice to taste instead; salt; a small bunch of fresh lovage; 3 litres water; sour cream, to serve. Finely chop the onion, grate the carrot and cut the orache leaves into thin strips. Put the water and peppercorns in a large pot with the onion, carrot and orache, bring to the boil and simmer for 20 minutes. Add the rice and simmer for 10 minutes more, until it is tender. Heat the borș in a small pan until it just boils, then stir it into the soup a little at a time, tasting, until it is as sour as you like. Whisk the egg and pour it slowly into the boiling soup, stirring all the time, so it sets in ribbons. Season well with salt, turn off the heat and stir in the chopped lovage. Serve hot, with sour cream on the side.
recipes.title: Romanian orache soup (ciorbă de lobodă)

recipes.method: Washed garden orache leaves, on their own or with green lettuce; 1 garlic clove, roughly chopped; a pinch of salt; a scant 5 ml (1 tsp) Dijon mustard; 10 ml (2 tsp) plum jam, or any other jam; 60 ml (4 tbsp) rice wine vinegar; 120 ml (½ cup) extra-virgin olive oil. Blend the garlic, salt, mustard, jam, vinegar and oil until smooth. Dress the leaves with it and add other chopped vegetables if you like.
recipes.title: Garden orache salad with plum jam dressing

recipes.method: About 2 cups of garden orache leaves, washed and roughly chopped; 1 onion, chopped, or garlic instead; 15–30 ml (1–2 tbsp) olive oil; salt and pepper; 2 cups hot cooked pasta, preferably a twisted shape; optional: toasted pine nuts or walnuts, crumbled blue cheese or grated parmesan. Fry the onion in the oil over a moderately high heat until soft. If you are using garlic, add it now, with the orache, salt and pepper, so it does not burn. Cook until the leaves wilt, about 2 minutes. Toss with the hot pasta and any of the extras, and serve.
recipes.title: Pasta with garden orache

summary.text:
Atriplex hortensis, known as garden orache, red orache or simply orache (also spelled orach), mountain spinach, French spinach, or arrach, is a species of plant in the amaranth family used as a leaf vegetable that was common before spinach; it is still grown as a warm-weather alternative to spinach. It is native to eastern Europe and western and central Asia.
In New Zealand it has been recorded wild since 1958, in Hawke's Bay and Wellington and in Canterbury and Central Otago, mostly near gardens. Herbarium specimens come mainly from Canterbury, with one from Marlborough. It was presumably brought here to eat but is not commonly grown; the reddish purple cultivar 'Rubra' is sometimes grown and has gone wild with the commoner green form. An early New Zealand record of patience dock (Rumex patientia), a European pot herb unknown here, was probably this plant.
New Zealand heritage seed companies sell green and red forms as a leaf vegetable, and the ruby-and-gold cultivar 'Ruby Gold' is sold for flower gardens for its seed heads, which dry well.
hortensis comes from the Latin hortus 'garden' and means growing in gardens.

warnings: Plants grown on fertilised ground can concentrate harmful amounts of nitrate in their leaves.
The seed contains saponins: cook it thoroughly, changing the water once, and do not eat it in large quantities.
The seeds and fruits are purgative and can cause vomiting.
In herbal medicine the leaves are classed as diuretic, emetic and purgative.

identification.text:
Garden parsley is a bright green, biennial plant in temperate climates, or an annual herb in subtropical and tropical areas.
Where it grows as a biennial, in the first year, it forms a rosette of tripinnate leaves 10–25 cm long with numerous 1–3 cm leaflets, and a taproot used as a food store over the winter. In the second year, it grows a flowering stem to 75 cm tall with sparser leaves and flat-topped 3–10 cm diameter umbels with numerous 2 mm diameter yellow to yellowish-green flowers.
The seeds are ovoid, 2–3 mm long, with prominent style remnants at the apex. One of the compounds of the essential oil is apiole. The plant normally dies after seed maturation.

recipes.method: Written for purslane, with chickweed, parsley and calendula petals; the author gives no amounts. Tear leafy salad greens — lettuce, mizuna, rocket, chickweed, parsley — into a bowl and add chopped purslane, cherry tomatoes and alfalfa sprouts. Decorate it with heartsease pansy flowers and calendula petals, and dress it with lemon juice, olive oil and salt.
recipes.title: Purslane salad

recipes.method: Written for chickweed, nasturtium and onion weed. Soak 500 ml (2 cups) chickpeas overnight, drain and rinse them well, and sprout them for 48 hours, rinsing twice a day, until the tails are as long as the peas; or cook them, as the author also allows. 500 ml (2 cups) sprouted chickpeas; 185 ml (¾ cup) tahini (the author grinds whole sesame seeds instead); 2–4 garlic cloves, minced; the juice of 2 large lemons and 1 orange; 125 ml (½ cup) olive oil; 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt; 5 ml (1 tsp) cumin; a big handful of chickweed, some nasturtium leaves, a small bunch of onion weed leaves and a sprig of parsley or another herb. Process the chickpeas with the citrus juice until still slightly chunky, then add everything else and process to the consistency you want.
recipes.title: Raw chickpea hummus with wild greens

recipes.method: The author's weeds were chickweed, nasturtium, dandelion, pūhā, ox-eye daisy and plantain, with parsley and garden herbs (the page does not say which plantain). She also adds a handful of New Zealand spinach; it is At Risk and its page says to blanch it first, so it is left out here. 5 rosemary sprigs about 12 cm long; a handful of parsley; a big handful of chickweed; 4 large nasturtium leaves; a handful of thyme sprigs 5 cm long; a few dandelion leaves; a small pūhā plant; 10 ox-eye daisy leaves; 8 plantain leaves; 5 sage leaves; 6 garlic cloves; 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt; about 30 ml (⅛ cup) cider vinegar; 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) olive oil, starting with the smaller amount; 5 ml (1 tsp) honey, or to taste; the juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml (½ cup) walnuts. Strip the leaves from the thyme and rosemary and wash any leaves that need it. Blend everything in a high-speed blender or food processor until smooth, pushing it down with the tamper. Keep it in the fridge or freezer.
recipes.title: Wild weed pesto

recipes.method: Written for plantain and dandelion, with celery leaves and parsley (the page does not say which plantain). A small handful of celery leaves; 4 branches of parsley (go easy: it can take over); 4 leaves each of plantain, dandelion and kale. Blend the greens in 750 ml–1 litre (3–4 cups) water, then add 1 banana, 250 ml (1 cup) frozen blueberries, 1 kiwifruit and ½ avocado and blend again.
recipes.title: Thick and creamy green smoothie

habitat.text: Pasture, paddocks and farmland above all, and lawns, gardens, parks and golf courses; also field edges, roadside verges and rank, nutrient-rich waste ground. It lives on dead plant material, in pasture on dead grass and old roots, and one came up on bare, glyphosate-sprayed soil between the vines of a Marlborough vineyard. It turns up occasionally in open woodland and clearings, and in New Zealand has been recorded among needle litter on a forest floor and with macrocarpa. It grows singly, in groups or in rings, and often reappears in the same place for years.

identification.text:
A large ball sitting on the ground with no stem, round, flattened, cushion-shaped or irregularly lobed, usually 15–50 cm across and sometimes much more. It is held to the soil by a cord-like strand of mycelium at the base, which often breaks.
The skin is white and smooth to slightly lumpy when young, with a leathery feel, sometimes wrinkled near the base. With age it turns cream, buff, then yellow-brown, dries, cracks into large plates and flakes away.
Cut it in half from top to bottom. A young one is firm, even, pure white flesh all the way through, like a dense, damp sponge or marshmallow, with no stem, cap, gills or any other shape inside: this is the only stage to eat. As the spores ripen, almost the whole ball turns from white to yellowish olive, then to a dry, powdery, olive-brown to dark brown spore mass.
Small white puffballs (Lycoperdon and other Calvatia species) are also common in New Zealand. Earthballs, stinkhorn eggs and the egg stage of the death cap can look like a young puffball from outside; see the warnings and the lookalike card.

lookalikes.howToTell: A young death cap starts as a white egg inside a veil, and these eggs have been mistaken for puffballs. Cut every puffball in half from top to bottom: a giant puffball is solid, even, pure white flesh with no structure inside, while a death cap egg shows the outline of a cap, gills and stem. Death caps grow with trees, especially oak. Size and an all-white outside do not separate them; only the cut does, so cut every one.
lookalikes.name: Death cap

preparation.text:
Cut every puffball in half from top to bottom before you cook it, and use it only if the inside is pure white throughout. Brush off any dirt, trim the base and peel off the skin, which can get leathery; then slice it into steaks or dice it.
The taste is mild, like a field or button mushroom, and the texture like tofu or a soft marshmallow. It soaks up flavour and a great deal of butter or oil, and a squeeze of lemon or a dash of vinegar lifts it. Fry or grill slices until browned (overcooked, they turn tough), coat them in breadcrumbs, since the outside can turn a little slimy when cooked, or add diced puffball to sauces, stir-fries, soups, scrambled eggs and pasta.
It keeps for 4 to 5 days in the fridge. To freeze it, fry the cubes in a little butter until their moisture has cooked off and they start to brown, then cool and freeze them; or crumb raw slices, freeze them flat and fry them from frozen within 3 months.

recipes.method: A giant puffball; bacon; garlic; devilled kidneys, to roast it whole. Thickly slice a giant puffball and fry the slices like steaks with bacon and garlic. Or hollow out a smallish one, fill it with devilled kidneys, wrap it in bacon and roast it whole — the author's favourite. Good as a creamy addition to a mushroom risotto, diced.
recipes.title: Giant puffball, fried or roasted whole

recipes.method: Written for mixed wild mushrooms — the author's are puffball (giant or common), dried porcini (cep) and chanterelles. Serves 4. 2 litres good chicken or vegetable stock; 30 g dried porcini; 150 g chanterelles; 1 large onion, finely diced; 3 garlic cloves; 3 bay leaves; 1 courgette, finely diced; 1 small leek, finely diced; 100 g butter; a few sprigs of thyme; 300 g unwashed carnaroli or arborio rice; 300 ml dry white wine; 150 g puffball, peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes; 300 g parmesan, finely grated; 75 ml double cream; a handful of parsley and tarragon, finely chopped; the juice of 1 lemon; a few drops of truffle oil; a sprinkle of hairy bittercress (optional). Heat 2 litres of good chicken or vegetable stock in a separate pan and add 30 g dried porcini to soak and enrich it. Sweat 150 g chanterelles in a frying pan until they give up their juice, and strain the juice into the stock. In a heavy pan, sweat 1 finely diced large onion, 3 garlic cloves, 3 bay leaves, and 1 courgette and 1 small leek (both finely diced) in 50 g of 100 g butter until soft and translucent. Add a few sprigs of thyme and 300 g unwashed carnaroli or arborio rice and stir over a medium heat for a couple of minutes. Add 300 ml dry white wine and keep stirring as it absorbs. Add 150 g puffball, peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes, and the soaked porcini with a little hot stock. Keep stirring briskly, adding the stock a ladleful at a time; when about half is in, add the chanterelles. Season, and stop when the rice keeps a hint of bite (no chalkiness) and the risotto is like a very thick soup — you may not need all the stock. Off the heat, stir in half of 300 g finely grated parmesan, the remaining 50 g butter, 75 ml double cream and a handful of finely chopped parsley and tarragon. Cover and rest for a few minutes. Stir in the juice of 1 lemon, check the seasoning and add a little more stock if needed. Serve in shallow bowls with a few drops of truffle oil, the rest of the cheese on the side, and, if you like, a sprinkle of hairy bittercress for a sharp note.
recipes.title: Ultimate wild mushroom risotto

recipes.method: Serves 4. 2 tbsp oil; 4 slices of giant puffball, peeled, each about 2 cm thick and 10 cm square; 35 g sweet rice flour or plain flour; ½ tsp salt; 1 tsp pepper, divided; 2 eggs; 25 g finely grated parmesan; 40 g instant polenta or fine cornmeal; ½ tsp garlic powder; 250 ml or more tomato pasta sauce; about 150 g grated mozzarella. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Mix the flour with the salt and half the pepper in one shallow bowl, beat the eggs in a second, and mix the parmesan, polenta, garlic powder and the rest of the pepper in a third. Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Coat each slice in flour, then egg, then the parmesan mixture, covering every surface, and fry for 2–3 minutes a side until deep golden. Lay them in a baking dish with a little space between them, spoon a generous 60 ml of tomato sauce down the middle of each and pile about 60 ml of mozzarella on top. Bake for 30 minutes, until the cheese is bubbling and golden in spots. To freeze, lay the crumbed, uncooked slices apart on baking paper, freeze them solid, then bag them for up to 3 months; fry them from frozen, then add the sauce and cheese and bake.
recipes.title: Puffball parmigiana

recipes.method: Serves 4. 2 tbsp oil; 1 tbsp minced ginger; 3 garlic cloves, minced; 1 jalapeño with its seeds, minced (or 1–2 Thai chillies, or ¼–½ tsp dried chilli flakes); 1 onion, diced; 1 red capsicum, in 2 cm pieces; 450 g giant puffball, peeled, in 2 cm cubes; 375 ml chicken stock, divided; 60 ml soy sauce; 3 tbsp dark brown sugar; 2 tbsp white vinegar; 2 tbsp cornflour; 4–5 spring onions, sliced on a steep diagonal; 125 ml roasted salted peanuts or cashews, roughly chopped; cooked rice to serve. Heat the oil over medium heat in a large heavy pan, add the garlic, ginger and chilli, and stir for 1 minute. Add the onion and capsicum and cook for 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until the onion is translucent, then add the puffball. Mix 250 ml of the stock with the soy sauce, sugar and vinegar, pour it over, bring to the boil and cook for 5 minutes, stirring now and then. Stir the cornflour into the remaining stock, stir it into the bubbling pan with the spring onions and cook until thickened, about 30 seconds. Sprinkle with the nuts and serve over rice.
recipes.title: Sweet and sour puffball

recipes.method: Slices of giant puffball 1–2 cm thick, peeled (whole rounds for large pizzas, smaller pieces for single serves or bites); olive oil; tomato pasta or pizza sauce; dried oregano; your choice of thinly sliced toppings (ham, salami, onion, capsicum, tomato); grated mozzarella; grated parmesan (optional). Brush both sides of each slice with olive oil, then cook the slices until browned and a little dried out, so they are firm enough to hold the toppings: grill them on a barbecue over medium heat for about 10 minutes a side, roast them on a rack over a baking tray at 220 °C for 30 minutes, turning once, or fry them in a little extra oil until golden and drain on paper towels. They can be kept in the fridge for several days, or frozen and topped straight from frozen. Lay them on a baking tray, spread with a thin layer of sauce, sprinkle with oregano, add the toppings, cover with mozzarella and a little parmesan, and bake at 200 °C for 15–20 minutes, until the cheese is bubbling and golden in spots. Leave for 5 minutes before serving.
recipes.title: Puffball pizza

recipes.method: Serves 4–6. 3 tbsp butter; 1 onion, diced; 4 garlic cloves, minced; ½ tsp salt, plus more to taste; 450 g giant puffball, peeled, in 2.5 cm cubes; ¼ tsp pepper; grated zest and juice of half a lemon; 60 ml chopped fresh parsley. Heat the butter in a large heavy frying pan, add the onion, garlic and salt and cook for 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until the onion is translucent. Add the puffball and cook, stirring occasionally, until it has shrunk and is golden brown in spots, 5–10 minutes. Add the pepper and lemon zest and cook for 1 minute more, then squeeze over the lemon juice, scatter with parsley, toss and season to taste. Serve with chicken, fish or pork.
recipes.title: Sautéed puffball with lemon and garlic

recipes.method: Serves 4–6. 450 g giant puffball, peeled; 35 g sweet rice flour or plain flour; ½ tsp salt; 2 eggs; 45 g finely grated parmesan; 80 g instant polenta or fine cornmeal; 1 tsp garlic powder; 1 tsp pepper; a dipping sauce. Heat the oven to 220 °C. Cut the puffball into thick chips about 1 cm square and 7.5 cm long. Mix the flour and salt in one shallow bowl, beat the eggs in a second, and mix the parmesan, polenta, garlic powder and pepper in a third. Coat each chip in flour, then egg (tap off the excess), then the parmesan mixture, covering every surface. Lay them apart on an ungreased baking tray and bake for 15–18 minutes, until golden, or fry them in a few tablespoons of oil, turning until golden on every side. To freeze, lay the coated, uncooked chips apart on baking paper, freeze them solid and bag them for up to 3 months; baked from frozen they take a minute or two longer.
recipes.title: Puffball fries

recipes.method: Serves 6. 2–3 tbsp butter or oil; 450 g giant puffball, peeled, in 2.5 cm cubes; ½ tsp salt; 450 g short pasta (macaroni, fusilli or shells); 750 ml tomato- or cream-based pasta sauce; 100 g grated aged cheddar; 300–400 g grated mozzarella. Heat the oven to 180 °C and grease a 23 x 33 cm baking dish. Cook the pasta in boiling salted water until about 2 minutes short of done, still firm in the centre; keep 125 ml of the cooking water and drain. Meanwhile heat the butter or oil in a large frying pan, add the puffball and salt (the pan will be very full, but the puffball shrinks) and cook, stirring now and then, until it has given up its moisture, the liquid has evaporated and the cubes are golden in spots, about 10 minutes. Toss the puffball with the pasta, sauce, reserved water and cheddar, tip into the dish and cover with a thick layer of mozzarella. Bake for about 30 minutes, until the cheese is bubbling and golden in spots.
recipes.title: Cheesy puffball pasta bake

recipes.method: Written for puffball; the page does not name the species. 1 large slice of puffball, about 4 cm thick, peeled; 2 garlic cloves, crushed; 2 tbsp light olive oil; salt to taste. Mix the oil and garlic and brush it generously over the slice. Grill it on a barbecue or grill over medium heat until golden brown and shrunk to about 2 cm thick. Overcooked, it turns tough. Season with salt.
recipes.title: Grilled puffball with garlic oil

recipes.method: Written for puffball; the page does not name the species. 1 small puffball, peeled and cubed (about 500 ml); 1 medium shallot, finely chopped; 4 eggs, well beaten; 3 tbsp butter; salt and pepper or cayenne to taste. Soften the shallot in some of the butter until translucent, add the puffball and sauté until it starts to colour; set it aside. Melt the rest of the butter in a frying pan over medium heat, pour in the eggs, draw in the sides and let the egg spread out again, then spoon the puffball over one half. Cook slowly, fold the other half over, cook briefly and serve, seasoned to taste.
recipes.title: Puffball omelette

recipes.method: Serves 4. 1 giant puffball, peeled and sliced into steaks; 250 ml aquafaba (the liquid from a tin of chickpeas); 250 ml breadcrumbs; 125 ml hot sauce. Heat the oven to 200 °C and line a baking tray with baking paper. Put the aquafaba in one shallow bowl and the breadcrumbs in another. Dip each slice in aquafaba, coat it in breadcrumbs and lay it on the tray with a little space around each piece so they crisp. Bake for about 30 minutes, then brush with hot sauce. It can also be cooked in batches in an air fryer, and barbecue, teriyaki or sweet chilli sauce can replace the hot sauce.
recipes.title: Crispy baked puffball "chicken"

recipes.method: Written for giant puffball or king oyster mushrooms. Serves 4–6. 450 g giant puffball; 4 tbsp butter; 2 tbsp olive oil; 1 tbsp fresh thyme leaves; leaves from 4 sprigs of fresh rosemary, kept in small bunches; 3 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste; 2 tsp freshly ground black pepper. Wipe the puffball clean with a damp paper towel, trim the base so only white flesh remains, peel it if it is large (the skin can get leathery) and cut it into large slices about 6 mm thick. Stud the slices with the rosemary and season with half the salt and pepper. Melt the butter and oil in a large frying pan over medium heat until foaming, lay in the slices and fry until well browned, about 3–4 minutes. Turn them, season with the rest of the salt and pepper, sprinkle with thyme and brown the other side. Serve at once with steak or grilled chicken, or on their own with salad and bread.
recipes.title: Sautéed giant puffball with rosemary and thyme

recipes.method: Serves 3–4. 1 giant puffball, about 24 cm across; about 1 tbsp garlic purée, divided between batches; olive oil or butter for frying; 2 large eggs, beaten; a large handful of plain flour. Southern fried coating (or a ready-made one): 100 g breadcrumbs; a pinch of salt; ½ tsp turmeric; ½ tsp paprika; a pinch of black pepper; 1 level tsp dried oregano; ½ tsp garlic powder; ½ tsp onion powder; a pinch each of dried fennel and dried rosemary. Mix the coating ingredients. Cut the puffball into slabs about 4 cm thick. Heat some oil or butter with a little garlic purée in a frying pan over medium-high heat and fry the slabs in batches until lightly golden on both sides; set them aside. Put the flour, egg and coating in three bowls and dip each slab in each in turn, coating it thoroughly. Return them to the pan and fry on both sides until golden.
recipes.title: Southern fried giant puffball

Not used: 'Some people experience a laxative effect' (its Arora citation is tagged 'Verify source': 'Arora was cited to Clitocybe gigantea'); Lindley's sixty million cells a minute and seven quintillion spores (dropped with the old verbatim text); 'deciduous forests' as a habitat beyond the verbatim first sentence (First Nature: occasionally open woodland).

My favourite recipe is to hollow smallish ones out, fill with devilled kidneys, wrap with bacon and roast whole'. 'Ultimate wild mushroom risotto' (06/11/2011, https://gallowaywildfoods.com/ultimate-wild-mushroom-risotto/): 'Puffballs (giant or common)'; '150g puff ball – peeled and diced into 1cm cubes'; amounts as on porcini. Not used: its claim that Waipukurau 'takes its name from the fungus (Wai = water + pukurau)' (Wikipedia 'Ileodictyon cibarium', citing Vennell 2023, suggests the town may be named for basket fungus soaked there before eating). Biota of NZ 'Calvatia gigantea (Batsch) Lloyd 1904' https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/1cb18049-36b9-11d5-9548-00d0592d548c — Exotic, Present; Māori vernacular names Poketara, Pukurau, Rope atua; basionym Lycoperdon giganteum Batsch 1786, synonym Langermannia gigantea; associations with Agrostis capillaris and Cupressus macrocarpa (PDD); 'recorded by Arnold and Brien (1961) as causing "fairy rings" on greens and fairways in golf courses in New Zealand'; 'common in pastures throughout New Zealand' (summary, habitat). Geoff Ridley, Spores, moulds, and fungi 'Vineyards and giant puffballs' (04/07/2011) https://sporesmouldsandfungi.wordpress.com/2011/07/04/vineyards-and-giant-puffballs/ — not native, 'probably arrived in imported seed used to establish pastures in the nineteenth century'; largest New Zealand find Christchurch 1986, 8 kg, about 40 cm; oldest New Zealand collection Taranaki 1923; Cunningham: 'extremely common in pastures during autumn'; less common now, perhaps from changing farming and land use; pastures and gardens in New Zealand; rots dead grass and old roots; one fruited on glyphosate-treated soil in a Marlborough vineyard; inside turns to a dry khaki spore mass, skin turns brownish, cracks and flakes away; the ripe ball can detach and blow along like a tumbleweed (summary, identification, habitat, warning 4).

Owner's links, continued: The Hidden Forest 'Calvatia gigantea' https://www.hiddenforest.co.nz/fungi/family/lycoperdaceae/lycop05.htm — typically 200–500 mm, exceptionally over 600 mm; globose, lobed, often flattened or cushion-shaped; white, smooth or slightly uneven, ageing cream, buff or yellow-brown, cracking into large plates; firm and fleshy young, brittle and papery when mature; gleba 'When young, white, firm, and homogeneous, this is the edible stage', mature yellow-brown to dark brown and powdery; farmland, parks, golf courses; saprobic on ground; New Zealand; autumn to early winter; exotic; 'Edible: Yes when young'; spore print brown (identification, habitat, edible parts, months). Not used: 'Subgleba: Well developed, forming a thick sterile base' (First Nature: 'virtually the whole of this puffball is filled with fertile spore mass'). Stuff 'Stunned farming family finds giant puffball in Tokoroa paddock' (05/04/2017) https://www.stuff.co.nz/oddstuff/91146712/giant-puffball-found-in-tokoroa-paddock (read through r.jina.ai) — about 50 cm across and 5 kg; Ian Hall: usually in paddocks in late summer and autumn, 'most likely unintentionally brought to New Zealand by settlers', 'found all around the country', the largest he has seen nearly a metre across; edible if the inside is solid white without 'the silhouette of a cap-type mushroom' (summary, habitat, months, death cap card).

Owner's recipe links, 29/10/2026, metric (1 cup = 250 ml, 1 inch = 2.5 cm, the authors' own °C): Kitchen Frau 'The Mighty Mushroom Hunters (and Some Giant Puffball Recipes)' (29/09/2016) https://www.kitchenfrau.com/puffball-recipes/ (ingredient lists read from the page HTML, which r.jina.ai partly dropped) — six recipes used: Puffball Parmigiana, Sweet and Sour Asian Style Puffball, Puffball Pizza, Sauteed Puffball with Lemon and Garlic, Puffball Fries, Cheesy Puffball Pasta Bake. Also used: slice vertically and check for 'markings of gills or a stem inside'; peel the rind; any colour but pure white, don't use it; keeps 4 to 5 days in the fridge; sauté cubes until the moisture cooks out and freeze; freeze crumbed slices up to 3 months; texture like a dense damp sponge, cooked like tofu or a sugarless marshmallow (identification, preparation, warning 1, death cap card). Not used: 'Amanitas also stay small, so if you collect puffballs that are larger than your fist, and the flesh is evenly white inside, you can be assured' (size is no test; only the cut is); 'The rind can cause gastrointestinal upset in some people' (not found elsewhere; peeling is kept on Food52's leathery skin); its Canadian season. summary.text:
Calvatia gigantea, commonly known in English as the giant puffball, is a puffball mushroom found in meadows, fields, and deciduous forests in late summer and autumn.
It is not native to New Zealand. It probably arrived with imported grass seed used to sow pasture in the nineteenth century, and the oldest New Zealand collection is from Taranaki in 1923. It is now found throughout the country, mostly in pasture: the mycologist G. H. Cunningham called it extremely common in pastures in autumn, though it seems less common today, perhaps because farming and land use have changed. With other Calvatia puffballs it has been recorded making fairy rings on New Zealand golf greens and fairways. New Zealand finds of about 40–50 cm across and 5–8 kg have been reported, from Christchurch in 1986 and a Tokoroa paddock in 2017.
Māori names recorded for it include pukurau, poketara and rope atua; pukurau is used for puffballs in general. Māori also used puffballs to stop bleeding and to ease burns. It has also been called Langermannia gigantea and, when first described in 1786, Lycoperdon giganteum; Calvatia means a bald head or skull. A single large fruitbody makes trillions of spores; when it is ripe the skin cracks and flakes away, and the whole ball can break free and roll across the ground in the wind, scattering them.

warnings: Eat it only while it is white all the way through. Once the flesh turns yellowish, olive or brown, the spores are forming and it can upset your stomach; the fruitbody grows in a few weeks and soon starts to rot. Throw out any that are discoloured inside, soft or crumbling.

Earthballs (Scleroderma) can look like a small puffball, and two are common in New Zealand, the potato earthball (S. bovista) and S. macrosporum. Most earthballs are not edible, and the common earthball is poisonous. An earthball's skin is very thick and tough, the ball is much firmer, and its inside turns dark purplish-black, marbled with white, while it is still young. Earthballs grow with trees and shrubs.

A white ball with a layer of jelly inside is a stinkhorn egg, not a puffball. In New Zealand it is usually the basket fungus (tūtae kēhua, Ileodictyon cibarium), whose white eggs grow up to 7 cm across in gardens, parks and forest.

Don't pick giant puffballs from busy roadside verges, where they are likely to be contaminated by toxins from vehicle exhausts, or from ground that may have been sprayed: they can come up on herbicide-treated soil.

identification.text:
A dense, viciously spiny shrub up to 4 m tall; the spines are the leaves. Bright yellow pea-shaped flowers, strongly scented of coconut on a warm day, present most of the year with a peak in spring. Black seed pods that crack open audibly in summer heat.
Shrub up to 2 m high; main stems erect or spreading, densely branched in younger parts but eventually bare at base; young twigs and spines somewhat glaucous; hairs usually grey. Leaves of seedlings not spinous but with 3 hairy leaflets; spines branched; terminal and lateral spines rigid, deeply furrowed, 15–30 mm long; secondary spines subtending lateral up to 12 mm long. Flowers solitary; bracteoles acute to more or less rounded, 1.5–3 mm wide. Calyx greenish yellow, with more or less patent hairs; calyx teeth connivent. Corolla clear yellow or golden yellow, 13–20 mm long; wings > keel. Pod villous, turning dark brown to black, 13–25 mm long; seeds smooth and rounded, brown or greenish brown, shiny, few per pod.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: French (Montpellier) broom has no spines, and its leaves have three leaflets all its life; gorse is sharply spiny, and on a grown plant its leaves are reduced to spines, the main ones rigid, furrowed and 15–30 mm long. French broom's flowers are 9–13 mm long, in clusters of 4–7 at the ends of short side branches; gorse's are single, 13–20 mm long. Gorse seedlings have leaves of three hairy leaflets, so a seedling's leaves do not separate it from broom. Broom flowers are not eaten.
lookalikes.name: French broom

lookalikes.howToTell: Sweet broom has no spines, and its leaves have three silky leaflets all its life; gorse is sharply spiny, and on a grown plant its leaves are reduced to spines, the main ones rigid, furrowed and 15–30 mm long. Sweet broom's flowers are 13–18 mm long, 10–30 or more together in elongated racemes at the ends of the shoots; gorse's are single, 13–20 mm long. Gorse seedlings have leaves of three hairy leaflets, so a seedling's leaves do not separate it from broom. Broom flowers are not eaten.
lookalikes.name: Sweet broom

lookalikes.howToTell: Scotch broom has no spines; its green twigs are more or less five-angled, and its leaves have three leaflets on older twigs, often one or two on young twigs. Gorse is sharply spiny, and on a grown plant its leaves are reduced to spines, the main ones rigid, furrowed and 15–30 mm long. Both have yellow pea flowers, usually single, and their length overlaps (gorse 13–20 mm, Scotch broom 16–25 mm), so flowers do not separate them. Scotch broom's pods are 15–60 mm long and hairy only along the edges; gorse's are hairy all over and 13–25 mm long. Gorse seedlings have leaves of three hairy leaflets, so a seedling's leaves do not separate it from broom.

preparation.text: Pick flowers with gloves. Scatter fresh over salads, steep for tea or cordial, or infuse in spirits. A garnish and a flavouring, not a bulk food.

recipes.method: Written for gorse in Ireland; the page names no species. 2 litres gorse flowers; 1 kg sugar; 2 lemons, preferably unwaxed; 2 oranges; 4.5 litres filtered water; champagne yeast or a general-purpose white wine yeast. Pick fresh, fully open flowers, ideally on a calm, sunny day. Start the yeast as the sachet directs. Simmer the flowers in the water for 15 minutes, then stir in the sugar until it dissolves. Let it cool a little, pour it into a bucket and add the thinly pared rind and the juice of the lemons and oranges. When it has cooled to lukewarm (about 35–37 °C), add the yeast, mix well and cover with a cloth. Stir it every day for 3–4 days, then strain off the solids through a fine sieve into a demijohn, fit an airlock and leave it to ferment for at least five months. Rack it into a clean demijohn, topping it up to the full amount with boiled and cooled water, and leave it another month. Filter it, or leave it until completely clear, then bottle it in sterilised bottles; if it is too dry at bottling, add more sugar. It can take up to nine months to mature. The authors find champagne yeast (they use 5 g of Lalvin EC-1118) clears the wine much faster than general-purpose yeast.
recipes.title: Gorse flower wine

recipes.method: Written for gorse in Ireland; the page names no species. 250 ml white wine vinegar; 100 g sugar; the zest of 1 orange; the zest of 1 lemon; gorse flowers, as many as the vinegar will cover. Bring the vinegar and sugar to the boil. Take it off the heat and add the orange and lemon zest and as many gorse flowers as you can keep submerged. Leave it to infuse overnight at least, or longer. The author mixes it with an equal amount of oil to marinate fillets of white fish, such as John Dory, as a ceviche.
recipes.title: Gorse-infused vinegar

recipes.method: Written for gorse in Ireland; the page names no species. Serves 2. 2 tablespoons (30 ml) fresh gorse flowers; hot water. Wear thick gloves to pick. Take the flowers off the prickly stalks and leave them somewhere cool outdoors for a few hours so the insects living in them can leave. Give the flowers a little squeeze to bruise them and put them in a small teapot. Pour on hot water and leave to infuse for 7–10 minutes, then strain and serve, hot or as iced tea. Dried flowers work too: use 1 tablespoon (15 ml) instead of 2.
recipes.title: Gorse flower tea

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) gorse flowers; 1 litre water; 375 ml (1½ cups) sugar; 15 ml (1 tbsp) grated lemon, lime and/or orange zest; and the juice of 1 lemon, lime or orange. Pick the flowers on a sunny day — the author finds them a little bitter otherwise — plucking small clusters gently; gloves help with the spines. Bring the sugar, water and zest to the boil and simmer for 5 minutes. Take it off the heat, stir in the juice and the flowers, and leave until cool, or overnight. Strain through muslin into a sterilised bottle, cap it and keep it in the fridge. To keep it longer than a month, bring it back to a simmer and pour it into a warm sterilised bottle; it seals as it cools. To drink, stir 45–60 ml (3–4 tbsp) into 500 ml of hot, cold or fizzy water.
recipes.title: Gorse flower cordial

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) gorse flower cordial (the recipe above); 500 ml (2 cups) water — or 250 ml water and 250 ml coconut milk or cream; 10 ml (2 tsp) agar powder; and the juice of 1 lime (optional); coconut yoghurt or whipped cream, to serve. Put the cordial and water in a pot and sprinkle in the agar. Bring it to the boil, stirring so the agar dissolves evenly, then simmer for 2 minutes. Take it off the heat, add the lime juice and pour into cups, small bowls or ramekins. Let it set at room temperature as it cools, or in the fridge. Serve with coconut yoghurt or whipped cream. They keep 1–2 weeks covered in the fridge.
recipes.title: Gorse flower jelly cups

recipes.method: Written for the author's mixed wild leaves. Of his lists, this catalogue covers dandelion and bittercress (pungent), chickweed and hawthorn leaf (mild), and gorse flowers and flowering currant blossom (extras). He warns to be extra careful identifying leaves before the plants flower. Pungent leaves; mild leaves; a few extras; walnut oil; elderberry vinegar; salt and pepper; a little mustard; fermented greens; pickled buds. Mix pungent and mild leaves about 1 to 3, then scatter a few extras over the top. Dress simply with walnut oil, elderberry vinegar, salt, pepper and a little mustard; he finishes it with fermented greens and pickled buds.

summary.text:
New Zealand's most hated weed has coconut-scented yellow flowers that are edible in small amounts — the one good thing to say about it.
In New Zealand: Gorse has been widely used in New Zealand as a hedging plant and is still used in some areas. The species is now a common and persistent weed in many parts of New Zealand, particularly in rough foothills and less-intensively farmed areas. It was first recorded naturalised here in 1867.

warnings: The pods and seeds are toxic; only the flowers and flower buds are eaten.
The flowers may contain small amounts of toxic alkaloids, so eat them in small quantities and not often — a handful in a salad, not a bowlful.

identification.text:
Shrub to small tree; twigs sharply angled, more or less glabrous to densely hairy. Leaves reduced to phyllodes, alternate; phyllodes glabrous, linear, symmetric or curved, acute and shortly mucronate or obtuse, entire, (30)–40–80–(120) × 3–8–(10) mm, usually with 3 prominent veins; stipules lanceolate, about 1 mm long or inconspicuous in mature plants. Flowers 4-merous, numerous and solitary in axillary, medium to pale yellow, cylindric spikes; spikes shorter than or equal to leaves. Pod glabrous, somewhat curved, 50–100 × about 4 mm; aril not much folded, thickened and cup-shaped below seed.
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Racosperma floribundum (Vent.) Pedley]
Its long, thin phyllodes and flowers in spikes set it apart from most other wattles naturalised in New Zealand. Told from Sydney golden wattle (Acacia longifolia), the most similar, by its much narrower phyllodes (see the lookalikes).

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the width of the phyllodes (the leaves). Gossamer wattle's are linear, 3–8 mm wide (up to 10 mm); Sydney golden wattle's are narrowly elliptic to obovate, 6–22 mm wide, and its coastal subspecies sophorae has broader ones still. A phyllode wider than 10 mm is Sydney golden wattle and one narrower than 6 mm is gossamer wattle; between 6 and 10 mm use the other signs. Gossamer wattle's phyllodes are 40–80 mm long (30–120 mm at the extremes), Sydney golden wattle's 80–130 mm (from 60 mm), so length only helps at the ends of the ranges. Gossamer wattle's twigs can be densely hairy; Sydney golden wattle's are hairless or sparsely hairy. Golden-yellow spikes point to Sydney golden wattle; gossamer wattle's are medium to pale yellow, and both can be pale. Gossamer wattle's pods are 50–100 mm long and somewhat curved; Sydney golden wattle's are 80–120 mm, straight or slightly curved, and subspecies sophorae's are dark reddish brown and extremely contorted. What does not separate them: both are shrubs or small trees with sharply angled twigs, phyllodes with 2–4 prominent veins, 4-merous flowers in cylindric spikes no longer than the phyllodes, pods about 4 mm wide, and the same cup-shaped aril below the seed, and both flower in late winter (Sydney golden wattle July–August, gossamer wattle August–September). Sydney golden wattle's seeds are eaten cooked (see its page).

summary.text:
Gossamer wattle (Acacia floribunda), also called Sally wattle or white sallow wattle, is a shrub or small tree of the pea family (Fabaceae), native to eastern Australia and naturalised in New Zealand.
In New Zealand: North Island: above the lower Huia Dam (west Auckland), established in coastal Wellington Province at Paraparaumu, Pukerua Bay and Plimmerton. Naturalised from eastern Australia, first recorded in 1981. Herbarium specimens of wild plants have since been collected in Canterbury, Nelson and Taranaki too.
Like all the naturalised wattles, it is grown in New Zealand as an ornamental or for shelter and firewood. In late winter it carries many spikes of pale yellow flowers.
It produces numerous hard seeds, spread by birds and ants. In Australia it has spread from gardens into bushland in southern Victoria and Tasmania, where it is an emerging environmental weed. It is not on the Department of Conservation's list of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024.

warnings: Its record as food is thin: one Australian nursery list of local wattles with edible seeds, repeated on a gardening blog, with no method for this species, so it is not given as food here.

Many wattles are considered poisonous, and 13 wattle species are naturalised in New Zealand. Gossamer wattle looks like Sydney golden wattle, whose seeds are eaten, so check the phyllodes before picking any wattle seed (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Especially rather moist open places such as river beds, seepage areas on hillsides, drains, and anywhere subject to water runoff from buildings, also drier areas, particularly open modified situations such as roadsides, waste places and coastal sands.
It is a common weed of lawns, pastures (especially run-down ones) and waste places. It copes with compaction, waterlogging and trampling better than narrow-leaved plantain, so it is often the commoner of the two on sports fields and in pasture gateways.
On New Zealand's national wetland plant list it is rated facultative upland: it sometimes grows in wetlands but usually on dry ground.

identification.text:
Hairy or occasionally glabrous short-lived perennial herb with stout caudex and many large adventitious roots, occasionally with persistent, well-developed primary roots. Leaves all radical, rosulate; petiole 1–20–(30) cm long, broadened at base, channelled. Lamina to 21 × 16 cm, ovate to suborbicular (somewhat narrower in small-leaved plants), generally puberulent, at least on the main veins beneath, sometimes glabrate or glabrous, entire or remotely dentate; main veins 5–7; base truncate to cordate in more typical large-leaved plants but often cuneate to attenuate in smaller, and especially narrower-leaved forms; apex rounded to obtuse. Scapes about 5–80 cm long, not ribbed, generally hairy, at least towards base, sometimes glabrous or nearly so. Spikes dense, 1.5- about 30 cm long, narrow-cylindric. Bracts ovate, longer than calyx, herbaceous and keeled, glabrous, sometimes with membranous margin. Sepals 1.5–2.1 mm long, broad-ovate; keel green and herbaceous, otherwise sepal scarious. Corolla tube equal to or slightly shorter than calyx; lobes 1–1.3 mm long, ovate to elliptic-ovate, reflexing. Stamens glabrous, long-exserted. Style long-exserted, puberulent. Capsule usually 2.5–4 mm long, broad-ellipsoid, 6–16-seeded. Seeds 1–1.8 mm long, slightly trigonous but also rather irregular, rugose, dark red, brown, dark brown or black. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
A rosette of broad, oval to almost round leaves, up to 21 cm long and 16 cm wide, each on a channelled stalk that widens at the base, with five to seven strong veins running from base to tip. Large leaves have a squared-off or heart-shaped base; small plants have narrower leaves that taper into the stalk. The tiny flowers are packed into a long, narrow spike, 1.5–30 cm, on an unribbed stalk, with long stamens sticking out; the flowers are cream to green. The fruits run a long way down the spike. It flowers from July to April. In winter the plant often turns yellowish and sickly. Leaf and spike size vary enormously. There is no single taproot: a crown just below the surface sends many roots straight down.

lookalikes.howToTell: Narrow-leaved plantain's leaves are long and narrow, 0.5–4.8 cm wide, tapering into a short, ill-defined stalk; greater plantain's are broad ovals up to 16 cm wide on a distinct stalk. Narrow-leaved plantain's flower stalk is strongly ribbed and carries a short, dense head, to about 6 cm, with the brown fruits clustered near the tip; greater plantain's stalk is not ribbed, and its fruits run much further down a spike up to 30 cm long. Small greater plantains can have narrower leaves that taper into the stalk, so check the flower stalk too. Both have veins running the length of the leaf and both flower from July to April, so neither of those tells them apart.
lookalikes.name: Narrow-leaved plantain

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp plantain's leaves are lance-shaped to broadly elliptic, up to 8 cm wide, and taper into the stalk, which is often purple; greater plantain's large leaves are oval to almost round, up to 16 cm wide, with a squared-off or heart-shaped base. Small greater plantains can have narrower, tapering leaves, so look at the flowers: swamp plantain's petals, 2.5–3 mm long, curl up into a small, pointed, upright cone, and its stamens are usually hidden; greater plantain's petals are 1–1.3 mm and bent back, with long stamens sticking out. Swamp plantain flowers from November to January only. Both can have fine hairs on the veins underneath, both have an unribbed flower stalk, and their spikes overlap in length, so none of those separates them.
lookalikes.name: Swamp plantain

lookalikes.howToTell: Water plantain grows in or at the edge of water — ponds, ditches, drains, swamps and slow streams — and is hairless. Its oval leaves, 8–23 cm long with a rounded or slightly heart-shaped base, stand upright on long stalks that are D-shaped in cross-section, and they die back over winter. From November to February it sends up a branched flower stalk up to about 1 m tall, with whorls of branches and many pale lilac or white, three-petalled flowers up to 1 cm across. Greater plantain's tiny flowers are packed into a dense, unbranched spike, and its leaves usually have fine hairs on the veins underneath, though some plants are hairless. Greater plantain also grows in moist places and drains, so where it grows does not separate them. Water plantain is poisonous raw.
lookalikes.name: Water plantain

preparation.text:
Pick young, tender leaves; they soon turn tough and fibrous. The leaves are rather bitter, and the stringy strands are tedious to pull out; leave out the leaf stalk, which is stringier still. Blanching the leaves in boiling water makes them more tender for salads. Cook older leaves in stews, or oil and bake them into crisps, which also gets rid of any lingering stringiness. The dried leaves make a passable tea.
The seeds have a nutty flavour. Eat them raw or cooked, grind them into a meal to mix with flour, or boil them whole like sago. They are tiny and tedious to gather.

recipes.method: Written for kopakopa (greater plantain). For 24 large leaves: 10 ml (2 tsp) olive oil, 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt and 2.5 ml (½ tsp) seasoning, such as a Moroccan spice mix or garlic powder. Heat the oven to 150 °C. Wash the leaves and dry them well, then toss them in the oil until coated. Spread them in a single layer on a baking tray, sprinkle with the salt and seasoning, and bake for about 10 minutes, until crisp.
recipes.title: Kopakopa chips

recipes.method: Written for plantain seeds, greater or narrow-leaved. 1 handful of plantain seeds; 3 handfuls of pumpkin seeds; 3 handfuls of sesame seeds; a generous splash of tamari or soy sauce. Mix 1 handful of plantain seeds with 3 handfuls of pumpkin seeds and 3 of sesame seeds. Toast them lightly in a non-stick frying pan, then add a generous splash of tamari or soy sauce, toss to coat, and let any excess cook off. Tip into bowls and eat as a snack.
recipes.title: Spiced plantain seed mix

recipes.method: Written for greater plantain (Plantago major). Plantain leaves; 15 ml (1 tbsp) sesame oil; 15 ml (1 tbsp) soy sauce; 1 garlic clove; a sprinkle of sesame seeds. Boil the leaves in salted water for 4 minutes, then drop them straight into iced water. Drain, and dress with 15 ml (1 tbsp) sesame oil, 15 ml (1 tbsp) soy sauce, 1 garlic clove and a sprinkle of sesame seeds. Mix and let it rest for 5 minutes. The recipe leaves them with something of the texture and translucence of seaweed.
recipes.title: Plantain side dish

summary.text:
Plantago major, the greater plantain, is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae.
Greater plantain is native to almost all of Europe (Iceland excepted), northern and central Asia, and northern and southern Africa, and has become widely naturalised elsewhere in the world.
The ability of greater plantain to survive frequent trampling and colonise compacted soils makes it important for soil rehabilitation. Its roots break up hardpan surfaces, while simultaneously holding together the soil to prevent erosion. The seeds are a common contaminant in cereal grain and other crop seeds. As a result, it now has a nearly worldwide distribution.
As a result of its wide occurrence, Plantago major has many vernacular names. In addition to greater plantain, other recorded vernacular names include broadleaf plantain, common plantain, broad-leaved plantain, cart track plant, dooryard plantain, greater plantago, healing blade, hen plant, lambs foot, roadweed, roundleaf plantain, snakeroot, waybread, wayside plantain, and white man's footprint. Plantago major is believed to be one of the first plants to reach North America after European colonisation. Reportedly brought to the Americas by Puritan colonists, greater plantain was known among some Native American peoples by the name "white man's footprint", because it thrived in the disturbed and damaged ecosystems surrounding European settlements.
In New Zealand it is also called broad-leaved plantain, cart-track plantain, white-man's foot and kopakopa. It came from Eurasia and was first recorded growing wild here in 1832; most New Zealand plants are subspecies major. It is very common throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands, and grows on the Kermadec and Chatham Islands. Stock eat it, but a pasture with more of it than grass is usually a run-down one. Kopakopa is recorded as its Māori name since at least 1907. It is a rongoā: Māori used the leaves on ulcers, boils, burns, cuts, wounds and insect bites, most often heating a leaf over embers for a moment and squeezing the juice onto the sore, or laying the bruised leaf on as a pack.
It has long been eaten in spring, before the garden vegetables are ready. The young leaves are a good source of vitamin C and carotenoids and are low in oxalic acid and nitrate. It is wind-pollinated, and one plant can set up to 20,000 seeds. The name Plantago is an old Latin name for flat-leaved plants, and major means greater. Farmers group it with dandelion and similar rosette weeds as 'flat weeds'. A variegated form, with cream or yellow leaf edges, is sold by New Zealand nurseries as a garden plant.

warnings: Plants beside busy roads can hold high levels of lead and cadmium. Pick away from traffic.
Plantains are easily killed by common lawn and pasture herbicides (2,4-D, mecoprop, MCPA), so lawns, sports fields and paddocks may have been sprayed for them. Pick from ground you know.

identification.text:
Annual loose tufts or solitary shoots, (18)–25–65–(90) cm. Leaf-sheath papery, glabrous, finely ribbed, light green, light brown or purplish. Ligule 2–4–(5) mm, glabrous, denticulate, centrally tapered. Leaf-blade (2.2)–5–23 cm × 2–8 mm, thin, flat, finely ribbed, gradually tapered to fine acicular tip, abaxially occasionally sparsely prickle-toothed on ribs, adaxially ribs usually finely scaberulous; margins finely scaberulous. Culm (12)–20–50 cm, erect or geniculate at base, internodes glabrous. Panicle (2.2)–4–13–(16) cm, secund, nodding, of 1–12, rarely to 18, papery spikelets; branches few, sparsely scabrid, pedicels filiform, 0.5–2–(3) cm. Spikelets 1–2–(2.5) × 0.6–1.5 cm, 8–15-flowered, silvery, light green to golden-brown, often dark purplish at base. Glumes subequal, 5–6–(6.6) mm, (5)–7–9-nerved, spreading, firmly membranous, concave, suborbicular, smooth, often purplish. Lemma 6.5–8.5 mm, 7–9–(11)-nerved, centrally hardened and concave, glabrous, base cordate, sometimes with minute glandular hairs especially on auricle-like extensions, and appressed fine hairs on broad, firmly membranous margins, apex subacute. Palea 3–4 mm, to ⅔ length of lemma, orbicular, keels finely winged and densely short-ciliate, interkeel glabrous. Lodicules (1)–2–3 mm, lanceolate, obtuse. Anthers 1.5–2 mm. Gynoecium: ovary about 1 mm; stigma-styles 2 mm. Caryopsis 2.5–3 × 1.5–2 mm; embryo 0.7–1 mm; hilum linear, 1.2–1.5 mm.
[From: Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

edibleParts.text: Young leaves, raw or cooked. They are bitter, and a few mixed into a salad add a slight aromatic tang. They can be cooked like spinach, added to soups or used as a flavouring, and a herb tea is made from the fresh or dried leaves. Before hops, it was the most common flavouring in beer. The flowers have almost no flavour and add colour to a salad, and the leaves can stand in for thyme or rosemary.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Usually in shady places below trees and around buildings.
G. hederacea thrives in moist shaded areas, but also tolerates sun very well. It is a common plant in grasslands and wooded areas or wasteland.  It also thrives in lawns and around buildings, since it survives mowing.

identification.text:
Herb; non-flowering stems hairy, creeping and rooting at nodes. Petiole slender. Lamina 1–3.5 × 1–4.5 cm, suborbicular to reniform, sparsely to densely hairy, especially beneath, shallowly to deeply crenate; base cordate. Calyx about 5 mm long, 15-nerved; nerves hairy; teeth triangular-acuminate. Corolla 1–1.5 cm long, blue or blue-violet, hairy outside; lower lip with purple spots. Nutlets not seen. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Crushed, the leaves smell strongly, earthy and spicy. The square stems are often reddish, and the leaves are often purplish beneath; young leaves can be tinged violet-brown. The leaves among the flowers are like the other leaves, each on its own stalk. Leaf stalks vary with the site, from about 1 cm in grassland to more than 20 cm under dense woodland. It grows as a low mat, and the runners can be more than a metre long. The flowers sit one to four together, often all on one side of the stem; they are sometimes pink or white, and some plants bear only smaller flowers with no pollen.

lookalikes.howToTell: Red deadnettle is an annual with ovate to almost round leaves, the upper ones purplish, and purple or deep pink flowers in a whorl near the stem tip. Ground-ivy is a creeping perennial whose stems root at the joints; its leaves are round to kidney-shaped, and its blue or blue-violet flowers sit in twos or threes in the leaf joints on the upper stem. Both grow in gardens and around buildings, and both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Red deadnettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Henbit is an annual whose leaves among the flowers have no stalk and clasp the stem; its flowers are pinkish purple, on a long, narrow, upright tube. Ground-ivy is a creeping perennial whose stems root at the joints; every leaf, even among the flowers, is on its own slender stalk, and its flowers are blue or blue-violet. Both grow on disturbed ground around buildings, and both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Henbit deadnettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Self-heal's leaves are ovate, 1.7–6 cm long and 0.7–2.3 cm wide, usually untoothed or only shallowly toothed, with a wedge-shaped to rounded base, and its flowers, usually violet, rarely pink or white, form a dense spike at the stem tip among broad bracts fringed with white hairs and often tinged purple. Ground-ivy's leaves are round to kidney-shaped, 1–4.5 cm wide, with scalloped edges and a heart-shaped base, each on a slender stalk, and its blue or blue-violet flowers sit in twos or threes in the joints of ordinary leaves. Flower colour does not reliably separate them, both creep, and both grow in lawns and under trees at woodland edges. Self-heal's leaves and flowers are eaten raw or cooked; allergic reactions to it have been reported.
lookalikes.name: Self-heal

lookalikes.howToTell: Bird's-eye speedwell's leaves are ovate, 6–35 mm long, with 3–8 pairs of coarse teeth and a squared-off base; its flowers are flat, 8–12 mm across, with four sky-blue lobes striped dark, each alone on a long, slender stalk, and its seed capsules are two-lobed and broader than long. Ground-ivy's leaves are round to kidney-shaped with a heart-shaped base and scalloped edges, and its flowers are tubular and two-lipped, 1–1.5 cm long, with purple spots on the lower lip. Both creep and root at the joints and both have blue flowers, so neither tells them apart. Bird's-eye speedwell's young leaves and shoots are eaten, but its record as food is thin.
lookalikes.name: Bird's-eye speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Out of flower the two are easily confused: both creep and root at the joints, have round to kidney-shaped, scalloped, hairy leaves and grow in lawns. Creeping speedwell's stems carry shorter hairs than ground-ivy's, and are not four-angled. Creeping speedwell's leaves are 3–8 mm long and 5–12 mm wide, with a squared-off to slightly heart-shaped base; ground-ivy's are usually larger, 1–3.5 cm long and 1–4.5 cm wide, with a deeper heart-shaped base and deeper, rounder scallops. Creeping speedwell's flowers are flat, with four blue lobes, 8–10 mm across, each alone on a thread-like stalk 15–40 mm long; ground-ivy's are tubular and two-lipped, 1–1.5 cm long, blue or blue-violet with purple spots on the lower lip, almost stalkless in clusters in the leaf joints. No food use of creeping speedwell has been confirmed; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Creeping speedwell

preparation.text: Pick the young leaves before the plant flowers. Use them sparingly raw, as they are bitter; otherwise cook them as a vegetable, add them to soups, or steep fresh or dried leaves in hot water for tea. The taste is aromatic and a little bitter, with a stronger, peppery bite as the leaves age, so a little goes a long way. For tea, pour boiling water over a handful of leaves and keep it covered while it steeps, so the aroma stays in; sweeten it to taste. The leaves fry well in a thin batter, and fried leaves make a crunchy garnish. To dry it, pick it when it is free of rain and dew, spread it in one layer in the open air for several days, and store it out of the light. Pick away from sprayed ground and from spots dogs use.

recipes.method: Serves 3. 2 handfuls of ground-ivy; 150 g plain flour; 1 tbsp cornflour; 1 egg; 300 ml cold water; a pinch of salt; 100 g rapeseed oil; soy sauce, honey or both, to serve. Pick the leaves off 2 handfuls of ground-ivy. In a chilled bowl, mix 150 g plain flour, 1 tbsp cornflour, 1 egg, 300 ml cold water and a pinch of salt into a thin batter. Heat 100 g rapeseed oil until very hot. Dip the leaves one at a time until well coated, fry until lightly crisp, and drain on kitchen paper. Serve with soy sauce, honey or both.
recipes.title: Ground-ivy tempura

recipes.method: Serves 6. 200 g butternut squash, in 1 cm dice; ½ tbsp olive oil; salt and pepper; 100 g diced bacon; 3 eggs; 300 ml double cream; a handful of ground-ivy; a blind-baked pastry case; 100 g grated cheddar. Toss 200 g butternut squash, in 1 cm dice, with ½ tbsp olive oil, salt and pepper, add 100 g diced bacon, and roast on a tray at 180 °C for 20–25 minutes, turning halfway, until the squash is soft and the bacon crisp; let it cool. Beat 3 eggs with 300 ml double cream. Keep back about 12 leaves from a handful of ground-ivy and roughly chop the rest. Spread the squash and bacon over a blind-baked pastry case, scatter over the chopped ground-ivy and 100 g grated cheddar, pour in the egg and cream, and dot the kept leaves on top. Bake at 180 °C for about 25 minutes, until golden and just set, and let it cool to warm before serving.
recipes.title: Ground-ivy, butternut squash and bacon quiche

recipes.method: 2.3 kg malted barley; 15 litres water in all; 85 g dried ground-ivy; 900 g brown sugar; yeast; ½ tsp sugar for each bottle. Mash 2.3 kg malted barley in water at 65 °C for 90 minutes, then sparge, slowly adding boiling water until 15 litres in all has gone in. Add 85 g dried ground-ivy and boil for an hour. Strain, stir in 900 g brown sugar until it dissolves, cool to 21 °C, pour into the fermenter and add the yeast. Ferment for about a week, until it has finished, then siphon into bottles each primed with ½ tsp sugar, cap and store. Ready in 10 days to two weeks.
recipes.title: Ground-ivy ale

recipes.method: Plenty of fresh ground-ivy; apple cider vinegar. Fill a bottle of apple cider vinegar with plenty of fresh ground-ivy — leaves, stems and flowers — and leave for a day or more. The author keeps a 5-litre bottle going and uses it as the vinegar in his pickles, especially pickled mushrooms. The recipe needs no heating.
recipes.title: Ground-ivy vinegar

recipes.method: Ground-ivy leaves; apple cider vinegar; a sugar syrup. Half fill a jar with ground-ivy leaves and top up with apple cider vinegar. Leave for at least 24 hours, better 48. Strain, and mix with a sugar syrup, starting at about 60 parts vinegar to 40 syrup and adjusting until it is sharp but not harsh. The author's syrup is burdock root, washed and finely sliced, steeped for at least 24 hours in a syrup of 2 parts sugar to 1 part water. Use the shrub in cocktails or as a pickling liquor.
recipes.title: Ground-ivy shrub

summary.text:
Glechoma hederacea is an aromatic, perennial, evergreen creeper of the mint family Lamiaceae.
European settlers carried it around the world, and it has become a well-established introduced and naturalized plant in a wide variety of localities. It is also considered an aggressive invasive weed of woodlands and lawns in some parts of North America, being considered a non-native plant in the United States, and invasive in some U.S. states. It has invaded wild areas, sometimes choking out native wildflowers. Part of the reason for its wide distribution is its rhizomatous method of reproduction.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1878 and grows locally in many places in the southern North Island and the South Island, and at Halfmoon Bay on Stewart Island. It is commonly grown in gardens, often as a variegated form, which occasionally grows wild too. No seed has been found on New Zealand plants.
It is also called alehoof, gill-over-the-ground, field balm and run-away robin, and creeping Charlie; the brewing names come from its use in ale before hops. Seed rarely forms even where it is native: a patch may be a single plant spread by its runners, and the flowers need pollen from another plant.

warnings: It is poisonous to horses that eat a lot of it, fresh or in hay: they sweat, drool, breathe with difficulty and sometimes get fluid on the lungs. Keep horses off it. No other livestock are known to be affected.

It is advised against in pregnancy and when breast-feeding, in epilepsy and in kidney disease. It contains pulegone, which makes up most of pennyroyal oil, though its volatile oil is less than a thirtieth as concentrated as pennyroyal's, and its effects on people have been little studied.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand – Seed Plants, Heenan 2020): The hairy and glabrous silique forms of C. hirsuta are both common weeds of parks and gardens in urban areas, of disturbed habitats such as roadsides, waterways and industrial areas, and sometimes of open areas of indigenous vegetation.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Weed of cultivation, waste places and bush remnants.
In New Zealand (Julia's Edible Weeds): found all over the country, often coming up in nursery container plants, and in damp gardens, driveways and cultivated or disturbed soil.
In Britain: bare ground such as vegetable beds, paths, pots, greenhouse borders, gravel drives, dunes and walls.

identification.text:
Depending on the climate C. hirsuta may complete two generations in a year, one in the spring and one in the fall; also depending on the climate, the seeds may germinate in the fall and the plants may remain green throughout the winter before flowering in the spring. It often grows a rosette of leaves at the base of the stem, while there may be leaves on the upright stem, most of the leaves will be part of the basal rosette. The leaves in this rosette are pinnately divided into 8–15 leaflets which have short stems connecting them to the petiole. These basal leaves are often 3.5–15 cm long. The leaflets are round to ovate in shape and may have smooth or dentate edges. The leaflet at the tip of the leaf (terminal leaflet) will be larger than the other leaflets and round to reniform in shape. The cauline (attached to the upright stem) leaves are also pinnately divided, with fewer leaflets, and generally smaller than the basal leaves; these leaves will be borne on a petiole and are 1.2–5.5 cm long. The stems, petioles, and upper surfaces of the cauline leaves are sparsely hairy.

Plants of this species are usually erect and grow to no more than about 30 centimetres from a stem which is either unbranched or branched near the base. The small white flowers are borne in a raceme without any bracts, soon followed by the seeds and often continuing to flower as the first seeds ripen. The flowers have 4 white petals (which may be lacking but are mostly present) which are 1.5–4.5 mm long and spatulate shaped. The flowers also have 4 stamens of equal height instead of the 6 which are found in most closely related plants. Pollen grains are elongated, approximately 32 microns in length.

Below the flowers there are 4 sepals which are oblong shaped and 1.5–2.5 mm long and .3–.7 mm wide. The seeds are borne in upright pointing siliquae which are straight and 1.5–2.5 cm long and 1–1.4 mm in diameter. When the fruit is ripe the valves on the siliquae will coil tightly from the bottom to the top after being touched and burst explosively, sending the seeds flying far from the parent plant. This seed dispersal strategy is referred to as ballochory and is a type of rapid plant movement.

Hairy bittercress is very similar to Cardamine flexuosa. It usually has only 4 stamens, while C. flexuosa has 6 stamens, and the fruits of C. hirsuta overtop the flowers whereas in C. flexuosa the fruits do not overtop the younger flowers. The fruits grow in a thin pod arranged as a single row.
Cardamine hirsuta has a chromosome number of 2n = 16.
Cardamine hirsuta and C. flexuosa can sometimes be confused. The two species are easily separated by stamen number, with C. hirsuta having mostly four stamens and C. flexuosa predominantly six stamens. However, stamen number in C. hirsuta can be variable, as noted by Cheo et al. (2001), who report that about 80% of the plants in C. hirsuta they examined have flowers with four stamens and 18% have five stamens. For C. flexuosa they report that 97% of plants have six stamens. In New Zealand a hairy silique form of C. hirsuta is distinguished from the glabrous silique form of C. hirsuta, and this is supported by nrDNA ETS sequence data (Heenan 2017).
Quick check (NZ Plant Conservation Network): the flowering stem is not zigzag, unlike wavy bittercress, which often grows with it. Rosettes can reach about 10 cm across as the plant comes into flower, with the leaflets more widely spaced (Julia's Edible Weeds, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Stamens are the best single test, seen with a hand lens on several flowers: hairy bittercress mostly has 4 and wavy bittercress 6, but stamen number varies; in one study about 80% of hairy bittercress plants had four-stamened flowers and 18% had five, while 97% of wavy bittercress plants had six. The flowering stem of hairy bittercress is straight; that of wavy bittercress is usually flexuous (zigzag), though it can also be straight. Hairy seed pods point to hairy bittercress, whose hairy-podded form grows mainly in the east of the North, South and Stewart Islands; wavy bittercress pods are hairless, but so are those of the common form of hairy bittercress. Sepals are 0.3–0.7 mm wide in hairy bittercress and 0.7–1.4 mm in wavy bittercress. In Britain the fruits of hairy bittercress overtop the flowers, while those of wavy bittercress generally do not. Wavy bittercress is found more often in damper sites. Stem hairiness, petal size, the style on the pod and the number of leaflets overlap and do not separate them. Wavy bittercress is eaten the same way, as a raw cress-flavoured leaf.
lookalikes.name: Wavy bittercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small rosette-forming weeds of cultivated ground with tiny white four-petalled flowers, and shepherd's purse looks a bit like bitter cress. The pods separate them: hairy bittercress has long, narrow, erect pods (10–)15–20(–25) mm long and only 1–1.3 mm wide, while shepherd's purse has flat, notched, triangular to heart-shaped pods 5–10 mm long and 4–7 mm wide. Hairy bittercress rosette leaves are pinnate, divided into separate stalked, bluntly lobed leaflets; shepherd's purse leaves range from unlobed to deeply cut but are not divided into separate leaflets, and are very variable, so check the pods. Shepherd's purse tends to grow larger. Shepherd's purse leaves are eaten raw or cooked; avoid it in medicinal amounts when pregnant — see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Shepherd's purse
