preparation.text: Mostly eaten raw. Pick it young and whole: lift the rosette, cut off the roots, and wash it by soaking in a bowl so the grit sinks, then chop it, then use it in salads, egg dishes, salsas and pesto, or a few sprigs as a garnish or flavouring. It is also used as a potherb, but cooking seems to remove the flavour. The taste is milder in winter and much more peppery once the plant flowers, and in summer the leaves can become a bit tough. Use the leaves in sandwiches in place of rocket (cheese sandwiches especially), fold them through potato salad, blend them into pesto with garlic, nuts and olive oil, or stir them into a herb butter. The flavour is like a milder watercress; the plants are small and strong-tasting, so for a big salad mix them with milder leaves.

recipes.method: Written for the author's mixed wild leaves. Of his lists, this catalogue covers dandelion and hairy bittercress (pungent), chickweed and young hawthorn leaves (mild), and gorse flowers and flowering currant blossom (extras). He warns to be extra careful identifying leaves before the plants flower. Pungent leaves; mild leaves; a few extras; walnut oil; elderberry vinegar; salt and pepper; a little mustard; fermented greens; pickled buds. Mix pungent and mild leaves about 1 to 3, then scatter a few extras over the top. Dress simply with walnut oil, elderberry vinegar, salt, pepper and a little mustard; he finishes it with fermented greens and pickled buds.
recipes.title: Wild summer salad

recipes.method: Written for hairy bittercress (Cardamine hirsuta). Serves 4. 4 beetroot (about 500 g); 50 g sunflower and/or pumpkin seeds; 15 ml (1 tbsp) honey; 30 ml (2 tbsp) olive oil; 15 ml (1 tbsp) lemon juice; 40 g bittercress; sea salt. Lift the bittercress whole, cut off the roots, rinse and chop it. Wash the beetroot and boil it until a skewer goes in easily, about 45–50 minutes. Dry-roast the seeds in a frying pan for about 8 minutes, stirring. Whisk the honey, oil, salt and lemon juice together. Peel the beetroot while still warm, cut it into bite-sized pieces and toss everything together in a bowl.
recipes.title: Warm beetroot and bittercress salad

recipes.method: Written for cleavers, violet leaves, chickweed, red deadnettle and bittercress. A small handful of cleavers; 4 violet leaves; a handful of chickweed; 3 or 4 stems of red deadnettle; a small handful of bittercress; a big handful of bok choy, kale or silverbeet; 1 banana, peeled; 1 apple (whole without the stalk if organic, otherwise peeled); 1 mandarin (with its peel if organic, otherwise peeled); 1 or 2 kiwifruit, peeled; 1 small or ½ large avocado; 500 ml (2 cups) water, more if the blender struggles. Wash the weeds and greens, put them in the blender, snip them up a bit with scissors and add the water. Blend on low until the greens break down, then on high until smooth. Add the fruit and avocado and blend again, low and then high, until creamy.
recipes.title: Winter health boosting smoothie

recipes.method: Written for hairy bittercress (Cardamine hirsuta). 1 red pepper, roasted and skinned; 5 ml (1 tsp) coriander seeds; 5 ml (1 tsp) cumin seeds; 5 ml (1 tsp) caraway seeds; 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter; 1 red onion, finely chopped; 5 garlic cloves, roughly chopped; 1 fresh red chilli, finely chopped; 3 dried bird's eye chillies, finely chopped; 30 ml (2 tbsp) tomato purée; juice of 1 lemon; 40 g raw hairy bittercress, chopped; a pinch of salt. Toast the cumin, caraway and coriander seeds in a dry pan just until they start to pop, then grind them to a powder. Soften the onion and chillies in the butter, add the garlic and cook until soft. Put everything in a bowl and blend with a stick blender, chunky or smooth. To serve, spread it thickly over white fish fillets, cover and chill for at least 2 hours (4 is better), then fry the fillets in butter or oil about 2 minutes a side.
recipes.title: Hairy bittercress harissa

recipes.method: Written for hairy bittercress (Cardamine hirsuta). No amounts are given. Hairy bittercress; tomatoes; red onion; lemon juice; olive oil; for the fuller version, feta, chickpeas and a little agave syrup. Soak the bittercress in a bowl of water so the dirt sinks, and cut off the roots. Toss it with the tomatoes and red onion and dress with lemon and olive oil. For a fuller salad add feta and chickpeas, and sweeten the dressing with a little agave syrup against the pepper.
recipes.title: Bittercress, tomato and red onion salad

summary.text:
Cardamine hirsuta, commonly called hairy bittercress, popping cress, common bittercress, hoary bittercress, hairy wood-cress, small bittercress, pepperweed, shotweed, or snapweed, is an annual or biennial species of plant in the family Brassicaceae, and is edible as a salad green.
It is commonly found in damp, recently disturbed soil, open ground, turf and waste places and native to Europe, the Middle East, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Central Asia, North Africa, Central Africa, and the Horn of Africa.
These conditions are prevalent in nursery or garden centre plants, and hairy bittercress seeds may be introduced with those plants. Once established, it is difficult to eradicate. The tiny flowers are attractive to a few early butterflies, including (in the United States) spring azure (Celastrina ladon) and falcate orange-tip (Anthocharis midea).
Cardamine hirsuta has been introduced in many countries across the world. Its range includes but is not limited to: Argentina, Australia, Canada, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Gabon, Great Britain, India, Japan, Laos, Madagascar, Mexico, Pakistan, Panama, Peru, Philippines, South Africa, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Turkmenistan, United States, Venezuela, and Vietnam.
The 1889 book The Useful Native Plants of Australia records that it was also called "Lady's Smock" and that "This and other species afford excellent pot-herbs when luxuriant and flaccid. The present one is a common weed almost throughout the world."
Cardamine hirsuta is naturalised in New Zealand, and is originally from Europe. The glabrous silique form of C. hirsuta occurs throughout New Zealand (including offshore islands). The hairy silique form of C. hirsuta occurs predominantly in eastern areas of the North, South and Stewart Islands.
Other names in New Zealand use include lamb's cress, spring cress, shot weed and flick weed. Cardamine comes from kárdamon, a Greek name for an Indian spice; hirsuta is Latin for hairy, probably for the hairy leaves.
It grows and sets seed within a few weeks, so several generations can follow one another in a year; in Tauranga it starts to flower in August. In New Zealand it has been recorded flowering and fruiting in every month.
Kirk (1899) gave the first New Zealand record, and also treated four native bittercresses as varieties of C. hirsuta, so older names such as C. hirsuta var. corymbosa and var. debilis refer to native plants, not this weed. The 1901 date sometimes given comes from a list of garden weeds with no locality and no voucher. Most of Landcare Research's databased herbarium specimens come from Wellington (63) and Canterbury (50), then North Auckland 14, Southland 13, Otago 11, Nelson 5, Hawke's Bay 4, South Auckland 4, Gisborne 2, Marlborough 2, Westland 2 and Taranaki 1.

warnings: Several native New Zealand bittercresses, including Cardamine corymbosa, C. forsteri, C. grandiscapa, C. heleniae and C. unicaulis, also grow in weedy places, so not every small white-flowered bittercress in a garden or track edge is an introduced one; the native species are keyed out on characters such as leaf hydathodes, sepal width and pod style length. The native New Zealand bittercress, C. corymbosa, is itself a weed of lawns, path edges, concrete drains, glasshouses and potted plants; it is a perennial whose flowers sit singly or in small flat-topped clusters on stalks 5–50 mm long, where hairy bittercress is an annual with 6–12 flowers in each lengthening spike on stalks (4–)6–10(–13) mm long, so stalk length alone does not separate them.
It is a common weed of gardens and lawns, where herbicides may be used to control it. Pick it only where you know none has been used.

habitat.text:
Lowland, montane, and lower subalpine forest.
It is notably more common in montane forest than in lowland forest, often on poor or immature, skeletal soils, or on sites naturally stressed by drought or by extreme swings in temperature.
Along with kaikawaka, Hall’s tōtara is the dominant mountain tree in regions where beech is absent (Mt Taranaki, central Westland and Stewart Island).

identification.text:
Tree up to 20 m, trunk up to 1.25 m diameter, bark thin, papery, branchlets slender, of juveniles somewhat drooping. Leaves brownish green, of juveniles 2.5–5 cm × 4–5 mm, linear-lanceolate; of adults 2–3 cm × 3–4 mm, narrow-linear to linear-lanceolate, acute to acuminate, rather rigid, coriaceous, pungent, midvein usually evident. Male strobili 1–2.5 cm long, solitary or up to 5 on a common peduncle, with about 4 scales; apiculus obtuse. Ovules solitary or paired; receptacles usually red, swollen and succulent. Seed 3–5 mm long, narrow-ovoid, pointed, nutlike.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1, as Podocarpus hallii Kirk.]
The leaf bud at the shoot tip is clearly wider than the branchlet, like a meatball on a stick, and is surrounded by broadly ovate, papery bracts that soon fall. The bark is generally thin, papery and freely flaking, reddish-grey. The leaves, especially on juvenile and young trees, are longer and broader than tōtara's, with a very sharp, prickly tip. Male and female cones grow on separate trees. The red, swollen, succulent receptacle under the seed is formed from 2–4 scales.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaf bud at a shoot tip: Hall's tōtara's bud is clearly wider than the branchlet, like a meatball on a stick, with broadly ovate bracts; tōtara's bud is no wider than the branchlet, with narrow, lance-shaped bracts. The bracts soon fall, so look at fresh shoots. Look at the bark: Hall's tōtara's is generally thin, papery and freely flaking; tōtara's is thick, corky, furrowed and somewhat stringy. On young trees, Hall's tōtara's leaves are longer and broader, 2.5–5 cm long and 4–5 mm wide, against about 2 cm long and 1–2 mm wide on young tōtara, with a very sharp tip. Adult leaves overlap (Hall's tōtara 2–3 cm × 3–4 mm, tōtara 1.5–3 cm × 3–4 mm), so adult leaf size does not separate them. Both carry the seed on a red, swollen, succulent receptacle formed from 2–4 scales, and both grow in lowland, montane and lower subalpine forest, sometimes together, so the fruit and the place do not separate them. They often hybridise, and hybrids can be told apart only by the bud and its bracts. Tōtara's red receptacle is eaten (see its page).

summary.text:
Podocarpus laetus, Hall's tōtara, mountain tōtara or thin-barked tōtara, is a species of conifer in the family Podocarpaceae. Previously known as Podocarpus hallii and Podocarpus cunninghamii, in 2015 it was realised that the much earlier name P. laetus has priority. Its common name results from the species being named after J. W. Hall, a New Zealand pharmacist.
It is endemic to New Zealand.
It is found from Northland to Stewart Island. At the time of Māori settlement in the South Island, Hall’s tōtara formed extensive forests on the eastern side and in Central Otago. These were burnt some 500–750 years ago, and grassland appeared in their place.
It grows on the North, South and Stewart Islands and is assessed Not Threatened. It hybridises with tōtara and with snow tōtara; where its range overlaps snow tōtara's, fertile hybrid swarms are sometimes common.

warnings: Yew, which is poisonous, also has red, fleshy 'berries' and needle-like leaves. Check how the seed sits and where the leaf joins the shoot before eating (see the yew page).
Only the red flesh is recorded as eaten. No record of the seed being eaten was found, so whether it is safe is not known.
It grows with tōtara, whose red receptacle is eaten, and often hybridises with it. Check the leaf bud before taking a tree for tōtara (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text: The jumping spider Trite planiceps lives predominantly in the rolled-up leaves of this species. Phormium tenax is a coastal cover plant associated with significant habitat such as the breeding habitat for the endangered yellow-eyed penguin.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Leaves 1–3 m. × 5–12 cm., stiff and more or less erect, at least in lower part; butt heavy and usually brightly coloured. Inflorescence to 5–(6) m. tall; peduncle about 2–3 cm diameter, usually erect, dark, terete, glabrous. Flowers 2.5–5 cm long, predominantly dull red; tips of inner tepals only slightly recurved. Ovary erect; carpels straight. Capsule usually shorter than 10 cm long, often much less, erect, trigonous, abruptly contracted to tip, not twisted, remaining firm and dark in age. Seeds about 9–10 × 4–5 mm., more or less elliptic, plate-like but more or less twisted. 2n equal to 32.
[From: Moore and Edgar (1970) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 2.]

recipes.method: Written for kawakawa leaves, which grow spicier and more peppery dried, with nasturtium leaves and harakeke seed; the author takes it from Michael Daly's Find It, Eat It. 200 g coarse sea salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) dried kawakawa leaves; 30 ml (2 tbsp) dried nasturtium leaves; 15 ml (1 tbsp) black harakeke (flax) seed. Grind the dried leaves and the seed to a powder in a coffee grinder. Grind the salt smooth in the grinder or a mortar, mix in the powders, and keep it in a dry, labelled glass jar with a tight lid.

NZPCN's distribution reads 'Indigenous to New Zealand and Norfolk Island', but its status on Norfolk Island is disputed: Coyne 2009 (Cunninghamia 11) notes that Norfolk Island fossil pollen has no Phormium, and a 2022 plastid-genome study (New Zealand Journal of Botany, https://doi.org/10.1080/0028825X.2022.2032212) found the Norfolk Island plants 'nested well within the wider diversity of P. tenax', consistent with introduction there by early East Polynesian voyagers. summary.text: Phormium tenax (called flax in New Zealand English; harakeke in Māori; New Zealand flax outside New Zealand; and New Zealand hemp in historical nautical contexts) is an evergreen perennial plant native to New Zealand and Norfolk Island that is an important fibre plant and a popular ornamental plant. Its Norfolk Island plants may have been brought there by East Polynesian voyagers, and New Zealand's registers count it as endemic.

identification.text:
Perennial with slender to stout rootstock. Stems ascending, not branching, (2)-10-50 cm tall, glabrous or with sparse 2-fid hairs. Leaves all basal, linear to linear-oblanceolate, simple and distantly dentate to pinnatifid with triangular spreading to recurved lobes, (2)-6-16-(25) × (0.2)-0.6-1.5-(3) cm; hairs 2-(3)-fid at tip, sparse to dense. Stem bracts 0-(1). Capitula turbinate, nodding in bud. Involucral bracts linear-lanceolate, acute, glabrous or with 2-fid hairs; outer bracts about ⅓ length of inner bracts; inner bracts (7)-10-15 mm long. Florets yellow, about 1½× length of involucre. Stigmas yellow. Achenes pale brown; outer achenes smooth or finely muriculate, not beaked, cylindric, 3-4 mm long, with a pappus of scales about 0.7 mm long; inner achenes muricate, shortly beaked, fusiform, 4-5 mm long, with a pappus of 2 rows of bristles, the outer row short, simple, the inner row 5-7 mm long, plumose, widened at base.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In the field (NatureSpot, a UK guide): at least some of the leaf hairs are forked, which separates it from catsear and autumn hawkbit; the outer florets are usually greyish violet underneath, a band Wildflowers of Ireland also describes; the unbranched stem usually carries a few scale-like bracts, where Flora of New Zealand allows no more than one. The plant varies in how hairy it is, and in every other feature.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both send up a leafless, unbranched stem with a single yellow head, so branching does not separate them. A dandelion's flower stem is stout and hollow, and so are its leaf stalk and the base of its midrib; hawkbit's stem is thin and solid. Under a hand lens, hawkbit's leaf hairs fork at the tip into two or three, sparse to dense; a dandelion's leaves are hairless or have sparse short hairs, mostly on the midrib above. In seed, every dandelion seed carries a parachute of fine white hairs on a slender beak 7–10 mm long, while hawkbit's outer seeds have only a ring of tiny scales. Both have rosettes of lobed leaves and milky sap. The dandelion's leaves, flowers and roots are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Dandelion

lookalikes.howToTell: The two hawkbits differ in their hairs, stems and buds. Hawkbit's leaf hairs fork into two, sometimes three, at the tip; autumn hawkbit's are simple, sparse or absent. Hawkbit's stem is unbranched, with one head and none to a few small scale-like bracts, and its buds nod; autumn hawkbit's stems branch, carry many small bracts, and hold their buds erect. Hawkbit's stigmas are yellow, autumn hawkbit's greyish green. Turned over, hawkbit's outer florets are usually greyish violet underneath, autumn hawkbit's striped red. In seed, all autumn hawkbit's achenes are alike, unbeaked, with one row of feathery hairs; hawkbit's outer achenes carry only tiny scales and its inner ones are shortly beaked. Both have yellow heads, basal rosettes of lobed leaves and milky sap. Autumn hawkbit's leaves are used like dandelion leaves (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Autumn hawkbit

lookalikes.howToTell: Out of flower, catsear is strikingly similar to hawkbit. The test is the leaf hairs, under a hand lens: hawkbit's fork into two, sometimes three, at the tip; catsear's are simple, stiff and pale. Catsear's stems are usually branched, with a few tiny bracts, and can carry several heads; hawkbit's stem is unbranched, with one head and none to a few small scale-like bracts — but some catsear stems are unbranched, so branching alone does not settle it. Inside the head, catsear has thin scales among the florets on the flower base; hawkbit has none. Both have hairy rosette leaves that are often lobed, yellow heads and milky sap. Catsear's young leaves and roots are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Catsear

lookalikes.howToTell: Both carry a single yellow head on an unbranched stem with no more than one small bract, and stem heights and leaf sizes overlap. With a hand lens, hawkbit's leaf hairs fork into two, sometimes three, at the tip, and its leaves are distantly toothed to cut into triangular lobes; mouse-ear hawkweed's leaves are untoothed or very obscurely toothed, with long simple hairs above and a very dense coat of star-shaped hairs that makes the underside white, and the plant spreads by creeping runners. Hawkbit's inner achenes are 4–5 mm, shortly beaked, with a feathery inner pappus; mouse-ear hawkweed's are about 2 mm, unbeaked, with simple bristles. No food use of mouse-ear hawkweed is recorded; its traditional uses are medicinal (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mouse-ear hawkweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Both send up a leafless, unbranched stem with a single yellow head and have nodding buds, leaves all in a basal rosette that may be toothed or lobed, and milky sap, so the stem and leaf shape do not separate them. With a hand lens, hawkbit's leaf hairs fork into two, sometimes three, at the tip; microseris's leaves are hairless or have scurfy, scaly hairs beneath. In seed, hawkbit's outer achenes carry only a ring of tiny scales and its inner ones are shortly beaked with feathery hairs; microseris's achenes are unbeaked and ribbed, with stiff, brownish, minutely barbed hairs. Microseris is a native plant whose roots are edible, though eating them rests on two tastings and no Māori food use is recorded; murnong, the Australian 'yam daisy' eaten for its tuber, is a different species (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Microseris

summary.text:
Leontodon saxatilis is a species of hawkbit known by the common names lesser hawkbit, rough hawkbit, and hairy hawkbit. It is native to Europe and North Africa but can be found in many other places across the globe as an introduced species and often a noxious weed. This is a dandelion-like herb growing patches of many erect, leafless stems from a basal rosette of leaves.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Northland, Auckland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty, East Cape, Hawke's Bay, Taranaki, Manawatu, Wairarapa, Wellington; S.: throughout; St.; K., Ch., C. Naturalised from Europe and western Asia, first recorded in 1867.
L. taraxacoides has also been referred to in N.Z. as Apargia hispida, L. hirtus, L. hispidus, L. nudicaulis, and Thrincia hirta.

habitat.text:
Old hedgerows, shelter belts, roadsides and scrub, especially in Canterbury and Otago where it has naturalised widely.
Lowland to montane, on ground of low to moderate fertility: low forest and its margins, disturbed forest, scrub, hill-country and other pasture, waste places and roadsides (NZPCN, restated).
Invades disturbed forest, shrubland and forest margins, fernland, wetland margins, short tussockland and cliffs, and tolerates salt, wind, semi-shade and damp to dry ground (Weedbusters, restated).
In Canterbury it is locally abundant in lowland forest remnants and grows with matagouri on grazing land, spreading in lightly grazed pasture (New Zealand Journal of Ecology 1986, restated).

Weedbusters, 'Hawthorn' (restated)
Flora of New Zealand Online, 'Crataegus' (genus)
identification.text:
A small tree or dense shrub with sharp thorns along the branches. Leaves are small and deeply lobed, like tiny oak leaves. Masses of white five-petalled blossom in late spring, then dark red berries (haws) about 1 cm across in autumn, each with a single hard stone.
Flora of New Zealand: spines up to 12–(20) mm long; leaves 25–70 mm, deeply cut into 3–7 lobes that are usually smooth-edged in the lower half and sparingly toothed near the pointed tip, hairless, paler beneath. Flowers many together in flat clusters, petals 4–8 mm, usually white, rarely red-pink, with pink anthers and usually a single style. Fruit 7–11 mm across, dark red and shining, crowned by the bent-back sepals, holding usually one stone (restated).
The flowers are sweet-scented, 6–15 to a cluster, and the haws have little flesh around the single stone (Weedbusters).
Crataegus laevigata, usually grown as pink, double-flowered garden cultivars, is recorded in New Zealand only as a casual escape (Weedbusters; Flora of New Zealand).

lookalikes.howToTell: Hawthorn's leaves are deeply cut into 3–7 lobes; barberry's are unlobed, mostly 2.5–7.5 cm long, smooth-edged or spiny-toothed, and very variable on one plant. Hawthorn loses its leaves in winter; barberry is evergreen or partly so. Hawthorn's flowers are white, rarely pink; barberry's are yellow and smell unpleasant. Hawthorn's haws are dark red and shining, 7–11 mm across, crowned by the bent-back sepals and holding usually one stone; barberry's berries are reddish black under a heavy whitish bloom, with dark red juice. Hawthorn's spines are single, up to 12–(20) mm; barberry's are single or three-parted, up to 2.3 cm. A thorny hedge shrub with berries in autumn does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Hawthorn's leaves are 25–70 mm and deeply cut into 3–7 lobes; boxthorn's are small, 5–43 mm long, unlobed and oblong to spoon-shaped, mostly in clusters on short spurs along the rigid branch spines. Hawthorn loses its leaves in winter; boxthorn is evergreen. Hawthorn's flowers are white, rarely pink, open and five-petalled, many together in flat clusters; boxthorn's are tubular, pale mauve or cream, 10–13 mm long, one to three together. Hawthorn's haws are dark red and crowned by the bent-back sepals, holding usually one stone; boxthorn's berries are scarlet, round or slightly egg-shaped, on stalks up to 2 cm long. Boxthorn's orange-red berries are probably poisonous. A thorny hedge shrub with red berries does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Boxthorn

Eatweeds, 'Hawthorn jelly recipe' (restated)
Herbal Reality, 'Hawthorn flower cordial' (restated)
preparation.text: Haws are dry and mealy raw. Simmer, sieve out the stones, and make jelly or a ketchup. Young leaves and blossom go in salads. Ripe haws are deep red and a little pithy, like an overripe apple; watch for the thorns when picking. To strip a bunch, roll the stalked clusters between your hands and the haws come off. For a clear jelly let the juice drip through the bag without squeezing. Pick blossom in the morning, and rinse off insects and dirt.

recipes.method: Written for hawthorn berries in general; the page names no species. 1 kg haws; 200 ml lemon juice; 500 g sugar; water, to cover. Take the stalks off the haws and rinse them. Put them in a pan, cover with water and boil for about 10 minutes, then lower the heat and simmer for about an hour, until the berries change colour and are tender. Strain through a fine sieve or muslin, mashing to press out as much liquid as you can, leaving the stones and skins behind. Return the liquid to the pan with the sugar and lemon juice, bring it back to the boil and simmer until the sugar has dissolved and it forms a clear syrup. Take it off the heat and pour it into a bottle. It keeps about 3 months in the fridge.
recipes.title: Hawthorn berry syrup

recipes.method: Written for hawthorn in British hedgerows; the page names no species. 2–3 sprigs of hawthorn blossom per pot (with a couple of leaves); boiling water. Pick the sprigs carefully, watching for the thorns. Wash them and put them in a teapot. Pour on boiling water and leave for a few minutes, until it turns pale gold. To dry sprigs for later, lay them on a tray or a sheet of baking paper, cover them with another sheet and leave them somewhere warm and airy for a day or so, until dry and slightly crisp; store them in a paper bag or jar and use one sprig per mug or pot, straining if needed. The author finds the fresh tea floral and sweet, like jasmine tea, and the dried tea stronger, more like green tea; the scent fades with storage.
recipes.title: Hawthorn blossom tea

recipes.method: Written for Crataegus monogyna, C. laevigata or C. pinnatifida in Tasmania. 1 kg ripe haws, washed; 1 kg apples, peeled and chopped; a couple of strips of lemon rind; 125 ml water; honey or maple syrup, to taste; fresh ginger, grated or juiced (optional). Cut five pieces of baking paper to fit your dehydrator or oven trays. Put the haws, apples, lemon rind and water in a large pot over a low to medium heat. Stir often so all the fruit cooks and none of it sticks. When the fruit is mushy and the liquid almost all absorbed, take it off the heat. Pass the fruit through a sieve fine enough to hold back the stones, and throw the stones away whole. Sweeten the pulp to taste with honey or maple syrup, adding ginger if you are using it. Spread the pulp on the baking paper about 4 mm thick, thick enough that it isn't see-through. Dry it in a dehydrator at about 55 °C, or in the oven on its lowest setting, about 50 °C, for several hours until the leather is dry. Keep the sheets whole, or cut them into strips and roll them, and store in an airtight container.
recipes.title: Hawthorn and apple fruit leather

recipes.method: Written for the author's mixed wild leaves. Of his lists, this catalogue covers dandelion and bittercress (pungent), chickweed and hawthorn leaves (mild), and gorse flowers and flowering currant blossom (extras). He warns to be extra careful identifying leaves before the plants flower. Pungent leaves; mild leaves; a few extras; walnut oil; elderberry vinegar; salt and pepper; a little mustard; fermented greens; pickled buds. Mix pungent and mild leaves about 1 to 3, then scatter a few extras over the top. Dress simply with walnut oil, elderberry vinegar, salt, pepper and a little mustard; he finishes it with fermented greens and pickled buds.
recipes.title: Wild summer salad

recipes.method: Written for Crataegus monogyna. Makes 1 jar; scale up for more. 680 g (1½ lb) ripe haws; 850 ml (1½ pints) water; sugar, 450 g for every 570 ml (1 pint) of juice; juice of 1 lemon. Strip the haws off their stalks by rolling the clusters between your hands, then wash and drain them. Put them whole in a heavy pan with the water, bring to the boil and simmer for 15 minutes. Strain overnight through muslin or a jelly bag; leave it to drip rather than squeezing if you want a clear jelly. Measure the juice and weigh out the sugar. Put the juice, sugar and lemon juice in a heavy pan and stir over the heat until the sugar dissolves, then boil hard for about 10 minutes, until it reaches setting point. Skim off any foam, pour into warm sterilised jars and seal. It can be eaten straight away, with cheese or meat.
recipes.title: Hawthorn jelly

recipes.method: Written for hawthorn blossom in Britain (Crataegus spp.). Makes about 1 litre. 200 g hawthorn blossom; 200 g caster sugar; 1 litre water. Pick the blossom in the morning, then rinse it, removing any insects and dirt. Heat the sugar and water gently in a clean pan, stirring until the sugar has dissolved. Take the pan off the heat and add the flowers, bruising them slightly for a stronger floral flavour. Cover and leave to infuse, up to an hour for a mild cordial or up to four hours for a stronger one. Strain through muslin into a jug and pour into sterilised bottles. Keep it in the fridge and throw it out at any sign of mould. Serve with tonic or soda water, ice and a slice of lemon or lime, or pour a little over ice cream or fruit.
recipes.title: Hawthorn flower cordial

recipes.method: Written for Crataegus monogyna in Oregon. Makes about 2 litres. About 1 litre (4 US cups) fresh ripe haws, picked off their stalks; 2 vanilla pods; 2 cassia cinnamon sticks; 1 tablespoon cardamom pods; 1.75 litres brandy; about 240 ml (1 cup) honey, to taste. Put the haws, whole, with the vanilla, cinnamon and cardamom in a 2-litre jar and pour the brandy over. Leave to infuse for 4 to 6 weeks, shaking every day. Strain into another jar, then stir in the honey until it dissolves, adding more or less to taste. Bottle it.
recipes.title: Hawthorn brandy

recipes.method: Written for hawthorn berries in general; the page names no species. 500 g haws; 300 ml cider vinegar; 300 ml water; 170 g sugar; salt and black pepper. Take the stalks off the haws and rinse them. Put them in a pan with the vinegar and water, bring to the boil and simmer for about 30 minutes, until the berries change colour and split. Strain through a fine sieve or muslin, leaving the stones behind, and return the liquid to the pan. Add the sugar and warm gently, stirring until it dissolves, then bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, stirring often. Season with salt and pepper, take it off the heat and pour it into a bottle. Keep it in the fridge once opened.
recipes.title: Hawthorn ketchup

recipes.method: Written for Crataegus monogyna in the Netherlands, from a Danish family recipe. 1 litre haws; 300 g sugar; water. Mash the haws into a purée without cracking the stones (see Warnings). Add the sugar and heat to about 70 °C, steaming hot but not boiling, then strain out the stones. Use the purée as it is, or dilute 1 part purée with 10 parts water for hawthorn juice.
recipes.title: Hawthorn purée and juice

recipes.method: Written for Crataegus monogyna in the Netherlands, from a Danish family recipe. 500 ml hawthorn juice (from the hawthorn purée and juice recipe); 750 g apples, peeled, cored and quartered; 100 g prunes, roughly chopped; sugar, to taste. Cook the apples and prunes in the hawthorn juice until the apples turn to pulp and the prunes are swollen and soft, then sweeten to taste. Thicken with a little pectin if you like. Eat it straight away or store it in sterilised jars.
recipes.title: Hawthorn with apples and prunes

summary.text:
A thorny hedgerow tree with white spring blossom and red autumn haws — mealy fruit that makes a good jelly, so long as the stones are strained out.
Also called whitethorn or white hawthorn. Native to Europe, it was brought to New Zealand as an ornamental and planted by early settlers for hedges and fences; it was recorded naturalised in 1899. Birds and possums spread the seed, and it forms dense thickets that keep out native seedlings. It is named on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and in Auckland it must not be sold, distributed, released or planted. In Southland it is under a site-led programme for Stewart Island/Rakiura: it must not be kept on or taken to Rakiura or the other islands in the site-led area, any found there must be reported to Environment Southland, and it must not be sold, propagated or otherwise spread.
The genus name comes from the Greek krataigos, 'flowering thorn', thought to refer to the hardness of the wood.

warnings: The stones contain trace amounts of cyanide. Strain them out and never crush them into a preparation.

Hawthorn acts on the heart and circulation and may interact with heart and blood-pressure medicines such as digoxin and beta-blockers; anyone taking them should check with a doctor before using it regularly. Side effects of hawthorn preparations include dizziness, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Little is known about whether it is safe in pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Roadsides, shelter belts, waste land.
It is found on roadsides, wasteland and as a weed of arable land.
In New Zealand it is mostly a weed of crops, but it also grows in waste places and sometimes in pastures.
It is found throughout New Zealand in pasture, cultivated land, gardens and roadsides, and comes up in lawns, garden beds and roadside verges, getting in at the edges of thin or compacted lawns.
In Britain it grows in hedgerows and hedge banks, by roads and paths, on waste ground and field margins, around walls and buildings and on disturbed urban ground; it does best in nutrient-rich, disturbed soil, often in places much used by people. It favours fertile soil with a high pH (over 6) and plenty of calcium, which it finds in the mortar dust and concrete crumbs of towns, where its wind-blown seeds collect in cracks in pavements and rubble.
In the Mediterranean it is usually found near streams and in places that get a lot of rain.

identification.text:
Annual herb. Stem erect, hairy, to 1 m tall. Leaves and petioles with fine stiff hairs. Rosette leaves deeply lyrate-pinnatifid to lyrate-pinnate, (3)–7–25–(30) × (1.5)–2–9–(12) cm; terminal leaflet not lobed or 2–3-lobed, broadly toothed, ovate to reniform; lateral leaflets in 2–6 pairs, more or less deflexed, triangular. Upper stem leaves smaller, deeply lyrate-pinnatifid to lyrate-pinnate; terminal leaflet narrow-oblong; lateral leaflets in 1–2 pairs, spreading or more or less deflexed. Uppermost stem leaves becoming simple and hastate to narrow-triangular. Racemes ebracteate, suberect to spreading, hairy, (10)–20–30–(40) cm long. Pedicels about 3 mm long, hairy. Sepals hairy, about 2 mm long, not horned. Petals yellow, 3–4 mm long. Anthers about 0.5 mm long; filaments longer than sepals. Silique hairy or glabrous, appressed to stem, tapering evenly from base, 10–15–(20) × 1–2 mm; style about 0.5 mm long. Seeds oblong, brown, about 1 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The rosette leaves are deeply lobed, with a large rounded end lobe and side lobes that point back toward the base; they tend to wither before the plant flowers. The flowering stems are tough and wiry and branch widely, the side branches at almost right angles. The tiny yellow flowers sit at the tips, and the short pods are pressed flat against the stem, so they are easy to miss. The stems carry downward-pointing hairs, and the side branches curve upward. The plant has a deep taproot. As a seedling it is almost identical to eastern rocket.

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild radish's flowers are much larger: petals 13–20 mm long, usually pale yellow or white and veined with mauve, against hedge mustard's yellow 3–4 mm. Wild radish's pods are (10)–20–60–(80) × (2)–3–8–(9) mm, pinched between the seeds, on stout stalks 1–2 cm long; hedge mustard's are slender, 10–15–(20) × 1–2 mm, on stalks about 3 mm long and pressed flat against the stem.
lookalikes.name: Wild radish

lookalikes.howToTell: The rosettes are easily confused; tell them apart once they flower. Hedge mustard's petals are yellow and 3–4 mm long; field mustard's are bright yellow and 6–10 mm. Hedge mustard's pods are 10–15–(20) × 1–2 mm and pressed flat against the stem; field mustard's are (30)–40–60 × 2–5 mm, end in a seedless beak 6–10 mm long, and stand out from the stem. Hedge mustard's stem is hairy and its upper stem leaves are still deeply lobed, only the topmost becoming simple and arrow-shaped to narrowly triangular; field mustard's stem is hairless and its upper leaves are smooth, bluish-green, not lobed and clasp the stem.
lookalikes.name: Field mustard

lookalikes.howToTell: As seedlings the two are almost identical. In the rosette, eastern rocket's end lobe is longer and more pointed; hedge mustard's is short and rounded. In flower, eastern rocket's petals are 6–10 mm long, against hedge mustard's 3–4 mm, and its sepals 3–5 mm, against about 2 mm. Eastern rocket's pods are much longer, (40)–60–100 × 1–1.5 mm, and spread away from the stem; hedge mustard's are 10–15–(20) mm long and pressed flat against it.
lookalikes.name: Eastern rocket

preparation.text: Pick it young: once it grows past the early stage it turns tough and spindly, and older plants are more bitter and more peppery. Use the young leaves and shoots raw, as a flavouring in salads or mixed with milder greens, or cook them as a potherb or green vegetable; they can also go chopped into soups, sauces and savoury dishes. In parts of the Levant it is eaten with yoghurt. In Palestine, where it is called hwerneh, the leaves and tender stalks are washed four or five times to get the dirt off, the thick stalks removed, and the rest cut into thin strips, rubbed with salt and left in a strainer for 6–8 hours to draw out the bitterness; then it is squeezed hard, a handful at a time, and stirred into yoghurt to ferment slightly. Squeezed, it keeps in the freezer. Use the flowers as a small garnish, or infuse them, fresh, dried or frozen, in a hot drink. Dried for tea, the plant leaves a sour aftertaste. Grind the seed to a powder and use it as a mustard-like flavouring in soups, or make it into a mustard paste.

recipes.method: Serves 2. 30 ml (2 tbsp) vegetable oil; 1 shallot, finely sliced; 2 garlic cloves; 5 g laver seaweed; 50 g shiitake mushrooms, sliced; 100 g fresh hedge mustard leaves; 115 g jasmine rice; 30 ml (2 tbsp) miso; 60 ml (4 tbsp) mirin; 1 litre water; 2 cm galangal or ginger; 2 lemongrass stalks; 4 makrut lime leaves; 2 Thai green chillies. Heat the oil in a large saucepan and gently fry the shallot and mushrooms until the shallot is soft. Add the lemongrass, galangal, chillies and lime leaves and fry for 30 seconds. Stir in the miso and 1 litre of boiled water until the miso dissolves, then simmer for 10 minutes. Add the rice, the finely chopped hedge mustard and the laver, stir well and simmer for 15 minutes. Take the pan off the heat, stir in the mirin and leave it for 5 minutes. Take out the lime leaves and lemongrass before serving; chew the galangal slices but do not swallow them. The source lists the garlic but its method doesn't use it.
recipes.title: Hedge mustard and laver rice soup

recipes.method: Makes about 1 litre. 1 litre water; zest of ½ lemon; 1 apple, sliced, unpeeled; 20 g fresh ginger, peeled and cut in pieces; 1–2 fresh okra pods, sliced; 30 ml (2 tbsp) honey; 15 ml (1 tbsp) hedge mustard flowers, fresh, dried or frozen; 10 ml (2 tsp) hedge mustard seeds. Put the water, apple, lemon zest, ginger and okra in a saucepan, bring to the boil, then cover and simmer over a low heat for 8–10 minutes. Take it off the heat and let it cool to about 60 °C, then add the hedge mustard flowers and seeds and leave them to infuse. Drink it hot, warm or cold; served cold, it can go in a jug with pieces of fruit, like sangria, but without ice. The source lists the honey but its method doesn't use it.
recipes.title: Hedge mustard flower and seed drink

recipes.method: Fresh hedge mustard; salt; 1 litre (4 cups) Greek yoghurt; olive oil and warm pita bread, to serve. Wash the hedge mustard four or five times to get rid of the dirt on the leaves. Take off the thick stalks, keeping the leaves and tender stalks, and cut them into thin strips. Sprinkle generously with salt and massage it into the leaves. Leave them in a strainer over a bowl for 6–8 hours, in the fridge if the weather is hot, until they wilt. Squeeze out as much liquid as you can, a handful at a time; the squeezed greens can be frozen in a freezer bag at this point. Stir 250 ml (1 cup) of the squeezed hedge mustard into the yoghurt in a jar or bowl until evenly mixed. Keep it in the fridge for at least 24 hours, better 2–4 days, so the hedge mustard flavours the yoghurt and it ferments slightly. Serve with a drizzle of olive oil and warm pita bread.
recipes.title: Hwerneh (hedge mustard in yoghurt)

recipes.method: The author's greens, picked in August, were storksbill, hedge mustard and chickweed. A big handful of these wild greens; the juice of 1 lime and 1 lemon; 5 ml (1 tsp) of her herb-steeped cider vinegar; 5 ml (1 tsp) of her wild salt and pepper (sea salt ground with dried kawakawa and nasturtium leaves and harakeke seed); 60 ml (¼ cup) sunflower seeds; 60 ml (¼ cup) almonds. Put everything in a high-speed blender or small food processor and blend on low, pushing the mix onto the blade with the tamper, until it is as smooth or chunky as you like.
recipes.title: Winter wild-greens pesto

summary.text:
Sisymbrium officinale, the hedge mustard, (formerly Erysimum officinale) is a plant in the family Brassicaceae.
Once indigenous to North Africa and southern Europe, but found in Ireland, Wales and England and also in the highlands of Scotland. It is now well-established throughout the world.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) it is widespread throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands, the Kermadecs and the Chathams, naturalised by 1855 from western, central and southern Europe, north-west Africa and Asia Minor. Plants with hairless pods, once called var. leiocarpum, turn up here and there throughout its range here, and it has also been recorded in New Zealand as Erysimum officinale.
It can germinate at any time of year, though mostly in spring or autumn, and grows first as a rosette, then sends up flowering stems a metre or more tall. In some parts of the country it is wrongly called wireweed, a different plant. In crops such as peas its tough stems can clog harvesters. Its tiny flowers are usually self-pollinated, each pod holds around 15 tiny wind-dispersed seeds, and a few seeds stay viable for five years.
Its species name, officinale, comes from the Latin officina, a word that first meant a workshop and later a monastic storeroom, herb room or pharmacy; it refers to the plant's medicinal value. In Britain it was long thought native, but it is now regarded as an archaeophyte, a plant introduced in ancient times.
In folk medicine it was used to soothe sore throats and lost voices, which earned it the name singer's plant. Its Italian name, erisimo, comes from the Greek for 'I save the singing', and its old French name, herbe aux chantres, means roughly 'singers' herb'; in the nineteenth century opera singers took it before performing.
It has long dropped out of traditional cooking except in northern Europe, where it is widely used as a condiment.

warnings: Do not gather it from heavily fertilised ground or places that catch run-off: the leaves may be full of nitrates, which are toxic in high doses.
It grows mostly by roadsides and on waste ground, and the plant tends to collect and hold dust, so leaves from beside roads or other polluted places are seldom fit to eat.
In pastures it is controlled with herbicides such as MCPB, MCPA, 2,4-D and flumetsulam, and in lawns with MCPA, dicamba, picloram or triclopyr. Pick it only where you know none has been used.
It contains heart-acting glycosides like those of digitalis. No poisonings are recorded, but take care if you take digoxin or are low in potassium.
Eat it in ordinary food amounts, not in excess: like other cabbage-family plants it contains active mustard compounds.

Brassicaceae plants are known for their tendency to accumulate heavy metals, a trait that makes them valuable for the phytoremediation of contaminated soils. However, this same ability necessitates careful monitoring, as the accumulation of heavy metals can also pose potential health risks.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Shaded places along forest margins, amongst scrub and around hedges.
It grows in dappled shade at the edge of woods, in hedgerows and on rough ground.
It grows best in part to full shade and moist, rich soil, and also takes dry shade, under hedges and larger shrubs.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous, strongly aromatic or foetid perennial herb, to 80–(100) cm tall, densely hirsute, with many glandular hairs, also with sessile, white, glandular scales. Petioles to 7 cm long in lower leaves, often much less in upper leaves. Lamina 5–10 × 3–6 cm, usually ovate, sometimes oblong-ovate, deeply crenate-serrate and teeth often mucronulate; base cordate; apex acute. Bracts remotely toothed or entire, very different from foliage leaves. Calyx 6–8 mm long; tube longer than teeth; teeth about 3 mm long, narrow-triangular, acuminate, more or less purple. Corolla 12–16 mm long, reddish purple with whitish markings on the downward curved, spathulate, lower lip; tube exserted from calyx; upper lip hooded, with dense simple and glandular hairs outside; lower lip about 9 mm long × 8 mm across lateral lobes, longer than upper lip. Nutlets about 1.5–2 mm diameter, broad-obovoid or suborbicular, trigonous, smooth, almost black. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The crushed leaves give off a strong, foetid smell, unpleasant to some people; pressed longer between the fingers, they smell of mushrooms (ceps). It looks like a nettle but does not sting.
The leaves are light green and feel thick and furry. The smell comes only when a leaf or stem is crushed, not from the standing plant.

lookalikes.howToTell: Stinging nettle is covered in stinging hairs, and its flowers are tiny, green and tassel-like at the leaf joints; hedge woundwort does not sting, smells strongly foetid when crushed, and has reddish-purple two-lipped flowers 12–16 mm long, with white markings on the lower lip, in whorls up a spike. Both are perennials that spread by rhizomes, with opposite, toothed, heart-based leaves; nettle grows in thickets and along fence rows, hedge woundwort along forest margins, in scrub and around hedges. Both are eaten; nettle must be cooked or dried first.

preparation.text: Pick the shoot tops before the plant flowers. Wash and chop the leaves; they can go raw into salads, where they bring their strong flavour, but are better cooked, in soups, cream sauces, spreads and pasta fillings. The leaves freeze as they are. For tea, use the upper leaves and flowering tops, as a hot tea or a cold infusion; to dry them, take the leaves off the stems so they dry evenly and dry them at a low heat (about 38 °C).

recipes.method: Written for Stachys sylvatica in Belgium. 2 large onions; 2 large potatoes; 3 big handfuls of washed hedge woundwort leaves; 1 tbsp butter; 1 tbsp flour; a stock cube; milk; a little cream (optional); croutons, pumpkin or sunflower seeds, or the flowers, to garnish. Chop 2 large onions, and peel and chop 2 large potatoes. Roughly chop 3 big handfuls of washed hedge woundwort leaves. Soften the onions in 1 tbsp butter for a few minutes, add the potatoes and cook 5 minutes over a medium heat, then add the leaves for 30 seconds and stir in 1 tbsp flour. Add a stock cube and pour in milk, stirring, then simmer gently for 15 minutes, stirring now and then and adding a little water if it gets too thick. Blend for 1–2 minutes until smooth, add a little cream if you like, and season. Garnish with croutons, pumpkin or sunflower seeds, or the flowers.
recipes.title: Hedge woundwort velouté

recipes.method: Written for Stachys sylvatica in Belgium. 3 shallots; 50 ml olive oil; 300 ml chicken stock; 300 ml crème fraîche; 2 good handfuls of washed, drained hedge woundwort leaves; chicken, fish or pasta, to serve. Finely chop 3 shallots and sweat them in 50 ml olive oil in a small pan. Add 300 ml chicken stock and let it reduce, then pour in 300 ml crème fraîche, heat through and season. Add 2 good handfuls of washed, drained hedge woundwort leaves, cook 5 minutes, then blend. Serve with chicken, fish or pasta.
recipes.title: Hedge woundwort cream sauce

recipes.method: Written for Stachys sylvatica in Belgium. 50 g sunflower seeds; 50 g walnut halves; 2 handfuls of young hedge woundwort leaves; 1 small onion; 2 tbsp rapeseed oil; a pinch each of flaky salt and pepper. The night before, soak 50 g sunflower seeds and 50 g walnut halves in water; drain them the next day. Wash 2 handfuls of young hedge woundwort leaves well and chop them finely. Fry 1 small onion for a few minutes, add the leaves and cook about 5 minutes. Blend everything with 2 tbsp rapeseed oil and a pinch each of flaky salt and pepper. Keep it in a jar in the fridge and spread it on toast or bread like a vegetable pâté.
recipes.title: Hedge woundwort and seed spread

recipes.method: Written for Stachys sylvatica in Belgium. Serves 8. Malfatti: 130 g young hedge woundwort leaves; a little olive oil; 350 g ricotta; 1 egg; 60 g grated parmesan, plus more to serve; 60 g flour, plus more for coating; salt and pepper. Sauce: 200 ml cream (or plant cream); 20 g young hedge woundwort leaves. Finely chop 130 g of young hedge woundwort leaves and soften them for a few minutes, steamed or in a pan with a little olive oil; squeeze out as much liquid as you can and let them cool. Bring 200 ml cream (or plant cream) to the boil with the remaining 20 g of leaves, blend, season and leave to infuse. Mix the chopped leaves with 350 g ricotta, 1 egg, 60 g grated parmesan, 60 g flour, salt and pepper, and chill 15 minutes until firm. With wet hands, roll walnut-sized balls, coat them in flour and lay them on a floured cloth. Drop them one at a time into a large pan of boiling salted water and lift them out with a slotted spoon as soon as they rise, like gnocchi. Serve under the hot sauce with more parmesan and black pepper.
recipes.title: Hedge woundwort malfatti

summary.text:
Stachys sylvatica, commonly known as hedge woundwort, whitespot, or sometimes as hedge nettle, is a perennial herbaceous plant growing to 80 cm tall in woodland and unmanaged grassland.
Hedge woundwort is native to Europe and central and western Asia.
It has been introduced into New York state, Ontario, and New Zealand.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1935. It is widespread in the North Island, especially common in the southern half; in the South Island it is generally uncommon, in scattered places as far south as the Otago Peninsula.
It spreads quickly on underground runners and by seed, and can form a dense ground cover that crowds out other plants; it can be invasive in damp places. It is also called hedge stachys.

warnings: Avoid it when pregnant: once it flowers, it may be slightly abortifacient. This rests on a single wild-food guide.

identification.text:
Erect annual or biennial, with a foetid smell when crushed. Stems hollow, striate, up to 2–(3) m high, usually light green and purple spotted or blotched, sometimes tinged purplish or pink, particularly toward the base. Leaves 2–4-pinnate; ultimate segments narrowly or broadly ovate to deltoid, pinnatisect or serrate, 5–40 mm long; leaf stalks light green and purple blotched when mature; stem leaves similar to basal, but with short stalks and 1–3-pinnate. Umbels 1–8 cm in diameter; rays 4–16; bracts about 4–8, narrow-triangular, acuminate, reflexed; bracteoles 3–6, triangular, confined to the outer side of the small umbels. Flowers numerous, white, about 2 mm in diameter. Fruit dark brown, 2.5–3 mm long; ribs slender, light brown, often crenulate. Flowers September–January.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In its first year it is a large rosette of finely divided, fern-like leaves, dark green above and grey-green underneath. In the second year it sends up a tall branching flower stem, often holding the white flowers a metre or more above the ground, and dies after flowering. The stems and leaf stalks have no hairs. Crushed, it smells musty or mouse-like.

lookalikes.howToTell: Fennel's leaves are divided into thread-fine segments, its flowers are yellow, the plant is aromatic and its leaves smell of aniseed, and its leaf stalks extend into a thin ribbed sheath along their whole length; there are no bracts under its umbels. Hemlock's leaf segments are broader — narrowly to broadly ovate or triangular, toothed or cut — its flowers are white, it has a few narrow, down-turned bracts under each umbel, and it smells foetid or musty when crushed. Hemlock's stem is usually spotted or blotched purple, especially toward the base, but not always, so an unspotted stem does not prove fennel. Both are hairless, so a smooth stem does not separate them. Check every one of these on every plant.
lookalikes.name: Wild fennel

lookalikes.howToTell: Look under the umbels: hemlock has about 4–8 narrow, pointed, down-turned bracts beneath each umbel and 3–6 bracteoles on the outer side of each small umbel; sea celery usually has none, occasionally a single bract that falls early. Hemlock is erect, up to 2–(3) m, with hollow stems usually spotted or blotched purple; sea celery is prostrate to ascending, its sprawling stems 0.3–1.2 m long. Hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided and sea celery's three-parted to 1–2 times divided with lobed, toothed segments that are narrow in some plants, so leaf shape alone does not separate them. Hemlock smells foetid or musty when crushed and sea celery has a celery-like aroma, but no source here treats smell as a reliable test on its own. Sea celery is mostly coastal but also grows beside lakes and streams inland, and hemlock grows in damp waste ground and riverbeds, so place does not rule hemlock out. Both have white flowers in compound umbels, though sea celery's petals can be off-white to cream.
lookalikes.name: Sea celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild carrot's stem is bristly-hairy and more or less solid, up to 120 cm tall, and sometimes tinged purple; hemlock's is hairless and hollow, up to 2 m (rarely 3 m), and usually spotted or blotched purple — but sometimes only tinged purplish or pink, so a stem without blotches does not rule hemlock out. Wild carrot's leaves are sparsely to moderately hairy; hemlock is hairless throughout. Under the umbel, wild carrot has numerous bracts divided into narrow linear segments; hemlock has about 4–8 narrow-triangular bracts that bend back. A few central flowers of a wild carrot umbel are sometimes red or purple. Wild carrot's root smells of carrot; crushed hemlock smells foetid and musty. Every one of these must agree before you treat a plant as wild carrot.
lookalikes.name: Wild carrot

lookalikes.howToTell: Alexanders has yellowish flowers and leaves divided in threes into flat, shiny, lobed and toothed leaflets. Hemlock has white flowers and leaves divided two to four times into finely divided segments. Hemlock's stem is hollow and usually spotted or blotched purple, sometimes tinged purplish or pink, particularly toward the base, but an unmarked stem does not rule it out. Alexanders' stem starts solid but becomes hollow and grooved with age, so a hollow stem does not separate them either. Purple on the leaf stalks is no help: alexanders' are purple-striped, and hemlock's are purple-blotched when mature. Crushed hemlock smells foul and mousy. Ripe hemlock fruits are dark brown, 2.5–3 mm; alexanders' are black, 6.5–8 mm. Check every character on every plant, and if the flowers are white or the leaves finely divided, do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Alexanders

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have finely divided, fern-like leaves and flat-topped heads of small white flowers, both grow in waste places throughout New Zealand, and their flowering seasons overlap. Hemlock's flowers are separate, about 2 mm across, on the spokes of open umbels (4–16 rays), several umbels to a much-branched stem; yarrow's are tiny daisy heads about 5–10 mm across with 4–7 short rays, packed into one dense, flat cluster. Hemlock's stem is hairless, hollow, up to 2–3 m and usually purple-spotted or blotched (sometimes only tinged purplish or pink); yarrow's is ribbed, hairy especially above, and up to about 80 cm. Hemlock's leaves are larger, triangular and parsley-like with broader toothed segments; yarrow's are narrow and feathery, with tiny awl-shaped segments not in one plane. Hemlock smells foetid and musty when crushed; yarrow is strongly aromatic. Young hemlock is closer to yarrow than a tall flowering plant. Yarrow is edible in small amounts but carries its own cautions (daisy-family allergy, pregnancy) — see its entry.
lookalikes.name: Yarrow

lookalikes.howToTell: Garden celery is found wild in New Zealand in damp waste places, where hemlock grows too. Look under the umbels: hemlock has about 4–8 narrow, pointed, down-turned bracts beneath each umbel and 3–6 bracteoles on the outer side of each small umbel; celery has none, though its umbels sit almost without a stalk opposite a leaf and so can look as if they had a bract. Hemlock grows up to 2–(3) m, its hollow stems usually purple spotted or blotched, but not always; celery reaches 80–(100) cm. Hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided into segments 5–40 mm long, celery's 1–2 times divided into lobed segments 2–4 cm long. Hemlock's flowers are white, about 2 mm across, and its fruit 2.5–3 mm long; celery's flowers are greenish white, about 1 mm across, and its fruit 1.5–2 mm long. Hemlock smells foetid when crushed and celery smells strongly of celery, but no source here treats smell as a reliable test on its own.
lookalikes.name: Celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Both begin as rosettes of divided leaves, and both grow in waste places and riverbeds. Hemlock's leaf stalks have no hairs; musky storksbill is densely covered in glandular hairs and feels sticky. Crushed hemlock smells foetid; musky storksbill usually smells of musk, though not always strongly. Leaf shape does not separate them: hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided into ovate to triangular, toothed or cut segments 5–40 mm long, and musky storksbill's carry stalkless leaflets that are themselves lobed and toothed. Stem colour does not either: hemlock's stems are usually spotted or blotched purple, and musky storksbill's can be green to purple. Both carry their flowers in umbels. Grown on, hemlock stands erect, up to 2–(3) m, with hollow stems and white flowers about 2 mm across; musky storksbill lies along the ground or rises to about 60 cm, with pink or mauve-pink flowers, petals 4.5–8 mm long, about 12 to a cluster, followed by fruits with a beak 3–3.5 cm long. If a rosette is hairless or smells foul, leave it. Musky storksbill's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Musky storksbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Both begin as rosettes of finely divided, fern-like leaves, and both grow in waste places and riverbeds. Hemlock is hairless throughout; common storksbill's leaves and stems are hairy, sometimes densely so. Crushed hemlock smells foetid; common storksbill has no scent. Leaf shape alone is not enough: hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided into segments 5–40 mm long, and common storksbill's stalkless leaflets are themselves deeply and finely cut. Stem colour is not either: hemlock's stems are usually spotted or blotched purple, and common storksbill's can be red. Grown on, hemlock stands erect, up to 2–(3) m, with hollow stems and many white flowers about 2 mm across; common storksbill lies along the ground or rises to about 50 cm, with (2–)5–12 flowers to a cluster, petals 4–6 mm long, usually pink or mauve-pink but rarely white, followed by fruits with a beak 3–3.5 cm long. If a rosette is hairless or smells foul, leave it. Common storksbill's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Common storksbill

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conium_maculatum Puts a number on the lethal dose, which is the most useful thing a deterrence page can carry: 'Ingesting more than 150–300 milligrams of coniine, approximately equivalent to six to eight hemlock leaves, can be fatal for adult humans.' The toxic alkaloids are coniine and γ-coniceine; coniine resembles nicotine in structure and acts on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the central nervous system. Two facts that cut against assuming a given plant is mild: the alkaloids are volatile and drying loses a large part of them, but plants grown in sunny conditions can be twice as poisonous as those from wet, cloudy ground. Poisoning is recorded across pigs, cattle, turkeys, horses, rabbits, cats and dogs.

summary.text:
The tall, purple-blotched umbellifer that kills people who think they have found fennel, parsley or wild carrot. Every part is poisonous if eaten.
Hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand, and probably the commonest of all the naturalised members of the carrot family (Apiaceae) here. Edible plants that can be confused with it include cultivated and wild carrot, parsnip, fennel and parsley, with potentially fatal results; in New Zealand pasture it is probably most likely to be confused with wild carrot.
Native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, it was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1872. It is very common throughout the North and South Islands, though only occasional on the West Coast of the South Island, and is also recorded at Halfmoon Bay on Stewart Island and on the Chatham Islands.
Most livestock recognise it as poisonous and leave it alone; poisoning is most likely when animals are pushed hard to eat it or after it has been sprayed, which seems to attract them. In the Auckland region it is a pest plant under the Regional Pest Management Plan, set for sustained control. The name maculatum is Latin for 'blotched'.

warnings: Every part — leaf, stem, root, seed — is poisonous if eaten. The poison paralyses the breathing muscles and can kill.
Wear gloves if you pull it, and do not eat with unwashed hands after handling it. Children have died after using the hollow stems as blowpipes, and dead stems stay poisonous for up to three years.
If you suspect any contact with food, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766 immediately.

edibleParts.text: The young leaves and shoots can be eaten raw or cooked, as can the stems and flowers. Henbit dead-nettle has a slightly sweet and peppery flavour, similar to celery. Young leaves are added to salads or used as a potherb. The leaves, stems and flowers can also be made into a tea.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Waste places such as roadsides, railway yards and building sites, also on arable land.
It is found growing in open areas, gardens, fields and meadows, and widely in uncultivated areas in urban habitats.
In New Zealand it is a common weed of cropping land, especially in the South Island.
It grows into slightly drier places than red deadnettle, which takes a little more shade.

identification.text:
Annual herb with hairy or nearly glabrous, more or less erect stems to about 30 cm, but often shorter than 5 cm high in dry situations. Petioles long and slender. Lamina 5–20 × 5–20 mm, ovate or oblong-ovate, crenate, sometimes more deeply cut, sparsely to moderately clothed in usually more or less appressed hairs; base broad-cuneate, truncate to cordate. Bracts to about 2.5 × 2 cm, very broadly ovate, hairy; base cordate, amplexicaul. Calyx 5–7 mm long, with more or less silky tomentum; teeth linear-subulate, about equal to tube. Corolla about 15 mm long, pinkish purple; tube erect, narrow, long-exserted, glabrous inside; upper lip 3–5 mm long, tomentose outside, with 3 purple blotches inside; lateral lobes of lower lip 0 (sometimes flowers cleistogamous and corolla remaining closed and included in calyx). Nutlets 1.8–2.2 mm long, patterned white, sharply angled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is often found alongside Lamium purpureum (red dead-nettle), for which it is easily mistaken, because the two species bear not only similar leaves, but also similar bright pink to purple flowers. They can, however, be distinguished from one another by the form of the leaves on their respective flowering stems; those of red dead-nettle are petiolate, while those of henbit dead-nettle are sessile.
Some N.Z. populations are almost or completely cleistogamous whilst in other places the flowers are chasmogamous and conspicuous.
In the field: the stem is square and often purplish, and the leaves are aromatic when rubbed. The lower leaves have long stalks and the lower leaf pairs are set wide apart; the upper leaves are stalkless, and a pair can look almost joined into one leaf wrapped round the stem. The leaves have a few deep, rounded teeth and a crinkled surface. The flowers, often with darker spots, come from the top of the stem and usually stand above the highest leaves. After flowering the calyx teeth close up. The lower stems can root at the joints.
Seedlings: the seed leaves are round with a flat tip and a notched base, on stalks.

lookalikes.howToTell: Henbit's bracts — the leaves under the upper flower clusters — are stalkless, broadly ovate and clasp the stem, unlike its lower leaves; red deadnettle's bracts are like its leaves and short-stalked. Henbit's flower tube is long, narrow and hairless inside; red deadnettle's has a conspicuous ring of hairs inside near the base. Henbit's flowers usually stand above its top leaves, which are held upright; red deadnettle's flowers sit under the top few pairs of leaves, which droop and give the stem tip a pagoda-like look. Henbit's leaves have fewer, deeper and blunter teeth. Both grow in the same waste places and crops, and both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Red deadnettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Henbit's bracts — the leaves under the upper flower clusters — are stalkless, broadly ovate and clasp the stem; cut-leaved deadnettle's bracts are like its deeply toothed leaves, with short stalks. Henbit's flower is about 15 mm with a long, narrow tube; cut-leaved deadnettle's is 11–15 mm. Both grow on waste ground and in gardens.
lookalikes.name: Cut-leaved deadnettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Field woundwort's flowers are small — 6–7 mm long, with a small upper lip that is not hooded and is shorter than the lower lip, the tube no longer than the calyx; henbit's are about 15 mm long with a hooded upper lip, on a long, narrow tube. Field woundwort's stem is much hairier. Henbit's leaves among the flowers are stalkless, broad and kidney-shaped, clasp the stem and look unlike its other leaves; field woundwort's are stalkless too, but oblong, oval or nearly round, like its upper leaves — so stalkless leaves alone do not separate them. Both are weeds of gardens, crops and waste places, and young plants are easily confused. Field woundwort poisons livestock (staggers); no record of it being eaten by people has been found, so do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Field woundwort

lookalikes.howToTell: Ground-ivy is a creeping perennial whose stems root at the joints; every leaf, even among the flowers, is on its own slender stalk, and its flowers are blue or blue-violet. Henbit is an annual whose leaves among the flowers have no stalk and clasp the stem; its flowers are pinkish purple, on a long, narrow, upright tube. Both grow on disturbed ground around buildings, and both are eaten. Ground-ivy is local in the southern North Island and the South Island.
lookalikes.name: Ground-ivy

preparation.text: Pick it young and tender: older plants are not harmful but get tough and woody. The hairy leaves put some people off eating them raw. Its flavour has a musty edge, which goes well with mushrooms. To freeze, blanch it as you would kale.

recipes.method: Written for henbit in the United States. About 1 litre (4 cups) of henbit shoots; 45 ml (3 tbsp) butter; 5 ml (1 tsp) curry powder; 2 whole cloves; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground cinnamon; 30 ml (2 tbsp) flour; 185 ml (¾ cup) sour cream. Chop the henbit shoots, cover with water and boil for 10 minutes. In another pan melt the butter with the curry powder, cloves and cinnamon, cook for a minute, stir in the flour and cook a minute more. Whisk in 125 ml (½ cup) of the henbit's cooking water until smooth, then add the drained henbit and the sour cream and cook on low for 15 minutes.
recipes.title: Spicy henbit

recipes.method: Written for henbit. Serves 4. Noodles: about 225 g henbit leaves; 1 garlic clove; 2 eggs; 15 ml (1 tbsp) olive oil; 250 ml (1 cup) plain flour, plus 125 ml (½ cup) for dusting; 185 ml (¾ cup) semolina. Sauce: 250 ml (1 cup) chopped mushrooms; 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter; salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) flour; 250 ml (1 cup) mushroom or other stock; a little thyme; 125 ml (½ cup) light cream; 60 ml (¼ cup) grated parmesan, plus more to serve. Wilt the henbit leaves in 60 ml (¼ cup) water over medium heat, about 5 minutes; drain, cool under cold water and squeeze dry. Purée with the garlic, eggs and olive oil. Mix the 250 ml flour (keep the dusting flour aside) with the semolina, make a well, work in the purée and knead for 10 minutes into a dough that no longer sticks. Rest it under a damp cloth for 30 minutes, roll each quarter thin, roll up loosely and cut into noodles 6–12 mm wide. For the sauce, cook the mushrooms in the butter with salt until their liquid has evaporated, stir in the flour for 2 minutes, then add the stock a splash at a time with the thyme until thick; finish with the cream. Boil the noodles in salted water for 3 minutes, drain, toss with the sauce and the parmesan, and serve with more cheese.
recipes.title: Henbit noodles with mushroom sauce

recipes.method: Written for henbit in Tennessee. Serves about 6. 4 garlic cloves, chopped; 1 onion, chopped; 30 ml (2 tbsp) olive oil; 1.5 litres (6 cups) chicken or vegetable stock; a 440 g can of cannellini beans, drained and rinsed; 250 ml (1 cup) small pasta; 375 ml (1½ cups) chopped henbit; parmesan to serve, if you like. Fry the garlic and onion in the olive oil until translucent, about 10 minutes. Add the stock and bring to the boil, then add the beans and pasta and boil until the pasta is tender, 8–10 minutes. Add the henbit and cook a few minutes until wilted. Season with salt and pepper and serve with parmesan.
recipes.title: Cannellini bean and henbit soup

summary.text:
Lamium amplexicaule, commonly known as henbit dead-nettle, is a species of Lamium native to most of Europe, Asia and northern Africa.
Henbit dead-nettle is native to most of Europe, Asia and North Africa, and has since been spread around the world by human activity.
It is widely naturalised in eastern North and South America, New Zealand, South Africa and Tasmania. Its attractive appearance, edibility, and readiness to grow in many climates often mean it is permitted to grow when other weeds are not.
Its status in Great Britain and Ireland is disputed; some sources give it as native, while others cite it as an archaeophyte.
It propagates freely by seed, where it becomes a key part of a meadow ecosystem; sometimes entire fields will be reddish-purple with its flowers before spring ploughing.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1880 and is widespread and common in the North and South Islands.
Besides its open flowers it makes small ones that never open and pollinate themselves, often in the cooler part of the year when few pollinators are about.
It is also called fairy horns: a plucked flower can be blown like a little horn.

warnings: Henbit is listed as poisonous in New Zealand. The poisonings on record are of grazing animals: sheep, and probably cattle and horses, develop staggers — staggering after exercise, stiff hind legs, rapid shallow breathing, shivering and trembling — mostly after grazing cereal stubble holding mature plants.
It is a weed of cropping land, where it is sprayed with herbicides. Pick from ground you know has not been sprayed.

Field woundwort (staggerweed), which poisons livestock, grows in the same places and looks alike when young. Check for henbit's long flower tube and the broad leaves clasping the stem under the flowers; field woundwort's leaves there are stalkless too, but oblong to oval like its upper leaves.

identification.text:
Annual or biennial hairy taprooted herb, with a characteristic scent. Stems decumbent to spreading, to about 50 cm long, lax, often red where exposed to strong light, sometimes with base thickened; internodes short and leaves rosette-like. Petioles long and slender on lower leaves, often reddish, glabrous or hairy. Lamina palmate, to about 9 × 10 cm, broad- or triangular-ovate, usually becoming red with age; lobes 3–5, at least the terminal petiolulate, pinnately divided to varying degrees, more or less appressed-hairy; ultimate segments usually mucronulate. Inflorescence very diffuse; flowers paired; peduncles usually longer than pedicels; peduncles and pedicels with long- and short-stalked glands. Sepals (at anthesis) 6.5–8 mm long including apical awn, ovate, prominently 3-nerved, with hairs as on pedicels. Petals (7.5)–10–11.5 mm long, obovate-oblanceolate, pink or rose except for white margin of claw; limb equal to claw; apex rounded. Filaments pinkish; anthers orange. Mericarps 2.5–3 mm long, glabrous or hairy, with 4–6 transverse ridges. Seed smooth. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Small herb Robert is an annual or biennial, hairy, taprooted herb with a characteristic scent; its stems are sprawling to nearly upright and reach about 30 cm; its leaves are 1.5–5–(7) × 2–6–(8) cm, cut very deeply into 5 lobes; its flowers are paired, with pink to rose petals 6–9 mm long; its anthers are yellow; its fruit segments are 2.5–3 mm long, with many close cross-ridges on their upper two-thirds. Herb robert is an annual or biennial, hairy, taprooted herb with a characteristic scent; its stems reach about 50 cm; its leaves reach about 9 × 10 cm, with 3–5 lobes; its flowers are paired, with pink or rose petals (7.5)–10–11.5 mm long; its anthers are orange; its fruit segments (mericarps) are 2.5–3 mm long, with 4–6 cross-ridges. They are separated on the petals, usually 10–11.5 mm in herb robert and 6–9 mm in small herb Robert, and the anthers, orange in herb robert and yellow in small herb Robert. The two have sometimes been confused; small petals, yellow pollen and more, closer ridges on the fruit segments together are the signs of small herb Robert, which is also generally more upright, with smaller leaves. No single sign settles it: herb robert's petals can be as short as 7.5 mm, inside small herb Robert's range, and both species have yellow pollen, so anther colour alone can be hard to read. Both are scented, both have paired pink flowers and deeply divided leaves that turn red, and their fruit segments are the same length. No source read records small herb Robert as food.

preparation.text: The fresh leaves are put in a mug of hot water as a tea, or the leaves and flowers dried for tea in winter.

recipes.method: 30 g herb robert; 30 g basil leaves; 1 garlic clove, crushed; olive oil; 40 g Parmesan or Pecorino, finely grated; the juice of half a lemon; salt and black pepper. Blend 30 g herb robert, 30 g basil leaves and 1 crushed garlic clove with enough olive oil to make a loose purée. Stir in 40 g finely grated Parmesan or Pecorino and the juice of half a lemon, then season with salt and black pepper to taste. Keeps well frozen in ice-cube trays.
recipes.title: Herb robert and basil pesto

recipes.method: Written for plantain, herb Robert, nasturtium seeds, oxtongue or rosemary, singly or together (the page does not say which plantain). Chop the plant material and pack it loosely in a jar. Fill the jar with apple cider vinegar to cover the plants completely, let it sit a little, and poke out any air bubbles under the leaves with a chopstick. Cap it, with a piece of plastic under a metal lid so the vinegar doesn't eat the metal, label it and leave it in a cool place for 2–6 weeks, then strain the vinegar into a bottle. Use it in salad dressings, soups and pestos, or sweetened with honey by the spoonful.
recipes.title: Herbal vinegar

recipes.method: The author's greens were the leaves of Indian, alpine (woodland) and garden strawberries, red deadnettle, wall lettuce, herb Robert and nasturtium. A handful of mixed strawberry leaves, stems removed (they are tough); a handful of beetroot leaves and stems; several stems of red deadnettle with their flowers; 5 wall lettuce leaves; 5 herb Robert leaves; red nasturtium flowers and several leaves; a few celery and small kale leaves, optional. Blend the leaves and flowers with 500–750 ml (2–3 cups) water, then add 1 punnet of strawberries, 1 red apple, 2 kiwifruit and 2 bananas and blend again.
recipes.title: Wild and tame strawberry smoothie

summary.text:
Geranium robertianum, commonly known as herb-robert or, in North America, as Robert's geranium, is a species of cranesbill that is widespread throughout the northern hemisphere and introduced to some countries in the southern.
The main areas of distribution of herb-robert are throughout Europe northwards to the Baltic and eastwards as far as Russia. It also occurs in north Africa and it is considered also to be native in north America, although in some western states it is regarded as a weed.
The IUCN has not assessed the threat status of this species, but in some countries it is classified as Least Concern.
It grows at altitudes from sea level to 700 m at Great Dun Fell in England and up to 2,400 m in Kashmir.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island; South Island: widely naturalised but commonest in the North Island. It has been recorded as naturalised since 1878 (NZPCN).

warnings: In Cantabria, Spain, it is regarded as poisonous and handled with care, though the records name no case of poisoning and no toxic compound.
Its safety has not been established in pregnancy or while breastfeeding.
