identification.text:
Shrub to 2–(3) m high; stems hollow, glabrous, green, glaucous at first. Petiole 0.5–2–(5) cm long, purplish, with hairy groove on upper side. Lamina 4–14–(24) × 1.5–8–(12) cm, ovate or broad-ovate, mostly entire, sometimes 5–9-lobed (rarely divided almost to midrib) with rounded sinuses, becoming glabrous except for midrib and bases of main veins; base rounded to cordate; apex long-acuminate. Inflorescence 3–8 cm long at flowering. Bracts mostly 1–3 cm long, sessile, broad-ovate, aristate-acuminate, more or less glandular-hairy, usually deep reddish purple. Calyx small, hidden by bracts; lobes very unequal. Corolla about 1.5 cm long, funnelform, white; lobes rounded at apex, much shorter than tube, with glandular-hairy margins. Stamens shortly exserted. Style longer than stamens. Berry 7–10 mm diameter, subglobose, dark brownish purple, glandular-hairy. Seed 1.1–1.5 mm long, obovoid-ellipsoid, shining brown, minutely white-dotted. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Leycesteria formosa, the pheasant berry, is a deciduous shrub in the family Caprifoliaceae, native to the Himalayas and southwestern China.
L. formosa includes within its wide range of distribution the areas of all the other known species of the genus. From the North-West Frontier Province and the Punjab it ranges the whole length of the Himalaya eastwards to south-eastern Yunnan, where it was collected by Henry near Mengtze, and north-eastwards to Szechuan and eastern Tibet, where Rehder's var. stenosepala appears to replace very largely the typical form.
A Revision of the Genus Leycesteria
— H.K. Airy-Shaw

The species is native to Pakistan, India, Nepal, East and West Himalaya,  Southwestern China (Sichuan, Yunnan and Guizhou), Tibet and Myanmar.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Lowland to high montane grassland and open habitats, such as cliffs, river banks, lakesides, sometimes in swampy ground.
From the coast to alpine country it is a sparse part of grassland and other open places such as cliffs, river banks, lake sides and grey scrub, and occasionally grows in swampy ground (NZPCN, restated).
It is found sparsely in grassy fields and open land generally. It inhabits an elevation range from coastal to alpine, within a range of sea level to 1,400 metres.

identification.text:
Mentha cunninghamii shares a mint odour with other species within the Mentha (mint) genus, but in appearance is very distinct from many other mints. It has been suggested that it may actually be more closely related to members of the Micromeria genus.
It is a slender, wiry, prostrate perennial plant, with a creeping rhizome. The plant is much branched, often matted, with numerous stems arising from the rhizome, diffusely branched, pubescent, growing from 5 to 30 cm long. Its leaves are shortly petiolate or nearly sessile, 4 to 13 mm long, broadly ovate or almost orbicular, obtuse, entire or with an obscure notch on each side, and glandular-dotted. Its flowers are small, white, axillary, usually solitary but sometimes with two to three in each axil. Its peduncles are slender and variable in length. Its calyx are about 3 mm long, tubular-campanulate in shape, densely hairy, with teeth villous within. Its corolla-lobes are almost equal, flat and spreading, with the upper one shortly bifid. Its stamens protrude equally with the corolla or are slightly exserted.
Gynodioecious perennial; stems more or less creeping, very slender, branched, puberulent, especially on angles. Leaves sessile or with short hairy petioles to 4 mm long. Lamina 2–15 × 2–15 mm, broad-ovate to suborbicular, not rugose, entire or shallowly crenate, dotted with glands and usually glabrous except for nerves on lower surface; base broad-cuneate or truncate; apex rounded. Flowers axillary, in clusters of 1–2–(3); pedicels prominent, puberulent. Calyx 3–4 mm long, narrow-campanulate, densely hairy and with glandular dots; teeth triangular, ciliate, much shorter than tube, acute. Corolla about 6 mm long, white, glabrous; tube not exserted; lobes subequal; uppermost lobe more or less 2-fid. Stamens more or less exserted. Nutlets 1–1.3 mm long, more or less broad-ellipsoid, slightly angled, smooth.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It looks quite unlike any of the naturalised mints in New Zealand; in a sward of native turf it is often first noticed by its mint smell (NZPCN, restated).
It forms loose patches up to 300 mm across, with purple to purple-red stems, bright green to yellow-green leaves and fragrant flowers (NZPCN fact sheet, restated).

summary.text:
Mentha cunninghamii, known commonly as New Zealand mint or Māori mint, is a species within the Mentha (mint) genus, endemic to New Zealand.
Mentha cunninghamii is endemic to the four islands of North Island, South Island, Chatham Island and Stewart Island in New Zealand.
Sources variously describe its flowering season as beginning in the Southern Hemisphere in either September or November, ending in April.
As of 2018, New Zealand's Department of Conservation's New Zealand Threat Classification System (NZTCS) assesses Mentha cunninghamii's conservation status as "At Risk: Declining." The system uses the Declining status to indicate populations that currently possess large populations, but are experiencing declines that could eventually lead to a listing as "Threatened."
Its biostatus is endemic, and the 2023 assessment of New Zealand vascular plants (de Lange et al. 2024) keeps it At Risk – Declining, as in 2017 and 2012 (NZTCS, restated).
It is threatened by habitat degradation from livestock, irrigation and drainage, and by weed competition (NZPCN, restated).
Māori used the leaves for scent, including as one ingredient of a scent compound made with taramea gum, and used the plant to induce sweating (Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga, restated).

warnings: No food record for hioi was found. Māori use is recorded for the scented leaves and as a medicine to induce sweating, not as food, and no edible use of it is recorded.

edibleParts.text: Root, raw or cooked, before the plant flowers; once it flowers the root usually turns tough. Flowers, raw, in salads. Leaves, raw or cooked, picked before the flowers appear; they turn bitter after that. Leaves and flowers can be bitter, though the leaves can also taste of cabbage and mustard. The seed and green seed pods are not listed here: see Warnings.

identification.text:
Biennial, roots often swollen. Stems erect, leafy, hairy, branching above, to 1 m tall. Leaves cordate, acute, dark green, hairy, bluntly or coarsely dentate; lower leaves petiolate, opposite, 5–10–(20) × 3–5–(15) cm; upper leaves subsessile, alternate, 3–5–(8) × 1.5–3–(4) cm. Racemes to 30 cm long. Sepals hairy, 7–9 × 1.5–2.5 mm. Petals purple, rarely white, 15–22 × 6–8 mm. Silicle elliptic (lanceolate when immature), 2.5–4 × 2–3 cm, obtuse at both ends; carpophore 8–15 mm long; style 5–8 mm long. Seeds dark brown, 5–8 mm diameter 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
When a silique is ripe and dry, a valve on each of its sides readily falls off, and its seeds fall off a central membrane which has a silvery sheen, 3–8 cm in diameter; the membrane can persist on a plant throughout a winter depending on the weather.

lookalikes.howToTell: Honesty has heart-shaped, dark green, hairy leaves with blunt or coarse teeth, on a biennial plant, and its fruit is a broad, flat, elliptic disc 2.5–4 × 2–3 cm. Stock has narrow, lance-shaped leaves that are entire to shallowly lobed, densely felted and grey-green, tufted at the tips of stout woody stems that carry conspicuous leaf-base scars, and its pod is long and narrow, 50–120 × 3–5 mm. Flower colour and size do not separate them: honesty petals are purple (rarely white), 15–22 mm, and stock petals are pink to purple, 18–25 mm. Stock flowers are eaten as a vegetable or used as a garnish.

summary.text:
Lunaria annua, commonly called honesty or annual honesty, is a species of flowering plant in the cabbage and mustard family Brassicaceae.
Lunaria annua is native to southern Europe from Spain to Romania, and has been introduced to many other parts of the world with temperate climates.
In New Zealand it is recorded from Auckland, Palmerston North, Horowhenua and Wellington in the North Island; Canterbury (Christchurch, Banks Peninsula, Ashburton) and Dunedin in the South Island; and Stewart Island. It is native to south-eastern Europe and was first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1940.
New Zealand plants belong to subsp. annua. White-flowered cultivars are sometimes referred to as var. albiflora, but do not merit varietal rank.
Lunaria annua L. (Brassicaceae) is an ornamental plant newly identified in Europe as a promising industrial oilseed crop for its valuable very-long-chain monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs), especially erucic acid (EA) and nervonic acid (NA).

warnings: Do not eat the seed or the seed pods. The seeds accumulate toxic lunarine and lunaridin alkaloids. Several foraging sources list the seed as a mustard substitute and the green pods as a horseradish-hot vegetable, but none of them mention the alkaloids, and no source gives a safe amount.

Before it flowers, honesty is easy to confuse with several other species, and the leaves and roots are best taken at that stage. Make sure of the plant from its heart-shaped, toothed, hairy leaves, and leave it if in doubt.

identification.text:
Spreading deciduous tree, to about 10 m high and sometimes much taller, usually armed with stout spines on the trunk and branches; the spines are simple or branched, 2–10 cm long and sometimes up to 18 cm. Leaves alternate, 15–20 cm long, either once divided (pinnate) with 5–15 pairs of leaflets or, more often, twice divided (bipinnate) with 2–7 pairs of side branches each carrying 12–30 leaflets; leaflets elliptic to egg-shaped, mostly 10–35 mm long and 5–12 mm wide, sparsely toothed; leaf stalk 3–5 cm long, it and the leaf axis more or less hairy. Flowers small and inconspicuous, greenish or creamy-yellow, petals 4–6 mm long, in golden-hairy spikes 5–10 cm long in the leaf joints, in spring after the new leaves have formed. Pod flat, slightly curved, 15–40 cm long and 3–4 cm wide, dark brown or reddish-brown when ripe, not splitting open, with 15–25 dark brown, egg-shaped seeds about 10 mm long set in pulpy tissue.
Thornless forms are widely planted as street and garden trees, and some cultivars set few or no pods.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers, the pods and the leaves. Black locust's flowers are white, 15–23 mm long, many to a cluster; honey locust's are small, greenish or creamy-yellow, with petals 4–6 mm long, in golden-hairy spikes 5–10 cm long. Black locust's pods are 35–80 mm long with 2–8 seeds; honey locust's are 15–40 cm long and 3–4 cm wide, dark brown when ripe, with 15–25 seeds set in pulp. Black locust's leaves are once divided, with 4–10 pairs of leaflets; honey locust's are more often twice divided, though some are once divided with 5–15 pairs. Black locust's spines are up to about 1 cm long, scattered on the twigs; honey locust's are 2–10 cm long or more, often branched, on the trunk and branches. Both are planted in forms without spines and in golden-leaved forms, so missing spines or leaf colour do not tell them apart. Black locust's seeds, bark and leaves are poisonous; only its flowers are eaten (see its page).

Young seeds, cooked young pods and roasted seeds as a coffee substitute have each been recorded in one source only, so they are not given here.

summary.text: Honey locust, a deciduous tree of the pea family (Fabaceae) from eastern North America, planted in New Zealand as a street, shade and ornamental tree. It is exotic here and only sometimes found wild: it reproduces by seed, its long-lived seed is held for years in pods that stay on the tree, and seedlings and suckers come up near planted trees. On farms it is grown for stock shade and its pods as fodder. Most garden and street trees are thornless forms, and some cultivars bear few or no pods; the thornless weeping cultivar 'Emerald Kascade' was introduced by a New Zealand nursery in 1992. In Australia it forms dense thorny thickets along rivers and in pasture and is a declared weed; in New Zealand it is not on DOC's 2024 environmental weed list.

warnings: The typical form carries long, rigid spines on the trunk and branches, simple or branched, 2–10 cm and up to 18 cm long. They can cause serious injuries, and they stay dangerous on dead wood. Thornless forms are common in planting.
Eat only the pod pulp. The plant contains potentially toxic compounds: the twigs and leaves contain alkaloids, one of which, gleditschine, causes stupor and loss of reflexes.

Black locust, a pea-family tree with divided leaves also planted in New Zealand streets and parks, has poisonous seeds, bark and leaves, and only its flowers are eaten. Make sure of the tree before eating any pod (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text: On wood, in dense groups: round the bases of standing dead broadleaved trees and on their fallen trunks and branches, on stumps and logs, and on the ground from buried wood and roots. It grows in southern beech and podocarp–broadleaf forest, and also in pine plantations, orchards, and town parks and gardens, often round old stumps.

identification.text:
It grows in dense clusters on wood, the stem bases swollen and joined together. The cap is 3–8 cm across, olive-buff to olive-brown, with a sprinkling of very small dull brown scales at the centre. It is convex at first with a strongly down-rolled edge, then flat or shallowly dished; when fresh it is moist and clearly lined (striate) at the edge, and it dries matt. The flesh is creamy white.
The gills run a little way down the stem, or are notched just before it, and are moderately crowded with many short ones between; they are creamy white, turning dull fawn. The stem is 4–7 cm long and 4–8 mm thick, tough and solid, often tapering to the base; it is fawn above a thin ring that soon disappears, and brown to dark purplish brown below. The spore print is white.
In infected wood, look for white sheets or fans of mycelium under the bark and black bootlace-like strands.
The lemon honeycap (A. limonea), endemic to the North Island and northern South Island, is larger and brighter: its cap is 8–13 cm across, lemon yellow, thickly scattered at the centre with dark brown tufted scales, and its stem has a substantial cottony ring. Its spore print is also white. Its edibility is uncertain: it has been eaten without ill effect, but it is also recorded as bitter and inedible.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both grow on rotting wood, including southern beech, and both can have a ring on the stem, so place and ring do not separate them. Wood nipple fungus belongs to the group of the deadly Galerina marginata and probably carries the same toxins. It is much smaller and more slender: its cap is 1–2.5 cm across, often with a prominent pointed bump in the centre, on a stem 2–4 mm thick, and it grows singly or in loose groups, rarely in tight clumps. A honey mushroom's cap is 3–8 cm across on a tough stem 4–8 mm thick, in dense clusters with the stem bases joined together. Look at the gills: rusty orange to cinnamon in the Galerina, creamy white to dull fawn in the honey mushroom. A spore print settles it: cinnamon-brown for Galerina, white for the honey mushroom.

preparation.text:
Never eat it raw or undercooked. Cut the mushrooms high on the stem, or trim off the tough lower stems. Rinse them well, or soak them briefly: the lower caps in a cluster catch grit, bark and spores from the ones above. Then parboil them: cover with cold salted water, bring to the boil, skim off the foam and simmer for 15–20 minutes, then pour the water away. After that, fry, stew or pickle them, or add them to sauces and soups; the caps stay firm and chewy even after long simmering. Keep small button caps whole for pickling, and chop large open ones for frying.
To keep them, freeze them after boiling, or pickle them. Dried ones stay tough when soaked again.

recipes.method: Written for honey mushrooms (Armillaria) in general. Serves 4. 1 kg fresh honey mushrooms; 1 litre water; 4 tbsp (60 ml) white vinegar, 9% acidity; 2 tbsp sugar; 1½ tbsp non-iodised salt; 4 garlic cloves; 8–10 black peppercorns; 3 bay leaves; 3–4 whole cloves. Sort and clean the mushrooms, cut off the tough lower stems and wash them in several changes of cold water. Put them in a large pot, cover with cold water and bring to the boil, skimming off the foam. Simmer for 15–20 minutes, then drain and rinse them in a colander. For the marinade, bring the litre of water to the boil, add the salt, sugar, peppercorns, bay leaves and cloves and simmer for 3–5 minutes. Add the parboiled mushrooms and cook over medium heat for another 15 minutes. Slice the garlic thinly, add it with the vinegar and simmer 2–3 minutes more, then turn off the heat. Ladle the hot mushrooms and marinade into sterilised jars, keeping the mushrooms covered by the liquid, seal with sterilised lids, cool to room temperature and refrigerate. They are ready in about 24 hours and better after a few days. To serve, drain them and toss with a little olive or sunflower oil and chopped spring onion or red onion.
recipes.title: Marinated honey mushrooms

recipes.method: Written for honey mushrooms (Armillaria) in general. Serves 2. 500 g honey mushrooms; 1 large onion (about 120 g); 3 tbsp vegetable oil; 20 g butter; 1 garlic clove; salt and black pepper; fresh parsley. Clean the mushrooms, put them in a pot of salted water, bring to the boil and simmer for 15 minutes. Drain well and pat them as dry as you can with paper towels. Cut the onion into half-rings and mince the garlic. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat, add the mushrooms and fry for 10–12 minutes, stirring now and then, until their moisture has gone and they start to brown. Add the onion, lower the heat to medium and cook 8–10 minutes more, until soft and caramelised. In the last 2 minutes add the butter, garlic, salt and pepper and toss to coat. Sprinkle with chopped parsley. Good with fried or boiled new potatoes.
recipes.title: Sautéed honey mushrooms with onion

recipes.method: Written for honey mushrooms (Armillaria) in general. Serves 4. 600 g honey mushrooms; 250 g sour cream, at least 20% fat, at room temperature; 2 medium onions; 40 g butter; 1 tbsp plain flour; 50 ml water or mushroom stock; salt and pepper; a small bunch of fresh dill. Clean the mushrooms, boil them in salted water for 15–20 minutes and drain well; chop large ones and leave small ones whole. Finely dice the onions. Melt the butter in a deep frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions until translucent, 5–7 minutes. Add the mushrooms and sauté for about 10 minutes, until lightly golden. Sprinkle over the flour and stir for 1–2 minutes. Lower the heat, add the sour cream and the water or stock and stir until smooth, adding a little more water if it is too thick. Season, cover and simmer gently for 5–7 minutes without letting it boil hard, or the sour cream may split. Stir in the chopped dill, turn off the heat and leave 5 minutes before serving, with buckwheat, mashed potato or egg noodles.
recipes.title: Honey mushrooms in sour cream

recipes.method: Written for honey mushrooms (Armillaria) in general. Serves 4. 400 g honey mushrooms; 1.5 litres water; 3 medium potatoes; 1 medium carrot; 1 medium onion; 2 tbsp vegetable oil; 1 bay leaf; 4–5 black peppercorns; salt; fresh dill or parsley. Wash the mushrooms well and trim the stems. Put them in a large pot with the cold water, bring to the boil, skim off the foam, add a pinch of salt and simmer over medium-low heat for 20 minutes. Meanwhile peel the potatoes and cut them into medium cubes; add them to the pot and cook 10–15 minutes until tender. Finely dice the onion and coarsely grate the carrot. Fry the onion in the oil until soft, add the carrot and cook 5 minutes more until golden, then add them to the soup with the bay leaf and peppercorns. Check the salt and simmer gently for 5 minutes. Turn off the heat, take out the bay leaf, cover and leave 10–15 minutes. Serve hot, with sour cream and dark rye bread.
recipes.title: Honey mushroom soup

recipes.method: Written for honey mushrooms (Armillaria) in general. Serves 4. 300 g linguine or spaghetti; 400 g honey mushrooms; 3 garlic cloves; 4 tbsp extra virgin olive oil; 60 ml dry white wine; 20 g butter; 50 g grated Parmesan; a handful of chopped fresh parsley; salt and red pepper flakes. Clean the mushrooms, parboil them in salted water for 15 minutes, drain well and pat dry. Cook the pasta in plenty of well-salted boiling water until al dente, keeping 125 ml of the cooking water before draining. Slice the garlic thinly. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat, add the garlic and a pinch of pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, without letting the garlic brown. Turn the heat to medium-high, add the mushrooms and sauté for 7–8 minutes, until crisp and golden at the edges. Pour in the wine, scrape up the browned bits and let it reduce by half, about 2 minutes. Stir in the butter, add the drained pasta and toss well, adding a splash of the pasta water if it seems dry. Stir in the parsley and half the Parmesan, season with salt and serve with the rest of the cheese.
recipes.title: Honey mushroom pasta

summary.text:
Armillaria novae-zelandiae is a species of mushroom-forming fungus in the family Physalacriaceae.
In te reo Māori it is harore, and in English the olive honeycap. It is native: one of four Armillaria species in New Zealand, alongside the lemon honeycap (A. limonea), A. hinnulea and A. aotearoa, and also found in Tasmania and eastern Australia, Papua New Guinea, Argentina and Chile, and parts of Indonesia, Malaysia and Japan. It is common here, with 1,858 research-grade iNaturalist records.
It is a white-rot fungus of wood and a root-rot pathogen of living trees. It spreads underground by black, bootlace-like strands (rhizomorphs) from buried wood and old stump roots, and by wind-borne spores. When native forest was cleared and planted in Pinus radiata, it survived in the old stumps and killed young pines around them, and from the 1970s to the 1990s it caused heavy losses in pine plantations and kiwifruit orchards. The cap sometimes glows in the dark.
In Mātauranga Māori, harore appearing in autumn forests foretells the future, a good fishing season or a famine depending on the region's tradition. It is a traditional Māori food, still collected by Tūhoe in Te Urewera. Because the mushrooms vanish soon after they come up, the whakataukī 'he harore rangitahi', a one-day mushroom, describes something fleeting, or a person who helps with work only briefly.

warnings: Never eat honey mushrooms raw or undercooked; raw, they cause severe stomach upset. Even well cooked, they disagree with some people, causing allergic reactions, fever-like symptoms, diarrhoea or other stomach and gut upsets. These reactions are recorded for the northern honey fungus (Armillaria mellea) and its relatives; no account of reactions to the New Zealand species was found.

Other mushrooms that grow in clusters on stumps and logs in New Zealand have brown spore prints. The spectacular rustgill (Gymnopilus junonius), common here, is inedible: it is bitter and contains neurotoxins. It is bright yellow-orange, ageing orange-brown or reddish brown, with yellow flesh, a frail ring dusted with rusty orange spores, and a rusty brown spore print. Scalycaps (Pholiota) have coarser scales that stand out and are firmly attached, and a brown spore print. A honey mushroom's spore print is white: check it before eating any.

identification.text:
Glabrous, short-lived perennial; taproot often thick; stems rather slender, branched, spreading to erect, to about 100 cm long. Petiole shorter than lamina, especially in uppermost leaves. Lamina of basal and cauline leaves (2.5)–6–22 × (0.5)–1–5 cm, linear, lanceolate-oblong, or oblong, generally with 2 rounded lobes at base, sometimes not lobed, sometimes oblique; margin not or somewhat undulate; base truncate to cordate, rarely cuneate; apex acute to long-acuminate. Inflorescence usually with leaves in the lower axils; flowers in distant whorls of 3–12, bisexual, strongly protandrous, extending downwards for ⅔ or more of stem. Pedicels prominently jointed, elongating and deflexed at fruiting. Perianth segments 1.5–2.5 mm long; outer segments lanceolate to ovate, acuminate or aristate, often tinged red, more or less spreading at fruiting; inner segments more or less broad-ovate, toothed, enlarging at fruiting. Fruiting valves about 2 × 2 mm (excluding terminal hooked spine), very broadly ovate, strongly reticulate, with about 5, red, hooked spines 2 mm long on each side; tubercles 0. Nut 2–2.5 mm long, deep glossy brown, acutely angled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The fruit valves carry red hooked spines that lock the fruiting branches together, making them look tangled, and catch on fur, hair and clothing.

lookalikes.howToTell: New Zealand dock never has hooked fruit: its valves have 1–4 straight teeth on each edge (an older Flora described them as minutely hooked), while hooked dock's carry about five red hooked spines, 2 mm long, on each side. New Zealand dock's fruiting stems zig-zag strongly into a tangled mass; hooked dock's only look tangled because the hooked fruit lock together. New Zealand dock's leaves are usually brown, narrow (up to 3 cm wide) and often wavy or curled; hooked dock's are up to 5 cm wide, usually with two rounded lobes at the base. New Zealand dock grows in bogs, wet flushes and by lakes and streams, mostly from the central North Island south; hooked dock on dry cliff tops, roadsides and stony ground, mostly in the north and in Marlborough and Nelson.

summary.text: Hooked dock, also called swamp dock, is native to south-eastern Australia and was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1948. Its hooked fruit hitch rides on passing animals, and it seems to have spread quickly in the 20th century. It has been confused with, and recorded as, the native New Zealand dock, which never has hooked fruit.

warnings: It contains oxalic acid, which gives the leaves their sharp taste. A little is fine, but large amounts can lock up calcium and other minerals in food; cooking lowers the oxalic acid. Take particular care, or leave it alone, if you are prone to rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.
Large amounts of dock leaves that are not properly cooked can cause nausea, stomach cramps, vomiting and headache.

edibleParts.text: Young shoots and young leaves, cooked; young leaves are also eaten in salads. Only the tender tip of a shoot is used: below it the bine becomes tough and fibrous. The dried female cones (the hops) are used as a flavouring and preservative in beer, and a tea is made from the leaves and cones. The fleshy rhizomes are sometimes eaten. The cones also flavour syrups, sweets, relishes and baking.

identification.text:
Dioecious or monoecious climber, with extensive roots. Stems striate, up to 10 m long and clothed in rough deflexed hairs. Leaves broadly ovate, not lobed or deeply 3–5-lobed; lobes acute to acuminate, serrate, more or less glabrous to sparsely hairy above, more or less glabrous to moderately hairy with yellow glandular hairs below. Petiole usually more or less equal to leaf blade. Stipules 2 per node and 2-fid or 4 per node and entire. Bracts of female flowers triangular, hairy, green, elongating and becoming yellowish at fruiting to form a cylindric-ovoid infructescence (the hop) with yellow glandular hairs especially at base of bracts. Calyx of male flowers ovate-triangular, green, hairy. Achene ovate-ellipsoid, covered by glandular calyx. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The female cones have a distinctive smell (Weedbusters).

preparation.text: Pick shoots shortly after they come up and before the leaves unfurl; the first 20 cm or less of a young shoot is tender. Shoots about 10 cm long can be blanched and eaten like asparagus. Later in the season only the growing tips stay tender, and they can be picked until the cones form. Rinse and cook lightly and quickly: steam or blanch and serve with butter and salt, boil in salted, acidulated water or cook in butter in a covered pan until tender, or fry. They go well with eggs (frittata, omelette) and in risotto. Shoots keep for about a week in a bag with a damp cloth, and can be frozen after light cooking or pickled. Pick cones when they are springy and papery with visible yellow lupulin, dry rather than damp, slightly sticky and fragrant; plants in more sun ripen sooner; orange, rancid-smelling cones are spoiled. Dry them at no more than 60 degrees and store airtight and out of the light. Hop tea is bitter.

recipes.method: Serves 2–4. Ingredients: about 55 g (2 oz) fresh hop shoots, tender parts only; about 55 g (2 oz) bacon (optional); 4 large eggs; 60 ml (¼ cup) cream or half-and-half; 2 tablespoons chopped chives or a mix of fresh herbs such as parsley, dill and coriander; salt and pepper; chive flowers to garnish (optional). Heat the oven to 150 °C (300 °F). Beat the eggs with the herbs, a pinch of salt and pepper and the cream, and set aside. In a 25 cm (10 inch) cast-iron or similar pan, cook the bacon to render its fat. Add the hop shoots, cover and cook on medium heat just to wilt them; season with a little salt. Add the egg mix and cook, stirring and swirling the pan to spread the egg. Put the pan in the oven for a minute or two to dry the top, and serve as soon as the egg sets, garnished with chive flowers if using.
recipes.title: Hop shoot frittata

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1 bunch wild hop shoots; about 225 g (½ pound) Carnaroli rice; 2–3 strawberries; 2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil; 4 tablespoons Parmesan; a small knob of butter; salt; 125 ml (½ cup) dry white wine; 1.5 litres (6 cups) boiling water or vegetable stock. Wash and chop the hop shoots and fry them very slowly in the olive oil for about 2 minutes. Add the rice, turn up the heat and stir for about 2 minutes until slightly translucent, then add the wine and let the alcohol evaporate. Add a first ladle of hot water and a good pinch of salt, lower to a simmer, and keep adding ladlefuls, stirring and letting each be absorbed before the next, for about 15 minutes. The source uses no onion or stock so the hops are not overpowered. When the rice is soft but still has a slight bite, take it off the heat, stir in the strawberries in pieces, the butter and the Parmesan, cover and rest for 3 minutes until creamy. Serve straight away, garnished with hop tips and strawberry.
recipes.title: Risotto with hop shoots and strawberries

recipes.method: Makes 2. Ingredients: 2 buckwheat crêpes; 1 bunch wild hop shoots; 1 carrot; 1 small onion; pink peppercorns in brine (about a dozen, crushed); 2 eggs; stracchino or another soft fresh cheese; butter; salt. The source gives no amount for the cheese. Soften the chopped onion and carrot with a pinch of salt and a little water for a couple of minutes, then cover and cook another 5 minutes. Rinse and chop the hop shoots and add them to the pan with the crushed pink peppercorns; cook a few minutes more. Meanwhile fry the eggs in a knob of butter so they are ready with the vegetables. Spread cheese on each crêpe, spoon the vegetables over, top with a fried egg and fold the edges towards the centre, leaving the yolk uncovered. If needed, warm for no more than a minute in a hot oven so the yolk stays runny.
recipes.title: Crespelle with hop shoots

recipes.method: Ingredients: 200 g (1 cup) sugar, or honey; 250 ml (1 cup) water; enough hop cones, picked green and closed, to sit under the syrup. Make as much syrup as you need to cover the hops. Warm the sugar and water until the sugar dissolves, without letting it boil, which changes the syrup's texture. Add the hops and leave them to infuse for at least 30 minutes; the source takes it off the heat after about 15 minutes and lets it finish infusing cold. Strain and keep in the fridge. For a thinner syrup use 1 part sugar to 2 parts water. Use it in soft drinks or tea, or with rum and a ginger syrup made the same way for a bitter cocktail.
recipes.title: Hop syrup

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1–2 dried or fresh hop cones; 500 ml (2 cups) boiling water; honey to taste (optional). Put the cones in a teapot, pour over the boiling water and infuse for 5 minutes. Sweeten if you like, strain, and drink warm or let it cool and bottle it. Hop tea is bitter, and hops make you drowsy.
recipes.title: Hop tea

recipes.method: Ingredients: 500 ml (2 cups) milk of your choice; 1–2 dried or fresh hop cones; 1 teaspoon ground turmeric; ½ teaspoon ground cinnamon; ¼ teaspoon ground ginger; 1 cardamom pod; 1 teaspoon vanilla; 1–2 tablespoons honey. Heat the milk with everything else in a small pan and simmer for 10 minutes. Strain into cups. The source drinks it at bedtime; hops make you drowsy.
recipes.title: Golden hop milk

recipes.method: Makes 20 or more. Ingredients: 125 ml (½ cup) beer (the source uses an IPA); 6 dried hop cones (the source uses the Centennial variety); 200 g (1 cup) sugar; 125 ml (½ cup) light corn syrup; a little butter; lollipop sticks. You need a sugar thermometer. Butter the backs of one or two baking trays well. Heat the beer to a light simmer, break the hop cones apart into it and take it off the heat; leave to steep for up to 10 minutes, tasting as you go, since hops vary a lot in strength. Strain and measure out 80 ml (⅓ cup) of the beer. In a heavy saucepan mix the sugar, corn syrup and measured beer, bring to the boil over medium-high heat and stir often until it reaches 150 °C; watch it closely from about 138 °C, as the temperature climbs fast and it can burn. Take it off the heat and stir constantly for about a minute as it cools and thickens. Working quickly, drop 1–3 teaspoons at a time onto the buttered trays, lay a stick flat into each with its tip near the centre and twirl it so the candy coats it. Cool completely, lift off and wrap.
recipes.title: Hop beer lollipops

recipes.method: Makes about 1.4 litres (3 US pints). Ingredients: 900 g (2 lb) pickling cucumbers, cleaned; 1 small onion, peeled; 1 small red capsicum; 500 ml (2 cups) vinegar; 1 large handful dried hop 'leaves' (the author's word for the broken-up cone petals) or 2 handfuls fresh; 60 ml (¼ cup) pickling salt; 3 garlic cloves, crushed or minced; 1 teaspoon mustard seed; ½ teaspoon celery seed; ½ teaspoon crushed chilli or 1–2 fresh jalapeños; ¼ teaspoon dill seed; ¼ teaspoon turmeric. You need sterilised jars, new lids and a large pot for processing. Cut the cucumbers, onion and capsicum into 2–3 cm pieces and chop finely in a food processor. Fill the large pot with at least 15 cm of water and bring it to the boil. In another heavy pot bring the vinegar to the boil, add the hops, mash them about and simmer for 5–10 minutes, tasting often. When it is as bitter as you want, lift out all the hops with a slotted spoon, add the vegetables and everything else and bring back to the boil. Ladle the boiling relish into the jars, leaving about 6 mm headspace, wipe the rims, put on the lids and process in the boiling water for 15 minutes. Lift out and leave to cool overnight. Check the seals next morning: any lid that pops when pressed has not sealed, so keep that jar in the fridge and use it within a few weeks. Chill well before eating.
recipes.title: Hoppy dill pickle relish

recipes.method: Serves 14; start the hop extract a week ahead. Hop extract (from the same author's 'Homemade Hop Extracts', https://celebrationgeneration.com/homemade-hop-extracts/): put 250 ml (1 cup) fresh hops, gently rinsed, or 180 ml (¾ cup) dried hop 'leaves' (cone petals) in a clean jar, pour over 500 ml (2 cups) good vodka, close tightly and shake. Keep it in a cool dark place, shaking a couple of times a day, for about a week, then taste: it should be a strong flavouring like vanilla extract, not something to drink. Strain through a fine sieve and then a coffee filter and bottle. Crust: 375 ml (1½ cups) graham cracker crumbs; 50 g (¼ cup) sugar; 5 tablespoons melted butter. Filling: 900 g (2 lb) cream cheese at room temperature; 300 g (1½ cups) sugar; 250 ml (1 cup) sour cream; 250 ml (1 cup) cream; 6 large eggs; juice of 1 lemon; 1 tablespoon hop extract. Topping: 250 ml (1 cup) citrus marmalade; juice and zest of 1 lemon; 1 teaspoon hop extract; a pinch of salt. Mix the crumbs, sugar and butter until moistened, press firmly over the base and partway up the sides of a 23 cm (9 inch) springform tin, and chill for at least 1 hour. Heat the oven to 220 °C. Beat the cream cheese and sugar just until smooth, add the sour cream, cream, eggs, lemon juice and extract and beat on low just until smooth. Pour into the crust and chill 10 minutes. Bake 15 minutes, then turn the oven down to 160 °C and bake 50 minutes more. Turn the oven off and leave the cake inside to cool for 2 hours without opening the door, then chill for at least 3 hours. For the topping, whisk everything together in a small pan over medium heat just until smooth and liquid, pour over the cold cake and chill at least 10 minutes before slicing.

summary.text:
Humulus lupulus, the common hop or hops, is a species of flowering plant in the hemp family, Cannabaceae.
The plant is native to Europe, western Asia and North America.
It is a perennial, herbaceous climbing plant which sends up new shoots in early spring and dies back to a cold-hardy rhizome in autumn.
It grows best in the latitude range of 38°–51° in full sun with moderate amounts of rainfall.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Waikato, Bay of Plenty, Lake Waikaremoana, Taupo, Wellington Province; South Island: common in Nelson, North Westland, Central and South Canterbury, also recorded from Blenheim, Otago Peninsula, and Riverton (Southland). Native of Europe, West and Central Asia; first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1872. Both cultivated and wild plants in New Zealand fall within H. lupulus var. lupulus. This variety is cultivated for the glandular female infructescence which is used in brewing; plants escaped from cultivation are now well-established, persistent weeds in some areas.
It was introduced to New Zealand for agriculture (New Zealand Plant Conservation Network), and New Zealand's commercial hop varieties are grown in the Nelson region (Kiwiherb).
It grows and matures fast and takes root where its stems touch the ground, and it forms a dense canopy that stops native plants establishing (Weedbusters).
The name hop is thought to come from the Anglo-Saxon hoppan, to climb, and lupulus from the Latin lupus, wolf. Pliny wrote of hops as a garden plant whose new shoots were harvested for eating (Herb Federation of New Zealand).

warnings: Handling hops causes dermatitis in sensitive people, long known among hop pickers; about 1 in 30 people who handle the plant are affected. Hairs dislodged from the plant can irritate the eyes. The bines and cones carry scratchy hooked hairs, so wear gloves when picking a lot.

Hop cones are sedative: the hairs on them contain lupulin, a sedative and hypnotic substance. Hop preparations may impair the ability to drive or use machines, and are best not taken in large quantities within a couple of weeks of a procedure using anaesthetic. Do not combine hops with alcohol, check with a health professional before taking them with sedatives or sleep medicine, and avoid them if you have depression.

Safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and medicinal use of hop cones at these times, or when trying to conceive, is not recommended; use in children under 12 is not recommended for lack of data. Hops contain xanthohumol, which gut bacteria convert to a phytoestrogen (8-prenylnaringenin) that may bind to oestrogen receptors; people with hormone-sensitive conditions such as breast cancer or endometriosis should avoid hops.

Hops are toxic to dogs: signs are panting, high body temperature, seizures and death. Of five dogs (4 of them Greyhounds) that ate spent hops, 4 died despite treatment. Keep hops, including spent hops from brewing, away from dogs.

When picking shoots, other climbers can grow tangled through the hops, including field bindweed, which is common in New Zealand in the same waste places. None has the light green cones, so the risk is with the shoots: check every shoot has hop leaves (in opposite pairs, 3 to 5 lobes, toothed margins, rough to touch) and no tendrils. Field bindweed leaves are arrow- or spear-shaped and untoothed, apart from often a pair of teeth near the base.
It is controlled as an environmental weed with herbicide (metsulfuron or triclopyr sprays, or glyphosate or metsulfuron gel on cut stems). Pick only where you know it has not been sprayed.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Take a few leaves per shrub. DOC permission is needed to collect plants on public conservation land. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In the Auckland region (Regionally Critical), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it. In Northland (Regionally Naturally Uncommon), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text: Small shrub with leathery oval leaves blotched red, pale blue-green underneath. Chewing a fragment produces a strong chilli-like burn; lowland horopito, with unblotched glossy leaves, is only somewhat pungent.

lookalikes.howToTell: Lowland horopito's leaves are dark green and glossy above with no red blotches; horopito's are dull green and blotched with red, at least in exposed places. Lowland horopito's leaves are usually larger, 6–10 × 3–6 cm against 2–6 (rarely 8) × 1–3 cm, and pale to glaucous underneath but not white, where horopito's are glaucous to white and often pink-flushed. Lowland horopito's ripe fruit is usually bright red, rarely dark; horopito's is dark red to black. Horopito's leaves are very pungent to taste, lowland horopito's only somewhat pungent. Hybrids between the two are frequent where they meet, so some plants fit neither description.
lookalikes.name: Lowland horopito

lookalikes.howToTell: Feel the leaf: horopito's is leathery, mountain alseuosmia's thin. Mountain alseuosmia's leaves are glossy, widest towards the tip and narrowed wedge-like to the base, with a tiny point at the tip and the edge entire or with a few minute teeth, on rather stout stalks up to 10 mm long; horopito's are dull, elliptic to broadly elliptic with a wavy edge, on slender stalks 5–10 mm long. Both can show red: mountain alseuosmia's leaves are often red-edged and sometimes flecked red, horopito's blotched red in exposed places, and their leaf sizes overlap. Mountain alseuosmia is a shrub up to about 50 cm tall, unbranched or with one or two branches; horopito grows to 2 m, sometimes 3.5 m, but a small plant could be either. In flower, mountain alseuosmia's flowers are tubular, about 8–10 mm long, with five fringed lobes, white to yellowish or reddish and sweet-scented; horopito's have 5–6 separate greenish-yellow petals 4–5 mm long. Mountain alseuosmia's berries are oval, about 9–12 × 5–6 mm, bright shining red; horopito's are round, dark red to black, 3–6 mm across. Mountain alseuosmia grows in montane forest, in the North Island from Te Moehau and Mt Pirongia south, and in the South Island in the west, from North-West Nelson to near Okarito; horopito grows on the North, South and Stewart Islands, east of the main divide too. No record of mountain alseuosmia as food was found (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mountain alseuosmia

lookalikes.howToTell: Northland horopito is known only from Mt Manaia and Bream Head at Whangārei Heads and from Logues Bush near Wellsford, so elsewhere it is not Northland horopito. Horopito's leaves are dull green and blotched with red, at least in exposed places, with the midvein inconspicuous above; Northland horopito's are glossy, without blemishes or blotches, with a conspicuous pale cream to yellow-green midvein above and a red midvein beneath. Both have white leaf undersides; horopito's are often pink-flushed, and Northland horopito's leaf buds and young leaves are usually hairy. Northland horopito's leaves are usually larger, 3.5–11 × 1.8–4.5 cm against 2–6 (rarely 8) × 1–3 cm, though the sizes overlap. Northland horopito is an upright shrub or small tree up to 7 m tall; horopito is a shrub up to 2 m, sometimes 3.5 m. Northland horopito's ripe fruit is black, egg-shaped to oblong, 6.4–9.8 mm long; horopito's is round, dark red to black, 3–6 mm across. Northland horopito is Threatened – Nationally Critical, and no record of it as food was found (see its page).

preparation.text: Dry and grind as a pepper substitute, or use the leaves fresh, whole or torn into large pieces, and lift them out before serving — they are thick and leathery and do not soften much when cooked. Very potent — start with far less than you think.

recipes.method: Written for wild horopito; the page names no species. 1 cup (250 ml) coarse pink sea salt; the zest of 1 lemon; the zest of 1 orange; 5 fresh horopito leaves; 2 tablespoons (30 ml) dried oregano; 1 tablespoon (15 ml) dried garlic granules. Spread the horopito leaves and the lemon and orange zest in a shallow dish and leave them on a warm windowsill for about a week, until completely dry; or dry them on a small baking tray in the oven at 80 °C for 2 hours. Put everything in a food processor and pulse to a coarse salt flecked with herbs, or pound it in a mortar and pestle. Store it in an airtight jar and sprinkle it over roast vegetables, meat or fish. The author calls it a horopito-infused citrus salt.
recipes.title: Horopito spice rub

recipes.method: Written for fresh horopito leaves in New Zealand. 190 ml water; 60 ml vinegar; 125 ml sugar; 1 teaspoon salt; a good handful of fresh horopito leaves; 3–6 garlic cloves, to taste; ¼ red capsicum; ⅓ medium carrot; 1 tablespoon cornflour; 10–15 cm piece of fresh ginger. Bring the water, vinegar, sugar and salt to a simmer in a saucepan. Add the horopito leaves, tearing them a little so they give up their heat and flavour, and simmer for 5–10 minutes. Meanwhile, finely chop or mince the garlic, deseed the capsicum and chop it as finely as you can, and finely grate the carrot. Strain out the horopito. Add the garlic, capsicum and carrot to the liquid and simmer for another 5–10 minutes. Mix the cornflour with a little more water, stir it into the hot liquid and simmer for about a minute, until it turns translucent. Take the pan off the heat. Grate the ginger, squeeze the juice out of the gratings by hand into the pan and stir it in. Pour the hot sauce into hot sterilised jars and seal. It keeps sealed in a cool, dark place for up to 6 months; refrigerate it to be sure. The author uses it as you would sweet chilli sauce.
recipes.title: Sweet horopito sauce

recipes.method: Written for dried horopito in New Zealand. Serves 4. For the granita: 125 ml golden caster sugar; 1½ teaspoons dried horopito; 100 ml cold water; 500 g strawberries, hulled and halved. For the vanilla cream: 250 g crème fraîche; 250 ml cream; 3–4 tablespoons golden icing sugar, sifted; 3 teaspoons vanilla extract or paste; edible flowers to serve (optional). Put the sugar, horopito and water in a saucepan and bring to the boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Turn off the heat and leave to infuse for at least 10 minutes, then strain through a fine sieve. Blend the strawberries with the horopito syrup until smooth, pour into a shallow tray and freeze. After 30 minutes, scrape the ice crystals from the edges into the middle with a fork. Freeze for another 30 minutes and scrape again, and repeat twice more, about 2 hours in all, then keep it frozen until you serve. Whip the crème fraîche, cream, icing sugar and vanilla to soft peaks. Spoon or pipe the cream into glasses, top with the granita and any flowers, and serve straight away.
recipes.title: Strawberry and horopito granita with vanilla cream

summary.text:
Fiercely hot native leaf — a genuine NZ spice.
In New Zealand it grows on the North, South and Stewart Islands, from latitude 36° 30′ south.

warnings: The heat is genuine and builds gradually, so you may not feel it at first, and milk does not cool it. Do not chew a whole leaf to test it.
Horopito can numb some of your taste buds for a while, so what you eat or drink afterwards tastes odd; the more you have, the stronger the effect.

identification.text:
A large tree with big compound leaves of five to seven leaflets spread like fingers from one stalk. Upright cones of white flowers in spring. The nuts sit one or two to a thick green husk covered in short spikes, and are large, glossy and rounded with one pale patch. Sweet chestnut husks are densely bristly like a hedgehog and hold two or three flattened nuts with a pointed tuft.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Tree 10–15–(about 25) m tall. Twigs stout, glabrous with prominent leaf scars and large reddish brown, very viscid buds. Leaflets 5–7, sessile; central leaflets mostly 15–35 × 6–14 cm (basal leaflets smaller), obovate […], irregularly crenate-serrate. Panicles to about 30 cm high, broad-cylindric. […] Petals 1–1.7 cm long including narrow claw; limb more or less broad-oblong, white with yellow to red spot near base, very undulate and recurved. […] Capsule to 6 cm diameter, subglobose, echinate. Seeds 1–2, 3–5 cm diameter, usually more or less subglobose, often somewhat asymmetric, dark shining brown with prominent, elongated, white hilum.
A fertile hybrid, A. × carnea, is commonly cultivated in New Zealand, but spontaneous trees have not been reported. It has scarcely viscid buds, deep pink flowers and the capsules have few prickles.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaves first. Sweet chestnut's are single, long (about 15–32 cm), oblong and boldly toothed; horse chestnut's are hand-shaped, with five to seven leaflets spreading from one stalk. Horse chestnut's leaflets are toothed too, so teeth alone do not separate them. Both cases are spiny; sweet chestnut's is covered in many long, fine spines, horse chestnut's in short, more widely spaced spikes. Sweet chestnut's case usually holds two or more nuts with a tufted tip; horse chestnut's usually holds one round, glossy, dark brown conker with a large pale scar, sometimes two. Some grafted sweet chestnut varieties bear a single large nut, so nut count alone does not decide it. Sweet chestnut is edible.

summary.text:
Conkers. The park tree whose shiny brown nuts look like sweet chestnuts and are poisonous.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): South Island: Canterbury, occasional, but nowhere fully naturalised. Horse chestnut is very commonly cultivated in both North and South Islands, especially in cooler areas.

warnings: Contains aesculin. Eating horse chestnuts causes stomach pain, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea; children who ate them have become weak, drowsy and unsteady, with muscle twitching and paralysis, and in adults 1–4 seeds have caused massive vomiting, facial swelling, low blood pressure and collapse. Keep children from eating the seeds from fallen cases.
Never roast a nut you found under a tree with hand-shaped leaves.

habitat.text: Grass on rich soil: pasture and paddocks, lawns, parks and other urban grassland, and forest margins, singly or in groups, and often in rings. In New Zealand it has been collected among browntop and Chewings fescue, on bare soil under stone-fruit trees, and once each under pine and oak. A Waikato forager finds it in paddocks that have not been cropped and resown for some years. Elsewhere it is known from well-manured fields, beside stables and bridle paths, on roadside verges and along wood edges and hedgerows.

identification.text:
A large, stout, white mushroom with a thick ring and a strong smell of aniseed or almond. The cap is usually 8–20 cm across, sometimes to 25 cm (Canterbury collections were 4–12 cm); egg-shaped or hemispherical when young, it opens convex and then almost flat. It is smooth and silky to finely fibrous, white to cream, and turns yellowish with age and where it is bruised or handled, most at the edge; old caps may crack or grow pale brownish scales. The edge is rolled under when young and often keeps scraps of veil.
The gills are free of the stem and crowded. They are pale when young — whitish, pale grey or pale pink — and stay pale for a long time, then turn grey-brown and finally dark chocolate brown. The spore print is dark brown.
The stem is 5–15 cm long and 1.5–3 cm thick, cylindrical, sometimes with a slight bulb at the base, white, turning yellowish below the ring with age and where bruised. The ring is the best feature: large, thick, double and persistent, and in a closed cap its underside is a circle of thick, cogwheel-like patches around the stem. There is no sac (volva) at the stem base.
The flesh is white and firm and changes little when cut. It yellows slowly where bruised, but the cut stem base never turns bright chrome yellow straight away. The smell — aniseed, almond or marzipan, from benzaldehyde — is the key test: smell every one.
Similar Agaricus in New Zealand: Agaricus crocodilinus has been confused with it. A native forest mushroom, an undescribed Agaricus of deep leaf litter in Auckland podocarp–broadleaf forest (the Hidden Forest's 'forest arvensis'), looks like it but has a simple, single ring with no cogwheel underneath, no almond smell and no strong yellowing; its edibility is unknown.

lookalikes.howToTell: Death cap's gills are white, turning cream, sometimes with a faint pink tinge, as it ages, but never the chocolate brown of a mature horse mushroom. Its swollen stem base sits in a white, sack-like volva that may be buried, so dig up the whole base of every mushroom. Young horse mushroom gills also stay pale for a long time, so pale gills alone do not separate them: check for a volva, look under the ring for horse mushroom's thick cogwheel patches, and smell it — horse mushroom smells strongly of aniseed or almond, while young death caps have almost no smell. A spore print confirms it: horse mushroom dark chocolate brown, death cap white. Cap colour and the ring do not separate them: death caps are usually yellow-green, olive or bronze, but an all-white form occurs, and both have a ring. Death cap grows with trees, especially oak; horse mushroom is a grassland mushroom, but it also grows at forest margins and has been collected under oak and pine in New Zealand, so grass near trees is no guarantee. Half a mature cap is reportedly a lethal dose for an adult.
lookalikes.name: Death cap

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are white Agaricus with pale gills that turn pink, then brown, a large ring and a dark brown spore print, both can have a bulbous base, and both turn yellow where bruised, so yellowing alone does not tell them apart. Scratch the cap edge and cut through the very base of the stem. Yellow stainer turns bright chrome yellow almost at once, most strongly at the stem base (most marked in young, fresh mushrooms), and smells of ink, phenol or iodine, strongest at the cut base and stronger again when cooked. Horse mushroom yellows only slowly and faintly, its cut stem base does not flash bright yellow, and it smells of aniseed or almond. A mushroom that turns chrome yellow fast or smells chemical is yellow stainer or one of its yellow-staining relatives — throw it out.
lookalikes.name: Yellow stainer

lookalikes.howToTell: Field mushroom is smaller, its gills are pink when young, its ring is thin and simple and often disappears, and its cut flesh blushes reddish. It smells pleasant but not of aniseed, and does not turn yellow. Horse mushroom is bigger and stouter, with a thick double ring that has cogwheel-like patches underneath, it yellows slowly where bruised, and it smells of aniseed or almond.
lookalikes.name: Field mushroom

lookalikes.howToTell: From a distance the two look very alike: both are big and pale with a large ring. Skirt webcap grows in soil under mānuka, kānuka or beech; its gills start pale straw or mustard and turn rusty brown, not pink then chocolate; rusty spores stain its ring and stem; young ones are wrapped in a thick web-like veil; and it has no smell. Its edibility is unknown and close relatives contain lethal toxins. Horse mushroom grows in grass, sometimes at forest margins, with pink-to-chocolate gills, a dark chocolate spore print, a thick double ring with cogwheel-like patches underneath, and a smell of aniseed or almond.

preparation.text:
Brush off any dirt; they soak up water, so if you rinse them, pat them dry and leave them in the fridge for a few hours before cooking. Twist or cut the stem out of the cap and chop it into the dish.
The flavour is rich, with a sweet note of aniseed, and the texture firm and meaty, though older ones can be a little tough. Use them in any recipe that calls for large flat or portobello mushrooms: stuffed and baked whole, in risotto, omelettes, soups and sauces. To fry, slice them and cook in a little oil or butter over medium heat for 5–7 minutes, stirring now and then, until they give up their juice and turn golden; season.
Mature caps picked after rain can release so much water that they stew rather than fry. Pour the liquid off, keep it for stock or reduce it, add a little more fat and carry on.

recipes.method: Serves 2 as a starter. 2 large horse mushrooms; 2 shallots, finely diced; a little butter; a handful of sweet cicely leaves; 2 tbsp cream cheese; a little olive oil; 2 slices of sourdough; any other mushrooms you found; a few wild herbs and flowers. Carefully twist the stems out of 2 large horse mushrooms — still domed, with pale gills and firm caps — without damaging the caps, and chop the stems finely. Fry them gently with 2 finely diced shallots in a little butter for 4 minutes. Finely shred a handful of sweet cicely leaves, keeping a few fronds to garnish, and mix with the stems, shallots and 2 tbsp cream cheese; season. Stuff the caps, set them on a baking tray, season, drizzle with a little olive oil and bake in a medium oven for 10 minutes. Meanwhile toast 2 slices of sourdough and sauté any other mushrooms you found. Put a cap on each toast (on a slice of a big mushroom, if you have one) and dress with the smaller mushrooms and a few wild herbs and flowers. The author says tarragon works instead of the sweet cicely.
recipes.title: Horse mushrooms stuffed with sweet cicely

recipes.method: Written for horse mushrooms in the Waikato; vary the amounts to taste and to how many mushrooms you have. Horse mushrooms; olive oil; 5 garlic cloves; 1 small red chilli, seeds removed; 1 onion; parsley; 2 big tomatoes; salt and black pepper; 1 tsp honey; Parmesan. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Cut the stems off as close to the caps as you can and chop them to add to the topping. Finely chop the garlic and chilli and fry them gently in a little olive oil; add the onion, finely chopped, and fry together. Add the tomatoes, finely chopped, season, and add the parsley. Stir in the honey and cook for about 10 minutes, until reduced. Turn the caps in a dish of olive oil, spooning it over them, then lay them on a baking tray and bake for about 5 minutes. Take them out, spoon the tomato mixture generously over them and top with grated Parmesan. Grill for 6–7 minutes, watching closely, and serve at once. Bacon or other ingredients can go into the topping.
recipes.title: Grilled spicy horse mushrooms with tomato

recipes.method: Use large horse mushrooms that are still rounded, not yet flattening out. 2 large horse mushrooms; ½ red onion, chopped; 1 tbsp butter; 1 tbsp Stilton; 1 tbsp breadcrumbs; olive oil; flaky salt and black pepper; a small bunch of herbs, such as parsley, coriander, dill, chives and thyme. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Clean the mushrooms, take out the stems and chop them. Set the caps gill side up on a baking tray, put half the butter in each, season, and add a sprig of thyme to each (just the leaves if the stalks are woody). Bake for 10 minutes. Meanwhile fry the onion in a little olive oil for a minute, add the chopped stems and cook until soft, and chop the herbs. Spoon the onion and stem mixture into the baked caps and scatter over half the herbs. Crumble the Stilton on top, sprinkle with the breadcrumbs, drizzle with olive oil and bake for about 5 minutes more, until the cheese is melted and bubbling. Serve scattered with the rest of the herbs.
recipes.title: Stuffed and baked horse mushrooms with Stilton

recipes.method: 450 g horse mushrooms, cleaned and sliced; 225 g linguine or fettuccine; 2 tbsp olive oil; 4 garlic cloves, minced; 1 small onion, finely chopped; 240 ml double cream; 120 g grated Parmesan, plus extra to serve; 2 tbsp chopped parsley, plus extra to serve; salt and pepper. Cook the pasta until al dente and drain. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat and fry the garlic and onion until the onion is translucent. Add the mushrooms and cook for about 5 minutes, until they give up their juice and start to brown. Pour in the cream, bring to a simmer and cook for about 5 minutes, until slightly thickened. Stir in the Parmesan and cook for 2 minutes more, until the sauce is smooth. Toss the pasta through the sauce, season, add the parsley and toss again. Serve hot with more Parmesan and parsley.
recipes.title: Creamy horse mushroom pasta

recipes.method: Serves 4 as a first course. About 700 ml (3 US cups) shredded green cabbage, lightly salted; about 240 ml (1 US cup) sliced horse mushroom; 1 tbsp umeboshi (Japanese pickled plums, about 5), stoned; 2 tbsp vegetable oil; 2 tsp dark sesame oil; ½ tsp sugar; salt. Heat both oils in a large frying pan over medium heat, add the mushroom and sauté for 1 minute. Add the cabbage and stir until just wilted, then stir in the sugar and plums and cook for 1 minute more. Serve hot or at room temperature. Without umeboshi, use a dash of sour vinegar and 1 tbsp minced rhubarb. The author likes to add about 80 ml (⅓ US cup) of fresh or rehydrated hijiki seaweed.
recipes.title: Cabbage and horse mushroom with pickled plums

recipes.method: Serves 1, from Ralph Jackson, Lincolnshire. 1 large horse mushroom; 2 thin slices of cooked or smoked ham; 1 spring onion, roughly chopped; 1 tomato, sliced; 1 celery stick, thinly sliced; a knob of butter; cress; black pepper. Take out the stem and put the butter in its place. Lay the ham on the cap, then the spring onion, tomato and celery. Microwave for 2 minutes, less if the mushroom is smaller than a dinner plate's width. Garnish with cress and black pepper.
recipes.title: Ralph's horse mushroom feast

recipes.method: Written for cultivated white flat mushrooms, which large horse mushroom caps can replace. Serves 4. Mushrooms: 6 flat mushrooms; 60 ml (¼ cup) olive oil; juice of ½ lemon; 2 tbsp harissa paste. Flatbreads: 250 ml (1 cup) thick Greek yoghurt; 1 cup self-raising flour. Yoghurt dip: 125 ml (½ cup) thick Greek yoghurt; juice of ½ lemon; a handful of soft herbs, such as mint, coriander, flat-leaf parsley or dill, finely chopped. Stir the dip ingredients together and chill. Mix the oil, harissa and lemon juice, toss the mushrooms in it and leave to marinate for at least 30 minutes. Mix the yoghurt and flour into a smooth dough, adding flour if it is sticky, divide it into 4 and roll each out on a well-floured surface. Cook the flatbreads on a barbecue or in a dry frying pan over medium-high heat for 2–4 minutes a side, until charred in spots and golden, and keep them warm in a tea towel. Cook the mushrooms on a hot barbecue or in a frying pan for 4–5 minutes a side, until golden and cooked through. Spread the flatbreads with the yoghurt dip and top with the mushrooms, whole or sliced, and more herbs. Without harissa, mix tomato paste, olive oil, garlic, salt, cumin, chilli flakes and coriander seed; shop-bought wraps can replace the flatbreads.
recipes.title: Harissa mushrooms with yoghurt in flatbread

recipes.method: Written for cultivated small portobello mushrooms, which sliced horse mushrooms can replace. Serves 2. Pastry: 225 g flour, sifted; ½ tsp salt; 150 g cold butter, cubed; 60 ml ice water. Filling: 40 g butter; 1 onion, finely chopped; 2 garlic cloves, finely chopped; 120 g goat's cheese, crumbled; 200 g ricotta; 2 tbsp finely chopped thyme; 125 ml (½ cup) finely chopped basil, plus extra to serve; grated rind of 1 lemon; 2 eggs, lightly beaten; salt and pepper; 250 g mushrooms, thickly sliced; a drizzle of olive oil. Pulse the flour, salt and butter in a food processor to fine crumbs, add the ice water and pulse until it just comes together. Knead gently into a dough, wrap and chill for at least 30 minutes. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Roll the pastry out 3 mm thick on a floured surface, cut a 30 cm round, put it on a lined tray and chill for 15 minutes more. Meanwhile, sauté the onion and garlic in half the butter until tender, 2–3 minutes, and set aside. Melt the rest of the butter and sauté the mushrooms for 2–3 minutes, until soft; drain off the juice. Mix the onion and garlic with 80 g of the goat's cheese, the ricotta, thyme, basil, lemon rind and half the egg; season. Spread it over the pastry, leaving a 3 cm border, lay the mushrooms on top, drizzle with oil and fold the edges in. Brush the pastry edge with the rest of the egg and bake for 20–25 minutes, until crisp and golden. Serve warm with the rest of the goat's cheese and more basil.
recipes.title: Mushroom, thyme and goat’s cheese galette

recipes.method: Written for field mushrooms. Serves 4. 4 chicken breast fillets; dry white wine; 500 g mushrooms; spring onions; salt and pepper; fillo pastry; melted butter. Marinate the chicken in white wine for 3 hours. Chop the mushrooms with spring onions and season. Brush a strip of fillo with melted butter, lay a chicken fillet diagonally across one corner, add a generous spoonful of the mushrooms and fold it up into a neat triangle. Wrap each parcel in a second sheet of fillo and set them on a baking tray. Bake at 190 °C for 35 minutes, until the pastry is crisp and brown.
recipes.title: Chicken and mushroom fillo parcels

Owner's links, 29/10/2026 (all retrieved 29/10/2026): The Hidden Forest 'Agaricus arvensis' https://www.hiddenforest.co.nz/fungi/family/agaricaceae/agari10.htm — cap 80–200 mm, white to cream, yellowing at the margin, brownish scales with age; gills free, crowded, pink young, dark chocolate-brown; stipe 80–150 × 15–30 mm, sometimes slightly bulbous, bruising yellowish; ring large, double, thick, persistent, cog-wheel-like scales below; flesh slowly yellowing in the stipe base and cap margin when cut; odour strong almond/anise, 'a key character'; pasturelands, urban greenspaces, forest margins; widespread and common; autumn; introduced, long established; edible; spore print dark brown; A. crocodilinus 'claimed to be often mistaken for A. arvensis' (identification, habitat, summary). The Hidden Forest 'Agaricus species' (Forest Arvensis) https://www.hiddenforest.co.nz/fungi/family/agaricaceae/agari01.htm — endemic, Auckland, lowland podocarp–broadleaf forest, deep leaf litter; simple ring, no cog-wheel; no almond odour; no strong yellowing; edibility 'Dont know' (identification). Landcare Research Fungal Guide image PK 7007 https://fungalguide.landcareresearch.co.nz/WebForms/ViewLargerImage.aspx?isGenus=false&PK=7007 — cap up to 20 cm or more, introduced, always on grass in parks, cap 'sometimes stains slightly yellowish with age, but the flesh inside the stalk never stains yellow', edible and good (identification, habitat).

Number 8 Network, 'Mushrooms galore!' (Annette Taylor, pictures and 'mushroom wrangler' David Riddell, Gordonton, Waikato, 19/04/2017) https://www.number8network.co.nz/2017/04/19/lashings-of-delicious-mushroom/ — 'the biggest of the local mushroom varieties', 15 cm or more; 'deliciously rich flavour with a hint of aniseed'; mushrooms from mid-May one year, early April the next; harvested once fully open; rinse, pat dry, fridge several hours; look in areas not cropped and regrassed in recent years (summary, habitat, preparation, recipe). Also read (29/10/2026): Pat O'Reilly, First Nature 'Agaricus arvensis — Horse Mushroom' https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/agaricus-arvensis.php — 'In New Zealand this species is commonly known as the Snowball Mushroom'; name from horse manure or perhaps size; cap 8–20 cm, exceptionally over 30 cm, yellowing with age and where bruised; double cog-wheel ring; stem base 'does not rapidly turn bright yellow', unlike the yellow stainer; aniseed smell; manured meadows, bridle paths; copper and cadmium, 'an occasional treat'; use in any recipe calling for large (portobello) mushrooms, risotto, omelettes, soups, sauces; check gills pink or brown, not white (summary, identification, habitat, warning 1, preparation, death-cap card). summary.text:
Agaricus arvensis, commonly known as the horse mushroom, is a mushroom-forming fungus of the genus Agaricus.
It is introduced in New Zealand and long established: it was first recorded here by Berkeley in 1855, and in 1899 Massee knew it from the North Island, growing in pasture. A Waikato forager calls it the biggest of the local mushrooms, and First Nature says it is often called the snowball mushroom in New Zealand. The Hidden Forest calls it widespread and common, but most herbarium collections and 11 of its 15 research-grade New Zealand iNaturalist records are from Canterbury. The name is usually put down to its liking for fields manured by horses, though some say it refers to its size.

warnings: Like other Agaricus, horse mushrooms take up heavy metals, notably cadmium and copper, from contaminated ground. Don't pick them from busy roadsides or from lawns and parks that may be sprayed or fertilised, and treat them as an occasional treat rather than a staple.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Mostly waste places, also other disturbed sites, coastal areas, forest margins and pasture.

identification.text:
Erect annual or biennial herb, up to 2–(2.5) m tall. Stems ridged, moderately to densely softly hairy, often becoming sparsely hairy below. Cauline leaves usually obovate to narrow-oblanceolate, rarely linear, more or less flat, apetiolate and cuneate, acute, often shallowly 1-pinnatifid or remotely serrate, sometimes entire especially above, sparsely to densely scaberulous, ciliate, (20)–35–120–(250) × 4–20–(45) mm; uppermost leaves smaller, usually narrow-oblanceolate or narrow-elliptic. Inflorescence a leafy pyramidal panicle with dominant main axis. Capitula 1.5–2 mm diameter; receptacle usually with distinct flanges between pits, sometimes with short flanges or more or less smooth. Inner involucral bracts lanceolate, green, usually hairy at least toward apex, 4–5.5–(6) mm long; outer bracts moderately to densely hairy. Outer florets filiform, cream, usually becoming reddish. Achenes obovoid, sparsely hairy, 1–1.2–(1.4) mm long; pappus hairs fawn or dirty white. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Conyza albida Spreng.]
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand, as Conyza albida): C. albida is easily distinguished from C. bonariensis by its later flowering time, larger size, broader, more-toothed, flat leaves, pyramidal inflorescence, broader inflorescence leaves, smaller capitula, green bracts and smaller seeds.
It starts as a rosette of unlobed leaves, a little like narrow-leaved plantain but with teeth along the margins that point toward the leaf tip, before bolting into tall stems that branch near the top; it has no yellow flowers. Canadian fleabane has slightly smaller heads with less hairy bracts (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated).

summary.text:
Erigeron sumatrensis (syn. Conyza sumatrensis) is an annual herb probably native to South America, but widely naturalised in tropical and subtropical regions, and regarded as an invasive weed in many places.It is a perennial in the Western Cape of South Africa.
It probably originates from South America, but is now naturalised in North America, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australasia. It poses a significant threat to wildlife conservation areas and other reserves. In Britain, of the non-native former Conyza species, it is the second most abundant (after Erigeron canadensis) and is typically found in London and the South East of England. It was first recorded in London by Brian Wurzell in 1984,
and noted in France at Saint-Sozy (Dordogne) in 2006.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand, as Conyza albida): N.; S.: Nelson, Marlborough, S. Westland, Banks Peninsula and vicinity of Christchurch; St.; Ch. Naturalised from subtropical South America, first recorded in 1957; it was confused with wavy-leaved fleabane until then, and the first record may in fact be as early as 1864.
Known in New Zealand as broad-leaved fleabane, it is a common weed that has become more common on farms in recent years; animals are reluctant to graze it, and its tall stems along fence lines can short out electric fences. It has developed resistance to glyphosate in vineyards and orchards in Europe (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated).

warnings: Its record as food is thin: a little-used vegetable in one West Javan village, a leafy vegetable in Ogun State, south-western Nigeria, and a one-line note that the leaves may be used as a vegetable in South-East Asia. No New Zealand, European or Australian food use of this species was found.

Foraging advice for 'horseweed' — young leaves boiled, dried leaves as a seasoning — is written for Canadian fleabane (Erigeron canadensis), a different species that is rare in New Zealand; it does not apply to this plant.
Suspected of poisoning livestock and of tainting milk.
A weed of roadsides, farms, fence lines and orchards that is sprayed with herbicides such as glyphosate. Gather only where you know it has not been sprayed.

habitat.text: Zealandia pustulata is widespread and commonly described as both a lithophyte and epiphyte. They are evident across a range of wet sclerophyll forest and rainforest, as well as more open, subalpine environments, with preferred growing conditions being in ferneries or gullies in partial- to full shade. Within these forested environments, the species is described as a middle-storey inhabitant, but is able to grow anywhere from the forest floor to the canopy.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Zealandia pustulata' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text: This epiphytic fern species seems to climb onto suitable substrates (fallen logs, rocks, growing plants etc.) via long, creeping grey-green rhizomes. The rhizomes have clathrate, ovate scales which are 3-7 mm long and 1-2 mm wide. Generally, the species exhibits 1-9 pairs of lobed, glossy-green fronds which are erect to pendant and can range from 5-50 cm in length. The texture of the fronds is leathery, and they have thick, wavy margins. They have distinct, relatively large (approximately 3-4 mm wide) circular sori on their abaxial surface. The spores themselves are 45–62.5 μm long, 20–32.5 μm wide, pale, with wart-like protuberances. The species can grow to a maximum height of approximately 30 cm and a maximum width of approximately 120 cm.

summary.text:
Zealandia pustulata is a species of fern native to eastern Australia and New Zealand.
Zealandia pustulata ranges from southeastern Queensland through New South Wales to Victoria on the Australian mainland, and to Tasmania, Lord Howe Island, Norfolk Island,  New Zealand's North and South Islands, and the Chatham, Kermadec, and Antipodes islands.
There are two subspecies, Zealandia pustulata ssp. pustulata, the type species which is present across the plant's mainland and insular ranges; Z. pustulata ssp. howensis is uniquely endemic to Lord Howe Island.

identification.text:
C. foetidissima grows as a small open branched tree or shrub, typically up to 3 m tall, but in the Auckland Islands reaching heights of 6 m, with a trunk up to 45 cm in diameter. The bark is dark brown, and the branchlets are glabrous (lacking hairs). The interpetiolar stipules are shorter than those of many other coprosma species and taper to a conspicuous tooth fringed by fine short hairs and with uneven tufts of hairs at the tips. Leaves are thin, 30-50 mm long, 14-20 mm wide, somewhat leathery-textured, and shaped obovate to oblong to broadly ovate. Leaf tips may be rounded or have a small tapered point. The leaves lie in a single plane on the branchlet. The leaves of C. foetidissima (and many other species of Rubiaceae) have domatia, small indentations on the underside that may be occupied by potentially beneficial insects such as mites and other arthropods.
C. foetidissima is dioecious, meaning that male and female flowers are borne on separate plants. Flowering occurs between October and November. The flowers are solitary and occur on the ends of branchlets. The calyx of male flowers is  cup-like with four or five teeth; the corolla is bell-shaped, 4 or 8 lobed to the middle; and anthers are large, elongate-oblong in shape, and as long as the corolla. Female flowers have a short, narrowly ovoid, tubular, and toothed calyx and the corolla is a curved tube with 4 or 5 splits extending one-third to halfway down. The styles are long and substantial. Fruiting occurs between March and July. The drupes are 7–10 mm in length with an oblong shape. They are yellow to orange-red in colour, and are dispersed primarily by birds.
Crushed leaves smell strongly of dung.

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long.
