lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; Hūpiro's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

summary.text:
Coprosma foetidissima, commonly known as stinkwood or hūpiro (Māori), is a species of flowering plant in the family Rubiaceae, native to mainland New Zealand as well as Stewart Island and the Auckland Islands.
C. foetidissima is endemic to New Zealand and found from the Coromandel Peninsula southwards to Stewart Island, and on the Auckland Islands.

edibleParts.text: The ripe fruit, raw, dried, or blended with other fruit into fruit leather. It looks like a strawberry but is usually described as dry and insipid, with very little flavour, likened to watermelon bitten close to the rind; its appeal is its colour and crunchy texture. The leaves, cooked as a potherb, raw in salads or dried for tea; young leaves are mild, faintly of cucumber. The flowers, as a garnish.

identification.text:
Herb with short stock, somewhat flaccid, up to 10–(15) cm high at flowering; runners greenish, slender, pilose, up to about 50 cm long and rooting at nodes and tips to form new rosettes. Basal leaves several in rosette; petiole 30–80–(160) mm long, densely pilose; leaflets obovate to narrowly ovate, subacute, obtuse to cuneate at base, bright green above, paler below, usually sparsely to moderately pilose on both surfaces especially along veins, sometimes with only scattered hairs on upper, with margins crenate to obscurely lobed; terminal leaflet 15–55 × 12–30 mm; lateral leaflets equal to terminal or slightly smaller; petiolules 1–5 mm long, pilose. Scape often only slightly exceeding leaves, pilose. Epicalyx segments broadly obovate, pilose, deflexed at fruiting, with 3–5 purple-tipped teeth. Sepals ovate-triangular, about 6–10 mm long, acuminate, purple-tipped, pilose. Petals narrowly obovate, 4–8 mm long, more or less equal to epicalyx segments and sepals, shallowly emarginate to rounded, spreading, bright yellow. Achenes uniformly scattered over and projecting from receptacle; receptacle red, swollen, up to 12 mm long, often slightly constricted near base.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Woodland strawberry has white petals, where Indian strawberry's are bright yellow. Its epicalyx segments (the leafy bracts just beneath the sepals) are narrow and more or less entire; in Indian strawberry they are broadly obovate with 3–5 purple-tipped teeth, about as long as the petals and sepals, and bent back under the fruit. Woodland strawberry leaflets are coarsely serrate in the upper half to two-thirds; Indian strawberry leaflets are crenate to obscurely lobed. Woodland strawberry fruit is usually red, occasionally white, juicy, sweet and fragrant; Indian strawberry fruit is red, dryish and semi-fleshy, with very little flavour. Woodland strawberry can carry 1 to several flowers on a stalk, so a single flower does not separate them, but Indian strawberry flowers are solitary. What does not separate them: both form rosettes with runners rooting at the nodes and tips, both have three-part leaves of overlapping size, petals up to 8 mm long and sepals of overlapping length, both have achenes scattered over and projecting from a swollen red receptacle of similar size, both grow on roadsides, wasteland and forest margins or clearings, both are recorded from Nelson, Canterbury and Dunedin, and both fruit from November to April. Woodland strawberry fruit is edible raw, cooked or as preserves, and its young leaves are also eaten.

preparation.text: Pick the fruit when fully red and firm and use it soon, as it bruises easily. Eat the berries raw, or scatter them over salads, fruit platters, cakes or yoghurt. They can be mixed with other berries to stretch a jam or jelly, and on their own make a mild jelly or juice. To keep them, air-dry or dehydrate the berries, or blend them with more flavourful fruit and dry into fruit leather. Pick young leaves for salads; older leaves are better cooked or dried for tea, and the leaves are usually used sparingly. Leaves can be folded through omelettes, wilted in butter or stirred into soups at the end of cooking.

recipes.method: Ingredients for 6 ice pops: about 250 ml (1 cup) Indian strawberries, 375–500 ml (1½–2 cups) vanilla Greek yoghurt and 2 tablespoons honey. In a food processor, blend three-quarters of the berries with a few spoonfuls of the yoghurt until smooth. Add the rest of the berries and pulse a couple of times to chop them roughly. Tip into a bowl and stir in the honey and enough yoghurt to fill the ice-pop moulds (the author's hold 500 ml in all). Fill the moulds and freeze. The berries taste faint, so use plenty; the vanilla and honey carry their flavour.
recipes.title: Indian strawberry yoghurt ice pops

summary.text:
Potentilla indica, known commonly as false strawberry, mock strawberry, or Indian strawberry, (also snakeberry in North America) is a flowering plant in the family Rosaceae, native to West Asia to India, East Asia, and Southeast Asia. It has ternate foliage and an aggregate accessory fruit, similar to true strawberries of the genus Fragaria. Unlike the white or slightly pink flowers of true strawberries, Potentilla indica has yellow flowers, as do many other Potentilla species. It is native to eastern and southern Asia, but has naturalized in many regions worldwide.
Many sources consider this plant part of the genus Potentilla due to evidence from chloroplast genetic sequence data that the genus Duchesnea is included within Potentilla, though some still list it as Duchesnea indica.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: frequent, especially in hill country from Kaitaia (N. Auckland) south to near New Plymouth and Bay of Plenty, Wellington (Bunnythorpe, Hutt Valley, Wellington City); S.: Nelson (Motueka, Nelson City), Canterbury Plains, Dunedin. First recorded wild in New Zealand in 1935.
Grown in gardens for ground cover and as an ornamental, this species occasionally escapes into the wild. It flowers and fruits for much of the year and locally can become a very persistent pasture pest.
Also known in New Zealand as wild strawberry. Herbarium specimens come from the North Auckland, South Auckland, Taranaki, Wellington, Nelson, Canterbury and Otago land districts, including one collected in 2021 at Bastia Hill, Whanganui.

warnings: The berries are sometimes described as poisonous. A US poison-centre review of mostly small ingestions by young children found that mock strawberries produce no toxicity and that allergic reactions are rare; one child developed hives that resolved after antihistamine.
Use the leaves sparingly; 50 raw leaves may be too many. This advice rests on a single foraging source and names no compound or case of harm.
It is a lawn and garden weed that is controlled with broad-spectrum weedkillers. Pick only from unsprayed ground away from roadsides.

identification.text:
Woody shrub up to 2–(4) m high, much-branched from base. Stems clothed in very fine stellate hairs when young, becoming more or less glabrous when older. Leaves densely clothed in fine stellate hairs, triangular to suborbicular, cordate to obtuse at base, (3)–5–7-palmately lobed to about 1/2 radius, coarsely crenate, 2–15–(20) cm diameter; petioles 3–15 cm long; stipules triangular, 3–5 mm long, deciduous. Flowers in axillary clusters of 1–4–(5); fruiting pedicels 20–50 mm long; epicalyx segments ovate-triangular, united for lower ⅓, usually about 1/2 as long as calyx, unchanged at fruiting; calyx long-tubular; calyx teeth much shorter than tube, triangular, acuminate, densely clothed in stellate hairs, somewhat recurved at fruiting; petals magenta with darker veins, 30–40 mm long. Mericarps 7–9 per fruit, glabrous or sparsely to moderately hairy, smooth on back, but a single low longitudinal rib usually present; edges sharply angled or slightly rounded.
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Lavatera assurgentiflora Kellogg]
The species is distinguished by the long-tubular calyx.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Both have palmately lobed, toothed leaves whose sizes overlap (island mallow 2–15(–20) cm across, cheeseweed mallow 1–8 cm), so use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Island mallow's petals (30–40 mm) and common mallow's (12–30 mm) only meet at 30 mm, and both are pink to purple with darker veins or markings, so the flower colour does not separate them; check the calyx, long and tube-shaped in island mallow, and the fruit, smooth with one low rib against strongly net-veined. Leaf size overlaps. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Both have palmately lobed, toothed leaves whose sizes overlap (island mallow 2–15(–20) cm across, dwarf mallow 1–7(–8) cm), so use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. They differ in the epicalyx (longer than the calyx and enlarged in fruit in tree mallow, shorter and barely changed in island mallow), the fruit segments, the calyx (shallowly bell-shaped in tree mallow, long and tube-shaped in island mallow) and the petals (15–20 mm against 30–40 mm). Both are tall, both grow at coastal sites, and both have lobed leaves up to 20 cm across and pink to purple flowers with darker veins, so the leaves and flower colour do not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Tree mallow

summary.text:
Malva assurgentiflora, formerly classified as Lavatera assurgentiflora, the island mallow, mission mallow, royal mallow, malva rosa island mallow, island tree mallow or malva rosa ('pink mallow') in Spanish, is a species of flowering plant in the mallow family.
It is endemic to southern California, where it is native only to the Channel Islands. It can also be found growing as an escapee from cultivation in localised spots in coastal mainland California and Baja California, as well as sparingly in locations in Guatemala, cooler regions in mountainous or Mediterranean areas in western South America, New Zealand and Australia.
In New Zealand it is locally established on the east coast of the South Island from Marlborough to Otago. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1940.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Cultivation escape, on shady banks, walls, amongst rocks, mostly in the vicinity of buildings.
The original habitat for Cymbalaria muralis was narrow niches in rock faces and cliffs. It is considered very characteristic of the vegetation that grows on walls.
Common on cliffs and walls around Wellington and throughout New Zealand; it does well in full sun as well as shade (Garnock-Jones). Also on paths (Kiwicare).

identification.text:
Glabrous herb; stems often purplish. Petioles slender, to 4 cm long. Lamina 1–2.7 × 1–3.5 cm, 5-lobed, often with 2 subsidiary lobes on basal pair, more or less reniform, more or less purplish on lower surface; base cordate; lobes usually mucronate. Pedicels slender, 1–3 cm long at anthesis. Calyx 2–3 mm long; lobes lanceolate, extending nearly to base. Corolla 10–12 mm long from obtuse apex of spur to rounded apices of lower lobes, pale mauve with yellow or whitish pouch and dark lines on the upper lip. Capsule slightly longer than calyx. Seeds 0.7–0.9 mm diameter, broad-ovoid or subglobose, with prominent sinuate ridges. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The trailing stems root at the nodes and can reach about 80 cm (Kiwicare; Julia's Edible Weeds). Leaves grown in shade are bigger and slightly fleshy (Garnock-Jones). The mouth of the flower is closed by two yellow knobs, with a long nectar spur behind; once a flower is pollinated its stalk lengthens and curves down below the leaves, holding the fruit close to the ground or pushing it into a crevice (Garnock-Jones; Wikipedia).

preparation.text: Mix a few leaves into a salad with other greens. They taste pungent and acrid, like cress, and can be rather bitter and unpleasant; the taste has also been likened to raw garden peas, or called bitter with a sharp numbing feel. Scatter the flowers over the top. Because the leaves stay green all year, they are a winter green.

summary.text:
Cymbalaria muralis, commonly called ivy-leaved toadflax, is a low, spreading, trailing plant with small purple flowers, native to rocky habitats in southern Europe.
It is often cultivated in New Zealand as a pot or rock garden plant. The species has been recorded previously in New Zealand as Linaria cymbalaria.
Other names: coliseum ivy, Kenilworth ivy, mother of thousands, Oxford ivy and wandering sailor (Wikipedia). It probably came to New Zealand as a garden plant and was first reported naturalised here in 1904 (Garnock-Jones, citing Flora of New Zealand vol. IV; NZPCN).

warnings: Some caution is advised: the plant might be slightly toxic. This rests on a single British reference on poisonous plants, which deals mainly with livestock.
Its record as food is thin: salad use in southern Europe, and once as a vegetable in one Pyrenean valley. It is seldom listed in wild-food manuals.
Weedkillers are sold for spraying it on paths, driveways, walls and garden beds, including long-lasting ones that stop it coming back for an extended period. Pick from ground you know.

habitat.text: Occasional escape from cultivation, regenerating in the vicinity of planted trees, particularly in modified forest, as well as in and around plantations. Wild seedlings and saplings have been collected on a limestone cliff above tawa–rimu forest, on a track edge under a eucalypt plantation and at the edge of shrubland. Planted trees do best on deep, well-drained soils below about 600 m with good, evenly spread rainfall; they do not like dry conditions or waterlogged ground.

identification.text:
Medium to large tree. Trunk ridged or somewhat buttressed towards base. Bark reddish brown, peeling in long strips. Crown dense. Juvenile leaves 0.8–1.8–(2.2) cm long, subulate, often red in winter. Adult leaves (from coning branches) 5–15 mm long (excluding adnate, decurrent base), subulate with broad base, directed forwards, shining green; apex acute. Male strobili densely clustered at apices of small shoots, 2.5–5 mm long. Female cones 1–1.7 cm diameter when open. Bract scale apex pungent. Ovuliferous scales with about 6 spiny processes 2–3 mm long. Seed 4–5 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The persistently juvenile cultivar 'Elegans' is the commonest form in gardens and can produce cones, but no spontaneous plants of this form have been reported.

summary.text:
Japanese cedar is the only species of Cryptomeria, a genus in the cypress family (Cupressaceae); the name comes from the Greek kryptos, 'hidden', and meros, 'a part'. It is native to Japan and China.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1957, in the North Island in North Auckland (Omahuta, Trounson Park) and the Wairarapa (Kiriwhakapapa), and in the South Island in Marlborough (near Kahutara River) and Westland (Mahinapua). Japanese cedar is abundant in cultivation throughout New Zealand, especially in gardens, parks and domains, but also sometimes as a plantation tree. Herbarium specimens collected since record it wild in the Taumatatotara Range near Waitomo (1989), in Lismore Forest near Whanganui (1994) and at Masons Bay on Stewart Island (2009). In New Zealand it is mostly grown for shelter, and farm foresters have planted many small blocks for its timber.

warnings: Its pollen is a major cause of hay fever: around 30% of people in Japan are allergic to it.

identification.text:
Deciduous, spreading to erect tree, 4–12–(15) m high when mature, not armed; trunk tall. Lf petiole (14)–20–32–(40) mm long, glabrous or occasionally with sparse hairs; blade usually thin, usually broadly ovate to broadly elliptic, occasionally oblong or narrowly obovate, (70)–80–130–(155) × (40)–45–60–(65) mm, acuminate to long-acuminate at apex, usually rounded to subcordate or occasionally cuneate at base, glabrous above and below, with lower surface slightly paler, serrate with teeth aristate and often gland-tipped; stipules long-triangular, early deciduous. Inflorescence a corymbose cluster of (2)–3–4–(6) flowers, on short lateral shoots, sometimes clustered near branchlet tips, up to 45–(80) mm long, more or less pendent; flowers not fragrant; pedicels (10)–14–(35) mm long, glabrous, subtended by serrate bracts. Hypanthium narrowly campanulate; sepals 4–7–(8) mm long, lanceolate or subulate, acuminate, glabrous, greenish to magenta, erect to spreading or occasionally reflexed. Petals 5 or many, more or less spreading at anthesis, broadly obovate to orbicular, (12)–14–18–(20) × 9–14 mm, undulate and notched, white or pink-flushed to rose. Stamens shorter than petals; filaments whitish or flushed pale pink. Fruit shorter than 15 mm diameter, globose, glabrous, black-purple, bitter; stone smooth. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Taiwan cherry's flowers are deep pink to rose-magenta and more or less bell-shaped, the lower part of each petal staying semi-erect while the upper part eventually spreads, with magenta to dark deep red sepals; Japanese cherry's petals are white or pink-flushed to rose and more or less spread open, and its sepals are greenish to magenta. The bell-shaped flower is what sets Taiwan cherry apart. Fruit: Taiwan cherry's is glossy scarlet and egg-shaped to ellipsoid, up to 12 × 10 mm; Japanese cherry's is round, black-purple and bitter, under 15 mm across — but Japanese cherry fruit can also be red, so a red fruit does not settle it. Leaf teeth: Japanese cherry's end in a bristle and are often gland-tipped; Taiwan cherry's are pointed. Flowering overlaps: Taiwan cherry July to September, Japanese cherry August to October. Leaf size, leaf-stalk length and flower-stalk length overlap, and neither has spines.

preparation.text: Owing to their bitter taste, the raw sakuranbo is unpalatable and rarely eaten; instead, the seed inside is removed and the fleshy part preserved.

recipes.method: About 50 g cherry blossoms (around 5 very loosely packed cups); 2 tsp flaky or fine sea salt, plus 5 g (1 tsp) more if needed; 240 ml rice vinegar; 2 tsp umezu (Japanese plum vinegar), if you have it. Pick from an unsprayed tree, choosing flowers that are just starting to open. Soak them gently in clean water, stirring lightly with your hands, then lay them out to dry or give them a quick, gentle spin in a salad spinner. Layer the flowers in a small jar, sprinkling each layer with salt, and refrigerate for 3 days. Cover with the vinegar and refrigerate for another 3 days. To keep them as a pickle, simply leave the flowers in the vinegar in the fridge; they keep 6 months or more but fade. To dry them, drain off and keep the vinegar, then spread the flowers on a tray lined with a soft cloth in a warm, dry place out of direct sun, checking once a day — about three days on average — or dry them in a dehydrator at about 35 °C for 6–8 hours. Keep the heat low, or they turn brown. Toss flowers left a little moist with a further 5 g (1 tsp) sea salt. Use the pink sakura vinegar, which is salty, like a seasoned vinegar, for example in sushi rice. They keep, dried, at room temperature, out of direct sun, for about a year; the vinegar keeps in the fridge for 6 months or more. Makes about 1 cup of flowers and 240 ml of vinegar.
recipes.title: Preserved cherry blossoms (sakura no shiozuke) and sakura vinegar

recipes.method: A handful of clean, fresh cherry blossoms with the stalks removed; water; and white sugar. Put the blossoms in a dish, pour over enough water just off the boil to cover them, cover the dish and leave to infuse for 24 hours. Strain the liquid through a fine sieve, muslin or a paper filter into a small pan and add the same quantity of sugar — 500 g sugar to 500 ml of liquid. Heat gently until the sugar dissolves, bring to the boil and simmer for 3 to 5 minutes. Funnel into a sterilised bottle and seal. Once opened, keep it in the fridge and use within 2 months. Use it as you would a subtle orgeat or maraschino, in drinks.
recipes.title: Cherry blossom syrup

recipes.method: About 2 cups of fresh cherry blossoms and about 475 ml raw apple cider vinegar. Pick flower buds and open blooms from a tree you know has not been sprayed or contaminated, leaving the leaves behind — the author advises against harvesting leaves with the flowers. Fill a glass jar about two-thirds full of flowers and top up with the vinegar. If the jar has a metal lid, put a piece of parchment or wax paper between jar and lid so the vinegar does not eat the metal. Leave to infuse for at least 2–4 weeks; pink blossoms turn it a golden fuchsia. Strain, and use it in salad dressings, marinades, soda water or cocktails.
recipes.title: Cherry blossom vinegar

recipes.method: For one drink: 75 ml sake; 15 ml dry gin; 15 ml of the cherry blossom vodka; 1 tsp cherry blossom syrup; a salted cherry blossom (or a small pinch of salt). Infused vodka: a handful of clean fresh cherry blossoms; vodka. First infuse the cherry blossoms in vodka for a couple of days, then fine-strain. Stir with ice, strain, and garnish with a fresh or salted cherry blossom.
recipes.title: Sakura martini

recipes.method: Put cherry blossoms in a jar, cover them with good mirin and leave for four days, then strain out the flowers and keep the mirin in the fridge. The author drizzles it over mild, crunchy salads and spoons it over silken tofu as a dessert.
recipes.title: Cherry blossom mirin

recipes.method: 1 Japanese or 5 Persian cucumbers, 1 tbsp (15 ml) sesame seeds toasted in a pan, 3 tbsp (45 ml) cherry blossom mirin (above), 2 tsp (10 ml) rice vinegar, ¼ tsp sea salt, and cherry blossoms to scatter. Crush the cucumbers lightly with the back of a knife or a rolling pin, break them into chunks and put them in a bowl. Roughly crush the sesame seeds in a mortar. Whisk the mirin, vinegar and salt together in a small bowl, add them to the cucumber with the sesame seeds and toss well. Turn onto a serving dish, scatter over the blossoms and serve at once. If you like, leave the salad to macerate in the mirin mixture for an hour to develop its flavour, but add the sesame seeds and blossoms just before serving.
recipes.title: Cucumber and cherry blossom salad

summary.text: Prunus serrulata or Japanese cherry is a species of cherry tree that grows wild in Japan, China, Korea and Vietnam.

warnings: The plant (especially the seed and young shoots) contains cyanogenic glycosides, especially amygdalin and prunasin. When ingested, these compounds break down in the digestive tract to release cyanide.

Eat the blossoms only in small amounts, particularly raw: cherry flowers, leaves, twigs and bark contain cyanogenic compounds that release cyanide when chewed or crushed. Leave the leaves behind when picking flowers.

habitat.text: It prefers to invade areas that have been disturbed, such as roadsides or floodplains. It will generally only invade forests when the canopy has been opened by logging or fallen trees, as it grows less vigorously in the shade.

identification.text:
Vigorous climber, evergreen, or semi-evergreen in cold districts. Stems mostly purplish and hirsute when young. Leaves dimorphic: those produced in colder weather in early spring sinuate to deeply lobed; summer leaves and those on reproductive shoots entire. Petiole to 1.3 cm long, densely hirsute. Lamina of entire leaves 2.5–12 × 1.5–6 cm, ovate-oblong, ovate or ovate-elliptic, usually deep more or less shining green or sometimes yellowish green above, lighter green below, sometimes mottled yellow, densely hairy to glabrous on veins beneath; midrib above glabrous or hairy; base rounded, truncate or subcordate; apex obtuse to acute; leaves subtending flowers similar but smaller, all free. Flowers in axillary pairs, fragrant; peduncles 0.5–2.5 cm long, densely hirsute. Bracteoles more or less oblong-obovate, much shorter than ovaries. Calyx lobes very small, more or less narrow-triangular, fringed with long hairs. Corolla 2–4.5–(5) cm long, usually white, becoming yellow after anthesis, often flushed pink on reverse, glandular-hairy outside; tube 1–3 cm long, cylindric; limb 2-lipped; single linear lobe of lower lip recurving; upper lip 4-toothed. Stamens and style shorter than to equal to corolla limb. Ovaries separate. Berry (4)–5–7 mm diameter, broad- ovate to suborbicular, glossy black. Seed about 2 mm diameter 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are fragrant climbers whose white flowers can be flushed pink and whose fruit is a glossy black berry of much the same size, and the flower tubes overlap in length, so fruit and tube size do not separate them. Japanese honeysuckle's leaves are simple and entire, though leaves produced in colder weather in early spring are wavy-edged to deeply lobed; pink jasmine's leaves are pinnate, with (5)–7 stalked leaflets. Japanese honeysuckle's flowers come in pairs in the leaf axils, are two-lipped, turn yellow after opening and are glandular-hairy outside; pink jasmine carries many flowers together in panicles, each a narrow tube opening to flat, elliptic lobes, usually pink in bud. Pink jasmine has no food record and is not treated as food.

summary.text:
Lonicera japonica, known as Japanese honeysuckle and golden-and-silver honeysuckle, is a species of honeysuckle native to East Asia, including many parts of China.
The flowers can also be a significant source of food for deer, rabbits, hummingbirds, and other wildlife.
Japanese honeysuckle has become naturalized in Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Mexico, New Zealand, and much of the United States, including Hawaii, as well as a number of Pacific and Caribbean islands. It is classified as a noxious weed in 46 states, being prohibited to be bought and sold in Connecticut, Illinois, Massachusetts, and Vermont, and banned in Indiana and New Hampshire. It is on the New Hampshire invasive species list.
Lonicera japonica was initially brought to the U.S. from Japan in the early 1800s as an ornamental plant. It is still deliberately planted in the U.S. for reasons such as erosion control or forage for deer, but has become invasive in many areas.
Once it has invaded an area, Lonicera japonica grows rapidly and outcompetes native plants for sunlight and nutrients. It proliferates using both sexual and vegetative reproduction, producing seeds that are spread by animals and expanding locally via rhizomes. Eventually, it will form a dense thicket which prevents other plant species from germinating in that area. Due to its suppression of germination in the understory, Lonicera japonica also prevents the regeneration of trees.
Management of invasive Lonicera japonica has been achieved through a variety of means. Small patches can be removed by hand, or using simple digging tools, but all plant parts including roots and rhizomes must be removed to prevent resprouting. Larger patches can be removed through repeated mowing, but application of herbicide is also recommended to prevent regrowth. There has been some study of using controlled burns to remove L. japonica, but the underground portion of the plant is usually able to survive and resprout, limiting the effectiveness of this method. Browsing by herbivores may limit its growth, but is unlikely to eliminate it.

Biological control
The EPA of New Zealand approved the release of Limenitis glorifica butterflies in 2013 as a biological control for Lonicera japonica. This butterfly is host specific for Japanese honeysuckle, but it may incidentally feed on other closely related plants, including Himalayan honeysuckle Leycesteria formosa. Oberea shirahatai is a Japanese honeysuckle host-specific beetle that feeds on the stems and leaves of Japanese honeysuckle. It was released in New Zealand in 2018 as another L. japonica-specialist biological control.

harvestEthics.text: It is a National Pest Plant Accord species: it must not be sold, bred or distributed anywhere in New Zealand. In the Waikato it is illegal for anyone but the regional council to remove or disturb it — don't pick it there; report it on 0800 800 401. Auckland Council manages every known site and asks you to report it (pestfree@aucklandcouncil.govt.nz) rather than control it. Elsewhere, check your regional council's rules first, and carry no living piece anywhere new.

identification.text:
The flowers are small, cream or white, produced in erect racemes 6–15 cm long in late summer and early autumn. Japanese knotweed has hollow stems with distinct raised nodes that give it the appearance of bamboo, though it is not related. While stems may reach a maximum height of 3–4 m each growing season, it is typical to see much smaller plants in places where they sprout through cracks in the pavement or are repeatedly cut down. The leaves are broad oval with a truncated base, 7–14 cm long and 5–12 cm broad, with an entire margin. New leaves of Reynoutria japonica are dark red and 1 to 4 cm long; young leaves are green and rolled back with dark red veins; leaves are green and shaped like a heart flattened at the base, or a shield, and are usually around 12 cm long.
Mature R. japonica forms 2-to-3-metre-tall, dense thickets. Leaves shoot from the stem nodes alternately in a zigzag pattern. Plants that are immature or affected by mowing and other restrictions have much thinner and shorter stems than mature stands, and are not hollow. The below-ground rhizome network acts as a long-lived storage system; it is often concentrated in the upper metre of the soil profile, but may extend well beyond the visible stand.


Similar species
Japanese knotweed may be confused with other plants suspected of being knotweed owing to the similar appearance of leaves and stems. Dogwood, lilac, houttuynia (Houttuynia cordata), ornamental bistorts such as red bistort (Persicaria amplexicaulis), lesser knotweed (Koenigia campanulata), Himalayan balsam (Impatiens glandulifera), broad-leaved dock (Rumex obtusifolius), bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis), bamboo, Himalayan honeysuckle (Leycesteria formosa), and Russian vine (Fallopia baldschuanica) have been suspected of being Reynoutria japonica.

recipes.method: Young knotweed shoots; a little sugar and water; Greek yoghurt, to serve. Avoid patches that may have been sprayed; the author watches a patch for at least a year before eating from it. Pick young shoots under 50 cm long. Chop the whole shoot without peeling it — the author doesn't peel them — stew it with a little sugar and water until soft, and pass it through a fine sieve. Serve with Greek yoghurt, or make a fool. Cook or burn every trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings). He also says it is high in oxalic acid and to eat it sparingly if you have a kidney complaint or have been told to avoid spinach or rhubarb.

recipes.method: Juice whole raw young stems. Drink the green juice in smoothies, or pass it through a fine cloth for a clear purple juice — the author uses it as a gin mixer. Don't compost the pulp, as the author does — cook or burn it, or bag it for the transfer station (see Warnings).

recipes.method: Chopped young knotweed shoots; chopped sweet cicely seeds, leaves and stems; vodka. Fill a jar a third full with chopped young knotweed shoots, then to halfway with chopped sweet cicely seeds, leaves and stems, and top up with vodka. Leave for at least 2 months, shaking daily for the first 2 weeks, then strain. Sweeten to taste after steeping rather than before. Cook or burn every trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).

summary.text:
Reynoutria japonica, synonyms Fallopia japonica and Polygonum cuspidatum, is a species of herbaceous perennial plant in the knotweed and buckwheat family Polygonaceae.
It is native to East Asia in Japan, China and Korea. In North America and Europe, the species has successfully established itself in numerous habitats, and is classified as a pest and invasive species in several countries. Spread in invaded ranges is mainly vegetative, through rhizome pieces, stem fragments and soil contaminated with plant material; waterways, construction activity and garden waste can move these propagules over longer distances. Many introduced populations are dominated by male-sterile clonal plants, but seed set, hybridisation with giant knotweed and the production of viable seed by Bohemian knotweed have also been reported.

warnings: Even small fragments of stem or root grow into new plants. Never put any of it in compost or garden waste. Cook or burn everything you bring home; bag any other pieces securely so nothing escapes, and take them to a refuse transfer station or landfill.

It is controlled with herbicide gels and sprays (glyphosate, metsulfuron-methyl, triclopyr, picloram), and a sprayed patch can keep sending up shoots. Pick only where you know it has not been treated.

identification.text:
Arborescent shrub to about 3 m high; stems few and with terminal crown of leaves. Leaves to about 40 cm long, sessile, composed of 5–9 pairs of sessile (except the terminal) leaflets, the basal pair smaller and stipule-like, the terminal leaflet largest. Leaflets of main pairs 4–7.5 × 2–3.5 cm, ovate, rigidly coriaceous, with 2–5 spiny teeth on margins; apex spiny. Racemes lax and spreading, to about 20 cm long; basal scales to 1.5 cm long, broadly ovate, membranous, dark brown. Bracts ovate, slightly shorter than pedicels at anthesis. Perianth segments to 9 mm long, ovate, imbricate except for short outermost whorl. Stamens included, shorter than inner perianth segments; filaments entire. Style very short. Berry 8–10 mm long, more or less broadly obovoid, blue-black and pruinose.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Mahonia japonica (Thunb.) DC.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Japanese mahonia's leaves are stalkless, and their lowest pair of leaflets is small and stipule-like; Oregon grape's leaves have no such pair and usually sit on a dark red stalk up to 4 cm long. Japanese mahonia has few stems to about 3 m, each crowned with leaves; Oregon grape is many-stemmed and suckering, usually about 1 m. Japanese mahonia's flower clusters are lax, spreading and up to about 20 cm; Oregon grape's reach 6–7 cm. Japanese mahonia's berries are broadly egg-shaped, 8–10 mm long; Oregon grape's round, about 10 mm across. Leaflet counts overlap (5–9 pairs against 3–7), and blue-black bloomed berries do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Oregon grape

lookalikes.howToTell: Japanese mahonia's flower clusters are lax and spreading; leatherleaf mahonia's stand upright, 7–26 cm long. Japanese mahonia's main leaflets are 4–7.5 cm long and 2–3.5 cm wide; leatherleaf mahonia's leaflets are wider, 2–6 cm, so only a wide leaflet tells. Japanese mahonia's berries are 8–10 mm long; leatherleaf mahonia's up to 15 mm. Leaflet counts (5–9 pairs against 4–10), a small lowest pair, spiny teeth and blue-black bloomed berries do not separate them. The two have long been confused: leatherleaf mahonia has been listed as a form of B. japonica ('Bealei'), so a garden label does not settle it. The two have hybridised in gardens and many seedlings are hybrids, so intermediate plants are fairly common. Some plants grown as leatherleaf mahonia in the United States have loose, spreading to hanging flower clusters and narrow leaflets, so on a planted or escaped shrub neither trait settles it.
lookalikes.name: Leatherleaf mahonia

lookalikes.howToTell: Japanese mahonia's leaves carry 5–9 pairs of ovate leaflets with 2–5 spiny teeth; mountain grape's carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped ones. Japanese mahonia's flower clusters are lax and spreading; mountain grape's dense and upright. Blue-black berries with a bloom do not separate them, and neither test settles the garden hybrid B. × hortensis ('Charity', 'Winter Sun'), whose parents are these two species.

recipes.method: Written for the berries of Japanese and leatherleaf mahonia. Base: 375 ml flour, 440 ml rolled oats, 125 ml chopped walnuts, 250 ml packed dark brown or coconut sugar, 1 tsp baking powder, ½ tsp fine salt, 1 tsp vanilla and 250 ml melted butter. Topping: 625 ml mahonia berries, 250 ml sugar, 2 tsp grated orange or lemon zest and two lavender buds. Heat the oven to 180°C and line a 20–23 cm square tin with baking paper, leaving it overhanging the sides. Stir the dry ingredients together, then work in the melted butter until crumbly. Press three-quarters of it firmly into the tin and bake for 10 minutes. Cook the berries with the sugar, zest and lavender over low heat for 15 minutes, until they pop open; cool for 5 minutes and take out the lavender. Pour over the base, scatter the rest of the crumble on top and bake for 30–40 minutes, until golden. Cool completely in the tin, lift out by the paper and cut into 12 large bars or 24 squares.

summary.text:
Berberis japonica is a species of flowering plant in the family Berberidaceae, native to Taiwan. Despite the name, it is not native to Japan, though it has been known in cultivation there for centuries.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): South Island: known from 2 sites only, Botanical Hill (Nelson), just north of Clarence Bridge (coastal Marlborough).
M. japonica is fairly common in old gardens throughout New Zealand and persists for a long time without cultivation. Wild plants are presumably the result of dispersal of the fruit by birds.
Berberis bealei, native to mainland China and also widely cultivated, is usually treated as a separate species, but in the past has been listed as a cultivar of Berberis japonica. Its most obvious differences from B. japonica are in shorter, upright flowering racemes and wider leaflets.
Where it grows wild is not settled. Kew's Plants of the World Online gives Taiwan; the NZPCN says the origin is uncertain, probably southern China or northern Taiwan; Bean (Trees and Shrubs Online) doubts the Taiwan record, which rests on treating the Taiwanese M. tikushiensis as the same species; and Useful Temperate Plants suggests it may be known only in cultivation.

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.

identification.text:
It is a deciduous tree growing to 20 m tall, rarely 30 m, and 40–80 centimetres stem diameter, with light grey bark. The leaves are pinnate, 50–90 cm long, with 11–17 leaflets, each leaflet 7–16 cm long and 3–5 cm broad. The whole leaf is downy-pubescent, and a somewhat brighter, yellower green than many other tree leaves.
The male flowers are inconspicuous yellow-green catkins produced in spring at the same time as the new leaves appear. The female flowers have pink/red pistils. The fruit is a nut, produced in bunches of 4–10 together; the nut is spherical, 3–5 cm long and broad, surrounded by a green husk before maturity in mid-autumn.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both edible; this is about which you have. Count and feel the leaflets: Japanese walnut has 9–17, finely toothed though the teeth are often sparse, the end leaflet about the size of the side ones; walnut has 5–9 with smooth (untoothed) edges, the end leaflet the largest and the lowest pair much smaller. Seedling walnuts can have toothed leaflets, so check an adult tree. Japanese walnut's fruits hang 10–22 together in long strings; walnut's sit in clusters of 1–3 close on the twig. Japanese walnut's fruit is 2.5–4 cm, egg-shaped, beaked, sticky and rusty-hairy; walnut's is 3.5–5 cm, nearly round, smooth and green with gland dots, not beaked. Japanese walnut's thick shell has raised seams that split with difficulty and an often sharp tip; walnut's splits easily in half along its seams when ripe.

identification.text:
Trailing herb. Stem prostrate, terete, glabrous. Leaves terete or weakly 3-angled, obtuse and mucronate at apex, clavate, tapering to shortly connate base, (5)–20–30–(50) × (4)–5–6–(10) mm; margins papillate. Flowers 2–4 cm diameter. Calyx glabrous; sepal keels smooth. Petals purple with white base, in 2 rows, 10–30 mm long. Stamens 5–7 mm long; filaments hairy at base; anthers whitish yellow. Capsule 5–12 mm diameter, valves with widely divergent expanding keels; placental tubercle 2-lobed. Seeds pale brown to brown, weakly rugose or smooth, about 1 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The white bases of the petals turn purple when dry.

lookalikes.howToTell: Native ice plant's leaves are 3-angled and sharp-pointed, often with a small point, where this plant's are club-shaped, round or only weakly 3-angled in section, and blunt with a small point. Its petals are uniformly white to deep pink, in 3–5 rows, against purple with a white base, in 2 rows, here. Native ice plant grows on coasts throughout New Zealand, mostly on cliffs, rock stacks and boulder or cobble beaches and more rarely in saltmarsh, so the two can meet in South Island saltmarshes.

preparation.text: Cook the leaves as a green, add them to salads or stir-fries, or pickle them. Raw, they can be dressed in a little oil and laid on cooked fish.

recipes.method: Serves 1. Fish: 180 g snapper fillet; 1 tablespoon vegetable oil; 30 g butter; 3 lemon myrtle leaves. Buttermilk sauce: 1 shallot, finely sliced; 20 g ginger, in fine matchsticks; 200 ml vegetable stock; 1 nori sheet; 100 ml buttermilk; ¼ teaspoon xanthan gum; salt and white pepper. Leek: ½ leek; 20 g butter; vegetable stock to cover; salt and white pepper. Lemon myrtle oil (makes 500 ml): 500 ml grapeseed or other neutral oil; 10 g dried lemon myrtle leaves; 100 g spinach. To serve: a handful of jellybean ice plant leaves. For the sauce, cook the shallot and ginger gently in a pot until soft, add the stock and nori and simmer gently for 30 minutes, strain, and stir the liquid into the buttermilk; thicken with the xanthan gum using a stick blender and season. For the leek, cut it into 7 cm lengths and halve them lengthways, lay them flat in a small pan with the butter, cover with stock and simmer gently for 10–15 minutes until just tender, then lift out. For the oil, warm the lemon myrtle leaves in the oil over a low heat for 10 minutes without letting it get hot enough to scorch them, add the spinach and blend with a stick blender, then strain through an oil filter and remove any water from the spinach. For the fish, heat the oil in a pan until lightly smoking, put in the fish and turn the heat to low; cook for about 4 minutes on one side, until about 70% of the flesh has turned white, add the butter and lemon myrtle leaves and cook 1 minute more, then turn the fish, baste for 1 minute and rest it for 2 minutes. To serve, put the leek in the middle of a bowl, warm the sauce gently without boiling and pour about 125 ml (½ cup) into the bowl, and set the fish on the leek. Dress the ice plant leaves in 1 tablespoon of the lemon myrtle oil and pile them on the fish, then drizzle another tablespoon of oil over the sauce.
recipes.title: Snapper with lemon myrtle butter, buttermilk sauce and jellybean ice plant

summary.text:
Disphyma clavellatum, the jellybean ice plant or jellybeans, is a trailing succulent herb in the ice plant family Aizoaceae, native to Australia and New Zealand. Australian botanists treat it as a subspecies of round-leaved pigface, Disphyma crassifolium subsp. clavellatum.
In New Zealand it is presumed to be a natural arrival from Australia within roughly the last 50 years, and it is classed as a Non-resident Native – Coloniser, secure overseas. It was first collected here in 1984. The Flora of New Zealand (1988) recorded it at the New River Estuary near Invercargill, and NZPCN lists it from Waimea Inlet and Riverton Estuary; iNaturalist records also come from Sandy Point near Invercargill, the Otago coast at Aramoana, Karitāne and Waikouaiti, and around Nelson and Tasman.
It is easily grown from rooted pieces, division of whole plants or fresh seed, but it is not a usual nursery plant, and it should not be planted in estuaries beyond its known New Zealand sites, where it could compete with local saltmarsh plants; native ice plant is the usual garden choice.

habitat.text: Lowland forest, often dominant in swamp forest. It grows throughout New Zealand on moist, fertile soils, and is the dominant tree of swampy lowland areas. It was formerly dominant on frequently flooded or poorly drained alluvial soils, and occasionally extends into lower montane forest. A light-loving pioneer, it establishes fairly easily on moist sites and regenerates among mānuka and gorse, overtopping them within two or three decades; small groups of young trees are sometimes seen on farmland. Planted, it does best in moist to wet sites.

identification.text:
Kahikatea is a stout conifer 50–65 m tall, New Zealand's tallest native tree, with male and female cones on separate trees. The trunk is 1–2 m across, often fluted and buttressed at the base, and bare of branches for about three-quarters of its length. Young adult trees have a distinctive narrow, columnar form, with branches starting a third to half of the way up the trunk. The bark is grey to dark grey and falls in thick, wavy flakes; the wood is white and has no smell. Near the base the roots are typically buttressed and grooved, and trees growing in clusters develop interlocking root islands that may help stop single trees falling in high winds. It lives about 600 years and reaches maturity after 250–450 years. The branchlets are slender and drooping.
Seedlings carry juvenile foliage until they are 1–2 m tall, and juvenile, semi-adult and adult foliage often grow together on the same tree. Juvenile leaves are narrow, slightly sickle-shaped and sharply pointed, 3–7 × 0.5–1 mm, spreading in two rows, and red, wine-red or dark green to green; those of young adults are up to 4 mm, dark green or red. Adult leaves are only 1–2 mm long, keeled and scale-like, pressed tightly overlapping against the stem, and brown-green or blue-grey with a waxy bloom.

As a conifer, kahikatea has no flowers. Male cones grow at the branch tips, oblong and about 10 mm long, with pale yellow pollen. Each seed sits alone at a branchlet tip on a fleshy, oblong, flattened, warty receptacle 2.5–6.5 mm long, yellow to orange-red. The seed is broadly egg-shaped to round, 4–6 mm across, purple-black and thickly covered in a waxy bloom. A male tree glows faint orange when its cones are mature, and a female tree turns red when its receptacles are ripe.

For most of the year the tree carries no cones or fruit, and in forest it is usually too tall for its foliage to be seen, so bark and tree form are the main field characters; it sheds foliage and branchlets fairly constantly, so fallen foliage can confirm it. The bark of young trees is not distinctive, but that of a mature tree is unlikely to be confused with any native conifer except miro, which usually has no buttresses and very different foliage. The columnar form of young adults, the buttressed and fluted trunk base, the scale leaves and the round seeds at the branchlet tips separate kahikatea from all other native conifers.

lookalikes.howToTell: The bark of a mature kahikatea is easily mistaken for miro's: both are grey to grey-brown and fall in thick flakes, so bark alone does not separate them. Look at the base: kahikatea's trunk is often fluted and buttressed; miro usually has no buttresses. Look at the foliage: adult kahikatea leaves are tiny scales 1–2 mm long pressed tightly against the stem (juvenile leaves 3–7 mm); miro's are flat, dark green leaves 1.5–2.5 cm long and 2–3 mm wide, spreading in two rows. Look at the fruit: kahikatea's is a round, purple-black seed 4–6 mm across on a fleshy, yellow to orange-red receptacle 2.5–6.5 mm long; miro's is a plum-like fruit up to 20 mm long, with no separate fleshy receptacle. Miro's fruit is eaten too (see its page).

summary.text:
Dacrycarpus dacrydioides, commonly known as kahikatea (from Māori) and white pine, is a large coniferous tree in the family Podocarpaceae, endemic to New Zealand.
Kahikatea is endemic to the North, South, and Stewart Islands of New Zealand, and is the only member of the genus Dacrycarpus found in the country.
It was once the dominant tree of a distinct swamp forest type that is now all but extinct in the North Island; the best examples remain on the West Coast of the South Island. Its white, odourless timber was used extensively for butter boxes in the late 1800s and early 1900s, which all but eliminated kahikatea swamp forest from the North Island and northern South Island. It is assessed Not Threatened, but very few intact kahikatea-dominated forests remain in the North Island. Riccarton Bush in Christchurch is a surviving remnant.
It is commonly sold by nurseries and is a popular garden tree; a form with distinctly blue-grey foliage is sometimes offered.
Its pollen has three air sacs, a shape distinctive in the New Zealand flora, so it is easily identified. Kahikatea has a diploid chromosome count of 20. Several different glycosides have been isolated from the leaves; the tricetin 3',5'-di-O-/β-glucopyranoside and 3'-0-β-xylopyranoside have been found only in kahikatea. The receptacles and seeds have been found to contain anthocyanins, rare in gymnosperms, which it was suggested in one 1988 paper make the fruit as a whole more attractive to prospective animal dispersers.

warnings: Only the fleshy receptacle is recorded as eaten. No record of the seed being eaten was found, so whether it is safe is not known.

habitat.text: Forest understorey and sheltered, shady places, from the coast up to montane and cloud forest. Where rainfall is high it can make up much of the shrubland and regenerating forest, and it is often common along the edges of logging tracks and roads.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to about 6 m tall; trunk slender (not always developed); branches and branchlets rather stout, glabrous. Leaves on petioles about 2–5 cm long. Stipules tapering from rather broad base to 2 conspicuous denticles, glabrous. Lamina membranous to subcoriaceous, subglossy green above, paler below, broadly elliptic to obovate; apex subacute, sometimes apiculate; rather gradually narrowed to petiole; (10)–15–20 × (5)–7–10 cm.; margins sometimes waved, sometimes more or less crenulate. Reticulations close, conspicuous or evident on both surfaces. Flowers in clusters on trichotomously branched peduncles up to about 6 cm long. male with 4–5-toothed cupular calyx; corolla narrow-funnelform, lobes usually 5, acute, shorter than tube; stamens usually 5. female usually with small stipulate bracts at axils of branches; calyx-teeth usually 5, small, acute; corolla tubular, lobes 5, narrow-triangular, acute, more or less equal to tube. Drupe reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1 as Coprosma australis (A.Rich.) Robinson]

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Leaf thickness separates them: shining karamū's are thick, kanono's rather thin. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; Kanono's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Those figures fit the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa; the North Island's wild subsp. minor has thinner, papery leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) on stalks about 10–18 mm long, and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Māmāngi's young twigs are hairy; Kanono's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Mingimingi's young twigs are more or less hairy; Kanono's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Swamp coprosma's young twigs are hairy; Kanono's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. summary.text: Coprosma autumnalis or C. grandifolia according to earlier Colenso authority,  (In Māori: kanono, raurēkau or kawariki) is a native forest shrub of New Zealand. It is widespread in both the North Island and in the northern South Island, and has the largest leaves of any New Zealand coprosma. The name kawariki was applied after its leaves resembling those of the tropical Terminalia catappa which was once planted as shade for noble chiefs (ariki).

habitat.text: Coastal to lowland shrubland, regenerating forest and forest margins, also montane forest and ultramafic shrubland, and very occasionally subalpine shrubland. It tolerates winter cold, drought and a wide range of soils. In gardens it copes with coastal sites, wind, wet ground and long dry spells.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Some kānuka are still ranked separately by the New Zealand Threat Classification System. Kunzea sinclairii and K. toelkenii are Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable: do not harvest them unless it is a life-or-death situation and you absolutely must. K. amathicola, K. linearis, K. salterae, K. tenuicaulis and K. triregensis are At Risk: if you harvest them, take only a little, and never in a way that kills them or stops them from reproducing and spreading.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text: Shrub of diverse habit, or tree up to 15 m tall or more; trunk up to 60 cm or more in diameter; bark brown, thin, shedding in long flakes. Branchlets sparsely to rather densely clad in appressed hairs when young. Leaves in fascicles of 3–5 or solitary, ± 4–12 × 1–2 mm, linear to narrow-lanceolate, acute, not pungent, glabrous or sparsely silky-hairy when young; margins sometimes ciliolate. Flowers 3–5–(7) mm in diameter, axillary, on slender pedicels up to c. 5 mm long, in 2–5-flowered cymes to solitary. Receptacle narrow-turbinate; sepals ovate, acute, persistent; petals suborbicular, ± 2 mm in diameter, shortly clawed. Capsules about equalling to slightly exceeding receptacle-rim, 2–4 mm in diameter.

lookalikes.howToTell: Feel the leaves: mānuka's are rigid and end in a sharp, prickly point; kānuka's are not sharp-pointed and are soft to grasp. Mānuka's flowers are usually borne singly in the leaf axils; kānuka's are usually in small clusters. Mānuka's sepals soon fall, and its woody capsule stands clearly above the rim of the flower cup and stays on the plant for a long time; kānuka's sepals persist, and its capsule is about level with, or only slightly above, the rim. Both have white, occasionally pink, flowers, and bark is not a reliable test: both shed it in long strips or flakes. Mānuka's leaves are brewed as a tea (see its page).

summary.text:
Kunzea ericoides, commonly known as kānuka or white tea-tree, is a tree or shrub in the myrtle family, Myrtaceae and is endemic to New Zealand.
Kānuka is abundant throughout most of New Zealand, including many northern islands. It ranges from small, many-stemmed trees about 4 m tall to trees over 30 m tall. A fairly long-lived successional tree, it is one of the few native trees that regenerates widely after fire, and it tends to form pure stands through which other trees later regenerate. Forest clearance since human settlement has greatly widened the disturbed ground it colonises, and it is probably more widespread and abundant now than it has ever been. Once treated largely as a farm weed or cut for firewood, it is now valued for honey and essential oil, and it is a key plant in restoration and erosion-control planting, especially on steep land. New Zealand nurseries sell it for coastal planting, revegetation, shelter and screening.
It was first named Leptospermum ericoides and was moved to Kunzea in 1983. Flora of New Zealand treats all New Zealand kānuka as this one species, Kunzea ericoides in a broad sense, following a 2023 genetic study that recognised a single species; the ten species named in 2014, such as Kunzea robusta, are treated as its synonyms. The New Zealand Plant Conservation Network and the New Zealand Threat Classification System still list those species separately.

warnings: A strong brew of the leaves can make you vomit.
If you drink it regularly over a long time, keep it away from meals: its tannins may reduce how well minerals are absorbed.
Kānuka essential oil is strong. Don't take it internally except under the supervision of a qualified medical herbalist, and it should not be used by pregnant or breastfeeding women.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corynocarpus_laevigatus Names the toxin class and describes the processing this entry tells the reader not to attempt. The seeds 'contain highly toxic glucosides of 3-nitropropionic acid, such as karakin'; initial symptoms are diarrhoea, nausea and restlessness, developing into more severe gastrointestinal and neurological problems. The traditional process: seeds dropped each autumn were collected into open-weave kete, washed in water to remove the outer pulp, then baked and sun-dried, which removed the toxicity. It was one of the most grown pre-European Māori food crops, alongside kūmara and aruhe — the bracken rhizome, which has its own entry here — and in Māori tradition the tree came from Hawaiki. The flesh tastes sickly sweet, of apricots or dates, and the fruit is a valuable food for kererū and the Chatham Islands pigeon.

summary.text: Listed so you can recognise it and leave it alone. The kernel is severely poisonous without traditional processing.

warnings: The kernel is poisonous unless it has been through the traditional cooking and steeping. Do not attempt it yourself: the raw kernel can cause convulsions and paralysis.
The kernel contains karakin. Poisoning can cause seizures and paralysis; symptoms include nausea and vomiting, and muscle spasms may begin several weeks later.
The orange flesh is not the hazard — the kernel inside is, and separating them reliably is not a beginner's task.
Fallen karaka fruit is a recognised poisoning risk for children and dogs. Learn the tree so you can steer them away from it.

habitat.text: Coastal, lowland and lower montane shrubland, and open places within forest, from sea level to about 1,200 m. Hardy: it copes with infertile, poorly drained and exposed ground, in full sun or shade, wind and frost. Also grows in city green spaces.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to 6 m tall; branches and branchlets spreading, stout, glabrous. Leaves opposite on rather stout petioles about 10–20 mm long. Stipules connate towards base, obtuse, glabrous, crowned by 1–2 prominent sharp denticles. Lamina coriaceous, dullish dark green above, paler below, glabrous; elliptic to elliptic-oblong to broad-ovate, acute or obtuse, more or less mucronate, gradually narrowed to petiole, about 7–12 × 3–4–(5) cm.; reticulated veins usually conspicuous on both surfaces. male in axillary many-flowered glomerules on short peduncles, glomerules again divided into dense clusters. Calyx-teeth minute; corolla subcampanulate, lobes triangular, acute, shorter than tube. female in compound clusters on trichotomously branched axillary peduncles 10–15 mm long. Calyx minute, truncate, sometimes with 1–2 teeth; corolla about 5 mm long, narrow-funnelform, lobes acute or obtuse, oblong-triangular, shorter than tube. Drupe dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrow-ovoid, 8–9 × 4–5 mm.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Leaf shape and stipule separate them: shining karamū's leaves are widest above the middle and its stipules acute; karamū's are elliptic to ovate with tapering, long-pointed (acuminate) stipules. Shining karamū's leaf is glossy, karamū's rather dull. Shining karamū's roots and inner bark are yellow, karamū's dull brown, and shining karamū lacks karamū's foul smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; Karamū's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Leaf width and fruit length separate them: karamū's leaves about 35–42 mm wide with fruit 8–9 mm long; large-seeded coprosma's about 40–80 mm wide with fruit 10–25 mm long. Widths meet at about 40 mm, so take both tests together. Those tests fit only the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa: the North Island's wild subsp. minor has leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long, so neither test separates it from karamū. Karamū's leaf margin is minutely toothed; subsp. minor's is not. Those tests fit only the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa: the North Island's wild subsp. minor has leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long, so neither test separates it from karamū. Karamū's leaf margin is minutely toothed; subsp. minor's is not. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Māmāngi's young twigs are hairy; Karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Mingimingi's young twigs are more or less hairy; Karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm.
