Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Sand coprosma's young twigs are hairy; Karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

summary.text:
Coprosma robusta, commonly known as karamū, is a flowering plant in the family Rubiaceae that is endemic to New Zealand.
Karamū is endemic to New Zealand. However, it is gradually becoming naturalised in areas of the south-east coast of Australia such as Victoria and Tasmania and has been rated as a weed threat there.
It is widely distributed across New Zealand in both the North and South Islands. On the Chatham Islands between Waitangi and Owenga, there is a small area where karamū has become naturalised.
Judging from the distribution map on New Zealand Plant Observation, the distribution of karamū increases with the differentiation in lower altitude which means more karamū in the North Island.
In Canterbury, karamū is found on Banks Peninsula in fragments of regenerating native bush and bush remnants. Additionally it is also found in forest margins and edges of the montane and lowland forests in the southern alps at the start of the Canterbury plains.

habitat.text:
Lowland and hill forest throughout the North Island and the wetter parts of the South Island, looping between trees in dense, dark tangles.
It grows from the coast to the mountains, usually in forest but occasionally in swamps, where it sprawls through flax and fern, and it is common in limestone country around sinkholes and cave entrances.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. The vine is a food and rongoā plant for mana whenua, and a DOC permit is required on conservation land. Take a few tips from a large tangle, not every tip from one plant, and never cut the vine.

identification.text: Thick, smooth, dark brown to black woody vines that loop and tangle through the understorey. In spring the growing tips are soft, pale green to reddish shoots the thickness of a pencil that snap cleanly when bent. Leaves are glossy, oval and opposite, on the older growth. Berries are bright red.

preparation.text: Snap off the tender tip — if it bends rather than snaps it is too old. Eat raw, or steam briefly like asparagus.

recipes.method: Serves 4. 20 young kareao shoots, cut crosswise on an angle; 20 kawakawa leaves, blanched and squeezed of excess water; 1 lemon, zested and juiced; 250 g brown butter, melted; 6 egg yolks; 1 tbsp boiling water; 250 ml (1 cup) canola oil for the yolks, plus a little for frying; sea salt. Warm the 250 ml of oil in a small saucepan to just above body temperature, slip in 4 of the yolks and hold the oil at that temperature until serving; add a spare yolk or two in case any break. Blend the other 2 yolks at high speed for 10 seconds, add the boiling water and blend 20 seconds more. With the motor running, drizzle in the brown butter very slowly so the sauce thickens without splitting. Add the kawakawa, lemon zest and juice and blend until bright green and smooth, then season with salt. Heat a frying pan until hot, add a little oil and then the kareao, and sauté until just tender; season with salt. Spread 3 tbsp of the emulsion into a circle about 5 cm across in the middle of each plate. Lift the yolks from the oil with a slotted spoon, dab off the oil, set one in the centre of each circle with a pinch of salt and arrange the shoots around it.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Karengo is a taonga species with deep customary significance, and specific beds are managed by hapū. Check for rāhui before harvesting, cut rather than tear so the holdfast survives, and take only what you will use. Some areas are subject to customary management under the Fisheries Act — ask locally.
In the Kaikōura Marine Area karengo may be gathered by hand only, within a daily limit, and the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998 protects it from commercial harvesting within Ngāi Tahu's traditional seaweed-gathering grounds.

identification.text:
Thin, translucent, almost membranous fronds in purple-brown to olive, clinging flat to rock. Only one cell layer thick, so it feels like wet tissue paper rather than rubber.
In New Zealand (Nelson 2013): Blades circular to folded rosettes, strongly attached centrally by rhizoidal holdfast. Blades (1.5) 4–12 (42) cm in diameter. Colour purple to grey, bleaching to khaki-green on upper edges. It is the only species of Pyropia present on mainland shores with a marked rosette-like growth form.

preparation.text: Rinse in seawater, dry thoroughly, then toast. Use as you would nori, or crumble into soups and boil-ups.

recipes.method: Fresh karengo; 15 ml (1 tbsp) sunflower, olive or coconut oil, or more as needed; salt; lime juice, tamari, paprika or cumin, if you like. Wash the karengo well to get rid of sand and stones. Dry it, either spread out in the air for a few days or patted with a tea towel. Toss it with just enough oil to coat it lightly. Spread it over a baking tray and roast at 150 °C until crisp, turning it often so it toasts evenly; it shrinks a lot, so you may want two trays going. Watch it closely, as it burns quickly. Season with a sprinkle of salt, and with lime juice, tamari, paprika or cumin if you like. Eat straight away, on their own or with a dip. The author finds they go chewy again if kept, so grinds leftovers into sea salt or seals them in a glass jar.
recipes.title: Crisped karengo

recipes.method: Dried karengo; a little olive oil; flaky sea salt, the same amount as the crushed karengo. Fry the dried karengo gently in the olive oil. Crush it and mix it with an equal amount of flaky sea salt. Keep it in an airtight container.
recipes.title: Karengo salt

recipes.method: Fresh karengo; olive oil; 1 garlic clove, crushed; the juice of 1 orange. Wash the karengo, picking over the fronds to remove sand and any small animals. Pinch off and discard the holdfast, where the frond gripped the rock. Tear the fronds into palm-sized pieces, or shred them more finely with a knife. Spread them in a shallow ovenproof dish, drizzle with olive oil, scatter over the garlic, pour over the orange juice and toss together. Bake at 180 °C for about 20 minutes, longer for thicker kinds, until the lower layers are soft and the top is slightly crisp.
recipes.title: Baked karengo with garlic and orange

recipes.method: Written for laver (Porphyra), the European relative of karengo; the author's are purple, tough and winter laver. Laver; fresh water; a little apple cider vinegar. Rinse the laver thoroughly of sand and silt. Put it in a pan with fresh water — just a little if it is fresh or already soaked, as it gives off plenty more, but more if it is dried. Cover and keep it at a bare simmer for about 3 hours, adding water so it never boils dry; a little apple cider vinegar shortens the cooking and helps it keep. When very soft, drain and squeeze it, keeping the liquid: reduced further, it is a rich stock to freeze in ice-cube trays for soups, sauces and glazes. Spread the paste left behind — the laverbread — on toast, fry it into patties (with or without oats), or use it in stews, soups, tarts and pâtés. Freeze what you won't use soon in small tubs, as it doesn't keep well.
recipes.title: Laverbread

recipes.method: Written for laver (Porphyra), the European relative of karengo; the author's are purple, tough and winter laver. Cooked, drained laverbread; pinhead oatmeal; soy sauce, miso, sea lettuce or chopped fried mushrooms; a squeeze of lemon juice; fat for shallow-frying — bacon fat is best. Blitz cooked, drained laverbread (see the laverbread recipe), then stir in pinhead oatmeal — between half and an equal volume of oatmeal to laver — until thick enough to shape. Season to taste with soy sauce, miso, dried sea lettuce or chopped fried mushrooms, and add a squeeze of lemon juice for acidity. Leave for at least an hour, better overnight, so the oatmeal swells. Shape into patties with wet hands and shallow-fry in hot (not smoking) fat — bacon fat is best — pressing them flat with a spatula until the oatmeal bronzes into a crust. They keep well frozen once cooled, and reheat in the oven.
recipes.title: Laverbread patties

Wikipedia contributors. 'Pyropia', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyropia Supports the 'native nori' description and explains the double genus name on this entry. Pyropia is a genus of red algae of intertidal zones and shallow water worldwide, and several of its species are what nori is made from — a two-billion-dollar industry centred on China, Korea and Japan — with nori carrying substantial vitamin B12. Many species now in Pyropia sat in Porphyra until recently, and New Zealand material drove some of that: 2013 research on New Zealand plants moved Pyropia plicata out of Porphyra. Both names are therefore in circulation for the same seaweeds, which is why this entry lists both.

summary.text:
Aotearoa's native nori — a taonga species, traditionally dried on rocks and traded inland.
In New Zealand (Nelson 2013): North Island, South Island and Chatham Islands; not found on the Three Kings Islands, Stewart Island or the subantarctic islands. For many years it was incorrectly known as Porphyra columbina.

warnings: Harvest only from clean, wave-exposed coast — never from harbours, marinas, or near stormwater or wastewater outfalls.
Seaweed concentrates whatever is in the water around it.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Kawakawa is a significant rongoā (medicinal) plant. Tikanga around its harvest matters: take only what you need, never strip a plant, and seek guidance from mana whenua. Do not harvest on DOC land without a permit.

preparation.text: Traditionally, leaves with holes eaten by caterpillars were considered the best to use. Dry and steep as a tea, or use fresh leaves to wrap food. Use as a flavouring, not a bulk green.

recipes.method: Serves 4. 10 kawakawa leaves; 1 lemon; 60 ml (4 tbsp) honey; 1.25 litres (5 cups) cold water. Wash the leaves. Slice 6 of them and keep the other 4 whole for serving. Chop the sliced leaves and boil them in the water for 5 minutes. Let it cool a little, then pour it into a plunger. Add the lemon juice and honey, stir, and leave for 2 minutes. Serve in cups with a slice of lemon and a whole leaf, or let it cool and serve over ice as a summer drink. The author takes only the large leaves, leaving the young ones and those about to shoot.
recipes.title: Kawakawa tea

recipes.method: 125 ml (½ cup) caster sugar; 4 fresh kawakawa leaves, finely chopped. Mix the sugar and chopped kawakawa together in a small bowl. Make it a few days ahead if you can and keep it in a sealed jar, so the kawakawa flavours the sugar. The author rolls freshly fried mini kūmara doughnuts in it.
recipes.title: Kawakawa sugar

recipes.method: 8 kawakawa leaves; 15 ml (1 tbsp) salt flakes. Lay the leaves on a perforated baking tray and dry them in the oven at 60 °C for 5 hours. Crumble them by hand and rub them through a sieve, or grind them in a spice grinder. Mix the dried kawakawa into the salt. The recipe serves it with green-lipped mussel fritters.
recipes.title: Kawakawa salt

recipes.method: Kawakawa leaves; 500 ml (2 cups) sunflower or canola oil; a pinch of bread to test the oil. Wash the leaves — holed ones look prettiest — and dry them very thoroughly. Heat the oil in a deep pot over medium heat until a pinch of bread sizzles as soon as it goes in. Fry the leaves 2 or 3 at a time, holding a light pot lid or splatter screen over the pot as they go in, because they spit. They puff up and turn translucent within seconds and stop spitting almost at once; lift them out gently and drain on paper towels. The author serves them on grilled salmon, one crisp on each fillet with extras on the side.
recipes.title: Kawakawa crisps

recipes.method: The author's greens, picked from roadsides around Whangaroa Harbour, were nasturtium, kawakawa, fennel, samphire, fat hen, wild mustard, cleavers and clover. The author warns that New Zealand roadsides are still sprayed with glyphosate, so pick with care. 1 garlic clove (or 4 peeled onion weed bulbs); 60 ml (¼ cup) macadamia nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) grated parmesan, dairy or plant-based (or 125 ml, ½ cup, macadamias and no parmesan); 750 ml (3 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml extra-virgin olive oil; salt and pepper. Makes about 350 g. Blend in a food processor to the texture you like. Good on crackers or toast, as a side, or stirred through soup, pasta or rice.
recipes.title: Wild Whangaroa pesto

summary.text:
New Zealand's native pepper tree — a rongoā plant first and a flavouring second.
In New Zealand it is common from Te Paki south to about Ōkārito, North Canterbury and Banks Peninsula, and also grows on the Chatham Islands.

warnings: Kawakawa essential oil contains myristicin, a deliriant when consumed in high concentrations. Because of potential toxicity, be careful how much you drink as tea.

habitat.text:
On the Kermadec Islands it is the dominant canopy tree of Raoul Island, from the coastline to the highest peaks, and the main tree of both dry and wet forest.
It occurs from almost sea level to 516 m above sea level, ranging from the coastline to the highest altitudes of the islands. M. kermadecensis is commonly associated with Alsophila kermadecensis and Rhopalostylis baueri in the forests.
On the New Zealand mainland it is widely planted, especially in the North Island, and is sold in most garden centres. It sometimes comes up wild from planted trees: a herbarium specimen was collected from crevices in a boulder sea wall at New Plymouth.
In gardens it tolerates coastal exposure and prefers free-draining soil and sun. It is frost-tender, so young plants need shelter.

harvestEthics.text:
There is no reason to pick this plant. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text:
Tree up to 20 m tall in the wild (in cultivation to 10 m tall), with large canopies, often multi-trunked from base. Branches spreading, and often bearing aerial roots. Bark firm, grey to grey-brown. Branchlets very hairy, becoming hairless with age. Sometimes branches spreading and rooting where touching the ground.
Leaves arranged in opposite pairs, each pair being at right angles to the pair below, leathery, sub-orbicular, broadly ovate to elliptic-oblong, (20–)25–50 mm long, 10–20(–30) mm wide, upper surface dark green, paler below (mainly due to thick layer of grey-white hairs), leaf surface flat, not puckered, upper surface at first hairy, becoming hairless with age, lower surface mostly velvety, midrib raised, oil glands not readily visible on either surface; margins entire, but slightly rolled downwards (revolute), tips rounded or notched, leaf stalks ± 7–9 mm long, hairy.
Flowers in rounded terminal clusters, cluster-branchlets often 3-flowered, or flowers solitary on cluster axis. Flowers ± 6–8 mm in diam., mature flower stalks absent to ± 2 mm long, ± 1.5 mm wide, petals 5, crimson; sepals 5, tips free, persistent, stalks and base of flowers and outer surface of sepals all with long, copious hairs; stamens crimson (rarely pink), filaments 10–23 mm long, much longer than petals. Main flowering period: throughout the year.
Fruit dry, densely hairy, ± 5–8 mm wide, capsule dome raised above the calyx tube, calyx tube as wide as fruit, seeds released through open valves.
Of the New Zealand species M. kermadecensis is most similar to M. excelsa in that both have velvety lower leaf surfaces, but differs in that the former possesses smaller leaves and relative to its length, wider leaves (up to 50 mm long and up to 30 mm wide, as opposed to up to 120 mm long and up to 60 mm wide), and shorter stamens (filaments 10–23 mm long as opposed to 30–40 mm long).

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stamens, the long threads of the flower: pōhutukawa's are 30–40 mm long, Kermadec pōhutukawa's 10–23 mm, and its flowers are smaller (about 6–8 mm across against 8–12 mm). Pōhutukawa's leaves are larger, 25–100 mm long (sometimes to 120 mm) and 30–50 mm wide (sometimes 15 mm or up to 60 mm), elliptic to egg-shaped-oblong, with tips pointed rather abruptly or rounded but never notched; Kermadec pōhutukawa's are 25–50 mm long (sometimes 20 mm) and 10–20 mm wide (to 30 mm), almost round, broadly egg-shaped to elliptic-oblong, with rounded or notched tips. Leaves 25–50 mm long occur on both, and pōhutukawa on the Three Kings Islands has smaller leaves close to Kermadec pōhutukawa's, so go by the stamens. Kermadec pōhutukawa often has some flowers through the year but rarely flowers en masse; pōhutukawa flowers mainly in late spring and early summer, though from August to March at the extremes. On the mainland Kermadec pōhutukawa is a planted tree, mostly a slow-growing large shrub or compact tree, to 10 m in cultivation and rarely if ever a big tree; pōhutukawa grows to about 20 m. Both have leaves velvety with grey-white hairs beneath, crimson flowers and densely hairy capsules. Kermadec pōhutukawa is often sold mislabelled as pōhutukawa, and the two hybridise in cultivation. Pōhutukawa's flower nectar and stamens are used (see its page).

summary.text:
Metrosideros kermadecensis, commonly known as the Kermadec pōhutukawa, is a species of tree in the family Myrtaceae. It is endemic to the Kermadec Islands of New Zealand.
Endemic to the northern Kermadec Island group. However, widely cultivated in New Zealand (North Island especially), also in Australia and Norfolk Island. Widely planted in mainland New Zealand from, seemingly, a single clone. The clone is slow growing and forms large shrubs, or compact trees with time. Hybridises in cultivation with M. excelsa.
It is sold in most New Zealand garden centres, often mislabelled as pōhutukawa (Metrosideros excelsa). In 2017, it was reported that myrtle rust, an invasive species of fungus, was discovered growing on M. kermadecensis. It is assessed At Risk – Naturally Uncommon (2023), as an island endemic found at one location.
A variegated form, M. kermadecensis 'Variegata', is sold by New Zealand nurseries, sometimes under the name Metrosideros excelsa 'Variegata'.

warnings: No record of Kermadec pōhutukawa as food was found, so it is not given as food here.

It is often sold as pōhutukawa, and the two hybridise in cultivation, so a planted tree labelled pōhutukawa may be this species or a hybrid. Check the stamens and leaves before using the flowers (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
Woody but brittle perennial climber attached by roots to trunks of forest trees or in large masses on ground. Stems about 4 cm diameter, branched, marked with scars of old leaves. Leaves more or less tufted towards ends of stems, spirally arranged, to about 150 × 2–2.5 cm.; sheathing bases pale; tips long-attenuate, triangular in T.S.; margins, and midrib abaxially, minutely and distantly spinulose. Spadices simple and solitary in axils of several more or less foliaceous bracts at stem apex; bracts thick and succulent towards base, white to purplish. Peduncle 1–4 cm long, glabrous, whitish; spadix at flowering about 7 × 1.5 cm., cylindrical or slightly flattened, the axis quite hidden by tightly packed flowers. male of several stamens each with a long filament, ovate anther and cop. more or less confluent pollen surrounding a small rudimentary ovary; limits of individual flowers not easily determined. female with 6–12 purplish staminodes at base of flattened, vertically elongated ovary about 2–4 × 1 mm. × 2 mm tall, the long sides grooved between the staminodes; stigmas about 6–12, sessile, arranged around a long groove; locule narrow, placentae forming ridges projecting into it. Infructescence to about 15 × 3 cm on stiff woody peduncle. Individual frs (phalanges) about 8 × 2 × 10 mm., compressed laterally, thin-walled proximally, broadest about ⅓ from base and almost woody towards top. Seed about 1 mm long, narrow, on long, slender funicle.
[From: Moore and Edgar (1970) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 2.]

identification.text:
Rhizomes short-creeping, up to 100 m long (in herbarium material), bearing scales. Rhizome scales narrowly ovate, 5–21 mm long, 1–2 mm wide, chestnut-brown, concolorous or occasionally slightly bicolorous with paler margins. Fronds strongly dimorphic; fertile and sterile fronds with similar habit, arching upwards or outwards; sterile fronds 185–2780 mm; fertile fronds on same plant equalling or shorter than the sterile, 210–2250 mm long. Sterile fronds. Stipes 35–1150 mm long, sometimes black-brown at extreme base but mostly yellow-brown, bearing narrowly ovate chestnut-brown concolorous scales and bicolorous scales with a conspicuous dark spot around the point of attachment. Rachises yellow-brown, grooved adaxially, scaly. Laminae 150–2125 mm long, 65–740 mm wide, 1-pinnate, elliptic to obovate, with an undivided apical segment, bright green, similar colour on both surfaces, red-tinged when young, coriaceous; scales on abaxial pinna costae with a dark spot around the point of attachment, but becoming concolorous towards the pinna apices and on the distal pinnae. Pinnae in 7–53 pairs, closely spaced, narrowly oblong, straight or slightly falcate, markedly reduced to small, rounded lobes at the lamina base; the longest pinnae above the middle, 32–400 mm long, 9–30 mm wide, apices acuminate, margins shallowly crenate, bases auricled, short-stalked; the basal pinnae opposite. Veins free. Fertile fronds. Stipes 100–900 mm long. Laminae 135–1350 mm long, 65–280 mm wide. Pinnae in 8–45 pairs, linear, straight or curled basiscopically, 48–320 mm long, 2–6 mm wide; short, sterile, proximal flanges present on the middle pinnae; 2–9 pairs of pinnae at the base of the lamina replaced by short, rounded, sterile lobes. Sori and indusia in one row either side of costa, continuous along most of the length of the pinna except for the proximal sterile flanges.
Note: Measurements given above are from herbarium specimens. Larger fronds are known to occur in the wild. CHR 199087, from Moumoukai, South Auckland, comprises parts of a frond said to measure 3000 mm long.

edibleParts.text:
The fruit can be eaten by people and is a traditional food for Māori: the gum from the stem was also chewed. The seeds have a peppery taste.
Fruit. The reddish pulp surrounding the seeds is eaten. The orange, subglobose fruit is around 25 - 30mm in diameter. An edible gum is obtained from the stem.

identification.text:
Vigorous, dioecious, high-climbing vine, glabrous except for slightly hairy young stems. Leaves simple; petioles (0.8)–1–2 cm long, eglandular; stipules minute or 0; lamina (4)–5–12–(14) × (1.8)–2–4–(5.5) cm, lanceolate to narrow-ovate or elliptic, coriaceous, dark glossy green above, entire, acute to acuminate. Flowers (1)–3–4 in cymes, fragrant. Pedicels 5–15 mm long. Bracts more or less subulate, caducous. Hypanthium 0. Perianth 4-merous; segments 5–6 mm long, more or less oblong, yellowish green; corona threads 2.5–3.5 mm long. male flowers with 4 stamens; filaments 5–6 mm long forming a short androphore bearing an abortive ovary. female flowers with short staminodes. Ovary glabrous; styles (2)–3, about 2 mm long. Fruit (2)–2.5–3 cm diameter, subglobose or broad-ellipsoid, orange; pulp reddish, sparse. Seeds 3–7 mm long, flattened, wrinkled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia's leaves are undivided and leathery and its flowers under 2 cm across, while banana passionfruit (P. tripartita)'s leaves are 3-lobed. Kōhia is dioecious: only female plants bear fruit, and only after pollen reaches them from a male plant, so a vine without fruit can still be kōhia; use the leaves. Both are edible.

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube about 6–8 cm long (published figures run from up to 6 cm to 8 cm), with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and published lengths run from up to 9 cm to 14 cm. Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia's leaves are undivided and leathery and its flowers under 2 cm across, while banana passionfruit (P. tarminiana)'s leaves are 3-lobed. Kōhia is dioecious: only female plants bear fruit, and only after pollen reaches them from a male plant, so a vine without fruit can still be kōhia; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia's leaves are undivided and leathery and its flowers under 2 cm across, while black passionfruit's leaves are 3-lobed. A young black passionfruit's leaves are undivided too, so on a young plant go by texture: kōhia's are leathery, black passionfruit's thin. Kōhia is dioecious: only female plants bear fruit, and only after pollen reaches them from a male plant, so a vine without fruit can still be kōhia; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Black passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Pink-flowered passionfruit has downy young shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, grey- or white-felted underneath and dark shining green above; its stipules are pinnate, with dark thread-like segments almost to the base of a very narrow central strip; its flowers have a floral tube (4)–4.5–5 cm long, pink petals and violet-blue corona threads; its fruit is 4–7 cm across, round or slightly flattened, yellow and finely downy. Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia's leaves are undivided and leathery and its flowers under 2 cm across, while pink-flowered passionfruit's leaves are 3-lobed. Kōhia is dioecious: only female plants bear fruit, and only after pollen reaches them from a male plant, so a vine without fruit can still be kōhia; use the leaves. Both are edible.

Lookalike cards among the five Passiflora entries (written by the assistant on the owner's instruction (owner, 22/10/2026: /goal "find all you can about Passiflora and fill in following the rules")): each card restates the two species' descriptions and Flora of New Zealand's Passiflora key — Webb, C.J. et al. 1988, Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Flora of New Zealand Series, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/0e0cc34b-28b7-4b4a-8a94-9b059b1af976 — couplet 1 'Hypanthium cylindric and strongly elongated' against 'Hypanthium 0 or saucer-shaped and inconspicuous'; couplet 2 'Stipules pinnate with filiform segments; fr. ± globose' (pinnatistipula) against 'Stipules simple, ovate and toothed or subulate and entire; fr. ellipsoid'; couplet 3 '× rosea' 'Stipules with lanceolate rachis; stamens abnormal and ± petaloid'; couplet 6 'Lvs entire, coriaceous; perianth < 2 cm diam. when fresh' (tetrandra) against 'Lvs lobed, membranous or submembranous; perianth > 4 cm diam. when fresh'. Descriptions: Webb 1988 for P. edulis, P. pinnatistipula, P. tetrandra and P. mollissima (= P. tripartita var. mollissima; Flora of New Zealand Online files Webb's P. mollissima description under that name); for P. tarminiana, which Webb did not separate, Wikipedia 'Passiflora tarminiana' (revision 1352787405, CC BY-SA 4.0), NZPCN's P. tarminiana page (all rights reserved; facts restated) and Flora of New Zealand Online's weed profiles (CC BY 3.0 NZ: tube '6-7 cm' for P. tarminiana, '8-10 cm' and leaves 'moderately to densely hairy on the upper surface' for P. tripartita var. mollissima). The tarminiana–tripartita test follows Wikipedia's 'distinguished from P. tripartita var. mollissima' paragraph and NZPCN ('Can be distinguished from P. tarminiana by the large persistent stipules, and the long hypanthium'); var. azuayensis 'leaves glabrous to glabrate on upper surface' is NZPCN after Heenan & Sykes 2003; the hybrid is iNaturalist taxon 1645626, Passiflora tarminiana × tripartita (43 wild New Zealand records on 22/10/2026). Blue passionflower: NZPCN 'Most similar to P. caerulea in flower'; Webb 1988 'Lvs 5-lobed almost to base', 'pulp scanty and inedible'. × rosea: Webb's key and NZPCN's P. pinnatistipula page. Kōhia's fruit only on female plants: Wikipedia 'Passiflora tetrandra' (revision 1324332696). Risk `edible` every way, because every page carries a food record. Not carded: black passionfruit ↔ pink-flowered passionfruit — Webb gives black passionfruit 'N.: N. Auckland … Great Barrier Id; K.' and pink-flowered 'S.: Banks Peninsula (widespread), Otago (Palmerston)', so their wild ranges do not meet in the Flora. Blue passionflower, P. × rosea, P. mixta and P. antioquiensis have no entries (owner, 22/10/2026: blue passionflower 'Skip it').

summary.text:
Passiflora tetrandra (Māori: kōhia), also known as New Zealand passionflower, New Zealand passionfruit, or kohe, is a climbing vine found in New Zealand. Of the c. 500 species of passionflower, this is the sole species native to New Zealand.
It occurs throughout the North Island and in parts of the South Island as far south as Banks Peninsula.

identification.text:
Biennial, sometimes short-lived perennial. Stems branched above, (20)–40–60–(90) cm tall. Rosette leaves deeply lyrate-pinnatifid, sparsely hairy, especially on petiole and margins, or glabrous, (3)–7–25 × (1)–2–6 cm; terminal lobe ovate to oblong; lateral lobes in (4)–5–8 or more pairs, the distal pair usually wider than the terminal lobe; margins entire, sinuate, toothed or lobed. Upper stem leaves deeply pinnatifid with deflexed lobes at base; terminal lobe narrow-oblong or cuneiform, usually 3-lobed or 3-fid; lateral lobes in (1)–2 pairs, linear. Racemes to 30 cm tall; pedicels erecto-patent at fruiting, about 5 mm long. Sepals glabrous, 3–4 × 0.8–1.5 mm. Petals 6–8 × 2–3 mm. Silique erecto-patent, (30)–40–70 × 1.5–2.5 mm; style 1–1.5 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In plain terms: seeds usually germinate in autumn and form a rosette that stays green through winter. Its leaves are hairless or sparsely hairy, deeply divided into rounded lobes, and smell of mustard when crushed. The next season it sends up upright stems, branched above, with clusters of bright yellow four-petalled flowers, then long, thin pods angled upwards. In New Zealand it flowers and fruits mainly from October to December, sometimes from August and as late as May.

lookalikes.howToTell: Bog yellow cress has much smaller flowers: its yellow petals are only about as long as the sepals (1.5–2.5 mm), against 6–8 mm in land cress. Its pods are short and plump, 2–7 mm long, with the seeds in two rows; land cress's are long and narrow, 30–70 mm, with the seeds in one row. Both have yellow flowers and deeply lobed leaves with lobes at the base, and both can grow by rivers and streams, so colour, leaves and place do not separate them. Bog yellow cress's young leaves and stems are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Bog yellow cress

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping yellowcress has smaller flowers, with yellow petals 3–5 mm long against 6–8 mm in land cress. Its pods, when they form, are 10–15 mm long with the seeds in two rows; land cress's are 30–70 mm with the seeds in one row. Creeping yellowcress often sets no pods at all, and it spreads into patches by creeping underground parts, where land cress grows from a stout taproot. Both have yellow flowers and deeply lobed leaves, and both grow on riverbeds and cultivated or waste ground, so colour, leaves and place do not separate them. Creeping yellowcress has no reliable food record.
lookalikes.name: Creeping yellowcress

lookalikes.howToTell: Watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, and grows in streams, ditches and drains; land cress has yellow flowers on upright stems from a stout taproot, and grows on river banks, roadsides and waste land. Land cress's pods are 30–70 mm long; watercress's are 8–18 mm. Both have lobed leaves and a hot, cress-like taste, so taste does not separate them. Watercress is edible; cook it if it comes from water below grazing land.
lookalikes.name: Watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Some farmers wrongly call twin cress 'land cress', but the plants are easy to tell apart. Twin cress lies along the ground, smells foetid when crushed, has tiny white petals shorter than the sepals (or none) and tiny paired pods about 1.5 mm long. Land cress is an erect biennial (20–)40–60(–90) cm tall with yellow petals 6–8 mm long and long thin pods (30–)40–70 mm long. Twin cress leaves are eaten raw or cooked for their hot, cress-like taste; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Twin cress

lookalikes.howToTell: Narrow-fruited watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, and grows in streams, ditches and drains; land cress has yellow flowers on upright stems from a stout taproot, and grows on river banks, roadsides and waste land. Narrow-fruited watercress's pods are (10–)15–25(–30) mm long; land cress's are (30–)40–70 mm. Both have lobed leaves, so the leaves alone do not separate them. Narrow-fruited watercress is edible; cook it if it comes from water below grazing land.
lookalikes.name: Narrow-fruited watercress

preparation.text: Use the young leaves raw in salads and sandwiches, or cook them like spinach or in soups. The taste is strongly peppery, hotter than watercress, so raw it is usually mixed with milder leaves; the leaves are hotter in summer. As a potherb the leaves are parboiled, rinsed, then cooked until tender with fat and salt. The young flowering shoots are the hottest part; wilting them over very low heat for a short time softens their bite and bitterness. The leaves grow hotter and more bitter as the season goes on, and old leaves from a rosette that has overwintered can be fibrous and strong: pick the tender new leaves, and add stronger ones to milder cooked greens. Sautéing or steaming mellows them. Cook the young flowering stem like broccoli raab while it is still tender; once it toughens, use the yellow flowers to garnish salads and other dishes. Sprout the seeds for salads.

recipes.method: Serves 4. Ingredients: 1 medium onion, chopped; 340 g potatoes, peeled and chopped; 55 g butter; 100 g land cress; 850 ml vegetable or chicken stock; 280 ml milk; 100 ml double cream; salt and pepper. Sweat the onion and potato gently in the butter in a covered pan for 5 minutes. Add the land cress and cook 5 minutes more, then add the stock and simmer for about 20 minutes, until the potatoes are cooked. Add the milk and cream and blend, but only briefly: over-blending makes the potato gluey. Season to taste and serve with a few small leaves and a swirl of cream. The source advises against using watercress instead.
recipes.title: Land cress and potato soup

recipes.method: Written for creasy greens, the Appalachian name for land cress. Ingredients: half a pound (about 225 g) of chopped land cress leaves; half to 1 yellow onion, diced; 2–3 tablespoons (30–45 ml) of oil or fat (the author's grandmother used bacon fat); 2 tablespoons (30 ml) of pepper vinegar; salt. Rinse the leaves. Heat the fat in a frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion until caramelised. Add the leaves and sauté for a few minutes, until they darken and soften. Add a few splashes of pepper vinegar, cook 1 minute more, take off the heat and salt to taste.
recipes.title: Greasy creasies

recipes.method: Written for mixed wild greens; wintercress (land cress), wild turnip (field mustard) and purple dead nettle (red deadnettle) are the author's choices. Serves 5. Ingredients: half an onion; 4 cloves garlic; 4 cups (about 1 litre) washed, coarsely chopped wild greens; 2 cups (about 500 ml) raw, coarsely chopped chickweed tops; 120 ml extra virgin olive oil; 60 ml tahini; 125 ml freshly toasted whole pecans; 85 g feta; salt. (The source's list also names a further half cup, about 125 ml, of chickweed.) Sauté the onion and half the garlic in some of the olive oil until the onion begins to turn translucent. Add the greens and sauté until tender, then take off the heat and let cool. Put the chickweed, pecans, the rest of the oil, the tahini, the feta and the remaining garlic in a blender or food processor. Add the cooled greens a little at a time, blending between additions, until the pesto is coarsely ground; don't overload the blender. Add more oil for a creamier pesto, and salt to taste. For a milder pesto use more chickweed and fewer mustard greens. Serve as a dip, spread on flatbread or pizza, or toss through pasta or vegetables.
recipes.title: Wild greens, pecan and feta pesto

recipes.method: Written for creasy greens, naming both land cress and its relative Barbarea vulgaris. Ingredients: about 1.4 kg land cress, with stems; 4 litres water; 250 ml vinegar; 2 Tabasco peppers; 8 cloves garlic (the source says only '8 garlic'); 30 ml black pepper; 1 onion, quartered; 2 chunks smoked fatback. Strip the leaves from the stems and keep the stems. Wash the leaves in two changes of water, then put them in a pot with everything else. Bring quickly to the boil, then simmer slowly for two to four hours. Lift out the greens, strain the liquid and serve the greens. For the pot likker, put the stems into the strained liquid and cook a few hours more, adding more fatback and vinegar if you like. Take out the stems, cool the liquid and skim the fat from the top; use it as a base for soups and stews or drink it as a broth.
recipes.title: Creasy greens and pot likker

summary.text:
Barbarea verna is a biennial herb in the family Brassicaceae.
Common names include land cress, American cress, bank cress, black wood cress, Belle Isle cress, Bermuda cress, poor man's cabbage, early yellowrocket, early wintercress, scurvy cress, creasy greens, and upland cress. It is native to southern Europe and western Asia, and naturalized elsewhere It has been cultivated as a leaf vegetable in England since the 17th century.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) it is recorded from Northland, Auckland, Waikato, Rotorua, Taranaki, Wairarapa and Wellington, and from Nelson, Canterbury and Otago, naturalised by 1869 from southern, western and central Europe. It has also been called Barbarea praecox in New Zealand. Miller first named it Erysimum vernum in 1768; Ascherson moved it to Barbarea in 1860. Other New Zealand names are American cress and upland cress, and the NZ Plant Conservation Network lists it as winter cress. The genus is named after St Barbara, to whom wintercress was dedicated.
Te Papa holds a Wellington specimen, collector and date unknown, identified by Phil Garnock-Jones in 1979 (SP062053). Manaaki Whenua's herbarium has about 37 databased New Zealand records: Canterbury 8, Wellington 8, Nelson 5, Otago 2, one each from North Auckland and Westland, and 12 not placed in a region.

warnings: It can grow tangled with creeping buttercup, which is toxic: make sure every leaf you pick is land cress.

Avoid places that may have been sprayed or polluted, and pick at least 9 m from roads. Fields that look abandoned may still be sprayed, and some weedkillers take about a week to kill a plant, so sprayed greens can still look healthy.

habitat.text: A saprobic fungus, Morchella importuna fruit bodies grow in wood chips, gardens, fire pits, planters, and almost any disturbed ground in urban areas. Kuo suggests that it has mycorrhizal tendencies when grown in an environment with trees. Known primarily from northern California and the Pacific Northwest region of the United States, it has been reported from British Columbia (Canada), California, Washington, Nevada, and Oregon, although there have been a few isolated reports of the morel from the Midwestern United States and from eastern North America. Fruiting occurs in the spring, from March until May. Identified as phylogenetic species "Mel-10", Morchella importuna has also been found in Turkey and China, but it remains unclear whether dispersal between these distant locations occurred naturally or through accidental introduction by humans.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Morchella importuna' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The fruit bodies of M. importuna are 6–20 cm high. The cap is 3–15 cm high and measures 2–9 cm wide at its widest point. It is conical to widely conical or occasionally egg-shaped. Its surface has pits and ridges, with 12–20 primary vertical ridges and numerous transecting horizontal ridges, creating a laddered appearance. The cap is attached to stipe with a sinus about 2–5 mm both deep and wide. The ridges are smooth or finely velvety and colored pale to dark gray when young, becoming dark grayish brown to nearly black in age. They are bluntly rounded when young, but later become sharpened or eroded. Pits are vertically elongated in all stages of development. They have a smooth or finely velvety texture. The pits open and deepen with development, progressing from gray to dark gray when immature to grayish brown, grayish olive or brownish yellow at maturity. The stipe measures 3–10 cm high and 2–6 cm wide, and is often somewhat thicker near the base. Its whitish to pale brownish surface is smooth or finely mealy with whitish granules. It develops longitudinal ridges and grooves (particularly near the base) as the fruit body matures. The flesh is whitish to watery tan, measuring 1–3 mm thick in the hollow cap; in the stipe, this tissue is sometimes arranged as chambers or layers. The sterile inner surface of the cap is whitish and pubescent (covered with short soft "hair").

The ascospores are elliptical, smooth, and measure 18–24 by 10–13 μm. The cylindrical, hyaline (translucent), asci are eight-spored, measuring 220–300 by 12–25 μm. Paraphyses are septate, measuring 150–250 by 7–15 μm. They are cylindrical with variably shaped tips: rounded to roughly club-shaped, pointy, or fuse-shaped. Elements on the sterile ridges are septate and measure 25–300 by 10–30 μm. Terminal cells are cylindrical with a rounded tip that is variably shaped similar to the paraphyses. Both the paraphyses and the terminal cells are hyaline or brownish in dilute (2%) potassium hydroxide.
As a member of the Morchella elata group of black morels, M. importuna is sought after as a choice edible mushroom. Raw morels are poisonous and should always be cooked.


Similar species
The rare Pacific Northwest morel Morchella hotsonii, known only from its type collection, is quite similar in appearance to M. importuna. The former species is distinguished by its finely velvety surface.

habitat.text: Grassland, scrub and open forest. Montane and subalpine, on sites of low fertility, including tussockland; it grows in harsh conditions where there has been no grazing, oversowing or topdressing. It does not tolerate frost at the spring flush, dense shade or poor drainage, tolerates partial shade and is slightly intolerant of drought; it regrows after damage if some green foliage remains, and fire kills plants under 2 m. Planted, it needs light and well-drained soils, prefers natural shelter and slopes that shed cold air, and grows productively up to 900 m.

identification.text:
Small or medium-sized tree (large in cultivation), pyramidal when young, irregular in shape later. Branchlets more or less drooping. Bark grey, pinkish below, fissured and forming small plates. Long shoots yellow, glabrous, appearing ribbed because of elongated, pad-like persistent leaf bases. Short shoots stout, about 5 mm long, grey. Leaves on short shoots in fascicles of 40–65, 1.5–4 cm × about 0.5 mm at 1/2 way along leaf, grass-green, very soft; midrib raised on either side. Male and female strobili or cones surrounded by thin, brown bud scales with dense marginal tuft of curly brown hairs. Female cones about 1 cm long at anthesis; bract scales prominent, crimson, with subulate, green apical point. Mature cone 1.5–3.5 × 1.7–2.5 cm when open, broadly ovoid-oblong; ovuliferous scales 40–50, broad-ovate or suborbicular, not prominently recurved, vertically striated with outer margin rounded; bract scales usually concealed at maturity, sometimes a small part of subulate tip exposed. Seed with large, broad, asymmetric wing.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The leaves are needle-like, light green, 2–4 centimetres long which turn bright yellow before they fall in the autumn, leaving the pale yellow-buff shoots bare until the next spring.
Male cones are yellow and hang from the lower sides of the branchlets; female cones are crimson red and upright, maturing to brown.
Japanese larch is best distinguished from L. decidua by the greenish conelets and the recurved margins of the mature ovuliferous scales which give an almost rosetted appearance to the cone. Japanese larch also has less dense, more regular needle clusters.

preparation.text: Steep the young needles in hot water for tea, or make a cordial (see the recipe). Use them on the day you pick them, as their aroma fades quickly.

recipes.method: Written for European larch. The author makes it by his nettle cordial method, with young larch needles in place of the nettle. Equal parts water and white sugar (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar); at least a cupful (about 250 ml) of young larch needles, pressed down; a little citric acid or lemon juice, or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar. Pick the young needles in spring, while they are bright, almost luminous green and taste sharp, like sorrel. Make a syrup of equal parts water and white sugar (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar), heating gently and stirring until the sugar dissolves. Add at least a cupful (about 250 ml) of needles, pressed down, or more. Keep it on the heat until steaming hot, but don't let it boil. Strain out the needles. Stir in a little citric acid or lemon juice, or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar, until it tastes slightly sharp. It keeps for several weeks in the fridge.

summary.text:
European larch (Larix decidua) is a rather open-branching deciduous conifer in the pine family (Pinaceae), native to Europe and western Asia and widely planted in New Zealand.
The seeds are an important food for some birds, notably siskin, redpoll, and citril finch, while the buds and immature cones are eaten by capercaillie.
Larch needles (including L. decidua and L. sibirica) are the only known food for caterpillars of the case-bearer moth Coleophora sibiricella; its cone scales are used as food by the caterpillars of the tortrix moth Cydia illutana.
Larch canker is a major disease in Europe but is not present in New Zealand.
In New Zealand it is naturalised in the South Island in inland high country areas, especially the Amuri Range (North Canterbury) and Mackenzie County (South Canterbury); it was first recorded wild in 1919. Larch or European larch is mainly grown as a forest and plantation tree in colder parts of New Zealand, especially in the Rotorua area and the high country of the South Island. In the Mackenzie Basin it has become so extensively naturalised and aggressive that control measures have become necessary. It was introduced as an ornamental, is grown in parks and gardens, and has been planted on a small scale for timber, as farm shelter and to control erosion in the high country, where it tends to spread unless grazed. It is listed as an environmental weed, and regional pest management plans put it under progressive containment in Waikato, Bay of Plenty, Hawke's Bay, Wellington, Tasman-Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago and Southland, site-led control in Gisborne, and list it as an organism of interest on the Chatham Islands. The seed is spread by the wind, with 130,000–170,000 seeds per kilogram of cones, and stays viable for 3–5 years in dry storage; trees live more than 80 years. Hybrid larch, the cross between European and Japanese larch, is sterile and does not spread as wildings.

warnings: Larch bark taken by mouth, or larch oil spread over large areas of skin, may cause kidney damage. Allergies such as hives, rashes and contact dermatitis are possible.
Take extra care in pregnancy: many sources recommend against eating or drinking any conifer while pregnant.
Try only a little the first time: allergic reactions to conifers are not common, but are more likely than with most foods.
Do not pick from trees that may have been sprayed: wilding conifers are controlled with herbicide.

identification.text:
Suillus grevillei is a mushroom with a 5–10 cm cap colored from citrus yellow to burnt orange, that is at first hemispherical, then bell-shaped, and finally flattened. It has a sticky skin, often with veil remnants on the edge, short tubes of yellow (possibly staining brownish) which descend down to the bottom of its cylindrical stalk (6–10 x 1–2 cm), which is yellowish above the ring area with streaks of reddish brown below. The flesh is yellow, staining brown.
Taste mild to slightly astringent to bitterish; odor none to somewhat metallic.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to 5–(10) m. tall; branches and branchlets stout, glabrous. Leaves on stout petioles about 12–25 mm long. Stipules connate into broad membranous sheath tipped by long sharp denticle. Lamina subcoriaceous, broad- to elliptic-ovate, obtuse or subacute to mucronulate, about 9–13 × 4–8 cm. Midrib prominent, secondary veins and reticulations evident. male in compound glomerules on axillary peduncles 10–15 mm long; calyx-teeth minute; corolla about 9 mm long, subcampanulate, lobes ovate-triangular, acute, shorter than tube. female 2–5 together, on simple or branched peduncles 20–70 mm long; calyx-teeth acute; corolla tubular, widening above, lobes acute, shorter than tube. Drupe orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Leaf width and fruit length separate them: karamū's leaves about 35–42 mm wide with fruit 8–9 mm long; large-seeded coprosma's about 40–80 mm wide with fruit 10–25 mm long. Widths meet at about 40 mm, so take both tests together. Those tests fit only the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa: the North Island's wild subsp. minor has leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long, so neither test separates it from karamū. Karamū's leaf margin is minutely toothed; subsp. minor's is not. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; large-seeded coprosma's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Māmāngi's young twigs are hairy; large-seeded coprosma's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Mingimingi's young twigs are more or less hairy; large-seeded coprosma's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

identification.text:
Large, narrow-pyramidal tree; branches usually present to near ground and more or less drooping towards the apex. Bark thick, fibrous, reddish brown, fissured. Branchlets in horizontal sprays, green or, less commonly more or less glaucous (mostly glaucous in cultivation), aromatic when bruised. Sapling quickly passing into adult condition. Scale leaves appressed; facial pairs on lateral shoot systems (excluding 1–3 year terminal brown shoots) mostly 1–2 mm long, broad-ovate, subacute, with gland on back elongated and appearing as a translucent dot in transmitted light; lateral pairs similar but mostly 1.5–2.5 mm long, with whitish stomatal lines on lower side more or less evident when fresh. male strobili 2–5 mm long; pollen sacs deep pink to crimson. female cones blue when young, brownish with bluish bloom and 6–9 mm diameter when mature; scales 8; umbo a small ridge. Seeds 2–4 on each scale, with conspicuous resin tubercles; wing narrower than or equal to to seed.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The combination of acute scale leaves with translucent glands, obviously larger lateral than facial leaves, and bright crimson male cones, distinguishes C. lawsoniana from C. obtusa and C. pisifera, which are cultivated abundantly in New Zealand, in the adult stage.
It can reach 50 m. Cypresses (Cupressus) look similar but do not have its flattened branchlet sprays; Thuja has flattened sprays too, but its cones of both sexes are quite different. Of the several Chamaecyparis species grown in New Zealand, Lawson's cypress is the one with brightly coloured male cones.

summary.text:
Lawson's cypress, also called Port Orford cedar, is a conifer in the cypress family (Cupressaceae), brought to New Zealand as an ornamental.
The species is native to southwestern Oregon and northwestern California, and grows from sea level up to 1,500 metres in the valleys of the Klamath Mountains, often along streams. It fares best at the north end of its range.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1940. Lawson's cypress is a very common cultivated garden, park, domain and windbreak tree. There are a number of cultivars grown in New Zealand, mainly differing in habit and foliage colour, but spontaneous plants usually have green foliage and the typical narrow-pyramidal habit.
It spreads by seed: a female cone holds up to 32 seeds, and a mature tree may carry as many as 10,000 cones. It was on the Department of Conservation's 2008 consolidated list of environmental weeds but is not on the 2024 list.
North Island; South Island: scattered localities throughout, especially cooler areas with a moderate to high rainfall.

warnings: Lawson's cypress has been queried as a cause of abortion in cattle, like macrocarpa, but there is little hard evidence for it.
Cypresses are more likely than needled conifers to cause allergic reactions, including skin rashes.

habitat.text:
Lawns and other open turf, typically dry and poor but also wet or rich ground, and urban areas; also disturbed or regenerating native vegetation, often on track edges, rarely in dense forest. Coast to subalpine (to 1100 m), mostly lowland.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Open rocky slopes, rock crevices, stony ground, old screes, short turf, poor or open pastures and tussockland, open scrub, cliff faces, river beds, beaches, waste places, lawns, plantations, cultivated ground, common to abundant, sea level to c. 1500 m.

identification.text:
Perennial; primary root slender to stout, occasionally to about 10 mm thick. Stems glabrous to densely hairy (hairs usually antrorse, occasionally dense and patent), more or less filiform, creeping, prostrate or nearly so, rooting at nodes, much-branched and often mat-forming. Leaves 3-foliolate. Petiole 5–40 mm long, with patent or antrorse hairs, these sparse to dense; stipules adnate, truncate or rounded at apex. Petiolules very short. Lamina of leaflets equal, 1–9 × 1.5–12 mm, obcordate, sometimes broadly so, with width greater than length, with narrow to broad sinus and rounded lobes, glabrous or hairy above, glabrate or with appressed hairs beneath, ciliate or eciliate, often purplish below; calli 0. Flowers solitary, rarely paired; peduncle glabrate to densely clothed in antrorse hairs, generally geniculate at apex; pedicel (4)–8–25 mm long. Bracts 1–3 mm long, more or less linear-subulate, hairy, situated at base or at middle of pedicels; calli 0. Sepals 2.3–3.5–(4) mm long, oblong-lanceolate, oblong, or ovate-elliptic, glabrate or with antrorse hairs; calli 0. Petals 4.5–9–(13) mm long, more or less oblong-obovate, yellow, often pink-flushed outside, glabrous. Stamens at 2 levels, glabrous or nearly so; filaments united at base, those of longer whorl about 1.5 mm long. Styles shorter than or longer than longer stamens, densely hairy. Capsule (3)–7–10–(13) mm long excluding styles, broadly cylindric, cylindric-ovoid or conic, glabrous to densely hairy; hairs short, patent or retrorse, sometimes glandular. Seed 1–1.3–(1.5) mm long, broad-ellipsoid; transverse ridges 7–13, subacute, sometimes white-topped; grooves deep. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Least yellow sorrel creeps: its stems are more or less thread-like, prostrate or nearly so, root at the nodes and often form mats. Bermuda buttercup appears stemless, with its leaves all rising from the base on stalks 6–22 cm long, and grows from a bulb with underground runners that bear many small bulbils. Measure a leaflet and a petal, remembering the ranges almost meet: least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long and its petals 4.5–9 mm (up to 13 mm); Bermuda buttercup's leaflets are 10–32 mm long and its golden petals 2–2.8 cm (from 1.5 cm). Least yellow sorrel's flowers are solitary, rarely paired, and it sets a capsule 7–10 mm long (3–13 mm at the extremes); Bermuda buttercup usually carries 3–18 flowers (occasionally 1) hanging on a stalk 15–45 cm long (from 7 cm), and no capsule has been seen on it in New Zealand. Yellow flowers, notched leaflets and purple in the leaf do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Bermuda buttercup

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping wood sorrel looks like a larger least yellow sorrel, with much the same leaves, creeping stems and yellow flowers, so size and flower count are the tests, and size changes with growing conditions. Creeping wood sorrel's leaflets are 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm) and up to 23 mm wide, and its leaves are normally about 20 mm across; least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long and its leaves typically under 10 mm across. Count the flowers on a stalk: creeping wood sorrel carries 1 to 5, usually at least two; least yellow sorrel's are solitary, rarely paired. Creeping wood sorrel's capsule is mostly 10–18 mm long, least yellow sorrel's mostly 7–10 mm, though the ranges meet. Creeping wood sorrel is more often in garden beds and nurseries, least yellow sorrel in lawns. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. White clover's leaflets are 5–25 mm long, least yellow sorrel's 1–9 mm long. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves or stems: both creep and root at the nodes, both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually stalkless on the leaves beneath it, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Red clover's hairy stems stand erect or lie along the ground at the base and do not root at the nodes; least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats. Red clover's leaflets are 15–40 mm long, least yellow sorrel's 1–9 mm long. Out of flower, leaflet size is a guide, as the published ranges do not meet. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Alsike clover's hairless stems stand erect or rise from the base and do not root at the nodes; least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats. Alsike clover's leaflets are 10–35 mm long, least yellow sorrel's 1–9 mm long. Out of flower, leaflet size is a guide, as the published ranges do not meet. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have small yellow flowers and three small leaflets that are often notched at the tip, and both grow in lawns. Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long. Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Suckling clover's stems lie along the ground or rise a little and do not root at the nodes; least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats. On most suckling clover leaves the middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the side ones (under 1 mm); least yellow sorrel's three leaflets are equal, on very short stalks. Leaflet size does not separate them: suckling clover's are about 3–12 mm long, least yellow sorrel's 1–9 mm. Season does not either: suckling clover is an annual that flowers from October to June, and least yellow sorrel flowers in every month. Suckling clover has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Suckling clover

preparation.text: Add the leaves to salads, cook them as a pot herb with milder greens, or use them to give a sour taste to other food. The flowers can be eaten raw in salads. The leaves are very small and fiddly to pick.

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) lemon juice and 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) maple syrup or honey. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the sorrel and stir for 1–2 minutes, until it wilts. Put it in a blender or food processor with the lemon juice and the syrup or honey and blend until well combined. Serve it straight away, or refrigerate it and warm it before use; the author finds it even better the next day. The author serves it on fish, or as a dipping sauce for grilled prawns.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel sauce

recipes.method: About 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, stems or flowers, or a mix, about 250 ml (1 cup) water, and maple syrup or another sweetener to taste. The amounts are rough: use as much sorrel as you like and enough water to cover it. Blend the sorrel and water until well combined, strain through a fine sieve and sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel 'lemonade'

recipes.method: Equal parts wood sorrel, sugar, and water; the author usually uses 250 ml (1 cup) of each. Put everything in a saucepan and bring it to a simmer, stirring. Simmer for 15–30 minutes, strain through muslin (cheesecloth) and pour into sterilised bottles. The author uses it in tea, topped up with soda water, over ice cream or fresh strawberries, or in vinaigrettes and marinades.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel syrup

recipes.method: The recipe uses one part leaves to three parts water. Fresh wood sorrel leaves; boiling water; sweetener to taste (optional). Put the leaves in a container, pour the boiling water over them and leave to steep for 5–15 minutes. Strain out the leaves and sweeten to taste if you like. Drink it hot, or pour it over ice for an iced tea.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel tea

recipes.method: 2 cloves garlic, minced; olive oil for cooking; 2 spring onions, chopped; 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock; 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish; 3 medium mint leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk; salt and pepper. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks. Heat a little olive oil in a small saucepan and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the spring onions. Cover with the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, then add the sorrel for about 30 seconds. Take it off the heat, add the mint and blend smooth with a stick blender (or an ordinary blender). Stir in the coconut milk and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until well chilled, a couple of hours, and serve garnished with the sorrel flowers.
recipes.title: Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

recipes.method: About 450 g (1 lb) Italian or breakfast sausage; 1 medium spaghetti squash; several cups of wood sorrel, washed and drained, stems removed (the recipe gives no closer amount); olive oil; 1 red onion, halved and sliced; 1 egg; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk or any milk; 1 garlic clove, minced; 15 ml (1 tbsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) tarragon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) black pepper; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground sage. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Halve the squash, spoon out the seeds and stringy threads, set the halves cut side up on a baking tray, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and bake for 20–25 minutes, until the flesh gives a little when pressed. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts. Take the squash out of the oven and scrape out the flesh with a fork (careful, it will be hot). Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.
recipes.title: Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel

recipes.method: Two handfuls of wood sorrel, chopped; potato and kūmara, boiled first and sliced; cream. Layer the sorrel with the sliced potato and kūmara in a baking dish, pour cream over the top and bake at 180 °C until it starts to brown.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel, kūmara and potato gratin

recipes.method: Chop a big handful of wood sorrel leaves, stalks and flowers and mix them through a potato salad dressed with a cream dressing.
recipes.title: Potato salad with wood sorrel

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: The author's greens were puha, sow thistle, nasturtium, onion weed, wild fennel, oxalis, wild mustard and wild celery; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 1 diced onion; 1 potato, scrubbed and diced; 2 sliced garlic cloves; 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 1.3 litres water; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked pepper; extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil, to serve; edible weed flowers. Serves 4. Cut the vegetables and greens to similar sizes. Fry the onion in the oil for a minute, then add the potato and garlic (the method also adds fennel bulb and celery stalks, which the ingredient list leaves out) and fry for another minute. Add the water, cover, bring to the boil and simmer until the potato is soft. Add the greens with the salt and yeast and cook for 3 minutes, until just tender — added at the end, they keep their colour. Blend until smooth (push it through a sieve if your blender isn't powerful), season with the pepper and more salt if needed, and serve drizzled with extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil and scattered with edible weed flowers.
recipes.title: Wild greens soup
