Recipes copied 16/10/2026 from creeping-wood-sorrel (owner: "yeah copy the recepies to the sorrels", after "the recipies are interchangeble betwwen sorrel species"). None is written for Oxalis exilis: seven are written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally, and the gratin and potato salad for Oxalis incarnata. This page records no edible parts of its own; the recipes rest on the owner's word that wood sorrel recipes are interchangeable. Provenance as recorded on creeping-wood-sorrel: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (cups at 250 ml, 1 tbsp = 15 ml, 1 tsp = 5 ml; every page all rights reserved; retrieved 15/10/2026; supplied by the owner). None is written for this species: each is written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally. The sauce, 'lemonade' and syrup from Kate MacQuarrie, 'Wood Sorrel Recipes', PEI Untamed, 09/07/2023 (https://www.pei-untamed.com/post/wood-sorrel-recipes) — written for 'the Wood Sorrels' of Prince Edward Island, no species named; 'grilled shrimp' given as prawns; the lemonade's 'leaves, stems, and/or flowers' and its note that the author does not measure are kept. 'Wood sorrel cooler' is Sunny Savage's 'Oxalis Cooler' as given in Green Deane, 'Oxalis: How To Drown Your Sorrels', Eat The Weeds (dated 16/01/2018 on the page, with reader comments from 2012; https://www.eattheweeds.com/oxalis-how-to-drown-your-sorrels/; the owner's second link, https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/oxalis-deppei/, is a tag page showing the same article) — written for Oxalis generally, the article naming the Florida species including O. corniculata; 1 US quart is about 946 ml; the recipe does not strain the drink and neither does this. 'Wood sorrel tea' from Jesse, 'Wood Sorrel: Identification, Uses, and Precautions', Feral Foraging, 11/07/2024 (https://feralforaging.com/wood-sorrel/) — written mainly for O. stricta and O. violacea; the page gives the ratio only as '1:3' after 'Gather wood sorrel leaves' and 'Pour over boiling water', without saying by volume or by weight, so 'one part leaves to three parts water' is this guide's reading. 'Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup' from Valerie Zemba, 'Chilled Lemony Wood Sorrel Soup', Very Vegan Val, 03/07/2019 (https://veryveganval.com/chilled-lemony-wood-sorrel-soup/) — written for 'Oxalis stricta and others'; scallions given as spring onions, vegetable broth as stock; the rinsing and stripping step is from the page's prose above the recipe card. 'Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel' from Chosen Weeds Farm, 'Cooking With Wood Sorrel', 15/03/2017 (https://thechosenweeds.com/cooking-with-wood-sorrel/) — written for the purple-leaf wood sorrel that grows in the author's south-east Texas garden; 400 °F given as 200 °C, 1 lb as about 450 g; 'Several cups' of sorrel kept because the page gives no closer amount; the page says only 'Combine mixture with the egg' after forking out the squash, and the method keeps that wording rather than saying where the squash goes. Not used from the recipe pages (15/10/2026): the casserole page's 'If you are short on time you can skip the oven step', because skipping the final bake would leave the stirred-in egg uncooked; Feral Foraging's statements that all species of wood sorrel are edible and can be used in similar ways (genus-level claims), its estimate that about 30 g a day, several times a week, is safe and its view that oxalate warnings are overblown (it contradicts every other page read here and is not a trusted source for a safety amount), and its cold-infusion and dried-leaf variants; Green Deane's statements that cooking reportedly renders oxalic acid harmless, particularly with calcium, that eating a lot raw can leach calcium from the bones, and that the juice curdles milk for cheese, and that all parts including the root bulb are edible (said of the Florida species as a group); the casserole page's medicinal and vitamin claims; the reader comment on Eat The Weeds suggesting more sorrel for a sharper cooler. Two of the owner's links have no recipe: Rachel Lambert, 'Wild Food: Wood Sorrel family', Wild Walks Southwest, 07/05/2021 (https://wildwalks-southwest.co.uk/wild-food-wood-sorrel-family/), and Diego Bonetto, 'How to identify and eat wood Sorrel', 10/08/2021 (https://www.diegobonetto.com/blog/wood-sorrel-id-forage-edible-weed) — both name O. corniculata among the species they describe. Lambert says all of them have a lemony, tart flavour and uses them in salads, in soups and as an edible decoration; Bonetto says the stalks, flowers and leaves are eaten raw or cooked, in salads and as a garnish; recorded here for edibleParts and preparation, which were empty on creeping-wood-sorrel when this was written (15/10/2026). The post was first written as O. acetosella; a commenter (AJB, 26/11/2009) identified the plant pictured as 'the South African Ox. incarnata', which the author accepted, and the title now names O. incarnata. The blog covers Wellington and the Wairarapa; the post does not say where the plant grew. Not used as recipes: adding it to apple, peach or pear pie and a jelly (suggestions, not made by the author); its use to curdle milk for cheese (the author had not got it to work).

summary.text: Oxalis exilis, the least yellow sorrel or shady woodsorrel, is a small herbaceous plant found in Australia and New Zealand.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

edibleParts.text:
Fruit - raw or cooked. A pleasant acid flavour, it is nice when added to muesli or porridge. Unfortunately, there is relatively little flesh and a lot of seeds.
Berberis bealei has berries that are used in pies, jellies, jams, beverages and confections. The yellow flowers are eaten or used to make a lemonade-like drink.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand: native and exotic forest, forest margins and shrubland, most likely near gardens or historic sites (Environment Canterbury, for the four mahonias growing wild here); recorded growing wild in the Christchurch Botanic Gardens.
In the south-eastern United States, where it is naturalised: open woodlands and shrublands, 100–500 m (Flora of North America).
In its native range: Forests, forest margins, weedy slopes, streamsides, roadsides and thickets; at elevations from 500 - 2,000 metres.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Berberis bealei' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Berberis bealei is a multi-stemmed, evergreen shrub or small tree with irregular, strong upright stems that have limited branching. It grows up to 8 metres tall, is upright, and is scarcely branching. The leaves are up to 50 centimetres long, with 4–10 pairs of leaflets, plus a much larger terminal leaflet. The sessile leaflets have spines and the terminal leaflets are larger than others.
The flowers are borne in an erect raceme up to 30 cm long. The berries are blue or dark purple colored egg-shaped berries, up to 15 millimetres long, that turn bluish black with a grayish bloom. Fruits hang in grapelike clusters and are glaucous, covered with a white waxy coating. The erect stems are stiff and unbranched.

lookalikes.howToTell: Leatherleaf mahonia's leaves are up to about 50 cm long with 4–10 pairs of leaflets and a much larger terminal one; Oregon grape's are up to about 25 cm with 3–7 pairs. Leatherleaf mahonia's flower clusters stand upright, 7–26 cm long; Oregon grape's reach 6–7 cm. Its berries are egg-shaped and up to 15 mm long; Oregon grape's round, about 10 mm across. Leatherleaf mahonia has stiff upright stems and can reach 8 m; Oregon grape is a low, many-stemmed, suckering shrub, usually about 1 m. Leaflet counts overlap at 4–7 pairs, and dark bloomed berries and spiny leaflets do not separate them. Leatherleaf mahonia's berries are also described as globose, so shape alone does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Oregon grape

lookalikes.howToTell: Leatherleaf mahonia's flower clusters stand upright, 7–26 cm long; Japanese mahonia's are lax and spreading. Leatherleaf mahonia's leaflets are wider, 2–6 cm, against Japanese mahonia's 2–3.5 cm, so only a wide leaflet tells. Leatherleaf mahonia's berries reach 15 mm long; Japanese mahonia's are 8–10 mm. Leaflet counts (4–10 pairs against 5–9), a small lowest pair, spiny teeth and blue-black bloomed berries do not separate them, and leatherleaf mahonia has been listed as a form of B. japonica ('Bealei'). The two have hybridised in gardens and many plants raised from seed are hybrids, so intermediate plants seem to be fairly common in gardens. Plants grown under the name leatherleaf mahonia in the United States are also described with loose, spreading to hanging flower clusters and narrow leaflets, so on a planted or escaped shrub neither trait settles it.
lookalikes.name: Japanese mahonia

lookalikes.howToTell: Leatherleaf mahonia's leaves carry 4–10 pairs of broad leaflets, roundish to ovate and 2–6 cm wide; mountain grape's carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped ones, 1–2.5 cm wide. Leatherleaf mahonia's berries are up to 15 mm long; mountain grape's up to 8 mm. Upright flower clusters, a tall habit and dark blue bloomed berries do not separate them, and the garden hybrid 'Arthur Menzies' has both as parents.

preparation.text: The berries can be eaten raw but the seed to pulp ratio is large so most of these berries are boiled and strained.

recipes.method: Written for the berries of Japanese and leatherleaf mahonia. Base: 375 ml flour, 440 ml rolled oats, 125 ml chopped walnuts, 250 ml packed dark brown or coconut sugar, 1 tsp baking powder, ½ tsp fine salt, 1 tsp vanilla and 250 ml melted butter. Topping: 625 ml mahonia berries, 250 ml sugar, 2 tsp grated orange or lemon zest and two lavender buds. Heat the oven to 180°C and line a 20–23 cm tin with baking paper, leaving it overhanging the sides. Stir the dry ingredients together, then work in the melted butter until crumbly. Press three-quarters of it firmly into the tin and bake for 10 minutes. Cook the berries with the sugar, zest and lavender over low heat for 15 minutes, until they pop open; cool for 5 minutes and take out the lavender. Pour over the base, scatter the rest of the crumble on top and bake for 30–40 minutes, until golden. Cool completely in the tin, lift out by the paper and cut into 12 large bars or 24 squares.

summary.text:
Berberis bealei, also known as leatherleaf mahonia, Beale's barberry, is a species of evergreen shrub native to mainland China. The species has been regarded as the same species as Berberis japonica, native to Taiwan, but the two differ consistently in certain floral and leaf characters. Both species are widely cultivated in many countries as ornamentals.
Berberis bealei is one of approximately 70 species that were once classified in genus Mahonia. Thus, older sources refer to this species as Mahonia bealei or M. Japonica.
In New Zealand: Flora of New Zealand Online and NZPCN list it as exotic, as Berberis bealei with the synonym Mahonia bealei; neither describes it.
Biota of New Zealand records it as a casual exotic (growing wild but not naturalised), after Heenan, de Lange et al. (2004). In the south-eastern United States it has escaped gardens and naturalised, and North Carolina lists it as invasive; it spreads by seed and by suckers, which can form a colony, and birds eat the fruit.

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.
The berries contain berberine, which can upset the stomach, especially in children. Eating the poisonous parts (bark, leaves, roots and sap) can cause stomach upset, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous, lemon-scented herb with branched puberulent stems ascending to about 60 cm. Leaves and bracts petiolate. Lamina 2–8.5 × 1–7 cm, elliptic to broad-ovate, hairy, sometimes only sparsely hairy above, prominently crenate-serrate; base more or less truncate in larger lower leaves, cuneate in upper smaller leaves and bracts. Verticels generally 3–10-flowered. Calyx about 8 mm long; nerves prominent, with long, white, pilose hairs; upper teeth broad-triangular, aristate; lower narrow-triangular, aristate. Corolla 12–15 mm long, white (sometimes tinged pink); lobes hairy outside. Nutlets 1.7–2 mm long, almost black.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Crushed leaves smell strongly of lemon. The mints share its square stems but smell of mint.
Large bushy plants lacking the characteristic lemon scent were found in the Kauaeranga Valley, Thames district. They are not foetid, although the mint-like scent is quite different to the ordinary lemon balm.

lookalikes.howToTell: Lemon balm and spearmint both have square stems and opposite leaves, and both are aromatic. Spearmint's flowers are in narrow spikes at the stem tips, the central spike 4–12 cm long. Its calyx is 1.5–2.2(–3.5) mm long and nearly regular, and its mauve or pinkish corolla is 3–5 mm long with 4–5 nearly equal lobes. Lemon balm's flowers are in whorls of generally 3–10 among stalked, leaf-like bracts. Its calyx is about 8 mm long, with prominent nerves, long white hairs and unequal teeth, and its corolla is 12–15 mm long, clearly two-lipped, with a curved tube. Spearmint's leaves are stalkless or very shortly stalked; lemon balm's leaves are stalked. Crushed lemon balm leaves usually smell strongly of lemon, and spearmint has a strong spearmint smell. But lemon balm plants without the lemon scent, smelling of mint, have been found in New Zealand, so smell is a clue, not a test. The flower tests are the surest. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Wild spearmint

preparation.text: Use the leaves mainly as a flavouring: in salads and cooked foods, fish dishes, pesto and ice cream. A lemon-flavoured tea is made from the fresh or dried leaves. The flavour is delicate and fades fast, and does not stand up to strong flavours: add the leaves at the last minute, even to cooked dishes. Use them in place of mint; in green, fruit, cucumber, potato and chicken salads; chopped into soups and stews; or stirred into scone and muffin dough with a pinch of lemon zest. To scatter over food, tear the leaves by hand: chopped, they soon taste of grass clippings. The fresh leaves bruise and brown easily, and tender leaves turn black when cooked, so for a jam infuse them in the sugar instead. They go well in black or green tea, and can be frozen in ice cubes for summer drinks; cover tea while it brews to keep in the aromatic oils. The leaves are best freshly picked, but dry well if dried gently, as heat and light take their aroma: spread stems and leaves in a single layer with good airflow, out of the light, at about 25 °C for the first day and no more than 35 °C after that, and strip the leaves once they are crisp. Plants cut back hard after flowering put up a fresh flush of leaves.

recipes.method: Tender lemon balm leaves; equal parts sugar and water; lemon juice, citric acid or the lemon balm vinegar below. Use the tender leaves. For a syrup, infuse them into a syrup of equal parts sugar and water by heating gently, without boiling. Cool, and keep in sterilised jars in the fridge for a couple of weeks. Pour it over puddings or use it in cocktails. For a cordial, sharpen the syrup to taste with lemon juice, citric acid or the lemon balm vinegar below; it keeps better and gains a pleasing sharpness. Dilute to drink, or use it for a gimlet.
recipes.title: Lemon balm syrup and cordial

recipes.method: Tender lemon balm leaves; cold apple cider vinegar; lemon balm syrup or cordial, or honey. Use the tender leaves. Infuse them straight into cold apple cider vinegar for a week, then strain. Use it in salad dressings or as a pickling liquor. Mix the vinegar with lemon balm syrup or cordial for a shrub, or with honey for an oxymel, to give cocktails a gentle acidity.
recipes.title: Lemon balm vinegar and shrub

recipes.method: Tender lemon balm leaves; vodka; lemon balm cordial, syrup or shrub. Use the tender leaves. Infuse them in vodka for no more than 3 days, strain, and sweeten to taste with lemon balm cordial, syrup or shrub.
recipes.title: Lemon balm liqueur

recipes.method: The author's elderflower champagne with lemon balm leaves in place of the elderflowers, or added to them. He gives no amount for the leaves. 650 g sugar; 4.5 litres of cold water; lemon balm leaves, or elderflowers and lemon balm leaves; the juice and quartered skin of 1 lemon; 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar. Dissolve 650 g sugar in 4.5 litres of cold water — warm a little of the water to dissolve the sugar, cool it, then mix it into the rest. In a large bucket or bowl, combine the sweetened water with the flowers or leaves, the juice and quartered skin of 1 lemon, and 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar. Cover and leave for 4 days, somewhere cool; if mould forms, scrape off the mat of flowers on top and carry on. Fine-strain into clean screw-top plastic fizzy-drink bottles, leaving a few centimetres of air at the top. Never use corked bottles, and avoid glass flip-tops: you can't feel the pressure through them, and they are far more dangerous if they burst. Leave at room temperature for 6–14 days. From day 6, check the bottles regularly by squeezing them, and as soon as the bases start to round out, ease the caps to let off some (not all) of the pressure — a forgotten bottle can explode. Once it tastes right, move it to the fridge to slow the fermentation, and keep checking the pressure. The author drinks it between 2 and 4 weeks: it is lightly alcoholic after a week and starts turning vinegary at 5–6 weeks. The recipe's yeast comes from the flowers, so in a cool room it can take a while to get going.
recipes.title: Lemon balm champagne

recipes.method: Lemon balm leaves; wood sorrel (oxalis) leaves; a little sugar; crab-apple verjuice; cracked ice; gin; soda. Muddle lemon balm and wood sorrel (oxalis) leaves with a little sugar and crab-apple verjuice. Add cracked ice, then gin and soda to taste.
recipes.title: Wild mojinto

recipes.method: Lemon balm; 70 ml gin; 35 ml elderflower limoncello; 35 ml dry vermouth; 15 ml pineapple weed shrub (pineapple weed vinegar mixed with syrup); a splash of lemon balm champagne; lemon balm and elderflowers, to garnish. Muddle lemon balm in a glass with 70 ml gin, 35 ml elderflower limoncello, 35 ml dry vermouth and 15 ml pineapple weed shrub (pineapple weed vinegar mixed with syrup). Top up with a splash of lemon balm champagne, to taste. Garnish with lemon balm and elderflowers placed so that you smell them as you drink.
recipes.title: The Elderbalm

recipes.method: Written for green or purple amaranth (Amaranthus viridis or A. lividus), with galinsoga, dandelion and lemon balm. A bunch of amaranth; several stems of galinsoga; 2 or more dandelion leaves; 2 beetroot leaves; a small bunch of lemon balm; 375–500 ml (1½–2 cups) water; 1 banana; 1 kiwifruit; 1 peeled tangelo; 250 ml (1 cup) blueberries; 15 ml (1 tbsp) chia and a sprinkle of pumpkin seeds, ground in a coffee grinder with 2 cardamom pods or 2 star anise. Blend the greens in the water until well broken down, then add the fruit and the ground seeds and spice and blend again. Drop a few whole blueberries into the glass to chew on.
recipes.title: Blueberry amaranth smoothie

recipes.method: Fresh lemon balm leaves, or 1–2 tsp dried leaves per 250 ml water; simmering water; sugar or honey, to taste. Fill a jar with fresh leaves, or put the dried leaves in a cup. Pour on simmering water and cover the top straight away with a saucer, so that the aromatic oils stay in the tea. Leave it to steep until it is cool enough to drink, then sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Lemon balm tea

recipes.method: Fresh lemon balm leaves; 1 lemon, thinly sliced; cold water. Fill a jar with the leaves and the lemon slices, top it up with cold water and refrigerate for several hours before drinking.
recipes.title: Lemon balm water

recipes.method: 1 egg white; a little water; lemon balm leaves; sugar. Beat the egg white with a very little water. Dip each leaf in it, then in sugar, and lay the leaves on a baking tray lined with baking paper. Dry them in the oven at about 95 °C until they look dry but not browned: check after 20 minutes, then every 5–10 minutes. Use them to garnish ice cream or tarts.
recipes.title: Candied lemon balm leaves

recipes.method: 60 g (4 tbsp) softened butter; a pinch of finely chopped lemon balm; honey. Mix the lemon balm into the butter and add a drizzle of honey to taste. Spread on hot fresh bread or scones.
recipes.title: Lemon balm honey butter

recipes.method: Serves 2. Pickled shallot: 1 large shallot; 1 tbsp honey; 30 ml vinegar; 60 ml water; ½ tsp salt; ¼ tsp pepper. Salad: 1 large telegraph (English) cucumber; virgin sunflower oil or extra virgin olive oil; salt and pepper; 5–6 lemon balm leaves, to taste. Bring the honey, vinegar, water, salt and pepper to the boil, then turn off the heat. Peel and trim the shallot, slice it into 3 mm rings and pour the hot liquid over them; chill. Halve the cucumber lengthways, scrape out the seeds with a spoon and slice it 6 mm thick. Arrange the slices on a chilled plate, season with salt, pepper and oil, scatter over the pickled shallot, then tear the lemon balm into roughly 1 cm pieces over the top and serve at once. An ordinary cucumber works too, peeled and seeded. A variation: salt the sliced cucumber, drain off the water it gives, and dress it with a little yoghurt.
recipes.title: Cucumber salad with lemon balm and pickled shallot

recipes.method: 250 ml packed lemon balm leaves; 1 litre chilled white sugar; 500 ml water. Tear the leaves by hand rather than cutting them, so they don't bruise. Pulse them with the sugar in a food processor just until the sugar turns bright green — a few pulses only: over-processed, it loses colour and aroma. Freeze the sugar in dated, labelled containers, for sorbets or drinks. For a syrup (about 875 ml), stir the lemon balm sugar into the water until it dissolves, leave it in the fridge overnight to infuse, then strain out the leaf, label and date it, and keep it in the fridge. Add a splash to lemonade, iced tea or cold desserts.
recipes.title: Lemon balm sugar and cold-infused syrup

recipes.method: Makes 5–6 jars of about 250 ml. 900 g raspberries; 1.1 litres (4½ cups) white sugar; 1 bunch lemon balm, flowers removed; the juice of 1 lemon (listed in the recipe, though its steps do not say when to add it). A day ahead (12–14 hours), rub the lemon balm leaves and stalks into the sugar until it is fragrant, cover, and leave it to sit: tender leaves turn black when cooked, so the herb flavours the sugar instead. Pick out the stalks and any loose leaves. Sterilise the jars, lids and any equipment, and get a water bath ready. Heat the raspberries gently in a large non-reactive pan, pressing them against the pan, for about 10 minutes, until very soft and juicy. Push 250 ml of the fruit through a fine sieve to take out some of the seeds, and return it to the pan. Add the sugar and stir over low heat until it dissolves, then boil rapidly for 10–15 minutes, until the jam passes the wrinkle test or reaches 104 °C. Take it off the heat for at least 3 minutes, fill the sterilised jars, and process them in the water bath for 10 minutes.
recipes.title: Raspberry and lemon balm jam

recipes.method: Makes 2 glasses. 2 stalks fresh lemongrass; 125 ml fresh lemon verbena leaves, plus a sprig for each glass; 125 ml fresh lemon balm leaves; the zest of 1 lemon; about 1 tbsp sugar; 500 ml boiling water; 250 ml brewed black tea, not too strong, cooled. Trim the lemongrass, peel off a couple of the tough outer layers and chop the core. Put the lemongrass, lemon verbena, lemon balm and zest in a heatproof jug, pour over the boiling water and steep for about 20 minutes. Strain, stir in the sugar, and pour into 2 glasses full of ice. Top each with about 125 ml of the tea and a sprig of lemon verbena.
recipes.title: Sunset Palmer

recipes.method: After a recipe in Janet Ross's Leaves from our Tuscan Kitchen (1899). 60 ml olive oil, divided; 1 garlic clove; a handful of lemon balm leaves, torn or roughly chopped; 500 g drained, cooked cannellini beans; 1 tbsp white wine vinegar; salt and plenty of pepper; 80 g finely grated Parmesan; 1 egg, beaten; 250 ml dried breadcrumbs; 2 tbsp butter. Warm half the oil with the garlic and lemon balm in a wide frying pan over low to medium heat for 5 minutes to infuse. When the garlic is golden, add the beans and stir them through the herbs, then add the vinegar, salt and pepper and cook gently for 5–10 minutes, until some of the liquid has cooked off. Off the heat, mash the beans, mix in the Parmesan and chill until completely cold and firm. Roll tablespoons of the mixture into walnut-sized balls, then into little cylinders, and coat each in egg and then breadcrumbs. Heat the rest of the oil with the butter over medium heat and pan-fry the croquettes in batches until golden; if loose crumbs burn in the pan, wipe it out and start again with fresh oil and butter. Serve hot or warm.
recipes.title: Cannellini bean croquettes with lemon balm

recipes.method: Serves 2. 500 ml sliced red radishes; 500 ml loosely packed herb leaves, equal parts basil, mint, lemon balm and dill; 250 ml small cherry tomatoes; 250 ml very ripe quartered strawberries; 4 tbsp plain yoghurt; 2 tbsp pure maple syrup. Mix the radishes, herbs, tomatoes and strawberries in a bowl. Stir the yoghurt and maple syrup together, pour over the salad, mix well and serve at once.
recipes.title: Radish and herb salad with tomatoes and strawberries

summary.text:
Lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) is a perennial herbaceous plant in the mint family.
Melissa officinalis is native to south-central Europe, the Mediterranean Basin, Central Asia and Iran, but is now naturalized in the Americas and elsewhere around the world.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands: scattered localities throughout. Naturalised from Eurasia, first recorded in 1904. Lemon balm has been widely cultivated in New Zealand since the early period of European settlement. The strongly lemon-scented leaves are used for flavouring and once were used medicinally.
Other names include melissa and sweet balm, and it is sometimes called bee balm too.
It is not to be confused with bee balm (genus Monarda).

warnings: Taken as a medicine to aid sleep, lemon balm leaf may in theory cause drowsiness and impair your ability to drive or use machines, and the risk may increase with alcohol, other sedatives or large doses.
Its safety in pregnancy and breast-feeding has not been established, so medicinal use then is not recommended. Medicinal use in children under 12 is not recommended either, for lack of data.

In laboratory and animal studies, water extracts of the leaf may inhibit thyroid-stimulating hormone; whether this matters in people is not known. As a precaution, avoid large amounts if you have an underactive thyroid or take thyroid hormone medicine.

habitat.text:
Pittosporum eugenioides is found throughout the South Island and North Island in low lying forests. It is found in forest clearings and along forest margins up to 600 m above sea level.

Pittosporum eugenioides can be found in a cooler, mature, lowland and subalpine forest climate zone throughout New Zealand. The species can be found in regenerating areas of forest, both young and old. It has proved to be a great plant for establishing a quick canopy.

At home in the garden, P. eugenioides prefers a sunny to part shade position, does not mind the wind, and thrives in soil with good drainage.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

identification.text:
Polygamodioec. tree with spreading branches, up to 12 m tall, trunk up to 6 dm. diameter, bark pale. Leaves alt., often approximate, 5–10–(15) × 2.5–4 cm., on rather slender petioles 1–2 cm long. Lamina subcoriac., glossy, scented, elliptic to elliptic-oblong, acute to subacute, narrowed to petiole; margins usually undulate, midrib pale. Flowers fragrant, in terminal compound umbels, subcorymbosely arranged. Peduncles and pedicels with scattered hairs; peduncles 1–2 cm long, pedicels about 5 mm long. Sepals ovate to narrow-ovate, pale, membranous, about 2 mm long; petals narrow-oblong, yellowish, 5–7 mm long. Capsules glabrous, finely granulate, ovoid to elliptic in outline, 5–6 mm long; valves 2 or sometimes 3; seeds immersed in viscid pulp, remaining more or less covered by papery endocarp at dehiscence.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

summary.text:
Pittosporum eugenioides, commonly known as tarata or lemonwood, is a species of evergreen tree endemic to New Zealand.
Pittosporum eugenioides is endemic to New Zealand. There are "about 200 trees and shrubs" in the genus located in neighbouring parts of the world. Places where the genus is found include Africa, Australia, some Pacific islands, southern and eastern Asia, and New Zealand.
A reason for this endemic occurrence is due to the isolation of New Zealand over a long period of time.
This species, along with other Pittosporum, are making their way in to the average household gardens. Nurseries and garden centres are stocking this native because it is suited to New Zealand conditions where it naturally grew many years ago.

identification.text:
Plants openly branched, 1–1.5 m tall. Stems grooved, with sparse to dense cobwebby eglandular and subsessile glandular hairs, rarely glabrous or farinose. Basal leaves deltoid to broadly deltoid, green and sparsely hairy above, whitish and densely felted beneath, (15)–25–40–(55) × (10)–13–30–(35) cm; base cordate; apex subacute to obtuse; margin crenate to bluntly dentate with apiculate vein endings; petioles hollow. Upper leaves similar to basal, becoming smaller. Inflorescence racemose; peduncles 0–1–(3) cm long. Capitula (12)–15–20 × (14)–20–30 mm. Involucral bracts straw yellow, greenish or purplish, glabrous or with sparse to dense cobwebby hairs; margins with short, stiff, tapered, forwardly directed denticles, at least on the innermost bracts. Florets equal to or longer than involucral bracts; corolla reddish purple. Achenes 5–7 mm long; pappus 1.5–3.5 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In its first year it is only a rosette of large leaves over a long, deep taproot; the flowering stem rises in the second year or later, and the plant dies once it has flowered and set seed. The pale undersides of the leaves have fuzzy, raised, light-coloured veins. The flower heads look like small thistles: reddish-purple centres in a spiky green ball of bracts. As the heads dry the bracts harden into hooks, and the burs cling to clothes, fur and wool. It flowers from January to April and fruits from February to May.
Greater burdock (A. lappa) has larger, longer-stalked flower heads and solid stalks to its lower leaves; lesser burdock's are hollow. In New Zealand greater burdock is known only around Morrinsville and at scattered sites in Canterbury and Otago. Coltsfoot looks like a burdock rosette, but its leaves are broadly heart-shaped with the veins spreading from the base like fingers, not triangular. Winter heliotrope has large kidney-shaped basal leaves and flower heads like burdock's that never form burs.

lookalikes.howToTell: Broad-leaved dock's leaves are oblong ovals, often finely downy beneath, especially on the veins, with smooth, slightly wavy edges and a papery sheath (ochrea) round the base of each stalk; lesser burdock's basal leaves are broadly triangular, 25–40 cm long (up to 55), whitish and densely felted beneath, with scalloped to bluntly toothed edges and hollow stalks. Dock leaves are glossy; burdock's are matt.
lookalikes.name: Broad-leaved dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Foxglove is deadly. Its rosette leaves are lance-shaped to oval, 10–25 cm long and 3.5–12 cm wide, and narrow gradually into a long, winged stalk; lesser burdock's basal leaves are broadly triangular, 25–40 cm long (15–55) and 13–30 cm wide, with a heart-shaped base and a hollow stalk. Foxglove's side veins curve forward to run almost parallel with the midrib. Both are felted grey or white beneath and have scalloped edges, so neither of those tells them apart. In flower there is no confusion: foxglove flowers from October to January in a tall spike of hanging bells, burdock from January to April in thistle-like heads that turn into burs. If a leaf narrows into a winged stalk, leave it.
lookalikes.name: Foxglove

preparation.text:
Dig roots from first-year rosettes, before any flowering stem appears; once it rises, much of the root's food value is gone and it turns woody. The taproot runs deep and is hard to get out whole: dig a deep hole beside the plant and lever the root sideways into it, or settle for the top part. Plants in soft, rich soil give thicker roots than those in stony ground. Wash and peel the roots and cut away the tough top few centimetres; on large roots, cut off the outer layer and use the core, as the outside stays woody even when cooked. Cut root darkens fast, so drop the pieces into water with a little vinegar or lemon as you go, but don't leave them there overnight or they curl. Small roots and the thin tips are good raw. Cut the rest into thin matchsticks to stir-fry or simmer, or slice and boil or roast them like carrot or parsnip. Washed roots keep for up to a couple of months in a closed container in the fridge.
Cut flowering stems while they are young and slice easily with a knife, before the flower heads form; later they cook up stringy and fibrous. Strip off the leaves, peel off the thick outer skin with a knife and then the stringy fibres beneath with a vegetable peeler, and keep the peeled stems in lemon water. Simmer them in stock until tender, 30–45 minutes, then brown them in butter or add them to soups; raw, they can be shaved very thin and crisped in iced water. Unpeeled stems keep for weeks in the fridge.
Cut leaf stalks before the flowering stem rises. Scrub off the bitter coating, slice them thinly and boil until very tender.

recipes.method: Written for lesser burdock. 1–3 large burdock roots; a little vinegar; 1–2 tsp sesame oil (or another oil); salt and pepper. Heat the oven to 200 °C and grease a baking tray. Wash and peel 1–3 large roots, slice them into 1 cm rounds, and drop them into water with a little vinegar as you go. Drain, pat dry and toss in 1–2 tsp sesame oil (or another oil). Spread in one layer and roast for 20–30 minutes, turning once halfway. Season with salt and pepper.
recipes.title: Roasted burdock root

recipes.method: Written for lesser burdock. 1 burdock root; 1 litre of water. Fresh root: wash, peel and grate 1 root into 1 litre of boiling water, simmer 10 minutes, then take it off the heat and leave to steep 15–20 minutes. Dried root: wash, peel and cut the root into small pieces and dry them in a dehydrator, or the oven on its lowest setting, for 3–4 hours until hard. Grind 1–2 tsp per cup as you need it.
recipes.title: Burdock root tea

recipes.method: Written for greater and lesser burdock. Thin strips of burdock root; oil; sea salt; cornflour and sesame seeds, for a sesame version. Clean the roots, peeling large ones a little, and slice them into thin strips. Line a plate or two with kitchen paper. Heat oil in a frying pan over a medium-high heat; it is ready when a test piece floats up and the oil bubbles. Fry the strips for a few minutes, until crisp and lightly browned, lift them onto the paper with a slotted spoon and sprinkle with sea salt. For a sesame version, dip the raw strips in cornflour before frying, and toss the hot chips in sesame seeds mixed with a little salt; serve straight away.
recipes.title: Burdock root chips

recipes.method: Written for burdock root generally — the author treats lesser and greater burdock roots as interchangeable in recipes. 225 g burdock root (1 large); 225 g carrot (1 large); 1 tbsp maple syrup or sugar; 1 tbsp mirin or apple cider vinegar; 2 tbsp soy sauce; 1 tsp fish sauce (optional); 310 ml (1¼ cups) water; 2 tbsp toasted sesame oil; ½ tsp finely grated ginger (optional); 2 tsp toasted sesame seeds and 2 tsp sliced Chinese chives (both optional), to garnish. Wash the burdock well, trim the ends and cut it into 15 cm lengths. Peel each length, cut it on the diagonal into 5 mm-thick ovals, stack a few and cut into 5 mm matchsticks, dropping them into cold water as you go. Cut the carrot the same way and keep it separate. In a 25 cm pan or wok, bring the burdock and 250 ml of the water to the boil, cover and cook 5 minutes, then pour off the water. Add the carrot, maple syrup, mirin or vinegar, fish sauce, soy sauce, ginger, half the sesame oil and the remaining 60 ml water, and stir-fry over a high heat until the pan is nearly dry. Off the heat, stir in the rest of the sesame oil and the chives. Garnish with the sesame seeds; serve warm, cool or at room temperature.
recipes.title: Kinpira gobo

recipes.method: Written for burdock root generally — the author treats lesser and greater burdock roots as interchangeable in recipes. 225 g cleaned, peeled burdock root; 225 g mild fresh mushrooms; 2 tbsp soy sauce; 2 tbsp apple cider or rice wine vinegar; a good pinch of chilli flakes (optional); 2 tbsp ghee, lard or cooking oil; a small handful of sliced fresh herbs such as coriander, mint or basil; 30 g sliced spring onions or green garlic; salt. Cut the burdock on the diagonal into 5 mm rounds, stack them and cut into 5 mm matchsticks; slice the mushrooms 5 mm thick. Boil the burdock in water for 5 minutes and drain well. Heat the fat in a wide pan and cook the burdock and mushrooms until the mushrooms are cooked. Add the soy sauce, chilli and vinegar and cook down, tossing. Season with salt and chilli, toss in the spring onions and herbs, fry a minute more and serve hot. To serve it cold as a salad, use oil (sesame oil is good) instead of ghee or lard.
recipes.title: Braised burdock and mushrooms

recipes.method: Written for burdock root generally — the author treats lesser and greater burdock roots as interchangeable in recipes. Lemon juice, for the peeling water; 170 g burdock root; 500 ml (2 cups) cream; 900 g floury potatoes; 2 tbsp unsalted butter, plus a knob to serve; salt and white pepper; some sliced chives, to serve. Peel the roots into water sharpened with lemon juice, then slice them thinly. Heat the oven to 120 °C. Bring the burdock and cream to a simmer in a small non-reactive pot, season lightly, then cover and bake until the burdock is tender, 30–45 minutes. Blend until smooth, adding a little water if needed, and pass through a sieve; the purée can be made a day or two ahead, or frozen (blend it again after thawing). Peel the potatoes and boil them in lightly salted water until tender, about 15 minutes. Rice them, stir in the burdock cream and the butter, and season. Serve with a knob of butter and some sliced chives.
recipes.title: Burdock mashed potatoes

recipes.method: Written for burdock root generally — the author treats lesser and greater burdock roots as interchangeable in recipes. 225 g burdock root; 60 ml (¼ cup) water; 190 ml (¾ cup) rice or apple cider vinegar; 1 tsp salt or 1 tbsp soy sauce; 4 tbsp sugar. Optional spices: a few slices of fresh ginger, 2 tsp turmeric (or 1 tbsp carrot or beetroot powder, for colour), 1 tsp Sichuan peppercorns, 2 dried hot chillies, 1 large garlic clove, 1 tsp yellow mustard seed, 2 makrut lime leaves, 5 allspice berries and a small handful of dill. Peel the burdock and cut it into 7.5 cm lengths. Bring everything else to the boil, then cool, and take out the dill. Spoon the spices into the bottom of the jar or jars, pack in the burdock, and pour in the liquid, leaving 1 cm headspace; put the lids on. Lower the jars into a large pot of boiling water that covers them by 5 cm, cover, and once it is back at the boil, process for 10 minutes. Lift out, label, date and store in the pantry.
recipes.title: Yamagobo (pickled burdock root)

recipes.method: Written for burdock root generally — the author treats lesser and greater burdock roots as interchangeable in recipes. 900 g pork spare ribs in 2–3-bone pieces; 250 ml (1 cup) carrots, quartered and sliced 5 mm; 250 ml (1 cup) each diced onion, leek (white and tender green) and fennel; 500 ml (2 cups) puréed canned whole tomatoes; 2 litres chicken stock; 750 ml (3 cups) peeled burdock root sliced into 5 mm rounds; 225 g shiitake caps sliced 5 mm; 2 tbsp minced fresh ginger; 60 ml (¼ cup) oil; salt; a bouquet garni (5 allspice berries, 5 cloves, 2 star anise, 2 fresh bay leaves and a halved bulb of garlic); cooked millet to taste (or quinoa, wild rice, sorghum or lentils); hot chilli oil, or sesame oil and chopped chilli, to serve; fresh coriander. Sweat the leek, onion and ginger in the oil, add everything else and simmer gently for about 2 hours, until the meat comes off the bones. Season with salt and cool quickly, then pick the meat off the ribs, chop it and return it to the soup. Just before serving, add cooked millet to taste (or quinoa, wild rice, sorghum or lentils). Serve with hot chilli oil, or sesame oil and chopped chilli, and fresh coriander. The author says to treat the amounts as a rough guide.
recipes.title: Pork rib and burdock soup

recipes.method: Written for the flower stalks of greater and lesser burdock. 450 g peeled burdock flower stalks (see Preparation); 1 small carrot; 1 celery stick; 1 small onion; about 1 litre (4 cups) vegetable stock, enough to cover; a sprig of fresh thyme; 1 bay leaf; fresh herbs; salt; 125 ml (½ cup) white wine if you like; butter, for browning (optional). Cut the vegetables into 7.5 cm pieces. Put everything in a pan, bring to a simmer, season the liquid lightly with salt, and cook gently until the burdock is just tender, 30–45 minutes. Let the stalks cool in the liquid, then strain out and discard the aromatic vegetables, keeping the burdock and the liquid (it can cook another batch, or be the broth for a vegetable stew). Keep the cooked stalks in a sealed container in the fridge. To serve, cut them into 1 cm pieces and reheat them in their liquid, or brown them in butter. To serve with roast meat, use red wine for half the stock; it stains them purple.
recipes.title: Burdock flower stalks à la barigoule

recipes.method: Written for the flower stalks of greater and lesser burdock. 225 g peeled carrot and 225 g peeled burdock flower stalk, each roll-cut into pieces about 2 cm (slice on the diagonal, turn the piece half a turn, slice again); lemon water; 1 small garlic clove; a good pinch of sugar; 2 tbsp butter; salt and black pepper; and, optionally, a small handful of greens such as parsley, and chives, mint or basil to finish. Keep the peeled stalks in the lemon water. Bring a small pot of lightly salted water to the boil. Blanch the carrots about 30 seconds, until just al dente, and cool them in cold water; blanch the stalks 60 seconds (less for very young ones) and cool them too. Drain both. Crush the garlic and warm it in the butter for a minute or two, without letting it burn. Add the vegetables and cook until tender, seasoning with the sugar, salt and pepper. Toss in the greens and herbs and serve hot.
recipes.title: Burdock flower stalks with carrots

recipes.method: Written for the flower stalks of greater and lesser burdock. 4 thick sections of flower stalk about 15 cm long, skinned and peeled; 1 litre (4 cups) vegetable stock; ¼ lemon; salt; a little oil or fat; sesame oil, sliced hot chilli and sesame seeds, to finish. Shave the stalks as thin as you can into long noodles with a vegetable peeler or a mandoline. Simmer gently in the stock with the lemon, seasoned lightly with salt, until just tender, 15–20 minutes, and drain. Warm a little oil or fat in a pan and cook the noodles over a medium-low heat until very lightly browned; they turn grey as they cook, which is normal. Finish them with sesame oil, sliced hot chilli and sesame seeds, as the author did. Makes two small servings.
recipes.title: Burdock flower stalk noodles

recipes.method: Written for the flower stalks of greater and lesser burdock. 115 g each of carrot, onion and celery; 225 g peeled burdock flower stalks; 1–2 bay leaves; 3 tbsp flavourless oil; about 1 litre (4 cups) really good stock, enough to cover; optionally 115 g diced mushrooms or 250 ml (1 cup) chopped cooked meat; salt; a dash of lemon juice; fresh herbs such as chives or parsley; olive oil or another flavoured oil, to serve. Dice the vegetables, and cut the burdock into slightly larger pieces, keeping it in lemon water until needed. Sweat the vegetables (and the mushrooms, if using) in the oil, then add the stock, burdock and bay leaves and simmer until tender, about 20 minutes. Add the meat, if using, and warm it through. Season with salt, add the lemon juice and herbs, and serve with a drizzle of olive oil or another flavoured oil.
recipes.title: Burdock flower stalk soup

summary.text:
Arctium minus, commonly known as lesser burdock, little burdock, louse-bur, common burdock, button-bur, cuckoo-button, or wild rhubarb, is a biennial plant native to Europe.
The plant is native to Europe, but has become introduced elsewhere such as Australia, North and South America, and other places.
In New Zealand it is also called burdock or common burdock; its older scientific name is Lappa minor. It comes from Europe and western Asia, arrived by accident, and was first recorded growing wild here in 1894. It is occasional throughout the North and South Islands except Westland. Each plant makes many seeds, carried by wind and water and on animals and people. The specific name minus is Latin for smaller.
DOC lists it among New Zealand's environmental weeds (2024). In Auckland it is under sustained control across the region and is a pest in the Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area: it must not be bred, distributed, released, sold or planted there. Gisborne's regional pest plan has it under progressive containment, and Canterbury and Otago list it as an organism of interest. The burs tangle in sheep's wool and can injure livestock.
Its relative greater burdock (A. lappa) is grown in Japan as a root vegetable, gobo. Lesser burdock has been gathered from the wild for food, and for fibre to make paper.

warnings: The tiny hairs on the seeds are irritating and toxic if breathed in: take care with ripe burs, and don't collect the seed in any quantity. Handling the plant can also cause contact dermatitis.

Burdock is a pest plant under control throughout the Auckland region and in pest plant strategies elsewhere, and may be sprayed with herbicide, so pick it only where you know no herbicide has been used.

habitat.text: Pasture, meadows, lawns and rough grassland on rich, acidic soil, most often where sheep or cattle have been grazing. It does not typically grow directly on the dung. It grows singly or in groups. In New Zealand it grows in high-altitude grasslands.

identification.text:
Cap 5–25 mm across and about as tall, sharply conical to bell-shaped, and usually tipped with a small distinct nipple. Colour shifts with moisture: ochre to pale brown or dark chestnut brown when damp, with the gill lines showing through the margin, fading to pale buff as it dries. A damp cap is tacky, with a gelatinous skin that peels away if you bend the margin back.
Gills are narrow and moderately crowded, pale brown at first, darkening to purple-brown with paler edges. The stipe is 4.5–14 cm long but only 1–3.5 mm thick, slender, often wavy, and has no ring. Spore print is dark purple-brown.
Any part handled or bruised stains bluish.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both grow in grass, so habitat does not separate them. Cap shape is the first check but not a certain one. A liberty cap is sharply conical to bell-shaped, often tipped with a small nipple, and keeps that shape as it ages. A mower's mushroom is conical or bell-shaped when young but opens out to broadly convex and lacks the liberty cap's point. A liberty cap stains bluish where it is handled or bruised, and its stem is sometimes blue towards the base. The mower's mushroom's flesh does not change colour when cut. Bend back a piece of a damp liberty cap and a thin gelatinous skin peels away (not once the cap has dried out); the mower's mushroom is not described as having this skin. Mower's mushroom gills are broad and often go mottled as the spores ripen. A liberty cap's gills are narrow and moderately crowded, darkening to dark grey or purple-brown. Both can have paler gill edges, so the edges do not separate them. The spore print will not decide it either: liberty cap very dark purple-brown, mower's mushroom dark brown, sometimes purplish to nearly black.

The legal claims on this page, checked against the Act rather than a summary of it. Schedule 1 (Class A controlled drugs) lists Psilocine, Psilotsin and Psilocybine by name and formula. Section 7(1)(a) makes it an offence to procure, possess, consume, smoke or otherwise use a controlled drug, and section 7(2)(a) sets the penalty at 'imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months or to a fine not exceeding $1,000 or to both where a Class A controlled drug was the controlled drug' — which is what this entry's warning says. Note that section 7(2) applies 'without prejudice to any liability under section 6', the dealing provision, which carries life imprisonment for a Class A drug: the same handful of mushrooms can be charged either way depending on quantity and circumstance. Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, read on legislation.govt.nz 06/10/2026. https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1975/0116/latest/DLM436100.html

The fungus itself is a prohibited plant, which is a second offence this page did not mention. Section 2 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 defines 'prohibited plant' to include 'any fungus of the genera Conocybe, Panaeolus, or Psilocybe from which a controlled drug can be produced or which contains a controlled drug' — so cultivating it is an offence under section 9, separately from possessing it under section 7. summary.text:
A small, sharply conical grassland mushroom with a nipple-tipped cap that bruises blue. It contains psilocybin, which makes it a Class A controlled drug in New Zealand.
Like other Psilocybe species it feeds on decaying organic matter; it is thought to live on the decaying root remains of grasses.

warnings: Magic mushrooms, and the psilocybine and psilocine in them, are Class A controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. Picking or carrying one is possession of a Class A drug.

Maximum penalties are six months' imprisonment and/or a $1,000 fine for possession, and life imprisonment for supplying or manufacturing. This entry is here so you can recognise the species, not so you can collect it.

habitat.text:
Occasional in the vicinity of planted trees, mainly in scrub or on waste ground.
It can establish in existing forest under low light. In the Auckland region it grows in forest, plantations, roadsides and gardens. Herbarium collections record self-sown seedlings in regenerating forest, a swamp-forest remnant and a shaded stream gorge, some far from any parent tree, and among garden shrubs.

harvestEthics.text:
An Unwanted Organism and National Pest Plant Accord species: it must not be bred, distributed, released or sold anywhere in New Zealand. Birds carry its seed into native forest, which it can invade. Harvest as much as you like, and do not spread the seed: put it in green waste or landfill.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text:
Tree (6–15 m high in cultivation). Leaves very aromatic when crushed; petiole usually c. 5 mm long. Lamina 4–12–(15) × 2–5–(8) cm, ovate or elliptic-ovate, coriaceous, glossy above, dotted with glands below; veins parallel and prominent below; base cuneate or narrow-cuneate; apex obtusely cuspidate or acuminate. Flowers shortly pedicellate. Hypanthium (including pseudopedicel) 3–5 mm long; calyx lobes 4, deciduous. Petals 4, c. 2 mm long, forming a small calyptrum, whitish. Stamens to c. 3 mm long, whitish. Fruit subglobose to broad-oblong or obovoid, often slightly flattened, usually 1–1.7–(3) cm diameter, pinkish mauve or white, with apical cavity. Seed large.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Acmena smithii (Poir.) Merr. & L.M.Perry.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Brush cherry's fruit is crimson to crimson-purple, oblong to obovoid and glossy, with its calyx lobes (2–4 mm long) still on the tip; lilly pilly's fruit is pinkish mauve or white, nearly round to broadly oblong or obovoid and often slightly flattened, with a hollow at the tip, and its calyx lobes fall off. Brush cherry's flowers are showier, with petals about 4 mm across and stamens to about 13 mm long; lilly pilly's petals are about 2 mm long and its stamens to about 3 mm. Lilly pilly's leaves are broader for their length (ovate or elliptic-ovate, usually 2–5 cm wide); brush cherry's are often narrowly elliptic, mostly 1–3.5 cm wide, on branchlets that more or less hang down. In New Zealand lilly pilly flowers from October to January, brush cherry from January to July. Look at the young branchlets: only brush cherry has a small pocket just above where each pair of leaves joins the stem; lilly pilly has none. Angles alone do not separate them, as both can be four-angled or shortly four-winged. Otherwise the two are very similar, with glossy, aromatic leaves, parallel veins and reddish new leaves. Brush cherry's fruit is eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Brush cherry

lookalikes.howToTell: Magenta lilly pilly's flowers are showier, with free, spreading petals 4–5 mm long and stamens 6–15 mm long; lilly pilly's petals are about 2 mm long, joined into a small cap, and its stamens reach about 3 mm. Magenta lilly pilly's fruit is round to egg-shaped, with somewhat swollen calyx lobes at the tip; lilly pilly's is nearly round to broadly oblong or obovoid and often slightly flattened, with a hollow at the tip where the calyx lobes have fallen. Lilly pilly's leaves are broader for their length: ovate or elliptic-ovate and usually 2–5 cm wide, against magenta lilly pilly's lanceolate to obovate leaves 1.5–3 cm wide that taper to the base. Fruit colour does not separate them: magenta lilly pilly's is usually magenta but can be white, pink or purple, and lilly pilly's is pinkish mauve or white. Cut a fruit open: magenta lilly pilly's single large seed usually shows lines of division marking its many embryos, which sets it apart from the other Syzygium species in New Zealand. Magenta lilly pilly's fruit is eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Magenta lilly pilly

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: tree privet's berries are bluish or purplish black with a powdery bloom, no more than 6 mm long, in dense clusters, each with a ribbed seed about 5 mm long; lilly pilly's fruit is pinkish mauve or white, usually 1–1.7 cm across (up to 3 cm), with a hollow at the tip and one large seed. Lilly pilly's new leaves are reddish, unlike tree privet's. Tree privet's flowers are small and tubular, with a white tube about 1.5 mm long, four reflexed lobes 2–2.5 mm long and only two stamens; lilly pilly's four tiny petals, about 2 mm long, are joined into a small cap that falls, and it has numerous stamens. Lilly pilly's leaves are very aromatic when crushed and dotted with glands underneath, on stalks usually about 5 mm long; tree privet's are not described as aromatic or gland-dotted, and their stalks are mostly 1–2 cm long. Lilly pilly's twigs are often four-angled or shortly four-winged; tree privet's shoots are more or less round, with prominent lumpy warts. Both are evergreen trees with glossy, opposite leaves of overlapping size (lilly pilly usually 4–12 cm long, tree privet 5–13 cm), and both grow in scrub and on waste ground, so leaf shape and place do not separate them. Tree privet's berries are poisonous.
lookalikes.name: Tree privet

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: swamp maire's is deep crimson and glossy, 10–15 mm across, with its very short, broad calyx lobes still on the tip; lilly pilly's is pinkish mauve or white, usually 1–1.7 cm across (up to 3 cm), with a hollow at the tip where the calyx lobes have fallen. Swamp maire's white stamens are long, 5–12 mm (up to 15 mm), so its flowers look brushy; lilly pilly's stamens reach only about 3 mm. Swamp maire's leaves are mostly 2.5–6 cm long and 1–2.5 cm wide, with wavy edges; lilly pilly's are usually larger, 4–12 cm long (up to 15 cm) and 2–5 cm wide, so small lilly pilly leaves overlap swamp maire's in size. Otherwise the leaves look much alike, thin, shiny, elliptic and in opposite pairs on both, so go by the fruit and flowers. With a hand lens, swamp maire's anther sacs are usually parallel; lilly pilly's anther lobes spread apart. Both have small white or whitish petals, about 2–3 mm, joined into a cap that falls, and lilly pilly sometimes grows with swamp maire in urban forest remnants, so place does not separate them. Swamp maire's fruit is edible, but it is a threatened native tree: do not pick it unless your life depends on it (see its page).

preparation.text: Eaten fresh, or made into jams, jellies or drinks. Each fruit holds one large seed.

recipes.method: 2 litres (8 cups) lilly pilly fruit; about 625 ml (2½ cups) sugar; 3 lemons. Wash the fruit well, throwing out any underripe fruit, stems and leaves. Put it in a pot and add just enough water to cover it, holding the floating fruit down with a plate or lid while you measure. Bring to the boil and boil for an hour; the fruit will fade to a pale mauve. Pour the fruit and liquid into a bowl lined with a large cheesecloth, tie the cloth into a bag and hang it over the bowl for several hours or overnight to drip. Squeeze it only lightly, or the juice turns cloudy. Measure the juice and, for each cup (250 ml), add 1 cup of sugar and the juice of 1 lemon. Heat slowly, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then boil, skimming off the foam. Stay with it: after about 15–20 minutes the bubbles turn thick and syrupy and pop slowly. Lower the heat so it doesn't scorch, and test by putting a teaspoonful on a plate in the freezer for 5 minutes: if it wrinkles when pushed, it is ready; if not, boil a few minutes more and test again. No pectin is needed. Pour into hot, sterilised jars and seal at once with the lids. Makes about 2 × 375 ml jars.

summary.text:
An evergreen tree of the myrtle family from eastern Australia. In New Zealand it is commonly grown as an ornamental tree and windbreak in warmer parts, and has been naturalised since 1982 in the Bay of Islands, the Whangārei area and Auckland. Self-sown seedlings have also been collected near Te Puke in the Bay of Plenty and in Whanganui. Its New Zealand name is monkey apple; lilly pilly is the Australian name, sometimes used here.
It is an Unwanted Organism and a National Pest Plant Accord species, and is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. Birds, kererū among them, carry its seed into native forest, where it can establish in shade, outcompete native trees and become a dominant canopy tree. Its sale and propagation are banned nationwide, but trees and hedges planted before the ban are still common in gardens. It is very susceptible to myrtle rust.

warnings: Tree privet, a weed tree with poisonous purple-black berries, can look similar. Lilly pilly's berries are white to pink and its new leaves are reddish; tree privet's new leaves lack that red colour.

identification.text:
Stout annual herb up to 80–(100) cm high. Stems glabrous, usually simple or sometimes somewhat branched at base. Stem leaves always alternate, glabrous, lanceolate to linear, usually obovate or oblong at base of stem, acuminate, 3-nerved, entire, (5)–10–40 mm long; leaves subtending inflorescence-branches single, similar to stem leaves but usually somewhat smaller. Inflorescence of few to numerous flowers in a diffuse compound dichasium or corymb; sepals elliptic to suborbicular, acuminate, (5)–6–10 mm long, shorter than capsule, with glabrous entire margins; petals white or pale to dark blue, 2–3× as long as sepals, (10)–12–18–(20) mm long; styles united for about ⅓ length. Capsule glabrous, subglobose, indehiscent or subdehiscent, (6)–8–10–(12) mm diameter; seeds elliptic and narrowed to base, shiny light to dark brown, 4–5 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

edibleParts.text: Ripe fruit, eaten raw or cooked: sweet and juicy, tasting like a cross between apricot and plum with a citrus tang. It is good fresh, in fruit salads, stewed for breakfast, in pies, puddings and baking, as jam or cordial, and in savoury sauces, pickles and chutneys. Leaves, brewed as a tea (biwa-cha, a traditional Japanese herbal tea of dried loquat leaves). The seeds are not eaten (see Warnings).

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Hillsides, scrub, plantations, wasteland near sites of cultivation.
It grows in forest, shrublands, coastal slopes, roadsides, wastelands, plantations and gardens (Auckland Council), and invades disturbed forest and shrubland and inshore islands, mainly in the northern North Island. It tolerates wet to dry conditions, hot to moderately cool temperatures, most soils and moderate shade (Weedbusters).

identification.text:
Tree up to 8 m high when mature;  trunk well developed;  primary stems erect;  secondary stems spreading;  young stems stout, white-tomentose; older stems with prominent leaf scars, becoming greyish brown and transversely calloused.  Leaves near branch tips;  petiole  about 15 mm long, stout;  blade oblanceolate to narrowly elliptic, 150–350–(400) × 75–100–(130) mm, acute, tapering to cuneate or slightly auriculate base, very coriaceous, more or less rugose, dark green and glossy above, thinly grey- or brown-tomentose below (very young leaves completely brown-tomentose), serrate at least in upper 1/2 (sometimes obscurely);  stipules long-triangular, more or less attenuate, pilose.  Inflorescence of many flowers;  pedicels 5–8 mm long, brownish tomentose.  Sepals fused for most of length;  lobes 2–4 mm long, brown-tomentose.  Petals white or ivory, oblong,  about 7–8 × 3–4 mm, shallowly emarginate.  Fruit pyriform to broadly ellipsoid-oblong or subglobose, up to 50 × 35 mm;  skin yellow, more or less tomentose;  flesh sweet. 
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The seeds are large and brown (Weedbusters). The flowers, borne from late autumn into winter, are strongly scented, with a vanilla-almond fragrance (NZ Tree Crops Association).

preparation.text: Pick when golden and ripe: yellow-orange with no green left and soft to the touch; before that it is too tart. Cut the clusters off with snips rather than pulling single fruit, which tears the skin; picking in bunches with the stalks on helps. The fruit spoils fast once picked, so use it within a day or two and keep it in the fridge, as it browns quickly. Remove the large seeds and the membrane around them (for jam the membrane can be left in); the seeds stain fingers and nails black, so wear gloves for a big batch. The skin peels off easily but is thin enough to leave on for jam and chutney. Eat fresh, stew with a little sugar, or use in pies, sauces, chutney and jam; slightly underripe fruit has enough pectin to set a jelly. To freeze, halve and seed the fruit, blanch it to stop it browning, cool, freeze in a single layer on a tray, then bag it. For leaf tea, scrape the furry hairs off the underside of the leaves first, as they can irritate the throat.

recipes.method: 2.5 kg loquats; 1.25 kg white sugar; juice of half a lemon; 1/8 tsp ground cinnamon (optional); jam setting sugar (optional). For smaller batches keep the ratio of 2 parts fruit to 1 part sugar by weight. Wash the loquats, cut off the flower end and halve them; scoop out and discard the stones and the papery sack around them. Cut each half into quarters, weigh, and put in a large pan with half that weight of sugar; leave for about an hour for the juices to run. Add the lemon juice and cinnamon if using. Stir over a medium heat until the sugar dissolves, bring to the boil, then simmer for about 60 minutes until it is a golden slurry. Let it cool, blend with a stick blender to the texture you like, then bring back to the boil until thick, adding a tablespoon or two of jam setting mix if it is still too runny. Pour into sterilised jars and seal. Makes about 2.5 litres.
recipes.title: Loquat jam

recipes.method: Filling: 1 kg loquats with the seeds removed; 7 tbsp sugar; 1 tbsp flour; 1/4 tsp almond essence; 1 tsp cinnamon; 2 tsp lemon juice. Topping: 1 cup (250 ml) flour; 1 tsp baking powder; 1/4 tsp baking soda; 1/2 tsp salt; 1/2 cup (125 ml) sugar; 3/4 cup (185 ml) milk; 3 tbsp butter; 3 tbsp brown sugar to finish. Mix the filling ingredients and leave for half an hour (the source does not name the dish; use a baking dish). Pulse the topping ingredients in a food processor until combined, spoon over the filling and sprinkle with the brown sugar. Bake at 180 °C for 20–30 minutes. Serve hot with whipped cream, yoghurt or ice cream.
recipes.title: Loquat cobbler

recipes.method: 680 g loquats, washed, seeded and cut small; 450 g onion, chopped; 225 g apples, grated; 450 g sugar; 2 tsp mustard; 2 tsp sea salt; 1 tsp curry powder; 1 tbsp mustard seeds, crushed; 1 tbsp molasses; 2 tbsp fresh ginger, peeled and cut into thin strips; 500 ml apple cider vinegar; 500 ml water; 60 ml raisins or currants. Put everything in a large pot and bring to the boil, then cook gently, stirring often so it does not stick, for about 1–1½ hours until soft and well coloured. Pour into hot sterilised jars, leaving about 1 cm headroom, seal, and process the jars for 10 minutes in a boiling-water bath; refrigerate and use any that do not seal. The sealed jars keep in a cool dark place for 9 months.
recipes.title: Loquat chutney

recipes.method: 900 g loquats (about 600 g once stoned); 1 cup (250 ml) soft brown sugar; 3 cups (750 ml) malt vinegar; 1 onion, chopped; 2 cloves garlic; 1/2 tsp salt; 1/2 tsp black pepper; 1/4 tsp cayenne pepper; 6 whole cloves (or 1/2 tsp ground cloves). Wash, halve and stone the loquats. Put them in a large saucepan with everything else, bring to a low boil, then simmer for about an hour, stirring now and then, until the liquid has reduced and the fruit has collapsed. Cool slightly, blend until smooth (take care, hot sauce burns), pour into sterilised jars and seal. Makes about 1 litre; good with chicken.
recipes.title: Loquat barbecue sauce

recipes.method: Topping: 2 tbsp unsalted butter, melted; 3/4 cup (150 g) brown sugar; about 25 medium loquats, halved and seeded. Cake: 1 3/4 cups (220 g) plain flour; 1 1/2 tsp baking powder; 1/2 tsp baking soda; 1/2 tsp salt; 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon; 110 g unsalted butter; 3/4 cup (150 g) sugar; 2 tsp vanilla extract; 2 large eggs at room temperature; 3/4 cup (180 ml) milk. Heat the oven to 190 °C. Mix the melted butter with the brown sugar. Lay the loquats cut side down in a greased cake pan and pour the butter-sugar over them. Sift the flour, baking powder, soda, salt and cinnamon together. Cream the butter and sugar for 4–5 minutes until smooth, beat in the eggs and vanilla, mix in the dry ingredients, then the milk, without overmixing. Pour the batter over the loquats and bake for about 40 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean. Cool for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a plate before the caramel sets; serve warm or at room temperature. Serves 8.
recipes.title: Loquat upside-down cake

recipes.method: 3 cups (750 ml) loquats, washed and seeded; 1 tsp fenugreek seeds; 2 tsp mustard seeds; 1 tsp red chilli powder, or to taste; 1 tsp salt, or to taste. Tempering: 2 tsp oil; 1/2 tsp mustard seeds; 2 pinches asafoetida. Dry the washed loquats well, halve, seed and cut into long wedges (peeling is optional). Toast the fenugreek seeds in a dry pan for 45 seconds to a minute until light brown, then pop the 2 tsp mustard seeds in the same pan; grind both to a fine powder. Heat the oil, pop the 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, add the asafoetida and take off the heat. Mix the loquats with the chilli powder, salt, ground spices and the tempering and leave for an hour. Mix again, adjust the salt and chilli, and leave another 30 minutes before serving with rice and dal or yoghurt rice. Keeps in the fridge for up to a week.
recipes.title: Instant loquat pickle

recipes.method: 4 medium loquat leaves (or about 1 tbsp crushed dried leaves per cup); 3 cups (750 ml) water; sweetener, optional. Pick fresh, medium-sized green leaves, rinse and dry them. Scrape the furry hairs off the underside with a small knife (they can irritate the throat), cut out the thick middle vein, and slice or tear the leaves into small pieces. Put them in a pot with the water, bring to the boil, then simmer gently for 10 minutes. Turn off the heat, cover and steep for another 10 minutes. Strain and drink hot, or over ice; the longer it simmers, the darker and stronger it gets. For dried leaves, air-dry or oven-dry young leaves, crush and store in a jar.
recipes.title: Loquat leaf tea

recipes.method: A guide rather than a strict recipe: scale it to your dish. Base: crushed Weet-Bix and pitted dates, bound with a little fruit juice. Filling: cottage cheese, Greek yoghurt and thick loquat purée, sweetened to taste. Blitz the base ingredients in a food processor, bind with juice and press into a greased flan dish. Blend the filling ingredients and pour over the base. Refrigerate until firm and serve with extra fruit and yoghurt.
recipes.title: Loquat cheesecake (no-bake)

summary.text:
The loquat (Eriobotrya japonica, Chinese: 枇杷; Pinyin: pípá) is a large evergreen shrub or tree grown commercially for its orange-coloured fruits.
The plant is originally from China, where related species can be found growing in the wild. It grows in places where suitable winter temperatures are generally above -12°C, such as Georgia, Argentina, Armenia, Afghanistan, Australia, Azerbaijan, Bermuda, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Greece, Kenya, Syria, India, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Türkiye, Israel, Palestine, Jordan, South Africa, the whole Mediterranean Basin, Pakistan, New Zealand, Réunion, Tonga, Central America, Mexico, South America and warmer parts of the United States such as Hawaii, California, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, with a maximal range comprising coastal Oregon and Washington, southern Tennessee, and most of North Carolina, in places with a favorable humid subtropical climate with relatively mild winters.
E. japonica is widely grown in warm temperate countries for its attractive appearance and edible fruit and is very common north of the Volcanic Plateau in New Zealand. On a hillside behind Paihia (Bay of Islands), a large wild population occurs with fruits ranging from pyriform to subglobose.
Also called Japanese plum, Chinese plum or Japanese medlar. It is native to the hills of south-central China and has been cultivated in Japan for more than 1000 years; the genus name comes from the Greek for 'wool' and 'cluster', and the Chinese name pipa likens the fruit to the lute of that name. Early New Zealand cookery writers such as Aunt Daisy give recipes for it, so it is not a recent arrival (NZ Tree Crops Association).
Birds, especially kererū, spread the seed, as do people and dumped garden waste; gardens, wastelands and exotic plantations are common seed sources. It forms tall stands that replace native low-canopy and mid-tier species (Weedbusters) and can invade intact native forest canopy (Auckland Council). It is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.
In Auckland it is a sustained-control pest across the whole region and a pest under the Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area Notice. Since 1 September 2022 it may not be bred, distributed, released, sold or planted there (an existing plant may be moved within the same property), and a loquat planted in breach of these rules must be destroyed if an authorised person directs it (Auckland Council).
The NZ Plant Conservation Network and DOC's 2024 weed list use the name Rhaphiolepis bibas; Biota of New Zealand keeps Eriobotrya japonica as the current name.

warnings: The seeds contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide: raw seeds hold 2–5% amygdalin, so a single seed of about 2 g can carry 2.4–5.9 mg of cyanide. They are hard and bitter and unsuitable to eat; remove them. Do not take powdered loquat seed, home-made or bought, unless analysis has confirmed it safe: products on sale have tested high enough in cyanide that a teaspoon could exceed the safe acute dose.
The leaves also contain cyanogenic glycosides, though much less than the seeds; drinking a leaf infusion carries a low risk of cyanide poisoning. Amygdalin has also been recorded in the fruit peel.
Eat only ripe fruit: a 5-year-old child who ate 4 unripe loquats became drowsy and dazed and was back to normal after about 2 hours (a single reported case).
It is controlled as an environmental weed with herbicide (metsulfuron sprays, metsulfuron gel on cut stumps, or basal bark spray). Pick only where you know it has not been sprayed.

identification.text:
Erect shrub or tree up to 8 m tall, bark dark. Leaves on slender petioles ± 2 cm long; lamina elliptic-oblong to elliptic-obovate to ovate-oblong, 6–10 × 3–6 cm, obtuse to subacute, rather coriaceous, dark green and glossy above, glaucous below, somewhat pungent to taste; midrib and veins evident below. Flowers ± 1 cm diameter, in axillary fascicles of 3–5–(10) on pedicels 5 mm to 1 cm long or more; calyx subentire to shallowly lobed; petals 5–6, greenish yellow, narrow-oblong to narrow-obovate, 5–6 mm long; stamens 6–15; carpels 3–6; fruits red (rarely dark), 5–6 mm diameter, mesocarp slightly fleshy; seeds 3 to 6, black, angled.
Leaf undersides are pale to glaucous but not white, leaf edges are wavy, and the ripe fruit is orange to red. Told from horopito by its leaves, which are not blotched and are glossy above, and by its fruit, usually bright red.

lookalikes.howToTell: Horopito's leaves are dull green and blotched with red, at least in exposed places; lowland horopito's are dark green and glossy above with no red blotches. Horopito's leaves are usually smaller, 2–6 (rarely 8) × 1–3 cm against 6–10 × 3–6 cm, and glaucous to white underneath and often pink-flushed, where lowland horopito's are pale to glaucous but not white. Horopito's ripe fruit is dark red to black; lowland horopito's is usually bright red, rarely dark. Horopito's leaves are very pungent to taste, lowland horopito's only somewhat pungent. Hybrids between the two are frequent where they meet, so some plants fit neither description.
lookalikes.name: Horopito

lookalikes.howToTell: Feel the leaf: lowland horopito's is rather leathery, mountain alseuosmia's thin. Both have glossy leaves, but mountain alseuosmia's are often red-edged and sometimes flecked red, while lowland horopito's have no blemishes or blotches. Mountain alseuosmia's leaves are widest towards the tip and narrowed wedge-like to the base, with a tiny point at the tip, 2–2.5 cm wide (sometimes 3.5 cm), on rather stout stalks up to 10 mm long; lowland horopito's are elliptic-oblong to elliptic-obovate or ovate-oblong, 3–6 cm wide, with a wavy edge, on slender stalks about 2 cm long. Leaf lengths overlap: usually 7 cm (2.5–10 cm) against 6–10 cm. Mountain alseuosmia is a shrub up to about 50 cm tall, unbranched or with one or two branches; lowland horopito grows to 7–8 m, but small lowland horopito plants closely resemble mountain alseuosmia. In flower, mountain alseuosmia's flowers are tubular, about 8–10 mm long, with five fringed lobes, white to yellowish or reddish and sweet-scented; lowland horopito's are about 1 cm across, with 5–6 separate greenish-yellow petals 5–6 mm long, often several together in the leaf joints. Both have red berries: mountain alseuosmia's are oval, about 9–12 × 5–6 mm; lowland horopito's are round, 5–6 mm across. Mountain alseuosmia does not grow north of Te Moehau and Mt Pirongia. No record of mountain alseuosmia as food was found (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mountain alseuosmia

lookalikes.howToTell: Northland horopito is known only from Mt Manaia and Bream Head at Whangārei Heads and from Logues Bush near Wellsford, and until 2003 its plants were taken for lowland horopito or for hybrids between lowland horopito and horopito. Both are upright shrubs or small trees, to 7–8 m, with glossy leaves without blotches and a conspicuous pale midvein above. Turn a leaf over: Northland horopito's underside is white with a red midvein; lowland horopito's is pale to glaucous but not white, with a pale midvein. Northland horopito's leaf stalks are 4–11 mm long, red-brown to maroon; lowland horopito's are slender, about 2 cm long. Northland horopito's leaf buds and young leaves are usually hairy on the edges, undersides and stalks; lowland horopito is hairless. Leaf sizes overlap: 3.5–11 × 1.8–4.5 cm against 6–10 × 3–6 cm. Northland horopito's flowers are single or in twos or threes, with cream petals; lowland horopito's are greenish yellow, often several together. Northland horopito's ripe fruit is black, 6.4–9.8 mm long; lowland horopito's is red to orange-red, rarely dark, 5–6 mm across. Northland horopito is Threatened – Nationally Critical, and no record of it as food was found (see its page).

summary.text:
Lowland horopito (Pseudowintera axillaris), also called lowland pepper tree, is a pungent-leaved shrub or small tree of the Winteraceae, endemic to New Zealand.
It grows on the North and South Islands from latitude 35° south, extending to 42° in the South Island west of the main divide; it is scarce north of Auckland and reaches to near Westport. The Winteraceae is one of the most primitive families of flowering plants. Lowland horopito hybridises frequently with horopito (P. colorata) where the two meet, and browsing animals find it unpalatable. Te Arawa call the fruit matou. It is grown from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in March–April, and its seeds are spread by birds. It is ranked Not Threatened (2023).

warnings: The heat builds gradually, so you may not feel it at first, and milk does not cool it. Nibble lightly on a leaf before you use more. A leaf infusion can leave a burning feeling in the throat and chest.

Horopito can numb some of your taste buds for a while, so what you eat or drink afterwards tastes odd; the more you have, the stronger the effect. A brew of lowland horopito leaves strongly dulls the taste of sweet, and possibly bitter, things, but not of salt or sour.
