harvestEthics.text: Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text: A dense, bushy, upright tree to 15 m tall, with a trunk up to 35 cm across and brown bark that is flaky to hard, rough and fissured. Young stems have smooth internodes above and below the nodes. The leaves are opposite, lanceolate to oval and widest above the middle, 30–100 mm long and 15–30 mm wide, with a tapered, sharp-pointed tip and a wedge-shaped base, on stalks 2–10 mm long. They are hairless, glossy green above and paler below, with numerous side veins, a vein inside the leaf margin that is usually visible, and small, rather scattered oil glands. New growth is coppery. The flowers come in clusters at or near the ends of young branches, mainly from summer to early autumn: the funnel-shaped calyx is green at first and turns red, the round white petals are 4–5 mm long, free and spreading, and the numerous white stamens are 6–15 mm long, longer than the petals. The fruit is berry-like, round to egg-shaped, 15–25 mm wide and magenta, occasionally white, pink or purple. It holds a single large seed, which usually shows lines of division marking its many embryos; this sets its fruit apart from the other Syzygium species in New Zealand.

lookalikes.howToTell: Lilly pilly's flowers are smaller: its petals are about 2 mm long, joined into a small cap, and its stamens reach about 3 mm; magenta lilly pilly has free, spreading petals 4–5 mm long and stamens 6–15 mm long. Lilly pilly's fruit is nearly round to broadly oblong or obovoid and often slightly flattened, with a hollow at the tip where the calyx lobes have fallen; magenta lilly pilly's is round to egg-shaped, with somewhat swollen calyx lobes at the tip. Lilly pilly's leaves are broader for their length: ovate or elliptic-ovate and usually 2–5 cm wide, against magenta lilly pilly's lanceolate to obovate leaves 1.5–3 cm wide that taper to the base. Fruit colour does not separate them: lilly pilly's is pinkish mauve or white, and magenta lilly pilly's is usually magenta but can be white, pink or purple. Cut a fruit open: magenta lilly pilly's single large seed usually shows lines of division marking its many embryos, which sets it apart from the other Syzygium species in New Zealand. Lilly pilly's fruit is eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Lilly pilly

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the strong young shoots: brush cherry's are more or less four-winged, the wings running down from each leaf stalk and joining just above the next pair of leaves in a small pocket or hump; magenta lilly pilly's shoots are at most angled, with smooth internodes and no pocket. This works even on young plants. Cut a fruit open: magenta lilly pilly's seed usually shows lines of division marking its several embryos; brush cherry's seed has a single embryo. Magenta lilly pilly's fruit is round to egg-shaped and usually magenta, but can be white, pink or purple; brush cherry's is oblong to obovoid and crimson to crimson-purple, so colour alone is not reliable. Leaf size and the white flowers overlap. Magenta lilly pilly is sometimes sold in New Zealand under brush cherry's scientific name, so a garden label does not settle it. Brush cherry is much less often planted than magenta lilly pilly, and its wild seedlings are uncommon. Brush cherry's fruit is eaten too (see its page).

preparation.text: Eaten fresh, or cooked into jams; it also makes a cordial and a cold fruit drink. Each fruit holds a single large seed.

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) magenta lilly pilly fruit; 2 tablespoons sugar; 750 ml (3 cups) boiling water; ice (optional). Wash the fruit, put it in a bowl and sprinkle over the sugar. Pour over the boiling water and leave to stand until almost cold. Mash with a potato masher to crush out the juice, then pour the fruit and juice through a sieve into a jug to remove the stones and pulp. Chill in the fridge, or add a few ice blocks, to serve. Serves 2.
recipes.title: Lilly pilly summer drink

recipes.method: 1 kg magenta lilly pilly fruit; 750 ml (3 cups) water; juice of 2 lemons; 750 ml (3 cups) sugar; 3 teaspoons citric acid. Put the washed fruit in a large saucepan with the water and bring to the boil, then cover and simmer for 20 minutes until cooked. Let cool. Line a sieve with a jelly bag or flannelette and set it over a large clean saucepan; tip in the cooked fruit and its juice and pour in the lemon juice. Gather the bag around the fruit and squeeze and twist it until all the juice is forced out, then discard the remains. Bring the liquid to a rapid boil, stir in the sugar and citric acid, and when they have completely dissolved, pour through a funnel into hot, clean bottles and seal. To drink, put 1–2 tablespoons in a glass and dilute with tap or soda water. Refrigerate after opening. Makes about two 750 ml bottles.
recipes.title: Lilly pilly cordial

recipes.method: 550 g magenta lilly pilly fruit, weighed after the stones are removed; 385 g white sugar; 1–2 lemons; 2 apples. The evening before, juice the lemons and soak their pips overnight in a little water to draw out pectin. Wash the fruit and take the stone out of each one (a cherry pitter helps). Weigh the pitted fruit and add sugar at 70% of its weight (700 g sugar per 1 kg fruit); stir and leave to stand until juicy. Slice the apples thinly into a small pot, cover with about 1 cm of water and simmer until the water has halved and turned light golden, then strain off this liquid and add it to the fruit. Put the fruit mixture in a heavy-based pot with the lemon juice and the soaking water from the pips (without the pips). Bring to the boil, then simmer: after about 12–15 minutes the fruit turns translucent and the jam thickens. Test a drop on a chilled plate; if it is still runny, simmer a little longer and test again. Ladle into hot, sterilised jars and seal while hot. Makes about 2 × 350 ml jars.
recipes.title: Magenta lilly pilly jam

summary.text: A tree of the myrtle family from coastal rainforest in New South Wales, where it is uncommon in the wild and listed as threatened, but it is widely cultivated. In New Zealand it is planted in parks and gardens or for shelter, and self-sows freely; it grows in lowland areas of the North Island and is uncommon in the South Island. Biota of New Zealand lists it as a casual exotic, not fully naturalised. It is often sold in New Zealand under the name S. australe (brush cherry), a name once misapplied to this species, and the two are commonly confused. It is not on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.

identification.text: It is a small, bushy tree reaching 8–12 m in height with a trunk diameter of 20–50 cm. The branches are closely set, with slender branchlets. Adult leaves are somewhat glossy and hairless; they are dark green or yellow-green above and often mottled with maroon or purple and a pale wine-red underneath. The fruit is a fleshy white drupe, broadly oblong, 6–8 mm long. The flowers have insignificant petals and are wind pollinated, with long anthers and stigmas. The thin, mottled leaves have a small pit where the veins join. Young plants have small spoon-shaped leaves like those of Coprosma spathulata; run a finger along a young branchlet: in māmāngi it feels smooth, while in C. spathulata it is finely wrinkled and feels like a cat's tongue.

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Kanono's young twigs are hairless; Māmāngi's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Karamū's young twigs are hairless; Māmāngi's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Shining karamū's young twigs are hairless; Māmāngi's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Both can have a rounded or notched leaf tip, so the tip does not separate them; taupata's leaf is very glossy, māmāngi's only somewhat glossy. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Those figures fit the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa; the North Island's wild subsp. minor has thinner, papery leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) on stalks about 10–18 mm long, and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma's young twigs are hairless; Māmāngi's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Hūpiro's young twigs are hairless; Māmāngi's are hairy. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Swamp coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

habitat.text:
Grows throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands, from the coast to low alpine areas up to about 1800 m, in many kinds of habitat, including wetlands, river gravels and dry hillsides, often forming extensive thickets. Once established it tolerates drought, waterlogging, strong wind and frost, and it grows on poorer, colder, wetter and more acidic ground than kānuka.
In gardens it does best in full sun and well-drained soil.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text:
A shrub or small tree, usually up to about 4–5 m tall but recorded to about 12 m; low-growing and creeping forms are also found in the wild. The bark is grey, dark grey or reddish and peels in papery flakes that are reddish underneath. Young branchlets are hairy, losing their hairs with age. The leaves are alternate, narrow to oval, 5–20 mm long and 1–8 mm wide, stiff, with rough or finely scalloped edges, and almost stalkless; most end in a long, stiff, prickly point, so they are prickly to grasp. The flowers are borne singly in the leaf axils, usually 10–20 mm across (8–25 mm), with five white petals, sometimes flushed pink, and usually a red centre; the five sepals soon fall, and the many stamens are shorter than the petals. The fruit is a hard, dry, woody capsule about 5–8 mm wide with a domed top, and it stays on the plant for a long time, so mature plants nearly always carry some.
Mānuka is often confused with kānuka. Its hard, long-lasting, nut-like capsules, sepals that soon fall, sharp-tipped leaves and flowers that appear to be borne singly tell it apart.

lookalikes.howToTell: Feel the leaves: kānuka's are not sharp-pointed and are soft to grasp; mānuka's are rigid and end in a sharp, prickly point. Kānuka's flowers are usually in small clusters; mānuka's are usually borne singly in the leaf axils. Kānuka's sepals persist, and its capsule is about level with, or only slightly above, the rim of the flower cup; mānuka's sepals soon fall, and its woody capsule stands clearly above the rim and stays on the plant for a long time. Both have white, occasionally pink, flowers, and bark is not a reliable test: both shed it in long strips or flakes.

summary.text:
Mānuka or kahikātoa (Leptospermum scoparium) is a shrub or small tree in the myrtle family, Myrtaceae. It is indigenous to New Zealand and is also found in Australia, especially Tasmania, whose plants are very similar to some South Island forms but have a lignotuber, wider leaf bases and longer, more prickly leaf tips; there is evidence that mānuka in the strict sense is endemic to New Zealand, but more study is needed. Captain Cook called it 'tea tree' because the leaves were brewed as a substitute for tea. It is a very variable species, with two varieties currently accepted: var. incanum, whose young shoots and buds are covered in long silky grey hairs and whose flowers are pink-white or pink, is confined to the north of the North Island.
Mānuka is one of the few New Zealand native species adapted to fire: it responds by opening its seed capsules and spreading seed onto recently disturbed ground. It is often one of the first plants back on cleared land, and its shade and shelter make a nursery for slower-growing native plants, which in time overtop it and shade it out. Sheep, cattle and goats seldom eat it, so it is widely used in restoration plantings. It is also grown in commercial plantations for oil and honey, and in gardens, especially cultivars with pink, red or double flowers.
Pests and diseases
The adult mānuka beetle (Pyronota festiva) and its larvae feed on Leptospermum scoparium in New Zealand. The scale insect, Eriococcus orariensis, is a sap-sucking insect that feeds on L. scoparium. Plants are sometimes covered with sooty mould, a black fungus that feeds on the honeydew of scale insects.

Pollinators
The sweet-smelling flowers are an important source of pollen and nectar for native bees, flies, moths, beetles and geckos.

Chemistry
Australian populations of Leptospermum scoparium are shown to be chemically distinct from their New Zealand counterparts, with significantly higher levels of cinteole and monoterpines. Chemotypical variations also exist between different populations within New Zealand, leading some to suggest that L. scoparium be divided into three subspecies: those with high pinenes, high triketones, and high sesquiterpenes. Recently, however, new research suggests that plant-to-plant variation far outstrips the variation seen between geographically isolated manuka sites, at least with regard to nectar chemistry.

warnings: A strong brew of the leaves can make you vomit.
Avoid taking large amounts with meals over a long time: its tannins may reduce how well minerals are absorbed.

habitat.text: Lowland forest, frequent except on Stewart Island. It favours fertile, well-drained soils, and like tōtara can grow where there is low rainfall. It is often found in drier climates, where it can dominate alluvial soils that are waterlogged or flooded in winter and dry in summer, and it seems to prefer base-rich soils. In the North Island it grows from sea level to 760 m, and in the South Island to 300 m.

identification.text:
Tree up to 25 m, trunk up to 1.25 m in diameter, bark dark, falling in thick flakes. Juveniles with slender, flexuous, divaricating branchlets, leaves brownish, 5–10 × 1–2 mm, acute. Adults with leaves 1–1.5 cm × 1–2 mm, subdistichous, linear, straight to subfalcate, obtuse, often apiculate, coriaceous, dark green, more or less glaucous below. Male strobili in spikes, 3–5 cm long, 10–30 per spike, perpendicular to the axis; apiculus subacute. Ovules 3–10 per spike about 4 cm long, on short axillary branchlets; peduncle not swollen. Seeds 5–9 mm long, subglobose, apiculus obtuse; black, drupaceous.
Young mataī look so different from the mature trees that early botanists failed to recognise they were the same species. Mataī begins life as a divaricating shrub – a tangle of interlaced branches with tiny brown leaves. Growing slowly in shaded forest, it may take 50 years to reach 2 metres, and eventually reaches 3–5 metres in height. After this, as it continues to grow, it develops a cylindrical trunk and rounded crown. Mature trunks have a hammer-marked appearance, caused by circular pieces of bark flaking off.
Bark dark brown to almost black, falling in thick round flakes that leave hammer-like scars on the trunk. Ripe fruit a fleshy, oily, aromatic, purple-black drupe with a waxy bloom; the stone inside is roughly round, 6–8.5 mm across (sometimes 5.5 mm), and pale orange-yellow.
Small mataī and miro trees look similar, but can be distinguished because miro oozes resin from its bark when it receives an injury.

lookalikes.howToTell: Small mataī and small miro trees look similar. Miro oozes resin from its bark when it is injured, which distinguishes them. Very young mataī is a tangled, divaricating shrub of slender, flexible, interlaced branchlets with tiny brownish leaves 5–10 mm long; young miro looks like a miniature adult, with dark green, feathery leaves up to 3 cm long, flattened into two rows. Look at the stone inside the fruit: mataī's is roughly round, 6–8.5 mm across (sometimes 5.5 mm), and pale orange-yellow; miro's is 11–17 mm long and dark brown to black-brown. Mataī's whole fruit is 5–9 mm long and black to purple-black with a waxy bloom; miro's is up to 20 mm long and usually red or pink-red, but can be purplish with a waxy bloom, so colour alone does not separate them. Mataī's ovules are borne 3–10 on a spike about 4 cm long; miro's are single, rarely paired, on a short branchlet about 1 cm long. On male trees, mataī's pollen cones are in spikes 3–5 cm long with 10–30 cones; miro's are single in the leaf joints, 0.5–1.5 cm long. Adult leaf size only partly separates them: mataī's are 1–1.5 cm long and 1–2 mm wide, miro's 1.5–2.5 cm long and 2–3 mm wide. On big trees, mataī's bark is dark brown to almost black and falls in thick round flakes that leave hammer-like scars; miro's is grey to grey-brown and falls in thick, wavy flakes. Miro's fruit flesh is eaten (see its page).

preparation.text: Eat raw. The ripe fruit is sweet, fragrant and rather slimy; the flesh is oily and aromatic, with a terpene taste. Mataī beer is the sap tapped from the heartwood cracks of old trees and drunk as it is, a rich brown, refreshing drink.

summary.text:
Mataī (Prumnopitys taxifolia) grows to 30 metres tall and the trunk to 2 metres in diameter. It is found throughout lowland forests of the North and South islands. It is most common in the central North Island and locally abundant in the South Island. The extent of mataī has been reduced after the conversion of lowland forest to farmland. Mataī live for about 1,000 years.
Male and female cones are borne on separate trees. Heavy seeding years occur infrequently. Mataī produces hard-coated seeds, each enclosed in a fleshy purple cover. They are dispersed by forest birds, which digest the outer covering and excrete the seeds. By contrast, introduced mammals such as rats, pigs and possums destroy mataī and other podocarp seeds as they feed.
It is endemic to New Zealand, on the North, South and Stewart islands (uncommon on Stewart Island). It is assessed Not Threatened, but mataī forest has been greatly reduced by widespread logging, and very few intact mataī-dominated forests remain. The fruits take 12–18 months to mature. It is a very popular garden tree. It grows slowly: planted trees reach about 13 m tall and 19 cm across after 60 years. Young plants need protecting from frost. When Page (2019) moved miro to the new genus Pectinopitys, he kept mataī in Prumnopitys.
Other names: black pine; young trees are called kāī, māī or kākāī.

warnings: Only the fruit flesh is recorded as eaten. No record of the stone being eaten was found, so whether it is safe is not known.

identification.text: Climber with annual stems up to 10 m long, sparsely covered in harsh hairs, and tendrils branched into 3–5. Leaves grey-green, ovate to broadly ovate in outline, 3.5–19.5 × 4.5–20 cm, heart-shaped at the base with a broad, open notch (the basal lobes do not overlap), shallowly to deeply 5- or 7-lobed, the lobes broadly triangular and pointed, the edges toothed, rough to the touch on both sides. Male flowers white, 5-lobed, 4.5–7.8 mm across, 8–19 along a stalk 2.5–15.5 cm long; female flowers smaller, 2.5–3.5 mm across, 8–11 together in a head. Fruit egg-shaped, about 6–10 mm long, densely covered in spines 1.6–3.6 mm long with backward-pointing barbs. Seeds ellipsoid, 4–5.5 mm long, brown. It flowers and fruits throughout the year in suitable conditions.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: māwhai's are only about 6–10 mm long, egg-shaped, and densely covered in spines 1.6–3.6 mm long with backward-pointing barbs; choko's is a pear-shaped, pale green fruit 10–25 cm long holding a single large, flattened stone, and even the spiny kinds grown in New Zealand carry only small spines. The two have been confused when not in fruit: choko's leaves are larger and darker green, heart-shaped and 10–25 cm wide; māwhai's are grey-green, 3.5–19.5 × 4.5–20 cm, sharply 5- or 7-lobed with toothed edges and rough to the touch, and its stems carry harsh hairs. Māwhai's white male flowers, 4.5–7.8 mm across, come 8–19 along a long stalk, and its female flowers 8–11 together in a head; choko's male flowers are in clusters and its female flowers single. Both grow in the northern North Island: māwhai in coastal and lowland forest, scrub and bracken, and spreading into farmland and urban wasteland; choko near gardens and over hedges and fences. Choko's fruit, seed, shoots and root are eaten (see its page).

summary.text:
Māwhai (Sicyos australis), also called native cucumber, is an annual climbing vine of the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae), native to New Zealand and also found in Australia, and formerly on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands.
In New Zealand it grows in the northern North Island: Northland, Auckland, Waikato and the Bay of Plenty. It seems to have established recently, presumably by natural means, and is spreading into farmland, plantation forestry and urban wasteland. It shares the name māwhai with the endemic Sicyos mawhai, a rarer coastal vine now found mainly on offshore islands. Both have been confused with choko, especially when not in fruit. Flora of New Zealand also lists the Māori name pōhue for it, a name better known for bindweed, whose roots Māori ate; the two plants are unrelated, and no record of māwhai being eaten was found. It is ranked At Risk – Naturally Uncommon (2023), and Regionally Critical in Northland and Auckland. It can catch cucumber, watermelon and zucchini yellow mosaic viruses, though less readily than S. mawhai, and is secure at most known sites.
It is easily grown from seed, though the seed can take several months to germinate, and is occasionally sold by commercial nurseries.

warnings: No record of māwhai as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
When not in fruit it has been mistaken for choko, so check for choko's pear-shaped fruit before picking choko shoots or leaves (see the lookalikes).
The fruits are densely covered in sharply barbed spines; avoid touching them.

identification.text:
Under ideal circumstances, the deciduous plant grows up to 8 metres tall. Generally, it is shorter and more shrub-like than tree-like. With a lifespan of 30–60 years, the tree is rather short-lived. Its bark is greyish brown with deep vertical cracks forming rectangular plates that tend to lift off.
The wild form of M. germanica is mostly a thorny, more shrub-like than tree-like plant, which is between 1.5 and 4 m high. In the cultivated forms, the thorns are usually reduced or even completely absent. In general, the medlar is a small, deciduous tree with an overhanging, almost round crown. The trunk is irregularly shaped. The tree has a height between 1 and 6 m, but can become significantly larger in culture. The diameter at breast height is usually between 20 and 25 cm, but in exceptional cases it can be up to 50 cm. The roots are heavily branched and far-ranging, with a somewhat fibrous root system.
The winter buds are pointed, ovoid and up to 5 millimetres long. The leaves are dark green and elliptic, 8–15 centimetres long and 3–5 cm wide. The leaves are densely hairy (pubescent) below, and turn red in autumn before falling.
Medlar flowers are 2–5 cm in diameter, have a short stalk and are terminal and single on short side shoots. They have five elongated, narrow sepals and five free, white or pale pink petals. The flowers are hermaphrodite and pollinated by bees. Normally, self-pollination occurs in this plant. The flower then develops flattened, reddish-brown, hairy fruits with juicy flesh. The reddish-brown fruit is a pome, 2–3 cm diameter, with wide-spreading persistent sepals around a central pit, giving a 'hollow' appearance to the fruit. In cultivated forms the diameter is even between 3 and 8 cm.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): It is a small, deciduous tree with large, solitary, white flowers and a large, brown, depressed-globose pome-like fruit.
The fruit is about 25 mm across, apple-like, smooth matt brown, open at one end and crowned with a ring of persistent calyx lobes. Old trees grow branches bent again and again at right angles, and the leaves turn russet in autumn (Otago Daily Times).
The leaves have very short stalks and toothed edges, dull green above and felted beneath. The flowers are about 5 cm wide, usually single, sometimes paired. Branches are thorny, though cultivated trees may be thornless (Oregon State University).
The fruit is borne at the tips of shoots and usually holds 5 pips (The Polyculture Project).

preparation.text: Leave the fruit on the tree as long as possible into winter, preferably until after a frost, and pick when it comes away easily, once the leaves have fallen; never pull it off roughly. Fruit that is already soft when picked can be eaten straight away. Store the hard fruit in a single layer, stalk upward, in a cool, dry place until the skin darkens and wrinkles and the flesh turns brown and very soft, which takes from about two weeks to a few months. Scoop out the flesh and discard the skin and pips, or cook the fruit whole and sieve it for jelly or medlar cheese.

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1.4 kg bletted medlars; 1 green apple; 1/2 lemon; 600 g sugar. Rinse and quarter the medlars and put them in a large pot with skins and seeds. Chop the apple, core and seeds included, and add it with the lemon half. Add enough water for the medlars to float, about 2 litres. Bring to the boil, then keep at a low boil for 45 minutes. Ladle into a colander lined with several layers of cheesecloth over a deep bowl and leave to drip overnight without pressing, or the jelly will be cloudy. Next day you should have about 1 litre of liquid. Put a small plate in the freezer. Add the sugar to the juice and cook until it reaches 104°C or sets; test by chilling a spoonful on the cold plate for a few minutes: it is done if it wrinkles when pushed. A few drops of lemon juice can offset the sweetness. Ladle into clean jars.
recipes.title: Medlar Jelly

recipes.method: Ingredients: about 3 kg bletted medlars, about 300 ml water, sugar at half the weight of the pulp (600 g to each 1.2 kg batch of pulp), and for flavour either the juice of one lemon or a heaped teaspoon each of ground ginger and cinnamon with a level teaspoon of nutmeg. Rinse the medlars, mash them into the water in a large pan, bring to a slow boil and simmer 30–40 minutes to free the pulp from the skins and seeds. Press the mush through a colander with a spatula. Warm the pulp until it bubbles gently, add the sugar slowly while stirring until it dissolves, then boil and reduce to a rolling simmer, stirring almost constantly for about an hour, until it is much darker and thick enough to leave trails and cling to the spatula. The pulp spits hot globs: stir gently, wear long sleeves and eye protection. Spoon into sterilised jars, seal and leave to set. The leftover skins and seeds, with about 500 g of whole medlars, can be boiled for a medlar jelly.
recipes.title: Medlar Cheese

recipes.method: Pastry: 240 g plain flour, a pinch of salt, 60 g white cooking fat, 60 g butter, 1 egg lightly beaten, 1–2 tbsp cold water. Filling: about 450 g bletted medlars (to give 300 g purée), 1 tsp ground ginger, 1 tsp ground cinnamon, a grating of nutmeg, 100 g soft light brown sugar, grated zest and juice of 1 orange and 1 lemon, 2 eggs well beaten. Remove the skins and pips from the medlars, push the flesh through a sieve to a smooth purée and mix in the spices. Heat the oven to 200°C. Rub the fats into the flour and salt, add the egg (and water if needed) to form a ball. Line a greased 22 cm loose-bottomed flan tin with two-thirds of the pastry and chill 30 minutes; keep the rest for decoration. Blind bake 15 minutes with foil and beans, remove them, brush the base with egg and bake 5–10 minutes more; trim when cool. Lower the oven to 190°C. Whisk the sugar with the fruit juices (the method also lists honey, which the ingredients omit, without an amount), add the zests and eggs, then beat in the purée. Pour into the case, bake about 25 minutes until partly set, add the pastry decorations and bake another 30–35 minutes until golden and a skewer comes out clean. Cool 10–15 minutes in the tin. Based on Robert May's 1660 recipe; serves 6–8.

summary.text:
Mespilus germanica, known as the medlar or common medlar, is a large shrub or small tree in the rose family Rosaceae.
From an extensive study of literature and plant specimens, Kazimierz Browicz concluded that the true homeland of M. germanica is only in the southeastern part of the Balkan peninsula, in Asia Minor, on the Caucasus, Crimea, northern Iran, and possibly also in Turkmenistan. It is also found in southeastern Europe, especially the Black Sea coasts of Bulgaria and Turkey. Fossil remains, however, have been reported from a wider area, including from Oriolo, Italy (c. 800 kya thousand years ago) and Burgtonna, Germany (130-115 thousand years ago), dating from the Pleistocene.
It is found across southern Europe where it is generally rare. It is reported to be naturalised in some woods in southeast England, but is found in few gardens.
When the genus Mespilus is included in the genus Crataegus, the correct name for this species is Crataegus germanica (L.) Kuntze.
The fruit of this tree, also called medlar, has been cultivated since Roman times. It is usually available in winter and eaten when bletted. It may be consumed raw and in a range of cooked dishes.
The species requires temperate and sub-mediterranean climate conditions with warm summers and mild winters. Air temperatures of 18 to 20 °C are mentioned as favourable for growth, cold of as low as −20 °C is tolerated and late frosts hardly cause any damage. The wild form was observed in dry areas with annual precipitation of 700 mm and at altitudes from 0 to 1,100 m. The species grows in a wide range of soil types and prefers fresh, well-drained loamy soils with a pH that is between 6 and 8.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Mespilus germanica L., medlar, is only seen as a rather uncommon relic of cultivation.
Once popular as a fruit tree, it has fallen out of favour and is now grown more as a picturesque ornamental. It is self-fertile, and within the rose family is most closely allied to Cotoneaster, Amelanchier and hawthorn (Otago Daily Times).
The name germanica means 'of Germany', although Germany is not part of its native range (Oregon State University).
Birds eat the fruit, and the occasional medlar growing wild in a hedge has probably come from bird-spread seed (The Polyculture Project).
The wood has a fine texture, but is very hard. It has a white, slightly pink-tinted sapwood. The core is brownish. The annual rings are clearly visible.
Sexual reproduction is the norm in wild forms of the medlar. The resulting seeds have a germination capacity lasting from 18 to 20 months. The seeds are distributed by various animals such as birds, squirrels and deer. Some varieties are sterile and can therefore only be propagated vegetatively.
The number of chromosomes is given as 2n = 32 or 2n = 34.
Dunedin Botanic Garden has a mature tree (Otago Daily Times, restated).

warnings: The pips contain hydrocyanic acid and should not be eaten in quantity.
Unbletted fruit is hard, acidic and harsh, with a high tannin content; it is eaten only after bletting.
Bletted fruit has dark, wrinkled skin and brown flesh and can look spoiled. Fruit whose skin has burst is open to bacterial and fungal infection.

identification.text:
Perennial with short, vertical, much-branched caudex and numerous fleshy taproots. Leaves all basal, glabrous or furfuraceous, entire to denticulate to pinnatifid. Scapes more or less furfuraceous, naked, unbranched, striate. Bracteoles deltoid to elliptic or lanceolate, obtuse to acuminate. Florets yellow, conspicuously exceeding phyllaries. Achenes narrowed to base, distinctly ribbed, the ribs smooth. Pappus-hairs about 14–24, stiff, brownish, widened to membranous base, barbellate above.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]
Genus (Flora of New Zealand): Capitula solitary on fistular scapes, many-flowered, homogamous. Phyllaries in 1 series, with a few bracteoles at base; receptacle nude, alveolate. Florets perfect, ligulate. Achenes usually glabrous, striate, not beaked; pappus-hairs dilated and paleaceous at base, barbellate above. Scapigerous herbs with milky juice.
Key to the dandelion tribe (Flora of New Zealand vol. IV): Leaves glabrous or with scaly hairs beneath; stellate hairs absent. Involucral bracts with dark eglandular hairs or glabrous; achenes terete; pappus hairs widened to membranous base, pale brown, bristly.
The plant is very variable, with intermediates between its forms: the leaves range from about 1 mm wide (forma linearis), through cut into narrow spreading lobes (forma pinnatifida) and obovate-spathulate (forma obovata), to 10–25 cm long (forma major), and the flower stems reach about 40 cm. Its roots are several, fleshy, cylindrical or long-tapered and usually branched shortly below the leaves; it has no tuber. Its flower heads stay open for only an hour or two, at least in Victoria.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaves with a hand lens: hawkbit's carry hairs that fork into two, sometimes three, at the tip, sparse to dense; microseris's leaves are hairless or have scurfy, scaly hairs beneath. In seed, microseris's achenes are not beaked and are distinctly ribbed, with about 14–24 stiff, brownish pappus hairs, widened at the base and minutely barbed above, not feathery; hawkbit's outer achenes carry only a ring of tiny scales, and its inner ones are shortly beaked, with an inner row of feathery hairs 5–7 mm long. Both send up a leafless, unbranched stem with a single yellow head, both have nodding buds, leaves all in a basal rosette that may be toothed or cut into lobes, and milky sap, so the stem and the leaf shape do not separate them. Hawkbit's leaves are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Hawkbit

lookalikes.howToTell: Autumn hawkbit's stems branch and carry many small narrow bracts, especially near the top; microseris's flower stems are leafless and unbranched, with a single head. Autumn hawkbit holds its buds erect; microseris's buds nod. Autumn hawkbit's outer involucral bracts are about half as long as the inner ones, and its florets are a darker yellow; microseris has a single row of involucral bracts with a few small bracteoles at the base. In seed, autumn hawkbit's achenes carry a single row of feathery hairs; microseris's pappus hairs are stiff, brownish and minutely barbed, not feathery. Leaf hairs do not separate them: autumn hawkbit's leaves are hairless or sparsely hairy, microseris's hairless or scurfy. Both have yellow heads, leaves all in a basal rosette, often toothed or lobed, and milky sap. Autumn hawkbit's leaves are used like dandelion leaves (see its page).

Hawkbit characters from the same description (hairs '2-(3)-fid at tip, sparse to dense'; 'Stems ascending, not branching'; 'Stem bracts 0-(1)'; 'nodding in bud'; outer achenes 'not beaked … with a pappus of scales c. 0.7 mm long'; inner achenes 'shortly beaked … the inner row 5-7 mm long, plumose'); microseris characters from Flora of New Zealand vol. I ('Lvs all basal, glab. or furfuraceous, entire to denticulate to pinnatifid', 'Scapes … naked, unbranched', 'distinctly ribbed', 'Pappus-hairs c. 14-24, stiff, brownish, widened to membranous base, barbellate above'; genus 'not beaked', 'milky juice') and the vol. IV Lactuceae key ('Lvs glabrous or with scaly hairs beneath'; pappus 'bristly', not plumose). Milky latex: the tribe description.

Microseris ↔ autumn hawkbit card (02/11/2026): Flora of New Zealand vol. IV, 'Leontodon autumnalis' (Webb et al. 1988, CC BY-NC-SA, https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/a0f22db2-57c5-49e3-ba23-427498a76666), retrieved 02/11/2026: 'may sometimes resemble forms of the native Microseris scapigera, but is distinguished by the branching stems bearing stem bracts, the outer involucral bracts c. 1/2 the length of inner bracts, the darker yellow florets and plumose pappus hairs'; its description ('Stems erect, branching'; 'Stem bracts numerous, especially above'; 'erect in bud'; 'hairs simple, sparse or 0'; 'Pappus in 1 row; hairs plumose'). Microseris: nodding buds (Webb's hawkbit note), 'Phyll. in 1 series, with a few bracteoles at base' (Allan, genus), leaves 'glab. or furfuraceous' (Allan). Both occur in the South Island (Flora distributions). Autumn hawkbit's edibility from its own entry.

Not carded: catsear, dandelion and native dandelion — no source read names them as confused with Microseris scapigera (Flora of New Zealand's notes name only the two hawkbits). Walsh 2016 suggests Aboriginal people at Coranderrk may have recognised a similarity between Hypochaeris glabra and Microseris, a conjecture about food use, not an identification note.

Crowe sought, 02/11/2026: Useful Temperate Plants' and Plants For A Future's line 'The root tastes like a sweet potato with an occasional hot taste' cites reference [173], Crowe, A. (1990) Native Edible Plants of New Zealand (Hodder and Stoughton). Neither that book nor Crowe's A Field Guide to the Native Edible Plants of New Zealand (1981; 1997; 2004) could be read: no copy on the Internet Archive or Open Library (catalogue records only, no scan), and Google Books blocked access; a Goodreads reader review confirms only that the field guide includes Microseris scapigera. So it is not known whether Crowe wrote the line about the New Zealand plant or about murnong, and it is not used. No New Zealand record of the plant as food was found: Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga has no Microseris record; Papers Past's journals (37 hits for 'Microseris', mostly Transactions of the New Zealand Institute plant lists) mention it only in species lists; Ferdinand von Mueller, Select Extra-tropical Plants (1880, Internet Archive), calls 'Microseris Forsteri' 'The Native Scorzonera of extra-tropical Australia and New Zealand' but records food use only by 'The Australian aborigines'; Lyons, Plant Names (1900), has only 'Australia and New Zealand. Native Scorzonera. Root esculent.' under the old broad name; Cooper & Cambie, New Zealand's Economic Native Plants (1991), lists 'native scorzonera (Microseris scapigera)' beside cranesbills and onion orchid on page 100, but the book is borrow-only and the sentence around it could not be read; Tim Entwisle (Talking Plants, 01/07/2013) found no Māori name and suspected 'yam' was 'borrowed more recently from Australia'. Edible parts stay 'None.' — the owner may borrow Crowe or Cooper & Cambie to settle it.

Owner's links checked 05/11/2026 for a food record — none found for this species: NZPCN, Biota of New Zealand, Flora of New Zealand Online and Plants For A Future (already cited above; no NZ food or Māori use); Atlas of Living Australia, 'Microseris scapigera' (APC concept https://id.biodiversity.org.au/taxon/apni/51268669): common names 'Yam Daisy', 'Murrnong', 'Native Dandelion', 'Yam', no use notes; Victorian Resources Online, 'Native yam daisy' (https://soilhealth.ccmaknowledgebase.vic.gov.au/vro_archive/statewide/pages/sip_salt_native_yam.html): 'Microseris spp. (syn. M. scapigera, M. lanceolata)', roots 'an important food source for indigenous peoples' — the pre-2016 broad name, so not assignable (Walsh 2016); Warndu, 'Murnong' (https://warndu.com/blogs/first-nations-food-guide/murnong): murnong 'is any of the plants Microseris walteri, Microseris lanceolata and Microseris scapigera', describes tubers, no source, New Zealand not mentioned; Slow Food Ark of Taste, 'Yam daisy' (https://www.fondazioneslowfood.com/en/ark-of-taste-slow-food/yam-daisy/): names M. scapigera and M. lanceolata but M. walteri as 'the correct name' for the cultivated plant, south-eastern Australia only. All three describe tubers, which Walsh 2016 gives to M. walteri and not to M. scapigera, so they describe murnong. nativeplants.nz, 'Microseris scapigera' (https://www.nativeplants.nz/microseris-scapigera.html): no food use; its 'dense, stiff tufts', 'flowering panicles' and '1000 to 2000 meters' contradict Flora of New Zealand (solitary heads on naked scapes; lowland to subalpine), so it is not used. Edible parts stay 'None.'

Owner answer 05/11/2026 ('yes', after asking 'is it the same species as the australian one? if so there is no reason why it would be only edible in one country and not the other'): caution doNotEat → careRequired; edible parts 'None.' → roots, raw or cooked; preparation, harvest ethics (Not Threatened sentence plus NZPCN regional cautions), warnings and both reverse cards updated. Same species in New Zealand and Australia: Walsh 2016 (basalt plains of western Victoria and elevated Tasmania), Australian Plant Census via ALA, Flora of New Zealand Online. Food evidence for M. scapigera in the post-2016 sense: Walsh 2016's raw tasting, and Campanelli, M., Muir, J., Mora, A., Clarke, D.R. & Griffin, D. 2018, 'Re-Creating an Aboriginal Earth Oven with Clayey Heating Elements: Experimental Archaeology and Paleodietary Implications', EXARC Journal 2018/2 (CC BY 4.0), https://exarc.net/issue-2018-2/ea/re-creating-aboriginal-earth-oven-clayey-heating-elements-experimental-archaeology-and-paleodietary, retrieved 05/11/2026 — nursery-grown M. scapigera '(used in place of the traditional M. walteri)', '1-3 tapered roots, up to 2 g each, and about 6 cm long'; the 'crunchy and bitter roots' cooked about 18 hours in an earth oven 'had become soft, almost creamy, and palatable, with a particular sweet-smoky smell and a nutty taste'. No report of harm found. The 02/11 line recording edible parts 'None.' and doNotEat is superseded. No recipes: the root harvest kills the plant, the national status rests on poor data, and the owner chose careRequired with no recipes. Months left empty (year-round): the roots of this perennial (Flora of New Zealand) are present all year.

summary.text:
Microseris scapigera is a yellow-flowered daisy, a perennial herb, found in New Zealand and Australia. It is the only New Zealand species of Microseris, and one of three Australian species along with Microseris lanceolata and Microseris walteri. It is classified into a group of plants, the tribe Cichorieae, that includes chicory and dandelion.
The murnong or "yam daisy" has been referred to as M. scapigera, M. lanceolata, or M. forsteri, but is now classified as M. walteri.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North, South and Stewart Islands, not recently recorded north of about latitude 37°. Forma linearis grows from latitude 38° 30' southwards, forma pinnatifida from latitude 39° 30' southwards, forma obovata between latitudes 41° and 42°, and forma major on the Ure River, Marlborough. The forms are informal, there are intermediates, and the distribution and status of the complex need further study.
Its national conservation status (2023) is Not Threatened, with low confidence for lack of data on population size and trend. Regionally it is ranked extirpated in Northland and Regionally Critical in the Wellington region. An unnamed plant on the Brothers Islands, Microseris aff. scapigera, is ranked At Risk – Naturally Uncommon.
Unlike murnong, whose tuber was a staple food in south-eastern Australia, it has no tuber.

warnings: Murnong or yam daisy, the Australian plant whose sweet tubers were a staple food, is a different species (Microseris walteri) and is not a New Zealand plant. This plant has no tuber; its roots are small, fleshy and slightly bitter. Eating them rests on two tastings by researchers; no traditional use of them as food has been confirmed.
Its single yellow heads on leafless, unbranched stems, with buds that nod, look like hawkbit's. Check the leaf hairs and the seed hairs to be sure which plant you have (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
Unmistakable: the flowering stem passes straight through the centre of a single round, saucer-like leaf, with a small spray of white flowers rising from the middle. Nothing else in NZ looks like it.
Fleshy taprooted annual. Stems erect or ascending, 10–30 cm tall. Rosette leaves entire; lamina rhomboid to spathulate to broadly ovate, subacute or acute, (5)–10–30 × (5)–10–35 mm; petiole (1.5)–5–15 cm long. Stem leaves 2, united to form a 1–3 cm wide suborbicular involucre to the inflorescence. Inflorescence a (1)–5–15-flowered bracteate raceme with 1–5 basal flowers, all flowers clustered at first. Bracts obovate, subacute, 3–6 × 1–4 mm. Pedicels (3)–5–15 mm long. Sepals persistent, broadly ovate, 1.5–2.5 mm long. Petals 5, white, entire or notched, 2–3–(6) mm long. Stamens 5, opposite the petals. Capsule subglobose, shorter than the sepals. Seeds 1–(3) per capsule, elliptic, smooth, shiny, black with white aril, 1.2–1.5 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

preparation.text: Raw. It is a salad green and cooking wastes it.

recipes.method: Makes about 360–480 ml. 480 ml (2 cups) miner's lettuce; 1 large garlic clove, chopped; 15 ml (1 tbsp) fresh lemon juice; 60 ml (¼ cup) olive oil; 15 ml (1 tbsp) nutritional yeast; 80 ml (⅓ cup) fresh or frozen peas; 60 ml (¼ cup) raw cashews. Wash the miner's lettuce and put it in a blender or food processor with everything else. Blend until smooth, adding a little water if it is too thick to turn over. Taste and adjust with salt, more nutritional yeast, lemon juice or garlic. The author serves it as a dip with crackers and raw vegetables, or stirs it through pasta.
recipes.title: Miner's lettuce pesto

recipes.method: Serves 4. 60 ml (¼ cup) pine nuts or sesame seeds; 15 ml (1 tbsp) olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) rice vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) chopped fresh basil, or 10 ml (2 tsp) dried; about 1 litre (4 cups) miner's lettuce, stems and flowers included, rinsed and crisped; salt and pepper. In a small frying pan, 15–20 cm across, stir the nuts in the oil over low heat until golden, 3–4 minutes. Add the vinegar and leave to cool. Tip the nut mixture into a wide bowl, add the basil and miner's lettuce, toss, and season with salt and pepper.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In the Auckland region (Regionally Vulnerable), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it. In Northland (Regionally Declining), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.
On the Chatham Islands, where the variety var. martinii grows (At Risk – Naturally Uncommon), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text:
Shrub up to 3–(6) m. tall, sometimes depressed or prostrate. Branches divaricate; branchlets more or less pubescent, more or less interlacing, becoming glabrous. Leaves opposite or in opposite fascicles on slender pubescent petioles 1–2 mm long. Stipules subacute to obtuse, pubescent, sheath short, cilia absent or very few, denticle solitary. Lamina linear- to broad-oblong, obtuse to subacute, coriaceous, dark green above, paler below; (7)–10–14–(16) × 2–3–(5) mm. Reticulations of veins evident, at least below. male 1–4 axillary clusters on very short arrested branchlets; calyx minutely toothed; corolla narrow-funnelform, lobes ovate-oblong, acute, shorter than tube. female solitary, terminal on short branchlets; calyx-teeth short, obtuse; corolla-tube short, lobes long, acute. Drupe pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, globose, about 7 mm long.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Kanono's young twigs are hairless; Mingimingi's are more or less hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Karamū's young twigs are hairless; Mingimingi's are more or less hairy. Mingimingi freely hybridises with karamū and can form extensive hybrid swarms: the hybrids have glossy, trowel-shaped leaves 3–5 cm long, and backcrosses have intermediate leaves, some as small as 2 cm. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Shining karamū's young twigs are hairless; Mingimingi's are more or less hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Those figures fit the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa; the North Island's wild subsp. minor has thinner, papery leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) on stalks about 10–18 mm long, and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma's young twigs are hairless; Mingimingi's are more or less hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Hūpiro's young twigs are hairless; Mingimingi's are more or less hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Both are twiggy shrubs with wide-angled, interlacing branches and more or less hairy young twigs, so neither the branching nor the twig hairs separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Swamp coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. The leaf veins separate them: mingimingi shows the midrib and the net of veins, sand coprosma the midrib alone. Sand coprosma's leaves are yellowish green, mingimingi's dark green. Both have pale blue fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Sand coprosma

summary.text:
Coprosma propinqua is a New Zealand plant of the genus Coprosma in the family Rubiaceae.
It is one of the most widely-distributed Coprosma species in New Zealand, ranging from Mangōnui in the North Island to as far south as Stewart Island, (var. propinqua) and in the Chatham Islands (var. martinii).

habitat.text: Lowland to montane forest. The tree prefers moist, well-drained soils, and fine specimens grow on the deep pumice soils of the central North Island. It is found wherever rimu grows, up to about 1000 m in the North Island, 750 m in the South Island and 300 m on Stewart Island. It grows on most soil types but does poorly on waterlogged or droughty sites, and survives in quite low light, though mature trees also grow in full light.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

identification.text:
Tree up to 25 m, trunk up to 1 m in diameter, bark grey-brown, falling in thick flakes. Leaves of juveniles up to 3 cm long, narrow-linear, acute; of adults 1.5–2.5 cm × 2–3 mm, dark green, distichous, patent, subfalcate, subsessile, acute to subacute, midvein distinct, margins recurved. Male strobili solitary, axillary, almost sessile, 0.5–1.5 cm long, furnished at base with several scales; apiculus broadly triangular, subacute. Ovules solitary or rarely paired on short branchlets about 1 cm long, densely furnished at base with triangular scales, not succulent. Seeds broadly oblong to subspherical, drupaceous, purplish, with glaucous bloom, up to 20 mm long.
Bark thick and grey, falling in thick, wavy flakes. Foliage feathery, dark green to bronze-green. Ripe fruit a broadly oblong to almost round, red or pink-red, oily drupe up to 20 mm long; the stone inside is 11–17 mm long and dark brown to black-brown. The feathery foliage and red, plum-like fruit are unlike any other New Zealand conifer, but young plants can be confused with yew; miro's leaves have no stalks.
Young plants look like miniature versions of adults. They have dark green, feathery, needle-like leaves flattened into two rows. Small mataī and miro trees look similar, but can be distinguished because miro oozes resin from its bark when it receives an injury.

lookalikes.howToTell: Young yew and young miro look alike. Look at where each leaf joins the shoot: yew's leaves have a short yellowish-green stalk; miro's are stalkless or nearly so, each leaf blade running straight into the stem. Miro's shoots are yellow; yew's are green and ribbed. Look at the fruit: miro's is a plum-like drupe up to 20 mm long, red to pink-red or purplish with a waxy bloom, with a single large stone 11–17 mm long enclosed in the flesh; yew's is a red, fleshy cup 10–15 mm long that almost surrounds the seed and is open at the end. Leaf size does not separate them: miro's adult leaves are 1.5–2.5 cm long and 2–3 mm wide, yew's 1.2–2.5 cm long and 1.5–2 mm wide. Nearly every part of yew is poisonous, including the seed inside the red flesh. Check the leaf base on every plant.
lookalikes.name: Yew

lookalikes.howToTell: The bark of a mature miro is easily mistaken for kahikatea's: both are grey to grey-brown and fall in thick flakes, so bark alone does not separate them. Look at the base: miro usually has no buttresses; kahikatea's trunk is often fluted and buttressed. Look at the foliage: miro's adult leaves are flat, dark green, 1.5–2.5 cm long and 2–3 mm wide, spreading in two rows; adult kahikatea leaves are tiny scales 1–2 mm long pressed tightly against the stem (juvenile leaves 3–7 mm). Look at the fruit: miro's is a plum-like fruit up to 20 mm long with no separate fleshy receptacle; kahikatea's is a round, purple-black seed 4–6 mm across on a fleshy, yellow to orange-red receptacle 2.5–6.5 mm long. Kahikatea's receptacle is eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Kahikatea

lookalikes.howToTell: Small miro and small mataī trees look similar. Miro oozes resin from its bark when it is injured, which distinguishes them. Young miro looks like a miniature adult, with dark green, feathery leaves up to 3 cm long, flattened into two rows; very young mataī is a tangled, divaricating shrub of slender, flexible, interlaced branchlets with tiny brownish leaves 5–10 mm long. Look at the stone inside the fruit: miro's is 11–17 mm long and dark brown to black-brown; mataī's is roughly round, 6–8.5 mm across (sometimes 5.5 mm), and pale orange-yellow. Miro's whole fruit is up to 20 mm long and usually red or pink-red, but can be purplish with a waxy bloom; mataī's is 5–9 mm long and black to purple-black with a waxy bloom, so colour alone does not separate them. Miro's ovules are single, rarely paired, on a short branchlet about 1 cm long; mataī's are borne 3–10 on a spike about 4 cm long. On male trees, miro's pollen cones are single in the leaf joints, 0.5–1.5 cm long; mataī's are in spikes 3–5 cm long with 10–30 cones. Adult leaf size only partly separates them: miro's are 1.5–2.5 cm long and 2–3 mm wide, mataī's 1–1.5 cm long and 1–2 mm wide. On big trees, miro's bark is grey to grey-brown and falls in thick, wavy flakes; mataī's is dark brown to almost black and falls in thick round flakes that leave hammer-like scars. Mataī's fruit flesh is eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mataī

summary.text:
Miro (Pectinopitys ferruginea) grows to 25 metres tall and its trunk to 1 metre in diameter, forming a round-headed tree. It is widely distributed in lowland and high-altitude forests from north Auckland to Stewart Island, and is most common on the West Coast.
Each year miro produces a regular crop of fleshy, bright red seeds, which smell strongly of turpentine. The seeds are an important food for forest birds in winter.
It is endemic to New Zealand. It was long known as Prumnopitys ferruginea, and before that Podocarpus ferrugineus; Page (2019) moved it to the new genus Pectinopitys.
It is assessed Not Threatened, but miro forest has been greatly reduced by widespread logging, and very few intact miro-dominated forests remain. The fruits take 12–18 months to mature. The large, oily fruits are an important food of the kererū, the only living native bird able to disperse them, and Māori hunters snared kererū at miro trees, setting water troughs nearby.
Other names: brown pine; Biota of New Zealand also lists the Māori name toromiro.

warnings: Young miro looks like young yew, which is poisonous. Check where the leaf joins the shoot before eating (see the lookalikes).
Only the flesh is recorded as eaten. No record of the stone being eaten was found, so whether it is safe is not known.

habitat.text: Usually only a minor escape from cultivation in open or much disturbed sites in the vicinity of planted trees, occasionally extensively naturalised in scrub and herbaceous vegetation on slopes down-wind from plantations or forests. A plant of coastal and lowland sites of low fertility, growing in scrub and forest margins, shrubland, short tussockland, sand dunes, cliffs and bluffs. It tolerates drought but not shade or frost, and dislikes waterlogged ground.

identification.text:
Medium-sized to very large tree; habit variable, generally more or less spreading, with foliage in dense terminal clusters. Bark thick, deeply fissured and ridged in mature trees, dark grey on surface, reddish brown beneath. Shoots brown or greyish brown, occasionally somewhat glaucous when young, glabrous. Buds cylindric or cylindric-ovoid, thinly resinous; scales appressed, chestnut-brown. Leaves 3 per fascicle, (3)–6–15 cm × 1.2–2 mm, deep or dark green, more or less spreading, moderately rigid; resin canals median; sheath initially long but rarely > 1 cm long on mature leaves, persistent. Male strobili 0.7–1.5 cm long, cylindric. Conelets stalked, cylindric, scales with short mucro. Mature cones sessile or subsessile, 1–about 6 in a cluster, backward pointing but not pendent, long-persistent, eventually falling intact, 6–13 × 4.5–8.5 cm when closed, more or less ovoid, brown at maturity; base asymmetric; apophyses on upper side enlarged and rounded; umbo usually not armed at maturity. Seed wing more or less oblong, only slightly wider towards apex, 1.5–2 cm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Spontaneous hybrids with a closely related species from coastal California, P. attenuata, knobcone pine, are recorded in New Zealand. Plants attributable to this hybrid, P. ×attenuradiata, have very strongly reflexed cones which lie parallel to the branch, and the umbos erect and then inflexed.
Male cones cluster at the ends of new shoots in spring, light brown to pinkish; they are borne on the lower branches and the seed cones on the upper part of the tree.

summary.text:
Pinus radiata (syn. Pinus insignis), the Monterey pine, insignis pine or radiata pine, is a species of pine native to the Central Coast of California, and the Guadalupe and Cedros islands of Mexico.
In the United States, it is native to three very limited areas located in Santa Cruz, Monterey, and San Luis Obispo Counties of California.
In Mexico, it is found on two islands in the Pacific Ocean, Guadalupe Island and Cedros Island.
Edward Palmer and Francescho Franceschi were the first to discover the pines on Guadalupe Island. When Franceschi visited in 1892, he noted that they extended all over the northern and northwestern part of the island, comprising a very thick forest, with some of the finest trees growing with the Guadalupe palm.
On Cedros Island, the pines are more abundant, being found in far greater numbers partly due to the lack of feral goats. (Goats were exterminated on Guadalupe island by 2007.) They are found at lower elevations than on Guadalupe, at around 285 to 690 m, on the windward ridges and canyons of the north and central parts of the island. In both cases, the pines seem to be heavily dependent on locations with a high frequency of fog.
In Australia, New Zealand, and Spain it is the leading introduced tree and in Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Kenya, and South Africa it is a major plantation species. It is also an introduced tree on the world's most remote inhabited island, Tristan da Cunha.
On Guadalupe Island, located 280 km off the mainland coast, the pines are found on the steep northern end of the island, at elevations of around 500 to 1,200 m, where they follow the ridgetops and steep slopes.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1904. Pinus radiata is by far the most important timber tree in New Zealand and is the usual species planted for shelter as well, so much so that there are few settled areas where its dark green crowns are not a characteristic feature of the landscape. In view of its success and abundance in cultivation throughout lowland New Zealand it is perhaps surprising that it is not more extensively naturalised.
Throughout lowland New Zealand, to nearly 1000 m on Mt Tarawera in the North Island and to 500 m in the Amuri Range in the South Island, probably commonest north of the Waikato, but even occasionally reported from the wettest western areas (e.g., Big Bay in westernmost Otago).
One of the first recorded in New Zealand was planted at Mt Peel Station in South Canterbury in 1859, and within ten years large quantities of seed were coming from California; it became the standard Canterbury firewood and shelter tree. The Grey Pine at Geraldine, planted in 1860, is 48 m tall and one of the largest of its species in the world.

warnings: In New Zealand, cows late in pregnancy have aborted after eating its needles, especially where pines had been pruned or thinned, though much of the evidence is circumstantial. Its foliage contains isocupressic acid, a compound that causes abortion in cattle, at lower levels than ponderosa pine's.
Take extra care in pregnancy: many sources recommend against pine needle tea, and any conifer, while pregnant.
Pine wood, sawdust and resin can cause dermatitis in sensitive people.
Try only a little the first time: allergic reactions to conifers are not common, but are more likely than with most foods.
Do not pick from trees that may have been sprayed. Wilding conifers are controlled with herbicide, and urban trees may have been sprayed with pesticides or exposed to other pollutants.

habitat.text:
Around gardens, in waste places, plantations and other modified habitats.
It also grows on coastal and lowland cliffs and bluffs. It invades intact and disturbed forest and forest margins, tracks, coastline, dunes, cliffs, shrubland, mangroves, orchards and urban areas, and almost any frost-free habitat; it tolerates shade, drought or damp, wind, salt and many soil types, but is frost tender.

identification.text:
Vigorous liane with twining puberulent stems. Petioles to about 4 cm long, densely puberulent or whitish tomentulose. Lamina 2.7–12 × 1.5–6 cm, ovate-oblong or oblong, dark green and becoming glabrous above except for midrib, glaucous-white tomentulose beneath; base deeply cordate with acute sinus, or truncate on flowering shoots; apex rounded and mucronate. Flowers usually 2–4. Peduncles and pedicels to about 1.5 cm long, tomentulose. Bracts usually shorter than the longer pedicels, linear or linear-oblong. Calyx 8–15 mm long; segments ovate, imbricate, tomentulose. Corolla (1.7–)2–2.5 × 1.5–2 cm, deeply campanulate, white, sometimes strongly streaked with pinkish mauve inside. Gynostegium ½–⅔ length of corolla tube. Follicle to 10(–12) × 7 cm, oblong-ovoid or ovoid, green, thick and leathery, minutely tomentulose, with carpel groove down inner face. Seeds 7–8 mm long, oblong-spathulate, dark brown, tuberculate; silken apical tuft 3–5 cm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
A rampant evergreen vine up to 10 m tall, with smelly, milky sap; the stems are woody near the base. The leaves are in opposite pairs, dull and hairless on top and greyish-downy underneath. The flowers come from December to May. The pear-shaped, choko-like pods hold kapok-like pulp and split open to release many black, thistledown-like seeds on the wind. Seedlings are best told by their sticky sap.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at how it climbs: choko holds on with tendrils on the stem; moth plant's stems twine. Look at the leaves: choko's are heart-shaped, 10–25 cm wide and more grape-like; moth plant's are 1.5–6 cm wide, ovate-oblong or oblong, in opposite pairs, dark green above and glaucous-white and downy underneath. Cut the fruit open: choko's holds a single large, flattened stone in firm green to white flesh; moth plant's thick, leathery pod holds kapok-like pulp and many dark brown seeds, 7–8 mm long, each with a silky tuft 3–5 cm long. In flower, moth plant's are white, deeply bell-shaped, about 2–2.5 cm long, sometimes streaked pinkish mauve inside, usually 2–4 together; choko's are small, white or greenish, the male ones in clusters and the female ones single. The fruits are of much the same pear shape and size (choko's 10–25 cm long, moth plant's pods up to 10, sometimes 12, cm long), and both grow around gardens and over hedges in the Auckland area and the Bay of Plenty. Choko's fruit, shoots and root are eaten (see its page).

summary.text:
Moth plant (Araujia sericifera, called Araujia hortorum by New Zealand botanists), also known as kapok vine, cruel plant and wild choko vine, is a poisonous climbing vine of the dogbane family (Apocynaceae) from southern Brazil and Argentina, introduced to New Zealand.
It is cultivated throughout New Zealand but naturalised only in warmer areas: occasionally throughout the North Island, especially around Auckland and the coastal Bay of Plenty, and near Blenheim; it was first recorded wild in 1888. Its flowers trap and kill visiting moths, butterflies and bees in a sticky secretion. Each pod holds about 400 wind-borne seeds, which stay viable for at least 5 years.
It is an Unwanted Organism and a National Pest Plant Accord species, is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and is in most regional pest management plans. It grows quickly up into the canopy and smothers and kills the plants beneath, preventing native plants from establishing.

warnings: Do not eat any part of moth plant. The white milky sap in every part of the plant is poisonous, so its green, choko-like pods should never be put in the mouth.
The sap causes dermatitis and can sting the skin and eyes: protect your skin from it when pulling or handling the vine.
Choko, which is eaten, has similar pear-shaped fruit and climbs over hedges and fences around gardens in the same districts. Check the leaves and how it climbs before picking (see the lookalikes).
