identification.text:
Glabrous shrub up to c. 5 dm tall, unbranched or occasionally with 1–2 branches, rarely taller and more branched; branchlets dark purple. Leaves on rather stout petioles up to 10 mm long. Lamina obovate, cuneately narrowed to base, obtuse, apiculate, (2.5)–7–(10) × 2–2.5–(3.5) cm, submembranous, entire or with a few minute teeth. Inflorescence of usually solitary flowers on glabrous peduncles. Calyx 5-lobed; lobes deltoid, acute. Corolla ± 8–10 mm long, yellowish to reddish; lobes 5, fimbriate. Berry ellipsoid, ± 9–12 × 5–6 mm, bright shining red.
It is inconspicuous unless in flower or fruit. The leaves are glossy, often red-edged and sometimes flecked red; the flowers are white, tubular and sweet-scented, and the red berries fleshy and conspicuous. Its leaves are strikingly like horopito's. Told from horopito and lowland horopito by its thin, not leathery, leaves, its tubular flowers with fringed lobes, and its oval berries 9–12 mm long.

lookalikes.howToTell: Feel the leaf: mountain alseuosmia's is thin, horopito's leathery. Horopito's leaves are dull, elliptic to broadly elliptic with a wavy edge, on slender stalks 5–10 mm long; mountain alseuosmia's are glossy, widest towards the tip and narrowed wedge-like to the base, with a tiny point at the tip and the edge entire or with a few minute teeth, on rather stout stalks up to 10 mm long. Both can show red: horopito's leaves are blotched red in exposed places, mountain alseuosmia's often red-edged and sometimes flecked red, and their leaf sizes overlap. Horopito grows to 2 m, sometimes 3.5 m; mountain alseuosmia is a shrub up to about 50 cm tall, unbranched or with one or two branches, but a small plant could be either. In flower, horopito's flowers have 5–6 separate greenish-yellow petals 4–5 mm long; mountain alseuosmia's are tubular, about 8–10 mm long, with five fringed lobes, white to yellowish or reddish and sweet-scented. Horopito's berries are round, dark red to black, 3–6 mm across; mountain alseuosmia's are oval, about 9–12 × 5–6 mm, bright shining red. Horopito grows on the North, South and Stewart Islands; mountain alseuosmia does not grow on Stewart Island, nor north of Te Moehau and Mt Pirongia, and in the South Island only in the west, from North-West Nelson to near Okarito. Horopito's leaves are eaten as a spice (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Horopito

lookalikes.howToTell: Feel the leaf: mountain alseuosmia's is thin, lowland horopito's rather leathery. Both have glossy leaves, but lowland horopito's have no blemishes or blotches, while mountain alseuosmia's are often red-edged and sometimes flecked red. Lowland horopito's leaves are elliptic-oblong to elliptic-obovate or ovate-oblong, 3–6 cm wide, with a wavy edge, on slender stalks about 2 cm long; mountain alseuosmia's are widest towards the tip and narrowed wedge-like to the base, with a tiny point at the tip, 2–2.5 cm wide (sometimes 3.5 cm), on rather stout stalks up to 10 mm long. Leaf lengths overlap: 6–10 cm against usually 7 cm (2.5–10 cm). Lowland horopito grows to 7–8 m; mountain alseuosmia is a shrub up to about 50 cm tall, unbranched or with one or two branches, and closely resembles small lowland horopito plants. In flower, lowland horopito's flowers are about 1 cm across, with 5–6 separate greenish-yellow petals 5–6 mm long, often several together in the leaf joints; mountain alseuosmia's are tubular, about 8–10 mm long, with five fringed lobes, white to yellowish or reddish and sweet-scented. Both have red berries: lowland horopito's are round, 5–6 mm across; mountain alseuosmia's oval, about 9–12 × 5–6 mm. Mountain alseuosmia does not grow north of Te Moehau and Mt Pirongia. Lowland horopito's leaves are used as a spice (see its page).

summary.text:
Mountain alseuosmia (Alseuosmia pusilla), matukuroimata, is a small shrub of the Alseuosmiaceae, endemic to New Zealand.
In the North Island it grows from Te Moehau and Mt Pirongia south, mainly in the mountains; in the South Island it grows only in the west, from North-West Nelson to near Okarito. It is the least variable New Zealand species of its genus. Its leaves are strikingly like horopito's, and it has been studied as a possible mimic of horopito, which is chemically defended; toropapa (Alseuosmia) shrubs in general are often confused with horopito and other unrelated shrubs. No record of it being eaten was found. It is ranked Not Threatened (2023).

warnings: No record of mountain alseuosmia as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
Its leaves are strikingly like horopito's and the two grow together, so check every plant before picking horopito leaves (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
C. indivisa is very distinctive. The species can be distinguished from all other Cordyline species by its very broad blue-grey leaves, and its smaller, tightly compacted inflorescence which is produced from beneath the foliage. It forms a stout tree up to 8 metres tall, with a trunk from 40–80 centimetres in diameter. The stem is usually unbranched, or has very few branches. The foliage, which droops with age, is blue-green and shaped like a broad sword, with a broad and conspicuous midrib which is often tinged red, orange red or golden. The inflorescence is a panicle that arises from the base of the growing points underneath the leaves.
Plant to about 8 m high; stems massive, rather sparingly branched. Leaves to 1–2 m × 10–15 cm, broadly ensiform, narrowed above base to short petiole; midrib and several nerves conspicuous, reddish. Panicle tightly compact, 60–160 cm long. Flowers long-pedicelled, more or less fleshy; segments 7–8 mm long. Berry bluish.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cabbage tree grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Mountain cabbage tree (Cordyline indivisa) grows to about 8 m with massive, rather sparingly branched stems; its leaves are up to 1–2 m × 10–15 cm, broadly sword-shaped, drooping only with age, glaucous underneath, narrowed above the base to a short stalk, with a broad, conspicuous midrib that is often reddish, the stronger nerves often reddish too; its panicle is tightly compact, 60–160 cm long, its crowded, rather fleshy flowers on longer stalks than in the other species, and its berries are bluish, about 6 mm across. Mountain cabbage tree stands apart from all the others on its leaves: up to 10–15 cm wide, glaucous underneath, with a strong, often reddish midrib and main nerves, and a tightly compact flower cluster. The other species' leaves are rarely over 10 cm wide, often much less, not or scarcely glaucous underneath, and their flower clusters are lax and open. Garden plants sold as 'Cordyline indivisa' or 'Dracaena indivisa' are often young cabbage trees, so a nursery label does not settle it.
lookalikes.name: Cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Forest cabbage tree grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Mountain cabbage tree (Cordyline indivisa) grows to about 8 m with massive, rather sparingly branched stems; its leaves are up to 1–2 m × 10–15 cm, broadly sword-shaped, drooping only with age, glaucous underneath, narrowed above the base to a short stalk, with a broad, conspicuous midrib that is often reddish, the stronger nerves often reddish too; its panicle is tightly compact, 60–160 cm long, its crowded, rather fleshy flowers on longer stalks than in the other species, and its berries are bluish, about 6 mm across. Mountain cabbage tree stands apart from all the others on its leaves: up to 10–15 cm wide, glaucous underneath, with a strong, often reddish midrib and main nerves, and a tightly compact flower cluster. The other species' leaves are rarely over 10 cm wide, often much less, not or scarcely glaucous underneath, and their flower clusters are lax and open. Kirk (1874) listed 'dubious forms' among New Zealand cabbage trees, some intermediate between these two.

Leaves sometimes steamed and fleshy part eaten. The kāuru, or upper part of the trunk, sometimes eaten prepared as tī, but doesn't seem to have been much appreciated. Outside of kāuru cut off before steaming.

Cordyline indivisa is a monocot tree endemic to New Zealand.

identification.text:
Erect annual to short-lived perennial herb. Mid cauline leaves almost glabrous or with few scattered hairs on both surfaces, apetiolate or cuneately narrowed to appear petiolate, narrow-oblong, elliptic, or narrow-obovate, shallowly pinnately lobed and denticulate to lyrate-pinnatifid or 1-pinnatifid with more or less oblong, few-toothed (rarely many-toothed) segments, amplexicaul and dentate at base or rarely not amplexicaul, (4)–6–13 × (1)–2–5 cm. Uppermost leaves smaller, often lanceolate, usually 1-pinnatifid, sometimes only dentate or entire. Supplementary bracts 3–6, 1–2 mm long. Involucral bracts (8)–12–13–(14), glabrous, 6–7–(8) mm long. Ray florets 0. Disc yellow, 2–3 mm diameter. Achenes subcylindric, narrowed to and constricted below apex, glabrous or with scattered hairs in 1–3 rows in narrow grooves between broad ribs, (2.2)–3–4–(5) mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Stems simple or sparingly branched, sulcate, nearly glabrous, up to about 50 cm tall, usually shorter. Capitula often few, about 9 mm long. Pappus hairs fine, white, about 6 mm long.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]
Its sap is watery, not milky. The heads carry two kinds of tiny tubular florets and no strap-shaped ones, and the achenes are sparsely papillate.

lookalikes.howToTell: Break a stem or leaf: nipplewort's sap is milky, mountain fireweed's is watery. Look at a flower head: nipplewort's florets are all strap-shaped and yellow, about 1.5 times as long as the involucre; mountain fireweed has no strap-shaped florets, only a yellow disc 2–3 mm across of tiny tubular ones. In seed, mountain fireweed's achenes are sparsely papillate, sometimes with a few hairs in the grooves, and topped with fine white pappus hairs about 6 mm long; nipplewort's are hairless, pale and have no pappus. Both can have lyre-shaped, lobed leaves and yellow heads in a loose spray, with involucres of much the same length, and both grow at forest margins and in disturbed places, so leaves and habitat do not separate them. Nipplewort's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Nipplewort

lookalikes.howToTell: Break a stem or leaf: wall lettuce's sap is milky, mountain fireweed's is watery. Wall lettuce's heads have usually 5 or fewer strap-shaped, pale yellow florets; mountain fireweed has no strap-shaped florets, only a yellow disc 2–3 mm across of tiny tubular florets of two kinds. Wall lettuce's leaves are thin, coarsely toothed, with prominent water pores (hydathodes) at the tooth tips; mountain fireweed's are thicker, with more rounded teeth. In seed, wall lettuce's achenes are dark brown to black; mountain fireweed's are paler and sparsely papillate. Both are hairless or nearly so, have lobed leaves that clasp the stem higher up and achenes topped with fine white pappus hairs, and both grow at forest margins and by streams, so hairiness, pappus and habitat do not separate them. Wall lettuce's leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they can taste extremely bitter (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Wall lettuce

summary.text:
Mountain fireweed (Senecio wairauensis) is a herb of the daisy family found only in New Zealand.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island; South Island: throughout; Stewart Island. Endemic.
S. wairauensis is very variable in leaf shape, with entire forms approaching S. dunedinensis and more dissected forms approaching S. biserratus. Material from Stewart Island and parts of Fiordland is quite distinctive in having very dissected leaves, short achenes (2.2–3 mm) and long bracts (7–8 mm), and should perhaps be accorded taxonomic recognition. Montane and alpine plants from northern South Island have less divided leaves than typical S. wairauensis, but do not differ in other characters; they probably do not merit taxonomic recognition. S. wairauensis was treated by Allan (1961) within Erechtites as E. wairauensis.
The epithet wairauensis refers to the Wairau Valley; the type locality is Lake Rotoiti, Nelson.
Its national conservation status (2023) is Not Threatened, and Otago ranks it Regionally Not Threatened (2025). It grows easily from fresh seed and can become invasive.

warnings: Do not eat it. No record of it being eaten has been found, and its chemistry has not been tested. It is a Senecio, a genus known for pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which poison livestock by damaging the liver; the damage builds up over months and is irreversible. All Senecio species should be treated as toxic, though not every species studied contains these alkaloids.

Its lobed leaves and small yellow heads look like nipplewort's and wall lettuce's, both eaten, and all three grow at forest margins. Break a stem: its sap is watery, theirs is milky (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
The leaves are under 2 metres in length while those of P. tenax range from 1 to 3 metres in length. The scape is much shorter than that of P. tenax, rising up to 2 metres in height while that of P. tenax is around 5 metres in height. The colour of the inner tepals is green while the outer tepals are yellow to red. In contrast the tepals of P. tenax are a dull red, with the tips of the inner tepals being less strongly recurved. The capsules of P. colensoi, unlike those of P. tenax are twisted and pendulous, and may be twice as long (up to 20 cm in length). The numerous seeds in each pod are glossy black, flat and elongated with a frilled margin 
Phormium colensoi has two distinct geographic forms, one occurring in lowland parts of the North Island, and the other in the southern and mountainous areas of the South Island as well as ranges in the North Island. The lowland form has green or yellow tepals and the mountain form has red tepals. In the Cook Strait area, both forms and intermediates can be found.

identification.text:
Berberis oiwakensis is a shrub or tree up to 7 m tall. Leaves are up to 45 cm long, compound with 12-20 pairs of leaflets plus a larger terminal one, dark green above, yellow-green below. The inflorescence is a fascicled raceme up to 25 cm long. The berries are egg-shaped, dark blue, sometimes almost black, up to 8 mm long.
In recent times another Chinese species, M. lomariifolia Takeda, has become very popular for New Zealand gardens. It is easily distinguished from M. japonica by the leaves which have 14–20 pairs of broad-lanceolate leaflets.
In gardens it grows upright, on mostly unbranched, cane-like stems, and its lightly scented yellow flowers come in dense clusters at the stem tips (San Marcos Growers, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain grape's leaves, up to 45 cm long, carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped leaflets; Oregon grape's carry 3–7 pairs of ovate ones, 2.5–5 cm wide. Mountain grape grows to 7 m; Oregon grape is a low, many-stemmed shrub, usually about 1 m. Mountain grape's flower clusters reach 25 cm; Oregon grape's 6–7 cm. Mountain grape's berries are egg-shaped, up to 8 mm long; Oregon grape's round, about 10 mm across. Dark blue bloomed berries and spiny-edged leaflets do not separate them.

lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain grape's leaves carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped leaflets; Japanese mahonia's carry 5–9 pairs of ovate ones. Mountain grape's flower clusters are dense and upright; Japanese mahonia's lax and spreading. Blue-black bloomed berries do not separate them, and neither test settles the garden hybrid B. × hortensis ('Charity', 'Winter Sun'), whose parents are these two species.

lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain grape's leaves carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped leaflets, 1–2.5 cm wide; leatherleaf mahonia's carry 4–10 pairs of broad ones, roundish to ovate and 2–6 cm wide. Mountain grape's berries are up to 8 mm long; leatherleaf mahonia's up to 15 mm. Upright flower clusters, a tall habit and dark blue bloomed berries do not separate them, and the garden hybrid 'Arthur Menzies' has both as parents.

summary.text:
Berberis oiwakensis is a species of plant in the barberry family, Berberidaceae. It is native to Taiwan, China (Guizhou, Hong Kong, Sichuan, Xizang (Tibet) and Yunnan) and Myanmar, where it occurs at elevations of 600 to 3800 m. It has recently been found naturalized in South Africa.
Berberis oiwakensis is one parent of the important garden hybrid Berberis × hortensis, which includes popular cultivars such as 'Charity', 'Winter Sun' and 'Lionel Fortescue' (the other parent is Berberis japonica).
Other names: Mahonia lomariifolia; Flora of New Zealand Online files it as Berberis lomariifolia; Auckland Council calls it Chinese holly grape.
Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and casual, not naturalised, from eight databased collections, all in Canterbury; its English names there include mountain grape and Chinese holly grape. In the wild it is Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (Wikipedia). It has been grown in the West since 1931, from seed collected near Tengchong, Yunnan, and raised in England (San Francisco Botanical Garden); birds favour its berries (San Marcos Growers).
Environment Canterbury reported it showing invasive tendencies in Christchurch in 2006; mahonia seed is spread by birds.

identification.text:
Stolons slender, with numerous long simple eglandular hairs and dense stellate hairs. Rosette leaves dull glaucescent green above, white-hairy beneath, oblanceolate, sessile or shortly petiolate, entire or very obscurely dentate, (1.5)–2.5–5–(7) × 0.6–1.5–(1.8) cm, subacute and often apiculate, cuneate at base; upper surface with scattered coarse simple hairs 4–6 mm long; lower surface with fine eglandular hairs 1–2 mm long and very dense stellate hairs. Stem leaf 0–(1), scale-like. Flowering stems erect, (2)–5–10–(15) cm tall, with 0-few simple eglandular hairs, numerous short glandular hairs and dense stellate hairs. Capitula solitary; involucre 8–13 mm long; bracts with dense stellate hairs and varying proportions of simple eglandular and glandular hairs. Florets yellow, often with red stripe on outer face, about 2× length of involucre. Achenes dark, about 2 × 0.5 mm. Pappus 5–6 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Hieracium pilosella L.]
The scapes of mouse-ear hawkweed are usually short at flowering but elongate up to about 5× at fruiting. It is distinguished from other species by its large solitary pale yellow capitula and the dense stellate pubescence on stolons and leaves beneath. (Flora of New Zealand)
It is very common on sunny banks and walls, and in dry pastures, and is well distinguished from all other British plants of the order, by its creeping scions or runners, which are thrown out in the same manner as in the strawberry, by its small rosettes of hairy, undivided leaves, greyish green above and hoary beneath, with a dense white coat of stellately branched hairs, and by its bright lemon-coloured flowers, which are borne singly on the almost leafless stems, which are only a few inches high. (Grieve, A Modern Herbal)

lookalikes.howToTell: Turn a leaf over: mouse-ear hawkweed's leaves are white beneath with a very dense coat of star-shaped hairs and carry long bristly hairs above, and they are untoothed or only very obscurely toothed. A dandelion's leaves are toothed, usually cut into back-pointing lobes, and hairless or with sparse short hairs, and the leaf stalk and the base of the midrib are hollow. Mouse-ear hawkweed spreads by slender creeping runners (stolons), as several other hawkweeds in New Zealand do. In seed, a dandelion's achene carries a slender beak 7–10 mm long; mouse-ear hawkweed's achenes are about 2 mm and not beaked. A dandelion head is 3–5 cm across, with the outer bracts bent sharply back. Both make rosettes with one yellow head on a leafless stem, leaf lengths overlap at 5–7 cm, and stem heights overlap, so a single head on a bare stem does not separate them. The dandelion's leaves, flowers and roots are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Dandelion

lookalikes.howToTell: Catsear's leaves are usually cut into shallow to deep lobes, rarely just toothed, and carry moderately dense pale bristly hairs; mouse-ear hawkweed's are untoothed or very obscurely toothed, with a very dense coat of star-shaped hairs that makes the underside white, and the plant spreads by creeping runners. Catsear's stems are usually branched; mouse-ear hawkweed has a single head on each stem. Pull a head apart: catsear has thin scales among the florets on the flower base, mouse-ear hawkweed has none. In seed, catsear's achenes are 8–16 mm and beaked (the outer ones sometimes shortly or not beaked, and then shorter), with feathery inner pappus hairs; mouse-ear hawkweed's are about 2 mm, unbeaked, with simple bristles. Both form hairy rosettes with yellow heads and milky sap, catsear's stems can be as short as 4 cm, and leaf lengths overlap, so size alone does not settle it. Catsear's young leaves and flower buds are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Catsear

lookalikes.howToTell: Both carry a single yellow head on an unbranched stem with no more than one small bract, and their stem heights and leaf sizes overlap. Look at the leaves with a hand lens: hawkbit's are distantly toothed to cut into triangular lobes and their hairs fork into two, sometimes three, at the tip; mouse-ear hawkweed's are untoothed or very obscurely toothed, with long simple hairs above and a very dense coat of star-shaped hairs that makes the underside white. Mouse-ear hawkweed spreads by creeping runners. In seed, hawkbit's inner achenes are 4–5 mm, shortly beaked, with a feathery inner pappus, and its outer ones 3–4 mm with a crown of short scales; mouse-ear hawkweed's are about 2 mm, unbeaked, with simple bristles. Hawkbit's leaves are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Hawkbit

lookalikes.howToTell: Autumn hawkbit's stems are 20–75 cm tall, branched, with numerous small bracts, and carry several heads; mouse-ear hawkweed has one head on a stem with no more than one scale-like leaf, (2)–5–10–(15) cm tall at flowering, though the stem lengthens up to about five times as the seed ripens, so height alone does not settle it in seed. Autumn hawkbit's leaves are usually cut into narrow lobes, rarely just toothed, with sparse simple hairs or none; mouse-ear hawkweed's are untoothed or very obscurely toothed, with a very dense coat of star-shaped hairs that makes the underside white, and the plant spreads by creeping runners. Autumn hawkbit's achenes are 4–5 mm, with one row of feathery pappus hairs; mouse-ear hawkweed's are about 2 mm, with simple bristles. Both have yellow heads and milky sap. Autumn hawkbit's leaves are eaten in salads or cooked (see its page).

summary.text:
Pilosella officinarum (synonym Hieracium pilosella), known as mouse-ear hawkweed, is a yellow-flowered species of flowering plant in the daisy family Compositae ( equal to Asteraceae), native to Europe and northern Asia.
It is a known allelopathic plant, whose roots secrete several substances inhibiting root growth, including its own. It can be controlled through rotation with clover and grasses where possible.
Recent research claims that Pilosella officinarum exhibits an atavism by the reemergence of sexual reproduction.
The plant has been found as an invasive species in Sphagnum peatlands disturbed by peat extraction in southern Patagonia.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Rotorua, Volcanic Plateau, Lake Waikaremoana, Kaimanawa and Ruahine Ranges, Hawke's Bay; S.: Marlborough, Canterbury, Westland (Douglas R.), Otago, Southland. H. pilosella is a prominent weed of high country pastures and tussock grasslands.
It is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and is an Unwanted Organism under the National Pest Plant Accord (restated).

warnings: Its rosettes and single yellow heads can be mistaken for dandelion, catsear or the hawkbits. Mouse-ear hawkweed spreads by creeping runners, and its small, untoothed leaves are white beneath with a dense coat of star-shaped hairs.

Medicinal preparations of mouse-ear hawkweed are not to be used by anyone hypersensitive to plants of the daisy family. Their safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and they are not recommended then; use in children and teenagers under 18 has not been established either.
The herb is strongly diuretic.

habitat.text: Lawns, playing fields, verges and grazed pasture, especially where the grass has been fertilised. One of the commonest mushrooms of mown grass, and it often fruits in large numbers.

identification.text:
Cap 1–4 cm across, conical at first then opening out to convex — it does not hold the sharp point a liberty cap keeps, and it has no nipple. Hygrophanous like a liberty cap: brown when moist, drying tan from the centre outwards, which often leaves a two-tone cap. No peelable gelatinous skin is described on it.
Gills are broad and attached, brown with paler edges, going distinctly mottled or blotchy as the spores ripen rather than an even colour. Stipe 3–8 cm by 1–3 mm, fragile and hollow, beige to light brown, with no ring. Spore print is deep brown, sometimes with a purplish cast.
It does not bruise blue anywhere.

lookalikes.howToTell: A liberty cap is sharply conical to bell-shaped, often tipped with a small nipple, and keeps that shape as it ages. A mower's mushroom is conical or bell-shaped when young but opens out to broadly convex and lacks the liberty cap's point. A liberty cap stains bluish where it is handled or bruised, and its stem is sometimes blue towards the base; the mower's mushroom's flesh does not change colour when cut. Bend back a piece of a damp liberty cap and a thin gelatinous skin peels away (not once the cap has dried out); the mower's mushroom is not described as having this skin. A liberty cap's gills are narrow and moderately crowded, darkening to dark grey or purple-brown. The mower's mushroom's are broad and often go mottled as the spores ripen. Both can have paler gill edges. Do not try to separate them on spore print or on where they grow. A liberty cap prints very dark purple-brown and a mower's mushroom dark brown, sometimes purplish to nearly black, and both come up in grass.
lookalikes.name: Liberty cap

lookalikes.howToTell: Both come up in lawns and other short grass. Make a spore print: a mower's mushroom's is deep brown, sometimes purplish, a fairy ring champignon's white. A mower's mushroom's gills are brown with paler edges and go mottled as the spores ripen; a fairy ring champignon's are white to cream and widely spaced. A mower's mushroom's stem is fragile and hollow; a fairy ring champignon's is tough and pliant and bends without snapping.

edibleParts.text: The leaves and flowers can be added to salads. The seeds are also edible. Leaves - raw or cooked. The leaves are mucilaginous and fairly bland. Flowers - raw. identification.text:
Erect perennial herb. Stems moderately hairy with only simple hairs. Leaves sparsely to moderately hairy with simple hairs and rarely a few stellate hairs below, more or less glabrous above; lower leaves reniform, shallowly 3–5-palmately lobed and crenate, 5–8 cm diameter; upper stem leaves deeply divided more or less to base with usually 5, 2-pinnatifid lobes; ultimate segments more or less linear; petiole 1–20 cm long; stipules linear to lanceolate, 5–8 mm long. Flowers solitary in lower axils and racemose at apex; fruiting pedicels (8)–10–50 mm long; epicalyx segments linear or narrow-ovate, shorter than calyx; calyx teeth ovate, acute to acuminate, moderately hairy with simple and stellate hairs, enlarged at fruiting; petals usually pink, sometimes white, 2–4× as long as calyx, (15)–20–30 mm long. Mericarps about 15–20 per fruit, densely hairy, smooth on back; edges rounded.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The rounded mericarps of M. moschata are densely covered in long hairs.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. They are separated by the upper stem leaves (cut almost to the base in musk mallow, shallowly lobed in common mallow) and the fruit (densely hairy and smooth-backed against usually hairless and net-veined). Petal lengths overlap ((15–)20–30 mm against 12–30 mm), so the flower does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.

Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. summary.text:
Malva moschata, the musk mallow or musk-mallow, is a species of flowering plant in the family Malvaceae. It is native to Eurasia and has been introduced elsewhere, being cultivated as an ornamental plant.
In New Zealand it is known from scattered places in South Auckland, Taranaki and Wellington, and in the South Island from Tākaka and the Taieri Plain, with one collection from Southland. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1904.

warnings: When grown on nitrogen rich soils (and particularly when these are used inorganically), the plant tends to concentrate high levels of nitrates in its leaves.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Roadsides, railways, waste places, building sites, quarries, riverbeds, lawns and pastures, and cultivated ground.
It needs bare soil to establish, such as turf opened up by drought or other damage, or pasture opened up by dryness, overgrazing or insect damage. It grows on more fertile sites than common storksbill, which tends to grow in drier, less fertile places.

identification.text:
Annual, at first stemless, later usually with several stems, extremely variable in size according to habitat, from prostrate to about 60 cm high and about 1 m across, densely glandular and more or less musk-scented. Leaves to about 30 cm long, pinnate, with petiole sometimes equal to leaf rachis. Leaflets sessile, pinnately lobed; lobes more or less ovate, serrate. Stipules broad-ovate or suborbicular, membranous, silvery, obtuse. Umbels about 12-flowered; bracts broad, membranous, obtuse; peduncles and pedicels densely glandular, shorter than to slightly longer than calyx at anthesis. Sepals 4.5–6 mm long, lanceolate-oblong, densely glandular, mucronate. Petals 4.5–8 mm long, pink or mauve-pink; claw very short; limb more or less elliptic-oblong, sometimes almost obovate. Stamens 3–4 mm long; filaments widened at base, white or pink, usually with a small membranous tooth on 1 or both sides, rarely without teeth; anthers dark purple. Staminodes lanceolate. Fruit beak 3–3.5 cm long, puberulent. Mericarps densely hirsute with hairs of differing length; apical pits prominently glandular, with 1 broad, glabrous furrow beneath.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In dry, stony and similar habitats plants are often reddish and extremely depauperate and only 1–2 cm diameter, whereas in fertile soils and amongst taller herbs the plants are green and the rank-growing stems can attain lengths of nearly 1 m. Plants are usually musk-scented to some extent.
Musk stork's-bill is distinguished from other British stork's-bills by its smell, its once-pinnate leaves and the glands in the apical pits on the fruit.
It begins as a rosette whose leaves, each made of a row of leaflets, radiate from a growing point at ground level; in good conditions the leaves grow long and the rosettes large enough to be seen from a distance. When it flowers it sends out stems along the ground with small purple-pink flowers 1–1.5 cm across, followed by seed heads shaped like a stork's head; each fruit has a long, spirally twisted awn.
Common storksbill (Erodium cicutarium) looks very similar. It has no musky smell when bruised, is usually much less clammy to the touch, has finely divided, fern-like leaves whose leaflets are deeply cut into narrow lobes, and its stipules and bracts are acute to short-pointed; musky storksbill's leaflet lobes are more or less ovate and its stipules and bracts only slightly pointed to rounded. The fertile stamens separate them too: musky storksbill's filaments usually have a small tooth on one or both sides of the widened base (rarely none), common storksbill's have none. Common storksbill also has glandless pits at the top of each seed segment.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both begin as rosettes of divided leaves, and both grow in waste places and riverbeds. Musky storksbill is densely covered in glandular hairs and feels sticky; hemlock's leaf stalks have no hairs. Crush a leaf: hemlock smells foetid; musky storksbill usually smells of musk, though not always strongly, so smell alone is not enough. Leaf shape does not separate them: hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided into ovate to triangular, toothed or cut segments 5–40 mm long, and musky storksbill's carry stalkless leaflets that are themselves lobed and toothed. Stem colour does not either: hemlock's stems are usually spotted or blotched purple, and musky storksbill's can be green to purple. Both carry their flowers in umbels. Grown on, hemlock stands erect, up to 2–(3) m, with hollow stems and white flowers about 2 mm across; musky storksbill lies along the ground or rises to about 60 cm, with pink or mauve-pink flowers, petals 4.5–8 mm long, about 12 to a cluster, followed by fruits with a beak 3–3.5 cm long. If a rosette is hairless or smells foul, do not eat it. Hemlock is deadly poisonous; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: Both start as flat rosettes whose leaves, each made of a row of leaflets, radiate from a growing point at ground level; both later send stems along the ground, and both come up on bare soil on roadsides, in waste places and on cultivated ground. Crush a leaf: twin cress smells foetid; musky storksbill usually smells of musk, though not always strongly. Musky storksbill is densely covered in glandular hairs and feels sticky; twin cress is hairless or nearly so. Twin cress's leaflets are lopsided, with more lobes on one side than the other; musky storksbill's leaflets are stalkless, with more or less ovate, toothed lobes. In flower they differ clearly: musky storksbill has clusters of about 12 pink or mauve-pink flowers, petals 4.5–8 mm long, followed by fruits with a beak 3–3.5 cm long; twin cress has tiny white petals shorter than its 0.5 mm sepals, or none, and paired pods about 1.5 mm long. Twin cress leaves are eaten raw or cooked for their hot, cress-like taste; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Twin cress

lookalikes.howToTell: Common storksbill looks very similar and comes up in the same places, though it tends to grow on drier, less fertile sites. Crush a leaf: musky storksbill usually smells of musk, though not always strongly; common storksbill has no musky smell. Musky storksbill is densely glandular and clammy; common storksbill is usually much less clammy. Musky storksbill's leaflets are lobed into more or less ovate, toothed lobes; common storksbill's are deeply and finely cut into narrow, linear to lanceolate lobes, giving fern-like foliage. Musky storksbill's stipules and bracts are blunt to rounded; common storksbill's end in an acute to short-pointed tip. In flower, musky storksbill's fertile stamens usually have a small tooth on one or both sides of the widened base (rarely none); common storksbill's have none. Petal colour and the 3–3.5 cm fruit beak do not separate them. Common storksbill's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked; see its own entry.

Caution 'careRequired' (re-checked 02/11/2026): cooked leafy tops of this species are recorded as food by three independent field surveys with vouchered specimens — Yalova, Turkey (Koçyiğit & Özhatay 2008–2009, cooked with rice), the Datça peninsula, Turkey (Akbulut & Yilmaz 2022, roasted and added to pastries) and the Jbala of northwest Morocco (Ben Sbih et al. 2025, stems and leaves in mixed cooked wild greens) — and by Ertuğ's Bodrum study as reviewed by Dogan (2012, fried, in pastry fillings). Raw use rests on Yanovsky (1936, 'used like E. cicutarium'), Useful Temperate Plants and Eat The Weeds, which are not independent of each other. The only known hazard is photosensitisation in sheep that eat large amounts (Stroebel 2002; Connor 1977 as cited by Collett 2019); none is recorded in people. None of the records is from New Zealand.

Habitats: grassland (lawns and pastures), urban (roadsides, railways, building sites), disturbed (waste places, quarries, cultivated ground, bare soil). Riverbeds not tagged wetland (sweep precedent).

summary.text:
Erodium moschatum is a species of flowering plant in the geranium family known by the common names musk stork's-bill and whitestem filaree. This is a weedy annual or biennial herb which is native to much of Eurasia and North Africa but can be found on most continents where it is an introduced species.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands and the Chatham Islands, common in the lowlands throughout. Naturalised from Europe, North Africa and western Asia, first recorded in 1869. It flowers mainly from September to November, occasionally from January and into December. It is also called musky crowfoot.
It is a weed of turf, where it forms large, unsightly rosettes, and of pasture, where its sharply pointed fruits can pierce the skin of sheep and work into the flesh, though much less often than those of barley grass or common storksbill. It is sometimes a weed of crops. The long awn of each fruit winds and unwinds with the humidity, burying the seed in the soil.
Sheep that eat large amounts of it can become sensitive to sunlight (photosensitisation). In South Africa sheep grazing a paddock where it grew abundantly developed severe photosensitivity, and sheep fed the pulped plant for 7 days developed mild photosensitivity. Photosensitisation has also been seen in lambs grazing herbage that was mainly storksbill in Australia and New Zealand (North Canterbury and Hawke's Bay); the agent responsible has not been identified.

warnings: Before eating, confirm it by its sticky glandular hairs, musky smell, pink to mauve flowers in clusters and long beaked fruits. Its rosette of divided leaves resembles that of hemlock, which is deadly; hemlock's leaf stalks are hairless and it smells foetid. If a rosette is hairless or smells foul, do not eat it (see the lookalikes).

Sheep that eat large amounts can become sensitive to sunlight (photosensitisation) and suffer skin damage. The substance responsible has not been identified, and whether it affects people is not known.

Its food use is recorded mostly as cooked leafy tops, in field surveys from Turkey and Morocco; raw use rests on plant databases and a foraging page that treat it like common storksbill. No source gives a safe quantity.
The half-ripe green seeds have been eaten raw only as a children's nibble, and they apparently caused a lot of constipation; the seeds are not given here as food.
In lawns and pastures it is controlled with herbicides such as MCPA, 2,4-D, dicamba, picloram with triclopyr, and bentazone. Pick it only where you know none has been used.

edibleParts.text: Leaves - raw or cooked. Delicious in salads, they start off being sweet and then develop a fairly strong garlic-like flavour, they are liked by most people who try them. Bulb - raw or cooked. Rather small but a very nice mild garlic flavour. Flowers - raw or cooked. Excellent in salads, making them look attractive as well as adding a strong onion flavour.

In New Zealand: Garden escape.
In its native Mediterranean range: Dry grassy places and fields. Macchie, phrygana, rocky places, weedy banks, rivulets, ruins, often in shade; at elevations from sea level to 1,035 metres.

identification.text: Bulb globose, 1–2 cm diameter, with non-stipitate offset bulbs. Leaves 2–3, about 25 × 1–2 cm, flat, margins finely toothed or ciliate. Scape 20–60 cm high, sheathed at base only, subtriquetrous with 2 angles acute, almost winged, the third more obtuse. Umbels 5–8 cm diameter, many-flowered, more or less flat-topped; pedicels about 3 times length of flowers, rigid; spathe-valve 1, persistent. Flowers white, 8–10 mm long, about 10 mm diameter, campanulate; segments ovate-elliptic, obtuse. Stamens about ½ length of perianth; filaments simple without appendages. Capsule about 7 mm long, more or less globose, papery, few-seeded. Seeds black, angled, 2–3 mm long.

lookalikes.howToTell: Onion weed's flowers are white with a green stripe down the centre of each segment; Naples garlic's are pure white. Onion weed's flower stalk is sharply three-angled; Naples garlic's has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one. Onion weed carries 3–15 flowers on drooping stalks; Naples garlic carries a many-flowered, roughly flat-topped umbel 5–8 cm across on stiff stalks. Onion weed's leaves are strongly channelled; Naples garlic's are flat, with finely toothed or hairy-edged margins. The onion-garlic smell, a 20–60 cm flower stalk, white flowers and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Onion weed

lookalikes.howToTell: Rosy garlic's flowers are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves; Naples garlic's are pure white. Rosy garlic often carries bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among its flowers, though plants without bulbils also occur. Rosy garlic's flower stalk is round in section; Naples garlic's has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one. Flat leaves, the garlic smell, an umbel 5–8 cm across and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Rosy garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild garlic's leaves are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical; Naples garlic's are flat, with finely toothed or hairy-edged margins. Wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils; Naples garlic carries a many-flowered umbel 5–8 cm across of white flowers 8–10 mm long. Wild garlic's flower stalk is slender and rush-like; Naples garlic's has two sharp, almost winged angles. The garlic smell does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Wild garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Snowflake has none of Naples garlic's garlic smell. Snowflake carries 3–7 flowers (sometimes 1–2), 1.5–2 cm long, with green-tipped segments; Naples garlic carries a many-flowered, roughly flat-topped umbel 5–8 cm across of white flowers 8–10 mm long on stiff stalks. Snowflake's flower stalk is hollow and somewhat flattened; Naples garlic's has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one. Flat leaves of similar width (8–15 mm against 1–2 cm), a 30–60 cm flower stalk against 20–60 cm, white bells and flowering at the same time (snowflake July–October, Naples garlic September) do not separate them. If a plant does not smell of garlic or onion when crushed, leave it.
lookalikes.name: Snowflake

lookalikes.howToTell: False garlic has none of Naples garlic's garlic smell, or only a faint one. False garlic carries 8–20 dull white flowers 1–1.5 cm long, each segment with a greenish base and a reddish midvein, above two bracts joined at the base and tinged red; Naples garlic carries a many-flowered, roughly flat-topped umbel 5–8 cm across of pure white flowers 8–10 mm long on stiff stalks, above a single bract that stays on. False garlic's flower stalk is round in section and hollow; Naples garlic's has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one. Flat leaves of overlapping width (5–15 mm against 1–2 cm), a 20–60 cm flower stalk, offset bulbs and white bells do not separate them. If a plant does not smell of garlic or onion when crushed, leave it. False garlic has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: False garlic

preparation.text:
Of the bulbs: Sliced up, they make a delicious addition to salads and can also be used as a vegetable or as a flavouring in cooked foods. The bulbs, harvested once the plant dies down, will store for 6 months or more.
In Cyprus it is eaten fresh with olives, onions and bread.
In Jódar, in Spain's Sierra Mágina, people out in the fields also commonly ate it, and then preferred the white bases of the leaves.
The leaves keep well chopped and frozen, and the bulbs store like other garlic. The flowers are only good while in bloom, before the seed capsule in the middle starts to swell.
Dried bulbs can stand in for cultivated garlic, with a less pungent flavour.

recipes.method: Written for Naples garlic by a Chilean forager, who says it suits onion weed too. A cauliflower (or broccoli, or another vegetable in season); the stems, leaves and bulbs of the Naples garlic; 3 eggs; salt and pepper; grated cheese (optional). Cook a cauliflower (or broccoli, or another vegetable in season) in very little water until soft. Meanwhile chop the stems, leaves and bulbs of the Naples garlic small and fry them gently. Drain the cauliflower, chop it small and mix it in a bowl with 3 eggs, the fried Naples garlic, and salt and pepper to taste. Pour into a dish and bake at 180 °C for about 30 minutes, until the top is golden; grated cheese on top is optional. Cut into pieces and serve with a salad or a grain. The source gives no amounts for the cauliflower or the Naples garlic.
recipes.title: Naples garlic and cauliflower bake

recipes.method: Recorded in Jódar, in Spain's Sierra Mágina, where it was prepared the same way as wild leek. The bulbs, the white bases of the leaves, or both; a little salt; egg (optional); a little vinegar (optional). Cut up the bulbs, the white bases of the leaves, or both, as you prefer. Boil them first with a little salt. Then fry them and eat them as they are, or scramble them with egg, or make them into an omelette. Or let the boiled pieces cool to room temperature and dress them with a little vinegar.
recipes.title: Boiled and fried Naples garlic, Jódar style

recipes.method: From a Roman garden club's note on Naples garlic: make a frittata with the leaves, the tender stems and the flower clusters. The source gives no amounts or method beyond that.
recipes.title: Naples garlic frittata

recipes.method: From the same Roman note. Ricotta; a good handful of Naples garlic flowers; salt; olive oil; cooked pasta. Mix ricotta with a good handful of Naples garlic flowers, salt and olive oil, and toss it through cooked pasta. The source gives no other amounts.
recipes.title: Pasta with ricotta and Naples garlic flowers

recipes.method: From the same Roman note. Boil Naples garlic leaves together with chicory, which tones down their flavour. Or fry cooked chicory in a pan with the leaves, in place of a garlic clove.
recipes.title: Chicory with Naples garlic leaves

summary.text:
Allium neapolitanum is a bulbous herbaceous perennial plant in the onion subfamily within the Amaryllis family.
Its native range extends across the Mediterranean Region from Portugal to the Levant. The species is cultivated as an ornamental and has become naturalized in many areas, including Pakistan, Australia, New Zealand, and in southern and western parts of the United States. It is classed as an invasive species in parts of the U.S., and is found primarily in the states of California, Texas, Louisiana, and Florida.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N. Auckland City; Gisborne - Opotiki; Hawkes Bay - Napier, abundantly naturalised; Wellington - Palmerston North. S. Canterbury - Rangiora.
Other names (Flora of New Zealand Online, NZPCN): daffodil garlic, flowering onion, Naples onion.

warnings: Although no individual reports regarding this species have been seen, there have been cases of poisoning caused by the consumption, in large quantities and by some mammals, of certain members of this genus. Dogs seem to be particularly susceptible.

Every part is mildly poisonous: its sulfides may cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Garlic and wild garlic carry the same low-severity rating, so this is a caution for the genus, not a reason to doubt the edible leaves and bulbs.

identification.text:
Perennial stoloniferous herb. Stems trailing, glabrous, up to 1 m long. Leaves glabrous, all similar but becoming smaller near inflorescence, pinnate, petiolate, 2–10–(25) × 1–5 cm; basal auricles very small; leaflets rounded, ovate; margins entire or sinuate. Pedicels glabrous, slender, erecto-patent, spreading to deflexed at fruiting, (8)–12–20–(30) mm long. Sepals 2.5–3.5 × 1 mm. Petals white, (4)–5–6 × 1.5–2.5 mm. Silique glabrous, narrow-oblong to linear, curved, (10)–15–25–(30) × about 1.5 mm; valves with distinct midrib at least below; style about 1 mm long. Seeds in about 1 row per locule, brown, about 1 mm long, reticulate with 100–150 polygonal depressions per face. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Rorippa microphylla (Rchb.) Hylander]
A bright green, sturdy herb that creeps or stands upright, with small white flowers from spring through summer. The leaves smell peppery when crushed, and turn brown or purple in autumn and winter. It is very like watercress, and the surest difference is in the seeds: see Lookalikes.

lookalikes.howToTell: The two are very alike and the leaves do not separate them. The surest test is the ripe seeds: narrow-fruited watercress has them in a single row in each half of the pod, each seed with 100–150 small pits per face; watercress has them in two distinct rows, with 20–50 coarse pits. Narrow-fruited watercress also tends to have larger flowers (petals 5–6 mm long against 4–6 mm), longer flower stalks (12–20 mm against 10–15 mm) and narrower pods (about 1.5 mm wide against 2–2.5 mm). Its leaves turn brown or purple in autumn and winter. Both grow in the same streams and drains. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Water celery's leaflets are toothed, in 2–8 pairs; narrow-fruited watercress's are rounded, with smooth or wavy edges, and smell peppery when crushed. In flower, water celery has small compound umbels of tiny white flowers on short stalks opposite the leaves, with 4–8 small bracteoles under each small umbel; narrow-fruited watercress has white flowers in spikes, followed by narrow curved pods. Both grow in streams and drains. Water celery is edible, but it is an umbellifer, and deadly hemlock — another umbellifer — also grows on damp ground in New Zealand, so be certain of the identification.
lookalikes.name: Water celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Bog yellow cress has yellow petals only about as long as the sepals (1.5–2.5 mm), usually stands upright from a taproot, and its leaves are deeply lobed with toothed edges. Narrow-fruited watercress has white petals, about twice as long as the sepals, and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, with rounded leaflets with smooth or wavy edges. Bog yellow cress's pods are short and plump, 2–7 mm long; narrow-fruited watercress's are slender, 10–30 mm. Both grow in wet places, so place does not separate them. Bog yellow cress's young leaves and stems are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Bog yellow cress

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping yellowcress has yellow flowers on upright stems and spreads by creeping underground parts; its upper leaves are cut into narrow, toothed or untoothed lobes. Narrow-fruited watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, with rounded leaflets with smooth or wavy edges. Both grow in wet ground and both have petals about twice as long as the sepals, so place and petal length do not separate them. Creeping yellowcress has no reliable food record.
lookalikes.name: Creeping yellowcress

lookalikes.howToTell: Land cress has yellow flowers on upright stems from a stout taproot, and grows on river banks, roadsides and waste land; narrow-fruited watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, and grows in streams, ditches and drains. Land cress's pods are (30–)40–70 mm long; narrow-fruited watercress's are (10–)15–25(–30) mm. Both have lobed leaves, so the leaves alone do not separate them. Land cress's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Land cress

preparation.text: Raw only if it comes from water with no sheep or cattle grazing above it; otherwise cook it, which kills liver fluke. The plant is very sensitive to pollution, so pick only from clean water. For mustard, grind the seeds and mix with cold water: the heat develops over 10–15 minutes. Hot water, vinegar or salt stops that reaction and gives a mild but bitter mustard.

recipes.method: Serves 4. 500 g meaty pork ribs; 1 bunch watercress, washed thoroughly; 6 dried Chinese dates, red or black; a 2 cm piece of ginger, sliced lengthwise and smashed; 2 tsp salt; 1 tsp sugar. Cover the ribs with water by about 5 cm in a large pot and bring to a rolling boil, then drain in a colander to get rid of fat and scum and return the ribs to the pot. Trim the watercress, separate the leaves from the stems and chop the stems small. Add about 2 litres of water, the watercress stems, dates and ginger and bring to the boil over high heat. Cover and simmer gently over medium heat for 45 minutes to an hour, until the ribs are tender. Add the leaves and simmer about 10 minutes more, until they turn dark green. Stir in the salt and sugar and serve straight away.
recipes.title: Pork rib and watercress soup

recipes.method: Written for wild watercress (Nasturtium officinale) by an American chef. Serves 4. 450 g (1 lb) fresh watercress; salt; soft salted butter or extra virgin olive oil; lemon wedges or vinegar, to serve. Wash the watercress, picking out insects and debris, and dry it well, ideally in a salad spinner. Put a thin film of water in a large pot, fill the pot with the watercress and cover it. Set it over medium-high heat for a few minutes until the pot is very hot, then lift the lid and stir. Cover again for a minute or two, stir, and repeat until the watercress has wilted. Keep cooking and tasting, adding a splash of water if it dries out, until it is tender: young shoots are quick, older leaves can take 15 minutes or more. Turn off the heat and pour off what little water is left. Toss with a drizzle of olive oil and salt, taste, and serve with lemon or a dash of vinegar, or butter at the table. The author also steams it in a steamer basket over 5–8 cm of boiling water, covered on low heat, until tender, but prefers the pot method for watercress.
recipes.title: Steamed watercress

recipes.method: Fills a 30 cm tart tin. Pastry: 125 g very cold butter; 250 g sieved plain flour; 50 g finely grated parmesan; 1 tsp icing sugar; salt; plenty of black pepper; just enough water. Filling: 500 g watercress leaves, with some white flowers kept for garnish; 20 g butter; the juice of 1 orange; 3 large eggs plus 2 extra yolks; 300 ml double cream; 200 g grated parmesan; salt and pepper; 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts. Heat the oven to 180 °C. For the pastry, grate 125 g very cold butter into 250 g sieved plain flour, 50 g finely grated parmesan, 1 tsp icing sugar, salt and plenty of black pepper. Rub together lightly, keeping it cool, then add just enough water to form a rough ball (less water, less shrinking). Chill for 30 minutes, roll out and line the tin, patching where needed. Prick the base, chill for 20 minutes, then blind-bake with baking paper and beans for 15 minutes; remove them and bake on until lightly toasted. For the filling, strip 500 g watercress leaves from the fibrous stalks (some stalk is fine — just a coarser tart), keeping some white flowers for garnish. Melt 20 g butter in a large heavy pan over a medium heat, add the watercress and the juice of 1 orange, and sweat gently for 10 minutes, stirring often. Blitz it with its juices, then beat it hard with 3 large eggs and 2 extra yolks, 300 ml double cream, all but a handful of 200 g grated parmesan, and plenty of salt and pepper — the more air, the more it rises. Pour into the case, sprinkle with the reserved parmesan and 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts, and bake for 20–25 minutes, until bronzed and only slightly wobbly in the middle. Cool a little and scatter the watercress flowers on top.
recipes.title: Watercress and parmesan tart

summary.text:
Nasturtium microphyllum, the onerow yellowcress, is an aquatic plant species widespread across Europe and Asia, and naturalized in the United States, Canada, Mexico, Central America, Australia, New Zealand and other places.
In New Zealand it is called one-rowed watercress; its seeds sit in a single row in each half of the pod. It is an exotic from Europe, brought in as a culinary herb and recorded naturalised in 1954. It is common throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands, and commonest in the South Island. It spreads by seed and by pieces of stem that break off and root. It grows with watercress in New Zealand's cold springs, where a 1976 study looked at the two together. The name microphyllum means 'small leaf'.

warnings: Liver fluke risk: plants in water draining from land where sheep or cattle graze can carry Fasciola hepatica. Cooking kills it; eating raw does not.

identification.text:
Scrambling perennial; stems glabrous, angled, broadly winged. Leaves glabrous; tendril branched in upper leaves, sometimes simple in lower leaves; leaflets in 1 pair, usually lanceolate to linear, rarely narrowly elliptic, narrowly acute to acuminate, 50–130 mm long; veins parallel; stipules lanceolate to linear, with 1 narrow basal lobe, less than 1/2 as wide as stem (about 1–3 mm wide), (5)–10–20 mm long. Inflorescence longer than leaves, (2)–5–8-flowered; pedicels 4–10 mm long. Calyx glabrous, slightly or not gibbous at base; calyx teeth unequal, narrowly triangular, shorter than tube. Corolla purple-pink, 13–17 mm long. Pod glabrous, brown, 8–15-seeded, 40–70 mm long; seeds reticulate-rugose.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Broad-leaved sweet pea (Lathyrus latifolius), much more commonly naturalised, is very similar; it has larger flowers, (15)–20–30 mm long, usually elliptic leaflets, and broad stipules, (3)–5–15 mm wide, at least half as wide as the stem.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stipules, the leafy flaps where each leaf joins the stem: narrow-leaved everlasting pea's are lance-shaped to linear, about 1–3 mm wide and less than half as wide as the stem; broad-leaved sweet pea's are broader, (3)–5–15 mm wide, usually about as wide as the stem or wider and at least half as wide. Narrow-leaved everlasting pea's flowers are smaller, 13–17 mm long, (2)–5–8 to a stalk; broad-leaved sweet pea's are (15)–20–30 mm long, (4)–8–14 to a stalk. Narrow-leaved everlasting pea's leaflets are usually lance-shaped to linear, rarely narrowly elliptic, 50–130 mm long; broad-leaved sweet pea's are narrowly to broadly elliptic, 30–100 mm long (to 120 mm), but its shoots late in the flowering season may have narrow, almost linear leaves and as few as 2 flowers, so go by the stipules. Narrow-leaved everlasting pea's calyx teeth are all shorter than the calyx tube; broad-leaved sweet pea's lower teeth are as long as the tube or longer. Narrow-leaved everlasting pea's pods are 40–70 mm long, broad-leaved sweet pea's 60–110 mm. Both are scrambling perennials with broadly winged stems, one pair of leaflets and branched tendrils, and broad-leaved sweet pea also grows in South Canterbury and Otago, where narrow-leaved everlasting pea is established. Neither is eaten.

summary.text: Narrow-leaved everlasting pea, also called flat pea (Lathyrus sylvestris), is a scrambling perennial of the pea family, Fabaceae, native to Europe, north-west Africa, Asia Minor and the Caucasus, and first recorded in New Zealand in 1958. It is established only locally, in South Canterbury and North and Central Otago, and is rarely recorded. It is very similar to the much more commonly naturalised broad-leaved sweet pea (Lathyrus latifolius), from which it differs in its smaller flowers and narrower leaflets and stipules.

warnings: Narrow-leaved everlasting pea is not given here as food. No record of it as food was found, and its seeds are recorded as toxic.
Its seeds contain a nerve-active amino acid, diaminobutyric acid, in very high concentration, and the same toxin is found in its leaves.

All parts of the plant, but especially the seed, contain a toxic amino acid, made at about the time the seed starts to develop. Eaten in quantity it can cause lathyrism, a very serious disease of the nervous system: paralysis of the muscles below the knees and back pain, followed by weakness and stiffness of the legs and growing loss of coordination.
It is poisonous to livestock: sheep fed hay cut when the plant was bearing seed developed a potentially fatal nervous illness, with seizures, muscle trembling and twisting of the neck.

Plants For A Future / Useful Temperate Plants, 'Tropaeolum majus' (Ken Fern; facts restated) — leaves, flowers and young seed pods raw
edibleParts.text: Leaves, flowers, flower buds, stems and young shoots, and green seed pods. The flowers have a peppery bite likened to Sichuan pepper, or to radish.

sources: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb, Sykes & Garnock-Jones 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY-NC-SA), 'Tropaeolum majus L.'
habitat.text:
Garden escapes, banks, coastal waste ground, roadside dumps of garden waste.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Waysides and waste places, especially moist and shady situations, also river banks and other waterways in built-up areas, and around many gardens and parks.

sources: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb, Sykes & Garnock-Jones 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY-NC-SA), 'Tropaeolum majus L.' — abbreviations spelled out ('Lvs' leaves, 'c.' about, 'diam.' diameter, 'Fls' flowers, 'Frs' fruits, '±' more or less), parts cut marked […]; NZPCN 'Tropaeolum majus' (similar taxa, restated)
identification.text:
Unmistakable round shield-shaped leaves with the stem joining at the centre, and bright orange, yellow or red spurred trumpet flowers. Sprawling, often smothering.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Glabrous aromatic annual or short-lived perennial with long trailing or scrambling, succulent stems, sometimes climbing to 2 m high. Leaves simple, peltate. Petioles to about 30 cm long, usually not coiling. Lamina to about 18–(21) cm diameter, suborbicular, often slightly asymmetric, entire but often sinuate, glaucescent beneath. Flowers usually solitary, sometimes in clusters of 2–3 […]; spur 2.5–3.3 cm long, more or less curved, tapering, usually pale orange. Corolla moderately irregular, (2)–3–4 × (1.7)–2.2–3.3 cm, usually yellow or orange to scarlet, sometimes semi-double with 7–8 petals […]. Fruits dry […], remaining green until abscission.
No species is easily confused with it in New Zealand (NZPCN).
