Palmers (New Zealand), 'Nasturtium Recipes'. https://www.palmers.co.nz/blogs/recipes/nasturtium-recipes
preparation.text: Leaves and flowers raw in salads. Green seed pods brined and pickled as 'poor man's capers'. If the flowers taste too strong, use only the petals: the centre carries most of the flavour. Turn the leaves over to check for aphids and caterpillar eggs, and shake the flowers to dislodge insects. Leaves and flowers keep their pepperiness when dried, and keep about a year in a jar. Pick from plants you know have not been sprayed. Flower buds can be pickled like the green seeds. For winter shoots, sow saved seed thickly in a tray indoors or on heat and cut the shoots at 6–8 cm for salads and stir-fries.

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) nasturtium seed pods, picked young and light green; 60 ml (¼ cup) salt; 500 ml (2 cups) water; 250 ml (1 cup) apple cider vinegar; 15–30 ml (1–2 tbsp) sugar; 1 bay leaf. Split the pods into single seeds and rinse off any dirt. Dissolve the salt in the water in a jar and add the seeds; the brine tames their strong mustardy bite. Keep them under the brine — a plastic bag pushed down into the jar works — and leave at room temperature for a couple of days. Lift them out, soak them in cold water for an hour, and drain. Warm the vinegar and sugar in a small pan until the sugar dissolves and the vinegar just simmers. Pack the seeds into hot sterilised jars, pour the hot vinegar over, add the bay leaf and seal. Use them wherever you would use capers. The author keeps them in the fridge and says they last indefinitely there.
recipes.title: Pickled nasturtium seed pods

recipes.method: 3 cups (about 750 ml) nasturtium leaves, well rinsed; a bowl of iced water; 60 ml (¼ cup) olive oil; 1 medium shallot, finely diced; the juice of 1 lemon. Bring a pot of water to the boil, drop in the leaves, turn off the heat and let them wilt for about 30 seconds. Scoop them straight into the iced water, leave them 2 minutes, then spread them on a clean tea towel to dry. Blend the leaves with the olive oil in a food processor until smooth and bright green. Strain through a colander lined with paper towel, letting the oil drip through. Stir in the shallot and a squeeze of lemon juice just before serving. Keep it in a clean jar in the fridge and use within 3 days. The author drizzles it over fish or prawns, swirls it through pumpkin or potato soup, or stirs it into mayonnaise or yoghurt.
recipes.title: Nasturtium leaf oil

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard. 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: The author's greens were dock, onion weed, nasturtium, plantain, baby wild mustard, dandelion, sow thistle and a violet leaf. 2 crushed garlic cloves; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 500 ml (2 cups) firmly packed wild greens, sliced very thinly; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper; 125 ml (½ cup) roughly chopped pistachios, walnuts, almonds or brazil nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp hearts, pumpkin or sunflower seeds; and 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, hemp seed oil or a mix. Makes about 750 ml (3 cups). To slice the greens, sort them into similar shapes, bunch and twist a few leaves together and slice as thinly as you can — this suits the tougher, stringier ones such as plantain, mustard and dock. Toss everything together. Good as a side or salad, in a wrap or sandwich, or with pasta, risotto, eggs, or sausages and mash. It keeps at least 4 days in a sealed jar in the fridge.
recipes.title: Weedolata (wild-greens gremolata)

recipes.method: The author's greens were puha, sow thistle, nasturtium, onion weed, wild fennel, oxalis, wild mustard and wild celery. 1 diced onion; 1 potato, scrubbed and diced; 2 sliced garlic cloves; 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 1.3 litres water; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked pepper; extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil, to serve; edible weed flowers. Serves 4. Cut the vegetables and greens to similar sizes. Fry the onion in the oil for a minute, then add the potato and garlic (the method also adds fennel bulb and celery stalks, which the ingredient list leaves out) and fry for another minute. Add the water, cover, bring to the boil and simmer until the potato is soft. Add the greens with the salt and yeast and cook for 3 minutes, until just tender — added at the end, they keep their colour. Blend until smooth (push it through a sieve if your blender isn't powerful), season with the pepper and more salt if needed, and serve drizzled with extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil and scattered with edible weed flowers.
recipes.title: Wild greens soup

recipes.method: Written for nasturtium and nipplewort together. 6 large field mushrooms; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil plus another 60 ml for frying; the leaves of 1 rosemary stalk, chopped; salt and pepper; 600 g nasturtium and nipplewort leaves, roughly chopped; 250 ml water; 1 onion (the method uses one, though the ingredient list leaves it out); 4 crushed garlic cloves; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 250 ml (1 cup) roughly chopped walnuts; 240 g cream cheese, plant-based or dairy; 1 slice of bread, broken into small pieces. Serves 4. Toss the mushrooms with the first 60 ml of oil, the rosemary, 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper and leave them to marinate. Cook the greens in a lidded pot with the water and 5 ml (1 tsp) salt on high heat for 5 minutes, turning them, until wilted; cool them under cold running water, squeeze out the water and chop again. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Fry the mushrooms in the second 60 ml of oil, open side down, for 4 minutes, then 4 minutes on the other side, until golden, and set them open side up in a baking dish. In the same pan soften the onion for 5 minutes, add the garlic, greens, lemon zest and juice and cook a minute, then stir in the walnuts, cream cheese, bread, 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper off the heat. Pack the filling into the mushrooms, drizzle with olive oil and bake for 20 minutes until golden. Good on soft polenta or mashed kūmara and potato.
recipes.title: Nasturtium and nipplewort stuffed mushrooms

recipes.method: 400 g dried pasta and 5 ml (1 tsp) salt for the water. Sauce: 1 litre (4 cups) nasturtium flowers, 375 ml (1½ cups) ricotta or soaked cashews, 30 ml (2 tbsp) parmesan or nutritional yeast, 2 garlic cloves, 1 chilli (optional), 1 tomato, 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, the zest and juice of 2 lemons, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) salt, 5 ml (1 tsp) black pepper and 80 ml (⅓ cup) water from the pasta pot. To finish: 1 bunch asparagus, ends snapped off; 4 roughly chopped tomatoes; 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil; salt and pepper; 80 ml (⅓ cup) grated parmesan or hemp parmesan; 80 ml (⅓ cup) finely chopped parsley; a few more nasturtium flowers and leaves. Serves 4. Boil the pasta in the salted water for about 8 minutes, until just cooked, adding the asparagus for the last 2 minutes. Meanwhile blend the sauce ingredients until smooth. Drain the pasta, take out the asparagus and cool it briefly under cold water, then return the hot pasta to the pot and stir in the sauce. Season the tomatoes with salt, pepper and the second measure of oil. Top the pasta with the asparagus, tomatoes, parsley, parmesan and a few more nasturtium flowers and leaves.
recipes.title: Nasturtium flower pasta

recipes.method: 1 litre (4 cups) flour; 500 ml (2 cups) warm water; 3 tsp dried yeast; 1 tsp salt; 1 tsp sugar; 1 Tbsp oil; 500 ml (2 cups) nasturtium leaves. Blend the leaves with 125 ml of the warm water, then mix in the rest of the water. Pour it into a bowl, whisk in the sugar and yeast, and leave 5–10 minutes to activate. In a large bowl mix the flour, oil and salt, add the green liquid half at a time and mix, then knead for 1–2 minutes. Put the dough in an oiled bowl, cover and leave somewhere warm to rise for 1–2 hours. Bake on a lightly greased or non-stick tray at 180 °C for 20 minutes, or until lightly golden. The leaves turn the bread green.
recipes.title: Nasturtium bread

recipes.method: Makes 8. 450 g self-raising flour; 1 tsp salt; 100 g cold butter; 250 g grated parmesan; 3 Tbsp nasturtium leaves; 120 ml cold milk; 120 ml cold water; 1 egg. Heat the oven to 220 °C. Mix the flour and salt, grate in the cold butter and rub it in with your fingertips until crumbly. Stir in the cheese and the leaves, then gradually mix in the milk and water until the dough comes away from the bowl in a ball. Tip it onto a lightly floured surface and cut it into 8. Set them close together on a baking tray so they rise rather than spread, brush with the egg and bake for 15 minutes, until golden. Serve warm with butter.
recipes.title: Nasturtium and parmesan scones

recipes.method: 4 medium oranges; 1 litre (4 cups) sugar, plus 2 Tbsp; 2 Tbsp pectin; 25 nasturtium flowers. Peel 2 of the oranges and cut them into small cubes. Finely cut the other 2 with their peel on, and put all the orange in a pan. Gently wash the flowers and tear the petals into the pan. Mix the pectin with the 2 Tbsp of sugar and add it. Cook over medium heat, stirring now and then, until it boils. Add the rest of the sugar and boil for 10 minutes. Skim off the foam and pour into jars. The author does not say to sterilise or seal the jars, or how long the jam keeps.
recipes.title: Nasturtium petal and orange jam

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) nasturtium flowers, closely packed; 1 garlic clove; 1 chilli; 500 ml apple cider vinegar. Wash the flowers and put them in a sterilised jar. Peel and slice the garlic and add it, then the chilli, slit in half. Fill the jar with the vinegar, put on the lid and shake well. Keep it in a cool, dark place for a week, then strain through a sieve lined with kitchen paper into small sterilised bottles. Use it as you would chilli sauce or Tabasco.
recipes.title: Nasturtium flower hot sauce

recipes.method: 12 nasturtium flowers; 125 ml (½ cup) cream cheese; 1 Tbsp finely chopped herbs, two kinds, such as dill and chives; salt and pepper. Dip the flowers in cool water and leave them a moment to clear out dirt and insects, then shake them gently. If you are not filling them straight away, keep them between paper towels in a container in the fridge. Mix the herbs into the cream cheese and season. Take the stamens out of the middle of each flower, especially for anyone with allergies or hay fever. Spoon about a teaspoon of the mixture into each flower and serve. The author says to know where your flowers came from, so you can be sure they have not been sprayed with pesticide.
recipes.title: Cream cheese stuffed nasturtium flowers

recipes.method: 250 ml (1 cup) nasturtium flowers, with some leaves and buds if you like; 1 litre boiling water. Put the flowers, leaves and buds in a jug and pour over the boiling water. Cover and leave to brew for 15 minutes, then strain and drink. The author lists only flowers but also adds leaves and buds in the method.
recipes.title: Nasturtium flower tea

recipes.method: Makes about 250 ml. 500 ml (2 cups) nasturtium leaves, packed; 250 ml (1 cup) nasturtium flowers, packed; 180 ml (¾ cup) olive oil; 180 ml (¾ cup) walnuts, lightly toasted and cooled; 125 ml (½ cup) grated parmesan; a pinch of salt. Pick leaves and flowers without blemishes. If you have few flowers, leaves alone are fine. Wash and dry them well, and tear larger leaves in half. Blend everything in a blender or food processor until smooth. Spoon it into a jar and pour a little olive oil over the top to stop it browning.
recipes.title: Nasturtium and walnut pesto

recipes.method: Serves 1, with rim salt for 6–8 glasses. 60 ml tequila; 15 ml orange liqueur; petals from 3–4 nasturtium flowers; ice; 60 ml orange juice; 15 ml lime juice; 15 ml agave nectar; 60 ml (¼ US cup) flaky sea salt; 1 Tbsp granulated sugar; petals from 6–8 more nasturtium flowers. For the rim, pulse the salt, sugar and the petals from the 6–8 flowers in a small food processor until the petals are finely chopped, and spread it on a small plate. Wet the rim of the glass with a little lime or orange juice, press it into the salt-sugar, and add ice. Muddle the tequila, orange liqueur and the petals from the 3–4 flowers in a cocktail shaker. Add ice, the orange juice, lime juice and agave, and shake hard. Strain into the glass, garnish with a nasturtium flower if you like, and serve straight away.
recipes.title: Nasturtium margarita

recipes.method: Nasturtium leaves, flowers or both, as many as you like; any salt, sea, rock or table, the same weight as the dried nasturtium powder; a clean, dry jar with a lid. Turn the leaves over to check for caterpillar eggs and aphids, and shake the flowers to dislodge insects. Dry them in a dehydrator following its instructions, or in an oven on a low setting with the door open. Grind them to a powder in a blender, food processor or mortar. It need not be fine. Mix in an equal weight of salt, crushing lumpy salt finer first. Store it in a labelled jar in a cool, dark place. It keeps about a year. Good in marinades, sauces and salad dressings, and on chips. Made with leaves only it is green, and flowers add yellow and red flecks.
recipes.title: Spicy nasturtium salt

recipes.method: Nasturtium flowers, enough to fill a jar loosely; cider vinegar, or another light vinegar such as white wine or white balsamic, to fill the jar; a light weight to hold the flowers under, such as folded greaseproof paper. Shake each flower to dislodge aphids and fill the jar loosely. Fill the jar with vinegar, weigh the flowers down and put on the lid. Glass or stone preserving weights are too heavy for these flowers. Leave it in a cool, dark place for 2–4 weeks: the longer it infuses, the stronger it tastes. Strain through a muslin-lined sieve into a clean, labelled jar. The vinegar turns rose pink. Use it in salad dressings, sauces and dips.
recipes.title: Nasturtium flower vinegar

recipes.method: 1 litre nasturtium flowers, loosely packed; 1 litre vodka; a large clean jar. Shake the flowers to dislodge insects and put them in the jar. Pour in the vodka and close the lid. Leave it in a cool, dark place for 3 days to a week, then strain through a muslin-lined sieve and bottle it. Equal volumes of flowers and vodka is the rule, so a teacup of each makes a small batch. It comes out a fiery pink. The author mixes it with lime juice and tonic water, or uses it in a martini or a Bloody Mary.
recipes.title: Nasturtium vodka

recipes.method: A bunch of nasturtium leaves (as many as you like); a little good salt (optional). Dry the leaves, stopping before they lose their colour. Grind them in a spice mill or coffee grinder. Use it like pepper or in salad dressings, on its own or mixed with the salt. The author finds it tastier than fresh nasturtium, without the bite. The author dried the leaves in a microwave, in a single layer between paper towels for 2 minutes, but the same trick set a single leaf alight within 30 seconds, so this guide does not suggest it.
recipes.title: Nasturtium leaf powder

recipes.method: About 360 ml (1½ cups) elderflower syrup; 45 nasturtium flowers; 3 Tbsp pectin mixed with 2 Tbsp sugar. Have clean glass jars ready. Mix everything in a pot and boil over medium heat for 10 minutes, skimming off any foam. Fill the jars and let them cool, then store them in a cold, dark place. The author makes the elderflower syrup first, from a separate recipe.
recipes.title: Nasturtium and elderflower jam

recipes.method: Written for garden nasturtiums from unsprayed plants; the recipe is by Ashley Adamant. Makes 5–6 jars of about 240 ml. 475–950 ml (2–4 US cups) fresh nasturtium flowers, rinsed; 950 ml (4 US cups) water; 60 ml (¼ US cup) bottled lemon juice, or 1 tsp citric acid; 1 box (about 50 g) regular powdered pectin, or 6 Tbsp bulk pectin; 1.2 litres (5 US cups) granulated sugar. Bring the water to the boil and pour it over the flowers, pushing them under. Cover and steep for at least an hour, or overnight in the fridge. Strain through a fine sieve, pressing gently, and top up with water to 950 ml. Put this tea in a large pot with the lemon juice and whisk in the pectin until it dissolves. Bring to a full rolling boil over high heat, stirring all the time, and boil for 1 minute. Add all the sugar at once and stir to dissolve. Return to a full rolling boil and boil hard for exactly 1 minute. Take it off the heat and skim off the foam. Ladle into prepared jars, leaving 6 mm of headspace, wipe the rims, and put on the lids and bands fingertip-tight. Process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes, turn off the heat and leave the jars 5 minutes. Leave them undisturbed for 12–24 hours before checking the seals.
recipes.title: Nasturtium flower jelly

recipes.method: Written for garden nasturtiums by John Mitzewich (Chef John). Serves 8. 120 ml (½ US cup) nasturtium petals, washed and patted dry; a pinch of salt; 60 ml (¼ US cup, about 55 g) unsalted butter, at room temperature. Pound the petals with the salt in a mortar and pestle to a paste. Stir the paste into the butter until well combined. Put the butter on plastic wrap, roll it into a small log and chill until firm, at least 30 minutes. Slice off a pat to melt over grilled fish, chicken or vegetables. The author says it has a slight radish-like taste.
recipes.title: Nasturtium butter

recipes.method: 100 g nasturtium leaves, stems, shoots and flowers; 50 g toasted nuts or seeds, such as pine nuts, cashews, walnuts, hazelnuts, peanuts, sunflower or pumpkin seeds; 50 ml olive or sunflower oil; 1–2 garlic cloves; salt and pepper. Blend everything in a food processor or blender. Scrape it into a jar and pour a little oil over the top to keep it fresh. It keeps 10 days to 2 weeks in the fridge. For winter, freeze it in ice cube trays, then tip the cubes into a labelled freezer bag. Good with pasta, as a dip, stirred through rice or couscous, or spread over roasted vegetables. The author seasons it with nasturtium salt and says raw nuts work too, though toasting gives a richer flavour.
recipes.title: Nasturtium pesto with stems and shoots

recipes.method: Written for chickweed, nasturtium and onion weed. Soak 500 ml (2 cups) chickpeas overnight, drain and rinse them well, and sprout them for 48 hours, rinsing twice a day, until the tails are as long as the peas; or cook them, as the author also allows. 500 ml (2 cups) sprouted chickpeas; 185 ml (¾ cup) tahini (the author grinds whole sesame seeds instead); 2–4 garlic cloves, minced; the juice of 2 large lemons and 1 orange; 125 ml (½ cup) olive oil; 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt; 5 ml (1 tsp) cumin; a big handful of chickweed, some nasturtium leaves, a small bunch of onion weed leaves and a sprig of parsley or another herb. Process the chickpeas with the citrus juice until still slightly chunky, then add everything else and process to the consistency you want.
recipes.title: Raw chickpea hummus with wild greens

recipes.method: The author's greens were the leaves of Indian, alpine (woodland) and garden strawberries, red deadnettle, wall lettuce, herb Robert and nasturtium. A handful of mixed strawberry leaves, stems removed (they are tough); a handful of beetroot leaves and stems; several stems of red deadnettle with their flowers; 5 wall lettuce leaves; 5 herb Robert leaves; red nasturtium flowers and several leaves; a few celery and small kale leaves, optional. Blend the leaves and flowers with 500–750 ml (2–3 cups) water, then add 1 punnet of strawberries, 1 red apple, 2 kiwifruit and 2 bananas and blend again.
recipes.title: Wild and tame strawberry smoothie

sources: Langlands, Peter. Foraging New Zealand (Penguin Random House NZ, 2024), 'Nasturtium' entry.
Knox, Johanna. A Forager's Treasury: A New Zealand guide to finding and using wild plants (Allen & Unwin, 2013), 'Nasturtium' entry.

Origin checked 20/10/2026 (owner: "find the bio status all shipped species and label them accordingly"), retrieved 20/10/2026: NZ Organisms Register 'Tropaeolum majus' (https://data.nzor.org.nz/names/search?query=Tropaeolum%20majus): NZFLORA biostatus Exotic, Present; NZPCN 'Tropaeolum majus' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/tropaeolum-majus/): Biostatus Exotic, year naturalised 1883, Environmental Weed (2024). Origin set to 'pest' (was 'introduced'): named in DOC's List of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024 (McAlpine & Howell, Science for Conservation 340, https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/sfc340.pdf). Auckland Council's pest search (https://www.tiakitamakimakaurau.nz/protect-and-restore-our-environment/pests-in-auckland/pest-search/tromaj/) says 'Not a legally declared pest'; the DOC listing alone makes it a weed here.

Recipes from The Veggie Tree (Anna, Northland, New Zealand; no licence stated), added 25/10/2026 (owner: 'I want you to cross reference our cataloge against the recepies there'): 'Wild Whangaroa pesto' from 'Wild Whangaroa Pesto' (09/07/2020, updated 15/08/2023, https://www.theveggietree.com/single-post/2020/07/09/edible-weeds-pesto-recipe-indentification-and-health-benefits); 'Green goddess dip' from 'Green Goddess Dip' (10/08/2021, updated 03/12/2025, https://www.theveggietree.com/single-post/green-goddess-dip-foraging-recipes); 'Weedolata (wild-greens gremolata)' from 'Weedolata Gremolata with a twist' (22/09/2021, https://www.theveggietree.com/single-post/weedolata-gremolata-with-a-twist); 'Wild greens soup' from 'Wild Greens Soup' (22/09/2021, updated 03/12/2025, https://www.theveggietree.com/single-post/wild-greens-soup); 'Nasturtium and nipplewort stuffed mushrooms' from 'Nasturtium and Nipplewort Stuffed Mushrooms' (15/09/2021, updated 03/12/2025, https://www.theveggietree.com/single-post/nasturtium-and-nipplewort-stuffed-mushrooms); 'Nasturtium flower pasta' from 'Nasturtium Flower Pasta' (04/12/2025, updated 15/12/2025, https://www.theveggietree.com/single-post/nasturtium-flower-pasta). Restated in my words, metric (NZ 250 ml cup, 15 ml tablespoon), every amount checked against the page retrieved 25/10/2026; the author's health claims are not used. A recipe is on this entry only because the author made it with this plant, not because it is named as a substitute.
Recipe: Sue, 'Poor Man's Capers: Nasturtium Pickles', Life's Bounty (New Zealand, 30/11/2024). Retrieved 27/10/2026. https://lifesbounty.co.nz/2024/11/poor-mans-capers-nasturtium-pickles/

Recipe: Yield Press, 'Nasturtium oil: turning a garden rambler into a kitchen gem', Shelf to Table, Yield Press & Media (30/08/2025 NZ time). Retrieved 27/10/2026. https://yieldpress.substack.com/p/nasturtium-oil-turning-a-garden-rambler

Recipe 'Nasturtium leaf salt' (offered 27/10/2026 in place of the owner's 'Nasturtium seed pepper', which needs mature seeds the entry does not list as edible): Honke, Dina. 'Nasturtium butter and nasturtium salt', Olive Oil and Lemons (Canada), 17/07/2019. All rights reserved. summary.text:
Garden escapee with peppery leaves, edible flowers, and seed pods that pickle into passable capers.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: warmer lowland parts, especially in coastal areas; South Island: mainly northern coastal areas but occurring south to Southland; Stewart Island: Halfmoon Bay; Kermadec Islands: Raoul Island, occasional. Native to the northern Andes, it was first recorded naturalised here in 1883. The species is very commonly cultivated and there are many cultivars differing in flower colour, extent of petal doubling and habit; many such forms have not yet been found wild.

warnings: Strongly peppery, and it can irritate the lining of the stomach and gut; it is not advised for infants or small children, or for people with stomach ulcers or kidney disease.

identification.text:
Perennial rosette herb. Leaves all basal, linear to oblong or linear- oblanceolate, simple, usually dentate, sometimes runcinate-pinnatifid, glabrous or with sparse multicellular hairs, especially above, (3)–5–15–(30) × (0.7)–1–1.5–(4.5) cm; terminal lobe narrowly deltoid to oblong, obtuse, truncate at base; lateral lobes triangular, deflexed or recurved, entire or toothed on distal margin; petiole and proximal part of midrib hollow. Scape stout, hollow, usually sparsely cobwebby above, sometimes glabrous, (2)–5–20–(30) cm tall. Capitula 1.5–3–(4) cm diameter. Involucral bracts glabrous; outer bracts lanceolate to ovate, more or less attenuate, green or reddish, erect at flowering, suberect to patent at fruiting, with scarious margins; inner bracts narrowly triangular to linear, acute, green, erect, with scarious margins. Florets usually golden yellow, rarely paler. Achene body usually orange-brown to dull greenish brown, rarely cream, ribbed, clavate-fusiform, 2.5–4 mm long; ribs each with (3)–5–7 teeth on distal ⅓-⅔, the distal teeth slightly longer than the proximal; cone tapering or narrowly cylindric, (0.5)–1–2 mm long, concolorous with the body. Beak usually pale, sometimes dark, slender, 4.5–8 mm long. Pappus white, 4–7 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Check the bracts under the flower head. The native dandelion's outer bracts are erect at flowering and usually have pale papery margins; the introduced dandelion's are strongly bent back at flowering and fruiting and have no papery margins. The seed differs too: (3)–5–7 teeth on each rib over the top third to two-thirds of the native dandelion's achene, against 3–(5) teeth on the top third in the introduced dandelion. Both have a hollow, leafless flower stem with a single head, hollow leaf stalks, and hairless or sparsely hairy leaves, so none of those separates them; nor does leaf shape, since some native dandelions have deeply lobed leaves. The introduced dandelion's heads are usually the larger, 3–5 cm across against 1.5–3 cm (sometimes 4 cm). The introduced dandelion's leaves, flowers and roots are eaten (see its page).

summary.text:
Biota of New Zealand and the New Zealand Plant Conservation Network name it Taraxacum zealandicum and treat it as endemic; Flora of New Zealand calls it Taraxacum magellanicum, a species also native to South America. Biota of New Zealand notes that 'The taxonomic status of T. zealandicum needs to be thoroughly investigated' (Heenan 2004).
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Tongariro National Park, Kaweka Range, Kaimanawa Range, Ruahine Range, Tararua Range; S.: throughout; St.: N.W. coast; Ch., Ant., A., C.
It is now scarce over much of its former range. Its 2023 national assessment is At Risk – Declining; it was assessed Not Threatened from 2004 to 2017 (NZPCN, restated).
Flora of New Zealand describes three forms: over most of its range, plants of damp montane to alpine grassland and herbfield whose leaves are not often deeply lobed; in lowland South Canterbury and the Chatham Islands, plants with deeply lobed leaves, in lowland grassland, river terraces, forest remnants and damp coastal sites; and on Stewart Island, plants of coastal sand dunes with usually simple, toothed leaves (sometimes deeply lobed), very pale seeds and pale yellow florets (restated).

habitat.text:
In New Zealand it is abundant on coastal banks, rocks and cliffs.
It grows mostly on cliff faces, rock stacks and boulder or cobble beaches, and only rarely inland. On the Kermadec Islands it grows on rock stacks, cliff faces, banks, and cobble and boulder beaches, and near bird nesting grounds.
Planted, it needs full sun and free-draining soil, is not fussy about fertility or moisture and tolerates long dry spells, though young plants can be frost-sensitive.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. On the Kermadec Islands the plants are subspecies stricticaule, which is at risk: if you harvest it there, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Trailing herb. Stem terete, glabrous. Leaves 3-angled, acute, often mucronate, tapering to connate base, (6)–20–30–(40) × 4–6–(9) mm; margins usually smooth, rarely papillate. Flowers 2–4 cm diameter. Petals uniformly white to deep pink, in 3–5 rows, 1–3 cm long. Stamens 4–6 mm long; inner filaments hairy at base. Stigmas (5)–6–8–(10). Capsule valves with parallel or more or less divergent expanding keels; placental tubercle rounded or 0. Seeds brown, obovoid, rugose, about 1 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Chilean sea fig is larger in every part. Its flowers are 6.5–8 cm across, with purple petals paler near the base, against 2–4 cm and uniformly white to deep pink here. Its leaves are 35–90 × 5–12 mm, against mostly 20–30 mm long (6–40 mm) and 4–6 mm wide (up to 9 mm) here. Its stems are 2-angled and woody at the base, not round in section, and its fruit stays closed, where this plant's fruit is a capsule whose cells have lids. Plants with purplish flowers 4–5.2 cm across may be hybrids between the two.
lookalikes.name: Chilean sea fig

lookalikes.howToTell: Jellybean ice plant's leaves are club-shaped, round or only weakly 3-angled in section, and blunt with a small point at the tip, where this plant's are 3-angled and sharp-pointed. Its petals are purple with a white base and sit in 2 rows, against 3–5 rows of petals uniformly white to deep pink here. In New Zealand it is known only from a few South Island saltmarshes and estuaries, often in places flooded at high tide; this plant grows mostly on cliffs, rock stacks and boulder or cobble beaches, and more rarely in saltmarsh.
lookalikes.name: Jellybean ice plant

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stem: native ice plant's is round and smooth; Chatham Island ice plant's is flattened, 2-angled and rough with tiny pimples (papillae). Native ice plant's leaf edges are usually smooth but rarely pimply, where Chatham Island ice plant's are pimply, so go by the stem; on the Kermadec Islands native ice plant (subspecies stricticaule) has pimply leaf edges but still a round, smooth stem. Native ice plant's leaves are mostly longer, 20–30 mm (6–40 mm) against mostly 10–15 mm (4–30 mm), but the ranges overlap. Native ice plant's seeds are brown and wrinkled; Chatham Island ice plant's are yellowish brown to brown and distinctly pimply; both are about 1 mm long. Both are trailing succulents with 3-angled, pointed leaves and flowers 2–4 cm across with 3–5 rows of petals, white to deep pink here and white to purple on Chatham Island ice plant, so flower colour does not separate them. Both grow on the coasts of the Chatham Islands, and Chatham Island ice plant grows nowhere else, so any ice plant picked there needs the stem check. Chatham Island ice plant was once counted as part of native ice plant. No record of Chatham Island ice plant as food was found (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Chatham Island ice plant

summary.text:
Disphyma australe, horokaka or New Zealand ice plant, is a trailing succulent herb in the ice plant family Aizoaceae, endemic to New Zealand.
Subspecies australe grows on coasts throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands and on the Three Kings and Chatham Islands. Subspecies stricticaule grows only on the Kermadec Islands, where it is widespread and common. In the 2023 national assessment subspecies australe is Not Threatened, and subspecies stricticaule is At Risk – Naturally Uncommon, as an island endemic.
It forms natural hybrids with both naturalised ice plants, South African ice plant and Chilean sea fig. The hybrid with South African ice plant, ×Carpophyma mutabilis, has mostly sterile pollen and forms no fruit. The Chatham Island ice plant, Disphyma papillatum, was once counted as part of this species.
Its fleshy capsules are spread by animals that eat them, and possibly by wind and water. It is grown in gardens as a fast-growing groundcover over rocks and the edges of retaining walls, and in coastal plantings to help hold sand. It is easily raised from rooted pieces and fresh seed.

habitat.text:
On rocks or stones between the tides, on both sheltered and exposed shores — most often on rock platforms and in rock pools, where it gets plenty of light and enough seawater not to dry out.
In New Zealand it is common at mid-tide level, often in dense mats.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Keep off the mats as much as you can: trampling damages them, and heavy trampling can almost wipe them out.
Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.

identification.text: Branched chains of hollow beads joined to one another by thin constrictions, attached to the rock by a small disc. Plants are up to 30 cm long, sometimes 50 cm. Yellow-green to grey-brown. Bead size varies with the habitat and how exposed the shore is. The fertile structures are scattered over the beads and show clearly as small bumps.

preparation.text:
Eat the beads raw while fresh, or slice the tender tips into salads or over cream cheese on crackers. Heated, the beads turn bright green, which makes them a garnish. They also pickle well in a sweet vinegar brine; rinse them well in fresh water first to remove sand and small animals.
It spoils quickly once picked, so eat or process it the same day; kept in seawater in the fridge it lasts a little longer.

recipes.method: Makes four 250 ml jars (or two 500 ml jars). 1 kg Neptune's necklace; 500 ml (2 cups) white wine vinegar; 250 ml (1 cup) fine caster sugar; 500 ml (2 cups) water; 1 slice fresh ginger; 5 ml (1 tsp) coriander seeds; 5 ml (1 tsp) wild peppercorn berries; 5 ml (1 tsp) mustard seeds. Sterilise the jars: wash them well in soapy water, put them in a cold oven and heat it to 110 °C, then leave them for 10 minutes once it gets there, or until completely dry. Rinse the Neptune's necklace thoroughly in fresh water to remove any sand or tiny stowaways. Put the ginger and spices in the jars, then pack in the seaweed. Warm the vinegar, sugar and water in a saucepan over low heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then bring to the boil and take off the heat. Fill the jars with the hot liquid so it covers the seaweed completely and sits 1–2 cm below the rim; let them stand a few minutes and top up if needed. The seaweed turns brighter green. To make sure the jars are well sealed, turn them upside down for a few minutes while still warm. Sealed jars keep up to a year in a cool, dry place away from sunlight; once opened, up to 4 weeks in the fridge. Use as any other pickle — with cheese, roast vegetables, or a roast sesame dressing.

summary.text:
Neptune's necklace (Hormosira banksii), also called bubbleweed, is a native brown seaweed made of branched chains of hollow, olive-brown beads, common on rocky shores between the tides.
In New Zealand it grows around the North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands. It is also native to Australia, including Lord Howe and Norfolk Islands.
It forms a canopy over the rock that shelters many small shore animals; where the canopy is removed, almost all the species living with it are lost.
It is assessed as Not Threatened in New Zealand, with low confidence because the data are poor.
The name sea grapes is also used for it, and for Caulerpa (sea grapes in this catalogue).

warnings: Neptune's necklace is a brown seaweed, and brown seaweed can contain very high levels of iodine. High levels of iodine can cause thyroid problems, so eating it more than every once in a while may be unsafe, especially when pregnant or breastfeeding.
Harvest only from clean water — never near stormwater drains, in harbours, or where there is heavy boat traffic, and not straight after a storm, when stormwater carries city debris into the sea.
Neptune's necklace takes up metals from the seawater around it.
Cut from higher up the plant — never pull it off the rock by its base.

identification.text:
Opposite, coarsely toothed, heart-shaped leaves on a square stem, covered in stinging hairs. Small green tassel-like flower clusters at the leaf joints.
A perennial up to 1.5 m tall that spreads by creeping underground stems (rhizomes), often into large patches that come back year after year; the stems seldom branch, and the plant dies down in winter. Leaves are 5–25 cm long, the end tooth longer than the teeth beside it. Male and female flowers are in separate clusters up to 9 cm long, usually on separate plants.
Dwarf nettle (Urtica urens), the commoner nettle in New Zealand, is a branched annual up to 60 cm with a short taproot and no rhizomes. Its leaves are 2–8 cm, the end tooth about as long as its neighbours, and its short flower clusters, up to 3 cm, usually carry male and female flowers together.

lookalikes.howToTell: Ongaonga (tree nettle) is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m tall; common nettles are herbs — Urtica urens an annual to 60 cm, Urtica dioica a perennial to 1.5 m — so height alone will not separate a tall Urtica dioica from a small ongaonga. Ongaonga's leaves are pale green, triangular to ovate-triangular and coarsely toothed, and it carries white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long on the leaf teeth, young stalks and leaf veins; ongaonga's stinging hairs are long-stalked and common nettles' short-stalked. Ongaonga has 2 stipules at each node, common nettles 4. Its sting has killed: in 1961 a young man died of paralysis and breathing problems several hours after walking through tree nettles, and stung dogs and horses have developed convulsions and breathing distress within minutes, often dying within hours. Young ongaonga can be confused with other native nettles, so do not touch a stinging plant unless you are sure it is not woody.
lookalikes.name: Ongaonga

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf nettle is a branched annual up to 60 cm with a short taproot; stinging nettle is a perennial up to 1.5 m that spreads by rhizomes into patches and seldom branches. Dwarf nettle's leaves are 2–8 cm and rounder, the end tooth about as long as the teeth beside it; stinging nettle's are 5–25 cm, the end tooth longer. Dwarf nettle's flower clusters, up to 3 cm long, usually carry male and female flowers together; stinging nettle's clusters, up to 9 cm, are one sex, usually on separate plants. Both sting, and both are eaten young and cooked.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf stinging nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush nettle is a native herb 15–60 cm tall with light green, triangular leaves 2–6 cm long (sometimes up to 12 cm); stinging nettle grows to 1.5 m with leaves 5–25 cm long. Bush nettle carries male and female flowers on the same plant, the lowest clusters all male and the upper all female; stinging nettle's male and female flowers are usually on separate plants. Bush nettle grows in forest, forest margins and shaded places; stinging nettle in waste places, cultivated land and grassland.
lookalikes.name: Bush nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Southern nettle is a stout, bushy native up to about 1 m whose branches lie down and root before turning upright, with broadly ovate, dark green leaves 10–20 cm long, the leaf stalk often carrying a pair of small leaflets near its base; its stinging hairs are mainly on the leaf edges and the veins underneath, and are often few or none. Stinging nettle spreads by long underground rhizomes into patches, and its male and female flowers are usually on separate plants; southern nettle carries both, female clusters above male. Leaf size does not separate them: stinging nettle's are 5–25 cm. Southern nettle grows only in Fiordland, the islets of Foveaux Strait, Stewart Island and the Chatham and subantarctic islands, where stinging nettle is rare (on Stewart Island it is recorded only at Port Pegasus). No record of southern nettle being eaten has been found, and it is At Risk – Declining.
lookalikes.name: Southern nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Hedge woundwort does not sting, smells strongly foetid when its leaves are crushed, and has reddish-purple two-lipped flowers 12–16 mm long, with white markings on the lower lip, in whorls up a spike; nettle stings, and its flowers are tiny, green and tassel-like at the leaf joints. Both spread by rhizomes and have opposite, toothed, heart-based leaves; hedge woundwort grows along forest margins, in scrub and around hedges. It is eaten too.
lookalikes.name: Hedge woundwort

preparation.text: Wear gloves. Soaking in water or cooking removes the stinging chemicals, so the leaves can then be handled and eaten; blanching in salted water until wilted, 30–60 seconds, is enough. Soup, pesto, or dried for tea. Steaming keeps more of the flavour than blanching; leaves to be dried need no blanching first. To freeze, blanch, drain, squeeze out the water and bag.

recipes.method: Makes 1 jar. 50 g walnuts; 50 g nettle leaves (weighed after picking); 20 g pine nuts; 2 garlic cloves, minced; 30 g basil (stalks and all); the juice of 1 lemon; salt and black pepper; 125–175 ml extra virgin olive oil. Roast 50 g walnuts at 180 °C (fan) for 7–8 minutes, until lightly browned, and let them cool. Wearing gloves, pick the leaves off the nettles, discard the thick stalks and wash the leaves well. Blanch 50 g of leaves (weighed after picking) in boiling salted water for 20–30 seconds, until just wilted, lift them into iced water, then squeeze out as much water as you can — they no longer sting. Blend the walnuts and nettles with 20 g pine nuts, 2 minced garlic cloves, 30 g basil (stalks and all), the juice of 1 lemon, salt and black pepper, drizzling in 125–175 ml extra virgin olive oil until almost smooth. Keeps up to a week in an airtight jar in the fridge.
recipes.title: Nettle pesto

recipes.method: 1 litre water; a large handful of fresh nettle tops (or half a handful of dried); half a lemon, sliced; a little honey (optional). Bring 1 litre of water to a simmer. Add a large handful of fresh nettle tops (or half a handful of dried) and half a lemon, sliced. Take it off the heat and let it brew for 5–10 minutes. Sweeten with a little honey if you like.
recipes.title: Nettle tea

recipes.method: Makes 6 × 750 ml bottles. 1 kg nettle tops; 4 litres water; 750 g sugar; the juice of 1 lemon; 25 g cream of tartar; a sachet of ale yeast. Sterilise everything first — pots, demijohn, bottles and siphon tube. Wash and drain 1 kg nettle tops. Bring 4 litres of water to the boil, add the nettles, boil hard for 15 minutes, then strain into a clean pot. Stir in 750 g sugar, the juice of 1 lemon and 25 g cream of tartar until dissolved, and leave to cool to room temperature. Sprinkle a sachet of ale yeast over the surface, cover with muslin or a tea towel and leave overnight. Next day pour it into a demijohn with a bung and airlock and leave to ferment for up to 6 days. Siphon into brown bottles, cap them and chill in the fridge for a week before drinking.
recipes.title: Nettle beer

recipes.method: Written for common stinging nettle (Urtica dioica and similar nettles) in North America. Serves 6. About 225 g nettles; 1 cup diced celery; 2 cups diced leeks; 2 diced shallots; 1 small diced onion; 3 tbsp butter; about 1 litre chicken stock; 2 cups diced potato; 120 ml cream; salt and white pepper; crème fraîche and chopped dill or mint, to serve. Blanch about 225 g nettles in salted boiling water until just wilted, about 30 seconds, cool them in cold water, squeeze dry and finely chop a handful to finish the soup. Sweat 1 cup diced celery, 2 cups diced leeks, 2 diced shallots and 1 small diced onion in 3 tbsp butter over medium heat for 5 minutes. Add about 1 litre chicken stock and 2 cups diced potato and simmer until tender, about 15 minutes. Add the blanched nettles and blend, then stir in the chopped nettles and 120 ml cream and season with salt and white pepper. Serve with crème fraîche and chopped dill or mint.
recipes.title: Classic stinging nettle soup

recipes.method: Written for common stinging nettle (Urtica dioica and similar nettles) in North America. Serves 2. About 225 g young nettle tops; 3 large garlic cloves, crushed; 3 tbsp olive oil, plus more to serve; salt and pepper; a pinch of chilli flakes; ½ cup ricotta; lemon wedges, to serve. Wash about 225 g young nettle tops and steam them, covered, over boiling water for 2–3 minutes until tender. Meanwhile warm 3 large crushed garlic cloves in 3 tbsp olive oil over medium heat for at least 10 minutes until browned, then discard the garlic. Add the steamed nettles to the oil, season with salt, pepper and a pinch of chilli flakes, gently fold in ½ cup ricotta and warm through. Serve warm or at room temperature with olive oil and lemon wedges.
recipes.title: Steamed nettles with ricotta

recipes.method: Written for stinging nettle in Britain; the recipe does not name the species. Serves 6. 25 g butter; 150 g nettle leaves, washed; 200 g feta, crumbled; 50 g parmesan, grated; the zest and juice of a lemon; 1 egg, beaten; grated nutmeg; seasoning; 7 filo sheets; 75 g melted butter; 1 tbsp sesame seeds. Brown 25 g butter in a large frying pan, add 150 g washed, still-damp nettle leaves and cook for about 6 minutes until wilted; cool, squeeze out the liquid and chop roughly. Mix with 200 g crumbled feta, 50 g grated parmesan, the zest and juice of a lemon, two-thirds of a beaten egg, grated nutmeg and seasoning. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan). Lay 3 filo sheets end to end, overlapping by about 5 cm, brush with some of 75 g melted butter, add 3 more sheets and more butter, then a seventh sheet in the middle. Spoon the filling in a line about 2 cm wide along one long edge, tuck in the ends, roll into a long sausage and coil it into a spiral about 20 cm across in a shallow round pan or on a buttered baking tray. Brush with the rest of the egg, scatter with 1 tbsp sesame seeds and bake for 40–45 minutes until golden.
recipes.title: Nettle spanakopita

recipes.method: Written for stinging nettle in Britain; the recipe does not name the species. Serves 4. 200 g nettle leaves; 1 tbsp olive oil; a 200 ml tub of crème fraîche; 1 tsp wholegrain mustard; 140 g blue cheese, crumbled; seasoning; 4 slices of sourdough. Wilt 200 g nettle leaves in 1 tbsp hot olive oil for 1 minute, cool briefly and chop roughly. Mix with a 200 ml tub of crème fraîche, 1 tsp wholegrain mustard, half of 140 g crumbled blue cheese, and seasoning. Toast 4 slices of sourdough on both sides under the grill, spread with the nettle mix, top with the rest of the cheese and grill until golden and bubbling.
recipes.title: Nettle and blue cheese rarebit

recipes.method: Written for common stinging nettles in North America. Serves 6. About 450 g tender nettle tops; 3 tbsp melted butter; 60 ml cream, warmed; ¼ tsp salt; black pepper; a little grated nutmeg; 4 large eggs; 1 tbsp oil; 3 tbsp grated parmesan; a little tomato sauce, to serve. Steam about 450 g tender nettle tops for at least 5 minutes, until thoroughly wilted, in batches if your pot is small. Chop them finely and, while still warm, mix in 3 tbsp melted butter, 60 ml warmed cream, ¼ tsp salt, black pepper and a little grated nutmeg, then work in 4 large eggs — the mixture will look stiff. Heat the grill. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a 20 cm cast-iron pan until nearly smoking, pack the mixture in and press it down, cover, turn the heat to medium and cook for 5 minutes. Uncover, scatter over 3 tbsp grated parmesan and grill for 5–10 minutes, until the cheese melts and the centre puffs slightly. Rest for 10 minutes before cutting into wedges; good with a little tomato sauce.
recipes.title: Nettle frittata

recipes.method: Written for common stinging nettles in North America. Serves 4 as a starter. About 115 g nettles, washed; 1 egg; 2 egg yolks; ½ cup grated parmesan, plus more to serve; a little nutmeg; a pinch of salt; ¾ cup (about 85 g) fine dry breadcrumbs, plus more if needed; flour for dusting; 4 tbsp butter; 1½ tbsp thinly sliced mint; salt and pepper; 60 ml dry white wine; about 1 cup warm tomato sauce. Steam about 115 g washed nettles for 2–3 minutes, spread them on a tray to cool, then chop roughly and purée in a food processor with 1 egg, 2 egg yolks, ½ cup grated parmesan, a little nutmeg and a pinch of salt. Mix in ¾ cup (about 85 g) fine dry breadcrumbs, cover and rest for an hour; the dough should be firm, not sticky — knead in more crumbs if it is. With floured hands roll it into 1 cm logs, cut them on the diagonal and dust with flour (they can be frozen at this point). Boil in lightly salted water until they float, then a couple of minutes more, 3–5 minutes in all. Meanwhile brown 4 tbsp butter in a frying pan, add 1½ tbsp thinly sliced mint with salt and pepper for 20 seconds, then 60 ml dry white wine, and take it off the heat. Toss the gnocchi in the butter and serve on warm tomato sauce (about 1 cup) with grated parmesan.
recipes.title: Nettle and breadcrumb gnocchi

recipes.method: Written for common stinging nettles in North America. Makes 6. For the batter: about 85 g young nettles; 250 ml milk; 1 egg; 2 tbsp butter; ¼ tsp salt; 1 cup sifted flour; oil for the pan. For the filling: about 115 g young nettles; 225 g soft goat cheese or ricotta; 55 g grated parmesan; half a beaten egg; nutmeg; salt and pepper. To finish: parmesan for sprinkling; ½ tbsp butter for each crêpe; about 170 g more nettles. Batter: blanch or steam about 85 g young nettles for 60 seconds, squeeze dry and chop, then blend until very smooth with 250 ml milk, 1 egg, 2 tbsp butter, ¼ tsp salt and 1 cup sifted flour; rest for 30 minutes. Cook thin crêpes, about 60 ml of batter each, in a very hot, lightly oiled 20 cm pan, turning each for just a second once the first side is light golden. Filling: steam about 115 g young nettles for 2 minutes, cool, squeeze dry and chop medium-fine, then mix with 225 g soft goat cheese or ricotta, 55 g grated parmesan, half a beaten egg, nutmeg, salt and pepper. Spread a scant ¼ cup over each crêpe, fold in half and in half again, lay them on a lightly greased lined tray, sprinkle with parmesan, dot each with ½ tbsp butter and bake at 190 °C for 15 minutes, until hot through and slightly puffed. Serve with about 170 g more nettles, steamed for 5 minutes and blotted dry.
recipes.title: Nettle crêpes with goat cheese

recipes.method: Written for broad-leaved dock and dandelion, with stinging nettle as a swap for them (pick only the top six or so leaves, before the nettle flowers) and dried nettle in the coating. Makes about 35 small puddings or one large one. 400 g pearl barley; 4 eggs, for hard-boiling; 2 large leeks; a little oil; about half a supermarket bag of dock and dandelion leaves, washed; 3 raw eggs, plus 1–2 more if needed; seasoning; flour; 1 beaten egg; 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs; 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle (optional); garlic mayonnaise, to serve. Boil 400 g pearl barley until tender, drain and cool. Hard-boil 4 eggs and chop finely. Finely chop 2 large leeks and soften them in a little oil. Blanch about half a supermarket bag of washed dock and dandelion leaves in boiling water for 20 seconds, then plunge into iced water (skip this and the puddings are more bitter and less green); squeeze out every drop of water and chop finely. Mix the chopped eggs, leeks, barley and greens with 3 raw eggs, and season very well. Wrap the mixture tightly in a tray covered with cling film, set in a larger tray of hot water, or seal it in a pudding bowl with baking paper, foil and string and stand it in a pan of water reaching at least halfway up. Steam for 45–60 minutes, in a 160 °C oven or on the hob, until it holds together; if it won't roll into balls, mix in 1–2 more raw eggs and steam longer. Turn out and serve as one pudding, or roll into small balls while warm and chill them (they freeze individually at this stage). Roll the chilled balls in flour, then in 1 beaten egg, then in 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs (mixed, if you like, with 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle), and deep-fry for 1–2 minutes until browned; or simply flour and fry them. Serve warm, with garlic mayonnaise.
recipes.title: Dock, dandelion and nettle puddings

recipes.method: Water and white sugar in equal parts (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar); at least a cupful (about 250 ml) of nettle tops, pressed down, or more; citric acid or lemon juice, or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar (optional). Make a syrup of equal parts water and white sugar (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar), heating gently and stirring until the sugar dissolves. Add a load of nettle tops — the top 3 or 4 pairs of leaves and their stem, picked with gloves — at least a cupful (about 250 ml) pressed down, or more. Keep it on the heat until steaming hot, but don't let it boil. Leave to cool, then strain out the nettles (the author dries them in a dehydrator as nettle sweets). Stir in small amounts of citric acid or lemon juice until it tastes slightly sharp — or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar — or leave it as a syrup. It keeps for several weeks in the fridge. The recipe works with dried nettles too, with a slightly different flavour.
recipes.title: Nettle cordial

recipes.method: Nettle cordial; gin, up to equal parts with the cordial; ice; a squeeze of lime juice or a pinch of citric acid (optional); a splash of soda or tonic (optional). Mix nettle cordial with gin, up to equal parts, to taste, and stir over ice. Add a squeeze of lime juice or a pinch of citric acid if it is too sweet. Strain into a chilled coupe, or, less classically, top with a splash of soda or tonic; the author likes a little vermouth in his.
recipes.title: Nettle gimlet

recipes.method: Written for nettles: the author eats both perennial and annual (dwarf) nettle, and gives this soup from Richard Mabey's Food for Free (1972). 4 large handfuls of nettle tops, picked with gloves; 1 large onion; 50 g butter or coconut oil; 2 potatoes; 1 litre vegetable stock; 15 ml (1 tbsp) crème fraîche or yoghurt; salt, pepper and grated nutmeg. Strip the nettles from the thicker stalks and wash them. Melt the butter and cook the chopped onion gently until translucent. Add the nettles and the chopped potatoes and cook 2–3 minutes, then add the stock and simmer 20 minutes, crushing the potatoes now and then with a wooden spoon. Season, with a little grated nutmeg, and finish with a swirl of crème fraîche or yoghurt; blend it first if you want a smoother soup.
recipes.title: Nettle and potato soup

recipes.method: The author's greens, picked in spring, were cleavers, chickweed, herb Robert, stinging nettle (the page does not say which nettle), onion weed, speedwell, pūhā and lemon balm; she gives no amounts for them. She blends the nettle raw; the nettle page says to cook it, so blanch it first. Chop the greens into the blender with 2 cabbage leaves, stalks removed, the juice of 1 large grapefruit, 125 ml (½ cup) kombucha and 500 ml (2 cups) water, and blend until the greens are broken down. Add 2 small bananas or 1 large, 1 apple, 1 kiwifruit (hairs scrubbed off, top and bottom trimmed), 1 whole orange, and 15 ml (1 tbsp) chia seeds and 5 ml (1 tsp) pumpkin seeds ground in a coffee grinder, and blend again. Decorate it with onion weed and viola flowers and a piece of orange.
recipes.title: Spring clean smoothie

summary.text:
It has a flavour similar to spinach when cooked — and a genuinely dangerous native relative.
Introduced from the northern temperate regions and first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1870, it grows here only at scattered places — much less often than dwarf nettle — and Auckland Council manages it as a pest plant across the region.

warnings: Only harvest soft, herbaceous nettle. Never harvest from a woody shrub.

Stop harvesting once the plant flowers. Older leaves develop gritty crystals (cystoliths) that cooking does not dissolve; they are widely held to irritate the kidneys, though that has not been shown medically, and old leaves can be laxative.
Auckland Council controls it as a pest plant with herbicide. Pick from ground you know.

If you are stung, wash the skin with lukewarm water and soap and don't scratch; the sting usually fades within about 10 minutes but can last 12 hours or more. Rubbing it with dock leaves has no known chemical effect.
Nettle is widely advised against in pregnancy because it may stimulate uterine contractions and cause a miscarriage; whether it does in people is not known.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Lowland to montane grassland, open places, especially bogs, wet flushes, lake and streamsides.
It prefers damp, boggy ground that can be flooded for months at a time.
Look for it from the mountains of the central North Island southwards, down to sea level in parts of the South Island and on Stewart Island, and on Campbell Island; it is mostly uncommon in the north.
On the national wetland plant list it is a facultative wetland plant: usually found in wetlands, occasionally on drier ground.

identification.text:
Glabrous, much-branched, divaricately spreading herb with stout tap-root; branches and branchlets together up to about 50 cm long, rather slender. Lower leaves with slender petioles from longer than to much shorter than lamina. Lamina (1)–3–15–(17) × (0.2)–0.4–2.5–(3) cm, linear to narrow-oblong or elliptic, usually brown, rarely green; margins more or less undulate and often crisped or even crenulate; base cuneate to truncate or cordate, sometimes widened; apex obtuse or subacute. Upper leaves smaller, linear to ovate-oblong, gradually decreasing to 2 cm long or less. Inflorescence of numerous, rather distant whorls of 6–12, bisexual, protandrous flowers; leaves subtending whorls gradually reduced towards inflorescence apex; pedicels rather slender, glabrous, often short. Perianth segments 1.5–3 mm long; outer segments lanceolate or narrow-ovate, apiculate, more or less spreading at fruiting; inner segments ovate to almost rhombic, acuminate. Fruit valves strongly reticulate, with (1)–2–3–(4) straight teeth on each margin; tubercles usually 0, sometimes 1, narrow and towards base. Nut (1.5)–1.8–2.3 mm long, pale brown, lustrous, sharply angled. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Its leaves are bronze-green; the young rosette leaves reach about 15 cm, and the leaves up the zig-zag flowering stems shrink to under 5 cm as the stems spread to about half a metre. Hooked dock looks similar, but New Zealand dock never has hooked fruit.
It flowers from November to April. The tiny flowers are greenish-yellow to brown, with cream anthers.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hooked dock's fruit valves carry about five red hooked spines, 2 mm long, on each side, which catch on clothing; New Zealand dock never has hooked fruit — its valves have 1–4 straight teeth on each edge (an older Flora described them as minutely hooked). Hooked dock's leaves are up to 5 cm wide, usually with two rounded lobes at the base; New Zealand dock's are usually brown, narrow (up to 3 cm wide) and often wavy or curled. Hooked dock grows on dry cliff tops, roadsides and stony ground, mostly in the north and in Marlborough and Nelson; New Zealand dock in bogs, wet flushes and by lakes and streams.
lookalikes.name: Hooked dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Curled dock stands upright, with stems to about 1 m and erect branches whose flower whorls are mostly packed together; New Zealand dock is low and spreads sideways, its slender zig-zag branches together about 50 cm long, with many small whorls (6–12 flowers each) spaced well apart. Curled dock's lower leaves are larger, 6–30 × 1.5–6.5 cm, and taper into the stalk; New Zealand dock's are 3–15 × 0.4–2.5 cm, usually brown and only rarely green. Both have wavy, curled leaf edges, so the edges don't separate them. In fruit, curled dock's valves are 3–4.5 mm with smooth or finely scalloped edges and 1–3 deep red swellings (tubercles); New Zealand dock's have 1–4 straight teeth on each edge and usually no tubercle. Curled dock's nut is dark brown; New Zealand dock's pale brown.
lookalikes.name: Curled dock

lookalikes.howToTell: Broad-leaved dock's lower leaves are big ovals up to 35 × 15 cm (rarely 50 × 20) with a heart-shaped to rounded base, on erect stems 30–100 cm tall with flower whorls usually packed together; New Zealand dock's are narrow, 3–15 × 0.4–2.5 cm, usually brown and only rarely green, on low, sideways-spreading zig-zag branches with small whorls spaced well apart. Both have teeth on the fruit valves, but broad-leaved dock's valves (3.5–5 mm) carry one prominent rosy swelling (tubercle) 2–2.5 mm long; New Zealand dock's usually have none.
lookalikes.name: Broad-leaved dock

summary.text: New Zealand dock is endemic and very closely related to the Australian Rumex dumosus. Its species name, flexuosus, means winding; older names for it are Rumex brownianus and Rumex cunninghamii. It has been confused with the naturalised hooked dock, and old records based on that confusion (including one from the Kermadecs) gave it a misleading range. Old museum records place it on Kawau Island, in Northland and near Auckland, but there are no recent ones, and it is now regionally extinct in Auckland; an engineer's record of it in the Waitākere Ranges was never confirmed by a museum specimen or any other record. Because it is mistaken for the introduced docks, it is both crowded out by them and pulled out as a weed. Its national status is Not Threatened (2023). Māori names: runa (explained in 1899 as 'water or juice from the dock plant'), rungarunga.

warnings: Like other docks, it can be harmful if too much is eaten at one time. Eat only a little.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.
Kelp that has come loose and washed ashore is the gentlest to collect; even then, take a little from several places, as the piles on the beach are also habitat. If you cut a living plant, use a sharp knife and leave the holdfast so it can regrow.
Attached plants may not be taken from the East Otago taiāpure; only unattached kelp cast ashore may be taken there. Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.

identification.text:
Grows to about 1 m. A single large blade, deeply divided into lobes, smooth or wrinkled, on a cylindrical, unbranched, trunk-like stipe. The holdfast is a clump of finger-like cylindrical branches (haptera). Golden brown. Reproductive tissue shows as darker patches on the lobes. The blade is rough and leathery, often with many small raised bumps, and has no midrib.
Told from wakame by the midrib: wakame has a strap-like midrib up the blade once it is larger than about 10 cm, a flattened stipe, a smooth, thin blade and, when mature, a frilly reproductive structure at the base of the stipe. Young plants are difficult to tell apart before wakame's midrib develops.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look down the middle of the blade: wakame has a strap-like midrib, continuing from the stalk, once the plant is larger than about 10 cm (it starts to show from about 5 cm); this kelp has no midrib. This kelp's stipe is cylindrical and trunk-like; wakame's is flattened and strap-like. This kelp's blade is rough and leathery, often with many small raised bumps; wakame's is smooth, thin and fragile. Mature wakame has a frilly reproductive structure (the sporophyll) at the base of the stalk, thicker and often darker brown than the blade and deeply folded, spiralling round the stalk when big; this kelp has none, and its reproductive tissue shows as darker patches on the lobes. Young plants are difficult to tell apart before wakame's midrib develops. Lobes, colour and holdfast do not separate them: both have a blade that can be deeply divided into lobes, both can be golden brown, and both have a holdfast of finger-like branches. Size does not either: this kelp grows to about 1 m, wakame to 1 m and up to 3 m. Both grow from the low intertidal into the subtidal. Wakame grows on any hard surface, including wharf piles, ropes, moorings, boat hulls and concrete, and is found in almost all of New Zealand's international ports and harbours; this kelp grows on moderately exposed or exposed coasts.

preparation.text: Take kelp that is freshly washed up, soon after high tide or a storm, and rinse off all the sand in fresh water. Use it fresh: trim off the tough stems and slice the blade into thin ribbons for pickling, or blanch for 10–30 seconds, when it turns bright green, and add it to soups or stir-fries. Or dry it: in the sun it takes 2–3 days and turns from golden brown to dark green, or use a dehydrator in cold, damp weather; then chop or grind it and add it towards the end of cooking. Dried pieces flavour stock and dashi: put them in tepid water and warm it gradually without boiling. Dried blades can be softened in water and wrapped round fish to bake. Soaking seaweed in water, with or without heat, lowers its iodine content, by up to 90%.

recipes.method: Written for common kelp (Ecklonia radiata) washed up on the south coast of New South Wales. Makes 4 × 250 ml jars. 1 kg fresh kelp; 650 ml water; 250 ml white wine vinegar; 100 g white sugar; 1 tsp black peppercorns; 1 tsp coriander seeds; 1 tsp mustard seeds. Sterilise the jars and lids: 20 minutes before you need them, heat the oven to 110 °C and line an oven tray with baking paper; boil the jars and lids in a large pot of water for 10 minutes, drain, and stand them upside down on the tray in the oven until completely dry, without touching the rims or insides. Keep them in the oven until you fill them. Rinse the kelp thoroughly in fresh water to get rid of any sand, trim off any tough stems, and slice it into thin ribbons. Bring the water, vinegar, sugar and spices to the boil in a saucepan; once the sugar has dissolved, take it off the heat. Add the kelp to the hot pickling liquid: it turns vivid green at first, then quickly dulls. Pack it firmly into the jars, top up with the pickling liquid so the kelp is completely covered, and seal. The page gives no keeping time.
recipes.title: Pickled kelp

recipes.method: Written for dried New Zealand kombu leaves (the blade of Ecklonia radiata). Serves 2. 2 large dried kelp blades, softened in water; 2 pieces of salmon; tamari or soy sauce; 1 lemon, thinly sliced; a handful of fresh herbs (dill, thyme, tarragon or fennel); salt (kelp or seaweed salt if you have it) and pepper. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Line an oven tray with baking paper and lay the 2 softened blades on it. Put a piece of salmon on each and drizzle with tamari. Cover with the lemon slices and herbs, season, and wrap each blade diagonally round its fish. Bake for about 10 minutes, until the fish is just cooked, and serve straight away. Other fish fillets can be cooked the same way.

summary.text:
A native kelp, known in New Zealand as common kelp or paddle weed and sold dried as kombu. It grows around the Three Kings, North, South, Stewart and Snares Islands; it is absent from the Chatham Islands but found on Mernoo Bank, 200 km east of the South Island, and also grows in Australia, South Africa, Madagascar, West Africa and Oman. In northern waters it dominates the marine forests. It is the preferred food of kina, which sometimes mass together and graze a whole forest bare; in northern New Zealand, at least, it grows back rapidly. It is assessed Not Threatened, and secure overseas.
The kombu of Japanese cooking is a different kelp, Saccharina japonica; the kombu sold in New Zealand is dried Ecklonia radiata, harvested from the North Island.

warnings: This is a brown seaweed, and brown seaweed can contain very high levels of iodine. Wild New Zealand Ecklonia radiata has been measured at 3,990 mg of iodine per kg dry weight, the highest of the seaweeds tested in a New Zealand study, and the safe upper limit for adults is 1.1 mg a day. High levels of iodine can cause thyroid problems, so eating it more than every once in a while may be unsafe, especially when pregnant or breastfeeding.
Collect only from clean coast, away from cities, wastewater outfalls and farm run-off. Seaweed from water contaminated with human sewage can carry norovirus.

harvestEthics.text: Leave it where it stands. This is an endemic beech associate listed At Risk – Naturally Uncommon, known from three sub-populations, and the forest it was first described from has already been cleared for pasture. Photograph it, note where it was, and submit the record to iNaturalist NZ. Picking is prohibited in reserves and on conservation land, and there is no reason to take one.

identification.text:
Cap 5.5–13 cm across, convex when young and flattening or sinking in the centre with age, dry and finely powdered to velvety under a lens; dark brown to almost black, sometimes with salmon patches, and without concentric zones. Gills light orange to salmon with dark brown edges, thick, moderately crowded, up to 9 mm deep, attached to slightly running down the stem. Stem 4.5–8 cm long and 1.3–2.8 cm thick, more or less even, coloured like the cap. The milk is viscid, white, unchanging in the air, and dries pale cream. The flesh is granular and white at first, then runs through pink, salmon and orange-red to wine red where it is cut or broken. Gills taste mild and the flesh turns slowly faintly acrid; no distinctive smell. Spore print ochraceous. Solitary or in groups under beech.

Lactarius novae-zelandiae McNabb, described from New Zealand, is a similar large and dark brown to brownish black species from this subgenus. The species differs by the lamellae that are moderately crowded and have dark brown edges, a character that was not observed in L. megaplinthogalus. The latex in this New Zealand species is unchanging and not staining the lamellae pinkish to blackish. The context does change to pink, salmon, and orange-red to finally vinaceous on exposure to air. The pseudocystidia are sparse and scattered. The spores are larger (9–12 × 8.2–10.5 µm).

The macroscopic appearance of this taxon is striking, and the fact that there was a 44-year gap between the initial records (1968–1971) and subsequent records (2015–2018) suggests it is uncommon.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white, does not change, and dries pale cream. Its flesh does change, slowly, from white through pink, salmon and orange-red to wine red where cut - so judge the milk, not the cut flesh. Its cap is dark brown to almost black and unzoned, often with dull salmon patches near the centre, where saffron milk cap's is orange, often with darker rings. It grows under beech; saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine.

The endemic it is most easily confused with, and that confusion has no page here. McNabb's own note separates this species from Lactarius sepiaceus, another New Zealand endemic under beech: both are dark greyish brown to brownish black, dry and finely bloomed, azonate and wrinkled, with white unchanging latex and dark brown gill edges. The differences are that L. sepiaceus has pale creamy-white to cream gills rather than light orange to salmon ones, flesh that stays white apart from very faint salmon tints rather than running through pink and orange-red to wine red, a white spore print rather than an ochraceous one, and prominently apiculate reticulate spores. L. sepiaceus has no iNaturalist NZ records and so no entry in this catalogue. Manaaki Whenua Landcare Research, Virtual Mycota, 'Lactarius sepiaceus', description attributed to McNabb (1971), restated not quoted. Checked 06/10/2026. https://virtualmycota.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/vM_Species_Details.aspx?pk=5189

How many Lactarius New Zealand actually has, which is more than the iNaturalist list shows. The Virtual Mycota carries twelve described species for the region — the ten with entries here, plus two further endemics with full McNabb (1971) descriptions and no iNaturalist NZ observations at all: Lactarius sepiaceus (pk 5189) and Lactarius maruiaensis (pk 5183, solitary under beech, recognisable by its pale yellow cap and stem and reticulate spores). Three more names are indexed with no biostatus recorded (L. helvus, L. oculatus, L. pusillus). summary.text:
This striking milkcap is endemic of New Zealand, where it is apparently ectomycorrhizal with Fuscospora truncata, growing in relatively mature forests.

There has been extensive surveying of the Russulaceae by Ross McNabb in the 1960/70s and by Jerry Cooper and Pat Leonard from 2005 onwards, and there are three known and extant sub-populations of this species. The single original locality from which the species was described (Karamea) has been lost due to the conversion of forest habitat to pasture.

Since 2017, two additional locations in Nelson and Buller have been identified and confirmed from sequence data. These locations significantly change the value of the area of occupancy (AOO of known sites), making the 2017 IUCN assessment of Endangered no longer appropriate. The distribution of records suggests some degree of regional restriction, but as an associate of beech, the potential distribution of this species remains considerable, and there is no reason to suspect population decline. For that reason, the panel re-assessed this species as Naturally Uncommon.

habitat.text:
Wet coastal cliffs and talus, rarely on sand or salt meadow.
On the coast, usually on cliff faces in or around damp seepages, often with the blue-green alga Nostoc and the fern Blechnum blechnoides, and mostly on base-rich rock such as basalt, calcareous mudstone, siltstone, limestone or apatite-rich greywacke. On some offshore islands it extends up into coastal scrub and coastal herbfield, and it occasionally grows on stabilised sand dunes.

harvestEthics.text: This species is at risk. If you harvest it, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In Northland (Regionally Critical), the Auckland region (Regionally Endangered), Otago (Regionally Endangered) and the Wellington region (Regionally Vulnerable), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it.

identification.text:
Biennial to perennial. Roots tap and fibrous; taproot swollen above. Stem erect, simple or branching above, finely grooved or ribbed, glabrous, (5)–15–60–(100) cm tall. Leaves thick, glaucous, dull, glabrous, lanceolate to narrowly oblong to linear-oblanceolate, (3)–8–20–(55) × (1)–3–6–(15) cm; margins dentate. Rosette and lower stem leaves tapering to base, pinnatifid to less than 1/2 way to midrib; lobes broadly triangular, spreading or slightly deflexed. Upper leaves not lobed, narrowly triangular to linear or narrowly oblanceolate, with more or less rounded amplexicaul auricles at base. Inflorescence cymose to umbellate; capitula few to many. Involucre 10–15 mm long, turbinate to cylindric; bracts imbricate, recurved at fruiting, glabrous or sometimes the outer with a row of median broad-based trichomes, occasionally densely white-tomentose at base. Receptacle glabrous. Florets 1½× length of involucre; corolla tube slightly longer than ligule; ligules spreading, yellow. Achenes elliptic, brown, strongly flattened, (3)–3.5–4 × 1.3–1.8 mm, 3-ribbed on each face, winged; spaces between ribs smooth; wings and ribs smooth. Pappus fine, white, about equal to involucre.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In the field: very large, thick, dull blue-grey leaves that are not spiny set it apart from the introduced sow thistles. All parts bleed white latex when broken, and the stem is hollow. The rosette spreads 30–40 cm, with broader, more lettuce-like leaves than the introduced sow thistles, and the flowering stem stands up to about 1 m.

lookalikes.howToTell: New Zealand sow thistle's leaves are thick, dull and blue-grey, with toothed margins that are not spiny; common pūhā's (Sonchus oleraceus) are soft, edged with small spine-tipped teeth, and range from mid or dark green to blue-grey, so leaf colour alone does not separate them. New Zealand sow thistle's upper leaves are not lobed and clasp the stem with more or less rounded lobes; common pūhā's upper leaves are usually lobed and clasp the stem with pointed lobes. New Zealand sow thistle lives two years or more from a taproot swollen at the top; common pūhā is an annual. In seed, New Zealand sow thistle's achenes are winged and smooth between the ribs; common pūhā's are not winged and are finely wrinkled crosswise. Common pūhā is edible: its leaves are widely eaten as greens.
lookalikes.name: Pūhā / Sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: New Zealand sow thistle's leaves are thick, dull and blue-grey, with toothed margins that are not spiny; prickly sow thistle's (Sonchus asper) are firm, more or less shiny and usually green (rarely blue-grey), with prickly-spined teeth. Both have upper leaves that clasp the stem with rounded lobes, and both have winged achenes, smooth between the ribs, so neither the leaf base nor the seed separates them. New Zealand sow thistle's taproot is swollen at the top; prickly sow thistle's taproot is not described as swollen. Prickly sow thistle is edible: it is recorded as a popular Māori food (pūhā tiotio).
lookalikes.name: Prickly sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: Perennial sow thistle spreads by creeping roots; New Zealand sow thistle (Sonchus kirkii) grows from a taproot swollen at the top. New Zealand sow thistle's leaves are thick, dull and blue-grey; perennial sow thistle's are firm, dark green and paler beneath. Perennial sow thistle's involucre is 15–18 mm long and its bracts carry tangled short white hairs and long yellow glandular bristles (an Australian description allows hairless bracts too); New Zealand sow thistle's is 10–15 mm, its bracts hairless, sometimes with a row of broad-based hairs on the outer ones or densely white-woolly at the base. Both clasp the stem with rounded lobes, so the leaf base does not separate them. In seed, perennial sow thistle's achenes have 5 ribs on each face, are not winged and are closely wrinkled; New Zealand sow thistle's have 3 ribs, are winged, and are smooth between the ribs. Perennial sow thistle is edible: its young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Perennial sow thistle

preparation.text: Eat raw or cooked. The leaves are tougher and more bitter than common pūhā's (Sonchus oleraceus). Squeezing them under running water washes out some of the bitter juice, and blanching them for a minute in salted boiling water calms the bitterness.
