summary.text:
Sonchus kirkii, also known as New Zealand sow thistle, or shore puha is a herb in the Asteraceae family.
Endemic to New Zealand: the Three Kings, North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands. Its conservation status is At Risk – Declining (2023). The introduced prickly sow thistle and common pūhā grow faster and can take over the places it prefers. It probably once grew in a wider range of habitats and has retreated to coastal cliffs where weeds compete less. It is declining over most of its range, especially in the North Island; on the south Wellington coast it was very common until the mid-1980s and has since gone from many sites, through weeds and rock quarrying but also from apparently stable native habitats, for reasons not yet known. Auckland and Otago both rate it Regionally Endangered (2025).
It is thought to be the pūhā Māori ate before European settlement; common pūhā, from Europe, was naturalised by 1832 and has taken its place as the everyday pūhā.
It grows easily from fresh seed and is short-lived, best treated as an annual.

Frequent but rather local on coastal sands, dunes and stony beaches.
In New Zealand: the coastal strand — beaches among driftwood and seaweed, sand dunes, boulder and cobble beaches, cliff faces and rock ledges. It also turns up in landfills and as a casual weed in towns, and some coastal plants may have started from garden waste.

identification.text:
Herb with decumbent branching stems, softly woody towards base. Leaves on petioles up to 2 cm long; lamina ovate-rhomboid to triangular, obtuse to subacute, entire to slightly sinuate or shallowly lobed, more or less densely papillose. Flowers solitary or occasionally paired, occasionally unisexual, sessile or nearly so, about 7 mm in diameter; perianth yellowish. Calyx tube broad-turbinate, lobes broad-triangular, obtuse. Stamens 10–20. Ovary 3–8-celled, styles 3–8. Fruit 8–10 mm long, subturbinate, angled; seeds 4–10; horns 2–4, hardened.
The plant cultivated as New Zealand spinach has much larger leaves than the wild plant.

lookalikes.howToTell: Beach spinach is most reliably told apart when fruiting: its fruit is a round, succulent berry 5–8 mm long, pink to dark red, with no horns and 1–3 seeds, where this plant's is typically top-shaped and angled, 8–10(–15) mm long, with 2–4 hardened horns and 4–10 seeds. Out of fruit, look at the flower stalks: beach spinach's flowers sit on slender stalks, 5–30 mm long, against the stalkless or nearly stalkless flowers here. Do not go by leaf shape, the papillae on the thick leaves or the yellow flowers; the two share all of these.

summary.text:
Tetragonia tetragonioides, commonly called New Zealand spinach, warrigal greens or by its Māori name of Kōkihi, is a flowering plant in the fig-marigold family (Aizoaceae). It is often cultivated as a leafy vegetable.
It is a widespread species, native to eastern Asia, Australia, and New Zealand. It has been introduced and is an invasive species in many parts of Africa, Europe, North America, and South America.
In New Zealand it is indigenous to the Kermadec, Three Kings, North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands, where it grows on the coastal strand. Its 2023 national assessment is At Risk – Naturally Uncommon.

warnings: The leaves are high in oxalates, higher than spinach, and boiling leaches much of the soluble oxalate into the water. Blanch the leaves in boiling water for one to two minutes, discard the water and refresh them in cold water before cooking. People with a history of kidney stones should eat it only in moderation.

identification.text:
Annual herb. Stems erect, branched above, finely ribbed, with fine crisped eglandular hairs especially below, 15–100–(150) cm tall. Leaves glabrous or sparsely to densely hairy; margins ciliate. Rosette and lower stem leaves petiolate, lyrate-pinnatifid; terminal lobe large, broadly ovate to deltoid to orbicular, bluntly dentate, (1.5)–3–8 × (1.5)–3–8 cm; lateral lobes in (0)–1–3 pairs, the distal pair equal to or less than width of terminal lobe, the proximal pairs successively smaller, all dentate. Upper leaves undivided, becoming sessile, linear-lanceolate to ovate, sharply dentate to serrate, smaller than lower leaves. Capitula in diffuse corymbose panicles; peduncles longer than 2× length of involucre. Involucre 5–8 mm long; bracts glabrous except for ciliate apex, strongly veined or keeled, erecto-patent; outer bracts 1–1.5 mm long. Florets few, about 1.5× length of involucre; corolla yellow; tube shorter than ligule. Achenes fusiform, glabrous, pale, about 20-ribbed, 3–5 mm long; pappus 0. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The small pale-yellow flower heads open only in sunlight and close in the afternoon.

lookalikes.howToTell: Wall lettuce is hairless all over; nipplewort's stems carry fine crinkled hairs, especially low down, and its leaf margins are fringed with hairs, though the leaf surfaces range from hairless to densely hairy. Count the florets: wall lettuce's heads have usually 5, nipplewort's 8 to 15. Wall lettuce's leaf end-lobe is large, triangular or kidney-shaped and itself three-lobed, coarsely toothed with prominent water pores (hydathodes) at the tooth tips; nipplewort's is broadly ovate to triangular to round, bluntly toothed and not three-lobed. Under the head, nipplewort's bracts are strongly veined or keeled; wall lettuce's inner bracts are linear, strictly erect and often purplish, with 2–4 very short outer ones. In seed, wall lettuce's achenes are dark brown to black, shortly beaked and topped with a white pappus; nipplewort's are pale, without beak or pappus. Both have milky sap, lyre-shaped lower leaves with a large end lobe, small yellow heads in a loose branched spray, and grow at forest margins and roadsides. Wall lettuce's leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they can taste extremely bitter (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Wall lettuce

lookalikes.howToTell: Break a stem or leaf: nipplewort's sap is milky, mountain fireweed's is watery. Nipplewort's florets are all strap-shaped and yellow; mountain fireweed has no strap-shaped florets, only a yellow disc 2–3 mm across of tiny tubular ones. In seed, nipplewort's achenes are hairless, pale and have no pappus; mountain fireweed's are sparsely papillate and topped with fine white pappus hairs about 6 mm long. Both can have lyre-shaped, lobed leaves and yellow heads in a loose spray and grow at forest margins and in disturbed places, though mountain fireweed grows mostly from 600 to 1500 m. Mountain fireweed is a native plant with no food record, and its genus, Senecio, is known for liver-damaging pyrrolizidine alkaloids (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mountain fireweed

preparation.text: Add the young leaves to salads, cook them like spinach, or put them in soups and casseroles; wilted down, they stand in for spinach or silverbeet. The taste is bitter or radish-like, and the tiny hairs make some prefer it mixed with other vegetables. On Ikaria, Greece, the rosettes are boiled or baked into pies, and there nipplewort counts among the non-bitter greens. In Sicily the tender shoots are eaten raw and cooked. For cooking, take the larger lobed leaves from low on the plant rather than the small ones at the top; a 20-minute soak in water with a little vinegar cleans them and takes the edge off any bitterness, and they cook down a great deal. The rosette leaves taste like lettuce and, like lettuce, turn more bitter once the flower stalk forms; they are soft and wilt quickly, so pick them just before you use them. Try them in salads, or anywhere you would use parsley, as in tabbouleh.

recipes.method: Written for nasturtium and nipplewort together. 6 large field mushrooms; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil plus another 60 ml for frying; the leaves of 1 rosemary stalk, chopped; salt and pepper; 600 g nasturtium and nipplewort leaves, roughly chopped; 250 ml water; 1 onion (the method uses one, though the ingredient list leaves it out); 4 crushed garlic cloves; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 250 ml (1 cup) roughly chopped walnuts; 240 g cream cheese, plant-based or dairy; 1 slice of bread, broken into small pieces. Serves 4. Toss the mushrooms with the first 60 ml of oil, the rosemary, 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper and leave them to marinate. Cook the greens in a lidded pot with the water and 5 ml (1 tsp) salt on high heat for 5 minutes, turning them, until wilted; cool them under cold running water, squeeze out the water and chop again. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Fry the mushrooms in the second 60 ml of oil, open side down, for 4 minutes, then 4 minutes on the other side, until golden, and set them open side up in a baking dish. In the same pan soften the onion for 5 minutes, add the garlic, greens, lemon zest and juice and cook a minute, then stir in the walnuts, cream cheese, bread, 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper off the heat. Pack the filling into the mushrooms, drizzle with olive oil and bake for 20 minutes until golden. Good on soft polenta or mashed kūmara and potato.
recipes.title: Nasturtium and nipplewort stuffed mushrooms

recipes.method: Written for nipplewort with other New Zealand weeds. 250 ml (1 cup) millet; a squeeze of lemon juice; 2 small beetroot, cut small; 4 asparagus spears, cut in pieces; 2 onion weed leaves; 2 large nipplewort leaves; 2 stems each of chickweed and nettle; 8 cleavers tips; 625 ml (2½ cups) cold water; salt. The night before, soak the millet in warm water with the lemon juice, and soak the cleavers tips in the cold water. Next day strain the millet, pour the cleavers water over it in a saucepan, bring to the boil and simmer for 10–15 minutes, until the millet is cooked but still soupy; salt to taste. Cook the beetroot until soft. Steam the asparagus until just tender, then add the chopped onion weed, nipplewort, chickweed and nettle and steam until wilted and cooked. Drain the beetroot and asparagus and add them to the millet, with some of their cooking water if you want it thinner. Top with the cooked herbs, and onion weed flowers if you have them.
recipes.title: Spring herb millet soup with nipplewort

recipes.method: Written for nipplewort (Lapsana communis) in Seattle. About 450 g nipplewort leaves, the larger lobed ones from low on the plant; 4 garlic cloves, minced; 45 ml (3 tbsp) sesame oil; 30 ml (2 tbsp) soy sauce; 15 ml (1 tbsp) raw sugar; 500 ml (2 cups) cooked noodles, such as soba; about 30 ml (2 tbsp) vinegar for soaking; toasted sesame seeds, chopped spring onions or umeboshi to finish. Cook the noodles, rinse them in cold water and set aside. Strip as much stem from the leaves as you can and soak the leaves for about 20 minutes in water with the vinegar. Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat and add the garlic. Drain the leaves and squeeze out the water. When the garlic sizzles, after 3–5 minutes, add the nipplewort and stir until wilted, about 5 minutes. Add the soy sauce and sugar and stir for another 5 minutes, then tip it all over the noodles and add the garnishes.
recipes.title: Wilted sesame nipplewort noodles

recipes.method: The author's wild greens were dandelion, nipplewort, chickweed, herb Robert, plantain and cleavers (the page does not say which plantain). 1 large handful of these wild greens; 2 cavolo nero or other kale leaves; chia and pumpkin seeds (no amount given), soaked in 125 ml (½ cup) water; 5 large strawberries; 125 ml (½ cup) grapefruit juice; 1 kiwifruit, hairs scrubbed off; 1 banana; 1 peeled tangelo; 250 ml (1 cup) water. Blend the greens and the soaked seeds with their water, the extra water and the juice, then add the fruit and blend again. Thin it with more water if it is too thick.
recipes.title: Strawberry green smoothie

recipes.method: Written for nipplewort, used in place of the usual parsley. 250 ml (1 cup) fresh nipplewort leaves, whole if young, chopped if stringier; 2 garlic cloves; the zest and juice of a small lemon; about as much olive oil as lemon juice; salt and pepper. Blitz everything in a food processor for about 20 seconds. Serve it with any savoury dish, or put a spoonful in soup; it keeps a couple of days in the fridge. Other young spring greens can go in too, and orange in place of lemon makes it sweeter and less sharp.
recipes.title: Nipplewort gremolata

recipes.method: Written for nipplewort or mixed greens. 1 onion; a little coconut oil; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) nigella seed; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) ground turmeric; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) ground cardamom; 1 or 2 garlic cloves, crushed; 200 ml (¾ cup) coconut milk; about 200 g nipplewort (a colander full); 250 ml (1 cup) chopped tomato, cherry tomatoes halved or quartered if you have them; salt and pepper. For the cornmeal: 1 litre water, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) salt and 200 g yellow cornmeal (polenta). Chop the onion and fry it gently in the coconut oil until it turns translucent, then add the nigella, turmeric, cardamom and garlic and fry gently a few minutes more. Add the coconut milk, nipplewort and tomato, season, and cook gently for 10–15 minutes. Meanwhile bring the water to the boil, add the salt and whisk in the cornmeal so it doesn't go lumpy, cover and cook gently until done (precooked cornmeal takes very little time). Spoon the cornmeal into a large dish or 4 bowls, make a hollow in the middle and fill it with the greens. Rice, millet or another grain can stand in for the cornmeal, and fat hen, orache or spinach for some of the nipplewort.
recipes.title: Zanzibari-style nipplewort with cornmeal

recipes.method: Written for nipplewort picked in an English garden. The author gives no amounts — use what suits you: butternut squash, peeled and cubed; brown basmati rice; freshly picked nipplewort, chopped; onion and garlic; fresh sage and thyme; vegetable or mushroom stock; olive oil; salt and pepper. Heat the oven to 180–200 °C and start the rice (for brown basmati, put it in cold salted water, bring it to the boil, then simmer 25–30 minutes; it can go into the oven part-cooked, with more stock, to finish). Toss the squash with olive oil in a large oven dish and roast it. When it starts to brown, stir in the chopped onion; when the onion turns translucent, add the garlic and herbs, taking care not to burn them. When the garlic just colours, add the nipplewort and some stock and cook about 5 minutes more, until the leaves wilt. Stir in the cooked rice and seasoning, with a little more stock if needed to moisten the rice rather than make soup, and return it to the oven until the rice is hot and has soaked up most of the liquid. Take out any herb stalks and serve. Mushrooms roasted with the squash, or chickpeas or other beans, go in well too.
recipes.title: Baked butternut and nipplewort rice

summary.text:
Lapsana communis, the common nipplewort, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae.
Away from its native area, Lapsana communis is common throughout the British Isles, naturalised, and sometimes considered an invasive species, in many areas around the world, including Australia, Chile, New Zealand, Greenland, and most of Canada and the United States.
The English name 'nipplewort' was coined in the 17th century as an equivalent of papillaris (from Latin papilla, meaning a nipple), the name used by German apothecaries, since the plant was used to treat cracked nipples and ulcerated breasts, especially under the doctrine of signatures on account of the flower buds' resemblance to nipples.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Northland, Auckland, Bay of Plenty, Urewera National Park, Waikato, Volcanic Plateau, Manawatu, Wellington; South Island: Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago; Stewart Island: Halfmoon Bay; Kermadec Islands. Naturalised from Eurasia and North Africa, first recorded in 1869.

identification.text:
Shrub or small tree up to 7 m tall, with upright trunks and branches and red-brown to maroon-black twigs. Leaves 35–110 × 18–45 mm, broadly obovate, oblanceolate, elliptic or almost round, leathery, glossy dark green to yellow-green above with no blemishes or blotches, and with a conspicuous pale cream to yellow-green midvein; white underneath, the midvein there red. Leaf stalks 4–11 mm long, red-brown to maroon. Leaf buds and expanding leaves are usually hairy on the margins, undersides and stalks. Flowers in the leaf joints, single or in clusters of 2–3, with 5–8 free cream petals 3.8–7 mm long and 13–22 stamens. Fruit a black berry, egg-shaped to oblong, 6.4–9.8 mm long, with 1–4 seeds.
Told from horopito and lowland horopito by its upright small-tree habit, its glossy leaves without blotches, its conspicuous pale cream to yellow-green midvein, and its black fruit. Unlike horopito's, its leaves are not particularly peppery to taste.

lookalikes.howToTell: Northland horopito is known only from Mt Manaia and Bream Head at Whangārei Heads and from Logues Bush near Wellsford; horopito grows on the North, South and Stewart Islands. Northland horopito's leaves are glossy, without blemishes or blotches, with a conspicuous pale cream to yellow-green midvein above and a red midvein beneath; horopito's are dull green and blotched with red, at least in exposed places, with the midvein inconspicuous above. Both have white leaf undersides; horopito's are often pink-flushed, and Northland horopito's leaf buds and young leaves are usually hairy. Horopito's leaves are usually smaller, 2–6 (rarely 8) × 1–3 cm against 3.5–11 × 1.8–4.5 cm, though the sizes overlap. Horopito is a shrub up to 2 m, sometimes 3.5 m; Northland horopito is an upright shrub or small tree up to 7 m tall. Horopito's ripe fruit is round, dark red to black, 3–6 mm across; Northland horopito's is black, egg-shaped to oblong, 6.4–9.8 mm long. Horopito's leaves are eaten as a spice (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Horopito

lookalikes.howToTell: Northland horopito is known only from Mt Manaia and Bream Head at Whangārei Heads and from Logues Bush near Wellsford, and until 2003 its plants were taken for lowland horopito or for hybrids between lowland horopito and horopito. Both are upright shrubs or small trees, to 7–8 m, with glossy leaves without blotches and a conspicuous pale midvein above. Turn a leaf over: Northland horopito's underside is white with a red midvein; lowland horopito's is pale to glaucous but not white, with a pale midvein. Northland horopito's leaf stalks are 4–11 mm long, red-brown to maroon; lowland horopito's are slender, about 2 cm long. Northland horopito's leaf buds and young leaves are usually hairy on the edges, undersides and stalks; lowland horopito is hairless. Leaf sizes overlap: 3.5–11 × 1.8–4.5 cm against 6–10 × 3–6 cm. Northland horopito's flowers are single or in twos or threes, with cream petals; lowland horopito's are greenish yellow, often several together. Northland horopito's ripe fruit is black, 6.4–9.8 mm long; lowland horopito's is red to orange-red, rarely dark, 5–6 mm across. Lowland horopito's leaves are used as a spice (see its page).

summary.text:
Northland horopito (Pseudowintera insperata) is a shrub or small tree of the Winteraceae, endemic to New Zealand.
It once grew on the high points around the northern Whangārei Harbour, from Maungatapere to Bream Head, and at Logues Bush near Wellsford; it is now known only from Mt Manaia, Bream Head and Logues Bush. About 50 adult plants survive at two sites and a single plant at Logues Bush, all within less than 1 ha, though it is easily overlooked. It was recognised as distinct in 2003 and described in 2006; before that these plants were usually taken for lowland horopito (P. axillaris) or for hybrids between lowland horopito and horopito (P. colorata). No record of it being eaten was found. It is ranked Threatened – Nationally Critical (2023). In gardens it is more likely to reach 2–3 m and stands pruning; trial plantings have grown in both high light and dense shade, it does best in well-drained soil, and planting it away from other horopito is advised so that it does not cross with them. It grows from semi-hardwood cuttings, slowly, and from fresh seed, which can take 1–2 years to come up.

warnings: No record of Northland horopito as food was found, so it is not given as food here.
Until it was recognised as a distinct species in 2003 these plants were taken for lowland horopito or hybrids, so check any horopito-like shrub within its range before picking (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text: Lactarius quietus is found growing exclusively at the base of oak trees, solitarily or in scattered groups, in soil. It is ectomycorrhizal, feeding symbiotically exclusively with oak, though studies have suggested it is also able to feed saprotrophically, growing from organic soil matter.

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to pick this mushroom. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Lactarius quietus' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Lactarius quietus typically has a convex cap of 5 to 8 centimetres across, which later flattens or develops a small depression in the centre. In colour, the cap is a dull reddish brown with a tint of cinnamon, sometimes with darker concentric bands or spots. This zoning is one of the most distinctive features of the species. The cap is dry and matt, and not sticky when moist. It features a thick layer of firm, whitish-buff flesh. The stem measures from 4 to 9 centimetres in height, and is typically 10 to 15 millimetres thick. It is cylindrical in shape, but is sometimes furrowed lengthways, and it lacks a ring. It is concolorous with the cap, or a little darker, and is sometimes hollow. The brownish-white gills are slightly decurrent, and change colour with age to a pale reddish brown with mauve hints. The milk is white or cream in colour. The mushroom has a distinctive, strong oily smell, which has also been likened to bedbugs and wet laundry. The spores are oval, with plentiful warts joined by numerous ridges, forming a well-developed network. The spores typically measure 7.5 to 9 by 6.5 to 7.5 μm, and leave a cream print.


var. incanus
Lactarius quietus var. incanus is typically slightly larger than the nominate variety, and younger specimens feature a whitish bloom, after which the variant is named. It has a sweet smell reminiscent of maple syrup, and can be commonly found under oak trees. It can be confused with L. aquifluus and L. mutabilis, but both of these species are found in coniferous woodland.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Oakbug milkcap's milk is white or cream. Its cap is dull, matt reddish brown with a cinnamon tint and stays dry, not sticky, when moist, and it has a strong oily smell likened to bedbugs or wet laundry. Oakbug milkcap grows with oak; in New Zealand and Australia, saffron milk cap grows only with pine. Both can show concentric zones on the cap, so zoning is not the difference.
lookalikes.name: Saffron milk cap / Pine mushroom

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a little flesh and smell it. Oakbug milkcap has a strong oily smell likened to bedbugs or wet laundry; rufous milkcap has no smell. Rufous milkcap's cap often has a small central boss, and its milk is watery white. In New Zealand rufous milkcap is reported only with pines, oakbug milkcap with oak. Cap colour does not separate them: both are matt reddish brown.

summary.text:
Lactarius quietus (commonly known as the oak milkcap, oakbug milkcap or southern milkcap) is a mushroom of the genus Lactarius.

It can be found very commonly throughout autumn months. In the United Kingdom, it is one of the one hundred most commonly encountered mushroom species. L. quietus var. incanus is found commonly in eastern North America.
In New Zealand it is currently known only from a single site, where it grows with oak (Quercus).

sources: Useful Temperate Plants, Ken Fern, temperate.theferns.info (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0)
edibleParts.text:
Seed - cooked. It has a floury texture and a mild, somewhat creamy flavour. It can be used as a staple food crop in either savoury or sweet dishes. Used as a cereal, it is probably best known as the breakfast cereal porridge but it can also be used in many other ways. The seed can be sprouted and used in salads, the grain can also be ground into a flour and used in making biscuits, sourdough etc. The roasted seed is a coffee substitute.
Dried oat straw — the green stems and leaves — is made into a tea or infusion.

identification.text:
Erect, green to glaucous tufts, 50–150 cm. Leaf-sheath glabrous or slightly hairy. Ligule (2)–3–5 mm, more or less rounded, finely denticulate, abaxially finely scabrid. Leaf-blade 15–40 cm × (2.5)–7–15 mm, more or less finely scabrid on ribs; margins finely scabrid, sometimes with a few scattered hairs. Culm erect or decumbent and rooting at base, internodes glabrous. Panicle 14–32 cm, very variable in shape, loose or contracted, equilateral to secund; branches horizontal to more or less erect, slender, finely scabrid. Spikelets (15)–20–30–(40) mm, 2–(3)-flowered, pendulous on fine unequal pedicels; falling intact at maturity. Glumes 9–11-nerved. Lemma 10–18 mm, ovate-lanceolate, glabrous, or with a few hairs towards base, apex obtuse or shallowly notched, red-brown, grey, yellow, white or blackish, usually awnless, but lowest or sometimes all florets in certain cultivars bearing a weak, straight or curved awn, not geniculate and scarcely twisted at base. Palea keels with 1 row of cilia, interkeel scabrid or glabrous. Anthers 2–4.2 mm. Caryopsis 4–9 × 1.5–3 mm.
[From: Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are edible; this is about which you have. When ripe, the cultivated oat's spikelet falls as a whole, where slender oat's breaks apart below each floret. Slender oat's lemma has long, stiff reddish hairs below the awn, and each of its two tip-lobes is drawn out into a fine bristle 2–3 mm long; the cultivated oat's lemma is hairless or has a few hairs near the base, with a blunt or shallowly notched tip. Slender oat's lemmas carry an awn 30–36 mm long, bent at a knee and twisted, with a very dark brown lower part; the cultivated oat's are usually awnless, and any awn is weak, straight or curved, and not bent. Slender oat is often a very slender plant with very fine panicle branches, but the cultivated oat's pedicels are fine too, so build is only a clue.
lookalikes.name: Slender oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Both edible; this is about which you have. Look at the awn: winter wild oat's lowest one or two florets each carry an awn bent at a knee and twisted in its lower part, 25–50 mm long in subsp. ludoviciana and 60–70 mm in subsp. sterilis; the cultivated oat is usually awnless, and where an awn is present it is weak, straight or curved, not kneed and scarcely twisted. Winter wild oat's lemmas are hairy below the awn; the cultivated oat's are hairless or have a few hairs near the base. Size helps but overlaps: cultivated oat spikelets are (15)–20–30–(40) mm with 2–(3) florets, winter wild oat's 3.5–6 cm with 2–3 florets (subsp. ludoviciana) or 6–8 cm with 3–5 (subsp. sterilis).
lookalikes.name: Winter wild oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild oat's spikelets break up at maturity, separating below each floret; the cultivated oat's spikelets fall intact. Wild oat's lemma is stiffly hairy below where the awn joins, though sometimes hairless, and carries a stout awn 30–40 mm long, bent at a knee, with a twisted dark-brown lower column. The cultivated oat's lemma is hairless or has a few hairs near the base, and is usually awnless; any awn is weak, straight or curved, not bent at a knee and scarcely twisted. Spikelet length does not separate them cleanly: wild oat's are 35–50 mm, the cultivated oat's usually 20–30 mm but 15–40 mm at the extremes. None of these tests holds for fatuoids, or false wild oats — a mutant form that turns up in oat crops: their florets look like wild oat's, with a bent, twisted awn and a horseshoe-shaped callus bordered by hairs, and the spikelet breaks below every floret. Occasional hybrids between wild oat and the cultivated oat may occur within an oat crop or where oats have been grown, though few are found.

preparation.text: Oats are harvested when grain is in the hard dough stage and straw is slightly green (when the moisture content of the grain is 14% or less). If too ripe, shattering causes seed loss. Seeds are threshed and cleaned by winnowing, and artificially dried to below 14% moisture for storage. The seed, when harvested and dried, can store for several years. Harvested oats go through multiple stages of milling. The first stage is cleaning, to remove seeds of other plants, stones and any other extraneous materials. Next is dehulling to remove the indigestible hull, leaving the seed or "groat". Heating denatures enzymes in the seed that would make it go sour or rancid; the grain is then dried to minimise the risk of spoilage by bacteria and fungi. For home use such as making porridge, oats are often rolled flat to make them quicker to cook.

recipes.method: About 60 ml of dried oatstraw; boiling water to fill a 1 litre jar. Put about 60 ml of dried oatstraw in a 1 litre jar, fill with boiling water and cover. Leave it to steep several hours or overnight, then strain. Drink through the day.
recipes.title: Oatstraw infusion

recipes.method: Built on the infusion above. 375 ml (1½ cups) milk — dairy, almond or soy; 2 tbsp honey; ½ tsp cinnamon; ¼ tsp maca powder; 190 ml (¾ cup) strained oatstraw infusion. Warm the milk in a pot with the honey, cinnamon and maca, stirring until it is warmed through and smooth. Pour it into a jar with the infusion, cover and shake well before serving.

summary.text:
The oat (Avena sativa), sometimes called the common oat, is a species of cereal grass (Avena) grown for fodder and for its seed, which is known by the same name (usually in the plural).

Oats tolerate cold winters less well than cereals such as wheat, barley, and rye, but need less summer heat and more rain, making them important in areas such as Northwest Europe that have cool, wet summers. They can tolerate low-nutrient and acid soils. Oats grow thickly and vigorously, allowing them to outcompete many weeds, and compared to other cereals are relatively free from diseases.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.; S.; Foveaux Strait on Pig Id; St.; C. Naturalised from Eurasia.

warnings: Claviceps purpurea is an ergot fungus that grows on the ears of rye and related cereal and forage plants. Consumption of grains or seeds contaminated with the survival structure of this fungus, the ergot sclerotium, can cause ergotism in humans and other mammals. It affects oats only rarely.

Oat products are frequently contaminated by other gluten-containing grains, mainly wheat and barley, requiring caution in the use of oats if people are sensitive to the gluten in those grains. Use of pure oats in a gluten-free diet offers improved nutritional value, but remains controversial because a small proportion of people with coeliac disease react to pure oats.

edibleParts.text: Fruit, once cured. Both green-ripe (full-sized, before colouring) and fully ripe (dark red to purplish black) olives are cured. Wild olives in New Zealand are small-fruited: wild European olive (oleaster) fruit is fleshy and 12–14 mm long, African olive fruit thinly fleshy and 7–10 mm long. African olive fruit is edible but bitter; no curing method written for it was found.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Open coastal scrub and modified areas near indigenous forest margins.
In Auckland feral olive grows in open areas, on cliffs and sand dunes, in forest gaps and margins, and on roadsides (Auckland Council, restated). Wild European olive (oleaster) is locally naturalised mainly on some Auckland volcanic cones and inner Hauraki Gulf islands, near where it has been planted. African olive is the most abundant woody weed of the coastal bush slope in front of the Treaty House grounds at Waitangi, and self-sown trees come up in gardens and hedges beside the planted street trees at Panmure, Auckland (Cameron 2017, restated).
Olive is also planted in New Zealand as street and avenue trees and as hedges and screens.

identification.text:
Dense bushy shrub or small tree to about 7 m high; bark becoming rough. Shoots angular, lepidote when young. Leaves shortly petiolate. Lamina 5–11 × 0.8–2 cm (juvenile leaves smaller), lanceolate or narrow-elliptic, sparsely to densely lepidote beneath and appearing pale green or slightly silvery, dark green and lepidote or elepidote above; base attenuate; apex mucronate. Panicles axillary. Calyx 1–1.5 mm long; lobes broad-triangular, glabrous or somewhat lepidote. Corolla lobes 3–4 mm long, whitish, more or less oblong, almost fleshy, patent at first, ultimately reflexed. Stamens slightly shorter than corolla. Drupe 5–8 mm diameter, globose to broad-ovoid, glossy, becoming red and ultimately black. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Telling the two wild subspecies apart: African olive seedlings are not divaricating, its leaves are green or yellowish-brown beneath with tips often hooked, and its fruit is spherical, thinly fleshy and 7–10 mm long. Wild European olive (oleaster) seedlings are strongly divaricating, its leaves are whitish-green beneath with tips rarely hooked, and its fruit is ovoid, fleshy and 12–14 mm long. Cultivated European olives, grown on grafted rootstock, have large fruit (Cameron 2017, restated).

preparation.text: Raw olives are too bitter to eat and must be cured to leach out the bitter compound. Pick by hand, with as little stem as possible, and put the olives gently into the bucket so they don't bruise; don't gather fallen olives from the ground, as bruised olives have an off flavour. For green olives the tree is ready when the first few start turning purple or black; for black olives wait until most have turned. Remove leaves, stems and damaged fruit and rinse. Green olives turn brown in air, so keep every olive under the liquid while curing. Don't mix kinds or ripeness in one container, and cure at 15–30 °C, ideally about 25 °C. The usual cures are water, brine, dry salt or lye. Water curing: cut or crack each olive, soak in fresh water changed daily for a week or more, then put the olives in a salt-and-vinegar finish brine; they stay slightly bitter. Brine curing ferments the olives in salt brine and takes at least 3 months, sometimes 6 months or longer. Dry-salt curing of fully ripe olives takes about 5 to 6 weeks. Lye curing is the fastest but needs strict safety precautions (see warnings).

recipes.method: Ingredients: firm, fully coloured (dark red to purplish black) olives picked before the first frost, preferably an oil-rich kind; pickling salt; red wine vinegar; olive oil. Sort the olives by size if you like and discard bruised or damaged fruit. Rinse and drain. With a clean, sharp knife make 2 lengthwise cuts about 3 mm deep in each olive. Put them in a food-grade plastic or glass container, cover with fresh cool water, keep them under with a heavy plate or a sealed bag of water, and close the lid loosely. Every 24 hours drain and cover with fresh cool water, for 8 to 10 days (up to 20 days for less bitter olives); over-soaking makes them soft and washed-out. For the finish brine, dissolve 450 g (1½ cups) pickling salt in 3.8 litres (1 US gallon) cool water and add 1 litre (4 cups) red wine vinegar — enough for about 4.5 kg of fresh olives. Drain the olives, cover with the finish brine, pour 6–10 mm of olive oil over the top, close firmly and keep at about 16–27 °C for about a month to develop the flavour. Kept airtight in a cool, dark place or the fridge they last about a year.
recipes.title: Kalamata-style water-cured olives

recipes.method: Ingredients: green-ripe olives of any kind; pickling salt; white wine vinegar; optional chopped oregano, lemon slices and garlic cloves. Sort and discard bruised or damaged fruit; rinse and drain. Strike each olive with the flat of a mallet or a rolling pin just to crack the flesh, without breaking or removing the stone. Put the cracked olives in a food-grade container, cover with fresh cool water, weigh them under and close the lid loosely. Drain and replace the water every 24 hours for 6 to 7 days (a few days more for less bitter olives). For the finish brine, dissolve 450 g (1½ cups) pickling salt in 3.8 litres (1 US gallon) cool water and add 500 ml (2 cups) white wine vinegar — enough for about 4.5 kg of fresh olives. Drain the olives, cover with the finish brine, add the seasonings if using, close firmly and refrigerate. They must be kept in the fridge; they are ready after 4 days and keep up to a year in the finish brine.
recipes.title: Mediterranean-style cracked green olives

recipes.method: Ingredients: firm, fully coloured (dark red to purplish black) olives picked before the first frost; pickling salt. Sort by size so they cure evenly and discard bruised or damaged fruit. Pack into jars or containers that can be made airtight (a 1-quart, about 1-litre, jar is the smallest recommended). Make a medium brine of 225 g (¾ cup) pickling salt per 3.8 litres (1 US gallon) cool water, cover the olives, close the lids loosely and keep at about 16–27 °C. After 7 days replace it with a strong brine of 450 g (1½ cups) salt per 3.8 litres water and close the lids firmly. Keep the olives in brine for at least 2 months; for less bitter olives replace the strong brine monthly for 2 or 3 months. If lids bulge from fermentation gas, loosen them carefully to let it out and close again; top up any lost brine with fresh strong brine. Eat after 2 months if you like them fairly bitter, or after at least 3 months for milder olives. Kept airtight in a cool, dark place they last at least a year; refrigerate after opening. To make them less salty, soak overnight in water before eating, then dress with a little olive oil.
recipes.title: Greek-style black olives in brine

recipes.method: Ingredients: fresh green or purple olives; unprocessed salt (rock or sea salt); rainwater or other unchlorinated water; a little olive oil (optional). Pick with as little stem as possible and put the olives gently into the bucket so they don't bruise. There is no need to cut or crack them. At home put them in a container big enough to hold them all (a chilly bin with a drain plug makes the daily draining easier) and cover with water; it doesn't matter if they float. Every day drain, give them a rinse and cover with fresh water, for at least 12 days and up to 15 for larger olives; they give off a foamy, slimy liquid as the bitterness leaches out. On the last day drain and rinse well. Put the olives in clean food-grade buckets with lids and measure how much water it takes to cover them. Make a 10% brine: 100 g salt for every litre of that water — take out a few litres, heat them, dissolve all the salt in it, cool completely, then pour back and stir. Pour a thin layer of olive oil over the top, or weigh the olives under with a plate, so none touch the air. Close and keep in a cool, dark place for at least 3 months, then taste: leave longer if they are still hard; if too salty, pour off a little brine and top up with water. Up to 10% vinegar can be added to the brine for flavour. They keep for at least a year in the same brine; spoon into jars as needed, covered with brine, and top up the oil layer. If any mould appears, throw out the whole batch.
recipes.title: Sicilian-style olives in brine

recipes.method: Ingredients: green or black (ripe) olives; coarse or cooking salt; olive oil; optional garlic, basil, oregano, thyme or chilli. For green olives, pick once some olives on the tree begin to turn black. Strip the fruit by hand onto cloth sheets laid under the tree, remove all stems and leaves and rinse in clean water. Straight away put the olives in a bucket of salt water, 125 ml (½ cup) coarse salt to every 2.5 litres (10 cups) water, with a clean plate on top so that every olive stays under. Every day (at a stretch every second day) pour the water away and replace it with fresh salt water, for about 20 days for green olives or about 14 days for black. Bite one to test: they are ready when the bitterness has nearly gone. Measure the last lot of water you pour off, to know how much brine you need. Dissolve salt in that much fresh warm water at 250 ml (1 cup) salt to every 2.5 litres (10 cups) water, bring to the boil and leave to cool. Pack the olives into bottles, pour the brine over until they are completely covered, top with 1 cm of olive oil and seal. They are ready to eat straight from the brine and keep at least 12 months in a cool cupboard. For extra flavour, put some in a clean jar with garlic, basil, oregano, thyme or chilli and cover with olive oil.
recipes.title: Salt-water-leached olives in brine

recipes.method: Ingredients, for each 1 kg of cured olives: 250 ml white wine vinegar (red wine vinegar for black olives); 5 g dried chopped garlic; 2 g each dried thyme, basil and oregano (or 5 g mixed herbs); 2–4 whole cracked dried red peppers; 5 g dried rosemary; 4 bay leaves, whole or cut into strips; 100 ml extra virgin olive oil; rind and juice of 1 lemon; cracked pepper to taste. Mix the olives with the vinegar, garlic, herbs, peppers, oil and pepper, and pack into the container they will be kept in, adding the bay leaves and the lemon rind and juice there. Alternatives for the herbs: 5 g fennel seeds, 5 g rosemary and lemon slices, with grapevine leaves laid over the surface of the olives. Marinated olives keep up to 12 months.
recipes.title: Herb and garlic marinated olives

summary.text:
Olea europaea is the tree species that includes the cultivated olive, and five other subspecies.
Two wild olives grow in New Zealand. The European olive (subsp. europaea) is widely cultivated in parts of New Zealand for olive oil and table olives; its seed-grown wild form, the oleaster, is small-fruited and locally naturalised near where it has been planted. Introduced for agriculture, it was first recorded naturalised in 1970 and its fruit is spread by birds (NZPCN, restated). The African olive (subsp. cuspidata), native to eastern and southern Africa and south-western Asia east to Yunnan in China, has been locally naturalised in parts of northern New Zealand for many decades; on Raoul Island in the Kermadecs it has been all but eradicated, the last plant being detected in 2011. The 1988 Flora referred all naturalised olives to the African olive; Heenan et al. (1999) showed that the naturalised olives of Auckland and the Hauraki Gulf are European olive (Cameron 2017, restated).
Auckland Council lists feral olive as not a legally declared pest plant, though it may be invasive in some situations (Auckland Council, restated).

warnings: Raw olives are very bitter and astringent from oleuropein; they are not palatable until cured.

Lye (sodium hydroxide, caustic soda) is extremely corrosive: it can cause severe burns, permanent injury or scarring to skin and eyes. Wear safety goggles and intact rubber gloves, always add lye to water and never water to lye, and never use aluminium, tin, lead or zinc-galvanised containers or utensils: lye corrodes them and gives off hydrogen gas, and zinc dissolved from galvanised coatings may make the olives poisonous.

If olives become mouldy, soft or bad-smelling at any stage of curing or storing, do not eat or even taste them. Mould shows as raised, fuzzy or cotton-like patches on the surface, white, green, blue, black, orange or pink, often with a musty or rotten smell; if any appears, throw out the whole container. Lye-cured, non-fermented olives are low-acid, and olives canned improperly at home have caused botulism: olives can only be canned safely in a pressure canner, never in a boiling-water bath or steam canner.

identification.text:
A rubbery, shell- to fan-shaped mushroom growing from dead wood, singly or in overlapping tiers, with a short stem off to one side. The cap is 1–7 cm wide, flat to gently domed, smooth and moist but not slimy, and dark violet to deep brownish violet, keeping its colour when dried; depending on how much light it gets it can also be brown, olive or yellow-green. The margin is slightly rolled under when young and straight when mature; older caps can be ragged.
The gills are pale silvery grey, thin and crowded, and run down the stem. The stem is short (0.5–1.5 cm) and solid, white to lilac-grey with yellowish tints at the base. The flesh is thin and grey, and tears easily with a slightly rubbery feel. The spore print is white. It has no particular smell or taste.
Darker brown oyster mushrooms can look similar but are not rubbery and their gills are not grey; the other New Zealand oyster mushrooms have cream to brown caps, never dark and polished.

lookalikes.howToTell: Brown oyster is not rubbery, and its gills are cream to yellow. Olive oyster is rubbery, with a dark brown to purplish-brown polished cap and pale grey gills. Darker brown oyster caps can become dark brown and shiny, so check the texture and the gill colour, not the cap. Brown oyster is commonest in the upper North Island, mostly on mānuka, kānuka and gorse; olive oyster mostly grows on dead southern beech and is commoner in the South Island.

preparation.text: Use it in place of a shop-bought mushroom, in stir-fries, soups, pies, pasties, tacos and burgers. To dry it, spread it in a single layer on a baking tray and fan-bake at 70 °C with the oven door slightly open for a few hours, until dry and crisp. Store it whole or ground to a powder in an airtight jar; to use, cover with boiling water and leave 20–30 minutes.

recipes.method: Written for oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus) generally, mixed with button mushrooms. Serves 4. Gnocchi: 500 g potatoes; 175 g plain (type 00) flour; 8 g fine salt. Sauce: 300 g oyster mushrooms, cleaned; 300 g button mushrooms; 100 g prosciutto in one thick slice; 1 garlic clove; 1 fresh chilli; rosemary; salt and black pepper; olive oil. To finish: 150 g aged Valtellina Casera cheese (or another semi-hard cow's cheese), diced; 30 g grated Grana Padano; butter. Boil the potatoes, starting in cold water, for 30–40 minutes. Meanwhile tear the oyster mushrooms into rough pieces, slice the button mushrooms about 5 mm thick and dice the prosciutto. In a large pan fry the garlic and rosemary in a little oil for 1–2 minutes, add the prosciutto and the halved chilli and fry on higher heat for 3–4 minutes. Add the mushrooms, salt and pepper and cook gently for about 15 minutes; take out the garlic and chilli. Mash the hot potatoes, work in the flour and salt to a soft but firm dough, roll it into ropes about 2 cm thick and cut them into pieces; roll each over a fork or gnocchi board. Boil the gnocchi in plenty of water until they float, drain them into the mushroom pan and toss over high heat for a few seconds. Layer half the gnocchi and half the diced cheese in an oiled baking dish, then the rest of each; dot with butter, scatter the Grana and grind over pepper. Bake in a 200 °C fan oven for 10 minutes, then grill for 3 minutes to brown.
recipes.title: Baked mushroom gnocchi

recipes.method: Written for oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus) generally, with a few honey mushrooms. Serves 4 as a side. 400 g oyster mushrooms; 100 g honey mushrooms; 100 g stale bread; the grated zest of ½ lemon and 4 lemon slices; 30 g olive oil; parsley; 1 garlic clove; 8 g fine salt. Trim the dirtiest part of the stems and wipe the mushrooms with a damp cloth; rinse quickly only if very dirty, without soaking. Slice the oyster mushroom caps and stems about 3 mm thick and leave the honey mushrooms whole. Blitz the bread to crumbs and mix in chopped parsley and garlic, the lemon zest and the salt. Lay the mushroom slices on a lined tray, slightly overlapping, drizzle with half the oil, spread the crumbs over, drizzle with the rest of the oil and top with the lemon slices. Bake at 180 °C (no fan) for 15 minutes, then 10 minutes more on fan at 180 °C. Eat straight away.
recipes.title: Oyster mushroom gratin with lemon crumbs

recipes.method: Written for a mix of oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus), button mushrooms and porcini. Serves 4. 220 g oyster mushrooms; 250 g button mushrooms; 220 g porcini; 150 g plain (type 00) flour; 190 g water; 150 g dried breadcrumbs; salt; 1 litre peanut oil for frying. Wipe the mushrooms clean with a damp cloth. Cut the base off the oyster mushroom cluster and separate the caps; trim the button mushroom stems and halve them lengthwise; scrape the porcini stems clean and halve them lengthwise. Whisk the flour and water to a smooth batter and season with salt. Heat the oil to about 170 °C. Dip each mushroom in the batter, let the excess drip off and roll it in the breadcrumbs. Fry a few pieces at a time for about 3 minutes, turning, until evenly golden; drain on paper towels, salt and serve hot.
recipes.title: Crumbed fried mushrooms

Also read (found by web search, 29/10/2026): Jess, 'Identifying NZ Oyster Mushroom (Pleurotus purpureo-olivaceus)', Woodland Folk (NZ; the live site no longer resolves; read via the Internet Archive copy of https://woodlandfolkforaging.com/?p=129, captured 28/11/2022) — 'an indigenous edible species of oyster mushroom' (edible parts); dark grey to brownish-grey cap, paler grey gills, white stipe far to one side, larger ones a little smaller than palm size, about 60 × 70 mm, an ideal size for harvesting; smooth, not slimy or gelatinous, tear-able, slightly rubbery; older ones ragged-edged; singly spreading en masse or in clusters (identification, edible parts); mostly on fallen trunks and limbs of black beech, common in lowland dry areas (habitat); fruiting autumn through winter (months); the closest lookalike is the shoehorn oyster (Hohenbuehelia), told by a gelatinous layer under the cap cuticle (warning); stir-fries, soups, pies, pasties, tacos, burgers; drying at 70 °C fan-bake, door ajar, rehydrating 20–30 minutes in boiling water (preparation). summary.text:
Pleurotus purpureo-olivaceus is a gilled fungus native to Australia and New Zealand.
It is one of four Pleurotus species indigenous to New Zealand, and is commoner in the South Island, where its range follows southern beech. It is the earliest-branching lineage of the oyster mushroom genus, set apart from every other known Pleurotus, and New Zealand populations differ very little genetically. Unlike brown oyster it has no asexual stage, so its caps do not carry the black, slimy coremia. Its name may change: some of the old collections it was described from may in fact be brown oyster. Mycologic NZ lists it as a native species that can be grown in New Zealand.

warnings: Shoehorn oysters (Hohenbuehelia) can look like it at a glance. They are usually smaller, with crowded gills, and have a gelatinous layer under the cap skin that makes them tough to break. Their gills carry large, thick-walled cells (metuloids) that show under a hand lens and clearly under a microscope, so check the gills before eating.

identification.text: A woody shrub or small tree, usually about 2 m and up to 3 m tall, with a main stem up to 12 cm thick at the base. Leaves are pale green and thin, 8–12 cm long and 3–5 cm wide (up to 15 cm on young plants), in opposite pairs, ovate to triangular or lance-shaped, with coarsely toothed edges, on stalks up to 5 cm long. Stiff white stinging hairs 6 mm long or more sit at the tip of each tooth and along the midrib, leaf stalks and young stems. In some southern places it drops some or all of its leaves in winter. Common nettles are soft herbs — dwarf nettle up to 60 cm, stinging nettle up to 1.5 m — with short-stalked stinging hairs. A young ongaonga can be confused with the other native nettles.

lookalikes.howToTell: Common nettles are herbs: Urtica urens is an annual to 60 cm and Urtica dioica a perennial to 1.5 m, so not always below waist height. Both have short-stalked stinging hairs and 4 stipules at each node. Ongaonga is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m, with long-stalked white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long and 2 stipules at each node. Young ongaonga can be confused with other native nettles, so size is not reliable on a young plant. If it is woody, walk away. Young common nettle leaves are eaten cooked.
lookalikes.name: Stinging nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf nettle is a soft, branched annual herb up to 60 cm, with short-stalked stinging hairs and 4 stipules at each node. Ongaonga is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m, with long-stalked white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long and 2 stipules at each node. Young ongaonga can be confused with other native nettles, so size is not reliable on a young plant. If it is woody, walk away. Young dwarf nettle leaves are eaten cooked.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf stinging nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush nettle is a soft native herb 15–60 cm tall, spreading by rhizomes, with light green triangular leaves 2–6 cm long (sometimes up to 12 cm, overlapping ongaonga's); its sting is generally less painful than other native nettles'. Ongaonga is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m, with long-stalked white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long and 2 stipules at each node. Young ongaonga can be confused with other native nettles, so size is not reliable on a young plant. If it is woody, walk away. Young bush nettle leaves are eaten cooked.
lookalikes.name: Bush nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Southern nettle is a stout herb up to about 1 m, somewhat woody only at the base, whose branches lie down and root before turning upright, with broadly ovate, dark green leaves 10–20 cm long; its stinging hairs are few and short-stalked, mainly on the leaf edges and the veins underneath, and are often sparse or absent. Ongaonga is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m, with numerous long-stalked white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long. Both grow on Stewart Island. If it is woody with long white stinging hairs, walk away. No record of southern nettle being eaten has been found and it is At Risk – Declining.
lookalikes.name: Southern nettle

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urtica_ferox Corrects the death count on this page from one to two, and locates both: 'two recorded human deaths from contact with U. ferox. One death occurred in 1961, when a young hunter died five hours after walking through a patch of U. ferox bushes in the Ruahine Range. In 2002, another young man's death in the Ruahine Range was retrospectively attributed to U. ferox by a pathologist.' Endemic to New Zealand, a woody shrub or small tree to 3 m, covered in trichomes carrying the toxins; stings can also cause ataxia, blurred vision, confusion, polyneuropathy, respiratory distress and hypersalivation, lasting days to weeks, and are strong enough to kill cattle, dogs and horses. Not closely related to the other New Zealand native nettles — its sister species is the South African U. lobulata — and its ferocity has been hypothesised as a response to browsing by moa.

summary.text:
Urtica ferox, commonly known as tree nettle and ongaonga, is a species of nettle endemic to New Zealand. It is a large woody shrub or small tree that can grow to a height of 3 metres. Its trichomes can cause painful stings, with effects that can last several days or weeks; the sting is strong enough to kill cattle, dogs, and horses. Two human deaths have been caused by contact with the plant.
Urtica ferox is endemic to New Zealand, where it is found throughout the North and South Islands. The southernmost limit of the plant is Stewart Island, according to a 2011 book on the flora of New Zealand. The plant varies in abundance throughout its distribution area, being especially common near Wellington and Christchurch, whereas it is uncommon or absent north of Auckland (as noted by botanist Lucy Moore in 1978). The 2023 assessment of U. ferox in the New Zealand Threat Classification System was not threatened, but in the Northland Region, it has been assessed as regionally critical, meaning regionally endangered, with an estimated 250 mature U. ferox plants in the region.
The plant is the primary host for the larvae of the endemic mainland New Zealand red admiral (Vanessa gonerilla subsp. gonerilla), which begin laying eggs in early spring (September). Populations of V. gonerilla have had a potential decline, possibly in part because of people treating U. ferox as a weed and removing it.
Not the nettle you make soup from.
It also occurs inland, including in the Canterbury Region on the Harper Hills near Glentunnel. The plant can be found on alluvial soils in the Taramakau Valley within Arthurs Pass National Park.

warnings: The sting causes pain, a rash and numbness. Serious stings can also cause loss of coordination, blurred vision, confusion, drooling and breathing difficulty, lasting days to weeks. Two people have died from it, both in the Ruahine Range: in 1961 a young hunter died five hours after walking through a patch, and a 2002 death was later attributed to it by a pathologist.
Do not push through it on a track. Do not touch it to test the sting.
Seek medical help for widespread stings or any weakness, blurred vision or breathing difficulty.

It has killed dogs, horses and cattle. A dog can be poisoned by running through it, or by licking or eating it, and signs — trembling, vomiting, drooling, breathing difficulty, incoordination, seizures or collapse — can start within minutes. Call a vet straight away, and keep dogs on a lead where it grows.

edibleParts.text: Leaves, flowers, flower stalks and the small bulbs.

sources: NZPCN 'Allium triquetrum' and Weedbusters 'Onion weed' (facts restated)
habitat.text:
Damp shady ground: roadsides, stream banks, under hedges and trees, neglected gardens. Forms dense carpets in winter and spring.
In New Zealand it invades disturbed forest and shrubland, streamsides, herbfields and bare land, especially after spraying or other clearing.

identification.text: Strap-like leaves and a flower stalk with three distinct edges — roll it between your fingers and you feel the triangle. Nodding white bell flowers, each petal with a fine green stripe down the middle, in late winter and spring. Crush any part: a strong onion smell. No smell, not onion weed.

lookalikes.howToTell: Snowflake has none of onion weed's strong garlic-onion smell. Its flower stalk is hollow and somewhat flattened, with winged edges; onion weed's is three-angled. Snowflake's white bells have green-tipped segments; onion weed's have a green stripe down the centre. Strap-shaped leaves, nodding white bells and damp ground do not separate them, and they can flower at the same time (snowflake July–October, onion weed October–November). If a plant does not smell of onion when crushed, leave it.
lookalikes.name: Snowflake

lookalikes.howToTell: Naples garlic's flowers are pure white; onion weed's have a green stripe down the centre of each segment. Naples garlic's flower stalk has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one; onion weed's is sharply three-angled. Naples garlic carries a many-flowered, roughly flat-topped umbel 5–8 cm across on stiff stalks; onion weed carries 3–15 flowers on drooping stalks. Naples garlic's flat leaves have finely toothed or hairy-edged margins; onion weed's are strongly channelled. The onion-garlic smell, a 20–60 cm flower stalk, white flowers and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Naples garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Rosy garlic's flowers are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves; onion weed's are white with a green stripe down the centre of each segment. Rosy garlic's flower stalk is round in section; onion weed's is sharply three-angled. Rosy garlic often carries bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among its flowers; onion weed's umbel has none. Plants of rosy garlic without bulbils also occur, so no bulbils does not rule rosy garlic out. Rosy garlic's leaves are flat; onion weed's are strongly channelled. The onion-garlic smell, a flower stalk of similar height (30–60 cm against 20–60 cm) and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Rosy garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild garlic's leaves are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical; onion weed's are solid and strongly channelled. Wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils, its few flowers about 5 mm long, green to white and often purplish; onion weed carries 3–15 white flowers 10–15 mm long (up to 20) and no bulbils. Wild garlic's slender, rush-like stalk is sheathed by the leaves for a third to a half of its length; onion weed's is three-angled and sheathed only at the base. The garlic smell and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Wild garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: False garlic has none of onion weed's strong garlic-onion smell, or only a faint one. Its flower stalk is round in section and hollow; onion weed's is sharply three-angled. Its leaves are flat, dull and light green; onion weed's are strongly channelled. False garlic's dull white bells have a greenish base and a reddish midvein on each segment, 8–20 to a head on erect or spreading stalks; onion weed's have a green stripe down the centre of each segment, 3–15 to a head on drooping stalks. Flower size, a 20–60 cm flower stalk, offset bulbs, garden ground and flowering at the same time (false garlic October–December, onion weed October–November) do not separate them. If a plant does not smell of garlic or onion when crushed, leave it. False garlic has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: False garlic
