preparation.text: Use like spring onion or chives, raw or cooked. Flowers scatter well over salads. Milder than it smells.

recipes.method: Written for three-cornered leek, as onion weed is called in Britain. Makes about 500 ml. 2 big handfuls of nettle tips; 1 Babington leek, green part only; 4–5 sprigs of mint; 1 bunch of onion weed leaves; 2 chard leaves, stalks removed; the zest of ½ lemon; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 100 g pumpkin seeds; 150 ml olive oil. Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry frying pan over medium heat until they start to colour, then tip them into a cold dish to cool. Put the washed nettle tips and Babington leek greens in a heatproof bowl, pour boiling water over and stir for about 30 seconds. Scoop the greens into a blender and keep the nettle water. Add the mint leaves, onion weed and chard, then the salt, lemon zest and 15 ml (1 tbsp) of the oil, and blend until roughly chopped. Add the cooled seeds and most of the remaining oil and blend again, stopping before it is a smooth paste. Tip it into a bowl and loosen it with about 150 ml of the nettle water. Season to taste, spoon into a jar and refrigerate. The author served it over roast carrots and suggests stirring it through pasta or into mayonnaise.
recipes.title: Onionweed salsa verde

recipes.method: Written for three-cornered leek, as onion weed is called in Ireland. 40 g onion weed; 100 g butter; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) nigella seeds. Melt the butter in a deep pot over medium heat until it foams; it is ready when it goes quiet and smells nutty. Meanwhile, wash the onion weed well and pat it dry with a clean tea towel. Let the butter cool a little, add the onion weed and leave it to infuse for about 30 minutes. Blend the butter and onion weed for 2–3 minutes, until the butter turns bright green, then strain it through a fine sieve and discard the pulp. Stir in the nigella seeds and chill until set. The author puts ½ tsp on each shucked oyster and cooks them on a very hot barbecue for about 2 minutes, until the butter bubbles.
recipes.title: Onionweed herb butter

recipes.method: Serves 4–6. A couple of big handfuls of onion weed flowers, with their stems; 250 ml (1 cup) plain flour and 125 ml (½ cup) cornflour, or 250 ml (1 cup) gluten-free flour mix in place of both; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) black pepper; 300 ml ice-cold soda water; 1 litre rice bran oil. Whisk the flour, salt and pepper together in a large bowl, then whisk in the soda water only briefly, leaving it a little lumpy, and let it rest. Heat the oil to 180 °C in a deep fryer or large wok. Gather three flower heads together, dip them in the batter and lower them into the oil. Turn them so they cook evenly and lift them out with a slotted spoon or spider when light golden. Drain on a rack over a tray and season with salt. The author serves them as a starter with sweet chilli sauce and an onion weed mayonnaise.
recipes.title: Onionweed flower tempura

recipes.method: Written for three-cornered leek in Cornwall. Onion weed bulbs; 1.25 litres apple cider vinegar; 250 ml water; 5 ml (1 tsp) peppercorns; 15 ml (1 tbsp) salt; 15 ml (1 tbsp) sugar; 2 bay leaves; 5 ml (1 tsp) each of fennel seeds, coriander seeds and cumin seeds; 2 onions, finely chopped. Warm the fennel, coriander and cumin seeds in a saucepan for a few minutes to bring out their flavour. Add the vinegar and the rest of the pickling ingredients and bring to a simmer. Stand the bulbs upright in sterilised jars and pour the hot vinegar over them. Seal well and leave for about a fortnight before eating.
recipes.title: Pickled onionweed bulbs

recipes.method: Written for three-cornered leek (onion weed). Serves 4. 6 eggs; 3 tbsp milk or cream; salt and pepper; 50 g grated hard cheese (Parmesan, Gruyère or aged Cheddar); 2 tbsp olive oil; a thinly sliced courgette (optional); 80 g roughly chopped onion weed leaves and stems; a small handful of raw onion weed flowers. Heat the grill. Beat 6 eggs with 3 tbsp milk or cream, season well, and stir in most of 50 g grated hard cheese (Parmesan, Gruyère or aged Cheddar). Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a 24 cm ovenproof frying pan over medium heat; if you like, soften a thinly sliced courgette in it for 3–4 minutes. Add 80 g roughly chopped onion weed leaves and stems and stir for 1 minute, until just wilted. Pour in the eggs and cook undisturbed on medium-low for 5–6 minutes, until the edges set. Scatter the rest of the cheese over and grill 3–4 minutes, until set and lightly golden. Scatter a small handful of raw onion weed flowers over the top and serve in wedges, warm or at room temperature.
recipes.title: Onion weed frittata

recipes.method: Written for three-cornered leek (onion weed). Serves 4. A diced white onion; 2 tbsp olive oil or butter; 2 sliced garlic cloves; a peeled, diced potato (or a small cauliflower); 1 litre of vegetable or light chicken stock; 300 g onion weed leaves and stems; 3 tbsp crème fraîche (or coconut cream), plus more to serve; the juice of half a lemon; salt and white pepper; a few onion weed flowers. Soften a diced white onion in 2 tbsp olive oil or butter for 8 minutes. Add 2 sliced garlic cloves and a peeled, diced potato (or a small cauliflower) and cook 2 minutes. Add 1 litre of vegetable or light chicken stock and simmer 12–15 minutes, until the potato is tender. Stir in 300 g onion weed leaves and stems and cook exactly 3 minutes, to keep the colour. Off the heat, add 3 tbsp crème fraîche (or coconut cream) and the juice of half a lemon, and blend smooth straight away. Season with salt and white pepper and serve at once, with more crème fraîche and a few flowers; it loses colour if it sits.
recipes.title: Onion weed soup

recipes.method: Written for three-cornered leek (onion weed). Onion weed, enough to fill 2 cups (about 500 ml) when cut; a quarter of a cucumber, thinly sliced; 1 tsp red pepper flakes; 1 tsp sugar; 1 tsp sesame seeds; 1 tsp salt; 1 tbsp sesame oil; 1 tbsp white vinegar. Cut onion weed into pieces about 4 cm long, enough to fill 2 cups (about 500 ml). Toss them in a bowl with a quarter of a cucumber, thinly sliced, 1 tsp each of red pepper flakes, sugar, sesame seeds and salt, and 1 tbsp each of sesame oil and white vinegar. Serve straight away while crunchy, or leave a few minutes to marinate. Good with fishcakes, grilled meat or rice.
recipes.title: Korean-style onion weed salad

recipes.method: Written for three-cornered leek (onion weed). A large bunch of onion weed flower stalks with their buds; some butter; sea salt; lemon juice. Pick the flower stalks with their buds before the buds open. Melt some butter in a pan, add a large bunch of the stalks, cover to keep the moisture in, and stir; they cook very quickly. Finish with sea salt and lemon juice.
recipes.title: Buttered onion weed flower stalks

recipes.method: From an Italian wild-herb cookbook, written for aglio triangolo (Allium triquetrum). A generous bunch of onion weed, bulbs, leaves and flowers; extra-virgin olive oil; a little water; tagliatelle; 500 g cherry tomatoes (optional). Stew the bulbs and leaves of a generous bunch of onion weed in extra-virgin olive oil with a little water, keeping the flowers aside. Toss tagliatelle cooked al dente through it and add the flowers. Or toss the tagliatelle for 10 minutes with 500 g cherry tomatoes before adding the flowers. The authors prefer it plain to taste the garlic best.
recipes.title: Tagliatelle with onion weed

recipes.method: Written for lágrimas de la Virgen (Allium triquetrum). A bunch of wild asparagus; a dozen onion weed flower heads; 2 eggs; salt and black pepper; a little olive oil. Cut the tenderest part of a bunch of wild asparagus into pieces, and leave a dozen onion weed flower heads whole; the flowers give a very mild garlic flavour. Beat 2 eggs with salt and black pepper, mix in the asparagus and flowers, and pour into a frying pan with a little olive oil. When set underneath, turn it over with a plate and cook a few minutes more.
recipes.title: Onion weed and wild asparagus omelette

recipes.method: Written for onion weed, kawakawa and kelp together. 250 ml (1 cup) onion weed stems and leaves, sliced 5 mm thick; 8–10 kawakawa leaves; 2 hand-sized pieces of kelp or other seaweed (the author forages hers, and says bought seaweed works); and 125 ml (½ cup) rock salt. Makes about 200 g. If you can, dry the kawakawa for a few days beforehand. Spread each ingredient in a single layer on its own tray, because they dry at different speeds — in a dehydrator, or on a lined perforated tray in a 50–60 °C oven — until crisp to the touch, 2 to 4 hours. Grind them with the salt in batches, in a spice grinder or with a mortar and pestle, to the texture you like, and keep it in a sealed jar. The author says it lasts indefinitely. Good on anything, or in place of stock.
recipes.title: Onion weed, kawakawa and kelp super salt

recipes.method: 10 onion weed bulbs with their white parts, finely chopped; 60 ml aquafaba (the liquid from cooked chickpeas) with 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cream of tartar, or 1 egg yolk; 30 ml (2 tbsp) mustard; 5 ml (1 tsp) sugar or honey; 100 ml rice bran oil and 50 ml extra-virgin olive oil; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 10 ml (2 tsp) apple cider vinegar; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt and a pinch of black pepper. Makes about 250 ml. Blend the onion weed, aquafaba or yolk, mustard and sugar in a mini food processor, then add the oils a little at a time, blending well after each addition. Once it has emulsified, blend in the lemon, vinegar, salt and pepper. The author serves it with the tempura flower clusters, and with the more bitter wild greens.
recipes.title: Onion weed mayo

recipes.method: Batter (as for the tempura flower clusters): 250 ml (1 cup) plain flour and 125 ml (½ cup) cornflour, or 250 ml (1 cup) gluten-free flour mix; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) black pepper; 300 ml ice-cold soda water. Fritters: 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped onion weed flowers; 60 ml (¼ cup) grated parmesan (dairy or not); 300 g mashed tofu, if you like; for frying, 30 ml (2 tbsp) rice bran or another neutral oil with 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) sesame oil. Serves 4–6. Whisk the batter, then stir in the onion weed, parmesan and tofu. Heat the oils in a frying pan over medium-high heat and fry the fritters about five at a time until golden on both sides. Move them to a cooling rack and repeat until the mixture is used up. Serve with sweet chilli sauce and avocado mayo, or the onion weed mayo.
recipes.title: Onion weed fritters

recipes.method: Dressing: 10 onion weed bulbs with their white parts, roughly chopped; 60 ml aquafaba (the liquid from cooked chickpeas); 15 ml (1 tbsp) mustard; 5 ml (1 tsp) sugar or honey; 150 ml extra-virgin olive oil; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 10 ml (2 tsp) apple cider vinegar; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt and a pinch of black pepper. Salad: 3–4 kūmara; 3–4 potatoes (a waxy kind such as peruperu); 60 ml (¼ cup) capers; 375 ml (1½ cups) cooked chickpeas; 125 ml (½ cup) rice bran oil; 1 finely sliced celery stick; 1 finely sliced fennel bulb; 60 ml (¼ cup) finely sliced daikon or radish; the juice of half a lemon; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and a pinch of pepper; the rest of the onion weed stems and flowers. Dressing: blend the onion weed, aquafaba, mustard and sugar in a mini food processor, add the oil a little at a time, blending well between additions, and once it has emulsified blend in the rest. Salad: scrub 3–4 kūmara and 3–4 potatoes (the author prefers a waxy kind such as peruperu), cut them into bite-sized pieces, steam until cooked and let them cool. Drain and pat dry 60 ml (¼ cup) capers and 375 ml (1½ cups) cooked chickpeas, fry them in 125 ml (½ cup) rice bran oil until crisp, and drain on paper towel. In the salad bowl, mix 1 finely sliced celery stick, 1 finely sliced fennel bulb, 60 ml (¼ cup) finely sliced daikon or radish, the juice of half a lemon, 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and a pinch of pepper, and leave it a couple of minutes while you slice the rest of the onion weed stems and flowers. Add everything to the bowl, pour the dressing over generously, toss and serve. Serves 4–6.
recipes.title: Potato, kūmara and crispy chickpea salad with onion weed dressing

recipes.method: Chilli oil (makes 250 ml): 250 ml (1 cup) rice bran or another neutral oil; 45 ml (3 tbsp) chilli flakes; 30 ml (2 tbsp) Sichuan pepper; 2 star anise; 1 cinnamon quill broken in half; 2 kawakawa or horopito leaves, torn (optional); and 2 garlic cloves, squashed and peeled. Put everything except the oil in a heatproof bowl. Heat the oil to 180 °C and pour it over carefully — the fresh leaves and garlic spit and bubble. Leave it to cool and infuse; blend it if you don't want large pieces, and keep it in a lidded jar in the pantry. The dish (serves 4 as a side): a colander full of onion weed flower clusters, about 1 litre (4 cups); 3–4 fresh wood ear (hakeke) or shiitake mushrooms, thinly sliced (optional); 6 flowering tops of ruruhau, mizuna, wild mustard or broccoli (optional); 15 ml (1 tbsp) rice bran or extra-virgin olive oil; 15 ml (1 tbsp) butter, plant-based or dairy; 30 ml (2 tbsp) tamari or light soy sauce; the juice of half a lemon or lime; and 60 ml (¼ cup) crushed salted peanuts (optional). Heat the oil and butter on high, add the mushrooms and cook for 1 minute; add the onion weed and the flowering tops and cook another minute; add the tamari and cook 2 minutes more. Spoon over as much chilli oil as you like, squeeze over the citrus and top with the peanuts. Serve on noodles or as a side dish.
recipes.title: Dandan onion weed flowers with chilli oil

recipes.method: Fritters: a quarter of a pumpkin, peeled and grated; 200 g feta (or goat's cheese), cubed or crumbled; 1 crushed garlic clove; a handful of onion weed flowers (or chives), chopped; 100 g sprouted, cooked or canned chickpeas; 250 ml (1 cup, 120 g) chickpea flour; 60 ml (¼ cup, 30 g) tapioca starch; 10 ml (2 tsp) baking powder; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper; 100 ml milk (dairy or not); 2 eggs (or 30 ml (2 tbsp) ground flaxseed soaked 10 minutes in 80 ml (⅓ cup) water); 80 ml (⅓ cup, 90 g) yoghurt; 50 ml rice bran oil for frying. Makes about 23 fritters; serves 4–6. Salsa: 1 capsicum; 1 diced tomato; a quarter of a cucumber, cubed; a handful of finely chopped parsley; 3 sprigs of finely chopped mint; 125 ml (½ cup) lentil sprouts; 1 diced avocado; the juice of half a lime; 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt and some pepper. Start the chickpea and lentil sprouts a couple of days ahead. Mix the dry ingredients with the pumpkin, feta, garlic, onion weed and chickpeas, make a well, and mix in the milk, eggs and yoghurt. Heat 30 ml (2 tbsp) of the oil at a time in a frying pan. Shape fritters from 2 tablespoons of mix, fry 2–3 at a time, pressed with a spoon to just under 1 cm thick, over gentle heat until golden on both sides. Salsa: char 1 capsicum under the grill or over a gas flame until the skin is black, steam it in a covered bowl, peel and dice it (a few charred bits are fine). Mix it with 1 diced tomato, a quarter of a cucumber, cubed, a handful of finely chopped parsley, 3 sprigs of finely chopped mint, 125 ml (½ cup) lentil sprouts, 1 diced avocado, the juice of half a lime, 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil, 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt and some pepper. Serve the fritters with the salsa.
recipes.title: Pumpkin and feta fritters with onion weed flowers

recipes.method: 1 crushed garlic clove; the zest and juice of 1 lemon and of 1 orange; 45 ml (3 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil or hemp seed oil; 15 ml (1 tbsp) honey or coconut nectar; 1–2 finely sliced fennel bulbs; 1 finely sliced radicchio; 60 ml (¼ cup) shelled pistachios; 6 finely sliced onion weed leaves (or 1 spring onion); a handful of roughly chopped coriander; a handful of roughly chopped basil, dandelion tips, baby wild mustard or nasturtium leaves; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper. In the salad bowl, mix 1 crushed garlic clove, the zest and juice of 1 lemon and of 1 orange, 45 ml (3 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil or hemp seed oil, and 15 ml (1 tbsp) honey or coconut nectar. Add 1–2 finely sliced fennel bulbs, 1 finely sliced radicchio, 60 ml (¼ cup) shelled pistachios, 6 finely sliced onion weed leaves (or 1 spring onion), a handful of roughly chopped coriander, a handful of roughly chopped basil, dandelion tips, baby wild mustard or nasturtium leaves, 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper. Toss well and serve. Serves 4.
recipes.title: Fennel and radicchio salad with onion weed

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard. 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: The author's greens were dock, onion weed, nasturtium, plantain, baby wild mustard, dandelion, sow thistle and a violet leaf. 2 crushed garlic cloves; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 500 ml (2 cups) firmly packed wild greens, sliced very thinly; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper; 125 ml (½ cup) roughly chopped pistachios, walnuts, almonds or brazil nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp hearts, pumpkin or sunflower seeds; and 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, hemp seed oil or a mix. Makes about 750 ml (3 cups). To slice the greens, sort them into similar shapes, bunch and twist a few leaves together and slice as thinly as you can — this suits the tougher, stringier ones such as plantain, mustard and dock. Toss everything together. Good as a side or salad, in a wrap or sandwich, or with pasta, risotto, eggs, or sausages and mash. It keeps at least 4 days in a sealed jar in the fridge.
recipes.title: Weedolata (wild-greens gremolata)

recipes.method: The author's greens were puha, sow thistle, nasturtium, onion weed, wild fennel, oxalis, wild mustard and wild celery. 1 diced onion; 1 potato, scrubbed and diced; 2 sliced garlic cloves; 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 1.3 litres water; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked pepper; extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil, to serve; edible weed flowers. Serves 4. Cut the vegetables and greens to similar sizes. Fry the onion in the oil for a minute, then add the potato and garlic (the method also adds fennel bulb and celery stalks, which the ingredient list leaves out) and fry for another minute. Add the water, cover, bring to the boil and simmer until the potato is soft. Add the greens with the salt and yeast and cook for 3 minutes, until just tender — added at the end, they keep their colour. Blend until smooth (push it through a sieve if your blender isn't powerful), season with the pepper and more salt if needed, and serve drizzled with extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil and scattered with edible weed flowers.
recipes.title: Wild greens soup

recipes.method: The author's greens, picked in spring, were cleavers, chickweed, herb Robert, stinging nettle (the page does not say which nettle), onion weed, speedwell, pūhā and lemon balm; she gives no amounts for them. She blends the nettle raw; the nettle page says to cook it, so blanch it first. Chop the greens into the blender with 2 cabbage leaves, stalks removed, the juice of 1 large grapefruit, 125 ml (½ cup) kombucha and 500 ml (2 cups) water, and blend until the greens are broken down. Add 2 small bananas or 1 large, 1 apple, 1 kiwifruit (hairs scrubbed off, top and bottom trimmed), 1 whole orange, and 15 ml (1 tbsp) chia seeds and 5 ml (1 tsp) pumpkin seeds ground in a coffee grinder, and blend again. Decorate it with onion weed and viola flowers and a piece of orange.
recipes.title: Spring clean smoothie

recipes.method: Written for chickweed, nasturtium and onion weed. Soak 500 ml (2 cups) chickpeas overnight, drain and rinse them well, and sprout them for 48 hours, rinsing twice a day, until the tails are as long as the peas; or cook them, as the author also allows. 500 ml (2 cups) sprouted chickpeas; 185 ml (¾ cup) tahini (the author grinds whole sesame seeds instead); 2–4 garlic cloves, minced; the juice of 2 large lemons and 1 orange; 125 ml (½ cup) olive oil; 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt; 5 ml (1 tsp) cumin; a big handful of chickweed, some nasturtium leaves, a small bunch of onion weed leaves and a sprig of parsley or another herb. Process the chickpeas with the citrus juice until still slightly chunky, then add everything else and process to the consistency you want.
recipes.title: Raw chickpea hummus with wild greens

Sources: Flora of New Zealand Online (Manaaki Whenua, CC BY 3.0 NZ), factsheet Leucojum aestivum https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Leucojum-aestivum.html (saved sweep/pages/flora-Leucojum-aestivum.txt) | Flora of New Zealand Online (Manaaki Whenua, CC BY 3.0 NZ), factsheet Allium triquetrum https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Allium-triquetrum.html (saved sweep/pages/flora-Allium-triquetrum.txt) | Wikipedia, Leucojum aestivum https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leucojum_aestivum (sweep/pages/wiki-Leucojum.txt) — 'The flowering stem (scape) is hollow and has wings with translucent margins'; 'All species of Leucojum are poisonous, as they produce the alkaloids lycorine and galantamine' — supports risk 'toxic' | Weedbusters, Onion weed https://www.weedbusters.org.nz/what-are-weeds/weed-list/onion-weed/ (sweep/pages/wb-onion-weed.txt) — 'strong garlic smell'; '3-sided flower stalk'; 'white with green stripes on each petal'; flowers Oct–Nov; 'Snowflake (Leucojum aestivum) and Nothoscordum inodorum lack garlic odour' | Wikipedia, Allium triquetrum https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allium_triquetrum (sweep/pages/wiki-Allium-triquetrum.txt) — leaves 'have a strong onion smell when crushed'; 'All parts of the plant, from the bulb to the flowers, are edible' UNRESOLVED: 'two winged edges' and 'green spot' weakened to source wording. Snowflake toxicity rests on Wikipedia only (Connor & Fountain not fetched). Damp-ground habitat for snowflake is Wikipedia (overseas range). The catalogue entry is 'Snowflake and daffodil leaves', but this card's text covers only Leucojum; daffodil is not addressed. Weedbusters names an odourless lookalike, Nothoscordum inodorum, with no card.

Origin checked 20/10/2026 (owner: "find the bio status all shipped species and label them accordingly"), retrieved 20/10/2026: NZ Organisms Register 'Allium triquetrum' (https://data.nzor.org.nz/names/search?query=Allium%20triquetrum): NZFLORA biostatus Exotic, Present; NZPCN 'Allium triquetrum' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/allium-triquetrum/): Biostatus Exotic, year naturalised 1899, Environmental Weed (2024). Origin 'pest' stands: named in DOC's List of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024 (McAlpine & Howell, Science for Conservation 340, https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/sfc340.pdf). Auckland Council's pest search (https://www.tiakitamakimakaurau.nz/protect-and-restore-our-environment/pests-in-auckland/pest-search/alltri/) says 'Not a legally declared pest'; the DOC listing alone makes it a weed here.

Lookalike cards among the four Allium entries (written by the assistant on the owner's instruction (owner, 22/10/2026: /goal "do a web search n find all about Allium fill it in make sure to follow our rules")): every test restates Flora of New Zealand's Allium key and its four species descriptions — Healy, A.J.; Edgar, E. 1980: Flora of New Zealand vol. III, Adventive Cyperaceous, Petalous & Spathaceous Monocotyledons (Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), genus https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/e23ad601-5985-4d12-b57c-e857fa0b9872, A. neapolitanum https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/022db9e0-b367-4b23-9c7b-c1e98616ca34, A. roseum subsp. bulbiferum https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/e6412c78-1898-44b9-a2bb-de8530146681, A. triquetrum https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/1273be45-2515-4e18-b2f1-33dafb094bfe, A. vineale https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/df84645f-9b6f-471c-a853-a17e8c11b797 — retrieved 22/10/2026; every number was checked mechanically against those pages. The key separates wild garlic first (leaves hollow, ± cylindrical, against solid, flat or channelled), then onion weed (stems sharply triquetrous, perianth white with a green stripe, against subtrigonous or terete stems and a pure white or pink perianth), then rosy garlic (pink) from Naples garlic (white). Not used: stamen length, because the key gives rosy garlic's stamens as c. ¼ the perianth and its description as c. ⅔. 'Spring flowering' rests on FL. 9 (Naples), FL. 10–11 (the other three). All four share Auckland City in the Flora's distribution lines, so every pair was carded. Risk 'edible' everywhere: all four pages list edible parts. Not carded, no entry: Nothoscordum inodorum, which the Flora says 'In general aspect … resembles an Allium but lacks the characteristic onion smell'; chives, which Wikipedia compares with wild garlic's leaves. On this shipped page the three new cards open drafts until the owner ships them.

summary.text: Three-cornered leek. A weedy wild onion with a triangular stem and drooping white bell flowers that smells unmistakably of onion — the smell is the whole identification.

warnings: The onion smell is the test. Every leaf you pick should smell of onion when crushed — bulb lookalikes cause vomiting.

Although no individual reports regarding this species have been seen, there have been cases of poisoning caused by the consumption, in very large quantities and by some mammals, of certain members of this genus. Dogs seem to be particularly susceptible.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous perennial with hairy, usually branched, purplish stems about 60 cm tall. Leaves shortly petiolate, 1.2–3 × 0.6–1.8 cm, ovate, or rhombic to suborbicular, entire or obscurely serrulate, ciliate, hairy and dotted with glands below, often becoming glabrous above. Inflorescences dense, corymbose or paniculate, terminal and axillary; bracts 3–5 mm long, ovate, glabrous, often purple. Calyx about 2.5 mm long, often purple, hairy outside, and with a prominent, long, white, pilose tuft in throat; teeth 0.5–1 mm long, almost regular, triangular. Corolla 4–7 mm long, pink or purplish, hairy outside; tube longer than calyx; limb 4–6 mm diameter; upper lip emarginate. Stamens exserted, lacking in the occasional female plants.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Sweet marjoram (Flora of New Zealand, genus Origanum): The generic description includes sect. Marjorana (Miller) Vogel, 1 species of which is widely cultivated in New Zealand but has not been reported wild. This is O. marjorana L. (usually known as Marjorana hortensis), sweet marjoram or knotted marjoram, with grey-tomentose leaves and a 1-lipped calyx deeply slit on one side.
Nutlets (Flora of China; Flora of Pakistan): brown, about 0.6 mm long (Flora of China), or oblong, about 0.8–1 × 0.5 mm (Flora of Pakistan).

preparation.text: Use the leaves fresh or dried; the flavour can be more intense dried than fresh. They suit salad dressings, vegetables and legumes, and strongly flavoured dishes with chillies, garlic and onions. To dry and store, cut the whole plant (not the roots) in late summer, when aroma compounds are much higher than earlier in the season, and dry it gently: hotter, longer drying loses more of the aroma. Plain Origanum vulgare and plants from cooler climates can taste milder than oregano from southern Europe, and climate, season and soil all change the flavour. Pick fresh, unwilted leaves. Wash and dry them quickly, as wet leaves soon turn brown; it is easiest to wash them still on the stem and spin or pat them dry. The stems are woody and unpleasant to eat: strip the leaves by pinching the thick end of a stem and pulling your fingers along it. The stems still carry flavour, so steep them for tea or tie them into soups, stews and stocks. Fresh leaves darken to brown or black when baked, and wet leaves blacken, so dry them well first.

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1¼ cups (about 310 ml) fresh oregano leaves, ¼ cup (about 60 ml) fresh parsley, 1 clove garlic, ¼ cup (about 60 ml) chopped walnuts, ¼ cup (about 60 ml) walnut oil (or olive oil), ¼ cup (about 60 ml) grated parmesan. Blend everything except the cheese until smooth, then add the parmesan and stir through hot pasta. It is a robust pesto, so use it more sparingly than basil pesto. The source (Kimberly Gallagher, from Barbara Radcliffe Rogers's Fresh Herbs) gives no amount of pasta and no salt.
recipes.title: Oregano pesto

recipes.method: Ingredients: 750 g plain flour plus extra for dusting, 7 g active dried yeast, 1 teaspoon sugar, 100 g extra virgin olive oil, 1 teaspoon honey, 2 teaspoons sea salt, 1–1½ cups (250–375 ml) water, about 1 tablespoon dried oregano, and 1 teaspoon coarse sea salt for the top. Stir the yeast into ½ cup (125 ml) warm water with the sugar and 5 tablespoons of the flour; cover and leave somewhere warm for about 30 minutes. With a dough hook, mix the olive oil, salt and honey into the remaining flour, add the yeast mixture, then slowly add about 1 cup (250 ml) warm water and knead for 5 minutes. Cover tightly and leave somewhere warm to prove for an hour. Punch down, shape into a ball on generously floured baking paper, and sprinkle the top with the dried oregano, the coarse salt and a little flour; cover and rest 30 minutes. Meanwhile heat the oven to 230 °C with a large lidded cast-iron pot inside (the source uses a 5-quart Dutch oven) for 30 minutes. Lift the dough on its paper into the hot pot and bake covered for 30 minutes, then uncovered for 10–15 minutes until golden and baked through. Cool slightly before slicing.
recipes.title: Greek bread with oregano and olive oil

recipes.method: Ingredients: 3 cups (about 750 ml) fresh oregano leaves, 1 small–medium white onion, finely diced, ¼ cup (about 60 ml) extra virgin olive oil, ½ cup (about 125 ml) fresh lemon juice, a pinch of salt. Rinse the oregano while it is still on the stem, then pat or spin it dry and strip the leaves from the stalks. Roughly chop any large leaves, but not too finely. Toss the leaves with the onion, oil, lemon juice and salt, adjusting the dressing to taste. Serve with bread to mop up the juices.
recipes.title: Fresh oregano salad (zouba)

recipes.method: Ingredients — dough: 290 ml warm water (cool enough to hold a little finger in), 2½ teaspoons dried active yeast, 1 teaspoon maple syrup, 480 g plain flour plus extra for dusting, 2 tablespoons olive oil, 1½ teaspoons salt; filling: 3 cups (about 750 ml) fresh oregano leaves, dried well and finely chopped, 1 medium onion, finely chopped, 2 tablespoons fresh lemon juice, 2 tablespoons olive oil plus more for brushing, ½ teaspoon salt. Mix the warm water, maple syrup and yeast and leave 10 minutes until frothy. Stir in the oil and salt, then the flour, and knead for 5 minutes. Cover in an oiled bowl and leave somewhere warm for about an hour, until doubled. Meanwhile mix the filling ingredients and divide into 3. Heat the oven to 190 °C (fan). Divide the dough into 3, keeping the rest covered. Roll one piece 3–4 mm thick, spread with a third of the filling, leaving a small gap at the top edge, roll up from the bottom and slice into 3.5 cm pieces. Repeat, then set the scrolls just touching in a greased dish and brush with oil if you like. Bake 35–40 minutes until golden (start checking at 35) and cool 5 minutes. The oregano turns dark brown or black in the oven, which is normal. Keeps 3 days sealed at room temperature or 5 days in the fridge.
recipes.title: Oregano bread scrolls

recipes.method: Ingredients: 2 cups (about 500 ml) ground dried oregano, 2 cups (about 500 ml) ground sumac, 2 cups (about 500 ml) raw sesame seeds, 1 teaspoon salt (to taste). To dry your own oregano, strip the leaves from the stalks, wash them and spin them completely dry, then hang them in a breathable cloth bag in the sun until fully dry, which takes 5–10 days depending on the weather; a dehydrator or low oven also works. The source does not say how to grind the dried leaves. Dry-toast the sesame seeds over medium-high heat until golden, add the oregano, sumac and salt, and stir over the heat for 5–10 minutes until well combined and aromatic. Let it cool completely before jarring, as a warm mix causes condensation and spoils the blend. Keeps several months in an airtight jar in the pantry.
recipes.title: Za'atar with oregano

recipes.method: Ingredients: 2 tablespoons fresh oregano (or to taste), 1 cup (250 ml) boiling water, 1 teaspoon maple syrup or other sweetener (optional). Pick and wash the oregano, put it in a mug or pot, pour over the boiling water and steep 5–10 minutes. Sweeten if you like. For a stronger tea, steep for hours or overnight.
recipes.title: Fresh oregano tea

summary.text:
Oregano (Origanum vulgare), sometimes called wild marjoram, is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae.
Along with its close relative O. majorana (sweet marjoram), oregano is widely used as a culinary herb. Although once used in folk medicine, there is no clinical evidence that oregano provides any health or anti-disease effects.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): South Island: rather scattered but common locally, abundant in Queenstown area (Central Otago). Native to Europe and western Asia; first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1944. A number of subspecies and varieties have been described for this very popular culinary herb. A greater range of forms are found in cultivation in New Zealand than occur wild.
Herbarium specimens held by Manaaki Whenua come from the Canterbury, Hawke's Bay, Nelson, Otago and Wellington land districts (Biota of NZ).

warnings: Not for medicinal use in pregnancy; small culinary amounts are considered safe.
Avoid large medicinal doses: oregano is strongly sedative, though mild teas are soothing. This rests on a single source.
The essential oil can irritate the skin, and there is no clinical evidence that the oil or extracts are safe or effective for health.
Systemic allergic reactions to eating oregano and thyme are on record (a single-patient case report), and mint-family (Lamiaceae) herbs such as marjoram, mint, sage and hyssop appear to cross-react.
Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed. Pick from ground you know.

edibleParts.text:
Fruit - raw or cooked. The fruit is almost as large as a blackcurrant and is produced in large bunches so it is easy to harvest. It has an acid flavour, but it is rather nice raw and is especially good when added to a porridge or muesli. Unfortunately, there is relatively little flesh and a lot of seeds, though some plants have larger and juicier fruits. The cooked fruit tastes somewhat like blackcurrants. The fruit can also be dried and stored for later use.
Flowers - raw. They can also be used to make a lemonade-like drink.
The small purplish-black fruits, which are quite tart and contain large seeds, are edible raw after the season's first frosts.

Roadsides, semi-shade by plantation margins or beneath deciduous trees.

identification.text:
Shrub 0.5–1–(2) m high, many-stemmed and stoloniferous. Leaves to about 25 cm long, composed of 3–7 pairs of sessile (excluding the terminal) leaflets, without basal pair of stipule-like leaflets; petiole (0)–1–4 cm long, dark red. Most leaflets 5–9.5 × 2.5–5 cm, ovate or elliptic-ovate, glossy above, prominently reticulate; margins undulate and spinose-dentate; apex spiny. Scales at base of fascicled racemes 5–10 mm long, membranous, brown. Racemes eventually to 6 or 7 cm long. Bracts broadly ovate, much shorter than pedicels at anthesis. Perianth segments to 7 mm long, ovate to obovate, imbricate; segments of innermost whorl shorter and emarginate. Stamens included; filaments with 2 teeth. Stigma sessile. Berry about 10 mm diameter, globose, blue-black, pruinose.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Mahonia aquifolium (Pursh) Nutt.]
Environment Canterbury describes the New Zealand plant as up to 2 m tall with few branches but often many upright stems, its leaves usually of 3–4 pairs of shiny, dark green, holly-like leaflets (restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Oregon grape's leaves are compound, up to about 25 cm long, of 3–7 pairs of holly-like leaflets 5–9.5 cm long plus one at the tip, and its stems carry no spines; Darwin's barberry has simple leaves 1–3 (rarely 3.5) cm long in clusters, with five-parted spines on the stems. Oregon grape's berries are about 10 mm across; Darwin's barberry's 5–7 mm, with a conspicuous style 1.5–3 mm long at the tip. Glossy, spiny-edged foliage, dark berries with a bloom and yellow to orange flowers do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Darwin's barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Oregon grape's leaves have no pair of small, stipule-like leaflets at the base, and usually sit on a dark red stalk up to 4 cm long; Japanese mahonia's leaves are stalkless and their lowest pair of leaflets is small and stipule-like. Oregon grape is a many-stemmed, suckering shrub, usually about 1 m and rarely 2 m; Japanese mahonia has few stems to about 3 m, each topped by a crown of leaves. Oregon grape's flower clusters reach 6–7 cm; Japanese mahonia's are lax, spreading and up to about 20 cm. Oregon grape's berries are round, about 10 mm across; Japanese mahonia's broadly egg-shaped, 8–10 mm long. Leaflet counts overlap (3–7 pairs against 5–9), and blue-black bloomed berries and spiny leaflets do not separate them. Most plants grown as Oregon grape are casual hybrids with Mahonia repens, so expect in-between plants.
lookalikes.name: Japanese mahonia

lookalikes.howToTell: Oregon grape's leaves are up to about 25 cm long with 3–7 pairs of leaflets; leatherleaf mahonia's are up to about 50 cm with 4–10 pairs and a much larger terminal leaflet. Oregon grape's flower clusters reach 6–7 cm; leatherleaf mahonia's stand upright, 7–26 cm long. Oregon grape's berries are round, about 10 mm across; leatherleaf mahonia's are egg-shaped and up to 15 mm long. Oregon grape is a low, many-stemmed, suckering shrub, usually about 1 m; leatherleaf mahonia has stiff upright stems and can reach 8 m. Leaflet counts overlap at 4–7 pairs, and dark bloomed berries and spiny leaflets do not separate them. Leatherleaf mahonia's berries are also described as globose, so shape alone does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Leatherleaf mahonia

lookalikes.howToTell: Oregon grape's leaves carry 3–7 pairs of ovate leaflets, 2.5–5 cm wide; mountain grape's, up to 45 cm long, carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped ones. Oregon grape is a low, many-stemmed shrub, usually about 1 m; mountain grape grows to 7 m. Oregon grape's flower clusters reach 6–7 cm; mountain grape's up to 25 cm. Oregon grape's berries are round, about 10 mm across; mountain grape's egg-shaped, up to 8 mm long. Dark blue berries with a bloom and spiny-edged leaflets do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Mountain grape

preparation.text:
They were included in small quantities in the traditional diets of Pacific Northwest tribes, mixed with salal or another sweeter fruit. Today, they are sometimes used to make jelly, alone or mixed with salal.
The berries are rather sour straight off the plant but make excellent jellies.

recipes.method: Written for Oregon grape (Mahonia aquifolium, or its low relative M. nervosa) by a preserving author in Oregon. About 1.6 kg Oregon grape berries; water; about 450 g (2¼ cups) sugar. Pick about 1.6 kg berries once they are evenly dark; sliding your fingers down a bunch drops them into the basket. Simmer the berries, covered, with half their volume of water for 15 minutes, mashing them after the first 10. Let the juice drip through a jelly bag for several hours, then boil it for 10 minutes to reduce it a little. Combine about 720 ml (3 cups) juice with about 450 g (2¼ cups) sugar in a wide, heavy, non-reactive pan over medium heat and stir until the sugar dissolves. Raise the heat and boil, skimming now and then, until it begins to jell, which takes only a few minutes: drops falling from a tipped metal spoon thicken and run together. Skim, pour into three sterilised half-pint (about 240 ml) jars and process in a boiling-water bath for 5 minutes; it should be firm by the next day. The author advises against doubling the batch. Metric amounts are converted from the source's pounds and cups.
recipes.title: Oregon grape jelly

summary.text:
Berberis aquifolium, the Oregon grape, holly-leaved barberry, or Mahonia, is a North American species of flowering plant in the family Berberidaceae. It is an evergreen shrub growing up to 3 metres tall and 1.5 m wide. It has pinnate leaves consisting of spiny leaflets, exhibiting dense clusters of yellow flowers followed by dark bluish-black berries.
Berberis aquifolium is invasive in parts of Western Europe, having escaped cultivation in parks.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: occasional, particularly in the Wellington area; S.: fairly common but scattered throughout, particularly Canterbury and Otago.
Oregon grape was introduced to N.Z. in the early days of European settlement and is often found around old gardens and churchyards, where it may persist long after the area has been abandoned.
Most plants grown under this name are casual hybrids with Mahonia repens. This species is easily confused with Mahonia pinnata, with which it also hybridizes.
It spreads by stolons into colonies, and a lone plant with no other nearby to pollinate it fruits poorly, if at all (Missouri Botanical Garden, restated).

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.

edibleParts.text: Young leaves and shoots, flower buds, flower heads and the root. The leaves are eaten raw or cooked; the young shoots are finely chopped into salads and, being pungent, are best used sparingly or mixed with other salad plants. The leaves taste aromatic and slightly lemony, and the plant can be bitter, so the youngest plants are best. Young shoots and buds can also be lightly steamed. Unopened flower buds are marinated or pickled in vinegar and used like capers. Flower heads are eaten raw in salads or used as a garnish; the yellow disc is mild and almost crunchy. The root is eaten raw — a use that rests on a single source.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Waste places, especially roadsides, grasslands, riverbeds, and forest margins.
In New Zealand it is most common in waste places, especially along roadsides, and also grows in dairy pasture (Massey University, restated), often in poorer or wetter dairy pastures (Stuff, restated).
It is a typical grassland perennial wildflower, growing in a variety of plant communities including meadows and fields, under scrub and open-canopy forests, and in disturbed areas. It grows in temperate regions where average annual rainfall exceeds 750 mm, and often where soils are heavy and damp. It is often a weed of degraded pastures and roadsides.

identification.text:
Scarcely scented, perennial herb. Stems erect, up to about 1 m tall, usually sparsely to densely villous below and glabrous above, rarely hairy or glabrous above and below, striate, simple or branched at base or sometimes above, rooting toward base. Basal and lower cauline leaves long-petiolate, elliptic, obovate or spathulate, obtuse at apex, cuneate, coarsely 1–2-serrate, crenate, or shallowly 1–(2)-pinnatifid, usually glabrous, sometimes sparsely hairy on petiole and midrib, very rarely moderately hairy, up to 12–(18) × 2–(4) cm; cauline leaves similar to basal but above becoming smaller, apetiolate, narrow-oblong, amplexicaul, with few distant teeth or sometimes entire, and often auriculate at base. Involucral bracts 3–8 mm long, glabrous; margins and apex brown, membranous; inner bracts with extended, broad, apical flap. Capitula solitary or few in corymbs, (25)–30–60–(65) mm diameter; ray florets (9)–18–33; ligules white; disc florets numerous, yellow. Achenes about 2.5 mm long, dark brown with pale ribs; achenes of disc florets mostly more or less terete, with 10 more or less equal ribs, and corona 0; achenes of ray florets similar to those of disc florets, but sometimes flattened with lateral ribs somewhat extended, 3 ribs on outer surface and 5 ribs on inner surface, rarely achene 3-angled, sometimes with irregular corona about 0.3 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It varies somewhat in hairiness, and in the number, size, and shape of the ligules. Much of this variation can be seen within a single population, and all forms are easily distinguished from L. maximum.
Leucanthemum maximum, the other naturalised Leucanthemum in New Zealand, has narrow-elliptic, evenly toothed basal and lower stem leaves, stems hairless or with a few scattered hairs, and heads (50)–70–120 mm across (Flora of New Zealand key, restated).
It grows as a rosette at first, then as taller clumps with upright, leafy flower stems (Massey University, restated).
While it is small it can be confused with the common lawn daisy, with stinking mayweed (stinking chamomile) and with scentless chamomile (Stuff, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Lawn daisy's flower stalk is leafless, 3–15 cm long (up to 25 cm), and rises from a flat rosette with a single head 15–25 mm across. Ox-eye daisy's flowering stems are leafy and erect, up to about 1 m tall, with one or a few heads usually 30–60 mm across (25–65 mm at the extremes), so the two meet only at about 25 mm. Ox-eye's upper stem leaves are stalkless, narrow and clasp the stem, often with ear-like lobes at the base; its basal leaves are long-stalked, coarsely toothed, scalloped or shallowly lobed, and up to 12 cm long (rarely 18 cm). Lawn daisy's leaves are spoon-shaped to oblong, usually 20–60 mm long (10–80 mm at the extremes), with 2–6 pairs of shallow teeth and one main vein. Lawn daisy's rays are often tinged pink to reddish purple underneath or at the tip; ox-eye's are white. What does not separate them: white rays around a yellow disc, and young rosettes — both have spoon-shaped, scalloped basal leaves, though ox-eye's rosettes grow into taller clumps while lawn daisy's stay small and flat. Common lawn daisy is eaten too — its young leaves, flower buds and petals (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Common lawn daisy

lookalikes.howToTell: Leaves separate them best: stinking mayweed's are cut three times into narrow, almost thread-like segments with a somewhat feathery look, while ox-eye daisy's basal leaves are long-stalked and coarsely toothed, scalloped or at most shallowly lobed, and its upper stem leaves are narrow, stalkless and clasping, with a few distant teeth or none. Stinking mayweed is a strongly foetid annual; ox-eye daisy is a scarcely scented perennial whose stems root towards the base. Stinking mayweed's receptacle carries narrow, pointed scales among the inner florets; ox-eye daisy's has none. What does not separate them: head size overlaps (stinking mayweed about 15–30 mm across, up to 35 mm; ox-eye usually 30–60 mm, 25–65 mm at the extremes), so heads of 25–35 mm need the leaf, smell or scale tests; ray number overlaps (8–21 against 9–33); both have white rays around a yellow disc, and both grow on roadsides, waste places and pasture. Stinking mayweed is not a food plant: its juice is acrid, touching or eating it can cause allergies in some people, the foliage may irritate skin, and there are reports of toxicity.
lookalikes.name: Stinking mayweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Roman chamomile is a low, creeping, sweetly aromatic perennial whose hairy stems lie along the ground or rise to about 20 cm; ox-eye daisy's flowering stems stand erect, up to about 1 m. Roman chamomile's leaves are cut three times into narrow segments with a feathery look, 15–50 mm long; ox-eye's are coarsely toothed, scalloped or shallowly lobed, the basal ones up to 12 cm long (rarely 18 cm). Roman chamomile's receptacle carries small, blunt scales among the florets; ox-eye's has none. Heads: Roman chamomile's are about 8–20 mm across (up to 30 mm), ox-eye's usually 30–60 mm (25–65 mm at the extremes), so they meet only between 25 and 30 mm. What does not separate them: white rays around a yellow disc, and place — both grow on roadsides, waste places and pasture. Roman chamomile's fresh or dried flowers are used for herb tea and its young sprigs as a seasoning (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Roman chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: Leaves separate them best: ox-eye daisy's basal leaves are long-stalked and coarsely toothed, scalloped or at most shallowly lobed, and its upper stem leaves are narrow, stalkless and clasp the stem; scentless chamomile's are cut about three times into thread-like segments with a feathery look. Cut a head in half: ox-eye's receptacle is flat or slightly domed, scentless chamomile's conical. Ox-eye daisy is a perennial that roots at the base of its stems and spreads by short rhizomes; scentless chamomile is an annual or biennial. What does not separate them: smell — both are almost scentless; head size — ox-eye usually 30–60 mm across (25–65 mm at the extremes), scentless chamomile about 30–50 mm; white rays around a yellow disc; and place — roadsides, waste places and pasture. There is no record of scentless chamomile being eaten.
lookalikes.name: Scentless chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: Leaves separate them best: ox-eye daisy's basal leaves are long-stalked, elliptic, obovate or spoon-shaped, coarsely toothed (sometimes doubly), scalloped or shallowly lobed, and up to 12 cm long (rarely 18 cm); Shasta daisy's are narrow-elliptic, evenly toothed with single teeth, and up to about 30 cm long. Heads: ox-eye's are usually 30–60 mm across (25–65 mm at the extremes), Shasta daisy's usually 70–120 mm (50 mm at the smallest), so they meet only between 50 and 65 mm. Ox-eye's stems are usually hairy below, rarely hairless; Shasta daisy's are hairless or have a few scattered hairs. What does not separate them: both are scarcely scented perennials up to about 1 m tall, with white rays around a yellow disc, narrow, stalkless upper leaves that clasp the stem, and no scales on the receptacle, and both grow on roadsides, waste places and pasture. Shasta daisy is a garden escape, occasional in the wild; it has no reliable record as food, is listed as mildly toxic if eaten, and can irritate the skin (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Shasta daisy

preparation.text: Pick the youngest plants. Chop the leaves into salads, sandwiches, omelettes, raita or tabbouleh, or cook them in soups, stews and sauces; steam young shoots and buds lightly. For capers, pack unopened buds into jars and cover them with strained, spiced vinegar; they can be eaten after a day but are best left a month. Use only fresh flower heads, not wilted or browning ones, and check them for insects.

recipes.method: Makes two 0.25 litre jars. 500 ml brown rice wine vinegar; 1 teaspoon sea salt; 1 teaspoon red peppercorns; 1 teaspoon mace; 2 garlic cloves, chopped; enough oxeye daisy flower buds to fill two 0.25 litre screw-top jars. Put the vinegar in a small saucepan with everything except the buds, bring it to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes. Take it off the heat and leave it for at least an hour, until warm or cold. Meanwhile pack the buds into the jars as tightly as you can. Strain the vinegar through a sieve to remove the spices, pour it into the jars to the top and cap them. They can be eaten after 24 hours but are best left to mature for a month.
recipes.title: Oxeye daisy capers

recipes.method: Serves 2; to go with curry and other spicy food. 20 g oxeye daisy leaves; 150 ml coconut milk; 150 g natural yoghurt; the juice of half a lime. Roughly chop the leaves, put them in a bowl with the yoghurt, coconut milk and lime juice, mix thoroughly and leave at room temperature for 10 minutes before serving.
recipes.title: Oxeye daisy raita

recipes.method: Serves 2; quinoa replaces the usual bulgur wheat. ½ cup (125 ml) cooked quinoa, cold; a handful of chopped parsley; a handful of chopped oxeye daisy leaves; ¼ cup (about 60 ml) chopped fresh mint; 4 medium tomatoes, chopped; ¼ cup (about 60 ml) light olive oil; the juice of 1 lemon; ½ teaspoon sea salt; 1 garlic clove, finely chopped. Put the cold quinoa in a bowl, add the parsley, oxeye daisy leaves, mint and garlic, mix well and leave for 30 minutes or until you are ready to serve. Just before serving add the tomatoes, oil, lemon juice and salt, mix well, leave for 15 minutes and serve.
recipes.title: Oxeye daisy tabbouleh

recipes.method: Serves 2 as a light lunch. A handful of young oxeye daisy greens, chopped; 2 garlic cloves, crushed; 14 cherry tomatoes, quartered; 1 teaspoon red wine vinegar; olive oil; salt and pepper; rustic bread. The page gives no amount of oil and does not say when the daisy greens go in; its title and serving step call it a 'tomato and oxeye daisy mix'. Put the ripe, room-temperature tomatoes in a bowl with the garlic and vinegar, mix, season with salt and pepper and leave for 15 minutes. Slice and lightly toast the bread, drizzle it generously with olive oil, top with the tomato and oxeye daisy mix and serve at once.
recipes.title: Oxeye daisy bruschetta

recipes.method: Serves 2 as a main, inspired by Vietnamese street food. 800 g firm tofu; 1 tablespoon lemon juice or vinegar; 3 garlic cloves, crushed; 300 g fresh tomatoes, diced; 100 g oxeye daisy greens, chopped; 2 tablespoons 'gia vi' seasoning (grind 2 teaspoons sugar, 1 teaspoon sea salt, 1 teaspoon ground black pepper and 1 teaspoon dried onion pieces to a powder); 2 lemongrass stalks; 4 tablespoons tamari; 1 tablespoon sesame oil; ½ teaspoon chipotle chilli flakes; 100 ml water; oil for frying. Bring 500 ml water to the boil, add the cubed tofu and the lemon juice and simmer for 10 minutes; drain and pat dry. Heat the oven to 200 °C (fan 180 °C). Bake the tofu cubes on baking paper for 20 minutes. Gently fry the garlic in 2 tablespoons of oil for about 30 seconds, stirring so it does not burn, then add the tomatoes and the baked tofu and stir well. Stir in 2 tablespoons of the gia vi and ¼ teaspoon of the chilli flakes (the ingredient list gives ½ teaspoon). Bruise the lemongrass until it splinters and add it with the chopped daisy greens. Pour in the 100 ml water and simmer for about 15 minutes until the sauce thickens. Off the heat, stir in the sesame oil and serve on millet or rice. The ingredient list includes tamari but the steps never say when to add it.
recipes.title: Oxeye daisy greens and baked tofu

recipes.method: The author's weeds were chickweed, nasturtium, dandelion, pūhā, ox-eye daisy and plantain, with parsley and garden herbs (the page does not say which plantain). She also adds a handful of New Zealand spinach; it is At Risk and its page says to blanch it first, so it is left out here. 5 rosemary sprigs about 12 cm long; a handful of parsley; a big handful of chickweed; 4 large nasturtium leaves; a handful of thyme sprigs 5 cm long; a few dandelion leaves; a small pūhā plant; 10 ox-eye daisy leaves; 8 plantain leaves; 5 sage leaves; 6 garlic cloves; 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt; about 30 ml (⅛ cup) cider vinegar; 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) olive oil, starting with the smaller amount; 5 ml (1 tsp) honey, or to taste; the juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml (½ cup) walnuts. Strip the leaves from the thyme and rosemary and wash any leaves that need it. Blend everything in a high-speed blender or food processor until smooth, pushing it down with the tamper. Keep it in the fridge or freezer.
recipes.title: Wild weed pesto

summary.text:
Leucanthemum vulgare, commonly known as the ox-eye daisy, oxeye daisy, dog daisy, marguerite (French: Marguerite commune, "common marguerite") and other common names, is a widespread flowering plant native to Europe and the temperate regions of Asia, and an introduced plant to North America, Australia and New Zealand.
The species is native to Europe, and to Turkey and Georgia in Western Asia.
The species is widely naturalised in many parts of the world, including North America, and is considered to be an invasive species in more than forty countries.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands: throughout, lowland to montane; Stewart Island: Halfmoon Bay area; Campbell Island. Native range temperate Eurasia; naturalised in New Zealand by 1867.
The oxeye daisy is a common and conspicuous roadside weed. The species has been previously known in New Zealand as Chrysanthemum leucanthemum.
In New Zealand it can be troublesome in dairy pasture because cows tend not to eat it, but never where sheep graze, as they eat it readily; it is not susceptible to the selective herbicides normally used in pasture, and its short rhizomes make it hard to control (Massey University, restated).
Sheep, goats and horses eat it, but cows and pigs dislike its bitter taste, so beef and dairy farmers can lose a good deal of pasture where it takes hold (Stuff, restated).
The Department of Conservation lists it among New Zealand's environmental weeds (2024), as a fully naturalised plant with more than minor impacts in natural ecosystems.

warnings: Eat it sparingly: the leaves are pungent and can be bitter, very large amounts can cause sickness, and eating many of the yellow flower centres may cause indigestion.

Ox-eye daisy contains sesquiterpene lactones, strong inducers of allergic contact dermatitis, sometimes with sensitivity to sunlight; allergy to daisies usually shows as contact dermatitis, and people sensitised to other daisy-family plants (Asteraceae) may cross-react.

In New Zealand dairy pasture it is controlled with herbicides — 2,4-D, clopyralid, aminopyralid, metsulfuron, thifensulfuron-methyl, flumetsulam or triclopyr/picloram, often as spot treatments, or glyphosate in a weed wiper — so pasture plants may have been sprayed.

habitat.text:
Bush, gardens, roadsides, disturbed sites, also along the seaside. Tolerates shade well.
In New Zealand: waste places and gardens, especially in shady disturbed sites, on banks, beneath hedges, windbreaks, and forest margins.

identification.text:
Perennial, almost glabrous herb with thick fleshy contractile root; main bulb about 2 cm long, subterranean; tunic brown, with scale nerves inconspicuous; secondary aerial bulbs or bulbils small, common in branch axils. Stems spreading to sub-erect, glabrous, with many flexuous, slender branches. Leaves 3-foliolate, glabrous. Petiole 2–7–(12) cm long; stipules forming a narrow to broad wing. Lamina of leaflets subequal, subsessile, 4–16 × 5–22 mm, mostly broadly obcordate, with more or less divergent lobes, finely reticulate beneath, with a submarginal irregular row of orange calli; base more or less narrow-cuneate, often slightly hairy. Flowers solitary; peduncles 2.5–12 cm long, filiform. Bracts about 1/2 way along pedicel, 2–2.8 mm long, linear-subulate; calli prominent. Sepals 4.5–5.5 mm long, ovate-oblong, often slightly hairy; calli 2, apical, prominent, orange. Petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes becoming almost white, glabrous; limb broad-obovate. Stamens in 2 whorls; filaments hairy, dilated towards base, shorter than 4 mm long. Styles much longer than longer whorl of stamens, hairy except near apex. Capsule not seen. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Its stems creep along the ground and root at the nodes. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: white clover's leaflets are c. 5–25 mm long, can be notched at the tip and often carry light or dark markings, so leaflet size, shape and markings overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually without a stalk, sitting among the top leaves, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Its leaf stalks and leaflet undersides are usually moderately hairy, and its leaflets, c. 15–40 mm long, usually carry a crescent-shaped mark towards the base. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless. Red clover's leaflets are mostly larger, but the ranges meet at 15–16 mm, so use size only as a guide. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Its stems are erect or ascending and do not root at the nodes, and its leaflets are c. 10–35 mm long. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Leaflet size overlaps between 10 and 16 mm, so it does not separate them. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Shamrock wood sorrel: a hairy, clump-forming plant with all its leaves in basal rosettes on stalks (3)–7–30 cm long, and no leafy stem. Its flowers come (4)–7–35 together in a branched cluster on a stalk up to c. 35 cm tall; petals 9–16 mm long, usually rose with darker veins, rarely white. Its leaflets are usually 8–35 mm long, up to 55 mm. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless. Its petals can be as short as 10 mm, so petal size alone does not separate them, and both can be pale or white. Several flowers on one stalk point to shamrock wood sorrel, but a single flower does not rule it out: its clusters can hold anything from 1 to at least 30 flowers. Look for a leafy, branched stem, which only pale-pink wood sorrel has. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Shamrock wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Pink shamrock has no leafy stem: its leaves all rise from the base, from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, and it carries 3–7 or 10–18 flowers in a cluster on a stalk up to 35 cm long. Pale-pink wood sorrel has leafy stems, spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and each flower stalk carries a single flower. Pink shamrock's leaflets are hairy beneath and its flower clusters carry long curly hairs; pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless. Petals do not separate them: pink shamrock's are 1.5–2 cm long, pink to rose; pale-pink wood sorrel's 1.7–2.2 cm, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Leaflet size overlaps (pink shamrock 10–35 mm long, pale-pink wood sorrel 4–16 mm), and both have orange dots near the leaflet edge. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pink shamrock

lookalikes.howToTell: Fishtail oxalis has no leafy stem: its leaves all rise from the base, from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, and it carries about 5–15 (up to 20) flowers in a cluster on a stalk about 10–50 cm tall. Pale-pink wood sorrel has leafy stems, spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and each flower stalk carries a single flower. Fishtail oxalis's petals are about 1.2–1.5 cm long, pink; pale-pink wood sorrel's are 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white, but can be as short as 10 mm, so petal size alone does not separate them. Fishtail oxalis's leaflets are broadly fishtail-shaped, with no orange dots or only faint ones; pale-pink wood sorrel's carry an irregular row of orange dots just inside the edge. Leaflet size overlaps: fishtail oxalis's are 12–50 mm long, pale-pink wood sorrel's 4–16 mm. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. The tests above that do not rest on leaflet shape or petal colour still hold for it. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Fishtail oxalis

lookalikes.howToTell: Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long; its stems are sparsely to densely hairy, lie along the ground or rise a little, and do not root at the nodes. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and it is almost hairless. Out of flower, do not rely on leaflet size: suckling clover's are about 3–12 mm long, pale-pink wood sorrel's 4–16 mm. On most suckling clover leaves the middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the side ones. Suckling clover has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Suckling clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Purple wood sorrel has no stem above ground: its leaves all rise from the base. Its leaf stalks and the undersides of its leaflets are hairy, the leaflet edges fringed with long hairs, and its leaflets are 10–35 mm long (up to 45 mm), broadly obovate with a rounded tip, sometimes slightly notched; the dots and streaks on them turn black when dry. Each flower stalk, 1–11 cm long, carries a single flower forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base; its sepals carry a dense fringe of long white hairs and have no orange dots at the tip. Pale-pink wood sorrel has leafy stems, spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils; it is the only oxalis in New Zealand with bulbils above ground. It is almost hairless. Its leaflets are 4–16 mm long, mostly broadly heart-shaped, with an irregular row of orange dots just inside the edge, and each sepal has two prominent orange dots at its tip (in some plants they look light brown). Each flower stalk, 2.5–12 cm long, carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. What does not separate them: both carry a single flower on each stalk, and the stalk lengths overlap. Petal length overlaps too, as either plant's petals can be as short as 10 mm, so only petals longer than 2.2 cm point to purple wood sorrel. Leaflet length overlaps between 10 and 16 mm. Look for a leafy, branched stem and orange dots on the sepal tips, which only pale-pink wood sorrel has. Do not eat purple wood sorrel; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Purple wood sorrel

preparation.text: Eat the young leaves fresh and in small amounts: in salads, finely chopped as a garnish or in green pestos. Toss the leaves and flowers through a green salad, or use the flowers as a garnish; pick the flowers by day, when they are open.

recipes.method: Two handfuls of wood sorrel, chopped; potato and kūmara, boiled first and sliced; cream. Layer the sorrel with the sliced potato and kūmara in a baking dish, pour cream over the top and bake at 180 °C until it starts to brown.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel, kūmara and potato gratin

recipes.method: Chop a big handful of wood sorrel leaves, stalks and flowers and mix them through a potato salad dressed with a cream dressing.
recipes.title: Potato salad with wood sorrel

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) lemon juice and 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) maple syrup or honey. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the sorrel and stir for 1–2 minutes, until it wilts. Put it in a blender or food processor with the lemon juice and the syrup or honey and blend until well combined. Serve it straight away, or refrigerate it and warm it before use; the author finds it even better the next day. The author serves it on fish, or as a dipping sauce for grilled prawns.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel sauce

recipes.method: About 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, stems or flowers, or a mix, about 250 ml (1 cup) water, and maple syrup or another sweetener to taste. The amounts are rough: use as much sorrel as you like and enough water to cover it. Blend the sorrel and water until well combined, strain through a fine sieve and sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel 'lemonade'

recipes.method: Equal parts wood sorrel, sugar, and water; the author usually uses 250 ml (1 cup) of each. Put everything in a saucepan and bring it to a simmer, stirring. Simmer for 15–30 minutes, strain through muslin (cheesecloth) and pour into sterilised bottles. The author uses it in tea, topped up with soda water, over ice cream or fresh strawberries, or in vinaigrettes and marinades.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel syrup

recipes.method: The recipe uses one part leaves to three parts water. Fresh wood sorrel leaves; boiling water; sweetener to taste (optional). Put the leaves in a container, pour the boiling water over them and leave to steep for 5–15 minutes. Strain out the leaves and sweeten to taste if you like. Drink it hot, or pour it over ice for an iced tea.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel tea

recipes.method: 2 cloves garlic, minced; olive oil for cooking; 2 spring onions, chopped; 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock; 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish; 3 medium mint leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk; salt and pepper. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks. Heat a little olive oil in a small saucepan and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the spring onions. Cover with the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, then add the sorrel for about 30 seconds. Take it off the heat, add the mint and blend smooth with a stick blender (or an ordinary blender). Stir in the coconut milk and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until well chilled, a couple of hours, and serve garnished with the sorrel flowers.
recipes.title: Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

recipes.method: About 450 g (1 lb) Italian or breakfast sausage; 1 medium spaghetti squash; several cups of wood sorrel, washed and drained, stems removed (the recipe gives no closer amount); olive oil; 1 red onion, halved and sliced; 1 egg; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk or any milk; 1 garlic clove, minced; 15 ml (1 tbsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) tarragon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) black pepper; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground sage. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Halve the squash, spoon out the seeds and stringy threads, set the halves cut side up on a baking tray, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and bake for 20–25 minutes, until the flesh gives a little when pressed. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts. Take the squash out of the oven and scrape out the flesh with a fork (careful, it will be hot). Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: The author's greens were puha, sow thistle, nasturtium, onion weed, wild fennel, oxalis, wild mustard and wild celery; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 1 diced onion; 1 potato, scrubbed and diced; 2 sliced garlic cloves; 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 1.3 litres water; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked pepper; extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil, to serve; edible weed flowers. Serves 4. Cut the vegetables and greens to similar sizes. Fry the onion in the oil for a minute, then add the potato and garlic (the method also adds fennel bulb and celery stalks, which the ingredient list leaves out) and fry for another minute. Add the water, cover, bring to the boil and simmer until the potato is soft. Add the greens with the salt and yeast and cook for 3 minutes, until just tender — added at the end, they keep their colour. Blend until smooth (push it through a sieve if your blender isn't powerful), season with the pepper and more salt if needed, and serve drizzled with extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil and scattered with edible weed flowers.

The post was first written as O. acetosella; a commenter (AJB, 26/11/2009) identified the plant pictured as 'the South African Ox. incarnata', which the author accepted, and the title now names O. incarnata. The blog covers Wellington and the Wairarapa; the post does not say where the plant grew. Not used as recipes: adding it to apple, peach or pear pie and a jelly (suggestions, not made by the author); its use to curdle milk for cheese (the author had not got it to work).

Edibility sources (16/10/2026; warnings added 16/10/2026, preparation filled 03/11/2026 from the two sources below; edible parts since written by the owner, 'Leafs, flowers and stems.', spelling regularised 16/10/2026) — no openly licensed source found that records this species as edible (Useful Temperate Plants has no record; Plants For A Future returned no entry; Wikipedia and Flora of New Zealand say nothing of use). The only species-specific source is Johanna Knox's Wild Picnic post above (all rights reserved, so not quoted), which records: raw leaves and stalks have a bright, sour taste and suit sweet and savoury dishes; leaves and flowers in a green salad, flowers as a garnish; it goes with root vegetables, fish, chicken and cream; used in place of lemon. Its caution: high oxalic acid levels, so not too much, and avoid it if you have gout, kidney trouble or rheumatoid arthritis and are avoiding high-oxalic-acid foods. Knox's A Forager's Treasury and Langlands' Foraging New Zealand (both owned, cited above) are the book routes. Not copied from creeping-wood-sorrel, whose text is about Oxalis corniculata. Species-specific, all rights reserved, facts only: (1) Heartland Folk, 'Pale Wood Sorrel ~ Oxalis incarnata', Wild Food Wednesday issue 10 (Substack, 2026, Central Highlands of Victoria, Australia), https://heartlandfolk.substack.com/p/pale-wood-sorrel-oxalis-incarnata — all aerial parts edible, leaves and flowers; young leaves sour, eaten fresh in salads, chopped as a garnish or in green pestos in small amounts; best used fresh in small amounts because of its oxalic acid; pick young tender leaves, flowers by day when open; harvest only from unsprayed sites away from roadsides; clovers named as close lookalikes; the plant goes dormant in heat and drought. Its leaflet size (1.5–3 cm long) is larger than Flora of New Zealand's 4–16 mm and is not used. (2) PictureThis, 'Pale pink-sorrel (Oxalis incarnata)' (plant-identification app wiki, author not named), https://www.picturethisai.com/wiki/Oxalis_incarnata.html — leaves edible but not in large amounts because of oxalic acid; not used further, no named author. (3) EdiblePlantDB, 'Oxalidaceae' family page, https://edibleplantdb.org/families/Oxalidaceae — lists O. incarnata with edible parts leaves and stems; an aggregated list with no author or primary source given. It is a genus-wide flag, not a finding about this species, but it is the only source found that says not to eat it.
