The seven recipes from 'Wood sorrel sauce' onward were copied 16/10/2026 from creeping-wood-sorrel (owner, 16/10/2026: "the recipies are interchangeble betwwen sorrel species"); none is written for this species. Their provenance, as recorded there: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (cups at 250 ml, 1 tbsp = 15 ml, 1 tsp = 5 ml; every page all rights reserved; retrieved 15/10/2026; supplied by the owner). None is written for this species: each is written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally. The sauce, 'lemonade' and syrup from Kate MacQuarrie, 'Wood Sorrel Recipes', PEI Untamed, 09/07/2023 (https://www.pei-untamed.com/post/wood-sorrel-recipes) — written for 'the Wood Sorrels' of Prince Edward Island, no species named; 'grilled shrimp' given as prawns; the lemonade's 'leaves, stems, and/or flowers' and its note that the author does not measure are kept. 'Wood sorrel cooler' is Sunny Savage's 'Oxalis Cooler' as given in Green Deane, 'Oxalis: How To Drown Your Sorrels', Eat The Weeds (dated 16/01/2018 on the page, with reader comments from 2012; https://www.eattheweeds.com/oxalis-how-to-drown-your-sorrels/; the owner's second link, https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/oxalis-deppei/, is a tag page showing the same article) — written for Oxalis generally, the article naming the Florida species including O. corniculata; 1 US quart is about 946 ml; the recipe does not strain the drink and neither does this. 'Wood sorrel tea' from Jesse, 'Wood Sorrel: Identification, Uses, and Precautions', Feral Foraging, 11/07/2024 (https://feralforaging.com/wood-sorrel/) — written mainly for O. stricta and O. violacea; the page gives the ratio only as '1:3' after 'Gather wood sorrel leaves' and 'Pour over boiling water', without saying by volume or by weight, so 'one part leaves to three parts water' is this guide's reading. 'Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup' from Valerie Zemba, 'Chilled Lemony Wood Sorrel Soup', Very Vegan Val, 03/07/2019 (https://veryveganval.com/chilled-lemony-wood-sorrel-soup/) — written for 'Oxalis stricta and others'; scallions given as spring onions, vegetable broth as stock; the rinsing and stripping step is from the page's prose above the recipe card. 'Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel' from Chosen Weeds Farm, 'Cooking With Wood Sorrel', 15/03/2017 (https://thechosenweeds.com/cooking-with-wood-sorrel/) — written for the purple-leaf wood sorrel that grows in the author's south-east Texas garden; 400 °F given as 200 °C, 1 lb as about 450 g; 'Several cups' of sorrel kept because the page gives no closer amount; the page says only 'Combine mixture with the egg' after forking out the squash, and the method keeps that wording rather than saying where the squash goes. Not used from the recipe pages (15/10/2026): the casserole page's 'If you are short on time you can skip the oven step', because skipping the final bake would leave the stirred-in egg uncooked; Feral Foraging's statements that all species of wood sorrel are edible and can be used in similar ways (genus-level claims), its estimate that about 30 g a day, several times a week, is safe and its view that oxalate warnings are overblown (it contradicts every other page read here and is not a trusted source for a safety amount), and its cold-infusion and dried-leaf variants; Green Deane's statements that cooking reportedly renders oxalic acid harmless, particularly with calcium, that eating a lot raw can leach calcium from the bones, and that the juice curdles milk for cheese, and that all parts including the root bulb are edible (said of the Florida species as a group); the casserole page's medicinal and vitamin claims; the reader comment on Eat The Weeds suggesting more sorrel for a sharper cooler. Two of the owner's links have no recipe: Rachel Lambert, 'Wild Food: Wood Sorrel family', Wild Walks Southwest, 07/05/2021 (https://wildwalks-southwest.co.uk/wild-food-wood-sorrel-family/), and Diego Bonetto, 'How to identify and eat wood Sorrel', 10/08/2021 (https://www.diegobonetto.com/blog/wood-sorrel-id-forage-edible-weed) — both name O. corniculata among the species they describe. Lambert says all of them have a lemony, tart flavour and uses them in salads, in soups and as an edible decoration; Bonetto says the stalks, flowers and leaves are eaten raw or cooked, in salads and as a garnish; recorded here for edibleParts and preparation, which were empty on creeping-wood-sorrel when this was written (15/10/2026).

summary.text:
Oxalis incarnata is a species of flowering plant in the woodsorrel family known by the common names pale pink-sorrel and crimson woodsorrel. It is native to southern Africa, but it can be found on other continents where it is an introduced species, often the descendant of garden escapees. It is grown and kept as an ornamental plant.
In New Zealand: North Island: especially common in coastal towns and cities; South Island: from Marlborough to Southland, but never more than locally common south of Marlborough, occasional on the West Coast; Stewart Island: Halfmoon Bay. Naturalised from South Africa, first recorded in 1944.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

Prostrate to low-growing shrub up to about 15 cm tall or more, forming extensive dense patches; branches decumbent to ascending; branchlets close-set, minutely puberulous when young, densely clad in erect imbricate leaves. Lamina sessile or subsessile, coriaceous, glabrous, usually brownish green above, paler below, finely nerved, about 4–9 × 1–2 mm., obovate-oblong; margins scarious to cartilaginous, finely ciliolate; abruptly narrowed to pungent tip about 2 mm long. Inflorescence of axillary solitary sessile flowers; bracts minute, apiculate. Flowers small; calyx-lobes acute. Corolla-tube cylindric. longer than twice length calyx; lobes short, acute, densely hairy on upper surfaces. Fruit orange to yellow, broad-oblong in outline, 8–9 mm long.
[From:  Allan  (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1 as Cyathodes fraseri (A.Cunn.) Allan]

identification.text: Hericium novae-zealandiae has a relatively large (10 cm + diameter), white fruiting body, initially described (as Hydnum nova zealandia) as looking somewhat like a cauliflower nearing flowering. Lacking a pileus or defined stipe, basidiomata are highly and irregularly branched. Growing from a short, corkish stem, culminating in numerous, densely arranged, fine tips. The hymenium (spore bearing surface) is located on the surface of the fine tips, there is no delineation between the stipe and the hymenium until spore maturity when tips become reddish.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Common to abundant in wet pastures, by rivers and lakesides, also in drier places, including bare lava and backs of sandy beaches.
It is mainly a weed of moist pastures and lawns. It tolerates some summer dryness but takes over only where rain is reliable for much of the year or the soil is poorly drained.
Wetland status (NZPCN, from the national wetland plant list, Clarkson et al. 2021): facultative — commonly found both in wetlands and on dry ground.

identification.text:
Perennial with prostrate creeping and ascending stems to about 30 cm long, hairy when aerial, glabrous when submerged. Leaves petiolate, sometimes shortly so; lamina of vegetative shoots usually 0.6–2 × 0.4–1 cm, ovate, elliptic to suborbicular, not rugose, entire or sparingly and shallowly toothed, usually glabrous when submerged, hairy and densely dotted with glands when aerial; base attenuate to rounded; apex rounded to acute. Leaves subtending the axillary verticels similar, but often smaller, hairy. Verticels axillary, spaced, with densely packed, shortly pedicellate flowers. Calyx about 3 mm long, campanulate, purple, hairy and dotted with glands outside, with prominent white hairy tuft in throat; teeth more or less forming 2 lips, acuminate, ciliate, shorter than the tube at anthesis. Corolla 4–6 mm long, mauve, hairy outside, well exserted. Stamens usually exserted at anthesis. Nutlets 0.5–0.6 mm long, bluntly angled, oblong.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The strong mint smell of the crushed foliage is the best way to recognise it. In flower, its purplish-blue flowers cluster around the bases of the leaves. The stems creep and root along the ground, with only the ends of flowering stems turning upright, and it forms dense mats in pasture and lawns. Out of flower it looks very like turf speedwell, which grows in the same places but has no mint smell.

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: pennyroyal smells strongly of mint; self-heal has no minty smell. Self-heal's flowers are usually violet, 10–15 mm long, in a dense head at the stem tip among broad bracts fringed with white hairs; pennyroyal's are mauve to purplish-blue, 4–6 mm long, packed in spaced rings in the joints of the leaves along the stem. Self-heal's leaves are larger, 1.7–6 cm long, puckered and coarsely hairy; pennyroyal's are usually 0.6–2 cm long, not puckered and dotted with glands. Both creep, root along the stems and form mats in damp lawns and pasture. Self-heal's leaves and flowers are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Self-heal

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: turf speedwell has no mint smell, pennyroyal smells strongly of mint. In flower, turf speedwell's flowers are pale blue fading to whitish, flat with four lobes, 3–5 mm across, up a spike at the stem tips; pennyroyal's mauve flowers, 4–6 mm long, crowd in rings around the stem at the leaf bases. Out of flower they look very alike: both creep and root along the ground, have small paired leaves of much the same shape and size, and grow in damp lawns and pasture. Turf speedwell's record as food is thin, so it is not given as food here.
lookalikes.name: Turf speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Smell does not separate them: crushed pennyroyal leaves have a very strong fragrance like spearmint. Look at where the flowers are: pennyroyal's are densely packed in spaced rings in the leaf joints along the stem, with a cluster of leaves at the shoot tip; spearmint's are in narrow spikes at the stem tips, the central spike 4–12 cm long. Pennyroyal's stems creep along the ground and ascend, to about 30 cm long; spearmint's ascend to about 80 cm. Pennyroyal's leaves are stalked, sometimes shortly, usually 0.6–2 cm long and not wrinkled; spearmint's are stalkless or very shortly stalked, 2.5–9 cm long, flat or wrinkled. Both have mauve flowers of similar size (pennyroyal's corolla 4–6 mm long, spearmint's 3–5 mm) and a purple or purplish calyx, so flower colour does not separate them, and both grow in damp grassy places. Wild spearmint's leaves are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Wild spearmint

lookalikes.howToTell: Smell does not separate them: crushed pennyroyal leaves have a very strong fragrance like spearmint. Apple mint is often spearmint-scented too. Look at where the flowers are: pennyroyal's are densely packed in spaced rings in the leaf joints along the stem, with a cluster of leaves at the shoot tip; apple mint's are in several narrow, densely hairy spikes at the stem tips, the central spike to about 8 cm long. Pennyroyal's stems creep along the ground and ascend, to about 30 cm long; apple mint's are erect, to about 70 cm tall. Pennyroyal's leaves are stalked, sometimes shortly, not wrinkled, usually 0.6–2 × 0.4–1 cm; apple mint's are stalkless or nearly so, broad, wrinkled, 1.5–4.5 × 0.8–3 cm, often grey-woolly beneath, with a heart-shaped or nearly heart-shaped base that often clasps the stem, so the smallest apple mint leaves overlap pennyroyal's in size. Pennyroyal's calyx is purple and its corolla mauve, 4–6 mm long; apple mint's calyx is more or less green and its corolla pale pink or whitish, 3–3.5 mm long. Both grow in pasture. Apple mint's leaves are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Apple mint

summary.text:
Mentha pulegium, commonly (European) pennyroyal, or pennyrile, also called mosquito plant and pudding grass, is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae, native to Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. Pennyroyal is a traditional folk remedy, emmenagogue, abortifacient, and culinary herb, but is toxic to the liver and has caused some deaths.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North, South and Stewart Islands. Naturalised from Europe, North Africa and Macaronesia, first recorded in 1883. Flowering November to May. Pennyroyal is so abundant in some pastures that they appear completely purple from a distance when it is flowering. It is disliked by some farmers because the strong aroma can taint milk.
Livestock avoid it, so it can take over damp pasture, and some people grow it in lawns for the smell when mowing.

warnings: Do not eat pennyroyal or make tea from it. It contains pulegone, which damages the liver. As little as 10 ml of the oil has caused moderate to severe liver damage, larger amounts have killed, and a baby given home-brewed mint tea from plants containing pennyroyal oil died of liver failure. It has a history as a flavouring and a tea, but safe amounts are not known.
It can cause miscarriage. Never use it in pregnancy.
Its crushed leaves smell strongly of mint. In damp lawns and pasture it grows among self-heal, so check every plant before picking (see the lookalikes).

edibleParts.text:
Leaves, raw or cooked, with a strong peppermint flavour, used as a flavouring in salads and cooked foods. Fresh or dried leaves make a herb tea, alone or with other herbs, and peppermint flavours ice cream, sweets and preserves. The leaves go well with new potatoes and strawberries and can be used sparingly in green and fruit salads.
The lemon-scented form, bergamot mint, has a very pungent flavour that is too aromatic for most tastes.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Streams, rivers, drains and lakes, particularly in still or slow-flowing water. Plants of peppermint are often submerged or partly so and may form dense stands. Bergamot mint grows around rivers, streams, drains and lakes, particularly in still or slow-moving water, and is often submerged or partly so.
Wetland status (NZPCN, from the national wetland plant list, Clarkson et al. 2021), for both varieties: facultative wetland — usually a wetland plant, occasionally found on dry ground.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous perennial; stems glabrous or sparsely hairy, to 60 cm or more tall, often submerged; aerial stems erect, often purple. Leaves very variable, petiolate; lamina 1–6 × 1–3.5 cm, lanceolate-elliptic, elliptic, oblong-ovate, ovate, or suborbicular, aerial leaves somewhat rugose, serrate, hairy or glabrous; base cuneate to rounded; apex sharply acute. Inflorescence of a terminal, more or less rounded head and 1–3 distinct verticels of shortly pedicellate flowers below, or an oblong spike, sometimes with 1–4 distinct verticels below, often glabrous except for calyx teeth. Calyx 3–4 mm long, tubular, purple, dotted with oil glands; teeth equal, ciliate, narrow-acuminate, much shorter than tube at anthesis. Corolla 5–6 mm long, mauve or lilac, glabrous; tube exserted. Stamens small, included. Nutlets not formed. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Leaves usually distinctly petiolate, sometimes subsessile on shoots in water, peppermint- or lemon-scented.
Var. piperita (peppermint): Leaves on flowering shoots elliptic-lanceolate or narrow-elliptic, sometimes elliptic, smelling of peppermint when bruised; inflorescence oblong or broad-oblong, nearly always longer than wide, rarely interrupted.
Var. citrata (bergamot mint): Leaves on flowering shoots broad-ovate or sometimes broadly oblong-ovate, lemon-scented when bruised; inflorescence subglobose or at least head-like, sometimes interrupted with lowest verticels discrete. Bergamot mint is more like M. aquatica than var. piperita, but lacks the hairy pedicels and calyx of this parent, as well as the exserted stamens.

lookalikes.howToTell: No single character separates every plant, so use several together. Peppermint's leaves usually have a distinct stalk, though shoots growing in water can have nearly stalkless leaves; spearmint's are stalkless or very shortly stalked. Crush a leaf: peppermint smells of peppermint, or of lemon in the bergamot-mint form; spearmint is not peppermint- or lemon-scented and often smells of spearmint. Peppermint's calyx is 3–4 mm long and its mauve or lilac corolla 5–6 mm long; spearmint's calyx is 1.5–2.2(–3.5) mm long and its mauve or pinkish corolla 3–5 mm long, so the largest spearmint flowers overlap. Peppermint's flowers are in a rounded head or an oblong spike, often with a few separate whorls below; spearmint's are in narrow spikes, the central one 4–12 cm long. Both have a purple calyx, both often have purplish or red-tinged stems, and their leaf sizes overlap (peppermint 1–6 × 1–3.5 cm, spearmint 2.5–9 × 0.7–2 cm), so these do not separate them. Peppermint is a hybrid of spearmint and water mint, and both hybridise freely with other mints, so in-between plants occur. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Wild spearmint

lookalikes.howToTell: No single character separates every plant, so use several together. Apple mint's calyx is more or less green and 1.5–2.5 mm long, and its corolla pale pink or whitish, 3–3.5 mm long; peppermint's calyx is purple and 3–4 mm long, and its corolla mauve or lilac, 5–6 mm long. Apple mint is densely hairy, its leaves often grey-woolly at least beneath; peppermint's stems are hairless or sparsely hairy and its leaves hairy or hairless. Apple mint's leaves are stalkless or nearly so, with a heart-shaped or nearly heart-shaped base that often clasps the stem; peppermint's usually have a distinct stalk (nearly stalkless on some shoots in water) and a tapered to rounded base. Crush a leaf: peppermint smells of peppermint, or of lemon in the bergamot-mint form; apple mint is not peppermint- or lemon-scented and has a fruity, minty flavour. Their leaf sizes overlap (apple mint 1.5–4.5 × 0.8–3 cm, peppermint 1–6 × 1–3.5 cm), so size does not separate them. Both are edible.

preparation.text: For drying, pick the leaves and flowering tops as soon as the flowers begin to open. For tea, steep fresh or dried leaves in hot water. Cook plants picked from water that drains grazed land (see the warnings).

recipes.method: 250 ml peppermint leaves; 125 ml lemon balm leaves; 750 ml water; honey or sugar to taste (optional). Pull the leaves from the stems and rinse them well. Tear them roughly by hand into a jar or jug; a French press works well. Bring the water to the boil, take it off the heat and pour it over the leaves. Steep for 10 minutes, or longer for a stronger flavour. Strain, sweeten if you like, and drink hot or chilled. The amounts are approximate, and the ratio of peppermint to lemon balm is up to you.
recipes.title: Peppermint and lemon balm tea

recipes.method: 32 g fresh peppermint leaves; 300 g whole milk; 300 g cream (heavy cream); 35 g light corn syrup; 100 g sugar; ¼ teaspoon xanthan gum; ½ teaspoon fine sea salt; 2 tablespoons dried milk powder; 90 g dark chocolate (60–70 percent cocoa solids); 2 teaspoons vegetable oil. Wash and dry the leaves. Bring the milk and cream to a simmer in a small saucepan, turn off the heat, stir in the leaves, cover and steep at room temperature for 2 hours. Strain, squeezing the leaves into the dairy, and return it to the pan with the corn syrup. Whisk the sugar, xanthan gum, salt and milk powder together, add them, and cook over medium-low heat, whisking, until just steaming and the sugar has dissolved. Cover, cool to room temperature, then refrigerate for 8–24 hours; the mint flavour strengthens as the base sits overnight. Churn in an ice cream machine. Melt the chocolate with the oil and drizzle it in during the last minute of churning, aiming for small chips. Freeze for at least 4 hours.

summary.text:
Peppermint (Mentha × piperita) is a hybrid species of mint, a cross between watermint and spearmint. Indigenous to Europe and the Middle East, the plant is now widely spread and cultivated in many regions of the world.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): there are two distinct forms of this hybrid growing wild. Var. piperita, peppermint: North, South and Stewart Islands: common in nearly all localities; native to Europe, first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1864. Var. citrata, bergamot mint, also known as eau de Cologne mint: North and South Islands: scattered localities throughout, commonest north of the Volcanic Plateau; native to Europe, first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1846. Flowering January to May. Nutlets are not formed. M. aquatica has been recorded for New Zealand, but no specimens have been seen; records were probably based on plants of bergamot mint.

warnings: Peppermint's essential oil is toxic in large doses. In large quantities, especially as the extracted oil, peppermint can cause abortion. The amounts used in food are likely safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding, but medicinal amounts have not been shown to be safe then, so avoid them.

Peppermint can bring on or worsen heartburn and acid reflux. People with reflux should avoid peppermint preparations, and people with gallstones or other bile-duct problems should take care with them.

Peppermint leaf preparations are not recommended for children under 4, for lack of data. Never put peppermint oil on the face of a baby or young child: breathing in the menthol can cause serious side effects.
Rarely, peppermint causes allergic reactions; anyone sensitive to peppermint or menthol should not use it. The long-term safety of drinking large amounts of peppermint tea is not known.

Liver fluke risk: mints growing in water are among the plants recorded as sources of human liver fluke (Fasciola) infection, caught by eating them raw; this is recorded for mints in general, not for this species. Peppermint often grows in streams and drains, so do not eat it raw from water draining land where sheep or cattle graze. Cooking kills the cysts.
Peppermint hybridises freely with other mints, so wild plants may not match the description exactly.
Never eat plants from sites with polluted water.

identification.text:
Subshrub to about 75 cm tall, smelling strongly of peppermint. Stems, leaves and inflorescence with more or less velvety white tomentum, and glandular scales beneath hairs. Petiole to about 30 cm long. Stipules ovate-acuminate, brown and membranous. Lamina to 12 × 15 cm, broadly obovate, rather shallowly 3-lobed with each lobe usually lobulate, serrate-dentate and extending 1/4–1/2 way to midrib; base usually shallowly cordate, sometimes deeply so. Inflorescence of several umbels, each with 5–8 flowers; hairs dense, mostly long and simple but some short and glandular; peduncles often equal to petioles; pedicels 2–3.5 cm long, generally radiating widely in umbels of 6–8 flowers. Sepals 5.5–6.5 mm long, more or less triangular-ovate, green, with copious long white hairs; calyx spur about 2 mm long. Corolla white or pinkish; upper 2 petals 7–8.5 mm long, more or less oblong, usually with asymmetric base, crimson-purple-marked in lower 1/2; lower 3 petals 8–10.5 mm long, linear or ligulate. Style crimson or purplish, about 4 mm long; stigmas crimson or purplish. Mericarps not seen.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is easily recognised by its rather large, velvety hairy leaves, strongly smelling of peppermint.

lookalikes.howToTell: Rose geranium (P. ×asperum) is a strongly aromatic, densely hairy subshrub to about 75 cm, with more or less triangular leaves up to about 7 × 10 cm that are deeply divided into 3 toothed lobes, lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib and rough above; its pink flowers, the upper 2 petals with more or less prominent purple markings and a white central patch, sit about 10 to an umbel on stalks 1–6 mm long, with a calyx spur about 3 mm long. Peppermint geranium is a subshrub to about 75 cm that smells strongly of peppermint, with more or less velvety white hairs and broad leaves up to 12 × 15 cm, rather shallowly three-lobed, the lobes reaching a quarter to half way to the midrib; its flowers are white or pinkish, 5–8 to an umbel, on stalks 2–3.5 cm long that generally radiate widely, with a calyx spur about 2 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates rose geranium by its leaves (lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib; a quarter to half way in peppermint geranium), and the two descriptions also differ in the flower stalks (1–6 mm against 2–3.5 cm). Peppermint geranium's flowers are white or pinkish, rose geranium's pink, so a pink flower does not separate them. A crushed leaf of peppermint geranium smells strongly of peppermint; Flora of New Zealand calls rose geranium only "strongly aromatic". The leaf test works without flowers.
lookalikes.name: Rose geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Rose-scented geranium is a sprawling plant whose leaves are strongly undulate and velvety, generally lobed more than half way to the midrib, with more or less oblong lobes; its pink flowers, the larger upper pair of petals marked purple, sit in dense heads on almost no stalks, with a calyx spur 4–5 mm long. Peppermint geranium is a subshrub to about 75 cm that smells strongly of peppermint, with more or less velvety white hairs and broad leaves up to 12 × 15 cm, rather shallowly three-lobed, the lobes reaching a quarter to half way to the midrib; its flowers are white or pinkish, 5–8 to an umbel, on stalks 2–3.5 cm long that generally radiate widely, with a calyx spur about 2 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them by the umbels (dense, with almost stalkless flowers, in rose-scented geranium; diffuse, with long flower stalks, in peppermint geranium) and the calyx spur (4–5 mm against about 2 mm). Leaf lobing meets at about half way, so it does not settle a plant on its own. Both plants are hairy, and flower colour does not separate them (Wikipedia gives rose-scented geranium white through pink to purple flowers). A crushed leaf of peppermint geranium smells strongly of peppermint; rose-scented geranium's scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. Most of these tests need flowers.

preparation.text: A peppermint-flavoured tea is infused from the fresh leaves. Line the tin with the leaves before baking a chocolate cake. The leaves also flavour puddings, jellies and hot or cold drinks.

recipes.method: Written for rose geranium leaves; the author suggests mint-scented geranium as a substitute. 250 ml water, 200 g sugar and about five sprigs of peppermint geranium 10–13 cm long. Put the water, sugar and sprigs in a small saucepan, bruising the leaves against the side of the pan with a spoon. Bring to the boil over moderate heat, cover, take off the heat and leave to stand for at least 30 minutes. Lift out the leaves and squeeze them into the syrup. Keeps in the fridge for up to a month, or frozen for up to a year. The source uses it in a chocolate dessert.
recipes.title: Peppermint geranium syrup

recipes.method: Written for scented geranium leaves, "preferably with a lemon scent"; no species named. 2–3 scented geranium leaves; about 250 g sifted icing sugar; a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese; 2 teaspoons softened butter; 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind; lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel, to decorate (optional). Tear 2–3 scented geranium leaves into small pieces and mix them with about 250 g sifted icing sugar in a small bowl. Leave somewhere warm overnight so the sugar takes up the scent, then pick out and discard the leaf pieces. Beat a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese, 2 teaspoons softened butter and 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind, gradually adding the scented icing sugar, until smooth. Spread over a cooled carrot cake and decorate, if you like, with lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel.
recipes.title: Scented geranium and lemon icing

summary.text:
Pelargonium tomentosum, the peppermint-scented geranium, is a pelargonium species native to South Africa.
In New Zealand, Flora of New Zealand (1988) recorded it wild at Eastbourne and Paekākāriki, near Wellington; it was first recorded growing wild here in 1944. Peppermint geranium is fairly commonly cultivated and can be expected to occur wild at other suitable coastal localities.

edibleParts.text: This mushroom contains toxins and is usually considered inedible. It has been used as a condiment in many countries, with the Italian chef Antonio Carluccio recommending it be used only to add its peppery flavour to other mushrooms.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Chalciporus piperatus' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
Fruit bodies of Chalciporus piperatus occur singly, scattered, or in groups on the ground. The fungus occurs naturally in or near coniferous or beech and oak woodlands, often on sandy soils. Fruit bodies appear in Europe in late summer and autumn from August to November. The fungus is widespread across North America, fruiting from July to October in the eastern states and from September to January on the Pacific Coast. It is found in Mexico and Central America. In Asia, it has been collected from Pakistan, West Bengal (India), and Guangdong Province (China). In South Africa, it is known from the southwestern Cape Province and the eastern Transvaal Province.
Chalciporus piperatus grows in conifer plantations associated with the fly agaric (Amanita muscaria) and the chanterelle (Cantharellus cibarius). It has been recorded under introduced loblolly pine (Pinus taeda) plantations in Santa Catarina and Paraná states in southern Brazil, and under introduced trees in the Los Lagos Region of Chile. It has also spread into native forest in northeastern Tasmania and Victoria, having been found growing with the native myrtle beech (Nothofagus cunninghamii). The rare variety hypochryseus occurs only in Europe, including Austria, Czechia, Greece, Italy, and Spain. Also rare, variety amarellus is widespread in European coniferous forests, where it usually found near pines, spruce, and sometimes fir.
Fruit bodies can be parasitised by the mould Sepedonium chalcipori, a highly specialised mycoparasite that is only known to infect this bolete. Infections result in necrotic mushroom tissue and the production of copious yellow conidia.
Initially thought to be ectomycorrhizal (symbiotic with plants, like most Boletaceae), C. piperatus has not been confirmed as such in multiple synthesis studies or in isotope fractionation studies. There is some speculation that C. piperatus is a mycoparasite on the mycorrhiza of A. muscaria. In New Zealand, A. muscaria is thought to have been introduced with Pinus radiata, and has made a host jump to the native Nothofagus trees; C. piperatus has since been observed fruiting near Nothofagus trees with A. muscaria associations.  Buchwaldoboletus lignicola is in the same clade as C. piperatus and is thought to be a parasite as well, strengthening the evidence that C. piperatus and its relatives may be mycoparasites.

identification.text:
One of the smaller boletes, Chalciporus piperatus  has an orange-fawn 1.6–9 cm cap that is initially convex before flattening out in age. The cap surface can be furrowed; shiny when dry, it can be a little sticky when wet, and may crack with age. The colour of the pore surface ranges from yellowish to dark reddish brown in maturity. When bruised, the pore surface stains brown. Individual pores are angular, measuring about 0.5–2 mm wide, while the tubes are 3–10 mm deep. Slender for a bolete, the stipe measures 4–9.5 cm long by 0.6–1.2 cm thick, and is either roughly the same width throughout its length, or slightly thicker near the base. The colour of the stem is similar to the cap, or lighter, and there is yellow mycelium at the base. The flesh is yellow, sometimes with reddish tones, maturing to purplish brown. It has no odour. The spore print is brown to cinnamon. Variety hypochryseus is essentially identical to the main form except for its bright yellow tubes and pores. Variety amarellus has pinker pores and a taste that is bitter rather than peppery.

The spores are smooth, narrowly fusiform (fuse-shaped), and measure 7–12 by 3–5 μm. The basidia (spore-bearing cells) measure 20–28 by 6–8 μm and are hyaline (translucent), four-spored, and narrowly club-shaped, with many internal oil droplets. The cystidia are fusiform, sometimes with a rounded tip, and have dimensions of 30–50 by 9–12 μm. Some are more or less hyaline, while others are encrusted with a golden pigment. The cap cuticle is a trichodermium, an arrangement in which the outermost hyphae emerge roughly parallel, like hairs, perpendicular to the cap surface. These hyphae are 10–17 μm wide and have elliptical to cylindrical cells at their ends that are not gelatinous. Clamp connections are absent from the hyphae.


Similar species
The fruit body of the North American species Chalciporus piperatoides are similar, but can be distinguished by its flesh and pores staining blue after cutting or bruising. It has a less peppery taste. Another mild-tasting relative, C. rubinellus, has brighter colours than C. piperatus, including completely red tubes. One European species, C. rubinus, has a shape similar to C. piperatus, but has red pores and a stem covered in red dots.

lookalikes.howToTell: Do not decide on the tree. The endemic grows under native beech, but this introduced peppery bolete, usually found with fly agaric under pines and introduced broadleaved trees, also turns up in beech forest where fly agaric has become naturalised. Cap colour helps but the ranges meet at orange. The endemic's cap is golden yellow, apricot or occasionally reddish orange, dry and finely felted. This one's is fawn to light brown, brownish orange or cinnamon brown, and slightly slimy when wet. Look at the stem. This one's stem is golden yellow at the base, with yellow flesh. The endemic's matches the cap or is reddish, pale yellow at the very top, with pale reddish-brown flesh. A crumb of this one, chewed and spat out, is acrid and peppery; the endemic's taste is not distinctive.

identification.text:
The plant grows up to 1.5 metres in height, with leaves 10–35 cm long and 4–14 cm wide. It produces conspicuous yellow flowerheads about 3–5 cm wide, which are visited by various types of insects—especially hoverflies of the genus Eristalis.
It is perennial, spreading from deep-seated rhizomes, and plants often show the previous year's leaves, stems or stem bases.

lookalikes.howToTell: Perennial sow thistle lives for years and spreads by creeping roots; common pūhā (Sonchus oleraceus) is an annual with a taproot. Perennial sow thistle's flower heads are 3–5 cm wide; common pūhā's are 1.5–2.5 cm. Under the flower head, perennial sow thistle's involucre is 15–18 mm long and its bracts carry tangled short white hairs and long yellow glandular bristles (an Australian description allows hairless bracts too); common pūhā's involucre is 10–15 mm long and its bracts are usually hairless, rarely with a few pale bristles. Perennial sow thistle's upper leaves clasp the stem with rounded lobes; common pūhā's clasping lobes are pointed. In seed, perennial sow thistle's achenes are 3.5–3.8 mm long with 5 ribs on each face; common pūhā's are 2.5–3 mm with 3 ribs. Neither is winged. Common pūhā is edible: its leaves are widely eaten as greens.
lookalikes.name: Pūhā / Sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: Perennial sow thistle lives for years and spreads by creeping roots; prickly sow thistle (Sonchus asper) is an annual or biennial with a taproot. Perennial sow thistle's flower heads are 3–5 cm wide; prickly sow thistle's are 1.5–2.5 cm. Perennial sow thistle's involucre is 15–18 mm long and its bracts carry tangled short white hairs and long yellow glandular bristles (an Australian description allows hairless bracts too); prickly sow thistle's is 10–15 mm, its bracts hairless or rarely with tangled white hairs and sparse long pale glandular hairs. Prickly sow thistle's leaf teeth are prickly-spined; perennial sow thistle's margins are coarsely toothed and are not described as prickly. Both clasp the stem with rounded lobes, so the leaf base does not separate them. In seed, perennial sow thistle's achenes have 5 ribs on each face, are not winged and are closely wrinkled; prickly sow thistle's have 3 ribs, are winged, and are smooth between the ribs. Prickly sow thistle is edible: it is recorded as a popular Māori food (pūhā tiotio).
lookalikes.name: Prickly sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: Perennial sow thistle spreads by creeping roots; New Zealand sow thistle (Sonchus kirkii) grows from a taproot swollen at the top. New Zealand sow thistle's leaves are thick, dull and blue-grey; perennial sow thistle's are firm, dark green and paler beneath. Perennial sow thistle's involucre is 15–18 mm long and its bracts carry tangled short white hairs and long yellow glandular bristles (an Australian description allows hairless bracts too); New Zealand sow thistle's is 10–15 mm, its bracts hairless, sometimes with a row of broad-based hairs on the outer ones or densely white-woolly at the base. Both clasp the stem with rounded lobes, so the leaf base does not separate them. In seed, perennial sow thistle's achenes have 5 ribs on each face, are not winged and are closely wrinkled; New Zealand sow thistle's have 3 ribs, are winged, and are smooth between the ribs. New Zealand sow thistle is edible: its leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they are tougher and more bitter than common pūhā's.

recipes.method: Written for the sow thistles of British Columbia's Sea to Sky region, where perennial and annual sow thistle both grow; the card does not say which. Serves 4. A large bunch of sow thistle leaves; a quarter of a red onion, minced; olive oil; a clove of garlic, minced; about 60 ml chicken or vegetable stock; salt and pepper; a couple of tablespoons of crumbled goat cheese; some pine nuts. Rinse and chop a large bunch of leaves, boil for a few minutes and drain. Sauté a quarter of a red onion, minced, in olive oil in a large frying pan for 3 minutes, add a minced clove of garlic and cook a minute more. Turn the heat to medium and add the leaves a handful at a time, stirring, as they shrink. Add about 60 ml chicken or vegetable stock, cover and simmer for 10 minutes. Season with salt and pepper, then stir in a couple of tablespoons of crumbled goat cheese, or to taste, and some pine nuts.
recipes.title: Sow thistle with red onion, goat cheese and pine nuts

summary.text:
Sonchus arvensis, the field milk thistle, field sowthistle, perennial sow-thistle, corn sow thistle, dindle, gutweed, swine thistle, or tree sow thistle, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae.
Sonchus arvensis is native to Eurasia, where it is widespread across most of the continent. It has also become naturalized in many other regions, and is considered an invasive noxious weed in some places, such as North America (including Prince Edward Island), Russia and Australia.
A study conducted in 2003 has shown that with future global atmospheric carbon levels, S. arvensis shows increased growth with increased atmospheric carbon which could potentially expand its range and outcompete native species.
In New Zealand: North Island: Hawke's Bay (near Taradale); South Island: Canterbury (vicinity of Christchurch, Springston), Otago (Waipiata, Catlins River mouth). Naturalised here since 1855. Herbarium specimens have since come from North Auckland, Wellington, Marlborough, Canterbury and Westland.
The name arvensis means growing in arable fields.

warnings: The plant can contain toxic nitrates. It is one of the weeds that naturally build up nitrate, and plants hold more of it on heavily fertilised ground, after drought, or in low light.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Waste land. A 2013 Te Papa collection came from a green-waste discard area in dunes at Koitiata, near Turakina. It is also grown in gardens, where it self-seeds freely.
It is a ruderal plant of roadsides and waste ground. It generally grows in places where there is full sunlight and requires moderately damp soils with a slightly alkaline reaction and moderately fertile conditions. It is tolerant of occasional salinity, which allows it to grow on the upper part of beaches and along salt-treated road verges.

identification.text:
Perennial wall-rocket is a glabrous herb with an erect or sprawling habit, that grows up to 1.3 m tall, with a solid, almost woody terete stem and spreading branches.
The deeply pinnate leaves are up to 12 cm long and often rather fleshy, with a peppery taste and a musty smell.

The inflorescence is a branched raceme up to 30 cm long with up to 30 flowers, each of which has 4 free bright yellow petals up to 15 mm long, and 4 free yellow/brown sepals up to 7.5 mm long. Each flower has 6 stamens and a single style.

The fruit is a straight, flat silique (pod) up to five centimeters long. The pedicels are shorter than the fruits and ascend at an acute angle to the stem. Above the receptacle is a short (2 mm) stalk (or stipe) below the pod (a useful feature for separating this species from annual wall-rocket). The seeds are arranged in 2 rows, or staggered in a zigzag pattern, towards the centre of the pod, which in turn consists of 2 valves, so a cross-section of the fruit shows 4 seeds in total. This is a distinguishing feature of the genus Diplotaxis, although it is not always easy to see, as plants are not self-pollinating, so ripe seeds do not always develop.
In Britain it is most likely to be confused with annual wall-rocket, but it does not have a basal rosette, the leaves are divided more than halfway to the midrib, and the fruit has a short stalk (stipe) above the sepal scars.
The Diplotaxis species can be separated from most other crucifers by the double row of seeds in each valve of the fruit (although this is a difficult feature to see in unfertilised plants) and a seedless beak to the silique.

Perennial, not foetid; stems erect, stout, branching, leafy, glabrous, 30–100 cm tall. Leaves mostly cauline, variable, petiolate, glabrous, linear-lanceolate to lanceolate and toothed, to broadly triangular in outline and deeply pinnatifid, 4–20 × 1–4–(10) cm; upper leaves becoming smaller. Racemes glabrous, (10)–30–60 cm tall. Pedicels 1.5–4 cm long. Sepals triangular, glabrous or rarely sparsely hairy, 4.5–6 × 2–3.5 mm. Petals yellow, spathulate, shortly clawed, 7–12 × 3–5 mm. Silique 20–30–(45) × 1.5–2 mm, on short gynophore (0.5)–1–2 mm long; beak seedless. Seeds oblong, brown, 1–1.5 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

In plain terms: the leaves are thin and serrated to deeply lobed, the flowers buttercup-yellow. Garden plants may not behave as perennials: in New Zealand they can last only one season, or two to three years under favourable conditions, so a short-lived plant is not ruled out. The cultivar 'Dragon's Fire' has deeply lobed leaves streaked with red veins.

lookalikes.howToTell: Annual wall-rocket's pod has no stalk between the sepal scars and the pod; perennial wall-rocket's pod sits on a short stalk (gynophore) (0.5–)1–2 mm long. Annual wall-rocket's petals are 3–7 mm long against 7–12 mm, so flowers with petals about 7 mm long are not separated by size. Annual wall-rocket is foetid and its leaves are mostly basal, forming a rosette; perennial wall-rocket is not foetid and its leaves are mostly on the stem. Leaf division does not reliably separate them in New Zealand: annual wall-rocket's leaves run from sinuate-margined to pinnatifid, and perennial wall-rocket's from toothed to deeply pinnatifid. Height (annual (10–)30–40(–60) cm, perennial 30–100 cm) and pedicel length (annual 0.5–2 cm, perennial 1.5–4 cm) overlap. Both have yellow petals, a seedless beak and seeds in two rows in each half of the pod. Annual wall-rocket's leaves are eaten raw in salads and in cooked dishes.

preparation.text: The leaves have a hot, peppery, cress-like flavour, like salad rocket but stronger: they make a good addition to a mixed salad but are too strong to eat in quantity on their own. They can be used in all the same ways as salad rocket — in salads, on pizza, in pesto, or as a cooked leaf added to stir-fries and stews or lightly cooked. The heat is mustardy, with a sesame note. In Auckland the plant stays in leaf almost all year, but the most succulent, best-flavoured leaves come in spring and early summer. For a simple salad, toss the leaves with a little lemon juice and olive oil, season, and finish with shavings of parmesan. Scatter them over a pizza straight from the oven, or fold them into pasta at the last minute. As a pesto it can take the place of basil, and goes well with oily fish. A light wilting keeps the bite; longer cooking softens the pepperiness into something rounder, as in the Puglian orecchiette below.

recipes.method: Ingredients: 400 g orecchiette; 300 g wild rocket; 10 small red tomatoes; 2 cloves garlic; 10 black olives; extra virgin olive oil, chilli and salt. Clean and wash the rocket thoroughly, keeping only the leaves and the most tender shoots. Boil it in plenty of salted water for five minutes, then drain well, keeping the water. In a large pan, soften the halved tomatoes, the chilli and the minced garlic in olive oil. Cook the orecchiette in the rocket water, drain, and toss with the rocket, the tomato base and the olives. Wild rocket is much stronger than the bagged cultivated leaf; with a milder leaf, the source says to use more.

summary.text:
Diplotaxis tenuifolia is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by the common name perennial wall-rocket.
It is native to parts of Europe, reaching in the east to Turkey and Syria. It is extinct from Morocco and Algeria, but has been introduced in a number of regions: Cyprus, the Caucasus, the Levant, Yemen, Japan, Australia, New Zealand, New Caledonia, Canada (Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia), the United States, Costa Rica, Argentina and Uruguay.

Within Europe, its native range covers much of France, the Low Countries, Italy, the Pannonian Basin and the western Balkans up to Macedonia, with generally more thinly scattered populations in northern Greece, Bulgaria, Romania, Crimea, Sicily, Malta, Sardinia, Corsica and parts of Spain. It has extensively been introduced further north from its native range. In the British Isles the plant is an archaeophyte, with industrial regions and ports still at the centre of the distribution. It is established especially in parts of England and Wales (some believing the plant could even be native to the south-east). Its range has been expanding to the west since the 19th century, but it is still very rare in Scotland and Ireland. It has also been introduced into much of Central Europe: throughout Switzerland, Austria, Germany and Poland, with more scattered instances on the southern shores of Norway and Sweden (where it is found in fewer areas than in the recent past), the Baltic States, Belarus and a few locations further east in Ukraine and European Russia. It has also been introduced on Menorca and near Lisbon in Portugal.
In recent years it has increasingly been cultivated to produce salad leaves, which are marketed as wild rocket in Britain or arugula in the U.S. It is easily confused with garden rocket, which has similar uses.
This species is also sometimes called wild rocket, sand rocket, Lincoln weed (mainly in Australia) and white rocket; the seeds are sometimes marketed as "wild Italian arugula" or "sylvetta arugula".
In New Zealand it was first recorded naturalised in 1924; the Flora of New Zealand (1988) knew it, as sand rocket, from one Wellington City collection and as occasional in Canterbury and Otago (Flora of New Zealand, restated).
The New Zealand Plant Conservation Network also calls it sand rocket, gives its origin as southern and central Europe, north-west Africa and Asia Minor, and explains the name tenuifolia as thin, slender leaves (restated). Te Papa holds New Zealand specimens from Karaka Bay (30/09/1922) and Breaker Bay (28/10/1934) in Wellington, and from dunes at Koitiata near Turakina (Leon Perrie and Colin Ogle, 30/03/2013). The seed is sold in New Zealand as wild rocket, including a red-veined cultivar, 'Dragon's Fire'.

warnings: The leaves can accumulate high levels of nitrate, depending on growing conditions: cultivated perennial wall-rocket has stored up to 9000 mg per kg fresh weight or more, often above the maximum limits set by European law. No figures for wild New Zealand plants were found.

In Australia, where it is a weed called Lincoln weed, it has been reported to be poisonous to livestock, and on occasion suspected of causing the death of both livestock and people. No case, dose or toxin is described, and the same plant is grown and eaten widely as a salad leaf, but the report has not been ruled out: eat it in salad amounts, not as a bulk vegetable.

identification.text: A soft, upright weed 5–40 cm tall with smooth oval leaves and odd, cup-like green flowers with no petals at the top of the stem. The test is the sap: snap any stem and it bleeds white milky latex immediately. No milky sap is recorded for chickweed.

lookalikes.howToTell: Chickweed's stem is round and weak, with a single line of hairs down one side (very occasionally two), and its leaves are in opposite pairs; its flowers have white petals split almost to the base. Petty spurge has a hairless stem, alternate leaves, small green flower heads with no petals, and white milky sap; no milky sap is recorded for chickweed. Missing petals alone does not prove spurge, because chickweeds rarely lack them too — check the leaves, the hairs and the sap together. Snap a stem from every clump before picking.

summary.text: The small garden weed that grows through chickweed and bleeds a milky sap that burns skin and eyes. Snap a stem before you pick a mat.

warnings: The latex is a severe irritant: it blisters skin and can damage the cornea. Wash hands before touching your face.
Eating it can cause severe vomiting and diarrhoea, and the milky sap of spurges can burn the lining of the mouth.
If sap gets in an eye, rinse it with water for 15 minutes and get urgent medical attention.

habitat.text:
Damp shaded native forest floor and gullies, often under tree ferns.
It grows under kauri, podocarp, broadleaved and beech forest and under tall mānuka and kānuka, in the wetter and more shaded places: on the forest floor, in gullies, among rocks or tree roots, on banks, streamsides and river terraces, on both acidic and base-rich soils. It is a common species of the forest ground layer, especially in high-rainfall areas, from the coast to the subalpine zone.

harvestEthics.text: Take no more than one or two fronds per plant and move on. Pikopiko is culturally significant and slow-growing; commercial demand has already stripped accessible stands. Seek permission from mana whenua and the landowner. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In Otago (Regionally Naturally Uncommon), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text:
Finely divided lacy fronds, usually with tiny bulbils (plantlets) growing on the upper surface of mature fronds — the 'chickens' that give it its name. Harvest only the tightly curled, still-unfurling koru at the tip.
Rhizomes short, stout, erect or occasionally short-creeping, bearing scales. Stipes brown on the underside, green on the upper side, bearing ovate scales with short apical projections. Laminae 2-pinnate to deeply 2-pinnate-pinnatifid, light to mid-green on both surfaces, bearing scattered scales, lacking hairs, usually bearing bulbils on the upper surface.
Asplenium bulbiferum is usually readily recognised by the presence of bulbils on the upper surface of the lamina. However, similar bulbils also occur in A. gracillimum, albeit less frequently.
[From: Flora of New Zealand Online, eFlora ferns.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Bracken has long-creeping underground rhizomes and forms extensive stands, mostly in the open — rough pasture, road cuttings and banks, forest margins and clearings — though it also grows under forest and in scrub. Its fronds carry hairs and no scales, and its stalks become woody and chestnut brown at the base. Pikopiko grows from a short upright rhizome in wetter, shaded forest-floor places; its stalks and fronds carry scales, its fronds lack hairs, and they usually bear bulbils. Do not eat bracken shoots: bracken fern (studied as the northern-hemisphere Pteridium aquilinum) is possibly carcinogenic to humans, with sufficient evidence of cancer in animals, and its constituent ptaquiloside caused tumours in rats. Bracken rhizome was a major traditional Māori food and the young shoots were occasionally eaten, but the young fronds have been found to be highly carcinogenic.

summary.text:
The curled young fronds are a native delicacy — and one of the easiest species to over-harvest.
Pikopiko is a Māori word for the young curled shoots of ferns, and it may refer to a range of fern species; mouku (Asplenium bulbiferum, hen and chicken fern) is the most widely eaten. Hen and chicken fern is endemic to New Zealand, on the North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands, and is Not Threatened (2023).

warnings: Harvesting plant material on public conservation land is prohibited without a DOC permit. Most accessible native forest in NZ is DOC land.
Taking every frond kills the plant. It cannot photosynthesise without them.
Pikopiko is a name for the young shoots of several ferns, and only about seven of New Zealand's roughly 200 ferns are edible. Pick only fronds you are sure are hen and chicken fern.

The leaves and tender stems are edible too, with a slightly fruity chamomile flavour and a little bitterness; the leaves may turn bitter by the time the plant flowers, and older stems are tough and chewy.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Waste places especially roadsides, grassland, cultivated land, gardens, and disturbed areas such as vehicle tracks in farmland and montane areas.
The plant thrives in disturbed areas, especially those with poor, compacted soil.
Waysides and waste places, especially along tracks, paths and by trampled gateways.
In Southland: sun-baked, compacted soil, gravel tracks, garden edges and farm gateways.

identification.text:
Aromatic herb. Stems erect or ascending, 5–20–(40) cm tall, striate, glabrous or with a few hairs below capitula, usually much-branched from base. Basal and lower cauline leaves appearing shortly petiolate but usually with very reduced leaflets along sheath, narrow-obovate to elliptic, usually glabrous, sometimes sparsely hairy when young, 2–3-pinnatisect, 2–8 × 0.5–2 cm; ultimate segments narrow-linear or subulate, more or less all in one plane; cauline leaves similar to basal but above becoming smaller, with fewer segments, ovate, and apetiolate. Corymb diffuse, of 1-many capitula. Involucral bracts glabrous, 3–5 mm long; margins pale, membranous. Capitula 4–10 mm diameter; ray florets 0; disc florets numerous, dull yellow to greenish yellow, 4-toothed. Achenes about 1.5 mm long, very pale brown, narrow-obovoid; inner surface with usually 4 narrow ribs, the outer 2 with glandular groove for longer than 1/2 length; outer surface smooth; corona shorter than 0.1 mm long or 0. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
This species is distinguished by the pineapple scent, rayless conic capitula, and the distinctive achenes.
Before it flowers it looks like stinking mayweed; crush it — rayless chamomile smells of pineapple, stinking mayweed very strongly and unpleasantly.

lookalikes.howToTell: Stinking mayweed nearly always has 8–21 white rays around a yellow disc, its heads 15–30 mm across (up to 35); pineappleweed has no rays and heads 4–10 mm across — but rayless forms of stinking mayweed occur rarely, so a rayless head is not proof on its own. Before flowering the two look alike, so smell is the test then. Crush it: stinking mayweed smells strongly foetid, pineappleweed of pineapple. Stinking mayweed has narrow, pointed scales between the florets on the inner part of the receptacle; pineappleweed has none. Stinking mayweed's leaf segments do not all lie in one plane, giving a feathery look; pineappleweed's lie more or less in one plane. Stinking mayweed is not eaten in this guide: its acrid juice can blister skin and it has been reported as toxic.
lookalikes.name: Stinking mayweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Roman chamomile has 13–20 white rays around a yellow disc; pineappleweed has no rays and its heads are 4–10 mm across. Roman chamomile has scales between the florets on its receptacle; pineappleweed has none. Roman chamomile creeps, and its stems are moderately to densely hairy; pineappleweed's stand upright or rise from the base and are hairless or carry a few hairs below the heads. Roman chamomile's leaf segments do not all lie in one plane, which makes its leaves look feathery; pineappleweed's lie more or less in one plane. Roman chamomile is sweetly aromatic, pineappleweed smells of pineapple. Roman chamomile's flowers are used for tea, with care for people allergic to the daisy family.
lookalikes.name: Roman chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: Pineappleweed's heads have no white rays and are 4–10 mm across; scentless chamomile's have white rays and are about 30–50 mm. Before flowering, crush a leaf: pineappleweed smells of pineapple, scentless chamomile is almost scentless. Pineappleweed's leaf segments lie more or less in one plane; scentless chamomile's do not, so its leaves look more feathery. What does not separate them: finely divided leaves, and roadsides and waste places. There is no record of scentless chamomile being eaten.
lookalikes.name: Scentless chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are low weeds of roadsides, waste places and cultivated land with finely divided leaves, and twin cress can be mistaken for pineappleweed. Crush a leaf: twin cress smells foetid, pineappleweed smells of pineapple. Twin cress stems usually lie along the ground, and it has tiny white or petal-less flowers followed by paired pods about 1.5 mm long; pineappleweed has erect or ascending stems and rayless, cone-shaped, greenish-yellow flower heads 4–10 mm across. Leaf division alone does not separate them. Twin cress leaves are eaten raw or cooked for their hot, cress-like taste; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Twin cress

preparation.text: It grows along paths and driveways, so pick from ground you know is clean. Cut it with scissors, refresh it in cold water for 15 minutes, drain, roll it in a towel and keep it in a bag in the fridge until you use it. Eat the flower heads raw as a nibble or in salads, or scatter them over roasting vegetables. For tea, pour boiling water over fresh or dried flower heads or sprigs and leave for 5–10 minutes; flowers alone give the strongest tea, and dried ones a less fruity one. The flowers also infuse well into syrups, cordials and vinegar. To dry it, wash and dry the plants the same way, then dry them in a dehydrator on its lowest heat (32–38 °C) until brittle and keep them in a jar.

recipes.method: Pineapple weed flower tops; apple cider vinegar; sugar or honey (optional). Half fill a jar with pineapple weed flower tops, top it up with apple cider vinegar, and leave for a couple of weeks. The author uses it as a base for salad dressings and as the vinegar in pickles. Sweeten it with sugar for a shrub, or with honey for an oxymel, for cocktails or for diluting with cold or hot water as a long drink.
recipes.title: Pineapple weed vinegar

recipes.method: Ingredients: 250 ml (1 cup) boiling water; 1–2 tablespoons pineapple weed flowers, or small sprigs including stems; 1 teaspoon honey, to taste (optional). Serves 1. Put the flowers in a mug and pour the boiling water over. Leave to infuse for 5–10 minutes and sweeten with honey if you like; straining is optional. With dried flowers, use ½–1 tablespoon, or just a few sprigs. Leaves and stems can go in, but flowers alone give the strongest infusion.
recipes.title: Pineapple weed tea

recipes.method: Ingredients: 85 g (3 cups) fresh pineapple weed, or 125 ml (½ cup) dried; 250 ml (1 cup) water; 500 ml (2 cups) sugar. Mix them and bring to the boil, then take off the heat and cool. Leave to infuse overnight, then strain and store in a jar in the fridge. Makes about 500 ml (2 cups), for drinks and desserts.
recipes.title: Pineapple weed syrup

recipes.method: Ingredients: 30 g butter; 75 g digestive biscuits (about 6), crushed; 50 g pineapple weed flower heads; 300 ml double cream; 75 g caster sugar; 3 tablespoons lemon juice. Serves 4. Melt the butter over a gentle heat, take it off the heat and stir in the crushed biscuits; press the crumbs into the bottom of 4 small glasses or ramekins and chill for half an hour. Crush the flower heads thoroughly in a mortar and pestle (or in a bowl with a potato masher). Put the cream, crushed flower heads and sugar in a small pan over a medium heat and bring to the boil, stirring gently to dissolve the sugar, then lower the heat and simmer for 3 minutes. Take off the heat, whisk in the lemon juice, and strain through a fine sieve into a jug. Pour over the chilled bases, leave to cool, then chill for at least 3 hours. For the purest pineapple flavour, pick the flower heads carefully and leave out the leaves.
recipes.title: Pineapple weed posset pots

recipes.method: Ingredients: 250 ml (1 cup) pineapple weed flowers, or 750 ml–1 litre (3–4 cups) leaves and flowers, fresh or dried, for each 3.8 litres (1 US gallon) of water; pineapple weed syrup, to taste; fresh lemon juice, to taste. Make a large batch of pineapple weed tea: pour the boiling water over the flowers and leave for 5–10 minutes. Season it to taste with pineapple weed syrup and fresh lemon juice, and drink it cold. Or just add fresh flowers, gently squeezed to release their aroma, to your usual lemonade.
recipes.title: Pineapple weed lemonade

recipes.method: Ingredients: a bunch of pineapple weed (the more flowers, the sweeter the ice cream); 250 ml double cream; 250 ml full-fat milk; 2 teaspoons honey; 250 ml Greek yoghurt. Chop the pineapple weed and put it in a pan with the cream, milk and honey. Bring to a simmer and simmer for 10 minutes, then leave to cool and infuse overnight. Warm it slightly so it runs, strain it through a sieve, and squeeze the stems to get out as much flavour as you can. Leave to cool and stir in the yoghurt. Churn in an ice cream maker for about 30 minutes, until frozen, or freeze it in a shallow tub and whisk it every 2 hours until smoothly frozen. Eat it within 6 months.
recipes.title: Pineapple weed ice cream

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1 litre (4 cups) pineapple weed, in two halves; 500 ml (2 cups) vodka; 375 ml (1½ cups) water; 375 ml (1½ cups) sugar. Put half the pineapple weed and the vodka in a glass jar, cover it and shake it, and keep it out of direct sun, shaking it once a day. After two or three days, when the vodka smells distinctly of pineapple, strain it into a jar with a tight lid. Meanwhile, shake the other half of the pineapple weed with the sugar in a lidded container and leave it overnight. The next day, tip the sugar and pineapple weed into a saucepan, add the water, bring to a low boil and simmer for 2–3 minutes. Take it off the heat, cover it and leave it overnight, then strain the syrup into a jar with a tight lid. When both are ready, stir them together in equal amounts and bottle the liqueur. Leftover syrup goes on ice cream.
recipes.title: Pineapple weed liqueur

summary.text:
Matricaria discoidea, commonly known as pineappleweed, wild chamomile, disc mayweed, and rayless mayweed, is an annual plant native to North America, northern Asia, and Europe where it grows as a common herb of fields, gardens, and roadsides.
It occurs across Canada and the United States, especially as a common weed in Alaska, the Yukon, and the Northwest Territories. However, there is disagreement over whether it originated in North America or in Siberia. This species has been introduced to Europe, Asia, Iceland, South America, and New Zealand and is now widespread and naturalized in Britain, where it has become one of the fastest-spreading plants of the 20th century.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: throughout; South Island: Nelson, Kaikoura, Canterbury, Otago, Southland; Stewart Island: Halfmoon Bay; Chatham Islands. (Northeast Asia, western North America; first recorded 1883.) Its New Zealand name is rayless chamomile (Flora of New Zealand, NZ Flora Online, NZPCN and Te Papa's herbarium); the alternative common name pineapple weed is often used. It is a widespread weed in the Northern Hemisphere and its native range is not known with certainty. It has sometimes been known in New Zealand as M. suaveolens or M. matricarioides.
Bayer's New Zealand weed guide says it resists cold, trampling and many herbicides.

warnings: Some people are allergic to it. Avoid it if you are allergic to chamomile, and try only a little the first time.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Swamps, lakesides, banks, forest margins, roadsides, waste places.
It grows on lowland forest margins and in shrubland, forming tangled masses where it has nothing to climb, and in coastal and lowland regenerating vegetation, often along the margins of wetlands; it very rarely reaches montane forest. It has spread into towns, where it can be very aggressive.
Look for it in the North Island, where it is very common in many areas, and on the South, Stewart, Chatham, Kermadec and Three Kings Islands; it becomes less common in the south.

harvestEthics.text: Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.

identification.text:
Rhizomes extensive. Stems glabrous or puberulent at first. Petioles 1.5–8 cm long, generally puberulent. Lamina 3–14–(17) × 2.5–9–(11) cm, usually triangular- or ovate-sagittate, glabrous or puberulent near base; sinus deep and rounded, usually with diverging sides; basal lobes usually rounded or obtuse, rarely acute, sometimes with small subsidiary lobule; apex acute to short-acuminate. Flowers solitary; peduncles 3–12 cm long, puberulent or glabrous, ridged or very narrowly winged. Bracts 1.25–3 × 1–1.5 cm, broad-ovate, not imbricate or only slightly so; base rounded or cordate; apex usually obtuse and mucronate. Sepals 12–15 mm long, lanceolate-ovate. Corolla (3)–5–6–(7) cm long; limb 4–6 cm diameter, usually pink with white mid-petaline bands, rarely all white. Stamens 2–2.5 cm long; filaments hairy in lower half. Ovary 1-locular. Style longer than stamens. Capsules about 1 cm long, subglobose. Seed more or less triangular-ovoid with rounded outer surface and more or less flat on inner faces, dark brown to almost black.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It twines anticlockwise up other plants to about 3 m from thickened white roots and far-creeping rhizomes, and every part bleeds white milky sap. The thin, dull, arrowhead-shaped leaves have a deep notch at the base. Single pink trumpet flowers with white stripes, 5–7 cm long, stand on long stalks, their base hidden by two large green bracts that barely touch.
Other bindweeds here differ: large bindweed has bracts that clearly overlap and white flowers about 6 cm or more across; New Zealand bindweed has leaves usually under 4 cm long and orange seeds; shore bindweed lies along the ground with fleshy, kidney-shaped leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Climbing dock's stems are ribbed and it scrambles over its support rather than twining round it. Its flowers are tiny (1.5–2 mm), green to pink, in large branched clusters at the top of the plant, followed by masses of papery, heart-shaped, three-winged fruit, yellow, pink or crimson. Its leaves are 3–8 cm long with pointed basal lobes and a broad, rounded notch, and it grows from brown tubers with yellow flesh. Pink bindweed's stems are smooth and twine round other plants; its flowers are single pink trumpets, usually 5–6 cm long (3–7 cm), each with two large bracts hiding its base; its leaves are 3–14 cm long (rarely 17), the basal lobes usually rounded and the notch deep; its roots are white. Both have arrowhead-shaped leaves and both smother hedges and scrub on coastal, lowland and town land, so leaf shape alone does not separate them.

summary.text:
Pōhue, or pink bindweed, is a native twining vine of the morning glory family, first collected in New Zealand by Banks and Solander in 1769. Since 2025 it is often named Convolvulus sepium subsp. roseata, after its genus was merged into Convolvulus; Flora of New Zealand and most guides call it Calystegia sepium.
It is summer-green, regrowing each year from far-creeping rhizomes, and is aggressive and weedy. It hybridises readily with the introduced large bindweed and with New Zealand bindweed, and most bindweed gathered in towns is the hybrid with large bindweed. Its other Māori names include pōhuehue, pōpōhue, panahi and rauparaha.
Māori once dug its thick, fleshy roots, which were dried and stored, then soaked and steamed, and leaves were eaten in the Tūhoe district. Since it has interbred with large bindweed, the roots are no longer recommended as food.

warnings: Do not eat it. Pink bindweed here has interbred with the introduced large bindweed, whose roots are highly purgative, and the hybrids also have pink flowers with white stripes, so a safe plant cannot be picked out by eye. Even the native form's roots are purgative, though more mildly.
Most bindweed gathered in towns is the hybrid with large bindweed.

identification.text:
Vigorous vine; young shoots angular, downy. Leaves 3-lobed; petioles 1–3 cm long, white-lanate, with (2)–4–8 glands almost hidden in indumentum; stipules pinnate with dark filiform segments almost to the base of the very narrow-linear rachis; lamina lobes 5–9 cm long, extending ?-3/4 distance in from margin; middle lobe largest, 3–8 × 1.5–3 cm, lanceolate to elliptic-ovate, dentate, grey- or white-tomentose below, glabrate above except when young, dark shining green, more or less rugose, acute or mucronate. Flowers ☿, solitary. Pedicels much longer than petioles, hairy. Bracts free, 1.5–2.3 cm long, ovate, hairy or glabrate outside, serrate with teeth setose. Hypanthium (4)–4.5–5 cm long, tomentulose. Sepals 3–4.8 cm long, elliptic, green outside, with tomentulose band, white or very pale pink inside, with short horn near apex; petals similar to sepals but all pink; corona threads violet-blue, about 1/2 perianth. Filaments 1.3–1.7 cm long, much longer than anthers; anthers 6–9 mm long. Ovary white-villous. Fruit 4–7 cm diameter, globose or depressed globose, yellow, tomentulose; pulp sweet and edible, orange. Seeds 5–6 mm long, ellipsoid-ovoid, dark brown or dark red, alveolate. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Pink-flowered passionfruit has downy young shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, grey- or white-felted underneath and dark shining green above; its stipules are pinnate, with dark thread-like segments almost to the base of a very narrow central strip; its flowers have a floral tube (4)–4.5–5 cm long, pink petals and violet-blue corona threads; its fruit is 4–7 cm across, round or slightly flattened, yellow and finely downy. Pink-flowered passionfruit's stipules are pinnate, with thread-like segments, and its fruit is more or less round; a banana passionfruit's stipules are simple — either ovate and toothed or awl-shaped and untoothed — and its fruit is ellipsoid. Both have pink flowers and edible orange pulp, so flower colour does not separate them. A hybrid, Passiflora × rosea, which has no entry here, looks very like pink-flowered passionfruit, but the central strip of its stipules is lanceolate and its stamens are usually abnormal. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Pink-flowered passionfruit has downy young shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, grey- or white-felted underneath and dark shining green above; its stipules are pinnate, with dark thread-like segments almost to the base of a very narrow central strip; its flowers have a floral tube (4)–4.5–5 cm long, pink petals and violet-blue corona threads; its fruit is 4–7 cm across, round or slightly flattened, yellow and finely downy. The flower splits the genus first: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: kōhia's leaves are undivided and leathery and its flowers under 2 cm across, while pink-flowered passionfruit's leaves are 3-lobed. Kōhia is dioecious: only female plants bear fruit, and only after pollen reaches them from a male plant, so a vine without fruit can still be kōhia; use the leaves. Both are edible.

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube about 6–8 cm long (published figures run from up to 6 cm to 8 cm), with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and published lengths run from up to 9 cm to 14 cm. Pink-flowered passionfruit has downy young shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, grey- or white-felted underneath and dark shining green above; its stipules are pinnate, with dark thread-like segments almost to the base of a very narrow central strip; its flowers have a floral tube (4)–4.5–5 cm long, pink petals and violet-blue corona threads; its fruit is 4–7 cm across, round or slightly flattened, yellow and finely downy. Pink-flowered passionfruit's stipules are pinnate, with thread-like segments, and its fruit is more or less round; a banana passionfruit's stipules are simple — either ovate and toothed or awl-shaped and untoothed — and its fruit is ellipsoid. Both have pink flowers and edible orange pulp, so flower colour does not separate them. P. tarminiana's stipules soon fall, so look for them on young growth. A hybrid, Passiflora × rosea, which has no entry here, looks very like pink-flowered passionfruit, but the central strip of its stipules is lanceolate and its stamens are usually abnormal. Both are edible.

summary.text:
Passiflora pinnatistipula, commonly known as poro poro or gulupa (Colombia), is a climbing perennial that grows in the Cajamarca region of Peru.
S.: Banks Peninsula (widespread), Otago (Palmerston). On Banks Peninsula this is the commonest sp. in the Tacsonia group.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Secondary forest margins, scrub, waste ground, abandoned gardens.
In Auckland it grows in forest, forest margins and gaps, wasteland, roadsides, disturbed sites and fence-lines, and over abandoned structures (Auckland Council, restated).
In the Bay of Plenty it grows in open and intact forest and forest margins, on coastlines and cliffs, in shrublands and along streamsides, and can invade cold-climate forest under a dense canopy (Bay of Plenty Regional Council, restated).

identification.text:
When supported, the plant can grow up to 6 metres in height. The compound leaves with 5 to 9 leaflets are dark green on the upper surface and a lighter green beneath, with glabrous, terete or angular branches. The terminal leaflet is noticeably larger than the other leaflets.
The species is heterostylous, meaning that a few distinct flower morphs (forms) are available, though each plant bears only one morph. In late winter and early spring it produces an abundance of reddish-pink flower buds, followed by fragrant five-petalled starry white flowers which are about 2 cm in diameter. The bracts are subulate (tapering to a point), 1-6 mm. Each flower is carried by a pedicel (single stalk) of 0.5 - 2.5cm The calyx forms a 1-2 mm tube terminating in 5 triangular or subulate-linear lobes, only 2 mm long, and a corolla, white, with a red underside and red buttons. The fruit is a black, globular berry.
Almost glabrous, evergreen climbing shrub. Stems more or less terete. Leaves opposite, pinnate, with (5)–7 leaflets; petioles from about 5–30 mm long. Terminal leaflets 3–7 × 0.8–2.5 cm, lanceolate to ovate, entire, with hairy tufts in axils of basal veins beneath, sometimes ciliolate; base subcordate to rounded, or sometimes oblique; apex acuminate; petiolules to 10 mm long. Lateral leaflets smaller, otherwise similar; petiolules less than 5 mm long. Cymes terminal or axillary in uppermost axils, forming many-flowered panicles of very fragrant flowers; pedicels 8–20 mm long, slender. Calyx 3–4 mm long; teeth subulate, equal to or slightly shorter than the tube. Corolla white, usually pink in bud; tube 1.5–2.5 cm long, narrow-cylindric; lobes 1–1.8 cm long, elliptic, glabrous, with more or less rounded, mucronulate apex. Style exserted. Fruit 5–8 mm diameter, broad-ellipsoid to globular, glossy black, not often produced; pulp dark red.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Stems round, tough and very long, rooting at the nodes; flowers up to 25 mm across (NZPCN, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are fragrant climbers whose white flowers can be flushed pink and whose fruit is a glossy black berry of much the same size, and the flower tubes overlap in length, so fruit and tube size do not separate them. Pink jasmine's leaves are pinnate, with (5)–7 stalked leaflets; Japanese honeysuckle's leaves are simple and entire, though leaves produced in colder weather in early spring are wavy-edged to deeply lobed. Pink jasmine carries many flowers together in panicles, each a narrow tube opening to flat, elliptic lobes, usually pink in bud; Japanese honeysuckle's flowers come in pairs in the leaf axils, are two-lipped, turn yellow after opening and are glandular-hairy outside. Japanese honeysuckle's shining black berries are not poisonous, but eating a lot of them can upset the stomach.
