summary.text:
Jasminum polyanthum (Chinese: 多花素馨; pinyin: Duōhuāsùxīn), the many-flowered jasmine, pink jasmine, or white jasmine, is a species of flowering plant in the olive family Oleaceae, native to China and Myanmar.
The plant is native to the mountainous areas of Southwest China, particularly Guizhou, Sichuan and Yunnan, as well as Myanmar.
It lives in valleys and forests at elevations between 1,400 and 3,000 m.
In New Zealand it is naturalised in the North Island: North Auckland, Auckland, Bay of Plenty (Opotiki district), Gisborne. Jasminum polyanthum is now the most commonly cultivated species in New Zealand and thrives in all but the colder North Island and South Island areas. The vines are often very rampant and layer themselves extensively, and so spread over some distance, e.g., about a hectare of low forest between Waiwera and Warkworth is reported to be mostly covered by this species. However, unlike the Italian jasmine, Jasminum polyanthum is intolerant of more than a few degrees of frost and only grows vigorously in warm areas.
This species of jasmine spreads rapidly as it can grow from any small section of stem material. The stems layer profusely and runners spread long distances. It is highly shade tolerant and can flower under a full canopy. It forms dense ground cover, preventing the growth of native seedlings, and smothers all other vegetation up to mid-canopy level.
Auckland's Regional Pest Management Plan lists it for sustained control across the whole region (Auckland Council, restated).
Other names in New Zealand: jasmine, climbing jasmine (NZPCN, Biota of New Zealand); nurseries also sell it as winter jasmine, a name used for other jasmines too.
It was recorded as naturalised in New Zealand in 1980 and can live 15 to 20 years in the wild (Bay of Plenty Regional Council). Seed was once rare here but is now found on plants in some areas, and birds spread it (NZPCN); most spread is from stem pieces dumped in green waste from gardens, roadsides, vacant land, cemeteries and bush tracks (Bay of Plenty Regional Council, restated). Bush or a backyard full of it does not support native birds and other wildlife (Pest Free Kaipātiki).
The Bay of Plenty lists it as an advisory pest: the council does not enforce its control, which is left to landowners (Bay of Plenty Regional Council, restated).

warnings: No reliable food record for pink jasmine was found, and the evidence conflicts: its fresh buds and flowers are sometimes used to scent tea, but it is also described as not edible, eating it may cause mild stomach upset, and a poisons information centre reportedly told a caller it is toxic, can cause stomach problems and should not be used for tea. Jasmine tea and jasmine water are usually made with Arabian jasmine (Jasminum sambac), a different species. Do not treat pink jasmine as food on this evidence.

Carolina or yellow jessamine (Gelsemium sempervirens), a garden climber whose genus name comes from the Italian word for jasmine, is not a jasmine and is highly poisonous in its bark, flowers, fruit, leaves and roots; poisoning causes sweating, nausea, muscular weakness, dilated pupils, lowered temperature, convulsions and respiratory failure.
The strong perfume of the flowers is highly allergenic to some people.

Pink jasmine is a pest plant throughout Auckland, where it must not be planted, distributed, released or sold. It can grow from any small piece of stem and is spread by dumped garden waste, so do not move cuttings or prunings. It is controlled with metsulfuron gel painted on cut stems and, on large infestations, by foliar spraying, so vines in reserves and bush may have been treated.

identification.text:
Perennial acaulous herb with thick, fleshy, glassy white, contractile root below the main bulb which is surrounded by numerous small bulbils; tunic brown; scales 3-nerved. Leaves 3-foliolate. Petiole usually 7–20 cm long, glabrate or with scattered long hairs; stipular wing broad, membranous, hairy. Petiolule about 1 mm long, hairy. Lamina of leaflets equal or nearly so, 10–35 × 12–48 mm, broadly obcordate, 2-lobed, rounded, with rather narrow sinus, glabrous or nearly so above, hairy beneath, finely punctate with raised orange calli beneath, especially round the margin. Inflorescence to 35 cm long, cymose, 3–7- or 10–18-flowered, with long curly hairs; pedicels more or less deflexed, very variable in length. Bracts at base of pedicels, 2–3 mm long, with calli present but these often small. Sepals 4–5 mm long, more or less elliptic, slightly hairy; calli 2–(4), prominent, orange, apical. Petals 1.5–2 cm long, oblong-obovate, pink to rose, glabrous. Stamens at 2 levels; filaments patently hirsute, dilated towards base, the longer 5–6 mm long. Styles either slightly shorter than the shorter stamens or intermediate between stamen whorls, densely and patently hirsute. Capsule not seen.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are pink-flowered sorrels with no leafy stem, their leaves all rising from the base, and heart-shaped leaflets with orange dots or an orange band near the edge; both carry several flowers on a stalk up to about 35 cm tall. So the leaves and the flower clusters do not separate them. Look at the base of the plant: pink shamrock grows from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, with a thick, fleshy, glassy white root below it; shamrock wood sorrel grows from a short, thick, fleshy rhizome, rough with old leaf-base scars, and has no true bulbils. Look at the petals: pink shamrock's are pink to rose, 1.5–2 cm long and hairless; shamrock wood sorrel's are 9–16 mm long, usually rose with darker veins, with a band of flattened hairs on the outside. The petal lengths meet at 15–16 mm. Pink shamrock's leaflets are hairless or nearly so on top; shamrock wood sorrel's have flattened hairs on both faces. Flower number overlaps: pink shamrock carries 3–7 or 10–18 on a stalk, shamrock wood sorrel (4)–7–35. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Shamrock wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are pink-flowered sorrels with no leafy stem, growing from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, with a thick, fleshy, glassy white root below it, and both are weeds of cultivated and waste ground. They are alike in size and flower colour; the orange dots under the leaflets settle it. Fishtail oxalis's leaflets are broadly fishtail-shaped, shallowly and broadly two-lobed, 12–50 mm long and 18–80 mm wide, hairless except near the base, with no orange dots or only faint ones; pink shamrock's are broadly heart-shaped and rounded, 10–35 mm long and 12–48 mm wide, with a rather narrow notch, hairy beneath and finely dotted underneath with raised orange spots, especially round the edge. Fishtail oxalis's flower clusters are hairless or nearly so; pink shamrock's carry long curly hairs. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. Its leaflet shape and flower-cluster hairs then match pink shamrock's, but it still has no orange dots under the leaflets. Petals do not separate them safely: fishtail oxalis's are about 1.2–1.5 cm long, pink; pink shamrock's 1.5–2 cm, pink to rose. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Fishtail oxalis

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel has leafy stems, spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and each flower stalk carries a single flower. Pink shamrock has no leafy stem: its leaves all rise from the base, from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, and it carries 3–7 or 10–18 flowers in a cluster on a stalk up to 35 cm long. Pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless; pink shamrock's leaflets are hairy beneath and its flower clusters carry long curly hairs. Petals do not separate them: pale-pink wood sorrel's are 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white; pink shamrock's 1.5–2 cm, pink to rose. Leaflet size overlaps (pale-pink wood sorrel 4–16 mm long, pink shamrock 10–35 mm), and both have orange dots near the leaflet edge. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pale-pink wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Purple wood sorrel carries a single flower on each stalk, 1–11 cm long, forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base. Its leaflets are broadly obovate with a rounded tip, sometimes slightly notched, and its sepals have no orange dots. Pink shamrock carries 3–7 or 10–18 flowers in a cluster on a stalk up to 35 cm long, the cluster with long curly hairs, its petals 1.5–2 cm long, pink to rose. Its leaflets are broadly heart-shaped, two-lobed with a rather narrow notch, and finely dotted underneath with raised orange spots, especially round the edge, and each sepal has two (sometimes four) prominent orange dots at its tip. What does not separate them: both have no leafy stem, with all the leaves rising from the base; both have leaflets hairy underneath; both grow from bulbs that make bulbils, though purple wood sorrel's outer bulb scales are dark brown or blackish, shining and sticky and pink shamrock's are brown. Leaflet length overlaps (pink shamrock 10–35 mm, purple wood sorrel 10–35 mm, up to 45 mm). Purple wood sorrel's petals can be as short as 10 mm, so petal length points to purple wood sorrel only when the petals are longer than 2 cm. Do not eat purple wood sorrel; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Purple wood sorrel

A pleasant acid flavour, they make an ornamental addition to a mixed salad' (Ken Fern's own notes), 'Root - raw. Sweet, crisp and succulent'; 'sometimes harvested from the wild for its edible leaves, flowers and root'. Second, independent source: Hawaiian Plants and Tropical Flowers, 'Oxalis debilis var. corymbosa – Pink Wood Sorrel' (all rights reserved, facts only), http://wildlifeofhawaii.com/flowers/1358/oxalis-debilis-var-corymbosa-pink-wood-sorrel/, retrieved 03/11/2026 — 'The flowers, leaves, and roots are edible, but this plant should only be consumed in small amounts because it contains oxalic acid'. Both are written for O. debilis (Flora of New Zealand treats var. corymbosa within it). Caution careRequired, as on the other eaten sorrels. Plants For A Future has no page for it.

Bulbil warning: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (cited above), 'Dispersal of the numerous small bulbils during cultivation can result in a dense infestation'; Royal Horticultural Society, 'Oxalis' weed page (all rights reserved, facts only), https://www.rhs.org.uk/weeds/oxalis, retrieved 03/11/2026 — O. debilis bulbils 'are easily dislodged and spread when digging', 'can remain viable in the soil for several years', 'Being mindful of where you dig'.

Months (03/11/2026): leaves, flowers and roots are eaten, so the window is the union of the flowering window, Flora of New Zealand 'FL Nov–May' (NZFO 'Flowering: Nov.–May.'), and the months with iNaturalist research-grade wild NZ records at or above a quarter of the peak month (peak October, 6 records; July to December have 2 or more): July to May. June has 1 record and is left out. The record count is small (22), so the leaf window is thin evidence; no NZ source dates the leaves.

Origin checked 03/11/2026: NZTCS has no record (findNztcsSpeciesByCriteria 'Oxalis debilis', 0 results); NZ Organisms Register (https://data.nzor.org.nz/names/search?query=Oxalis%20debilis): Exotic, Present, New Zealand; NZPCN 'Oxalis debilis' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/oxalis-debilis/): Biostatus Exotic, year naturalised 1958; NZ Flora Online Biostatus Exotic. Not on DOC's List of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024 (McAlpine & Howell, Science for Conservation 340) and not in Wildland Consultants 2021 Contract Report 5396 for the PCE, Appendix 2 (text searched: only Oxalis pes-caprae), so not a pest. summary.text:
Oxalis debilis, the large-flowered pink-sorrel or pink woodsorrel, is a perennial plant and herb in the family Oxalidaceae. Its original distribution is South America but it has become a cosmopolitan species, occurring in all continents except Antarctica. It can be found in both temperate and tropical areas.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands: widespread. Naturalised from northern South America and probably Central America and the West Indies, first recorded in 1958. O. debilis is generally the commonest of the stemless, bulbil-bearing, pink-flowered oxalis. Dispersal of the numerous small bulbils during cultivation can result in a dense infestation and it is thus regarded as a serious weed in many places.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

It spreads by the many small bulbils around its bulb, which come away easily and are scattered when the soil is dug or moved; spreading them during cultivation can produce a dense infestation, and they can stay alive in the soil for several years. Dig it only where you mean to clear it, and do not move soil it grows in.
It grows with shamrock wood sorrel and fishtail oxalis, pink-flowered sorrels that look very like it (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text:
Lawns, paths, paddocks, roadsides and any compacted ground. Everywhere.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Generally open modified places, particularly poor pastures, also a pioneer of river beds, landslips, coastal sands and talus, and cliff faces, common on many small offshore islands and often in remote coastal areas where very few other naturalised species occur.
It copes with drought better than greater plantain.
On New Zealand's national wetland plant list it is rated facultative upland: it sometimes grows in wetlands but usually on dry ground.

identification.text:
A flat rosette of narrow, lance-shaped leaves with three to seven prominent parallel veins running their length; tear a leaf across and the veins pull out like strings. The flower is a short brown head on a tall leafless stalk, ringed with pale stamens. Greater plantain (Plantago major) has wider, oval leaves and a longer flower spike and is used the same way.
The flower stalk is 12–70 cm tall and strongly ribbed, and the dense head is up to about 6 cm long, with the brown fruits clustered near its tip. A tuft of silky white hairs, often purplish, sits at the base of each leaf stalk. New Zealand plants have either white or yellow anthers; both are common. It flowers from July to April. It has a persistent taproot. Each small capsule holds one or two seeds, 2–3 mm long and medium to dark brown.

lookalikes.howToTell: Buck's-horn plantain's leaves usually have one to four pairs of narrow lobes or teeth, like antlers, a single main vein, and are 1–5 mm wide (up to 10); narrow-leaved plantain's are entire or only slightly toothed, 5–48 mm wide, with 3–7 veins running their length. Buck's-horn's flower stalk is not ribbed and is 3–45 cm long; narrow-leaved plantain's is strongly ribbed and 12–70 cm long. Both are hairy rosettes that flower from July to April, so neither tells them apart.
lookalikes.name: Buck's-horn plantain

lookalikes.howToTell: Greater plantain's leaves are broad ovals, up to 16 cm wide, on a distinct stalk; narrow-leaved plantain's are long and narrow, 0.5–4.8 cm wide, tapering into a short, ill-defined stalk with a tuft of silky white hairs at the base. Greater plantain's flower stalk is not ribbed, and its fruits run far down a spike up to 30 cm long; narrow-leaved plantain's stalk is strongly ribbed, with a short, dense head, to about 6 cm, and the brown fruits clustered near the tip. Small greater plantains can have narrower leaves, so check the flower stalk too. Both have veins running the length of the leaf and both flower from July to April, so neither of those tells them apart.
lookalikes.name: Greater plantain

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp plantain's flower stalk is round, not ribbed, and densely hairy near the top, and its narrow spike is usually more than 10 cm long when mature; narrow-leaved plantain's stalk is strongly ribbed and its head is short and dense, to about 6 cm. Swamp plantain's petals curl up into a small, pointed, upright cone and its stamens are usually hidden; narrow-leaved plantain's stamens stick out around the head. Swamp plantain grows in swamps, bogs, lake and river edges and wet grassland, and flowers only from November to January. Leaf widths overlap — up to 8 cm in swamp plantain, 0.5–4.8 cm in narrow-leaved plantain — and both have parallel veins, so leaves alone do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Swamp plantain

preparation.text:
Young leaves shredded finely into salads, or cooked — older ones are stringy and best in soup or as a tea.
Pull the stringy ribs out of the leaves; the very youngest leaves are least fibrous. The unopened flower heads can be eaten raw, and taste of raw button mushrooms, or simmered into a stock. Cook the seeds, or grind them into flour. The green seeds rub off the heads easily; if they don't come away, the heads are still in flower.

recipes.method: Serves 3. 6 handfuls young ribwort plantain leaves, torn; 3 aubergines, cut into 4 mm slices; 1 onion, sliced; 4 garlic cloves, sliced; 1 avocado, halved and sliced; 400 g Greek strained yoghurt; 400 g passata; rapeseed oil; grated cheddar; cracked black pepper. Boil the plantain leaves for 3 minutes, drain, squeeze out the water, chop them finely and set aside. Blanch the aubergine slices in salted water, drain and set aside. Fry the onion and garlic in a little oil until soft, stir in the plantain for 30 seconds, then add the passata and cook down to a thick sauce; season with black pepper. Lay half the aubergine in an ovenproof dish and cover it with the avocado slices. Pour on half the sauce and spread the yoghurt over it. Add the rest of the aubergine, then the rest of the sauce, and scatter cheese on top. Bake at 160 °C for about 30 minutes, until done. The author gives the oven only as '160 degree'; it is read here as °C.
recipes.title: Aubergine and avocado bake with ribwort plantain

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard (the page does not say which plantain). 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Use it as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: The author's greens were dock, onion weed, nasturtium, plantain, baby wild mustard, dandelion, sow thistle and a violet leaf (the page does not say which plantain). 2 crushed garlic cloves; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 500 ml (2 cups) firmly packed wild greens, sliced very thinly; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper; 125 ml (½ cup) roughly chopped pistachios, walnuts, almonds or brazil nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp hearts, pumpkin or sunflower seeds; and 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, hemp seed oil or a mix. Makes about 750 ml (3 cups). To slice the greens, sort them into similar shapes, bunch and twist a few leaves together and slice as thinly as you can — this suits the tougher, stringier ones such as plantain, mustard and dock. Toss everything together. Serve as a side or salad, in a wrap or sandwich, or with pasta, risotto, eggs, or sausages and mash. It keeps at least 4 days in a sealed jar in the fridge.
recipes.title: Weedolata (wild-greens gremolata)

recipes.method: Made with narrow-leaved plantain seeds; the author suggests greater plantain's longer heads if you find them. Makes about 28. 135 g pumpkin seeds, 20 g linseeds, 20 g (about 125 ml) green plantain seeds, 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt or seaweed salt, 100 g plain flour, 100 g wholemeal or spelt flour, 7 g nettle powder (optional), 50 ml vegetable oil, 200 ml just-boiled water. Rub the green seeds off the heads. Mix 135 g pumpkin seeds, 20 g linseeds, 20 g (about 125 ml) green plantain seeds, 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt or seaweed salt, 100 g plain flour and 100 g wholemeal or spelt flour, plus 7 g nettle powder if you like. Stir in 50 ml vegetable oil and 200 ml just-boiled water; it will look like stiff, soggy porridge. Heat the oven to 140 °C (120 °C fan). Roll the dough out between two sheets of baking paper to the thickness of one seed, cut it into rectangles about 5 × 2 cm, and lift them onto two baking trays. Bake for an hour or a little more, until light brown and crisp. Cool, and keep in an airtight container.
recipes.title: Plantain seed crackers

recipes.method: Written for plantain seed heads, greater or narrow-leaved; the author's own plant is narrow-leaved plantain. The brown seed heads of plantain, with or without their stalks; butter or olive oil; thyme; salt. Pick the brown seed heads, with or without their stalks. Heat enough butter or olive oil to coat a cast-iron pan over medium-high heat, add the heads and toss them for 2 minutes. Add thyme and a sprinkle of salt and cook 1–2 minutes more, stirring now and then, until the heads are toasted and the seeds just begin to fall off; add more fat if they look dry. Serve straight away; the stalks make handles, but are too tough to eat.
recipes.title: Plantain seed heads with butter and thyme

recipes.method: Written for plantain seeds, greater or narrow-leaved. 1 handful of plantain seeds; 3 handfuls of pumpkin seeds; 3 handfuls of sesame seeds; a generous splash of tamari or soy sauce. Mix 1 handful of plantain seeds with 3 handfuls of pumpkin seeds and 3 of sesame seeds. Toast them lightly in a non-stick frying pan, then add a generous splash of tamari or soy sauce, toss to coat, and let any excess cook off. Tip into bowls and eat as a snack.
recipes.title: Spiced plantain seed mix

recipes.method: Written for plantain, herb Robert, nasturtium seeds, oxtongue or rosemary, singly or together (the page does not say which plantain). Chop the plant material and pack it loosely in a jar. Fill the jar with apple cider vinegar to cover the plants completely, let it sit a little, and poke out any air bubbles under the leaves with a chopstick. Cap it, with a piece of plastic under a metal lid so the vinegar doesn't eat the metal, label it and leave it in a cool place for 2–6 weeks, then strain the vinegar into a bottle. Use it in salad dressings, soups and pestos, or sweetened with honey by the spoonful.
recipes.title: Herbal vinegar

recipes.method: The author's weeds were chickweed, nasturtium, dandelion, pūhā, ox-eye daisy and plantain, with parsley and garden herbs (the page does not say which plantain). She also adds a handful of New Zealand spinach; it is At Risk and its page says to blanch it first, so it is left out here. 5 rosemary sprigs about 12 cm long; a handful of parsley; a big handful of chickweed; 4 large nasturtium leaves; a handful of thyme sprigs 5 cm long; a few dandelion leaves; a small pūhā plant; 10 ox-eye daisy leaves; 8 plantain leaves; 5 sage leaves; 6 garlic cloves; 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt; about 30 ml (⅛ cup) cider vinegar; 60–125 ml (¼–½ cup) olive oil, starting with the smaller amount; 5 ml (1 tsp) honey, or to taste; the juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml (½ cup) walnuts. Strip the leaves from the thyme and rosemary and wash any leaves that need it. Blend everything in a high-speed blender or food processor until smooth, pushing it down with the tamper. Keep it in the fridge or freezer.
recipes.title: Wild weed pesto

recipes.method: Written for plantain and dandelion, with celery leaves and parsley (the page does not say which plantain). A small handful of celery leaves; 4 branches of parsley (go easy: it can take over); 4 leaves each of plantain, dandelion and kale. Blend the greens in 750 ml–1 litre (3–4 cups) water, then add 1 banana, 250 ml (1 cup) frozen blueberries, 1 kiwifruit and ½ avocado and blend again.
recipes.title: Thick and creamy green smoothie

Leaf widths meet at 5–10 mm, so width is given with its range, not as a test on its own. Flowering 'Jul.–Apr.' for both (Flora Online), hairs and rosettes in both — ruled out. Ranges overlap: buck's-horn on coasts, lake margins and waste places (NZPCN), narrow-leaved plantain on lawns, roadsides and disturbed ground throughout. IV (Webb et al. 1988, via Flora of New Zealand Online https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Plantago-lanceolata.html) describes New Zealand plants as '3–7-veined'; Minnesota Wildflowers (https://www.minnesotawildflowers.info/flower/english-plantain) agrees, '3, 5 or 7 prominent veins'. The commoner '3–5' (Wikipedia 'Plantago lanceolata' after Blamey's Wild Flowers of Britain and Ireland; Illinois Wildflowers) and NSW Flora's '5-veined' all fall inside the Flora of New Zealand range, so they undercount rather than contradict it.

summary.text:
Ribwort. The lawn weed with the stringy, parallel-veined leaves — a tough but reliable green, and a traditional folk remedy, crushed fresh, for insect bites and stings.
It is also called English plantain, lamb's tongue, rib-grass and ripple grass. It came from Eurasia and was first recorded growing wild in New Zealand in 1855, and is now common to abundant throughout the North, South and Stewart Islands, and grows on the Kermadec, Chatham and Campbell Islands. Farmers sow improved cultivars, such as Agritonic, in pasture mixes: stock eat it, it carries more copper and zinc than ryegrass or clover, and it helps reduce nitrate leaching from grazing animals. It is pollinated mostly by the wind, and only now and then by bees. 100 g of fresh leaves give about 22 kcal, with 2.1 g of protein and 3.7 g of fibre.

warnings: Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed. Pick from ground you know.
Plants beside busy roads can hold high levels of lead and cadmium. Pick away from traffic.

habitat.text:
Coastal forest, and occasionally inland around lake margins; in the far north it is sometimes found with kauri forest, and in some northern places pōhutukawa forms a forest type of its own.
The tree is renowned as a cliff-dweller, able to maintain a hold in precarious, near-vertical situations. Like its Hawaiian relative the ʻōhiʻa lehua (M. polymorpha), the pōhutukawa has been shown to be efficient in the colonisation of lava plains – notably on Rangitoto, a volcanic island in the Hauraki Gulf.

harvestEthics.text:
Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In the Auckland region (Regionally Declining), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text:
Pōhutukawa grow up to 20 metres high, with a spreading, dome-like form. They usually grow as a multi-trunked spreading tree. Their trunks and branches are sometimes festooned with matted, fibrous aerial roots. The oblong, leathery leaves are covered in dense white hairs underneath.
The tree flowers from November to January with a peak in early summer (mid to late December), with brilliant crimson flowers covering the tree, hence the nickname New Zealand Christmas tree. The first published reference to pōhutakawa as a Christmas tree was in 1857, in a newspaper report of a feast held by Eruera Patuone. There is variation between individual trees in the timing of flowering, and in the shade and brightness of the flowers. In isolated populations genetic drift has resulted in local variation: many of the trees growing around the Rotorua lakes produce pink-shaded flowers, and the yellow-flowered cultivar 'Aurea' descends from a pair discovered in 1940 on Mōtītī Island in the Bay of Plenty.
Tree up to 20 m tall; trunk up to 2 m in diameter; branches spreading; branchlets stout, tomentose. Leaves on short stout petioles; lamina (2.5)–5–10 × 2.5–3–5 cm, elliptic to oblong, acute or obtuse, coriaceous, thick, clad in white tomentum below (young plants occasionally glabrous below). Inflorescence of broad compound cymes with numerous flowers; pedicels stout, tomentose. Receptacle obconic; sepals deltoid; petals crimson, oblong. Stamens numerous, crimson, 3–4 cm long. Ovary adnate to receptacle. Capsules 7–9 mm long, tomentose, distinctly exserted, loculicidally 3-valved.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stamens, the long threads of the flower: pōhutukawa's are 30–40 mm long, Kermadec pōhutukawa's 10–23 mm, and its flowers are smaller (about 6–8 mm across against 8–12 mm). Pōhutukawa's leaves are larger, 25–100 mm long (sometimes to 120 mm) and 30–50 mm wide (sometimes 15 mm or up to 60 mm), elliptic to egg-shaped-oblong, with tips pointed rather abruptly or rounded but never notched; Kermadec pōhutukawa's are 25–50 mm long (sometimes 20 mm) and 10–20 mm wide (to 30 mm), almost round, broadly egg-shaped to elliptic-oblong, with rounded or notched tips. Leaves 25–50 mm long occur on both, and pōhutukawa on the Three Kings Islands has smaller leaves close to Kermadec pōhutukawa's, so go by the stamens. Kermadec pōhutukawa often has some flowers through the year but rarely flowers en masse; pōhutukawa flowers mainly in late spring and early summer, though from August to March at the extremes. On the mainland Kermadec pōhutukawa is a planted tree, mostly a slow-growing large shrub or compact tree, to 10 m in cultivation and rarely if ever a big tree; pōhutukawa grows to about 20 m. Both have leaves velvety with grey-white hairs beneath, crimson flowers and densely hairy capsules. Kermadec pōhutukawa is often sold mislabelled as pōhutukawa, and the two hybridise in cultivation. No record of Kermadec pōhutukawa as food was found (see its page).

preparation.text: Draw the nectar out of the flower with a reed. For drinks, use the stamens, the long, slender stalks in the middle of the flower; there are plenty in the fallen flowers on the ground under the tree.

recipes.method: 1 litre (4 cups) pōhutukawa stamens (stripped from the flowers); 250 ml (1 cup) crushed strawberries; the flowers of 1 elderflower head (optional); 375 ml (1½ cups) golden sugar; 1 sliced lemon; 2.5 litres water. Makes 2.5 litres. The fizz comes from the wild yeasts on the flowers and strawberries, so use spray-free strawberries and don't wash either; keep as much of the pollen as you can when picking. Stir the sugar, water and lemon in a large jar until the sugar dissolves, then add the stamens, elderflowers and strawberries and push them under. Cover with muslin held by a rubber band, and date it. Stir hard every day for 3–4 days; it is fermenting when the flowers rise and bubbles appear as you stir. Strain through muslin into flip-top bottles and leave at room temperature for 1–2 days, checking the fizz, then refrigerate once it is as fizzy as you like. Serve cold; the cold slows the fermentation, so it keeps a long time in the fridge.
recipes.title: Pōhutukawa fizzy drink

recipes.method: Makes 1 litre. 300–400 g pōhutukawa stamens (the long, slender stalks in the middle of the flower); 1 litre water; 100 g sugar. Bring the water to the boil, then turn it down to a simmer. Add the sugar and simmer until it has dissolved. Turn off the heat, add the stamens and leave them to steep overnight, like tea. Next day strain out the stamens, pressing them gently but not squeezing, and bottle the cordial in a clean bottle. Serve with bubbles or gin.
recipes.title: Pōhutukawa stamen cordial

summary.text:
Pōhutukawa (Metrosideros excelsa), also known as the New Zealand Christmas tree, or iron tree, is a coastal evergreen tree in the myrtle family, Myrtaceae, that produces a brilliant display of red (or occasionally orange, yellow or white) flowers, each consisting of a mass of stamens.
The pōhutukawa's natural range is the coastal regions of the North Island of New Zealand, north of a line stretching from New Plymouth (39° S) to Gisborne (38° S), where it once formed a continuous coastal fringe. By the 1990s, pastoral farming and introduced pests had reduced pōhutukawa forests by over 90%.

edibleParts.text: Cap and stem. Trim any maggot-riddled stem base.

habitat.text: Mycorrhizal with introduced trees: oak, birch, pine and sweet chestnut. Look along the drip line of mature street and park trees and in old shelter belts, especially in Canterbury. It does not grow with native bush trees, so a bolete under native beech or kānuka is something else.

identification.text:
Cap 8–30 cm, tan to chestnut brown, smooth and slightly tacky when wet, often with a fine pale line at the rim. Underneath is a sponge of tiny pores, never gills: white and firm when young, ageing to yellow then olive. The stem is thick and club-shaped, pale brown, with a fine white net (reticulation) at least over the top third — look closely, it is subtle. Flesh is white; when cut or bruised it does not change colour, or turns only very light brown or light red. Blueing rules porcini out. Taste a crumb of raw cap and spit it out: it should be mild and nutty, never bitter.

Turn the mushroom over. Porcini's pore surface is white, yellow or olive. If it is red, orange or any warm colour, stop. Cut the cap in half and watch for a minute: if the flesh blues, stop.

preparation.text: Cook before eating. Brush clean rather than wash, slice, and check the stem for maggots. Sauté in butter, or slice thinly and dry for stock — the flavour concentrates.

recipes.method: Serves 1. 100 g porcini, cleaned and sliced; 1 shallot, peeled and finely chopped; 1 garlic clove, peeled and finely chopped; a few sprigs of tarragon, chopped; 15 ml (1 tbsp) finely chopped curly parsley; 22 ml (1½ tbsp) butter; 15 ml (1 tbsp) cold-pressed rapeseed oil; 25 ml double cream; 1 slice of good sourdough; a knob of butter or bacon fat for the bread, if you like; a few watercress leaves; a splash of Madeira, if you like; salt and pepper. Warm the oil with 15 ml (1 tbsp) of the butter in a medium frying pan and cook the shallot for a minute or two until soft but not coloured. Stir in the garlic and give it another minute. Add the porcini and the rest of the butter and cook for a couple of minutes, tossing the pan if you can. Stir in the cream, tarragon, parsley, salt and pepper, taste, and add the Madeira if you want it. Keep cooking until the porcini are cooked through, then check the seasoning. Toast the sourdough on a chargrill, or fry it in butter or bacon fat. Spoon the porcini over the toast, scatter with the watercress leaves and serve.
recipes.title: Porcini on toast

recipes.method: Fresh porcini; a food dehydrator; boiling water for soaking. Wipe the caps and stems clean with a damp cloth, without soaking them, as they can turn slimy. Peel off the brown cap skin if you prefer; if it won't come away easily, pull it off the slices after cutting. Slice no more than 6 mm thick and spread the slices on dehydrator racks. Dry at 55–60 °C for two to six hours, depending on how thin the slices are and how many racks you are running. Stop when they are light and brittle to slightly bendy, with nothing soft left. Let them cool to room temperature, then seal them in a jar or airtight container and keep them out of the light. To use, cover a handful with boiling water. Use both the softened porcini and their soaking broth in risotto, pasta, sauces and other savoury dishes. You can also drop the dried slices straight into a sauce or stew and let its liquid soften them. The author finds dried porcini keep for at least one to two years.
recipes.title: Dried porcini and their stock

recipes.method: Written for mixed wild mushrooms — the author's are dried porcini (cep), puffball and chanterelles. Serves 4. 2 litres of good chicken or vegetable stock; 30 g dried porcini; 150 g chanterelles; 1 finely diced large onion; 3 garlic cloves; 3 bay leaves; 1 courgette, finely diced; 1 small leek, finely diced; 100 g butter; a few sprigs of thyme; 300 g unwashed carnaroli or arborio rice; 300 ml dry white wine; 150 g puffball, peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes; salt and pepper; 300 g finely grated parmesan; 75 ml double cream; a handful of finely chopped parsley and tarragon; the juice of 1 lemon; truffle oil; hairy bittercress (optional). Heat 2 litres of good chicken or vegetable stock in a separate pan and add 30 g dried porcini to soak and enrich it. Sweat 150 g chanterelles in a frying pan until they give up their juice, and strain the juice into the stock. In a heavy pan, sweat 1 finely diced large onion, 3 garlic cloves, 3 bay leaves, and 1 courgette and 1 small leek (both finely diced) in 50 g of 100 g butter until soft and translucent. Add a few sprigs of thyme and 300 g unwashed carnaroli or arborio rice and stir over a medium heat for a couple of minutes. Add 300 ml dry white wine and keep stirring as it absorbs. Add 150 g puffball, peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes, and the soaked porcini with a little hot stock. Keep stirring briskly, adding the stock a ladleful at a time; when about half is in, add the chanterelles. Season, and stop when the rice keeps a hint of bite (no chalkiness) and the risotto is like a very thick soup — you may not need all the stock. Off the heat, stir in half of 300 g finely grated parmesan, the remaining 50 g butter, 75 ml double cream and a handful of finely chopped parsley and tarragon. Cover and rest for a few minutes. Stir in the juice of 1 lemon, check the seasoning and add a little more stock if needed. Serve in shallow bowls with a few drops of truffle oil, the rest of the cheese on the side, and, if you like, a sprinkle of hairy bittercress for a sharp note.
recipes.title: Ultimate wild mushroom risotto

recipes.method: Written for mixed wild mushrooms; the author strongly recommends that some be dried porcini, for their intensity. 1 kg fresh mushrooms, or 250 g dried, or a mix; butter or oil; 200 g finely grated parmesan or another strong hard cheese; up to 500 g cream cheese; a large handful of sorrel leaves or a squeeze of lemon juice; salt and pepper. Use 1 kg fresh mushrooms, or 250 g dried (soaked for 30 minutes in boiling water and drained), or a mix. Chop roughly and cook thoroughly in butter or oil over a medium heat until all the moisture has gone (the juice can be strained off as a mushroom broth). Cool, then squeeze out any remaining moisture. Blend in a food processor, then add 200 g finely grated parmesan or another strong hard cheese, up to 500 g cream cheese (less for a more mushroomy pâté), a large handful of sorrel leaves or a squeeze of lemon juice, and salt and pepper, in stages, tasting as you go. Optional extras: dried porcini powder cooked with the mushrooms, black garlic, finely chopped pickled walnuts stirred through at the end, miso, soy sauce or dried seaweed powder. Pack into small tubs and label each with the species you used. Keeps for a week in the fridge, or freeze it.

identification, second paragraph: moved verbatim from the former 'Red-pored boletes' entry when that page was split into the species it stood for. It was a rule rather than a species, so it could carry no photograph, and the catalogue now requires one.

The red-pored boletes European guides warn about are not on record in New Zealand. iNaturalist NZ holds 0 observations of Rubroboletus satanas and 0 of Suillellus luridus, and has no Neoboletus taxon; the New Zealand Organisms Register returns nothing for either genus. Checked 07/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/observations?taxon_id=48702&place_id=6803&view=species

Blueing flesh is not by itself a danger sign here. Xerocomellus cisalpinus, the bluefoot bolete, has 163 New Zealand records and is eaten in Europe. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/xerocomellus-cisalpinus.php

warnings: Wild Food UK, 'Identifying Boletus mushrooms' — 'All content and photography © 2026 Wild Food UK', so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.wildfooduk.com/articles/identifying-mushrooms-and-plants/identifying-boletus-mushrooms/ Gives the beginner's bolete rules this page's deleted red-pore warning was a version of: confirm it is a bolete — pores not gills, growing from soil not wood; avoid any red colouring on stem, pores or cap; and cut it lengthwise and avoid it if the flesh turns vivid blue quickly. It names the bitter bolete, Tylopilus felleus, as the look-alike for the penny bun, separated on stem reticulation.

warnings: Stephenson, K., EdibleWildFood.com, 'How to identify boletes' — 'All information, photographs and web content contained in this website is Copyright © EdibleWildFood.com 2020', so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.ediblewildfood.com/blog/2017/08/how-to-identify-boletes/ The same two rules, put more strongly — 'stay away from anything with red colouring (even if only a tiny amount)' — while noting that the pore surface of some edible boletes does discolour green or blue, and that it is rapid change in the flesh that matters. It asks for at least three credible sources before eating any identification.

warnings: both of the above are United Kingdom and North American beginner heuristics, and this catalogue has already found one New Zealand species they would wrongly condemn: bluefoot-bolete, Xerocomellus cisalpinus, 163 iNaturalist NZ records, red-stemmed, strongly blueing, and called edible by three sources. Whatever sentence replaces the deleted red-pore warning has to hold both facts at once.

summary.text: A stout brown-capped bolete with a sponge of pores instead of gills, white flesh that stays white when cut, and a pale net over the top of the stem. In Aotearoa it fruits under introduced oak, birch and pine in autumn.

warnings: Cut every cap and stem lengthwise before it goes in the basket: white flesh that stays white, and a white, yellow or olive pore surface. Blueing, or any strong colour change, means put it down.
Check the pore surface of every specimen, not just the first — mixed patches under the same tree are common.

Forest margins, slips, regenerating scrub, coastal banks. A fast coloniser of disturbed ground.
Coastal to montane (0–400 m), usually in disturbed successional habitats: shrublands, gullies, riversides, forest margins and reverting pasture, often appearing after fires. A common urban weed in many parts of the country.

identification.text: Soft-wooded shrub to 3 m with large deeply lobed leaves and showy purple flowers with yellow centres. Fruit is an oval berry ripening from green through orange to a soft deep orange.

lookalikes.howToTell: Black nightshade is a herb to about 75 cm, usually hairy, where poroporo is a hairless, soft-wooded shrub to about 3 m. Its flowers are 10–13 mm across, usually white, sometimes pale mauve, in clusters that are usually few-flowered; poroporo's are usually 4–5 cm and violet, though the other poroporo, Solanum aviculare, can have white flowers from 10 mm. Its berries are 7–10 mm across and round, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow; poroporo's are 23–30 mm long, egg-shaped, usually yellow or pale orange. The unripe green berries hold the most toxin, but eating mature leaves raw may also cause poisoning, so no part is safe to assume.

summary.text:
Native nightshade with genuinely good fruit — but only when fully ripe, and never before.
Poroporo is native to New Zealand's North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands and to south-eastern Australia and Tasmania. It is often confused with the much less common Solanum aviculare, which shares the name poroporo. The ripe berry was a traditional Māori food, and early European settlers stewed the fruit and made pies or jams with it.

warnings: Unripe green fruit contains solasodine and is genuinely poisonous. This is not a case of 'a bit sour' — wait for full ripeness.
Leaves and stems are toxic at every stage.

Yellow berries are poisonous as well as green ones; only ripe orange berries lose much of their toxicity. Symptoms are often delayed up to 6–12 hours and may include fever, sweating, nausea and abdominal pain.

identification.text:
Angelica pachycarpa is a short-lived, stout fleshy plant. It grows about one meter tall, with very glossy dark green foliage. It has creamy-white to greenish-white flowers in flat umbels that are ten to twenty centimeters wide. The foliage and hollow stems have a faint aniseed odor.  The stems are grooved.  The base foliage is two to three pinnate and noticeable petiolate; the stem leaves are one to three pinnate with very short petioles.  The fruit are up to twelve millimeters long, brown with lighter colored wings, and have a pepper-like scent.
Angelica pachycarpa is found growing in the Crithmo-Armerion maritimae (Géhu 1968) community of plants in Spain and Portugal which includes these species also: Armeria berlengensis, Armeria euscadiensis, Armeria maritima subsp. miscella, Armeria pubigera subsp. depilata, Armeria pubigera subsp. pubigera, Centaurea borjae, Daucus gingidium subsp. atlanticum, Leucanthemum ircutianum subsp. crassifolium, Leucanthemum merinoi, Leucanthemum pluriflorum, Rumex acetosa subsp. biformis, Rumex rupestris, Sesamoides suffruticosa subsp. latifolia, Silene uniflora, Spergularia rupicola subsp. rupicola, Trifolium occidentale.

identification.text:
Annual or biennial. Stem erect, branching above, finely grooved, glabrous or with patent coarse spinous bristles up to 3–4 mm long below, 50–150–(250) cm tall. Leaves glaucous; rosette and lower stem leaves tapering to base, with stiff hairs and spinous bristles especially on veins beneath, 5–30 × 2–12 cm, deeply runcinate-pinnatifid to undivided; margins finely dentate to bristly ciliate, usually sinuate. Upper leaves becoming glabrous, triangular to obovate to linear, sometimes triangularly 3-lobed at apex, with oblong amplexicaul auricles at base. Inflorescence diffusely paniculate. Capitula numerous, cylindric. Involucre 8–13 mm long; bracts imbricate, suberect to reflexed at fruiting; outermost bracts triangular to ovate, subacute, 1/4-⅓ length of innermost bracts; inner bracts lanceolate to linear, obtuse to acute. Florets about 1½× length of involucre; corollas erect to erecto-patent, yellow. Achenes pale brown to grey, sometimes dark-spotted, 5–9-ribbed on each face, obovate, flattened, finely spiny distally on ribs; body 2.5–3 mm long; beak pale, equal to body. Pappus fine, white. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Some plants have undivided leaves; in New Zealand they have been called var. integrata, but they differ in nothing else.
The leaves get progressively smaller as they reach its top. They are oblong or lanceolate, often pinnately lobed and (especially for the lower leaves), waxy grey green. Fine spines are present along the veins and leaf edges. The undersides have whitish veins. They emit latex when cut.
The flower heads are 1–1.5 cm wide, pale yellow, often tinged purple, with 12–20 ray flowers but no disc flowers. The bracts are also often tinged purple. The achenes are grey, tipped with bristles. The pappus is white with equal length hairs.
Lactuca serriola is known as the compass plant because in the sun the upper leaves twist round to hold their margins upright, pointing roughly south or north from the stem. The twist is a response to direct sun: plants grown in shade do not do it.
Similar to Mycelis muralis but showing more than 5 florets.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at a basal leaf. Prickly lettuce's ends in a triangular to ovate lobe, and its side lobes are narrow, about as wide as the gaps between them and not toothed (though they may be fringed with bristles) on the edge nearer the leaf base; wild lettuce's ends in a small, rounded lobe, and its side lobes are broader than the gaps and toothed along the outer edge and most of the inner edge. Prickly lettuce's leaves are grey-green; wild lettuce's are green and darken markedly as they dry, which prickly lettuce's do not. Up the stem, prickly lettuce's leaves tend to be held on their sides (in sun the upper ones twist to stand edge-up, roughly north–south), wild lettuce's flat. In seed, prickly lettuce's achenes are pale brown to grey, sometimes dark-spotted, with a body 2.5–3 mm long; wild lettuce's are very dark brown or black, with a body 4–5 mm long. Prickly lettuce's involucre is 8–13 mm long and wild lettuce's (11)–13–15 mm, so they overlap at 11–13 mm. Wild lettuce's stem carries pale spines up to 4 mm long, especially low down; prickly lettuce's is hairless or bristly below, so a spiny stem does not separate them. Both have spiny bristles under the leaf midrib, yellow heads in a loose branched spray and milky sap. Wild lettuce is not one to eat: eight people in Iran were taken to hospital after eating it (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Wild lettuce

lookalikes.howToTell: Turn over a rosette or lower leaf: prickly lettuce has stiff hairs and spiny bristles on the veins underneath, especially the midrib, while common pūhā's leaves are hairless, their only spines the small ones tipping the marginal teeth. Prickly lettuce's upper leaves become hairless, so check the lower ones, and young lettuce plants can lack the midrib bristles. Prickly lettuce's stem is hairless or carries coarse bristles up to 3–4 mm long low down; common pūhā's is hairless. Prickly lettuce carries numerous narrow, cylindrical heads in a loose, much-branched spray; sow thistle heads are usually larger. In seed, prickly lettuce's achenes have a pale beak about as long as the body, under the white pappus; common pūhā's have no beak. The involucre does not separate them: 8–13 mm long in prickly lettuce, 10–15 mm in common pūhā. Both have milky sap, lobed leaves that clasp the stem and yellow heads of strap-shaped florets. Common pūhā is edible: its leaves are widely eaten as greens.
lookalikes.name: Pūhā / Sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: Prickly edges do not separate them: prickly sow thistle's leaf margins have prickly-spined teeth and prickly lettuce's are finely toothed to bristly. Turn a rosette or lower leaf over instead: prickly lettuce has stiff hairs and spiny bristles on the veins underneath, especially the midrib, while prickly sow thistle's leaves are hairless. Prickly lettuce's upper leaves become hairless, and young lettuce plants can lack the midrib bristles. Prickly sow thistle's leaves are firm, more or less shiny and usually green; prickly lettuce's are grey-green. Prickly sow thistle's stem is hairless; prickly lettuce's is hairless or carries coarse bristles up to 3–4 mm long low down. In seed, prickly sow thistle's achenes are winged and have no beak; prickly lettuce's have a pale beak about as long as the body. The involucre does not separate them: 8–13 mm long in prickly lettuce, 10–15 mm in prickly sow thistle. Both have milky sap, lobed leaves that clasp the stem and yellow heads of strap-shaped florets. Prickly sow thistle is edible: it is recorded as a popular Māori food (pūhā tiotio).
lookalikes.name: Prickly sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the florets in a head: wall lettuce has 5 or fewer, prickly lettuce usually more (12–20). Under the head, wall lettuce's bracts are in two distinct rows, a few very short outer ones and a row of linear inner ones; prickly lettuce's are in more than two rows of gradually changing length. Wall lettuce is hairless, its lower leaves stalked and lyre-shaped with a large triangular or kidney-shaped, three-lobed end lobe and 1–3 pairs of small side lobes; prickly lettuce's lower leaves taper to the base and carry stiff hairs and spiny bristles on the veins beneath, especially the midrib. Wall lettuce's achene is shortly beaked; prickly lettuce's beak is about as long as its body. Both have milky sap and small yellow heads in a loose, branched spray. Wall lettuce's leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they can taste extremely bitter (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Wall lettuce

preparation.text: Pick the young leaves from the rosette, while the plant is very young and tender, before the prickles harden. Raw, they go in a mixed salad with milder greens and a good dressing; trim off the spines first. As a pot-herb they need very little cooking. Bitter leaves should be blanched or boiled, but they stay bitter, and the lines of prickles on the midrib and leaf edges soften only slightly. In Spain the leaf rosettes and the lower part of the stem were gathered before flowering and boiled briefly, and the leaves were also stewed or eaten in salads. The young shoots are cooked like asparagus. The unopened flower buds are much less bitter than the leaves and can be nibbled raw.

recipes.method: Written for wild lettuces in general; the author says prickly lettuce is good to eat only when very young in spring, before the prickles harden. 225 g tender prickly lettuce leaves, picked from the stems and washed; 30 g (2 tablespoons) butter; 250 ml (1 packed cup) finely chopped spring onion leaves; 1 stalk of rhubarb, finely sliced (about 115 g); 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable or chicken stock; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt, or to taste; 250 ml (1 cup) buttermilk. Serves 2 as a meal or 4 as a starter. Boil the leaves in a large pot of water for 2–3 minutes, until still bright green but tender at the midrib; drain, refresh at once in cold water, squeeze dry and chop. In the pot, cook the spring onion and rhubarb in the butter over medium-low heat until the rhubarb is soft, about 5 minutes; add the stock, bring to a simmer and turn off the heat. Let it cool a little, then blend with the chopped leaves until very smooth, salt to taste and chill. Serve with 60 ml (¼ cup) buttermilk drizzled over each bowl and swirled in. Instead of the rhubarb, add 15 ml (1 tablespoon) lemon juice or a handful of raw sorrel leaves in the blender.

summary.text:
Lactuca serriola, also called prickly lettuce, milk thistle (not to be confused with Silybum marianum, also called milk thistle), compass plant, and scarole, is an annual or biennial plant in the tribe Cichorieae within the family Asteraceae.
Lactuca serriola is native to Europe, Asia, and North Africa, and has become naturalized elsewhere.
It has a slightly fetid odor and is commonly considered a weed of orchards, roadsides and field crops. It is the closest wild relative of cultivated lettuce (Lactuca sativa L.).
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Auckland, Bay of Plenty, Waikato, Hawke's Bay, Wairarapa, Wellington; South Island: Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago. Naturalised from Eurasia and North Africa, first recorded in 1914.
The genus name is from the Latin lac, milk, for the white juice. Lactuca scariola is treated as a synonym.
One plant can produce up to 100,000 seeds, which are spread by the wind, and it is a serious weed of grain crops in Australia.

warnings: Eat it in moderation: large quantities upset the stomach, and the mature plant is mildly toxic. The latex may be toxic.

The milky sap contains lactucarium, which acts like a feeble opium; there is little in young plants and most when the plant comes into flower (prickly lettuce has less than wild lettuce). Do not take the sap or the flowering plant as a medicine without a skilled practitioner: even normal doses cause drowsiness, excess causes restlessness, and an overdose can kill through cardiac paralysis.

identification.text:
Erect or spreading shrub up to about 5 m tall; bark black, branchlets divergent. Leaves coriaceous, patent or reflexed, sessile to very shortly petioled, glaucous below, 6–15–(20) × 0·5–1 mm.; margins more or less recurved, ciliolate; apex with fine pungent tip about 1 mm long; veins 3–7, branched above. Inflorescence of solitary axillary flowers on recurved peduncles about 5 mm long. Bracts imbricate, ovate-oblong, investing peduncle, up to about 1 mm long. Flowers 3–4 mm long; calyx-lobes ovate-oblong, about 3 mm long, ciliolate. Corollatube hardly longer than calyx, whitish green; lobes spreading, whitish green, acute or subacute, usually glabrous on upper surface. Fruit white to pink to red to crimson to dark purple; 4–7–(9) mm. diameter, globose; locules 5.

identification.text:
A large cactus up to about 5 m tall, often with a thick cylindrical trunk; larger plants droop. The stem segments (pads) are flattened and egg-shaped, up to about 30 cm long, and attached at the narrow end. Spines come out one to six together from the areoles, which also carry numerous glochids (tiny barbed bristles). Yellow flowers up to 7 cm across grow on the edges of the pads. The fleshy fruit is up to 7.5 × 3.5 cm and can be yellow, orange or red. A wild plant collected at Himatangi Beach had no spines.
Told from drooping prickly pear (O. monacantha), the commoner wild prickly pear in New Zealand, by its blue-green stems, up to six spines in each cluster and completely yellow flowers: drooping prickly pear has green stems, never more than two spines per cluster and red-tinged flowers. Robust cactus (O. robusta) has 1–12 spines per cluster and almost completely round segments, up to 40 cm across.

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the spines in each cluster on the pads: drooping prickly pear never has more than two, prickly pear has one to six, so clusters of three or more point to prickly pear, while ones and twos do not separate them. Drooping prickly pear's stems are green and its yellow flowers have a red tinge or a red stripe on the outside of the outer petals; prickly pear's stems are blue-green and its flowers completely yellow. The fruit does not reliably separate them: drooping prickly pear's is reddish purple, prickly pear's can be yellow, orange or red. Both are large cacti of beaches and coastal places, up to about 5 m tall, with flat egg-shaped pads up to about 30 cm long and a drooping habit when large. Drooping prickly pear's ripe fruit is eaten.

preparation.text: The small spines on the fruits are removed by rubbing them on an abrasive surface or sweeping them through the grass. Before consumption, they are peeled. The young pads are sliced into strips, skinned or unskinned, and cooked; they are watery and very mucilaginous, with a texture and flavour like green beans. Handle pads with gloves or tongs, and twist the fruit off the pads with tongs. Burning the glochids off the fruit over a gas flame gives the flesh a slightly smoky taste. To clean a pad, hold it with tongs over newspaper and pare the spines off with a potato peeler, out of any draught, as the finest spines can become airborne; then roll up the newspaper and throw it away. Slice off the knobs that carry the spines and glochids, outdoors so they do not cling to the kitchen bench, or burn the glochids off over a gas flame or with a kitchen torch; the thick skin protects the fruit or pad underneath. Harvest the pads young and tender.

recipes.method: 25–30 prickly pears (about 2 litres of pulp); 200 ml lemon juice; 1.5 kg sugar; a 3 cm piece of ginger, cut crosshatched; 30 g pectin. Wearing good gloves, twist the fruit off the pads with tongs. Turn each fruit over a gas flame until every surface is scorched and the prickles are burnt off. Halve the fruit lengthwise, scoop out the seeds with a teaspoon and keep them, flatten the halves and gently scrape the flesh from the skin, then blend it. Press the seeds through a sieve with a spoon or the back of a plate until what is left is a paste, add the juice to the flesh, and strain the pulp through a sieve to remove all the seeds. Mix the pectin with the lemon juice, add the sugar and ginger, and stir it into the pulp; the squeezed lemon skins can go in too. Bring to the boil in a large heavy-based pan, stirring regularly, then boil rapidly for 3 minutes, to 105 °C on a jam thermometer. To test the set, put a teaspoon of jam on a plate chilled in the freezer or a spoon chilled in iced water: after 2–3 minutes it should be set. Pour into clean jars heated in a 100 °C oven for a few minutes. It is best after a few months.
recipes.title: Prickly pear jam

recipes.method: 6 young cactus pads (nopales); 1 white onion, thinly sliced; 2 tablespoons canola or other vegetable oil; ¼ teaspoon salt. Cover the bench with newspaper, hold each pad with tongs and peel off the spines with a potato peeler, out of any draught; roll up the newspaper carefully and throw it away. Rinse the pads and cut them into 1 cm squares. Heat the oil over a medium heat and sauté the pads for 13 minutes, until they colour a little and most of the liquid has evaporated. Add the onion and salt and cook until the onion is soft and translucent but not brown. Adjust the salt and serve straight away.
recipes.title: Nopalitos sautéed with onion

recipes.method: Makes 1.5 litres. 50 g water kefir grains; 80 g cane sugar; 1.2 litres water; 1 dried fig; 2 tablespoons lemon juice; 2 prickly pears; 10 sprigs coriander. Dissolve the sugar in the water in a fermentation jar and add the grains, fig and lemon juice. Leave at room temperature for 24–48 hours, until the fig rises to the surface, then strain, keeping the grains for the next batch. Wearing gloves, peel the prickly pears, purée them and divide between two bottles with 5 coriander sprigs in each, then top up with the kefir. Leave at room temperature for about 24 hours, until it is as fizzy as you like, then refrigerate. The fruit carries a lot of yeast and makes the kefir much fizzier: open the bottles carefully and keep them cool. A little grated lime zest in the glass is optional.
recipes.title: Prickly pear and coriander water kefir

summary.text:
Opuntia ficus-indica, the Indian fig opuntia, fig opuntia, or prickly pear, is a species of cactus that has long been a domesticated crop plant grown in agricultural economies throughout arid and semiarid parts of the world.
It belongs to the cactus family, Cactaceae, and is also called Barbary fig or Indian fig. Native to Mexico, it was brought to New Zealand as an ornamental and was first recorded as naturalised here in 2000. Wild plants have been recorded in Canterbury, Hawke's Bay, Nelson and Manawatū–Whanganui. Herbarium specimens come from Waipara in North Canterbury, where young plants had grown from broken pieces, from a green-waste dump at Himatangi Beach, and from a river cliff in Whanganui below houses it had probably escaped from. It spreads by pieces of stem and by seed, which people, birds and gravity disperse. Auckland Council's Regional Pest Management Plan lists it, with drooping prickly pear (Opuntia monacantha) and robust cactus (O. robusta), for sustained control across the whole region. It is not on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds, unlike drooping prickly pear. Bay of Plenty Regional Council lists prickly pear cacti (Opuntia spp.), naming this species and drooping prickly pear as the two common naturalised ones, as advisory pest plants, which it does not require landowners to control.

warnings: The pads and fruit carry tufts of tiny barbed bristles (glochids) as well as spines. They come away at a touch, stick in the skin, are hard to see and remove, and can cause considerable discomfort.

identification.text:
Like pūhā but the leaves are dark, glossy and edged with stiff spiny teeth that actually prick, and the leaf bases wrap around the stem in rounded, curled lobes. Yellow dandelion-like flowers, and the same milky sap when snapped.
Prickly sow thistle is variable: some plants come close to common pūhā (Sonchus oleraceus) in leaf shape and colour and have few prickles, and those can be told apart with certainty only by the seed — smooth between the ribs in prickly sow thistle, finely wrinkled crosswise in pūhā.
Sow thistles are not true thistles: their flower heads are made only of strap-shaped florets and the plant is full of milky latex, while true thistles (Cirsium) have heads of tubular florets and no latex. Prickly sow thistle's spines are much less fierce than a true thistle's.

lookalikes.howToTell: Prickly sow thistle's leaves are firm and somewhat shiny, with prickly-spined teeth on wavy margins, and its upper leaves clasp the stem with rounded lobes. Common pūhā (Sonchus oleraceus) has soft leaves with small spine-tipped teeth, and its clasping leaf bases have pointed lobes. Rounded clasping lobes do not separate prickly sow thistle from native pūhā (Sonchus kirkii), whose upper leaves also clasp the stem with more or less rounded lobes; S. kirkii's leaves are thick, dull and blue-grey, with toothed margins that are not spiny. Prickly sow thistle is variable, and plants close to common pūhā in leaf shape and colour, with few prickles, can be separated from it with certainty only by the achenes. In seed, prickly sow thistle's achenes are winged with smooth spaces between the ribs; S. oleraceus's are not winged and are finely wrinkled crosswise; S. kirkii's are winged, so the seed does not separate it from S. kirkii. Common pūhā is edible: its leaves are widely eaten as greens.
lookalikes.name: Pūhā / Sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: New Zealand sow thistle's leaves are thick, dull and blue-grey, with toothed margins that are not spiny; prickly sow thistle's (Sonchus asper) are firm, more or less shiny and usually green (rarely blue-grey), with prickly-spined teeth. Both have upper leaves that clasp the stem with rounded lobes, and both have winged achenes, smooth between the ribs, so neither the leaf base nor the seed separates them. New Zealand sow thistle's taproot is swollen at the top; prickly sow thistle's taproot is not described as swollen. New Zealand sow thistle is edible: its leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they are tougher and more bitter than common pūhā's.
lookalikes.name: New Zealand sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: Perennial sow thistle lives for years and spreads by creeping roots; prickly sow thistle (Sonchus asper) is an annual or biennial with a taproot. Perennial sow thistle's flower heads are 3–5 cm wide; prickly sow thistle's are 1.5–2.5 cm. Perennial sow thistle's involucre is 15–18 mm long and its bracts carry tangled short white hairs and long yellow glandular bristles (an Australian description allows hairless bracts too); prickly sow thistle's is 10–15 mm, its bracts hairless or rarely with tangled white hairs and sparse long pale glandular hairs. Prickly sow thistle's leaf teeth are prickly-spined; perennial sow thistle's margins are coarsely toothed and are not described as prickly. Both clasp the stem with rounded lobes, so the leaf base does not separate them. In seed, perennial sow thistle's achenes have 5 ribs on each face, are not winged and are closely wrinkled; prickly sow thistle's have 3 ribs, are winged, and are smooth between the ribs. Perennial sow thistle is edible: its young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Perennial sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: Prickly edges do not separate them: prickly sow thistle's leaf margins have prickly-spined teeth and prickly lettuce's are finely toothed to bristly. Turn a rosette or lower leaf over instead: prickly lettuce has stiff hairs and spiny bristles on the veins underneath, especially the midrib, while prickly sow thistle's leaves are hairless. Prickly lettuce's upper leaves become hairless, and young lettuce plants can lack the midrib bristles. Prickly sow thistle's leaves are firm, more or less shiny and usually green; prickly lettuce's are grey-green. Prickly sow thistle's stem is hairless; prickly lettuce's is hairless or carries coarse bristles up to 3–4 mm long low down. In seed, prickly sow thistle's achenes are winged and have no beak; prickly lettuce's have a pale beak about as long as the body. The involucre does not separate them: 8–13 mm long in prickly lettuce, 10–15 mm in prickly sow thistle. Both have milky sap, lobed leaves that clasp the stem and yellow heads of strap-shaped florets. Prickly lettuce's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they are bitter (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Prickly lettuce

lookalikes.howToTell: Prickly edges do not separate them: prickly sow thistle's leaf margins have prickly-spined teeth and wild lettuce's are toothed to bristly. Wild lettuce's stem carries pale spines up to 4 mm long, especially low down; prickly sow thistle's stem is hairless. Turn a leaf over: wild lettuce has spiny bristles under the midrib, often on the side veins too; prickly sow thistle's leaves are hairless. Young lettuce plants can lack the midrib bristles. In seed, wild lettuce's achenes are very dark brown or black, with a body 4–5 mm long and a pale beak about as long; prickly sow thistle's are pale brown, 2.5–3 mm long, winged and without a beak. The involucre does not separate them: (11)–13–15 mm long in wild lettuce, 10–15 mm in prickly sow thistle. Both have milky sap, lobed leaves that clasp the stem and yellow heads of strap-shaped florets. Wild lettuce is not one to eat: in Morocco a person died after eating wild lettuce mistaken for common sow thistle, and eight people in Iran were taken to hospital after eating it (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Wild lettuce

preparation.text:
Cook as for pūhā — boil and change the water to cut the bitterness. Wear gloves to pick; the spines soften once cooked.
To eat the stems, bruise them and wash out the bitter milky juice first; peeled, they can be eaten raw like celery.
Leaves picked too old can stay prickly even after cooking.

recipes.method: 5 prickly sow thistle shoot tips per person; creamy salted butter. Pick the shoot tips just as the flower buds start to appear, allowing 5 tips per person. Steam them for about a minute and serve with creamy salted butter.
recipes.title: Steamed prickly sow thistle tips with butter

recipes.method: Written for common sow thistle (Sonchus oleraceus) in Croatia; the recipe names prickly sow thistle as edible too, and any edible greens can stand in. Makes 6 fritters (2–3 portions). 140 g sow thistle leaves; 2 tbsp water or 1 tbsp oil; 250 g cooked chickpeas, with 150 ml of their cooking liquid (aquafaba); 100 g spelt flour; a pinch of baking soda; a pinch of salt; a pinch of black pepper or other spices; 1–2 tbsp oil for frying. Wash and coarsely chop 140 g leaves. Heat 2 tbsp water or 1 tbsp oil in a pan over low to medium heat, add the leaves and cook until tender, a minute or two. Drain 250 g cooked chickpeas, keeping 150 ml of their cooking liquid (aquafaba). Whisk the aquafaba with 100 g spelt flour, a pinch of baking soda and a pinch of salt. Mash the chickpeas with a fork, mix in the cooked leaves and a pinch of black pepper or other spices, then stir in the batter. Heat 1–2 tbsp oil in a pan (or use a dry non-stick pan) over low to medium heat, spoon in ladlefuls and cook 2–3 minutes a side, until golden-brown on both sides.
recipes.title: Sow thistle and chickpea fritters

summary.text:
The spinier cousin of pūhā, glossy and sharp-edged. Just as edible once cooked; just less pleasant to pick.
Sonchus asper is native to Europe, North Africa, and western Asia. It has also become naturalised on other continents and is regarded as a noxious, invasive weed in many places. It was first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1870.

warnings: Roadside and verge plants are routinely sprayed. Pick from ground you know.

identification.text: Annual or short-lived perennial with green or brownish procumbent or decumbent branched stems often forming large mats. Petioles to c. 2.5 cm long, ± puberulent. Lamina 0.5–4–(6) × 0.3–2.25–(3) cm, sometimes larger on vegetative shoots, ovate, triangular-ovate, to rhombic, glabrous above except for midrib, sometimes puberulent on veins below, sometimes glabrate; base cuneate; apex obtuse to acute. Inflorescence a terminal spike, often interrupted; lateral branches below with short lateral spikes in upper leaf-axils. Bracteoles 1–1.5–(2) mm long, ovate, keeled, green, glabrous. Tepals 2–3, scarcely > bracteoles, oblong, linear-oblong, or oblong-spathulate, keeled, mucronate. Fruit ellipsoid, compressed, smooth, indehiscent, with 3 longitudinal lines, 1.5–2× perianth when mature. Seed 0.8–1–(1.1) mm diameter, broadly obovoid, dark brown, only occupying part of lower 1/2 of capsule.

summary.text:
Prostrate amaranth is a mat-forming annual or short-lived perennial of the amaranth family (Amaranthaceae), probably from tropical America and introduced to New Zealand.
It was first recorded wild here in 1896. In the North Island it is locally common to abundant from the Waikato southwards and less common northwards to North Auckland; in the South Island it is common or very common in Nelson, Marlborough and northern and central Canterbury, and less common southwards to Otago.

warnings: Its leaves accumulate nitrates, which are toxic in high doses. Amaranths, as a genus, concentrate nitrates in their leaves when grown on nitrogen-rich soil, especially where chemical fertilisers are used, so do not eat plants from fertilised ground.
Its record as food comes from South American books only. No New Zealand record, plant-database entry or record of Māori use of it as food was found.

identification.text:
Rosa gallica is a deciduous shrub forming large patches. The slender, straight prickles are various in size and frequency in this species. The leaves are pinnately-compound, with three to seven bluish-green leaflets. The flowers are clustered one to four together, on glandular pedicels. Each flower has five or more petals, sometimes producing double corollas. The flowers are fragrant and deep pink. The hips are globose to ovoid, 10–13 mm diameter, and orange to brownish.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Deciduous, erect shrub to about 1.5 m high, densely suckering and forming low thickets; stems many, sometimes with glandular hairs; armature of occasional, narrow, almost straight prickles and more abundant acicles. Leaves with 2-3 pairs of leaflets; petiole 20-55 mm long, usually with eglandular hairs, often with glandular hairs also, sometimes glabrate; stipules […] glabrous or with a few eglandular hairs, with numerous marginal glandular hairs. Lamina of leaflets (15)-25-60 × (10)-15-35 mm, broadly elliptic, glabrous and usually deep green and slightly shining above, hairy on lower part of midrib and veins beneath, otherwise glabrous, somewhat rugose; margins 1-2-serrate, with glandular hairs; base rounded or slightly subcordate; apex rounded or obtuse to acute. Flowers 1-3, double, 50-90 mm diameter, fragrant; pedicels usually with numerous glandular hairs and some acicles, occasionally glabrate. Sepals ovate, acute to long-acuminate, tomentose inside, with few to numerous small glandular hairs outside; outer sepals pinnatifid to pinnatisect with linear lobes. Petals about 20-30 mm long, broadly obovate, rose, crimson or purplish rose. Styles free, slightly exserted, hairy. Fruit not seen.
The double or semi-double flowers are 5–7 cm across, and fruit is not formed or only sparingly. Glandular hairs on the young shoots, flower stalks and calyx are never so dense that they look mossy.
The apothecary rose ('Officinalis') has spreading thorny stems to about 1 m. Its leathery, oval to elliptic leaflets are smooth and dull green above and hairier beneath. The strongly scented, semi-double, rose-pink to light red flowers are borne singly or two to four together.
