preparation.text: Scatter the petals over salads as a garnish, make them into jam, crystallise them or preserve them in syrup, or dry them to flavour tea, drinks and cakes. Rose water is made by cold-infusing the petals. Pick freshly opened flowers early in the morning and pluck the petals, removing leaves, insects and debris. For drying, pick on a dry day before the flowers are fully open, remove the stamens and dry the petals quickly so they keep their colour and scent; store them in a tin and use within four months. The white base of each petal is slightly bitter and is traditionally trimmed off. Petals contain no pectin, so jam needs added pectin. Rose water can also be made by simmering the petals until their colour fades. Sugared petals keep in the freezer.

recipes.method: Written for apothecary roses (Rosa gallica) and 'Charles de Mills'. Ingredients: 4 cups (1 litre) rose petals, cleaned and pressed down into the cup; 4 cups (1 litre) sugar; 2 cups (500 ml) cold water; juice of 2 lemons; 1 envelope liquid pectin; 2 tablespoons (30 ml) rose water, optional. Put the petals in a large bowl, mix in the sugar by hand, cover tightly and leave in a cool spot for 4 hours so the petals sweat. Tip into a large saucepan, add the water and stir until the sugar dissolves, then add the lemon juice. Heat over medium heat until it boils (about 10 minutes), stirring so it does not scorch, and boil for 1 minute. Add the liquid pectin, return to a rapid boil for 2 minutes and test the set; take off the heat when it gels and stir in the rose water if using. Skim off foam, ladle into clean half-pint (about 250 ml) jars leaving about 6 mm (1/4 inch) headspace, seal, and process in a water-bath canner for 10 minutes plus the altitude adjustment. The source gives the yield as 5 half-pint jars in the text but says 7 jars in the method. For jelly, strain through cheesecloth before adding the pectin.
recipes.title: Rose petal jam

recipes.method: Written with apothecary rose petals. Ingredients: 1 pasteurised egg white beaten with a little water (or simple syrup, or prepared meringue powder); granulated sugar; fragrant, unsprayed rose petals, rinsed and patted dry; a small watercolour brush. Cut off and discard the white base of each petal, which is bitter. Paint both sides of each petal with the egg wash, sprinkle both sides with sugar, and leave on baking or wax paper to dry overnight. Petals done with syrup hold their shape less well than with egg wash. Use as decorations on cakes, puddings, sweets, biscuits and pastries; store in the freezer if not using straight away.
recipes.title: Sugared rose petals

recipes.method: Written with apothecary rose petals. Ingredients: fragrant, unsprayed rose petals, rinsed and patted dry; sugar; a clean jar with a seal. Cut off and discard the white base of each petal. Sprinkle sugar over the bottom of the jar, then a layer of petals, and keep layering sugar and petals until the jar is full. Store in a cool, dark cupboard for several weeks; remove the petals before use if you like. Use to flavour or top pastries, biscuits and sweets, stir into tea or lemonade, or sprinkle over scones and shortbread.
recipes.title: Rose sugar

recipes.method: Written for unsprayed garden roses generally (damask roses suggested), not for this species. Ingredients: 1/2 cup (125 ml) fresh rose petals; 1–1 1/2 cups (250–375 ml) water. Pick the roses early in the morning. Put the petals in a saucepan, pour the water over, cover and bring to the boil, then simmer until the colour fades from the petals. Leave covered to cool completely, strain through cheesecloth or a fine strainer into a dark bottle, and keep in the fridge for up to several weeks. Use in cakes and biscuits or add to herbal tea.

summary.text:
Rosa gallica, the Gallic rose, French rose, or rose of Provins, is a species of flowering plant in the rose family, native to southern and central Europe eastwards to Turkey and the Caucasus.
R. gallica was one of the principal shrub roses cultivated by the early European settlers and soon became popular with Maori people also. Its suckering habit meant that it was easy to propagate. Several cultivars were grown; all those that have persisted and have been collected wild have fragrant, rather stiffly erect, flattened and double flowers and rarely form hips, even in cultivation. By far the commonest cultivars now wild are 'Charles de Mills', with crimson petals when first expanded, and 'Anais Segales' with purple-crimson petals from early anthesis. 'Officinalis' and 'Antonia d'Ormois' have also been recorded wild.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: North Auckland, Auckland; South Island: Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago. It is almost certainly more widely distributed than indicated above.
Rosa gallica was one of the first species of rose to be cultivated in central Europe.
It was naturalised in New Zealand by 1966. Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and wild, with herbarium records from Canterbury and North Auckland. It is one of the parents of the cabbage rose and the moss rose.
Its cultivar 'Officinalis' is the apothecary rose, also called the Red Rose of Lancaster and Old Red Damask; it was International Herb of the Year in 2012 and is sold by New Zealand rose nurseries.

warnings: Use petals only from roses that have not been sprayed. Florist roses, and roses sprayed with pesticides or fungicides, are not safe to eat.
If hips are found, the layer of hairs around the seeds just beneath the flesh irritates the mouth and digestive tract; remove it before eating.
Rose thorns can cause an infection in some people if they scratch the skin or break off in it.

identification.text:
The cap is 15–55 mm diam., broadly conic, expanding to broadly umbonate to more or less flattened, with edges becoming slightly upturned and often splitting; dry; lacking veil remnants; dark brown to yellow-brown, striate (radially lined) to edge, hygrophanous, drying to pale yellow-brown to straw-coloured; staining greenish-blue with damage or age; flesh white. The gills are adnate (broadly attached to the stem), close, greyish yellow-brown, maturing dark violaceous, with a conspicuous pale narrow margin. The stipe is 35-100 x 1.5–5 mm, cylindric, finely pruinose in the upper part and silky-fibrillose near the base, white, yellow or pinkish purple brown, with brownish flesh. Veil cortinoid and poorly developed, disappearing as caps mature. All parts staining deep greenish-blue or blackish-blue with damage. Spore print violet brown.
Spores measure (6.5-)7-9.5 x 4–5.5 x 3.5-4.5 μm, 8.1 x 4.9 x 4.3 μm average, ovate in face view, elliptic-ovate in side view; brown-walled and smooth, 0.5 μm thick with apical pore; Basidia 20-28 x 4.5-6 μm, cylindric, with 4 spores, clamped; Cheilocystidia 15-32 x 4-8 μm, ventricose-rostrate (swollen and uneven with a beak), with long, tapering, flexuous and sometimes bifurcate neck (forked in two), transparent, thin-walled, up to 12 μm long; Pleurocystidia 13-19 x 4.5-6 μm, scattered, similar to cheilocystidia but with shorter neck, up to 4.5 μm.

The legal claims on this page, checked against the Act rather than a summary of it. Schedule 1 (Class A controlled drugs) lists Psilocine, Psilotsin and Psilocybine by name and formula. Section 7(1)(a) makes it an offence to procure, possess, consume, smoke or otherwise use a controlled drug, and section 7(2)(a) sets the penalty at 'imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months or to a fine not exceeding $1,000 or to both where a Class A controlled drug was the controlled drug' — which is what this entry's warning says. Note that section 7(2) applies 'without prejudice to any liability under section 6', the dealing provision, which carries life imprisonment for a Class A drug: the same handful of mushrooms can be charged either way depending on quantity and circumstance. Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, read on legislation.govt.nz 06/10/2026. https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1975/0116/latest/DLM436100.html

The fungus itself is a prohibited plant, which is a second offence this page did not mention. Section 2 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 defines 'prohibited plant' to include 'any fungus of the genera Conocybe, Panaeolus, or Psilocybe from which a controlled drug can be produced or which contains a controlled drug' — so cultivating it is an offence under section 9, separately from possessing it under section 7. summary.text:
Psilocybe aucklandiae is a species of agaric fungus in the family Hymenogastraceae. As a blueing member of the genus Psilocybe it contains the psychoactive compounds psilocin and psilocybin. It has been recorded from Waipoua in Northland, and in Australia as Psilocybe sect. Zapotecorum, which is likely phylogenetically similar or the same.
It is phylogenetically similar to or almost the same as Psilocybe zapotecorum from Mexico and South America. As noted by Guzman et al. (1991), "P. aucklandii is very similar to P. zapotecorum R. Heim emend. Guzman, which is common in Mexico and known from South America. The two species are barely distinguishable microscopically, although comparison with published descriptions (Guzman 1983) show that P. aucklandii may have slightly narrower pleurocystidia and slightly wider spores. Published illustrations of P. zapotecorum (Guzman 1983) appear to show that P. aucklandii is a less robust species."

warnings: Magic mushrooms, and the psilocybine and psilocine in them, are Class A controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. Picking or carrying one is possession of a Class A drug.

Maximum penalties are six months' imprisonment and/or a $1,000 fine for possession, and life imprisonment for supplying or manufacturing. This entry is here so you can recognise the species, not so you can collect it.

habitat.text: Fruit bodies grow scattered or in groups on the fallen, rotting wood of southern beeches (genus Nothofagus), and are often encountered near lakes and picnic grounds.

harvestEthics.text: Picking it is possession of a Class A drug. It fruits on fallen beech wood, which is habitat in its own right, so leave the log as you found it.

identification.text:
The cap is initially conical to bell shaped, but as the mushroom grows, it expands to become convex with a prominent umbo, and attains a diameter of 15–55 mm. The cap surface is dry to slightly tacky. Its colour is yellow-brown to orange-brown, often paler towards the margin, which has fine striations corresponding to the gills on the underside. The flesh is white. Gills have an adnexed attachment to the stem, and are pale greyish brown. The whitish stipe is 30–60 mm long by 2–4 mm wide. It is cylindrical, with a surface of pressed silky fibrils. The base of the stem is often brownish, with white rhizoids present. The veil of young fruit bodies is cortinate—resembling the cobweb-like partial veil found in Cortinarius species. As the mushroom grows, its remnants often remain visible on the stem, but it never forms a complete ring. Both the cap and the stem stain greenish-blue when damaged.
The spore print is dark purplish brown. Spores typically measure 7.5–9.5 by 5.5–6.5 by 4.5–5.5 μm, averaging 8.7 by 6.0 by 5.3 μm. Its shape in face view is ovate (egg-shaped) to roughly rhomboid, while viewed from the side it appears elliptical. The spore wall is brown, smooth, about 0.8–1 μm thick, and has a germ pore. The basidia (spore-bearing cells) are four-spored and somewhat club-shaped, tapering slightly to the base; they are clamped, and measure 25–31 by 7–8.5 μm.
The cheilocystidia (cystidia on the gill edge) have dimensions of 18–26 by 6–9 μm, and a shape ranging from ventricose-rostrate (broad in the middle and tapering to a beaklike neck) to mucronate (ending abruptly in a short sharp point). They are hyaline (translucent), thin-walled, and clamped, with necks that are 3–5 μm long. The pleurocystidia (cystidia on the gill face) are similar in shape to cheilocystidia, but narrower (4–8 μm wide), and usually have a shorter neck measuring 2.5–4 μm. The cap cuticle is a cutis (characterised by hyphae that run parallel to the cap surface) of long-celled, 2–3 μm diameter, gelatinised hyphae. The hypodermium (the tissue layer under the cap cuticle) is filamentous, comprising 4–6 μm diameter cells with pale brown walls. Clamps are common. The subhymenium (the tissue layer under the hymenium) is poorly developed, containing 2–4 μm diameter cells with pale brown walls. The tissue comprising the hymenophore is made of short cylindric, 3–6 μm diameter hyaline cells.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small brown mushrooms with a bump in the centre of the cap, often more or less pointed, and both grow on fallen, rotting wood - P. makarorae on southern beech, and wood nipple fungus mainly on beech wood too - so shape and habitat do not separate them. Cap colour overlaps too: P. makarorae is yellow-brown to orange-brown, and wood nipple fungus ochre-yellow to bay or honey-coloured. Damage the cap or stem: P. makarorae stains greenish-blue, and no blue staining is recorded for wood nipple fungus. Look at the stem: wood nipple fungus has a well-developed ring, though in its close relative the ring often disappears with age. P. makarorae has only cobwebby veil remnants and never a complete ring. A spore print may help: wood nipple fungus drops cinnamon-brown, and Psilocybe prints generally run lilac-brown to dark purple-brown, though rusty-brown prints are known in at least one species. Wood nipple fungus has not been tested for toxins, but it sits in the group that includes the deadly Galerina marginata and probably carries the same amatoxins.

summary.text:
Psilocybe makarorae is a species of psilocybin mushroom in the family Hymenogastraceae.

Psilocybe makarorae is known only from New Zealand. The reported collection locations have been on both the North and South Islands, including the Bay of Plenty, Westland District, Central Otago, and Dunedin.
Like all Psilocybe species, it is saprobic, and feeds on decomposing organic matter.
Based on the bluing reaction to injury, P. makarorae is presumed to contain the psychedelic compounds psilocybin and psilocin. Although the potency is not known definitely, Paul Stamets suggests that, based on the degree of the bluing reaction, they are "probably moderately potent".
Psilocybe makarorae is related to Psilocybe weraroa and Psilocybe subaeruginosa, though not as closely as they are to each other.

warnings: Magic mushrooms, and the psilocybine and psilocine in them, are Class A controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. Picking or carrying one is possession of a Class A drug.

Maximum penalties are six months' imprisonment and/or a $1,000 fine for possession, and life imprisonment for supplying or manufacturing. This entry is here so you can recognise the species, not so you can collect it.

habitat.text:
Psilocybe subaeruginosa grows solitary to gregarious from wood debris in Australian native forests, pine plantations and is occasionally observed growing on dung. The species is also known from Australian native and Eucalyptus forests, and famously in New Zealand on wood chip.
In New Zealand: most often in gardens mulched with wood chip, and now and then on rotted wood in native bush.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Psilocybe subaeruginosa' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
The cap averages 12–50 mm in diameter. It is conical to conic-convex with slightly inrolled edges when young, and becomes convex, often slightly upturned, sub-gibbous, or sometimes with a small acute umbo. It is slightly tacky. There may be veil remnants at the margin when young. Coloured yellow-brown to orange-brown, paler towards the margin, which is a little striate, hygrophanous, fading in drying to pallid biscuit brown or pale orange-yellow. The cap stains greenish blue with age or handling and the flesh inside is whitish. The gills are moderately close, pale smoky brown when young, violet-brown or brownish fuscous in age, with narrow pale edges, slightly ventricose, in three series, the middle reaching halfway to the stipe, with an adnate or broadly adnexed attachment and lines sometimes running down the stipe. The stipe is 25–70 × 2–3.5(-5) mm, tall and slender, equal or slightly wider towards the cap, finely vertically lined, mealy at the top with fine fibrils below, the base somewhat swollen or becoming a mass of mycelium, hollow inside, cartilaginous, pale whitish streaked with dark greyish brown, staining greenish blue, flesh brownish. A white cortinate partial veil soon disappears, leaving traces as a raised area around the upper stipe.
Taste and odour are farinaceous and the spore print is purple brown.
The cheilocystidia are 17–29 x 5.5–11 μm, hyaline, fusoid-ventricose, subpyriform or mucronate, often with an elongated neck at the apex which is 2–4.5 μm.  The pleurocystidia measure 22–47 x 6–16 μm and is shaped like the cheilocystidia and also hyaline. The spores are smooth, subellipsoid, with an apical germ pore, measuring (10) 13.2–14.3 (15.4) x 6.6–7.7 x 6–7.5 μm.

lookalikes.howToTell: Never separate these on one character. The Galerina is deadly-suspect and both grow on rotting wood. Look for a ring. The common NZ Galerina has a well-developed ring on the stem, though in the related Galerina marginata the ring may disappear. P. subaeruginosa has only a short-lived cobweb-like veil that leaves at most a raised zone on the upper stem. Check the gills: cinnamon to rusty brown in the Galerina, pale smoky brown ageing to violet-brown in P. subaeruginosa. P. subaeruginosa's cap and stem stain greenish blue with age or handling. In the related Galerina marginata the gills do not bruise and the flesh does not change colour when cut. Cap shape and colour do not separate them. Both have yellowish to orange-brown caps, and P. subaeruginosa can also have a small pointed centre. A spore print confirms it: P. subaeruginosa purple-brown, Galerina cinnamon-brown. The Galerina's toxicity is unknown, but it sits in the group containing the deadly Galerina marginata and is thought likely to contain amatoxins.
lookalikes.name: Wood nipple fungus

lookalikes.howToTell: Both grow on wood-chip mulch in New Zealand gardens and both drop a purple-brown spore print, so neither the place nor the print separates them. Wine cap is an edible mushroom, often grown on purpose in wood-chip beds. It is far bigger and heavier: a wine-red to tan cap 4–14 cm or more across, a stem 1–2.5 cm thick, a thick ring split like a cogwheel underneath, and firm white flesh that does not change colour. Psilocybe subaeruginosa is small and slender, with a yellow-brown to orange-brown cap 1–5 cm across, a stem 2–3.5 mm thick, a veil that soon disappears, and cap and stem that stain greenish blue when handled.

So whether the NZ plants under this name are the Australian species at all is open; native is not supported, and neither is introduced. summary.text:
Psilocybe subaeruginosa is a species of agaric fungus in the family Hymenogastraceae described in 1927 and known from Australia and New Zealand.

It is common in southern parts of Australia from April to August. It is recorded as present in New Zealand, but DNA sequencing of collections so far indicates P. allenii and P. cyanescens there as well as P. subaeruginosa. Its tendency to live on wood chips, as well as on plants and in soil, contribute to the likelihood that these were the materials it was transplanted to the Northern Hemisphere on, and the transplantation led to a decrease in genetic diversity. This concept also led to the idea that they exist in disturbed areas, rather than natural.
As a blueing member of the genus Psilocybe it contains the psychoactive compounds psilocin and psilocybin.

warnings: Magic mushrooms, and the psilocybine and psilocine in them, are Class A controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. Picking or carrying one is possession of a Class A drug.

Maximum penalties are six months' imprisonment and/or a $1,000 fine for possession, and life imprisonment for supplying or manufacturing. This entry is here so you can recognise the species, not so you can collect it.

edibleParts.text: Young leaves and shoots. Older leaves turn tough and very bitter.

sources: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
Waste ground, gardens, roadsides, cultivated paddocks. Almost anywhere disturbed.
Waste land, grassland, coastal rocks, dunes and beaches, forest margins, crevices in walls and footpaths, gardens, pasture, roadsides, railway land.

harvestEthics.text: Abundant and introduced. Take freely, but leave plants that are flowering and setting seed on land you want to keep harvesting.

identification.text: Rosette of deeply lobed leaves with soft prickly margins, clasping the stem. Stems and leaves exude a white milky sap when broken. Small yellow dandelion-like flowers on a branched stem. The native S. kirkii is fleshier and coastal.

lookalikes.howToTell: Prickly sow thistle's leaves are firm and somewhat shiny, with prickly-spined teeth on wavy margins, and its upper leaves clasp the stem with rounded lobes. Common pūhā (Sonchus oleraceus) has soft leaves with small spine-tipped teeth, and its clasping leaf bases have pointed lobes. Rounded clasping lobes do not separate prickly sow thistle from native pūhā (Sonchus kirkii), whose upper leaves also clasp the stem with more or less rounded lobes; S. kirkii's leaves are thick, dull and blue-grey, with toothed margins that are not spiny. Prickly sow thistle is variable, and plants close to common pūhā in leaf shape and colour, with few prickles, can be separated from it with certainty only by the achenes. In seed, prickly sow thistle's achenes are winged with smooth spaces between the ribs; S. oleraceus's are not winged and are finely wrinkled crosswise; S. kirkii's are winged, so the seed does not separate it from S. kirkii. Prickly sow thistle is edible: it is recorded as a popular Māori food (pūhā tiotio), and its young leaves are described as mild-flavoured; bruise the stems and wash out the bitter milky juice.
lookalikes.name: Prickly sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: New Zealand sow thistle's leaves are thick, dull and blue-grey, with toothed margins that are not spiny; common pūhā's (Sonchus oleraceus) are soft, edged with small spine-tipped teeth, and range from mid or dark green to blue-grey, so leaf colour alone does not separate them. New Zealand sow thistle's upper leaves are not lobed and clasp the stem with more or less rounded lobes; common pūhā's upper leaves are usually lobed and clasp the stem with pointed lobes. New Zealand sow thistle lives two years or more from a taproot swollen at the top; common pūhā is an annual. In seed, New Zealand sow thistle's achenes are winged and smooth between the ribs; common pūhā's are not winged and are finely wrinkled crosswise. New Zealand sow thistle is edible: its leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they are tougher and more bitter than common pūhā's.
lookalikes.name: New Zealand sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: Perennial sow thistle lives for years and spreads by creeping roots; common pūhā (Sonchus oleraceus) is an annual with a taproot. Perennial sow thistle's flower heads are 3–5 cm wide; common pūhā's are 1.5–2.5 cm. Under the flower head, perennial sow thistle's involucre is 15–18 mm long and its bracts carry tangled short white hairs and long yellow glandular bristles (an Australian description allows hairless bracts too); common pūhā's involucre is 10–15 mm long and its bracts are usually hairless, rarely with a few pale bristles. Perennial sow thistle's upper leaves clasp the stem with rounded lobes; common pūhā's clasping lobes are pointed. In seed, perennial sow thistle's achenes are 3.5–3.8 mm long with 5 ribs on each face; common pūhā's are 2.5–3 mm with 3 ribs. Neither is winged. Perennial sow thistle is edible: its young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Perennial sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: Turn over a rosette or lower leaf: prickly lettuce has stiff hairs and spiny bristles on the veins underneath, especially the midrib, while common pūhā's leaves are hairless, their only spines the small ones tipping the marginal teeth. Prickly lettuce's upper leaves become hairless, so check the lower ones, and young lettuce plants can lack the midrib bristles. Prickly lettuce's stem is hairless or carries coarse bristles up to 3–4 mm long low down; common pūhā's is hairless. Prickly lettuce carries numerous narrow, cylindrical heads in a loose, much-branched spray; sow thistle heads are usually larger. In seed, prickly lettuce's achenes have a pale beak about as long as the body, under the white pappus; common pūhā's have no beak. The involucre does not separate them: 8–13 mm long in prickly lettuce, 10–15 mm in common pūhā. Both have milky sap, lobed leaves that clasp the stem and yellow heads of strap-shaped florets. Prickly lettuce's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they are bitter (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Prickly lettuce

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild lettuce's stem carries pale spines up to 4 mm long, especially low down; common pūhā's stem is hairless. Turn a leaf over: wild lettuce has spiny bristles under the midrib, often on the side veins too, and its upper leaves often have them on the midrib; common pūhā's leaves are hairless, their only spines the small ones tipping the marginal teeth. Young lettuce plants can lack the midrib bristles. Wild lettuce carries numerous narrow, cylindrical heads in a loose, much-branched spray; sow thistle heads are usually larger. In seed, wild lettuce's achenes are very dark brown or black, with a body 4–5 mm long and a pale beak about as long; common pūhā's are brown, 2.5–3 mm long and have no beak. The involucre does not separate them: (11)–13–15 mm long in wild lettuce, 10–15 mm in common pūhā. Both have milky sap, lobed leaves that clasp the stem and yellow heads of strap-shaped florets. Wild lettuce is not one to eat: in Morocco a person died after eating wild lettuce mistaken for common sow thistle, and eight people in Iran were taken to hospital after eating it (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Wild lettuce

lookalikes.howToTell: Feel the stem: smooth hawksbeard's carries slender white crinkly hairs, usually with stouter pale crinkly hairs as well, at least low down; common pūhā's stem is hairless. Turn a leaf over: smooth hawksbeard's leaves are often hairless, but may carry pale hairs about 0.5 mm long along the middle underneath, rarely on both surfaces; common pūhā's leaves are hairless. A hairy midrib points to hawksbeard, but a hairless leaf does not rule it out. Common pūhā's leaf margins have small spine-tipped teeth and are more prickly than smooth hawksbeard's. Smooth hawksbeard's upper stem leaves are stalkless, narrowly triangular to linear and not lobed, with teeth especially at the slightly eared base; common pūhā's upper leaves are usually lobed, with a broad triangular end lobe, and clasp the stem with pointed lobes, though they are sometimes unlobed. Young pūhā leaves tend to have a large end lobe, unlike hawksbeard's. Smooth hawksbeard's heads are bell-shaped, with inner bracts 5–8 mm long carrying short white tangled hairs and usually a few dark glandular hairs; common pūhā's involucre is 10–15 mm long and top-shaped to cylindrical, its bracts usually hairless, rarely with a few pale bristles. Smooth hawksbeard's yellow florets often have a pink or red stripe on the outer face; no stripe is recorded for common pūhā's. In seed, smooth hawksbeard's achenes are spindle-shaped, 10-ribbed and 2–2.5 mm long; common pūhā's are weakly flattened, 3-ribbed on each face, finely wrinkled crosswise and 2.5–3 mm long. Neither achene is beaked. Yellow heads on a leafy, branched stem do not separate them, nor do the white pappus, rosette leaves that can both be deeply lobed, or height (smooth hawksbeard (5)–15–45–(100) cm, common pūhā 50–120 cm). Smooth hawksbeard's leaves are eaten in Tuscany, Italy, where they are recorded as laxative (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Smooth hawksbeard

preparation.text:
Strip the leaves, boil and discard the water to cut the bitterness — traditionally boiled with pork bones. Young shoots can be eaten raw in small amounts.
Traditionally the stems were also pounded to squeeze out the bitter white juice and the stalks eaten raw, or the pūhā was cooked with eel or wild pig in an umu.
It is generally picked from early spring to midsummer and grows more bitter into autumn; cutting plants back in autumn often prolongs the picking. To prepare it, rub the stems and leaves together under running water, take off woody stalks and discoloured leaves, and use the leaves with the medium to thin stalks; the coarsest stalks can go into stock.

recipes.method: Written for pūhā; the recipe does not name the species. Serves 4. 2 kg pork bones; a large bunch of pūhā, rinsed well, flowers removed; 2 carrots, cut in chunks; 2 kūmara, cut in chunks; 4 small potatoes; 1 tbsp salt for the pot; 1 tsp salt for the vegetables. Put the bones in a large pot, cover with cold water, add the tablespoon of salt and bring to the boil with the lid off. Simmer gently for about an hour, until the meat is close to falling off the bone. Add the pūhā, put the lid on and cook for 15 minutes. Meanwhile steam or gently boil the carrots, kūmara and potatoes with the teaspoon of salt in a separate pot until soft. Plate the pork, pūhā and vegetables and pour a little of the stock over. The author gives watercress as an alternative to pūhā.
recipes.title: Boil-up with pūhā

recipes.method: Written for pūhā by New Zealand chef Geoff Scott as the topping for pork and pūhā sliders; the page does not name the species. 500 ml (2 cups) pūhā, washed; 60 ml (¼ cup) macadamia nuts; 1 garlic clove, grated; 45 ml (3 Tbsp) olive oil; 15 ml (1 Tbsp) grated parmesan. Cook the pūhā in boiling salted water for 30 seconds, drain it and tip away the water. Plunge it into iced water, then squeeze out as much water as you can. Blitz it to a paste in a food processor with the macadamias, garlic, olive oil and parmesan. The author spreads it on sliders of pork patties, rocket, bacon mayonnaise and pan-fried kūmara.
recipes.title: Pūhā and macadamia pesto

recipes.method: Written for sow thistle growing in Pennsylvania; the blog does not name the species. Serves 2. 225 g pork shoulder (pork butt); 1 tbsp soy sauce (or teriyaki sauce); 1 tbsp white cooking wine; a pinch of sugar; salt and pepper; a pinch of cornflour; half a shopping bag of sow thistle leaves; oil; ½ tsp grated ginger; 1 coarsely chopped spring onion. Slice 225 g pork shoulder (pork butt) into thin strips about 5 cm long and 3 mm thick. Toss with 1 tbsp soy sauce (or teriyaki sauce), 1 tbsp white cooking wine, a pinch of sugar, salt, pepper and a pinch of cornflour, cover and leave in the fridge for about 30 minutes. Clean and coarsely chop half a shopping bag of leaves. Heat oil in a frying pan and fry ½ tsp grated ginger on high heat for a few minutes, then add 1 coarsely chopped spring onion for a few minutes more. Add the pork and stir-fry for about 4 minutes, until no longer pink. Turn the heat to medium, add the leaves and keep stirring, adding a little water if needed, until tender, about 5 minutes. The source says chicken or beef can replace the pork.
recipes.title: Stir-fried sow thistle and pork

recipes.method: Written for sow thistle growing in Pennsylvania; the blog does not name the species. Serves 2. Half a shopping bag of sow thistle leaves; finely chopped garlic; oil; salt, pepper and nutmeg. Clean and coarsely chop half a shopping bag of leaves. Fry finely chopped garlic in oil for a few minutes, add the leaves and stir until tender. Season with salt, pepper and nutmeg.
recipes.title: Sautéed sow thistle

recipes.method: Written for sow thistle growing in Pennsylvania; the blog does not name the species. Serves 4. Half a shopping bag (packed) of sow thistle leaves; a quarter of a red onion, thinly sliced; olive oil; a clove of garlic, minced; about 60 ml chicken stock; salt, pepper and nutmeg; a couple of tablespoons of crumbled goat cheese; some pine nuts. Rinse and chop half a shopping bag (packed) of leaves, boil for a few minutes and drain. Sauté a quarter of a red onion, thinly sliced, in olive oil in a large pan for 3 minutes, add a minced clove of garlic and cook a minute more. Turn the heat to medium and add the leaves a handful at a time, stirring, as they shrink. Add about 60 ml chicken stock, cover and simmer for 10 minutes. Season with salt, pepper and nutmeg, then stir in a couple of tablespoons of crumbled goat cheese and some pine nuts.
recipes.title: Sow thistle with red onion, goat cheese and pine nuts

recipes.method: Written for sow thistle growing in Pennsylvania; the blog does not name the species. A stand-in for Hawaiian pork laulau, using big older leaves in place of taro. Serves 2. Two 115 g pieces of pork shoulder; salt and pepper; 1–2 garlic cloves, sliced; big old sow thistle leaves; 1 stalk of lemongrass, cut in pieces; 2 cans of coconut milk; rice, fish sauce and/or mirin, and fried onions, to serve. Season two 115 g pieces of pork shoulder with salt, pepper and slices of garlic (1–2 cloves). Lay each on a bed of big old leaves, fold the leaves into a parcel and tie with cooking twine. Put the parcels in a slow cooker with 1 stalk of lemongrass, cut in pieces, pour over 2 cans of coconut milk and cook on low for at least 8 hours, turning the parcels after 4. Serve with rice, drizzled with fish sauce and/or mirin, and fried onions.
recipes.title: Pork wrapped in sow thistle leaves, slow-cooked in coconut milk

recipes.method: Written for smooth sow thistle (Sonchus oleraceus) in Britain. Serves 4. 100 g hazelnuts; 60 g sow thistle leaves; 2 garlic cloves; 15 g parsley; ¼ tsp sea salt; 2 tsp Korean red chilli flakes; 4 tbsp olive oil; 10 chopped cherry tomatoes. Soak 100 g hazelnuts in boiling water for an hour, then drain and rinse well. Soak 60 g leaves in cold water for an hour, then strip the blades off the larger leaves and discard their stalks; small leaves can go in whole, as their stalks are not yet stringy. Crush 2 garlic cloves. Pulse the hazelnuts, shredded leaves, 15 g parsley, the garlic, ¼ tsp sea salt, 2 tsp Korean red chilli flakes and 4 tbsp olive oil in a food processor until chopped and thick, not runny. Spoon over 10 chopped cherry tomatoes and fork them through. Serve as a sauce with grilled meat, or with nut loaf, baked tempeh, roast vegetables or potatoes.
recipes.title: Sow thistle and hazelnut salsa

recipes.method: Written for common sow thistle (Sonchus oleraceus) in Croatia. Makes 6 fritters (2–3 portions). 140 g sow thistle leaves; 2 tbsp water or 1 tbsp oil; 250 g cooked chickpeas, with 150 ml of their cooking liquid (aquafaba); 100 g spelt flour; a pinch of baking soda; a pinch of salt; a pinch of black pepper or other spices; 1–2 tbsp oil for frying. Wash and coarsely chop 140 g leaves. Heat 2 tbsp water or 1 tbsp oil in a pan over low to medium heat, add the leaves and cook until tender, a minute or two. Drain 250 g cooked chickpeas, keeping 150 ml of their cooking liquid (aquafaba). Whisk the aquafaba with 100 g spelt flour, a pinch of baking soda and a pinch of salt. Mash the chickpeas with a fork, mix in the cooked leaves and a pinch of black pepper or other spices, then stir in the batter. Heat 1–2 tbsp oil in a pan (or use a dry non-stick pan) over low to medium heat, spoon in ladlefuls and cook 2–3 minutes a side, until golden-brown on both sides.
recipes.title: Sow thistle and chickpea fritters

recipes.method: Written for young common sow thistle (Sonchus oleraceus) leaves 5–10 cm long, picked while they are not bitter. 1–2 handfuls of young sow thistle leaves; butter or oil; a generous splash of beef stock or water; a pinch of nutmeg; 1 tsp flour; salt and pepper; another knob of butter. Heat butter or oil in a pan, add 1–2 handfuls of leaves and stir until coated. Add a generous splash of beef stock or water, cover and simmer for 5–10 minutes. Stir in a pinch of nutmeg, 1 tsp flour, salt and pepper, then melt in another knob of butter over low heat.
recipes.title: Buttered young sow thistle leaves

recipes.method: The author's greens were dock, onion weed, nasturtium, plantain, baby wild mustard, dandelion, sow thistle and a violet leaf. 2 crushed garlic cloves; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 500 ml (2 cups) firmly packed wild greens, sliced very thinly; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper; 125 ml (½ cup) roughly chopped pistachios, walnuts, almonds or brazil nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp hearts, pumpkin or sunflower seeds; and 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil, hemp seed oil or a mix. Makes about 750 ml (3 cups). To slice the greens, sort them into similar shapes, bunch and twist a few leaves together and slice as thinly as you can — this suits the tougher, stringier ones such as plantain, mustard and dock. Toss everything together. Good as a side or salad, in a wrap or sandwich, or with pasta, risotto, eggs, or sausages and mash. It keeps at least 4 days in a sealed jar in the fridge.
recipes.title: Weedolata (wild-greens gremolata)

recipes.method: The author's greens were puha, sow thistle, nasturtium, onion weed, wild fennel, oxalis, wild mustard and wild celery. 1 diced onion; 1 potato, scrubbed and diced; 2 sliced garlic cloves; 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 1.3 litres water; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked pepper; extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil, to serve; edible weed flowers. Serves 4. Cut the vegetables and greens to similar sizes. Fry the onion in the oil for a minute, then add the potato and garlic (the method also adds fennel bulb and celery stalks, which the ingredient list leaves out) and fry for another minute. Add the water, cover, bring to the boil and simmer until the potato is soft. Add the greens with the salt and yeast and cook for 3 minutes, until just tender — added at the end, they keep their colour. Blend until smooth (push it through a sieve if your blender isn't powerful), season with the pepper and more salt if needed, and serve drizzled with extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil and scattered with edible weed flowers.
recipes.title: Wild greens soup

recipes.method: Written for watercress and puha together. Balsamic reduction (makes about 600 ml; you need 45 ml): 1 litre balsamic vinegar; 150 g unrefined cane sugar; 1 rosemary stalk; half a diced red onion (optional). Maple walnuts: 125 ml (½ cup) walnuts; 5 ml (1 tsp) ground cinnamon; 30 ml (2 tbsp) maple syrup; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt. Salad (serves 4): half a finely sliced red onion; 45 ml (3 tbsp) balsamic reduction; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1 orange, peeled and segmented; 1 litre (4 cups) watercress; 250 ml (1 cup) young puha leaves, roughly chopped; 4 finely sliced radishes; 250 ml (1 cup) sprouts (ruruhau, mizuna, alfalfa or broccoli; optional); 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil. Raw watercress: use only watercress that is bought or cultivated, or picked from water with no sheep or cattle grazing above it (see the watercress entry's liver fluke warning). Balsamic reduction: stir until the sugar dissolves, bring to the boil, then simmer, stirring often, until reduced by half. Cool, remove the rosemary and bottle it. Maple walnuts: toast 125 ml (½ cup) walnuts on a lined tray in a 180 °C oven for 10 minutes, then stir through 5 ml (1 tsp) ground cinnamon, 30 ml (2 tbsp) maple syrup and 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and return to the oven for 2 minutes; cool. Salad (serves 4): scrunch half a finely sliced red onion with 45 ml (3 tbsp) balsamic reduction and 5 ml (1 tsp) salt in a large bowl and leave it while you prepare the rest, adding each to the bowl without mixing: 1 orange, peeled and segmented; 1 litre (4 cups) watercress, the stems finely chopped (they can be stringy) and the leaves roughly chopped; 250 ml (1 cup) young puha leaves, roughly chopped; 4 finely sliced radishes; and 250 ml (1 cup) ruruhau, mizuna, alfalfa or broccoli sprouts (optional). Drizzle with 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil, add the walnuts, toss and serve.
recipes.title: Watercress and puha salad

recipes.method: The author's greens, picked in spring, were cleavers, chickweed, herb Robert, stinging nettle (the page does not say which nettle), onion weed, speedwell, pūhā and lemon balm; she gives no amounts for them. She blends the nettle raw; the nettle page says to cook it, so blanch it first. Chop the greens into the blender with 2 cabbage leaves, stalks removed, the juice of 1 large grapefruit, 125 ml (½ cup) kombucha and 500 ml (2 cups) water, and blend until the greens are broken down. Add 2 small bananas or 1 large, 1 apple, 1 kiwifruit (hairs scrubbed off, top and bottom trimmed), 1 whole orange, and 15 ml (1 tbsp) chia seeds and 5 ml (1 tsp) pumpkin seeds ground in a coffee grinder, and blend again. Decorate it with onion weed and viola flowers and a piece of orange.
recipes.title: Spring clean smoothie

identification.text:
Glabrous or occasionally slightly hairy annual herb of spreading habit; stems procumbent. Leaves with slender petioles to 1/2 as long as blades. Lamina 1.25–5.5–(9) × 0.75–4–(7) cm (some plants with leaves only a few mm long), broadly ellipsoid, broadly ovate or obovate; base cuneate; apex emarginate or retuse, with prominent midrib prolonged to form an apical mucro. Inflorescence a terminal spike, usually also with short lateral spikes in the upper leaf axils. Bracteoles < 1 mm long at anthesis, oblong-ovate, acute, < 1/2 perianth, with green keel. Tepals 3, 1–1.5 mm long, to 2 mm long at fruiting, ± oblong; keel green; apex acute. Fruit subglobular, indehiscent, usually smooth, sometimes slightly wrinkled, slightly > perianth. Seed 1–1.2 mm diameter, globose, dark brown, occupying nearly all fruit cavity.
Plants vary greatly in stature and leaf size, but all specimens seen have at least most leaves with emarginate or retuse apices.

preparation.text:
Use the leaves raw or cook them as spinach. Cook the seed; it can stand in for a cereal in cakes and porridge. The seed is very small, about 1.2 mm across; cooked whole it becomes very gelatinous, and some of it is hard to crush in the mouth and passes through undigested.
The whole flower head can be blended into a smoothie.

recipes.method: Written for purslane with amaranth (in other posts the author names green and purple amaranth, Amaranthus viridis and A. lividus), sweet basil and galinsoga. A handful of purslane sprigs, stems and leaves, washed; 3–4 sprigs of amaranth, with or without seed heads; sprigs of sweet basil; 2 sprigs of galinsoga; 3 garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) sunflower seeds; olive oil; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt. Process the sunflower seeds, add the garlic, then the leaves and the salt, with 30 ml (2 tbsp) olive oil, and more if needed to bind it. The author spreads it on cucumber slices over cashew mayonnaise.

recipes.method: Written for green or purple amaranth (Amaranthus viridis or A. lividus), with galinsoga, dandelion and lemon balm. A bunch of amaranth; several stems of galinsoga; 2 or more dandelion leaves; 2 beetroot leaves; a small bunch of lemon balm; 375–500 ml (1½–2 cups) water; 1 banana; 1 kiwifruit; 1 peeled tangelo; 250 ml (1 cup) blueberries; 15 ml (1 tbsp) chia and a sprinkle of pumpkin seeds, ground in a coffee grinder with 2 cardamom pods or 2 star anise. Blend the greens in the water until well broken down, then add the fruit and the ground seeds and spice and blend again. Drop a few whole blueberries into the glass to chew on.

summary.text:
Purple amaranth is a sprawling annual weed of the amaranth family (Amaranthaceae), introduced to New Zealand.
Its accepted name is Amaranthus blitum subsp. oleraceus; it was long known in New Zealand as Amaranthus lividus, and has also been recorded here as A. oleraceus and A. lividus var. ascendens. It is widespread in tropical and subtropical regions and was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1870. It is fully naturalised but uncommon: scattered throughout the North Island, especially in towns and cities of warmer areas, and rare in the north of the South Island.

warnings: Amaranths, as a genus, concentrate nitrates in their leaves when grown on nitrogen-rich soil, especially where chemical fertilisers are used, so do not eat plants from fertilised ground.

Not every amaranth in New Zealand is food: redroot amaranth (Amaranthus retroflexus), one of the plants called redroot, is recorded as poisonous here. Purple amaranth is hairless or only slightly hairy, sprawls along the ground, and has most of its leaves notched at the tip with the midrib running out into a small point; A. retroflexus is hairy and upright, to about 1 m, with blunt leaf tips.

identification.text:
Apparently acaulous perennial, but with underground stem above bulb; bulb narrow-ovoid; outer scales dark brown or blackish, more or less shining, viscid, with inconspicuous nerves. Leaves radical, 3-foliolate. Petiole (1)–2–10–(20) cm long, hairy; stipules 3–7 mm long, appearing as a broad wing, sometimes ciliate. Lamina of leaflets sessile, somewhat unequal, the terminal larger and 10–35–(45) × 1–37–(45) mm, broadly obovate, sometimes broader than long, glabrous above, hairy beneath and densely marked with short, black, glandular dashes when dry; margins long-ciliate; base cuneate; apex rounded; lateral leaflets somewhat asymmetric at base. Flowers solitary, erect; peduncles 1–11 cm long, hairy. Bracts 2–3 mm long, linear-subulate, usually in lower 1/2 of pedicel; calli 0. Sepals 6–7.5 mm long, elliptic, with longitudinal black streaks when dried, with dense long, white cilia, otherwise glabrous; calli 0. Corolla forming a deep cup 2.5–4 × 2.5–3 cm, with a lower, tubular part; petals 2–4 cm long, more or less suborbicular, glabrous except for ciliate margins; lower part yellowish; limb usually rose or purplish, sometimes white flushed pink outside. Stamens at 2 levels, glabrous; filaments with broad membranous wing, often almost to apex in shorter stamens. Styles shorter than or longer than longer stamen whorl, hairy. Capsule not seen. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually without a stalk, sitting among the top leaves, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. It has leafy stems, erect or lying along the ground, and its leaflets usually carry a crescent-shaped mark towards the base. Purple wood sorrel: no stem shows above ground and the leaves all rise from the base. Each flower stalk, 1–11 cm long, carries a single flower forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base. Out of flower, do not rely on leaflet size (red clover's c. 15–40 mm long, purple wood sorrel's 10–35 mm, up to 45 mm), leaflet tips (both can be rounded or blunt) or hairs (both usually have hairy leaf stalks and leaflet undersides).
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel has leafy stems, spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils; it is the only oxalis in New Zealand with bulbils above ground. It is almost hairless. Its leaflets are 4–16 mm long, mostly broadly heart-shaped, with an irregular row of orange dots just inside the edge, and each sepal has two prominent orange dots at its tip (in some plants they look light brown). Each flower stalk, 2.5–12 cm long, carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Purple wood sorrel has no stem above ground: its leaves all rise from the base. Its leaf stalks and the undersides of its leaflets are hairy, the leaflet edges fringed with long hairs, and its leaflets are 10–35 mm long (up to 45 mm), broadly obovate with a rounded tip, sometimes slightly notched; the dots and streaks on them turn black when dry. Each flower stalk, 1–11 cm long, carries a single flower forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base; its sepals carry a dense fringe of long white hairs and have no orange dots at the tip. What does not separate them: both carry a single flower on each stalk, and the stalk lengths overlap. Petal length overlaps too, as either plant's petals can be as short as 10 mm, so only petals longer than 2.2 cm point to purple wood sorrel. Leaflet length overlaps between 10 and 16 mm. Look for a leafy, branched stem and orange dots on the sepal tips, which only pale-pink wood sorrel has. Pale-pink wood sorrel's leaves, flowers and stems are eaten (see its entry); do not eat purple wood sorrel.
lookalikes.name: Pale-pink wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Shamrock wood sorrel grows from a short, thick, fleshy rhizome, rough with old leaf-base scars, and has no bulbs or bulbils. Its flowers come (4)–7–35 together in a branched cluster on a stalk up to about 35 cm tall, its petals 9–16 mm long, usually rose with darker veins, rarely white. Its leaflets are broadly heart-shaped with a narrow notch up to a third of their length and a band of orange dots along the edge, and its bracts and sepals carry orange dots. Purple wood sorrel grows from a narrow egg-shaped bulb with dark brown or blackish, shining, sticky outer scales. Each flower stalk, 1–11 cm long, carries a single flower forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base. Its leaflets are broadly obovate with a rounded tip, sometimes slightly notched, and its bracts and sepals have no orange dots. What does not separate them: both have no leafy stem, with all the leaves rising from the base, and both are hairy. A single flower does not rule out shamrock wood sorrel, whose clusters can hold anything from 1 to at least 30 flowers. Purple wood sorrel's petals can be as short as 10 mm, so only petals longer than 16 mm point to purple wood sorrel. Shamrock wood sorrel's leaves and flowers are eaten (see its entry); do not eat purple wood sorrel.
lookalikes.name: Shamrock wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Pink shamrock carries 3–7 or 10–18 flowers in a cluster on a stalk up to 35 cm long, the cluster with long curly hairs, its petals 1.5–2 cm long, pink to rose. Its leaflets are broadly heart-shaped, two-lobed with a rather narrow notch, and finely dotted underneath with raised orange spots, especially round the edge, and each sepal has two (sometimes four) prominent orange dots at its tip. Purple wood sorrel carries a single flower on each stalk, 1–11 cm long, forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base. Its leaflets are broadly obovate with a rounded tip, sometimes slightly notched, and its sepals have no orange dots. What does not separate them: both have no leafy stem, with all the leaves rising from the base; both have leaflets hairy underneath; both grow from bulbs that make bulbils, though purple wood sorrel's outer bulb scales are dark brown or blackish, shining and sticky and pink shamrock's are brown. Leaflet length overlaps (pink shamrock 10–35 mm, purple wood sorrel 10–35 mm, up to 45 mm). Purple wood sorrel's petals can be as short as 10 mm, so petal length points to purple wood sorrel only when the petals are longer than 2 cm. Pink shamrock's leaves, leaf stalks, flowers and root are eaten (see its entry); do not eat purple wood sorrel.
lookalikes.name: Pink shamrock

lookalikes.howToTell: Fishtail oxalis carries about 5–15 (up to 20) flowers in an umbel-like cluster on a stalk about 10–50 cm tall, its petals about 1.2–1.5 cm long, pink. Its leaflets are broadly fishtail-shaped, shallowly and broadly two-lobed, 12–50 mm long and 18–80 mm wide, and its sepals are hairless, with two prominent orange dots at the tip. Purple wood sorrel carries a single flower on each stalk, 1–11 cm long, forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base. Its leaflets are broadly obovate with a rounded tip, sometimes slightly notched, with long hairs fringing the edges, and its sepals carry a dense fringe of long white hairs and have no orange dots. What does not separate them: both have no leafy stem, with all the leaves rising from the base; both grow from bulbs that make bulbils, though purple wood sorrel's outer bulb scales are dark brown or blackish, shining and sticky and fishtail oxalis's are brown or pale fawn-brown; and fishtail oxalis's leaflets have no orange dots or only faint ones, so leaflet dots do not help. Purple wood sorrel's petals can be as short as 10 mm, so petal length points to purple wood sorrel only when the petals are longer than 16 mm. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. The tests above that do not rest on leaflet shape or petal colour still hold for it. Fishtail oxalis's leaves, stems, flowers and bulbs are eaten (see its entry); do not eat purple wood sorrel.
lookalikes.name: Fishtail oxalis

That they look alike: SANBI PlantZAfrica, 'Oxalis purpurea' (Adam Harrower, Kirstenbosch NBG, December 2009; © SANBI, facts only), https://pza.sanbi.org/oxalis-purpurea, retrieved 16/10/2026 — it 'often occurs commonly in lawns (not to be confused with clover weed Trifolium pretense)'. Every test: Flora of New Zealand Online (Webb et al. 1988; CC BY 3.0 NZ), retrieved 16/10/2026: 'Oxalis purpurea', https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Oxalis-purpurea.html ('Apparently acaulous'; 'Lvs radical'; leaflets 10–35–(45) mm, apex rounded, hairy beneath; petiole hairy; 'Fls solitary'; peduncles 1–11 cm; corolla 'a deep cup'; petals 2–4 cm, 'lower part yellowish', limb 'usually rose or purplish, sometimes white flushed pink outside'), and 'Trifolium pratense', https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Trifolium-pratense.html (stems 'erect or decumbent'; leaflets c. 15–40 mm, 'usually obtuse', 'usually with a crescentic spot'; petioles and leaflet undersides usually moderately hairy; heads terminal, usually sessile; corolla 10–16 mm, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream). Ranges overlap: both are Exotic in New Zealand (Flora), and both habitat texts name grassy places, gardens and roadsides; SANBI says purple wood sorrel is 'most commonly found in lawns' in South Africa. Habitat: Plants of South Eastern New South Wales (Lucid), 'Oxalis purpurea', Where found, author Betty Wood, CC BY 4.0, https://apps.lucidcentral.org/plants_se_nsw/text/entities/oxalis_purpurea.htm, retrieved 16/10/2026 — first sentence verbatim; its Australian distribution ('Sydney district. Coastal. Occasionally elsewhere.') omitted. An Australian statement, not a New Zealand one. Tags grassland, urban, disturbed. Native-range facts, not quoted (© SANBI, cited on the card line): open, sunny soil; disturbed ground along the edges of paths and roads; most commonly in lawns. New Zealand fact, not quoted: Julia's Edible Weeds (cited below) saw it flowering through kikuyu in sandy soil and in a mown camp-ground lawn at Muriwai.

Summary sentences two and three: Wikipedia, 'Oxalis purpurea' (revision 1306452221; CC BY-SA 4.0), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxalis_purpurea, retrieved 16/10/2026, verbatim. Flora of New Zealand and Biota of New Zealand (https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/b7386169-5a69-4f1d-a212-c1f66cb6e0c9, retrieved 16/10/2026) give the New Zealand vernacular name 'Large-flowered oxalis'; Biota of New Zealand: Exotic, Wild (historic: Exotic, Cultivated).

SANBI (cited above) describes it as summer-dormant and winter-growing, its shoots appearing after the first good autumn rains. The months date the flowers; the leaves are up over the same season.

Infl. 7-26 cm long, an 8-15-flowered cyme, glabrous or hairy … Petals 9-15 mm long … whitish or very pale mauve-pink'; 'It is often confused with these 2 spp. [O. latifolia, O. debilis], but O. vallicola has paler fls'. summary.text:
Oxalis purpurea is a species of flowering plant in the woodsorrel family known by the common name purple woodsorrel. It is native to southern Africa, including South Africa, but it is known on most continents as an introduced species. It is cultivated as an ornamental plant.
In New Zealand: North Island: Auckland to Wellington, local; South Island: Nelson. A cultivation escape, naturalised from South Africa, first recorded in 1883.

warnings: Do not eat. It is toxic because of the oxalic acid it contains, and it has no reliable record as food.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand it grows on stony waste land, cultivated land, crops and gardens.
It also comes up in dry waste places, farm gateways, yards and bare ground, and in cracks in pavements, rocky crannies and gutters in towns. It prefers sunny, open places.

identification.text:
Glabrous taprooted annual herb. Stems reddish, prostrate to ascending, (5)–10–30–(45) cm long. Leaves alternate to subopposite, fleshy, shiny, often red-tinged, obovate to oblong, cuneately narrowed to a short petiole, obtuse to almost retuse, (5)–10–15–(30) × (2)–3–8–(10) mm; axillary hair-tufts short. Flowers shorter than 1 cm diameter, (1)–3–(7) in sessile terminal clusters soon overtopped by subapical branches, subtended by membranous, ovate-acuminate, pinkish bracts. Sepals green, hooded, overlapping, fleshy, falling at fruiting, 5 mm long. Petals yellow, soon falling. Stamens 6–15; anthers yellow. Style branches 3–6. Capsule 3–7 mm long, ovoid, circumscissile. Seeds many, ovoid, shining, dark red-black, finely tuberculate, 1 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

preparation.text: Young leaves go into salads; their mucilaginous quality also makes them a thickener for soups. Older leaves are cooked as a potherb. The taste is slightly sour and salty, and the leaves are crunchy and slippery. Cooked, it tastes a little stronger. Large or tough purslane can be blanched for a few seconds and cooled in cold water to tenderise it, though it changes colour; very thick stems are best left behind. The stems can be pickled in vinegar for winter. Boiling lowers the oxalate content and pickling lowers it a little (see warnings).

recipes.method: 1 small red onion, finely sliced; 30 ml (2 tbsp) pomegranate molasses; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; then 125 ml (½ cup) pitted green olives, 6 quartered tomatoes, 1 cucumber quartered lengthways and sliced, 250 ml (1 cup) finely chopped parsley and/or coriander, 5 sprigs of roughly chopped mint, 125 ml (½ cup) purslane tips and leaves, 125 ml (½ cup) roughly chopped walnuts, 15 ml (1 tbsp) sumac, 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked black pepper and 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil. Serves 4–6. Mix the onion, molasses, lemon and salt in a large bowl and leave it to marinate while you prepare the rest, adding each to the bowl as you go. Toss and serve.
recipes.title: Turkish-style salad with purslane

recipes.method: Written for purslane, with chickweed, parsley and mint. A small bunch each of purslane and chickweed; 4 parsley stems; 4 sprigs of fresh mint; 4 ripe plums; 1 banana; 250 ml (1 cup) blueberries; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk; 250 ml (1 cup) water. Blend the greens in the coconut milk and water, then add the fruit and blend again until smooth. Makes 1 litre.
recipes.title: Purslane smoothie

recipes.method: Written for purslane, with chickweed, parsley and calendula petals; the author gives no amounts. Tear leafy salad greens — lettuce, mizuna, rocket, chickweed, parsley — into a bowl and add chopped purslane, cherry tomatoes and alfalfa sprouts. Decorate it with heartsease pansy flowers and calendula petals, and dress it with lemon juice, olive oil and salt.
recipes.title: Purslane salad

recipes.method: Written for purslane stems. Fill a jar with chopped purslane stems and top it right up with raw apple cider vinegar. Let it sit, or poke it with a chopstick, to release the air bubbles, then close it with a piece of plastic under a metal lid, so the vinegar doesn't eat the metal and taint the pickle. Use it through the winter in salads or soups.
recipes.title: Pickled purslane

recipes.method: Written for purslane with amaranth (in other posts the author names green and purple amaranth, Amaranthus viridis and A. lividus), sweet basil and galinsoga. A handful of purslane sprigs, stems and leaves, washed; 3–4 sprigs of amaranth, with or without seed heads; sprigs of sweet basil; 2 sprigs of galinsoga; 3 garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) sunflower seeds; olive oil; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt. Process the sunflower seeds, add the garlic, then the leaves and the salt, with 30 ml (2 tbsp) olive oil, and more if needed to bind it. The author spreads it on cucumber slices over cashew mayonnaise.
recipes.title: Purslane and amaranth pesto

recipes.method: Written for purslane with watercress; the author says other greens can take the watercress's place. 225 g watercress; 225 g purslane; 2 large roma tomatoes; 60 ml (¼ cup) duck fat, or other poultry fat, lard or a flavourful oil; salt and black pepper; a few slices of jalapeño or serrano chilli (optional); 1 small garlic clove, minced; ¼ yellow onion, cut in 6 mm dice. Serves 4. Core the tomatoes, cut a cross in the other end, blanch them in boiling salted water for a minute or two, then chill them in iced water. Peel, halve and squeeze out the seeds, and cut them into 1 cm dice. In a 25–30 cm frying pan, heat the fat with the garlic, chilli and onion until the onion is translucent. Add the watercress, purslane and tomato and cook, stirring now and then, until the greens are well wilted. Season and serve straight away.
recipes.title: Braised purslane with tomatoes and duck fat

recipes.method: 115 g (500 ml, 2 cups) tender purslane, plus a few sprigs to garnish; 375 ml (1½ cups) sweet corn, roasted in the husk for 15 minutes at 175 °C, cooled and cut off the cob; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) freshly toasted and ground cumin seed; a few handfuls of cherry tomatoes; a few garlic scapes or spring onions; extra-virgin olive oil, lime juice, salt and pepper, chopped coriander and (optional) mint, all to taste. Serves 4. Heat a cast-iron pan until it smokes and char the tomatoes in it dry, 5–10 minutes, until they have black spots and are hot through; set aside. Char the scapes or spring onions the same way in large pieces, then slice them 6 mm thick. Mix everything and season boldly: it should be sweet, barely tart and herby. Garnish with purslane sprigs. To make it ahead, add the lime juice just before serving, as it discolours the greens. If the purslane is large or tough, blanch it for a few seconds first, cool it in cold water and dry it well.
recipes.title: Purslane and sweet corn salad

recipes.method: 85 g (about 375 ml, 1½ cups) washed and dried purslane, cut into 2.5 cm pieces, any larger tough stems removed; ½ a large cucumber; 1 large avocado; a small handful of sliced coriander, dill or mint; extra-virgin olive oil, lime or lemon juice, salt and black pepper, to taste. Serves 4. Quarter the cucumber lengthways, cut out the seeds, halve the quarters and cut them into 2.5 cm pieces. Cut the avocado into 1 cm cubes. Combine everything, season, check the citrus, herbs and salt, and serve cold; it starts to wilt after about 15 minutes. If the purslane is large or tough, blanch it for a few seconds first, cool it in cold water and dry it well.
recipes.title: Purslane, cucumber and avocado salad

recipes.method: 3 slices of good bread, preferably sourdough, 1.25 cm thick, left out overnight to go stale; 55 g red onion in 6 mm dice; 680 g ripe heirloom or other good tomatoes; 170 g cucumber (about half a large telegraph cucumber); 1 large garlic clove; salt and black pepper; 80 ml (⅓ cup) extra-virgin olive oil or sunflower oil; torn basil leaves; 140 g purslane tips, washed; champagne or another good vinegar, to taste; 115 g fresh mozzarella or burrata in 1 cm cubes (optional). Serves 6. Soak the onion in water. Core the tomatoes and cut them into rough 1 cm pieces; peel the cucumber, scrape out the seeds if it is mature, and cut it into 1.25 cm dice. Cut the crusts off the bread, toast it until crisp, let it cool, then rub it lightly with the garlic. Tear the bread into pieces the size of the tomato, combine everything and leave it for a few minutes so the juices soak into the bread. Toss, adjust the seasoning and serve.
recipes.title: Tomato and purslane panzanella

recipes.method: 285 g fresh purslane; 1 lemon, zest and juice; 45 ml (3 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil or sunflower oil; salt; roughly chopped soft herbs such as mint, coriander, dill or basil; 1 medium ripe tomato (about 170 g); feta to finish (the author gives no amount). Serves 6. Leave any very thick or dirty stems behind when you pick. Blanch the purslane in boiling salted water for about 60 seconds, until barely tender, then spread it on a tray to cool. Drain it well and chop it into rough 2.5 cm lengths. Dice the tomato small. Mix the purslane with the tomato, lemon, oil, herbs and salt, adjust the seasoning and finish with feta. Serve at room temperature or cool.
recipes.title: Blanched purslane salad with tomato, herbs and feta

Filled in the Caryophyllales fill round 07/11/2026: summary, habitat, edible parts, preparation, warnings, habitat tags and months. Sources, all retrieved 07/11/2026: Flora of New Zealand Series vol. Food Agric. Environ. 5(1): 124–128, abstract via US EPA HERO (https://hero.epa.gov/reference/511303/) — oxalate warning (raw not recommended for regular consumption by people prone to kidney stones; boiling −27%, pickling −16% total oxalate). Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga (https://rauropiwhakaoranga.landcareresearch.co.nz/names/5eba3799-c80c-4195-ab11-2ef5128cedf6) lists it under 'food plants - other' with no use text, so it is not counted as a record. The Wikipedia habitat text (world distribution and pre-Columbian America) is removed: the Flora covers New Zealand origin and habitat. The 'wetland' tag is removed: neither the Flora nor NZPCN puts it in wetlands, and it has no national wetland plant list rating; tags disturbed (waste land, cultivated land, bare ground) and urban (gardens, pavements, gutters) are added. The existing five recipes stay.

Months set to November–May in the fill round 07/11/2026: the leaves and stems of a frost-killed annual, eaten while the plant is up. Flora of New Zealand flowering and fruiting November–March (–April); Julia Sich: only in the heat of summer and autumn, killed by frost; iNaturalist NZ research-grade, non-captive observations Jan 91, Feb 100, Mar 71, Apr 68, May 14, Jun 2, Jul 1, Aug 4, Sep 2, Oct 3, Nov 7, Dec 45. The previous January–March was narrower than the evidence.

Looked at and not used in the fill round 07/11/2026: spurge (Euphorbia) as a lookalike — the only pages found naming purslane and spotted spurge as confused are US lawn-care and foraging blogs; University of Wisconsin Extension's spotted spurge page and UC IPM's spurge and purslane pest notes do not name the confusion. Spotted spurge (E. maculata) is naturalised in New Zealand (Flora vol. IV: locally common from Bay of Plenty and Waikato to Northland, Nelson and Christchurch, gardens and waste places, 'Possibly poisonous'), and nodding spurge (E. nutans, 'Poisonous') grows in Auckland and Bay of Plenty, but no trusted source names either as a purslane lookalike, so no card; the catalogue's petty spurge is not named as one either.

summary.text:
Portulaca oleracea (common purslane, also known as little hogweed, or pursley) is a succulent plant in the family Portulacaceae.
In New Zealand it is an introduced annual weed, also called wild portulaca, native to Europe and south-west Asia and first recorded as naturalised in 1869. It grows throughout the North Island, in Nelson, Canterbury and Otago in the South Island, and on the Kermadec Islands. It is common in the upper North Island and less common further south. It spreads over the ground only in the warmth of summer and autumn and is killed by frost. It is not listed as an environmental weed or in any regional pest management plan.

warnings: Purslane is high in oxalate, especially the leaves, so raw purslane is not recommended for regular eating by anyone prone to kidney stones. Boiling the leaves, stems and buds cut their total oxalate by about 27%, and pickling by about 16%, in one study; in the same study larger leaves held 40% more oxalate than small ones.

edibleParts.text: Fruit, cooked: made into jelly, jam, preserves and quince paste (quince cheese), stewed, baked or roasted, added to cooked apples, and used in cider, liqueurs and other alcoholic drinks. It is also poached in syrup, pot-roasted whole, and made into curd, marmalade and chutney. Fruit grown in warm climates can soften enough to eat raw, and a few varieties are eaten raw.

identification.text:
Large shrub or small tree up to 5–(8) m high and several m diameter when mature; trunk short or 0 and plants sometimes forming small suckering thickets; upper branches often arching; stems dark brownish red and felted when young. Petiole (4)–6–14 mm long; blade ovate to broad-elliptic, oblong or suborbicular, 30–80 × 25–50 mm, rounded to subacute at apex, obtuse at base, white-tomentose at first on upper surface, becoming glabrate and dull, white- to grey-tomentose below; margin entire; stipules lanceolate. Flowers 30–50 mm diameter. Sepals densely tomentose, persistent; lobes oblong, acute, glandular, sharply reflexed. Petals oblong, 12–25 mm long, rounded or slightly emarginate. Fruit pyriform or subglobose, usually 80–150 mm long, yellow, more or less finely tomentose, fragrant, with apical cavity. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Genus Cydonia (Flora of New Zealand): Flowers solitary and terminal on short, lateral, leafy shoots, 5-merous, bisexual, pedicellate, moderately large and showy. Petals more or less contorted in bud, suberect at anthesis, white to pink. Fruit a fleshy pome with leathery carpel wall and abundant stone cells in flesh; seeds many in each locule.
Pink buds open to large, cupped white or soft-pink flowers in spring. The fruit has a fuzzy white coat while green, and turns yellow and fragrant as it ripens.

lookalikes.howToTell: Flowering quince is a spiny shrub; quince is unarmed, or only rarely slightly spiny. Quince leaves have entire margins and are white- to grey-woolly beneath; flowering quince leaves are finely toothed, hairless, and more or less shining deep green above. Quince flowers sit singly at the ends of short leafy shoots, 30–50 mm across, with sharply bent-back, densely woolly sepals that stay on the fruit; flowering quince flowers come in clusters of (3)–4–5, 25–35 mm across, mostly before the leaves, with erect sepals. Quince fruit is usually 80–150 mm long and more or less finely downy; flowering quince fruit is up to 60 mm across, often misshapen and brown-speckled. Flower colour helps only at the red end: flowering quince can be white, pink or scarlet, quince white to pink. Height does not separate them (both are suckering shrubs that can form thickets, quince growing up to 5–(8) m and flowering quince up to 3–(4) m), and both fruits are yellowish and fragrant. Flowering quince fruit is eaten cooked, like quince.
lookalikes.name: Flowering quince

lookalikes.howToTell: Pear leaves are finely round-toothed, bright green, glossy and hairless above when mature, and only sometimes hairy beneath when young; quince leaves have entire margins and are white- to grey-woolly beneath. Pear flowers come in clusters of usually 5–10, white, with more or less purple anthers; quince flowers sit singly on short leafy shoots, 30–50 mm across, white to pink. Pear fruit is usually 40–80 mm long (longer in some cultivated plants), with green to yellow, sometimes brown skin, and is sweet when ripe; quince fruit is usually 80–150 mm long, yellow, more or less finely downy and fragrant, and stays hard when ripe. Shape does not separate them: both fruits can be pear-shaped or nearly round, both have gritty flesh, and size overlaps in cultivated pears. Pear fruit is eaten.
