preparation.text: Wipe or wash the down off the skin. For paste, peel, core and slice the fruit and cook it until tender; for jelly, chop it unpeeled and uncored, simmer it in water until it turns pink and soft, and strain off the juice. Long cooking with sugar turns the flesh pink to deep red. Ripe quinces stay hard but bruise easily. Pick the fruit once it has turned yellow and smells fragrant, or gather it as it drops; fruit that drops early while still green can still be cooked. Fruit left hanging into winter is damaged by frost. Raw quince is very hard, so cut it with a large sharp knife, and slice it just before cooking because the cut flesh browns quickly. Peeling is optional: the skin softens when cooked, especially if sliced thinly. The fruit is high in pectin, so jams and jellies set without added pectin. Store unblemished fruit in a single layer, not touching, somewhere cool, dark and airy and away from other fruit, which takes on its scent; it keeps for several weeks, up to two or three months. Sliced, cored fruit freezes well with the skin on.

recipes.method: Quinces must be cooked; the author warns not to bite into a raw one. Base: 175 g softened butter, 115 g unrefined cane sugar, 100 g (1 cup) plain flour, 50 g rice flour, 50 g cornflour and 100 g coarsely ground macadamia nuts. Filling: 370 g cream cheese at room temperature, 350 g ricotta, 60 g (¼ cup) liquid honey, 6 eggs, 250 g unrefined cane sugar, 5 ml (1 tsp) vanilla paste, and 30 ml (2 tbsp) cornflour mixed with 30 ml (2 tbsp) water. Topping: 2 quinces, the juice and zest of 1 lemon, 3 tamarillos and 125 g unrefined cane sugar. Makes one 26 cm cake. Line a 26 cm springform tin and heat the oven to 160 °C. Cream the butter and sugar, mix in the flours and nuts on slow speed until it just comes together, press it evenly into the tin, prick it and bake 20 minutes. Beat the cream cheese, ricotta and honey until smooth and scrape into a large bowl. Whisk the eggs, sugar and vanilla on medium-high for about 10 minutes, until light and fluffy; fold half into the cheese mixture, whisk in the cornflour paste, then fold in the rest gently so you keep the air. Pour onto the base (set on top, not coloured) and bake 1 hour 40 minutes, until set with a slight wobble. For the topping, peel, core and chop the quinces, cover with water and cook until soft, then add the lemon, the scooped-out tamarillo flesh and the sugar, simmer and stir 10 minutes, cool and blend or mash. When the cake is cold, remove the tin's ring, chill about an hour, move it to a plate and spread the purée on top.
recipes.title: Tamarillo and quince baked cheesecake

recipes.method: Ingredients: 700 ml water, the juice of 1 lemon, 1 kg quince (weighed after peeling and coring) and 1 kg sugar. Put the cold water and lemon juice in a saucepan. Wash the fluff off the quince skins, then peel, core and slice the fruit, dropping the pieces into the water so they don't brown. Tie the peelings and cores in a muslin or cheesecloth bag and add it to the pan. Cook over a medium heat until the quince is tender, about 30 minutes. Lift out the muslin bag and purée everything else in a food processor until smooth. Return the purée to the pan, add the sugar and cook over a low heat for 3 to 4 hours, until it turns deep ruby. Let it cool in the pan, then pour it into a 28 cm sponge-roll tin lined with greaseproof paper. Dry the paste for about 12 hours in an oven on fanbake with the heat off, or leave the tin on the bench for a few days. Store in an airtight tin.
recipes.title: Quince paste

recipes.method: Ingredients: up to 5 kg quinces, water and sugar (the source gives no fixed amounts; sugar is measured against the juice). Wipe the quinces clean and roughly chop them into medium cubes, unpeeled and uncored. Put them in a large pot with just enough water to cover, bring to the boil, then simmer gently with the lid on until the flesh turns pink and starts to break down. Pour the fruit and liquid into a muslin-lined sieve or a jelly bag over a large bowl, tie up the cloth, hang it and leave it to drip overnight. Next day discard the pulp and measure the juice; you need an equal volume of sugar. Put a small plate in the freezer. Bring the juice to the boil in a large pot, stir in the sugar until it dissolves, then boil hard for 10–15 minutes. Test by dropping a little onto the cold plate: it is ready when it forms a skin. Take off the heat, skim off any scum and pour into small warm jars to seal. Fruit picked early in the season sets more firmly; later, riper fruit gives a deeper red jelly. If jelly has failed before, the author suggests jam setting sugar instead: 1 kg for each litre of juice, boiled for 5 minutes.
recipes.title: Quince jelly

recipes.method: Serves 4. Poaching liquid: 720 ml cold water, 170 g (½ cup) liquid honey, 50 g (¼ cup) sugar, 4 whole cloves (optional), 1 cinnamon stick, two 5 cm strips of lemon peel with as little pith as possible, one 6 mm slice of unpeeled fresh ginger, 2 teaspoons vanilla extract or paste and a pinch of salt. Fruit: 2–3 quinces (about 700–800 g). Cut a round of baking paper just larger than a 4–5 litre saucepan, to lay on the surface of the liquid. Put all the poaching ingredients in the pan and bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then take it off the heat. Without peeling, halve the quinces lengthwise with a large sharp knife, cut out the cores with a sturdy melon baller or cut into quarters and trim the core with a small knife, and slice 6 mm thick. Put the slices straight into the hot liquid so they are mostly covered, lay the paper round on top and simmer very gently 15–25 minutes, turning once or twice, until tender; check from 10 minutes, as they keep cooking while they cool. Cool in the liquid, then take out the spices, peel and ginger. Serve with yoghurt or ice cream, or on pancakes, waffles or porridge. Keeps up to a week in the fridge in its liquid; the leftover syrup can poach more fruit.
recipes.title: Poached quince

recipes.method: Amanda Lawson's recipe, inspired by one of Stephanie Alexander's. Serves 4. Ingredients: 4 quinces, 1 orange cut into quarters, 1–2 lemons, 1 litre water, 500 g sugar and 2 cinnamon sticks. Heat the oven to 160 °C (140 °C fan). Wash the quinces (no need to peel them) and sit them snugly in a 1.5 litre casserole dish. Tuck the orange quarters around them and add the cinnamon sticks. Add the water and sugar and bring to the boil on the stove, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Move the dish to the oven and cook about 1½ hours, until a knife slides in easily; the fruit turns orange-pink in a deep pink syrup. Squeeze in the juice of one or two lemons before serving to cut the sweetness. Serve with porridge, yoghurt, custard or ice cream, or with roast pork or duck; purée some to spread on bread with goat's cheese, and mix the syrup with sparkling water. Keeps up to a week in an airtight container in the fridge.
recipes.title: Cinnamon pot-roasted quinces

recipes.method: Camilla Hawkins' recipe; she perfected it with ordinary quinces. Makes 500 ml (two 250 ml jars). Ingredients: 225 g prepared quince (peeled, cored and chopped; about 310 g whole, or 2 medium quinces), the finely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lemon, 1 tablespoon lemon juice, 200 g caster sugar, 55 g cold unsalted butter in cubes and 2 large eggs, beaten. Sterilise the jars: wash jars and lids in hot soapy water, fill the jars with boiling water, empty them and keep them hot in a 140 °C oven for 20 minutes; soak the lids in boiling water and drain. Put the quince in a small pan with 275 ml cold water, bring to the boil and simmer, covered, until tender, about 25–30 minutes. Drain off the water and blend the hot quince to a smooth purée with a stick blender. Put the purée, lemon juice, zest, butter and sugar in a medium pan, preferably non-stick, and stir with a wooden spoon over low heat until the sugar and butter have dissolved. Raise the heat to medium until it simmers, then pour in the beaten egg in a thin stream, whisking, and keep whisking up to a minute, until it thickens and coats the back of a spoon. Pour at once into the hot jars and screw on the lids. Cool, keep in the fridge and use within 3 weeks, always with a clean spoon.
recipes.title: Quince curd

recipes.method: Ingredients: 2.3 kg (5 lb) quinces, 800 g (4 cups) sugar, 1 large lemon and 950 ml (4 cups) water. Chop 1.4 kg (3 lb) of the quinces, skin and cores included, and keep the other 900 g (2 lb) aside. Simmer the chopped fruit in the water, covered, over low heat until soft, usually 30–45 minutes, stirring regularly. Tip it into a colander or jelly bag over a bowl and leave to drain overnight; pressing it to help it drain is fine. Next day, heat the juice with the sugar to a low simmer. Wash the reserved quinces well, rub off the down, and grate them on the large holes of a grater, skin on, discarding the cores. Add the grated fruit to the syrup with the zest and juice of the lemon (or two small limes) and simmer, stirring, about 30 minutes, until the grated fruit has softened. Keep cooking on low heat, stirring often so the bottom does not scorch, until thick and spreadable, or to 104 °C on a thermometer. To keep it, fill hot jars leaving 1 cm headspace and process 10 minutes in a boiling water bath. The author sometimes adds rosemary, and suggests cider in place of the water for the first simmer.
recipes.title: Quince marmalade

summary.text:
The quince (Cydonia oblonga) is the sole member of the genus Cydonia in the Malinae subtribe (which contains apples, pears, and other fruits) of the Rosaceae family.
It is a deciduous tree that bears hard, aromatic bright golden-yellow pome fruit, similar in appearance to a pear. Ripe quince fruits are hard, tart, and astringent. They are eaten raw or processed into jam, quince cheese, or alcoholic drinks.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Quince is commonly cultivated throughout New Zealand for its edible fruits and long persists in neglected or abandoned gardens. Naturalised in North Auckland – upper part of Hokianga Harbour and Kaipara Harbour at Oruawharo River; native to south-west Asia, first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1922.
It was introduced to New Zealand as a fruit crop and was once known here as Cydonia vulgaris. Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and wild, with herbarium records from North Auckland, Wellington and Canterbury. Cydonia was the ancients' name for the quince, which grew in abundance at Cydon in Crete; oblonga means oblong. The New Zealand cultivar 'Taihape' was raised from an old tree in Taihape.

warnings: Most quinces are too hard, tart and astringent to eat raw. In cooler climates the fruit stays hard and needs cooking before it is eaten.

The seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides (mainly amygdalin), which break down in the gut to release hydrogen cyanide. The levels in quince seeds are reported to be low, and the seeds are toxic only if eaten in large quantities.

edibleParts.text: The whole plant: young leaves, raw or cooked; young flower clusters, raw or cooked; young seed pods, raw or pickled; the seeds, raw or sprouted; and the root, raw or cooked. The leaves are hot and rather coarse, the flower clusters spicy and crisp, and the young pods crisp and juicy with a mild heat, tasting like a concentrated radish. Once a plant has flowered its root is usually too woody or fibrous to eat. Roasted, the root loses its peppery bite and turns sweeter and milder, with a texture like potato.

identification.text:
Annual or biennial. Taproot tuberous, napiform or cylindric, white or red, 1–3–(8) cm diameter. Stems often reddish, (10)–40–100 cm tall. Rosette and lower stem leaves lyrate-pinnate, rarely simple; terminal leaflet (2)–3–6 × (2)–3–6 cm, wider than rest of leaf; lateral leaflets in 1–4 distant pairs. Stem leaves simple, rarely with a pair of basal lobes, orbicular to lanceolate, 1–3 cm long. Racemes 15–40 cm long. Pedicels 1–2 cm long, stout at fruiting. Sepals 6–8 × 1–2 mm. Petals usually white, sometimes pink or mauve, rarely pale yellow, mauve-veined, 15–20 mm long. Silique (1)–5–12-seeded, ovoid to cylindric, not or scarcely constricted between seeds, not breaking into segments, veined or very weakly ribbed, tapering at apex, 20–60 × 8–15 mm. Seeds about 3 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild radish's ripe pods are narrower, (2)–3–8–(9) mm wide, pinched between the seeds, and break into one-seeded segments when ripe, though sea radish's do not break readily; radish's are fat, 8–15 mm wide, not or scarcely pinched, and do not break. Pods 8–9 mm wide fall in both ranges, so check the pinching rather than the width. Wild radish's rosette leaves have an end leaflet as wide as or narrower than the rest of the leaf, with 1–8 pairs of side leaflets; radish's end leaflet is wider than the rest, with 1–4 pairs. Wild radish's stems are usually green, radish's often reddish; wild radish's root is slender in subsp. raphanistrum, though sea radish's can be stout to swollen. Flower colour and size do not separate them: wild radish's petals are 13–20 mm long, radish's 15–20 mm, both white, pink or mauve with mauve veins, and either can be yellowish. The two can cross, so a plant in between may not be nameable. Both are eaten.

preparation.text: Use the leaves only while young, in small amounts in chopped salads, or cook them as greens. Add the young flower clusters to salads or cook them as a broccoli substitute. Pick the pods while still fresh and green but after the seeds inside start to form, when they bulge a little and grow fleshier; they are best raw, straight off the stem, or pickled. Left on the plant they dry, turn yellow or brown and split. The root is usually eaten raw; tougher ones can be steamed or roasted. To sprout the seed, soak it in warm water for 12 hours, then let it sprout for about 6 days. To roast the roots, halve or quarter them and cook at 200 °C for 35–40 minutes, until golden and a fork goes in easily; or fry them whole in foaming butter for about 10 minutes, turning, until glazed, soft and wrinkled.

recipes.method: Makes about 750 ml (3 cups). 250 ml (1 cup) water; 125 ml (½ cup) rice vinegar; 125 ml (½ cup) white wine vinegar; 125 ml (½ cup) sugar; 7.5 ml (½ tbsp) kosher salt; about 500 ml (2 heaping cups) green radish pods. In a small saucepan over a medium heat, stir 250 ml (1 cup) water, 125 ml (½ cup) rice vinegar, 125 ml (½ cup) white wine vinegar, 125 ml (½ cup) sugar and 7.5 ml (½ tbsp) kosher salt until the sugar and salt dissolve, then let the brine cool to room temperature. Pack about 500 ml (2 heaping cups) green radish pods into jars and pour the brine over, making sure the pods are fully covered. Leave at room temperature, out of direct sun, for at least 4 hours before serving, or overnight in the fridge for the best flavour. Use them like radishes in salads, tacos and wraps, or chop them like capers.
recipes.title: Pickled radish seed pods

recipes.method: Serves 2 as a side. 1 bunch of radishes, leaves kept; olive oil; salt and pepper; about 50 g dark green leek tops; 1 large garlic clove (or 2 small); 70 g cold, cubed butter. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Cut the leaves off 1 bunch of radishes and keep them. Halve or quarter the radishes, depending on size, spread them in one layer in an ovenproof dish, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and roast for 35–40 minutes, until golden and a fork goes in easily. Meanwhile, cut about 50 g of the dark green tops off a leek (keep the white part for another dish), chop them roughly, rinse off any soil and shake them dry; roughly chop the radish leaves. Blend the leek tops, radish leaves and 1 large garlic clove (or 2 small) until it looks like pesto, scraping down the sides now and then, then add 70 g cold, cubed butter, blend again and salt it. Warm the green butter in a pan over a low to medium heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring all the time, pour it over the roasted radishes and toss. Season with salt and pepper and serve straight away — with steak or fish, or piled on warm baguette.
recipes.title: Roasted radishes in radish-leaf garlic butter

recipes.method: Serves 4. 600 g radishes; 85 g butter; the juice of ½ lemon; sea salt. Trim the leaves off 600 g radishes. In a heavy frying pan just big enough to hold them snugly, heat half of 85 g butter until it foams and starts to turn nut-brown, then add the radishes and roll them in it. Fry for about 10 minutes, turning them every few minutes and adding the rest of the butter a small knob at a time, until they are glazed, soft and wrinkled. Turn the heat to full, add the juice of ½ lemon, let it sizzle for 1 minute, take the pan off the heat, season with sea salt and serve.
recipes.title: Brown butter basted radishes

recipes.method: Makes 2 × 400 ml jars. 500 g radishes; 10 ml (2 tsp) fine sea salt; 250 ml apple cider vinegar; 125 g caster sugar; a large pinch of chilli flakes (optional). Slice 500 g radishes very thinly, about 4 mm, into a non-metal bowl, mix in 10 ml (2 tsp) fine sea salt with your hands and leave for 30–45 minutes, until soft but not floppy. Meanwhile, gently simmer 250 ml apple cider vinegar, 125 g caster sugar and, if you like, a large pinch of chilli flakes until the sugar has just dissolved, then cool to room temperature. Stir the liquid that has collected under the radishes into the vinegar until any salt dissolves. Pack the radishes into sterilised jars, pour the cooled liquid over, seal and keep in the fridge. Ready after 24 hours; keeps up to a week in the fridge. The recipe works with daikon or carrots in place of the radishes.
recipes.title: Sweet-pickled radishes (amazuzuke)

recipes.method: Makes about 400 g. 300 g radishes, washed and finely sliced; ½ red pepper, finely chopped; 10 ml (2 tsp) sea salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) demerara sugar; 2 crushed garlic cloves; 1 red chilli, deseeded and finely chopped; still mineral water, if needed. Sterilise a jar first, and plan to check the ferment every day for 4–5 days. In a bowl, combine 300 g radishes, washed and finely sliced (a mandolin is best), and ½ red pepper, finely chopped, with 10 ml (2 tsp) sea salt and 2.5 ml (½ tsp) demerara sugar, and scrunch them hard with your hands to start the juices running. Leave for 1 hour, then squeeze again for about 10 minutes. Add 2 crushed garlic cloves and 1 red chilli, deseeded and finely chopped, and squeeze some more. Pack it into the jar, pressing down hard (the end of a clean rolling pin works) so there are no air pockets and the brine covers the vegetables, leaving 2–3 cm of space at the top. If the brine does not cover them, top up with still mineral water — they must be fully under liquid. Push a scrunched piece of baking paper firmly down on top to keep them under, cover with clean muslin held on with a rubber band, and leave on a cool, dark shelf for 4–7 days, to taste; it ferments faster when warm, slower when cold. Each day, lift off the muslin and paper to check it and let the gas escape, then cover it again. When it tastes right, take out the paper and muslin, put the lid on and refrigerate to stop the ferment; it keeps for months. Use it in salads, hot dogs and burgers.
recipes.title: Radish kraut

recipes.method: Serves 4 as a starter. Salsa verde: 2 anchovies in oil, drained; a large handful of parsley; a small handful of mint leaves; 15 ml (1 tbsp) capers; 45 ml (3 tbsp) good olive oil (plus a little more); 5 ml (1 tsp) Dijon mustard; 15 ml (1 tbsp) red wine vinegar. Radishes: 2 bunches of radishes (about 400 g), with a few of the youngest leaves; a little olive oil; sea salt. For the salsa verde, blitz 2 anchovies in oil (drained), a large handful of parsley, a small handful of mint leaves, 15 ml (1 tbsp) capers, 45 ml (3 tbsp) good olive oil, 5 ml (1 tsp) Dijon mustard and 15 ml (1 tbsp) red wine vinegar in a mini chopper or with a stick blender to a bright green sauce, adding a little more oil. Top and tail 2 bunches of radishes (about 400 g), keeping a few of the youngest, freshest leaves in iced water. Slice the radishes wafer-thin on a mandolin, using the guard, or with a knife. Pile the slices in a rough circle in the middle of 4 chilled plates, drain the leaves and scatter them around the outside, dot the salsa over the radishes and drizzle the leaves with a little olive oil. Season with sea salt and serve.
recipes.title: Radish confetti with salsa verde

recipes.method: Serves 4. 1 bunch of radishes; 1 minced garlic clove; 15 ml (1 tbsp) red wine vinegar; 5 ml (1 tsp) sesame oil; 5 ml (1 tsp) chilli oil; a pinch of salt; 5 ml (1 tsp) brown sugar; 60 ml (¼ cup) chopped peanuts; 1 finely sliced spring onion; 45 ml (3 tbsp) roughly chopped flat-leaf parsley. Trim 1 bunch of radishes. On a sturdy board, press each one with the base of a small pan or the flat of a large knife until it cracks open, and put them in a bowl. In another bowl, mix 1 minced garlic clove, 15 ml (1 tbsp) red wine vinegar, 5 ml (1 tsp) sesame oil, 5 ml (1 tsp) chilli oil, a pinch of salt and 5 ml (1 tsp) brown sugar. Toss the radishes in the dressing, stir in 60 ml (¼ cup) chopped peanuts, 1 finely sliced spring onion and 45 ml (3 tbsp) roughly chopped flat-leaf parsley, and serve fresh.

summary.text:
The radish (Raphanus sativus or Raphanus raphanistrum subsp. sativus) is a flowering plant in the mustard family, Brassicaceae. Its large taproot is commonly used as a root vegetable, although the entire plant is edible and its leaves are sometimes used as a leaf vegetable.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): recorded from the North, South and Kermadec Islands, naturalised by 1832; unknown in the wild, it probably arose in cultivation in Europe.
Herbarium specimens of it are held from the North Auckland, South Auckland, Gisborne, Hawke's Bay, Taranaki, Wellington, Canterbury and Southland land districts.

warnings: Japanese (daikon-type) radishes have more glucosinolate, which acts against the thyroid gland; it is probably best to peel them.

Brassicaceae plants are known for their tendency to accumulate heavy metals, a trait that makes them valuable for the phytoremediation of contaminated soils. However, this same ability necessitates careful monitoring, as the accumulation of heavy metals can also pose potential health risks.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Plants 1–3 m tall, usually growing in large colonies, summer-green. Rhizome to 3–4 cm diameter, fleshy, with ∞ membranous scale leaves. Lf-sheath often longer than 30 cm long; lamina 1–3 cm wide, more or less plano-convex at base, mesophyll spongy. Peduncle usually shorter than leaves, about 1 cm diameter. Inflorescence usually 30 cm or more long, the female part ultimately about 2.5 cm diameter, the male part narrower and either continuous with or separated more or less widely from the female. Bracteoles in male part more ∞ than stamens, about equal to anthers, narrow-linear proximally, broader at tip and there variously shortly laciniate, arising directly on axis and remaining more or less curled up after flowers fall. Male flower almost sessile; filaments at first shorter than anther-width, elongating later; anthers 1–3, tipped with blunt extension of connective; pollen clear yellow, grains single. Bracteoles in female part very few, absent from many flowers, about equal to gynophore hairs, filiform except for a few-celled expansion at tip. Female flowers very much smaller than male, several grouped on proximal part of a short compound pedicel. Ovary at flowering almost sessile, narrow-elliptic; style long, slender; stigma broader, spathulate, more or less concave; gynophore hairs very ∞, barely reaching base of stigma, stiff, filiform, very narrowly clavate at tip. Gynophore elongating at fruit to 1–2 times style-length, hairs then confined to proximal third of gynophore and in groups or more or less whorled; persistent stigmas brown. Carpodia oblong-obovate, tips just projecting between the hairs. Seed about 1.2 mm long, cuneate at base, truncate at tip, yellow. n equal to 30.
[From: Moore and Edgar (1970) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 2.]

summary.text:
Typha orientalis, commonly known as bulrush, cumbungi, or raupō, is a perennial herbaceous plant in the genus Typha.
The species is found across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand. The plant was introduced to the Chatham Islands of New Zealand by Māori.

edibleParts.text: Leaves and young flower heads, raw or cooked. The young flowers are also eaten raw in salads, and the petals, pulled apart, are sprinkled into salads or onto biscuits, cakes and desserts as a garnish. The seed can be sprouted and eaten in salads; sprouted, it is crisper and stronger in flavour than alfalfa.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Perennial; stems sparsely hairy below, moderately or densely hairy in upper parts, erect or decumbent, not rooting at nodes. Leaves usually moderately hairy on petioles and undersurface of leaflets, more or less glabrous or sparsely hairy on uppersurface; petioles up to about 200 mm long; leaflets ovate, elliptic or obovate, usually obtuse, sometimes acute or slightly emarginate, rarely shortly mucronate, cuneate to obtuse at base, usually more or less entire, usually with a crescentic spot toward base, about 15–40 mm long; lateral veins thin and more or less straight or somewhat recurved and thickened toward leaflet margin; petiolules 1–2 mm long, more or less equal; stipules ovate-oblong, acuminate. Inflorescences terminal, spicate, globose to ovoid, usually sessile, more or less equal to or longer than subtending leaves; flowers numerous, sessile; bracts 0, but an involucre present at base of inflorescence only and stipules of subtending leaves partly enfolding young inflorescence. Calyx moderately hairy, 10-veined, not inflated at fruiting; throat open, with a ring of hairs; calyx teeth unequal, much shorter than corolla, triangular with linear apex, spreading at fruiting; upper teeth more or less equal to tube; lowest tooth up to 1.5–2× as long as other 4, much longer than tube; sinuses narrowly obtuse. Corolla pink, purple-pink or rarely cream, persistent, 10–16 mm long. Pod glabrous, straight, shorter than calyx, thickened at apex, 2–3 mm long, 1-seeded; seeds about 2 mm diameter, with a blunt projection on one side.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Alsike's flower heads rise from the leaf axils on stalks, above the leaves; red clover's head is usually stalkless, sitting directly on the leaves beneath it, whose stipules partly wrap the young head. Alsike's stems and leaves are hairless, though its upper stem can be hairy; red clover's stems are sparsely hairy low down and moderately to densely hairy higher up, and its leaf stalks usually moderately hairy. Alsike's leaflets are described as unmarked, where red clover's usually carry a crescent-shaped spot towards the base. Alsike's corolla is 5–10 mm long, red clover's 10–16 mm. Colour is not a safe test: alsike is usually pink, red clover pink to purple-pink and rarely cream. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

lookalikes.howToTell: White clover's stems creep along the ground and root at the nodes, and its flower heads rise from the leaf axils on stalks, above the leaves; red clover's stems are erect or lie along the ground at the base but do not root at the nodes, they are hairy (sparsely low down, more densely higher up), and its flower head is usually stalkless, sitting directly on the leaves beneath it. White clover is more or less hairless. Red clover's leaflets usually carry a crescent-shaped spot towards the base and white clover's often carry light or dark markings, so the mark will not separate these two — use the stems and the flower stalk. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually stalkless on the leaves beneath it, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats; red clover's hairy stems stand erect or lie along the ground at the base and do not root at the nodes. Least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long, red clover's 15–40 mm long. Out of flower, leaflet size is a guide, as the published ranges do not meet. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Least yellow sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually stalkless on the leaves beneath it, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Creeping wood sorrel's stems lie along the ground or rise a little and often root at the nodes; red clover's hairy stems stand erect or lie along the ground at the base and do not root at the nodes. Creeping wood sorrel's leaflets are 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm), red clover's 15–40 mm long. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually without a stalk, sitting among the top leaves, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Its leaf stalks and leaflet undersides are usually moderately hairy, and its leaflets, c. 15–40 mm long, usually carry a crescent-shaped mark towards the base. Pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless. Red clover's leaflets are mostly larger, but the ranges meet at 15–16 mm, so use size only as a guide. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pale-pink wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Purple wood sorrel: no stem shows above ground and the leaves all rise from the base. Each flower stalk, 1–11 cm long, carries a single flower forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base. Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually without a stalk, sitting among the top leaves, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. It has leafy stems, erect or lying along the ground, and its leaflets usually carry a crescent-shaped mark towards the base. Out of flower, do not rely on leaflet size (red clover's c. 15–40 mm long, purple wood sorrel's 10–35 mm, up to 45 mm), leaflet tips (both can be rounded or blunt) or hairs (both usually have hairy leaf stalks and leaflet undersides). Do not eat purple wood sorrel; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Purple wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long. Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually stalkless on the leaves beneath it, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Both have hairy stems that do not root at the nodes, so the stems do not separate them. Red clover's leaflets are about 15–40 mm long, on more or less equal stalks 1–2 mm long, and usually carry a crescent-shaped spot towards the base; suckling clover's are about 3–12 mm long and on most leaves the middle one sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the side ones (under 1 mm). Out of flower, leaflet size is a guide, as the published ranges do not meet. Suckling clover has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Suckling clover

preparation.text: Pick the young leaves before the plant flowers and use them in salads and soups, or cook them like spinach; they can also be dried, powdered and sprinkled over food such as boiled rice. A mild tea is made from the fresh or dried flowers. The dried flowers and seed pods can be ground into a powder and used as flour.

recipes.method: A heaped handful of red clover leaves, 3 red clover flower heads, 4 tbsp prepared couscous, a quarter of a red pepper, chopped, half an onion and 2 cloves of garlic, finely chopped, the juice of half a lemon, a pinch of salt and 1 tbsp olive oil. Mix the garlic, lemon juice, olive oil and salt together. Rinse the clover leaves and chop them finely, then mix them in a bowl with the couscous, red pepper and onion. Stir in the garlic and lemon mixture and leave it to sit for 15 minutes. The page lists the flower heads but does not say how to use them.
recipes.title: Red clover tabbouleh

recipes.method: About 750 ml (3 cups) of flower heads, 1 litre of water, 250 ml lemon juice and 200 g sugar. Bring the flower heads and water to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes. Add the lemon juice and sugar and simmer another 5 minutes, stirring until the sugar has gone. Let it cool, strain the flowers out, and chill.
recipes.title: Red clover lemonade

recipes.method: About 500 ml of flower heads packed down, with no stems or leaves, 625 ml boiling water, 60 ml lemon juice, 800 g sugar and a packet of pectin. Pour the boiling water over the flower heads and leave them to infuse overnight, then strain. Put the infusion, lemon juice, sugar and pectin in a pot and boil for about 20 minutes. Test the set on a chilled saucer and boil longer if it has not set, then put it into a jar.
recipes.title: Red clover jam

recipes.method: 500 ml brown or wild rice; 1.5 litres water; 500 ml red clover florets pulled out of the flower heads; 125 ml butter; 1 tsp salt; 125 ml honey and some chopped nuts, for a sweet version. Cook the rice in 1.5 litres of water until done. While it is still hot, mix in the florets, butter and salt, and serve hot. For a sweet version, add 125 ml honey and some chopped nuts. The recipe works with quinoa or another grain in place of the rice.
recipes.title: Red clover rice

recipes.method: 500 ml rice, 1.5 litres water, 45 ml olive oil, 90 ml lemon juice, 1½ tsp salt, 6 spring onions minced, 250 ml walnuts or other nuts, 250 ml chopped dried fruit (raisins, cranberries, dates or apricots) and 500 ml red clover flowers pulled out of the flower heads. Cook the rice in 1.5 litres of water until done, without stirring it while it cooks or cools, and let it cool completely so it does not go sticky. Mix everything together thoroughly and serve chilled or at room temperature. For something special, use wild rice, alone or half and half with brown or white rice; boil the wild rice separately, since it cooks in a different time, and mix the two once cooked.
recipes.title: Red clover rice salad

recipes.method: About 1 litre of red clover blossoms; 1 litre water; 4 cups (about 800 g) sugar; if you like, half a lemon or orange chopped up, peel and all (leave the citrus out for the pure clover flavour); a tablespoon of beetroot or berry juice, for colour (optional). Put the blossoms and water in a pot and simmer gently for 15–20 minutes, then turn off the heat, cover and leave overnight. Next day, strain and press the liquid out of the spent flowers. Add the sugar and citrus and heat slowly, stirring now and then, for several hours, until it has reduced to a thick, honey-like syrup, then bottle it in jars. To colour it, add a tablespoon of beetroot or berry juice before bottling. The recipe gives a brownish syrup, like a light maple syrup. Makes a little over 500 ml.
recipes.title: Red clover blossom syrup

recipes.method: 250 ml wholemeal flour, 250 ml white flour, 1 tsp salt, 2 tsp baking powder, 2 eggs, 60 ml oil, 125 ml honey or red clover blossom syrup, 500 ml milk and 250 ml red clover flowers pulled out of the flower heads. Mix the dry ingredients first, then add all the wet ingredients before mixing them in thoroughly, which keeps the batter from going lumpy. Add a little milk or flour until the batter pours but is not runny. Cook on an oiled griddle and serve with butter and red clover blossom syrup.
recipes.title: Red clover pancakes

recipes.method: 500 ml wholemeal flour; 3 tsp baking powder; 60 ml butter; 125 ml almonds; 125 ml buttermilk; 2 eggs; ¼ tsp almond extract; 375 ml red clover flowers pulled out of the flower heads; butter and jam, to serve. Whizz the flour, baking powder and almonds in a food processor until the almonds are chopped fine, add the butter and whizz again to a crumbly mixture, then add the eggs, buttermilk, almond extract and clover and whizz just until the dough forms a lump. Shape into biscuits and bake on an ungreased tray at 230 °C for 10–15 minutes, until golden brown. Serve hot with butter and jam — they are sweet, dessert-like biscuits.
recipes.title: Red clover almond biscuits

recipes.method: A bunch of red clover blossoms and leaves; water just brought to the boil. Put a bunch of red clover blossoms and leaves in a large jar and cover them with water just brought to the boil. After about 15 minutes, strain out the flowers.
recipes.title: Red clover tea

recipes.method: The author's wild greens were creeping mallow, dandelion, plantain, chickweed and red clover flowers (the page does not say which plantain). 12 creeping mallow leaves; 6 dandelion leaves; 4 plantain leaves; 1 leaf of spinach, sugar beet or beetroot; 1 large sprig of sweet basil; a handful of chickweed; 3 red clover flowers; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) turmeric; 6 cardamom, freshly ground with 15 ml (1 tbsp) pumpkin seeds; a pinch of sea salt; 2 peaches; 1 banana; 30 ml (2 tbsp) Chilean guavas; ½ avocado; 10 ml (2 tsp) lemon juice; 750 ml (3 cups) water. Put the greens in the blender with the water, fruit, spices, salt and avocado and blend for about 60 seconds, until smooth. Taste it, and add a teaspoon of honey if it needs sweetening. Makes about 1 litre (4 cups).
recipes.title: Peaches and weeds smoothie

Cups and spoons converted at 250 ml a cup, 15 ml a tablespoon and 5 ml a teaspoon (the page does not say which cup it means; a US cup is about 237 ml); 4 cups of sugar as about 800 g, 1 quart taken as about 1 litre, 6 cups of water as 1.5 litres, ½-pint and 1-pint jars as 'jars', the yield 'a little more than 1 pint' as a little over 500 ml, and 450° (Fahrenheit, the page being American) as 230 °C. Hickory or black walnuts became walnuts (the page says any nuts will do), scallions spring onions, craisins cranberries, 'grill' a griddle and 'cookie sheet' a tray; the syrup's 'can in jars' became 'bottle it in jars', since the page gives no canning method.

Recipes 'Red clover tea' and 'Red clover sun tea', restated in this guide's own words: Jess Anderson, 'Jess' Adventures with Red Clover', CSA|365, 7 June 2016 (https://www.csa365.org/recipes/jess-adventures-red-clovers/), retrieved 15/10/2026, © CSA|365, all rights reserved; supplied by the owner. The page gives no quantities ('a bunch of the blossoms and leaves… in a large mason jar'); the sun tea is the farmer's mother's, as told on the page, which does not mention the water a sun tea is steeped in. Not used: its pregnancy precaution and its bloating 'in excess' (no source given), medicinal and smoking uses, its failed candied flowers, the clover vinegar and tincture (results not reported), Leda Meredith's soda bread (not on the page), and its drying method (300 °F oven switched off overnight) — a storage note, not a recipe.

summary.text:
Red clover (Trifolium pratense) is a perennial clover of the pea family (Fabaceae), native from Europe to western Asia and North Africa, and naturalised in New Zealand.
In New Zealand: North Island; South Island: common to abundant throughout; Stewart Island: Halfmoon Bay, South-West Muttonbird Islands; Kermadec, Chatham and Campbell Islands. Naturalised from Europe to western Asia and North Africa, first recorded in 1867. Red clover is widely cultivated and there are several described varieties and many cultivars. There is some variability within New Zealand naturalised material in hairiness, leaflet shape, flower colour, and calyx teeth length.

warnings: Due to its coumarin and flavonoid derivatives, T. pratense should be used with caution in individuals having coagulation disorders or prescribed with anticoagulation therapy.
Red clover contains isoflavones, also called phyto-oestrogens, which have structural similarity to oestrogens.
Diseased clover can contain toxic alkaloids, such as slaframine, even when it shows no sign of disease.
The seeds contain trypsin inhibitors, which can interfere with the digestion of proteins; they are normally destroyed if the seed is sprouted first.

edibleParts.text: Young leaves, raw or cooked as a potherb. Young plants have edible tops and leaves, which can be used in salads or stir-fried as a spring vegetable. When finely chopped, they can also be added to sauces. The flowers can be crystallised using sugar and egg white, and the leaves and flowers are scattered fresh on salads. The leaves do not seem to turn bitter as they age, so they can go in salads for as long as there are any.

identification.text:
Annual herb with lax, hairy, spreading to erect stems to about 50 cm long, often shorter than 7 cm long in dry situations. Petioles to about 6 cm long, slender. Lamina 2–4.5 × 1.5–3.2 cm (inflorescence leaves sometimes smaller), ovate to suborbicular, hairy, especially above, crenate; base truncate to cordate. Bracts similar to leaves but often larger and with short petioles. Calyx 4–9 mm long, accrescent, hairy; teeth more or less equal to tube, subulate, often purple. Corolla 10–14 mm long, purple or deep pink; tube with prominent ring of hairs inside near base; upper lip 3–4 mm long, tomentose outside; lower lip spotted dark purple, deeply emarginate, the lateral lobes very small and toothed. Nutlets 2.2–5 mm long, sharply angled, often patterned white. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
All its leaves are stalked, even those right under and over the flower whorls; the stems and upper leaves turn purplish, and the leaves around the flower whorls usually a deep purple. Its leaves have even, rounded teeth and its flower tube has a conspicuous ring of hairs inside near the base; cut-leaved deadnettle's leaves are deeply and irregularly toothed. Its main stem is sharply four-angled, and on a grown plant the lower part of it is often bare of leaves, the leaves crowding and overlapping towards the top. It does not sting.

lookalikes.howToTell: Henbit's bracts — the leaves under the upper flower clusters — are stalkless, broadly ovate and clasp the stem, unlike its lower leaves; red deadnettle's bracts are like its leaves and short-stalked. Henbit's flower tube is long, narrow and hairless inside; red deadnettle's has a conspicuous ring of hairs inside near the base. Henbit's flowers usually stand above its top leaves, which are held upright; red deadnettle's flowers sit under the top few pairs of leaves, which droop and give the stem tip a pagoda-like look. Henbit's leaves have fewer, deeper and blunter teeth. Both grow in the same waste places and crops, and both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Henbit deadnettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut-leaved deadnettle's leaves are irregularly and deeply toothed, and its flower tube has at most a faint ring of hairs inside near the base; red deadnettle's leaves have even, rounded teeth, and its flower tube has a conspicuous ring of hairs inside. Neighbouring teeth on a cut-leaved deadnettle leaf are often of different sizes. They look alike and often grow together, and cut-leaved deadnettle is probably often overlooked because it is so like red deadnettle.
lookalikes.name: Cut-leaved deadnettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Field woundwort's flowers are small — 6–7 mm long, with a small upper lip that is not hooded and is shorter than the lower lip, the tube no longer than the calyx; red deadnettle's are 10–14 mm long with a hooded upper lip. Field woundwort's stem is much hairier, and its bracts are stalkless. Both are weeds of gardens, crops, waste places and river beds, and young plants are easily confused. Field woundwort poisons livestock (staggers); no record of it being eaten by people has been found, so do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Field woundwort

lookalikes.howToTell: Ground-ivy is a creeping perennial whose stems root at the joints; its leaves are round to kidney-shaped, and its blue or blue-violet flowers sit in twos or threes in the leaf joints on the upper stem. Red deadnettle is an annual with ovate to almost round leaves, the upper ones purplish, and purple or deep pink flowers in a whorl near the stem tip. Both grow in gardens and around buildings, and both are eaten. Ground-ivy is local in the southern North Island and the South Island.
lookalikes.name: Ground-ivy

preparation.text: Pick the top 5–10 cm of the flowering stems. The leaves are fuzzy, so they are used sparingly raw and more often cooked; the earthy smell goes with cooking, and the taste is mild with a slightly bitter edge, the purple tops a little sweet. It is best mixed with other greens, in salads, pesto and soups; add it to soups near the end of cooking. The stems are tough and are not usually eaten, and the plant toughens once it has gone to seed. Ants often hide in the sprigs: turn each one upside down and tap it before taking it indoors. To keep it, dry the leaves — spread in one layer on a cloth for several days — or blanch and freeze them.

recipes.method: Written for Lamium purpureum in the United States. Serves 5–7. About 2 cups red deadnettle leaves; 2 tbsp butter; 1 large diced shallot; 2 minced garlic cloves; 1 cup long-grain rice; 1 tsp salt; 2 cups (about 500 ml) chicken stock. Rinse about 2 cups of red deadnettle leaves and pat dry. Melt 2 tbsp butter in a lidded saucepan, soften 1 large diced shallot for 4–6 minutes, add 2 minced garlic cloves for a minute or two, then stir in 1 cup long-grain rice to coat it in the butter. Add the leaves and cook until wilted, 3–5 minutes, with 1 tsp salt. Pour in 2 cups (about 500 ml) chicken stock, bring to the boil, cover and simmer for 15 minutes, then fluff with a fork.
recipes.title: Red deadnettle rice pilaf

recipes.method: Written for Lamium purpureum. Makes 4. 1 tbsp coconut oil (plus another 1 tbsp for frying); about 60 g finely chopped red deadnettle flowering tops; 2 minced garlic cloves; about 45 g finely chopped chickweed; 1 beaten egg. Melt 1 tbsp coconut oil in a frying pan over medium-low heat, add about 60 g finely chopped red deadnettle flowering tops and 2 minced garlic cloves and sauté for about 10 minutes, until the garlic just browns. Add about 45 g finely chopped chickweed and cook until tender, about 2 minutes. Tip into a bowl, mix in 1 beaten egg, add another 1 tbsp oil to the pan, and fry the mixture as 4 flattened fritters 5–7 cm across, 1–2 minutes a side, until brown and crisp.
recipes.title: Deadnettle and chickweed fritters

recipes.method: Written for Lamium purpureum. 1 tbsp butter or olive oil; 1 finely chopped smoked garlic clove; about 85 g red deadnettle flowering tops; 15 wild mint leaves; the juice of half a lime; salt and pepper; a few fresh deadnettle flowers. Warm 1 tbsp butter or olive oil over low heat and sauté 1 finely chopped smoked garlic clove for 1–3 minutes. Add about 85 g red deadnettle flowering tops and 15 wild mint leaves and cook for about 5 minutes. Season with the juice of half a lime, salt and pepper, and scatter a few fresh deadnettle flowers on top.
recipes.title: Deadnettle with mint and smoked garlic

recipes.method: Written for Lamium purpureum; stinging nettle, dandelion or spinach work too. Serves 4. 1 tbsp olive oil; 1 small chopped onion; 1 minced garlic clove; 1 cup (about 250 ml) washed, dried red deadnettle leaves; 1 cup cooked and cooled rice; 1 egg; 1 cup (250 ml) milk; ¼ cup grated cheddar; 1 tbsp soy sauce; 1 tsp salt; 1 tsp pepper. Heat the oven to 180 °C and grease a 20 cm square baking dish. Warm 1 tbsp olive oil in a heavy frying pan over medium heat and sauté 1 small chopped onion, 1 minced garlic clove and 1 cup (about 250 ml) washed, dried red deadnettle leaves for 2 minutes. Tip into a bowl and mix well with 1 cup cooked and cooled rice, 1 egg, 1 cup (250 ml) milk, ¼ cup grated cheddar, 1 tbsp soy sauce, and 1 tsp each of salt and pepper. Pour into the dish and bake for 30 minutes. Serve straight away.
recipes.title: Red deadnettle rice bake

recipes.method: Written for Lamium purpureum. 3 packed cups red deadnettle flowering tops; 5 garlic cloves; ⅓ cup nuts (pecans, walnuts or pine nuts); 1 tsp Italian seasoning; 2½ tbsp lemon juice; 2–4 pinches of sugar; ¾ cup grated parmesan; ½–1 cup (125–250 ml) olive oil. Pick the leafy flowering tops, rinse and dry them. In a food processor, blend 3 packed cups of the tops with 5 garlic cloves, ⅓ cup nuts (pecans, walnuts or pine nuts), 1 tsp Italian seasoning, 2½ tbsp lemon juice, 2–4 pinches of sugar and ¾ cup grated parmesan. Then drizzle in ½–1 cup (125–250 ml) olive oil until it is as thick as you like, then taste and adjust the seasoning. To freeze it, leave out the parmesan and stir it in after thawing.
recipes.title: Red deadnettle pesto

recipes.method: Written for cleavers, violet leaves, chickweed, red deadnettle and bittercress. A small handful of cleavers; 4 violet leaves; a handful of chickweed; 3 or 4 stems of red deadnettle; a small handful of bittercress; a big handful of bok choy, kale or silverbeet; 1 banana, peeled; 1 apple (whole without the stalk if organic, otherwise peeled); 1 mandarin (with its peel if organic, otherwise peeled); 1 or 2 kiwifruit, peeled; 1 small or ½ large avocado; 500 ml (2 cups) water, more if the blender struggles. Wash the weeds and greens, put them in the blender, snip them up a bit with scissors and add the water. Blend on low until the greens break down, then on high until smooth. Add the fruit and avocado and blend again, low and then high, until creamy.
recipes.title: Winter health boosting smoothie

summary.text:
Lamium purpureum (from Latin purpureus 'purple'), known as red dead-nettle, purple dead-nettle, or purple archangel, is an annual herbaceous flowering plant in the mint family (Lamiaceae).
Lamium purpureum is native and relatively common to Europe (including Britain and Ireland) and Asia but it can also be found in North America: especially in the western and eastern United States, and Canada.
Though superficially similar to species of Urtica (true nettles) in appearance, L. purpureum is not related to them, the genus Lamium belonging to the mint family, not the nettle family, the "dead" in the name "dead-nettle" referring to the inability of Lamium species to sting.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1878 and is now very common throughout the North and South Islands and on Campbell Island. It spread widely only recently: in 1940 it was known only from the northern half of the South Island. It is a weed of gardens and crops in most of the country.

warnings: It is a weed of crops and gardens, where it is sprayed with herbicides. Pick from ground you know has not been sprayed, away from roadsides.
Field woundwort (staggerweed), which poisons livestock, grows in the same places and looks alike when young. Check for red deadnettle's larger flowers with a hooded upper lip.
Avoid teas and tinctures of it when pregnant or nursing. This rests on a single herbal guide, which gives no reason.

edibleParts.text: Fruit - raw or cooked. The fruit can vary in colour - usually red in colour, it can range from white through to amber and is 5 - 20mm in diameter. Root - cooked. Young shoots - peeled and eaten raw or cooked like asparagus. They are harvested as they emerge through the ground and whilst they are still tender. A herb tea is made from the dried leaves.

identification.text:
Plants of Rubus idaeus are generally perennials, which bear biennial stems ("canes") from a perennial root system. In its second year (as a "floricane"), a stem does not grow taller, but produces several side shoots, which bear smaller leaves with three or five leaflets. In raspberries (various species of Rubus subgenus Idaeobatus), the drupelets separate from the core when picked, leaving a hollow fruit, whereas in blackberries and most other species of Rubus, the drupelets stay attached to the core.
Suckering, erect shrub, up to 1.5–(3) m high; stems erect when young, sometimes almost decumbent when older, terete, sparsely to densely hairy when young, soon becoming glabrous, somewhat pruinose, suckering by adventitious buds; armature of weak, more or less terete, erect prickles, these often very numerous (rarely almost 0) on young stems and sometimes sparse on older stems. Leaves usually imparipinnate with 2–(3) pairs of leaflets, rarely pinnately 3-foliolate, rugose, glabrescent, sometimes with whitish bloom on upper surface, densely white-tomentose on lower surface, 1–2-serrate; terminal leaflet ovate to ovate-oblong, sometimes slightly lobed, up to 115 × 85 mm, acuminate, truncate to cordate at base, petiolulate; stipules linear. Inflorescence a few-flowered leafy raceme; axis and branches pilose and prickly. Flowers 20–25 mm diameter. Sepals long-triangular, acuminate, tomentose, paler on margins, deflexed at fruiting. Petals narrow, flat, white. Stamen filaments white. Fruit of waxy, red or orange drupelets, cylindric, up to 15 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. Raspberry's leaves are pinnate, with side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk, where blackberry's are palmate, all leaflets spreading from one point; raspberry's are densely white-felted underneath. A ripe raspberry comes away from its core when picked and is hollow; a blackberry keeps its core.
lookalikes.name: Blackberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. Raspberry's leaves are pinnate, with side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk; bush lawyer's are palmate, all leaflets spreading from one point. Raspberry is an erect shrub with flowers 20–25 mm across; bush lawyer is a climbing liane with flowers 8–15 mm across, male and female on separate plants.
lookalikes.name: Bush lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. Both can be white-felted underneath, so the felt does not separate them: count the leaflets and see how they are attached. Raspberry's are pinnate, side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk; white-leaved lawyer's are palmate, usually three from one point. Raspberry is an erect shrub with flowers 20–25 mm across; white-leaved lawyer is a liane or a tangled mound with flowers 8–15 mm across, male and female on separate plants.

preparation.text: Aromatic and delicious when eaten out of hand, the fruit is also used in pies, preserves etc. The root, which should be neither too young nor too old, requires a lot of boiling.

recipes.method: Written for wild raspberries. Fills 2 jam jars. About 570 ml (1 UK pint) wild raspberries, pressed down, and about 285 ml (½ pint) sugar — half the volume of the berries. Put a small saucer in the freezer. Put the berries and sugar in a heavy-based pan, mash them gently with a potato masher and leave somewhere warm for half an hour so the sugar starts to dissolve in the juice. Stir well, then heat on low to medium, stirring until the last of the sugar has dissolved. Bring to a gentle boil; once bubbles cover the surface, skim off the froth and boil for 12 minutes (longer for a bigger batch). Take off the heat and drop a blob on the cold saucer: as it cools it should set to jam. If not, boil 2 minutes more and test again. Pour into sterilised jars and seal with sterilised lids. Keeps six months unopened in a cupboard; it is ready once cool. The recipe uses about half the sugar of many jams. The author says the cold mashing step keeps more of the flavour.
recipes.title: Wild raspberry jam

recipes.method: Written for raspberries; the page names no species. Serves 6. 800 g raspberries, 55 g icing sugar plus extra for dusting, 2 teaspoons rosewater, 2 drops vanilla essence, the finely grated zest of ¼ lemon and 450 ml cream (35% fat). Put 300 g of the raspberries into 6 glasses. Blend 350 g more with the icing sugar to a thick purée, then stir in the rosewater, vanilla and lemon zest. Set aside 170 g of the purée and drizzle a generous tablespoon of the rest over the berries in each glass. Whip the cream to soft peaks and fold the reserved 170 g of purée through it. Share this between the glasses, spoon over the last of the purée, top with the remaining raspberries and dust with icing sugar. The source serves it with home-made sponge fingers (6 eggs, 180 g caster sugar, 180 g plain flour, piped and baked at 220 °C for 7–9 minutes).

summary.text:
Rubus idaeus (raspberry, also called red raspberry or occasionally European red raspberry to distinguish it from other raspberry species) is a red-fruited species of Rubus native to Eurasia and commonly cultivated in other temperate regions.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1870. Flora of New Zealand (1988) lists it in the North Island at Hunua, Wellington City and the Hutt Valley, and in the South Island scattered through Canterbury's plains and foothills, Banks Peninsula and Mt Cook, at Gabriels Gully, Beaumont and Skippers in Otago, and in Southland's Eglinton Valley.

warnings: Safety of raspberry-leaf tea in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and its use at those times is not recommended.

identification.text:
Erect, ± hairy annual herb to c. 80 cm high, but plants often only a few cm high in impoverished conditions. Stem angular, ± hairy when young, red, especially towards base. Petiole to c. 7 cm long, often reddish, usually hairy. Lamina extremely variable according to habitat, 2–11 × 1–7 cm (smaller in inflorescence and very depauperate plants), ovate or rhombic-ovate, usually glabrate beneath and becoming glabrous above; base narrow-cuneate to attenuate; apex obtuse, sometimes mucronate. Panicles green, with elongated main spike to c. 25 cm long at fruiting, with shorter spikes in axils of uppermost leaves, the leaves sometimes very reduced. Longer bracteoles 4–8 mm long, ovate, with long subulate green tip; shorter bracteoles similar. Flowers 4–5-merous; tepals very unequal, especially in female flowers; female flowers with 1–2 longer and 3 shorter tepals, the longer 2.5–3–(4) mm, ± oblong, keeled, gradually tapering to the sharply acute or short-acuminate apex. Fruit subglobose, circumscissile, usually with prominent neck, not exceeding tepals except for the 3 persistent stigmas. Seed 1–1.5 mm diameter, lenticular, dark brown or black.
Told from Amaranthus retroflexus, also called redroot, best by the tip of the female flowers' tepals: sharply acute or short-acuminate in this plant, more or less truncate to rounded and cuspidate in A. retroflexus. In A. retroflexus the short side branches of the flower spike are densely arranged up the main spike; in this plant they are usually all towards its base, though this is not of much use for stunted plants in very poor soil.

lookalikes.howToTell: The best character is the tip of the female flowers' tepals: redroot's taper gradually to a sharply acute or short-acuminate tip; redroot amaranth's are more or less truncate to rounded and cuspidate, ending in an abrupt small point. In redroot amaranth the short side branches of the flower spike are densely arranged up the main spike; in redroot they are usually all towards its base, though this is not of much use for stunted plants in very poor soil. Both have stems red towards the base and both are called redroot, so the red colour does not tell them apart. Redroot amaranth is recorded as poisonous.
lookalikes.name: Redroot amaranth

summary.text:
Redroot is an upright annual weed of the amaranth family (Amaranthaceae), native to North America and introduced to New Zealand.
It was first recorded wild here in 1940 and is locally common to abundant throughout the North and South Islands. It has long been naturalised but has been confused with other species: the common name redroot is also applied to the closely related Amaranthus retroflexus, and plants of A. powellii have often been named A. hybridus, which is rare in New Zealand. It causes nitrate poisoning in stock but is also known as a potherb.

warnings: It causes nitrate poisoning in stock. Amaranths, as a genus, concentrate nitrates in their leaves when grown on nitrogen-rich soil, especially where chemical fertilisers are used, so do not eat plants from fertilised ground.

Redroot amaranth (Amaranthus retroflexus), also called redroot, is recorded as poisonous in New Zealand and is often confused with this plant. Check the tips of the female flowers' tepals before picking (see the lookalikes).

identification.text: Hairy, erect, annual herb to c. 1 m high, but very variable in size; stems reddish towards base, densely hairy above. Petioles c. 5 cm long. Lamina 2–10 × 1–4.5 cm, ovate-lanceolate, becoming glabrous above; veins persistently hairy below; margin undulate, usually ciliate; base cuneate; apex obtuse. Inflorescence dense, spike-like, to c. 20 cm high, with numerous short lateral branches. Longer bracteoles 4–5 mm long, lanceolate-subulate with green keel; shorter bracteoles similar. Tepals 4–5, 2–2.7–(3) mm long, oblong; keel green; apex ± truncate to rounded and cuspidate. Fruit broadly ellipsoid, circumscissile, with rounded apex, included within persistent perianth except for stigma apices. Seed 1–1.3 mm diameter, suborbicular or broadly ovoid, dark brown.

lookalikes.howToTell: The best character is the tip of the female flowers' tepals: redroot's taper gradually to a sharply acute or short-acuminate tip; redroot amaranth's are more or less truncate to rounded and cuspidate, ending in an abrupt small point. In redroot amaranth the short side branches of the flower spike are densely arranged up the main spike; in redroot they are usually all towards its base, though this is not of much use for stunted plants in very poor soil. Both have stems red towards the base and both are called redroot, so the red colour does not tell them apart. Redroot's young leaves and seeds are eaten.

summary.text:
Redroot amaranth is a hairy, upright annual weed of the amaranth family (Amaranthaceae), from tropical America and introduced to New Zealand.
It was first recorded wild here in 1869, and is widespread in the South Island and probably in at least some parts of the North Island. It is related to redroot (Amaranthus powellii), which shares its common name, and the two are often confused. It is recorded as poisonous.

warnings: Do not eat it. It is recorded as poisonous in New Zealand.
It is often confused with redroot, which is eaten and also has stems red towards the base. Check the tips of the female flowers' tepals before picking any redroot (see the lookalikes).

Cladonia confusa is a species of lichen, native to and found in New Zealand, Australia, Africa and South America.
In New Zealand, it is known from across both the North and South Island. It is also found on the Three Kings Islands. It is one of the most common lichens in the neotropics. It is found in Tasmania and South Australia, as well as on Lord Howe Island and Norfolk Island. It has also been found on the island of Réunion.

identification.text: Rhizomes erect, up to 70 mm long (in herbarium material), bearing scales. Rhizome scales linear to narrowly ovate, 5–12 mm long, 0.4–0.7 mm wide, dark brown, concolorous. Fronds strongly dimorphic; sterile fronds 120–700 mm long, forming a prostrate to suberect rosette; fertile fronds on same plant usually a little shorter, 85–620 mm long, positioned centrally, held erect. Sterile fronds. Stipes 10–140 mm long, red-brown, bearing a few scales proximally. Rachises yellow-brown, grooved adaxially, glabrous. Laminae 80–600 mm long, 15–115 mm wide, or very rarely to 125 mm wide, deeply pinnatifid to pinnatisect, narrowly elliptic to narrowly obovate, with a short apical segment, similar colour on both surfaces, red-tinged when young, herbaceous to coriaceous, glabrous. Pinnae in 7–54 pairs, closely spaced, narrowly oblong or narrowly triangular or triangular, straight or falcate, gradually reducing to short, rounded flanges at the lamina base; the longest pinnae at or above the middle, 14–60 mm long, or very rarely only 8 mm long or up to 68 mm long, 6–15 mm wide, or rarely only 4 mm wide, apices usually acute or rarely obtuse, margins shallowly crenate, bases adnate; the basal pinnae sub-opposite or alternate. Veins free. Fertile fronds. Stipes 20–250 mm long. Laminae 40–530 mm long, 10–70 mm wide. Pinnae in 15–52 pairs, linear, straight or falcate, 5–40 mm long, 1–3 mm wide, reducing to tiny sterile flanges at the lamina base. Sori and indusia in one row either side of costa, continuous along the length of the pinna.

identification.text:
Rimu is a conifer usually 35 m tall, sometimes up to 60 m, with male and female cones on separate trees. The stout trunk is 1.5–2 m across and, on adult trees, bare of branches for about three-quarters of its length. The bark is dark brown and falls off in large, thick flakes, leaving a wavy pattern of raised ridges like the contour lines on a map; the wood is dark red. Young trees are pyramid-shaped, with many slender branches and hanging branchlets; adults have few, spreading branches with slender, drooping branchlets, and the crown becomes domed.
The leaves overlap along the branchlets and are dark green, bronze-green, red-green or orange. On juveniles they are 4–7 mm long (sometimes to 10 mm) and 0.5–1 mm wide, keeled, narrow, pointed and slightly sickle-shaped; on subadults they are ascending and incurved, 4–6 mm long; on adults they are pressed against the branchlet, rigid, three-sided and only 2–3 mm long, so the foliage feels firm and spiky.
Cones first appear on subadult trees, which often bear fruit before they reach the adult form. Male cones are oblong, 5–10 mm long, single or paired at the branch tips, with yellow pollen. Each female ovule sits alone at the tip of an up-curved branchlet; when ripe it becomes a fleshy red or deep-orange cup 1–2 mm long holding the seed. The seed is oblong, flattened, 3–4 mm long, semi-glossy and dark brown. The fruit takes a year or more to ripen, so ripe fruit and young female cones are often on the tree together.
Rimu is very distinctive and is not confused with any other native conifer. Only very young seedlings look a little like seedlings of silver pine (Manoao colensoi), whose leaves are coarser, fewer and glossy rather than fine, numerous and dull red-green.
Rimu usually lives 600–800 years and can reach 1000.

preparation.text: Eat the receptacles raw. For spruce beer, small branches of rimu and mānuka were boiled in water for two to four hours, until the bark stripped off easily; the branches were taken out, molasses or sugar added, the brew brought back to the boil, an equal quantity of cold water added, and yeast added once it was lukewarm, then left for a few days.

recipes.method: Written for rimu, from the beer James Cook's crew brewed at Dusky Sound, Fiordland, in March 1773, scaled down from their 10 gallons of molasses to 240 gallons of brew (1 part molasses to 24 parts brew). Boil small branches of rimu and mānuka in water for two to four hours, until the bark strips off the branches easily, to make a strong brew. Take the branches out. Stir in 100 ml molasses for every 2.4 litres of brew (sugar can be used instead; the record gives no amount for it) and bring it back to the boil. Pour it into a clean fermenting vessel with an equal volume of cold water. When the whole is lukewarm, add yeast and leave it for a few days.
recipes.title: Rimu spruce beer

summary.text:
Dacrydium cupressinum, commonly known as rimu, is a species of conifer in the family Podocarpaceae, native to New Zealand.
It is endemic, found on the North Island from North Cape south, the South Island and Stewart Island, but is uncommon in large parts of the eastern South Island; on Banks Peninsula one natural tree is all that remains. Other name: red pine.
It is assessed Not Threatened, but rimu forest has been greatly reduced by widespread logging, and very few intact rimu-dominated forests remain in the North Island. It is commonly sold by nurseries and is a popular garden tree.
The first published mention of the species, by Georg Forster in 1786, described it only for its use in beer making.
Dacrydium cupressinum is known for exhibiting mast seeding, which is the synchronised periodicity of seed production. In the Pureora Forest and the Wanganui Forest, in the North Island and the South Island, respectively, seedfall data show clear yearly fluctuations in seed production in studied specimens. A 1988 study proposes that a combination of low seed production and cool temperatures two years before, followed by warm temperatures during seedfall are necessary, but not solely responsible for triggering a mast year in the tree. The relationship between seed production in one year and conditions from two years earlier also plays an important role. Canham et al. 2014 analysed D. cupressinum specimens growing in less fertile marine terrace sites had a higher seed production rate in comparison to specimens that grew on more fertile alluvial soils. Researchers suggested that the tree has adapted to seed production in less fertile soils rather than being displaced by other species.
Rimu has a diploid chromosome count of 20.
In terms of chemical composition, the foliage of D. cupressinum contains various sesquiterpenes, with their levels showing significant variation between specimens, which is similar to the differences observed in diterpene levels. There are twelve known sesquiterpenes in the tree that have been identified by a 1985 study, but none of which show any structural similarity to lauren-1-ene. The distinctive diterpene lauren-1-ene was first discovered in the foliage of the tree, however, the concentration of this compound, along with other diterpenes, also shows significant variation between D. cupressinum specimens.
Dacrydium cupressinum contains high levels of the unique sesquiterpene terpene compounds of 9-epi-β-caryophyllene. The tree also has a distinctive flavonoid glycoside profile; the tree possesses flavonol-3-O-rhamnoglucosides and also, to a lesser extent, 3-0-methyl-myricetin glycoside compounds.

warnings: The fruit can be somewhat constipating.
Only the red receptacle is recorded as eaten. No record of the seed being eaten was found, so whether it is safe is not known.

habitat.text: It can be found in wet woodland — pond edges, boggy ground and stream banks — growing by poplars, silver birch, willows, alders or oaks. The New Zealand collections so far are under poplar, silver birch and goat willow.

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to pick this mushroom. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.

identification.text: The cap is up to 6 cm, bright blood-red, carmine, dark red or reddish brown, often fading with age to apricot or ochre, and it is often cracked. The pores are pale yellow with an olive tint. The stipe is yellow, usually with fine red granules towards the base. The flesh is pale yellow, often red at the base of the stipe, and stains blue when injured.

lookalikes.howToTell: Bluefoot bolete's cap is usually ochre to brown, grey-brown or blackish brown, though it can have a reddish tint or be entirely red; riverine bolete's is bright red, carmine, dark red or reddish brown, often fading with age to apricot or ochre with a reddish tint. Cap cracking and blueing do not separate them: both caps often crack, both stain blue, and colour and cracking tend to intergrade between species in this group. Habitat may help: about half of bluefoot's New Zealand collections are under oak, and others under cedar, lime, beech, pine and silver birch; riverine bolete grows in wet woodland, and its New Zealand collections are under poplar, goat willow and silver birch.

identification, habitat: Kibby, G. (2023). 'Fungal Portrait 96: Xerocomellus cisalpinus and some lookalikes'. Field Mycology 24(4): 111–112, British Mycological Society. In copyright — facts restated, no text reproduced. X. ripariellus stains strongly and has striated spores like X. cisalpinus, but is separated by a bright blood-red, cracked cap and by habitat: it prefers wetter woodland — pond edges, boggy ground — with a variety of trees but especially Salix and Alnus, sometimes Quercus.

summary: Kibby, G. (2023). 'Fungal Portrait 96: Xerocomellus cisalpinus and some lookalikes'. Field Mycology 24(4): 111–112, British Mycological Society. In copyright — facts restated, no text reproduced. X. ripariellus, X. cisalpinus, X. chrysenteron and X. pruinatus have all been much confused and together formed the composite 'red-cracked bolete' of the older field guides.

lookalikes: carded against bluefoot-bolete, Xerocomellus cisalpinus, the congener it is most likely to be confused with here — 163 iNaturalist NZ records against this species' 47, both small bluing boletes. Risk recorded as unpalatable, the owner's judgement on that species.

REJECTED: PlantSnap, 'Xerocomellus ripariellus' (https://plantsnap.com/plant-care/xerocomellus-ripariellus). REJECTED for description: Hidden Forest, 'Xerocomellus ripariellus' (https://www.hiddenforest.co.nz/fungi/family/boletaceae/bolet12.htm). All rights reserved, and the description does not match this species: it gives a 'dry, yellow-brown to chestnut cap', the common name 'Red Cracking Bolete' and a late-summer season, against a bright blood-red to carmine cap (Kibby 2023; boletales.com) and an iNaturalist NZ season peaking in April.
