habitat: Biota of New Zealand, 'Xerocomellus ripariellus (Redeuilh) Šutara 2008'. Records it as exotic and present, confirmed by sequences from collections under poplar, and associated with silver birch (Betula pendula), poplar (Populus) and goat willow (Salix caprea). Nine collections: Auckland 3, Mid Canterbury 3, Wairarapa 2, Bay of Plenty 1. Checked 07/10/2026. https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/b57df96a-d1ba-43e5-ae14-71dcfa114479

identification: boletales.com, 'Xerocomus ripariellus'. Copyright © boletales.com, all rights reserved — facts restated, no text reproduced. Cap to 6 cm, bright red to carmine or dark red, dry and velvety, cracking and fading to apricot or ochre; tubes and pores pale yellow with an olive tint, blueing when injured; stipe yellow with fine red granules towards the base, blueing; flesh pale yellow, often red at the stipe base, blueing on exposure; spores 11–15 × 4–5.5 µm, striate; wet woodland, presumed mycorrhizal with poplar, alder, willow or oak. Note Ultimate Mushroom tracks this site closely, so the two are one source, not two. Checked 07/10/2026. https://boletales.com/genera/xerocomus/x-ripariellus/

REJECTED: griby.org, 'Xerocomellus ripariellus' (https://www.griby.org/en/xerocomellus_ripariellus.htm). The page labels its own text an 'AI-generated description', and it reads like one: a 3–6 cm reddish-brown to dark brown cracked cap, against the bright red to carmine cap of the protologue and of every human-written source. Third machine-written page found for this species after PlantSnap; they are now the commonest kind of result for a fungus with no Wikipedia article, which is exactly the kind this catalogue has to fill. Checked 07/10/2026.

SEARCH EXHAUSTED — no openly licensed description of this species exists in English. Routes run and closed, so nobody runs them again: (1) Wikipedia, no article in any language except French, which the translation ruling bars. (2) The new-record-paper route, twice — the Chilean Salix babylonica inventory lists it without describing it, and Pluzhnyk A.V. & Prydiuk M.P. (2025), 'New records of agaricoid fungi from the Kholodnyi Yar National Nature Park', Ukrainian Botanical Journal 82(4): 291–305, DOI 10.15407/ukrbotj82.04.291, is CC BY 4.0 and open but published in Ukrainian and describes only the two species new to Ukraine. Its record is still a fact, and an awkward one: oak-hornbeam forest with lime and maple, on soil, 11.08.2021, the second Ukrainian record — dry upland woodland, not the riparian ground the name and every other source give. One collection, so it widens the habitat rather than replacing it. (3) GBIF's species description endpoint, empty for all ten taxon keys. (4) Mexia S., et al. (2025), 'The genus Xerocomellus (Boletales, Boletaceae) in Mexico', Phytotaxa 689(1): 1–14, DOI 10.11646/phytotaxa.689.1.1, CC BY-NC 4.0 and therefore quotable under the non-commercial ruling — but this species appears in it only twice, both times as a GenBank accession in a table. Useful for genus-level Xerocomellus characters, not for this page. Checked 07–08/10/2026.

OPEN LEAD, needs a person and a licence ruling: Ladurner H., Pöder R., Rocabruna A. & Tabarés M. (2001). 'Boletellus catalaunicus Pöder, Moreno, Rocabruna et Tabarés: a synonym of Xerocomus ripariellus Redeuilh'. Revista Catalana de Micologia 23: 121–125. summary.text: This is a mushroom that was introduced from Europe. It is one of four red-cracked boletes that have long been confused with each other.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Forming small colonies in waste places, roadsides, pasture, and gardens.
In gardens it is grown in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil, kept out of waterlogged ground.

identification.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Sweetly aromatic, creeping, perennial herb. Stems decumbent to ascending, to about 20 cm tall, striate, moderately to densely hairy, much-branched from base. Basal and lower cauline leaves apetiolate, obovate, sparsely to moderately hairy, 3-pinnatisect, 15–50 × 5–15 mm; ultimate segments narrow-linear to subulate, entire, not all in one plane giving a feathery appearance; cauline leaves few, smaller than basal, oblong and becoming 1-pinnatisect. Involucral bracts sparsely hairy, 2–5 mm long; margins pale, membranous, often with an extended membranous flap at apex. Capitula solitary, about 8–20–(30) mm diameter; ray florets 13–20, female; ligules white; disc florets numerous, yellow. Receptacle scales elliptic-oblong, obtuse and often irregular at apex. Achenes 1.1–1.2 mm long, narrow-obovoid, narrowed to apex, brown, with 1–4 narrow ribs on inner surface.
Chamomile may be distinguished from Anthemis arvensis and A. cotula when mature achenes are not present, by the apex of the receptacle scales which is blunt and often irregular in C. nobile and acute to acuminate and entire in the 2 Anthemis species.
Although the plant is often confused with German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla), its morphology, properties and chemical composition are markedly different.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have scales between the florets, so check their tips with a hand lens: Roman chamomile's are blunt and often ragged at the tip, stinking mayweed's narrow and pointed. Crushed stinking mayweed smells strongly foetid; Roman chamomile is sweetly aromatic. Stinking mayweed's stems stand upright or rise from the base, usually 30–40 cm tall but from 5 cm to 60 cm; Roman chamomile creeps, its stems lying along the ground or rising to about 20 cm — so a small stinking mayweed can be as short. Stinking mayweed's stems range from almost hairless to moderately hairy and Roman chamomile's from moderately to densely hairy, so hairiness does not separate them; both have white rays around a yellow disc and feathery leaves. Stinking mayweed is not eaten in this guide: its acrid juice can blister skin and it has been reported as toxic.
lookalikes.name: Stinking mayweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Pineappleweed has no white rays — its heads are a dome of dull yellow to greenish-yellow florets, 4–10 mm across; Roman chamomile has 13–20 white rays around a yellow disc. Pineappleweed has no scales on its receptacle; Roman chamomile does. Pineappleweed's stems stand upright or rise from the base and are hairless or carry a few hairs below the heads; Roman chamomile's creep and are moderately to densely hairy. Pineappleweed's leaf segments lie more or less in one plane; Roman chamomile's do not, which makes its leaves look feathery. Crushed pineappleweed smells of pineapple, Roman chamomile sweetly aromatic. Pineappleweed's flower heads and leaves are eaten and made into tea.
lookalikes.name: Pineappleweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Common lawn daisy's leaves all grow in a basal rosette and are spoon-shaped to oval with a few rounded teeth and one main vein; Roman chamomile's leaves are divided three times into narrow, feathery segments. Lawn daisy's flower heads sit singly on hairy, leafless stalks from the rosette; Roman chamomile's stems are leafy, though the stem leaves are few and smaller than the basal ones. Lawn daisy's white rays are often tinged pink to reddish purple underneath or at the tip; Roman chamomile's are white — but a pure white head can still be a lawn daisy. Both grow in lawns and pasture, and their flower heads overlap in size (lawn daisy 15–25 mm, Roman chamomile 8–20 mm, up to 30), so place and size do not separate them. Common lawn daisy is eaten — its young leaves, flower buds and petals (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Common lawn daisy

lookalikes.howToTell: Yarrow carries many small flower heads, 5–10 mm across (as small as 3.5 mm), packed into a flat-topped or slightly domed cluster up to about 15 cm across, each head with only 4–7 rays, and its central florets are usually white as well; Roman chamomile carries its heads singly, 8–20 mm across (up to 30), with 13–20 white rays around a yellow disc. Yarrow's flowers can also be pink to deep red or purple. Yarrow's basal leaves are 6–15 cm long (up to 44), with 18–30 pairs of primary leaflets; Roman chamomile's are 15–50 mm. Yarrow's flowering stems are usually upright, up to about 80 cm; Roman chamomile's lie along the ground or rise to about 20 cm. Both have scales on the receptacle, feathery leaves and a scent, and both grow in lawns, so these do not separate them. Yarrow's young leaves are eaten in small amounts, and its leaves and flowers are made into tea (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Yarrow

lookalikes.howToTell: Roman chamomile is a low, creeping, sweetly aromatic, hairy perennial up to about 20 cm; scentless chamomile is an almost scentless, usually hairless annual or biennial with erect or ascending stems 15–100 cm tall. Roman chamomile has small, blunt scales among its florets; scentless chamomile has none. Roman chamomile's heads are about 8–20 mm across (up to 30 mm), scentless chamomile's about 30–50 mm. What does not separate them: leaves cut three times into narrow, feathery segments, and white rays around a yellow disc. There is no record of scentless chamomile being eaten or used for tea.
lookalikes.name: Scentless chamomile

preparation.text: Gather the flower heads when fully open and dry them; keep them no longer than 12 months. Make the tea in a covered vessel so the essential oil is not lost. For tea, 1–4 g of dried flower heads is infused in 100–150 ml of boiling water; adults take it 3 times a day between meals.

summary.text:
Chamaemelum nobile — chamomile, also called garden chamomile, perennial chamomile or Roman chamomile — is a low, creeping, sweetly aromatic perennial herb. It is exotic in New Zealand and grows wild here.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: scattered localities, commonest in Auckland and Northland; South Island: Nelson, Westland, one early collection from Bluff. (Western Europe, North Africa, Azores; first recorded 1867.) Chamomile has been previously recorded in New Zealand as Anthemis nobilis and A. mixta. C. nobile is widely cultivated as a lawn plant, and the florets are also used to make chamomile tea - it is sometimes known as perennial chamomile or as Roman chamomile.
New Zealand herbarium specimens come from North Auckland, South Auckland, Taranaki, Wellington, Nelson, Westland and Canterbury, so it has also been collected in Canterbury, outside the range the Flora gives.
New Zealand nurseries sell it for chamomile lawns, for planting between paving stones and for herb and cottage gardens; it can replace a lawn where foot traffic is light.

warnings: Do not use it if you are allergic to plants of the daisy family (Asteraceae). Allergic reactions to chamomile are commonly reported, including anaphylaxis after chamomile tea, and people allergic to ragweed, asters or chrysanthemums can cross-react.
Use in pregnancy and breastfeeding is not recommended: its safety has not been established.
Large doses of the single-flowered form can damage the lining of the stomach and bowels, and large amounts of the dried flower heads are reported to cause vomiting.

identification.text:
Soft-wooded subshrub up to about 75 cm tall, strongly aromatic, densely hairy. Stems with hairs deflexed. Stipules about 1 cm long, ovate, acuminate. Petioles of lower leaves to longer than 8 cm long. Lamina to about 7 × 10 cm on flowering plants, more or less triangular, deeply divided into 3 lobes; lobes toothed and sinuate, rough above; 2 side lobes to about 2 cm across, each with a secondary lobe near base; terminal lobe to about 2.5 cm across, with a pair of secondary lobes. Umbels about 10-flowered, densely covered in glandular hairs; peduncles 2–6 cm long; pedicels 1–6 mm long. Sepals 8–12 mm long, elliptic-lanceolate, green, densely hairy; calyx spur about 3 mm long. Corolla pink; upper 2 petals 1–1.6 × 0.5–0.8 cm, with more or less prominent purple markings and white central patch, and claw well developed; lower 3 petals 0.9–1.4 × 0.25–0.5 cm, with purple median line in lower 1/2, and claw not well differentiated. Style and stigmas becoming rose. Mericarps not seen.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Its parents are P. graveolens Aiton, which has a soft leaf indumentum and broader leaf lobes, and P. radens H. Moore (often known as P. radula) which has finely dissected leaves with linear lobes.

lookalikes.howToTell: Peppermint geranium is a subshrub to about 75 cm that smells strongly of peppermint, with more or less velvety white hairs and broad leaves up to 12 × 15 cm, rather shallowly three-lobed, the lobes reaching a quarter to half way to the midrib; its flowers are white or pinkish, 5–8 to an umbel, on stalks 2–3.5 cm long that generally radiate widely, with a calyx spur about 2 mm long. Rose geranium (P. ×asperum) is a strongly aromatic, densely hairy subshrub to about 75 cm, with more or less triangular leaves up to about 7 × 10 cm that are deeply divided into 3 toothed lobes, lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib and rough above; its pink flowers, the upper 2 petals with more or less prominent purple markings and a white central patch, sit about 10 to an umbel on stalks 1–6 mm long, with a calyx spur about 3 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates rose geranium by its leaves (lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib; a quarter to half way in peppermint geranium), and the two descriptions also differ in the flower stalks (1–6 mm against 2–3.5 cm). Peppermint geranium's flowers are white or pinkish, rose geranium's pink, so a pink flower does not separate them. A crushed leaf of peppermint geranium smells strongly of peppermint; Flora of New Zealand calls rose geranium only "strongly aromatic". The leaf test works without flowers.
lookalikes.name: Peppermint geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Rose-scented geranium is a sprawling plant whose leaves are strongly undulate and velvety, generally lobed more than half way to the midrib, with more or less oblong lobes; its pink flowers, the larger upper pair of petals marked purple, sit in dense heads on almost no stalks, with a calyx spur 4–5 mm long. Rose geranium (P. ×asperum) is a strongly aromatic, densely hairy subshrub to about 75 cm, with more or less triangular leaves up to about 7 × 10 cm that are deeply divided into 3 toothed lobes, lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib and rough above; its pink flowers, the upper 2 petals with more or less prominent purple markings and a white central patch, sit about 10 to an umbel on stalks 1–6 mm long, with a calyx spur about 3 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates rose geranium first, by leaves lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib; rose-scented geranium's lobes reach at least half way, and the key's other branch says "lobed to < 1/2 way", so a leaf cut between half and three-quarters is not decided by lobing alone. The calyx spur is a little longer in rose-scented geranium (4–5 mm against about 3 mm). Both have short-stalked heads of pink flowers with purple-marked upper petals, so the flowers do not separate them; rose geranium's leaves are described as rough above, rose-scented geranium's as velvety. Smell does not separate them: rose geranium is strongly aromatic and rose-scented geranium's scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. Flora of New Zealand notes that P. ×asperum is a hybrid of P. graveolens and P. radens; Wikipedia says P. capitatum hybridises readily, so in-between plants are possible and this card may not decide them.
lookalikes.name: Rose-scented geranium

preparation.text: The fresh leaves are brewed into a tea. The leaves are mostly used to scent food and then taken out: a leaf added to apple jelly as it boils, or a green sprig dropped into a syrup, custard or jelly and lifted out as soon as it thickens, before the leaves break up; leaves can also be layered in sugar or flour to flavour baking. Finely chopped leaves can be flecked through cakes, biscuits and puddings — 15–30 ml (1–2 tablespoons) of chopped leaves is enough for most dishes that serve six. Use them sparingly so they do not overwhelm a dish.

recipes.method: 250 ml water; 200 g sugar; 10–12 rose geranium leaves. Put 250 ml water, 200 g sugar and 10–12 rose geranium leaves in a small saucepan, bruising the leaves against the side of the pan with a spoon. Bring to the boil over moderate heat, cover, take off the heat and leave to stand for at least 30 minutes. Lift out the leaves and squeeze them into the syrup. Keeps in the fridge for up to a month, or frozen for up to a year. The source uses it in a chocolate dessert.
recipes.title: Rose geranium syrup

recipes.method: About 125 ml fresh rose geranium leaves and tender stems, firmly packed; 750 ml apple juice; one packet of powdered fruit pectin; 1.2 kg sugar. Firmly pack about 125 ml of fresh rose geranium leaves and tender stems. Bring them to the boil with part of 750 ml apple juice, take off the heat and steep for at least 15–20 minutes. Strain, add the rest of the juice and top up to 750 ml if needed. Put the juice in a heavy, large saucepan over high heat, add one packet of powdered fruit pectin and bring to a full rolling boil that cannot be stirred down. Add 1.2 kg sugar, keep stirring and bring back to a full rolling boil; boil hard for 1 minute, stirring all the time. Take off the heat, skim off the foam quickly and pour at once into sterilised jars — a whole leaf can be pressed into each jar. Seal and process for 5 minutes in a hot water bath, following the jar maker's instructions. Makes about eight 250 ml jars. Use it to fill or glaze cakes, as a sauce for fresh fruit, or with poultry. The source's ingredient list also has 30 ml lemon juice, but its method does not say when it goes in.
recipes.title: Apple and rose geranium jelly

recipes.method: 1 litre pineapple juice; 10 rose geranium leaves; 400 g sugar; 125 ml lime juice; scented geranium leaves and flowers, to garnish. Warm 1 litre pineapple juice slightly, add 10 rose geranium leaves and bruise them gently against the side of the container with a spoon. Cover and steep for 30 minutes, then take out the leaves. Stir in 400 g sugar and 125 ml lime juice until dissolved (warm it a little to speed this up). Cool, then freeze in an ice-cream maker, or pour into a shallow tray in the freezer and stir with a fork every 30–45 minutes until frozen. Garnish with scented geranium leaves and flowers.
recipes.title: Pineapple and rose geranium ice

recipes.method: 300 ml fresh cream; 4 tablespoons caster sugar; 4–6 rose geranium leaves; 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed); 250 g sour cream (or cream cheese). Heat 300 ml fresh cream, 4 tablespoons caster sugar and 4–6 rose geranium leaves in a pot, stirring often, until just short of boiling; do not let it boil. Take off the heat and cool. Mash 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed) to a purée. Beat 250 g sour cream (or cream cheese) until smooth, then beat in the purée. Strain the leaves out of the cream and fold the cream gently into the berry mixture with a spoon. Cover and chill for several hours or overnight. Serve on fresh berries or fruit salad instead of cream or yoghurt.
recipes.title: Rose geranium cream

recipes.method: Fruit: 6–8 rose geranium leaves; the juice and grated rind of two oranges; about 190 ml more orange juice; 10–12 trimmed rhubarb stalks; about 150 g brown sugar; 2 tablespoons cornflour. Topping: about 150 g brown sugar; about 90 g whole rolled oats; about 90 g fine rolled oats; about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds); 2 tablespoons soft butter. Roughly chop 6–8 rose geranium leaves and warm them gently with the juice of two oranges plus about 190 ml more orange juice; bring almost to the boil, take off the heat and leave to infuse as it cools. Cut 10–12 trimmed rhubarb stalks into 1 cm pieces — enough to fill, not overfill, the baking dish. In a large bowl mix about 150 g brown sugar, 2 tablespoons cornflour and the grated rind of the two oranges, tip in the rhubarb and mix well. Grease the dish and spread the rhubarb mixture back into it. Strain the juice over it. For the topping, mix about 150 g brown sugar, about 90 g whole rolled oats, about 90 g fine rolled oats and about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds), then rub in 2 tablespoons soft butter. Press the topping firmly over the rhubarb and around the edges. Bake at 180 °C for 45 minutes.
recipes.title: Rose geranium rhubarb crumble

recipes.method: Fill a dry glass jar with alternate layers of rose geranium leaves and caster sugar. Cover tightly and leave somewhere warm for a week or more, shaking it now and then. Sieve out the leaves before use, and sprinkle the sugar on custards, biscuits or sponge cakes.
recipes.title: Rose geranium sugar

recipes.method: 250 ml water; 200 g sugar; 10 clean rose geranium leaves; 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice; chilled water and ice, to serve; a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals, to garnish. Boil 250 ml water with 200 g sugar in a small pot. Take off the heat, add 10 clean rose geranium leaves and leave until cold, overnight if you can. Squeeze the leaves out well (repeat with fresh leaves for a stronger flavour). Add 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice, bottle and refrigerate; it keeps for up to two weeks. To serve, stir 1 tablespoon of the concentrate into each cup of chilled water and pour over ice, garnished with a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals.
recipes.title: Rose geranium lemonade

recipes.method: Makes 8 wedges. About 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter; about 60 g icing sugar; about 190 g plain flour; ¼ teaspoon salt; 1 teaspoon rose water; 8 large rose geranium leaves, washed and dried; 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar); fresh rose geranium leaves, to serve. Cream about 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter with about 60 g icing sugar until light and fluffy. Mix about 190 g plain flour with ¼ teaspoon salt, add it to the butter, then mix in 1 teaspoon rose water. Gather into a ball, wrap and refrigerate for 4–6 hours. Let it soften a little. Butter and flour the base of a 20 cm round tin. On baking paper, pat the dough out to the size of the tin. Press 8 large, washed and dried rose geranium leaves into the dough in a circle about 2.5 cm in from the edge, lay the dough in the tin leaf side down and pat it out to the edges. Score it lightly into 8 wedges, sprinkle with 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar) and chill for 45 minutes. Bake at 160 °C for about 20 minutes, until it just starts to colour. Cool in the tin, turn out, peel the baked leaves off the base, cut along the marks and serve with fresh rose geranium leaves.
recipes.title: Rose geranium shortbread

recipes.method: Written for scented geranium leaves, "preferably with a lemon scent"; no species named. 2–3 scented geranium leaves; about 250 g sifted icing sugar; a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese; 2 teaspoons softened butter; 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind; lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel, to decorate (optional). Tear 2–3 scented geranium leaves into small pieces and mix them with about 250 g sifted icing sugar in a small bowl. Leave somewhere warm overnight so the sugar takes up the scent, then pick out and discard the leaf pieces. Beat a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese, 2 teaspoons softened butter and 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind, gradually adding the scented icing sugar, until smooth. Spread over a cooled carrot cake and decorate, if you like, with lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel.
recipes.title: Scented geranium and lemon icing

IV (Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), 'Pelargonium ×asperum', https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/54414bb3-a4f0-405b-84d3-2de4eebebabe, retrieved 21/10/2026 (Webb's stray space in "P. radula )" closed); Wikipedia contributors, 'Pelargonium graveolens', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia, CC BY-SA 4.0, revision 1361378169, retrieved 21/10/2026, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelargonium_graveolens.

Name: "Rose geranium" — NZ Flora Online and NZPCN give no vernacular ("Pelargonium hybrid"); Wikipedia 'Pelargonium graveolens': "Both the true species and the cultivated plant may be called rose geranium", and its cultivated rose-scented P. 'Graveolens' is "possibly a hybrid between P. graveolens and P. radens or P. capitatum" — Webb's parents for P. ×asperum are P. graveolens × P. radens. That the cultivated rose geranium and Webb's P. ×asperum are the same plant is my reading, not a source's. iNaturalist calls it "Rose Storksbill". Close to "Rose-scented geranium" (P. capitatum), whose summary already says several species are called rose geranium.

Omitted on purpose: Webb's "It apparently spreads vegetatively - ripe mericarps have not been observed." — Colin Ogle's 2022 iNaturalist note on obs 231378051 (Whanganui) says "Commonly self-establishing from seed - becoming a weed in this garden!", and its photos show seedlings; a 1988 negative left out rather than contradicted.

Edibility, DECIDED 21/10/2026 (owner: "there are no edible parts and recipies") — option (1) of the earlier lead taken. Bridge: the Herb Society of America guide (2006) puts "P. graveolens and members of the P. 'Graveolens' cultivar group" among the culinary rose-scenteds, and says of that group "Members of this group were once classified as P. xasperum" — so the guide itself ties the culinary rose geranium to this name. Edible parts: Useful Temperate Plants 'Pelargonium graveolens' (Ken Fern, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Pelargonium+graveolens, retrieved 21/10/2026; cites Facciola, Cornucopia, and Bown; Known Hazards "None known") verbatim, citation markers dropped; Wikipedia 'Pelargonium graveolens' (CC BY-SA 4.0, revision 1361378169) Uses sentence verbatim. Both are written for P. graveolens / cultivated rose geranium, not for P. ×asperum by name. Preparation: UTP tea sentence verbatim; the rest restated from the HSA guide's Culinary Uses section (Madalene Hill and Gwen Barclay's kitchen tips, Susan Belsinger's "sparingly so that they don't overwhelm"), https://www.herbsociety.org/file_download/inline/2b2f9fc8-e827-446c-99da-1c1e8b6559d0. Not used: the guide's note that rose geranium oil is GRAS (oil, not leaves) and that "Most individual species, hybrids and cultivars do not have GRAS status". No warning added: no trusted source records a hazard for the leaves or flowers.

Recipes (all from the HSA guide above, © the named authors / HSA, all rights reserved — methods paraphrased, not quoted; written for "rose geranium" / "rose-scented geranium" leaves, which the guide does not tie to one species — that they suit this plant rests on the bridge above): 'Rose geranium syrup' — Susan Belsinger, the syrup in "Chocolate rose-scented soufflé", excerpted from Not Just Desserts (2005); 'Apple and rose geranium jelly' — Madalene Hill and Gwen Barclay, "Apple rose geranium jelly", The Flavour Connection (frozen apple juice "diluted according to directions" or bottled juice; the source lists 2 tablespoons lemon juice but never uses it in the method — said so on the page); 'Pineapple and rose geranium ice' — Ann Wilson, "Pineapple rose freeze". Conversions: 1 cup = 250 ml, 1 cup sugar ≈ 200 g, ½ pint jar ≈ 250 ml, 2 tbsp = 30 ml. summary.text:
This hybrid is very commonly cultivated and is the commonest of the scented-leaved geraniums to occur wild. In New Zealand it grows wild in coastal areas and on offshore islands of the North Island, and in the South Island at Nelson City, Gore Bay (North Canterbury) and Banks Peninsula; it was first recorded growing wild here in 1869. Most plants grown in N.Z. as P. graveolens are hybrids or represent other spp.
Many plants are cultivated under the species name "Pelargonium graveolens" but differ from wild specimens as they are of hybrid origin (probably a cross between P. graveolens, P. capitatum and/or P. radens). Both the true species and the cultivated plant may be called rose geranium – pelargoniums are often called geraniums, as they fall within the plant family Geraniaceae, and were previously classified in the same genus.

habitat.text: Its habitat is usually beach sand or other well-drained sandy soils. Its preferred habitat is on sand dunes, but it is a fast grower on any reasonable base, including hard clayey soil, so it readily colonises disturbed habitat.

identification.text:
Pelargonium capitatum is a low shrub up to about 100 cm in height and 1.5 m across. The stems are soft and coated in green, glandular hairs. Brushing against a bush releases a copious scent of the essential oil from damaged hairs. The scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. The flowers range from white through various shades of pink to purple.
P. capitatum differs from P. vitifolium in its sprawling habit, more undulate and velvety leaves, generally lobed more than 1/2 way to the midrib, and the typically more compact inflorescence. The flowers are very similar to those of P. vitifolium with the corolla irregular and the petals oblanceolate and pink with the larger upper pair marked purple.
Flora of New Zealand key: "Umbels dense; flowers subsessile; calyx spur 4-5 mm long"; "Habit sprawling; leaves strongly undulate, with more or less oblong lobes extending at least 1/2 way to the centre of the lamina".
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Peppermint geranium is a subshrub to about 75 cm that smells strongly of peppermint, with more or less velvety white hairs and broad leaves up to 12 × 15 cm, rather shallowly three-lobed, the lobes reaching a quarter to half way to the midrib; its flowers are white or pinkish, 5–8 to an umbel, on stalks 2–3.5 cm long that generally radiate widely, with a calyx spur about 2 mm long. Rose-scented geranium is a sprawling plant whose leaves are strongly undulate and velvety, generally lobed more than half way to the midrib, with more or less oblong lobes; its pink flowers, the larger upper pair of petals marked purple, sit in dense heads on almost no stalks, with a calyx spur 4–5 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them by the umbels (diffuse, with long flower stalks, in peppermint geranium; dense, with almost stalkless flowers, in rose-scented geranium) and the calyx spur (about 2 mm against 4–5 mm). Leaf lobing meets at about half way, so it does not settle a plant on its own. Both plants are hairy, and flower colour does not separate them (Wikipedia gives rose-scented geranium white through pink to purple flowers). A crushed leaf of peppermint geranium smells strongly of peppermint; rose-scented geranium's scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. Most of these tests need flowers.
lookalikes.name: Peppermint geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Rose geranium (P. ×asperum) is a strongly aromatic, densely hairy subshrub to about 75 cm, with more or less triangular leaves up to about 7 × 10 cm that are deeply divided into 3 toothed lobes, lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib and rough above; its pink flowers, the upper 2 petals with more or less prominent purple markings and a white central patch, sit about 10 to an umbel on stalks 1–6 mm long, with a calyx spur about 3 mm long. Rose-scented geranium is a sprawling plant whose leaves are strongly undulate and velvety, generally lobed more than half way to the midrib, with more or less oblong lobes; its pink flowers, the larger upper pair of petals marked purple, sit in dense heads on almost no stalks, with a calyx spur 4–5 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates rose geranium first, by leaves lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib; rose-scented geranium's lobes reach at least half way, and the key's other branch says "lobed to < 1/2 way", so a leaf cut between half and three-quarters is not decided by lobing alone. The calyx spur is a little longer in rose-scented geranium (4–5 mm against about 3 mm). Both have short-stalked heads of pink flowers with purple-marked upper petals, so the flowers do not separate them; rose geranium's leaves are described as rough above, rose-scented geranium's as velvety. Smell does not separate them: rose geranium is strongly aromatic and rose-scented geranium's scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. Flora of New Zealand notes that P. ×asperum is a hybrid of P. graveolens and P. radens; Wikipedia says P. capitatum hybridises readily, so in-between plants are possible and this card may not decide them.

preparation.text: No source gives a method written for this species. For rose-scented pelargoniums in general: steep the leaves in the syrup, jelly, custard or drink and lift them out before the leaves break up, and use them sparingly so they do not overwhelm the dish.

recipes.method: Written for "rose-scented geranium" leaves without naming a species. 1 litre pineapple juice; 10 rose-scented geranium leaves; 400 g sugar; 125 ml lime juice; scented geranium leaves and flowers, to garnish. Warm 1 litre pineapple juice slightly, add 10 rose-scented geranium leaves and bruise them gently against the side of the container with a spoon. Cover and steep for 30 minutes, then take out the leaves. Stir in 400 g sugar and 125 ml lime juice until dissolved (warm it a little to speed this up). Cool, then freeze in an ice-cream maker, or pour into a shallow tray in the freezer and stir with a fork every 30–45 minutes until frozen. Garnish with scented geranium leaves and flowers.
recipes.title: Pineapple and rose geranium ice

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. 300 ml fresh cream; 4 tablespoons caster sugar; 4–6 rose-scented geranium leaves; 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed); 250 g sour cream (or cream cheese). Heat 300 ml fresh cream, 4 tablespoons caster sugar and 4–6 rose-scented geranium leaves in a pot, stirring often, until just short of boiling; do not let it boil. Take off the heat and cool. Mash 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed) to a purée. Beat 250 g sour cream (or cream cheese) until smooth, then beat in the purée. Strain the leaves out of the cream and fold the cream gently into the berry mixture with a spoon. Cover and chill for several hours or overnight. Serve on fresh berries or fruit salad instead of cream or yoghurt.
recipes.title: Rose geranium cream

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. Fruit: 6–8 rose-scented geranium leaves; the juice and grated rind of two oranges; about 190 ml more orange juice; 10–12 trimmed rhubarb stalks; about 150 g brown sugar; 2 tablespoons cornflour. Topping: about 150 g brown sugar; about 90 g whole rolled oats; about 90 g fine rolled oats; about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds); 2 tablespoons soft butter. Roughly chop 6–8 rose-scented geranium leaves and warm them gently with the juice of two oranges plus about 190 ml more orange juice; bring almost to the boil, take off the heat and leave to infuse as it cools. Cut 10–12 trimmed rhubarb stalks into 1 cm pieces — enough to fill, not overfill, the baking dish. In a large bowl mix about 150 g brown sugar, 2 tablespoons cornflour and the grated rind of the two oranges, tip in the rhubarb and mix well. Grease the dish and spread the rhubarb mixture back into it. Strain the juice over it. For the topping, mix about 150 g brown sugar, about 90 g whole rolled oats, about 90 g fine rolled oats and about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds), then rub in 2 tablespoons soft butter. Press the topping firmly over the rhubarb and around the edges. Bake at 180 °C for 45 minutes.
recipes.title: Rose geranium rhubarb crumble

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. Fill a dry glass jar with alternate layers of rose-scented geranium leaves and caster sugar. Cover tightly and leave somewhere warm for a week or more, shaking it now and then. Sieve out the leaves before use, and sprinkle the sugar on custards, biscuits or sponge cakes.
recipes.title: Rose geranium sugar

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. 250 ml water; 200 g sugar; 10 clean rose-scented geranium leaves; 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice; chilled water and ice, to serve; a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals, to garnish. Boil 250 ml water with 200 g sugar in a small pot. Take off the heat, add 10 clean rose-scented geranium leaves and leave until cold, overnight if you can. Squeeze the leaves out well (repeat with fresh leaves for a stronger flavour). Add 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice, bottle and refrigerate; it keeps for up to two weeks. To serve, stir 1 tablespoon of the concentrate into each cup of chilled water and pour over ice, garnished with a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals.
recipes.title: Rose geranium lemonade

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. Makes 8 wedges. About 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter; about 60 g icing sugar; about 190 g plain flour; ¼ teaspoon salt; 1 teaspoon rose water; 8 large rose-scented geranium leaves, washed and dried; 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar); fresh rose-scented geranium leaves, to serve. Cream about 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter with about 60 g icing sugar until light and fluffy. Mix about 190 g plain flour with ¼ teaspoon salt, add it to the butter, then mix in 1 teaspoon rose water. Gather into a ball, wrap and refrigerate for 4–6 hours. Let it soften a little. Butter and flour the base of a 20 cm round tin. On baking paper, pat the dough out to the size of the tin. Press 8 large, washed and dried rose-scented geranium leaves into the dough in a circle about 2.5 cm in from the edge, lay the dough in the tin leaf side down and pat it out to the edges. Score it lightly into 8 wedges, sprinkle with 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar) and chill for 45 minutes. Bake at 160 °C for about 20 minutes, until it just starts to colour. Cool in the tin, turn out, peel the baked leaves off the base, cut along the marks and serve with fresh rose-scented geranium leaves.
recipes.title: Rose geranium shortbread

recipes.method: Written for scented geranium leaves, "preferably with a lemon scent"; no species named. 2–3 scented geranium leaves; about 250 g sifted icing sugar; a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese; 2 teaspoons softened butter; 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind; lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel, to decorate (optional). Tear 2–3 scented geranium leaves into small pieces and mix them with about 250 g sifted icing sugar in a small bowl. Leave somewhere warm overnight so the sugar takes up the scent, then pick out and discard the leaf pieces. Beat a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese, 2 teaspoons softened butter and 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind, gradually adding the scented icing sugar, until smooth. Spread over a cooled carrot cake and decorate, if you like, with lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel.
recipes.title: Scented geranium and lemon icing

summary.text:
Pelargonium capitatum is one of several species (including Pelargonium graveolens) known as rose geranium or rose-scented pelargonium in English.
It is found in fynbos along the coast of South Africa, from Lamberts Bay in the Western Cape east to Kwazulu-Natal.
It is a popular and convenient ornamental plant and it also is one of the species of Pelargonium cultivated as a source of essential oils.
Pelargonium capitatum is one of a number of related plants that have become a major problem in coastal regions of southwest Western Australia, where it invades banksia woodland and coastal heathland.
P. capitatum, rose-scented geranium, is occasionally wild in the Hokianga area of N. Auckland, as well as there being unconfirmed reports from Nuhaka, Poverty Bay and Napier. It seems to be less common in cultivation than the very closely-related P. vitifolium and the 2 spp. are often confused. P. capitatum is the main sp. used for the production of oil of geranium.

identification.text:
Thorny, rather erect shrub with compound leaves that smell of apples when crushed. Pink single flowers, followed by red or orange-red, oval to round hips.
Deciduous, rather erect, sometimes dense shrub 1–3–(5) m high, often with suckers; armature of few to numerous, unequal, flattened, moderately curved to strongly falcate prickles and pricklets. Leaves with 2–3–(4) pairs of leaflets; leaflets 12–40–(50) × 8–28–(35) mm, with numerous pale glands beneath; margins ± 2-serrate, with glandular hairs. Flowers 1–3–(6), single, (20)–25–40 mm diameter; petals pink or deep pink (especially in bud) except for whitish base. Fruit (10)–12–22–(28) × (8)–10–18–(20) mm, broadly ovoid to globose, red or orange-red, usually glabrous except at base, sometimes with dark red hispid glands.
From other wild roses except the rare R. micrantha it is immediately recognisable by the abundance of glands and the strong smell of apples (Flora of New Zealand).

preparation.text: Top, tail, halve and scrape out every seed and hair, or cook whole and strain through fine cloth. Into syrup, jelly or tea. The hips are mostly seed with a thin layer of flesh, so cooking them whole and straining is usually easier: simmer, mash and drain overnight through a teatowel or jelly bag, then strain the liquid again through four layers of muslin to catch the fine hairs. The taste is best after a frost.

summary.text:
Autumn fruit of a weedy wild rose, most abundant in the drier east.
Rosa rubiginosa (sweet briar, sweet brier or eglantine) is a species of rose native to Europe and western Asia. The foliage has a strong apple-like fragrance.
In New Zealand it grows in nearly all districts but is often scattered and uncommon in wetter areas in the west of the South Island, and is especially abundant in drier eastern areas from Hawke's Bay south (Flora of New Zealand, restated); it is a major scrub weed in Central Otago and inland Canterbury (Massey University, restated). Introduced as an ornamental, it had become wild by the 1860s (naturalised 1867) and by 1900 was common enough to be regarded as a noxious weed (Flora of New Zealand, restated). It is named on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds.
Marlborough, Canterbury and Central Otago are where it is especially common (Knox).

warnings: There is a layer of hairs around the seeds just beneath the flesh of the hip. They irritate the mouth and digestive tract if swallowed, and are used as itching powder: remove or strain them out completely.

identification.text: Bulb 2 × 1.5 cm, tunic scarious, outermost layer with prominent round pits, whitish-grey with stipitate offset bulbs. Leaves 2–4, about 35 × 1 cm, flat shorter than scape, light green to more or less glaucous; sheaths reddish-purple. Scape 30–60 cm high, cylindrical, sheathed by leaves at base. Umbels 5–8 cm diameter, more or less lax, with flowers and bulbils; pedicels 4–6 times length of flowers, or longer; spathe-valve 1, persistent. Flowers 10–12 mm long, about 12 mm diameter, pale pink, with deeper pink central nerves; segments more or less oblong, obtuse, margins slightly dentate. Stamens about ⅔ length of perianth; filaments entire, without appendages. Bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, shining. Capsule not seen.

lookalikes.howToTell: Onion weed's flowers are white with a green stripe down the centre of each segment; rosy garlic's are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves. Onion weed's flower stalk is sharply three-angled; rosy garlic's is round in section. Onion weed's umbel has no bulbils; rosy garlic often carries bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among its flowers, though plants without bulbils also occur, so no bulbils does not rule rosy garlic out. Onion weed's leaves are strongly channelled; rosy garlic's are flat. The onion-garlic smell, a flower stalk of similar height (20–60 cm against 30–60 cm) and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Onion weed

lookalikes.howToTell: Naples garlic's flowers are pure white; rosy garlic's are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves, often with bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among them (plants without bulbils also occur). Naples garlic's flower stalk has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one; rosy garlic's is round in section. Flat leaves, the garlic smell, an umbel 5–8 cm across and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Naples garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild garlic's leaves are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical; rosy garlic's are flat. Wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils, its few flowers about 5 mm long; rosy garlic carries a loose umbel 5–8 cm across of pale pink flowers 10–12 mm long. Both can carry bulbils in the flower head and both smell of garlic, so bulbils and smell do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Wild garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: False garlic has none of rosy garlic's garlic smell, or only a faint one. False garlic's flowers are dull white, each segment with a greenish base and a reddish midvein; rosy garlic's are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves, often with bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among them (plants without bulbils also occur). False garlic has two bracts below the head, joined at the base and tinged red; rosy garlic has a single one that stays on. Dug up, false garlic's offset bulbs are stalkless and its bulb skin is smooth and white; rosy garlic's offset bulbs sit on short stalks and the outer bulb skin has prominent round pits. A round flower stalk, flat leaves and spring flowering do not separate them. If a plant does not smell of garlic or onion when crushed, leave it. False garlic has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: False garlic

All four share Auckland City in the Flora's distribution lines, so every pair was carded. Risk 'edible' everywhere: all four pages list edible parts. summary.text:
Allium roseum, commonly called rosy garlic, is an edible, Old World species of wild garlic.
It is native to the Mediterranean region and nearby areas, with a natural range extending from Portugal and Morocco to Turkey and the Palestine region. It is cultivated widely, and has become naturalised in scattered locations in other regions outside its natural range.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) the plant recorded is subsp. bulbiferum, which carries bulbils among its flowers: N. Auckland City; Gisborne - Tahunga. S Canterbury - Christchurch. Of the other subspecies (Useful Temperate Plants): The sub-species Allium roseum roseum does not produce bulbils.

warnings: Although no individual reports regarding this species have been seen, there have been cases of poisoning caused by the consumption, in large quantities and by some mammals, of certain members of this genus. Dogs seem to be particularly susceptible.

identification.text:
Slender tufts. Corm about 1 cm diameter, globose, rounded at base where smooth brown tunic splits into acuminate teeth bent to one side. Leaves 10–30 cm × 1–2 mm, rush-like, compressed-cylindrical, narrowly grooved, dark shining green. Scapes hidden by sheathing leaf-bases, 2–4–(10) from each corm, 5–15 cm long, stouter than leaves, semiterete, arched over after flowering; spathe-valves 2, long-persistent, outer longer, greenish with fine brown veins, inner with membranous reddish-brown flecked margins. Flowers lilac-pink, rosy-cerise or magenta, with yellow centre and violet-blue band at throat, 1.5–2 cm long, to 3 cm diameter; tube very short; outer lobes greener on back than inner. Capsules about 1cm long, short-cylindrical, scapes straightening when capsules mature. Seeds 2 mm long, reddish-brown, globose-triangular.
[From: Healy and Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]

identification.text:
Plant to about 80 cm tall, very scabrid. Roots becoming very thick. Basal leaves with lamina very large, ovate to oblong; upper side especially densely covered with rigid, bulbous-based hairs; base cuneate to subcordate; cauline leaves similar but smaller, with the narrowly winged petiole not decurrent on stem; uppermost leaves subsessile or with short petiole. Cymes densely hispid. Calyx about 5 mm long at anthesis; lobes accrescent, extending nearly to base, lanceolate, usually subacute, rarely obtuse. Corolla 12 - 17 mm long, light purple or purplish blue at first, becoming blue, especially when dried; lobes about 1 mm long, rounded; scales narrowtriangular. Filament width usually less than anther width except at base; anthers equal to or shortly projecting beyond scales. Nutlets 3–5 mm long, finely rugose or granular. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

identification.text:
Tree up to 8–(12) m high, usually with an erect trunk and spreading branches; young shoots pilose, sometimes densely so, but soon becoming glabrate. Buds large; outer scales glabrous, purplish, inner scales densely covered with white hairs towards apex. Leaves imparipinnate with up to 8 pairs of leaflets; petiole 20–35–(45) mm long, green or brown to purplish, pilose, but hairs deciduous, sometimes with stalked glands; leaflets (excluding smaller ones near base) narrowly oblong or oblong-elliptic, sometimes lanceolate-elliptic, (20)–30–50–(60) × 8–20–(25) mm, obtuse to acute, more or less sessile, deep green and glabrous or finely hairy above, paler and finely to densely pilose below, serrate along whole length or sometimes in upper ⅔ only; leaflets of juvenile plants and suckering shoots narrowly elliptic to elliptic-ovate, deeply and jaggedly toothed; stipules more or less deciduous, small, acuminate. Inflorescence drooping, up to about 120 mm across; pedicels and branchlets white-villous, becoming glabrate by fruiting. Sepal lobes broadly triangular, 0.6–1.3 mm long, obtuse, white-villous, at least at base, sometimes glabrous in upper part; margin with several short glandular teeth. Petals 3–4.5 mm diameter, more or less orbicular with abbreviated claw, white. Fruit depressed-globose, sometimes more or less oblong-obovoid, 5–10 mm diameter, deep orange to scarlet, sometimes crimson, glossy. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Seedlings are very common in the vicinity of parents and have more deeply and jaggedly toothed leaflets.
The sepals persist as a black, five-pointed star on the ripe fruit.
Bark smooth, shiny and grey. The flowers come in October–November and have an unpleasant smell; the berries ripen from green through yellow to orange-red.

preparation.text: Cut whole clusters, knock them to shake out insects, wash, and pick the berries off the stalks. Cooking, freezing or drying breaks down the parasorbic acid that makes the raw berries bitter; berries picked after frosts are less bitter, and berries picked before any frost can be frozen overnight to the same effect. Discard any berries that look old, dark or fermented. For jelly, simmer the berries until soft and broken down and drip the juice through muslin, which also leaves the seeds behind; rowan jelly sets best with a pectin source such as crab apples or Bramley apple cores. The berries are also made into jam, compote, syrup, chutney, juice, wine and liqueur, or dried and ground into flour.

recipes.method: Written for rowan buds; they contain a cyanogenic glycoside (see Warnings), so treat this as a flavouring in small amounts. Young rowan flower buds and very young leaf buds; cold water; 100 g sugar per 100 ml of water, or up to twice that; 10% vodka (optional). Put young rowan flower buds and very young leaf buds in a pan and cover them with cold water, measuring the water. Add 100 g sugar per 100 ml of water, or up to twice that for a thicker syrup that keeps better. Heat, stirring to dissolve the sugar, and hold it at about 70 °C for a few minutes; the author simmers for no more than 5 minutes, as the almond flavour fades fast with heat. Leave to cool and strain into sterilised bottles, keeping the syrupy buds for the liqueur. Add 10% vodka to help it keep, or store it in the fridge, or freeze it in plastic bottles.
recipes.title: Rowan bud syrup

recipes.method: Written for rowan buds; they contain a cyanogenic glycoside (see Warnings), so treat this as a flavouring in small amounts. The syrup-coated buds left from the rowan bud syrup; cheap vodka; rowan bud syrup, to taste. Put the syrup-coated buds left from the rowan bud syrup in a jar, cover with cheap vodka and leave for about 4 weeks, shaking now and then. Strain, then sweeten to taste with the rowan bud syrup — the author aims for about 20–25% alcohol. Adding more fresh buds to the vodka strengthens the almond flavour, but also extracts more of the cyanogenic glycoside; the author says to drink correspondingly less.
recipes.title: Rowan bud liqueur

recipes.method: Written for rowan buds; they contain a cyanogenic glycoside (see Warnings), so treat this as a flavouring in small amounts. 20 ml rowan bud liqueur; 60 ml whisky (Scotch, or bourbon); ice; a rowan bud. Stir 20 ml rowan bud liqueur and 60 ml whisky (Scotch, or bourbon) over ice. Bruise a rowan bud and float it on top for its aroma.
recipes.title: The Godfather of Soil

recipes.method: Written for rowan buds; they contain a cyanogenic glycoside (see Warnings), so treat this as a flavouring in small amounts. 30 ml whisky (bourbon is best here); 30 ml rowan bud liqueur; 30 ml lemon juice; 10 ml rowan bud syrup (or to taste); 1 egg white; ice. Shake 30 ml whisky (bourbon is best here), 30 ml rowan bud liqueur, 30 ml lemon juice, 10 ml rowan bud syrup (or to taste) and 1 egg white with ice. Strain out the ice and shake again (a reverse dry shake, which makes the egg white creamy; leave it out if you prefer), then fine-strain into a glass.
recipes.title: The Godfather of Sour

recipes.method: 1.5 kg rowan berries; 1.5 kg crab apples (or Bramley apple cores); white sugar, 450 g for every 600 ml of strained juice; juice of 1 lemon. Chop the crab apples without peeling or coring and put them in a large heavy pan with the rowan berries. Just cover with water, bring to the boil, then simmer for about 20 minutes until the fruit is very soft and broken down. Tip the pulp and liquid into a muslin or clean cotton cloth over a large bowl, tie it up and let it drip for at least 4 hours or overnight; do not squeeze it or the jelly will be cloudy. Measure the juice into a pan, add 450 g sugar for every 600 ml, add the lemon juice and bring to the boil. Boil hard for about 10 minutes, then test: spoon a little onto a fridge-cold plate, leave a minute and push it with a finger — if the surface wrinkles it is set; if not, boil a few minutes more and test again. Take off the heat, pour into clean sterilised jars and seal. Serve with cheese, game or lamb.
recipes.title: Rowan and crab apple jelly

recipes.method: Ingredients: 2 cups (500 ml) fresh or frozen rowan berries (freeze fresh ones overnight first); 1/3 cup (80 ml) water; 125 g butter; 6 egg yolks; juice of 1 large orange (1/2 cup, 125 ml); 2/3 cup (160 ml) sugar. Bring the berries and water to the boil in a small pan, then simmer for 10 minutes, pressing the berries now and then to break the skins. Take off the heat and push the berries through a sieve, keeping the juice and pulp and discarding the skins and seeds; you need 2/3 cup (160 ml), topped up with the cooking liquid if short. Mix it with the orange juice. Melt the butter in a heavy pan over medium heat, add the juice, sugar and egg yolks, and cook, whisking often, until thick, 10–15 minutes. Cool completely; blend it if you want it extra smooth.
recipes.title: Rowan and orange curd

recipes.method: Juice: 140 g rowan berries, frozen then thawed; 500 ml water. Turkish delight: 1 tsp butter; 450 g sugar; 300 ml rowan juice; 1 tsp lemon juice; 25 g gelatine; 1/2 tsp vanilla essence; 1 tbsp rose water; 1 tbsp pistachios, crushed; 30 g (1 oz) arrowroot or cornflour. For the juice, bring the berries and water to the boil, crush the berries with a potato masher, then cover and simmer for about 45 minutes. Mash again and strain overnight through muslin in a sieve; you should have about 400 ml — make it up to 500 ml with water. Butter a 15 cm square tin. Boil the sugar, 300 ml rowan juice and lemon juice until a drop forms a hard ball in cold water, then take off the heat and leave 10 minutes. Dissolve the gelatine in 120 ml just-boiled water, add the vanilla, stir it well into the rowan syrup, and pour half into the tin. Scatter over the pistachios, stir the rose water into the rest and pour it on top. Cool, then refrigerate overnight. Turn out, cut into cubes and roll each in arrowroot or cornflour. Makes 20–30 pieces.
recipes.title: Rowan Turkish delight

summary.text:
Sorbus aucuparia, commonly called rowan and mountain-ash, is a species of deciduous tree or shrub in the rose family.
It can be found in almost all of Europe and the Caucasus up to Northern Russia and Siberia, but it is not native to Southern Spain, Southern Greece, Sardinia, the Balearic Islands, the Azores, and the Faroe Islands. The species was introduced as an ornamental species in North America.
It has naturalised in America from Washington to Alaska and eastward in Canada and the northeast of the US very successfully.
It is widespread from plains to mountains up to the tree line where it grows as the only deciduous tree species among krummholz. In the Alps it grows at elevations of up to 2,000 m. S. aucuparia appears north of the boreal forest at the arctic tree line; in Norway, it is found up to the 71st parallel north.
S. aucuparia is an undemanding species and can withstand shade. It is frost hardy and can tolerate winter dryness and a brief growing season. The plant is also resistant to air pollution, wind, and snow pressure. It mostly grows on soil that is moderately dry to moderately damp, acidic, low on nutrients, sandy, and loose. It often grows in stony soil or clay soil, but also sandy soil or wet peat. The plant grows best on fresh, loose, and fertile soil, prefers average humidity, and does not tolerate saline soil or waterlogging. It can be found in light woodland of all kinds and as a pioneer species over fallen dead trees or in clearcuttings, and at the edge of forests or at the sides of roads. The seeds germinate easily, so the plant may appear on inaccessible rock, ruins, branch forks, or on hollow trees.
Rowan is widely grown in gardens for both its attractive foliage and fruits and is particularly common in colder areas. Most New Zealand specimens have relatively short petioles, short and obtuse leaflets, and hairy sepals and can be referred to subsp. aucuparia. The species has been known in New Zealand as Pyrus aucuparia.
In New Zealand it was introduced as an ornamental and first recorded in the wild in 1904. Birds spread its plentiful, readily germinating seeds; it smothers and outcompetes native plants and is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds. It is not legally declared a pest, but is an organism of interest under the Canterbury, Otago, Southland and Tasman–Nelson pest plans (site-led in Tasman–Nelson), and Environment Canterbury suggests removing it from gardens.

warnings: The young leaves and buds contain a cyanogenic glycoside, which releases hydrogen cyanide as it is digested; their almond taste comes from it. Toxic in high doses — keep the amounts small.

Raw berries contain parasorbic acid, which irritates the stomach lining; in large amounts it causes indigestion and can affect the kidneys, and large quantities of raw fruit can cause vomiting, especially in people not used to it. Heating or freezing turns it into non-toxic sorbic acid — cook, freeze or dry the berries before eating.
The seeds contain the cyanogenic glycoside prunasin, which can release hydrogen cyanide; strain the seeds out when making jelly, juice or syrup rather than eating them.
Little is known about its safety in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, so avoid it then.

identification.text: The cap is up to 10 centimetres in diameter. It is dark brick, bay, or red-brown. At first it is convex, and often has a small central boss (umbo), but later flattens, eventually acquiring a shallow central depression. The surface is dry and matt. The concolorous, but paler stem often becomes hollow with age. The gills are slightly decurrent, cream, becoming coloured as the cap later, only paler. The spore print is creamy white, with a slight salmon tinge. The flesh is white, as is the (abundant) milk, which tastes mild initially, gradually becoming very hot, and acrid after a minute or so.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white and abundant. Its cap is dark brick, bay or red-brown, dry and matt, often with a small central boss. Both grow under pine, so habitat does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Saffron milk cap / Pine mushroom

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a little flesh and smell it. Rufous milkcap has no smell; oakbug milkcap has a strong oily smell likened to bedbugs or wet laundry. Rufous milkcap's cap often has a small central boss, and its milk is watery white; oakbug milkcap's milk is white or cream. In New Zealand rufous milkcap is reported only with pines, and oakbug milkcap is known from a single site, with oak. Cap colour does not separate them: both are matt reddish brown.

summary.text:
Lactarius rufus is a common, medium-sized member of the mushroom genus Lactarius, whose many members are commonly known as milkcaps.

It is frequent in the northern temperate zones in Europe and North America. It is common in northern California, and the Pacific Northwest from late summer to early winter.

warnings: Not recommended for eating: it carries toxins that may cause gastric upset and may be poisonous raw. It is eaten in Scandinavian countries after canning, and as of 1984 it was one of the most common wild mushrooms harvested for food in Finland.

edibleParts.text: Firm young caps.

habitat.text: Exclusively under pine, in plantation forest and shelter belts. Never in native bush.

harvestEthics.text: Cut rather than pull, and leave the smallest and the largest.

identification.text: Orange cap with darker concentric rings, often depressed in the centre. Orange gills that bruise dull green. The confirming test: cut the flesh and it bleeds bright carrot-orange latex, and the cut surface slowly stains green. Brittle, not fibrous, flesh. Test every cap for latex rather than reading the cap: other milk caps are zoned the same way, so the cap alone tells you nothing, and a spore print will not separate them either — the prints run white to ochre across the genus, this one's cream included.

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. Coconut milk cap's milk is white, rather watery and unchanging, its cap is greyish lilac, pale greyish brown or brownish grey with leaden tints rather than orange, and it smells of coconut - faintly, in the New Zealand description. It grows under silver birch; saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine.
lookalikes.name: Coconut milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Downy milk cap's milk is white and does not change colour or stain the flesh. Downy milk cap's cap margin is rolled in and bearded with coarse white hairs when young, and the cap is white to cream, reddening at the centre with age. Saffron milk cap's cap is orange to salmon, with an incurved margin. In New Zealand and Australia, downy milk cap grows with birch, saffron milk cap only with pine. Downy milk cap's milk and flesh taste acrid, and some authors consider it toxic.
lookalikes.name: Downy milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white, does not change, and dries pale cream, though its cut flesh slowly runs from white through pink, salmon and orange-red to wine red. Its cap is dark brown to almost black and unzoned, often with dull salmon patches near the centre. It is endemic, and recorded under beech.
lookalikes.name: New Zealand milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Oakbug milkcap's milk is white or cream. Its cap is dull, matt reddish brown with a cinnamon tint and stays dry, not sticky, when moist, and it has a strong oily smell likened to bedbugs or wet laundry. In Europe it grows only with oak; in New Zealand and Australia, saffron milk cap grows only with pine. Both can show concentric zones on the cap, so zoning is not the difference.
lookalikes.name: Oakbug milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white and abundant. Its cap is dark brick, bay or red-brown, dry and matt, often with a small central boss, which can sit in a shallow depression on older caps. Both grow under pine, so habitat does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Rufous milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Slimy milkcap's milk is white and plentiful and dries grey, and its cut gills turn grey-buff. Its cap is drab greenish-grey or olive-grey with rings of darker blotches, and slimy in wet weather. In Europe it grows with beech, very occasionally oak; in New Zealand and Australia, saffron milk cap grows only with pine. Its taste is bitter and hot.
lookalikes.name: Slimy milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white, sticky and unchanging, drying cream. Both species have zoned caps, so zoning does not separate them. Tawai's cap is a dull orange-brown or drab ochre with purplish-grey to reddish-brown bands. It is endemic, and recorded under beech.
lookalikes.name: Tawai milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Ugly milkcap's milk is white or creamy white, and old milk leaves its dirty-white gills stained olive-brown. Its cap is olive brown or yellow-green, often sticky or slimy in the middle, darkening to blackish with age. In New Zealand and Australia it grows with birch; saffron milk cap only with pine. Its milk tastes acrid, and it is reported to contain carcinogenic compounds.
lookalikes.name: Ugly milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white and unchanging, drying cream. Its cap is small, 1-3.5 cm across, where saffron milk cap's is 3-20 cm, so a small saffron cap can overlap. It is a dull salmon, greyish orange or pale orange-brown, and unzoned. It is an endemic of beech forest.
lookalikes.name: Umere milkcap

preparation.text: Dry-fry or roast hard — they release a lot of water and go slimy if cooked gently. Do not eat raw.

recipes.method: 12 medium caps, 15 ml olive oil, salt and pepper. Brush the caps clean — rinse only if they are really dirty — and pat them dry. Cut them to size, or leave the small ones whole. Get the oil hot in a skillet over medium-high, add the mushrooms, season, and stir now and then for about 5 minutes until they have shrunk down and cooked through. Serve hot alongside something else.
recipes.title: Sautéed saffron milk caps

recipes.method: 250 g caps, cleaned and sliced, 200 ml sherry or red wine vinegar, 200 ml water, 100 g sugar, 50 ml olive oil, 1 tsp salt, 5 black peppercorns, 3 cloves garlic, 3 juniper berries, 2 bay leaves, a sprig each of rosemary and thyme. To clean them first, soak them in 1.4 litres of water with 120 ml white vinegar. Bring everything but the mushrooms to the boil, add them, and simmer one minute. Off the heat, let it cool, then pack into a sterilised jar with the liquid above the mushrooms. Keeps up to 6 months in the fridge as long as they stay covered.
recipes.title: Pickled saffron milk caps

recipes.method: 400 g caps sliced, 4 cloves garlic chopped, oil, 80 ml white wine, 125 g cream cheese, 3 tbsp sour cream, 2 sage leaves, 2 sprigs thyme, salt and pepper, 1 sheet butter puff pastry, 1 egg yolk beaten with 1 tsp water. Fry the garlic a minute in oil over medium heat, add the mushrooms and cook 5 minutes, adding oil as they take it. Stir in the wine, cream cheese, sour cream, sage and thyme and cook until creamy and tender, then season and cool completely — this can be done a day ahead. Heap the filling down the centre of the pastry sheet, seal the edges with the egg wash, press the ends with a fork, and bake at 220 °C for 30 minutes until golden.
recipes.title: Saffron milk cap, sage and thyme strudel

recipes.method: An onion and 2 cloves garlic, finely diced, oil, 50 g butter, 3 tbsp flour, 200 g sliced caps, 3 tsp paprika, 600–700 ml chicken stock, 60 ml sour cream, parsley. Fry the onion and garlic in oil a few minutes until translucent, melt the butter into them, then stir in the flour. Add the mushrooms, paprika and stock and simmer about 10 minutes until the mushrooms are done. Serve with a spoonful of sour cream and parsley.
recipes.title: Hungarian mushroom soup

recipes.method: 125 ml olive oil; 2 tbsp butter; 300 g caps with the stems off and thinly sliced; 3 sprigs thyme; an onion; 105 g arborio rice; 1 litre chicken stock; a pinch of saffron; 165 ml dry white wine; 125 ml cream; 25 g blue cheese; chopped chives or parsley, to serve. Sauté the mushrooms in half the oil with the butter over medium-high until coated, season, and set aside. Soften the diced onion in the rest of the oil over medium heat for 5–8 minutes without browning, while the stock warms with the saffron in another pan. Stir the rice through the onion, then add the hot stock a ladle at a time, letting each one absorb, for 15–20 minutes until the rice is cooked. Stir in the wine, blue cheese and cream, fold through half the mushrooms, and season. Plate it with the remaining mushrooms on top and chopped chives or parsley.
recipes.title: Saffron milk cap risotto

recipes.method: Pastry: 480 ml plain flour, 150 g cold cubed butter, 240 ml finely grated parmesan, 2.5 ml fine salt, 1 egg, 120–160 ml ice water. Filling: 5 caps, 4 cloves garlic sliced, olive oil, 150 g ash brie sliced, 3 eggs, 240 ml cream, 240 ml parmesan, 2 sprigs thyme. Clean the mushrooms in 1.4 litres of water with 120 ml white vinegar. Pulse the flour, butter, cheese and salt in a food processor, add the egg and 120 ml water and run it until it starts to come together, then knead on a floured bench with more water if it needs it and rest it 30 minutes at room temperature. Line an oiled 31 × 21 cm loose-bottomed tart tin, trim, and chill 45 minutes or freeze 15. Meanwhile fry the garlic then the mushrooms — whole if small, sliced if not — in oil over medium heat only until they keep their bright orange, then season and cool a little. Blind bake at 200 °C under oiled foil and weights for 20 minutes, then 10–15 minutes uncovered. Drop the oven to 150 °C, whisk the eggs, cream and parmesan, pour it into the case, arrange the mushrooms and brie on top with the thyme, and bake 30–35 minutes until just set. Serve warm.
recipes.title: Saffron milk cap and ash brie tart

recipes.method: 500 g desiree potatoes, 125 g Italian 00 flour plus extra for the bench, 40 g chestnut flour (or just more 00), 2 tbsp oil, an onion sliced, 2 cloves garlic sliced thinly, 250 g caps with the stalks off and sliced, 150 g bacon or prosciutto (optional), 100 g roasted and peeled chestnuts, 100 g butter, salt and pepper. Boil the potatoes in their skins until tender, rice them, and cool completely before working the flours in. Roll the dough into logs, cut it into pieces, and shape each one against a fork. Boil them and lift them out as they float. Fry the onion and garlic until fragrant, add the mushrooms until the edges crisp, then the bacon, chestnuts and butter. Add the drained gnocchi and fry until golden all over, then season.
recipes.title: Saffron milk cap and chestnut gnocchi

Season. Plant & Food Research gives a January-to-May season for Lactarius deliciosus under Pinus radiata here; iNaturalist NZ holds only 11 research-grade records and they run March to July, peaking in May. March to June is where the two overlap, and is what this entry lists. Checked 06/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/taxa/155197

Which other New Zealand milk caps have zoned caps: Lactarius quietus ('darker concentric bands or spots'), L. blennius ('blotches of darker colouration in concentric bands') and the endemic L. tawai ('distinctly or indistinctly concentrically zonate'). The first two from Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0; the third from McNabb (1971) via the Virtual Mycota, restated. Checked 06/10/2026.

The eleven Lactarius taxa on record in New Zealand: Lactarius rufus, L. pubescens, L. turpis, L. glyciosmus, L. tawai, L. novae-zelandiae, L. umerensis, L. deliciosus, L. blennius, L. quietus, and the undescribed Lactarius sp. 'Hauroko' (6 records, no published name). All ten named species have entries here. Checked 06/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/observations?taxon_id=54597&place_id=6803&view=species

Downy milk cap belongs on the list of zoned caps too, which is why that count went from three to four. First Nature describes Lactarius pubescens with 'faint pinkish concentric bands and pinkish-brown centre zone' — fainter than this species' banding, but present, and it is a do-not-eat entry. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/lactarius-pubescens.php

lookalikes.howToTell: the three endemic milk cap cards (tawai-milkcap, new-zealand-milkcap, umere-milkcap) said those species had never been described in print. That is wrong — McNabb, R.F.R. (1971), 'The Russulaceae of New Zealand. 1. Lactarius', New Zealand Journal of Botany 9(1): 46–66 describes all three, and the Virtual Mycota reproduces it; what does not exist is an openly licensed description. All three were corrected to say that. The tawai-milkcap card was also rewritten to carry the two real separators — host tree (pine against beech, from the Hidden Forest and NZOR facts on that entry) and the point that both species have zoned caps, so zoning does not separate them, which is the limit this entry's own zonate-cap source already records. In copyright, so facts restated, no text reproduced. Written by the assistant on the owner's instruction, 08/10/2026; flagged here so it is greppable and reversible.

Cap colour added as dull orange-brown to dingy ochre. In copyright, so facts restated, no text reproduced. Written by the assistant on the owner's instruction; flagged here so it is greppable and reversible.

lookalikes.howToTell: the umere-milkcap and new-zealand-milkcap cards were rewritten 08/10/2026 once the full McNabb descriptions were read off the Virtual Mycota (pk=5192, pk=5184), in the same way as the tawai-milkcap card. Both endemics have white unchanging latex, which is a real separator from this species' carrot-orange; added with it are size (1–3.5 cm for umere), cap colour, the absence of zoning, and for L. novae-zelandiae the flesh running white to wine red on cutting. All three cards previously said no description was available, which was true only of openly licensed ones. In copyright, facts restated, no text reproduced. Written by the assistant on the owner's instruction; flagged here so it is greppable and reversible.

lookalikes.howToTell: two corrections to the cards written earlier on 08/10/2026, found by re-reading them against the sources. FIRST, the umere-milkcap card compared cap sizes as '1–3.5 cm against 4–15 cm'. THE 4–15 cm WAS NOT FROM ANY SOURCE — no source on this entry gives a cap size for Lactarius deliciosus at all — so the figure is removed and only the endemic's sourced measurement is given. SECOND, three cards said the endemics are 'never found under pine'. The sources record them under Nothofagus; they do not record an absence under pine, and that is a different claim. Reworded to 'recorded only from beech forest'. Corrected by the assistant, 08/10/2026.

summary.text: The best beginner's mushroom in NZ — it bleeds bright orange, and nothing dangerous does.

warnings: At least eleven Lactarius species are on record in New Zealand and this is one of them; others are undescribed or unnamed, and related milk-bleeding genera grow here too. Any milk cap bleeding white, cream or watery latex is a different species — some are considered toxic, and ugly milk cap contains a mutagen that boiling does not remove.
Only harvest from pine. A mushroom that looks similar in native forest is not this species.
Many plantation forests are private land or actively logged — get permission and check for harvesting operations.
Some plantations are aerially sprayed. Check with the forest manager.

edibleParts.text: Young leaves and shoots, raw or cooked: in salads, as a garnish, in dressings, sauces, soups and cold drinks, and to flavour vinegar, butter and cream cheese. It goes into herb vinegars and the traditional European green sauce, can stand in for basil or, in some recipes, mint, and chopped leaves stirred into yoghurt make a dressing. The leaves taste mildly of cucumber. The flowers can go into salads as a garnish; they have little flavour. Young seedlings are boiled and eaten, and a herb tea is made from the dried leaves.
