identification.text:
Herb with branching rhizomes; stems more or less erect, up to 35–(70) cm tall at flowering, glabrous to sparingly pilose, sparingly branched, greenish yellow to purplish, grooved. Lower leaves in basal rosettes; petiole short; blade oblong to narrowly oblanceolate, up to 150–(300) × 45 mm, imparipinnate; leaflets in (5)–7–10–(12) pairs, shortly petiolulate or subsessile, narrowly obovate to elliptic or orbicular, 5–12–(30) mm long, glabrous above, sparsely finely puberulent and often with a few longer hairs on veins beneath, deeply serrate, sometimes purplish especially towards margins or pale to more or less glaucous below. Cauline leaves few, similar to basal leaves but with fewer and narrower leaflets. Inflorescence a dense globose head, elongating somewhat at fruiting. Sepals ovate-oblong, (2)–3–4 mm long, free, more or less emarginate with a small cusp, green; margins whitish or pink to purple. Stamens numerous. Hypanthium usually broadly ellipsoid, rarely ellipsoid at fruiting, glabrous, almost glabrous or pubescent, (2)–4–5 mm long, usually sharply angled and winged, rarely obscurely winged; faces usually reticulate and the ridges with small projections, rarely faintly reticulate. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Crushed leaves smell of cucumber (Hands in the Dirt; Herb Federation of New Zealand).
The leaflets, up to 12 pairs, sit along the leaf stalk a little like the rungs of a ladder. The tiny green flowers are packed into small round heads at the stem tips, with red styles sticking out and longer yellow anthers hanging below (Totally Wild UK, restated).

preparation.text: Use the youngest leaves and new shoots; older leaves turn bitter and tough, and mature leaves are better added to soups. The leaves sometimes become bitter in hot dry summers (above about 25 °C) and are usually milder in winter, when it is one of the few salad herbs still green; plants on acid soil can taste distinctly bitter. Sources differ on timing: best before the plant flowers, or when it is just starting to flower. Cutting the foliage back as flower buds form, or removing the flower heads before they set seed, keeps new leaves coming; cutting off older leaves helps too. The cucumber flavour is best fresh and weakens when the leaves are dried or cooked at high temperatures. Cooked leaves taste more bitter, so salad burnet is best eaten raw. Sources differ on keeping: the leaves are best fresh and may not store, dry or freeze well, though chopped leaves can also be frozen and keep their flavour for up to a year, and leaves dried slowly keep their aroma for tea. Small leaflets make it a fiddly harvest.

recipes.method: Ingredients: 75 g butter; 1½ tablespoons chopped salad burnet; 1 tablespoon chopped spearmint; salt, black pepper and lemon juice to taste. Mix the chopped herbs. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the herbs and simmer on a very low heat for 10 minutes. Season with salt, pepper and lemon juice, and pour over grilled fish.
recipes.title: Salad burnet butter

recipes.method: Makes 2 sandwiches, about 10 minutes. Ingredients: 4 slices wholegrain bread (or wholegrain crackers); softened butter for spreading; 1 tablespoon whole fresh salad burnet leaves; 125 ml (½ cup) softened cream cheese; salt and black pepper. Butter each slice of bread. In a small bowl mix the whole leaves into the cream cheese (the leaves are too delicate to need mincing) and season with salt and pepper. Spread the mixture on two slices, top with the other two and cut into halves or quarters.
recipes.title: Cream cheese tea sandwiches with salad burnet

recipes.method: Serves 4 to 6. Ingredients: 1 wholegrain French baguette; a handful of salad burnet leaves; about 190 ml (¾ cup) chopped walnuts; good olive oil (the source gives no amount). Heat the oven to 190 °C (375 °F). Slice the baguette without cutting all the way through. Wash and chop the salad burnet, crush the walnuts into pieces, and divide both among the cuts. Drizzle olive oil into the cuts and over the top, bake 10 minutes and serve straight away.
recipes.title: French bread with walnuts and salad burnet

recipes.method: Ingredients: about 30 g each of cress, parsley, chives, salad burnet, sorrel, young borage leaves and chervil; 2 hard-boiled egg yolks; ¾ teaspoon prepared mustard; 125 ml (½ cup) sour cream (or yoghurt or crème fraîche). Whizz the herbs in a food processor until finely chopped, add the other ingredients and blend until smooth. Serve, or refrigerate and use within 2 days. Serve with fish (especially oily fish), chicken, hot new potatoes, asparagus or salads.
recipes.title: Traditional green sauce

summary.text:
Sanguisorba minor, the salad burnet, garden burnet, small burnet, burnet (also used for Sanguisorba generally), pimpernelle, Toper's plant, and burnet-bloodwort, is an edible perennial herbaceous plant in the family Rosaceae.
It is evergreen to semi-evergreen; in warmer climates grows all year around, and in cold climates it stays green until heavy snow cover occurs.
It has also naturalized in most of North America, in South America, Australia, and New Zealand.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): S. minor is a very variable species interpreted in a broad sense to include several subspecies sometimes treated as separate species. Two subspecies are found in New Zealand; the fruiting hypanthium provides principal distinguishing characters. S. minor may have entered New Zealand as a seed contaminant. Most records of Sanguisorba or Poterium naturalised in New Zealand are based on plants of S. minor subsp. muricata (sheep's burnet), native of South Europe, North Africa and South-West Asia and first recorded in New Zealand in 1877: North Island: Wellington (Marton, Martinborough, Wairarapa coast, Wellington City area); South Island: Nelson (Takaka, Nelson City), Marlborough (Blenheim, Fairhall, Renwick, Wither Hills), lowland Canterbury and inland North and South Canterbury, Otago (Benmore, Luggate). Subsp. lasiocarpa is known from one collection only, Delta Station, Wairau Valley, Marlborough, 1947. Records of subsp. minor, salad burnet, are not substantiated by specimens although this subspecies is cultivated in New Zealand as a culinary herb. It is distinguished from subsp. muricata by the angles of the hypanthium having short and obscure wings and the faces being merely reticulate.
The New Zealand Plant Conservation Network lists sheep's burnet as Sanguisorba minor subsp. balearica, with subsp. muricata as a synonym: native of southern Europe, North Africa and south-west Asia, naturalised in New Zealand in 1877.

warnings: The safety record for this species is thin: none of the sources checked records a hazard specific to salad burnet, which is not evidence that it is safe. For the related great burnet (Sanguisorba officinalis), people taking quinolone antibiotics are advised to avoid the plant.

Wild burnet in New Zealand is mostly the subspecies muricata (sheep's burnet; the New Zealand Plant Conservation Network now lists it as subsp. balearica). The culinary subspecies minor is grown in gardens, and records of it growing wild are not backed by specimens. Most of the food sources describe Sanguisorba minor as a whole; Eatweeds names its plant as the culinary subspecies minor. None separates the subspecies for eating.

identification.text:
Biennial with cylindric rootstock. Stems erect, weakly ribbed, glabrous or sometimes with sparse cobwebby tomentum above, 30–100 cm tall. Leaves linear- to lanceolate-subulate, entire, acuminate, 5–30–(40) × 0.5–1.5–(2) cm; base sheathing; margins undulate or flat. Capitula solitary; peduncles swollen beneath capitula ( longer than 5 mm thick at fruiting). Involucre glabrous at base; involucral bracts 6–8, lanceolate-acuminate, 3.5–6 × 0.5–1 cm at fruiting, glabrous, or tomentose near apex. Corolla mauve to purple, shorter than involucre. Achenes fusiform, ribbed, the outer coarsely muricate, the inner becoming smooth; body 8–13–(15) mm long; beak shorter than or up to 2× length of body, barely clavate at apex. Pappus sordid, 1.5–2 cm long, plumose, in 2 rows, seated on a distinct tomentose annulus. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It exudes a milky juice from the stems. The taproots can become 15–30 cm long and 2–5 cm thick.

preparation.text: Collect roots and leaves before the flower stalk appears: after flowering the root quickly turns fibrous, stringy and inedible. Wild plants often grow in compacted soil, so a garden fork or spade is needed to lift the long root. A broken root discolours and spoils quickly, and roots lose flavour soon after digging, so use them promptly. Scrape off the outer layers and dip the root in cold water to keep its colour; roots that are too tough can be boiled with a pinch of baking soda and a change of water. Boiling the roots for 15 minutes before frying softens them. Roots can be roasted with other root vegetables, made into a purée to go with fish, or added to soups, stews and stir-fries. The root's flavour is mild and sweet, likened to oysters or asparagus.

recipes.method: Ingredients: salsify roots, white wine, butter and garlic; the source gives no amounts. Steps: dig the roots (a spade helps in compacted soil) and clean them. Boil them for 15 minutes so they are not tough, then sauté them in white wine, butter and garlic. The source gives no frying time.

summary.text:
Tragopogon porrifolius is a species of plant commonly known as purple or common salsify, oyster plant, vegetable oyster, Jerusalem star, Jack go to bed, goatsbeard, or simply salsify.
Tragopogon porrifolius is a common biennial wildflower, native to southeast Europe, Mediterranean Turkey, and north Africa, but introduced elsewhere, for example, into the British Isles (mainly in central and southern England), other parts of northern Europe, North America and southern Africa, and in Australia. In the United States, it is now found growing wild in almost every state, including Hawaii, except in the extreme south-east.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Northland, Auckland, Bay of Plenty, Gisborne, Hawke's Bay, Manawatu; S.: Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago. Salsify is occasionally cultivated for its edible root.
Two yellow-flowered relatives are also naturalised in New Zealand, but are rare: Tragopogon dubius around Cromwell in Central Otago, and goatsbeard, T. pratensis, in Canterbury. Salsify is the one with mauve to purple florets (Flora of New Zealand, restated).

warnings: Out of flower salsify looks like grass, and its leaves resemble onion leaves. Cut or broken leaves, stems and fresh roots bleed a white, milky sap.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand it is common throughout in salt marsh or on coastal rock platforms and rock crevices.
It grows in intertidal places – estuaries, sandy and muddy shores, and rocks – where it can form a dense mat. It can grow on bare mud, but its roots are shallow, so it does not grow where water currents are strong. It also grows inland in Otago, where erosion leaves the soils salty when rain is scarce.
Planted, it grows best in full sun on free-draining sandy or rocky soil; once established it tolerates drought and salt spray.
On New Zealand's national wetland plant list it is rated facultative wetland: usually a wetland plant, occasionally found on dry ground.

identification.text:
A perennial subshrub with prostrate woody stems about 3–4 mm in diameter, up to 30 cm or more long; branches numerous, the plant forming extensive patches up to 60 cm or more in diameter. Branchlets mainly opposite, usually crowded, erect or ascending, completely invested by leaves, which are long-persistent in withered state. Leaves opposite, more or less translucent, succulent, green or flushed with red; the pairs completely fused to form a terete "joint" 5–6–(15) × 3–7 mm; apex free, forming a "collar" with 2 minute lobes. Flowers axillary, in upper portion of branchlets, forming a "spike" with shorter, thicker "joints"; the flowers sunk in axils, 5–10–(15) in a ring. Perianth fleshy, thickened, more or less urceolate, with 3–5 minute teeth; stamens 1–2; style branches 2, stigmatic portion linear, minutely papillose. Fruit more or less ovoid; seeds about 2 mm in diameter, with coriaceous testa clad in minute hooked hairs.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1, as Salicornia australis.]
Its small flowers are green and yellow and open in summer.

preparation.text:
Pick the tender new growth; the young stems are at their freshest in spring and summer. Each stem has a fibrous woody core, which makes the plant much less appealing as a vegetable or a pickle. It is used mainly as a pickle.
For glassworts (Salicornia) in general: use only the green, tender tips, and cut the hard, woody lower part off thicker stems, as with asparagus. Older stems can have a woody core partway up; serve those whole and nibble the soft flesh off by hand. Glasswort is very salty, so cook it without added salt. Soaking it in fresh water and boiling it in unsalted water draws out some of the salt; steaming draws out less. Very fresh, tender tips can go raw into salads; otherwise steam them and dress with oil and lemon, or boil until just tender and then sauté with oil, garlic and chilli. To freeze, blanch for 1–2 minutes, cool, dry and freeze.

recipes.method: The author's greens, picked from roadsides around Whangaroa Harbour, were nasturtium, kawakawa, fennel, samphire, fat hen, wild mustard, cleavers and clover; the author calls it marsh samphire, picked around the Whangaroa area. The author warns that New Zealand roadsides are still sprayed with glyphosate, so pick with care. 1 garlic clove (or 4 peeled onion weed bulbs); 60 ml (¼ cup) macadamia nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) grated parmesan, dairy or plant-based (or 125 ml (½ cup) macadamias and no parmesan); 750 ml (3 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml extra-virgin olive oil; and salt and pepper. Makes about 350 g. Blend in a food processor to the texture you like. Serve on crackers or toast, as a side, or stirred through soup, pasta or rice.
recipes.title: Wild Whangaroa pesto

recipes.method: Written for glassworts (Salicornia) in general; the page names no species. Serves 4. 140 g glasswort, 2 tablespoons (28 g) butter and 2 tablespoons (30 ml) freshly squeezed lemon juice. Rinse the glasswort well. Bring about 5 cm of unsalted water to the boil in a medium pot, add the glasswort and boil for 2 minutes, then drain in a colander. For a brighter green and a crisper bite, plunge it into iced water and drain again. Melt the butter and stir in the lemon juice. Toss tender glasswort in the lemon butter and serve it as a side; if the stems have a woody core, serve the lemon butter on the side as a dip and eat them by hand. Good with fish, shellfish and eggs. Cooked glasswort keeps up to a day in a sealed container in the fridge and can be eaten at room temperature or chilled; make the lemon butter just before serving.
recipes.title: Glasswort with lemon butter

recipes.method: Written for glassworts (Salicornia) in general; the page names no species. Trim the woody ends off thicker stems. Soak the glasswort in fresh water, then boil it for 3 minutes in unsalted water and drain. Sauté it in olive oil for 2 minutes. Serve it as a side with fish, such as a whole trout, or use it in a quiche or an omelette.

summary.text:
Salicornia quinqueflora, synonym Sarcocornia quinqueflora, commonly known as beaded samphire, bead weed, beaded glasswort or glasswort, is a species of succulent halophytic coastal shrub. Its Māori name is ureure. It belongs to the amaranth family, Amaranthaceae, and is indigenous to New Zealand but not endemic: it also grows in Australia.
In New Zealand it grows on the North, South and Chatham Islands. Nationally it is assessed Not Threatened (2023), with the qualifier Secure Overseas; the Wellington region ranks it Regionally Naturally Uncommon.
Allan's Flora of New Zealand (1961) treated it as Salicornia australis. Scott (1978) moved New Zealand plants to a new genus, as Sarcocornia quinqueflora subsp. quinqueflora; Flora of New Zealand Online now lists it again under Salicornia.
Nurseries sell it for coastal gardens, wetland margins, rock gardens and restoration plantings.

identification.text:
Low-growing, with slender flexible, sprawling to prostrate, interlacing branches and branchlets, forming a more or less cushion-like mass up to about 2 m in diameter, occasionally up to 2 m tall. Branchlets numerous, with yellowish brown bark, pubescent when young. Leaves in opposite pairs or fascicles, on yellowish petioles. Stipules rounded-obtuse to broadly triangular, more or less pubescent, ciliolate. Lamina coriaceous, yellowish green, linear, obtuse, 7–12 × 1–1.5–(2) mm. Midrib alone evident. Flowers solitary, terminal on short branchlets. Male flowers with calyx absent or vestigial; corolla funnelform, lobes ovate-oblong, subacute, about equal to the tube. Female flowers with acute, narrow-triangular calyx-teeth; corolla funnelform, lobes narrow-oblong, obtuse. Drupe translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, globose, about 7 mm in diameter.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Kanono's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Karamū's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Shining karamū's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Hybrids between taupata and sand coprosma are common (Coprosma ×kirkii), so plants in between exist; if a plant fits neither description, do not use this card. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Those figures fit the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa; the North Island's wild subsp. minor has thinner, papery leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) on stalks about 10–18 mm long, and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Large-seeded coprosma's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Hūpiro's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. The Flora's key separates them by the leaf veins: mingimingi shows the midrib and the net of veins, sand coprosma the midrib alone. Sand coprosma's leaves are yellowish green, mingimingi's dark green. Both have pale blue fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

habitat.text:
Gardens, paths, waste ground, dry banks and dunes.
In New Zealand: Common to abundant in cultivated land, waste places and most other open disturbed sites, especially stony and sandy areas, depleted and open pastures, coastal cliffs, dry river beds.

identification.text: Sprawling stems that are square in cross-section, with paired oval leaves — similar in size and shape to chickweed's. The flowers give it away: five salmon-orange petals (blue-flowered plants are blue pimpernel, now treated as a separate species), open in sunshine and closed in dull weather. Chickweed's flowers are white and its stem is round.

lookalikes.howToTell: Roll the stem: chickweed's is round with a single line of hairs, pimpernel's is four-angled and hairless. Any orange or orange-red flower means pimpernel — chickweed's petals are white, divided almost to the base, and rarely absent. Pimpernel carries its flowers singly in the leaf axils, chickweed in usually loose clusters at the stem tips. Pimpernel's leaves are stalkless and often indistinctly black-dotted underneath; chickweed's lower leaves are stalked. Leaf size and the sprawling habit do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Chickweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the petals: bird's-eye speedwell's flowers have four lobes, 8–12 mm across, usually sky-blue (rarely white) with dark stripes; scarlet pimpernel's have five, (2–)6–15 mm across, orange or orange-red. Bird's-eye speedwell's leaves have a short stalk and 3–8 pairs of coarse teeth; pimpernel's have no stalk, smooth edges and often faint black dots underneath. Speedwell's stem is round and hairy; pimpernel's is square and hairless. Both sprawl across the ground, carry their flowers singly on long, slender stalks, have leaves of overlapping size, flower all year and grow in gardens and crops, so none of these tells them apart. Bird's-eye speedwell's young leaves and shoots are eaten, but its record as food is thin.
lookalikes.name: Bird's-eye speedwell

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysimachia_arvensis Corroborates the saponins and the contact dermatitis, and gives the dose picture the entry's warning summarises: the herb and its seed contain saponins, and fresh material is strongly haemolytic; the root also yields cyclamin, a highly toxic triterpenoid glycoside. Experimental doses taken by mouth caused twenty-four hours of intense nausea, headache and bodily pain, and some people get dermatitis from handling the leaf. Experimental feeding to horses and dogs caused gastroenteritis and sufficiently high doses were fatal; it is also reported toxic to poultry and rabbits, and the seed to birds. Grazing stock avoid it — the plant is acrid and bitter — except under overgrazing.

identification.text:
Almost scentless, annual or biennial herb sometimes regrowing from old rootstock. Stems erect or ascending, 15–100 cm tall, ribbed, usually glabrous, sometimes sparsely hairy, branched only above to form inflorescence or sometimes also much-branched from base. Basal and lower cauline leaves appearing shortly petiolate, but usually with very reduced leaflets along sheath, usually narrow-obovate, sometimes ovate, glabrous, mostly 3-pinnatisect, 15–150 × 10–60 mm; ultimate segments filiform, entire, not all in one plane giving a feathery appearance; cauline leaves similar to basal, but apetiolate and above becoming smaller and with fewer segments. Corymb diffuse, of few to many capitula. Involucral bracts glabrous or with a few scattered hairs, 4–7 mm long; margins pale or dark brown, membranous. Capitula about 30–50 mm diameter; ray florets 12-numerous; ligules white; disc florets numerous, yellow. Achenes 1.7–2.5 mm long, brown, narrow-obpyramidal to cylindric; inner surface with 3 thick ribs; outer surface rugose, with 2, more or less globose or slightly elongated glands at apex; corona crenulate, about 0.1 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The achenes distinguish Tripleurospermum inodorum from all other naturalised New Zealand Anthemideae: they have 3 distinct ribs on the inner face and usually 2 conspicuous glands at the top of the outer face, and the receptacle is conical, especially in fruit, with no scales among the florets (Flora of New Zealand, restated).
The yellow disc grows from button-shaped to dome-shaped to nearly round as it matures, and the white rays droop as it expands until they point straight down. Cut a head in half: the disc is solid at the core (Minnesota Wildflowers, restated).
Seedlings form small, dense rosettes of very finely divided leaves rather like fern fronds, and are very hard to tell by eye from the seedlings of stinking mayweed and pineappleweed. Crush the foliage: pineappleweed smells of pineapple, stinking chamomile stinks, and scentless chamomile smells of almost nothing (PGG Wrightson, restated). Next to stinking mayweed (stinking chamomile) its flowers are slightly larger and its leaflets slightly finer (Massey University, restated).
Corn chamomile (Anthemis arvensis), also naturalised in New Zealand and also almost scentless, has scales on its receptacle — elliptic-lanceolate and long-pointed — and square achenes broadest at the top (Flora of New Zealand key, restated); in Washington State scentless chamomile spreads unnoticed because it looks so like corn chamomile.

lookalikes.howToTell: Leaves separate them best: scentless chamomile's are cut about three times into thread-like segments that do not lie in one plane, giving a feathery look; ox-eye daisy's basal leaves are long-stalked and coarsely toothed, scalloped or at most shallowly lobed, and its upper stem leaves are narrow, stalkless and clasp the stem. Cut a head in half: scentless chamomile's receptacle is conical, rising to a dome as it matures; ox-eye's is flat or slightly domed. Scentless chamomile is an annual or biennial with a taproot; ox-eye daisy is a perennial whose stems root towards the base and spread by short rhizomes. What does not separate them: smell — both are almost scentless; head size — scentless chamomile's about 30–50 mm across, ox-eye's usually 30–60 mm (25–65 mm at the extremes); white rays around a yellow disc; and place — both grow on roadsides and in waste places and pasture. Ox-eye daisy's young leaves and flower buds are eaten (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Ox-eye daisy

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: stinking mayweed smells strongly foetid; scentless chamomile is almost scentless. Look inside the head: stinking mayweed has narrow, pointed scales among the inner florets; scentless chamomile has none. Stinking mayweed's heads are about 15–30 mm across (up to 35 mm) with 8–21 rays; scentless chamomile's are about 30–50 mm with 12 to many rays, and its leaflets are slightly finer. What does not separate them: both have leaves cut three times into fine, feathery segments, white rays around a yellow disc, and both grow on roadsides, waste places and pasture; heads of 30–35 mm fall in both ranges. Stinking mayweed is generally the commoner of the two in the North Island, scentless chamomile in Canterbury and much of the South Island. Stinking mayweed is not a food plant: its acrid juice can blister skin and it is reported as toxic (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Stinking mayweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Roman chamomile is a low, creeping, sweetly aromatic perennial whose moderately to densely hairy stems lie along the ground or rise to about 20 cm; scentless chamomile is an almost scentless, usually hairless annual or biennial with erect or ascending stems 15–100 cm tall. Look inside the head: Roman chamomile has small, blunt scales among the florets; scentless chamomile has none. Roman chamomile's heads are about 8–20 mm across (up to 30 mm), scentless chamomile's about 30–50 mm. What does not separate them: both have leaves cut three times into narrow segments with a feathery look, and white rays around a yellow disc. Roman chamomile's flowers are used for herb tea (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Roman chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: In flower they are easy: pineappleweed's heads have no white rays — they are small greenish-yellow domes 4–10 mm across — while scentless chamomile's are 30–50 mm with white rays. Before flowering, crush a leaf: pineappleweed is aromatic and smells of pineapple, scentless chamomile is almost scentless. Pineappleweed's leaf segments lie more or less in one plane; scentless chamomile's do not, so its leaves look more feathery. Pineappleweed is usually 5–20 cm tall (up to 40 cm). What does not separate them: both have finely divided leaves and grow on roadsides and in waste places. Pineappleweed's flower heads are eaten and made into tea (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Pineappleweed

summary.text:
Tripleurospermum inodorum, common names scentless false mayweed, scentless mayweed, scentless chamomile, and Baldr's brow, is the type species of Tripleurospermum. It is an annual, or in some situations a short-lived perennial, found all over New Zealand and especially in Canterbury; in New Zealand it is also called false chamomile. Seeds germinate at any time of year when the soil is moist, lit and above 3 °C, mostly in spring and autumn, and one plant can set 10,000 to 200,000 seeds (PGG Wrightson, restated). Pollen is collected by solitary bees.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Auckland City, Wellington City, Hutt Valley; South Island: mainly dry eastern areas from Marlborough to Central Otago and Southland. Native range Mediterranean to Western Asia and southern Russia; first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1870.
Scentless mayweed, or scentless chamomile as it is sometimes called, is often abundant on roadsides and in waste places. It has previously been known in New Zealand as T. maritimum, Matricaria perforata, M. inodora, and Chrysanthemum inodorum.
In New Zealand stinking mayweed is generally the commoner of the two in the North Island, while scentless chamomile is the more common in Canterbury and several other parts of the South Island (Massey University, restated).

warnings: There is no record of scentless chamomile being eaten, and it is not one of the chamomiles used for tea. It looks very like them — check the receptacle and the smell (see the lookalikes).
It is not known to be toxic, but stock will not eat it and hens avoid it, and eaten in large amounts it can blister the muzzles of livestock.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand: waste places, scrubland, riverbeds, coastal areas.
In New Zealand it grows in lowland and montane places of low to high fertility, usually where rainfall is high, on acid soils but never on chalk: shrubland, tall and short tussockland, cliffs, bluffs and riverbeds, and disturbed ground such as pasture, waste ground and poorly grazed areas. It does not tolerate poor drainage.

identification.text:
Much-branched deciduous shrub up to 2–(2.5) m high; twigs glabrous, but sericeous when young, green, more or less 5-angled. Leaves variable, usually more or less glabrous above and sericeous below, and 3-foliolate and petiolate when mature or on older twigs; leaves of younger twigs often 1–2-foliolate and subsessile; young leaves often sericeous above and below but sometimes glabrous; leaflets apetiolulate, elliptic to obovate, usually acute, sometimes emarginate, 4–16–(20) mm long; terminal leaflet > lateral leaflets. Flowers usually solitary, rarely paired, axillary; pedicels (3)–5–13 mm long. Calyx glabrous, bilabiate, about 1/4 length of corolla; upper and lower lips more or less entire or shallowly toothed. Corolla usually golden yellow, rarely partly red or tinged mauve, 16–25 mm long. Pod black, oblong, many-seeded, 15–60 mm long, with hairy margins; seeds brown or greenish brown, ellipsoid, compressed, about 3 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Cultivated forms with a partly red standard, and also sometimes the keel and wings tinged red to reddish brown, are occasionally naturalised; the name C. scoparius f. andreanus is sometimes applied to these plants.
It flowers from September to April. The pods turn black as they ripen and burst explosively on warm days, scattering the seed and leaving the empty pod halves hanging in coils on the plant.

lookalikes.howToTell: French (Montpellier) broom's twigs are round and ribbed, it is usually evergreen, and its flowers are 9–13 mm long in clusters of 4–7 at the ends of short side branches, with a densely hairy calyx; its pods are densely hairy all over, about 18–20 mm long. Scotch broom's twigs are green and more or less five-angled, it loses its leaves, and its flowers are single or paired in the leaf angles, 16–25 mm long, with a hairless calyx; its pods are black, 15–60 mm long, hairy only along the edges.
lookalikes.name: French broom

lookalikes.howToTell: Sweet broom's twigs are rounded and ribbed, it is evergreen, and its flowers are 10–30 or more together in elongated racemes at the ends of the shoots, with a densely hairy calyx; its pods are densely hairy all over, 20–40 mm long. Scotch broom's twigs are green and more or less five-angled, it loses its leaves, and its flowers are single or paired in the leaf angles, with a hairless calyx; its pods are black, 15–60 mm long, hairy only along the edges. Flower length overlaps (sweet broom 13–18 mm, Scotch broom 16–25 mm) and does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Sweet broom

lookalikes.howToTell: Gorse is sharply spiny, and on a grown plant its leaves are reduced to spines, the main ones rigid, furrowed and 15–30 mm long. Scotch broom has no spines; its green twigs are more or less five-angled, and its leaves have three leaflets on older twigs, often one or two on young twigs. Gorse seedlings have leaves of three hairy leaflets, so a seedling's leaves do not separate it from broom. Both have yellow pea flowers, usually single, and their length overlaps (gorse 13–20 mm, Scotch broom 16–25 mm), so flowers do not separate them. Gorse's pods are hairy all over and 13–25 mm long; Scotch broom's are 15–60 mm long and hairy only along the edges.
lookalikes.name: Gorse

lookalikes.howToTell: Spanish broom's twigs are stout, rounded and finely grooved, and on adult plants are usually almost leafless; its leaves are simple, 15–25 mm long on mature branches. Scotch broom's twigs are more or less five-angled, and its leaves have three leaflets on older twigs but often only one or two on young twigs, so a single leaf on a young twig does not separate them. Spanish broom's calyx is one-lipped, split above, with five short teeth on one side, a shape that sets it apart from every other wild legume in New Zealand; Scotch broom's calyx is two-lipped. Spanish broom's flowers are fragrant and usually many together in racemes at the ends of the shoots; Scotch broom's are usually single, rarely paired, in the leaf angles. Spanish broom's pods become hairless and are 50–90 mm long; Scotch broom's are black, 15–60 mm long and hairy along the edges. Flower length overlaps (Spanish broom 22–28 mm, Scotch broom 16–25 mm) and does not separate them. Spanish broom flowers from December to May, Scotch broom from September to April.
lookalikes.name: Spanish broom

summary.text:
Scotch broom (Cytisus scoparius) is a much-branched, often almost leafless, deciduous shrub of the pea family, with flexible, ridged green stems and golden-yellow pea flowers.
In New Zealand: throughout the North and South Islands; on Stewart Island at Halfmoon Bay and the mouth of the Lords River; on the Chatham Islands and Campbell Island. It comes from Europe, Asia Minor and Russia and was first recorded wild here in 1872. Broom is a widespread and troublesome weed in many areas of New Zealand, particularly in less intensively farmed hill country and riverbeds. Broom has been known in New Zealand as Sarothamnus scoparius and Spartium scoparium. In New Zealand it is also called broom, English broom and wild broom.
It was brought here as an ornamental. Plants do not flower until at least two years old and are thought to live for 10–15 years. The pods burst on hot days and throw the seed, which is also carried by gravel, mud, animals, machinery, people, roads and water; seed buried deeper survives longer in the soil.
It copes with cold better than gorse, so it is the more troublesome of the two above 300 metres and in some southern districts, and it is one of the most troublesome weeds of plantation forests, where soil under pines has held up to 36,000 seeds per square metre.
As a legume it fixes nitrogen, changing which plants can grow where it has been and opening the way for other weeds; it forms pure stands that keep native seedlings from establishing in low-canopy habitats, and the extra nitrogen on gumlands and other poor soils harms specialised plants such as orchids, ferns and kauri. On braided riverbeds it binds the gravel, so the river forms fast-flowing channels that wading birds cannot feed in, and it covers the open ground riverbed birds nest on while giving cover to cats and stoats. It needs light, so where native seedlings are present taller native species eventually shade it out, though not in kauri or tānekaha forest; in a trial on a braided-river terrace on the Canterbury Plains, native trees and shrubs sown or planted under living broom germinated and survived better than where the broom had been mulched, root-raked or crushed.

warnings: The seeds are poisonous, especially if chewed or crushed before swallowing.

The pods are toxic, and the plant, flowers included, contains toxic alkaloids, chiefly sparteine and cytisine, that depress the heart and nervous system; only the flower buds and flowers are eaten. In large doses sparteine causes vomiting and purging, weakens the heart and lowers blood pressure, and in extreme cases it kills by impairing breathing.

The flower buds may be toxic to some people. Large doses of broom upset the stomach and bowels, and more than 30 g of it can poison, causing dizziness, headache, changes in heartbeat, weak legs, sweating, sleepiness and widened pupils.

Broom should not be eaten by pregnant women, as it might cause a miscarriage, or by breastfeeding women, or by people with high blood pressure, heart disease or kidney disease; it contains tyramine, which can raise or lower blood pressure.
Do not eat broom while taking MAOI antidepressants, which stop the body breaking down its tyramine and can lead to dangerously high blood pressure, or while taking lithium, haloperidol or quinidine.
Spanish broom, which is often confused with Scotch broom, is poisonous in all its parts, flowers included (see the lookalikes).

It is a pest plant in New Zealand: it is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and the regional pest management plans of Northland, Auckland, Waikato, Gisborne, Hawke's Bay, Manawatū-Whanganui, Taranaki, Tasman-Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, the West Coast, Otago, Southland and the Chatham Islands name it.

habitat.text:
Isolated populations grow in coastal scrub and around forest margins. It also grows in other shrubland and sometimes among rocks in the open, from sea level to 750 m.
Fuchsia perscandens's preferred habitats are river terraces and remnants of white pine swamp forest, but the species has also been found in limestone, for example in the Wairarapa or in Marlborough.
Lowland forest, especially in clearings, around margins and in remnant stands.
In gardens it is grown in partial shade or full sun, in fertile, free-draining soil kept moist but not waterlogged.

identification.text:
Gynodioecious, deciduous liane with stout main stems to about 5 m long and 5 cm diameter, sparingly branched, sprawling when lacking support; bark pale brownish orange, more or less flaking; branchlets hairy at first. Petioles 10–20 mm long, very slender. Lamina (10)–25–30 × (10)–20–25–(30) mm, broad-ovate to suborbicular, sinuate, membranous, remotely and obscurely dentate, green or dark green above, glaucescent below, glabrous except on veins and margins; base subcordate to truncate; apex subacute. Flowers solitary or occasionally 2–3 together; pedicels very slender, about 10 mm long. Floral tube 7–15 mm long. Sepals 6–10 mm long, narrow-ovate, green or nearly so, patent to reflexed. Petals dark purple, 1–5 mm long, narrow-oblong. Stamens of ☿ flowers exserted; filaments 10–15 mm long, purple. Stigma capitate. Berry 5–10 mm long, more or less broad-cylindric, dark purple.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stems: tree fuchsia is a tree or shrub to about 12 m with a distinct trunk to 60 cm thick, and keeps its trunked form even when it is much reduced in exposed places; scrambling fuchsia is a liane, with stout main stems to about 5 m long and 5 cm thick that sprawl when they lack support, and in the open it can form a ball-like shrub of interlacing branchlets. Look at the leaf shape: tree fuchsia's leaves are usually lance-shaped to narrowly egg-shaped or oblong, with a pointed to drawn-out tip and a rounded or wedge-shaped base; scrambling fuchsia's are broadly egg-shaped to almost round, with a slightly heart-shaped to squared-off base and a slightly pointed tip. Leaf size overlaps (tree fuchsia's 2–14 cm long, sometimes 1.5 cm; scrambling fuchsia's 25–30 mm, sometimes 10 mm), and tree fuchsia has smaller leaves in exposed places, so go by shape, not size. The flowers are alike, scrambling fuchsia's smaller, but the floral tube (tree fuchsia 7–20 mm, scrambling fuchsia 7–15 mm), the sepals (5–16 mm against 6–10 mm) and the dark purple berries (about 10 mm against 5–10 mm) overlap, so flowers and fruit do not separate them. Plants intermediate in size and habit between the two, Fuchsia ×colensoi, probably their hybrid though this is not confirmed, often grow with both. Tree fuchsia's ripe berries are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Tree fuchsia

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the main stems: scrambling fuchsia is a liane whose stout main stems, to about 5 m long and 5 cm thick, sprawl when they lack support; Fuchsia ×colensoi is usually a shrub or small tree whose branches may be slender and scrambling but not its main stems, though some plants are lianoid. Without support, both can form a somewhat similar ball-like shrub of interlacing branchlets. Look at the leaves: scrambling fuchsia's are broadly egg-shaped to almost round, usually 25–30 mm long, with a slightly heart-shaped to squared-off base; Fuchsia ×colensoi's are usually egg-shaped to broadly egg-shaped or oblong-egg-shaped, less often almost round, usually 3–8 cm long, with the base usually broadly wedge-shaped, squared-off or rounded, occasionally slightly heart-shaped. Leaf size overlaps (scrambling fuchsia 25–30 mm, sometimes 10 mm; Fuchsia ×colensoi 3–8 cm, sometimes 2 cm or 10 cm), so a plant with small, round leaves may be either. Flowers and berries do not separate them: the floral tube (scrambling fuchsia 7–15 mm, Fuchsia ×colensoi 8–20 mm), the sepals (6–10 mm against 6–14 mm) and the dark purple berries (5–10 mm against about 10 mm) overlap. Fuchsia ×colensoi is intermediate in size and habit between scrambling fuchsia and tree fuchsia, probably their hybrid though this is not confirmed, and in many areas grows with both. Fuchsia ×colensoi's food record is thin (see its page).

summary.text:
Fuchsia perscandens, commonly known as climbing fuchsia or scrambling fuchsia, is a species of plant endemic to New Zealand and belonging to the family Onagraceae.
It grows on the North and South Islands, from near Pipiwai in Northland to Southland, and is often uncommon over large parts of its range; in Otago, Southland and Fiordland it becomes increasingly rare and local southwards. It is assessed Not Threatened (2023).
New Zealand nurseries sell it for native and woodland gardens and for banks, where it spreads through the plants around it.

warnings: No record of people eating this species' berries was found. That they are harmless rests on a general record for all New Zealand's native fuchsias, not on a record for this one. Its berries are fewer than tree fuchsia's.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand it grows in salt marshes and on rocky and gravelly coasts within range of high tide, throughout, more or less local.
On New Zealand's national wetland plant list it is rated facultative: it commonly grows either in wetlands or on dry ground.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In the Wellington region (Regionally Critical), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it. In Northland (Regionally Naturally Uncommon) and the Auckland region (Regionally Declining), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text:
Perennial much-branched subshrub; stems woody, bearing persistent leaf-bases, more or less ascending, up to 30 cm or more long; branchlets grooved when dry. Leaves sessile, opposite, alternate, or fascicled (on same plant), approximate, patent; lamina fleshy, linear to narrow-oblong (occasionally narrow-obovate), more or less apiculate, 4–12 × 1–2 mm. Flowers axillary, (1)–3–(4) together, each subtended by 2 bracteoles. Perianth 5-lobed; lobes ovate, erect; stigmas 2–3; seeds horizontal, red-brown, glossy.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]
The New Zealand species has the flowers in the axils of undifferentiated foliage leaves (usually 1 large, between 2 small).
The flowers are green or white.

summary.text:
Sea blite (Suaeda novae-zelandiae) is a succulent, much-branched subshrub of salt marshes and rocky coasts, in the amaranth family, Amaranthaceae, and endemic to New Zealand.
It grows on the North and South Islands. Nationally it is assessed Not Threatened (2023); regionally it is ranked Regionally Critical in Wellington, Regionally Naturally Uncommon in Northland and Regionally Declining in Auckland, and Regionally Not Threatened in Otago.
It is related to S. maritima and S. australis. Before Allan named it in 1961, New Zealand plants were misidentified as S. maritima.
It is not sold by nurseries.

summary.text:
Silene uniflora is a species of flowering plant in the carnation family known by the common name sea campion.
Silene uniflora is a maritime species growing in many European countries, but almost entirely along the coasts bordering the Atlantic Ocean and Baltic Sea. In northern Europe, it is native to the coasts of Scandinavia including Finland, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, and Russia as far east as the Kola Peninsula. It is also listed as native to Poland by POWO. It is not found in, or native to, the Baltic States or Russia on the Baltic Sea. In western Europe, it is native to the west coast of France, the northern coast of Spain, and a limited area in northern Portugal. It grows all around the shores of Ireland and the United Kingdom, and is also found in some mountainous areas near fresh water, though only rarely. Further out in the Atlantic Ocean, it is native to the Azores, the Canary Islands, Madeira, and Iceland.
It has been introduced to Germany, Argentina, and New Zealand.

identification.text:
Procumbent to ascending, terrestrial perennial, not rooting at nodes. Leaves pinnately 3-foliolate to 1–2-pinnate; ultimate segments broadly or narrowly ovate to deltate, usually lobed and crenate, about 5–30 mm long; upper stem leaves similar to lower and basal leaves, but often reduced and 3-foliolate or simple. Umbels compound, usually sessile or subsessile, leaf-opposed; rays 2–10–(15); bracts and bracteoles 0. Flowers numerous, white. Fruit broadly ovoid, 1.5–2.5 mm long; ribs broad and spongy. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The sprawling stems are 0.3–1.2 m long and often climb up through the plants around them. The leaves are dark green to yellow-green and smell of celery when crushed; the petals are off-white to cream. A single bract sometimes sits under an umbel, but it usually falls early. Plants vary a great deal: some, mostly on muddy ground in saltmarshes and brackish ponds, have very slender leaves and purplish leaf stalks.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand; all parts are poisonous if eaten. Look under the umbels: hemlock has about 4–8 narrow, pointed, down-turned bracts beneath each umbel and 3–6 bracteoles on the outer side of each small umbel; sea celery usually has none, occasionally a single bract that falls early. Hemlock is erect, up to 2–(3) m, with hollow stems usually spotted or blotched purple; sea celery is prostrate to ascending, its sprawling stems 0.3–1.2 m long. Hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided and sea celery's three-parted to 1–2 times divided with lobed, toothed segments that are narrow in some plants, so leaf shape alone does not separate them. Hemlock smells foetid or musty when crushed and sea celery has a celery-like aroma, but no source here treats smell as a reliable test on its own. Sea celery is mostly coastal but also grows beside lakes and streams inland, and hemlock grows in damp waste ground and riverbeds, so place does not rule hemlock out. Both have white flowers in compound umbels, though sea celery's petals can be off-white to cream.
lookalikes.name: Hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: Look under the small umbels: water celery always has 4–8 small bracteoles there, and sea celery has none. Water celery's stems root at the lower nodes; sea celery's sprawling stems do not root. Water celery's leaves are once-pinnate, with 2–8 pairs of toothed leaflets 1–8 cm long (up to 12); sea celery's are three-parted to 1–2-pinnate, with lobed segments about 5–30 mm long. Water celery grows in fresh water — drains and the margins of rivers, streams, lakes and ponds — but sea celery also grows beside lakes and streams inland, so place does not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Water celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Garden celery is occasionally found wild. It is an erect biennial up to 80–100 cm tall with hollow, grooved stems; sea celery is prostrate to ascending, its stems sprawling 0.3–1.2 m long. Sea celery usually has no bracts or bracteoles under its umbels (at most a single bract that soon falls), and celery has none, so that check does not separate them. Celery's flowers are greenish white, about 1 mm across. The surest difference is the ripe fruit: celery's are dark brown with thread-thin ribs, sea celery's have broad, spongy ribs. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Celery

preparation.text: Use it as you would parsley or celery: in salads, soups, stocks, stews and quiches, in dressings, flavoured butter and white sauces, and with seafood. It is a strong herb, so use it sparingly so that it blends in rather than taking over. Dried leaves go into spice mixes.

recipes.method: Written for sea celery grown in a home garden in Perth, Western Australia; the page does not give the scientific name. Serves 2 with pasta. 60 g roasted macadamias; 40 g basil; 30 ml (2 Tbsp) extra virgin olive oil; 30 g pecorino; 1 large garlic clove; 3 large sprigs sea celery; 2 large sprigs seablite; 4–5 native mint leaves; 1 mountain pepper leaf. Chop the leafy ingredients finely first if you want a greener pesto. Pound everything in a mortar and pestle until mostly smooth but still a little chunky. Toss it through freshly cooked pasta, loosening it with a splash of the pasta water if needed. The authors serve it on their own wattleseed and peppermint gum malloreddus and warn to go easy on the mountain pepper. The authors' note allows extra basil or parsley in place of the fresh native herbs.
recipes.title: Sea celery and macadamia pesto

recipes.method: Written for dried sea parsley (Apium prostratum var. prostratum) sold by a Western Australian native-plant nursery. Serves 4 as a side. 45 ml (3 Tbsp) dried sea parsley; 1 whole cauliflower, broken into florets; 60 ml (4 Tbsp) wholegrain Dijon mustard; 30 ml (2 Tbsp) crushed garlic; 45 ml (3 Tbsp) lemon juice; olive oil; vegetable oil; salt and pepper; aioli, to serve. Heat the oven to 200 °C and line a baking tray with baking paper. Toss the cauliflower with the mustard, garlic, lemon juice and sea parsley, pour over plenty of olive oil, season with salt and pepper and toss again to coat. Spread it on the tray and bake for 25 minutes, turning once, until crisp and golden. Serve with spoonfuls of aioli. The author does not say how to dry the leaves, or what the vegetable oil is for.
recipes.title: Sea parsley baked cauliflower

recipes.method: Written for sea parsley (Apium prostratum var. prostratum) sold by a Western Australian native-plant nursery; the recipe is by RiverMint Dining. Serves 2. 350 g skin-on snapper fillets, scaled (keep the bones); 100 g warrigal greens; 200 ml vegetable purée, such as turnip, potato or pea; 150 g cold butter, cubed; 2 sticks celery; half an onion, roughly chopped; 3 lemons; 20 sprigs dried native lemongrass; 3 sprigs sea parsley; salt and pepper; olive oil. Season and dry the fillets and fry them skin side down in hot olive oil for 2 minutes, pressing down so they don't shrink; turn and cook 2 minutes more. Add a squeeze of lemon and 15 ml (1 Tbsp) butter to the pan, baste, then keep the fish warm in a low oven. For the sauce, put the juice of a lemon, 10 lemongrass sprigs, the snapper bones, onion and celery in a pan, cover with water, bring to the boil and simmer 15 minutes, skimming. Strain out the bones, return to the pan and reduce by half, adding more lemongrass to taste; season and strain again. Over medium heat, whisk in the cold butter a few cubes at a time until the sauce thickens. Bash the warrigal greens with a rolling pin, boil them for 2 minutes to remove oxalic acid, then drain and squeeze dry. Blanch the sea parsley on its stems for 15 seconds so it keeps its crunch, refresh in iced water, then pick and dry the leaves and season them. Sauté the sea parsley and warrigal greens in hot butter. Spread the purée on the plates, top with the greens and the snapper, crisp skin up, drizzle with the lemongrass sauce and garnish with the sea parsley. Warrigal greens are New Zealand spinach, which is At Risk in the wild in New Zealand; use cultivated ones.
recipes.title: Pan-fried snapper with sautéed sea parsley and warrigal greens

summary.text:
Apium prostratum, commonly known as sea celery, is a variable herb native to coastal Australia and New Zealand.
Commonly eaten by Māori in New Zealand, for whom it is known as tūtae kōau, sea celery was also an important vegetable for early explorers and colonists in Australia and New Zealand. Captain Cook ate sea celery at Botany Bay and gathered it in bulk along with Lepidium oleraceum at Poverty Bay in New Zealand in October 1769 to protect his crew from scurvy.
In New Zealand it grows on the Kermadec, Three Kings, North, South, Stewart, Chatham and Antipodes Islands, and it is also native to eastern and southern Australia and Tasmania. Three forms are recorded here. The common native form (subsp. prostratum var. filiforme) is Not Threatened (2023). Chatham Island celery (subsp. denticulatum) is endemic to the Chatham and Antipodes Islands; it is abundant there, but is listed At Risk – Naturally Uncommon (2023) because its range is so small. The Australian form (var. prostratum) is listed as exotic.

warnings: Hemlock, one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand, also has white flowers in compound umbels and grows in damp places. Before you pick, check under the umbels and along the stems as described in Lookalikes; the celery smell of a crushed leaf is not enough on its own.

On the Chatham and Antipodes Islands the plant is Chatham Island celery, which is at risk: if you harvest it there, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text: A plant of C. racemosa consists of a number of branches linked to stolons which are anchored to the sandy substrate by rhizoids. The branches are a few centimetres apart and can grow to a height of 30 centimetres. Many spherical or ovate side-shoots branch off these and give the seaweed its name of sea grapes. Like other members of the order Bryopsidales, each C. racemosa plant consists of a single enormous cell with a large number of nuclei. The chloroplasts containing chlorophyll are free to migrate from any part of the organism to another and there is a network of fibrous proteins that helps movement of organelles.

summary.text:
Caulerpa racemosa is a species of edible green alga, a seaweed in the family Caulerpaceae.
In 1926 a new form of the alga was reported off Tunisia, possibly an immigrant from the Red Sea, and this later spread to much of the eastern Mediterranean Sea. In 1990, a new, larger form with two vertical rows of branches on opposite sides of the stem was found off Libya. It spread widely, invading much of the Mediterranean Sea and becoming more widespread than the invasive species, Caulerpa taxifolia. It is known as var. cylindracea and may have originated from Australian waters. In America C. racemosa is found in shallow water in the Caribbean Sea, around Bermuda and along the eastern seaboard of America from Florida to Brazil.

identification.text:
Stems 10–30 cm tall, much-branched from base, stout, glabrous, sprawling to suberect, forking, not flexuous. Rosette leaves fleshy, narrow-oblong to ovate, shallowly crenate to pinnatifid, petiolate, 4–6 × 1–2 cm; margins entire, rarely crenate or sinuate; stem leaves smaller, crenate to pinnatifid, oblong to linear to linear-spathulate. Inflorescence axis straight, thickening and elongating at fruiting. Pedicels suberect to spreading, 1–3 mm long. Flowers about 1 cm in diameter, clustered. Petals 7–9 × 1–2 mm. Silique erect, (11)–13–16–(18) × 4–7 mm; upper segment mitre-shaped, tapering to a conic beak, acute, 4-angled, (8)–10–15 mm long; lower segment obconic, terete, 3–6 mm long, with 2 spreading to deflexed lateral horns at distal end.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Check the ripening fruit. In sea rocket the lower fruit segment has 2 spreading to deflexed horns at its tip and the upper segment is mitre-shaped, acute and 4-angled; in American sea rocket the lower segment has no horns and the upper segment is ovate, acuminate, notched at the tip, 4-angled or 8-ribbed, somewhat flattened, with a narrow winged beak. The flowering stem is straight in sea rocket and flexuous in American sea rocket, whose main stem is also often flexuous. Petals are 7–9 mm long in sea rocket against 4–6 mm, flowers c. 1 cm across against 6–8 mm, and rosette leaf margins are entire, rarely crenate or sinuate, against serrate. Sea rocket stems are 10–30 cm tall, American sea rocket's 30–60 cm. Fruit length and leaf lobing do not separate them: the fruit lengths overlap, and sea rocket plants can have entire or pinnatifid leaves. American sea rocket's leaves, young stems and pods are eaten in the same way.

preparation.text: Use very young leaves and stems raw in salads. Older leaves are more bitter: mix them with milder leaves as a potherb or use them in soups. Fresh flowers go into salads, and immature pods can be eaten raw. Sources disagree on cooking: the leaves are best cooked and eaten only in small quantities, yet cooking is also found to make them very bitter. For the root flour, dry and grind the root and mix it with cereal flour.

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1 large handful young sea rocket leaves and tender pods; 1 handful other coastal greens, such as sea celery leaves or New Zealand spinach (warrigal greens); 40 ml olive oil; 20 ml lemon juice; 5 ml agave or maple syrup; salt and pepper; 40 ml toasted sunflower seeds. Rinse the sea rocket well in cold water and dry it. If using New Zealand spinach, blanch it in boiling water for 1 minute, cool it in cold water and squeeze it dry. Toss the greens together in a bowl. Whisk the oil, lemon juice, syrup, salt and pepper into a dressing, toss the salad gently in it, and scatter the sunflower seeds over to serve.
recipes.title: Sea rocket salad with coastal greens

recipes.method: Ingredients: about 250 ml young sea rocket leaves, loosely packed; a splash of white vinegar; salt and pepper. Rinse the leaves and blend them with the vinegar and a little salt and pepper to a paste, tasting as you go. Serve it as you would mustard or wasabi.

summary.text:
Cakile maritima, sea rocket (Britain and Ireland) or European searocket (North America), is a common plant in the mustard family Brassicaceae. It is widespread in Europe, North Africa and western Asia, especially on coastlines. It can now be found in many other areas of the world where it has been introduced. It is present on the west and east coasts of North America, where it has the potential to become an invasive species. This is an annual plant which grows in clumps or mounds in the sand on beaches and bluffs. The shiny leaves are fleshy, green and tinted with purple or magenta, and long-lobed. It has white to light purple flowers and sculpted, segmented, corky brown fruits one to three centimetres long. The fruits float and are water-dispersed. It is pollinated by a wide range of insects, from Apis mellifera, Eristalis intricarius and Pieris rapae. As the seed oil contains a high level of erucic acid it can have pathological effects on the cardiac muscle of several animal species. However, orange-bellied parrots feed on its seed during their northward migrating journey from Tasmania and Australia. (Wikipedia)

In New Zealand it is naturalised from western Europe and the Mediterranean, first recorded as naturalised in 1940, and New Zealand plants belong to subsp. maritima; the Flora records it from Northland, Auckland, Bay of Plenty, East Cape, Gisborne and Hawke's Bay, and from the Kermadec Islands (Flora of New Zealand, restated). It was first collected in New Zealand in 1937, had spread to the northern tip of the North Island by 1973 and to its southernmost point by 2010, and has so far been collected only in the North Island; where it and American sea rocket have both grown, American sea rocket is now rarely found, which the authors read as one species displacing a close relative (Cousens & Cousens 2011, restated).

warnings: Eat the leaves only in small quantities.

Do not use the seeds or ripe fruit as food or for oil: the seed oil is high in erucic acid, which can damage heart muscle in several animal species, and caution is urged before using sea rocket seed oil for people or animals.

Evidence on oxalic acid in the leaves is mixed: one analysis found it particularly high compared with other edible wild halophytes, while a study of Italian plants found oxalate below detectable levels.
Do not gather near sewage outlets or other shoreline pollution.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Usually wet or rather damp pastures and lawns, forest margins and clearings, dry banks and riverbeds, particularly when modified and open, less common in other habitats.
It grows on roadsides, gardens, waste-places, and woodland edges, and usually in basic and neutral soils.
In New Zealand lawns it is typical of moist to wet ground but also tolerates dryness.
Wetland status (NZPCN, from the national wetland plant list, Clarkson et al. 2021): facultative upland — occasionally in wetlands, but usually on dry ground.

identification.text:
Perennial herb. Rhizome short; aerial stems long and decumbent, becoming erect and then often purplish. Petiole often equal to lamina in lower leaves, becoming short in leaves below inflorescence. Lamina 1.7–6 × 0.7–2.3 cm, ovate or ovate-oblong, hairy, especially on veins below, usually entire or shallowly toothed, or rarely upper leaves with narrow lobes (hybrids); base cuneate to rounded. Bracts 2–10 cm long, broad-ovate to broad-reniform, acuminate, the uppermost often acute, with prominent white cilia and often purple-tinged. Calyx 7–9 mm long, purplish; upper lip shallowly 3-toothed and mucronate; lower lobe of 2 lanceolate, acuminate teeth. Corolla 10–15 mm long, usually violet, rarely pink or white. Stamen appendages more or less straight. Nutlets 1.5–2 mm long, ellipsoid or ellipsoid-obovoid, shining brown.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Cut-leaved selfheal (Prunella laciniata) has been collected from a roadside at Ngaruawahia in the Waikato. It differs from P. vulgaris in that most or all leaves are pinnately and narrowly lobed, the plants are much hairier, the lower calyx teeth are linear-lanceolate, and the corolla is cream or pink. A few specimens with some pinnately lobed leaves are probably the hybrid P. × hybrida (P. laciniata × P. vulgaris).
The leaves are puckered and covered with short, coarse hairs, and seen from above each pair is set at right angles to the pair below.
The crushed leaves have no minty smell. Once flowering is over, self-heal's head turns brown. Mown, it stays low; left unmown in waste places it grows to about 30 cm.

lookalikes.howToTell: Ground-ivy's leaves are round to kidney-shaped, 1–4.5 cm wide, with scalloped edges and a heart-shaped base, each on a slender stalk, and its blue or blue-violet flowers sit in twos or threes in the joints of ordinary leaves. Self-heal's leaves are ovate, 1.7–6 cm long and 0.7–2.3 cm wide, usually untoothed or only shallowly toothed, with a wedge-shaped to rounded base, and its flowers, usually violet, rarely pink or white, form a dense spike at the stem tip among broad bracts fringed with white hairs and often tinged purple. Flower colour does not reliably separate them, both creep, and both grow in lawns and under trees at woodland edges. Ground-ivy's young leaves are eaten, but it is advised against in pregnancy and when breast-feeding and contains pulegone.
lookalikes.name: Ground-ivy

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: pennyroyal smells strongly of mint; self-heal has no minty smell. Pennyroyal's flowers are mauve to purplish-blue, 4–6 mm long, packed in spaced rings in the joints of the leaves along the stem; self-heal's are usually violet, 10–15 mm long, in a dense head at the stem tip among broad bracts fringed with white hairs. Pennyroyal's leaves are smaller, usually 0.6–2 cm long, not puckered and dotted with glands; self-heal's are 1.7–6 cm long, puckered and coarsely hairy. Both creep, root along the stems and form mats in damp lawns and pasture, so check every plant in a mixed patch. Pennyroyal is poisonous to the liver; do not eat it.

preparation.text: Add the leaves raw to salads, or cook them in soups and stews or as a potherb. The flavour is similar to romaine lettuce, but the leaves are somewhat bitter from tannin, which washing them can remove. The leaves are a little rough, so chop them very finely before mixing them with other salad greens or putting them in a sandwich. In China the young plants have long been eaten soaked to draw out the bitterness, then dressed with oil and salt. The flowers go into salads, and the leaves into pesto. A cold-water infusion of the freshly chopped, or dried and powdered, leaves makes a refreshing drink. Leaves and flower heads can be picked through summer; picking the heads and pinching out the centre stems keeps the plant bushy, with two new heads growing in place of each one taken. For tea, wash dried seed heads well in several changes of water to remove grit, and simmer rather than boil hard: the longer it brews, the more bitter it gets.

recipes.method: Written for self-heal with galinsoga. A bunch of galinsoga and a bunch of self-heal leaves; 2 garlic cloves; 125 ml (½ cup) cashew nuts; 45 ml (3 tbsp) lemon juice; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper, optional. Blitz the garlic and cashews in a food processor or blender, add everything else and process until well combined. Adjust the seasoning, and loosen it with a little water or more lemon juice if it is too thick.
recipes.title: Self-heal and galinsoga pesto

recipes.method: Made with dried self-heal seed heads (sold as xia ku cao in Chinese herb shops). 30 g dried self-heal; 2.5 litres water; 30 g sweetened winter melon (candied, from Asian supermarkets); 100 g carrot. Wash the self-heal in a bowl of cold water, squeezing out handfuls into a colander. Change the water and wash it twice more, and keep going until the water stays clear of grit. Peel the carrot and cut it into 2 cm chunks. Put the water, self-heal and carrot in a pot, bring to the boil, then simmer on medium heat for 30 minutes. Add the winter melon and boil for 5 minutes more. Turn off the heat and strain into a teapot. Serve hot, or chill in the fridge for a few hours. Keep it at a simmer rather than a hard boil. If it is too bitter, dilute it with water or sweeten it a little at a time; honey goes in after cooking.
recipes.title: Chinese herbal tea (liang cha)

summary.text:
Prunella vulgaris, the common self-heal, heal-all, woundwort, heart-of-the-earth, carpenter's herb, brownwort or blue curls, is an herbaceous flowering plant in the mint family (Lamiaceae).
Prunella vulgaris is a perennial herb native in Europe, Asia, Africa, and North America, and is common in most temperate climates.
Prunella vulgaris can spread aggressively through creeping stolons and roots, forming dense mats that can displace other plants. Because of its ability to outcompete other desirable vegetation, it can become weedy in lawns and damp shady locations. Prunella vulgaris is listed in Weeds of the Northeast and Weeds of the Great Plains. It was introduced to many countries in the 1800s and has become invasive in the Pacific Islands, including Australia, New Zealand, and Hawaii. In Ireland, it is generally abundant. It also grows in Kashmir where it is known as kalyuth and used as a decoction to wash and bathe in order to relieve muscle pain.
The conspicuous flowers are a favorite of bumblebees and butterflies.  Prunella vulgaris is a host species for the larvae of the  Clouded sulphur butterfly, Colias philodice.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands: common throughout. Naturalised from the northern temperate zone, first recorded in 1867.
Other names in New Zealand (Herb Federation of New Zealand, Massey University): selfheal, hookheal, sicklewort. It was brought to New Zealand as a garden plant (NZPCN) and is now a common weed of lawns throughout the country.

warnings: Self-heal is on the NZ Plant Conservation Network's list of plants known to be poisonous in New Zealand. The list gives no reason, toxin or part, and its source (Connor and Fountain, Plants that Poison, 2009) could not be checked. No poisoning from eating it has been found recorded. Large amounts can cause diarrhoea and stomach pain.

Allergic reactions to self-heal have been reported, including a case of contact dermatitis, though such reports are rare. Seek medical advice before using it in pregnancy, when breast-feeding or if you are prone to allergies.
Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed, and self-heal often regrows after lawn weedkillers, so a healthy-looking patch is no proof the ground was not sprayed. Pick from ground you know.

edibleParts.text: The cap and stem of young mushrooms, while the cap is still closed around the stem and pure white, with white or faintly pink gills. The stem is good too; its flavour has been compared to asparagus. Once the gills turn grey or black the mushroom is past its best: those parts soon turn bitter and slimy, so cut them away.

habitat.text: Grass and disturbed ground: lawns, parks, gardens, roadsides and verges, the edges of paths and gravel roads, pasture, and waste ground near towns, often on soil rich in organic matter such as compost. It grows from soil, not from wood or dung, singly or in troops, clusters or lines, and can push up through gravel and even asphalt. It also grows in open woodland.

identification.text:
A tall, white mushroom like a lawyer's wig. The young cap is a cylinder or narrow egg, usually 5–15 cm tall (up to 20 cm) and up to about 8 cm wide, wrapped down over most of the stem. It is white, with a smooth pale ochre to brown patch on top, and the rest breaks up into broad, shaggy, upturned white to buff scales; rain flattens them. The cap then opens into a bell, and from its lower edge upward it turns grey, then black, and melts into a black inky liquid, until only the stem is left with a small black disc on top.
The gills are free or almost free and very crowded. They are white at first, then pink, then black, and dissolve from the cap edge upward. The spore print is black.
The stem is 10–30 cm tall and 1–2.5 cm thick, white, smooth, brittle and hollow. Its base may be slightly swollen but has no sac (volva). A thin, loose ring sits on the stem; it slides up and down, is stained black by spores, and often slips to the base or falls off.
The flesh is white, thin and soft, and the taste mild. It always grows from the ground, never on wood.
