preparation.text:
Pick only as many as you can cook the same day, and cook them within a few hours: they begin to dissolve soon after picking, and even in the fridge they last only a day or two. Carry them in a wide, shallow basket, not piled on top of each other, because crushed or bruised ones break down fastest. Cut off the dirty stem base, then brush off any dirt or wipe them with a damp cloth; don't soak them.
Always cook them; raw they are bitter. They are mild and delicate and release a lot of water, so don't cut them small. Cook them gently, covered for about 5 minutes to draw out the liquid, then uncovered until it has evaporated and the butter starts to brown, or pour the liquid off and keep it for stock. Fry them in butter with onion or garlic and serve on toast, or use them in omelettes, soups, sauces, pasta, quiche and with chicken; very young, tight caps can be crumbed and fried.
To keep them, sauté them for 3–5 minutes, or blanch them in boiling water for 15–20 seconds and cool them in cold water, then freeze. Dried, they break up and never regain their texture, so use dried ones in soups, sauces and seasoning powder.

recipes.method: Serves 4. 900 g shaggy inkcaps; 1 tbsp extra virgin olive oil; 1 tbsp unsalted butter; 1 large onion, diced; 2 celery sticks, diced; ½ tsp fine sea salt, plus more to taste; 5 garlic cloves, minced; 3 sprigs fresh thyme; 1 litre low-salt chicken or vegetable stock; 250 ml full-fat coconut cream; freshly ground black pepper. Wipe the mushrooms clean with a damp cloth or paper towel rather than rinsing them. Cut each in half, then roughly chop into 2.5 cm chunks. Heat the oil and butter in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat until the butter melts and foams. Add the onion, celery and ½ tsp salt and sweat for 7–8 minutes, until the onion is soft and translucent. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds, until fragrant. Add the mushrooms and thyme and cook, stirring now and then, for about 10 minutes, until the mushrooms have released all their liquid. Pour in the stock, bring to a low boil, then cover and simmer on low for 30 minutes. Take out the thyme sprigs and purée the soup smooth with a stick blender, or carefully in a blender. Stir in the coconut cream and cook for about 5 minutes, until slightly thickened and hot through. Season with salt and pepper.
recipes.title: Shaggy inkcap soup

recipes.method: Serves 2. 400 g shaggy inkcaps; 50 g butter; salt; pepper; ½ tsp chopped parsley (optional); buttered bread, to serve. Cut away every dark, and also reddish, part of the mushrooms, generously, and clean them dry rather than washing them. Cut them lengthwise into halves or quarters. Melt the butter, add the mushrooms with salt and pepper, cover and cook for about 5 minutes, stirring several times, to draw out their water. Uncover and keep cooking until the liquid has evaporated and the butter starts to brown. Sprinkle with the parsley and eat at once, on buttered bread.
recipes.title: Fried shaggy inkcaps on buttered bread

recipes.method: Serves 6 as a first course. Shortcrust pastry for a 23 cm pie dish; 5–6 bacon rashers, cut into 2.5 cm pieces; 225–450 g shaggy inkcaps, sliced; 4 shallots or spring onions, minced; ½ cup (about 50 g) freshly grated provolone; ⅛ tsp ground nutmeg; ¼ tsp salt; a pinch of cayenne; 4 eggs, well beaten; 500 ml half-and-half (equal parts milk and cream). Roll the pastry out to a 25 cm round, line a 23 cm pie dish with it and crimp the edges. Fry the bacon until crisp, lift it out with a slotted spoon and drain it on paper towels. Pour off all but 2 tbsp of the fat and sauté the mushrooms and shallots in it until the shallots are translucent and most of the mushroom liquid has evaporated. Spread the bacon over the pastry, then the cheese, then the mushrooms and shallots. Beat the nutmeg, salt and cayenne into the eggs, add the half-and-half and pour the custard slowly over the filling. Bake in an oven preheated to 180 °C for about 35 minutes, until the custard is set and the top is brown.
recipes.title: Shaggy inkcap quiche

recipes.method: Serves 8 as a main course (16 crêpes). For the crêpes: 1 cup (125 g) plain flour; 3 eggs, beaten; ½ tsp salt; 500–625 ml milk; oil. For the filling: 700 g shaggy inkcaps, sliced; 60 g butter; 1 tbsp minced fresh basil; salt and pepper. For the sauce: 1 medium onion, minced; 1 tbsp butter; 250 ml chicken stock; 60 ml dry white wine; 250 ml half-and-half (equal parts milk and cream); salt and pepper. Stir the eggs into the flour, add the salt and enough milk to make a batter as thick as cream, and leave it to stand for at least an hour. Brush a crêpe pan or frying pan lightly with oil and heat it until a few drops of water sizzle in it. Pour in just enough batter to coat the base, tilt the pan to spread it thinly, and cook over moderate heat until the edges curl away from the pan; turn the crêpe out onto a tea towel. Repeat to make 16. For the filling, melt the butter and cook the mushrooms for 5 minutes, then add the basil, salt and pepper. Roll a spoonful or two of filling in each crêpe, fasten it with a toothpick and keep the crêpes warm in the oven. For the sauce, sauté the onion in the butter until translucent, add the stock, wine and half-and-half and boil hard until reduced by half; season. Pour the sauce over the crêpes and serve at once, with crisp steamed strips of carrot garnished with watercress.
recipes.title: Crêpes forestière

recipes.method: Serves 4–6 as a main course. 450 g shaggy inkcaps, halved; 60 g butter; 450 g cooked chicken or turkey; 1½ tbsp flour; 500 ml chicken stock; 250 ml half-and-half (equal parts milk and cream); ⅛ tsp ground nutmeg; salt and pepper; 60 ml dry sherry; 225 g vermicelli; ¼ cup (about 25 g) freshly grated Parmesan. Sauté the mushrooms in half the butter for 5–10 minutes, until browned; lift them out with a slotted spoon and mix with the chicken. Add the rest of the butter and the flour to the pan and cook, stirring, for 2–3 minutes. Whisk in the stock and keep whisking until the sauce is thick, then add the half-and-half, nutmeg, salt, pepper and sherry and cook until well blended. Take off the heat. Cook the vermicelli in plenty of boiling salted water until al dente and drain. Mix half the sauce with the chicken and mushrooms and the other half with the vermicelli. Layer the vermicelli and the chicken mixture in a buttered baking dish, sprinkle with the Parmesan and bake in an oven preheated to 180 °C for 20–30 minutes, until bubbling and brown.
recipes.title: Shaggy inkcap chicken tetrazzini

recipes.method: Very young shaggy inkcaps, caps still tight around the stem; flour; beaten egg; seasoned breadcrumbs. Clean the mushrooms, then roll them in flour, dip them in egg and coat them in seasoned breadcrumbs. Air-fry at 175 °C for 7 minutes, without preheating, until light, golden and crisp. Older, opened caps are too fragile for this.
recipes.title: Crumbed air-fried shaggy inkcaps

Also read (29/10/2026): Nowakowski, Naliwajko, Markiewicz-Żukowska, Borawska & Socha 2020, 'The two faces of Coprinus comatus — functional properties and potential hazards', Phytotherapy Research 34: 2932–2944, doi 10.1002/ptr.6741, CC BY 4.0, full text via Europe PMC PMC7754439 — confusion mainly with Coprinopsis atramentaria, which contains coprine; disulfiram-like reaction if alcohol is drunk 30 minutes to 3 days after eating it: flushing, vomiting, nausea, tachycardia, headache, dizziness, hypotension, palpitations; cited literature 'indicates that CC does not contain coprine' (Berger & Guss 2005; Carlsson et al. 1978; Michelot 1992 and others); edible only young; consume, process or ice within 4–6 hours, autolysis within 2 days of storage; mercury (144 mg/kg dry weight from a German mining area; 2.1–9.2 mg/kg elsewhere in Europe), cadmium rising with soil levels, aluminium, barium and vanadium even from unpolluted areas (warnings 1 and 3, edible parts, preparation). Its skin patch-test reactions in people with atopic dermatitis (Fischer et al. 1999) were not made a warning: they concern contact and airborne spores, not eating. Wikipedia 'Coprinopsis atramentaria' revision 1373248877 (CC BY-SA 4.0) — cap 3–10 cm, greyish or brownish-grey, furrowed; stem grey, lacks a ring; grows in tufts, commonly from buried wood; coprine reaction five to ten minutes after alcohol, including tingling in the limbs, up to three days after eating (warning 1). Pat O'Reilly, First Nature 'Coprinopsis atramentaria — Common Inkcap' https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/coprinopsis-atramentaria.php — from stumps or buried wood, in clusters; cap mostly smooth with a small central area of small flattened scales, grey or grey-brown; avoid alcohol for three days before and after (warning 1). summary.text:
Coprinus comatus, commonly known as the shaggy ink cap, lawyer's wig, or shaggy mane, is a species of fungus.
It is introduced in New Zealand, probably with grass seed, soil or dung, and long established: Massee described it from the North Island in 1899. It is now found throughout the country, with 969 research-grade iNaturalist records. It is the type species of Coprinus; most of the other inkcaps have since been moved to Coprinopsis, Coprinellus and Parasola. It lives on dead organic matter in the soil, and its threads can also trap and digest tiny nematode worms. Within hours of picking, or of shedding its spores, the cap digests itself into black ink, which was once used for writing; that is why it is never sold in shops. It is cultivated as food in China, and in New Zealand spawn is sold to start a patch in a lawn or garden bed. The name comatus means hairy, for the shaggy scales.

warnings: The common inkcap (Coprinopsis atramentaria) also grows in New Zealand, in grass, parks and gardens and on verges, and also melts into black ink. It contains coprine: eaten within about three days before or after drinking even a little alcohol, it causes flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, a racing or pounding heart and tingling in the limbs, starting within minutes of the drink. It is grey to grey-brown, not white; its cap is smooth and furrowed, with at most a few small flat scales in the centre and none of the shaggy scales; its stem has no ring; and it grows in tight clumps from stumps or buried wood. A shaggy inkcap is white and shaggy all over, has a loose ring on its stem and grows from soil. Shaggy inkcap itself contains no coprine.

The magpie inkcap (Coprinopsis picacea), recorded a few times in New Zealand, is poisonous and looks very like a young shaggy inkcap. It is covered in tiny white scales rather than large upturned shaggy ones, and as its cap opens and turns grey to dark brown the white scales stand out in separate patches, like a magpie's plumage.

Shaggy inkcaps take up mercury, cadmium and other toxic metals from the soil, and the more there is in the soil the more they hold. Don't pick them from busy roadsides, industrial or mining land, or lawns and parks that may be sprayed.

habitat.text: Rich soil with plenty of dead organic matter, often where it has been disturbed: compost heaps, woodchip and garden beds, garden debris, leaf and needle litter, parks, path edges and forest edges, usually in some shade near trees rather than in open pasture. It always grows from the ground, never from wood, singly, in troops or in fairy rings. In New Zealand it has been collected on the ground and in litter under radiata pine, macrocarpa, plum, rowan, kōwhai and Tecoma, and in sand under Metrosideros.

identification.text:
A large, stocky mushroom. The button is round, egg- or drumstick-shaped, with a smooth brown skin. As the cap opens, to a dome and then almost flat, 5–20 cm across, the skin breaks into coarse, shaggy brown scales on a white to cream, fibrous background, leaving a smooth brown patch in the centre; the edge is ragged and shaggy.
The gills are free of the stem, crowded and broad, white, becoming cream or pale brownish with age and often brown-edged. They never turn green. The spore print is white.
The stem is 6–20 cm tall and 1–3.5 cm thick, smooth, with no snakeskin pattern, whitish above the ring and brownish below, bruising orange-brown. It is tough and fibrous and swells into a bulb at the base. The ring sits high on the stem; it is thick, persistent, white above and brownish beneath, often double-edged, and can usually be slid up and down.
The flesh is white and thick. Cut or scratched, it turns saffron-orange to red within moments, most strongly in the stem and near its top, and then slowly darkens to wine-red or brown.
Cleland's parasol (Macrolepiota clelandii), a native parasol of grassland, open forest and bush edges, is recorded far more often in New Zealand (913 research-grade iNaturalist records). It is more slender, its stem has a snakeskin pattern of brown fibres, and its flesh does not change colour when cut. The green-spored Chlorophyllum molybdites, a frequent cause of poisoning overseas, is not known from New Zealand; a white spore print rules it out.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have free white gills, a ring, a swollen stem base and a white spore print, so a spore print does not separate them. Death cap's base sits in a ragged, white, sac-like volva, often hidden in leaf litter, and its cap is smooth, usually greenish, yellowish or bronze, with none of the coarse, shaggy brown scales of a shaggy parasol. Its buttons are white eggs inside a veil; shaggy parasol buttons are round, with a smooth brown skin. A shaggy parasol's base is a bulb with no sac (in C. brunneum it can be abruptly swollen with a rim on top), and its flesh turns orange to red within moments when cut. Dig up the whole base of every mushroom and check it.

preparation.text:
Always cook them thoroughly: raw or undercooked they can upset the stomach. Twist off the stems and brush the caps clean or wipe them with a damp cloth rather than washing them, which makes them soggy, and check the gills for insects.
Fry them slowly in oil or butter until deeply browned, crumb and fry them, stuff and bake the cupped young caps, or use them in soups, stews, sauces and egg dishes. Diced stems can go into the same pan earlier, or into a stuffing for the caps.
They dry and rehydrate well for soups, stews and sauces. To freeze them, sauté them lightly first, or crumb them, freeze them and fry them straight from frozen: once thawed they turn to mush.

recipes.method: 2 rashers bacon, chopped; 3 tbsp butter; 1 large leek, white part only, thinly sliced; 1 litre potatoes cut into 1 cm cubes; 500 ml chopped shaggy parasols; 875 ml chicken or vegetable stock; ⅛ tsp ground nutmeg; ⅛ tsp ground white pepper; ½ tsp salt; 375 ml cream; chopped fresh chives to garnish. Cook the bacon in a large saucepan over medium heat until almost crisp. Add the butter and sauté the leek until it is limp and turning yellow. Add the potatoes and mushrooms, stir and cook for a few minutes. Add the stock and spices, turn up the heat and boil for one minute, then reduce the heat to low, cover and simmer for 15–20 minutes, until the potatoes are quite tender. Take the pan off the heat, purée half the soup in a blender, return it all to the pan and stir in the cream. Garnish with chives.
recipes.title: Shaggy parasol and potato soup

recipes.method: 8 shaggy parasols picked before the caps open, brushed clean, stems peeled; freshly ground black pepper; 1 tbsp smoked paprika, or more to taste; 1 tsp garlic powder, or more to taste; 500 ml fine cornmeal; 500 ml coarse cornmeal (polenta); unsalted butter for frying; 4 large eggs; 1 tbsp water; salt; lemon wedges to serve (optional). Beat the eggs with the water. Mix the two cornmeals with the paprika, pepper and garlic powder. Halve the mushrooms. Melt a tablespoon or two of butter in a cast-iron or wide frying pan over medium heat. When it is hot, coat the mushrooms in the egg, dredge them thoroughly in the cornmeal, tap off the excess and put them in the pan. Season with salt and fry until golden and crisp, then turn them and brown the other side. When they are cooked and hot right through, about 5–10 minutes, drain them on paper towels and serve at once, with lemon wedges.
recipes.title: Cornmeal-fried shaggy parasols

recipes.method: Serves 4. 450 g shaggy parasols picked before the caps open, brushed clean, stems peeled; about 60 ml light olive oil or cooking oil, as needed; ½ tsp salt, to taste; 1 tsp minced garlic; 1 tbsp sliced fresh mint leaves; ¼ tsp crushed red pepper flakes; freshly ground black pepper; lemon wedges to serve (optional). Cut the mushrooms into large pieces; halve smaller ones. Heat half the oil in a cast-iron or wide frying pan over medium heat, add the mushrooms and cook them slowly, turning now and then. If they soak up the oil, add more. Take your time, until they are golden brown on both sides, seasoning with a pinch of salt halfway. Push them to the side of the pan, add the garlic and drag the mushrooms through it to coat them in the oil. Stir in the chilli flakes and mint, check the seasoning and serve with lemon wedges as a side dish.
recipes.title: Italian-style slow-fried shaggy parasols

recipes.method: Written for parasol mushrooms (Macrolepiota procera). Serves 3–4. 6–8 medium caps, still slightly cupped; 150 g cream cheese or ricotta; 50 g grated parmesan; 1 garlic clove, minced; 50 g fresh spinach, chopped; 3 tbsp panko breadcrumbs; 2 tbsp olive oil; salt and black pepper. Heat the oven to 190 °C. Brush the caps clean and twist off the stems to leave a cavity. Brush the outside of each cap with olive oil and set them gill side up on a baking tray lined with baking paper. Wilt the spinach in a drop of oil in a frying pan for 1–2 minutes and squeeze out the excess water. Mix the cream cheese, spinach, most of the parmesan and the garlic, season and spoon the mixture into the caps. Mix the panko with a teaspoon of oil and the rest of the parmesan and sprinkle it over. Bake for 15–20 minutes, until the mushrooms are tender and the topping golden and crisp. Leave them for 5 minutes before serving; the filling is very hot.
recipes.title: Stuffed shaggy parasol caps

recipes.method: Written for parasol mushrooms (Macrolepiota procera). Serves 2. 4 large eggs; 150 g mushroom caps, stems removed; 30 g butter; 1 small onion or shallot; 2 tbsp milk or cream; 1 tbsp chopped fresh chives; salt and pepper. Cut the caps into small bite-sized squares and finely dice the onion. Whisk the eggs with the milk, a pinch of salt and pepper until pale and slightly frothy. Melt half the butter in a non-stick frying pan over medium heat and soften the onion for 2–3 minutes. Add the mushrooms and cook for about 5 minutes, until tender and lightly browned. Lower the heat to medium-low, add the rest of the butter, then pour in the eggs. Let them sit a few seconds until the edges start to set, then push them gently from the edges to the centre with a spatula to form large, soft curds, until mostly set but still glossy. Take the pan off the heat, fold in the chives and serve at once.
recipes.title: Scrambled eggs with shaggy parasols

FungiAtlas 'Recipes with Parasol Mushrooms' https://fungiatlas.com/parasol-recipes/ — written for Macrolepiota procera, said so at the head of the two recipes used ('Stuffed Parasol Mushroom Caps', 'Scrambled Eggs with Parasol Mushrooms'); small Lepiota species resemble parasols and are severely poisonous; don't wash them, they act like sponges; check the gills for insects; lightly sauté and freeze, or freeze after breading (warning 3, preparation). Not used: its schnitzel, garlic-butter sauté and cream soup (near duplicates of the cornmeal-fried, Italian-style and potato-soup recipes, which are written for the shaggy parasol). Also read: FungiAtlas 'Shaggy Parasol (Chlorophyllum rhacodes)' https://fungiatlas.com/chlorophyllum-rhacodes/ — button spherical, egg- or drumstick-shaped; scales reddish-brown, cinnamon or dark brown, centre smooth and dark; margin shaggy; gills free, crowded, broad; stem without the snakeskin pattern, fibrous and tough; flesh 'instantly turns saffron-yellow, then orange-red, and finally dark red or wine-brown'; compost heaps, gardens, parks, wood edges; raw it can cause gastric upset; stems discarded or dried for powder; some people allergic even when cooked, try a very small amount first; C. brunneum 'Edible to some, but causes gastric upset in others' (identification, habitat, edible parts, preparation, warnings 1–2). Not used: its 'near ant hills' and European season (July–October/November).

Owner's links, continued: Ultimate Mushroom 'Chlorophyllum rhacodes: The Ultimate Mushroom Guide + 2 Recipes' https://ultimate-mushroom.com/edible/50-chlorophyllum-rhacodes.html — two recipes used, metric (1 cup = 250 ml, ½ inch = 1 cm): 'Shaggy Parasol and Potato Soup' and 'Cornmeal Fried Shaggy Parasols'. The cornmeal-fried recipe appears to be Alan Bergo's from Forager Chef (his page shows 'Cornmeal fried parasols (with woody stems, 2015)'; his current recipe card is the Italian one below); the source link stays with the page it was read from. Its description section repeats Kuo's MushroomExpert page word for word. Not used: 'also known as... the shaggy mane mushroom' (that is Coprinus comatus); caps 'up to 30cm'; 'prefers to grow in grassy areas, such as lawns and meadows' (Wikipedia: dislikes open pastures and fields); 'pale cream spores' (other sources white); its claim that C. brunneum 'is now considered poisonous' (see warning 1 for what the sources support); nutrition and traditional-medicine claims. Cascade Mycological Society 'The Shaggy Parasol' (05/2021) https://cascademyco.org/2021/05/the-shaggy-parasol/ — stems 'far too fibrous to eat', clip the caps; white spore print, tough fibrous stem, stem turning orange when scratched or cut; some people get gastrointestinal upset 'even those who have eaten them without problems in the past'; cook fully (edible parts, warning 2). Its Oregon habitat under Douglas fir and its batter-fried shaggy-mane recipe (Coprinus comatus) were not used.

Also read (29/10/2026): Michael Kuo, MushroomExpert.Com 'Chlorophyllum rhacodes' (11/2017) https://www.mushroomexpert.com/chlorophyllum_rhacodes.html — cap 5–16 cm, bald and brown in the button stage, then shaggy scales with brownish tips over a whitish background, centre smooth and brown; gills free, close to crowded, white to pale brownish, often brown-edged; stem 6–21 cm long, 1.5–3.5 cm thick, gradually swollen bulb, whitish above the ring, brownish below, bruising brown; ring high, double-edged, moveable, brownish beneath; flesh staining pinkish orange to reddish, then slowly brownish, especially near the stem apex; troops or fairy rings in lawns, gardens, roadsides; rhacodes from the Greek for ragged or tattered (identification, summary). Kuo 'Chlorophyllum brunneum' (07/2015) https://www.mushroomexpert.com/chlorophyllum_brunneum.html — 'a dead ringer' for C. rhacodes; abruptly swollen base, often rimmed; ring not two-layered (warning 1, death cap card). Kuo gives no edibility information. Alan Bergo, Forager Chef 'Foraging and Cooking Shaggy Parasol Mushrooms' (25/10/2025) https://foragerchef.com/the-shaggy-parasol-chlorophyllum-rhacodes/ (403 to curl; read from the Wayback Machine copy of 19/04/2026) — always from the ground, never from wood; very young ones 'nearly impossible to differentiate' from C. molybdites; learn your local Amanitas ('Amanita pantherina group'; there are no New Zealand research-grade iNaturalist records of panther cap, so the card is to death cap, 115 records); some people intolerant, 'enjoy small amounts at first'; stem tougher, needs longer cooking, can be diced or used in stuffing; 'dry and rehydrate very well'; recipe 'Italian Fried Shaggy Parasols' from its JSON-LD, metric (1 lb = 450 g, ¼ cup = 60 ml) (habitat, edible parts, preparation, warning 2, death cap card, recipe). Its Minnesota season was not used. Wikipedia 'Lepiota subincarnata' revision 1293035072 (CC BY-SA 4.0) — fatal dapperling, deadly parasol; cap light red to red-brown, cream toward the margin; gills whitish; flesh white to pinkish; contains alpha-amanitin (warning 3). Wikipedia 'Amanita phalloides' revision 1380615841 (CC BY-SA 4.0) — swollen, ragged, sac-like white volva, may be hidden by leaf litter; young ones emerge like a white egg covered by a universal veil (death cap cards).

Species in New Zealand, checked 29/10/2026. Jerry Cooper (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research) on iNaturalist NZ: observation 1072193 (Ashley Gorge Road, 02/03/2009, the owner's photo -1) and 1410704 (C. brunneum, South New Brighton, 16/02/2014) — 'Both IDs confirmed from sequence data'; observation 83343949 (Ian Dickie, Ilam, 17/06/2021), where Cooper replies that the double ring as a test is 'A myth in my opinion', cites a sequenced C. brunneum (PDD 96039) with a double ring, and writes 'I've never got any of the proposed macro characters to work based on sequenced material. Both species can sometimes have both sets of characters. The only character that seems to work is the shape of the cheilocystidia'; observation 265866379 (Methven Cemetery, 24/01/2024) — 'Sequence says this is C. olivieri and first confirmed observation from the southern hemisphere', 'not obviously identifiable to my eyes'; observation 268142958 (Dunedin North, 31/03/2025, woodchip) C. olivieri, Cooper: 'There are probably lots of records but just unrecognised' (summary, warning 1). iNaturalist NZ (place 6803, verifiable, wild): 1,220 Chlorophyllum records, of which research grade C. brunneum 7, C. rhacodes 3, C. olivieri 2, C. molybdites 0; needs-ID C. rhacodes 16, C. brunneum 15; the rest named only to genus. Lookalikes, research grade, wild: Macrolepiota clelandii 913 (identification note; no entry, so not a card), Amanita phalloides 115 (card, both ways), Lepiota subincarnata 4 (warning 3; no entry), Amanita pantherina 0, Macrolepiota procera 0. Warning 1's statement that the field tests fail rests on Cooper's comments.

Habitats set 29/10/2026 from [] to [forest, urban]: The Hidden Forest gives forest litter and forest edges as well as gardens, woodchip and compost; Biota's New Zealand records are under trees; Wikipedia says it prefers shade and dislikes open pastures, so grassland was not added, although lawns and parks fall under urban.

summary.text:
Shaggy parasol is the common name for three closely related species of mushroom: Chlorophyllum rhacodes, C. olivieri and C. brunneum, found in North America, Europe and Southern Africa.
This entry is Chlorophyllum rhacodes, the shaggy parasol in the strict sense. All three species are introduced to New Zealand and all three have been confirmed here by DNA sequencing: C. rhacodes and C. brunneum by Jerry Cooper of Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, and C. olivieri first at Methven cemetery in 2024, the first confirmed record from the Southern Hemisphere, and since in Dunedin. They look so alike that, of about 1,200 New Zealand iNaturalist records, almost all are named only to the genus Chlorophyllum (see the warnings). They are found throughout the country, for example at Te Mata Park in Hawke's Bay.
It was long called Lepiota or Macrolepiota rhacodes, until DNA showed it is closer to the green-spored Chlorophyllum molybdites than to the parasol mushroom, Macrolepiota procera. The name rhacodes comes from the Greek for ragged or tattered, for the shaggy cap; Vittadini spelled it rachodes when he described it in 1835, and some books still use that spelling. It lives on dead organic matter in rich soil, often growing in troops or fairy rings.

warnings: Three shaggy parasols grow in New Zealand — Chlorophyllum rhacodes, C. brunneum and C. olivieri — and they cannot be reliably told apart by eye. The field tests usually given (a double-edged ring and a gradually swollen stem base for C. rhacodes; a simple ring and an abruptly swollen, rimmed bulb for C. brunneum) do not hold up: New Zealand C. brunneum confirmed by DNA sequencing has had a double ring, both species can show both sets of features, and only a microscopic feature of the gill edge has worked to separate them. C. brunneum causes severe stomach upsets in some people and is considered toxic in some European countries, although no toxin has been identified; others eat it without trouble. Any shaggy parasol you pick may be C. brunneum.

Some people react badly to shaggy parasols even when they are well cooked, including people who have eaten them before without trouble, and some are strongly allergic to every Chlorophyllum. Eat only a small portion the first time, never eat them raw, and don't serve them to anyone who has not eaten them before.

Small parasol-like mushrooms can kill. The fatal dapperling (Lepiota subincarnata), recorded a few times in New Zealand, contains alpha-amanitin, the death cap's poison; its cap is light red to red-brown, cream towards the edge, its gills whitish and its flesh white to pinkish. Many of New Zealand's small parasol-like mushrooms have never been studied or named. Don't eat any small parasol-like mushroom.

Escape from cultivation. Gardens, roadsides and other disturbed areas, and sometimes native vegetation.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Usually waste places, roadside banks, grassy places, and open ground near habitations.

identification.text:
Clump-forming, hairy perennial; rhizomes short, thick, fleshy, sometimes with short offsets, rough from numerous leaf base scars. Leaves 3-foliolate, in basal rosettes. Petiole (3)–7–30 cm long, hairy or nearly glabrous; stipular wing inconspicuous, membranous, hairy. Lamina of leaflets often unequal, sessile, usually 8–35–(55) × 15–(60) mm, broadly obcordate with narrow sinus to ⅓ lamina, with appressed hairs above and below, with basal tuft of hairs; calli orange and forming marginal band; lobes 2, rounded. Inflorescence to about 35 cm tall, glabrate, a terminal cyme or panicle of (4)–7–35 flowers; pedicels more or less deflexed at first, later erect, very variable in length, with antrorse hairs. Bracts at base of pedicels 2–2.5 mm long, lanceolate to ovate, with 2 elongated orange calli. Sepals 3–5 mm long, ovate-elliptic or elliptic, with appressed hairs; calli 2, orange, terminal. Petals 9–16 mm long, oblique-obovate to oblong, usually rose above with darker veins and paler pink with band of appressed hairs outside, rarely white. Stamens in 2 whorls; filaments hairy, dilated and sometimes toothed in lower part, those of longest whorl 2–3 mm long. Styles usually much longer than longer stamen whorl at anthesis (if petals white, then much shorter than longer stamen whorl), densely hairy. Capsule not seen. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Shamrock wood sorrel: a hairy, clump-forming plant with all its leaves in basal rosettes on stalks (3)–7–30 cm long, and no leafy stem. Its flowers come (4)–7–35 together in a branched cluster on a stalk up to c. 35 cm tall; petals 9–16 mm long, usually rose with darker veins, rarely white. Its leaflets are usually 8–35 mm long, up to 55 mm. Pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless. Its petals can be as short as 10 mm, so petal size alone does not separate them, and both can be pale or white. Several flowers on one stalk point to shamrock wood sorrel, but a single flower does not rule it out: its clusters can hold anything from 1 to at least 30 flowers. Look for a leafy, branched stem, which only pale-pink wood sorrel has. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pale-pink wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Shamrock wood sorrel grows from a short, thick, fleshy rhizome, rough with old leaf-base scars, and has no true bulbils; pink shamrock grows from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, with a thick, fleshy, glassy white root below it. Shamrock wood sorrel's petals are 9–16 mm long, usually rose with darker veins, with a band of flattened hairs on the outside; pink shamrock's are pink to rose, 1.5–2 cm long and hairless, so the lengths meet at 15–16 mm. Shamrock wood sorrel's leaflets have flattened hairs on both faces; pink shamrock's are hairless or nearly so on top. Both have no leafy stem, leaves rising from the base, heart-shaped leaflets with orange dots or an orange band near the edge, and several flowers on a stalk up to about 35 cm tall: shamrock wood sorrel (4)–7–35, pink shamrock 3–7 or 10–18, so flower number does not separate them. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pink shamrock

lookalikes.howToTell: Shamrock wood sorrel grows from a short, thick, fleshy rhizome, rough with old leaf-base scars, and has no true bulbils; fishtail oxalis grows from a bulb surrounded by numerous small bulbils, with a thick, fleshy, glassy white root below it. Shamrock wood sorrel's leaflets are broadly heart-shaped with a narrow notch up to a third of their length, with flattened hairs on both faces, a tuft of hairs at the base and a band of orange dots along the edge; fishtail oxalis's are broadly fishtail-shaped, shallowly and broadly two-lobed, 12–50 mm long and 18–80 mm wide, hairless except near the base, with no orange dots or only faint ones. Shamrock wood sorrel's petals are 9–16 mm long, usually rose with darker veins, with a band of flattened hairs on the outside; fishtail oxalis's are about 1.2–1.5 cm long, pink and hairless, so length overlaps. Both have no leafy stem and carry several flowers on a tall stalk: shamrock wood sorrel (4)–7–35, fishtail oxalis about 5–15 (up to 20), so flower number does not separate them. Fishtail oxalis also has a pale form with broadly heart-shaped leaflets, up to 30 × 40 mm with a rather shallow notch, sometimes hairy beneath and with no orange dots, and whitish or very pale mauve-pink petals 9–15 mm long. The tests above that do not rest on leaflet shape or petal colour still hold for it. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Fishtail oxalis

lookalikes.howToTell: Purple wood sorrel grows from a narrow egg-shaped bulb with dark brown or blackish, shining, sticky outer scales. Each flower stalk, 1–11 cm long, carries a single flower forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base. Its leaflets are broadly obovate with a rounded tip, sometimes slightly notched, and its bracts and sepals have no orange dots. Shamrock wood sorrel grows from a short, thick, fleshy rhizome, rough with old leaf-base scars, and has no bulbs or bulbils. Its flowers come (4)–7–35 together in a branched cluster on a stalk up to about 35 cm tall, its petals 9–16 mm long, usually rose with darker veins, rarely white. Its leaflets are broadly heart-shaped with a narrow notch up to a third of their length and a band of orange dots along the edge, and its bracts and sepals carry orange dots. What does not separate them: both have no leafy stem, with all the leaves rising from the base, and both are hairy. A single flower does not rule out shamrock wood sorrel, whose clusters can hold anything from 1 to at least 30 flowers. Purple wood sorrel's petals can be as short as 10 mm, so only petals longer than 16 mm point to purple wood sorrel. Do not eat purple wood sorrel; see its own entry.

preparation.text: Use them to flavour salads, in moderation.

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) lemon juice and 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) maple syrup or honey. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the sorrel and stir for 1–2 minutes, until it wilts. Put it in a blender or food processor with the lemon juice and the syrup or honey and blend until well combined. Serve it straight away, or refrigerate it and warm it before use; the author finds it even better the next day. The author serves it on fish, or as a dipping sauce for grilled prawns.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel sauce

recipes.method: About 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, stems or flowers, or a mix, about 250 ml (1 cup) water, and maple syrup or another sweetener to taste. The amounts are rough: use as much sorrel as you like and enough water to cover it. Blend the sorrel and water until well combined, strain through a fine sieve and sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel 'lemonade'

recipes.method: Equal parts wood sorrel, sugar, and water; the author usually uses 250 ml (1 cup) of each. Put everything in a saucepan and bring it to a simmer, stirring. Simmer for 15–30 minutes, strain through muslin (cheesecloth) and pour into sterilised bottles. The author uses it in tea, topped up with soda water, over ice cream or fresh strawberries, or in vinaigrettes and marinades.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel syrup

recipes.method: The recipe uses one part leaves to three parts water. Fresh wood sorrel leaves; boiling water; sweetener to taste (optional). Put the leaves in a container, pour the boiling water over them and leave to steep for 5–15 minutes. Strain out the leaves and sweeten to taste if you like. Drink it hot, or pour it over ice for an iced tea.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel tea

recipes.method: 2 cloves garlic, minced; olive oil for cooking; 2 spring onions, chopped; 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock; 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish; 3 medium mint leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk; salt and pepper. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks. Heat a little olive oil in a small saucepan and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the spring onions. Cover with the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, then add the sorrel for about 30 seconds. Take it off the heat, add the mint and blend smooth with a stick blender (or an ordinary blender). Stir in the coconut milk and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until well chilled, a couple of hours, and serve garnished with the sorrel flowers.
recipes.title: Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

recipes.method: About 450 g (1 lb) Italian or breakfast sausage; 1 medium spaghetti squash; several cups of wood sorrel, washed and drained, stems removed (the recipe gives no closer amount); olive oil; 1 red onion, halved and sliced; 1 egg; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk or any milk; 1 garlic clove, minced; 15 ml (1 tbsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) tarragon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) black pepper; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground sage. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Halve the squash, spoon out the seeds and stringy threads, set the halves cut side up on a baking tray, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and bake for 20–25 minutes, until the flesh gives a little when pressed. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts. Take the squash out of the oven and scrape out the flesh with a fork (careful, it will be hot). Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.
recipes.title: Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel

recipes.method: Two handfuls of wood sorrel, chopped; potato and kūmara, boiled first and sliced; cream. Layer the sorrel with the sliced potato and kūmara in a baking dish, pour cream over the top and bake at 180 °C until it starts to brown.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel, kūmara and potato gratin

recipes.method: Chop a big handful of wood sorrel leaves, stalks and flowers and mix them through a potato salad dressed with a cream dressing.
recipes.title: Potato salad with wood sorrel

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: The author's greens were puha, sow thistle, nasturtium, onion weed, wild fennel, oxalis, wild mustard and wild celery; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 1 diced onion; 1 potato, scrubbed and diced; 2 sliced garlic cloves; 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 1.3 litres water; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked pepper; extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil, to serve; edible weed flowers. Serves 4. Cut the vegetables and greens to similar sizes. Fry the onion in the oil for a minute, then add the potato and garlic (the method also adds fennel bulb and celery stalks, which the ingredient list leaves out) and fry for another minute. Add the water, cover, bring to the boil and simmer until the potato is soft. Add the greens with the salt and yeast and cook for 3 minutes, until just tender — added at the end, they keep their colour. Blend until smooth (push it through a sieve if your blender isn't powerful), season with the pepper and more salt if needed, and serve drizzled with extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil and scattered with edible weed flowers.
recipes.title: Wild greens soup

summary.text:
Oxalis articulata, known as pink-sorrel, pink wood sorrel, windowbox wood-sorrel, sourgrass, is a perennial species of flowering plant in the genus Oxalis native to Northern Argentina, Southern Brazil and Uruguay.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island; South Island: around towns and cities throughout, especially in the lower part of the North Island, Nelson and the eastern coastal areas of the South Island; Stewart Island: Halfmoon Bay. Naturalised from eastern South America, first recorded in 1940.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

identification.text:
Scarcely scented, perennial herb. Stems erect, up to about 1 m tall, glabrous or with a few scattered hairs, striate, simple or branched at base or above. Basal and lower cauline leaves petiolate, narrow-elliptic, acute to obtuse at apex, cuneate, evenly 1-serrate, glabrous, up to about 30 × 4 cm; cauline leaves similar to basal but above becoming smaller, apetiolate, amplexicaul, the uppermost lanceolate to linear and sometimes almost entire. Involucral bracts 6–12 mm long, glabrous; margins and apex brown, membranous; inner bracts at least with extended apical flap. Capitula solitary, (50)–70–120 mm diameter; ray florets 20–40; ligules white; disc florets numerous, yellow. Achenes 2.5–4 mm long, dark brown with paler ribs; achenes of disc florets more or less terete or somewhat flattened, with 10 more or less equal ribs, and corona 0; achenes of ray florets similar to those of disc florets but with lateral ribs sometimes somewhat thicker, and an irregular corona up to about 1 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
L. maximum is part of the L. vulgare complex, but in New Zealand is easily distinguished from the oxeye daisy by its larger capitula and narrow-elliptic, regularly serrate leaves. Wild plants vary somewhat in capitulum diameter and all collections are single; a wide range of cultivars, including double forms, is cultivated.
Leucanthemum vulgare (ox-eye daisy), the other naturalised Leucanthemum in New Zealand, has elliptic, obovate or spoon-shaped basal and lower stem leaves that are coarsely toothed, scalloped or shallowly lobed, stems usually hairy below, and heads (25)–30–60–(65) mm across (Flora of New Zealand key, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Leaves and head size separate them best. Shasta daisy's basal and lower stem leaves are narrow-elliptic and evenly toothed with single teeth, up to about 30 cm long; ox-eye daisy's are elliptic, obovate or spoon-shaped, coarsely toothed (sometimes doubly), scalloped or shallowly lobed, and up to 12 cm long (rarely 18 cm), so a basal leaf longer than 18 cm is Shasta daisy. Shasta daisy's heads are usually 70–120 mm across (50 mm at the smallest); ox-eye's are usually 30–60 mm (25–65 mm at the extremes), so heads of 50–65 mm need the leaf test. Shasta daisy's stems are hairless or have a few scattered hairs; ox-eye's are usually sparsely to densely hairy below, but rarely hairless. Shasta daisy's heads are borne singly; ox-eye's singly or a few in a loose cluster. What does not separate them: both are scarcely scented perennials up to about 1 m tall, with white rays (20–40 against 9–33) around a yellow disc, narrow, stalkless upper leaves that clasp the stem, and no scales on the receptacle, and both grow on roadsides, waste places and pasture. Ox-eye daisy's young leaves, flower buds and flower heads are eaten (see its entry).

summary.text:
Shasta daisy (Leucanthemum maximum, synonym Chrysanthemum maximum) is a perennial herb of the daisy family, Asteraceae, sold by New Zealand nurseries as a garden plant, including double-flowered forms, and found wild as a garden escape. This species is one of the wild chrysanthemums Luther Burbank crossed to produce the popular garden hybrid known as the Shasta daisy, Leucanthemum × superbum.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North and South Islands: occasional throughout; Stewart Island: Halfmoon Bay area to Maori Beach. Native to the Pyrenees; naturalised in New Zealand by 1914.
The species is an escape from cultivation and is usually known as Chrysanthemum maximum. Hortus Third (1976) suggests that most of the material cultivated as C. maximum is probably C. × superbum J. Ingram, which is presumed to be a hybrid between C. lacustre Brot. and C. maximum. Other authorities treat all cultivated material as selections of C. maximum.

warnings: Do not eat Shasta daisy. The garden Shasta daisy, from which wild plants escape, is listed as mildly toxic, of low severity: eating it can cause drooling, mouth irritation, vomiting and diarrhoea, and the flowers, leaves, stems and roots are all listed as poisonous. The toxic principle listed is sesquiterpene lactones, which ox-eye daisy also contains. No report of anyone poisoned by it has been found. Plant databases record no food use; its record as food is a foraging blog and a gardening page about garden plants.
Handling the leaves and flowers can irritate the skin; wear gloves.
It grows with ox-eye daisy on roadsides, in waste places and in pasture, and looks very like it — check the leaves and the size of the heads before picking ox-eye daisy (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text:
Poor, acidic, dry soils: paddocks, roadsides, gravel, sand dunes, lawns that have given up.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Especially in open situations on poor, light, stony or sandy soils from sea level to about 1500 m, also in riverbeds, poor pastures, pavement cracks, gutters and cultivated ground.

identification.text:
A low plant with small arrow-shaped leaves — a narrow blade with two backward-pointing lobes at the base, like a spearhead. Flower stalks are slender and turn red; whole plants flush red in summer. It tastes sharply sour and lemony, but so do common sorrel and fiddle dock, so taste alone does not identify it.
It spreads by slender, branching, yellow underground stems. On poor, dry or stony soils plants are often stunted and deep red all over, and stands can turn the ground red with their flower spikes.

lookalikes.howToTell: Common sorrel is much bigger: leaf blades 3.5–12 cm long, with the two basal lobes pointing downwards, upper leaves partly clasping the stem, and stems to about 1 m. Sheep sorrel's blades are 1.5–5 cm, its basal lobes stand out at about right angles, and its flowering stems are 3–30 cm. On female plants, common sorrel's fruit is wrapped in round, winged, rose-red valves 2.8–4 mm across; sheep sorrel's valves are 1.2–1.5 mm and wingless. Both are sour and eaten the same way.
lookalikes.name: Common sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Fiddle dock's leaves are much bigger, 3–20 cm long and 1–8 cm wide, with two large rounded lobes at the base and pinched in above them like a fiddle; sheep sorrel's blades are 1.5–5 cm long and up to 2 cm wide, with a pair of narrow lobes sticking out sideways like a spearhead. Fiddle dock grows from a thick taproot to about 60 cm, with small leaves right to the branch tips; sheep sorrel is low (flowering stems 3–30 cm), spreads by slender yellow underground stems, and its flower spikes are nearly leafless. In fruit, fiddle dock's valves are 4.5–5.5 mm, spiny-edged with a lump on each; sheep sorrel's are 1.2–1.5 mm, smooth and without lumps. Don't use taste: both are sour.

preparation.text: A few leaves raw for sourness in a salad, or wilted into a sauce or soup as with garden sorrel. A seasoning more than a green.

recipes.method: Written for sheep sorrel (adapted from Anja Dunk's sorrel soup). Serves 4 as a side. 80–100 g sheep sorrel leaves (about 4 handfuls); 60 g spinach leaves (2 large handfuls); 40 g butter; 30 g plain flour; about 1 litre hot vegetable stock; 2 tbsp neutral oil; salt and black pepper. Put 80–100 g sheep sorrel leaves (about 4 handfuls) and 60 g spinach leaves (2 large handfuls) in a bowl of water, swish them about, let the dirt settle, then lift them out and dry them. In a saucepan over a medium heat, melt 40 g butter, add 30 g plain flour and stir for 3 minutes, until light tan. Whisk in about 1 litre of hot vegetable stock in a slow stream, then barely simmer for 10 minutes, until thickened. Meanwhile heat 2 tbsp neutral oil in a frying pan and wilt the greens for 60 seconds (the sorrel turns yellowish). Stir the greens into the soup, blend, and season with salt and black pepper.
recipes.title: Sorrel soup

recipes.method: Written for sheep sorrel (Alutiiq Museum, Kodiak, Alaska; recipe by Gayla Pedersen, there called a sauce or pesto); 60 ml of chopped leaves serves 2. 60 ml (¼ cup) chopped sheep sorrel; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 15 ml (1 tbsp) red wine vinegar; ½ tsp salt, or a pinch to taste. Rinse the leaves well in cool water and chop them finely. Put 60 ml (¼ cup) chopped sheep sorrel in a jar with 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil, 15 ml (1 tbsp) red wine vinegar and ½ tsp salt, or a pinch to taste, and stir. Scale it up or down keeping 3 parts oil to 1 part vinegar; use a blender for a larger batch. The recipe works with lemon or lime juice in place of the vinegar and any oil you like for the olive oil. Optional: 60 ml grated parmesan, 60 ml basil, ½ tsp black pepper, 1 tsp chilli flakes, or walnuts or oregano.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumex_acetosella Corroborates the oxalic acid and the dose caution: the plant contains oxalic acid and its derivatives, and is 'toxic in large amounts because of oxalates'. The Italian agronomist Nicola Onorati (1764–1822) first noticed that it damages the teeth of animals that graze it, for the same reason. On eating it: the leaves can be taken raw or cooked, with the water changed to reduce the strong taste, and are used as a garnish, a tart flavouring, a salad green and a curdling agent for milk in cheese-making — a lemony, tangy, rhubarb-like flavour. Note also that the similarly named Rumex acerosella likewise contains oxalic acid and should not be eaten in excess.

summary.text: A small sour weed of poor ground whose arrow-shaped leaves taste sharply of lemon. It is one of New Zealand's most abundant weeds, first recorded wild in 1867; it is poisonous to stock, though people eat it like sorrel in salads.

warnings: High in oxalic acid. Eat in small amounts, and avoid altogether if you have kidney problems or gout.

edibleParts.text: Young leaves, raw or cooked — best before the plant flowers, when they suit salads; they become more peppery with age, and once the plant has flowered the basal leaves are better cooked as greens. Young flowering shoots and flower tips, raw or cooked. Green seed stalks and the seedpods, which have a peppery taste and are used as a seasoning. The fresh seed heads and young leaves also go into salads and pesto. Seeds, raw or cooked or ground into a meal, though very small and fiddly to collect. The root, fresh or dried, as a ginger substitute; it is also grown and used in Korea as a root vegetable, though each root is small.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Common weed of cultivated and waste land throughout.
In New Zealand it is very common in crops and gardens throughout the country (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated).
Arable land, gardens, waste places etc, it is a common weed of cultivated soil and can even be found growing in situations such as cracks in pavements.
C. bursa-pastoris is common on cultivated ground and waysides and meadows.
Gardens, footpaths, cultivated land and bare ground (Common Weeds of New Zealand, restated); crops and waste areas (Rainbow & Brown, restated). In lawns it moves into thin or patchy turf, especially on compacted, low-fertility soil and damp open patches (New Zealand Lawn Addicts, restated). In Central Otago it often grows on dry, gravelly patches but also does well in rich soil (Herbal Culture, restated).

identification.text:
Annual herb. Stem erect, little- to much-branched above, (2)-15-30-(80) cm tall. Leaves and stems with spreading simple hairs and sparse to dense appressed stellate hairs. Leaves not lobed to runcinate-pinnatifid, very variable in shape, shallowly dentate or rarely subentire; lower leaves petiolate, (0.4)-5-15 × (0.2)-2-5 cm; upper leaves with sagittate or amplexicaul lobes at base, smaller, becoming entire. Racemes (2)-5-20-(45) cm long; pedicels erecto-patent at flowering, spreading at fruiting. Sepals glabrous or sparsely hairy, green or pinkish, 1-1.5 × 0.6-0.8 mm. Petals white, 2-2.5 × 0.7-1 mm, sometimes reduced or absent. Silicle narrowly to broadly obtriangular, emarginate, 5-10 × 4-7 mm; valves sharply keeled, reticulately veined, greenish brown; style about 0.5 mm long. Seeds pale brown, about 1 × 0.5 mm.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It starts as a rosette with very variable leaf shapes, which can make it hard to identify before it flowers; rosettes seldom grow much beyond 10–15 cm across, while the flowering stems often reach 20–30 cm in good conditions. It soon puts up a stem of small white flowers followed by many characteristic heart-shaped seed pods (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated).
In the rosette stage it can be told from other mustards by its lobed basal leaves, which are usually hairy, with the lobes more or less uniform on each side, and by its generally small size (Edible Wild Food, restated).
In plain terms: the rosette lies flat to the ground, with basal leaves 5–20 cm long, from deeply lobed to unlobed, narrowing towards the stalk; the seedling's first leaves are broader, spoon- to oblong-shaped. The stem leaves are arrow-shaped and toothed, with ear-like lobes clasping the stem. Even on small seedlings the leaves carry scattered star-shaped hairs, which you can see with a hand lens. The thin, branched flowering stem rises from the centre to about 15–30 cm, with white flowers 2.5–3 mm across, each with four small undivided petals and four green sepals half their length. The heart-shaped pods, 6–9 mm long and greenish-brown on long stalks, split into two halves when ripe to release many tiny pale brown seeds. The plant has a deep taproot (Common Weeds of New Zealand; Bayer Crop Science NZ; Rainbow & Brown, restated).
Before flowering the rosette can also be mistaken for Cape weed, which usually makes a larger rosette and is whitish under the leaf (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database; New Zealand Lawn Addicts, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Shepherd's purse is an erect annual; its lower leaves are very variable, unlobed to deeply lobed and usually shallowly toothed, its upper leaves clasp the stem with arrow-shaped lobes at the base, and its pod is flat, notched and triangular, 5–10 × 4–7 mm. Sweet alyssum is usually perennial, with stems lying down to ascending and branched from below, narrow untoothed leaves 12–30 × 2–3 (4) mm, flowers crowded in rounded heads, and a small, slightly inflated, oval pod 3–4 × 1.5–2.5 mm. White flowers of similar size do not separate them (shepherd's purse petals 2–2.5 mm, sometimes missing; sweet alyssum petals 2.5–3 mm, usually white, rarely purple). Sweet alyssum's young leaves, stems, flowers and green pods are eaten, mainly as a pungent flavouring.
lookalikes.name: Sweet alyssum

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small rosette-forming weeds of cultivated ground with tiny white four-petalled flowers, and bitter cress looks a bit like shepherd's purse. The pods separate them: shepherd's purse has flat, notched, triangular to heart-shaped pods 5–10 mm long and 4–7 mm wide, while hairy bittercress has long, narrow, erect pods (10–)15–20(–25) mm long and only 1–1.3 mm wide. Hairy bittercress rosette leaves are pinnate, divided into separate stalked, bluntly lobed leaflets with a round end leaflet, whereas shepherd's purse leaves range from unlobed to deeply cut but are not divided into separate leaflets; because shepherd's purse leaves are very variable, leaf shape alone is not reliable — check the pods. Hairy bittercress also tends not to grow as large. Hairy bittercress leaves are eaten raw as a cress.
lookalikes.name: Hairy bittercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Before flowering the two rosettes are easily confused: both are variable, toothed to deeply cut (runcinate-pinnatifid) rosettes of cultivated ground, and the leaf shape differs only slightly. Flowers separate them at once: smooth hawksbeard has yellow, dandelion-like flower heads (the outer face of the florets often striped pink or red) on branched, leafy stems, followed by fluffy white pappus; shepherd's purse has tiny white four-petalled flowers in loose spikes, followed by flat heart-shaped pods. Smooth hawksbeard leaves are often hairless or have pale hairs only along the middle of the underside, while shepherd's purse leaves and stems carry spreading simple hairs and star-shaped (stellate) hairs, which the Flora does not record for hawksbeard. Smooth hawksbeard leaves are eaten as a green; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Smooth hawksbeard

lookalikes.howToTell: Both begin as small rosettes on bare cultivated soil and are listed as similar weeds. Twin cress soon sends out stems that lie along the ground (to 40 cm long) and can form mats, its leaves are divided into leaflets that are usually lopsided, with more lobes on one side, and the crushed plant smells foetid; shepherd's purse sends up an erect flowering stem. The pods differ clearly: twin cress has tiny paired, finely warty pods only c. 1.5 mm long and broader than long, on stalks longer than the pod; shepherd's purse has flat heart-shaped pods 5–10 mm long. Petals do not separate them, as both can have tiny white petals or none. Twin cress leaves are eaten raw or cooked for their hot, cress-like taste; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Twin cress

preparation.text: Pick the young basal leaves for salads before the flower stalks appear; after flowering, cook the leaves as greens. Wash the plants thoroughly: soak them in water for 20–30 minutes so the grit sinks, rinse under running water, remove wilted yellow leaves and check the base of the roots for dirt. For cooked dishes, blanch briefly (10–20 seconds for soup, 45 seconds for a wonton filling), then squeeze out the water and chop. In Shanghai cooking the leaves are stir-fried with nian gao rice cakes or mixed into wonton fillings; in Korea they go into soybean-paste (doenjang) soups. The leaves carry small hairs, so mince them finely or cook them for at least five minutes. Add the fresh chopped leaves and seed pods in small quantities to soups, salads, vinaigrettes, steamed or sautéed greens, or pesto. Soaked mature seeds turn mucilaginous and thicken a soup a little. The leaves can also be dried for later use. To collect seed, wait until the pods turn tan, put the stems with pods in a bag and rub them by hand; the pods ripen from the bottom of the stem upwards, so not all are ready at once.

recipes.method:
Ingredients (serves 4): 170 g chicken breast cut into very small, thin strips, marinated with 1 teaspoon cornflour, 1 teaspoon Shaoxing wine, ½ teaspoon sesame oil, 1/8 teaspoon white pepper and 1/4 teaspoon salt; 2 tablespoons oil; 150 g shepherd's purse (the source uses frozen, washed, squeezed dry and finely chopped); 1/3 teaspoon salt, or to taste; 1/4 teaspoon white pepper; 1 teaspoon sesame oil; 340 g (12 oz) sliced rice cakes (nian gao), thawed and rinsed; 120 ml water or chicken stock.
Steps: Mix the chicken with its marinade and set aside while you prepare everything else. Heat the oil in a wok over high heat and stir-fry the chicken until opaque. Add the shepherd's purse, salt, white pepper and sesame oil and stir-fry for 30 seconds. Lay the rice cakes on top of the meat and greens so they don't touch the wok directly, pour in the water or stock, cover and cook for 2–3 minutes — no longer, or the greens turn yellow and the rice cakes go soggy. Once the rice cakes have softened, mix everything together and serve straight away.
recipes.title: Shanghai rice cake stir-fry with shepherd's purse

recipes.method:
Ingredients: 150 g minced pork; 150 g shepherd's purse, weighed after cleaning, blanching and squeezing; 1 packet shop-bought wonton wrappers; 1 spring onion; a small piece of ginger; 1 teaspoon salt; 1 teaspoon light soy sauce; 1 teaspoon sesame oil; 2 teaspoons oil; a pinch of sugar or a little chicken bouillon; white pepper; a small piece of dried seaweed to serve.
Steps: Clean the shepherd's purse and blanch it for 45 seconds. Squeeze out the water, weigh out 150 g (freeze the rest for later) and chop it finely. Blend the spring onion and ginger with 125 ml (1/2 cup) water to make ginger–spring onion water, and work it slowly into the pork with all the seasonings; leave to marinate about 10 minutes, then mix in the shepherd's purse. Put about 1/2 teaspoon of filling in the middle of each wrapper, fold and seal with a little water in any shape you like. Bring half a pot of water to the boil, add the wontons and cook for 3 minutes, add 2 tablespoons of water to calm the boil, and when it boils again they are cooked. Serve in hot broth with a little seaweed, or with red chilli oil, vinegar and soy sauce.
recipes.title: Shepherd's purse and pork wontons (ji cai hun tun)

recipes.method:
Ingredients (serves four): 1 litre water; 8–10 dried anchovies; a 3 × 4 cm piece of dashima (dried kelp); 80 g shepherd's purse (naengi); 20 g barley shoots (optional); 200 g littleneck clams (about 20); 1 clove garlic, sliced; 3 tablespoons doenjang (soybean paste); ½ bundle dallae (Korean wild chive).
Steps: Wipe any white powder off the kelp with a damp paper towel rather than rinsing it. Soak the shepherd's purse in water for 20–30 minutes so the dirt sinks, rinse under cold running water, and remove wilted yellow leaves and any dirt at the base of the roots. Scrub the clams 2–3 times under cold running water. Bring the water, anchovies and kelp to the boil, then simmer on low for about 15 minutes. Meanwhile blanch the shepherd's purse in boiling water for 10–20 seconds, rinse it under cold water, squeeze out the moisture and cut it into bite-sized pieces. Lift out the anchovies and kelp, and press the doenjang through a small sieve into the stock to dissolve it. Add the shepherd's purse, garlic, clams and barley shoots. When the soup boils and the clams open, sprinkle in the roughly chopped dallae and turn off the heat at once. Serve hot with rice.
recipes.title: Naengi-guk (Korean shepherd's purse and clam soup)

summary.text:
Capsella bursa-pastoris, commonly known as shepherd's purse or lady's purse, is a small flowering plant in the mustard family.
It was first named Thlaspi bursa-pastoris by Linnaeus and moved to Capsella by Medikus in 1792 (Biota of New Zealand). Capsella is Latin for a little box or case (NZ Plant Conservation Network); bursa means a bag or purse and pastoris 'of shepherds', after the purse-shaped pods (LearningHerbs, restated).
It is native to eastern Europe and Asia minor, but is naturalized and considered a common weed in many parts of the world, especially in colder climates, including the British Isles (where it is regarded as an archaeophyte), North America, and China, but also in the Mediterranean and North Africa.
Flora of New Zealand gives its region of origin as Europe and its first wild record in New Zealand as 1864; it is recorded from the North, South and Stewart Islands and the Kermadec, Chatham, Auckland and Campbell Islands (restated).
In New Zealand it is a fairly small annual weed that can germinate at most times of the year and is often noticed in winter, when more competitive summer annuals are absent. It can complete several generations in a year, and its seed can last in the soil for several decades under some conditions, so large seed banks build up (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated). Each plant can make thousands of seeds that fall close to it, so dense colonies form in lawns, paths and garden edges (New Zealand Lawn Addicts, restated). The plants are often infected with a white rust fungus (Common Weeds of New Zealand; Rainbow & Brown, restated).
Te Papa holds a specimen collected by Leon Perrie and Lara Shepherd on 12/01/2021 in Wellington, between Mount Cook and Brooklyn (SP111210). Manaaki Whenua's herbarium has about 114 databased New Zealand records: Canterbury 41, Wellington 28, Nelson 7, North Auckland 7, Marlborough 6, Gisborne 5, Hawke's Bay 5, South Auckland 4, Southland 4, Taranaki 4, Otago 2, and one without a district.
Shepherd's purse is a very common garden weed that can spread freely in cultivated ground. It is usually in flower and producing seed in all months of the year, unless the temperature drops below 5°c.
It is eaten as a leaf vegetable and cultivated as a commercial food crop in Asia. In China, where it is known as jìcài (荠菜; 薺菜) its use as food has been recorded since the Zhou dynasty. Today, it is commonly used in food in Shanghai and the surrounding Jiangnan region. The savory leaf is stir-fried with nian gao rice cakes and other ingredients or as part of the filling in wontons. It is one of the ingredients of the symbolic dish consumed in the Japanese spring-time festival, Nanakusa-no-sekku. In Korea, it is known as naengi (냉이) and used in the characteristic Korean dish, namul (fresh greens and wild vegetables).
The European Medicines Agency's herbal committee accepts shepherd's purse herb as a traditional herbal medicine for reducing heavy menstrual bleeding in women with regular cycles, after serious conditions have been excluded by a doctor (restated). During the First World War an extract of the plant was used to stop bleeding from wounds, in place of ergot (Herbal Reality; LearningHerbs, restated).
Its seeds become coated in mucilage when wet; this has been shown experimentally to trap nematodes, a form of 'protocarnivory'.

warnings: Avoid shepherd's purse teas and medicinal amounts when pregnant or breastfeeding. Extracts of the plant strongly contract the uterus in animal tests, it is traditionally used during childbirth, and its safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established — no reproductive-toxicity data exist for it.

It is an active medicinal plant: it is a traditional herbal medicine to reduce heavy menstrual bleeding, but only after a doctor has excluded serious causes, and medicinal use is not recommended under 18 years of age. If you take medicines for blood pressure, the heart or the thyroid, check with a doctor before medicinal use: animal studies suggest it can affect blood pressure, the heart and thyroid function, and interactions with medicines of similar or opposing effect should be considered, although how far this applies to people is unclear.

Like other mustard-family plants it contains glucosinolates, including sinigrin (most concentrated in the flowers); their breakdown products have been implicated in goitre when dietary iodine is insufficient, although there is no evidence that dietary glucosinolates cause goitre in people. Eat it in moderation.
Shepherd's purse accumulates metals from the soil — copper, cadmium, zinc, iron and chromium have been measured building up in it — so don't gather it from contaminated ground.

It tolerates many selective weedkillers but is controlled with MCPA, 2,4-D, glyphosate, amitrole or clomazone, and in lawns with MCPA, 2,4-D or glyphosate. Pick it only where you know none has been used.
The rosette is very variable in leaf shape and hard to identify before the plant flowers; confirm the flowering stem with its heart-shaped seed pods before eating rosette leaves.

habitat.text:
C. lucida is typically found in low coastal and montane forests. Smale et al. also noted that C. lucida can be found growing in geothermal soils of the Taupō Volcanic Zone.
C. lucida is an understory plant. C. lucida can also be found in forest gaps, at forest margins, and in regenerating forest sites. As an understory or sub-canopy plant, C. lucida is often associated with kauri forests. Additionally, C. lucida has been noted as an epiphyte, including as an epiphyte on tree ferns. After disturbance events, C. lucida is an early successional plant. Furthermore, C. lucida can be consistently found growing in geothermal zones. Due to the preference of C. lucida for coastal and montane habitats, the plant is present at altitudes ranging from sea level to 1130 metres.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to 3–(6) m. tall; branches and branchlets stout, glabrous; bark reddish brown. Leaves opposite on stout glabrous petioles 10–30 mm long; wing narrow, decurrent. Stipules short, triangular-truncate, more or less ciliolate; denticles 1–3, prominent. Lamina thick, coriaceous, glabrous, glossy dark green above, paler below, obovate to narrow-obovate to broad-elliptic, abruptly narrowed to produced midrib, cuneately narrowed to petiole; more or less (8) - 12–17 × 3–4 cm.; margins sometimes waved or distantly crenulate. Veins with close reticulations, evident below and often above. male in dense clusters on simple or branched peduncles 10–15 mm long, often with Iflike bracts at angles; calyx cupular, teeth 4–5, obtuse; corolla funnelform, lobes 5–6, acute, more or less equal to tube. female 3–4 per cluster, on trichotomously branched peduncles, main peduncle about 3 cm long; calyx cupular, teeth 5–6, short, triangular; corolla funnelform, tube about 2 mm., lobes 5–6, acute. Drupe orange-red, oblong 8–12 mm long.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Leaf thickness separates them: shining karamū's are thick, kanono's rather thin. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Leaf shape and stipule separate them: shining karamū's leaves are widest above the middle and its stipules acute; karamū's are elliptic to ovate with tapering, long-pointed (acuminate) stipules. Shining karamū's leaf is glossy, karamū's rather dull. Shining karamū's roots and inner bark are yellow, karamū's dull brown, and shining karamū lacks karamū's foul smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; shining karamū's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Those figures fit the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa; the North Island's wild subsp. minor has thinner, papery leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) on stalks about 10–18 mm long, and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Māmāngi's young twigs are hairy; shining karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Mingimingi's young twigs are more or less hairy; shining karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Swamp coprosma's young twigs are hairy; shining karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. summary.text:
Coprosma lucida, commonly known as shining karamū, karamū, kāramuramu, shiny karamū, or kakaramu, is a shrub or tree endemic to New Zealand.
C. lucida is found throughout both mainland islands of New Zealand and some smaller surrounding islands, extending as far south as Big South Cape Island. The latitudinal range of C. lucida in New Zealand is between 34.42°S and 46.75°S. However, C. lucida is rare on Stewart Island, where deer populations have drastically reduced the population.
C. lucida is a plant that lives in warm, temperate regions.
