identification.text: Terrestrial, rupestral, or epiphytic ferns. Rhizomes stout, erect, or short-creeping, sometimes forming a woody mass above ground, bearing scales. Rhizome scales ovate or narrowly ovate with filiform apices, 15–35 mm long, 1.5–8 mm wide, pale brown, shining, clathrate. Fronds 70–1400 mm long. Stipes 25–780 mm long, dark brown to pale brown or rarely green, densely covered in acicular or subulate scales with very long filiform apices. Rachises brown abaxially, green adaxially, or green on both surfaces, scaly. Laminae 1-pinnate, ovate or elliptic, narrowed to a long undivided or rarely lobed terminal segment with serrate margins similar to the primary pinnae; laminae 45–800 mm long, 25–450 mm wide, dark green on both surfaces, glossy on adaxial surface, herbaceous, bearing scattered scales on abaxial surface, lacking hairs (although scales becoming hair-like); laminae very rarely undivided, ovate or oblong, 60–70 mm long, 15–20 mm wide, apices acute or acuminate, margins serrate, borne on stipes 30–55 mm long. Primary pinnae in 0–22 pairs below an entire or lobed stalked apical segment, not overlapping, ovate or narrowly ovate or narrowly oblong, the longest at or below the middle, 10–260 mm long, 10–55 mm wide; pinna apices acuminate to acute or rarely obtuse or rounded in small fronds, margins serrate to almost entire, bases cuneate and stalked. Sori away from margins; indusia 4–35 mm long, straight or curved away from costae on largest fronds; free margins of indusia entire. Mean spore size 33–38 μm long, 20–24 μm wide; perispores reticulate.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Gravelly and sandy beaches, coastal turf and coastal banks.
It grows in damp coastal turf near streams and seepages, and in damp sand.
Look for it from the south Wellington coast and the shores of Cook Strait southwards, on Stewart Island, the Chatham Islands and most of the subantarctic islands; it is now common only on the Chathams and the subantarctic islands.
On the national wetland plant list it is a facultative wetland plant: usually found in wetlands, occasionally on drier ground.

identification.text:
Glabrous herb 1–12–(20) cm tall; rootstock long, stout, often branched above. Leaves in clusters, with flattened petioles to 6 cm long. Lamina (1)–2–9–(12) × (0.5)–1–3–(5) cm, narrow-oblong, oblong, or oblong-elliptic; margins subcrenate to sinuate; base cuneate to truncate; apex rounded to obtuse. Ochreae prominent, long. Inflorescence leaves narrower, decreasing in size upwards. Inflorescence of dense axillary clusters of up to about 16 bisexual flowers; axes 1–2-branched, short, stout; pedicels short or very short, glabrous. Outer perianth segments about 2 mm long, oblong, remaining forward pointing at fruiting; inner segments ovate-lanceolate. Fruit valves about 2.2–2.5 mm long, pale brown; margins entire or with a tooth or lobe; valves with an elongated tubercle. Fruit sharply angled, tightly invested by thickened perianth. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
A small creeping dock with broadly oval, fleshy leaves, bright green, or red or bronzed in strong sun, that hug the ground in dense tufts. Its short, simple flower spikes, 1–3 cm tall, rise from the leaf tufts, and each fruit is tightly wrapped in the thickened perianth — features that set it apart among New Zealand docks. It flowers from November to April.

summary.text: Shore dock is endemic to New Zealand and not closely related to any other dock in Australasia. Its species name, neglectus, means overlooked, and it is easy to overlook as it creeps low across the ground. Joseph Hooker had earlier treated it, in his Flora Antarctica, as a variety of another dock; Thomas Kirk named it as a species in 1877, and collected it on pebbly beaches near Wellington and on the Auckland Islands. It is at its most abundant on the subantarctic islands; on Enderby Island, where stock once grazed, it covered large areas, and other native plants took that ground back once the stock were removed. Its national status is Not Threatened (2023). Regionally it is ranked Regionally Critical in Wellington, its only North Island ground, and Regionally Declining in Otago (2025).

warnings: Like other docks, it can be harmful if too much is eaten at one time. Eat only a little.

habitat.text: Soil and leaf litter in native forest and scrub, as a root partner (mycorrhizal) of trees. In New Zealand it grows with mānuka and kānuka, and with beech — hard, black and mountain beech — and has been recorded once with kōhūhū. It often comes up in groups or clusters, sometimes beside tracks and roads under kānuka. In Australia it grows with eucalypts.

identification.text:
A big, stout, pale mushroom with a skirt-like ring. The cap is convex to flattened, whitish with brown tints, often with ragged scraps of veil hanging from the edge. Australian descriptions give 5–7.5 cm as typical, up to 30 cm; New Zealand observers have measured caps of 24–30 cm.
The gills are pale straw or mustard at first and attached to the stem, later almost free and rusty brown as the spores ripen; they can be up to 1 cm deep. The spores are rusty brown, and they stain the ring and the stem below it.
Young mushrooms are wrapped in a thick veil that runs from low on the stem over the whole cap. It is a cortina — the web-like veil of Cortinarius and its relatives — but its threads are so thick that it looks like the ring of a field or horse mushroom. Its remains usually stay on the stem as a ring until maturity, with shaggy patches of veil below. The stem is bulbous, up to 15 cm long and 3.7–6.2 cm thick, though often much smaller. It has no noticeable smell.

lookalikes.howToTell: From a distance the two look very alike: both are big and pale with a large ring. Horse mushroom grows in grass — pasture, lawns and parks, sometimes at forest margins — and has pale gills that turn pink, then chocolate brown, a dark chocolate spore print, a thick double ring with cogwheel-like patches underneath, and a strong smell of aniseed or almond. Skirt webcap grows in soil under mānuka, kānuka or beech; its gills start pale straw or mustard and turn rusty brown; rusty spores stain its ring and stem; young ones are wrapped in a thick web-like veil; and it has no smell.

summary.text:
Austrocortinarius australiensis, commonly known as the skirt webcap, is a species of mushroom in the family Cortinariaceae which is native to Australia and New Zealand.
It was described from Australia in 1918 as Rozites australiensis and was long known as Cortinarius australiensis; genomic work in 2022 moved it to a new genus. In New Zealand it is assessed Not Threatened, and secure overseas. It is one of the largest mushrooms here: caps can reach 30 cm across. It has 67 research-grade New Zealand iNaturalist records from Northland to Fiordland, and herbarium collections from Auckland, the Coromandel, Bay of Plenty, Taupō, Taranaki, Wairarapa, Nelson, Buller, Kaikōura and Mid Canterbury. In the jarrah forests of south-western Australia it is the largest native mushroom, and native mammals often eat it.

warnings: Do not eat it: its edibility is unknown, and some of its close relatives contain lethal toxins.

sources: Useful Temperate Plants, Ken Fern, temperate.theferns.info (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0)
edibleParts.text: Seed - cooked. Rather small. It has a floury texture and a mild, somewhat creamy flavour. It can be used as a staple food crop in either savoury or sweet dishes. The seed can be cooked whole, though it is more commonly ground into a flour and used as a cereal in all the ways that oats are used, especially as a porridge but also to make biscuits, sourdough bread etc. The seed can also be sprouted and eaten raw or cooked in salads, stews etc. The roasted seed is a coffee substitute. The seed is sometimes harvested from the wild for local use as a food - though usually only in times of shortage or mixed as a weed with other grain crops.

habitat.text: Near the sea, especially on cliffs, dry banks, and steep grassy slopes, occasionally inland on disturbed ground, roadsides and in pasture.

identification.text:
Tufts green to dark green, often very slender, 65–100–(170) cm, erect or drooping above in taller plants. Leaf-sheath smooth, or slightly scabrid above, occasionally red-tinged. Ligule 2.7–5–(9) mm, obtuse, denticulate, abaxially finely scabrid. Leaf-blade 12.5–30 cm × 2–8 mm, finely scabrid on ribs and margins. Culm internodes glabrous. Panicle (12)–18–40 cm, very lax, equilateral; rachis smooth, branches and pedicels very filiform, finely scabrid. Spikelets 40–50 mm, 2–(3)-flowered; disarticulation below each floret at maturity. Glumes 7–9-nerved. Lemma 12–18 mm, narrow-lanceolate, light brown, with long stiff reddish hairs below level of awn insertion, green and scabrid above, each lobe-tip produced to a fine bristle (2–3 mm); lemmas awned, awns 30–36 mm, geniculate, column very dark brown, twisted. Palea keels with 1–2 rows of cilia, interkeel glabrous, flanks sometimes sparsely scabrid. Callus long hairy, with horse-shoe shaped scar. Rachilla long hairy. Anthers 2–3 mm. Caryopsis 5–7 × 0.8–1.3 mm, light brown, silky hairy.
[From: Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are edible; this is about which you have. When ripe, the cultivated oat's spikelet falls as a whole, where slender oat's breaks apart below each floret. Slender oat's lemma has long, stiff reddish hairs below the awn, and each of its two tip-lobes is drawn out into a fine bristle 2–3 mm long; the cultivated oat's lemma is hairless or has a few hairs near the base, with a blunt or shallowly notched tip. Slender oat's lemmas carry an awn 30–36 mm long, bent at a knee and twisted, with a very dark brown lower part; the cultivated oat's are usually awnless, and any awn is weak, straight or curved, and not bent. Slender oat is often a very slender plant with very fine panicle branches, but the cultivated oat's pedicels are fine too, so build is only a clue.
lookalikes.name: Oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Size does not reliably separate them. Winter wild oat is a strong, rather stiff plant with heavy panicles, and slender oat is often very slender, but their measurements can overlap: slender oat's spikelets are 40–50 mm with awns 30–36 mm; winter wild oat's are 3.5–6 cm with awns 25–50 mm in subspecies ludoviciana (overlapping slender oat), and 6–8 cm with awns 60–70 mm in subspecies sterilis. Leaf width overlaps too (2–8 mm against 3–15 mm), and reddish hairs on the lemma occur in slender oat and in subspecies sterilis. Check how a ripe spikelet breaks up: slender oat's breaks apart below each floret, while winter wild oat's florets stay joined and fall together from above the glumes. Slender oat's lemma tip-lobes are each drawn out into a fine bristle 2–3 mm long; winter wild oat's lemma narrows to a papery, two-toothed tip, and only its lower one or two lemmas carry an awn. Both have edible seeds.
lookalikes.name: Winter wild oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Both shed below each floret and both have a bent, twisted awn — 30–36 mm in slender oat, 30–40 mm in wild oat — so the awn will not separate them. Look at the lemma tip: slender oat draws each lobe out into a fine bristle 2–3 mm long, while wild oat's narrows to a two-toothed papery tip, with no bristles described. Slender oat's lemma carries long, stiff, reddish hairs below the awn; wild oat's is stiffly hairy there or sometimes hairless, with no hair colour described. Slender oat's grain is narrower, 0.8–1.3 mm wide against 1.8–2.2 mm, and light brown and silky where wild oat's is light grey and densely hairy.
lookalikes.name: Wild oat

preparation.text: Ripe florets drop from the plant one at a time, so a stand is gathered as it ripens rather than after. The seed, when harvested and dried, can store for several years. No source gives a method written for this species. Written for the cultivated oat: Harvested oats go through multiple stages of milling. The first stage is cleaning, to remove seeds of other plants, stones and any other extraneous materials. Next is dehulling to remove the indigestible hull, leaving the seed or "groat". Heating denatures enzymes in the seed that would make it go sour or rancid; the grain is then dried to minimise the risk of spoilage by bacteria and fungi. For home use such as making porridge, oats are often rolled flat to make them quicker to cook.

summary.text:
Avena barbata is a species of wild oat known by the common name slender wild oat.
A. barbata is native to central Asia (as far east as Pakistan) and the Mediterranean Basin. As an introduced species it also occurs in other Mediterranean-like habitats of New Zealand, Australia, South Africa, Argentina, Chile, Brazil, and Uruguay. In Europe it has been reported in Finland, France, Germany, Norway, Bulgaria, and Austria. In North America it is an introduced species and noxious weed, where it is especially widespread in California. In California it has displaced native species of grass.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: North Auckland, South Auckland, Bay of Plenty (Opotoki), Hawke's Bay (near Napier), Wellington (Wanganui, Paekakariki and Wellington City). Naturalised from Mediterranean.

habitat.text: Lactarius blennius is very common and is found in broad-leaved woodland, favouring beech; it is most associated with Fagus sylvatica, the European beech, though it has also been observed growing in association with species of oak. It forms an ectomycorrhizal association with trees, and can grow on a wide variety of subsoil types, but is more typical of acidic soil.

identification.text: Lactarius blennius has a flattened convex cap that is 4–10 cm across that later becomes depressed in the centre. In colour, it is pale olive to a greenish grey, sometimes a dull green or pale grey-sepia, and has blotches of darker colouration in concentric bands, though the colour can vary greatly. Heavily spotted specimens are also known, and a very brown specimen similar to Lactarius circellatus was recorded in Scotland. The cap is very slimy when moist and has a margin that is curved inwards. The stem is a paler colour than the cap, but also very slimy, and measures from 4–5 cm tall by 1–1.7 cm thick, tapering a little towards the bottom. The flesh is whitish, similar in colour to the gills, which later become a creamy or pale buff colour. The gills turn a brownish-grey colour when wounded, and are crowded. In shape, they are slightly decurrent or adnate, meaning that they run a small way down the stem in attachment, or that they are attached to the stem by the whole depth of the gills. The milk is white and dries grey, and is very plentiful. L. blennius spores leave a creamy print, and are elliptic with low warts joined by ridges with a small number of cross-connections, measuring from 6–9 by 5.5–7 μm.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Slimy milkcap's milk is white and plentiful and dries grey, and its cut gills turn grey-buff. Its cap is drab greenish-grey or olive-grey with rings of darker blotches, and slimy in wet weather. In Europe it grows with beech, very occasionally oak; in New Zealand and Australia, saffron milk cap grows only with pine.

summary.text:
Lactarius blennius (commonly known as the slimy milkcap or beech milkcap) is a medium-sized mushroom of the genus Lactarius found commonly in beech forests in Europe, where it is mycorrhizal, favouring the European beech (though associations with other trees are known).

It is native to Europe. The distribution of the mushroom coincides with the distribution of beech. In the British Isles, the species is one of the one hundred most common mushrooms. Other areas in which it has been recorded include Sweden, France, Italy, and Poland.

warnings: Sources disagree on whether it is edible: it is given as edible when cooked but not recommended, and as inedible or even poisonous. Its milk tastes very hot and acrid.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suillus_luteus Corroborates the peeling rule and adds the field characters this entry was short of. Edible, 'but the slime/pileipellis must be removed', and 'the slime coating … may cause indigestion if not removed before eating' — which is this page's warning, independently. The cap is 4–10 cm and rarely to 20, conical then flattening, slimy, smooth and glossy even when dry, with a cuticle that peels off easily; the pores are initially yellow, turning olive to dark yellow. The three good field characters are the slimy brown cap, glandular dots on the upper stipe, and a prominent purplish ring. The frequent lookalike is S. granulatus — also common and also edible, yellow-fleshed and exuding latex droplets when young, but with neither a partial veil nor a ring. Regarded as low quality by some authors and a delicacy in Slavic cultures (maslyata, maslyuky), and often sold dried. Ectomycorrhizal with pine.

identification.text:
Taprooted annual, to over 30 cm tall, but often much less, densely clothed in short hairs. Stems decumbent to spreading, often branched from the base. Leaves with long eglandular, and short glandular hairs. Lower leaves long-petiolate. Lamina palmately lobed, 1–3.5 × 1.5–4.5 cm, reniform to almost orbicular; lobes 5–9, extending 3/4 way to petiole, 2–3-lobed; secondary lobes oblong to obovate. Upper leaves smaller and simpler with shorter petioles. Flowers numerous, often paired; peduncles short; pedicels usually longer than peduncles, curving upwards after flowering, densely clothed in glandular hairs. Sepals 2–3 mm long (to about 4 mm at fruiting), more or less ovate, densely clothed in long, white, pilose and short glandular hairs, mucronate. Petals 2.5–3.5 mm long, obovate, emarginate, pale mauve; claw short. Stamens 10, 4–5 reduced to staminodes (lacking anthers); filaments whitish; anthers mauvish brown. Mericarps 1.5–2 mm long, densely clothed in appressed hairs on outer face. Seed smooth. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Dove's-foot cranesbill is an annual densely covered in short or long hairs; its leaves are 1.5–5 × 1.5–6 cm, kidney-shaped to round, cut about 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes, usually with 3 rounded secondary lobes towards the tip; its sepals are 2–3.5 mm long and end in a short point; its petals are rosy pink or pink, (3)–4–6 mm long and deeply notched, its anthers mauve, and its fruit segments (mericarps) about 1.5 mm long, hairless, with prominent pale cross-ridges. Small-flowered cranesbill is a taprooted annual densely clothed in short hairs; its leaves are 1–3.5 × 1.5–4.5 cm, kidney-shaped to almost round, cut 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes that are themselves 2–3-lobed; its sepals are 2–3 mm long (to about 4 mm in fruit) and end in a short point; its petals are pale mauve, 2.5–3.5 mm long and notched; only 5–6 of its 10 stamens carry anthers (mauvish brown); and its fruit segments (mericarps) are 1.5–2 mm long, densely clothed in hairs pressed flat on the outer face. The two are similar in habit but can always be told apart by the fruit: small-flowered cranesbill's fruit segments (mericarps) are hairy but otherwise smooth, dove's-foot cranesbill's hairless with cross-ridges. Small-flowered cranesbill also has only 5–6 fertile anthers where dove's-foot cranesbill's 10 stamens all carry one, is usually less hairy, and generally has smaller petals (2.5–3.5 mm against (3)–4–6 mm). Both are hairy annuals with round leaves cut about 3/4 of the way into 5–9 lobes, so the leaves do not separate them. Dove's-foot cranesbill's fruits are recorded as eaten by young people in Spain as a nibble.
lookalikes.name: Dove's-foot cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Small-flowered cranesbill is a taprooted annual densely clothed in short hairs; its leaves are 1–3.5 × 1.5–4.5 cm, kidney-shaped to almost round, cut 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes that are themselves 2–3-lobed; its sepals are 2–3 mm long (to about 4 mm in fruit) and end in a short point; its petals are pale mauve, 2.5–3.5 mm long and notched; only 5–6 of its 10 stamens carry anthers (mauvish brown); and its fruit segments (mericarps) are 1.5–2 mm long, densely clothed in hairs pressed flat on the outer face. They are separated on the leaves and stamens: cut-leaved cranesbill's lower leaves are divided nearly to the base into linear segments, its sepals end in an awn and all 10 stamens are fertile; small-flowered cranesbill's are divided to about 3/4 of the way into oblong to ovate segments, its sepals end in a point under 0.5 mm, and 4–5 of its 10 stamens lack anthers. Both have hairy fruit segments (mericarps), so the fruit alone does not separate them, though cut-leaved cranesbill's hairs spread and small-flowered cranesbill's are pressed flat. Its petals are pink or rose and 3.5–5 mm long against small-flowered cranesbill's pale mauve 2.5–3.5 mm, and its anthers blue against mauvish brown. Cut-leaved cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food.

Geranium pusillum, commonly known as small-flowered crane's-bill or (in North America) small geranium, is a herbaceous annual plant of the genus Geranium.
Small geranium is native to Europe but is introduced in almost every region of the USA and Canada, where it is associated with ecologically disturbed sites.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Wellington area; South Island: mainly in Canterbury and Otago, also collected in Southland.
This species is similar in habit to G. molle, but can always be distinguished by its hairy but otherwise smooth mericarps. Also, G. pusillum has only 5-6 fertile anthers, is usually less hairy than G. molle and generally has smaller petals.

identification.text:
Annual or biennial, hairy, taprooted herb, with sprawling to suberect branched stems to about 30 cm long, and characteristic scent. Stem base sometimes short and thick with a rosette of leaves. Petioles to about 10 cm long, reddish where exposed to strong light, usually hairy along 1 side. Lamina very deeply palmately divided, 1.5–5–(7) × 2–6–(8) cm, more or less broad-ovate, with hairs scattered above, nearly glabrous below, often turning red with age; lobes 5, pinnatisect or less commonly pinnatifid; ultimate segments mucronate. Inflorescence very diffuse; flowers paired; peduncles and pedicels variable, with simple and glandular hairs, often with a line of hairs along 1 side. Sepals (at anthesis) 5–8 mm long including apical awn, ovate, with mostly glandular hairs, more or less reddish. Petals 6–9 mm long, more or less oblanceolate, pink to rose; claw a little longer than limb; apex rounded. Filaments pinkish; anthers yellow. Mericarps 2.5–3 mm long, with short hairs; upper ⅔ with many, close, transverse ridges. Seed smooth.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Herb robert is an annual or biennial, hairy, taprooted herb with a characteristic scent; its stems reach about 50 cm; its leaves reach about 9 × 10 cm, with 3–5 lobes; its flowers are paired, with pink or rose petals (7.5)–10–11.5 mm long; its anthers are orange; its fruit segments (mericarps) are 2.5–3 mm long, with 4–6 cross-ridges. Small herb Robert is an annual or biennial, hairy, taprooted herb with a characteristic scent; its stems are sprawling to nearly upright and reach about 30 cm; its leaves are 1.5–5–(7) × 2–6–(8) cm, cut very deeply into 5 lobes; its flowers are paired, with pink to rose petals 6–9 mm long; its anthers are yellow; its fruit segments are 2.5–3 mm long, with many close cross-ridges on their upper two-thirds. They are separated on the petals, usually 10–11.5 mm in herb robert and 6–9 mm in small herb Robert, and the anthers, orange in herb robert and yellow in small herb Robert. The two have sometimes been confused; small petals, yellow pollen and more, closer ridges on the fruit segments together are the signs of small herb Robert, which is also generally more upright, with smaller leaves. No single sign settles it: herb robert's petals can be as short as 7.5 mm, inside small herb Robert's range, and both species have yellow pollen, so anther colour alone can be hard to read. Both are scented, both have paired pink flowers and deeply divided leaves that turn red, and their fruit segments are the same length. Herb robert's leaves are eaten, though its use as food is thinly documented, and in Cantabria, Spain, it is regarded as poisonous (see its page).

summary.text:
Geranium purpureum, the little-robin, is a species of flowering plant in the geranium family Geraniaceae. It is native to Europe, Africa, and western Asia, and introduced on all continents except Antarctica. It is similar in appearance to Geranium robertianum, a close relative.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: commonest in the Auckland area, but occurring at least as far north as Whangaroa (North Auckland).
Because of the great similarity of this species to G. robertianum, the 2 species have sometimes been confused. The combination of small petals, yellow pollen, and more and closer ridges on the mericarps are diagnostic features of G. purpureum. Also, G. purpureum is generally more upright and has smaller leaves.

identification.text:
Annual, rarely perennial. Stems ascending to erect, sparingly branched or not branched, glabrous, 4–45–(60) cm tall. Leaves usually all basal, oblanceolate to linear-oblanceolate, simple and shallowly to deeply dentate, or pinnatifid, (0.6)–2.5–10–(15) × (0.1)–0.5–2–(3) cm, glabrous or sometimes with sparse short strigose hairs. Stem bracts few, minute; rarely whorls of rosette leaves formed on stems. Capitula narrowly cylindric. Involucral bracts narrow-oblong with subacute apex, glabrous, green, about 8 mm long at flowering; inner bracts with broad scarious margin, up to 20 mm long at fruiting. Florets yellow, about equal to involucre. Achenes dark brown, scabrid; outer achenes obconic, not beaked, 4–5 mm long; inner achenes fusiform, beaked, up to 8 mm long. Pappus in 2 rows, the outer hairs short, slender, scabrid, the inner up to 15 mm long, stout, plumose. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In the field (BSBI, a British account, restated): the leaves are shiny and pale green, often reddish, with shallow wavy margins, broadest near the tip and narrowing to the base; the stems carry no true leaves, only small scale-like bracts. The heads are 0.5–1.5 cm across, and they open in full sun and close by early afternoon. The bracts are purple-tipped, and the leaves sometimes have a purplish tint near the veins (Wikipedia).

lookalikes.howToTell: Turn the head over: catsear's bracts carry a row of stiff hairs along the midrib, dark near the tip and usually pale near the base — like a miniature cock's comb — while smooth cat's ear's bracts are always hairless. Smooth cat's ear's heads are narrowly cylindrical, with florets about as long as the bracts; catsear's are top- to bell-shaped, with florets about one and a half times as long. Smooth cat's ear's leaves are hairless or sometimes sparsely hairy; catsear's have moderately dense stiff pale hairs. Smooth cat's ear is an annual, rarely perennial; catsear is a perennial. Catsear's heads are larger, 2–4 cm across against 0.5–1.5 cm (measured on British plants). The seeds differ: catsear's are beaked and 8–16 mm long, though the outer ones are sometimes short- or unbeaked; smooth cat's ear's outer seeds are never beaked and 4–5 mm long, and only the inner ones carry a beak, up to 8 mm long. The two hybridise, so a plant with mixed features may be neither. Both have rosettes of toothed to lobed leaves, stems with a few minute bracts, yellow heads and milky sap. Catsear's young leaves and roots are eaten (see its page).

summary.text:
Hypochaeris glabra is a species of flowering plant in the tribe Cichorieae within the family Asteraceae known by the common name smooth cat's ear. It is native to Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East but it can be found on other continents where it is an introduced species and a widespread weed.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: Northland (Tokerau Beach), Auckland, Waikato, East Cape (Hicks Bay), Wairarapa (Palliser Bay), Wellington (south coast); South Island: Marlborough, Canterbury, Westland (Saltwater Lagoon), Otago; Kermadec and Chatham Islands. Naturalised from Europe, south-western Asia and North Africa, first recorded in 1869. Allan Herbarium specimens listed in Biota of New Zealand also come from the Nelson, Taranaki and Southland land districts.

A weed of turf, lawns, crops and newly sown pasture throughout New Zealand (Bayer New Zealand, restated).

identification.text:
Annual or biennial. Stems erect, branching, ribbed or grooved, (5)–15–45–(100) cm tall; hairs white, slender, crinkly; stouter pale crinkly hairs usually present also, at least below. Rosette and lower stem leaves thin, petiolate, oblanceolate to linear-oblanceolate, dentate to runcinate-pinnatifid, (2)–5–20–(30) × (0.3)–1–3–(6) cm, often glabrous or with pale hairs about 0.5 mm long confined to middle of leaf beneath or rarely distributed on both leaf surfaces. Upper stem leaves similar, becoming sessile and not lobed, narrowly triangular to linear, usually with narrowly triangular teeth especially at subauriculate base. Capitula campanulate; buds erect. Involucral bracts with sparse to dense short white tangled hairs and usually sparse dark glandular hairs on outer surface, glabrous on inner surface; outer bracts 6–10, linear, ?-1/2length of inner bracts; inner bracts linear, not keeled, 5–8 mm long, with pale to scarious more or less glabrous margins. Receptacle areoles with flat or depressed, glabrous margins. Corolla yellow, often with pink or red stripe on outer face of ligule. Achenes brown, 10-ribbed, fusiform, smooth or more or less scabrid, not beaked, 2–2.5 mm long. Pappus bristles in 2 rows, fine, white.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
In the field (BSBI Scotland, a British account, and Bayer New Zealand, restated): a rosette of toothed leaves like a dandelion's, usually smaller (5–25 cm), until it flowers; the flowering stems branch, carry a few strap-like leaves and grow up to 45 cm, with many small heads, each of about 40 bright yellow florets (Wikipedia: as many as 60), sometimes red underneath. The leaves are usually hairless and the stem usually hairy. Away from New Zealand the stems are often trailing along the ground but sometimes erect (Wikipedia).

lookalikes.howToTell: The seed separates them: beaked hawksbeard's achenes are all long-beaked and 6–9 mm long; smooth hawksbeard's are not beaked and are 2–2.5 mm. Beaked hawksbeard sometimes has outer achenes without a beak, so check the inner ones as well. Before seed, look at the rosette and lower stem leaves: beaked hawksbeard's are thick, with pale hairs 0.2–0.5 mm long on both surfaces and the margins, where smooth hawksbeard's are thin and often hairless, or hairy only along the middle beneath, rarely on both surfaces. Beaked hawksbeard's stems carry stout, straight, spreading red-based hairs as well as slender crinkly white ones; smooth hawksbeard's stem hairs are white and crinkly. Beaked hawksbeard's inner involucral bracts are usually longer, (6)–9–12 mm against 5–8 mm, but the ranges overlap at 6–8 mm, so bract length alone does not settle it. Both have yellow flowers that may carry a red or pink stripe on the outer face of the ligule — sometimes in beaked hawksbeard, often in smooth hawksbeard — and branching stems with erect buds, so none of those separates them. Beaked hawksbeard's leaves are eaten raw and taste bitter.
lookalikes.name: Beaked hawksbeard

lookalikes.howToTell: A dandelion sends up a hollow, leafless, unbranched stem with a single head, and its leaf stalk and the base of its midrib are hollow too; smooth hawksbeard's stem branches and carries narrow, stalkless leaves and several heads on multiple, branched flower stems, and its leaf stalk and midrib are solid. A dandelion's seeds carry a slender beak 7–10 mm long; smooth hawksbeard's have none and are only 2–2.5 mm. Out of flower the rosettes are alike — both can be cut into back-pointing lobes and be hairless. Both have yellow heads and milky sap. The dandelion's leaves, flowers and roots are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Dandelion

lookalikes.howToTell: Before flowering the two rosettes are easily confused: both are variable, toothed to deeply cut rosettes of cultivated ground and the leaf shape differs only slightly. Flowers separate them at once: shepherd's purse has tiny white four-petalled flowers in loose spikes followed by flat heart-shaped pods, while smooth hawksbeard has yellow, dandelion-like heads on branched, leafy stems followed by fluffy white pappus. Shepherd's purse leaves and stems carry spreading simple hairs and star-shaped (stellate) hairs, none of which are recorded for smooth hawksbeard; smooth hawksbeard leaves are often hairless or hairy only along the middle of the underside. Shepherd's purse leaves are eaten raw or cooked; avoid it in medicinal amounts when pregnant — see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Shepherd's purse

lookalikes.howToTell: Feel the stem: common pūhā's stem is hairless; smooth hawksbeard's carries slender white crinkly hairs, usually with stouter pale crinkly hairs as well, at least low down. Common pūhā's leaves are hairless, and their margins have small spine-tipped teeth that make them more prickly than smooth hawksbeard's. Smooth hawksbeard's leaves are often hairless too, but may carry pale hairs about 0.5 mm long along the middle underneath, rarely on both surfaces, so a hairy midrib points to hawksbeard while a hairless one settles nothing. Common pūhā's upper leaves are usually lobed, with a broad triangular end lobe, and clasp the stem with pointed lobes, though they are sometimes unlobed; smooth hawksbeard's upper stem leaves are stalkless, narrowly triangular to linear and not lobed, with teeth especially at the slightly eared base. Young pūhā leaves tend to have a large end lobe, unlike hawksbeard's. Common pūhā's involucre is 10–15 mm long and top-shaped to cylindrical, its bracts usually hairless, rarely with a few pale bristles; smooth hawksbeard's heads are bell-shaped, with inner bracts 5–8 mm long carrying short white tangled hairs and usually a few dark glandular hairs. Smooth hawksbeard's yellow florets often have a pink or red stripe on the outer face; no stripe is recorded for common pūhā's. In seed, common pūhā's achenes are weakly flattened, 3-ribbed on each face, finely wrinkled crosswise and 2.5–3 mm long; smooth hawksbeard's are spindle-shaped, 10-ribbed and 2–2.5 mm long. Neither achene is beaked. Yellow heads on a leafy, branched stem do not separate them, nor do the white pappus, rosette leaves that can both be deeply lobed, or height (common pūhā 50–120 cm, smooth hawksbeard (5)–15–45–(100) cm). Common pūhā's young leaves and shoots are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Pūhā / Sow thistle

summary.text:
Crepis capillaris, the smooth hawksbeard, is a species of flowering plant in the tribe Cichorieae within the family Asteraceae, and is native to Europe. It has become naturalized in other lands and is regarded as a weed in some places.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: throughout; S.: throughout; St.; K., Ch. Naturalised from southern and central Europe, first recorded in 1867.

warnings: The leaves are recorded as laxative in Tuscany, Italy, where they are also eaten.

habitat.text: Upper forest margins and subalpine scrub from lat. 36° 50' southwards, also lowland forest in Westland. It grows from montane to alpine levels, and in the North Island almost only in subalpine and alpine areas: common in open tussock grassland, subalpine scrub and herbfield, at the base of active scree, among boulderfalls, and on cliff faces and razorback ridges, sometimes extending down into beech forest and valley heads. In the Southern Alps it grows to 1,500 metres.

identification.text:
Podocarpus nivalis grows as a shrub of 20–40 cm. with spreading branches. It can also be semi-erect and up to 2 or 3m tall. Branches that contact the soil often root. It forms mats of a few square metres.
Leaves are thick, rigid and close together. They are arranged spirally and are a brownish green colour when they age. The leaves are 5–15 mm long and 2–4 mm wide and boat-shaped (naviculate) to ovate-linear. They may be curved outwards or down. The leaves are obtuse or mucronate at the apex. The seed (one, sometimes two, 3.5–7 mm long and green when fresh) sits on a red, swollen, fleshy receptacle 2.5–10 mm long, formed from two acute bracts.
Male and female cones grow on separate plants, so only some plants bear the red receptacles. Where snow tōtara grows with Hall's tōtara, tōtara or needle-leaved tōtara, fertile hybrids can be common, especially with Hall's tōtara. Hybrids are mostly more upright, often with drooping branches, and have much longer, narrower leaves that are not distinctly awl-shaped.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at how the seed sits. On yew, the single seed sits inside a red, fleshy cup (the aril) that almost surrounds it and is open at the end. On snow tōtara, the seed (one, sometimes two, green when fresh) sits on a receptacle of two acute, red, swollen bracts. Look at where each leaf joins the shoot: yew's leaves have a short yellowish-green stalk, lie more or less in two rows on horizontal shoots, and have two broad pale green bands beneath; snow tōtara's leaves are close-set and spirally arranged, rigid, with distinctly thickened margins. Snow tōtara's leaves are 0.5–1.5 cm long and yew's 1.2–2.5 cm, so short leaves point to snow tōtara, but the ranges overlap. Snow tōtara is a prostrate or spreading shrub, sometimes suberect to 3 m, whose branches root where they touch the ground; yew is a small tree to about 10 m, but a young yew can be small. Snow tōtara grows mostly in subalpine scrub, tussock grassland and rock, and yew in modified lowland sites, but snow tōtara also grows in lowland forest in Westland, so where it grows does not prove it. Nearly every part of yew is poisonous, including the seed inside the red flesh.
lookalikes.name: Yew

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaves. Snow tōtara's leaves are close-set, rigid and 0.5–1.5 cm long, with thickened margins and a blunt or barely pointed tip, and are usually bronze-green; adult tōtara leaves are 1.5–3 cm long and 3–4 mm wide with a sharp, prickly tip (juvenile tōtara leaves are about 2 cm long and 1–2 mm wide). Look at the plant: snow tōtara is a prostrate or spreading shrub, sometimes upright to 3 m, whose branches root where they touch the ground; tōtara grows into a tree to 30 m with thick, stringy, furrowed bark. Under the seed, snow tōtara's red receptacle is formed from two bracts and tōtara's from 2–4 scales. Where the two grow together, fertile hybrids are common; they are more upright, often with drooping branches and longer, narrower leaves, so a plant in between may be a hybrid. The red flesh of both is eaten.

summary.text:
Podocarpus nivalis, the mountain or snow tōtara, is a conifer of the family Podocarpaceae found only in New Zealand.
It grows in the North Island and South Island from Mt Hikurangi and Mt Pirongia south. Herbarium specimens come from the South Auckland, Gisborne, Hawke's Bay, Taranaki and Wellington land districts and from every South Island land district.

warnings: Yew, which is poisonous, also has red, fleshy 'berries' and needle-like leaves. Check how the seed sits and where the leaf joins the shoot before eating (see the lookalikes).
Only the red flesh is recorded as eaten. No record of the seed being eaten was found, so whether it is safe is not known.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Gaultheria antipoda' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text: This species is found in the North Island between 37° – 39°30'S in lowland to subalpine scrub habitat particularly on cliffs and rocky places.

sources: NZPCN, 'Gaultheria antipoda' — regional conservation statuses: Northland 2026 Regionally At Risk – Regionally Naturally Uncommon (Ford et al. 2026). https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/gaultheria-antipoda/
harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In Northland (Regionally Naturally Uncommon), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text:
Erect or rather spreading shrub, usually 0.5–2 m high; branchlets densely to rather sparsely setose, often puberulent also. Leaves alternate; petioles slender, to about 2 mm long. Lamina (5)–7–10–(20) × (3)–6–10–(20) mm, broadly elliptic-oblong or elliptic to orbicular, coriaceous, glabrous or nearly so; margins more or less undulate, crenulate-denticulate to serrate; base cuneate to rounded; apex rounded, mucronulate, sometimes more or less acute. Flowers solitary, axillary, but uppermost leaves sometimes so reduced that flowers appear racemosely arranged; pedicels glabrate to densely hairy; bracteoles 0.7–1.5 mm long, broadly ovate. Calyx lobes 1.5–2.5 mm long, ovate-triangular, subacute to acute. Corolla more or less urceolate; tube 1.5–2.5 mm long; lobes triangular. Fruit 4–6 mm diameter; calyx more or less fleshy, white to red or purplish. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

habitat.text:
Beside streams and rivers, usually within their flood zone, and around the plunge pools of waterfalls, mainly in native forest. Coast to montane, sometimes into the alpine zone. Usually in semi-shade; it can grow in full sun where the ground is permanently moist.
Lowland to subalpine regions, especially in damp places such as stream and lake sides, boggy areas, damp pastures, scrub and forest margins.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In the Auckland region (Regionally Endangered), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it. In Northland (Regionally Naturally Uncommon), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — abbreviations spelled out
identification.text:
Perennial, sometimes mat-forming. Stems to about 15 cm long, thin, creeping, glabrous, rooting at nodes. Leaves 3-foliolate, the rosettes in tufts at intervals, glabrous or hairy. Petiole (0.5)–1.5–5–(9) cm long, often dark reddish; stipules 3–5 mm long, broad and scarious. Lamina of leaflets equal, subsessile or nearly so, 2.5–9 × 2.5–9 mm, broadly obcordate, often dark reddish or deep purple below; sinus broad or narrow, rather shallow. Flowers solitary; peduncles slender, 1–6–(11) cm long, hairy. Bracts 2.5–4 mm long, linear-lanceolate, glabrate; calli 0. Sepals 3–5–(6) mm long, more or less elliptic, with more or less appressed hairs; calli 0. Petals 8–15–(20) mm long, broad-obovate, white, usually glabrous, sometimes ciliate. Stamens at 2 levels, glabrous; filaments not dilated at base. Styles slightly to obviously longer than longer stamens, glabrous. Capsule 4–5 mm diameter, globose. Seed 5–7 mm long, more or less ellipsoid-ovoid, with prominent raised reticulations. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

preparation.text: The flowers make a pleasant and decorative addition to salads. Use the leaves in moderation.

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) lemon juice and 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) maple syrup or honey. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the sorrel and stir for 1–2 minutes, until it wilts. Put it in a blender or food processor with the lemon juice and the syrup or honey and blend until well combined. Serve it straight away, or refrigerate it and warm it before use; the author finds it even better the next day. The author serves it on fish, or as a dipping sauce for grilled prawns.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel sauce

recipes.method: About 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, stems or flowers, or a mix, about 250 ml (1 cup) water, and maple syrup or another sweetener to taste. The amounts are rough: use as much sorrel as you like and enough water to cover it. Blend the sorrel and water until well combined, strain through a fine sieve and sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel 'lemonade'

recipes.method: Equal parts wood sorrel, sugar, and water; the author usually uses 250 ml (1 cup) of each. Put everything in a saucepan and bring it to a simmer, stirring. Simmer for 15–30 minutes, strain through muslin (cheesecloth) and pour into sterilised bottles. The author uses it in tea, topped up with soda water, over ice cream or fresh strawberries, or in vinaigrettes and marinades.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel syrup

recipes.method: The recipe uses one part leaves to three parts water. Fresh wood sorrel leaves; boiling water; sweetener to taste (optional). Put the leaves in a container, pour the boiling water over them and leave to steep for 5–15 minutes. Strain out the leaves and sweeten to taste if you like. Drink it hot, or pour it over ice for an iced tea.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel tea

recipes.method: 2 cloves garlic, minced; olive oil for cooking; 2 spring onions, chopped; 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock; 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish; 3 medium mint leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk; salt and pepper. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks. Heat a little olive oil in a small saucepan and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the spring onions. Cover with the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, then add the sorrel for about 30 seconds. Take it off the heat, add the mint and blend smooth with a stick blender (or an ordinary blender). Stir in the coconut milk and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until well chilled, a couple of hours, and serve garnished with the sorrel flowers.
recipes.title: Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

recipes.method: About 450 g (1 lb) Italian or breakfast sausage; 1 medium spaghetti squash; several cups of wood sorrel, washed and drained, stems removed (the recipe gives no closer amount); olive oil; 1 red onion, halved and sliced; 1 egg; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk or any milk; 1 garlic clove, minced; 15 ml (1 tbsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) tarragon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) black pepper; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground sage. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Halve the squash, spoon out the seeds and stringy threads, set the halves cut side up on a baking tray, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and bake for 20–25 minutes, until the flesh gives a little when pressed. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts. Take the squash out of the oven and scrape out the flesh with a fork (careful, it will be hot). Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.
recipes.title: Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel

recipes.method: Two handfuls of wood sorrel, chopped; potato and kūmara, boiled first and sliced; cream. Layer the sorrel with the sliced potato and kūmara in a baking dish, pour cream over the top and bake at 180 °C until it starts to brown.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel, kūmara and potato gratin

recipes.method: Chop a big handful of wood sorrel leaves, stalks and flowers and mix them through a potato salad dressed with a cream dressing.
recipes.title: Potato salad with wood sorrel

recipes.method: The author's greens were nasturtium, chickweed, onion weed, dandelion, oxalis, dock, plantain and wild mustard; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 125 ml (½ cup) cashews, soaked for an hour in the hottest tap water and drained; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 60 ml (¼ cup) apple cider vinegar; 60 ml (¼ cup) water, only if your blender needs it; 2 peeled garlic cloves; 60 ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil; 60 ml (¼ cup) hemp seed oil (or more olive oil); 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) pepper; and 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional). Blend in a high-speed blender until smooth. Makes about 500 ml; it thickens in the fridge. Good as a dip or dressing — with chips, steamed potatoes or kūmara, roast vegetables, an omelette or quiche, or stirred through pasta.
recipes.title: Green goddess dip

recipes.method: The author's greens were puha, sow thistle, nasturtium, onion weed, wild fennel, oxalis, wild mustard and wild celery; the page does not say which oxalis (written for oxalis generally). 1 diced onion; 1 potato, scrubbed and diced; 2 sliced garlic cloves; 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 1.3 litres water; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked pepper; extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil, to serve; edible weed flowers. Serves 4. Cut the vegetables and greens to similar sizes. Fry the onion in the oil for a minute, then add the potato and garlic (the method also adds fennel bulb and celery stalks, which the ingredient list leaves out) and fry for another minute. Add the water, cover, bring to the boil and simmer until the potato is soft. Add the greens with the salt and yeast and cook for 3 minutes, until just tender — added at the end, they keep their colour. Blend until smooth (push it through a sieve if your blender isn't powerful), season with the pepper and more salt if needed, and serve drizzled with extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil and scattered with edible weed flowers.
recipes.title: Wild greens soup

Recipes copied 16/10/2026 from creeping-wood-sorrel (owner: "yeah copy the recepies to the sorrels", after "the recipies are interchangeble betwwen sorrel species"). None is written for Oxalis magellanica: seven are written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally, and the gratin and potato salad for Oxalis incarnata. When they were copied this page recorded no edible parts of its own (it now has them, from Useful Temperate Plants, 'Oxalis magellanica'); the recipes rest on the owner's word that wood sorrel recipes are interchangeable. Provenance as recorded on creeping-wood-sorrel: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (cups at 250 ml, 1 tbsp = 15 ml, 1 tsp = 5 ml; every page all rights reserved; retrieved 15/10/2026; supplied by the owner). None is written for this species: each is written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally. The sauce, 'lemonade' and syrup from Kate MacQuarrie, 'Wood Sorrel Recipes', PEI Untamed, 09/07/2023 (https://www.pei-untamed.com/post/wood-sorrel-recipes) — written for 'the Wood Sorrels' of Prince Edward Island, no species named; 'grilled shrimp' given as prawns; the lemonade's 'leaves, stems, and/or flowers' and its note that the author does not measure are kept. 'Wood sorrel cooler' is Sunny Savage's 'Oxalis Cooler' as given in Green Deane, 'Oxalis: How To Drown Your Sorrels', Eat The Weeds (dated 16/01/2018 on the page, with reader comments from 2012; https://www.eattheweeds.com/oxalis-how-to-drown-your-sorrels/; the owner's second link, https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/oxalis-deppei/, is a tag page showing the same article) — written for Oxalis generally, the article naming the Florida species including O. corniculata; 1 US quart is about 946 ml; the recipe does not strain the drink and neither does this. 'Wood sorrel tea' from Jesse, 'Wood Sorrel: Identification, Uses, and Precautions', Feral Foraging, 11/07/2024 (https://feralforaging.com/wood-sorrel/) — written mainly for O. stricta and O. violacea; the page gives the ratio only as '1:3' after 'Gather wood sorrel leaves' and 'Pour over boiling water', without saying by volume or by weight, so 'one part leaves to three parts water' is this guide's reading. 'Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup' from Valerie Zemba, 'Chilled Lemony Wood Sorrel Soup', Very Vegan Val, 03/07/2019 (https://veryveganval.com/chilled-lemony-wood-sorrel-soup/) — written for 'Oxalis stricta and others'; scallions given as spring onions, vegetable broth as stock; the rinsing and stripping step is from the page's prose above the recipe card. 'Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel' from Chosen Weeds Farm, 'Cooking With Wood Sorrel', 15/03/2017 (https://thechosenweeds.com/cooking-with-wood-sorrel/) — written for the purple-leaf wood sorrel that grows in the author's south-east Texas garden; 400 °F given as 200 °C, 1 lb as about 450 g; 'Several cups' of sorrel kept because the page gives no closer amount; the page says only 'Combine mixture with the egg' after forking out the squash, and the method keeps that wording rather than saying where the squash goes. Not used from the recipe pages (15/10/2026): the casserole page's 'If you are short on time you can skip the oven step', because skipping the final bake would leave the stirred-in egg uncooked; Feral Foraging's statements that all species of wood sorrel are edible and can be used in similar ways (genus-level claims), its estimate that about 30 g a day, several times a week, is safe and its view that oxalate warnings are overblown (it contradicts every other page read here and is not a trusted source for a safety amount), and its cold-infusion and dried-leaf variants; Green Deane's statements that cooking reportedly renders oxalic acid harmless, particularly with calcium, that eating a lot raw can leach calcium from the bones, and that the juice curdles milk for cheese, and that all parts including the root bulb are edible (said of the Florida species as a group); the casserole page's medicinal and vitamin claims; the reader comment on Eat The Weeds suggesting more sorrel for a sharper cooler. Two of the owner's links have no recipe: Rachel Lambert, 'Wild Food: Wood Sorrel family', Wild Walks Southwest, 07/05/2021 (https://wildwalks-southwest.co.uk/wild-food-wood-sorrel-family/), and Diego Bonetto, 'How to identify and eat wood Sorrel', 10/08/2021 (https://www.diegobonetto.com/blog/wood-sorrel-id-forage-edible-weed) — both name O. corniculata among the species they describe. Lambert says all of them have a lemony, tart flavour and uses them in salads, in soups and as an edible decoration; Bonetto says the stalks, flowers and leaves are eaten raw or cooked, in salads and as a garnish; recorded here for edibleParts and preparation, which were empty on creeping-wood-sorrel when this was written (15/10/2026). Gratin and potato salad, as recorded on pale-pink-wood-sorrel: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (all rights reserved; retrieved 16/10/2026; supplied by the owner): Johanna Knox, 'Wood sorrel (Oxalis incarnata)', Wild Picnic, 16/07/2009, https://wildpicnic.blogspot.com/2009/07/wood-sorrel-oxalis-acetosella.html — the gratin and the potato salad. The post was first written as O. acetosella; a commenter (AJB, 26/11/2009) identified the plant pictured as 'the South African Ox. incarnata', which the author accepted, and the title now names O. incarnata. The blog covers Wellington and the Wairarapa; the post does not say where the plant grew. Not used as recipes: adding it to apple, peach or pear pie and a jelly (suggestions, not made by the author); its use to curdle milk for cheese (the author had not got it to work).

Edible parts, preparation and warning: Useful Temperate Plants (Ken Fern), 'Oxalis magellanica', https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Oxalis+magellanica, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, retrieved 16/10/2026 — Edible Uses 'Leaves - raw or cooked' (cited there to Crowe, Native Edible Plants of New Zealand, 1990, and Kunkel, Plants for Human Consumption, 1984), 'A pleasant acid flavour, but the leaves are rather small and they are also a bit chewy' and 'Use in moderation', 'Flowers - raw', 'A pleasant and decorative addition to the salad bowl' (the tasting notes are Ken Fern's own); General Information 'The plant is harvested from the wild for local use as a food.' Known Hazards (cited to Bown, Encyclopaedia of Herbs and their Uses) is word for word the text on Useful Tropical Plants 'Oxalis corniculata' (compared 16/10/2026), so the warning is the same sentence as on creeping-wood-sorrel and shamrock-wood-sorrel: oxalic acid, all right in small quantities but not in large amounts since it can bind the body's calcium, less after cooking, especial caution for rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity. Not used: its habitat 'Walls and stony places' (cited to the RHS Dictionary of Plants, a garden source, and not what NZPCN describes); the Chilean use of Oxalis juice to remove fruit stains (said of 'various species'); propagation. PFAF (https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Oxalis+magellanica, all rights reserved) is the same database. With edible parts now sourced for this species, the nine wood sorrel recipes copied here on the owner's word stay.

Habitat, paraphrased 16/10/2026 from the owner's link: NZPCN, 'Oxalis magellanica' factsheet (P.J. de Lange 2005; all rights reserved, facts only), https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/oxalis-magellanica/, retrieved 16/10/2026 — 'Coastal to montane where it is mainly confined to indigenous forested habitats, though sometimes extending into the alpine zone. A species of riparian habitats, usually found within the flood zone of streams and rivers, and around the plunge pools of waterfalls. Provided its habitat is permanently moist it may be found growing in full sun but it is more usually seen in semi-shaded situations.' and, under propagation, 'It does not cope with drying out.' Nelson Natives (owner's link, https://www.nelsonnatives.co.nz/oxalis-magellanica-white-oxalis) gives the same habitat text word for word, so it is not a second source. Tags [forest, wetland]: 'riparian' and 'flood zone' are the wetland definition's streamsides, 'indigenous forested habitats' is forest; coastal left out ('Coastal to montane' is an altitude range) and alpine left out ('sometimes'), the same rule as least-yellow-sorrel. NZPCN's wetland indicator rating is FAC (facultative).

Māori names: Biota of New Zealand (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research), 'Oxalis magellanica G.Forst.', owner's link, https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/30135eb8-6c4f-46a3-8bac-e6fbe28b025f, retrieved 16/10/2026 — vernacular names, Māori: Retireti, Tūtae kāhu, Tūtae kākā; English: White oxalis. Biota of NZ also gives Biostatus 'Indigenous, non-endemic'.

Months left empty (year-round) 16/10/2026: the leaves are the main part eaten. Flora of New Zealand gives 'Flowering: Jul.–Apr.'; NZPCN gives flowering 'September - March (sometimes year round)'; iNaturalist NZ (597 research-grade records, retrieved 16/10/2026) has flowering annotations Oct–Feb, peak Nov–Dec, none Mar–Sep; observations exist in every month (Jul 5, Aug 2). No source dates the leaves; this guide looked at three NZ research-grade photos from June–August (iNaturalist 379854858, Ōwhiro Bay, 07/07/2026; 369210339, Upper Waitati, 07/06/2026; 392865364, Mahoenui, 20/08/2026) and all three show green leaves — a reading of photos, not a source. Xera Plants (owner's link) says the cultivar 'Nelson' is 'Deciduous in most winters' in Oregon; not used (a garden cultivar, northern hemisphere).

Photos checked 16/10/2026 (iNaturalist API, one batch call, and by eye): 187094599 (Michael Berardozzi, Ōwhiro Bay, CC BY), 144746321 (Tyler McBeth, Lewis Pass, CC0), 150899728 (John Barkla, Lewis Pass, CC BY), 104312710 (Paul Bell-Butler, Marlborough, CC BY) — all research grade Oxalis magellanica; credits match the photo licences; captions match what the frames show.

Flora conflict recorded, not acted on (16/10/2026): Flora of New Zealand (Webb et al. 1988) gives 'Seed 5–7 mm long, ± ellipsoid-ovoid, with prominent raised reticulations' beside 'Capsule 4–5 mm diam.'; NZPCN gives 'Seeds smooth (without transverse ribs)' and the Victorian assessment 'seeds not transversely ribbed'. A seed longer than its capsule suggests a misprint in the seed size; the identification text is verbatim and is left as published.

Not used from the owner's links (16/10/2026): nativeplants.nz, 'Oxalis magellanica' (https://www.nativeplants.nz/oxalis-magellanica.html) — template text with no author and no species-specific facts ('Varies by habitat', 'Species-dependent'), and its 'well-drained soil' contradicts NZPCN's permanently moist habitat; Xera Plants, 'Oxalis magellanica Nelson' (https://xeraplants.com/plants/oxalis-magellanica-nelson/) — an Oregon nursery page for a double-flowered cultivar; Victorian Department of Environment, Land, Water and Planning, Threatened Species Assessment 'Oxalis magellanica Snowdrop Wood-sorrel', 09/06/2021 (https://bio-prd-naturekit-public-data.s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/species_assessments/Oxalis_magellanica_502385.pdf) — Australian: proposed Endangered in Victoria, habitat tall mountain forests, cool temperate rainforest and snow gum woodland, 'Flowers October-February (VicFlora, 2019)'; Nelson Natives' 'flowers that measure approximately 1 to 2 cm wide during the summer months' (Flora of New Zealand's petal lengths are on the page).

summary.text:
Oxalis magellanica or snowdrop wood-sorrel is an Oxalis species found in Chile, Argentina, New Zealand, and Tasmania.
In New Zealand it grows on the North, South, Stewart and Chatham Islands; it is also native to Australia and South America.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

identification.text:
Clumps of strap-shaped leaves and a hollow, somewhat flattened flower stalk with several nodding white bells, each petal tipped with a green spot. Crush a leaf: no onion smell at all. Onion weed has a triangular stalk, a green stripe down the whole petal, and smells strongly of onion.
Bulb ovoid, about 2.5 cm diameter. Leaves 3–6, about equal to scape, 8–15 mm wide, linear-lorate, bright green. Scape 30–60 cm high, hollow, more or less compressed. Flowers (1–2)–3–7, 1.5–2 cm long, less than 1.5 cm diameter, campanulate, white with green-tipped segments; spathe 3–5 cm long, green at apex. Capsule almost globose. Seeds black.
[From: Healy and Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Smell first: crushed onion weed smells strongly of garlic or onion; snowflake does not. Onion weed's flower stalk is three-angled; snowflake's is hollow and somewhat flattened with winged edges. Onion weed's white bells have a green stripe down the centre of each segment; snowflake's segments are green-tipped. Strap-shaped leaves, nodding white bells, damp ground and season do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Onion weed

lookalikes.howToTell: Crushed Naples garlic smells of garlic; snowflake does not. Naples garlic carries a many-flowered, roughly flat-topped umbel 5–8 cm across of white flowers 8–10 mm long on stiff stalks; snowflake carries 3–7 flowers (sometimes 1–2), 1.5–2 cm long, with green-tipped segments. Naples garlic's flower stalk has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one; snowflake's is hollow and somewhat flattened. Flat leaves of similar width, a similar flower-stalk height, white bells and season do not separate them.

summary.text:
A garden bulb that has gone wild along streams, with strap leaves and white bells much like onion weed's — but no onion smell, and a poisonous bulb.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): native to middle and southern Europe; first collected in 1953 in grass on a roadside north of Feilding, and recorded from Auckland, the Coromandel, Gisborne–Ōpōtiki, Feilding, Palmerston North, the Hutt Valley, Little Wanganui (Nelson) and Christchurch and Little River (Canterbury).

warnings: All snowflakes (Leucojum) are poisonous: they contain the alkaloids lycorine and galantamine, and in this species both are found in the bulbs and the leaves. Cases of poisoning in people are known for snowflakes and their relatives, daffodils and snowdrops. Symptoms of lycorine poisoning vary but include vomiting, diarrhoea and convulsions.

habitat.text:
Open lowland places, mostly near the coast in natural and partially modified grasslands, very occasionally in waste places.
In New Zealand: from the coast up into the montane zone (sea level to 600 m); it was once widespread in short tussock grassland, on lava fields and clay pans, and on rocky headlands by the sea (NZPCN, restated).

sources: NZPCN, 'Geranium solanderi' — regional conservation statuses: Northland 2026 Regionally Threatened – Regionally Critical (Ford et al. 2026); Auckland 2025 Regionally Threatened – Regionally Vulnerable (Simpkins et al. 2025); Wellington 2025 Regionally Threatened – Regionally Endangered (Enright et al. 2025). https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/geranium-solanderi/
harvestEthics.text: This species is at risk. If you harvest it, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In Northland (Regionally Critical), the Auckland region (Regionally Vulnerable) and the Wellington region (Regionally Endangered), do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you must eat it.

identification.text:
Perennial herb with napiform or cylindric taproot to about 2.5 cm diameter; caulorrhiza short and thick, bearing long weakly ascending flowering stems. Hairs variable; longer hairs straight to slightly curved; glandular hairs short and inconspicuous. Basal leaves: petiole to 30 cm long, with fine, straight or curved long hairs and shorter straight and crisped retrorse hairs; lamina to about 7 cm diameter, reniform to orbicular, lobed to 3/4-⅞ way to midrib, glabrous or densely hairy above; lobes (5)–7, obovate; larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; median and larger lateral teeth more or less oblong, usually obtuse. Cauline leaves similar to basal but smaller, usually 3–5-lobed; teeth usually 3–5 per lobe. Peduncle and pedicels with hairs as on petioles; bracteoles lanceolate or narrow-triangular; flowers usually in pairs, occasionally solitary. Sepals ovate or elliptic-ovate; outer sepals about 5.5 × 3.5 mm excluding mucro; inner sepals slightly narrower; hairs straight or slightly curved, antrorse and ascending. Petals to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm, obovate, rose-pink. Mericarp hairy; beak to about 15 mm long. Seed about 2 × 1.6 mm diameter, subglobular to oblong, dark reddish brown or almost black; dorsal alveolae deep, usually 4–6-sided, isodiametric or longer than wide.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
'Large petals' form (Flora of New Zealand vol. IV): Taproot napiform; lamina of leaf glabrous above except for margin and base; hairs of petioles and pedicels straight, to about 1.5 mm long, perpendicular to surface; petals usually longer than 7 × 4 mm; alveolae of seed mostly 5-6-sided, isodiametric.

lookalikes.howToTell: Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped or cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. They are separated on the hairs of the leaf and flower stalks: in turnip-rooted geranium they are sharply bent near the base, point backward and lie pressed flat; in Solander's geranium they are straight to curved, stand out or point backward, but never lie flat. Two further differences are the leaf lobes (usually linear-obovate in turnip-rooted geranium, obovate in Solander's geranium) and the seed: pits about 0.1 mm across against usually more than 0.1 mm. The root is often turnip-shaped in turnip-rooted geranium and more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot in Solander's geranium, but Solander's geranium can have a turnip-shaped root too, so the root alone does not settle it. Flower colour does not separate them: both can have pink petals, and both have petals up to about 8–9 mm long. No source read records turnip-rooted geranium as food, and it is Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable. The names do not separate them: turnip-rooted geranium, Matua-kūmara and pukupuku have each been given to both plants, so a record under any of them may mean either plant.
lookalikes.name: Turnip-rooted geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped or cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Three characters separate Australasian cranesbill from Solander's geranium: the middle teeth of its leaf lobes are about as long as broad (mostly longer than broad in Solander's geranium); the pale, see-through border of its inner sepals is mostly more than 0.3 mm wide near the tip (mostly less than 0.3 mm); and its seeds are red-brown with rather shallow rectangular pits (red-brown to dark brown, with rather deep rectangular to polygonal pits). Its sepals are mostly elliptic to obovate, against ovate. The lobing does not separate them (both are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way), and both have paired flowers. Australasian cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food.
lookalikes.name: Australasian cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped or cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Cinquefoil geranium and Solander's geranium are separated on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in Solander's geranium, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in Solander's geranium. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of Solander's geranium overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Cinquefoil geranium's root is recorded as food.
lookalikes.name: Cinquefoil geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped or cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. The first difference is the life form: cut-leaved cranesbill is an annual, usually with a thin fibrous taproot and glandular hairs prominent in the flower clusters, while Solander's geranium is a perennial with a rather stout to tuberous rootstock and no, very few, or short and inconspicuous glandular hairs on the flower clusters. Cut-leaved cranesbill's leaves are cut almost to the leaf stalk into linear segments; Solander's geranium's are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into broader lobes. Both have pink petals. Older floras placed Solander's geranium under Geranium dissectum (its synonyms include Geranium dissectum var. pilosum Hook.f. and var. australe Benth.), so older records may use that name. Cut-leaved cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food.
lookalikes.name: Cut-leaved cranesbill

Retrieved 23/10/2026. https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Geranium-solanderi.html — quoted verbatim. Flora of New Zealand vol. IV treats G. solanderi in a broad sense, as the two forms of Gardner (1984): 'Large petals' and 'Coarse hairs'. NZPCN says the 'coarse hairs' form is now Geranium gardneri (naturalised, probably from Australia). The NZ Flora Online description still covers both forms, so it is quoted as published. IV, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, URL as in the Summary line), quoted verbatim, its lead '(1) "Large petals" of Gardner (1984, loc. cit.).' replaced by the label. Why that form: Biota of New Zealand (owner's link, 23/10/2026) lists Geranium solanderi f. "large petals" among the synonyms of Geranium solanderi, and Gardner (1984, quoted there) says that form 'matches exactly the type'; NZPCN's Geranium gardneri page says gardneri 'Has been treated in New Zealand as Geranium solanderi “coarse hairs”'. NZPCN still describes the root as parsnip- or carrot-like where Webb gives the 'Large petals' form a napiform root; the cards keep both.

summary.text:
Geranium solanderi (common names - native geranium, Australian cranesbill, Austral cranesbill, Cut-leaf cranesbill, native carrot, and hairy geranium) is a species of plant in the family Geraniaceae. It is native to Australia (New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia, and Tasmania), and to New Zealand.
In New Zealand, in both 2004 and 2009 it was declared "Not threatened", but in 2012, under the New Zealand Threat Classification System it was declared "At Risk - Declining", with the qualifiers SO (safe overseas) and DP (data poor), and this status was reaffirmed in 2017.
Gardner, R. O., New Zealand J. Bot. 22: 131-134 (1984), stated that most N.Z. material of G. solanderi belongs to 1 or other of 2 forms. He did not give them taxonomic recognition because their distinctness is lost in Australia.
Its 2023 national assessment is At Risk – Declining. Regional assessments rate it Regionally Threatened – Regionally Critical in Northland (2026), Regionally Threatened – Regionally Endangered in Wellington (2025) and Regionally Threatened – Regionally Vulnerable in Auckland (2025), and Regionally Data Deficient in Otago (2025). Rabbit browsing and the spread of taller, faster-growing weeds have caused it to decline across large parts of its former range (NZPCN, restated).

edibleParts.text: The fruit and the leaves. The fruit is eaten raw when fully ripe, dried, or made into jam; it has very little flesh, its seeds sit in a sticky, sweet, jelly-like mucilage, and it tastes strongly astringent, salty and sour. Unripe fruit is very astringent. The fruit is also cooked in savoury dishes such as chilli, curry and chutney. The leaves are eaten raw or cooked, or pickled; raw, they are harshly astringent, mucilaginous and barely edible.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand it grows on cliffs and sand dunes, on the coast and inland on railway and roadside cuttings.
It favours hot, dry coastal places, and tolerates drought, wind, salt spray and sandy soils.

harvestEthics.text: It is a declared pest — an unwanted organism on the National Pest Plant Accord — under sustained control across the Auckland region and progressive containment on the Chatham Islands. It smothers native vegetation and hybridises with the native ice plant. Harvest as much as you like, and spread no stem fragments: they grow into new plants.
