identification.text:
Mat-forming trailing perennial herb. Stems to 6 m long, glabrous, 2-angled, subwoody at base. Leaves smooth, sharply 3-angled, linear, acute, scarcely tapered to connate base, 70–120 × 12–17 mm, 4–7× as long as wide; keel denticulate, at least near apex. Flowers 8–10 cm diameter. Calyx glabrous; longest sepals 40–55 mm long. Petals spreading, pale yellow, turning pinkish orange with age, 30–40 mm long. Stamens about 10 mm long; filaments yellow, hairy at base; anthers yellow. Stigmas (8)–10–12. Seeds brown, obovoid, 1–1.3 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Carpobrotus edulis (L.) L.Bolus]
Leaves bitter-tasting. Fruit indehiscent, fleshy, mucilaginous; locules as many as stigmas. [Genus description, from: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Fruit 2–3 cm across, turning yellowish to reddish-purple as it ripens.
Very similar to Chilean sea fig, but told from it when flowering by the yellow petals, which fade to dull pink; Chilean sea fig has smaller, purple flowers.
Hybrids with the native ice plant have weakly 2-angled stems, leaves 2–6 cm long and flowers 4.5–6 cm across, with petals either orange-pink or yellow to whitish, turning pink with a yellow base; their pollen is mostly sterile and they form no fruit.

lookalikes.howToTell: Best told apart in flower. Chilean sea fig has purple petals, paler near the base, on flowers 6.5–8 cm across; this plant's petals are pale yellow, turning pinkish orange or dull pink with age, on flowers 8–10 cm across. Its leaves are 35–90 × 5–12 mm, against 70–120 × 12–17 mm here, but the ranges overlap, so do not rely on leaves out of flower.

preparation.text: Pick the fruit when it has turned yellowish, wrinkled and leathery; it is best eaten dry and wrinkled. Bite off the base and suck out the jelly of seeds and pulp, or peel off the skin and the dried flower parts on top and eat the fruit raw or cook it. For jam, soak the fruit overnight in salted cold water, drain and peel it, then simmer it in a sugar syrup until thick and dark red. Blanching the leaves and soaking them in salted water before pickling takes out their astringency.

recipes.method: 1 kg sour figs; 1 teaspoon salt; 2 cups (about 500 ml) sugar; a few cinnamon sticks; 1 cup (about 250 ml) water. Cover the sour figs with cold water, add the salt and soak them overnight, then drain and peel them. Add the sugar and cinnamon to the water and boil until sticky. Add the sour figs and simmer until thick and the fruit is dark red. Bottle in sterilised glass jars.
recipes.title: Sour fig jam

recipes.method: 250 g leaves; table salt; 250 g white wine vinegar; 100 g honey; 100 g caster sugar; a pinch of chilli flakes; 2 cloves; 1 teaspoon caraway seeds. Put the leaves into a pan of boiling water for 2 minutes and strain. Toss them in a bowl with a few pinches of table salt, cover with cold water and leave for 6 hours. Repeat the boiling and salting once more and strain off any excess water. Bring all the other ingredients to the boil and pour the hot pickling liquor over the leaves. Put them into airtight containers or jars.
recipes.title: Ice plant gherkins

summary.text:
Carpobrotus edulis, the South African ice plant, sour fig or Hottentot fig, is a mat-forming succulent in the ice plant family Aizoaceae, native to South Africa and naturalised in New Zealand since 1883.
The sour fig grows on coastal and inland slopes in South Africa from Namaqualand in the Northern Cape through the Western Cape to the Eastern Cape. It is often seen as a pioneer on disturbed sites.
In New Zealand it is recorded from Northland, Auckland, Bay of Plenty, Wellington and Wairarapa, from Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago and Southland, and from Stewart Island and the Chatham Islands. It was brought in as a garden ornamental and planted for its hardiness in beach gardens. It spreads by seed, carried by animals that eat the fruit, and by creeping stems that root where they touch the ground; the stems travel in moved soil and dumped garden waste, and broken pieces grow into new plants. It is a declared pest: an unwanted organism on the National Pest Plant Accord, which bans breeding, distributing, releasing or selling it anywhere in New Zealand, and it may not be planted in the Auckland region; it is under sustained control across the Auckland region and progressive containment on the Chatham Islands, and is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. It smothers native vegetation, changes soil chemistry, and hybridises with the native ice plant, Disphyma australe; that hybrid is named ×Carpophyma mutabilis.
Carpobrotus species hybridise easily and are difficult to tell apart: a 2023 genetic study that sampled populations in New Zealand and six other countries found no clear features to identify the taxa by their form.

warnings: A syrup made from the fruit is said to be laxative, and eating the fruit is an old South African remedy for constipation.
It is a pest plant controlled with herbicide sprays such as triclopyr. Pick only where you know it has not been sprayed.

identification.text: Evergreen tree to 37 m tall, usually with a single trunk; bark grey, rough and thick. Twigs and buds densely red- or white-hairy. Leaves alternate, thick and leathery, narrowly to broadly elliptic, usually 13–20 × 6–10 cm, glossy bright green and hairless above, hairless to densely red-brown felted beneath, with smooth margins. Flowers at the tips of the twigs, 15–30 cm across, strongly lemon-scented, with creamy white, waxy tepals and many stamens with purple filaments. Fruit a cylindrical to somewhat egg-shaped cone of follicles, 7–10 × 3.5–5 cm, the follicles opening to show seeds with a red aril. A New Zealand herbarium specimen had white flowers up to 32 cm across with 9 cupped petals, and leaves shiny green above and rusty-felted beneath.

preparation.text: The flavour is strong, so the petals are not usually eaten raw. They are pickled, best in a sweet-sour pickle, and a petal is diced and used sparingly as a flavouring in salads; the flowers are also used as a spice and condiment. Flowers are best picked as they begin to open, before the petals turn brown. The leaves are used like bay leaf to flavour soups, cut into smaller pieces because they are large.

recipes.method: Written for magnolias in general; the page names no species, and the author's tree flowers in early spring before its leaves come, so it is a different magnolia. Makes 1 jar. Magnolia petals, enough to fill the jar once chopped; 1 cup (250 ml) rice wine vinegar or apple cider vinegar; ¼ cup (about 50 g) white sugar; a pinch of salt. Pull the petals off the centre of each flower, which is bitter, and throw the centre away. Leave the petals out for half an hour so any insects can crawl off, then rinse them in cold water. Chop or shred the petals and pack them into a clean jar. Warm the vinegar with the sugar and salt over low heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, pour it over the petals and press them down until covered. Let the jar cool to room temperature, then keep it in the fridge — this is a quick pickle, not a ferment. Taste after a few days. Use like pickled ginger, with sushi, in stir-fries or in sandwiches.
recipes.title: Pickled magnolia petals

recipes.method: Written for magnolias in general; the page names no species, and the author's tree flowers in early spring before its leaves come, so it is a different magnolia. 2 cups (500 ml) water; 2 cups magnolia petals, more for a stronger taste; 1 cup (about 200 g) sugar. Pull the petals off the bitter centre of each flower, leave them out for half an hour for insects to leave, and rinse in cold water. Dissolve the sugar in the water over low heat, stirring often, then bring it to the boil, add the petals and simmer on low for about 20 minutes. Lift out the petals and keep simmering the syrup until it is as thick as you want. Mix with cold water for a drink, or pour over pancakes or ice cream.
recipes.title: Magnolia syrup

recipes.method: Written for magnolias in general; the page names no species, and the author's tree flowers in early spring before its leaves come, so it is a different magnolia. Magnolia petals and a vinegar of your choice. Pull the petals off the bitter centre of each flower, leave them out for half an hour for insects to leave, and rinse in cold water. Chop the petals, pack them into a jar and cover with unheated vinegar. Leave at room temperature for a couple of weeks, then strain out the petals and keep the vinegar in the fridge between uses. Use in salad dressings and marinades. Infuse petals in vinegar, never in oil: fresh plant material in oil can grow the bacteria that cause botulism.

summary.text: Southern magnolia or bull bay (Magnolia grandiflora), also called laurel magnolia or evergreen magnolia, is a large evergreen tree in the magnolia family (Magnoliaceae), native to the south-eastern United States from North Carolina to Florida and Texas, where it grows in lowland woods, on wooded dunes and in river bottoms. It is widely cultivated in warmer areas around the world. In New Zealand it is planted in gardens, parks and streets and occasionally comes up self-sown from seed spread by birds; the New Zealand Organisms Register lists it as an exotic sometimes present in the wild, Biota of New Zealand records it as a casual exotic, and it is not listed as a pest plant.

warnings: Cut or crushed leaves can cause allergic skin rashes (contact dermatitis), especially in people already sensitive to daisy-family plants; the leaves contain parthenolide, a likely allergen. Damaging the leaf releases the allergen, and a dyer who boiled the leaves developed dermatitis of the hands and face.

identification.text:
Urtica australis (southern nettle) is a stout, dense, bushy, shrub that reaches 1 by 1 metre in diameter. The base can be somewhat woody. The plant can also be semideciduous. The petioles are up to 50 mm long.
Leaves are dark green, 100–150 mm long and 80–140 mm wide, with a heart-shaped base. The margins are usually coarsely toothed, sometimes nearly smooth, and rarely completely smooth. The stinging hairs or trichomes are mainly found along the leaf edges and veins on the underside, and may be sparse or absent. Flowering occurs from December to January. Fruits form from December to March. The achenes are 1.5–2 mm long, and pale brown.
It is told from all other New Zealand nettles by its big, broad, dark green leaves, 10–20 cm long, on a stout, bushy, partly deciduous plant whose branches lie down and root before turning upright. The leaf stalk often carries a pair of small leaflets near its base.

lookalikes.howToTell: Ongaonga is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m, with numerous long-stalked white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long and pale green, triangular to ovate-triangular leaves usually 7–12 cm long (4–18 cm, overlapping southern nettle's). Southern nettle is a stout herb up to about 1 m, somewhat woody only at the base, with few short-stalked stinging hairs and broad, dark green leaves 10–20 cm long with a heart-shaped base. Both grow on Stewart Island. Its sting has killed: in 1961 a young man died of paralysis and breathing problems several hours after walking through tree nettles. If it is a woody shrub with long white stinging hairs, walk away.
lookalikes.name: Ongaonga

lookalikes.howToTell: Stinging nettle spreads by long underground rhizomes and has broadly lanceolate or ovate leaves; southern nettle's branches lie down and root at the base before turning upright, and its leaves are broadly ovate to nearly round, dark green and 10–20 cm long. Stinging nettle is rare in southern nettle's range: on Stewart Island it is recorded only at Port Pegasus.
lookalikes.name: Stinging nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush nettle is a slender, erect herb 15–60 cm tall that spreads by rhizomes, with light green, triangular to triangular-ovate leaves (2–6 cm long, sometimes up to 12 cm). Southern nettle is stout and bushy, up to about 1 m, its branches lying down and rooting before turning upright, with broadly ovate, dark green leaves 10–20 cm long, the leaf stalk often carrying a pair of small leaflets near its base. Both grow on Stewart Island. Young bush nettle leaves are eaten cooked.
lookalikes.name: Bush nettle

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf nettle is a branched annual up to 60 cm with a short taproot and ovate or elliptic leaves 2–8 cm long (rarely 1–10 cm), and its short flower clusters, up to 3 cm, carry male and female flowers together. Southern nettle is a stout, bushy plant up to about 1 m whose branches lie down and root before turning upright, with broadly ovate, dark green leaves 10–20 cm long; most of its flower clusters are one sex, female above male. Both grow on the Chatham Islands. Young dwarf nettle leaves are eaten cooked.

summary.text:
Urtica australis, commonly known as southern nettle and onga, is a species of nettle endemic to New Zealand's southern and subantarctic islands.
Urtica australis is endemic to New Zealand. The species is found in the south-western coast of Fiordland (in the South Island). It is also found on Chatham, Stewart, and other main subantarctic islands. The 2023 assessment of U. australis in the New Zealand Threat Classification System was "At Risk – Declining".
Its specific epithet, australis, means 'southern'. It is also called Chatham Island nettle.
U. australis plays host to the Chatham Island red admiral (Vanessa gonerilla ida). It is the only known host plant of that endemic butterfly.
It also grows on islands in Foveaux Strait. It is uncommon on Stewart Island but weedy on the Chatham Islands, where it thrives on disturbance and large browsing animals hardly touch it.
It is common in damaged forest on the main Chatham Island (NZPCN, restated).

warnings: Its sting is milder than ongaonga's but still painful. The stinging hairs sit mostly along the leaf edges and on the veins under the leaf, and can be sparse.

identification.text:
Deciduous shrub up to 3 m high; twigs sparsely to moderately clothed in appressed hairs, becoming more or less glabrous, rounded, striate and glaucous-green to dark green. Mature branches with few leaves; leaves glabrous or sparsely to densely hairy, simple, entire, elliptic to oblong or more or less linear on mature branches, acute to obtuse, (8)–15–25 mm long, up to 45 mm long in shaded shoots or seedlings; petioles 1–2 mm long. Inflorescence with usually numerous fragrant flowers; pedicels 2–5 mm long; bract subtending pedicel narrowly triangular, 2–4 mm long; bracteole subtending calyx linear, about 2 mm long. Calyx more or less glabrous, unilabiate. Corolla 22–28 mm long. Pod becoming glabrous, oblong and flattened, 50–90 mm long; seeds smooth, dark brown.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The flowers are fragrant, and the unusually shaped calyx with 5 reduced teeth on one side distinguishes Spanish broom from all other wild New Zealand legumes. The stout, rounded green twigs are usually almost leafless in adult plants.
It flowers from December to May. The flowers are golden and grow in racemes at the ends of the shoots.

lookalikes.howToTell: Scotch broom's twigs are more or less five-angled, and its leaves have three leaflets on older twigs, often one or two on young twigs. Spanish broom's twigs are stout, rounded and finely grooved, usually almost leafless on adult plants, and its leaves are simple, 15–25 mm long on mature branches; a one- or two-leaflet leaf on a young Scotch broom twig can look like it. Scotch broom's calyx is two-lipped; Spanish broom's is one-lipped, split above, with five short teeth on one side, which sets it apart from every other wild legume in New Zealand. Scotch broom's flowers are usually single, rarely paired, in the leaf angles; Spanish broom's are fragrant and usually many together in racemes at the ends of the shoots. Scotch broom's pods are black, 15–60 mm long and hairy along the edges; Spanish broom's become hairless and are 50–90 mm long. Flower length overlaps (Scotch broom 16–25 mm, Spanish broom 22–28 mm) and does not separate them. Scotch broom flowers from September to April, Spanish broom from December to May.

summary.text:
Spartium junceum, known as Spanish broom, rush broom, or weaver's broom, is a species of flowering plant in the family Fabaceae and the sole species in the genus Spartium. It is native to the Mediterranean.
In New Zealand: North Island — Auckland City, locally common in Hawke's Bay, locally common to abundant in Wellington Province; South Island — Nelson City, Coverham (Marlborough), Port Hills and Christchurch, Otago Peninsula. It was first recorded wild here in 1940. Spanish broom is often cultivated as an ornamental in gardens and is used in plantings around cities.
It was brought here as an ornamental and reproduces by seed, of which it produces many. It is commonly grown in some areas but has not naturalised as widely as Scotch broom.
Its seeds are spread by gravity and by moving soil. It forms dense stands that reduce native plant cover, and as a nitrogen fixer it may change which plants grow there and help other exotic plants invade.
Since 1 September 2021 Auckland Council's rules ban breeding, distributing, selling or planting it anywhere in the Auckland region. The council controls it wherever it is known on Aotea / Great Barrier Island and asks that any seen there be reported.

warnings: All parts of Spanish broom are toxic. Every part contains the alkaloids cytisine and sparteine, which act on the nervous system; sparteine can affect heart rhythm.

Eating the flowers has poisoned people: three adults who ate rice cooked with Spanish broom flowers fell ill at once with abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea and tremors, and needed hospital treatment.

The seeds poison children, more severely the more are eaten: in one report a child who ate one or two seeds had no symptoms, one who ate four or five had digestive upset, and one who ate seven or eight had digestive and nervous-system symptoms.
In severe poisoning, symptoms can progress to seizures, muscle paralysis and respiratory failure, which can kill.
The seeds are probably poisonous, like those of Scotch broom.

It is a pest plant in New Zealand: it is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and the regional pest management plans of Auckland, Manawatū-Whanganui and Canterbury name it.

identification.text:
A pouch fungus around 20 by 60 mm that never opens out into gills. The cap is powder blue, purplish-blue or greenish, and smooth or pitted and furrowed. The stem is stout and solid, whitish to yellowish, often brighter yellow towards the base, widening where it meets the pouch.
Cut lengthways, the gleba inside is reddish-brown or orange, held in regular cell-like chambers behind a purple-brown sack-like wall. It does not bruise blue.

lookalikes.howToTell: Colour and shape do not separate them reliably. Spindle pouch is powder blue, purplish blue or greenish, usually elongated and tapering towards the tip. Weraroa is light brown when young, becoming french-grey or pale blue-grey (sometimes pale green), and can be roundish, egg-shaped or elongated. The stem is the better field check. Spindle pouch's is stout, solid, smooth and slippery, off-white to yellow and yellower towards the base, and widens towards the pouch. Weraroa's is slender, the same width throughout, fibrous and hollow, whitish to french-grey with a yellowish-brown base. Weraroa slowly bruises blue or greenish where injured, on both pouch and stem. Spindle pouch is naturally blue but does not blue when damaged. Cut one lengthways. Spindle pouch's gleba is brown to reddish-brown, rarely orange, in regular cell-like chambers inside a purple-brown sack-like layer. Weraroa's is sepia to chocolate-brown in contorted, gill-like chambers, with no sack.

The test that separates it from weraroa, which is the whole reason this page exists. Clavogaster virescens is *naturally* blue to greenish blue and has **no bluing reaction**, and contains no psilocybin; Psilocybe weraroa is a bluing Psilocybe containing psilocin and psilocybine. Because a secotioid cap never opens to show gills, the identification needs a cut through the fruitbody: in C. virescens the gleba is a reddish brown or orange chambered mass inside a sack-like structure within the peridium, and the stem is stout, smooth and slippery rather than fibrous, off-white to yellow, swollen at the top where it runs smoothly into the pouch and tapering to a yellower base. The taxonomy is why the two are tangled: the genus Weraroa was erected in 1958 for W. novae-zelandiae and this species was moved into it, and only in 2015 did it become Clavogaster virescens (Massee) J.A. Cooper again while W. novae-zelandiae became Psilocybe weraroa. Clavogaster holds two endemic species — this one and Clavogaster sp. identification.text:
Deciduous shrub or small tree to about 8 m high, often suckering extensively. Branchlets villous. Leaves pinnate, with 19–23 leaflets in mature plants, up to about 30 cm long; petiole and rachis villous or densely hairy, the hairs purple when young. Leaflets sessile, 4–12 × 0.8–2.5 cm, oblong-lanceolate (terminal leaflet more or less ovate), glabrate except for densely hairy midrib below, glaucous below, dull green above, serrate, acuminate at apex, becoming orange to crimson in autumn. Inflorescence terminal, villous, dense and conelike, to about 20 × 5 cm. Flowers greenish. Calyx segments lanceolate, long-ciliate. Petals 2–2.5 mm long. Fruit about 3 mm wide, broader than long, villous with long rose to crimson hairs. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

edibleParts.text: Seed - cooked. It has a floury texture and a mild, somewhat creamy flavour. It can be used as a staple food crop in either savoury or sweet dishes. The seed can be cooked whole, though it is more commonly ground into a flour and used as a cereal in all the ways that oats are used, especially as a porridge but also to make biscuits, sourdough bread etc. The seed can also be sprouted and eaten raw or cooked in salads, stews etc. The roasted seed is a coffee substitute. It is sometimes harvested from the wild or along with other cereal crops when growing wild with them.

identification.text:
Strong, rather stiff, erect green tufts to 150 cm, with heavy panicles. Leaf-sheath glabrous, or rarely with scattered soft hairs. Ligule 3–8 mm, truncate, or more tapered centrally, shortly denticulate, finely ciliate. Leaf-blade 15–45 cm × 3–15 mm, very finely scabrid on ribs, adaxially sometimes smooth, rarely with scattered hairs; margins minutely scabrid. Culm internodes glabrous. Panicle 20–40 cm, equilateral, lax; rachis smooth, branches few, widely spreading, filiform, scabrid. Spikelets often drooping; disarticulation above glumes; rachilla tough and continuous between florets. Glumes 9–11-nerved. Lemma elliptic-lanceolate, tough and hairy below level of awn insertion, greenish above and scabrid on nerves, narrowed to scarious bidentate apex; lower 1–2 lemmas awned; awn geniculate, column red-brown, twisted. Palea keels with 1–3 rows of cilia, interkeel usually minutely hairy above. Callus bordered by dense short hairs.

subsp. ludoviciana (winter wild oat): Spikelets 3.5–6 cm, 2–3-flowered, spreading. Lemma 18–20 mm, light brown or greyish, with more or less dense light brown or whitish hairs below awn insertion; awn more or less slender, 25–50 mm. Anthers 2–5 mm

subsp. sterilis: Spikelets 6–8 cm, 3–5-flowered, often drooping. Lemma 25–30 mm, light reddish brown, with dense stiff reddish brown hairs below awn insertion; awn very stout, 60–70 mm. Anthers 3–4 mm.
[From: Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Both edible; this is about which you have. Look at the awns: winter wild oat's lowest one or two florets each carry an awn bent at a knee and twisted in its lower part, 25–50 mm long in subsp. ludoviciana and 60–70 mm in subsp. sterilis, where the cultivated oat is usually awnless or has a weak, straight or curved awn that is not kneed and scarcely twisted. Winter wild oat's lemmas are hairy below the awn; the cultivated oat's are hairless or have a few hairs near the base. Winter wild oat's spikelets are usually larger — 3.5–6 cm or 6–8 cm against the cultivated oat's (15)–20–30–(40) mm — but the ranges meet, and floret number (2–5 against 2–3) overlaps.
lookalikes.name: Oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Size does not reliably separate them. Winter wild oat is a strong, rather stiff plant with heavy panicles, and slender oat is often very slender, but their measurements can overlap: slender oat's spikelets are 40–50 mm with awns 30–36 mm; winter wild oat's are 3.5–6 cm with awns 25–50 mm in subspecies ludoviciana (overlapping slender oat), and 6–8 cm with awns 60–70 mm in subspecies sterilis. Leaf width overlaps too (2–8 mm against 3–15 mm), and reddish hairs on the lemma occur in slender oat and in subspecies sterilis. Check how a ripe spikelet breaks up: slender oat's breaks apart below each floret, while winter wild oat's florets stay joined and fall together from above the glumes. Slender oat's lemma tip-lobes are each drawn out into a fine bristle 2–3 mm long; winter wild oat's lemma narrows to a papery, two-toothed tip, and only its lower one or two lemmas carry an awn. Both have edible seeds.
lookalikes.name: Slender oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have long, bent, twisted awns and both drop their seed, but differently. Wild oat's spikelet breaks up below each floret, so the florets fall one by one; winter wild oat's breaks above the glumes with the florets held together, so they fall as one unit. At the base of each floret, wild oat has a horseshoe-shaped scar densely bordered by long hairs; winter wild oat's is bordered by dense short hairs. Wild oat's awn column is dark brown, winter wild oat's red-brown. Size does not reliably separate them: wild oat's spikelets are 35–50 mm with 2–3 florets and an awn of 30–40 mm; in New Zealand, winter wild oat subsp. ludoviciana has spikelets 35–60 mm with 2–3 florets and awns 25–50 mm, and subsp. sterilis spikelets 60–80 mm with 3–5 florets and awns 60–70 mm.

preparation.text: Ripe florets drop from the plant together, as one unit, so a stand is gathered as it ripens rather than after. The seed, when harvested and dried, can store for several years. No source gives a method written for this species. Written for the cultivated oat: Harvested oats go through multiple stages of milling. The first stage is cleaning, to remove seeds of other plants, stones and any other extraneous materials. Next is dehulling to remove the indigestible hull, leaving the seed or "groat". Heating denatures enzymes in the seed that would make it go sour or rancid; the grain is then dried to minimise the risk of spoilage by bacteria and fungi. For home use such as making porridge, oats are often rolled flat to make them quicker to cook.

summary.text:
Avena sterilis (animated oat, sterile oat, wild red oat, winter wild oat; syn. Avena ludoviciana Durieu; Avena macrocarpa Moench; Avena sterilis ssp. sterilis; Avena sterilis ssp. ludoviciana) is a species of grass weed whose seeds are edible.
A. sterilis is native to the Mediterranean Basin and West, Central and South Asia, but is widely naturalized elsewhere. The species grows on all continents except Antarctica.

In North America, it grows as an introduced species in the U.S. states of California, Oregon, New Jersey, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec.

Because it thrives in the same conditions as many agricultural crops and has similar lifecycles, the grass directly competes with and reduces yield in arable crops.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): subsp. ludoviciana: N.: Feilding, Wellington City; S.: Nelson City, Blenheim, more common in Canterbury, North Otago (near Oamaru). Naturalised from Eurasia. subsp. sterilis: N.: North Auckland (near Whangarei), Auckland City, Waikato (Waerenga); Cook Strait (Stephens Id); S.: Dunedin. Naturalised from Mediterranean.

warnings: Claviceps purpurea is an ergot fungus that grows on the ears of rye and related cereal and forage plants. Consumption of grains or seeds contaminated with the survival structure of this fungus, the ergot sclerotium, can cause ergotism in humans and other mammals. It affects oats only rarely.

identification.text:
This is an annual herb growing from a slender taproot. It produces a branched stem up to 45 centimeters tall, with abundant glandular and non-glandular hairs. The leaves are opposite, hairy, up to 2 cm long, and the basal ones typically die back before flowering. The bracts are green, hairy and generally similar to the leaves.
The inflorescence bears as few as 3 or as many as 50 small, dioecious flowers arranged in a cyme and borne on very short pedicels. Each flower has 5 hairy green sepals which are occasionally red-tipped, and 5 white bifid petals which are a few millimeters long and generally about the same length as the sepals. The fruit is a capsule less than a centimeter long which is tipped with ten tiny teeth.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Waste places, especially roadsides, pasture, lawns.
In New Zealand it grows in spring-sown crops and in pastures that are thin in spring, often after treading damage over winter or when newly sown.
It also grows on roadsides, in farmyards and holding paddocks, and on bare or pugged soil.
Waste places usually on heavy soil.

identification.text:
An erect, bushy annual about 40 cm tall, with feathery, dark green leaves cut into awl-shaped segments and white daisy flower heads with a yellow centre; crushed or rubbed, it has a very strong smell.
Seedlings have stalkless seed leaves, pointed at the tip and tapered at the base.
Crush the foliage to tell it from its lookalike mayweeds: if it stinks, it is stinking mayweed; if it smells of pineapple, it is pineappleweed (rayless mayweed); if it smells of nothing, it is probably scentless chamomile.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Strongly foetid annual herb. Stems erect or ascending, (5)–30–40–(60) cm tall, striate, almost glabrous to moderately hairy especially above, usually much-branched from base, rooting in lower part. Basal and lower cauline leaves apetiolate, ovate to obovate-oblong, glabrous to sparsely hairy and glandular, 3-pinnatisect, up to 8 cm long; ultimate segments subulate to linear, entire, not all in one plane giving a somewhat feathery appearance to the leaf; cauline leaves similar to basal, smaller and less divided near capitula, usually ovate-oblong. Involucral bracts glabrous to moderately hairy, 2–6 mm long; margins and apex of at least inner bracts membranous. Capitula solitary, about 15–30–(35) mm diameter; ray florets 8–21, very rarely 0; ligules white, becoming reflexed; disc florets numerous, yellow. Scales usually confined to inner ⅔ of receptacle, linear, acute. Achenes 1.3–1.7 mm long, obconic, narrowed slightly at apex, circular in section, brown, obscurely ribbed; ribs usually prominently tuberculate, rarely whole achene almost smooth; pappus 0.
It can be distinguished from A. arvensis and Chamaemelum nobile, with which it has been confused in New Zealand, by the shape of the receptacle scales and achenes. The achenes are usually distinctly tuberculate, but in some forms the tubercules are scattered or altogether absent. Rarely rayless forms are found.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have feathery, finely divided leaves and grow in waste places, on roadsides, in pasture and in lawns. Stinking mayweed is a strongly foetid annual without rhizomes, with single daisy heads about 15–30 mm across (8–21 white rays, yellow centre); yarrow spreads by rhizomes into mats, lacks that strong smell, and has heads only about 5–10 mm across with 4–7 rays, usually white right across, packed many together in a flat cluster. Yarrow is edible in small amounts but carries its own cautions (daisy-family allergy, pregnancy) — see its entry.
lookalikes.name: Yarrow

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have scales between the florets, so check their tips with a hand lens: Roman chamomile's are blunt and often ragged at the tip, stinking mayweed's narrow and pointed. Roman chamomile is sweetly aromatic; crushed stinking mayweed smells strongly foetid. Roman chamomile creeps, its stems lying along the ground or rising to about 20 cm; stinking mayweed's stems stand upright or rise from the base, usually 30–40 cm tall but from 5 cm to 60 cm — so a small stinking mayweed can be as short. Roman chamomile's stems are moderately to densely hairy and stinking mayweed's almost hairless to moderately hairy, so hairiness does not separate them; both have white rays around a yellow disc and feathery leaves. Roman chamomile's flowers are used for tea, with care for people allergic to the daisy family.
lookalikes.name: Roman chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: Pineappleweed has no white rays — its heads are a dome of dull yellow to greenish-yellow florets, 4–10 mm across; stinking mayweed nearly always has 8–21 white rays and heads 15–30 mm across (up to 35), but rayless forms of stinking mayweed occur rarely, so a rayless head is not proof. Before flowering the two look alike, so smell is the test then. Crush it: pineappleweed smells of pineapple, stinking mayweed strongly foetid. Pineappleweed has no scales on its receptacle; stinking mayweed has narrow, pointed scales between the inner florets. Pineappleweed's leaf segments lie more or less in one plane; stinking mayweed's do not, which makes its leaves look feathery. Pineappleweed's flower heads and leaves are eaten and made into tea.
lookalikes.name: Pineappleweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Ox-eye daisy's lower leaves are long-stalked, spoon-shaped to oval and coarsely toothed or only shallowly lobed; stinking mayweed's are divided three times into fine, narrow segments. Ox-eye daisy has no scales on its flat or slightly convex receptacle; stinking mayweed has narrow, pointed scales between the inner florets. Ox-eye daisy is scarcely scented; crushed stinking mayweed smells strongly foetid. Ox-eye daisy's flower heads are usually 30–60 mm across (25–65 mm at the extremes) and stinking mayweed's 15–30 mm (up to 35), so a small ox-eye daisy and a large stinking mayweed overlap; both have white rays around a yellow disc and both grow on roadsides and in waste places. Ox-eye daisy is eaten — its young leaves, shoots and flower buds (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Ox-eye daisy

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: stinking mayweed smells strongly foetid; scentless chamomile is almost scentless. Look inside the head: stinking mayweed has narrow, pointed scales among the inner florets; scentless chamomile has none. Stinking mayweed's heads are about 15–30 mm across (up to 35 mm), scentless chamomile's about 30–50 mm, and scentless chamomile's leaflets are slightly finer. What does not separate them: both have finely divided, feathery leaves and white rays around a yellow disc, and both grow on roadsides and in waste places and pasture. Stinking mayweed is generally the commoner of the two in the North Island, scentless chamomile in Canterbury and much of the South Island. There is no record of scentless chamomile being eaten.
lookalikes.name: Scentless chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: Common lawn daisy has undivided, spoon-shaped leaves with 2–6 pairs of shallow teeth, all in a basal rosette, and a single head 15–25 mm across on a leafless stalk 3–15 cm long (up to 25 cm). Stinking mayweed is an annual with leafy stems, usually much-branched from the base and usually 30–40 cm tall (5–60 cm at the extremes), and its leaves are cut three times into narrow segments with a somewhat feathery look. Stinking mayweed's receptacle carries narrow, pointed scales, usually only in the inner two-thirds; lawn daisy's has none. Stinking mayweed is strongly foetid. What does not separate them: head size (stinking mayweed about 15–30 mm across, up to 35 mm; lawn daisy 15–25 mm), white rays around a yellow disc, and place — both grow in lawns and pasture. Lawn daisy's young leaves, flower buds and petals are eaten (see its entry).
lookalikes.name: Common lawn daisy

summary.text:
Anthemis cotula, known in New Zealand as stinking mayweed, stinking chamomile or mayweed, is a strongly foetid annual herb of the daisy family, native to Europe, North Africa and Caucasia to Iran and Iraq and naturalised in New Zealand by 1878.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: throughout; South Island: Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury. (Europe, North Africa, Caucasia to Iran and Iraq; first recorded 1878.) Stinking mayweed is a common plant of waste places. The Landcare Research herbarium also holds specimens from Otago and Westland, outside the Flora's range.
In New Zealand stinking mayweed is generally more common than scentless chamomile (Tripleurospermum inodorum) in the North Island, while scentless chamomile is the more common of the two in Canterbury and several other parts of the South Island. Once in a pasture, most livestock avoid it, which lets it dominate: cattle don't like it, and sheep graze it only when there is nothing else to eat. Its seedlings are weak and slow-growing, and it usually fades once a pasture sward thickens. Its seeds can germinate at any time of year if the soil is moist enough; plants usually die after setting seed, but plants mown while flowering may survive the winter.

warnings: The whole plant carries an acrid juice that can blister bare skin; prolonged contact with the flower heads and seeds is reported to cause dermatitis, and some people are allergic to it.

It is reported as toxic: it can poison poultry and may poison dogs, cats and horses, and most livestock avoid eating it; milk from cows that do can be tainted. The few records of it as a flavouring or a weak chamomile-like tea come with cautions about toxicity.
As a herbal remedy it is contraindicated in pregnancy and for nursing mothers.
It is easily mistaken for the chamomiles used for tea. Crush a leaf — stinking mayweed smells strongly foetid — and check the receptacle: its scales are narrow and pointed.

edibleParts.text: Flowers, eaten raw as a vegetable or used as a garnish, especially with sweet desserts; in China the dried flowers are sold as an edible flower and drunk as a tea. The seed pods are edible: freshly boiled pods are eaten in Puglia, Italy, though another record lists the pods only as a famine food, used when all else fails. No food use of the leaves was found in these sources.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): A garden escape, often firmly established on coastal cliffs and banks.
The plant prefers calcareous soils, and often grows on cliffs overlooking the sea, or on old walls. It is a plant of the coast, but it can be found, naturalized, even in the hinterland up to 600 m elevation.

identification.text:
Perennial. Stems hairy, branched, stout, erect, woody, to 80 cm tall, bearing conspicuous leaf-base scars below. Leaves tufted at branch tips, lanceolate, obtuse, entire, sinuate or shallowly pinnatifid, densely tomentose, glaucous, cuneate at base, (3)–8–15–(30) × (0.5)–1–2–(4) cm. Racemes 15–20–(30) cm long; pedicels erecto-patent, 1–2 cm long. Flowers fragrant, opening by day. Sepals densely hairy, 9–13 × 1.5–2.5 mm. Petals pink to purple, 18–25 × 5–10 mm. Silique flattened, 50–120 × 3–5 mm; stigma lobes 1.5–2 mm long, dorsally swollen but not horned; valves densely hairy. Seeds circular, brown, flattened, broadly winged, 2–3 mm in diameter.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The fragrant flowers are white, cream yellow, pink, red, purple or blue. Growers describe the scent as clove-like.
The other naturalised stock, Matthiola longipetala (night-scented stock), is annual, with slender, decumbent stems, flowers that open by night or on dull days, and a terete silique 1–2 mm wide; stock is perennial, with stout, erect stems, flowers that open by day, and a flattened silique 3–5 mm wide (Flora of New Zealand key, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Stock has narrow, lance-shaped leaves that are entire to shallowly lobed, densely felted and grey-green, tufted at the tips of stout woody stems with conspicuous leaf-base scars, and a long narrow pod 50–120 × 3–5 mm. Honesty has heart-shaped, dark green, hairy leaves with blunt or coarse teeth, on a biennial plant, and a broad, flat, elliptic disc-shaped fruit 2.5–4 × 2–3 cm. Flower colour and size do not separate them: stock petals are pink to purple, 18–25 mm, and honesty petals are purple (rarely white), 15–22 mm. Honesty's root, flowers and leaves are eaten; do not eat its seed or seed pods: the seeds accumulate toxic alkaloids.

summary.text:
Matthiola incana is a species of flowering plant in the cabbage family Brassicaceae. Common names include Brompton stock, common stock, hoary stock, ten-week stock, and gilly-flower. The common name stock usually refers to this species, though it may also be applied to the whole genus Matthiola. The common name "night-scented stock" or "evening-scented stock" is applied to Matthiola longipetala.
Matthiola incana is a common garden flower, available in a variety of colours, many of which are heavily scented and also used in floristry.
It is native to southern Europe from Spain to Greece, and is naturalized in the western part of the Mediterranean region, roughly in the same area as the olive tree.
Matthiola incana is widely used as an ornamental plant for summer bedding, and as a cut flower and aromatic plant. The species has been in cultivation since at least the 16th century.
In New Zealand it was first recorded naturalised in 1878; the Flora of New Zealand (1988) lists it from Northland, Taranaki (Oakura), Wairarapa (Castlepoint) and the Wellington coast in the North Island, and Nelson, Kaikoura, Christchurch and Dunedin in the South Island. New Zealand plants are subsp. incana (Flora of New Zealand, restated).
Flora of New Zealand Online also lists the names Brampton stock and Imperial stock. The species name incana means hoary, for the greyish-white hairs; the New Zealand Plant Conservation Network gives the plant's origin as southern and western Europe and Arabia, and its naturalisation year as 1878 (restated).

warnings: The food record is thin: the use of the flowers as a vegetable or garnish traces to one compilation, and the seed pods are listed elsewhere only as a famine food, used when all else fails.

Garden stock is often treated against aphids, caterpillars and powdery mildew with insecticides, fungicides or weekly Bt sprays. Pick flowers from a garden plant only if you know what it has been sprayed with.

identification.text:
Shrub or small tree with fissured bark (to about 10 m high in cultivation). Young shoots glandular-hairy. Leaves glabrous, with very short petioles. Lamina 4.5–9 × 2–3.5 cm, a little larger on vegetative shoots, elliptic to obovate, crenate-serrate to serrate, sometimes almost entire on flowering shoots; base cuneate; apex usually obtuse. Panicle usually 4–6 cm long; peduncles and pedicels glabrous or puberulent. Bracts ovate to lanceolate, conspicuous and often tinged reddish, shorter than or longer than pedicels. Calyx 2–3 mm long, often reddish; lobes broad, ciliate, obtuse. Corolla tube 7–8 mm long, white or pinkish, hairy towards apex; lobes broad, about 1 mm long. Filaments villous; anther awns aristate, curved. Style shortly exserted. Fruit 1.5–2 cm diameter, globose, orange-red or scarlet, with conic papillae giving a warty appearance. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Arbutus unedo, commonly known as strawberry tree, also called madrone, is an evergreen shrub or small tree in the family Ericaceae, native to the Mediterranean Basin and Western Europe.
Arbutus unedo is widespread in the Mediterranean region: in Portugal, Spain, and southeastern France; southward in Algeria, Morocco, Libya, and Tunisia, and eastward in Italy, Malta, Slovenia, Croatia, Montenegro, Greece, Turkey, Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria. It is also found in western France, Albania, Bulgaria, and southwestern Ireland.
A. unedo has been noted for its disjunct distribution, with isolated relict populations in southern and western Ireland in addition to its Mediterranean range. It is commonly cited as an example of the Lusitanian flora, a small assemblage of plants native to Iberia and South-Western Ireland, but generally absent from Britain. Recent genetic studies have suggested that A. unedo may not be truly native in Ireland, but a Chalcolithic introduction.
The red-flowered variant, named A. unedo rubra by William Aiton in 1785, was discovered growing wild in Ireland in 1835.

identification.text:
Annual; stems sparsely to densely hairy, procumbent or ascending, not rooting at nodes. Leaves glabrous to moderately hairy on petioles and undersurface of leaflets; petioles 1–5–(20) mm long; leaflets obovate, usually emarginate, occasionally obtuse, rarely some leaflets shortly mucronate, cuneate at base, finely serrate, about 3–12 mm long; lateral veins thin and straight to leaflet margin; petiolules distinctly unequal on most leaves; lateral petiolules less than 1 mm long; terminal petiolule up to 2–(3) mm long; stipules ovate, acute. Inflorescences axillary, racemose, cylindric to globose, pedunculate, much longer than leaves; flowers 5–20–(25); pedicels 0–1 mm long; bracts subtending flowers reduced to glandular hairs. Calyx more or less glabrous, occasionally sparsely hairy, 5-veined, not inflated at fruiting; throat open, glabrous; calyx teeth unequal, shorter than corolla, erect at fruiting; 3 lower teeth longer, lanceolate, more or less equal to or somewhat longer than tube; 2 upper teeth triangular and shorter than tube; sinuses obtuse. Corolla yellow, persistent, 2.5–4 mm long. Pod glabrous, straight, longer than calyx, 2–3 mm long, 1-seeded; seeds about 1–1.5 mm diameter.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Its leaflets are generally smaller than those of white clover and usually lack white crescent markings, but white clover's leaves can be very small under some mowing and growing conditions. Its stems, sometimes reddish, do not root along the ground. The middle leaflet usually sits on a slightly longer stalk than the other two. In flower it has small clusters of yellow florets.

lookalikes.howToTell: Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long. Its stems lie along the ground or rise a little and do not root at the nodes, and they are sparsely to densely hairy. White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish; its hairless stems creep and root at the nodes. Look at the leaflet stalks: on most suckling clover leaves the middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the two side leaflets (under 1 mm); white clover's three are about equal. Suckling clover's leaflets are about 3–12 mm long and usually lack the white crescent markings; white clover's are about 5–25 mm long and often carry light or dark markings. Size alone is not a safe test, as white clover's leaves can be very small under some mowing and growing conditions. White clover is eaten (see its own entry); suckling clover has no confirmed food record, so do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long. Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually stalkless on the leaves beneath it, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Both have hairy stems that do not root at the nodes, so the stems do not separate them. Suckling clover's leaflets are about 3–12 mm long and on most leaves the middle one sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the side ones (under 1 mm); red clover's are about 15–40 mm long, on more or less equal stalks 1–2 mm long, and usually carry a crescent-shaped spot towards the base. Out of flower, leaflet size is a guide, as the published ranges do not meet. Red clover is eaten (see its own entry); suckling clover has no confirmed food record, so do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long. Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Suckling clover's stems are sparsely to densely hairy and lie along the ground or rise a little; alsike clover's are hairless, erect or ascending. Neither roots at the nodes. On most suckling clover leaves the middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the side ones (under 1 mm); alsike clover's three are more or less equal. Leaflet size overlaps between 10 and 12 mm (suckling clover about 3–12 mm long, alsike clover about 10–35 mm), so it does not separate them. Alsike clover is eaten (see its own entry); suckling clover has no confirmed food record, so do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have small yellow flowers and three small leaflets that are often notched at the tip, and both grow in lawns. Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long. Least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats; suckling clover's stems lie along the ground or rise a little and do not root at the nodes. Least yellow sorrel's three leaflets are equal, on very short stalks; on most suckling clover leaves the middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the side ones (under 1 mm). Leaflet size does not separate them: least yellow sorrel's are 1–9 mm long, suckling clover's about 3–12 mm. Season does not either: suckling clover is an annual that flowers from October to June, and least yellow sorrel flowers in every month. Least yellow sorrel is eaten (see its own entry); suckling clover has no confirmed food record, so do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Least yellow sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have yellow flowers and three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and both grow in lawns and gardens. Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets, and sets cylindrical capsules (6)–10–18–(20) mm long. Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long, its florets staying on the head around tiny pods 2–3 mm long. Creeping wood sorrel's three leaflets are equal, on very short stalks; on most suckling clover leaves the middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the side ones (under 1 mm). Creeping wood sorrel's stems often root at the nodes; suckling clover's do not. Leaflet size overlaps (creeping wood sorrel (2.5)–5–18 mm long, suckling clover about 3–12 mm), and both have hairy stems that lie along the ground or rise a little. Creeping wood sorrel is eaten (see its own entry); suckling clover has no confirmed food record, so do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and it is almost hairless. Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long; its stems are sparsely to densely hairy, lie along the ground or rise a little, and do not root at the nodes. Out of flower, do not rely on leaflet size: pale-pink wood sorrel's are 4–16 mm long, suckling clover's about 3–12 mm. On most suckling clover leaves the middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the side ones. Pale-pink wood sorrel is eaten (see its own entry); suckling clover has no confirmed food record, so do not eat it.

summary.text:
Suckling clover (Trifolium dubium) is a small annual clover of the pea family (Fabaceae), native from Europe to the Caucasus and naturalised in New Zealand.
In New Zealand: North Island; South Island: common throughout; Stewart Island: disturbed lowland areas; Kermadec, Chatham and Campbell Islands. Naturalised from Europe to Caucasia, first recorded in 1869. Suckling clover is the most common of the 4 naturalised yellow-flowered clovers. Suckling clover is a troublesome lawn weed and is often an impurity in crop seed.
It is a winter annual: it mainly germinates in autumn, grows through the winter, flowers in spring, then sets seed and dies off as the soil dries out in early summer.

warnings: Suckling clover is not given here as food. It is not known to be poisonous, but no food use has been confirmed: plant databases record no edible uses, and its only record as food is one line in a list of edible turf weeds.

Its small yellow flower heads and three small, often notched leaflets look like least yellow sorrel's and creeping wood sorrel's, and it grows with them and with white clover in lawns. Check the flowers and the leaflet stalks before picking any of them (see the lookalikes).

sources: NZ Plant Conservation Network, 'Coprosma tenuicaulis' (paraphrased)
habitat.text: Swamps and boggy ground, poorly drained shrubland and forest beside streams and rivers, mostly in the lowlands and rarely in the mountains.

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to pick this plant. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.

identification.text:
Shrub up to about 3 m tall; branches slender, subdivaricate, usually more or less interlacing; branchlets slender, pubescent. Leaves on more or less winged slender pubescent petioles 3–5 mm long. Stipules small, triangular, subacute, more or less pubescent, ciliate, terminal tuft conspicuous. Lamina subcoriaceous, glabrous, orbicular-ovate, spathulate, obtuse, minutely apiculate, about 8–13 × 8–10 mm. Reticulations of veins evident on both surfaces. male in fascicles of 3–6; calyx 0; corolla funnelform, lobes more or less equal to tube, ovate, acute. female solitary or in axillary clusters of 2–4 along short branchlets; calyx-teeth minute; corolla funnelform, lobes ovate, acute, equal to or longer than tube. Drupe black, globose, 3–4 mm diameter
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]
In the field: the leaves have darker margins and a paler blotch in the middle of the upper surface; there is a small tuft of longer hairs (sometimes with a small dark tooth) on the hairy stem between each pair of leaf bases; the ripe fruit has dark reddish-black to black skin and dark purple flesh.

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Kanono's young twigs are hairless; swamp coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Karamū's young twigs are hairless; swamp coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Shining karamū's young twigs are hairless; swamp coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Those figures fit the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa; the North Island's wild subsp. minor has thinner, papery leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) on stalks about 10–18 mm long, and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long. Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Large-seeded coprosma's young twigs are hairless; swamp coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Hūpiro's young twigs are hairless; swamp coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Both are twiggy shrubs with wide-angled, interlacing branches and more or less hairy young twigs, so neither the branching nor the twig hairs separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

lookalikes.howToTell: Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Sand coprosma

habitat.text:
Lowland swamps and streamsides, forest or scrub.
It grows mostly in coastal and lowland forest beside streams and rivers on waterlogged ground, at the margins of swamps and on streamsides. It also grows in some montane and cloud forest in Northland (for example Tutamoe), the western Waikato (Pirongia, Taumatatotara and Tawarau) and the lower margins of Egmont National Park, where high rainfall and poor drainage let it establish on hill slopes, tablelands and karst.
Wetland status (NZPCN, from the national wetland plant list, Clarkson et al. 2021): obligate wetland — almost always in wetlands.

harvestEthics.text:
This species is Threatened (Nationally Vulnerable). Do not harvest it unless it is a life-or-death situation and you absolutely must eat it.
Myrtle rust, a fungal disease that only affects the myrtle family, to which this plant belongs, is in New Zealand. It shows as bright yellow to yellow-orange powdery pustules on young leaves, shoots, flowers or fruit, or as grey, fuzzy spore growth under the leaves. If you find it, don't touch it or collect samples, as this might spread the disease. Take clear photos, close up and of the whole plant, and report it on iNaturalist labelled as myrtle rust, noting the host plant. Wash your clothing, bag and shoes when you get home.

identification.text:
Tree to c. 12 m high, sometimes with pneumatophores; bark smooth, whitish or grey. Branchlets spreading, 4-angled. Petioles 5–10 mm long, slender. Lamina (1.5)–2.5–6 × 1–2.5 cm, usually elliptic, sometimes broadly elliptic, sinuate or undulate, shining. Cymes usually of 5–30 flowers, to c. 8 cm diameter. Pseudopedicels slender. Hypanthium 2–3 mm long at anthesis, obconic; calyx lobes very short and broad, persistent on fruit. Petals 2–3 mm diameter, orbicular, white, forming calyptrum in bud, caducous. Stamens 5–12–(15) mm long, white. Style shorter than the longest stamens. Ovary adnate to base of hypanthium. Fruit 10–15 mm diameter, subglobose, broad-ellipsoid or elliptic-ovoid, deep crimson, glossy. Seed 1, large.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Look for pale bark, sometimes upright breathing roots, pairs of yellowish-green, oval, pointed leaves that are glossy and often carry small galls and blisters, white brushy flowers in clusters, and red, blunt-tipped fruit. The single seed has a very hard coat covered in fibres.
Older trees can reach about 16 m, with a trunk up to 0.8 m across, often with knees at the base and, where the roots are exposed, orange-brown breathing roots standing up from the ground. The bark is pinkish grey, grey-brown or white and flakes off in soft or brittle, irregular pieces. The leaves are pale green underneath, with a strongly raised midrib.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: swamp maire's is deep crimson and glossy, 10–15 mm across, with its very short, broad calyx lobes still on the tip; lilly pilly's is pinkish mauve or white, usually 1–1.7 cm across (up to 3 cm), with a hollow at the tip where the calyx lobes have fallen. Swamp maire's white stamens are long, 5–12 mm (up to 15 mm), so its flowers look brushy; lilly pilly's stamens reach only about 3 mm. Lilly pilly's leaves are usually larger, 4–12 cm long (up to 15 cm) and 2–5 cm wide; swamp maire's are mostly 2.5–6 cm long and 1–2.5 cm wide, with wavy edges, so small lilly pilly leaves overlap them in size. Otherwise the leaves look much alike, thin, shiny, elliptic and in opposite pairs on both, so go by the fruit and flowers. With a hand lens, lilly pilly's anther lobes spread apart; swamp maire's anther sacs are usually parallel. Both have small white or whitish petals, about 2–3 mm, joined into a cap that falls, and lilly pilly sometimes grows with swamp maire in urban forest remnants, so place does not separate them. Lilly pilly's fruit is eaten too (see its page).

summary.text:
Syzygium maire, commonly known as the swamp maire, is an evergreen tree endemic to New Zealand. It is not related to other species called maire, which are in the genus Notelaea.
It grows in the North Island from Te Paki south, and locally in the South Island in Nelson and the Marlborough Sounds, to Rarangi near Blenheim. It is now often scarce or absent over large parts of its former range because swamp forest has been cleared.
It is ranked Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable (2023). Its status was raised to Nationally Critical in 2017 after myrtle rust arrived in New Zealand, and many populations survive only as remnants in partly drained farmland that was once riverside forest, where they are in slow terminal decline.
It is very susceptible to myrtle rust. It can be grown from seed, which germinates readily once the fruit has been soaked in water and the flesh left to rot off, or less reliably from cuttings. It does well in waterlogged ground in shade or sun, but it is frost tender and does not tolerate drought.

warnings: Lilly pilly, a weed tree with pinkish-mauve or white fruit, sometimes grows with swamp maire in urban forest remnants. Check the fruit colour and flowers to tell them apart (see the lookalikes).

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Usually in and around swamps, bogs, river banks, lakesides and in moist grassy areas, rarely in drier places such as coastal sands, up to 600 m in the North Island.
It also grows on the margins of lakes, ponds and wetlands and in wet pasture.
On New Zealand's national wetland plant list it is rated facultative: it grows as readily in wetlands as on dry ground.

identification.text:
Hairy perennial herb with short stout caudex and numerous adventitious roots. Leaves all radical, few to many in the rosette; petiole usually 1–20 cm long, often purple, sometimes very short and ill-defined with woolly tuft at base. Lamina about 2.5–30 × 7–8 cm, lanceolate, or obovate to broad-elliptic, hairy, especially beneath on the raised 5 or 7 main veins, entire or remotely dentate; base attenuate; apex obtuse. Scape about 5–60 cm long, more or less terete, densely hairy in upper part. Spike generally longer than 10 cm at maturity, narrow-cylindric. Bracts usually slightly shorter than sepals, ciliate, otherwise very similar to sepals. Sepals 2–3 mm long, broad-ovate, scarious except for central green or purple band, usually glabrous except for ciliate keel. Corolla tube equal to calyx; lobes 2.5–3 mm long, ovate, mostly soon curling involutely and forming a prominent, acute, erect, cone. Stamens glabrous, usually with small anthers and included (cleistogamous flowers), sometimes with large, long-exserted anthers (chasmogamous flowers). Style hairy, longer than corolla. Capsule 2.5–3.5 mm long, ovoid or ellipsoid-ovoid, 3-seeded. Seeds 1.8–2.2 mm long, ovoid-ellipsoid or oblong, generally deep olive green, sometimes brownish green or almost black. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
A hairy rosette of lance-shaped to broadly elliptic leaves, up to 30 cm long and 8 cm wide, tapering into the stalk, with five or seven raised parallel veins that are especially hairy underneath. The leaf stalks are often purple, sometimes with a woolly tuft at the base. The flower stalk, up to 60 cm tall, is round rather than ribbed and densely hairy near the top, and carries a narrow spike usually more than 10 cm long when mature. The petals curl inwards into small, pointed, upright cones, and the stamens are usually hidden inside. It flowers from November to January.

lookalikes.howToTell: Greater plantain's large leaves are oval to almost round, up to 16 cm wide, with a squared-off or heart-shaped base; swamp plantain's are lance-shaped to broadly elliptic, up to 8 cm wide, tapering into an often purple stalk. Small greater plantains can have narrower, tapering leaves, so look at the flowers: greater plantain's petals are 1–1.3 mm and bent back, with long stamens sticking out; swamp plantain's curl up into a small, pointed, upright cone and its stamens are usually hidden. Both can have fine hairs on the veins underneath, both have an unribbed flower stalk, and their spikes overlap in length, so none of those separates them.
lookalikes.name: Greater plantain

lookalikes.howToTell: Narrow-leaved plantain's flower stalk is strongly ribbed and carries a short, dense head, to about 6 cm, ringed with protruding stamens; swamp plantain's stalk is round, not ribbed, and densely hairy near the top, with a narrow spike usually more than 10 cm long when mature, its petals curled into small, pointed, upright cones and its stamens usually hidden. Narrow-leaved plantain flowers from July to April, swamp plantain only from November to January. Leaf widths overlap — 0.5–4.8 cm in narrow-leaved plantain, up to 8 cm in swamp plantain — and both have parallel veins, so leaves alone do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Narrow-leaved plantain

lookalikes.howToTell: Water plantain grows in or at the edge of water and is hairless. Its oval leaves, 8–23 cm long with a rounded or slightly heart-shaped base, stand upright on long, D-shaped stalks and die back over winter; swamp plantain's are lance-shaped to broadly elliptic, hairy on the raised veins underneath, and taper into the stalk. From November to February water plantain sends up a branched flower stalk up to about 1 m tall, with whorls of branches and many pale lilac or white, three-petalled flowers up to 1 cm across; swamp plantain's tiny flowers are packed into a dense, unbranched spike. Both grow in swamps and wet ground, so where it grows does not separate them. Water plantain is poisonous raw.
lookalikes.name: Water plantain

summary.text:
Swamp plantain (Plantago australis) is a plantain from southern North America and Central and South America, sometimes called Mexican plantain.
It was first recorded in New Zealand from the Waikato and is dated here from 1883, when Cheeseman recorded it by mistake as P. virginica, a related species with only 2-seeded capsules. By 1940 Allan still knew it only as an occasional plant of moist places in the northern half of the North Island, under the name P. hirtella. It probably arrived as a seed or soil contaminant; its seeds are spread by water, animals and machinery, and it is not controlled here. It grows from the North Cape peninsula southwards and on Stewart Island, but is usually rare in the east. Hoary plantain (P. media), once reported from damp places in both main islands, has never been confirmed by a New Zealand specimen and may have been swamp plantain recorded in error.

identification.text:
Lobularia maritima grows to 5–30 cm tall by 20–30 cm broad. The stem is very branched, with dense clusters of small flowers. The leaves are 1–4 cm long and 3–5 mm, broad, alternate, sessile, quite hairy, oval to lanceolate, with an entire margin. 
The flowers are about 5 millimetres in diameter, sweet-smelling, with an aroma similar to that of honey, with four white rounded petals (or pink, rose-red, violet. yellow and lilac) and four sepals. The six stamens have yellow anthers. The flowers are produced throughout the growing season, or year-round in areas free of frost. They are pollinated by insects (entomophily) as its sweet honey-like fragrance is attractive to bees, flower flies, stingless wasps and butterflies. The fruits are numerous elongated seedpods rather hairy, oval to rounded, each containing two seeds. The dispersal of seed is affected by the wind (anemochory).
Usually perennial, rarely annual. Stems decumbent to ascending, hairy, leafy, branched below, 10–30–(45) cm tall. Leaves entire, hairy, linear-lanceolate to lanceolate, subacute, 12–30 × 2–3–(4) mm. Racemes 4–15 cm long; flowers crowded in globose heads; pedicels spreading, hairy, 6–7 mm long. Sepals hairy, 1.5–2 × 0.5–0.8 mm. Petals glabrous, entire, usually white, rarely purple, 2.5–3 × 1.5–2 mm. Silicle obovate, subacute, slightly inflated, 3–4 × 1.5–2.5 mm; valves membranous, glabrous or sparsely hairy. Style about 0.6 mm long. Seeds brown, ovoid, compressed, very narrowly winged, about 1.2 × 1 mm, 1 per locule.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Sweet alyssum is usually perennial, with stems lying down to ascending and branched from below, narrow untoothed leaves 12–30 × 2–3 (4) mm, flowers crowded in rounded heads, and a small, slightly inflated, oval pod 3–4 × 1.5–2.5 mm. Shepherd's purse is an erect annual; its lower leaves are very variable, unlobed to deeply lobed and usually shallowly toothed, its upper leaves clasp the stem with arrow-shaped lobes at the base, and its pod is flat, notched and triangular, 5–10 × 4–7 mm. White flowers of similar size do not separate them (sweet alyssum petals 2.5–3 mm, usually white, rarely purple; shepherd's purse petals 2–2.5 mm, white, sometimes missing). Shepherd's purse young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.

preparation.text: Use the young leaves, stems and flowers to flavour salads or any dish where pungency is wanted; the flowers can also be candied. Eat the seed pods raw while still soft and green, in salads in place of radish or with meats in place of horseradish. Cook the leaves as mustard greens.

summary.text:
Lobularia maritima (syn. Alyssum maritimum) is a species of low-growing flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.
This plant is native to the Mediterranean Basin and the Macaronesia region: (Canary Islands, Madeira, Cape Verde). It is widely naturalized elsewhere in the temperate world, including the United States. There is an endemic subspecies in the local flora of the Columbretes Islands of the western Mediterranean.
In New Zealand it is naturalised in the North and South Islands. It is native to southern Europe and was first recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1840.
This species has also been referred to in New Zealand as Alyssum maritimum and as Koniga maritima.
Linnaeus first named it Clypeola maritima in 1753; Desvaux moved it to Lobularia in 1814.
It is also known as alyssum and sweet Alice.
The name of the species maritima refers to its preferred coastal habitat.
Te Papa holds a specimen collected in December 2021 from a roadside south of Featherston, at Waiorongomai (SP113633). Manaaki Whenua's herbarium has about 47 databased New Zealand records: Canterbury 9, Nelson 6, Wellington 6, Hawke's Bay 5, one each from North Auckland, Taranaki, Otago and Southland, and 17 not placed in a region.

warnings: Sweet alyssum is a common bedding plant; plants in flower beds may have been sprayed with pesticides, so ask the owner before picking.
The food evidence is thin: short notes on its use as a flavouring and as raw green pods, with no record of eating it in quantity.

identification.text:
Branched, evergreen shrub to small tree up to 6 m high; twigs sericeous, particularly when young, rounded and ribbed. Leaves sericeous on both surfaces but more densely below, petiolate, 3-foliolate; leaflets shortly petiolulate, elliptic to obovate, acute and shortly mucronate, 5–40 × 3–12 mm; terminal leaflet longer than lateral leaflets; stipules triangular, up to 2 mm long. Inflorescences elongate, with axis 10–130 mm long, terminal, racemose, 10–30–(40)-flowered; pedicels 2–6 mm long. Calyx densely hairy, bilabiate; upper lip deeply 2-fid; lower lip shortly 3-lobed. Corolla yellow, 13–16–(18) mm long; standard glabrous or somewhat hairy about midvein and apex. Pod densely villous, oblong, 3–10-seeded, 20–40 mm long; seeds black, orbicular and flattened, about 3 mm diameter.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Teline stenopetala (Webb & Berthel.) Webb & Berthel.]
The leaflets are coated with fine silky, silvery hairs, and the flowers are strongly scented.
It flowers from July to April. Its silky leaves give the shrub a silvery look.

lookalikes.howToTell: Sweet broom's flowers are in elongated racemes at the ends of the shoots, 10–30 or more on a stalk 10–130 mm long, and are 13–18 mm long; Montpellier broom's are in clusters of 4–7 at the ends of short side branches, on a stalk under 10 mm long, and are 9–13 mm long. Sweet broom can grow into a small tree up to 6 m high; Montpellier broom is a shrub up to 2.5 m. Both have leaves of three leaflets, and their hairiness overlaps, so leaves do not separate them. Plants with shorter, fewer-flowered racemes (stalk about 10–30 mm) are naturalised here; they may be the garden hybrid Cytisus × spachianus or hybrids between the two, and in hybrids the cluster stalk can reach about 4 cm, so a plant in between cannot be named from its flowers. Neither is eaten.
lookalikes.name: French broom

lookalikes.howToTell: Gorse is sharply spiny: on a grown plant the leaves are reduced to spines, the main ones rigid, furrowed and 15–30 mm long. Sweet broom has no spines, and its leaves have three silky leaflets all its life. Gorse's flowers are single, 13–20 mm long; sweet broom's are 13–18 mm long, 10–30 or more together in elongated racemes at the ends of the shoots. Gorse seedlings have leaves of three hairy leaflets, so a seedling's leaves do not separate it from broom.
lookalikes.name: Gorse

lookalikes.howToTell: Scotch broom's twigs are green and more or less five-angled, it loses its leaves, and its flowers are single or paired in the leaf angles, with a hairless calyx; its pods are black, 15–60 mm long, hairy only along the edges. Sweet broom's twigs are rounded and ribbed, it is evergreen, and its flowers are 10–30 or more together in elongated racemes at the ends of the shoots, with a densely hairy calyx; its pods are densely hairy all over, 20–40 mm long. Flower length overlaps (Scotch broom 16–25 mm, sweet broom 13–18 mm) and does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Scotch broom
