summary.text:
Genista stenopetala, the sweet broom, Easter broom or leafy broom (syn. Genista spachiana, Cytisus spachianus), is a species of flowering plant in the legume family Fabaceae, native to the Canary Islands, on La Palma and Tenerife.
In New Zealand: North Island — Auckland City, Gisborne City, New Plymouth, Palmerston North, Wellington City and coastal south-west Wellington Province; South Island — Tai Tapu (Canterbury) and Otago Peninsula; naturalised by 1940. T. stenopetala is only locally established as a garden escape. It has been previously known in New Zealand as Cytisus stenopetalus.
Some naturalised plants with shorter, fewer-flowered racemes (the axis about 10–30 mm long), but otherwise similar to T. stenopetala, are probably of horticultural origin and may be the plant usually called Cytisus × spachianus. Although these naturalised plants exactly match descriptions of the horticultural hybrid, it also seems possible that they are hybrids between T. monspessulana and T. stenopetala; certainly T. stenopetala is one of the parents, and in some areas T. stenopetala appears to intergrade with the hybrid.
Under the name Genista × spachiana, it has won the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.
The name stenopetala means 'with narrow petals', from the Greek stenos (narrow) and petalum (petal); Genista comes from the ancient Latin name for this plant.
Allan's 1940 handbook of New Zealand's naturalised plants recorded it as Cytisus stenopetalus and Cytisus maderensis; Cytisus racemosus is another old name for it.
Herbarium specimens of it are also held from the Marlborough, Westland and Southland land districts.
In New South Wales it is called Madeira broom; it is grown as an ornamental there and sometimes runs wild around Sydney, and it is naturalised in Victoria and South Australia too.

warnings: Parts of the plant are poisonous if eaten.
Montpellier broom, a close relative it hybridises with, carries quinolizidine alkaloids in its foliage and seeds, and its flowers, and perhaps all its parts, are toxic.

identification.text:
Long narrow leaves with sharply toothed edges. Nuts sit inside a dense casing covered in fine, sharp, needle-like spines — like a sea urchin — usually two or three flattened glossy brown nuts per case, each with a pointed tip and a tassel.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): sweet chestnut is distinguished by the erect male catkins and prickly cupule which completely encloses the fruit. The oblong-lanceolate, boldly toothed leaves are 15–32 cm long and 5–10 cm broad (Wikipedia).

lookalikes.howToTell: Horse chestnut has hand-shaped leaves of five to seven leaflets spreading from one stalk; sweet chestnut's leaves are single, long and boldly toothed. Horse chestnut's case has short, more widely spaced spikes rather than sweet chestnut's many long, fine spines, and usually holds one round, glossy, dark brown seed — a conker — with a large pale scar, sometimes two; sweet chestnut's usually holds two or more nuts with a tufted tip. Do not rely on nut count alone, because some sweet chestnut varieties bear a single nut. Raw horse chestnut seeds are toxic, with several toxic compounds including aesculin, and cause sickness when eaten.

preparation.text: Score each nut, then roast or boil. Never eat raw in quantity — the tannins are harsh.

recipes.method: Fresh sweet chestnuts; melted butter; salt. Heat the oven to 220 °C. Prick or score each shell so the nuts cannot burst, spread them on a baking tray and flick a few drops of water over them with your fingers. Roast on the bottom shelf for 10 minutes, then turn them so they roast evenly and carry on until cooked, when the kernel peels away easily. Peel, dip in melted butter and salt to taste.
recipes.title: Roasted sweet chestnuts

recipes.method: Fresh sweet chestnuts; a steamer; a coarse sieve; 500 g resealable freezer bags. Leave freshly gathered nuts somewhere dry for a few days to sweeten. On a chopping board, cut off the base and brown skin of each nut with a sharp knife, throwing out any that show signs of rot. Steam them for about 20 minutes. While they are hot, push them a few at a time through a coarse sieve with the end of a rolling pin to remove the brown inner skin; if they are very hard to push through, they need more steaming. The sieving dries them to a breadcrumb-like texture. Pack into 500 g resealable bags and freeze, and thaw before baking or cooking. Frozen processed chestnuts are best used within six months, and a 500 g bag is enough for a couple of meals for two.
recipes.title: Chestnut flour

recipes.method: Written for chestnuts in Britain; the page does not name the species. Serves 4. 3 tbsp olive oil, plus extra to finish; 15 g butter; 1 medium onion, chopped; 6 sage leaves, roughly chopped, plus extra to finish; 1 small garlic clove, finely chopped; 1 litre vegetable stock; 400 g cooked, peeled chestnuts; 100 ml crème fraîche; sea salt and black pepper. Warm 1 tbsp of the oil with the butter over medium-low heat and soften the onion for about 10 minutes until translucent. Stir in the sage and garlic for a minute. Add the stock and all but a handful of the chestnuts, season, raise the heat and simmer for 15 minutes, stirring now and then. Cool slightly and blend until very smooth. Return to the pan, stir in the crème fraîche, adjust the seasoning and warm through gently without letting it boil. Slice the reserved chestnuts. Fry the extra sage leaves in the remaining oil over medium heat for a few seconds until crisp and drain on paper towels. Serve topped with the sliced chestnuts and crisp sage, a trickle of olive oil and plenty of black pepper. The author notes fresh chestnuts work if blanched, peeled and simmered until tender first.
recipes.title: Chestnut soup

recipes.method: Written for chickweed, with sweet chestnuts. Makes 2. Boil chestnuts in water for 10 minutes, drain them and let them cool a little, then halve them and scoop out the flesh; process it to a fine flour. Mash a heaped 125 ml (½ cup) of this chestnut flour with ½ avocado and a little salt. Spread it on 2 nori sheets, add fenugreek sprouts and a bunch of chickweed, and roll them up.
recipes.title: Chickweed and chestnut nori wraps

summary.text: Worth the effort in autumn — but its ornamental namesake is toxic and far more commonly planted.

warnings: Check the case: sweet chestnut's has numerous long, fine spines; horse chestnut's has short, more widely spaced spikes and usually holds one round conker. Horse chestnuts are poisonous.
Many nuts in old plantings are grub-infested. Float them in water and discard any that float.
Chestnuts are tree nuts, and a tree nut allergy can cause severe reactions.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous perennial; aerial stems 0. Leaves all rosulate, with fine hairs above and beneath, (2)–4–8 × (2)–3–7 cm, broadly ovate-cordate, obtuse to subacute, with longer than 15 crenations each side; stipules linear to lanceolate, dentate, 1–2 cm long; petiole (3)–5–10–(20) cm long, with deflexed hairs. Peduncles erect, glabrous or hairy; bracts linear-acuminate, dentate, 5–10 mm long. Flowers 1.5–2.5 mm diameter. Sepals narrowly oblong, subacute to obtuse, 4–6 mm long; appendages 1–2 mm long. Petals violet or white or pink, exceeding sepals, the lateral bearded; spur 3–5 mm long, longer than sepal appendages. Style not geniculate at base, 2.5 mm long; stigma beaked. Capsule globose, hairy, about 1 cm long. Seeds obovoid, pale brown, 2.5 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

recipes.method: The author's greens and flowers were sweet violet leaves and flowers, chickweed, parsley, plantain, and dandelion leaves and flowers (the page does not say which plantain). A handful of chickweed; 2 sprigs of parsley; 1 plantain leaf; 2 dandelion leaves; the petals of 1 rose; 6 dandelion flowers; 6 violet flowers, keeping 2 to decorate; 7 violet leaves; 1 apple (whole if organic, otherwise peeled and cored); 1 banana; 5 ml (1 tsp) chia seeds; 5 ml (1 tsp) pumpkin seeds; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk, or yoghurt; 250 ml (1 cup) water, or water kefir, kombucha or rejuvelac. Blend the greens, flowers and liquid until smooth, then add the fruit and seeds and blend again. Pour it into glasses and decorate with the kept flowers.

summary.text:
Viola odorata is a species of flowering plant in the family Violaceae.
Viola odorata is native to Europe south of Scandinavia, northwest Africa (Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia), Macaronesia, the Caucasus, Western Asia, and Kazakhstan. It has been introduced to the Americas, Scandinavia, southern and eastern Asia, Australia, and New Zealand.

identification.text:
Sweet William grows in the mountains of southern Europe from the Pyrenees east to the Carpathians and the Balkans, with a variety disjunct in northeastern China, Korea, and southeasternmost Russia. It grows to 13–92 cm tall (depending on the variety), with green to glaucous blue-green tapered leaves 4–10 cm long and 1–2 cm broad. The flowers are produced in a dense cluster of up to 30 at the top of the stems (known as an umbel) and have a spicy, clove-like scent; Each flower is 2–3 cm in diameter, with five petals with serrated edges.
There are two varieties:

Dianthus barbatus var. barbatus. Southern Europe. Leaves broader, up to 2 cm broad.
Dianthus barbatus var. asiaticus Nakai. Northeastern Asia. Leaves slenderer, not over 1 cm broad.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand: waste land and scrubland, especially coastal areas; also shrubland, dry banks and riverbeds. It invades short tussockland, dry fernland and bare land, especially in warmer areas.
In the Auckland region it grows in open and disturbed places, coastal dunes, along streams and rivers, on dry banks and roadsides, in scrub and open forest, on waste land and in wetlands. It also invades young pine plantations and swamps such as the Kaimaumau swamps in Northland.
Planted, it grows in full sun in well-drained soil, does well in sandy, coastal and poor soils, and is drought tolerant once established; long wet spells reduce its vigour.

identification.text:
Shrub or small tree; twigs sharply angled, glabrous or sparsely hairy. Leaves reduced to phyllodes, alternate; phyllodes glabrous, narrowly elliptic to obovate, symmetric or slightly curved, acute or obtuse and usually shortly mucronate, entire, (60)–80–130 × 6–22 mm, with 2–(4) prominent veins; stipules lanceolate, 1–3 mm long, not always conspicuous in mature plants. Flowers 4-merous and solitary but closely packed in axillary, pale to golden yellow, cylindric spikes; spikes shorter than or equal to leaves. Pod glabrous or sparsely hairy, straight or slightly curved, 80–120 × about 4 mm; aril not much folded, thickened and cup-shaped below seed. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Racosperma longifolium (Andrews) Mart.]
Subspecies sophorae is distinguished by its broader phyllodes (typically only 3–4 times as long as wide), dark reddish brown, extremely contorted pods, and larger seeds.
Told from blackwood (Acacia melanoxylon) by its flowers in cylindrical spikes (blackwood's are in round heads) and, at fruiting, by the slightly folded, cup-shaped aril of the seed (blackwood's aril is large and folded).

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers: Sydney golden wattle's are pale to golden yellow, in cylindrical spikes; blackwood's are pale creamy yellow, in round heads. At fruiting, look at the seed: Sydney golden wattle's aril is not much folded, thickened and cup-shaped below the seed; blackwood's is large, pink to crimson or red, encircling and enfolding the seed. Sydney golden wattle's pods are straight or slightly curved, blackwood's twisted or spiralled, but Sydney golden wattle's coastal subspecies sophorae has extremely contorted pods, so pod shape does not always separate them. The leaves do not separate them: both have narrow, flat phyllodes with several prominent veins, Sydney golden wattle's (60)–80–130 × 6–22 mm with 2–4 veins, blackwood's (40)–60–100 × 8–20 mm with 3–4. Both grow in waste places, often near the coast. Blackwood's seeds and flowers are eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Blackwood

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the width of the phyllodes (the leaves). Sydney golden wattle's are narrowly elliptic to obovate, 6–22 mm wide, and its coastal subspecies sophorae has broader ones still; gossamer wattle's are linear, 3–8 mm wide (up to 10 mm). A phyllode wider than 10 mm is Sydney golden wattle and one narrower than 6 mm is gossamer wattle; between 6 and 10 mm use the other signs. Sydney golden wattle's phyllodes are 80–130 mm long (from 60 mm), gossamer wattle's 40–80 mm (30–120 mm at the extremes), so length only helps at the ends of the ranges. Sydney golden wattle's twigs are hairless or sparsely hairy; gossamer wattle's can be densely hairy. Golden-yellow spikes point to Sydney golden wattle; gossamer wattle's are medium to pale yellow, and both can be pale. Sydney golden wattle's pods are 80–120 mm long, straight or slightly curved, and subspecies sophorae's are dark reddish brown and extremely contorted; gossamer wattle's are 50–100 mm and somewhat curved. What does not separate them: both are shrubs or small trees with sharply angled twigs, phyllodes with 2–4 prominent veins, 4-merous flowers in cylindric spikes no longer than the phyllodes, pods about 4 mm wide, and the same cup-shaped aril below the seed, and both flower in late winter (Sydney golden wattle July–August, gossamer wattle August–September). Gossamer wattle's record as food is thin, so it is not given as food here.

summary.text:
Sydney golden wattle (Acacia longifolia) is a shrub or small tree, growing up to 8–10 m tall, of the pea family (Fabaceae), native to eastern Australia and naturalised in New Zealand.
In New Zealand: North Island: established locally in Northland, especially near Kaitaia, locally established in Auckland City and also reported for Ruakura (Hamilton), and Wellington City; South Island: established at Motueka Inlet, Nelson. Naturalised from eastern Australia, first recorded in 1897. Two subspecies are fully naturalised: subsp. longifolia and subsp. sophorae (coastal wattle).
It was brought here as an ornamental and to stabilise sand dunes, and is still sold by New Zealand nurseries as a fast-growing screening and shelter tree for coastal gardens.
It produces huge quantities of seed, which may stay viable for about 50 years, and tolerates frost, extended dry periods and salt spray. It is on the Department of Conservation's list of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024, under sustained control in Northland, Auckland and the Bay of Plenty, and an organism of interest in the Chatham Islands.
Its seeds are spread by wind, gravity and water, and in moved soil from waste places, old hedges and roadsides. It forms dense stands that keep native plants from establishing, threatening dune and wetland ecosystems, and is a problem in young pine plantations and in swamps such as the Kaimaumau swamps in Northland. As a nitrogen fixer it alters soils and nutrient cycling, harms plant communities of low-fertility ground (ferns, orchids, kauri) and may help other exotic plants invade.
Since 1 September 2021 Auckland Council's rules ban breeding, distributing, releasing, selling or planting it in the Auckland region (moving an existing plant within the same property is allowed), and a plant put in against the rules must be destroyed if an authorised person directs it.
A bud-galling wasp, Trichilogaster acaciaelongifoliae, was approved as a biological control in November 2022 and first released that year; its eggs, laid in flower and shoot buds, make large galls form instead of flowers and new shoots. Early signs are that it has established at the first release sites in Manawatū–Whanganui.
The common name Sydney golden wattle is also applied to Acacia pycnantha, which is cultivated in New Zealand but not naturalised.

warnings: Many wattles are considered poisonous, and 13 wattle species are naturalised in New Zealand. Be sure of the species before eating any wattle seed: blackwood (Acacia melanoxylon) has similar leaves, and gossamer wattle (Acacia floribunda) is also similar (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
Deciduous, small, spreading tree, 3–8 m high when mature (narrow in outline with more or less erect branches when young), not armed; trunk short. Lf petiole 12–20 mm long, glabrous; blade thin, obovate to broadly elliptic, (50)–60–130–(170) × 20–60–(90) mm, cuspidate, rounded or occasionally obtuse at base, with both surfaces glabrous with major veins obvious, serrulate with teeth acute; stipules short, triangular, laciniate, deciduous. Flowers in umbel-like clusters of (1)–2–3–(5), on very short shoots which elongate after anthesis, not fragrant, pendent; pedicels (8)–12–25 mm long, glabrous. Hypanthium narrowly campanulate; sepals triangular, 3–6 mm long, acute, magenta to dark deep red, glabrous, shining, at first erect but becoming spreading or reflexed. Petals 5, (5)–6–12 mm diameter, the lower parts remaining semi-erect and corolla appearing more or less campanulate; upper portion eventually spreading, more or less broadly elliptic-ovate to orbicular, narrowly emarginate, deep pink to rose-magenta. Stamens slightly shorter than to just longer than corolla; filaments flushed magenta to crimson. Fruit up to 12 × 10 mm, ovoid, ellipsoid or ovoid-oblong, glabrous, glossy scarlet; stone smooth. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Japanese cherry's petals more or less spread open and are white or pink-flushed to rose, its sepals greenish to magenta; Taiwan cherry's flowers are more or less bell-shaped, the lower part of each petal staying semi-erect while the upper part eventually spreads, deep pink to rose-magenta, with magenta to dark deep red sepals. The bell-shaped flower is what sets Taiwan cherry apart. Fruit: Japanese cherry's fruit is round, black-purple and bitter, under 15 mm across; Taiwan cherry's glossy scarlet and egg-shaped to ellipsoid, up to 12 × 10 mm. Japanese cherry fruit can also be red or black, so a red cherry is not proof of Taiwan cherry. Leaf teeth: Japanese cherry's end in a bristle and are often gland-tipped; Taiwan cherry's are pointed. Flowering overlaps (Taiwan cherry July to September, Japanese cherry August to October), as do leaf size and leaf-stalk and flower-stalk lengths; neither has spines.
lookalikes.name: Japanese cherry

lookalikes.howToTell: Cherry laurel is evergreen, with leathery leaves shining above and only a few distant, short teeth toward the tip; Taiwan cherry is deciduous, with thin leaves finely and sharply toothed along the edge. Cherry laurel's flowers are greenish white to cream, 20–35 on an erect spike 80–120 mm long (August–September); Taiwan cherry's are bell-shaped, deep pink to rose-magenta, and hang in clusters of 1–5 (July–September). Cherry laurel's fruit is dark purple, about 10 mm long, very bitter, and hangs in grape-like clusters along the spike; Taiwan cherry's is glossy scarlet, up to 12 × 10 mm. The fruits are of similar size, and cherry laurel fruits from November to January, when Taiwan cherry also fruits, so check the leaves and how the fruit is borne, not size. Cherry laurel's leaves and seeds release cyanide: do not eat any part of it.
lookalikes.name: Cherry laurel

summary.text:
Prunus campanulata is a species of cherry native to Japan, Taiwan, southern and eastern China (Guangxi, Guangdong, Hainan, Hunan, Fujian, and Zhejiang), and Vietnam.
The tree is an invasive plant species in some areas of New Zealand.

warnings: The plant (especially the seed and young shoots) contains cyanogenic glycosides, especially amygdalin and prunasin. When ingested, these compounds break down in the digestive tract to release cyanide.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Some regions rank it as more at risk. In the Auckland region (Regionally Declining), take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to 8 m tall, depressed to prostrate when very strongly insolated; branches stout, bark light brown; branchlets pubescent when young. Leaves on stout glabrous petioles 8–16 mm long. Stipules broad-triangular, subacute to subtruncate, glabrous; denticles several, conspicuous, central one prominent. Lamina thick, subfleshy, very glossy, dark green above, paler below; broad-oblong to broadly ovate-oblong, rounded to truncate to retuse or emarginate, sometimes apiculate; about 6–8 × 4–5 cm (shade leaves); 2–3 × 1·5–2 cm (sun leaves); margins recurved, sometimes inrolled. Reticulations evident above and below. Flowers in compound clusters on branched peduncles. male many per cluster; calyx-teeth minute; corolla funnelform, lobes 4–5, acute, more or less equal to tube. female usually 3 per cluster; calyx-teeth short, obtuse; corolla subfunnelform, about 5 mm long, lobes acute or obtuse, shorter than tube; stigmas stout. Drupe orange-red, depressed-obovoid, about 10 × 8 mm.
[From: Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Kanono's young twigs are hairless; Taupata's are hairy. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Karamū's young twigs are hairless; Taupata's are hairy. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Shining karamū's young twigs are hairless; Taupata's are hairy. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Those figures fit the Three Kings subsp. macrocarpa; the North Island's wild subsp. minor has thinner, papery leaves 45–90 × 35–50 mm (up to 140 × 100 mm) on stalks about 10–18 mm long, and yellowish to orange fruit 5–10 mm long. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Large-seeded coprosma's young twigs are hairless; Taupata's are hairy. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Both can have a rounded or notched leaf tip, so the tip does not separate them; taupata's leaf is very glossy, māmāngi's not or only slightly glossy. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Hūpiro's young twigs are hairless; Taupata's are hairy. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Swamp coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Hybrids between taupata and sand coprosma are common (Coprosma ×kirkii), so plants in between exist; if a plant fits neither description, do not use this card. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Sand coprosma

Fruiting counts 86 53 41 28 5 3 1 3 5 21 50 62; ripe photos 2/6 2/6 4/6 5/6 2/5 2/3 0.5/1 1/3 0/5 1/6 0/6 0/6. Estimated ripe Jan ≈29, Feb ≈26, Mar ≈27, Apr ≈23, then ≤3; Nov–Dec fruit is all green. summary.text:
Coprosma repens is a species of flowering shrub or small tree of the genus Coprosma, in the family Rubiaceae, native to New Zealand.
The species is native to the North Island, South Island and Three Kings Islands in New Zealand.
In Australia, it has become naturalised in coastal areas of Victoria, New South Wales, South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania, and it is now classified as an environmental weed.

habitat.text: Found on the ground under beech (Nothofagus), in beech forest, singly or in groups. Beech forest is the whole of its recorded habitat.

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to pick this mushroom. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.

identification.text: Cap 4–7.5 cm across, convex at first and sinking in the centre as it matures, and moderately to heavily sticky, especially when wet. Its ground colour is a muted orange-brown, sometimes closer to a drab ochre, and it is banded in concentric zones of purplish grey or reddish brown. Gills thin and crowded, running a little way down the stem, pale ochre with a pink tint. Stem 2–4 cm long and 1–1.8 cm thick, even or tapering towards the base, pale orange-cream to yellowish cream, often with a faint violet tint. Flesh brownish white, firm, and unchanging where cut. The milk is white and viscid, it does not change colour in the air, and it dries cream — this is the character that separates it from saffron milk cap, whose latex is carrot-orange. The gills taste slightly acrid, the flesh is mild, and there is no distinctive smell. The spore print is creamy-white.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white, sticky and unchanging, drying cream. Both species carry concentric bands on the cap, so zoning does not separate them. Saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine, this one under beech.
lookalikes.name: Saffron milk cap / Pine mushroom

Identification, habitat and summary: Manaaki Whenua Landcare Research, Virtual Mycota, 'Lactarius tawai' — biostatus 'Present in region - Indigenous. Endemic', and the morphological description, attributed to McNabb, R.F.R. (1971), 'The Russulaceae of New Zealand. 1. Lactarius', New Zealand Journal of Botany 9(1): 46–66. McNabb's text is still in copyright, so every fact here is restated and nothing is quoted. Checked 06/10/2026. https://virtualmycota.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/vM_Species_Details.aspx?pk=5190

The zonate-cap claim, and its limit. McNabb (1971), via the Virtual Mycota page above, calls this 'the only species found in New Zealand with a zonate pileus' — which holds for the native species he described. Three introduced milk caps with banded caps are on the iNaturalist NZ list now (Lactarius deliciosus, L. quietus, L. blennius), so a banded cap no longer separates this one. Checked 06/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/observations?taxon_id=54597&place_id=6803&view=species
Edibility: nothing published. McNabb's description records the taste (gills slightly acrid, flesh mild) and says nothing about edibility, and no later source does either. Checked 06/10/2026.

Season: iNaturalist NZ observations of 'Lactarius tawai' in New Zealand by month of year — 51 research-grade records, January to May carrying every month at or above a quarter of the April peak. The two December records fall below that, so December is not listed. Checked 06/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/taxa/382885

Habitat (the structured category only — the habitat prose is still blocked). The holotype agrees: collected under Nothofagus solandri at Whakapapaiti Stream, Tongariro National Park, 02/05/1967, PDD 26387. Beech forest is the whole of the habitat, so the category is forest. summary.text: This is a mushroom endemic to Aotearoa New Zealand. Whether it can be eaten has never been recorded.

sources: Bart Acres, 'Species Spotlight: Tawaka Mushrooms', MycoLogic (restated)
Wikipedia, 'Cyclocybe parasitica' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
SporeShift Mushrooms, 'Tawaka Mushroom Grain Spawn' (restated)
edibleParts.text: Caps and stems. Pick them when the veil is just about to drop or has just dropped, for the best flavour and texture. The stems are fibrous, more so in older mushrooms, and some people find them stringy.

sources: Biota of New Zealand, 'Cyclocybe parasitica' (Landcare Research): Stevenson 1982 and Gadgil 2005 descriptions (restated)
Bart Acres, 'Species Spotlight: Tawaka Mushrooms', MycoLogic (restated)
Wikipedia, 'Cyclocybe parasitica' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text: On the trunks, branches and logs of living and dead broadleaved trees, often from a wound, a hollow, a crevice or the ring-shaped scar where a branch has come off, at any height: look up as well as down. Native hosts include tawa, taraire, māhoe, houhere (lacebark), mānatu (ribbonwood), kānuka, karaka, tītoki, kohekohe, pōhutukawa, pukatea, putaputawētā, kawakawa and beech; introduced hosts include poplar, willow, oak, elm, ash, box elder, magnolia, rhododendron and coral tree, so it turns up in parks and street trees as well as native bush. It is seldom, if ever, on conifers. Recorded from Northland to Canterbury and found throughout the country.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

sources: Biota of New Zealand, 'Cyclocybe parasitica' (Landcare Research): Stevenson 1982 and Gadgil 2005 descriptions (restated)
Bart Acres, 'Species Spotlight: Tawaka Mushrooms', MycoLogic (restated)
Wikipedia, 'Cyclocybe parasitica' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
Large mushrooms, usually in clusters but sometimes single, growing out of trees. The cap is 5–25 cm across, flat-domed like a hamburger bun, pale buff to tawny brown and darker at the centre, velvety and dry when young, becoming smooth and leathery, often cracking as it dries. The flesh is white and firm. The gills are attached to the stem, moderately crowded, buff to clay or milky brown with a distinct white edge that later stains brown with spores; they look pinkish to dark brown. The stem is 8–20 cm long and 1–2 cm thick, tough and fibrous, white to pale buff above the ring and darker brown below, lined or with small dark speckles or flat scales. A thick veil stays pressed against the gills until the cap is well open, then falls free as a large, pleated ring high on the stem. The spore print is dark chocolate to cigar brown; the spores often dust the ring, the stem and the caps of lower mushrooms in a cluster. The smell has been described both as nutty, like yeast, and as strong and sour.

Similar species
The spectacular rustgill (Gymnopilus junonius) is more orange, with yellow flesh and a rusty brown spore print.

preparation.text: Cook it for a good while rather than flash-frying it, so the texture softens and the edges turn golden brown. To sauté, cook the mushrooms, sliced, halved or whole, on their own in a pan over medium-high heat with a little oil or butter and a pinch or two of salt to draw out their water. Once that water has cooked off, add a splash of wine or water if the pan gets dry; add garlic, herbs and more butter or olive oil near the end so they don't burn. Use it as you would a portobello: on toast, pizza, in pasta, risotto, soups, stews, gravies, pies and lasagne. Minced, it makes vegetarian sausages and burger patties, or can be mixed into meat ones; the stems can be pulled apart for a chicken-like texture.

recipes.method: Written for pioppino (Cyclocybe aegerita), tawaka's northern relative. About 500 ml (2 cups) of mushrooms; 3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil; 2 shallots, diced; 2 garlic cloves, minced; salt and black pepper; 60 ml dry white wine; juice of ½ lemon; a small handful (about 15 g) of flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped. Brush or wipe the mushrooms clean, cut the caps from the stems and slice both into bite-sized pieces. Warm the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat, add the shallots and garlic and cook for 1–2 minutes until fragrant. Add the mushrooms, stir to coat them in the oil and season. Sauté, stirring now and then, until tender and golden brown, about 4–6 minutes. Add the wine and lemon juice and keep cooking until the liquid has evaporated, 3–4 minutes. Take off the heat, season to taste and stir in the parsley just before serving.
recipes.title: Sautéed mushrooms with shallot, wine and lemon

recipes.method: Written for pioppino (Cyclocybe aegerita), tawaka's northern relative. 450 g pappardelle or fettuccine; 700 g mushrooms, cleaned and separated; 4 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil; 4 garlic cloves, thinly sliced; 125 ml dry white wine; 125 ml cream (optional); 40 g grated Parmesan; a handful of flat-leaf parsley, chopped; salt, black pepper and chilli flakes (optional). Cook the pasta until al dente. Meanwhile heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat and cook the mushrooms until golden brown, 6–8 minutes. Add the garlic for 1 minute, then pour in the wine and reduce it by half. Drain the pasta, keeping 250 ml of the cooking water, and add the pasta to the mushrooms with a splash of the water. Toss, adding the cream if using. Take off the heat, add the cheese and parsley, toss again and season with salt, pepper and chilli flakes. Serve at once with more cheese.
recipes.title: Mushroom pappardelle

recipes.method: Written for pioppino (Cyclocybe aegerita), tawaka's northern relative. 300 g arborio rice; 450 g mushrooms, cleaned and chopped; 1.5 litres warm mushroom or vegetable stock; 250 ml dry white wine; 1 large onion, finely diced; 3 garlic cloves, minced; 4 tbsp olive oil; 2 tbsp butter; 40 g grated Parmesan; 2 tbsp chopped parsley; salt and white pepper. Sauté the mushrooms in 2 tbsp of the oil until golden and set them aside. In the same pan heat the rest of the oil with the butter, cook the onion until translucent, then add the garlic and rice and stir for 2 minutes to toast the rice. Add the wine and stir until it is absorbed, then add the warm stock a ladle at a time, stirring and letting each addition be absorbed before the next, for 18–20 minutes until the rice is creamy and al dente. Fold in the mushrooms, cheese and parsley, season and serve at once with more cheese and a drizzle of olive oil.
recipes.title: Mushroom risotto

recipes.method: Written for pioppino (Cyclocybe aegerita), tawaka's northern relative. 900 g mushrooms, cleaned and left in small clusters; 60 ml extra-virgin olive oil; 1 large onion, sliced; 3 garlic cloves, crushed; 250 ml canned whole tomatoes, crushed by hand; 125 ml red wine; 2 bay leaves; a few thyme sprigs; salt and black pepper; fresh basil to finish. Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over medium heat and soften the onion for about 5 minutes. Add the garlic for 1 minute, then the mushrooms, and cook until they start to release their juices. Add the tomatoes, wine, bay leaves and thyme, season, bring to a simmer, then cover and braise on low for 25–30 minutes until the mushrooms are tender. Take out the bay leaves and thyme stems, adjust the seasoning and scatter with basil. Serve warm as a side, or over polenta, pasta or grilled bread.
recipes.title: Braised mushrooms with tomato and red wine

recipes.method: Written for pioppino (Cyclocybe aegerita), tawaka's northern relative. 700 g mushrooms, cleaned and kept in larger clusters; 60 ml extra-virgin olive oil; 2 garlic cloves, minced; 2 tbsp lemon juice; 2 tbsp chopped thyme, rosemary or oregano; salt and black pepper; lemon wedges to serve. Mix the oil, garlic, lemon juice and herbs in a large bowl, add the mushrooms, toss to coat and leave for 15–30 minutes. Heat a grill or barbecue to medium. Lift the mushrooms out of the marinade, season, and grill for 4–6 minutes a side until golden brown and tender. Serve straight away with lemon wedges and more herbs, as a starter, a side or in a salad.
recipes.title: Grilled mushroom clusters with lemon and herbs

recipes.method: Written for pioppino (Cyclocybe aegerita), tawaka's northern relative. 450 g mushrooms, separated into small clusters; 2 tbsp peanut oil; 2 garlic cloves, minced; 1 tbsp grated fresh ginger; 2 tbsp soy sauce; 1 tbsp rice wine or dry sherry; 1 tsp sesame oil; 2 spring onions, sliced; 1 tbsp sesame seeds; chilli flakes (optional). Heat the peanut oil in a wok or large frying pan over high heat and stir-fry the mushrooms until golden, about 4–5 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger and stir-fry 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the soy sauce and rice wine and toss to coat. Take off the heat, drizzle with the sesame oil and finish with the spring onions, sesame seeds and chilli flakes.
recipes.title: Mushroom stir-fry with ginger and soy

summary.text: Cyclocybe parasitica, also known as tawaka in Māori language or poplar mushroom, is a species of gilled mushroom in the genus Cyclocybe found in Australasia. Other Māori names are harore, paoke, piritawa and porotawa. Greta Stevenson described it in 1982 as Agrocybe parasitica, from a ribbonwood felled at Riccarton Bush, Christchurch; Colenso had collected it in 1891 under another name. It is a weak parasite that fruits from wounds on living trees and causes a heart rot. Its close relative the pioppino (Cyclocybe aegerita) is a prized mushroom in Europe and North America, but it cannot be grown in New Zealand for biosecurity reasons; tawaka is grown here instead, on logs or sawdust blocks, and sold at farmers' markets. It is reported to have been eaten by Māori for centuries and was used as a traditional medicine. A 1990 Lincoln University study found it about 20% protein by dry weight. It is listed as Indigenous and Not Threatened by the New Zealand Threat Classification System, though Biota of New Zealand gives its origin as uncertain, possibly an early introduction from Asia.

warnings: The spectacular rustgill (Gymnopilus junonius), common in New Zealand, also grows in large clusters on stumps, logs and the bases of trees and is inedible: it is bitter and contains neurotoxins. It is bright yellow-orange, ageing orange-brown or reddish brown, with a dry scaly cap, yellow flesh, a frail ring dusted with rusty orange spores, and a rusty brown spore print. Tawaka has a buff to tawny brown cap, white flesh, a thick pleated ring and a dark chocolate-brown spore print: check the flesh and take a spore print before eating any.

identification.text:
Small, densely branched shrub, with stellate tomentum, strongly aromatic. Leaves 0.8–3 cm long, sessile, revolute, grey, linear-lanceolate or linear, (linear leaves commonly forming axillary fascicles subtended by a larger linear-lanceolate leaf). Peduncle about equal to spike. Spike 1.5–3 cm long (excluding plume of sterile apical bracts), composed of very densely packed verticels of flowers. Fertile bracts 5–6 mm long, rhombic-cordate, green or brownish; sterile bracts 1–2 cm long, obovate or spathulate, mauve. Calyx 4–7 mm long, tubular, tomentose outside; teeth acute; appendage broad and more or less reniform. Corolla 5–8 mm long; tube longer than calyx; upper tube and lobes dark purple; lobes 1–1.5 mm long, broader than long, subequal. Nutlets about 2 mm long, broad-oblong, mucilaginous when wet.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Leaves entire; corolla dark purple.

lookalikes.howToTell: Topped lavender's leaves are entire; French lavender's are toothed or cut along the edges (pinnate-dentate), much less commonly only scalloped. Topped lavender's flowers are dark purple; French lavender's are mauve. Topped lavender's flower stalk is about as long as its spike; French lavender's, up to 30 cm, is much longer than its spike. The sterile bracts crowning the spike are 1–2 cm long in topped lavender, 7–10 mm in French lavender. Wetted, topped lavender's nutlets turn mucilaginous; French lavender's do not. Leaves that are often grey with star-shaped hairs, a strong aromatic smell and a crown of sterile bracts on the spike do not separate them: both belong to the same section of the genus.

preparation.text:
In Loja, in southern Spain, some people dress table olives with its leaves together with other herbs, and it has at times seasoned stews and other dishes such as roast meat. In the Alt Empordà, Catalonia, it is used as a culinary seasoning.
In Elche, in south-east Spain, the flowers are picked at full bloom, washed and dried, and kept in a bag or tin; to make a tea, boil water, add the flowers, then strain and let it cool.

summary.text:
Lavandula stoechas, the Spanish lavender or topped lavender (U.S.) or French lavender (U.K.), is a species of lavender native to the Mediterranean Basin.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): South Island: Kaiteriteri (Nelson), Birdlings Flat (Canterbury), Lake Wanaka (Central Otago). Allan (1940) recorded L. stoechas as "a somewhat persistent escape"; it seeds prolifically and germinates freely. It is a fairly common ornamental plant, particularly in eastern and central areas of the South Island, where its greater tolerance of frost makes it generally a more suitable plant to grow than L. dentata. The wild, and most cultivated plants in New Zealand, belong to subsp. stoechas from Spain eastwards to Greece.
Since its introduction into Australia, it has become an invasive species, widely distributed within the continent. It has been declared a noxious weed in Victoria since 1920.
Other names: bush lavender, French lavender, Spanish lavender (Flora of New Zealand Online); French lavender is the Flora of New Zealand's and NZPCN's name for it.

warnings: Potentially toxic to dogs and cats.
Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed. Pick from ground you know.

Lowland, montane and lower subalpine forest, sometimes dominant. Tōtara is commonly found in lowland areas where the soil is fertile and well drained.

On the West Coast, var. waihoensis is common in riparian and alluvial forest on poorly drained, flood-prone river terraces, seemingly preferring young soils over gravel.

identification.text:
Tōtara is a stout tree up to 30 m tall, with a trunk up to 2–3 m across. Its bark is thick, corky, furrowed and somewhat stringy, reddish-grey, and comes away in long, narrow strips. The leaves are brownish to dark green, stiff and leathery, narrow and tapering to a sharp, prickly tip, and sit directly on the shoot: 1.5–3 cm long and 3–4 mm wide on adult trees, about 2 cm long and 1–2 mm wide on juveniles. Male and female cones grow on separate trees. On a female tree, 2–4 scales, pointed and free at the tips, swell into a red, succulent, sweet receptacle that carries one, sometimes two, seeds 3–6 mm long on top; the seed is green to glaucous-green when fresh.
The largest known living tōtara, the Pouakani Tree, near Pureora in the central North Island, is over 35 m tall and nearly 4 m in trunk diameter at breast height. Bushmen discovered it in 1950. Other large trees are known in this area, while Whirinaki Forest, to the east, but also on deep recent volcanic soils, has groves of very tall tōtara (over 40 m in height).
It is most often confused with Hall's tōtara (Podocarpus laetus), with which it may grow and often hybridises. Tōtara's leaf bud is no wider than the branchlet and is surrounded by narrow, lance-shaped bracts; Hall's tōtara's bud is clearly wider than the branchlet, with broadly ovate bracts. Tōtara also has thicker bark and less sharply pointed leaf tips. Hybrids can be told only by the bud and its scales.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at how the seed sits. On yew, the single seed sits inside a red, fleshy cup (the aril) that almost surrounds it and is open at the end. On tōtara, the seed (one, sometimes two) sits on top of the swollen, usually red receptacle, which is made of 2–4 scales, acute and free at the tips. Look at where each leaf joins the shoot: yew's leaves have a short yellowish-green stalk, and its shoots are green and ribbed; tōtara's leaves are stalkless, joined by a narrow base. Adult tōtara leaves are 3–4 mm wide and yew's 1.5–2 mm, but tōtara's juvenile leaves are only 1–2 mm wide, so width separates only adult foliage. Mature tōtara has thick, stringy, furrowed bark; yew's bark is thin and peels in scaly, dark reddish-brown strips. Both have red, fleshy 'berries' and needle-like leaves of similar length (yew 1.2–2.5 cm, adult tōtara 1.5–3 cm), so colour and leaf length do not separate them. Nearly every part of yew is poisonous, including the seed inside the red flesh. Check the seed and the leaf base on every tree.
lookalikes.name: Yew

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaves. Adult tōtara leaves are 1.5–3 cm long and 3–4 mm wide with a sharp, prickly tip (juvenile leaves about 2 cm long and 1–2 mm wide); snow tōtara's are close-set, rigid and 0.5–1.5 cm long, with thickened margins and a blunt or barely pointed tip, and are usually bronze-green. Look at the plant: tōtara grows into a tree to 30 m with thick, stringy, furrowed bark; snow tōtara is a prostrate or spreading shrub, sometimes upright to 3 m, whose branches root where they touch the ground. Under the seed, tōtara's red receptacle is formed from 2–4 scales and snow tōtara's from two bracts. Where the two grow together, fertile hybrids are common; they are more upright than snow tōtara, often with drooping branches and longer, narrower leaves, so a plant in between may be a hybrid. The red flesh of both is eaten.
lookalikes.name: Snow tōtara

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaf bud at a shoot tip: tōtara's bud is no wider than the branchlet, with narrow, lance-shaped bracts; Hall's tōtara's bud is clearly wider than the branchlet, like a meatball on a stick, with broadly ovate bracts. The bracts soon fall, so look at fresh shoots. Look at the bark: tōtara's is thick, corky, furrowed and somewhat stringy; Hall's tōtara's is generally thin, papery and freely flaking. On young trees, tōtara's leaves are about 2 cm long and 1–2 mm wide, against 2.5–5 cm long and 4–5 mm wide on young Hall's tōtara, whose leaf tips are very sharp. Adult leaves overlap (tōtara 1.5–3 cm × 3–4 mm, Hall's tōtara 2–3 cm × 3–4 mm), so adult leaf size does not separate them. Both carry the seed on a red, swollen, succulent receptacle formed from 2–4 scales, and both grow in lowland, montane and lower subalpine forest, sometimes together, so the fruit and the place do not separate them. They often hybridise, and hybrids can be told apart only by the bud and its bracts. Hall's tōtara's red receptacle is eaten too (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Hall's tōtara

summary.text:
Tōtara (Podocarpus totara) is a podocarp tree found only in New Zealand, where it grows throughout, from lowland to mountain forest.
Tōtara is so commonly found on Northland farms that some farmers consider the tree to be a weed.
It is common throughout most of the North and South Islands, and present but extremely scarce on Stewart Island/Rakiura. It is assessed Not Threatened, though forest dominated by tōtara is all but gone from most of its former range.
A second variety, var. waihoensis, grows only on the West Coast of the South Island, from about the Waiho River south to the Cascades. It is a suckering tree to 10–15 m, usually with several stilt-like trunks from the base, slender branches and narrow leaves, and is thought to have arisen from hybrids between tōtara and needle-leaved tōtara (P. acutifolius). Its receptacle is also red, succulent and sweet.

warnings: Yew, which is poisonous, also has red, fleshy 'berries' and needle-like leaves. Check how the seed sits and where the leaf joins the shoot before eating (see the lookalikes).
Only the red flesh is recorded as eaten. No record of the seed being eaten was found, so whether it is safe is not known.

habitat.text:
Common in lowland to lower montane forest, especially on margins, in clearings and by streams.
It has a wide altitudinal range of 0–1050 m above sea level. F. excorticata prefers shaded areas but can still grow well in sunny areas.
In gardens it is grown in dappled light or partial shade, and adapts to full sun, in fertile, well-drained soil kept evenly moist but not sodden, sheltered from wind.

identification.text:
Gynodioecious, deciduous tree or shrub to about 12 m high; trunk to 60 cm diameter. Main branches stout, spreading; bark conspicuously light pinkish or brownish orange, very thin, peeling in strips; branchlets more or less puberulous. Petioles slender, 1–4 cm long. Lamina (1.5)–2–14 × (0.7)–1–6.5 cm, usually lanceolate to ovate-lanceolate or ovate-oblong, usually sinuate, obscurely toothed, glabrous except on veins and margins, thin, dark green above, pale glaucous to silvery below, sometimes suffused with red or purple; base rounded or cuneately narrowed; apex acute to acuminate. Flowers usually solitary, pendulous, often cauliflorous; pedicels filiform, to about 15 mm long. Floral tube 7–20 mm long, green to more or less purple at first. Sepals 5–16 mm long, ovate-lanceolate, green at first, the whole calyx turning red later, often eventually reflexing. Petals 2–5 mm long, dark purple, elliptic. Stamens of ☿ flowers well exserted; filaments 7–12 mm long, purplish. Style 20–35 mm long, much longer than stamens; stigma capitate. Berry about 10 mm long, ellipsoid-oblong, dark purple to almost black. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is deciduous in southern areas. The fruit is blunt at the tip and base.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the stems: scrambling fuchsia is a liane, with stout main stems to about 5 m long and 5 cm thick that sprawl when they lack support, and in the open it can form a ball-like shrub of interlacing branchlets; tree fuchsia is a tree or shrub to about 12 m with a distinct trunk to 60 cm thick, and keeps its trunked form even when it is much reduced in exposed places. Look at the leaf shape: tree fuchsia's leaves are usually lance-shaped to narrowly egg-shaped or oblong, with a pointed to drawn-out tip and a rounded or wedge-shaped base; scrambling fuchsia's are broadly egg-shaped to almost round, with a slightly heart-shaped to squared-off base and a slightly pointed tip. Leaf size overlaps (tree fuchsia's 2–14 cm long, sometimes 1.5 cm; scrambling fuchsia's 25–30 mm, sometimes 10 mm), and tree fuchsia has smaller leaves in exposed places, so go by shape, not size. The flowers are alike, scrambling fuchsia's smaller, but the floral tube (tree fuchsia 7–20 mm, scrambling fuchsia 7–15 mm), the sepals (5–16 mm against 6–10 mm) and the dark purple berries (about 10 mm against 5–10 mm) overlap, so flowers and fruit do not separate them. Plants intermediate in size and habit between the two, Fuchsia ×colensoi, probably their hybrid though this is not confirmed, often grow with both. No food record written for scrambling fuchsia was found (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Scrambling fuchsia

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the trunk and branching: tree fuchsia is a tree with a distinct trunk, to about 12 m high with a trunk to 60 cm thick, and keeps its trunked form even when it is much reduced in exposed places; Fuchsia ×colensoi is a shrub much-branched from the base, with slender branchlets that sometimes climb, or a small tree with a trunk to about 20 cm thick. Look at the leaves: tree fuchsia's are usually lance-shaped to narrowly egg-shaped or oblong, usually more than 5 cm long, with a pointed to drawn-out tip; Fuchsia ×colensoi's are usually egg-shaped to broadly egg-shaped or oblong-egg-shaped, less often almost round, usually less than 5 cm long, with a rounded to blunt tip ending in a short point, or a pointed to drawn-out one. Leaf size and shape overlap (tree fuchsia 2–14 cm long, sometimes 1.5 cm; Fuchsia ×colensoi 3–8 cm, sometimes 2 cm or 10 cm, and both can have oblong-egg-shaped leaves), and tree fuchsia has smaller leaves in exposed places, so leaves alone do not separate them. Flowers and berries do not separate them: the floral tube (tree fuchsia 7–20 mm, Fuchsia ×colensoi 8–20 mm), the sepals (5–16 mm against 6–14 mm) and the berries (both about 10 mm long, ellipsoid-oblong, dark purple to almost black) overlap. Fuchsia ×colensoi is intermediate in size and habit between tree fuchsia and scrambling fuchsia, probably their hybrid though this is not confirmed, and in many areas grows with both. Fuchsia ×colensoi's food record is thin (see its page).

summary.text:
Fuchsia excorticata, commonly known as the kōtukutuku and tree fuchsia, is a species of tree in the family Onagraceae that is endemic to New Zealand.
Fuchsia excorticata's fruits are dispersed by fruit-eating animals (frugivores). F. excorticata's fruits are an important food source for numerous New Zealand native birds, and they are an especially important food source for the kererū (Hemiphaga novaeseelandiae). Other birds, such as the tūī (Prosthemadera novaeseelandiae) and the New Zealand bellbird (Anthornis melanura) consume the fruits frequently. Beveridge (1964) estimated that a single dropping from an introduced blackbird (Turdus merula) produced 178 seedlings, thus proving the efficiency of blackbirds as seed distributors. The fruits of F. excorticata can also be part of the diet of the flightless kākāpō (Strigops habroptilus). German-born New Zealand explorer Julius von Haast said that he saw a kākāpō "sitting on a Fuchsia-tree, 3 m from the ground, and eating berries". Fuchsia excorticata has a gynodioecious breeding strategy, meaning individual trees are either hermaphroditic or female. According to Robertson et al. (2008), hermaphroditic individuals occur at a higher frequency than females. F. excorticata can be pollinated by birds, primarily by bellbirds and tūī. Other birds, such as stitchbirds (Pogonornis cincta) and silvereyes (Zosterops lateralis), as well as bumblebees (Bombus spp.) have been reported as visitors on F. excorticata flowers. Evidence presented by a 2012 study shows that the upland moa (Megalapteryx didinus) fed on the nectar. Green flowers stand out compared to the orange bark and produce more nectar, thus making them more attractive and rewarding to bird pollinators than red flowers. New Zealand botanist Eric Godley suggested that F. excorticata is capable of self-pollination "in the absence of pollinator visitors". The introduction of the common brushtail possum to New Zealand has led to a decline in this species. F. excorticata appears to be one of the possum's preferred food sources, and they will browse individual trees to the point of defoliation after which the trees can die. F. excorticata plays host to the endemic insect, the lemon tree borer (Oemona hirta). Wyman et al. (2011) investigated interactions between tree wētā (Hemideina spp.) and F. excorticata, finding that tree wētā consumes its seeds. F. excorticata has very low flammability rates. A 2025 study in the American Journal of Botany found that F. excorticata had a moderate ignition percentage, burn time, and burned amount of biomass.
Kōtukutuku is the name of the whole plant; its fruit is often called kōnini. It grows on the North, South, Stewart and Auckland Islands, and is assessed Not Threatened (2023). Other names recorded for the tree or its fruit include kōhutuhutu, kōhutuku, hōnā, māti and tākawa.
Māori gathered the berries by climbing the trees with baskets, or by shaking the branches so the berries fell onto mats; European settlers made them into jam, stewed them with honey and baked them in puddings.
New Zealand nurseries sell it as a garden tree. Its branches break easily, so it is best kept out of the wind.

warnings: Scrambling fuchsia, and plants intermediate between the two (Fuchsia ×colensoi), often grow with it and have similar flowers and dark purple berries. No food record written for either was found. Check the stems and leaf shape before eating (see the lookalikes).

edibleParts.text: Young leaves - raw or cooked. A mild flavour, but the leaves are dry and hairy and not that agreeable in quantity on their own. They can be used as part of a chopped mixed salad. The leaves are less palatable than those of common mallow unless cut very thinly, because of their velvety, hairy mouth-feel. The seeds are edible and are known in French as "petit pains", or "little breads".

Waste places and cultivated land, especially well-established at coastal sites.
It grows mainly on exposed coastal locations, often on small islands, only rarely any distance inland.

identification.text:
Stout biennial up to 2–(3) m high, usually with a single main stem. Stems moderately to densely clothed in stellate hairs when young, becoming more or less glabrous and woody at base when older. Leaves densely clothed in stellate hairs, velvety to touch, suborbicular, cordate at base, shortly 5–7-palmately lobed and crenulate, up to 20 cm diameter, rarely variegated; petioles 3–30 cm long; stipules narrow- to ovate-triangular, 4–8 mm long. Flowers in axillary and terminal clusters of 2–7–(10) or rarely in irregular racemes; fruiting pedicels 5–20–(30) mm long; epicalyx segments broadly ovate to suborbicular, united for lower ?-1/2, longer than calyx, distinctly enlarged and spreading at fruiting; calyx shallowly campanulate; calyx teeth more or less equal to tube, triangular, acute to acuminate, densely clothed in stellate hairs, usually more or less connivent at fruiting; petals lilac or deep pink with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long. Mericarps 6–8–(9) per fruit, usually glabrous, sometimes densely clothed in fine hairs, finely transversely ribbed on back; edges sharply angled.
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Lavatera arborea L.]
This robust species is most easily distinguished by the fused, enlarged, spreading fruiting calyx.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Both have round, palmately 5–7-lobed, round-toothed leaves, so the leaves do not separate them; use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. The flowers overlap: both are pink to purple with darker veins or markings, and tree mallow's 15–20 mm petals sit inside common mallow's 12–30 mm range. Use the epicalyx, which is longer than the calyx and enlarged in fruit in tree mallow but shorter than the calyx in common mallow (whose epicalyx segments may be somewhat joined at the base, so joining alone is not a test), and the fruit, ribbed crosswise against net-veined. Both have lobed leaves that can reach 20 cm across. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Both have round, palmately 5–7-lobed, round-toothed leaves, so the leaves do not separate them; use the petal length, the epicalyx and the fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. They differ in the epicalyx (longer than the calyx and enlarged in fruit in tree mallow, shorter and barely changed in island mallow), the fruit segments, the calyx (shallowly bell-shaped in tree mallow, long and tube-shaped in island mallow) and the petals (15–20 mm against 30–40 mm). Both are tall, both grow at coastal sites, and both have lobed leaves up to 20 cm across and pink to purple flowers with darker veins, so the leaves and flower colour do not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

preparation.text: Young leaves raw or cooked, cut very thinly or as part of a chopped mixed salad. In Andratx, Mallorca, it has been used to make omelettes and mallow salads dressed with oil and vinegar. Steam the leaves for longer than the 15–20 minutes a common-mallow recipe gives, or they stay furry, and chop them finely; they are not very slimy compared with other mallows. The young, green seed heads can be eaten fresh, when they taste a bit like raw peanuts, or fried for a few minutes, when they taste like fried sweetcorn.

recipes.method: Written for tree mallow (Lavatera arborea), on an Irish foraging blog. Young, green tree mallow seed heads; salt; ground cayenne pepper. Pick young, green seed heads (their texture is better). Take off the three leaf-like parts around each head before cooking, or while eating. Fry them for a few minutes, then season with salt and ground cayenne pepper. The author also toasts them in a popcorn maker.
recipes.title: Fried tree mallow seed heads

recipes.method: Written for tree mallow (Malva arborea), improvised by the author on molokhia, the Egyptian soup of jute mallow sometimes made with common mallow; the page gives no quantities. Tree mallow leaves, finely chopped; water; chopped onion; oil; garlic cloves; coriander seeds; salt and pepper; vegetable stock; lemon juice. Purée finely chopped raw tree mallow leaves in a blender with some water. Fry chopped onion in oil until soft. Crush garlic cloves, coriander seeds, salt and pepper in a mortar and add them with some vegetable stock and lemon juice, then add the puréed leaves. Simmer gently for a while, and purée again if it is not smooth enough. The author found tree mallow not very slimy, though the lemon is meant to offset the mucilage; one of the two tasters was not keen, possibly because of too much lemon.
recipes.title: Tree mallow and lemon soup (molokhia style)

summary.text:
Malva arborea (previously known as Lavatera arborea, or, more recently as Malva eriocalyx), the tree mallow, is a species of mallow native to the coasts of western Europe and the Mediterranean region, from Ireland and Britain south to Algeria and Libya, and east to Greece.
Malva arborea tolerates sea water to varying degrees, at up to 100% sea water in its natural habitat, excreting salt through glands on its leaves. This salt tolerance can be a competitive advantage over inland plant species in coastal areas. Its level of salinity tolerance is thought to be improved by soil with higher phosphate content, making guano enrichment particularly beneficial.
In New Zealand it has established on several seabird-dominated islands where it is considered to be a serious ecological weed and for which there are active eradication programmes, such as on North Brother Island in Cook Strait.
In New Zealand it is local throughout the North Island (not recorded from Taranaki) and throughout the South Island, and on Ruapuke Island and the Chatham Islands. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1870.

habitat.text:
Naturalised extensively in waste places, margins of remnant forest stands, coastal cliffs, and gardens.
In the Auckland region it grows in hedgerows, lowland and coastal forest, shrubland, disturbed sites, roadsides, wasteland and wetlands. It can invade most coastal and lowland forest types, intact or disturbed, as well as shrubland, fernland, cliffs and coastline, and it tolerates shade, frost, damp or drought, salt and wind.

An Unwanted Organism and National Pest Plant Accord species: it must not be bred, distributed, released or sold anywhere in New Zealand. Birds spread its seed. If you remove it, put the seed in green waste or landfill.

identification.text:
Glabrous, small or medium-sized, evergreen tree to c. 10 m high (taller in cultivation), sometimes a dense shrub. Shoots glabrous. Petioles mostly 1–2 cm long. Lamina 5–13 × 3–6 cm, ovate to elliptic-ovate, glossy above; base broad-cuneate to rounded; apex usually abruptly short-acuminate, sometimes acute. Panicles up to 25 × 20 cm, dense, broadly pyramidal; branches angular; pedicels very short. Bracts oblong or oblong-lanceolate; bracteoles much smaller, caducous. Flowers fragrant. Calyx 1–2 mm long; lobes indistinct. Corolla white; tube c. 1.5 mm long; lobes 2–2.5 mm long, oblong-elliptic, reflexed, with ± involute margins, acute. Stamens c. 4 mm long, exserted; anthers yellow. Style included. Fruit to 6 × 5 mm, ellipsoid-oblong, bluish or purplish black, ± pruinose. Seed c. 5 mm long, ± broadly ellipsoid, ribbed on back.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Shoots ± terete, prominently lenticellate. Leaves opposite, simple, entire. Inflorescence a terminal panicle of small, bisexual, usually scented flowers. Stamens 2, included or exserted, epipetalous; filaments short. [From the genus Ligustrum in Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The stems carry distinctive lumpy warts, the leaves are in opposite pairs, and the berries are coated with a powdery bloom. The fruit ripens in autumn. Chinese privet is a much shorter tree with smaller, more rounded leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: lilly pilly's is pinkish mauve or white, usually 1–1.7 cm across (up to 3 cm), with a hollow at the tip and one large seed; tree privet's berries are bluish or purplish black with a powdery bloom, no more than 6 mm long, each with a ribbed seed about 5 mm long. Lilly pilly's new leaves are reddish, unlike tree privet's. Look at the flowers: tree privet's are small and tubular, with a white tube about 1.5 mm long, four reflexed lobes 2–2.5 mm long and only two stamens, in dense clusters up to 25 × 20 cm; lilly pilly's four tiny petals, about 2 mm long, are joined into a small cap that falls, and it has numerous stamens. Lilly pilly's leaves are very aromatic when crushed and dotted with glands underneath, on stalks usually about 5 mm long; tree privet's are not described as aromatic or gland-dotted, and their stalks are mostly 1–2 cm long. Tree privet's shoots are more or less round, with prominent lumpy warts; lilly pilly's twigs are often four-angled or shortly four-winged. Both are evergreen trees with glossy, opposite leaves of overlapping size (lilly pilly usually 4–12 cm long, tree privet 5–13 cm), and both grow in scrub and on waste ground, so leaf shape and place do not separate them. Lilly pilly's fruit is eaten.
lookalikes.name: Lilly pilly

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the fruit: brush cherry's is crimson to crimson-purple and glossy, oblong to obovoid, usually 1–2 cm long (up to 2.5 cm), with its calyx lobes still on the tip and one or a few large seeds; tree privet's berries are bluish or purplish black with a powdery bloom, no more than 6 mm long, each with a ribbed seed about 5 mm long. Brush cherry's new leaves are reddish, unlike tree privet's. Brush cherry's flowers have free, round white petals about 4 mm across and numerous white stamens up to about 13 mm long, in clusters of 3–25; tree privet's are small and tubular, with four reflexed white lobes 2–2.5 mm long and only two stamens, in dense clusters up to 25 × 20 cm. Brush cherry's leaves are aromatic when crushed, mostly 1–3.5 cm wide (up to 4 cm), on stalks under 10 mm; tree privet's are not described as aromatic, are 3–6 cm wide, so the widths overlap a little, and sit on stalks mostly 1–2 cm long. Brush cherry's strong young shoots are more or less four-winged; tree privet's shoots are more or less round, with prominent lumpy warts. Both are evergreen trees with glossy, opposite leaves of overlapping length (brush cherry mostly 4–10 cm, up to 13 cm; tree privet 5–13 cm), and both grow on roadsides, in scrub and at forest margins. Brush cherry's fruit is eaten.

summary.text:
Ligustrum lucidum, the broad-leaf privet, Chinese privet, glossy privet, tree privet or wax-leaf privet, is a species of flowering plant in the olive family Oleaceae, native to the southern half of China and naturalized in many places. The name "Chinese privet" is also used for Ligustrum sinense.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island, in North Auckland, Auckland and coastal Bay of Plenty. Naturalised from China, first recorded in 1958. This is the largest species in New Zealand and is commonly used to form a tall hedge in warmer parts of the country; unclipped trees become widespreading and reach about 14 m high.
It is an Unwanted Organism and a National Pest Plant Accord species, and is on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. Birds spread its seed, and it forms dense stands that displace native plants and stop native seedlings establishing.

warnings: Do not eat any part of tree privet. Its berries are poisonous, as are the black, blue-black or dark purplish berries of every privet, and children may be tempted to eat them. The young shoots have been cooked as a famine food, but they contain a glycoside and are probably toxic.
Lilly pilly and brush cherry, which have edible fruit, can look similar and grow in the same places. Check every tree before picking (see the lookalikes).
