habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Wetlands in open turf and grassy places, pasture and lawns (usually damp), flushes and bogs. Recorded elevations range from 0 to 1281 m.
A weed of lawns that also grows in pasture, very common in New Zealand and best in moist places (Massey).
New Zealand's national wetland plant list rates it facultative: it is common both in wetlands and on dry ground (NZPCN).

identification.text:
Perennial herb to 0.25 m tall. Stems decumbent and rooting at nodes below, ascending to erect above, eglandular-hairy; hairs uniform, antrorse. Leaf bud indistinct; leaves separating while very small, opposite-decussate, erecto-patent to spreading; lamina thin, broadly ovate to broadly elliptic, to orbicular, 5–17 mm long, 4–15 mm wide, dull green above, paler beneath; midrib and 2–4 lateral veins evident; surfaces glabrous or sparsely minutely eglandular-puberulent; margin glabrous or sparsely ciliolate, shallowly crenate or crenate-serrate, rarely entire with marginal hydathodes, teeth in 3–8 pairs; apex and base more or less rounded; petiole 0.5–5.0 mm long. Inflorescence a terminal raceme, 20–60 (rarely to 110) mm long; flowers crowded at first, becoming distant, 3–12 (rarely to 60), all bisexual; bracts alternate or rarely the lowermost opposite, oblanceolate to elliptic, overtopping pedicels, the lowest leaf-like, becoming smaller above; pedicels erecto-patent, 1–3 mm long, shortly eglandular-puberulent all around. Calyx lobes 4, obtuse, more or less equal, 2–3 mm long, glabrous or sparsely eglandular-puberulent especially at base. Corolla 3–5 mm diameter, tube white and yellow, less than 1 mm long, shorter than calyx, hairy at throat; lobes 4, pale blue fading to whitish, or rarely white or blue, darker inside and on posterior lobe, sub-erect to erecto-patent, unequal, broadly ovate to orbicular, 2–3 mm long, obtuse to rounded, nectar guides dark blue or purple, on posterior and lateral lobes. Stamen filaments white, 1.5–2.0 mm long; anthers blue. Style blue, 1.7–2.0 mm long. Capsules angustiseptate, emarginate to obcordate, sparsely glandular ciliate on margins, 3.0–3.5 mm long, 3.5–4.0 mm wide at widest point. Seeds, ellipsoid, flattened, smooth, pale brown, 0.5–0.7 mm long.
Veronica serpyllifolia plants are distinctive among New Zealand species of Veronica. Characteristic features for their identification include the perennial habit with basal part of the stem decumbent and rooting at the nodes, short, antrorse stem hairs, almost glabrous dull green leaves, small, usually very pale blue corolla with a short anterior lobe, and rounded, emarginate capsule with marginal glandular cilia.
Veronica peregrina plants have a similar growth form, but differ in being annuals, completely glabrous, their flowers are almost sessile (pedicels less than 0.5 mm long), the corolla is pure white without nectar guides, the styles less than 0.2 mm long, and the capsules are a little smaller and more rounded.
Among the speedwells common in New Zealand lawns it is the only one with white flowers streaked blue; the others are blue streaked white. Its leaves are hairless, unlike the other lawn speedwells. Out of flower it looks very like pennyroyal, with a similar leaf shape and creeping stems; crush a leaf, as pennyroyal smells strongly of mint and turf speedwell does not (Massey).
Its flowers grow only in spikes at the ends of the stems, never in spikes from the leaf bases (NatureSpot).

lookalikes.howToTell: Bird's-eye speedwell's flowers are sky-blue, 8–12 mm across, each alone on a long, slender stalk; turf speedwell's are pale blue fading to whitish, 3–5 mm across, on short stalks (1–3 mm) up a spike at the stem tips. Bird's-eye speedwell's leaves are hairy, 6–35 mm long and coarsely toothed; turf speedwell's are almost hairless, 5–17 mm long, with shallow, rounded teeth. Bird's-eye speedwell is seldom in mown turf and is commoner in gardens and crops; turf speedwell is a perennial that stays below the mower in lawns and damp pasture. Both creep and can root at the joints, and both have paired leaves and dark-striped flowers, so neither tells them apart. Bird's-eye speedwell's young leaves and shoots are eaten, but its record as food is thin.
lookalikes.name: Bird's-eye speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a leaf: pennyroyal smells strongly of mint, turf speedwell does not. In flower, pennyroyal's mauve flowers, 4–6 mm long, crowd in rings around the stem at the leaf bases; turf speedwell's are pale blue fading to whitish, flat with four lobes, 3–5 mm across, up a spike at the stem tips. Out of flower they look very alike: both creep and root along the ground, have small paired leaves of much the same shape and size, and grow in damp lawns and pasture. Do not eat pennyroyal: it damages the liver.
lookalikes.name: Pennyroyal

lookalikes.howToTell: Field speedwell's leaves are hairy on both faces, at least on the veins, and its stems carry two kinds of hairs; turf speedwell's leaves are almost hairless. Field speedwell is an annual with no creeping stems; turf speedwell is a perennial whose lower stems creep and root at the joints. Field speedwell's flowers are bright blue, 2–3 mm across, almost stalkless; turf speedwell's are pale blue fading to whitish, 3–5 mm across, on stalks 1–3 mm long. Both grow low in lawns throughout New Zealand, with small paired, toothed leaves and four-lobed flowers in a spike at the stem tips, so habitat and leaf shape do not separate them. No record of field speedwell being eaten has been found.
lookalikes.name: Field speedwell

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping speedwell's leaves are hairy on both faces and edges; turf speedwell's are almost hairless. Creeping speedwell's flowers are blue, 8–10 mm across, each alone on a thread-like stalk 15–40 mm long; turf speedwell's are pale blue fading to whitish, 3–5 mm across, on short stalks (1–3 mm) up a spike at the stem tips. Creeping speedwell's stems lie flat, sometimes rising at the tips; turf speedwell's creep and root only at the base, then rise to flower. Creeping speedwell sets no fruit in New Zealand; turf speedwell sets small notched capsules. Both are perennials that creep, root at the joints and form mats in lawns, and their leaves overlap in size (creeping speedwell 3–8 mm long, turf speedwell 5–17 mm), so habit and leaf size do not separate them. No food use of creeping speedwell has been confirmed; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Creeping speedwell

summary.text:
Veronica serpyllifolia, the thyme-leaved speedwell or thymeleaf speedwell, is a perennial flowering plant in the plantain family. The species as a whole is native mostly to Eurasia & North America, and has three variants with their individual ranges; var. serpyllifolia has particularly spread beyond its native range.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: throughout. South Island: throughout. Stewart Island, Chatham Islands, Campbell Island. First recorded by Kirk in 1864.
It survives many common lawn weedkillers, so it often stands out after a lawn has been sprayed with the wrong one (Massey).
It is native to temperate Eurasia and was naturalised in New Zealand by 1864 (NZPCN). The name serpyllifolia means thyme-leaved, from the Latin serpyllum, thyme, and folium, leaf (Biota of New Zealand).

warnings: Its record as food is thin: one foraging page (leaves, flowers and stems raw in salads) and a database listing of food use with no part or method given, so it is not given as food here.
It survives many common lawn weedkillers, so a healthy-looking patch may still have been sprayed.

habitat.text:
T. versicolor commonly grows in tiled layers in groups or rows on logs and stumps of deciduous trees. It is a white rot fungus which degrades lignin from lignocellulosic materials, such as wood.
The species may be eaten by caterpillars of the fungus moth Nemaxera betulinella, maggots of the fly Polyporivora picta, and the fungus gnat Mycetophila luctuosa.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Trametes versicolor' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The fruiting body is somewhat tongue-shaped, with no discernable stalk, and the tough flesh is 1–3 millimetres thick. The cap is flat, up to 10 centimetres across. It is often triangular or round, with zones of fine hairs coloured rust-brown or darker brown, sometimes with black zones. Underneath a layer of tomentum is a black layer, topping the whitish flesh. Older specimens can have zones with green algae growing on them.
The bottom surface of the cap shows typical concentric zones of different colors, with the margin always the lightest. There are 3–5 pores per mm. They are whitish to light brown, with pores round and with age twisted and labyrinthine.


Similar species
One similar-looking mushroom is Stereum ostrea (false turkey tail).
Other similar species include Trametes betulina, T. hirsuta, T. ochracea, T. suaveolens, Bjerkandera adusta, Cerrena unicolor, Lenzites betulina, and Stereum hirsutum. Other species of Stereum are similar, typically with a smooth undersurface, as well as some species of Trichaptum.

recipes.method: Written for turkey tail with artist's bracket (Ganoderma applanatum) and shiitake. 2 onions with their skins, roughly chopped; 1 leek; 1 bulb of garlic, halved across; 2 celery sticks (ends and tops too); 2 carrots; 1 beetroot (optional); an 8 cm piece of fresh ginger, sliced; an 8 cm piece of fresh turmeric, sliced (or 30 ml/2 tbsp powder); 50 g dried or fresh mushrooms — turkey tail, artist's bracket pieces and shiitake; 8 g dried seaweed (kelp, kombu or wakame); 2.5 ml (½ tsp) crushed black peppercorns; 1 large stick of rosemary or 6 thyme sprigs; 4 bay leaves; 4 litres water; 5–10 ml (1–2 tsp) salt. Makes 2.5 litres. Put everything in a stockpot, bring to the boil uncovered and simmer gently for 1–1½ hours. Strain out the solids, keeping the mushrooms to slice and return to the liquid. Bring it back to the boil and bottle it into jars sterilised in a 150 °C oven; the lids pop as they seal. Store sealed jars in the pantry and opened ones in the fridge. Drink it as it is, or use it as a base for miso soup or with cooked noodles or rice.

Widely distributed in open habitats, especially in lowland grassland and scrub, on cliffs, often in modified communities of herbs.
In New Zealand: from the coast up into the lower montane zone (sea level to 400 m); it was once widespread in short tussock grassland, on lava fields and clay pans, and on rocky headlands by the sea (NZPCN, restated).

identification.text:
Perennial herb with napiform taproot about 3 cm diameter; caulorrhiza short, bearing a number of flowering stems. Hairs variable, the longer mostly curved or bent near base. Basal leaves with petioles to about 25 cm long with retrorse hairs. Lamina to 5 cm diameter, suborbicular to orbicular, lobed to about ⅞ way to midrib; lobes 5–7, linear, inconspicuously but uniformly hairy on both sides; larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; median and larger lateral teeth usually oblong, occasionally obovate to clavate, obtuse, subacute or mucronate. Cauline leaves smaller, with fewer lobes. Flowering stems with dense retrorse hairs or occasionally glabrescent; bracteoles linear to narrowly triangular; flowers usually in pairs, occasionally solitary. Sepals about 5 × 3 mm excluding awn, ovate or elliptic-ovate; awn to 1 mm long; hairs mostly short, appressed, longer on margins. Petals about 6 × 4 mm, obovate, white to pink. Mericarps hairy; beak to 14 mm long. Seed about 2 × 1.4 mm, oblong, dark; dorsal alveolae usually deep, 4–6-sided, more or less isodiametric.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (turnip-shaped or cylindrical, or more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. They are separated on the hairs of the leaf and flower stalks: in turnip-rooted geranium they are sharply bent near the base, point backward and lie pressed flat; in Solander's geranium they are straight to curved, stand out or point backward, but never lie flat. The leaf lobes (usually linear-obovate in turnip-rooted geranium, obovate in Solander's geranium) and the seed also differ: pits about 0.1 mm across against usually more than 0.1 mm. The root is often turnip-shaped in turnip-rooted geranium and more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot in Solander's geranium, but Solander's geranium can have a turnip-shaped root too, so the root alone does not settle it. Flower colour does not separate them: both can have pink petals, and both can have petals up to 8–9 mm long. Solander's geranium's root is recorded as food. The names do not separate them: Biota of New Zealand gives Solander's geranium the names turnip-rooted geranium, Matua-kūmara and pukupuku, and Flora of New Zealand Online gives the same three to turnip-rooted geranium, so a record under any of them may mean either plant.
lookalikes.name: Solander's geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Australasian cranesbill and turnip-rooted geranium are separated on three characters: the middle teeth of its leaf lobes are about as long as broad (mostly longer than broad in turnip-rooted geranium); the pale, see-through border of its inner sepals is mostly more than 0.3 mm wide near the tip (mostly less than 0.3 mm); and its seeds are red-brown with rather shallow rectangular pits (red-brown to dark brown, with rather deep rectangular to polygonal pits). Its sepals are mostly elliptic to obovate, against ovate. The lobing does not separate them (both are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way), and both have paired flowers. Australasian cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food.
lookalikes.name: Australasian cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Cinquefoil geranium and turnip-rooted geranium are separated on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in turnip-rooted geranium, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in turnip-rooted geranium. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of turnip-rooted geranium overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Cinquefoil geranium's root is recorded as food.

summary.text:
Geranium retrorsum is a species of Geranium known by the common name New Zealand geranium in the United States and common cranesbill in Australia. It is native to Australia and New Zealand but can be found on other continents as an introduced species which is often a noxious weed as well.
In New Zealand this species has been classified by the Department of Conservation as Threatened - Nationally Vulnerable.
Plants treated here as G. retrorsum were treated by Allan (1961) within his concept of G. pilosum.
Its 2023 national assessment is Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable (it was Not Threatened in 2004). Regional assessments rate it Regionally Threatened – Regionally Critical in Northland (2026), Wellington (2025) and Otago (2025), and Regionally Threatened – Regionally Vulnerable in Auckland (2025). It has become very uncommon over most of its North Island range, where it now grows mainly on northern offshore islands, but is still common in parts of the eastern South Island. Rabbits threaten it by digging the plants up for their roots, and taller exotic weeds now dominate the open places it favours. Besides the typical form, two other races grow in New Zealand: one on weedy sites around Canterbury, and one so far known only around Oakley Creek, Auckland, perhaps also at Tawa, Wellington; both are treated as indigenous for now (NZPCN, restated).
In Victoria (VicFlora): Most Victorian plants differ from the type form of Geranium retrorsum from New Zealand as circumscribed by Gardner (1984). Further assessment of this species may result in Victorian (?and Australian) material being reclassified at an infraspecific level.

habitat.text: Riverbeds, slips, forest margins, regenerating scrub. Extremely common nationwide.

harvestEthics.text: Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.

identification.text: Shrub or small tree with arching stems and glossy, strongly veined opposite leaves. Long drooping strings of small flowers followed by shiny purple-black fruit, each holding several small seeds. The fleshy purple 'petals' surround the seeds.

lookalikes.howToTell: Tutu is highly poisonous, and eating its fruit has been linked with deaths of children in New Zealand. Both have opposite leaves (tutu occasionally in whorls of three), so arrangement does not separate them. Elder's leaves are compound, of (3)–5–7 leaflets toothed except near the base, and its tiny white flowers are in large flat-topped clusters mostly 10–20 cm across, followed by berries 4–8.5 mm across, usually shining black. Tutu's leaves are simple, with flat or slightly wavy edges, and its flowers hang in slender drooping strings 10–30 cm long, followed by fruit of dark purple fleshy petals around the seeds. Season does not separate them: elder flowers November to January, tutu flowers October to March and fruits November to April. Elderflowers and cooked elderberries are eaten; raw elderberries can cause stomach upsets, and elder leaves and stems are poisonous. If you are unsure which you are looking at, harvest neither.

sources: Knox, Johanna. A Forager's Treasury: A New Zealand guide to finding and using wild plants (Allen & Unwin, 2013) — 'Common poisonous plants' chapter (Tutu).

Wikipedia contributors. 'Coriaria arborea', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriaria_arborea Corroborates the toxin and the single exception: endemic to New Zealand, growing to 7 m, and every part except the juice of the fruits contains tutin, 'which is highly poisonous to humans and livestock'. Poisoning can cause brain paralysis, convulsions, exhaustion, memory loss or death. It also records how Māori used it despite that: the petals were juiced after the poisonous seeds were filtered out through toetoe (Austroderia sp.) flower heads, making waitutu, drunk in quantity and used as a laxative, and fermented into a wine that European settlers took to as well. Leaves and young shoots treated wounds, sprains, strains and broken bones; stems of larger plants were made into flutes. Further recorded names: tāweku, tūpākihi, tāwehu, pūhou, pukou, puho, tuturakau. **The filtering is not a method to copy** — it is the context for why the warning on this page is absolute.

The honey regulation, which the warning now states precisely. New Zealand Food Safety: passion vine hoppers feeding on tutu excrete honeydew containing tutin; the resulting honey is 'chemically similar to floral honey and cannot be distinguished by taste, sight or smell' from safe honey; tutin is harmless to bees and toxic to mammals. The main risk period is January to April, over most of the North Island and the top third of the South Island. The Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code sets the maximum for tutin in honey and honeycomb at 0.7 mg/kg, and for the purposes of the Standard 'tutu' means Coriaria arborea and Coriaria sarmentosa. One compliance route is honey taken off hives by 31 December — which is where this entry's earlier 'December to April' came from, and it had the window wrong. The rules followed hospitalisations, including a family poisoned by their own honey in 2008. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.mpi.govt.nz/food-business/honey-bee-products-processing-requirements/managing-tutin-contamination-in-honey

sourcingNote: Owed a correction, not a book: the honey warning gives the risk window as December to April, and New Zealand Food Safety puts it January to April — 31 December is the end of the safe harvest window, not the start of the risky one. Evidence is in this entry's sources; the sentence is a person's to write.

summary.text: The most dangerous plant a New Zealand forager can meet. Learn it, then never touch it.

warnings: Every part of this plant except the fleshy petal is lethally toxic.
Contains tutin. Tutu has killed people, and it has killed circus elephants. Seeds, leaves and shoots are all lethal.

Toxic honey: bees do not visit tutu, but passionvine hoppers feed on it and excrete honeydew that bees collect. This produces genuinely poisonous honey and is the reason NZ regulates honey harvesting in tutu regions between December and April.
Never make a wine, cordial or jam from any purple-black wild berry in NZ unless you have positively identified the plant.

Leaves and stems, boiled or stewed together with other greens. The roots can be cooked, or ground and mixed with vinegar as a horseradish-like relish; the root use rests on a single source, and another source records only the leaves as used.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Waste land, roadsides, cultivated land, coastal shingly land.
In New Zealand it is more typically found in crops and gardens, wherever there is bare soil for seedlings to establish; on dairy farms it turns up mainly in young pastures and in open parts of paddocks such as around water troughs and gateways, and it is seldom found in dense, older pastures (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated). In lawns it takes hold in bare patches, compacted soil and areas damaged by drought or foot traffic (New Zealand Lawn Addicts, restated).
Waste places, roadsides, cultivated fields, frequently mown lawns etc. Roadsides, waste areas, lawns, pastures, fields, gardens, disturbed areas; at elevations up to 1,000 metres.

identification.text:
Lepidium didymum is an annual or biennial herb with decumbent or ascending and glabrous green stems, up to 40 centimetres long, radiating from a central position. The leaves are pinnate and alternate and can reach a length of 5 cm. The flowers are inconspicuous, with four very short white petals or none at all, and 2 (rarely 4), stamens. The fruits consist of two rounded valves, notched at the apex, with a very short style between them. They are wrinkled and contain orange or reddish brown seeds, that are 1–5 mm long.
Foetid annual or biennial with short-lived rosette and procumbent to ascending glabrous or sparsely hairy stems to 40 cm long. Leaves 1–2-pinnatifid, narrow-oblong to ovate, glabrous except for sparse spreading hairs on petioles of some basal leaves; rosette leaves petiolate, 6-10 × 1.5-2 cm; stem leaves smaller, usually pinnatifid, rarely 2-pinnatifid, 1-4 × 0.5-1.5 cm. Racemes (1)-3-5 cm; rachis with sparse spreading hairs; pedicels spreading, 2.5-4 mm long. Sepals about 0.5 mm long. Petals white, shorter than the sepals, or absent. Stamens usually 2, rarely 4. Silicle broader than long, emarginate, about 1.5 × 2-2.5 mm; valves finely warty or ridged, separating at maturity; stigma minute, almost sessile in apical notch of silicle. Seed comma-shaped, light brown, about 1 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Flora of New Zealand key to the two naturalised species: Silicles about 1.5 mm long, emarginate; pedicel longer than the silicle — twin cress (didymus). Silicles more than 2 mm long, apiculate; pedicel shorter than the silicle — wart cress (squamatus).
It begins as a flat rosette with its growing point at ground level; each leaf is made of several leaflets, and each leaflet has several lobes, usually more on one side than the other, so the leaflets are lopsided — unusual among weeds. As it matures it sends out stems along the ground that can form extensive mats, which from a distance look like wireweed. The flowers are tiny; the characteristic double pods confirm the identification, and the crushed foliage has a distinctive smell. The closely related wart cress (Lepidium squamatum) has pods that look like warts rather than twin pods (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Both begin as small rosettes on bare cultivated soil. Shepherd's purse sends up an erect flowering stem, (2–)15–30(–80) cm tall, and its leaves are not divided into separate lopsided leaflets; twin cress sends out stems that lie along the ground and can form mats, and smells foetid when crushed. The pods differ clearly: shepherd's purse has flat heart-shaped pods 5–10 mm long, twin cress tiny paired warty pods only about 1.5 mm long. Petals do not separate them, as both can have tiny white petals or none. Shepherd's purse leaves are eaten raw or cooked; avoid it in medicinal amounts when pregnant — see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Shepherd's purse

lookalikes.howToTell: Both form flat rosettes of narrow, deeply cut leaves on open ground, including near the sea, and twin cress can be mistaken for buck's-horn plantain. Buck's-horn plantain leaves all grow from the base, are linear with 1–4 pairs of narrow lobes or teeth, are hairy at least on the margins and have a silky tuft of hairs at the base; it flowers in dense cylindrical spikes on leafless stalks 3–45 cm long, with protruding stamens. Twin cress is hairless or nearly so, smells foetid when crushed, sends out leafy stems along the ground, and bears tiny white (or petal-less) flowers in short clusters followed by paired pods about 1.5 mm long. Buck's-horn plantain young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Buck's-horn plantain

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are low weeds of roadsides, waste places and cultivated land with finely divided leaves, and twin cress can be mistaken for pineappleweed. Crush a leaf: pineappleweed smells of pineapple, twin cress smells foetid. Pineappleweed stems are erect or ascending, 5–20(–40) cm tall, its leaves are 2–3 times divided into narrow-linear segments, and it bears rayless, cone-shaped, dull yellow to greenish-yellow flower heads 4–10 mm across. Twin cress stems usually lie along the ground, its leaves are 1–2 times divided, and it has tiny white or petal-less flowers followed by paired pods about 1.5 mm long. Leaf division alone does not separate them, since both can have twice-divided leaves. Pineappleweed flower heads and leaves are eaten raw or cooked; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Pineappleweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Yarrow and twin cress can both form low mats of divided leaves in pasture, lawns and waste places. Yarrow is strongly scented (aromatic rather than foetid) and hairy, its leaves are feathery — twice divided with the segments divided again, in 18–30(–37) pairs of leaflets, not all in one plane — and it spreads by rhizomes, sending up erect flowering stems to about 80 cm with flat-topped clusters of small white (sometimes pink) daisy-like heads. Twin cress is hairless or nearly so, smells foetid, has lopsided leaflets, stems lying along the ground, tiny white or petal-less flowers and paired pods about 1.5 mm long. Yarrow young leaves are eaten in small amounts but are bitter, and yarrow is not for use in pregnancy or by people allergic to the daisy family; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Yarrow

lookalikes.howToTell: Some farmers wrongly call twin cress 'land cress', but the plants are easy to tell apart. Land cress is an erect biennial (20–)40–60(–90) cm tall, with often glossy, deeply lyre-shaped rosette leaves that have an end lobe and (4–)5–8 or more pairs of side lobes, yellow petals 6–8 mm long, and long thin pods (30–)40–70 mm long. Twin cress lies along the ground, smells foetid when crushed, has tiny white petals shorter than the sepals (or none) and tiny paired pods about 1.5 mm long. Land cress young leaves are eaten raw or cooked for their hot, watercress-like flavour; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Land cress

lookalikes.howToTell: Both start as flat rosettes whose leaves, each made of a row of leaflets, radiate from a growing point at ground level, later send stems along the ground, and come up on bare soil on roadsides, in waste places and on cultivated ground. Crush a leaf: twin cress smells foetid; musky storksbill usually smells of musk, though not always strongly. Twin cress is hairless or nearly so; musky storksbill is densely covered in glandular hairs and feels sticky. Twin cress's leaflets are lopsided, with more lobes on one side than the other; musky storksbill's leaflets are stalkless, with more or less ovate, toothed lobes. In flower they differ clearly: twin cress has tiny white petals shorter than its 0.5 mm sepals, or none, and paired pods about 1.5 mm long; musky storksbill has clusters of about 12 pink or mauve-pink flowers, petals 4.5–8 mm long, followed by fruits with a beak 3–3.5 cm long. Musky storksbill's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked, but its record as food is thin; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Musky storksbill

preparation.text: Eat the leaves raw as a nibble or in salads, or cook them as a pot herb. The crushed plant smells foetid and opinions on its taste are mixed: many people boil the leaves and stems in several changes of water, while others eat it raw and never cook it. It can be used to stuff other foods such as fish. If grinding the root with vinegar as a relish, taste it before adding any salt.

summary.text:
Lepidium didymum, the lesser swine-cress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.
Lepidium didymum is of uncertain origin, but is often cited as native to South America, mainly Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay and Venezuela. It has been introduced elsewhere as a weed of cultivation. It has naturalised across the globe, from Africa, Europe, Asia, Australasia, North America and South America.
In Britain, it had been recorded from the wild by 1778, chiefly in England and the south of Ireland, growing on cultivated and waste ground, in gardens and lawns, by paths and roadsides.
Flora of New Zealand gives its region of origin as Europe and its first wild record in New Zealand as 1855; it is recorded from the North, South and Stewart Islands and the Kermadec, Chatham, Auckland and Campbell Islands. In New Zealand it has also been called Senebiera didyma and Coronopus didymus. Biota of New Zealand also lists Senebiera pinnatifida DC. as a former name and 'lesser swinecress' as an English name. The NZ Plant Conservation Network notes that the genus name Lepidium means scale-shaped, after the pods.
In New Zealand it can germinate at any time of year, but it establishes mainly in spring and autumn, starting as a rosette before it scrambles. In lawns its rosettes crowd out new grass seedlings and survive low mowing, and it looks most weedy over winter and early spring, when lawn grasses slow down.
Te Papa holds 32 specimens, the most recent collected by Leon Perrie on 29/12/2025 (SP129844). Manaaki Whenua's herbarium has about 89 databased New Zealand records: North Auckland 21, Wellington 21, Canterbury 17, Nelson 9, South Auckland 5, Southland 5, Gisborne 4, and two or fewer each from Hawke's Bay, Taranaki, Westland and Otago.
Although small and inconspicuous, it can cause major problems on dairy farms: milk from lactating cows that eat it develops a distinctive taint that processing companies do not want, and a company that detects it may refuse further milk from that farm until the problem is managed. Some farmers incorrectly call it land cress (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated).
The plant is harvested from the wild for local use as a food and a medicine. The dried plant material is sold for medicinal purposes in S. America. The plant also has potential for use in soil remediation projects.

warnings: Twin cress takes up lead from contaminated soil and stores it in its roots and, to a lesser extent, its leaves, and it often grows in unsavoury places — gather it only from clean ground.
In young pastures it is controlled with herbicides such as MCPB, MCPA and flumetsulam, and in lawns with MCPA, dicamba, picloram or triclopyr. Pick it only where you know none has been used.
The seeds contain erucic acid and glucosinolates; the recorded food parts are the leaves, stems and roots, not the seeds.
Its food use is thinly documented — a few foraging and plant-database sources and a single Spanish folk record — and none gives a safe quantity.
Confirm the identity by the tiny paired (twin) seed pods before eating: the young rosette resembles other rosette weeds such as musky storksbill, and from a distance its mats look like wireweed.

identification.text:
The cap is normally 4–20 cm in diameter. At first it has an involute margin and a somewhat depressed centre. The upper surface is olive brown or yellow-green and is often sticky or slimy in the middle. When young it has velvety zones and may be shaggy at the rim. Later it becomes funnel-shaped and the colour darkens to blackish. The gills are crowded, dirty white, stained olive-brown by old milk, which is initially white on contact with the air. They are somewhat decurrent. With potassium hydroxide or ammonia there is a purple reaction.
The stipe is up to about 7 cm tall by 3 cm in diameter and it is similar in colour to the cap, but much lighter. It may have shallow pits (scrobiculae). The flesh is a dirty white and tends to turn brown. The taste (especially the abundant milk) is acrid. There is little smell. The spores are about 7x6 μ and are ornamented with a pattern of ridges. The spore print is cream in colour.


Similar species
A similar species in Pacific Northwest conifer forests, as well as Sitka spruce forests, is L. olivaceoumbrinus. Usually found growing individually, it has a stronger olive-brown colour on its cap and stipe, with dark spots on the latter. Also similar is L. atroviridis.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Ugly milkcap's milk is white or creamy white, and old milk leaves its dirty-white gills stained olive-brown. Its cap is olive brown or yellow-green, often sticky or slimy in the middle, darkening to blackish with age. In New Zealand and Australia it grows with birch; saffron milk cap only with pine.

Manaaki Whenua Landcare Research, Virtual Mycota, 'Lactarius turpis' — the New Zealand record, with the description attributed to McNabb, R.F.R. (1971), 'The Russulaceae of New Zealand. 1. Lactarius', New Zealand Journal of Botany 9(1): 46–66. McNabb's text is in copyright, so the facts below are restated and nothing is quoted. Checked 06/10/2026. https://virtualmycota.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/vM_Species_Details.aspx?pk=5191 Biostatus 'Present in region - Exotic', and the entry's only New Zealand habitat statement: commonly associated with Betula pendula throughout the South Island. On New Zealand material: cap 7–23 cm, drab olive brown or dark brownish black with olive tints, paling towards an ochraceous, strongly inrolled and coarsely woolly margin; gills pale cream with dull brown edges at maturity, spotted and stained dull brown; latex copious, viscid, creamy white, unchanging; stem 3–7 cm by 2–3.5 cm, stout, often with greenish tints at the apex; spore print ochraceous buff; gills extremely acrid and flesh slightly acrid. KOH and ammonia turn the cap rapidly deep purple, which McNabb gives as characteristic. On edibility he reports it considered poisonous by European mycologists, and Pilát (1961) that it is poisonous raw or poorly cooked and edible though not recommended once the latex is soaked out.

First Nature, 'Lactarius turpis' (ugly milkcap) — © First Nature / Pat O'Reilly, all rights reserved, so facts only and nothing quoted beyond the short phrases marked. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/lactarius-turpis.php Cap dark olive brown with a paler margin, slimy when wet, 7–18 cm, convex then slightly depressed; gills cream to pale buff turning sepia-tinged when bruised, decurrent, narrow and crowded, releasing abundant white latex that dries olivaceous; stem 4–7 cm by 1–2.5 cm, no ring; spores 6.5–7.5 × 5.5–6 µm; spore print creamy white; no significant odour; taste hot and acrid. Mycorrhizal with birch in wet woodland on acid soils. Considered poisonous for its potential carcinogenic properties; the northern European practice of boiling it and using it as a seasoning is now discouraged. Lactarius blennius is the lookalike — lighter, smaller, and without the sepia-tinged gill patches.

The spore print, and why the disagreement is worth keeping. Wikipedia gives cream, First Nature creamy white, and McNabb — on New Zealand material — ochraceous buff. The spread is the point: saffron milk cap's page says a spore print cannot separate this genus because the prints run white to ochre across it, and this species runs the width of that range on its own. Checked 06/10/2026.

Which name is correct, because both are in use. McNabb sets out the dispute: Bulliard's 1791 Agaricus necator was redescribed by Persoon (1801) and revalidated by Fries (1821) against Persoon's rather than Bulliard's fungus, so most recent workers reject Bulliard's name for A. turpis Weinm., while Singer (1962) read the misinterpretation the other way and cited the species as Lactarius necator. This entry's summary already lists both, plus L. plumbeus. Checked 06/10/2026.

summary.text:
Lactarius turpis (also L. plumbeus or L. necator) is a Eurasian species of fungus, commonly known as the ugly milk-cap or green birch milk cap in English.

Lactarius turpis is found naturally in Europe and Siberia, and has been introduced to Australia and New Zealand. It can also be found in North America, in the northeast (July–September) and near the West Coast (September–November).

warnings: Contains the mutagenic compound necatorin. Boiling reduces it but does not eliminate it, so this is not a mushroom to eat however it is cooked — despite its use, after boiling, as a spice in northern and eastern Europe and Siberia, and for pickling in Russia.

identification.text: A small milk cap. Cap 1–3.5 cm across, convex when young, flattening or sinking in the centre with age, dry except in wet weather and finely powdered to the lens. Its colour is a muted salmon, sometimes closer to a grey-tinged orange or a washed-out orange-brown, and no concentric zoning is recorded on it. Gills pallid, crowded, moderately thick, up to 3 mm deep, attached to slightly or occasionally fully running down the stem. Stem 1–3 cm long and 4–7 mm thick, more or less even, coloured like the cap, solid at first and becoming chambered or hollow with age. Flesh pallid greyish orange and unchanging. The milk is white and does not change colour in the air. Gills and flesh both taste mild, and there is no distinctive smell. Found under beech.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white and does not change, drying cream. Its cap is 1-3.5 cm across, where saffron milk cap's is 3-20 cm, so a small saffron cap can overlap. It is dull salmon, greyish orange or pale orange-brown, and unzoned, where saffron milk cap is often ringed. It grows under beech; saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Roadsides, pastures, gardens, waste land.
In New Zealand it grows on alluvial flats, in stockyards and sheep camps and on other ground high in nitrogen, and invades pasture where summers are dry and winters moist and mild (Bay of Plenty Regional Council, restated).
Silybum marianum establishes itself in sunny, warm ruderal meadows in regularly disturbed places such as rubble deposits, at the foot of south-exposed walls or villages and on urban fallow land or on cattle pastures. However, it does not prefer dry, stony soils.

identification.text:
Annual or biennial. Stems branched above, ridged, with sparse mealy hairs at least above, 0.5–2 m tall, not winged. Leaves elliptic to lanceolate, lyrate-pinnatifid to pinnate, sinuate, coarsely dentate, green with conspicuous white markings along veins, (10)–20–60 × (5)–10–30 cm, with sparse short mealy hairs on lamina, and sparse long tangled multicellular hairs on midrib; base amplexicaul, auriculate, with very spinous margins; prickles marginal, yellowish, spreading, 5–12 mm long. Capitula ovoid, erect, 4–6 × 5–7 cm, solitary, terminal and pedunculate, and also sessile in axils of uppermost leaves; peduncles with appressed cobwebby tomentum. Involucral bracts sparsely covered with short mealy hairs; margins with sparse cobwebby hairs. Outer bracts leaflike, obovate with spinous apex and margins. Middle bracts oblong; appendage ovate, subulate, with spinous margins and a long spreading to recurved apical spine. Inner bracts lanceolate; appendage becoming linear-lanceolate, entire. Corolla reddish purple, 20–28 mm long; lobes unequal, 4–6 mm long. Anther filaments joined at margins into a tube which encloses the basal appendages of the anthers. Style exserted 1–2 mm beyond corolla lobes. Achenes brown or black-streaked, obovoid, weakly transversely flattened, smooth, about 6 × 3 mm; outer pappus bristles scabrid, about 15 mm long; inner hairs very fine. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

preparation.text: Gather leaves and stems before the plant flowers. Cut off the very sharp leaf spines first, which is fiddly. To peel a tender leaf, hold the base of its stalk in one hand and pull the other hand quickly and firmly from there to the tip; the peeled stalk and midrib can be eaten raw or cooked like cardoons. Young leaves are thick and mild and suit mixed salads, but can turn bitter in hot, dry weather; cooked, they stand in for spinach. Leaves and stems can be boiled with salt or added to stews. Peel the stems, and soak them to reduce their bitterness, then use them like asparagus or rhubarb or add them to salads. Use the buds before the flowers open: the flavour is mild, but they are small and more fiddly than globe artichokes. Boiled, the roots have a mild flavour and a somewhat mucilaginous texture.

summary.text:
Silybum marianum is a species of thistle.
Silybum marianum is native from around the Mediterranean and much of Europe to Central Asia and India; in Africa it reaches as far south as Ethiopia. It is possibly native near the coast of southeast England. S. marianum has been widely introduced outside its natural range, for example into North America, Hawaii, Australia, New Zealand, and Colombia where it is considered an invasive weed. It also spreads invasively in almost all of Europe as a consequence of field cultivation.
Milk thistle has been potentially observed to modify fire regimes in its invasive range. Its invasion into new habitats may also be encouraged by fire.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Northland, Auckland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty, East Cape, Volcanic Plateau, Wellington; S.: Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago, Southland; Chatham Islands. S. marianum has also been referred to in New Zealand as Carduus marianus.
It is a pest plant under regional pest management plans, among them Hawke's Bay (sustained control, with a boundary rule), Auckland (sustained control) and Bay of Plenty (progressive containment), and it is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds (restated).

warnings: Variegated thistle is recorded as poisonous. Its leaves can hold large amounts of nitrate, especially when heavy rain follows a long drought, after heavy fertiliser or after the plant has been sprayed with herbicide; in the gut nitrate is turned to nitrite, which stops the blood carrying oxygen. It grows especially on ground high in nitrogen, such as stockyards and sheep camps. Its leaves have poisoned cattle and sheep, and cattle that gorge on wilted plants (cut or sprayed) can die within 2 hours.

It may cause allergic reactions, particularly in people allergic to related plants such as ragweed, chrysanthemum, marigold and daisy, and in people allergic to artichokes. Medicinal preparations of the seed are not to be used by anyone hypersensitive to the daisy family; their reported side effects include dry mouth, nausea, upset stomach, diarrhoea, headache and allergic reactions, from skin rash and hives to asthma and anaphylaxis.
Safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and medicinal seed preparations are not recommended then.
The leaf margins carry stiff yellowish spines 5–12 mm long, and the flower-head bracts end in long spines.

identification.text:
It grows in tufts and clusters on wood, many caps rising from one base; now and then singly or in twos and threes. The cap is 1–8 cm across, rounded at first, then almost flat, sometimes with a slight bump in the centre. It is smooth and sticky to slimy, bright yellow to orange-brown with a darker, tawny centre, or yellowish brown all over. The flesh is thick at the centre and very thin at the edge, tinged yellow.
The gills are attached to the stem but notched just before it, broad, and white to pale yellow. The stem is 5–10 cm long and 6–8 mm thick, tough and rubbery, springing back when squeezed. It is yellowish at the top, orange-brown below and darker towards the base, which narrows into the wood, and it is finely velvety. It has no ring. The smell is mild and fresh, sometimes slightly fruity. The spore print is white.
The sticky yellow-orange cap with the dark velvety stem is the classic combination. On pine the caps are often dwarfed, though still in dense clusters.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small orange-brown mushrooms on rotting wood, so place and cap colour do not separate them. Wood nipple fungus belongs to the group of the deadly Galerina marginata and probably carries the same toxins. Look at the stem: velvet shank's is velvety and dark brown towards the base, with no ring. The Galerina's is slender, 2–4 mm thick, pale tan to rusty orange, with a thin ring high up that can soon fall away. Look at the gills: white to pale yellow in velvet shank, rusty orange to cinnamon in the Galerina. Velvet shank's cap is sticky, 1–8 cm across, and it grows in dense tufts from one base. The Galerina's cap is 1–2.5 cm across, often with a pointed bump in the centre, and it grows singly or in loose groups, rarely in tight clumps. A spore print settles it: white for velvet shank, cinnamon-brown for the Galerina.

preparation.text:
Never eat it raw: always cook it thoroughly. Cut off the dark lower half of the stems. Wipe the sticky caps with a damp cloth, and rinse them quickly only if they are dirty; peeling the skin off the cap before cooking is recommended. After frost, use only firm mushrooms, and throw away any that are soft, slimy or discoloured.
The sticky coating melts away in cooking and thickens broths. Velvet shanks keep a slight crunch after cooking and turn slippery in broth. They suit soups, noodle soups, ramen and hot pots, stir-fries with garlic, soy sauce and sesame, sauces, and risotto.
They dry well. Dried caps can be ground into a seasoning, and the tough stems can be dried and powdered.

recipes.method: Written for wild velvet shank. Serves 2. 200 g velvet shanks; 40 g cornflour; 40 g plain flour; 100 ml ice-cold water; 1 tsp salt; ½ tsp smoked paprika; vegetable oil for frying. Clean the mushrooms, cut off and discard the dark lower half of the stems and keep the caps and tender upper stems. Rinse briefly only if very dirty, then pat completely dry: dry mushrooms give a crisp shell. Whisk the cornflour, flour, salt and paprika, then whisk in the water a little at a time to a smooth, thin batter. Heat about 2.5 cm of oil in a deep frying pan or pot to 170 °C. Dip the mushrooms in the batter, let the excess drip off, and fry for 2–3 minutes a side until golden and crisp. Drain on a rack or paper towels and serve at once, with garlic aioli, spicy mayonnaise or sea salt, or on top of a winter soup.
recipes.title: Crispy fried velvet shank

recipes.method: Written for wild velvet shank. Serves 3. 200 g velvet shanks; 250 g very thinly sliced beef (ribeye, sirloin or flank); 2 tbsp soy sauce; 2 tbsp mirin; 1 tbsp sake or dry sherry; 1 tbsp sugar; 1 tbsp vegetable oil; sesame seeds. Clean the mushrooms and cut away the dark lower stems; halve or quarter large caps. Lay a slice of beef flat, put a few mushroom pieces at one end with the caps poking out, and roll it up tightly. Mix the soy sauce, mirin, sake and sugar until the sugar dissolves. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat and brown the rolls, seam side down first, turning them for 2–3 minutes. Pour in the sauce, lower the heat and let it bubble and thicken, rolling the bundles until glossy. Serve with the pan sauce, sesame seeds, steamed rice and pickled vegetables.
recipes.title: Velvet shank beef rolls

recipes.method: Written for wild velvet shank. Serves 4. 150 g velvet shanks; 800 ml dashi; 3 tbsp white or mixed miso; 150 g silken tofu; 1 tbsp dried wakame; 2 spring onions. Soak the wakame in cold water for 5 minutes and drain. Clean the mushrooms, discarding the tough lower stems; leave small caps whole and halve large ones. Cube the tofu and slice the spring onions. Bring the dashi to a gentle simmer, add the mushrooms and cook 3–4 minutes until tender and slippery. Add the tofu and wakame, simmer 1 minute, then turn off the heat. Dissolve the miso in a ladle of the hot broth and stir it in; do not boil the soup once the miso is in. Serve topped with the spring onions.
recipes.title: Velvet shank miso soup

recipes.method: Written for wild velvet shank. Serves 2–3. 150 g velvet shanks; 2 large eggs; 30 g carrot; 2 spring onions; ½ tsp salt; a pinch of black pepper; 2 tbsp vegetable oil. Clean the mushrooms, remove the tough lower stems, and chop the caps and upper stems into 1 cm pieces. Dice the carrot very small and slice the spring onions thinly. Beat the eggs, stir in the vegetables and mushrooms, and season. Heat the oil in a large non-stick frying pan over medium-low heat, spoon in small rounds 5–7 cm across and press them flat. Cook 2–3 minutes until golden, turn and cook 2 minutes more. Drain on paper towels and serve warm with a dipping sauce of 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp rice vinegar, a pinch of sugar and a few drops of sesame oil.
recipes.title: Velvet shank pancakes (jeon)

recipes.method: Written for wild velvet shank. Serves 2. 200 g velvet shanks; 20 g butter; 1 tbsp soy sauce; 1 garlic clove; 1 tbsp sake or white wine (optional); black pepper; 1 spring onion. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Clean the mushrooms, trimming off the tough velvety stem bases, and pile them in the centre of a 30 cm square of heavy foil (or a double layer). Scatter over the finely chopped garlic, dot with the butter, drizzle with the soy sauce and sake, and add pepper. Fold the edges together several times to seal the parcel tightly. Bake on a tray for 15 minutes, or cook on a barbecue over medium heat for 12–15 minutes. Open carefully (hot steam) and serve with the buttery juices and sliced spring onion.
recipes.title: Foil-baked velvet shank

recipes.method: Written for wild velvet shank. Serves 2. 450 g velvet shanks, cleaned and sliced; 2 large onions, sliced; 2 garlic cloves, crushed; 2 tbsp olive oil; salt and pepper; 1 cup (250 ml) quinoa; 500 ml water or chicken or vegetable stock; 125 ml (½ cup) chopped cherry tomatoes; 60 ml (¼ cup) chopped parsley; 2 tbsp balsamic vinegar; 1 tsp honey; 1 tbsp lemon juice. Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat and cook the onions about 10 minutes until soft and caramelised. Add the garlic for a minute, then the mushrooms; season and cook until tender, 5–7 minutes. Meanwhile rinse the quinoa, bring it to the boil in the water or stock, cover and cook on low about 20 minutes until tender and the liquid is absorbed. Mix the quinoa with the tomatoes, parsley, vinegar, honey and lemon juice and season. Serve the mushrooms and onions over the salad.
recipes.title: Velvet shank with caramelised onions and quinoa salad

recipes.method: Written for a mix of wild mushrooms; the author lists velvet shank (enokitake) among those that suit it. Serves 4. 1.5 litres mushroom or chicken stock; 170 g carrot in 2.5 cm matchsticks; 115 g spring onions in 2.5 cm pieces; one 5 mm slice of fresh ginger; 225 g fresh wild mushrooms in bite-sized pieces; 125 ml soy sauce, or to taste; a tiny pinch of chilli flakes; 115 g shredded spinach or other tender greens; salt. To serve: 570 g cooked soba noodles (about 140 g a person); toasted sesame oil; chopped coriander. Cook the soba ahead in lightly salted water, rinse in cool water and toss in a little sesame oil. Simmer the stock, carrot, spring onions, ginger, mushrooms, soy sauce and chilli in a 4-litre pot for 20 minutes, until the vegetables are tender. Add the greens and cook a minute more, then taste and add salt if needed. Warm the noodles in bowls, ladle the very hot soup over, and finish with sesame oil and coriander.
recipes.title: Wild mushroom soup with soba noodles

Not used: 'up to 10 cm tall and wide'; the European/North American seasons (Europe October to February, North America through May) and European hosts (elm, ash, beech, oak); cap flesh yellow, stem flesh brown; and the 'similar species' F. populicola, F. lupinicola, Marasmiellus dichrous and Xeromphalina tenuipes, none of which has a New Zealand iNaturalist record.

summary.text:
Flammulina velutipes, the velvet foot, velvet stem, velvet shank or wild enoki, is a species of gilled mushroom in the family Physalacriaceae.
William Curtis first described it from England in 1782, as Agaricus velutipes. Flammulina means 'little flame', for its colour. It is a winter mushroom: one of the few that fruit in really cold weather, often through frost.
In New Zealand it is naturalised and found over much of the country, less often in warm areas such as Northland; there are 1,547 research-grade iNaturalist records. It was recorded at Dannevirke in 1899. Whether it is native or was brought in is not settled: national registers list it as exotic, and it may have arrived early in colonisation in imported wood, but Horak (1971) hesitated to call it introduced and treated the New Zealand form as a distinct variety.
The white, long-stemmed enoki sold in shops is a different species, Flammulina filiformis, from Asia. The two were long treated as one, until DNA showed they are distinct. F. filiformis is not found wild in New Zealand. Grown in the dark with high carbon dioxide, it has long pale stems and tiny caps.
New Zealand also has an endemic Flammulina, F. stratosa, ranked Data Deficient; it has no iNaturalist records here.

warnings: Never eat velvet shank raw; always cook it thoroughly.

Rustgills (Gymnopilus) also grow in orange clusters on stumps and logs, and have brown spore prints. The spectacular rustgill (G. junonius), common in New Zealand, is inedible and contains neurotoxins. It is bright yellow-orange, ageing orange-brown or reddish brown, and its spore print is rusty brown. The common rustgill (G. penetrans), also recorded here, has crowded thin gills that get rusty spots as they age, a cap that is usually dry, and rusty spores. Velvet shank has a sticky cap, a dark velvety stem with no ring, white to pale yellow gills and a white spore print: check the print before eating any.

habitat.text:
Low intertidal to subtidal, on almost any hard surface: rock reefs and rock pools, wharf piles, seawalls, moorings, ropes, buoys and boat hulls.
In New Zealand it grows from about mid-low-water-neap level down to 15 m, occasionally 18 m. It is commonest in sheltered harbours and ports, but it also grows on wave-exposed coasts, including in native kelp forests, and it also grows attached to native seaweeds such as Carpophyllum flexuosum and Cystophora scalaris.

harvestEthics.text:
Wakame is an unwanted organism under the Biosecurity Act 1993 and on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds. Unless MPI permits it, it is an offence to knowingly spread or release it, to sell it or offer it for sale, or to propagate or breed it. Commercial harvest needs MPI permission, and plants growing on natural surfaces such as reefs may be harvested commercially only as part of a programme to control it.
Take it only from where it already grows. Carry no live plants or pieces to another place, never put any back in the sea elsewhere, and clean your gear, boat and anchor before you move on. On reefs take only the wakame: disturbing or removing the native seaweeds around it can help it spread.
Regional pest plans add their own rules. In Northland no one may knowingly transport material that may harbour it unless it has been removed or made non-viable; in Gisborne it may be disposed of only at a legal landfill or an authorised green-waste site; Auckland bans breeding, distributing, releasing or selling it live. Otago Regional Council asks for sightings to be reported, and in Fiordland MPI, DOC and Environment Southland are working to eliminate it from Te Puaitaha/Breaksea Sound; every vessel entering the Fiordland Marine Area must hold a Fiordland Clean Vessel Pass.
Some mātaitai reserves that ban taking seaweed exempt it: the Lyttelton Harbour/Whakaraupō and Rāpaki mātaitai reserves ban all seaweed other than Undaria, and the Makaawhio mātaitai reserves in South Westland all seaweed other than karengo and Undaria. Taking seaweed is banned in marine reserves and in some mātaitai, taiāpure and closed areas such as Pukerua Bay; check MPI's rules for the area first.

identification.text:
A kelp usually up to about 1 m long, sometimes 2 m, with one large, thin blade that is often deeply divided into lobes. A well-defined midrib runs up the middle of the blade and continues into the stalk. The holdfast is a clump of forked, finger-like branches. Colour ranges from pale golden brown to dark brown; mature plants look brown, green and yellow, and crinkly. Mature plants carry a reproductive structure, the sporophyll, at the base of the stalk: thicker and often darker than the blade, deeply folded and, when large, seeming to spiral around the stalk. Young plants do not have it yet.
Told from common kelp (Ecklonia radiata) by its midrib, more prominent than anything on Ecklonia's blade, by the folded sporophyll at the base of the stalk on mature plants, and by its thinner, membranous, slimy blade.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look for a midrib: wakame's blade has a well-defined midrib that runs up the middle and continues into the stalk, more prominent than anything on common kelp's blade. Mature wakame also has a reproductive structure at the base of the stalk, thicker and often darker than the blade, deeply folded and, when large, seeming to spiral around the stalk; common kelp's stalk is cylindrical and unbranched, and its reproductive structures show as darker patches on the blade lobes. Young wakame does not have the folded structure yet, so rely on the midrib. Wakame's blade is also thinner, membranous and slimy. Size, shape and colour do not separate them: both grow to about 1 m, both have a large blade deeply divided into lobes and a holdfast of finger-like branches, both can look wrinkled, and both are golden brown, wakame ranging to dark brown. Both grow from the low intertidal into the subtidal on hard surfaces, and their ranges overlap around the North and South Islands, Stewart and the Snares; common kelp is absent from the Chatham Islands, where wakame is found.

preparation.text: Rinse well. For salads, cut out the central stalk. Drop the blades into boiling water for about 30 seconds, until they turn from khaki to bright green, then shred and dress as a salad, or add to soups such as miso soup and Korean miyeok-guk. The stalks are chewy and a little crunchy: blanch them for 10 to 20 seconds and stir-fry them. Dried wakame is soaked in cold water before use.

recipes.method: Fresh wakame, choosing thin, tender blades; sesame oil; rice vinegar; tamari; mirin; cucumber. Cut out and discard the central stalks. Boil the blades until they change from khaki to emerald green, which takes only about 30 seconds. Shred them and dress them Japanese-style with sesame oil, rice vinegar, tamari and mirin. Serve with cucumber as a salad.
recipes.title: Wakame salad

recipes.method: Written for dried miyeok (wakame). Serves 2 to 3. 16 g dried miyeok, soaked in cold water for 30 minutes; 1.9 litres (8 US cups) water; 450 g beef brisket or skirt steak, cut into thin, small pieces; 4 garlic cloves, minced; 25 ml (1 tbsp plus 2 tsp) fish sauce, or salt and soy sauce to taste; 10 ml (2 tsp) toasted sesame oil. Rinse and drain the soaked miyeok, squeeze out the excess water and cut it a few times into bite-size pieces. Put it in a large, heavy pot with the water, cover and boil for about 10 to 12 minutes. Turn the heat down to medium, add the beef, cover and cook for 40 minutes. Stir in the garlic and fish sauce and cook another 10 minutes, until the beef is tender and the broth savoury. Stir in the sesame oil. Serve with rice and side dishes such as kimchi. It keeps in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 4 days.
recipes.title: Miyeok-guk (seaweed soup with beef)

recipes.method: Written for dried wakame. 60 ml (4 tbsp) unseasoned rice vinegar; 30 ml (2 tbsp) sugar; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) kosher salt, or half that of table salt, for the dressing; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) soy sauce; 15 ml (1 tbsp) dried wakame; 2–3 Japanese cucumbers; 5 ml (1 tsp) kosher salt, or half that of table salt, for the cucumbers; 7.5 ml (½ tbsp) toasted white sesame seeds. Warm the vinegar, sugar, salt and soy sauce in a saucepan over medium heat, whisking, until the sugar dissolves; take it off the heat and let it cool. Soak the wakame in a bowl of water for 5 minutes to rehydrate. Peel the cucumbers in alternate stripes and slice them thinly into rounds. Massage the salt into the cucumber and leave for 5 minutes. Squeeze the water out of the wakame and put it in a bowl; squeeze the liquid from the cucumber and add it. Add the sesame seeds, pour over the dressing, toss and serve.
recipes.title: Sunomono (cucumber and wakame salad)

recipes.method: Written for dried wakame. Dried wakame; 15 to 30 ml (1 to 2 tbsp) sesame or olive oil; 15 ml (1 tbsp) sesame seeds (optional). Cut the dried wakame into bite-size pieces. Warm the oil in a frying pan, add the wakame and stir-fry over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, tossing, until it turns green and crisp. Drain on paper towels and sprinkle with roasted sesame seeds to serve.
recipes.title: Seaweed chips

recipes.method: Written for dried wakame. Dried wakame; sesame seeds; parsley or coriander; spring onion; rice vinegar; soy sauce; sesame oil; 5 ml (1 tsp) sugar. Soak the wakame in warm water for about 30 minutes, longer if it is not yet soft. Meanwhile stir a splash each of rice vinegar, sesame oil and soy sauce with the sugar until it dissolves. Chop the spring onion and parsley or coriander finely. Drain the wakame, chop it to the size you like and return it to the bowl. Add the dressing, the greens and the sesame seeds and mix until everything is evenly coated.
recipes.title: Wakame sesame salad

recipes.method: Written for salted, packaged wakame stalks (miyeok julgi). Serves 8. 280 g salted wakame stalks; 5 ml (1 tsp) vegetable oil; 5 ml (1 tsp) sesame oil; 10 ml (2 tsp) chopped garlic; 15 ml (1 tbsp) cooking sake or mirin; about 1.5 ml (1/3 tsp) sea salt; about 1 ml (1/4 tsp) sugar; sesame seeds. Rinse the stalks in three changes of water to wash off the salt, then soak them in fresh water for 30 to 40 minutes, until they no longer taste salty, and drain. Heat both oils in a large frying pan over medium-high heat and sauté the stalks for 1 to 2 minutes until coated. Turn the heat to medium, add the garlic and sake and sauté about 1 minute. Add half the salt, taste and add more if needed, then the sugar, and turn off the heat. Do not cook too long or at too low a heat, or the stalks turn slimy. Sprinkle with sesame seeds and serve at room temperature or cold. It keeps in the fridge for up to a week.
recipes.title: Stir-fried wakame stalks (miyeok julgi bokkeum)

summary.text:
Wakame (Undaria pinnatifida), or Asian kelp, is an introduced kelp from north-east Asia, eaten there as wakame and in Korea as miyeok, and an unwanted organism in New Zealand.
It is native to Japan, Korea and China, and has also been introduced to the Mediterranean, the north-east Atlantic, Tasmania and Argentina. It was first found in Wellington Harbour in 1987 and has spread, largely on boat hulls, to many ports, harbours and coasts; it is now found around the North Island, South Island, Stewart, Chatham and Snares Islands. Often called 'the gorse of the sea', it can form dense underwater forests that displace native seaweeds and change native marine communities. It is an unwanted organism under the Biosecurity Act 1993 and on DOC's 2024 list of environmental weeds, and MPI runs programmes to remove it from Fiordland and the Chatham Islands.
Each plant lives about six months. Plants grow fast from winter to spring and break down in late summer and autumn, but in New Zealand some are present all year. At two months old a plant can release millions of spores.

warnings: Wakame grows readily in ports, marinas and harbours, on wharf piles and moorings. Harvest only from clean water, away from harbours and heavy boat traffic, and never near stormwater or wastewater outfalls.
Seaweed can carry contaminants from the water it grows in: lead where the shore takes industrial, sewage and drainage waste, and norovirus where wastewater flows into the sea.

Wakame is a brown seaweed, and brown seaweed can contain very high levels of iodine. High levels of iodine can cause thyroid problems, so eating it more than every once in a while may be unsafe, especially when pregnant or breastfeeding.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Forest and scrub, forest margins, roadsides, stream beds, pasture, lakeshores, almost always in shaded sites.
It grows in woodland, beech woodland in particular, and on lime-rich soils and substrates: wall mortar, the crack where a wall meets the pavement, and cemeteries. It avoids strong light and favours the shaded side of a wall.
On the national wetland plant list it is rated facultative upland: occasionally in wetlands, usually not.

identification.text:
Glabrous perennial. Stem usually single, erect, not branched or branching above, finely grooved, (20)–50–100 cm tall. Rosette and lower stem leaves petiolate, 7–20 × 3–10 cm, lyrate-pinnatifid with a large triangular or reniform ternatifid coarsely toothed terminal lobe and 1–3 pairs of small ovate-hastate coarsely toothed lateral lobes; hydathodes prominent at tips of teeth; lamina thin, bright green above, pale and glaucous beneath. Upper leaves similar, with petiole becoming broadly winged and amplexicaul-auriculate at base; uppermost leaves not divided, linear to oblong, amplexicaul. Inflorescence diffusely paniculate. Capitula numerous, narrowly cylindric. Outer involucral bracts 2–4, very short, ovate to lanceolate, 1/10-? length of inner bracts. Inner involucral bracts linear, strictly erect, often purplish, 5–7 mm long; margins scarious. Receptacle areoles with raised glabrous margins. Florets 1½× length of involucre; corolla pale yellow. Achenes usually 5 or fewer, dark brown to black, 10-ribbed, fusiform, flattened, very finely scabrid, shortly beaked, 3–4.5 mm long. Pappus bristles in 2 more or less unequal rows, fine, white.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Each head usually has five florets, which look like five petals, with five anthers sticking out of them; a stem carries a few hundred heads. The plant often shows red pigment.

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the florets in a head: wall lettuce has 5 or fewer, prickly lettuce usually more (12–20). Under the head, wall lettuce's bracts are in two distinct rows, a few very short outer ones and a row of linear inner ones; prickly lettuce's are in more than two rows of gradually changing length. Wall lettuce is hairless, its lower leaves stalked and lyre-shaped with a large triangular or kidney-shaped, three-lobed end lobe and 1–3 pairs of small side lobes; prickly lettuce's lower leaves taper to the base and carry stiff hairs and spiny bristles on the veins beneath, especially the midrib. Wall lettuce's achene is shortly beaked; prickly lettuce's beak is about as long as its body. Both have milky sap and small yellow heads in a loose, branched spray. Prickly lettuce's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they are bitter (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Prickly lettuce

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the florets in a head: wall lettuce has 5 or fewer, wild lettuce usually more. Under the head, wall lettuce's bracts are in two distinct rows, a few very short outer ones and a row of linear inner ones 5–7 mm long; wild lettuce's are in more than two rows of gradually changing length, the involucre (11)–13–15 mm long. Wall lettuce is hairless, its lower leaves stalked and lyre-shaped with a large triangular or kidney-shaped, three-lobed end lobe; wild lettuce's lower leaves taper to the base, carry spiny bristles under the midrib, and its stem has pale spines up to 4 mm long, especially low down. Wall lettuce's achene is shortly beaked; wild lettuce's beak is about as long as its body. Both have milky sap and yellow heads in a loose, branched spray. Wild lettuce is not one to eat: eight people in Iran were taken to hospital after eating it (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Wild lettuce

lookalikes.howToTell: Wall lettuce is hairless all over; nipplewort's stems carry fine crinkled hairs, especially low down, and its leaf margins are fringed with hairs, though the leaf surfaces range from hairless to densely hairy. Count the florets: wall lettuce's heads have usually 5, nipplewort's 8 to 15. Wall lettuce's leaf end-lobe is large, triangular or kidney-shaped and itself three-lobed, coarsely toothed with prominent water pores (hydathodes) at the tooth tips; nipplewort's is broadly ovate to triangular to round, bluntly toothed and not three-lobed. Under the head, nipplewort's bracts are strongly veined or keeled; wall lettuce's inner bracts are linear, strictly erect and often purplish, with 2–4 very short outer ones. In seed, wall lettuce's achenes are dark brown to black, shortly beaked and topped with a white pappus; nipplewort's are pale, without beak or pappus. Both have milky sap, lyre-shaped lower leaves with a large end lobe, small yellow heads in a loose branched spray, and grow at forest margins and roadsides. Nipplewort's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Nipplewort

lookalikes.howToTell: Break a stem or leaf: wall lettuce's sap is milky, mountain fireweed's is watery. Wall lettuce's heads have usually 5 or fewer strap-shaped, pale yellow florets; mountain fireweed has no strap-shaped florets, only a yellow disc 2–3 mm across of tiny tubular florets of two kinds. Wall lettuce's leaves are thin, coarsely toothed, with prominent water pores (hydathodes) at the tooth tips; mountain fireweed's are thicker, with more rounded teeth. In seed, wall lettuce's achenes are dark brown to black; mountain fireweed's are paler and sparsely papillate. Both are hairless or nearly so, have lobed leaves that clasp the stem higher up and achenes topped with fine white pappus hairs, and both grow at forest margins and by streams. Mountain fireweed is a native plant with no food record, and its genus, Senecio, is known for liver-damaging pyrrolizidine alkaloids (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Mountain fireweed

preparation.text: Use the leaves raw in mixed salads, or cook them. In Sicily, where it is called cardedda di muru, the leaves are commonly gathered and eaten both raw and cooked.

recipes.method: The author's greens were the leaves of Indian, alpine (woodland) and garden strawberries, red deadnettle, wall lettuce, herb Robert and nasturtium. A handful of mixed strawberry leaves, stems removed (they are tough); a handful of beetroot leaves and stems; several stems of red deadnettle with their flowers; 5 wall lettuce leaves; 5 herb Robert leaves; red nasturtium flowers and several leaves; a few celery and small kale leaves, optional. Blend the leaves and flowers with 500–750 ml (2–3 cups) water, then add 1 punnet of strawberries, 1 red apple, 2 kiwifruit and 2 bananas and blend again.
recipes.title: Wild and tame strawberry smoothie

summary.text:
Lactuca muralis, the wall lettuce, is a perennial flowering plant in the tribe Cichorieae within the family Asteraceae.
It has become naturalised in parts of Northern Ireland as long ago as 1913. It was first recorded in The Burren, where it is now frequent, in 1939.
Lactuca muralis is a native of Europe but has invaded shady roadsides, paths and logged areas of the Pacific Northwest and New England.
The specific Latin epithet muralis is interpreted as 'growing on walls'.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Coromandel southwards; S.: throughout; St. Naturalised from Europe, Asia Minor and North Africa, first recorded in 1899. M. muralis has also been referred to in N.Z. as Lactuca muralis.
Older floras placed it in Lactuca with the other lettuces. It is kept apart as Mycelis on a small difference in the seed hairs (in Mycelis the inner row is longer than the outer), and Stace (2019) has suggested returning it to Lactuca. Prenanthes muralis is its original name.
It overwinters with only a few green leaves and puts up new ones in late spring (Scotland). Its seeds fly on a pappus, but most seedlings come up within about 2 m of the parent.
Most of Landcare Research's databased herbarium specimens come from the South Island: Canterbury 14, Marlborough 9, Nelson 4, Otago 3, Westland 2 and Southland 1, against Wellington 4 and South Auckland 1. Auckland Museum holds one collected in the Rotorua Ecological District on 24/01/2016.

warnings: Its food record is thin: one plant database and one Sicilian field survey name the leaves, and no source gives a safe amount. The same database's other edition lists the raw root, not the leaves, as the edible part.

identification.text:
Large tree with compound leaves of five to nine leaflets, aromatic when crushed. Round green husks 3.5–5 cm long that split and blacken to release the familiar wrinkled shell.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Large tree to over 20 m high, with broad spreading crown. Shoots glabrous, stout, dark, with prominent, Y-shaped leaf scars; buds grey, more or less finely puberulent. Leaves to about 55 cm long; petiole and rachis to about 30 cm long on adult branches. Leaflets 5–9, densely glandular-puberulent when young, becoming glabrous except for axillary hair tufts on undersurface, entire; base cuneate to rounded; apex rounded to acute or cuspidate; lowest pair of leaflets much smaller; terminal leaflet largest. Lamina of terminal leaflet mostly 10–20 × 5–11 cm (sometimes larger on strong vegetative shoots), broad-elliptic or elliptic-obovate. Male catkins 5–11 cm long, puberulent. Female flowers in clusters of 1–3, sessile or subsessile, densely glandular-puberulent; stigmas to 3 mm long, pale green. Fruit 3.5–5 cm long, subglobose, glabrous but gland-dotted, green, not beaked. Shell thick or thin, rugose; sutures thick and easily dividing in half at maturity. Seed very convoluted. Wild or self-sown trees tend to have thick-shelled nuts.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both edible; this is about which you have. Count and feel the leaflets: walnut has 5–9 with smooth (untoothed) edges, the end leaflet the largest and the lowest pair much smaller; Japanese walnut has 9–17, finely toothed though the teeth are often sparse, the end leaflet about the size of the side ones. Seedling walnuts can have toothed leaflets, so check an adult tree. Walnut's fruits sit in clusters of 1–3 close on the twig; Japanese walnut's hang 10–22 together in long strings. Walnut's fruit is 3.5–5 cm, nearly round, smooth and green with gland dots, not beaked; Japanese walnut's is 2.5–4 cm, egg-shaped, beaked, sticky and rusty-hairy. Walnut's shell splits easily in half along its seams when ripe; Japanese walnut's thick shell has raised seams that split with difficulty and an often sharp tip.
