preparation.text: Gather fallen nuts promptly, husk them (wear gloves — the husk stains skin brown and the stain is very hard to remove), then dry for several weeks before storing.

recipes.method: Written for walnuts by New Zealand growers; the page does not name the species. 1 kg fresh green walnuts; 250 g salt; 2 litres boiling water, in two lots; 1 litre malt vinegar; 400 g brown sugar; 1 tsp salt; 1 tsp pickling spice; 1 tsp black peppercorns; ½ tsp whole cloves. Pick the nuts early, around Christmas, while they are green and before the shell forms: push a sturdy needle through each and throw out any that will not pierce easily. Wear gloves, as the juice stains skin and is very hard to remove. Prick the walnuts all over with a fork and put them in a large bowl. Dissolve half the salt in 1 litre of boiling water, pour it over to cover and leave in a cool place for a week. Drain, cover with a second brine made the same way and leave another week. Drain and spread the nuts in one layer on a tray, and set them outside in a sunny spot for 3–4 days, bringing them in at night, until black and dry. Bring the vinegar, sugar, teaspoon of salt and spices to the boil and simmer about 5 minutes to dissolve the sugar, then cool and strain out the spices. Bring the liquid back to the boil, pack the walnuts into clean jars and pour it over so every nut is covered. Cover and keep somewhere dark for at least a month before eating; the growers find them better after 4 months. Use vinegar-proof lids, or put a layer of cling film between lid and liquid, as vinegar corrodes metal lids and taints the walnuts.
recipes.title: Pickled green walnuts

recipes.method: Written for walnuts; the page does not name the species. 500 ml (2 cups) walnuts; ½ tsp salt. Heat the oven to 150 °C, or 140 °C if your oven runs hot. Spread the walnuts on a baking tray and toast for 12–15 minutes, watching that they do not burn, until toasted and fragrant. Let them cool. Process with the salt in a food processor until they turn into a smooth, runny butter.
recipes.title: Walnut butter

recipes.method: Written for walnuts; the page does not name the species. Makes about 375 ml (1½ cups). 250 ml (1 cup) toasted walnuts, roughly chopped; 250 ml (1 cup) parsley; 1 garlic clove; 250 ml (1 cup) grated parmesan; 1 tsp lemon zest and 2 tbsp lemon juice; ¼ tsp salt, and pepper; 125 ml (½ cup) olive oil; 4 slices bruschetta and some blue cheese, to serve. Blitz the walnuts, parsley, garlic, parmesan, lemon zest and juice, salt and pepper in a food processor until combined. Add the oil and blend again. Keep in a jar and use as needed. To serve it the author's way, heat the oven to 170 °C, spread the pesto thickly on the bruschetta, scatter with crumbled blue cheese and bake for 4 minutes to just melt the cheese; serve warm.
recipes.title: Walnut pesto

identification.text:
Procumbent to ascending, aquatic or amphibious perennial, rooting at lower nodes. Stems hollow, grooved, striate, up to 180 cm long. Basal leaves 1-pinnate, with a leaf stalk; leaflets in 2–8 pairs, ovate to lanceolate, serrate, sometimes lobed, particularly the end leaflet, 1–8–(12) cm long, without stalks; stem leaves similar to basal, but the uppermost often reduced to 3–5 leaflets. Umbel 2–4 cm in diameter, compound, almost without a stalk or shortly stalked, opposite a leaf; rays 4–14; bracts 0–2, linear to lanceolate; bracteoles 4–8, ovate-triangular. Flowers numerous, white, 1–2 mm in diameter. Fruit ovoid, dark brown, 1.5–2.5 mm long; ribs light brown, slender or slightly thickened. Flowers November–February.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Apium nodiflorum.]
A sprawling water plant up to a metre tall, with glossy, bright green leaves of paired, toothed leaflets and white flowers close to the leaf bases. Crushed, it smells of raw carrot; watercress smells of cress. Watercress also has rounded leaflets, a peppery taste, and four-petalled white flowers in spikes, not umbels; see Lookalikes.

lookalikes.howToTell: Watercress belongs to the cabbage family: its small white flowers have 4 petals and grow in stalked spikes (racemes) that lengthen into narrow, curved pods 8–18 mm long, and its leaves have a hot, mustardy taste. Water celery is an umbellifer: its tiny white flowers, 1–2 mm across with 5 petals, sit in small compound umbels 2–4 cm across on short stalks opposite the leaves. Watercress's leaflets are rounded with smooth or wavy edges; water celery's are toothed, and its crushed leaves smell of carrot. Water celery grows in shallow ponds, drains and the margins of slow streams and can be mistaken for watercress, so habitat does not separate them. Watercress from water draining grazed land can carry liver fluke and should be cooked.
lookalikes.name: Watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Look under the small umbels: water celery always has 4–8 small bracteoles there, and celery has none. Water celery lies along the ground or rises from it and roots at its lower nodes; celery stands erect, up to 80–(100) cm, and does not root at the nodes. Water celery's leaves are once-pinnate, with 2–8 pairs of toothed leaflets 1–8 cm long; celery's are 1–2-pinnate, with lobed segments 2–4 cm long. Both grow in wet ground, so place does not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Narrow-fruited watercress's leaflets are rounded, with smooth or wavy edges, and smell peppery when crushed; water celery's are toothed, in 2–8 pairs. In flower, narrow-fruited watercress has white four-petalled flowers in spikes, followed by narrow curved pods; water celery has small compound umbels of tiny white flowers on short stalks opposite the leaves, with 4–8 small bracteoles under each small umbel. Both grow in streams and drains, so place does not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Narrow-fruited watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Look under the small umbels: water celery always has 4–8 small bracteoles there, and sea celery has none. Water celery's stems root at the lower nodes; sea celery's sprawling stems do not root. Water celery's leaves are once-pinnate, with 2–8 pairs of toothed leaflets 1–8 cm long; sea celery's are three-parted to 1–2-pinnate, with lobed segments about 5–30 mm long. Sea celery is mostly coastal but also grows beside lakes and streams inland, so place does not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Sea celery

summary.text:
Fool's watercress. A streamside umbellifer that smells of raw carrot when crushed and is mistaken for watercress and grows in the same wet ground as hemlock. Eaten in Europe.
Helosciadium nodiflorum (synonym Apium nodiflorum) is not poisonous to humans, and it has traditionally been gathered and eaten in Spain, Italy, Portugal and Morocco. Native to Britain, central and southern Europe, south-western Asia to Persia and North Africa, it was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1947, possibly arriving as a seed contaminant or with ornamental pond plants. Flora of New Zealand (1988) gives it as established locally throughout the North Island except Taranaki and collected once in eastern coastal Southland; NZPCN now gives a scattered distribution from Northland to Wellington, abundant in many areas, and established in the north and west of the South Island.
It regrows from broken-off shoots, which root readily, and from seed. It can be mistaken for watercress and collected and passed on as such. It is on the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds.

warnings: Pull watercress stem by stem and smell each one. Anything that smells of carrot, celery or parsley rather than cress is not watercress.
Hemlock, a deadly relative, also lacks the pepper smell.
Liver fluke risk: water plants growing where sheep, goats or cattle graze can carry Fasciola hepatica, caught by eating them raw. Do not eat it raw from water draining grazed land.

Almost glabrous annual herb; stems erect or suberect, to about 75 cm tall, often reddish; roots rather slender. Leaves on main stem similar to those on branches, subsessile or shortly petiolate. Lamina 1–12 × 0.3–2 cm, lanceolate or linear-lanceolate, bright or deep green, with small translucent glandular dots; margins ciliolate and more or less undulate; base cuneate to attenuate; apex obtuse to acuminate. Ochreae to 2 cm long, reddish brown, truncate, with 0-few fringing bristles, more or less flared at upper nodes. Racemes slender, spike-like, to about 7 cm long, at least partly curving downwards, the lower flowers often distant; pedicels short, enclosed by bracts at anthesis, later protruding. Perianth 1.5–3 mm long, prominently dotted with brownish glands, usually pink or rose, rarely white, accrescent; segments more or less broad-elliptic, strongly imbricate. Nut 2.5–3 mm long, trigonous or biconvex, dark brown or black, finely granular and appearing dull to moderately shining. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Polygonum hydropiper L.]

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): In muddy ponds, ditches, swamps and slow-flowing waters; abundant in some places but absent in others.
It grows standing in, or at the edge of, farm drains, roadside ditches, swamps, ponds, dams, water races, slow streams and rivers, estuaries and marshy pasture, in humus-rich soil. It grows in both nutrient-poor and nutrient-rich water and tolerates some brackish water. In shaded drains and other sheltered water some plants keep submerged leaves through winter.
It copes with water levels that rise and fall and with ponds that dry out in summer, grows in the open or in light shade, and does poorly among taller plants.
On New Zealand's national wetland plant list it is rated obligate wetland: it almost always grows in wetlands.

harvestEthics.text: Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.

identification.text:
Stems stout, erect, to 1 m high; rootstock short, stout. Leaves all basal, erect; laminae 8–20 × 3–10 cm, ovate, subacute, rounded or subcordate at base; petiole long. Inflorescence a large, much-branched panicle; branches whorled, more or less straight, usually ascending, basally bracteate. Flowers usually pale lilac, about 1 cm diameter, pedicels slender, bracteate; sepals oblong; petals rounded. Achenes about 20, about 2.5 mm long, rounded, compressed, in a dense circular head; persistent style from below middle of inner edge of achene, more or less straight; stigmatic portion occupying 1/8–1/5 of style-length.
[From: Healy and Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]
A hairless plant of pond and ditch edges, 0.5–1.8 m tall. Its broad, oval leaves, 8–23 cm long and 3–10 cm wide with a pointed tip and a rounded or heart-shaped base, stand upright in a rosette on long stalks that are D-shaped in cross-section; rarely, the leaves float or grow under water. The leaves above water die back over winter. From November to February it sends up a pyramid-shaped flower stalk up to about 1 m tall, with whorls of branches and many three-petalled flowers up to 1 cm across, pale lilac, pale pink or white with a yellow spot at the base of each petal. Each flower opens for only part of a day, in the afternoon. They are followed by rings of about 20 flat seeds which, seen from above, leave a gap in the middle.
Lance-leaved water plantain (Alisma lanceolatum), scattered from Gisborne to Wellington and in Canterbury and Otago, is very similar. Its leaves are lance-shaped or narrowly elliptic and taper gradually into the stalk; its petals are usually pale pink, often with pointed tips; and the seeds in its fruiting head touch and overlap in the middle, leaving no gap. Young plants without flowers can be hard to tell apart.

lookalikes.howToTell: Greater plantain's tiny flowers are packed into a dense, unbranched spike on a leafless stalk, and its leaves usually have fine hairs on the veins underneath, though some plants are hairless. Water plantain is hairless, its upright oval leaves sit on long, D-shaped stalks and die back over winter, and from November to February it carries a branched flower stalk up to about 1 m tall with whorls of pale lilac or white, three-petalled flowers up to 1 cm across. Greater plantain also grows in moist places and drains, so where it grows does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Greater plantain

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp plantain's tiny flowers are packed into a dense, unbranched spike, usually over 10 cm long, on a round stalk densely hairy near the top; its leaves are lance-shaped to broadly elliptic, hairy on the raised veins underneath, tapering into an often purple stalk. Water plantain is hairless, its upright oval leaves sit on long, D-shaped stalks and die back over winter, and from November to February it carries a branched flower stalk up to about 1 m tall with whorls of pale lilac or white, three-petalled flowers. Both grow in swamps and wet ground, so where it grows does not separate them.

summary.text:
Alisma plantago-aquatica, also known as European water-plantain, common water-plantain or mad-dog weed, is a perennial flowering aquatic plant widespread across most of Europe and Asia, and apparently spread elsewhere in both the Old and New World.
It is native to Europe, western Asia, northern and central Africa and Australia. In New Zealand it was first collected in the Waikato in 1929, perhaps escaping from ornamental ponds or arriving as a seed or soil contaminant. It is scattered and locally common from Northland to northern Southland, but absent from large parts of the southern and eastern North Island and the eastern South Island. It spreads by seed, carried by water and waterfowl, and by side shoots from the rhizome; the seeds can lie dormant, and in Scotland have been found to stay viable for ten years. In moving water it can be a nuisance, slowing the flow and trapping debris and silt. Despite the name it is not a plantain: it is a monocot in the water-plantain family, Alismataceae, named for its plantain-like leaves. The name mad-dog weed comes from its old use against rabies, and it was among the medicinal plants of Gerard's Herbal of 1597.
The starchy rootstock has been eaten after drying or long cooking, and the leaves and stalks after long boiling: heat or thorough drying destroys the poison in the fresh plant. Missouri's conservation department, writing of water plantains generally, says they can be dangerous to people and cattle and does not recommend eating them.
Like many water plants it takes up heavy metals from polluted water and stores them in its roots, and it has been suggested for cleaning stormwater and industrial wastewater.

warnings: Do not eat it. The fresh leaves and roots are poisonous, and its plantain-like rosette can be mistaken for a plantain, which is eaten raw.
The fresh leaves can irritate the skin.

habitat.text: Slow-moving fresh water: the margins of shallow streams, ditches, drains and spring-fed creeks, growing submerged, floating, or spread over mud. Often in dense floating mats. At Te Waikoropupū Springs it grows in water up to 6 m deep.

identification.text: Hairless compound leaves of rounded leaflets with smooth or wavy edges, the end leaflet larger than the rest. Hollow stems that trail, float or sprawl over mud and root at the leaf nodes. Small four-petalled white flowers, from spring through summer, followed by narrow, curved pods about 12–15 mm long with the seeds in two rows. Sharp peppery taste. Narrow-fruited watercress is almost identical: see Lookalikes.

lookalikes.howToTell: Water celery's leaflets are toothed, in 2–8 pairs, and its crushed leaves smell of carrot; watercress's leaflets are rounded with smooth or wavy edges and have a hot, mustardy taste. In flower, water celery has small compound umbels of tiny 5-petalled white flowers on short stalks opposite the leaves; watercress has 4-petalled white flowers in racemes followed by narrow curved pods. Water celery grows in shallow ponds, drains and the margins of slow streams, and it can be mistaken for watercress and collected and passed on as such. Water celery's young leaves and shoots are eaten in Mediterranean countries, but it is an umbellifer, and deadly hemlock — another umbellifer — also grows on damp ground in New Zealand, so be certain of the identification.
lookalikes.name: Water celery

lookalikes.howToTell: The two are very alike and the leaves do not separate them. The surest test is the ripe seeds: watercress has them in two distinct rows in each half of the pod, each seed with 20–50 coarse pits per face; narrow-fruited watercress has them in a single row, with 100–150 small pits. Watercress also tends to have smaller flowers (petals 4–6 mm long against 5–6 mm), shorter flower stalks (10–15 mm against 12–20 mm) and wider pods (2–2.5 mm against about 1.5 mm). Narrow-fruited watercress's leaves turn brown or purple in autumn and winter. Both grow in the same streams and drains. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Narrow-fruited watercress

lookalikes.howToTell: Bog yellow cress has yellow petals only about as long as the sepals (1.5–2.5 mm), usually stands upright from a taproot, and its leaves are deeply lobed with toothed edges. Watercress has white petals, about twice as long as the sepals, and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, with rounded leaflets with smooth or wavy edges. Bog yellow cress's pods are short and plump, 2–7 mm long; watercress's are narrow, 8–18 mm. Both grow at the edges of streams and other wet places, so place does not separate them. Bog yellow cress's young leaves and stems are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Bog yellow cress

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping yellowcress has yellow flowers on upright stems and spreads by creeping underground parts; its upper leaves are cut into narrow, toothed or untoothed lobes. Watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, with rounded leaflets with smooth or wavy edges. Both grow in wet ground and both have petals about twice as long as the sepals, so place and petal length do not separate them. Creeping yellowcress has no reliable food record.
lookalikes.name: Creeping yellowcress

lookalikes.howToTell: Land cress has yellow flowers on upright stems from a stout taproot, and grows on river banks, roadsides and waste land; watercress has white flowers and trailing hairless stems that root at the leaf nodes, and grows in streams, ditches and drains. Land cress's pods are 30–70 mm long; watercress's are 8–18 mm. Both have lobed leaves and a hot, cress-like taste, so taste does not separate them. Land cress's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.
lookalikes.name: Land cress

preparation.text: Raw only if it is bought or cultivated, or from water with no sheep or cattle grazing above it; otherwise cook it — soups, blanched as a green, or wilted. Pick from above the waterline. It is at its best before or just as it comes into flower; the taste gets hotter as the season goes on, and plants grown in damp soil rather than water are hotter still. If cooked leaves taste bitter, cook them in two changes of water. For mustard, grind the seeds and mix with cold water: the heat develops over 10–15 minutes. Hot water, vinegar or salt stops that reaction and gives a mild but bitter mustard.

recipes.method: Written for cultivated watercress by a commercial grower; use it raw only if bought or cultivated, or picked from water with no sheep or cattle grazing above it (see this entry's liver fluke warning). 1 bunch watercress (about 75 g); 1 garlic clove; 1 tbsp toasted pine nuts or sunflower seeds; 50–75 ml olive oil; 50 g fresh parmesan, finely grated; salt and pepper. Pulse the watercress, garlic and pine nuts lightly in a food processor. Drizzle in the oil until the pesto is slightly runny. Turn it into a bowl, stir in the parmesan and season with salt and pepper.
recipes.title: Watercress pesto

recipes.method: Serves 4. 500 g meaty pork ribs; 1 bunch watercress, washed thoroughly; 6 dried Chinese dates, red or black; a 2 cm piece of ginger, sliced lengthwise and smashed; 2 tsp salt; 1 tsp sugar. Cover the ribs with water by about 5 cm in a large pot and bring to a rolling boil, then drain in a colander to get rid of fat and scum and return the ribs to the pot. Trim the watercress, separate the leaves from the stems and chop the stems small. Add about 2 litres of water, the watercress stems, dates and ginger and bring to the boil over high heat. Cover and simmer gently over medium heat for 45 minutes to an hour, until the ribs are tender. Add the leaves and simmer about 10 minutes more, until they turn dark green. Stir in the salt and sugar and serve straight away.
recipes.title: Pork rib and watercress soup

recipes.method: Written for wild watercress (Nasturtium officinale) by an American chef. Serves 4. 450 g (1 lb) fresh watercress; salt; soft salted butter or extra virgin olive oil; lemon wedges or vinegar, to serve. Wash the watercress, picking out insects and debris, and dry it well, ideally in a salad spinner. Put a thin film of water in a large pot, fill the pot with the watercress and cover it. Set it over medium-high heat for a few minutes until the pot is very hot, then lift the lid and stir. Cover again for a minute or two, stir, and repeat until the watercress has wilted. Keep cooking and tasting, adding a splash of water if it dries out, until it is tender: young shoots are quick, older leaves can take 15 minutes or more. Turn off the heat and pour off what little water is left. Toss with a drizzle of olive oil and salt, taste, and serve with lemon or a dash of vinegar, or butter at the table. The author also steams it in a steamer basket over 5–8 cm of boiling water, covered on low heat, until tender, but prefers the pot method for watercress.
recipes.title: Steamed watercress

recipes.method: The recipe uses raw watercress: use only watercress that is bought or cultivated, or picked from water with no sheep or cattle grazing above it (see this entry's liver fluke warning). Balsamic reduction (makes about 600 ml; you need 45 ml): 1 litre balsamic vinegar; 150 g unrefined cane sugar; 1 rosemary stalk; half a diced red onion (optional). Maple walnuts: 125 ml (½ cup) walnuts; 5 ml (1 tsp) ground cinnamon; 30 ml (2 tbsp) maple syrup; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt. Salad (serves 4): half a finely sliced red onion; 45 ml (3 tbsp) balsamic reduction; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 1 orange; 1 litre (4 cups) watercress; 250 ml (1 cup) young puha leaves; 4 finely sliced radishes; 250 ml (1 cup) sprouts (ruruhau, mizuna, alfalfa or broccoli; optional); 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil. Balsamic reduction: stir until the sugar dissolves, bring to the boil, then simmer, stirring often, until reduced by half. Cool, remove the rosemary and bottle it. Maple walnuts: toast 125 ml (½ cup) walnuts on a lined tray in a 180 °C oven for 10 minutes, then stir through 5 ml (1 tsp) ground cinnamon, 30 ml (2 tbsp) maple syrup and 2.5 ml (½ tsp) salt and return to the oven for 2 minutes; cool. Salad: scrunch half a finely sliced red onion with 45 ml (3 tbsp) balsamic reduction and 5 ml (1 tsp) salt in a large bowl and leave it while you prepare the rest, adding each to the bowl without mixing: 1 orange, peeled and segmented; 1 litre (4 cups) watercress, the stems finely chopped (they can be stringy) and the leaves roughly chopped; 250 ml (1 cup) young puha leaves, roughly chopped; 4 finely sliced radishes; and 250 ml (1 cup) ruruhau, mizuna, alfalfa or broccoli sprouts (optional). Drizzle with 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil, add the walnuts, toss and serve.
recipes.title: Watercress and puha salad

recipes.method: Fills a 30 cm tart tin. Pastry: 125 g very cold butter; 250 g sieved plain flour; 50 g finely grated parmesan; 1 tsp icing sugar; salt; plenty of black pepper; just enough water. Filling: 500 g watercress leaves, with some white flowers kept for garnish; 20 g butter; the juice of 1 orange; 3 large eggs plus 2 extra yolks; 300 ml double cream; 200 g grated parmesan; salt and pepper; 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts. Heat the oven to 180 °C. For the pastry, grate 125 g very cold butter into 250 g sieved plain flour, 50 g finely grated parmesan, 1 tsp icing sugar, salt and plenty of black pepper. Rub together lightly, keeping it cool, then add just enough water to form a rough ball (less water, less shrinking). Chill for 30 minutes, roll out and line the tin, patching where needed. Prick the base, chill for 20 minutes, then blind-bake with baking paper and beans for 15 minutes; remove them and bake on until lightly toasted. For the filling, strip 500 g watercress leaves from the fibrous stalks (some stalk is fine — just a coarser tart), keeping some white flowers for garnish. Melt 20 g butter in a large heavy pan over a medium heat, add the watercress and the juice of 1 orange, and sweat gently for 10 minutes, stirring often. Blitz it with its juices, then beat it hard with 3 large eggs and 2 extra yolks, 300 ml double cream, all but a handful of 200 g grated parmesan, and plenty of salt and pepper — the more air, the more it rises. Pour into the case, sprinkle with the reserved parmesan and 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts, and bake for 20–25 minutes, until bronzed and only slightly wobbly in the middle. Cool a little and scatter the watercress flowers on top.
recipes.title: Watercress and parmesan tart

recipes.method: Written for wild watercress by an American chef; the soup is cooked, and the raw sprigs on top follow this entry's preparation. Serves 4. 115 g fresh watercress, chopped (about 4 cups); 1 large floury potato (225 g), peeled and chopped; 2 small carrots (115 g), grated; 1 medium onion (115 g), chopped; 15 g ramp leaves, chopped, or a small garlic clove and a few spring onions; 60 g unsalted butter; 1 tsp salt; about 1 litre chicken or vegetable stock; 60 ml dry white wine; olive oil, black pepper and a few watercress sprigs, to serve. Sweat the onion, potato and half the carrot in the butter for a few minutes until just tender, without letting the pan colour, then add the wine and cook it off. Add the stock and salt, bring to the boil, then turn the heat down low and cook for 20 minutes. Add the watercress and the ramp leaves or garlic and spring onions, and blend with a stick blender, leaving it a little coarse. Add the rest of the grated carrot and pulse a few times so there are still pieces of carrot and watercress in the soup. Let it stand a few minutes, or warm it through briefly, so the carrot softens, check the seasoning, and serve with watercress sprigs on top, black pepper and a drizzle of olive oil. The author's method adds a little sugar with the stock that his list leaves out; ramp leaves are his choice when he has them, garlic and spring onions his stand-in.
recipes.title: Watercress soup with carrots

recipes.method: Written for wild watercress by an American chef, who cooks it partly to rule out liver fluke. Serves 2–4. 2 large carrots (280 g); 2 very generous handfuls of watercress (115 g), trimmed into small clusters; 45 g unsalted butter; a handful of chopped ramp leaves or a few sliced spring onions (30 g); 1 tbsp maple syrup or a couple of pinches of sugar; a 2.5 cm piece of fresh ginger, finely grated (optional); 240 ml chicken stock or water; ½ tsp salt, plus more to taste. Peel the carrots and cut them on the diagonal into 5 mm coins, or halve large ones lengthways first and cut half-moons. Put the carrots, stock or water, ginger, butter, salt and syrup or sugar in a wide pan, about 30 cm, cover and bring to the boil, then take off the lid and keep cooking. When the liquid is thick and syrupy and the carrots are tender, lower the heat, keeping the pan from drying out. Add the watercress and the ramp leaves or spring onions, cover for a few moments to wilt it, then toss, check the seasoning and serve: buttery, salted, and only a little sweet. The author also makes it with young nettles.
recipes.title: Glazed carrots with watercress

recipes.method: Written for wild watercress by an American chef; the omelette is cooked but the salad on the side is raw, so use watercress that is bought or cultivated, or from water with no sheep or cattle grazing above it (see this entry's liver fluke warning), or serve cooked watercress on the side instead, as the author suggests. Serves 2. 115 g fresh watercress (two large handfuls), divided in half; 2 large eggs plus 1 yolk; 30 ml cream; a sprinkle of parmesan (optional); salt and black pepper; 2 tbsp bacon fat or light olive oil; a few fresh herbs such as coriander or basil; lemon juice or vinegar; a dash of extra virgin olive oil; a few rashers of bacon (optional). Heat the oven to 150 °C. Roughly chop half the watercress and blend it with the eggs, yolk, cream and a pinch of salt and pepper until very smooth, 15–30 seconds. Heat the bacon fat in a 25 cm non-stick pan over a medium heat, add the green egg mixture and cook gently for a minute or two, tucking in the sides, without letting it colour. Sprinkle on the cheese if using, then put the pan in the oven for a few moments, just to set the top. Loosen the edge with a spatula, roll the omelette up gently and cut it in two. Serve on warm plates with the rest of the watercress tossed with lemon juice, the herbs, salt, pepper and oil, and the bacon if using. The author says the herbs are what make the dish.
recipes.title: Watercress green omelette

recipes.method: Serves 4. 800 g potatoes, peeled and cut into 2 cm slices; a small bunch of spring onions, trimmed and sliced; 2 bunches of watercress, washed, large stalks removed; a splash of flavourless oil; 150 g crème fraîche; 200 ml skim milk; 250 g smoked kahawai or trout, skinned, boned and flaked; a squeeze of lemon; salt and black pepper. Heat the oven to 180 °C. Simmer the potatoes in a large pan of salted water for 5–7 minutes. Meanwhile heat a generous splash of oil over a medium-high heat in a lidded pan big enough for the watercress, add the watercress and toss until it starts to wilt, then cover for a minute so the stalks soften. Uncover, pour in the milk, bring to a simmer, add the crème fraîche, and blend it all in a food processor to a green-flecked sauce. Drain the potatoes and cool them under cold water so they stop cooking. Toss them with the sauce, season, and spoon half into a baking dish that holds them all snugly. Mix the fish with the spring onions and lemon, spread it over the potatoes, cover with the rest of the potatoes and pour over any sauce left. Bake for 25–30 minutes, until the potatoes are cooked through.
recipes.title: Watercress potatoes with smoked kahawai

Travel Med. 2008, was a New Zealander infected on a business trip abroad). The new rule: CDC, 'About Fasciola' (https://www.cdc.gov/liver-flukes/fasciola/index.html, retrieved 25/10/2026): 'do not eat raw watercress and other freshwater plants, especially from areas where livestock feed on land covered by grass (grazing areas)'; Useful Temperate Plants 'Nasturtium officinale' (https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Nasturtium+officinale, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, retrieved 25/10/2026), Known Hazards: 'Any plants growing in water that drains from fields where animals, particularly sheep, graze should not be used raw', 'Cooking the leaves, however, will destroy any parasites' (citing Phillips & Foy 1990). summary.text:
Peppery and everywhere in NZ waterways — but the water it grows in is the whole problem.
Also called true cress. A perennial of the mustard family from Eurasia and North Africa, brought to New Zealand as a culinary herb and recorded naturalised in 1852. It is common throughout the North, South and Chatham Islands, and commonest in the North Island. It spreads by seed and by pieces of stem that break off and root, and it has become a serious river weed here. It is also grown commercially as a salad crop. The name officinale comes from the Latin officina, a workshop that came to mean a monastery's herb store or pharmacy, for the plant's old medicinal use.

warnings: Liver fluke risk: watercress in waterways grazed by sheep or cattle can carry Fasciola hepatica. Cooking destroys it — raw does not.
Check the waterway for agricultural runoff and toxic algae before harvesting. LAWA publishes water quality and algal bloom status for monitored sites.
Never harvest from a stream below a farm, dairy shed or urban stormwater outfall.
Eating a lot of it can upset the stomach.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand – Seed Plants, Heenan 2020): Cardamine flexuosa predominantly occurs in damp or wet and often shaded sites, where it can be found as a garden weed, within or on the margins of disturbed or open indigenous forest and scrub, in wasteland and exotic plantations, along the margins of stream banks, and at the edge of road cuttings and tracks.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Weed of cultivation and bush remnants. C. flexuosa is found more often in damper sites than C. hirsuta.
In Britain: damp, shady places, from muddy puddles to streamsides and marshes, as well as gardens.

identification.text:
This is a small flowering plant growing to a height of no more than 30 cm, usually annual or short-lived perennial, with few short, erect stems. The leaves pinnate, mostly at the base, each with about 5 pairs of rounded leaflets. Flowers very small, white, 3–4 mm across with 6 stamens. Fruits of C. flexuosa generally do not overtop the flowers, a feature distinguishing it from Cardamine hirsuta.
Annual or biennial herb, single rosette or with short lateral branches. Petals 4; 2.5–4.0 × 1.0–1.7 mm, white, limb obovate; apex obtuse; base cuneate, tapering to a 0.8–1.0 mm long claw. Stamens 6(–4); median filaments 4, 2.3–2.4 mm long; lateral filaments 2, 2.6–2.7 mm long; anthers 0.3–0.5 mm long, pale yellow, when dehiscent held at a similar height to or slightly below the stigma. Siliques 12.0–28.0 × 1.0–1.5 mm, glabrous, style 0.3–1.0 mm long; valves green at maturity and when dehiscent; replum 0.3–0.5 mm wide.
Stems erect, flexuous, hairy especially below, green, rarely purplish, (10)-15-30-(40) cm tall.
Quick check (NZ Plant Conservation Network): the flowering stem zigzags at each flower node, which is what flexuosa (flexuous) refers to; New Zealand Flora Online notes that it can also be straight. Leaves are up to 12 cm long.

lookalikes.howToTell: Stamens are the best single test, seen with a hand lens on several flowers: wavy bittercress has 6 and hairy bittercress mostly 4, but stamen number varies; in one study 97% of wavy bittercress plants had six, while about 80% of hairy bittercress plants had four-stamened flowers and 18% had five. The flowering stem of wavy bittercress is usually flexuous (zigzag), though it can be straight; that of hairy bittercress is straight. Hairy seed pods mean hairy bittercress (its hairy-podded form grows mainly in the east of the North, South and Stewart Islands); hairless pods do not separate them. Sepals are 0.7–1.4 mm wide in wavy bittercress and 0.3–0.7 mm in hairy bittercress. In Britain the fruits of wavy bittercress generally do not overtop the flowers, while those of hairy bittercress do. Wavy bittercress is found more often in damper sites. Stem hairiness, petal size, the style on the pod and the number of leaflets overlap and do not separate them. Hairy bittercress is eaten the same way, raw as a peppery cress-flavoured leaf.

preparation.text: Used like cress, mainly raw as a flavouring in salads. The flavour is very similar to hairy bittercress, and the two can be added to salads together. Best eaten raw, as a garnish or in salads; its peppery taste stands up to strong flavours and to sharp or sweet dressings. A large picking can be wilted like a vegetable or made into a soup in the way of watercress soup.

summary.text:
Cardamine flexuosa, commonly known as wavy bittercress or wood bitter-cress, is an herbaceous annual, biennial, or short-lived perennial plant in the cabbage family (Brassicaceae).
It is native to the British Isles, Europe, North Africa, Turkey and Iran and widely introduced elsewhere.
Naturalised in New Zealand, originally from Europe. Cardamine flexuosa occurs throughout the North Island and is more locally distributed in the South Island.
The specimen (CHR 70259) supporting the first record was collected from Marokopa River, near Te Anga, Kāwhia County (South Auckland), in 1947 (Healy 1957; see also Garnock-Jones 1979).
Other names include woodland, wood, greater, flexuous and bending bittercress. Cardamine comes from kárdamon, a Greek name for an Indian spice; flexuosa means flexuous, for the zigzag stem.
It is recorded from Northland, Auckland, the Volcanic Plateau, Gisborne, Taranaki and the southern North Island; from western Nelson, the Sounds, Westland, Canterbury and Otago; and from Chatham Island. The first South Island collection was from Dunedin in 1951. In New Zealand it has been recorded flowering and fruiting in every month.
Most of Landcare Research's databased herbarium specimens come from Wellington (36) and Canterbury (23), then North Auckland 10, South Auckland 6, Otago 4, Gisborne 3, Nelson 3, Westland 3, Taranaki 2 and Marlborough 1.

warnings: Several native New Zealand bittercresses, including Cardamine corymbosa, C. forsteri, C. grandiscapa, C. heleniae and C. unicaulis, also grow in weedy places, so not every small white-flowered bittercress in a garden or track edge is an introduced one; the native species are keyed out on characters such as leaf hydathodes, sepal width and pod style length. The native New Zealand bittercress, C. corymbosa, is itself a weed of lawns, path edges, concrete drains, glasshouses and potted plants. It is a perennial whose flowers sit singly or in small flat-topped clusters; in flower they are larger and pure white, often with fewer than four petals, each on its own thread-like stalk rising from the base and flopping sideways, where wavy bittercress is an annual or biennial with several flowers spaced along a fairly stiff flowering stem.

Cardamine occulta, an Asian bittercress once included in this species, is naturalised in Westland and possibly more widespread; it is told from wavy bittercress by its narrower sepals (0.4–0.5 mm wide) and smaller petals (1.8–2.3 mm long). No food record for it was found.

habitat.text: It grows in lowland mixed rainforest near Wellington and Auckland. The species is typically found on decaying wood buried in forest leaf litter (either solitary or crowded), often on the rotting branches of māhoe (Melicytus ramiflorus). It has also been found fruiting on rotted cabbage trees (Cordyline australis) and associated with decaying tree-fern fronds, native to the forests of New Zealand.

harvestEthics.text: Endemic to New Zealand and a fungus of the forest. Picking it is possession of a Class A drug. Leave it standing. Photograph it, note the place, and take nothing.

identification.text: Pileus (Peridium) 3–5 cm long by 1.5–3 cm wide, roundish, ovate (wider at the base and tapering towards the end, egg-shaped) or elongated and elliptic (tapered at the base and apex with a swollen mid-section), base decurrent (extending down the stem below the insertion) or rounded and blunt, margin folded and often torn, light brown when young, becoming french-grey or pale blue-grey, sometimes pallid green in age, longitudinally fibrillose causing a finely striated appearance, becoming smooth, polished, glabrous, tacky and leathery in age, slowly bruising blue or greenish when injured, drying yellow to dingy brown. Stipe up to 40 mm long by 6 mm in diameter, slender, equal in width, whitish to french-grey, bruising blue or greenish with damage, yellowish-brown at the base, initially fibrillose but becoming smooth, polished and cartilaginous in age excluding at the base, hollow, flesh yellow-orange, thickening at the internal apex. Gleba sepia-brown to chocolate-brown, cellular, coarsely shaped, often elongated, laterally compressed, sparse, chambered and gill-like. Spores 11–15(17) x 5–8 μm in size, smooth, sepia-coloured to purple-brown, elliptic-ovate or elliptical in shape, rounded at one end with a thin epispore.

lookalikes.howToTell: Colour and shape do not separate them reliably. Spindle pouch is powder blue, purplish blue or greenish, usually elongated and tapering towards the tip. Weraroa is light brown when young, becoming french-grey or pale blue-grey (sometimes pale green), and can be roundish, egg-shaped or elongated. Spindle pouch's stem is stout, solid, smooth and slippery, off-white to yellow and yellower towards the base, and widens towards the pouch. Weraroa's is slender, the same width throughout, fibrous and often hollow, whitish to french-grey with a yellowish-brown base. Weraroa slowly bruises blue or greenish where injured, on both pouch and stem. Spindle pouch is naturally blue but does not blue when damaged. Cut one lengthways. Spindle pouch's gleba is brown, reddish-brown or lighter red, rarely rust-coloured or orange, in regular cell-like chambers inside a purple-brown sack-like layer. Weraroa's is sepia or chocolate-brown to purple-brown in contorted, gill-like chambers, with no sack.

summary.text:
Psilocybe weraroa, formerly Weraroa novae-zelandiae, is a secotioid fungus in the family Hymenogastraceae.
It is endemic to New Zealand, where it grows in native forests from rotting wood and woody debris. As a bluing member of the genus Psilocybe it contains the psychoactive compounds psilocin and psilocybin.
It is fairly abundant in the early winter and spring months. The mushroom can be difficult to see, often buried under leaves or eaten by slugs, and it is sometimes hard to find mature specimens that are not partially eaten.

warnings: Magic mushrooms, and the psilocybine and psilocine in them, are Class A controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. Picking or carrying one is possession of a Class A drug.

Maximum penalties are six months' imprisonment and/or a $1,000 fine for possession, and life imprisonment for supplying or manufacturing. This entry is here so you can recognise the species, not so you can collect it.

habitat.text:
Suillus lakei is indigenous to the Rocky Mountains and western parts of North America. Its range extends south into Mexico. Fruit bodies grow solitarily or in groups on the ground in young conifer stands or grassy parkland. Fruiting occurs in the late summer and autumn, later on the West Coast. Suillus lakei forms ectomycorrhizae with Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), and its distribution coincides with this tree. It is one of the most common bolete species found in northwestern Montana and Idaho. In a study of host specificity in pure culture in the laboratory, S. lakei failed to form healthy ectomycorrhizas with Eucalyptus roots; the hyphae were covered in mucilage-like deposits and appeared to be collapsed.  It has also been noted to prefer poor, exposed soil such as that found on road banks and campgrounds. It can often be found with the mushroom Gomphidius subroseus, another species that associates with Douglas-fir.
Both Douglas-fir and S. lakei are non-native introduced species in Europe. The fungus has been found in several central and south European countries following the intentional introduction of Douglas-fir. These include Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Italy, and Slovakia. It is considered endangered in the Czech Republic. Suillus lakei has also been reported in South America (Argentina and Chile) and in the South Island of New Zealand.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Suillus lakei' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The cap of S. lakei is up to 15 cm in diameter and initially convex, but flattens out somewhat in maturity. The cap is fleshy, dry, yellowish to reddish-brown but fades with age. It is covered with pressed-down hairs or minute tufted scales in the center, with the yellowish flesh visible between the scales. Heavy rain can wash the fibrils off the cap surface, leaving a sticky, glutinous layer behind. Older specimens may be nearly smooth in age. Remnants of the partial veil sometimes hang from the edge of the cap. The cap margin is initially curved or rolled inwards, but unrolls as it grows and in maturity may be curled upward.

The tubes that comprise the pore surface on the underside of the cap are 5–12 mm deep; the angular pores are up to 2.5 mm wide and radially arranged. The pores range in color from yellow to brownish-yellow to ochre, and stain brownish or reddish-brown when bruised. They are covered by a partial veil in young specimens. The flesh is thick, yellow, and either unchanged in color when bruised or broken, or turns pinkish-red. The stem is 6 to 12 cm long and usually 1–3 cm thick, yellow, sometimes with reddish streaks (particularly below the ring zone), and solid and yellow within. The species usually lacks the glandular dots on the stem that are characteristic of some Suillus species. The stem is either equal in width throughout its length, or tapered downwards. The tissue of the stem base may weakly stain bluish-green when cut, although this reaction is not usually apparent in mature specimens. The ring is delicate and floccose (resembling woolly tufts), and soon disappears or leaves a thin whitish ring on the stem. The spore print is cinnamon to brown in color. The variety calabrus, found in Italy, has a light yellow cap and purple-red scales. Variety pseudopictus has a cap that is redder and more scaly than the more common form.
The spores are spindle-shaped to elliptical, have a smooth surface, and dimensions of 8–11 to 3–4 μm. There are both two- and four-spored basidia (spore-bearing cells), and they are club-shaped, hyaline (translucent), with dimensions of 28–36 by 10–12 μm. Cystidia are plentiful, and are found in bundles lined along the tube mouths (as cheilocystidia), or more commonly, singly along the sides of the tubes (as pleurocystidia). These structures are thin-walled, cylindrical, and measure 48–60 by 7–9 μm. The scales on the cap surface comprise more or less erect hyphae with tips that are clustered together. Clamp connections are rare in the hyphae.


Similar species

Mushrooms with an appearance similar to S. lakei can often be distinguished by their associations with trees. For example, the eastern North American species S. spraguei grows in association with Eastern White Pine. The cap of S. spraguei has red fibrils on a yellow background. S. cavipes and S. ochraceoroseus always grow with Larch. S. ponderosus, which grows in mixed coniferous forests, has a gelatinous veil. Smith and Thiers note that it is difficult to tell the difference between the two if S. ponderosus has lost its veil, since the colors of the species intergrade and cannot reliably be used to distinguish them. S. decipiens has a cap that is orangish to pink-orange with hairs or scales. S. caerulescens is a similar species in western North America; it can be distinguished by the strong blue staining that develops when the stem is injured.

identification.text:
Perennial; stems glabrous, creeping, rooting at nodes. Leaves more or less glabrous; petioles up to 140–(200) mm long; leaflets obovate to elliptic or suborbicular, obtuse to obcordate, cuneate at base, finely serrate, often with light or dark markings, about 5–25 mm long; lateral veins thin or somewhat thickened and more or less straight to leaflet margin; petiolules up to about 1 mm long, more or less equal; stipules oblong, acuminate. Inflorescences axillary, racemose, globose, pedunculate, longer than leaves; flowers numerous; pedicel up to 5 mm long; bracts subtending flowers free. Calyx more or less glabrous, 10-veined, not inflated at fruiting; throat open, glabrous; calyx teeth somewhat unequal (2 upper longer), shorter than corolla, triangular to narrowly triangular, shorter than tube, erect at fruiting; sinuses acute. Corolla usually white, occasionally pink to reddish, persistent, 8–12 mm long. Pod glabrous, straight, longer than calyx, 4–5 mm long, 2–5-seeded; seeds about 1 mm diameter.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Many cultivars are grown and wild plants also vary in leaflet shape and markings, and in flower colour. White clover is distinguished from alsike clover (Trifolium hybridum) by the stoloniferous habit and the acute sinuses of the calyx teeth.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are hairless or nearly so on stem and leaf with round heads on stalks above the leaves, so separate them by habit: white clover creeps and roots at the nodes, while alsike stands erect or ascending and does not root at the nodes. White clover's leaflets often carry light or dark markings; alsike's are described as unmarked. Alsike's head is usually pink; white clover's is usually white but occasionally pink to reddish, so do not lean on colour alone. With a hand lens, alsike's calyx teeth are usually much longer than the calyx tube, white clover's shorter than it. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover's flower head is usually stalkless, sitting directly on the leaves beneath it, and its stems (sparsely below, more densely above) and usually its leaf stalks are hairy; its stems are erect or lie along the ground at the base but do not root at the nodes. White clover's heads rise from the leaf axils on stalks, above the leaves, its stems creep and root at the nodes, and it is more or less hairless. Colour is a guide only: red clover is pink to purple-pink, rarely cream; white clover usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Red clover's leaflets usually carry a crescent-shaped spot towards the base and white clover's often carry light or dark markings, so the mark will not separate these two. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: If it is flowering, look at the flower: white clover packs numerous flowers, each with a corolla 8–12 mm long, usually white and occasionally pink to reddish, into a globe-shaped head, while Bermuda buttercup has separate golden flowers with petals (1.5)–2–2.8 cm long, usually 3–18 (occasionally 1) hanging together at the top of a stalk (7)–15–45 cm long. Without flowers, check how it grows: white clover's stems creep along the ground and root at the nodes; Bermuda buttercup grows upright, its leaves rising from a short vertical stem at the soil surface (or above it in shade or dense growth) over an underground bulb, and its bulbil-bearing runners are underground. Leaf shape and size do not separate them: white clover's leaflets are obovate to elliptic or nearly round with a blunt to notched tip and c. 5–25 mm long, Bermuda buttercup's are shallowly to deeply two-lobed and 10–32 mm long. Leaf markings do not separate them either — both are often marked. Season is no help: in New Zealand white clover flowers July to March and Bermuda buttercup is recorded flowering in every month. Bermuda buttercup is high in oxalic acid and is mildly toxic to people in larger quantities, so eat it only in modest amounts.
lookalikes.name: Bermuda buttercup

lookalikes.howToTell: Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long, white clover's 5–25 mm long. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves or stems: both creep and root at the nodes, both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Least yellow sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Creeping wood sorrel's leaflets are 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm), white clover's 5–25 mm long. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves or stems: both creep and root at the nodes, both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Its stems creep along the ground and root at the nodes. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: white clover's leaflets are c. 5–25 mm long, can be notched at the tip and often carry light or dark markings, so leaflet size, shape and markings overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pale-pink wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Suckling clover: its flowers come 5–20 (up to 25) together in a small round to cylindrical head on a stalk well above the leaves, each a yellow pea-type floret 2.5–4 mm long. Its stems lie along the ground or rise a little and do not root at the nodes, and they are sparsely to densely hairy. White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish; its hairless stems creep and root at the nodes. Out of flower, look at the leaflet stalks: on most suckling clover leaves the middle leaflet sits on a longer stalk (up to 2–3 mm) than the two side leaflets (under 1 mm); white clover's three are about equal. Suckling clover's leaflets are about 3–12 mm long and usually lack the white crescent markings; white clover's are about 5–25 mm long and often carry light or dark markings. Size alone is not a safe test, as white clover's leaves can be very small under some mowing and growing conditions. Suckling clover has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Suckling clover

preparation.text: Pick the young leaves before the plant flowers and use them in salads and soups, or cook them like spinach; the leaves are best cooked. The dried flower heads make a tea. The dried flowers and seed pods can be ground into a powder and used as flour, or sprinkled over cooked food such as boiled rice. The dried leaves give a vanilla flavour to cakes.

recipes.method: 225 g margarine or butter, 150 g brown sugar, 120 ml apple sauce, 30 ml milk, 375 g flour, 1 tsp baking soda, 120 ml of fresh white clover, chopped and 150 g diced strawberries. Heat the oven to 180°C. Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the apple sauce and milk, then work in the flour and baking soda. Fold the clover and strawberries through last. Roll the dough into small balls on a lined baking tray and bake for 13–15 minutes, until golden.
recipes.title: White clover and strawberry cookies

recipes.method: About 500 ml of white clover blossoms (snip the petals from the flower heads and throw out any browned ones), 15 ml (1 tbsp, or one sheet) of unflavoured gelatine, 250 ml water, 125 ml freshly squeezed orange juice (about two large oranges), 60 ml honey, 250 ml cream whipped stiff or 250 ml full-fat Greek yoghurt, and a pinch of salt. Dissolve the gelatine in 60 ml of water. In a small saucepan, slowly bring the blossoms, water, orange juice, honey and salt to the boil. Take it off the heat, stir in the gelatine until it has completely dissolved, and leave it to stand for 10 minutes. Cover and refrigerate until it begins to set, then fold in the whipped cream or yoghurt, spoon it into a serving bowl and refrigerate until set.
recipes.title: White clover pudding

recipes.method: About 1 litre (4 cups) of fresh white clover blossoms, stems removed, 1 litre water, 60 ml bottled lemon juice (or 1 tsp citric acid), one 50 g box of regular powdered pectin and 1.25 kg (5 cups) sugar. Pour the water, just boiled, over the blossoms, push them under and steep for 15–20 minutes. Strain, pressing the blossoms gently, and top the tea up with water to 1 litre if it is short. Stir in the lemon juice and bring it to the boil, then whisk in the pectin until it has dissolved and boil hard for a full minute. Only then add all the sugar at once — added earlier, the jelly will not set — stir until dissolved, return to a full rolling boil for exactly 1 minute, take it off the heat and skim. Ladle into prepared jars, leaving 5 mm headspace, and process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes. Cool undisturbed for 24 hours before checking the seals; refrigerate any that did not seal, and refrigerate after opening. Do not leave out the lemon juice: it helps the set and makes the jelly acidic enough to can.
recipes.title: White clover jelly

recipes.method: Pick white clover blossoms; leaves and stems can stay in, but they taste stronger, so separate them out for a milder flour. Pick roughly 8 times the volume you want: it shrinks a lot — about 1 litre of blossoms with stems gave 500 ml of blossoms and about 125 ml of flour. Lay the blossoms out to dry on a screen somewhere well ventilated and out of direct sun (sun dries them in a few hours, but can cost them nutrients). Grind them in batches in a small blade coffee grinder, or all at once in a food processor on high for about 5 minutes. Use it for up to a quarter of the flour in a recipe: it will not hold baked goods together on its own. The recipe gives a flour that tastes mildly sweet and green, like spring peas, with a spongy texture that suits biscuits and soft baking.
recipes.title: White clover flour

recipes.method: About 225 g blackberries, 225 g blueberries, 250 ml fresh white clover flowers, 125 ml orange juice and 500 ml tequila. Lightly muddle the berries in a jug, add the clover flowers, pour in the tequila and orange juice and stir. Add plenty of ice, and water to taste.
recipes.title: White clover berry punch (alcoholic)

Card to/from Bermuda buttercup, rewritten 11/10/2026 after the owner required every claim to rest on a trusted source. Each test and its source: white clover's flowers (numerous, in a globose head; corolla 8–12 mm, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish), leaflets (obovate to elliptic or suborbicular, obtuse to obcordate, c. 5–25 mm long, often with light or dark markings), creeping stems rooting at the nodes and flowering Jul.–Mar.: Flora of New Zealand Online (Webb et al. 1988; CC BY 3.0 NZ), retrieved 11/10/2026, https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Trifolium-repens.html. Bermuda buttercup's flowers, leaflets and Jan.–Dec. flowering: Flora of New Zealand Online (Webb et al. 1988; CC BY 3.0 NZ), retrieved 11/10/2026, 'Oxalis pes-caprae'. Its single short vertical stem, mostly underground, loose basal rosette, purple-dotted leaves and runner that can form a new aboveground plant: UC IPM Pest Notes 7444, 'Creeping Woodsorrel and Bermuda Buttercup' (LeStrange, Cudney & Elmore, 06/2010; © Regents of the University of California, facts only), https://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7444.html. That it can be mistaken for clover when not in flower: Weeds Australia (all rights reserved). CORRECTION: the first version of this card (10–11/10) said white clover's leaflets are 'elliptic to egg-shaped' while Bermuda buttercup's are two-lobed, as a test. Flora of New Zealand gives white clover's as up to obcordate, so leaflet shape is NOT a test, and the card now says so. This page's identification text (Wikipedia) says 'elliptic to egg-shaped'; the NZ Flora description is the wider one. Risk edible because the Bermuda buttercup page says the plant is palatable and eaten, with an oxalate warning.

Recipe 'White clover pudding', restated in this guide's own words, metric: Danielle Prohom Olson, 'White Clover Pudding: A Recipe for Comfort & Healing', Gather Victoria, 9 June 2015 (https://gathervictoria.com/2015/06/09/white-clover-pudding-a-recipe-for-comfort-healing/), retrieved 15/10/2026, no licence stated so all rights reserved assumed; supplied by the owner. The author adapted an old recipe written for sweet clover (Melilotus) to white clover, so this one is written for Trifolium repens. Cups and spoons converted at 250 ml a cup, 15 ml a tablespoon and 5 ml a teaspoon (the page does not say which cup it means; a US cup is about 237 ml). The page lists 1 cup of water and separately dissolves the gelatine in 1/4 cup; it does not say whether that quarter comes out of the cup, and the method keeps both as given.

Not used from the Gather Victoria page: its medicinal claims (anti-inflammatory, anti-bacterial, blood and lymph cleanser), its folklore, its claim that bees prefer white clover to red, and a reader's comment that browning clover blossoms ferment into warfarin — the author replied she believed that applies to sweet clover (Melilotus), not white clover, and neither claim was checked. The author's own instruction to discard browned petals is in the method.

Recipe 'White clover jelly', restated in this guide's own words, metric: Ashley Adamant (recipe card; the tasting notes are signed Cami), 'Clover Jelly', Creative Canning, first published 28/06/2024, updated 09/06/2026 (https://creativecanning.com/clover-jelly/), retrieved 15/10/2026, all rights reserved. Written for red, white or crimson clover. Cups converted at 250 ml (the site is American; a US cup is about 237 ml), 1.75 oz pectin as one 50 g box, 5 cups sugar as about 1.25 kg, 1/4 inch as 5 mm. Its altitude adjustment (15 minutes above 6,000 ft), low-sugar pectin variants, 'pantry shelf for 12 to 18 months' and blind-tasting flavours were not used. Found while answering the owner's question whether red and alsike clover recipes are interchangeable (15/10/2026).

summary.text:
White clover (Trifolium repens) is a creeping perennial clover of the pea family (Fabaceae), native to Europe, northern and western Asia and North Africa, and naturalised in New Zealand.
In New Zealand: North Island; South Island: abundant throughout; Stewart Island: locally common in open disturbed areas, and South-West Muttonbird Islands; Kermadec, Chatham, Auckland and Campbell Islands. Naturalised from Europe, northern and western Asia and North Africa, first recorded in 1864. White clover is widely cultivated as a pasture plant, but its stoloniferous habit also makes it a troublesome weed in many situations.

warnings: Most white clover cultivars bred in or grown successfully in New Zealand are highly cyanogenic: crushing or chewing the leaves or stems releases hydrogen cyanide. The flowers release it only occasionally, and at low levels.
White clover plants vary in their cyanogenic glycosides: in the leaves and flowers of some forms, a glycoside releases cyanide when it meets the enzyme linamarase.
Drying, soaking and cooking reduce the cyanide in cyanogenic plant foods.

identification.text:
Liane with stout stems, or a dense, mound-like shrub of intertwining branchlets; stems terete, finely tomentose especially when young; armature of small, reddish prickles, or 0. Leaves palmate; leaflets 3–(5), glabrous or almost glabrous and rugose on upper surface, usually white- to brown-tomentose on lower surface and sometimes greyish or glaucous, sometimes glabrous to almost glabrous on lower surface also, coarsely serrate; terminal leaflet lamina usually narrow- to broad-ovate, oblong or lanceolate, rarely linear or narrow-linear, 25–70 × 4–40 mm, with petiolule 10–30–(50) mm long. Inflorescence a many-flowered, sometimes compact, panicle, up to 10–(25) cm long. Petals white to cream. Drupelets yellowish or orange.
R. schmidelioides is very variable in leaflet shape and indumentum. The leaflets of mature leaves are typically narrow-ovate or lanceolate and tomentose beneath, but leaflets of juvenile plants are much narrower and usually glabrous. In lowland E. South Id mature plants often retain this juvenile leaflet form in open habitats; such plants are then easily distinguished from R. cissoides and R. australis by the narrow leaflets.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. The flowers separate them: blackberry's are 15–60 mm across and have stamens and carpels together, while white-leaved lawyer's are 8–15 mm across, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Ripe blackberry is black and white-leaved lawyer's yellow to orange or red, but blackberry is red before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit. The native lawyers lack the long, glandular, bristly hairs some introduced brambles carry on their young stems; not every blackberry has them, so their absence does not rule blackberry out.
lookalikes.name: Blackberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Both can be white-felted underneath, so the felt does not separate them: count the leaflets and see how they are attached. Raspberry's are pinnate, side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk; white-leaved lawyer's are palmate, usually three from one point. Raspberry is an erect shrub with flowers 20–25 mm across; white-leaved lawyer is a liane or a tangled mound with flowers 8–15 mm across, male and female on separate plants.
lookalikes.name: Red raspberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Leaves: bush lawyer's end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, hairless except often on the veins and margins, with fewer than 10 coarse or irregular teeth on each side; white-leaved lawyer's is felted underneath or, if hairless (mostly in the lowland eastern South Island), narrow-lanceolate or linear and coarsely toothed. Juvenile white-leaved lawyer leaflets are much narrower and usually hairless. Their fruit colours overlap, so fruit does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Bush lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet; white-leaved lawyer's have three or more. Young plants and flowering shoots of other brambles sometimes have single-leaflet leaves too, so judge by the leaves on mature stems.
lookalikes.name: Creeping lawyer

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. Makes 6 jars of 250 ml. The recipe is somewhere between a jam and a jelly: the juice is pressed rather than dripped through a bag, so it sets cloudy. 1 litre berry juice (fresh or thawed frozen berries put through a cold-press juicer), 300 ml cold-pressed apple juice, the juice of 3 lemons, 1.3 kg white sugar, 10 whole cloves and the zest of an orange. Wash the jars and dry them, open end up, in a 120 °C oven for about 15 minutes, leaving them in the warm oven until needed; boil the lids for 5 minutes and let them air-dry. Put the berry, apple and lemon juices and the sugar in a jam pan, dissolve the sugar over low heat, then bring to the boil. Add the cloves and orange zest, skim off foam as it rises, and boil to setting point — about 30 minutes for the author, giving a soft set. Ladle the hot jelly into the hot jars and seal.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry jelly

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. 400 g berries, 500 ml white wine vinegar and 100 g white sugar. Warm the vinegar with the sugar until it has dissolved. Put the berries in a large clean jar or a non-reactive bowl, pour the warm vinegar over them and leave overnight. Strain gently through a fine sieve or muslin and pour into a sterilised bottle or jar. The author uses it to quick-pickle wafer-thin slices of raw beetroot (3 tablespoons of vinegar and ¼ teaspoon of sea salt for 2 small beetroot, soaked at least 15 minutes) served with goat's cheese.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry vinegar

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. Muddle a big handful of berries (fresh or frozen) in a cocktail shaker, add 60 ml tequila blanco, 30 ml Cointreau, 60 ml fresh lime juice and 60 ml sugar syrup, shake hard over ice and pour. Strain it if you don't want the seeds.

summary.text:
Rubus schmidelioides, commonly called bush lawyer or white leaved lawyer, is a climbing plant species found commonly in New Zealand.
It is endemic to New Zealand, growing in the North Island from about Hikurangi and Dargaville south, and in the South and Stewart Islands (NZPCN, restated).
Noticing similarities to European wild blackberries, Early European settlers in New Zealand used tātarāmoa berries to create foods such as preserves or jams.
Rubus schmidelioides grows best during the mid-stages of succession when the tree canopies have not grown high. Juveniles struggle to grow in areas of low light where the canopy is already established.

warnings: Tātaramoa, or “bush lawyer”, has hooked thorns that snag clothing and rip or prick the skin.

identification.text:
Summer-green dioecious perennial, with woody crown; roots long, cylindrical, fleshy. Stems 60–120 cm high, bright green, stiffly erect, more or less woody below, branched above; shoots fleshy, edible. Scale-leaves scarious, 1–5 mm long, with short soft basal spur. Cladodes needle-like, 5–15 mm long, 2–8 at each node. Flowers axillary, 1–2–(4), greenish-yellow; pedicels drooping, 5–10 mm long; male flowers 5–6 mm long, stamens about 3 mm long, ovary rudimentary; female flowers shorter, about 4 mm long, stamens about 1.5 mm long, functionless. Berry globose, about 6–8 mm diameter, red. Seeds 1–9, about 3 mm diameter, black.
[From: Healy and Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]

identification.text:
Erect branching annual or biennial, with a slender white taproot. Stems hispid, more or less solid, ribbed, sometimes purple tinged, up to 120 cm high. Basal leaves sparsely to moderately hairy, 2–3-pinnate, with a leaf stalk; ultimate segments ovate to linear, pinnatisect or serrate, about 15–40 mm long; stem leaves similar to basal but reduced and segments more often linear. Umbels compound, 2–12 cm in diameter, usually strongly concave at fruiting; rays numerous; bracts numerous, 1-pinnate, with linear segments; bracteoles 5–9, usually simple and linear to triangular, those of outer small umbels sometimes pinnatisect. Flowers numerous, white or tinged pink, 1–7 mm in diameter, a few central flowers sometimes red or purple. Fruit ovoid, dark brown, 2.5–3 mm long; primary ribs sparsely ciliate, secondary ribs spinous; spines pale brown, rarely reflexed at tips. Flowers August–May.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The stems and leaves have fine hairs, and the root smells of carrot. The spiny fruit sets it apart from most other New Zealand umbellifers. Hemlock has bracts under its umbels too — narrow and bent back rather than divided — so the presence of bracts alone does not separate them; see Lookalikes.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock's stem is hairless and hollow, up to 2 m (rarely 3 m), and usually spotted or blotched purple, but sometimes only tinged purplish or pink, so a stem without blotches does not rule hemlock out. Wild carrot's stem is bristly-hairy, more or less solid, up to 120 cm, and sometimes purple-tinged itself. Hemlock is hairless throughout; wild carrot's leaves and leaf stalks are hairy. Under the umbel, hemlock has about 4–8 narrow-triangular bracts that bend back; wild carrot's are numerous and divided into narrow linear segments. Crushed hemlock smells foetid and musty; wild carrot's root smells of carrot. Check every plant for every feature. If any one does not fit, leave it.
lookalikes.name: Hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have finely divided leaves, hairy stems and flat-topped heads of small white or pinkish flowers, and both grow in waste places, grassland, cultivated land and gardens or lawns over the same months. Wild carrot's flowers are on the spokes of a true compound umbel 2–12 cm across, with forked bracts beneath it, sometimes a few red or purple flowers at the centre, and it curls into a concave 'bird's nest' as it fruits; yarrow's are tiny daisy heads with 4–7 short rays, packed together in a dense cluster. Wild carrot's root smells of carrot, and it has a slender white taproot; yarrow spreads by rhizomes into mats. Yarrow is edible in small amounts but carries its own cautions (daisy-family allergy, pregnancy) — see its entry.

preparation.text: Cook the roots while young, before they turn woody; dried, roasted and ground, they have been used to make a coffee substitute. The flower clusters can be battered and fried, or steeped (see the cordial recipe). The seeds flavour stews.

recipes.method: Written for wild carrot (Daucus carota) by a British forager. 20 wild carrot flower heads; 800 ml boiling water; 100 g honey or rapadura sugar; 100 ml cider vinegar. Lay the flower heads on newspaper for an hour so insects can leave; do not wash them. Put them in a saucepan, pour the boiled water over, stir and cover with a lid. Leave to infuse for 24 hours. Strain off the pink liquid and whisk in the honey or sugar until it dissolves. Stir in the cider vinegar and bottle it. The author's steps say 1 litre of water where his list says 800 ml, and he does not know how long the cordial keeps.
recipes.title: Wild carrot flower cordial

recipes.method: 50 g sunflower seeds; 50 g pumpkin seeds; 1–2 tbsp wild carrot seeds; 2 tbsp soy sauce. Warm a frying pan over medium heat and toast the sunflower and pumpkin seeds for a couple of minutes, stirring now and then so they don't burn, until they start to pop and turn golden. Add the wild carrot seeds and stir for 1–2 minutes more. Pour in the soy sauce, take the pan off the heat and keep stirring until the mix dries and clumps together. Let it cool before serving. The author also coats fish in flour and then dried wild carrot seeds before frying it.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daucus_carota Gives the hemlock separation feature by feature, which is what this page's warning demands and did not spell out: wild carrot has tripinnate leaves, **fine hairs on solid green stems and on the leaves**, a root that smells of carrot, and often a single red flower in the centre of the umbel; poison hemlock differs in **purple mottling on stems that are also hairless**. On the parts: the root is edible while young but quickly goes too woody, the flowers are sometimes battered and fried, and the leaves and seeds are edible. The seeds and flowers have been used as a contraceptive and abortifacient for centuries, but no research confirms the effect and there is no evidence of safety. Confirms the rash too — like many Apiaceae the leaves may cause phytophotodermatitis, and contact with wet foliage especially can irritate skin. Falcarinol, the plant's own antifungal compound, is toxic to mice and to Daphnia in the laboratory; normal consumption of carrots has no toxic effect in humans.
