summary.text:
Queen Anne's lace. An edible umbellifer with a hairy stem and a carrot smell — and hemlock's most dangerous double. Only for people who know hemlock cold.
Daucus carota is also called bird's nest and bishop's lace. It is native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, and cultivated carrots are its domesticated subspecies, Daucus carota subsp. sativus. It was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1854. It is common throughout the North Island and on the Kermadec Islands; in the South Island it is common in Nelson, Marlborough and Canterbury, and local in Otago and Westland. Most New Zealand plants belong to the typical subspecies. In New Zealand pasture, hemlock is probably most likely to be confused with wild carrot. The name carota comes through Latin from the Greek karoton, 'carrot'.

warnings: Confusing this with hemlock kills people. Do not harvest unless you can name every feature that separates them and have checked each one on the plant in your hand.
Handling the foliage, especially when it is wet, can irritate and blister the skin, and sap on the skin followed by sunlight can cause a rash.
Carrot causes allergic reactions in some people.
Do not eat the seeds or roots if you are pregnant. The seeds can cause miscarriage, and the wild root can bring on contractions of the womb.

summary.text:
Chervil (; Anthriscus cerefolium), sometimes called French parsley or garden chervil (to distinguish it from similar plants also called chervil), is a delicate annual herb related to parsley.
A member of the Apiaceae, the native distribution of chervil is uncertain due to its long history of cultivation, particularly by the Romans. The New Oxford Book of Food Plants limits its native range to the Caucasus, while Plants of the World Online cites it with a wider native range across central and southeastern Europe and southwestern Asia from Switzerland in the west, to Iran in the east.
The species is now naturalised through most of Europe and North Africa. It is also introduced and frequently grown in North America, where it is naturalised in many areas. These escapes differ from other Anthriscus species growing in North America (A. caucalis and A. sylvestris) by having lanceolate-linear bracteoles and a fruit with a relatively long beak.

identification.text:
Stout, aromatic, erect perennial. Stems more or less solid, striate, polished, up to about 2 m high. Basal leaves 3–5-pinnate, with a leaf stalk; ultimate segments filiform, acuminate, 3–50 mm long, not all in one plane; stem leaves similar to basal; leaf stalk extended along its whole length into a thin closely-ribbed sheath. Umbels 2–5 cm in diameter; rays 4–25, usually slightly incurved at fruiting. Flowers numerous, yellow, 1–2 mm in diameter. Fruit dark brown, 3–6 mm long, tasting of liquorice; ribs pale brown. Flowers November–May.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Crushed, it smells sweet, of aniseed or liquorice. Wild plants do not form the swollen bulb of shop fennel. Smell is not enough on its own: check the yellow flowers, thread-fine leaves and the absence of bracts under the umbels as well — see Lookalikes.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock is one of New Zealand's most poisonous plants, and every part is poisonous if eaten. Its stem is usually spotted or blotched purple, especially toward the base, but not always; its flowers are white; its leaf segments are broader than fennel's — ovate to triangular and toothed or cut; it has a few narrow, down-turned bracts under each umbel; and it smells foetid, musty or mousy when crushed. Fennel has yellow flowers, thread-fine leaf segments, no bracts under the umbels, and leaves that smell of aniseed. Both are hairless with finely ridged stems, and hollow versus solid stems are not reliable, so do not use the stem surface alone. Hemlock grows on roadsides, riverbeds, forest margins, damp ground and waste areas. If it does not smell of aniseed, do not treat it as fennel — and check the flowers, leaves and bracts as well as the smell.

preparation.text: Wash the green parts well, once or twice. Chop the softest fronds into salads, or scatter them over soups, roast vegetables, fish, potatoes and seafood stews; leaves and seeds go especially well with fish. Stems and fronds can be pickled. Collect the pollen on a dry day by shaking the yellow flower heads into a bag, and the seeds the same way from the dried heads in the months after; store both in airtight jars. Green seeds are best for cooking. Ripe seeds keep about a year: strip them from the dried heads and freeze them for a week first to kill any insects (see the seed recipe).

recipes.method: Written for wild fennel in New Zealand; the article does not give the species. 500 ml (2 cups) water; 250 ml (1 cup) sugar; 125 ml (½ cup) fennel fronds. Stir the water and sugar in a saucepan over low heat until the sugar dissolves. Bring to the boil, take it off the heat and add the fronds. Leave until completely cool, then strain into a jar or bottle and keep it in the fridge. The author uses it in citrus cocktails and vodka sours.
recipes.title: Fennel frond syrup

recipes.method: Written for wild fennel in California. Ripe fennel seed heads, dry on the stalk; a paper bag; a jar. Smell each plant first: fennel smells of anise or liquorice, hemlock smells musty. Snip off the seed heads carrying the biggest seeds into a paper bag; if they are not quite dry, finish drying them indoors so the seeds do not stick. At home, strip the seeds from each little cluster with thumb and forefinger into a wide, flat dish. Pick out the empty clusters, twigs, insects and other debris; tweezers help. Put the seeds in a jar and freeze for a week to kill any insects or eggs you missed. Keep them in the spice cupboard, where they last about a year, and use them as you would bought fennel seed. The author eats green seeds fresh and keeps brown ones for storage.
recipes.title: Fennel seed spice

recipes.method: Written for wild fennel in New Zealand; the article does not give the species. Wild fennel flower clusters in full yellow bloom; a paper bag or container; airtight jars. On a dry day, shake the flower clusters hard over a bag or container, straight off the plant. Or put whole flower heads in a bag and wait for the pollen to drop off by itself. Store the pollen in jars or airtight containers somewhere dry and dark. The author dusts it over mashed potatoes, pork dishes or baked cheese, and on cakes, biscuits, ice cream and popcorn.
recipes.title: Fennel pollen

recipes.method: The author's greens, picked from roadsides around Whangaroa Harbour, were nasturtium, kawakawa, fennel, samphire, fat hen, wild mustard, cleavers and clover. The author warns that New Zealand roadsides are still sprayed with glyphosate, so pick with care. 1 garlic clove (or 4 peeled onion weed bulbs); 60 ml (¼ cup) macadamia nuts; 60 ml (¼ cup) grated parmesan, dairy or plant-based (or 125 ml, ½ cup, macadamias and no parmesan); 750 ml (3 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; the zest and juice of 1 lemon; 125 ml extra-virgin olive oil; salt and pepper. Makes about 350 g. Blend in a food processor to the texture you like. Good on crackers or toast, as a side, or stirred through soup, pasta or rice.
recipes.title: Wild Whangaroa pesto

recipes.method: The author's greens were puha, sow thistle, nasturtium, onion weed, wild fennel, oxalis, wild mustard and wild celery. 1 diced onion; 1 potato, scrubbed and diced; 2 sliced garlic cloves; 500 ml (2 cups) roughly chopped wild greens; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 1.3 litres water; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 30 ml (2 tbsp) nutritional yeast (optional); 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) cracked pepper; extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil, to serve; edible weed flowers. Serves 4. Cut the vegetables and greens to similar sizes. Fry the onion in the oil for a minute, then add the potato and garlic (the method also adds fennel bulb and celery stalks, which the ingredient list leaves out) and fry for another minute. Add the water, cover, bring to the boil and simmer until the potato is soft. Add the greens with the salt and yeast and cook for 3 minutes, until just tender — added at the end, they keep their colour. Blend until smooth (push it through a sieve if your blender isn't powerful), season with the pepper and more salt if needed, and serve drizzled with extra-virgin olive or hemp seed oil and scattered with edible weed flowers.
recipes.title: Wild greens soup

summary.text:
Lines roadsides and railway banks over much of the country — and shares that ground with hemlock, one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand.
Native to southern and south-western Europe, fennel was first recorded wild in New Zealand in 1867. It is common throughout the North Island and on the Kermadec Islands, and in the South Island in Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, northern Westland and northern and central Otago; it is much less common in the south of the South Island and apparently absent from South Westland and Southland, and in the Stewart Island area it is recorded from Codfish Island. Useful Temperate Plants lists New Zealand among the places it is invasive.
A perennial, it dies back to a rootstock after flowering; its many seeds are blown a short way by wind or carried further on animals. Bronze forms are grown as ornamentals, and Florence fennel — a selected form with swollen leaf-stalk bases — as a vegetable. The name comes from the Latin foeniculum, 'hay', for its smell.

warnings: Check every plant before you pick it — yellow flowers, thread-fine leaves, aniseed smell — because hemlock grows in the same places. Crush and smell before every harvest, not just the first.
Roadside and railway verges are routinely sprayed. Avoid sprayed ground and places close to busy roads.
Skin contact with the sap can cause a rash, or make the skin sensitive to sunlight, in some people.

edibleParts.text: Leaves - raw or cooked. Rather stringy, they are used as a garlic substitute. Bulb - used as a flavouring. Rather small, with a very strong flavour and odour. Bulbils - raw or cooked. Rather small and fiddly, they have a strong garlic-like flavour. The leaves, flowers, and bulbs of Allium vineale are edible. While it has been suggested as a substitute for garlic, there is some difference of opinion as to whether there is an unpleasant aftertaste compared to that of common garlic (Allium sativum).

habitat.text: Occasional to locally abundant in pastures and waste places. Wild onion is occasional and difficult to detect in grassy waste land and on roadsides, and is usually grazed down when growing in adjacent grassland.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Series vol. III (Healy & Edgar 1980, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) — abbreviations spelled out
Wikipedia, 'Allium vineale' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
Bulb globose to ovoid, to 3 × 2.5 cm, tunic whitish, membranous, easily separated at base, with several stipitate offset bulbs. Leaves sub-cylindric, hollow, slender, shorter than scape, upper surface more or less grooved. Scape erect, slender, 30–90 cm high, sheathed for ½–⅓ its length. Umbels shorter than 2 cm diameter, with flowers and bulbils (var. vineale), or more commonly with bulbils and without flowers (var. compactum (Thuill.) Bor.); pedicels several times longer than flowers; spathe-valve 1, soon deciduous. Flowers about 5 mm long, green to white, often purplish, campanulate; segments lanceolate, acute, keeled. Stamens exserted, each inner filament with 2 prominent lateral appendages longer than anther, outer 3 filaments simple. Capsule not seen.
A. vineale may be recognised by the garlic-like odour, the slender, cylindrical rush-like stems and stipitate offset bulbs, and by the flowers being usually all replaced by bulbils.
Of the leaves (Wikipedia): Although similar to the leaves of Allium schoenoprasum (chives), they tend to be more fibrous, have more vertical grooves, and have better defined grooves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Onion weed's leaves are solid and strongly channelled; wild garlic's are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical. Onion weed carries 3–15 white flowers 10–15 mm long (up to 20) and no bulbils; wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils, its few flowers about 5 mm long, green to white and often purplish. Onion weed's flower stalk is three-angled and sheathed only at the base; wild garlic's is slender and rush-like, sheathed by the leaves for a third to a half of its length. The garlic smell and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Onion weed

lookalikes.howToTell: Naples garlic's leaves are flat, with finely toothed or hairy-edged margins; wild garlic's are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical. Naples garlic carries a many-flowered umbel 5–8 cm across of white flowers 8–10 mm long; wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils. Naples garlic's flower stalk has two sharp, almost winged angles; wild garlic's is slender and rush-like. The garlic smell does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Naples garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Rosy garlic's leaves are flat; wild garlic's are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical. Rosy garlic carries a loose umbel 5–8 cm across of pale pink flowers 10–12 mm long; wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils, its few flowers about 5 mm long. Both can carry bulbils in the flower head and both smell of garlic, so bulbils and smell do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Rosy garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: False garlic has none of wild garlic's garlic smell, or only a faint one. False garlic's leaves are flat; wild garlic's are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical. False garlic carries 8–20 dull white flowers 1–1.5 cm long; wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils, its few flowers about 5 mm long. Dug up, false garlic's offset bulbs are stalkless; wild garlic's sit on short stalks. Spring flowering does not separate them. If a plant does not smell of garlic or onion when crushed, leave it. False garlic has no confirmed record as food; see its page.
lookalikes.name: False garlic

preparation.text:
The leaves are used as an ingredient in minestrella soup, a complex blend of wild vegetables eaten in northwest Tuscany, Italy.
The bulbils can be used fresh, or air-dried as a crunchy seasoning, or sprouted for salads.
The stems can be washed, cut like chives and frozen in bags; they keep their scent. Cooking takes away its sharpness.

recipes.method: Written for wild garlic (Allium vineale). A 425 g tin of chickpeas; about 20 large wild garlic stems (more or fewer to taste); 2 tbsp lemon juice; 1 tbsp tahini; 125 ml olive oil, plus a little more to top; 1 tbsp nutritional yeast; salt. Drain and rinse a 425 g tin of chickpeas and put them in a food processor with about 20 large wild garlic stems, rinsed and with any dried stems removed (more or fewer to taste). Add 2 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tbsp tahini, 125 ml olive oil and 1 tbsp nutritional yeast, and process until completely smooth. Add salt, taste, and adjust any of the other ingredients. The author keeps the tahini light so it does not swamp the garlic, which is milder than a garlic bulb. Top with a little more olive oil and serve straight away, or chill.
recipes.title: Wild garlic hummus

recipes.method: Written for wild garlic (Allium vineale), whose bulbs are each about the size of one clove of garlic. 1.4 kg broccoli; 8 wild garlic bulbs; 60 ml lemon juice (from 2–4 lemons); 125 ml olive oil; salt and pepper. Cut 1.4 kg of broccoli into florets and simmer, covered, in 80–125 ml of water until tender, 10–15 minutes. Meanwhile peel and finely chop 8 wild garlic bulbs, and mix them with 60 ml lemon juice (from 2–4 lemons), 125 ml olive oil, and salt and pepper to taste. Toss the cooked broccoli in the dressing.
recipes.title: Broccoli with wild garlic and lemon

recipes.method: Written for wild garlic (Allium vineale) in Gers, France. A bunch of wild garlic stems; 100 g pine nuts, almonds or hazelnuts; the juice of a lemon; salt and pepper; olive oil. Rinse a bunch of stems in water with a little vinegar, then in clean water. Blend with 100 g pine nuts, almonds or hazelnuts, the juice of a lemon, and salt and pepper, pouring in olive oil in a thin stream until it is a soft paste. Keep in a jar in the fridge. Good with fish, pasta or on toast.
recipes.title: Wild garlic pesto

recipes.method: Written for wild garlic (Allium vineale). Serves 4. 4 potatoes; a bunch of wild garlic stems; 1 egg; seasoning; oil for frying; a spoonful of flour (optional). Peel and finely grate 4 potatoes. Rinse a bunch of wild garlic stems in water with a little vinegar, then in clean water, and snip them like chives. Mix the potato, the wild garlic and 1 egg, and season. For softer galettes, add a spoonful of flour. Heat a film of oil in a frying pan, drop in small spoonfuls and press them down lightly. Cook about 15 minutes, turning halfway, until golden and crisp, then drain on paper towel.
recipes.title: Potato and wild garlic galettes

recipes.method: From a French page on wild garlic (Allium vineale). 400 g wild garlic; 2 tbsp olive oil; 100 g flour; 2 litres water; a stock cube; salt; cream, croutons or cheese, to serve. Wash and cut 400 g of wild garlic and cook it in 2 tbsp olive oil, then stir in 100 g flour to thicken. Add 2 litres of water with a stock cube dissolved in it, and salt. Boil for 15 minutes. Serve with cream, croutons or cheese.
recipes.title: Wild garlic soup

summary.text:
Allium vineale (wild garlic, onion grass, crow garlic or stag's garlic) is a perennial, bulb-forming species of wild onion, native to Europe, northwestern Africa, and the Middle East.
The species was introduced in Australia and North America, where it has become an invasive species.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand), where the Flora calls it wild onion: N. North Auckland; Auckland - Auckland City, Miranda, Thames, near Hamilton; Wellington - Wanganui. S. Otago-Dunedin. It gives an unpleasant taint to meat and dairy products from animals which have grazed it.

warnings: There have been cases of poisoning caused by the consumption, in large quantities and by some mammals, of this species. Dogs seem to be particularly susceptible.
Every part is mildly poisonous to people, and potentially poisonous to livestock that eat a lot of it: it may cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Harvest only plants with a distinct onion smell.

identification.text:
Annual or biennial. Stem erect, branching above, finely grooved, with patent pale spines up to 4 mm long, especially below, (50)–100–280 cm tall. Leaves green; rosette and lower stem leaves tapering to base, with spinous bristles beneath on midrib and often on secondary veins, 8–25–(35) × 5–18 cm, deeply runcinate-pinnatifid to undivided; margins dentate to bristly-ciliate, usually sinuate. Upper leaves often with spinous bristles on midrib, oblong to obovate, often triangularly 3-lobed at apex, with oblong to rounded amplexicaul auricles at base. Inflorescence diffusely paniculate. Capitula numerous, cylindric. Involucre (11)–13–15 mm long; bracts imbricate, suberect to reflexed at fruiting; outermost bracts ovate to lanceolate, subacute, ?-1/2length of innermost bracts; inner bracts lanceolate to linear, subacute. Florets about 1½× length of involucre; corollas erect to erecto-patent, yellow. Achenes very dark brown or black, 5–8-ribbed on each face, obovate, flattened, finely spiny distally on ribs; body 4–5 mm long; beak pale, about equal to body. Pappus fine, white. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Stem leaves of L. serriola tend to be held on their sides whereas those of L. virosa are held flat. Young plants of L. virosa may be distinguished from L. serriola by the shape of their basal leaves, which have a small, rounded terminal lobe and broad lateral lobes which are broader than the sinus between them and toothed on the distal and most of the proximal margins. Basal leaves of L. serriola have a triangular to ovate terminal lobe and narrower lateral lobes which are about as broad as the sinus between them and not toothed (although they may be ciliate) on the proximal margin. Leaves of L. virosa darken markedly on drying whereas those of L. serriola do not.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at a basal leaf. Wild lettuce's ends in a small, rounded lobe, and its side lobes are broader than the gaps between them and toothed along the outer edge and most of the inner edge; prickly lettuce's ends in a triangular to ovate lobe, and its side lobes are narrow, about as wide as the gaps and not toothed (though they may be fringed with bristles) on the edge nearer the leaf base. Wild lettuce's leaves are green and darken markedly as they dry; prickly lettuce's are grey-green and do not. Up the stem, wild lettuce's leaves are held flat; prickly lettuce's tend to be held on their sides (in sun the upper ones twist to stand edge-up, roughly north–south). In seed, wild lettuce's achenes are very dark brown or black, with a body 4–5 mm long; prickly lettuce's are pale brown to grey, sometimes dark-spotted, with a body 2.5–3 mm long. Wild lettuce's involucre is (11)–13–15 mm long and prickly lettuce's 8–13 mm, so they overlap at 11–13 mm. Wild lettuce's stem carries pale spines up to 4 mm long, especially low down; prickly lettuce's is hairless or bristly below, so a spiny stem does not separate them. Both have spiny bristles under the leaf midrib, yellow heads in a loose branched spray and milky sap. Prickly lettuce's young leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they are bitter (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Prickly lettuce

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild lettuce's stem carries pale spines up to 4 mm long, especially low down; common pūhā's stem is hairless. Turn a leaf over: wild lettuce has spiny bristles under the midrib, often on the side veins too, and its upper leaves often have them on the midrib; common pūhā's leaves are hairless, their only spines the small ones tipping the marginal teeth. Young lettuce plants can lack the midrib bristles. Wild lettuce carries numerous narrow, cylindrical heads in a loose, much-branched spray; sow thistle heads are usually larger. In seed, wild lettuce's achenes are very dark brown or black, with a body 4–5 mm long and a pale beak about as long; common pūhā's are brown, 2.5–3 mm long and have no beak. The involucre does not separate them: (11)–13–15 mm long in wild lettuce, 10–15 mm in common pūhā. Both have milky sap, lobed leaves that clasp the stem and yellow heads of strap-shaped florets. Common pūhā is edible: its leaves are widely eaten as greens.
lookalikes.name: Pūhā / Sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: Prickly edges do not separate them: prickly sow thistle's leaf margins have prickly-spined teeth and wild lettuce's are toothed to bristly. Wild lettuce's stem carries pale spines up to 4 mm long, especially low down; prickly sow thistle's stem is hairless. Turn a leaf over: wild lettuce has spiny bristles under the midrib, often on the side veins too; prickly sow thistle's leaves are hairless. Young lettuce plants can lack the midrib bristles. In seed, wild lettuce's achenes are very dark brown or black, with a body 4–5 mm long and a pale beak about as long; prickly sow thistle's are pale brown, 2.5–3 mm long, winged and without a beak. The involucre does not separate them: (11)–13–15 mm long in wild lettuce, 10–15 mm in prickly sow thistle. Both have milky sap, lobed leaves that clasp the stem and yellow heads of strap-shaped florets. Prickly sow thistle is edible: it is recorded as a popular Māori food (pūhā tiotio).
lookalikes.name: Prickly sow thistle

lookalikes.howToTell: Count the florets in a head: wall lettuce has 5 or fewer, wild lettuce usually more. Under the head, wall lettuce's bracts are in two distinct rows, a few very short outer ones and a row of linear inner ones 5–7 mm long; wild lettuce's are in more than two rows of gradually changing length, the involucre (11)–13–15 mm long. Wall lettuce is hairless, its lower leaves stalked and lyre-shaped with a large triangular or kidney-shaped, three-lobed end lobe; wild lettuce's lower leaves taper to the base, carry spiny bristles under the midrib, and its stem has pale spines up to 4 mm long, especially low down. Wall lettuce's achene is shortly beaked; wild lettuce's beak is about as long as its body. Both have milky sap and yellow heads in a loose, branched spray. Wall lettuce's leaves are eaten raw or cooked, though they can taste extremely bitter (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Wall lettuce

summary.text:
Lactuca virosa is a plant in the Lactuca (lettuce) genus, often ingested for its mild analgesic and sedative effects.
It is related to common lettuce (L. sativa), and is often called wild lettuce, bitter lettuce, laitue vireuse, opium lettuce, poisonous lettuce, tall lettuce, great lettuce or rakutu-karyumu-so.
Lactucarium is the milky fluid secreted by several species of lettuce, especially Lactuca virosa, usually from the base of the stems. It is known as lettuce opium because of its sedative and analgesic properties.
Found coastally in Great Britain, rarely in the north-east of Ireland. Lactuca virosa is widespread across much of central and southern Europe. It can be found locally in the south east and east of England. In the rest of Great Britain it is very rare, and in Ireland it is absent. It is also found in the Punjab region of Pakistan and India and Australia where it grows in the wild.
In North America, it has been documented as introduced in California, Alabama, Iowa, and Washington, DC, and grows wild in other parts of the continent.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand, where it is called acrid lettuce): North Island: throughout; South Island: Marlborough (Rarangi and Blenheim). Naturalised from southern, western and central Europe, Asia and North Africa, first recorded in 1940.
Its Latin name says what it is: Lactuca is from lac, milk, for the white juice, and virosa means toxic.
Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and wild, with databased collections from Canterbury, Nelson and Marlborough in the South Island as well as across the North Island.

warnings: Not recommended for eating. In Morocco a person died after eating wild lettuce that had been mistaken for common sow thistle (pūhā). In northern Iran, where some people eat it raw as a vegetable unaware of its effects, eight people aged 12 to 38 were admitted to hospital with wild lettuce poisoning: dilated pupils, blurred vision, dizziness, vomiting, hallucinations, agitation, anxiety, urinary retention and, in some, loss of consciousness. All recovered; one spent 48 hours in intensive care. Two of them had eaten a great deal of it, and the poisoning was worse the more had been eaten. They had eaten it fresh, in May (spring there), before herbs are usually harvested, and the doctors who treated them thought that may be why it poisoned them.

The plant is classed as poisonous, though cases of poisoning are only very rarely recorded. It poisons livestock too: in Iran in 2019 a lamb that had eaten a large amount of it was left weak, unsteady, drowsy and blind. Its young leaves are eaten in some places, picked from the rosette in winter and early spring before they toughen, raw in salads or cooked with other greens, and are even more bitter than prickly lettuce's. No source gives a safe amount, and the poisonings above came from fresh leaves eaten in spring.

The milky sap, dried, is lactucarium or 'lettuce opium', sedative and pain-relieving; this species is probably its richest source. Even normal medicinal doses cause drowsiness, excess causes restlessness, and an overdose can kill through cardiac paralysis. Signs of overdose include dilated pupils, sensitivity to light, dizziness, sweating, hearing things that are not there, and an irregular heartbeat that upsets the heart and breathing. Three young drug users who injected wild lettuce extract with valerian root developed fever, chills, abdominal and low back pain, neck stiffness, headache and liver function disorders, and recovered in 3 days.

sources: Useful Temperate Plants, Ken Fern, temperate.theferns.info (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0)
edibleParts.text: Seed - cooked. It has a floury texture and a mild, somewhat creamy flavour. It can be used as a staple food crop in either savoury or sweet dishes. The seed can be cooked whole, though it is more commonly ground into a flour and used as a cereal in all the ways that oats are used, especially as a porridge but also to make biscuits, sourdough bread etc. The seed can also be sprouted and eaten raw or cooked in salads, stews etc. The roasted seed is a coffee substitute.

identification.text:
Tall, green or light green tufts to 1.5 m, robust, or sometimes with rather slender culms. Leaf-sheath slightly hairy, upper sheaths glabrous. Ligule 2–7 mm, truncate to oblong and obtuse, denticulate, abaxially scabrid. Leaf-blade 15–50 cm × 4–15 mm, scabrid on ribs and margins, often with scattered hairs, especially on margins. Culm erect or occasionally geniculate at base, internodes glabrous. Panicle (15)–20–38 cm, lax, equilateral, more or less nodding; branches widely spreading, slender, drooping, scabrid. Spikelets 35–50 mm, 2–3-flowered, pendulous on fine unequal pedicels; disarticulation below each floret at maturity. Glumes 9–11-nerved. Lemma 15–17.5 mm, narrow-lanceolate, light brown at first becoming tough and darker brown at maturity, stiffly hairy below level of awn insertion, or sometimes glabrous, scabrid on nerves above, narrowed to bidentate scarious apex; awn 30–40 mm, geniculate, stout, column dark brown, twisted. Palea keels with one row of cilia, interkeel scabrid. Callus with horse-shoe shaped scar densely bordered by long hairs. Anthers 2.5–3.5–(4) mm. Caryopsis 6–8 × 1.8–2.2 mm, light grey, densely hairy.
[From: Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: The cultivated oat's spikelets fall intact at maturity; wild oat's break up, separating below each floret. The cultivated oat's lemma is hairless or has a few hairs near the base and is usually awnless; any awn is weak, straight or curved, not bent at a knee and scarcely twisted. Wild oat's lemma is stiffly hairy below the awn, though sometimes hairless, and its awn is stout, 30–40 mm, bent at a knee, with a twisted dark-brown lower column. Spikelet length overlaps: the cultivated oat's are usually 20–30 mm but 15–40 mm at the extremes, wild oat's 35–50 mm. None of these tests holds for fatuoids, or false wild oats — a mutant form that turns up in oat crops: their florets look like wild oat's, with a bent, twisted awn and a horseshoe-shaped callus bordered by hairs, and the spikelet breaks below every floret. Occasional hybrids between wild oat and the cultivated oat may occur within an oat crop or where oats have been grown, though few are found.
lookalikes.name: Oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Both shed below each floret and both carry a bent, twisted awn — 30–36 mm in slender oat, 30–40 mm here — so the awn will not separate them. Use the lemma tip: slender oat draws each lobe out into a fine bristle 2–3 mm long, while wild oat's narrows to a two-toothed papery tip with no bristles described. Slender oat's lemma has long, stiff, reddish hairs below the awn; wild oat's is stiffly hairy there or sometimes hairless, with no hair colour described. Slender oat is often very slender, with very fine panicle branches, but wild oat is sometimes slender too; the grain widths do not overlap — 0.8–1.3 mm in slender oat against 1.8–2.2 mm here.
lookalikes.name: Slender oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Winter wild oat's spikelet breaks above the glumes with its florets held together, so they fall as one unit; wild oat's breaks below each floret, so they fall one by one. At the base of each floret, winter wild oat's callus is bordered by dense short hairs; wild oat has a horseshoe-shaped scar densely bordered by long hairs. Winter wild oat's awns, on the lowest 1–2 florets, have a red-brown twisted column; wild oat's column is dark brown. Size does not separate them: winter wild oat's spikelets are 3.5–6 cm with 2–3 florets and an awn of 25–50 mm in one subspecies (ludoviciana), and 6–8 cm with 3–5 florets and an awn of 60–70 mm in the other (sterilis); wild oat's spikelets are 35–50 mm with 2–3 florets and an awn of 30–40 mm.
lookalikes.name: Winter wild oat

preparation.text: Ripe florets drop from the plant one at a time, so a stand is gathered as it ripens rather than after. The seed, when harvested and dried, can store for several years. No source gives a method written for this species. Written for the cultivated oat: Harvested oats go through multiple stages of milling. The first stage is cleaning, to remove seeds of other plants, stones and any other extraneous materials. Next is dehulling to remove the indigestible hull, leaving the seed or "groat". Heating denatures enzymes in the seed that would make it go sour or rancid; the grain is then dried to minimise the risk of spoilage by bacteria and fungi. For home use such as making porridge, oats are often rolled flat to make them quicker to cook.

summary.text:
Avena fatua is a species of grass in the oat genus.
Indigenous to Europe, Central Asia and North Africa; now naturalised and a widespread weed in temperate regions of both Hemispheres.

This species and other wild oats can become troublesome in prairie agriculture when it invades and lowers the quality of a field crop, or competes for resources with the crop plants. It takes very few wild oat plants to cause a significant reduction in the yield of a wheat or cultivated oat field.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Auckland City, Bay of Plenty (Opotiki), Hawkes Bay (Takapau), more common in the Manawatu and Wairarapa, also from near Wellington City; S.: common in Canterbury, North and Central Otago, less so in Nelson, Marlborough, South Otago and Southland; Ch. Naturalised.

warnings: Claviceps purpurea is an ergot fungus that grows on the ears of rye and related cereal and forage plants. Consumption of grains or seeds contaminated with the survival structure of this fungus, the ergot sclerotium, can cause ergotism in humans and other mammals. It affects oats only rarely.

identification.text:
Annual, with short-lived rosette; stems erect or ascending, with short hairs or glabrous, 7–30 cm tall. Leaves (1)–2–6 cm long, glabrous or with short hairs, with 3–7 crenations each side. Basal leaves broadly ovate, truncately narrowed to long petiole; stipules short, linear-lobed. Stem leaves becoming narrow-elliptic, the uppermost cuneately narrowed to short petiole; stipules usually pinnatifid, 1/2–3/4 leaf length, with leaflike terminal lobe, and 3–7 linear lateral lobes. Peduncles erect, glabrous; bracts short, narrowly triangular. Flowers 1–2.5 cm diameter. Sepals narrowly triangular, acute, 5–8 mm long; appendages 2–3 mm long. Petals cream, the upper shorter than or equal to the upper sepals, the lowest with yellow or orange blotch and purple veins, the lowest and lateral bearded; spur about 3 mm long, equal to sepal appendages. Style geniculate at base, 1 mm long; stigma globose; ligule 0. Capsule ellipsoid, glabrous, 5–10 mm long. Seeds oblong, pale brown, 1.5 mm long. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

identification.text:
The parsnip is a biennial plant with a rosette of roughly hairy leaves that have a pungent odor when crushed. Parsnips are grown for their fleshy, edible, cream-colored taproots. The roots are generally smooth, although lateral roots sometimes form. Most are narrowly conical, but some cultivars have a more bulbous shape, which generally tends to be favored by food processors as it is more resistant to breakage. The plant's apical meristem produces a rosette of pinnate leaves, each with several pairs of leaflets with toothed margins. The lower leaves have short stems, the upper ones are stemless, and the terminal leaves have three lobes. The leaves are once- or twice-pinnate with broad, ovate, sometimes lobed leaflets with toothed margins; they grow up to 40 centimetres long.
The petioles are grooved and have sheathed bases. The floral stem develops in the second year and can grow to more than 150 cm tall. It is hairy, grooved, hollow (except at the nodes), and sparsely branched. It has a few stalkless, single-lobed leaves measuring 5 to 10 cm long that are arranged in opposite pairs.
The yellow flowers are in a loose, compound umbel measuring 10 to 20 cm in diameter. Six to 25 straight pedicels are present, each measuring 2 to 5 cm that support the umbellets (secondary umbels). The umbels and umbellets usually have no upper or lower bracts. The flowers have tiny sepals or lack them entirely, and measure about 3.5 millimetres. They consist of five yellow petals that are curled inward, five stamens, and one pistil. The fruits, or schizocarps, are oval and flat, with narrow wings and short, spreading styles. They are colored straw to light brown, and measure 4 to 8 mm long.
Despite the slight morphological differences between the two, wild parsnip is the same taxon as the cultivated version, and the two readily cross-pollinate. The parsnip has a chromosome number of 2n=22.

edibleParts.text: All the tender parts: young leaves, raw or cooked; flower buds and flowers; young seed pods, raw, cooked or pickled; the seeds, as a hot spice or mustard; and the root, peeled. The leaves are hot and peppery and soon turn bitter as they age; the pods are crisp and juicy but quickly turn tough and fibrous. Cooked, the peeled root is mild, like kohlrabi, not peppery.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): wild radish (subsp. raphanistrum) — Waste land, roadsides, disturbed soil. Sea radish (subsp. maritimus) — Coastal and on roadsides, waste land.
In New Zealand it is mainly a weed of waste places and disturbed ground. It also gets into cultivated fields and pastures, and grows best in well-drained soil, though it can take hold in poorer ground.

identification.text:
Annual to perennial. Taproot swollen or slender. Stems usually green, (10)–20–80–(100) cm tall. Rosette and lower stem leaves lyrate-pinnate; terminal leaflet 3–6–(10) × 3–6–(10) cm, as wide or narrower than rest of leaf; lateral leaflets in 1–8 pairs. Stem leaves simple or with 1 pair of basal lobes, orbicular to lanceolate, 1–6 cm long. Racemes 15–40–(60) cm long. Pedicels 1–2 cm long, stout at fruiting. Sepals 6–9 × 1–2 mm. Petals yellow, white, brownish, pink, or mauve, usually mauve-veined, 13–20 mm long. Silique (1)–2–8-seeded, cylindric, constricted between seeds, breaking into segments when ripe, weakly to strongly ribbed, tapering at apex, (10)–20–60–(80) × (2)–3–8–(9) mm. Seeds 1.5–3 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Key to the two subspecies: Silique (4)–6–8 mm wide; constrictions short; segments spherical or wider than long; apical portion rarely longer than 2× length of top segment — subsp. maritimus (sea radish). Silique (2)–3–4–(5) mm wide; constrictions long; segments longer than wide; apical portion (2)–3–4× length of top segment — subsp. raphanistrum (wild radish). Populations often display a petal colour polymorphism. All wild New Zealand material can be referred to 2 subspecies.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
When it sends up its flower stem, about 1 m tall, the stems and leaves stay bristly-hairy all the way up. The four petals are usually pale yellow or white, with distinct purplish veins. As the pods ripen they become deeply pinched around each seed, and later break into sections. Seedlings have stalked seed leaves, rounded at the base and notched at the tip; the first true leaves are long-stalked and already have side leaflets.

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild radish's flowering stems and their leaves stay bristly-hairy all the way up; field mustard's upper leaves are smooth (hairless), bluish-green, not lobed and clasp the stem, though its rosette leaves are bristly too, so a rosette alone does not separate them. Wild radish's petals are 13–20 mm long, usually pale yellow or white (also pink, mauve or brownish) and usually veined with mauve; field mustard's are bright yellow, without veins, and 6–10 mm long. Field mustard is also called wild turnip.
lookalikes.name: Field mustard

lookalikes.howToTell: Hedge mustard's flowers are tiny: its petals are yellow and 3–4 mm long, against wild radish's 13–20 mm. Its pods are slender, 10–15–(20) × 1–2 mm, on stalks about 3 mm long and pressed flat against the stem; wild radish's are (10)–20–60–(80) × (2)–3–8–(9) mm, pinched between the seeds, on stout stalks 1–2 cm long.
lookalikes.name: Hedge mustard

lookalikes.howToTell: Radish's ripe pods are fat, 8–15 mm wide, not or scarcely pinched between the seeds, and do not break into pieces. Wild radish's are (2)–3–8–(9) mm wide and pinched between the seeds, and break into one-seeded segments when ripe, though sea radish's do not break readily. Pods 8–9 mm wide fall in both ranges, so check the pinching rather than the width. Radish's rosette leaves have an end leaflet wider than the rest of the leaf and 1–4 pairs of side leaflets; wild radish's end leaflet is as wide as or narrower than the rest, with 1–8 pairs. Radish's stems are often reddish, wild radish's usually green, and radish usually has a swollen white or red root 1–3 cm (up to 8 cm) across, though sea radish's root can be stout to swollen too. Flower colour and size do not separate them: radish's petals are 15–20 mm long, wild radish's 13–20 mm, both white, pink or mauve with mauve veins, and either can be yellowish. The two can cross, so a plant in between may not be nameable. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Radish

lookalikes.howToTell: Eastern rocket's flowers are smaller: its petals are yellow and 6–10 mm long, against wild radish's 13–20 mm, usually pale yellow or white and usually veined with mauve. Eastern rocket's pods are slender, 1–1.5 mm wide and (40)–60–100 mm long, on stalks 3–5 mm long that lengthen to about 10 mm; wild radish's are (2)–3–8–(9) mm wide, pinched between the seeds, on stout stalks 1–2 cm long.
lookalikes.name: Eastern rocket

lookalikes.howToTell: Both can have white flowers. Black nightshade's are 10–13 mm across, usually white, sometimes pale mauve, with yellow anthers in the centre, and are followed by round berries 7–10 mm across, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow; the unripe green berries are the most toxic. Wild radish's flowers have four petals 13–20 mm long, usually veined with mauve, and its fruit are pods pinched between the seeds. Black nightshade's leaves are oval to lance-oval, entire to coarsely toothed, only sometimes slightly lobed; wild radish's rosette and lower leaves are divided into an end leaflet and 1–8 pairs of side leaflets, and are bristly.
lookalikes.name: Black nightshade

preparation.text: Use only young leaves; older ones soon turn bitter. Chop them finely into salads or use them as a potherb: like bok choy, fried or steamed for only a few seconds, which keeps more of their heat, or boiled in plenty of water for about 10 minutes. They shrink a lot as they cook. To keep them past their short season, blanch and freeze them. Steam the flower buds lightly, for no more than 5 minutes, as you would broccoli, and add the flowers to salads, or steep them in vinegar to flavour it. Pick the pods while they are young and tender, and eat them fresh, pickled or sautéed. The pods do not split open: wild radish's break into one-seeded segments when ripe, and sea radish's do not break readily. Use the seeds like mustard seed; to make mustard, pound them with a little liquid — vinegar if you want the paste to keep. For the root, peel off the tough outer layer, which comes away like a jacket, dice the inner core and boil it in plenty of salted water for about 45 minutes.

recipes.method: Written for sea radish (Raphanus raphanistrum subsp. maritimus), the coastal form of wild radish; the author borrowed a classic Turkish way with charlock. Wild radish leaves; onion; garlic; plenty of olive oil; yoghurt. Roast the leaves with onion and garlic in plenty of olive oil, then mix with yoghurt — stop cooking at this point or it will split. The author served it in toasted pitta with seared pheasant breast.
recipes.title: Roast wild radish leaves with yoghurt

recipes.method: For 625 ml (2½ cups) of pods: 185 ml (¾ cup) hot water; 125 ml (½ cup) cider vinegar; 15 ml (1 tbsp) sea salt; 90 ml (6 tbsp) sugar; 625 ml (2½ cups) wild radish pods, washed; 2 dried red chillies; 6 black peppercorns; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) yellow mustard seeds. In one jar, combine 185 ml (¾ cup) hot water, 125 ml (½ cup) cider vinegar, 15 ml (1 tbsp) sea salt and 90 ml (6 tbsp) sugar, and shake until everything has dissolved. Pack 625 ml (2½ cups) washed wild radish pods into a second jar, add 2 dried red chillies, 6 black peppercorns and 2.5 ml (½ tsp) yellow mustard seeds, and pour the vinegar mix over the pods. Leave for about two weeks before eating. Add the pods and their flowers to salads.
recipes.title: Pickled wild radish pods

recipes.method: From Turkey, where wild radish is called eşek turpu or turp ot. 1 bunch of wild radish; 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil; 2–3 garlic cloves; lemon juice; salt. Wash the leaves well, and pull off the older leaves and the thick lower part of the stems. Bring a pan of water to the boil, and meanwhile chop the leaves and young stems roughly. Drop them into the boiling water for only a few minutes, then lift them out and let them cool. Dress them with the garlic, chopped, the olive oil, lemon juice and salt.
recipes.title: Blanched wild radish salad

summary.text:
Raphanus raphanistrum, also known as wild radish, white charlock or jointed charlock, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.
It is native to temperate regions of North Africa, Europe and parts of Western Asia.
It is found in North Africa, within Macaronesia, Madeira Islands, Canary Islands, Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco and Tunisia. Within Western Asia it is found in the Caucasus, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Cyprus, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and Turkey. In eastern Europe, it is found within Belarus, Moldova and Ukraine. In middle Europe, it is in Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Netherlands, Poland, Slovakia and Switzerland. In northern Europe, in Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Isle of Man, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Sweden and United Kingdom. In southeastern Europe, within Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Italy, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia and Slovenia. Also in southwestern Europe, it is found in France, Portugal and Spain.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): wild radish, subsp. raphanistrum, naturalised by 1854 from Europe, Asia and North Africa, is recorded from Northland, Auckland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty and Wellington in the North Island and Nelson, Canterbury and Southland in the South Island. Sea radish, subsp. maritimus, from western and central Europe, the Mediterranean and Asia, naturalised by 1957, is recorded from Northland, Auckland, Bay of Plenty, Taranaki and Wellington, Nelson, Canterbury and Southland, and Stewart Island. Subsp. raphanistrum has also been called R. raphanistrum subsp. segetum here, and subsp. maritimus R. maritimus. Herbarium specimens of subsp. raphanistrum are databased from the North Auckland, Taranaki, Wellington and Nelson land districts.
It is frost hardy: even hard freezes only interrupt its flowering for a while. In Australia it is a major weed of canola crops; in New Zealand it does not seem to grow as commonly as wild turnip in many places.

warnings: Sea radish (subsp. maritimus), the coastal form, is classed as poisonous in New Zealand; the record gives no part or amount.
The seed is toxic: it contains an isothiocyanate formed from glucosinolates, and large quantities of seed may poison livestock.
Do not gather it from heavily fertilised ground or places that catch run-off: the leaves may be full of nitrates, which are toxic in high doses.
The leaves can upset some stomachs raw, and large amounts can cause stomach upsets.
In waste places it is controlled with herbicides such as glyphosate, amitrole, MCPA and 2,4-D. Pick it only where you know none has been used.

Brassicaceae plants are known for their tendency to accumulate heavy metals, a trait that makes them valuable for the phytoremediation of contaminated soils. However, this same ability necessitates careful monitoring, as the accumulation of heavy metals can also pose potential health risks.

edibleParts.text: Leaves, raw or cooked, used to flavour salads, cooked dishes and mint sauce, and fresh or dried in herb tea. Winter mint, the form of this species that stays evergreen throughout New Zealand, is the most commonly used culinary mint in the country. Sprigs are also added to the cooking water of new potatoes, and the leaves flavour drinks and desserts.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): An escape from cultivation along roadsides and in waste places near dwellings, especially in damp grassy places such as ditches and banks of streams running through settlements.
Wetland status (NZPCN, from the national wetland plant list, Clarkson et al. 2021), for subsp. spicata: facultative — commonly found both in wetlands and on dry ground.
Subsp. condensata (Flora of New Zealand, as subsp. tomentosa): An escape from cultivation on roadsides and river banks.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous perennial with branched more or less glandular-scaly stems ascending to about 80 cm, glabrous, glabrate or grey-villous, often tinged red. Leaves sessile to very shortly petiolate, 2.5–9 × 0.7–2 cm, lanceolate to elliptic or ovate-elliptic to ovate or oblong, plane or rugose, either with scattered hairs on veins below, or densely hairy above and persistently grey-villous below; base cuneate to cordate; apex obtuse to shortly acuminate. Inflorescence of rather narrow, short or long, terminal spikes, the central one 4–12 cm long, usually sparsely hairy, sometimes grey-villous. Flowers pedicellate. Calyx 1.5–2.2–(3.5) mm long, more or less purple, sparsely dotted with glands; teeth lanceolate or linear-subulate, ciliate, acuminate, slightly shorter than to equal to tube. Corolla 3–5 mm long, mauve or pinkish; lobes dotted with oil globules outside. Stamens included or exserted; anthers 0.35–0.4 mm long. Style long-exserted. Nutlets 0.5–0.7 mm long, broad-ovoid, minutely reticulate or granular, sometimes plant sterile. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Subsp. spicata: Stems glabrous or sparsely hairy. Leaves with hairs confined to veins on lower surface; lamina rounded to cordate at base. Inflorescence glabrous or sparsely hairy; spikes slender or fairly stout, often interrupted, especially in lower part. Corolla almost glabrous outside.
Subsp. condensata (called subsp. tomentosa in the 1988 Flora): Stems grey-villous. Leaves mostly grey-villous, but upper surfaces of mature leaves merely densely hairy; lamina cuneate or rounded at base. Inflorescence grey-villous; spikes narrow, usually interrupted in lower part. Corolla hairy outside. Nutlets present.
In New Zealand two distinct forms of subsp. spicata are naturalised. (1) This corresponds to the spearmint of north-west Europe and has lanceolate or narrow-elliptic, more or less plane leaves, is deciduous in colder areas, is very susceptible to mint rust disease and is sterile. (2) This is usually known as winter mint in New Zealand and has ovate, ovate-oblong or elliptic, rugose leaves, is evergreen in all parts of the country, is not badly infected with mint rust and produces fully formed nutlets.
The whole plant has a strong spearmint smell.

lookalikes.howToTell: No single character separates every plant, so use several together. Apple mint's leaves are broad, usually elliptic and wrinkled, 1.5–4.5 × 0.8–3 cm; spearmint's are lanceolate to ovate, 2.5–9 × 0.7–2 cm, so leaf sizes overlap. Apple mint is densely hairy and often grey-woolly beneath; spearmint ranges from nearly hairless to densely hairy and grey-woolly beneath, so hairiness alone does not decide it. Both have stalkless or nearly stalkless leaves; apple mint's leaf base is heart-shaped or nearly so and often clasps the stem, spearmint's ranges from tapered to heart-shaped. Apple mint's calyx is more or less green and its corolla pale pink or whitish; spearmint's calyx is more or less purple, its corolla mauve or pinkish, and its stems are often tinged red. Apple mint has a fruity, minty flavour, and spearmint a minty, green, cooling, spicy smell, but smell is a clue, not a test. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Apple mint

lookalikes.howToTell: Lemon balm and spearmint both have square stems and opposite leaves, and both are aromatic. Spearmint's flowers are in narrow spikes at the stem tips, the central spike 4–12 cm long. Its calyx is 1.5–2.2(–3.5) mm long and nearly regular, and its mauve or pinkish corolla is 3–5 mm long with 4–5 nearly equal lobes. Lemon balm's flowers are in whorls of generally 3–10 among stalked, leaf-like bracts. Its calyx is about 8 mm long, with prominent nerves, long white hairs and unequal teeth, and its corolla is 12–15 mm long, clearly two-lipped, with a curved tube. Spearmint's leaves are stalkless or very shortly stalked; lemon balm's leaves are stalked. Crushed lemon balm leaves usually smell strongly of lemon, and spearmint has a strong spearmint smell. But lemon balm plants without the lemon scent, smelling of mint, have been found in New Zealand, so smell is a clue, not a test. The flower tests are the surest. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Lemon balm

lookalikes.howToTell: Smell does not separate them: crushed pennyroyal leaves have a very strong fragrance like spearmint, and infants have been made ill by tea made from pennyroyal thought to be mint. Look at where the flowers are: spearmint's are in narrow spikes at the stem tips, the central spike 4–12 cm long; pennyroyal's are densely packed in spaced rings in the leaf joints along the stem, with a cluster of leaves at the shoot tip. Spearmint's stems ascend to about 80 cm; pennyroyal's creep along the ground and ascend, to about 30 cm long. Spearmint's leaves are stalkless or very shortly stalked, 2.5–9 cm long, flat or wrinkled; pennyroyal's are stalked, sometimes shortly, usually 0.6–2 cm long and not wrinkled. Both have mauve flowers of similar size (spearmint's corolla 3–5 mm long, pennyroyal's 4–6 mm) and a purple or purplish calyx, so flower colour does not separate them, and both grow in damp grassy places. Pennyroyal is poisonous to the liver; do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Pennyroyal

lookalikes.howToTell: No single character separates every plant, so use several together. Spearmint's leaves are stalkless or very shortly stalked; peppermint's usually have a distinct stalk, though shoots growing in water can have nearly stalkless leaves. Crush a leaf: spearmint is not peppermint- or lemon-scented and often smells of spearmint; peppermint smells of peppermint, or of lemon in the bergamot-mint form. Spearmint's calyx is 1.5–2.2(–3.5) mm long and its mauve or pinkish corolla 3–5 mm long; peppermint's calyx is 3–4 mm long and its mauve or lilac corolla 5–6 mm long, so the largest spearmint flowers overlap. Spearmint's flowers are in narrow spikes, the central one 4–12 cm long; peppermint's are in a rounded head or an oblong spike, often with a few separate whorls below. Both have a purple calyx, both often have purplish or red-tinged stems, and their leaf sizes overlap (spearmint 2.5–9 × 0.7–2 cm, peppermint 1–6 × 1–3.5 cm), so these do not separate them. Peppermint is a hybrid of spearmint and water mint, and both hybridise freely with other mints, so in-between plants occur. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Peppermint

preparation.text: Use the leaves fresh, dried or frozen; they can also be preserved in salt, sugar, sugar syrup, alcohol or oil. For drying, cut the stems just before or as the flowers open, because the leaves lose their aroma after the plant flowers. For tea, steep the fresh or dried leaves in hot water.

recipes.method: Four teaspoons of gunpowder green tea; 1.2 litres of water; four teaspoons of sugar; four sprigs of fresh spearmint. Boil the water. Put the tea leaves in the teapot, pour over a cup of the boiling water, swirl, then strain and discard that water. Add the spearmint and sugar to the rinsed leaves, fill the pot with the rest of the boiling water and steep for 5 minutes. Pour into glasses from a height to raise a frothy head. Serves 4.
recipes.title: Moroccan mint tea

recipes.method: About 25 fresh spearmint leaves; 1½ teaspoons demerara sugar; about 10–20 ml malt vinegar, to taste. Pick the leaves off and discard the stalks. Wash the leaves and chop them roughly, adding the sugar as you chop so it blends in. Put the mint and sugar in a small serving bowl, stir in enough vinegar to cover the mint, and chill until serving. Best made about 2 hours ahead so the vinegar softens the leaves. Serves 2, with roast lamb.
recipes.title: Spearmint sauce

recipes.method: About 28 g (1 ounce) fresh spearmint, about 1 cup chopped, stalks included if you like; 250 ml white sugar; 250 ml water. Wash and roughly chop the spearmint. Bring the sugar and water to the boil, lower the heat and cook 4–5 minutes until slightly reduced, then take off the heat. Stir in the chopped mint, cover and infuse 30–60 minutes. Strain into a glass jar. Keeps up to 1 month in the fridge; freeze for longer. For sweetening cold drinks.
recipes.title: Spearmint syrup

recipes.method: A large handful of dried spearmint leaves; about 1.9 litres of boiling water; 125 ml sugar. Pour the boiling water over the leaves and steep for about 20 minutes. Strain, stir in the sugar and serve poured over ice.
recipes.title: Iced spearmint tea

recipes.method: 2 tbsp olive oil; 450 g snap peas; 2 garlic cloves, peeled and minced; 2 tbsp minced fresh mint; 2 tsp lemon zest; 1 tbsp lemon juice; salt. Heat the oil in a wok or large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the peas and garlic and fry over high heat, stirring often, for about 5 minutes, until the peas are tender-crisp and starting to char or blister. Take off the heat and stir in the mint, lemon zest and juice and a pinch of salt. Taste, add more lemon juice if you like, and serve warm.
recipes.title: Charred snap peas with mint and lemon

recipes.method: Soup: 1 tbsp olive oil; 2 tbsp butter; 250 ml diced brown onion; 1 garlic clove, minced; 1 litre vegetable stock; 1.5 litres fresh or frozen peas; 2 spring onions, diced; 2 tbsp minced fresh mint; 60 ml sour cream; salt and pepper. Pesto: 125 ml parsley leaves; 60 ml mint leaves; 1 garlic clove, minced; 60 ml pine nuts; zest and juice of 1 lemon; 55 g Parmesan, grated; 2 tbsp olive oil. Heat the oil and butter in a large pot over medium-high heat and cook the onion 5–10 minutes until soft and clear. Add the soup garlic for a minute, then the stock, and bring to the boil. Add the peas, bring back to the boil and simmer 1–2 minutes. Off the heat, stir in the spring onions, mint, sour cream and a pinch of salt and pepper, then blend until smooth and season to taste. For the pesto, blend the parsley, mint, garlic, pine nuts and lemon zest and juice until smooth, blend in the Parmesan, then trickle in the oil. Serve warm or chilled, each bowl topped with a big spoonful of pesto.
recipes.title: Pea soup with mint pesto

recipes.method: Marinade: 4 tbsp low-salt tamari; 4 tbsp olive oil; 2 tbsp brown rice vinegar; 2 tsp minced garlic; 1 tsp dried thyme; 1 tsp paprika; ½ tsp chilli flakes; ½ tsp black pepper; 450 g sirloin steak. Pickles: 500 ml thinly sliced cucumber; 2 medium carrots, peeled and grated; 250 ml red onion in thin strips; 160 ml brown rice vinegar; 1½ tsp sugar; 1 tsp chilli flakes; 1 tsp sea salt. Sauce: 160 ml low-fat Greek yoghurt; 125 ml diced cucumber; 2 tbsp lime juice; 2 tbsp minced fresh mint; ½ tsp sea salt. To serve: 4 wholemeal tortillas, 25–30 cm across; 500 ml cooked basmati rice; a bunch of coriander. Mix the marinade, pour it over the steak in a glass or china dish and refrigerate 1–8 hours. An hour before cooking, mix the pickle ingredients in one bowl and the sauce ingredients in another. Grill the steak over medium-high heat 3–4 minutes a side, or to your liking, rest it 5 minutes and slice it thinly. Lay rice, steak and pickles down the middle third of each tortilla, scatter with coriander leaves and serve the yoghurt sauce alongside.
recipes.title: Steak wraps with pickled vegetables and minted yoghurt

recipes.method: 750 ml cubed seedless watermelon; 250 ml frozen strawberries; 500 ml rosé wine; 12 large mint leaves, plus sprigs to garnish. Freeze the watermelon cubes in a container. Just before serving, blend the frozen watermelon, strawberries, rosé and mint until smooth. Serve at once, each glass garnished with a mint sprig.
recipes.title: Watermelon mint frosé

summary.text:
Spearmint (Mentha spicata), also known as garden mint, common mint, lamb mint and mackerel mint, is native to Europe and southern temperate Asia, extending from Ireland in the west to southern China in the east.
M. spicata may be an allopolyploid derived from possibly M. longifolia and M. suaveolens and is only known as a cultivated plant or an escape from cultivation. Two subspecies occur in New Zealand.
Winter mint is the most commonly used culinary mint in New Zealand and must have been introduced before 1900.
Other names in New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand Online, NZPCN): mint, winter mint.

warnings: The essential oil in the leaves is toxic in large doses. Large quantities of mint essential oil can cause abortion; this caution is given for mints in general, not recorded for this species.
Spearmint hybridises freely with other mints, so wild plants may not match the description exactly.
Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed. Pick from ground you know.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Canterbury (small populations at White Rock, Loburn, and Rangitata River), Central Otago (common to dominant on dry slopes and terraces, especially in the Alexandra area).
NZ Flora Online weed profile habitats: bank, dry, flat, grassland, gravel, hill, open, pasture, river terrace, riverbed, roadside, rock outcrop, slope, stone, terrace.
Forms dominant scrub in cold, dry areas (NZPCN, restated). Prefers dry, stony soils, slopes, screes and terraces, and in Otago favours rabbit-disturbed sites; in the Rangitata Gorge it grows on very stony, dry lowland sites, spur brows, scree and north-facing lower slopes, and has spread down dry stony watercourses, but not into deeper soils (Canterbury Regional Pest Management Plan, restated). Grows on roadsides and waste ground from Roxburgh to Gibbston (Otago Daily Times, restated).
Very tolerant of cold and dry conditions (NZPCN, restated).

identification.text:
Small, hairy shrub to about 30 cm high. Shoots dense, erect or suberect, densely clothed in short hairs. Leaves sessile or subsessile, 3–8 × 0.5–3 mm, elliptic but appearing linear because of revolute margins, densely hairy, with abundant oil globules, tomentose along midrib below. Flowers in dense terminal heads; lower verticels often interrupted. Bracts similar to leaves, often somewhat wider, green, shorter than to longer than calyx. Calyx 3–4 mm long, campanulate, green or purplish, hairy, dotted with oil globules, with tuft of white hairs in throat; teeth of upper lip ovate, not ciliate; teeth of lower lip linear-subulate, long-ciliate. Corolla 4–6 mm long, white or mauve; tube not exserted, hairy outside; upper lip with large, broad, oblong-elliptic to obovate lobes, sparsely hairy or glabrous; lower lip at right angles to upper. Stamens not or scarcely exserted; anthers purplish. Nutlets … broad-ellipsoid to sub-spherical, dark brown. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The nutlets are about 1 mm wide (NParks Flora & Fauna Web).
Flora of New Zealand key to the two naturalised thymes: Prostrate herb; leaves not or scarcely revolute, elliptic — Thymus pulegioides (creeping thyme). Small erect shrub; leaves strongly revolute, appearing linear — Thymus vulgaris.
The stems and leaves are aromatic when crushed; creeping thyme has a much more prostrate form (NZPCN, restated).
The stems are square and semi-woody, with narrow, green, hairy leaves, and give off a strong, pleasant smell when crushed; the mauve or white flowers are in whorls on the upper stems (Environment Canterbury).

preparation.text: Strip the tiny leaves from the woody stems by scraping with the back of a knife or pulling the sprig through your fingers or a fork, and discard the stems. Central Otago wild thyme has much smaller leaves than garden thyme but a more intense flavour, and takes more work to gather and strip. To dry: rinse the sprigs, dry them in a salad spinner or tea towel, spread them on paper towels on a tray in a sunny window for a week or so, then rub them between your hands over a tray so the leaves fall off; pick out the stems and store in an airtight jar or tin. Oil content peaks just before flowering, the usual time to cut thyme for drying. Dried thyme is stronger than fresh and a little goes a long way. Thyme keeps its flavour on drying and in long, slow cooking; add it early, as its oils take a while to release. It goes well with mushrooms, courgettes, stocks, soups, stews and rabbit.

recipes.method: Ingredients: 2 tablespoons sesame seeds, 1½ tablespoons dried thyme or 2½ tablespoons fresh thyme, 2½ teaspoons sumac, ¼ teaspoon salt. Toast the sesame seeds in a dry frying pan over medium heat, tossing, until fragrant and starting to colour. When cool, grind them with the thyme, salt and sumac in a mortar and pestle. Sprinkle it with oil on flatbread before baking, use it as a dip with sourdough and olive oil, or scatter it on salads, eggs, labneh or yoghurt.
recipes.title: Za'atar with Central Otago wild thyme

recipes.method: Ingredients: 240 g oats, 50 g pumpkin seeds, 100 ml boiling water, 4 tablespoons butter (or lard, ghee or coconut oil), 20 g picked thyme leaves, 1 teaspoon sea salt plus extra to sprinkle; goat's cheese and honey to serve. Heat the oven to 165 °C. Blend half the oats with all the pumpkin seeds to the texture of wholemeal flour. Pour the boiling water over the butter and stir to melt. Mix all the dry ingredients in a bowl, then stir in the melted butter to make a soft dough. Roll it as thin as you can (about 2 mm) straight onto a baking-paper-lined tray, tidy the edges, mark squares and cut them diagonally into triangles. Sprinkle with sea salt and bake for 10–15 minutes until golden. Makes about 24. Serve with goat's cheese and honey. The source notes other herbs can be used.
recipes.title: Wild thyme oatcakes

recipes.method: Pluck the tiny wild thyme leaves and crush them gently in a mortar and pestle, then add roughly ground black pepper and extra virgin olive oil (the source gives no amounts). Trim the silver skin off a venison backstrap and cut it into manageable lengths. Rub in the seasoning, wrap tightly in cling film and leave at room temperature for an hour or so before cooking. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Heat a heavy ovenproof pan until smoking, sear the backstrap a couple of minutes on each side until browned, then roast for about eight minutes, turning it over four minutes in. Rest for a good ten minutes, carve into thin slices (about 5 mm), spoon over the juices and scatter with wild thyme leaves and a few sprigs. Venison tenderloin can be cooked the same way.
recipes.title: Venison backstrap with Central Otago wild thyme

recipes.method: Ingredients: 500 g golden caster sugar, 4 elderflower heads, 2 lemons, a small bunch of thyme. Put the sugar and 1 litre of water in a pan and bring to a simmer, making sure the sugar dissolves. Wash the elderflower heads gently under cold water and peel the rind of one lemon into strips. Take the syrup off the heat and add the elderflower, lemon strips, the juice of the peeled lemon and most of the thyme (keep 5 sprigs). Cool, cover and steep overnight. Strain through muslin or a clean tea towel; taste, and dilute with water and more lemon juice if too sweet (it should be a little sweeter than you like, as freezing dulls sweetness). Put a slice of the second lemon and a small thyme sprig in each of 10 ice-lolly moulds, pour in the liquid, add sticks and freeze overnight.
recipes.title: Thyme, elderflower and lemon ice lollies

recipes.method: Ingredients: 500 g shortcrust pastry, plain flour for dusting, 1 tablespoon olive oil, 2 garlic cloves (finely chopped), 4 large eggs, 300 ml double cream, 100 ml whole milk, 1 teaspoon Dijon mustard, 4 spring onions (sliced), 100 g soft goat's cheese (crumbled), leaves from 2 thyme sprigs, 200 g purple sprouting broccoli (tough outer stem peeled, blanched until tender). Roll the pastry on a floured surface to about the thickness of a coin, line a deep 24 cm tart tin, prick the base, trim and chill for 30 minutes. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan). Gently fry the garlic in the oil for 5 minutes until lightly golden. Line the pastry with baking paper and baking beans, bake 15 minutes, remove the paper and beans and bake 7–10 minutes more until very pale golden; turn the oven down to 160 °C (140 °C fan). Whisk the eggs, cream, milk and mustard, stir in the garlic and spring onions, pour into the case, scatter over the goat's cheese, thyme leaves and broccoli and press gently level. Bake 40 minutes until golden and just set, and cool completely before serving.
recipes.title: Purple sprouting broccoli and goat's cheese tart

recipes.method: Ingredients: 2 tablespoons vegetable oil, 2.5 kg lamb shoulder, 4 celery sticks, 2 carrots and 2 onions (all quartered), 6 garlic cloves, 1 bottle red wine, 1 litre lamb stock, ¼ bunch rosemary, ¼ bunch thyme. Season the lamb, brown it in the oil in a large frying pan, skin-side down first, for 4–5 minutes until browned on both sides, and move it to a large roasting tin. Heat the oven to 170 °C (150 °C fan). Brown the vegetables and garlic in the same pan for 3–4 minutes and add them to the tin. Bring the wine, stock, rosemary and thyme to a simmer in the pan and pour over the lamb. Cover with baking paper and foil and roast for 6 hours. Uncover, lift the lamb onto a platter and rest it loosely covered; strain the liquid, skim off the fat and simmer 5 minutes to reduce a little. Serve with the lamb.
recipes.title: Braised shoulder of lamb with thyme and rosemary

recipes.method: Ingredients: 3 teaspoons baking powder, 1 teaspoon sea salt, 350 g plain flour, 90 g cold unsalted butter (diced), 5 sprigs fresh thyme (finely chopped), 140 ml cold water. Mix everything in a mixer until it just forms a dough; do not overmix. Divide into 6 balls, wrap and chill for 1 hour. Bring the dough back to room temperature, then roll it through a pasta machine from the widest setting down to setting 2. Cut into long, thin triangles, lay them on a non-stick baking sheet and bake at 180 °C for 12 minutes. Cool and keep in an airtight container.
recipes.title: Thyme crackers

recipes.method: Ingredients: 1.2 kg floury potatoes (peeled and cut into chunks), 300 ml vegetable oil, 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 tablespoons fresh thyme, plus extra to garnish, salt and pepper. Parboil the potatoes in salted water for 8 minutes, drain, return to the pan and let them steam dry. Heat the oven to 250 °C and heat the vegetable oil in a large roasting tray until sizzling. Carefully toss the potatoes in the hot oil with the olive oil, thyme, salt and pepper until slightly roughed up. Turn the oven down to 180 °C and roast for 45 minutes to 1 hour, turning halfway, until crisp and golden. Garnish with more fresh thyme.
recipes.title: Thyme-roasted potatoes

summary.text:
Thymus vulgaris (common thyme, German thyme, garden thyme or just thyme) is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae.
The species is native to southern Europe from the western Mediterranean to southern Italy.
It is also the main source of the herb thyme, used as an ingredient in cooking and as a herbal medicine. It is slightly spicier than oregano and sweeter than sage.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Culinary thyme, often called wild thyme or simply thyme, was recorded in Central Otago by Cockayne in 1928. Elsewhere in New Zealand, as in many countries, it is cultivated as a culinary herb.
First recorded naturalised in New Zealand in 1926 (Flora of New Zealand, restated). Its arrival in Central Otago is usually credited to goldminers; Brian Patrick of the Central Stories Museum, Alexandra, and NZ Geographic credit the French miner, orchardist and winemaker Jean Desire Feraud, who planted it on his farm near Clyde in the 1860s. Unpalatable to sheep and rabbits, it now covers an estimated 2000 ha along the Clutha, Manuherikia and Kawarau valleys (Otago Daily Times; NZ Geographic, restated).
Wild thyme is a pest in the Canterbury Regional Pest Management Plan 2018–2038 under a site-led programme that aims to reduce its extent at listed sites by 50%; Environment Canterbury has hand-grubbed the Rangitata River infestation since 1981 and controls another near Loburn. Otago Regional Council lists thyme as an organism of interest, which is watch-listed but not a declared pest. DOC lists it among New Zealand's environmental weeds (2024) (Environment Canterbury; Otago Regional Council; NZPCN, restated).
It can form large, dense patches covering hillsides, crowding out native vegetation to become the dominant scrub; its seeds are spread mainly by gravity, soil movement and people (Environment Canterbury; NZPCN). Outside Canterbury's site-led areas, controlling it is the land occupier's responsibility (Environment Canterbury).
Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and wild in New Zealand under the names common thyme and wild thyme, with herbarium records from the Canterbury and Otago land districts.

warnings: Medicinal thyme (including medicinal-strength tea) is not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding, as its safety there has not been established, or for children under 12 (a few liquid extracts from age 4) for lack of data. Medicinal use can upset the stomach.
People allergic to plants of the mint family (Lamiaceae) should not take thyme medicinally, and systemic allergic reactions to eating thyme and oregano are on record (a single-patient case report).

Thyme essential oil can cause allergic reactions and irritation of the skin and mucous membranes, especially taken by mouth or put undiluted on skin; like all concentrated essential oils it can be harmful in large doses.

Wild thyme is a declared pest in Canterbury (site-led programme of the Regional Pest Management Plan), where selling, propagating or distributing it, or any part of it, is an offence under sections 52 and 53 of the Biosecurity Act. Do not spread seed or plants.
Lawns and verges are routinely sprayed. Pick from ground you know.

identification.text:
A big, chunky mushroom. The cap is usually 4–14 cm across, but it can reach 30 cm. It is bell-shaped or rounded at first, then broadly domed to flat. It is sticky when fresh, soon dry and glossy, smooth, and may crack when old; ragged scraps of veil can hang from the edge. Fresh caps are wine red to dark reddish brown. They fade to tan or yellowish brown, and almost white in dry weather; a white form also occurs. A faded cap is much harder to tell from other dull mushrooms.
The gills are attached to the stem and close to crowded. They are whitish to pale grey at first, then purplish grey, and finally purple-black.
The stem is 8–18 cm long and 1–2.5 cm thick, white, yellowing with age, and often wider at the base, where white mycelial threads cling to it. It carries a large, thick, white to yellowish ring. The ring is finely grooved on top, often blackened with spores, and split radially underneath like a cogwheel. The flesh is firm and white throughout and does not change colour when cut. The smell and taste are not distinctive. The spore print is dark purple-brown to purple-black.
The wine-red cap, the thick cogwheel ring and the dark purple-black print, on wood chip, together mark it.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both grow on wood-chip mulch in New Zealand gardens and both drop a purple-brown spore print, so neither the place nor the print separates them. Psilocybe subaeruginosa is a magic mushroom, a Class A controlled drug. It is small and slender: the cap is 1–5 cm across, yellow-brown to orange-brown, often with a small point, and the stem is 2.5–7 cm long and only 2–3.5 mm thick. Its veil soon disappears, leaving at most a faint raised zone on the stem. Cap and stem stain greenish blue when handled or as they age. Wine cap is far bigger and heavier: a wine-red cap 4–14 cm or more across, a stem 1–2.5 cm thick, a thick ring split like a cogwheel underneath, and white flesh that does not change colour.
lookalikes.name: Psilocybe subaeruginosa

lookalikes.howToTell: Wine cap can resemble Agaricus mushrooms, such as the field mushroom, which also have a ring and a dark spore print. A dark print does not separate them. The gills do: in Agaricus they are free of the stem and start white or pink, then turn chocolate brown. Wine cap's gills are attached to the stem and go from whitish or pale grey to purplish grey and purple-black. The field mushroom has a white cap, a short stem with a thin ring, and grows in open pasture. Wine cap has a wine-red to tan cap, a thick, grooved, cogwheel-like ring, and grows on wood chip and mulch.
