preparation.text:
Brush off any dirt or wood chips and wipe with a damp cloth. Rinse quickly only if very dirty, and pat dry. Trim the tough base of the stem. Always cook wine caps thoroughly; never eat them raw.
Young firm buttons suit roasting, stir-fries and pickling. Bigger, more open caps go spongy and soak up marinades, so they suit grilling, stuffing or thick slices. Sauté in butter, grill, roast, or add to risotto, pasta, soups and braises. Mature dark gills turn pale sauces and soups grey; scrape them out with a spoon if that matters.
Keep them in a paper bag in the fridge and use within 3–5 days. Drying can make them tough. Pickling, or part-cooking and freezing, keeps them better.

recipes.method: Serves 2. 300 g wine caps; 2 tbsp (30 g) butter; 1 tbsp olive oil; 2 garlic cloves; 2 sprigs parsley; salt; black pepper. Wipe the mushrooms clean, rinsing quickly and patting dry only if dirty, and slice caps and stems 5 mm thick; slice the stems of big mushrooms a little thinner, as they can be fibrous. Mince the garlic and chop the parsley. Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over medium-high heat and lay the mushrooms in one layer. Leave them for 4–5 minutes until deep golden underneath, then stir and cook 5 minutes more until their liquid has gone. Lower the heat, add the butter and garlic, and stir for 1–2 minutes until fragrant. Off the heat, season well and toss with the parsley.
recipes.title: Sautéed wine caps with garlic and parsley

recipes.method: Serves 4. 250 g arborio or carnaroli rice; 350 g wine caps; 1 litre vegetable or chicken stock; 2 shallots; 2 garlic cloves; 120 ml dry white wine; 50 g butter; 2 tbsp olive oil; 60 g grated parmesan; salt and pepper. Dice the mushrooms, chop the shallots finely and mince the garlic; keep the stock at a gentle simmer. Fry the mushrooms in 1 tbsp of the oil over medium heat for 7–8 minutes until golden, then lift them out. Add the rest of the oil and 20 g of the butter and cook the shallots 3–4 minutes until translucent, then the garlic for 1 minute. Stir in the rice and toast it 2–3 minutes. Add the wine and stir until it has gone. Add the hot stock a ladle at a time, stirring often and letting each be absorbed, for 15–18 minutes, until the rice is just tender. Fold the mushrooms back in. Off the heat, beat in the remaining 30 g of butter and the parmesan, and season. For more flavour, steep a small handful of dried mushrooms in the stock first.
recipes.title: Wine cap risotto

recipes.method: Serves 4. 300 g tagliatelle or pappardelle; 300 g wine caps; 150 ml cream; 1 small onion; 3 garlic cloves; 2 sprigs thyme; 30 g butter; 2 tbsp olive oil; 50 g grated parmesan; salt and pepper; chopped parsley to serve. Cook the pasta in plenty of well-salted boiling water until al dente, keeping 250 ml of the cooking water. Meanwhile slice the mushrooms, dice the onion and mince the garlic. Heat the oil and butter in a large frying pan over medium-high heat and cook the onion about 4 minutes until soft. Add the mushrooms and thyme and cook 6–8 minutes until browned and tender, then the garlic for 1 minute. Lower the heat, pour in the cream and simmer 2 minutes. Add the drained pasta and toss, adding splashes of the pasta water until the sauce is smooth and glossy. Off the heat, remove the thyme stalks, fold in the parmesan, season, and serve with more parmesan and parsley.
recipes.title: Wine cap tagliatelle with cream and thyme

recipes.method: Serves 4. 400 g wine caps; 700 ml vegetable or chicken stock; 150 ml cream; 150 g potatoes, peeled and diced; 1 large onion; 2 garlic cloves; 40 g butter; 1 tbsp olive oil; 1 tsp chopped thyme; salt and pepper. Roughly chop the mushrooms, dice the onion and mince the garlic. Heat the oil and butter in a heavy pot over medium heat and cook the onion about 5 minutes until translucent. Add the mushrooms and garlic and cook 8–10 minutes, stirring now and then, until shrunk and lightly browned. Stir in the thyme and potatoes, pour in the stock and bring to a gentle boil. Cover and simmer on low 15–20 minutes until the potatoes are tender. Blend about half the soup, leaving plenty of mushroom pieces. Stir in the cream and warm through on low without letting it boil. Season and serve with crusty bread.
recipes.title: Cream of wine cap soup

recipes.method: Serves 4. 4–6 large wine cap caps, stems removed (keep them for stock or a sauté); 4 tbsp olive oil; 2 tbsp balsamic vinegar; 1 tbsp soy sauce; 1 tsp garlic powder; ½ tsp dried oregano or thyme; ½ tsp black pepper; chopped parsley. Wipe the caps clean. Whisk the oil, vinegar, soy sauce, garlic powder, oregano and pepper, coat the caps all over and leave them 15–20 minutes. Heat a barbecue or grill pan to medium-high and oil the grill. Grill the caps gill side up for 4–5 minutes until marked and starting to soften, then turn them and grill 3–4 minutes more, brushing with the leftover marinade. Serve scattered with parsley, as a side or in a toasted bun with lettuce, tomato and garlic aioli as a vegetarian burger.
recipes.title: Grilled wine cap caps

recipes.method: Serves 2. 225 g wine caps, cut into even bite-sized pieces; 1 tsp minced garlic (or garlic greens); 2 tbsp tamari or soy sauce; 1 tsp balsamic vinegar; 2 tbsp vegetable oil; salt and pepper; fresh thyme or chive flowers to garnish (optional). Mix the garlic, tamari, vinegar and oil with salt and pepper in a bowl, add the mushrooms, toss, and leave to marinate for 30 minutes to 2 hours. Heat the oven to 220 °C. Tip the mushrooms and marinade onto a baking tray and roast about 20 minutes, until golden brown. Serve at once, with the garnish if you like.

summary.text:
Stropharia rugosoannulata, commonly known as the wine cap, wine-red stropharia, wine cap stropharia, garden giant, burgundy mushroom, or king stropharia, is a species of agaric mushroom in the family Strophariaceae found in North America. It is regarded as a choice edible.
It is also called the wine roundhead and, for its size, the godzilla mushroom. Its scientific name means 'wrinkled-ringed', for the ridged ring on its stem. It is native to North America and Europe and has been introduced to New Zealand, Australia and Asia. It is one of the world's ten most traded cultivated mushrooms, and is easy to grow on wood chip.
In New Zealand it is exotic. Specimens are held from Auckland, Waikato, Wellington, Nelson and Buller, and there are 328 research-grade iNaturalist records, most from Waikato, Auckland and the Bay of Plenty. Nearly all come from wood-chip mulch and garden beds; gardeners here grow it on purpose, and cultures can be imported for growing under an MPI permit.
It lives on rotting plant matter. It also traps and digests tiny nematode worms in the soil, using spiny cells called acanthocytes.

warnings: Always cook wine caps thoroughly; never eat them raw.

The redlead roundhead (Leratiomyces ceres) grows in large numbers on wood-chip mulch in New Zealand gardens (2,149 research-grade iNaturalist records) and also has a dark purple-brown spore print. It is not known to be edible. It is much smaller: a bright red to orange cap 2–6 cm across with thin flesh, a stem 0.5–1 cm thick, and only a thin, fragile ring that is sometimes missing in older mushrooms. Its red fades with age or heavy rain. Wine cap is chunky, with firm flesh, a stem 1–2.5 cm thick and a thick, cogwheel-like ring.
Pick wine caps only from clean wood chip, and never eat a mushroom from a garden bed that you cannot name for certain: other species come up in the same mulch.

identification.text:
Woody deciduous climber up to 30 m long; twigs densely hairy when young, becoming more or less glabrous. Leaves densely hairy when young, becoming more or less glabrous above when mature but usually remaining moderately clothed in appressed hairs below, petiolate; leaflets elliptic to obovate, acuminate, entire, in (3)–4–6 opposite pairs, 30–80 mm long, stipellate; petiolules 2–4 mm long; stipules inconspicuous. Raceme with numerous flowers; pedicels about 15–20 mm long. Calyx densely clothed in fine hairs; calyx teeth ovate-triangular, shorter than the tube. Corolla mauve to deep lilac, (15)–20–25–(28) mm long. Pod tomentulose, few-seeded, (6)–10–15 cm long; seeds smooth, brown, flattened, suborbicular.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Told from Japanese wisteria (Wisteria floribunda), also cultivated in New Zealand, by its stems twining anticlockwise; Japanese wisteria's twine clockwise.
Its deciduous foliage and long racemes of lilac pea-like flowers make it very distinctive. Wisteria venusta is very similar, but its most common cultivar is white-flowered and its mature foliage is much darker.

preparation.text: The flowers are eaten cooked: washed thoroughly, then boiled or made into fritters; cured in sugar and mixed with flour into cakes; or marinated in light salt brine as the filling for steamed or baked flower cakes.

recipes.method: Makes 5 litres. Use the flowers only; the rest of the plant is poisonous (see the warnings). The source does not say which wisteria; Chinese wisteria is the one recorded wild in New Zealand. 2–2.5 litres (8–10 cups) wisteria flowers, stripped from the stalks; 750 ml (3 cups) golden sugar; 4 lemons (2 sliced and the juice of the other 2); 5 litres water. Stir the sugar, water and lemon in a large jar until the sugar dissolves, add the flowers and push them under, leaving room in the jar because the mixture rises and falls as it ferments. Cover with muslin held by a rubber band, and date it. Stir hard every day for 3–4 days, until the flowers rise and bubbles appear when you stir. Strain through muslin into flip-top bottles, leave at room temperature for 1–2 days, checking the fizz, then keep it in the fridge and serve cold.

summary.text: Wisteria or Chinese wisteria, a woody deciduous climber of the pea family (Fabaceae) from East Asia, naturalised in New Zealand by 1981, on Great Barrier Island and at scattered places in the Bay of Plenty. Herbarium sheets also record it growing wild in West Auckland bush and in forest gaps and tree groves near Halcombe and Fordell in the Rangitīkei and Whanganui districts. Wisteria is widely cultivated in New Zealand and frequently persists in deserted gardens and at old house sites, but is rarely truly naturalised and seldom sets good seed. Naturalised plants are the result of vegetative spread, by layering and suckering, and it is spread by people dumping garden waste. New Zealand nurseries sell it for pergolas, fences, verandas and arches; it flowers slightly earlier than Japanese wisteria, often on bare wood, and mature vines need sturdy support.

warnings: The pods and seeds are poisonous.

Every part of the plant contains lectin and wisterin; the pods and seeds are the most toxic. Swallowed, they can cause a burning feeling in the mouth, stomach pain, vomiting and diarrhoea, lasting up to 2 days.
Two 13-year-olds who ate wisteria pods, flowers and seeds were vomiting and sweating heavily within 30 minutes and were admitted to hospital.

identification.text:
A stocky, fleshy mushroom with a bald cap, crowded gills and a short, thick stem with no ring or veil. Young ones are lilac to violet all over. The cap soon fades to tan or brown from the centre, while the gills and stem usually keep some violet; old ones can be buff all over, so colour alone is not a safe guide.
The cap is 3–15 cm across, convex with an inrolled edge when young, then flat and often wavy. It is smooth, almost suede-like, and slightly tacky when wet but never slimy. The gills are crowded, lilac fading to buff or pinkish-buff, and often notched where they meet the stem. The stem is 2–10 cm long and 1–2.5 cm thick, often swollen at the base, finely fibrous and pale violet; it usually comes up with a clump of leaf litter attached. The flesh is thick, soft and lilac to whitish.
The smell is fragrant and sweet, likened to frozen orange juice, perfume or lilac, or faintly of aniseed, though not every specimen has it. The spore print is white to pale pink, never rusty brown.
Two related species grow in New Zealand: Lepista luscina has grey or pale pinkish gills, a grey to pinkish cap often with darker spots, and lacks the earthy, fragrant smell; Lepista fibrosissima has violet gills but a dark brown, shaggy cap.

preparation.text: Cook blewits thoroughly, for at least 10 minutes. Brush or wipe them clean. They hold a lot of water, especially after rain, so dry-sauté them: put them in a pan with no fat over medium-low heat until they have given up their water and the pan looks dry, then add butter or oil, salt and chopped shallot. Keep small ones whole and cut big ones into large pieces to keep their firm, chewy texture. They suit butter, cream, shallots, leeks or onions, thyme and tarragon, and go well in omelettes, stews, soups and cream sauces, and with chicken, pork, cheese, rice or pasta. The violet colour fades after a day or two in the fridge, and in cooking. Blewits dry well for soups, stews and sauces, and young buttons make good pickles.

recipes.method: Written for blewits (pied bleu), wild or shop-bought. Serves 2. 100 g blewits; 2 eggs; 1 spring onion; 1 garlic clove; butter; olive oil; Parmesan; black pepper. Cut the caps into quarters, or eighths if large, and the stems into pieces of the same size. Slice the spring onion into thin rings, keeping the white and green apart. Fry the blewits in olive oil and butter for 5 minutes until well cooked, over moderate heat: too hot and they turn bitter. Add the white of the spring onion and the sliced or crushed garlic and fry a little longer, with more butter if needed. Turn the heat up, whisk the eggs well with the green of the spring onion and pour them into the pan. After a few seconds turn the heat right down and leave about 10 minutes, watching, until the egg is nearly set but still soft and runny on top. Serve on warm plates with grated Parmesan and black pepper.
recipes.title: Blewit omelette

recipes.method: Written for blewits. Serves 2. 115 g blewits; 15 ml (1 tbsp) finely diced shallot; a pinch of chopped fresh tarragon; salt; 15 ml (1 tbsp) neutral oil, or unsalted butter. Brush the blewits clean, or swish them in water and dry them on paper towels. Quarter large ones and halve or leave small ones whole. Heat a cast-iron pan until hot, add the blewits, season with salt and cook until they have wilted, browned lightly and given up their water. Add the oil, and a little more if the pan gets dry. Add the shallot, then the tarragon, and cook a minute or two; check the salt. Cook the blewits for at least 10 minutes in all. You can also toss the mushrooms with a small knob of unsalted butter.
recipes.title: Dry-sautéed blewits with shallot and tarragon

recipes.method: Written for any wild or shop mushrooms; the author made it with blewits. Chicken or other poultry can replace the pheasant. 250 ml (1 cup) pheasant, chicken or beef stock; 450 g fresh blewits; 45 g (3 tbsp) butter; 125 ml (½ cup) minced shallot; salt; 5 ml (1 tsp) dried thyme; 60 ml (¼ cup) brandy; 125 ml (½ cup) cream; 450 g pheasant breasts; 250 ml (1 cup) chopped spinach or other greens. Boil the stock down to about 60 ml and set it aside. Cut the pheasant into strips or chunks and salt it well. Cut the blewits into large pieces. Heat a large frying pan over high heat for 2 minutes, add the blewits and dry-sauté them, shaking the pan often, until they give up their water and it has almost gone. Add the butter and shallot and cook, stirring, until the shallot is translucent and the blewits start to brown. Sprinkle over the thyme and a little salt, pour in the brandy and scrape up the browned bits; cook on medium-high until the brandy has almost gone. Add the reduced stock, the cream and the pheasant, bring to a gentle simmer, then cover and cook on low for about 5 minutes, until the pheasant is just cooked through. Stir in the greens and serve with crusty bread, egg noodles or mashed potato.
recipes.title: Pheasant with blewits and cream

summary.text:
Collybia nuda, commonly known as the blewit, wood blewit or blue foot and previously described as Lepista nuda and Clitocybe nuda, is a species of fungi.
Biota of New Zealand still files it as Clitocybe nuda: since 2023 some mycologists put it in Collybia and others keep it in Clitocybe or Lepista. The name nuda, 'naked', refers to the stem, which never carries the cobweb-like veil of the webcaps.
It is native to Europe and North America and is grown commercially in Britain, the Netherlands and France; cultivated blewits are said to taste less good than wild ones. It is introduced in New Zealand, and several Clitocybe and Lepista species found here look like recent arrivals that have spread fast. Most of its 338 research-grade New Zealand iNaturalist records are from Christchurch and Wellington. In Australia it has formed a relationship with some eucalypts and gorse, and grows and looks slightly differently from European blewits; a young satin bowerbird there was seen collecting blewits to decorate its bower.
Soil under a blewit fairy ring in Swedish conifer forest held fourteen chlorinated and brominated organic compounds; it is unclear whether the fungus made them. A very pale form, glaucocana, grows in mountains in North America.

warnings: Never eat blewits raw: raw ones cause stomach upsets and vomiting. Even thoroughly cooked blewits disagree with some people, so eat only a small portion the first time.

Violet webcaps (Cortinarius), many of them poisonous, can look very like a blewit. New Zealand has violet ones such as the elegant blue webcap (Cortinarius rotundisporus), steely blue with a yellowish centre and lilac-tinged gills when young. Make a spore print every time: webcaps print rusty brown, blewits white to pale pink. Young webcaps have a cobweb-like veil over the gills that leaves threads or a rusty-brown band on the stem, and they often smell unpleasant; a blewit's stem is always bare.

edibleParts.text: The whole fruiting body.

habitat.text: Dead and dying wood in damp native bush, especially māhoe and other soft-wooded trees.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

identification.text: Ear-shaped rubbery brackets, brown to purplish, velvety on the outer surface and smooth within. Gelatinous and springy when fresh, shrinking to a hard flake when dry and rehydrating readily.

preparation.text: Rinse, slice and add to soups and stir-fries. Prized for texture rather than flavour. Dries and rehydrates well.

recipes.method: Written for dried black fungus (wood ear); the page does not name the species. Serves 2–4. 60 ml (¼ cup) dried wood ear; 1 tsp potato starch whisked smooth with 60 ml (¼ cup) cold water; 5 eggs; 1 tsp sesame oil; ½ tsp chicken stock powder or MSG; ½ tsp rice wine vinegar; 4 tbsp vegetable oil; 1 small green capsicum, cut in 3 cm pieces; 2 garlic cloves, thinly sliced; 3 thin slices ginger; 1 tbsp oyster sauce; 1 tsp Shaoxing wine; 1 tsp soy sauce; a good pinch of sugar. Soak the wood ear in hot water for 20 minutes, then drain, squeeze out the excess water, trim off the hard base and tear any large pieces smaller. Beat the eggs with the sesame oil, stock powder, vinegar and a generous drizzle of the starch slurry. Heat a wok over medium-high heat with 1 tbsp of the oil and stir-fry the capsicum, wood ear, garlic and ginger until the capsicum softens, then tip onto a plate. Add the rest of the oil and cook the eggs until barely set. Return the vegetables with the oyster sauce, Shaoxing wine, soy sauce and sugar, thicken with the remaining slurry, toss and serve straight away.
recipes.title: Stir-fried wood ear

recipes.method: Written for wood ear; the recipe does not name the species. Serves 4. For the soup: about 950 ml (4 cups) light chicken stock; ½ tsp grated ginger; a 6 mm slice of galangal (optional); 2 tbsp rice wine vinegar; 2 tsp red hot sauce such as sambal or chilli-garlic sauce, or to taste; 2 tbsp light-coloured mushroom ketchup, or soy or fish sauce; about 55 g small fresh yellowfoot chanterelles, or another fresh mushroom such as buna-shimeji or shiitake; 5 g dried wood ear or 125 ml (½ cup) fresh; a few drops of toasted sesame oil. For finishing: about 140 g firm tofu, diced 1 cm (optional); 2 tbsp cornflour mixed to a slurry with a splash of water; 1 large egg, beaten; a small handful of sliced spring onions; red chilli oil (optional); sliced culantro or coriander (optional). If using galangal, bruise it with the back of a knife. Cover dried wood ear with hot water for 15 minutes, then lift it out, discard the soaking water and cut it into 6 mm strips. Bring all the soup ingredients, mushrooms included, to a simmer and let it bubble gently for 10 minutes. Stir in the cornflour slurry and the tofu and let it thicken for a minute or two. Stir the soup briskly clockwise a few times, then drizzle in the egg slowly in the same direction while it is still swirling. When the egg has set in ribbons, add the spring onions and coriander, divide among four cups and drizzle with chilli oil if you like.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auricularia_cornea Corroborates the export story and adds the te reo name and the traditional preparation. In New Zealand it is known as hakeke; Māori traditionally cooked it by steaming in an earth oven and eating it with sow thistle — pūhā, which has its own entry here — and potatoes. It was collected and exported from New Zealand to China from the 1870s to the 1950s, which is the trade this entry's summary refers to. Commercially cultivated in China today, including a white unpigmented form, and used in Cantonese desserts and stir fries. Also called pepeiao ('ear') in Hawaii and taingang daga ('rat's ears') in the Philippines. A naming caution for anyone cross-checking: American authors have widely treated this species as a synonym of A. nigricans, and the misidentification persists.

habitat.text:
It grows on rotting wood.
In New Zealand: on rotting wood — trunks, branches and heaps of leaves, mainly of mountain beech — and on the ground.

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to pick this mushroom. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.

sources: Massee 1899, via Manaaki Whenua Virtual Mycota (public domain)
identification.text: Pileus thin, globose, then hemispherical, with a prominent elongated umbo, coarsely striate at the margin, remainder even, glabrous, 1-1.5 cm. high and broad, ochraceous-yellow ; gills emarginate, with a decurrent tooth, rather crowded, broad, ventricose, rusty-orange ; spores elliptical, 13-14 x 7-8 µ; stem about 5 cm. long and 2 mm. thick, equal, twisted, fibrillose, rusty-orange, fistulose. Distinguished by the prominent umbo.

lookalikes.howToTell: Never separate these on one character. The Galerina is deadly-suspect and both grow on rotting wood. Look for a ring. The common NZ Galerina has a well-developed ring on the stem, though in the related Galerina marginata the ring may disappear. P. subaeruginosa has only a short-lived cobweb-like veil that leaves at most a raised zone on the upper stem. Check the gills: cinnamon to rusty brown in the Galerina, pale smoky brown ageing to violet-brown in P. subaeruginosa. P. subaeruginosa's cap and stem stain greenish blue with age or handling. The gills of the related Galerina marginata do not bruise, and its flesh is unchanging when sliced. Cap shape and colour do not separate them. Both have yellowish to orange-brown caps, and P. subaeruginosa can also have a small pointed centre. A spore print confirms it: P. subaeruginosa purple-brown, Galerina cinnamon-brown. The Galerina's toxicity is unknown, but it sits in the group containing the deadly Galerina marginata and is thought likely to contain amatoxins.
lookalikes.name: Psilocybe subaeruginosa

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small brown mushrooms with a bump in the centre of the cap, often more or less pointed, and both grow on fallen, rotting wood - P. makarorae on southern beech, and wood nipple fungus mainly on beech wood too - so shape and habitat do not separate them. Cap colour overlaps too: P. makarorae is yellow-brown to orange-brown, and wood nipple fungus ochre-yellow to bay or honey-coloured. Damage the cap or stem: P. makarorae stains greenish-blue, and no blue staining is recorded for wood nipple fungus. Look at the stem: wood nipple fungus has a well-developed ring, though in its close relative the ring often disappears with age. P. makarorae has only cobwebby veil remnants and never a complete ring. A spore print may help: wood nipple fungus drops cinnamon-brown, and Psilocybe prints generally run lilac-brown to dark purple-brown, though rusty-brown prints are known in at least one species. Wood nipple fungus has not been tested for toxins, but it sits in the group that includes the deadly Galerina marginata and probably carries the same amatoxins.
lookalikes.name: Psilocybe makarorae

lookalikes.howToTell: Both grow on rotting wood, including southern beech, and both can have a ring on the stem, so place and ring do not separate them. The honey mushroom is much larger and stouter: its cap is 3–8 cm across, olive-buff to olive-brown, on a tough stem 4–8 mm thick, and it grows in dense clusters with the stem bases joined together. Wood nipple fungus has a cap 1–2.5 cm across, often with a prominent pointed bump in the centre, on a stem 2–4 mm thick, and grows singly or in loose groups, rarely in tight clumps. Look at the gills: creamy white to dull fawn in the honey mushroom, rusty orange to cinnamon in wood nipple fungus. A spore print settles it: white for the honey mushroom, cinnamon-brown for Galerina.
lookalikes.name: Honey mushroom

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small orange-brown mushrooms on rotting wood, so place and cap colour do not separate them. Velvet shank is edible cooked; wood nipple fungus belongs to the group of the deadly Galerina marginata. Velvet shank's stem is velvety and dark brown towards the base, with no ring; the Galerina's is slender, 2–4 mm thick, pale tan to rusty orange, with a thin ring high up that can soon fall away. Velvet shank's gills are white to pale yellow, the Galerina's rusty orange to cinnamon. Velvet shank has a sticky cap 1–8 cm across and grows in dense tufts from one base; the Galerina's cap is 1–2.5 cm across, often with a pointed bump, singly or in loose groups. A spore print settles it: white for velvet shank, cinnamon-brown for the Galerina.

summary.text:
Galerina patagonica is a species of agaric fungus in the family Hymenogastraceae. The toxicity of Galerina patagonica is unknown. However, it is phylogenetically nested within the Galerina marginata species complex, and thus likely contains deadly amatoxins.

It has a Gondwanan distribution, and is found in Australia, New Zealand, and Patagonia (South America).

warnings: This mushroom may contain toxins so do not consume.

Garden-grown alpine strawberries are smaller and less sweet than garden strawberries, with a tart edge. The fruit is also steeped in vinegar or spirits, macerated with sugar and balsamic vinegar, and used in baking. Young leaves, raw or cooked, and the fresh or dried leaves as a tea.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Roadsides, wasteland, forest clearings and damp banks up to about 1000 m. It is hardy to cold and wet but dislikes long dry spells, and spreads readily where there is enough moisture; it does best in well-drained, rich, loamy soil.
Typical habitat is along trails and roadsides, embankments, hillsides, stone- and gravel-laid paths and roads, meadows, young woodlands, sparse forest, woodland edges, and clearings. Often plants can be found where they do not get sufficient light to form fruit. It is tolerant of a variety of moisture levels (except very wet or dry conditions). It can survive mild fires and/or establish itself after fires.

identification.text:
Low-growing herb with short woody stock, up to about 15–(25) cm high; runners greenish, pilose, bracteate, up to about 80 cm long and rooting at nodes and tips to form new rosettes. Basal leaves several in rosette; petiole up to 15–(18) cm long, densely pilose; leaflets ovate to rhombic or elliptic, obtuse to subacute, cuneate at base, more or less thin, bright green above and usually sparsely to moderately silky pilose, rarely almost glabrous, paler below and usually silky pilose at least on veins, with margins coarsely serrate in upper 1/2-⅔ and pilose; terminal leaflets (15)–30–60–(90) × (10)–18–40–(50) mm; lateral leaflets slightly smaller; petiolules very short or 0, silky pilose; stipules triangular, 12–20 mm long, reddish brown, more or less pilose especially along axis. Scape (30)–60–180–(300) mm tall, more or less erect and often arching in upper part, finely pilose; inflorescence of 1-several flowers; pedicels 7–40 mm long; flowers 10–18 mm diameter. Epicalyx segments narrow, more or less entire. Sepals triangular, 4–6–(9) mm long, pilose, more or less acuminate, connate at base, deflexed at fruiting. Petals obovate, up to 8 mm long, sometimes only slightly longer than sepals, rounded, sometimes undulate, spreading, white. Achenes uniformly scattered over and projecting from the receptacle; receptacle usually red, occasionally white, swollen and juicy, sweet, fragrant, obconic, up to 15 × 12 mm. 
[From: Webb et al. (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Fragaria vesca L.]
Indian strawberry (Flora of New Zealand): Duchesnea closely resembles Fragaria but differs most obviously in having yellow rather than white petals, epicalyx segments wider and more coarsely toothed and in the drier, almost inedible fruits.

lookalikes.howToTell: Indian strawberry has bright yellow petals, where woodland strawberry's are white. Its epicalyx segments (the leafy bracts just beneath the sepals) are broadly obovate with 3–5 purple-tipped teeth, about as long as the petals and sepals, and bent back under the fruit; in woodland strawberry they are narrow and more or less entire. Indian strawberry leaflets are crenate to obscurely lobed; woodland strawberry leaflets are coarsely serrate in the upper half to two-thirds. Indian strawberry fruit is red, dryish and semi-fleshy, with very little flavour; woodland strawberry fruit is usually red, occasionally white, juicy, sweet and fragrant. Indian strawberry flowers are solitary; woodland strawberry can carry 1 to several flowers on a stalk, so a single flower does not separate them. What does not separate them: both form rosettes with runners rooting at the nodes and tips, both have three-part leaves of overlapping size, petals up to 8 mm long and sepals of overlapping length, both have achenes scattered over and projecting from a swollen red receptacle of similar size, both grow on roadsides, wasteland and forest margins or clearings, both are recorded from Nelson, Canterbury and Dunedin, and both fruit from November to April. Indian strawberry fruit is edible raw but dry and almost tasteless, and its leaves are eaten cooked.

preparation.text: Pick the fruit when ripe, before the birds get it; ripe berries often hide beneath the leaves and come away easily from the stem. They bruise and squash easily, so pinch or cut the stalk just above the berry and carry them in a container with breathable sides, or thread them onto a grass stem or straw as Scandinavian foragers do. Eat the fruit raw, cook it, or make it into jam or other preserves; the fruits are usually very small and fiddly to gather. Berries can be frozen in ice cubes for drinks. Add young leaves to salads or cook them as a potherb. Use fresh or fully dried leaves for tea; leaves for drying are picked in summer.

recipes.method: The author's greens were the leaves of Indian, alpine (woodland) and garden strawberries, red deadnettle, wall lettuce, herb Robert and nasturtium. A handful of mixed strawberry leaves, stems removed (they are tough); a handful of beetroot leaves and stems; several stems of red deadnettle with their flowers; 5 wall lettuce leaves; 5 herb Robert leaves; red nasturtium flowers and several leaves; a few celery and small kale leaves, optional. Blend the leaves and flowers with 500–750 ml (2–3 cups) water, then add 1 punnet of strawberries, 1 red apple, 2 kiwifruit and 2 bananas and blend again.
recipes.title: Wild and tame strawberry smoothie

recipes.method: Ingredients: 500 g wild strawberries, 500 g jam (gelling) sugar, 250 ml fresh redcurrant juice (made by cooking about 500 g redcurrants with just enough water to stop them catching for one or two minutes, then sieving). If possible do not wash the strawberries. Mix them with half the sugar and leave covered in the fridge overnight. Heat the rest of the sugar with the redcurrant juice until the sugar dissolves, add the strawberry mixture and cook for about 15 minutes. Pour straight into sterilised jars and close them tightly. The source suggests bulking out with homegrown strawberries if you cannot gather 500 g of wild ones.
recipes.title: Wild strawberry and redcurrant jam

recipes.method: Written for alpine strawberries, the cultivated form of this species. Ingredients: about 360 g alpine strawberries, 400 g sugar, 30 ml lemon juice; no added pectin. Put everything in a deep saucepan or jam pot and mash with the back of a spoon so some berries break up and release their juice. Bring to the boil over medium-high heat and boil hard, stirring often, for about 8 to 10 minutes until the jam reaches gel stage. Ladle into prepared jars leaving about 6 mm (1/4 inch) headspace. To keep on the shelf, process in a water-bath canner for 10 minutes; otherwise refrigerate and use within a few weeks. Makes about 500 ml (2 cups).
recipes.title: Alpine strawberry jam

recipes.method: From the Herb Federation of New Zealand's wild strawberry sheet. Ingredients: 500 g berries, 750 ml (3 cups) sugar, about 940 ml (3¾ cups) wine or cider vinegar. Put the berries in a saucepan, just cover with water and simmer, partly covered, for 30 minutes. Strain off the juice, ideally overnight, without squeezing the fruit or the vinegar will be cloudy. Add the vinegar and sugar to the juice and stir over the heat until the sugar dissolves, then bring to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes. Pour into sterilised bottles. Use it like a balsamic, for example in dressings.
recipes.title: Strawberry vinegar

recipes.method: The Italian fragoline di bosco al balsamico. Ingredients: about 250 g wild strawberries, 50–75 g caster sugar, 2–4 tablespoons good balsamic vinegar, a few sprigs of fresh mint. Coat the strawberries in the sugar and leave for up to an hour, then mix in the balsamic vinegar and the mint.
recipes.title: Wild strawberries with balsamic vinegar

recipes.method: Ingredients for 2 large bowls or 4 small glasses: 240 g (1 cup) Greek or thick yoghurt or whipped cream, 200 g (1 cup) wild strawberries, 100 g oats, a generous knob of butter, 2 tablespoons whisky or rum (leave it out for children), 2 tablespoons brown sugar or honey. Melt the butter in a large frying pan and toast the oats until they have soaked up the fat and turned golden brown; let them cool a little. Fold the sugar or honey and the whisky into the yoghurt or cream. Spread a layer of oats in the bowls or glasses, cover with the cream mixture, then a generous layer of strawberries, and repeat the layers until full. Finish with a few strawberries and a sprig of fresh mint.
recipes.title: Wild strawberry cranachan

recipes.method: Written for wild strawberries or garden strawberries. Ingredients: 400 g wild strawberries, 2–3 tablespoons honey, 2 tablespoons balsamic vinegar, 2 teaspoons freshly cracked black pepper; no pectin. Wash the strawberries (garden strawberries are hulled and quartered), mix everything in a shallow baking dish and leave while the oven heats to 120 °C. Roast for 2–3 hours, stirring a few times, until the berries have shrivelled and reduced to a syrup. Cool to room temperature, purée if you like it smooth, and keep in an airtight jar in the fridge for up to a few weeks.
recipes.title: Roasted wild strawberry jam with balsamic and pepper

recipes.method: Makes 12. Cupcakes: 115 g softened butter, 115 g golden caster sugar, 2 large eggs, ½ teaspoon vanilla extract, 115 g self-raising flour with a pinch of salt. Buttercream: 150 g softened butter, 300 g icing sugar, 1 teaspoon vanilla extract, 3 tablespoons milk. A handful of freshly picked wild strawberries. Heat the oven to 180 °C (160 °C fan) and line a 12-hole muffin tin. Beat the butter and sugar until pale, add the eggs gradually with the vanilla, then fold in the flour and salt. Divide between the cases and bake for about 15 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean. Beat the buttercream ingredients until smooth and spread on the cooled cupcakes. Top with sliced wild strawberries, and a single strawberry leaf pressed into the buttercream if you like.
recipes.title: Wild strawberry cupcakes

summary.text:
Fragaria vesca, commonly called the woodland strawberry, Alpine strawberry, wild strawberry, Carpathian strawberry or European strawberry, is a perennial herbaceous plant in the rose family that grows naturally throughout much of the Northern Hemisphere, and that produces edible fruits.
Woodland strawberry fruit is strongly flavored, and is still collected and grown for domestic use and on a small scale commercially for the use of gourmets and as an ingredient for commercial jam, sauces, liqueurs, cosmetics and alternative medicine.
In the southern part of its range, it can grow only in shady areas; further north it tolerates more sun.
Although F. vesca primarily propagates via runners, viable seeds are also found in soil seed banks and seem to germinate when the soil is disturbed (away from existing populations of F. vesca).
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): North Island: South Auckland (Thames), Opotiki, Volcanic Plateau; South Island: lowland and foothills in Nelson, Marlborough and Canterbury, Otago (Dunedin), Southland (Deep Cove)
It was brought to New Zealand as a garden plant and was first recorded growing wild in 1870. Herbarium specimens come from the South Auckland, Gisborne, Wellington, Nelson, Canterbury, Otago and Southland land districts. The name Fragaria comes from the Latin for strawberry, from fragrans, "fragrant", after the fruit.
Alpine strawberries, the cultivated form, are sold and grown in New Zealand gardens, including white-fruited forms that birds tend to leave alone. The large garden strawberry is a different plant, Fragaria × ananassa.

warnings: Woodland strawberry fruit carries the strawberry allergen Fra a 1 at levels similar to garden strawberries. People who react to strawberries should not eat it; about 30% of people sensitised to birch pollen (Bet v 1) report reactions after eating strawberries, mostly in the mouth. Reactions can include itching or a rash around the mouth, dermatitis, hives or hay-fever-like symptoms; birch-pollen-related food allergy can also cause more general reactions such as asthma or anaphylactic shock.
Strawberry leaf tea is laxative.
Use strawberry leaves fresh or totally dry, not wilted. This caution rests on a single foraging source written for strawberry leaf tea generally, which names no compound or case of harm.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): Mostly roadsides and waste places, also palustral and coastal sites, pasture, cultivated land, and lawns.
The plant grows from sea level to 3,500 m in elevation. Common yarrow is frequently found in the mildly disturbed soil of grasslands and open forests.
In New Zealand it is common in pastures and turf, and in waste areas and on roadsides, where it is better able to flower (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated).
Also on railways, industrial sites, arable land and marshy places (Common Weeds of New Zealand, restated).

identification.text:
Strongly scented, rhizomatous herb, with short non-flowering rosettes often forming dense mats. Stems usually erect, sometimes ascending, up to about 80 cm tall, ribbed and striate, hairy especially above, usually not branched except above to form inflorescence. Basal leaves petiolate, lanceolate, moderately hairy, 2-pinnate with segments again 1–2-pinnatisect, 6–15–(44) × 1–2–(4) cm; primary leaflets in 18–30–(37) pairs; ultimate segments subulate, not all in one plane giving a feathery appearance to leaf; rachis about 1–2 mm diameter, flattened, sometimes slightly winged, not toothed. Cauline leaves similar to basal, but above becoming apetiolate, less divided, smaller, and with fewer leaflet pairs. Corymbs usually more or less flat-topped or slightly convex, to about 15 cm across, with numerous, closely packed capitula. Involucral bracts glabrous to sparsely hairy, 1.5–4–(5) mm long; margin brown, hairy. Capitula (3.5)–5–10 mm diameter; ray florets 4–7; ligule and disc florets usually white, sometimes pink to deep red or purple. Achenes grey-brown, about 2 mm long; wings narrow, pale brown. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The flowers are usually white, but pale to deep pink forms occur forming small clonal patches within otherwise white-flowered populations. Some small populations may entirely comprise pink-flowered plants.
In turf it can be confused with Onehunga weed, but yarrow has about 15–20 leaflets down each side of a leaf against about 5–8 in Onehunga weed, and neither Onehunga weed nor stinking mayweed has yarrow's underground rhizomes (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated).
The plant smells pleasant when crushed. Each small head has 4–7 white, pink or red rays around 10–12 creamy disc florets, and the flat seeds have narrow wings and no pappus hairs (Common Weeds of New Zealand, restated).
Garden cultivars in other colours are sold in New Zealand, such as 'Butterscotch' with peach-toned flower clusters (The Plant Store); a plant by a garden may not be white or pink.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have finely divided, fern-like leaves and flat-topped heads of small white flowers, both grow in waste places throughout New Zealand, and their flowering seasons overlap, so leaf texture and flower colour alone do not separate them. Yarrow's flowers are tiny daisy heads about 5–10 mm across, each with 4–7 short rays, packed many together into one dense, flat or slightly domed cluster; hemlock's are separate flowers about 2 mm across on the spokes of open umbels (4–16 rays), with several umbels on a much-branched stem. Yarrow's stems are ribbed and hairy, especially above, and up to about 80 cm; hemlock's are hairless, hollow, up to 2–3 m, and usually spotted or blotched with purple — but sometimes only tinged purplish or pink, so a plain stem does not rule hemlock out. Yarrow's leaves are narrow (usually 1–2 cm wide), with many pairs of tiny awl-shaped segments that do not lie in one plane, giving a feathery look; hemlock's leaves are larger, triangular in outline and parsley-like, with broader, ovate to triangular, toothed or cut segments. Crushed, yarrow is strongly aromatic; hemlock has a foetid, musty smell. Hemlock is deadly poisonous in every part.
lookalikes.name: Hemlock

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have finely divided leaves and flat-topped heads of small white, sometimes pinkish flowers, and both grow in waste places, grassland, cultivated land and gardens or lawns, flowering over the same months; hairy stems do not separate them, since both have them, and flower colour does not either, since yarrow also has pink to deep red forms. Wild carrot's flowers sit on the spokes of a true compound umbel 2–12 cm across, with a ruff of forked bracts beneath it and sometimes a few red or purple flowers at the centre, and the umbel usually turns strongly concave, like a bird's nest, as it fruits; yarrow's flowers are tiny daisy heads, each with 4–7 short rays, packed together in a dense cluster. Wild carrot's leaf segments are ovate to linear, about 15–40 mm long; yarrow's are tiny awl-shaped segments not lying in one plane. Crushed, wild carrot smells of carrot. Wild carrot grows from a slender white taproot; yarrow spreads by rhizomes and forms mats. Wild carrot is edible, but it is itself easily confused with deadly hemlock — read its entry before eating it.
lookalikes.name: Wild carrot

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have finely divided leaves whose narrow, awl-shaped to linear segments do not lie in one plane, giving a feathery look, and both grow in waste places, on roadsides, in pasture and in lawns, so plants not in flower are easily confused. Stinking mayweed (stinking mayweed) is an annual with no underground rhizomes, its stems usually much-branched from the base; yarrow spreads by rhizomes and forms mats. Stinking mayweed is strongly foetid when crushed; yarrow's smell is pleasant, not foetid. In flower they differ clearly: stinking mayweed bears single daisy heads about 15–30 mm across, with 8–21 white rays around a yellow centre; yarrow's heads are only about 5–10 mm across, with 4–7 rays, and are usually white (sometimes pink) right across, packed many together in a flat cluster. Stinking mayweed's juice is acrid: touching or eating the plant can cause allergies in some people, and there are some reports of toxicity.
lookalikes.name: Stinking mayweed

lookalikes.howToTell: Roman chamomile carries its flower heads singly, 8–20 mm across (up to 30), with 13–20 white rays around a yellow disc; yarrow carries many small heads, 5–10 mm across (as small as 3.5 mm), packed into a flat-topped or slightly domed cluster, each with only 4–7 rays and usually white central florets too. Roman chamomile's basal leaves are 15–50 mm long; yarrow's are 6–15 cm (up to 44), with 18–30 pairs of primary leaflets. Roman chamomile's stems lie along the ground or rise to about 20 cm; yarrow's flowering stems are usually upright, up to about 80 cm. Both have scales on the receptacle, feathery leaves and a scent, and both grow in lawns, so these do not separate them. Roman chamomile's flowers are used for tea, with care for people allergic to the daisy family.
lookalikes.name: Roman chamomile

lookalikes.howToTell: Twin cress and yarrow can both form low mats of divided leaves in pasture, lawns and waste places. Twin cress is hairless or nearly so, smells foetid rather than aromatic, has lopsided leaflets, stems lying along the ground, tiny white or petal-less flowers and paired pods c. 1.5 mm long. Yarrow is strongly scented and hairy, with feathery, finely divided leaves in 18–30(–37) pairs of leaflets, and erect flowering stems with flat-topped clusters of small daisy-like heads. Twin cress leaves are eaten raw or cooked for their hot, cress-like taste; see its own entry.
lookalikes.name: Twin cress

preparation.text: Pick young leaves; they are slightly less bitter. The long leaves at the base of plants, away from the flowering stems, give the best yield. The bitterness stays whatever you do, so use a leaf or two: chop finely and mix with milder soft herbs such as parsley, chervil or tarragon. High heat destroys the flavour — add it at the end of cooking, off the heat, just to warm through. Simmering whole plants in stock gives a bitter broth. Young leaves are best picked before the plant flowers; pick flowers while it is in bloom, in the morning once the dew has dried. For tea, infuse the flowers and leaves. The flowers, fresh or dried, can be steeped hot or cold to flavour drinks, ice cream and custards such as crème brûlée; dried flowers make it possible out of season.

recipes.method: Serves 4. 8 oz (about 225 g) dried penne; 4 tablespoons finely chopped fresh garlic; kosher salt; 3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil; 3 tablespoons grapeseed or canola oil; 1 teaspoon crushed red pepper flakes, or more to taste; a large handful of yarrow leaves, picked from the stem and chopped to give 2 teaspoons; ¼ cup (about 60 ml) dry white wine; 4 anchovy fillets in oil, rinsed and chopped (optional); Parmesan to serve. Pile the chopped yarrow and the chilli flakes together and mince them finely. Bring a pot of water to the boil, salt it until it tastes like the sea, and cook the penne until al dente. Meanwhile, warm the garlic with both oils and the anchovy in a 10-inch (about 25 cm) sauté pan over low heat until fragrant and lightly browned; do not let the garlic burn. Take the pan off the heat, swirl it for a minute to cool, then add the wine. Drain the pasta, add it to the pan and toss to coat; cook for a minute to drive off the raw wine flavour. Add the yarrow and chilli mixture and toss just to heat through. Divide among 4 bowls, top with Parmesan and a little more olive oil if you like, and serve at once with a big green salad.
recipes.title: Penne aglio olio with yarrow

recipes.method: Makes about 85 g of tea blend. 28 g (1 oz) yarrow flowers; 28 g (1 oz) German chamomile flowers; 28 g (1 oz) peppermint leaves. Blend the herbs together and store them in an airtight container. For each cup (about 240 ml) of tea, use 1 teaspoon of the blend.
recipes.title: Yarrow, chamomile and peppermint tea

summary.text:
Achillea millefolium, commonly known as yarrow or common yarrow, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae.
Yarrow is native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, being found in Europe, Asia, and North America.
In North America, both native and introduced genotypes, and both diploid and polyploid plants are found.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.; S.: throughout, but more common in drier South Id areas; St.: local; K., Ch., A., C. Naturalised from Europe, Caucasia, Iran, Siberia and the Himalaya, first recorded in 1867.
It was once sown in New Zealand pastures for its tolerance of dry summers and its mineral content, and is still sold in pasture mixtures for organic farming; it becomes a problem weed when a paddock is cultivated and cropped, because its rhizomes survive cultivation (Massey University New Zealand Weeds Database, restated).
Other English names recorded in New Zealand include milfoil, nosebleed, sanguinary and thousand seal (Biota of New Zealand); it is also known as woundwort, staunch weed and carpenter's weed (Herbal Academy) — not to be confused with the woundworts (Stachys).
It is common throughout New Zealand and the offshore islands, especially in drier areas, and is readily grazed by stock (Common Weeds of New Zealand, restated).
The genus is named after Achilles, said to have treated his soldiers' wounds with it at Troy; millefolium is Latin for 'thousand-leaved' (NZPCN).

warnings: Do not eat or drink it if you are allergic to plants of the daisy family (Asteraceae), such as chamomile, arnica or marigold.

Skin reactions occur: touching the flowers can, in rare cases, cause an allergic rash with reddening and small blisters, and extended use, as medicine or food, can cause allergic skin rashes or sensitivity to sunlight in some people. (A tested extract of dried leaves and stalks was not phototoxic.)
Not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding: its safety has not been established, and it has a reputation as an abortifacient.

Keep to small, occasional amounts. The essential oil holds a trace of thujone — too little at medicinal doses of the flowers to be judged a risk — but large or frequent doses over a long period may be harmful.
Medicinal use in children under 12 has not been established.
Deadly hemlock is listed as a similar species, and mistaking one for the other can kill. Check the stem and flower heads on every plant — see the lookalike cards.

habitat.text:
Woods, lawns, gardens and hedgerows, most often under hedges and at the edges of parks and gardens, and on other disturbed soil, usually in small groups but sometimes singly. It can come up on the same lawns as field mushrooms.
In Australia it grows in groups in lawns and pastures, sometimes forming large rings.

identification.text: A white Agaricus, the young cap often boxy or flat-topped rather than domed, sometimes greying with age. Gills off-white at first, soon pink, then chocolate-brown. The test: cut or scratch the very base of the stem and watch for a few seconds — it turns bright chrome yellow almost immediately. The smell is phenolic, of ink, phenol or iodine, and gets stronger when cooked. Field mushroom stays white or blushes faintly pink and smells of mushroom.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut through the stem base of every mushroom in the basket. Bright chrome yellow almost at once (most marked in young, fresh mushrooms), with a smell of ink, phenol or iodine, points to yellow stainer or one of its yellow-staining relatives - discard it. Field mushroom does not turn yellow: its cut flesh reddens and it smells pleasant. Its stem narrows towards the base, where yellow stainer's is bulbous. A spore print will not help - both drop dark brown - and the white cap and pink-then-brown gills are shared.
lookalikes.name: Field mushroom

lookalikes.howToTell: Horse mushroom also turns yellow where bruised, so yellowing alone does not tell them apart: watch how fast, and where, and smell it. Scratch the cap edge and cut through the very base of the stem. Yellow stainer turns bright chrome yellow almost at once, most strongly at the stem base, and smells of ink, phenol or iodine, stronger when cooked. Horse mushroom yellows only slowly and faintly, its cut stem base does not flash bright yellow, and it smells of aniseed or almond. Both are large and white with pale gills that turn pink, then brown, a big ring and a dark brown spore print, and both can have a bulbous base.

summary.text: Agaricus xanthodermus, commonly known as the yellow-staining agaricus, yellow-staining mushroom or yellow-stainer, is a species of fungus in the genus Agaricus. It displays a strong yellow colouration at the base of the stem when cut. It has a strong 'sickeningly sweet' phenolic smell. It is poisonous for most people, causing gastric upset, but can be eaten by some without apparent negative effect. In New Zealand: the NZ Organisms Register lists Agaricus xanthodermus as recorded here in error, and iNaturalist has no verifiable New Zealand record. Other yellow-staining Agaricus are recorded here, among them the mildly poisonous mock meadow mushroom (A. californicus), whose yellowing is not always obvious.

warnings: Causes sweating, cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea within hours. Some people tolerate it, most do not — do not use someone else's experience as a test.
It can come up on the same lawns as field mushrooms, so cut the stem base of every mushroom you pick, every time.

identification.text:
Tufted or scrambling, prostrate annual; stem more or less glabrous. Leaves sparsely hairy; tendrils simple or branched; leaflets in (3)–4–7–(8) pairs, sometimes alternate, elliptic-oblong, 3–20 mm long; stipules entire or with 1–3, adaxial, basal lobes. Inflorescence much shorter than leaves, 1–(2)-flowered. Peduncle much shorter than flowers. Pedicel 1–2 mm long. Calyx somewhat gibbous at base; calyx teeth unequal; lower teeth more or less equal to tube; upper teeth much shorter than tube. Corolla pale yellow, sometimes tinged purple, 15–30 mm long; limb of standard more or less equal to claw. Pod moderately hairy, brown to black, 3–6-seeded, 25–40 mm long; seeds light brown with dark brown and black blotches.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Flowers or seeds are needed to identify vetches. Yellow vetch is very similar to common vetch (Vicia sativa) but has a yellow corolla and unequal calyx teeth.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the flowers and pods. Yellow vetch's corolla is pale yellow, sometimes tinged purple, and its calyx teeth are unequal: the lower teeth about as long as the calyx tube, the upper ones much shorter. Common vetch's corolla is usually purple, reddish purple or rose, sometimes white or pink, and its calyx teeth are more or less equal. Yellow vetch's pods are moderately hairy and hold 3–6 seeds; common vetch's are more or less hairless or finely downy and hold 5–12. The leaves do not separate them: both have tendrils and several pairs of leaflets, and leaflet sizes overlap, so flowers or seeds are needed. Both grow on Banks Peninsula, the only place yellow vetch is established. Common vetch is eaten (see its page).

summary.text: Yellow vetch (Vicia lutea) is a tufted or scrambling annual of the pea family, Fabaceae, introduced to New Zealand from southern and western Europe to the Caucasus and North Africa and first recorded here in 1904. In New Zealand it is established at several places on Banks Peninsula only. It is very similar to common vetch, and flowers or seeds are needed to tell them apart. It flowers in November and December. It is not a listed pest plant.

warnings: Its only food records are for the seeds: in Spain the unripe seeds were eaten raw as a snack, and the ripe seeds were milled with wheat flour for bread in times of shortage. No study of the seeds' chemistry was found, and vetch seeds can be toxic, so it is not given as food here.

The vetches grown as fodder are generally toxic to people and other animals with a simple stomach, at least if eaten in quantity. Common vetch and broad bean, and probably other vetches, contain compounds that can cause favism in people with G6PD deficiency.
It is very similar to common vetch, which is eaten. Check the flower colour and the calyx teeth before picking any vetch on Banks Peninsula (see the lookalikes).

identification.text:
Small tree to about 10 m high (larger in cultivation). Bark peeling in thin scaly strips, dark reddish brown. Trunk often short with main branches arising near the ground and tending to form a dense crown. Shoots green, ribbed. Leaves with short yellowish green petiole, radial on erect shoots, more or less 2-ranked on horizontal shoots. Lamina 1.2–2.5 cm × 1.5–2 mm, sometimes smaller in first leaves of season, dark green, more or less shining above, with 2 broad pale green stomatal bands beneath, revolute; midrib raised on both sides; apex acute or mucronate. Fruit (with aril) 10–15 × 8–11 mm, oblong, crimson; flesh viscid. Seed 5.5–7 mm long, ovoid-ellipsoid, angled, greenish brown.
The seed cones are modified, each cone containing a single seed, which is 4–7 mm long and almost surrounded by a fleshy scale which develops into a soft, bright red berry-like aril. The aril is 8–15 mm long and wide and open at the end. The arils mature 6 to 9 months after pollination.
The aril is gelatinous and very sweet tasting. The male cones are globose, 3–6 mm in diameter, and shed their pollen in early spring. Yews are mostly dioecious with male and female cones on separate trees, but occasional individuals can be variably monoecious, or change sex with time.

lookalikes.howToTell: Crush a few needles: yew's have no real scent; Douglas fir's smell of oranges. Turn a shoot over: yew's needles have two broad pale green bands beneath, never silver; Douglas fir's have two whitish, silvery bands. Yew's shoots are green and ribbed; Douglas fir's are light to dark brown with short hairs and end in long, narrow, sharply pointed, shining purplish-brown buds up to 1 cm long. Female yews carry soft crimson berry-like arils 10–15 mm long around a single seed, and yew has no woody cones; Douglas fir carries woody cones 4–10 cm long that hang down, with three-pointed bracts sticking out between the scales. Most yews are male or female trees, so a tree without red arils can still be yew. Needle size and arrangement do not separate them: yew's are 1.2–2.5 cm long and Douglas fir's 1.5–3.8 cm, and both can lie in two flat rows. Douglas fir's needles are used for tea and flavouring (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Douglas fir

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at how the seed sits. On tōtara, the seed (one, sometimes two) sits on top of the swollen, usually red receptacle, which is made of 2–4 scales, acute and free at the tips. On yew, the single seed sits inside a red, fleshy cup (the aril) that almost surrounds it and is open at the end. Look at where each leaf joins the shoot: tōtara's leaves are stalkless, joined by a narrow base; yew's leaves have a short yellowish-green stalk, and its shoots are green and ribbed. Adult tōtara leaves are 3–4 mm wide and yew's 1.5–2 mm, but tōtara's juvenile leaves are only 1–2 mm wide, so width separates only adult foliage. Mature tōtara has thick, stringy, furrowed bark; yew's bark is thin and peels in scaly, dark reddish-brown strips. Both have red, fleshy 'berries' and needle-like leaves of similar length (yew 1.2–2.5 cm, adult tōtara 1.5–3 cm), so colour and leaf length do not separate them. Tōtara's red receptacle is eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Tōtara

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at how the seed sits. On snow tōtara, the seed (one, sometimes two, green when fresh) sits on a receptacle of two acute, red, swollen bracts. On yew, the single seed sits inside a red, fleshy cup (the aril) that almost surrounds it and is open at the end. Look at where each leaf joins the shoot: snow tōtara's leaves are close-set and spirally arranged, rigid, with distinctly thickened margins; yew's leaves have a short yellowish-green stalk, lie more or less in two rows on horizontal shoots, and have two broad pale green bands beneath. Snow tōtara's leaves are 0.5–1.5 cm long and yew's 1.2–2.5 cm, so short leaves point to snow tōtara, but the ranges overlap. Snow tōtara is a prostrate or spreading shrub, sometimes suberect to 3 m, whose branches root where they touch the ground; yew is a small tree to about 10 m, but a young yew can be small. Snow tōtara grows mostly in subalpine scrub, tussock grassland and rock, and yew in modified lowland sites, but snow tōtara also grows in lowland forest in Westland, so where it grows does not prove it. Snow tōtara's receptacle is eaten, on thin evidence (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Snow tōtara

lookalikes.howToTell: Young miro and young yew look alike. Look at where each leaf joins the shoot: miro's leaves are stalkless or nearly so, each leaf blade running straight into the stem; yew's leaves have a short yellowish-green stalk. Miro's shoots are yellow; yew's are green and ribbed. Look at the fruit: miro's is a plum-like drupe up to 20 mm long, red to pink-red or purplish with a waxy bloom, with a single large stone 11–17 mm long enclosed in the flesh; yew's is a red, fleshy cup 10–15 mm long that almost surrounds the seed and is open at the end. Leaf size does not separate them: miro's adult leaves are 1.5–2.5 cm long and 2–3 mm wide, yew's 1.2–2.5 cm long and 1.5–2 mm wide. Miro's fruit flesh is eaten (see its page).
lookalikes.name: Miro

preparation.text: Eat raw, or cook into jam, jelly or fruit leather. Pull the flesh off each seed by hand, or with the blunt side of a fork, and throw the seed away before the flesh goes near your mouth or the pot. Do not put a whole fruit in your mouth to spit the seed out. Never crush, blend, juice or boil whole fruit to separate the seeds; take every seed out first.

recipes.method: Written for yew. 400 g yew aril flesh, seeds taken out; 1 sweet-sour apple; 1 vanilla pod; 200 g 2:1 jam-setting sugar. Rinse the fruit and pull the flesh off every seed by hand before anything is cooked. Peel, core and chop the apple. Cook the aril flesh with the apple and the vanilla pod for about 20 minutes. Take out the vanilla pod and purée. Stir in the jam-setting sugar, bring to the boil and boil hard for about 4 minutes, then pour hot into sterilised jars.
recipes.title: Yew aril and apple jam

recipes.method: Written for yew. Separate every aril from its seed by hand, using the blunt side of a fork; do not try to boil the seeds out. Put the seeded flesh in a pan with just enough water to cover, bring to the boil and simmer until it reaches a jam-like consistency, which comes quickly because the flesh is very gloopy. Mashed crab apple can be added to help it set, though it dulls the pink colour. If it is too sweet, add lemon juice to taste and simmer again to jam consistency. Spoon into a sterilised jar, lay a circle of greaseproof paper on top and screw on the lid. Eat on sourdough with something sour such as goat’s cheese, or freeze in ice cubes for drinks.
recipes.title: Yew aril jam

recipes.method: Written for wild fruit, yew included. Take the seed out of every yew aril before cooking. Cook the seeded flesh, alone or with other fruit such as chopped crab apples, in a large pan on low heat with just enough water to stop it sticking, until it is thoroughly mushy. Pass it through a fine sieve and add sugar or honey to taste. Spread the purée no more than 3 mm thick on lined baking trays and dry it overnight in a very low oven, no hotter than 50 °C, with the fan on or the door slightly open. Roll the leathers in cling film or cut them up into a sealed tub; they keep a month or two in the fridge.
recipes.title: Yew aril fruit leather

recipes.method: Written for yew. Makes two 10 cm tarts. Before you start: arum (Arum maculatum) is poisonous raw and edible only as flour from well-roasted root; cherry plum kernels contain cyanogenic glycosides (see cherry plum's page); the author himself calls yew berries and cherry plum kernels toxicologically ambiguous foods and the tart 'somewhat extreme and absurd'. Pastry: 150 g arum flour; 50 g sweet chestnut flour; 50 g wild oat flour; 50 g mixed wild grass seed flour; 100 g walnut oil or animal fat, or a mix; 15 ml (1 tbsp) yew aril juice concentrated three times, made from seeded flesh; 15 ml (1 tbsp) verjuice or staghorn sumac extract; a little cold water if needed. Sift the flours into a bowl, rub in the fat or oil with your fingertips until it looks like crumbs, make a well, pour in the verjuice or sumac and the yew syrup, and mix to a smooth dough without overworking it, adding a little cold water if needed. Wrap and chill for a couple of hours. Crème pâtissière: 570 ml cherry plum kernel milk; 1.8 litres water; a large handful of dried, sun-bleached carrageen seaweed; 100 g wild pear juice concentrated five times; 60 g arum flour. Boil the seaweed in the water for 30 minutes, cool slightly, strain through muslin, and simmer the liquid gently until about 280 ml is left; set aside to cool. For the kernel milk, grind two large handfuls of washed, dried cherry plum stones, stir into about 1.1 litres of hot water for a minute, leave 15 minutes, strain, boil the liquid down by half, mix in the pear concentrate and cool. Whisk the cooled kernel milk into the seaweed extract and chill. Topping: 300 g fully ripe yew arils; 5 sweet wild apples; 250 ml (1 cup) wild apple juice; 1 heaped teaspoon of jam and 15 ml (1 tablespoon) water for the glaze. To finish: roll each half of the pastry about 2 mm thick on a work surface dusted with arum flour and line two greased 10 cm loose-bottomed flan tins about 2.5 cm deep, leaving a 0.5 cm overlap that you crimp between finger and thumb. Rest the cases an hour in the fridge or freezer, prick the bases with a fork and bake 15 minutes at 180 °C until barely coloured. Juice three apples; peel, core and thinly slice the other two and stew the slices in the juice for a couple of minutes, then cool. Re-whisk the chilled crème and spread it in the cases, leaving room for the fruit. Take the seed out of each yew aril with tweezers without damaging the seed, and set the arils on the crème in shrinking circles from the edge, leaving a 4 cm circle of crème in the middle. Fan the apple slices over that. Heat the jam with the water until it thickens and brush or drip it over the tops.

summary.text:
Taxus baccata, English yew, is a conifer in the yew family, Taxaceae. It is native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia east to the Himalaya.
In New Zealand it grows wild in the North and South Islands, widespread but often scattered and rarely common, and was first recorded naturalised in 1968. Yew is a very common species in cultivation throughout New Zealand and persists in old gardens long after they have been allowed to revert to scrub or forest. The conspicuous crimson fruits are often eaten and dispersed by birds. All the mature wild plants recorded in the Flora were spreading or bushy small trees; none was the commonly grown Irish yew ('Fastigiata'), a female clone that fruits heavily and whose seeds germinate freely.
A notable Irish yew at Caccia Birch House, Palmerston North, planted about 1920, measured 14.5 m tall in 2012.

warnings: Eat only the red flesh. The seed inside is highly poisonous: chewing or crushing even a few seeds can cause severe heart poisoning, and there is no specific antidote.
A seed swallowed whole is not reliably harmless; it can be broken down in the gut and release the poison.
Never crush, blend, juice or boil whole fruit to separate the seeds. Drying and cooking do not destroy the poison.
The red flesh is not free of yew toxins: it contains small amounts of other yew taxanes, and no safe amount has been measured.
Every other part of the tree is poisonous. The poison acts on the heart, and the lethal dose for an adult is reported to be 50 g of needles. Eating the berries together with leaves has killed people.
Fresh or wilted yew foliage has caused many stock deaths in New Zealand. Dried yew material stays poisonous for several months, so fallen needles and clippings are poisonous too.
Children have died after eating whole yew berries with the seeds chewed. Keep children away from yew.

Symptoms start 1 to 5 hours after eating: vomiting, diarrhoea and stomach cramps, then heart rhythm problems, seizures and collapse. If a seed was chewed or swallowed, or leaves were eaten, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766 immediately.

Young yew can be mistaken for young miro, whose fruit is eaten, and its red fleshy fruit can be mistaken for the edible red receptacles of tōtara and snow tōtara. Check the leaf base and how the seed sits (see the lookalikes).
